2475.meaning_mnemonic: When a vocab is a single kanji all alone, it usually has the same meaning as its kanji parent. That goes for this vocab word as well. <kanji>Person</kanji> is <vocabulary>person</vocabulary>.
2475.reading_mnemonic:
When a vocab is a single kanji and all alone like this, it's usually going to use the kun'yomi. Since you don't know the kun'yomi reading for this kanji yet, let's use a mnemonic to learn it.

What does a <vocabulary>person</vocabulary> hate more than anything? They hate extreme <reading>heat</reading> (ひと). You can always put on more clothes to stay warm, but when the heat gets too high, you can only take off so much.

examples.en: This apartment is too big for two people.
examples.ja: このアパートは二人には大きい。

examples.ja: あの二人はバドミントンのダブルスのパートナーです。

examples.ja: せっかく二人のためにオーダーしたケーキなのに、なんで一人でたべちゃったの？

2476.meaning_mnemonic: When you have <kanji>two</kanji> and <kanji>person</kanji> and then put them together, what do you get? You get a <vocabulary>pair</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>two people</vocabulary>.
2476.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is quite strange. If you know 二つ's reading, you can use that to remember the 二 part (ふた). But, the り that is the 人 is a total exception, something you won't see too often (though you may have seen it in 一人). If you can use the reading of 一人 (aka if you've learned it already) then definitely use that. If not, do your best to remember the reading on your own. It's a strange one that doesn't connect to much else.

examples.en: For the first time, I went for a drive alone.

2477.meaning_mnemonic: When there's <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji>, what are they? Well, they're either just going to be simply <vocabulary>one person</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>alone</vocabulary>.
2477.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this vocab doesn't follow any rules you learned previously. It's an exception, which means you have to learn the reading separately too. Spend a few moments trying to remember this word, look away for 10 seconds, and then try to recall its reading. Could you do it? Try again, this time in thirty seconds. Did you do it again? Okay, go ahead and move on. You may know it now, though you'll need to recall it again in the next 5-10 minutes if you want to remember it for good.

Alternatively, if you know the reading for the vocab word 一つ (in the same level as this word), you can know that it uses the same reading!

examples.en: Are you American?
examples.ja: アメリカ人ですか？

examples.ja: アメリカ人が二人います。

examples.en: Michael is a friendly American.
examples.ja: マイケルは、フレンドリーなアメリカ人だ。

2478.meaning_mnemonic: The アメリカ part is pretty easy so long as you know katakana. It's the word for "America." You know that <kanji>人</kanji> means "person," so you can figure out that America + Person = <vocabulary>American person</vocabulary> — specifically a <vocabulary>person from the USA</vocabulary>.
2478.reading_mnemonic:
Often times, when two kanji come together to form a kanji compound (or jukugo), you use the on'yomi readings. This is similar to that, though instead of another kanji it's a foreign word. This pattern works with almost any country as well. Just add 人 to a country name and you've described the people who live there. You'll see more of these before you're finished here.

And since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: 

<vocabulary>Americans</vocabulary> absolutely love their <reading>jean</reading>s (じん), it's a well-known fact!

examples.en: According to word on the street, French people apparently drink beer too.
examples.ja: ウワサによると、フランス人はビールものむらしいよ。

2479.meaning_mnemonic: フランス is "France." So what is a "France person?" That would be a <vocabulary>French person</vocabulary>.
2479.reading_mnemonic:
Often times, when two kanji come together to form a kanji compound (or jukugo), you use the on'yomi readings. This is similar to that, though instead of another kanji it's a foreign word. This pattern works with almost any country as well. Just add 人 to a country name and you've described the people who live there. You'll see more of these before you're finished here.

And since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: 

As with all words for nationalities, the 人 here is pronounced じん. Like people of all other nationalities, a <vocabulary>French person</vocabulary> loves their <reading>jean</reading>s (じん) too!

examples.en: Jenny will go to an international school soon.
examples.ja: ジェニーはもうすぐインターナショナルスクールに入る。

examples.en: Michael went into karaoke alone.
examples.ja: マイケルは一人でカラオケに入った。

examples.en: I joined the ski club.
examples.ja: スキーのクラブに入ったんです。

2480.meaning_mnemonic: This vocab word has okurigana, which is the hiragana part that comes after the kanji. When a vocab's okurigana makes an "う/oo" sound (in this case, we have a る), it's often going to be a verb. So in this case, the kanji 入 is <kanji>enter</kanji>. The vocab 入る is <vocabulary>to enter</vocabulary>. We're just taking the kanji and using it in a verb!
2480.reading_mnemonic:
When a vocab is a single kanji with okurigana, chances are it's going to be the kun'yomi reading, which you don't usually learn in the kanji (you usually learn the on'yomi reading). So, let's learn the kun'yomi reading for this word using its meaning.

When you <vocabulary>enter</vocabulary> the room, what do you do? You say "<reading>Hi</reading>" (はい) to everyone to the point of absurdity. "Hi there. Oh hi Frank. Oh hi there Susan. Oh hi there lamp."

examples.en: I put water in a bottle every day.
examples.ja: 毎日ボトルに水を入れる。

examples.en: Did you put avocado in the sandwich?
examples.ja: サンドイッチにアボカド入れた？

examples.en: Please let me join the volunteer meeting.
examples.ja: ボランティアの会に入れて下さい。

2481.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji 入 means "enter," but this word does not mean "to enter" (which you already learned as 入る). Still, the meaning of 入れる is still related to the kanji's meaning: it means <vocabulary>to insert</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to put in</vocabulary>. It's something you do to another object, like inserting a key into a lock, or your hand into a glove.
2481.reading_mnemonic:
When a vocab is a single kanji plus some okurigana (hiragana stuck on the end of kanji) it's almost always going to be the kun'yomi reading. This is one of two kun'yomi readings you'll be learning for the kanji 入. As long as you know that this vocab means <vocabulary>to insert</vocabulary>, you can use that to remember the reading as well. 

Imagine inserting your hand into a hole and an <reading>ea</reading>gle (い) flies out, screaming: "<reading>い</reading>!" This is something that happens every time you insert your hand into something: an eagle comes out. You don't know why.

examples.en: This is an eight-page essay.
examples.ja: これは八ページのエッセイです。

examples.en: There are only eight rolls of toilet paper.
examples.ja: トイレットペーパーが八ロールしかない。

examples.en: Dad is an eight-ton truck driver.
examples.ja: パパは八トントラックのドライバーなんです。

2482.meaning_mnemonic: When a vocab is a single kanji it usually steals its meaning from its kanji as well. Same goes for this vocab word. It means <vocabulary>eight</vocabulary>.
2482.reading_mnemonic: When a vocab is a single kanji and all alone like this, it's usually going to use the kun'yomi. But, because this is a number (exception) it uses the on'yomi instead, meaning you already know the reading from when you learned the kanji!

examples.en: This curry has eight potatoes in it.
examples.ja: このカレーにはじゃがいもが八つ入っています。

examples.en: There are eight KitKats in my mouth.
examples.ja: キットカットが八つ、口に入ってます。

examples.en: My grandma has eight accounts on Instagram alone.
examples.ja: うちのおばあちゃんはインスタグラムだけで八つもアカウントをもってるんだ。

2483.meaning_mnemonic: This word follows the "number of things" pattern where there's a kanji for a number plus つ on the end. Whenever you see this, you know the word means "____ things." Knowing that, as long as you know the kanji (which you do) you can figure out what number of things it is. For this one, it's the kanji for <kanji>eight</kanji> plus つ. So, this one is <vocabulary>eight things</vocabulary>.
2483.reading_mnemonic: Since all the "number of things" words follow the same pattern (number + つ), you just have to remember the part before the つ. All their readings use kun'yomi. So far you've only seen the on'yomi reading for this kanji though, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it: Can you think of eight things that start with the sound "ya"? Yah (や), you can. Try listing them out loud. Even if you don't manage it, you'll remember the connection between eight and "ya." Oh, and see that small っ in the middle of the reading (やっつ)? It puts a little emphasis on the consonant that follows it, like yattttttsu. OK, not that much emphasis. More like yattsu.

examples.en: The size of the forces is different.
examples.ja: 力の大きさが、ちがう。

examples.en: At my house, my mom has a lot of power.
examples.ja: うちではママが大きな力をもってるんですよ。

examples.en: I want to relax, but I somehow get tense.
examples.ja: リラックスしたいのに、どうしても力が入ってしまう。

2484.meaning_mnemonic: When a vocab word is made up of a single kanji and that's it, it almost always takes the meaning from its parent kanji. So, this vocab word also means <vocabulary>power</vocabulary>.
2484.reading_mnemonic:
When a vocab is a single kanji and all alone like this, it usually uses the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn the kun'yomi reading with the kanji, so for this vocab word, we'll use a mnemonic:

You're going to need a lot of <vocabulary>power</vocabulary> if you want to win the <reading>chica ru</reading>n (ちから). You know, like a race just for chicas. You'll need the <vocabulary>strength</vocabulary> to face adversity, and the <vocabulary>ability</vocabulary> to outclass all the other tough chica runners. That's chica power for you.

examples.en: Ten grams of butter, please.
examples.ja: バターを十グラム下さい。

examples.en: I'll count to ten. One, two, three...
examples.ja: 十までカウントするよ。一、二、三...

examples.en: At the river, I flew a kite up to ten meters high.
examples.ja: 川で、たこを十メートルまで上げた。

2485.meaning_mnemonic: When a vocab is alone like this with no okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) it tends to steal its meaning from the kanji it came from. That means this vocab word also means <vocabulary>ten</vocabulary>.
2485.reading_mnemonic: When a vocab is alone and consists of a single kanji like this, usually it uses the kun'yomi reading for the kanji. But, numbers are an exception and they use the on'yomi reading (which you learned when you learned the kanji). That means you know that this word's reading is <reading>じゅう</reading> already.

examples.en: It's three dollars.
examples.ja: 三ドルです。

examples.en: Up to the first three lessons is a trial.
examples.ja: はじめの三レッスンまではトライアルです。

examples.en: There are three types of this kitchen model.
examples.ja: このキッチンには三タイプあります。

2486.meaning_mnemonic: When a vocab is a single kanji and alone like this, it usually steals its meaning from the parent kanji. That goes for this word too, making the meaning of this word <vocabulary>three</vocabulary>.
2486.reading_mnemonic: When a vocab is a single kanji and all alone like this, it's usually going to use the kun'yomi. Numbers are an exception, though, and use the on'yomi reading. You learned the on'yomi reading when you learned this kanji, so you already know that the reading for this vocab is <reading>さん</reading>.

examples.en: This suitcase can fit three melons.
examples.ja: このスーツケースにはメロンが三つ入る。

examples.en: You can fit three balls in here.
examples.ja: ここにボールを三つ入るよ。

examples.en: I ordered three cheeseburgers, and I will eat all three of them by myself.
examples.ja: チーズバーガーを三つオーダーしたけど、一人で三つたべます。

2487.meaning_mnemonic: This word follows the "number of things" pattern where there's a kanji for a number plus つ on the end. Whenever you see this, you know the word means "____ things." Knowing that, as long as you know the kanji (which you do) you can figure out what number of things it is. For this one, it's the kanji for <kanji>three</kanji> plus つ. So, this one is <vocabulary>three things</vocabulary>.
2487.reading_mnemonic:
Since all of the "number of things" words all follow the same pattern (number plus つ), you really just have to remember the part before the つ (and then remember that the つ is in all of these). All of the readings are the kun'yomi reading, which means we'll have to use a mnemonic to remember them (you know the on'yomi reading of the kanji portion).

What thing do you have three of? The <vocabulary>three things</vocabulary> that you have are actually three versions of yourself. "Who is the real one?" you ask yourself. "It's <reading>me</reading>!" "Wait, no, it's <reading>me</reading>!" Just remember that there are three of you, and they're all saying "me me me me me" to try and prove that they're the real you.

examples.en: I have three roommates.
examples.ja: 三人のルームメイトがいます。

examples.en: Is there a table for three?
examples.ja: 三人のテーブルありますか？

examples.en: Nicholas Cage, Keanu Reeves, and Tom Cruise. Out of these three, who's your type?
examples.ja: ニコラス・ケイジ、キアヌ・リーブス、トム・クルーズ。この三人で、だれがタイプ？

2488.meaning_mnemonic: You have the kanji for <kanji>three</kanji> and <kanji>person</kanji>. Common sense will tell you what this word is. It's <vocabulary>three people</vocabulary>.
2488.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo (kanji compound) word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Apparently, there are <vocabulary>three people</vocabulary> working as <reading>San</reading>ta-san at <reading>Nin</reading>tendo (さんにん)! It's a big company, so obviously they need three Santas.

examples.en: I want to do yoga on top of a mountain.
examples.ja: 山の上でヨガをしたいね。

examples.en: There is a kitchen on the floor above.
examples.ja: 上のフロアにキッチンがあります。

examples.en: There is a loft above the living room.
examples.ja: リビングルームの上にロフトがあります。

2489.meaning_mnemonic: When a vocab word is a single kanji and alone, it tends to steal the meaning from the kanji. Same goes for this one too. It means <vocabulary>above</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>up</vocabulary>.
2489.reading_mnemonic:
When a vocab is a single kanji and all alone like this, it's usually going to use the kun'yomi. Since you learned the on'yomi reading of the kanji, we'll need to use a mnemonic to learn the reading of this vocabulary word. 

<vocabulary>Above</vocabulary> you is a huge weight. You're holding it up and struggling (it's heavy!). You look up and try to crane your neck to see how much it <reading>weigh</reading>s (うえ), but you can't see the numbers on the side of it. How long can you hold it above your head like this?

examples.en: I lift a large blanket up to the loft.
examples.ja: 大きいブランケットをロフトに上げる。

examples.en: "Should I turn up the volume on the speaker?" "Yeah."
examples.ja: 「スピーカーのボリューム、上げる？」「うん。」

examples.en: What can I do to raise Pikachu's level?
examples.ja: ピカチュウのレベルを上げるには、どうしたらいいですか？

2490.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>above</kanji> and this verb is related to that meaning. It means <vocabulary>to lift something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to raise something</vocabulary>. It's a transitive verb, meaning that you do something to something else. You raise something. Like your hands!
2490.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to use the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn with the kanji. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

When you want <vocabulary>to lift something</vocabulary>, you always shout "<reading>Ah</reading>!" (あ) to get the extra power you need. Especially when you want to lift something over your head. Go ahead, try it now. Lift something up and shout "Ah!" Feels good, right?

examples.en: Fireworks get set off in August.
examples.ja: 八月に花火が上がる。

examples.en: Let's take the elevator up three floors.
examples.ja: 三フロア上までエレベーターで上がりましょう。

examples.en: My cholesterol has gone up from last year.
examples.ja: 去年よりコレステロールが上がってしまった。

2491.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>above</kanji>, and this verb means <vocabulary>to go up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to rise</vocabulary>.

It's an intransitive verb, so it doesn't take a direct object. For example: Prices go up. Temperatures rise. See? No direct object. You can remember this because stock prices always seems to go up when you see this one <reading>girl</reading> (がる). You don't know how this girl makes stock prices go up, she just does. Think of her as your lucky girl.
2491.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you can guess that it uses the kun'yomi reading. You've learned that reading, but here's a mnemonic in case you need a refresher:

You know this word means <vocabulary>to go up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to rise</vocabulary>. Imagine just rising into the air, sort of floating up all of a sudden. What would you say? You'd probably scream "<reading>Ah</reading>!" (あ) the moment you started to go up. You know, out of surprise. Going up? Ah!

examples.en: My roommate goes up to the loft.
examples.ja: ルームメイトはロフトに上る。

examples.en: The "up" button for the elevator is right here.
examples.ja: エレベーターの「上る」ボタンは、ここです。

examples.en: I saw salmon swimming upstream.
examples.ja: サケが川を上っているのをみた。

2492.meaning_mnemonic: This word means <vocabulary>to climb</vocabulary>. You can tell this word is a verb because it ends with an う sound (る, in this case). Its meaning is similar to the meaning of the 上 kanji, which is "above." So this word is all about moving "above" something (in other words, climbing!)
2492.reading_mnemonic:
上る consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, so it will use the kun'yomi reading of the kanji. For 上, there are multiple kun'yomi readings, and you didn't learn this one yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You want <vocabulary>to climb</vocabulary> the mountain, but a gruff old man grabs your shoulder and says "<reading>No bo</reading>y, you ain't climbing that thing, not today." If you're not a boy, think about how weird it is that he called you a boy. If you are a grown man, think how you wish he called you "dude" or something, not "boy." If you're a boy, well... think about how appropriate it is that he said "no boy."

examples.en: Oh, there's a hamster under the table!
examples.ja: あ、テーブルの下にハムスターがいる！

examples.en: Please come downstairs.
examples.ja: 下のフロアに、きてください。

examples.en: There's a large restaurant down the mountain.
examples.ja: 山の下に大きいレストランがあるよ。

2493.meaning_mnemonic: When a vocab is a single kanji with no okurigana (that's hiragana attached to the kanji) it tends to steal the meaning of the kanji it comes from. So, this one is <vocabulary>below</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>under</vocabulary>.
2493.reading_mnemonic:
When a vocab is a single kanji and is alone it tends to use the kun'yomi reading. You learned the on'yomi reading for this kanji, so now it's time to learn the kun'yomi reading to learn this vocabulary word.

What's <vocabulary>below</vocabulary> you? What's below your foot? Oh no. The worst thing possible: It's <reading>した</reading>.

examples.en: My mood is lower on rainy days.
examples.ja: 雨の日は気分が下がる。

examples.en: Excuse me. Your jeans are hanging down and I can see your panties.
examples.ja: すみません。ジーンズが下がってパンツが見えてますよ。

examples.en: Scores have dropped since last year.
examples.ja: 去年からスコアが下がった。

2494.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>below</kanji>, and 下がる means <vocabulary>to get lower</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to go down</vocabulary>.

It's an intransitive verb, so it doesn't take a direct object. For example: Prices fall. Temperatures come down. See? No direct object. You can remember this because your fever only goes down when a <reading>girl</reading> (がる) takes care of you. It has to be a girl if you want your fever to come down!
2494.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. Let's use a mnemonic to remember the reading of the kanji:

You know it means <vocabulary>to fall</vocabulary> so instead of using a <reading>sa</reading>w (さ) to cut down the tree, you decide to let it come to you. It has to come down all by itself. Picture yourself placing a saw at the foot of a tree then sitting back and waiting for it to drop itself at your knees. (This could actually work, don't you judge my methods!)

examples.en: Lower the lever as hard as you can!
examples.ja: 力いっぱいレバーを下げて！

examples.en: Let's lower it one level.
examples.ja: 一つレベルを下げよう。

examples.en: Oh, this rope is perfect for hanging bacon.
examples.ja: あっ、このロープ、ベーコンを下げるのにちょうどいい。

2495.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means below so the verb version of that is when you put something below you. It's to lower something. It can also mean to hang something, such as a lamp from the ceiling. This is a transitive verb, which means that the verb is done by one entity onto another. In other words, you lower something. Like your impossibly high expectations for yourself. Take it easy!
2495.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn with the kanji. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

You want <vocabulary>to lower something</vocabulary>. In this case, it's a tree, so you need a <reading>saw</reading> (さ). Lower the tree to the ground gently while you slowly saw it down!

examples.en: A miso ramen, please.
examples.ja: みそラーメン下さい。

examples.en: May I have seven apples?
examples.ja: りんごを七つ下さい。

examples.en: Please, give me some help.
examples.ja: どうか、力を下さい。

2496.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that the kanji 下 means <kanji>down</kanji>, and さい sounds like the word "sigh." You need to ask someone for something, so you look down, sigh, and say <vocabulary>please give me</vocabulary> that thing. You're ashamed that you have to ask. But you still need it. <vocabulary>Please</vocabulary>, please give it to me!

You only use this kanji version of ください when asking for something, which is why this is "please give me." If you're just saying "please," you don't need the kanji at all!
2496.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for 下 here is one you haven't learned. Just think about how it kind of sounds like you're saying <vocabulary>please</vocabulary>, <reading>could I</reading> (くだ) have this thing? Pretty please, could I have it? 

Alternatively, if you already knew the word ください beforehand, this shouldn't be too hard!

examples.en: There is some sauce on your mouth.
examples.ja: 口にソースがついていますよ。

examples.en: Please put this in your mouth.
examples.ja: これを口に入れてください。

examples.en: The mouth of this plastic bottle is too large.
examples.ja: このペットボトルは口が大きすぎる。

examples.en: If you don't take good care of your mouth, you won't have much luck with women.
examples.ja: ちゃんと口のケアをしないと、女にモテないだろ。

2497.meaning_mnemonic: When a vocab is made up of a single kanji with no okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) it's generally going to have the same meaning as the kanji it came from. From that, you know this word's meaning is <vocabulary>mouth</vocabulary>.
2497.reading_mnemonic:
When a vocab is a single kanji and all alone like this, it's usually going to use the kun'yomi, which you did not learn from learning the kanji. To remember this word, you should use a mnemonic. With your <vocabulary>mouth</vocabulary>, make a "<reading>kuchi</reading> kuchi kou" (くち) sound. Go ahead, make it. Focus on your mouth and try to imagine each shape it makes while zooming in on it. You're talking to a baby, which is why you're making all these ridiculous noises. Also, instead of "coo" at the end, you're saying "kou," because that's the reading of the kanji (こう).

くちくちこう！くちくちこう！ Sounds like something from Arrested Development, actually.

examples.en: Where is the entrance?
examples.ja: 入り口は、どこ？

examples.en: There are three entrances.
examples.ja: 入り口が三つあります。

examples.en: First, tell me the size of the entryway door of your apartment.
examples.ja: まず、あなたのアパートの入り口のドアの大きさをおしえて。

2498.reading_mnemonic:
This word is really two separate words put together to form one, so let's look at it in two parts:

The kanji 入 has り attached to it as okurigana (hiragana that comes after a kanji), so you can bet that 入り will use a kun'yomi reading for the kanji. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

The <vocabulary>entrance</vocabulary> you're going through is really <reading>eerie</reading> (いり). It has cobwebs and creepy figures carved into it, and it just gives you a really eerie feeling.

Since 入り uses the kun'yomi, you can guess that 口 will follow suit. You learned this reading with the vocabulary, but the く in くち changes to ぐ due to something called rendaku. Think of it as an eerie entrance into the <reading>Gucci</reading> (ぐち) store.

examples.en: A large melon, please.
examples.ja: 大きいメロンを下さい。

examples.en: These sandals are too big.
examples.ja: このサンダルは大きすぎる。

examples.en: Does this come in a larger size?
examples.ja: これよりも大きいサイズありますか？

2499.meaning_mnemonic: This is the adjective form of <kanji>big</kanji>. It has the same meaning, though it is a word for describing. Words that end with い are often adjectives, remember that for future words as well. So, as long as you know the meaning of this kanji, you can transfer that to the meaning of this word. It's the adjective <vocabulary>big</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>large</vocabulary>.
2499.reading_mnemonic: What do you do when you see something really, really <vocabulary>big</vocabulary>? You say <reading>おお</reading> because you can't believe your eyes. Imagine something really large and say おお out loud to help seal the memory in that brain of yours.

examples.en: These sandals are size 28 cm.
examples.ja: このサンダルの大きさは、28センチです。

examples.en: What surprised me about the United States? The size of the drinks.
examples.ja: アメリカでビックリしたこと？それはドリンクの大きさですよ。

examples.en: This chest freezer is big enough for two people or so.
examples.ja: このチェストフリーザーは二人くらい入る大きさですよ。

2500.meaning_mnemonic: In Japanese, さ on the end of a word is often the equivalent of "-ness" in English. In other words, if you replace the い on the end of an い-adjective with さ, you have a noun. In this case, the adjective is 大きい (big) and the noun 大きさ means "bigness", aka <vocabulary>size</vocabulary>.
2500.reading_mnemonic:
When a vocab has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) it is probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. Since you learned the on'yomi reading with the kanji 大, we'll have to use a mnemonic to remember this word.

When you saw the size of (pick something surprising), you said "<reading>おお</reading>*#$@!" Really imagine something surprising. Say the おお part out loud, as well. Think about the size of whatever you're looking at, too, and how <vocabulary>big</vocabulary> it is.

examples.en: It's no big deal.
examples.ja: 大したことじゃないよ。

examples.en: What!? Koichi's entering the major league? That's a big deal!
examples.ja: えっ！？コウイチが、メジャーリーグに入る？ それは、大したものだ！

examples.en: She had considerable nerve, dumping me.
examples.ja: このオレをふるなんて、大した女だったよ。

2501.meaning_mnemonic: した is the past tense form of する (which means "to do"). So, essentially this word is "did big." What is something that "did big"? It's something that's <vocabulary>great</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>considerable</vocabulary>.
2501.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for the 大 part is actually the on'yomi reading you learned when learning this kanji. Since 大 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

When something's <vocabulary>great</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>important</vocabulary>, you'd better wear a <reading>tie</reading> (たい) for it. No showing up without a tie to anything that's a <vocabulary>big deal</vocabulary>, okay?

examples.en: A ticket for an adult, please.
examples.ja: 大人のチケット下さい。

examples.en: PG-18 is content for adults.
examples.ja: PG-18は大人のためのコンテンツです。

examples.en: I am a model for a fashion magazine that caters to "mature women."
examples.ja: わたしは「大人の女」をテーマにしたファッションマガジンのモデルです。

2502.meaning_mnemonic: This word combines <kanji>big</kanji> and <kanji>person</kanji>. If you're a child, how do you think of adults? You just think of them like big people. That's why this combination of kanji means <vocabulary>adult</vocabulary>, and when used like an adjective, it means <vocabulary>mature</vocabulary>.
2502.reading_mnemonic:
Sometimes kanji have exceptional readings that are neither on’yomi, nor kun’yomi, and this is one of them. So here’s a mnemonic to help you remember this reading:

"I'm an <vocabulary>adult</vocabulary>, which means I have adult responsibilities, like… <reading>oh, toner</reading> (おとな)!" Are you an adult with your own toner printer? Ohhhh, toner…

examples.en: There are three women at the bar.
examples.ja: バーに三人の女がいる。

examples.en: Since "く + ノ + 一 = 女," a female ninja is called "kunoichi."
examples.ja: 「く + ノ + 一 = 女」なので、女のニンジャのことを「クノイチ」というんです。

examples.en: That woman is a very powerful female spy.
examples.ja: あの女は、とても力のある女スパイだ。

2503.meaning_mnemonic:
When a kanji is alone and doesn't have any okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) it's usually going to take the same meaning as the kanji it comes from. So in this case, you know that this word means <vocabulary>woman</vocabulary>.

But watch out! Using 女 on its own can often come off as blunt and disrespectful, especially in casual chats. We’ll introduce you to neutral equivalents soon!
2503.reading_mnemonic:
When a vocab is a single kanji and all alone like this, it's usually going to use the kun'yomi. You didn't learn the kun'yomi reading when you learned the kanji itself, so let's use a mnemonic to remember it:

Think about how this <vocabulary>woman</vocabulary> is <reading>onna</reading> (おんな) roll. She's winning left, right and center. She's unstoppable. Yep, she's truly onna roll!

examples.en: This is an artificial mountain.
examples.ja: これは人工の山だ。

examples.en: France's number one biggest mountain is Mont Blanc.
examples.ja: フランス一大きい山はモンブランです。

examples.en: I thought it was a mountain of trash, then I realized there was a bed underneath..
examples.ja: ゴミの山かとおもったら、下にベッドがあった。

2504.meaning_mnemonic: A vocab made of a single kanji all alone with no okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) usually has the same exact meaning as the kanji it's made from. So by that you know that this vocab's meaning is <vocabulary>mountain</vocabulary>.
2504.reading_mnemonic:
When a vocab is a single kanji and all alone like this, it's usually going to use the kun'yomi, which you didn't learn when you learned the kanji. To remember this word's reading we'll use a mnemonic.

What are you doing going up into the <vocabulary>mountain</vocabulary>s? You're hunting for <reading>yam</reading>s (やま). Go ahead, imagine yourself doing just that, climbing up the mountain (it's hard work!) and then digging in the ground with your hands, then pulling up that sweet, delicious yam! Mmm!

examples.en: Oh, it's Mt. Fuji!
examples.ja: あっ、ふじ山だ！

examples.en: Is Mt. Everest bigger than Mt. Fuji?
examples.ja: エベレスト山は、ふじ山より大きいですか？

examples.en: I want to propose to my girlfriend on the top of Mt. Fuji someday.
examples.ja: いつかガールフレンドにふじ山の上でプロポーズをしたいんです。

2505.meaning_mnemonic: Just look at this word. What do you think it means? That's right - it's a name (Fuji) plus the kanji for <kanji>mountain</kanji>. Put those together, and you have <vocabulary>Mount Fuji</vocabulary>. In English the "Mount(ain)" part comes first. In Japanese, it comes at the end, sort of like the name ender さん, ちゃん, and so on. You can add 山 to the end of any mountain's name too, not just Mount Fuji.
2505.reading_mnemonic: Normally ふじ would be in kanji, but I wanted you to see this kanji use in action since it's more useful than just being used on Mount Fuji. This is treated like a jukugo word (combo kanji word). In the case of jukugo, usually the on'yomi reading is used, meaning you just have to remember the on'yomi reading of 山. Luckily, you learned this when you were learning the kanji, so you should already know it!

examples.en: This river is the Amazon River.
examples.ja: この川はアマゾン川です。

examples.en: I want to BBQ by the river.
examples.ja: 川でバーベキューしたいなぁ。

examples.en: Oh. Are you going into the river in that bikini?
examples.ja: えっ。そのビキニで川に入るの？

2506.meaning_mnemonic: When a vocab is made up of a single kanji with no okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) it will usually take the same meaning as the kanji it comes from. So, from that you know that this word means <vocabulary>river</vocabulary>.
2506.reading_mnemonic: You're in luck — the reading you learned with the kanji is the same as the one you have to learn for this vocab!

examples.en: The samurai raised his sword out of the blue.
examples.ja: いきなりサムライが刀を上げた。

examples.en: I want to buy a sword in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本で刀をかいたいんです。

examples.en: Isn't this little sword so cute?
examples.ja: この小さい刀、かわいくない？

2507.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well!
2507.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. I'm hoping you already know this word - that will make everything much easier. It's <reading>かたな</reading> (you know what a katana is, right?).

examples.en: That tomato has some dirt on it.
examples.ja: そのトマト、土がついてるよ。

examples.en: This is soil from Mt. Fuji.
examples.ja: これはふじ山の土なんだよ。

examples.en: The mole was going into the ground.
examples.ja: モグラが土に入っていった。

2508.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

土 generally refers to <vocabulary>dirt</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>soil</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>earth</vocabulary>.
2508.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you to remember it: 

You look through the soil. You're trying to find something. As you dig and sift, you come across not one but <reading>two chee</reading>ses (つち). Pull them out of the ground and put them in your mouth. How do the two cheeses taste and compare?

examples.en: One liter is a thousand milliliters.
examples.ja: 一リットルとは、千ミリリットルのことだ。

examples.en: That French person is a one-in-a-thousand genius.
examples.ja: そのフランス人は、千に一人の天才です。

examples.en: It takes about 1,000 days.
examples.ja: 千日くらいかかりますね。

2509.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2509.reading_mnemonic: Normally a single kanji making up a word like this means it will use the kun'yomi readings. Numbers are generally the exception, though, which means this word uses the on'yomi reading. If you learned the kanji, then you should already know this!

examples.en: It's about one thousand.
examples.ja: 一千くらいです。

examples.en: Apparently, this toilet paper was 1,000 dollars!
examples.ja: このトイレットペーパー、一千ドルもしたんだって！

examples.en: We camped out on a 1,000-foot mountain.
examples.ja: 一千フィートの山の上でキャンプをした。

2510.meaning_mnemonic:
If you have <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>thousand</kanji>, you have... <vocabulary>one thousand</vocabulary>.

Simply saying 千 is the most common way to say 1,000, but sometimes you might use 一千 to emphasize or clarify the exact number.
2510.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The only thing that's a bit weird is the reading of the 一. The ち turns into a small っ, making the reading for this word <reading>いっせん</reading>.

examples.en: I saw the moon last night.
examples.ja: 夕べ、月をみた。

examples.en: Dinner last night was onion curry.
examples.ja: 夕べのディナーは玉ねぎのカレーでした。

examples.en: There's an event called "Wine Evening" in May.
examples.ja: 五月に「ワインの夕べ」というイベントがあります。

2511.meaning_mnemonic: I spent all <kanji>evening</kanji> in <reading>be</reading>(べ)d  <vocabulary>last night</vocabulary>. It was a really chill <vocabulary>evening</vocabulary>.
2511.reading_mnemonic: When hiragana is attached to a kanji, you can usually assume that that kanji is going to be read using the kun'yomi reading, which is exactly what's going on with this word as well. By learning this word's kanji you've also learned the reading for this word.

examples.en: The girl in the white dress is Rachel.
examples.ja: 白のドレスの女の子がレイチェルです。

examples.en: This girl is a five-year-old genius programmer.
examples.ja: この女の子は五才の天才プログラマーだ。

examples.en: I'm not a girl. I'm an adult woman. Got it?
examples.ja: わたしは女の子じゃない。一人の大人の女。わかった？

2512.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>woman</kanji> <kanji>child</kanji> is a <vocabulary>girl</vocabulary>.

This word has two kanji with hiragana stuck in the middle. That hiragana is the particle の. This time, it just means the noun before の is modifying the noun after it.

女の子 is a casual word for young girls, like kids or teenagers. Sometimes it can also refer to adult women, but only to playfully or affectionately highlight their youthful or girlish qualities.
2512.reading_mnemonic:
Since there's hiragana in here, you can bet that these kanji will use the kun'yomi readings. You already know the kun'yomi reading for 女. You might even remember the one for 子, but here's a mnemonic just in case:

When you need to remember the kun'yomi reading for 子, just think about how a child stole your <reading>co</reading>at (こ). You gave it to her because she looked cold, but then she ran off down the street and left you shouting, "Coat! Coat! That 子 has my coat!"

examples.en: That lion's child is called Simba.
examples.ja: そのライオンの子はシンバという。

examples.en: You aren’t my real child.
examples.ja: あなたは、わたしのほんとうの子ではないの。

examples.en: Don’t you think my kid looks similar to Beyoncé?
examples.ja: わたしの子、ビヨンセににているとおもわない？

2513.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2513.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word:

You saw a <vocabulary>child</vocabulary> and gave her your <reading>co</reading>at (こ). The kid looked all cold, so you gave her your coat. Children never want to wear proper warm clothing when they should, then they end up shivering their butts off and needing to wear a parent's oversized coat. Fortunately you were there to give this 子 your coat.

examples.en: The ladies' room is over there.
examples.ja: そっちは女子トイレですよ。

examples.en: I gave a women's professional wrestling ticket as a present.
examples.ja: 女子プロレスのチケットをプレゼントした。

examples.en: I was the captain of the women's volleyball team.
examples.ja: 女子バレーボールのチームキャプテンでした。

2514.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>woman</kanji> <kanji>child</kanji> is just a <vocabulary>girl</vocabulary>!

女子 is a relatively formal word commonly used in contexts where classification or categorization by gender is used, such as in sports or school settings.
2514.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Small tomatoes are delicious.
examples.ja: 小さいトマトはおいしいですよね。

examples.en: In this class, there are kids who are still small while there are kids who are as tall as adults.
examples.ja: このクラスには、まだ小さい子もいれば、大人のように大きい子もいる。

examples.en: This dress is too small for me.
examples.ja: このドレスは、わたしには小さすぎる。

2515.meaning_mnemonic: This kanji has hiragana attached and ends with an い sound. That means it's probably an adjective (and it is!). So, if you take the kanji 小 and its meaning (small), you can figure out the adjective version of it. What is the adjective version of "small?" Actually, it's the same thing: <vocabulary>small</vocabulary>.
2515.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember the ちい portion:

When you think of the word <vocabulary>small</vocabulary>, try to think of this <reading>chee</reading>se <reading>ea</reading>tery (ちい). You go inside, and all of their cheeses are so small. They hand you a magnifying glass to see all the cheeses. You look at them and exclaim: "Why are these cheeses so small???"

examples.en: They said their goodbyes, and another few years passed.
examples.ja: 別れを告げ、それから又数年が過ぎた。

examples.en: This form must be filled out with a black pen or ballpoint pen.
examples.ja: この書類は、必ず黒のペン又はボールペンで記入してください。

examples.en: "I'll be back," he said, and the cat hurried off.
examples.ja: 「僕又来ますね 」と言って、猫はそそくさと帰って行った。

2516.meaning_mnemonic:
The meaning of this word and the meaning of the kanji are the same: <vocabulary>Again</vocabulary>!

This is a very common word, but it's almost always written in kana in casual situations. However, it's often written in kanji in formal contexts, such as official paperwork and legal documents. You'll also see it in some literature, particularly stuff that was written around the time of Miyazawa Kenji and Natsume Soseki.
2516.reading_mnemonic: The reading you learned for the kanji is the same as the reading for this word. You hopefully won't have to learn it... again.

examples.en: Check here with a circle, please.
examples.ja: ここに丸でチェックして下さい。

examples.en: My type is someone who is good at drawing circles.
examples.ja: 丸をかくのが上手な人がタイプです。

examples.en: People get wide-eyed when someone proposes to them as a surprise.
examples.ja: 人はサプライズでプロポーズされると目が丸になるものなんです。

2517.meaning_mnemonic: This vocab word and the kanji that makes it have the same meaning: <vocabulary>Circle</vocabulary>.
2517.reading_mnemonic: The reading you learned for this kanji is the kun'yomi one. Since this vocab word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. Guess what? That means you already know it!

examples.en: I want a round ball.
examples.ja: 丸いボールがほしい。

examples.en: This restaurant only serves round-shaped fruit.
examples.ja: このレストランには丸いフルーツしかありません。

examples.en: Isn't this ball a bit too round?
examples.ja: この玉、ちょっと丸すぎませんか？

2518.meaning_mnemonic: With an い on the end, you can guess that this word is an い-adjective. What is the adjective version of the kanji <kanji>丸</kanji>? "Circle" becomes <vocabulary>circular</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>spherical</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>round</vocabulary>. This, compared to another similar word (円), is more general purpose and can be used with 3D spherical objects as well.
2518.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the reading you learned for the kanji <kanji>丸</kanji>, though you'll need to tack the い onto the end too.

examples.en: I am five years old.
examples.ja: わたしは五才です。

examples.en: My first kiss was when I was 16 years old.
examples.ja: ファーストキスは十六才のときでした。

examples.en: Dad's present for his fiftieth birthday was a mountain of Pokémon cards.
examples.ja: パパの50才のバースデープレゼントは、ポケモンカードの山でした。

2519.meaning_mnemonic:
Although this word consists of one kanji that is all alone, it doesn't share its meaning with the parent kanji. But the meanings are similar in a way. This word means <vocabulary>years old</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>age</vocabulary>. With more years comes more <kanji>talent</kanji>, right? That's why this word means "years old" and not "talent," like the parent kanji.

You can stick this word onto numbers to say how old someone is!

Special note for all of you advanced learners out there. When discussing age, 〜歳 is the original and correct kanji to use. Because 〜才 is easier to write and has the same reading, it became mainstream. You'll see it used in writing today, especially in elementary schools. In formal writing though, you'll always want to use 〜歳, which you'll learn later on.
2519.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned for the kanji, meaning you should already know it! Don't try to type the 〜 part though.

examples.en: Let's go inside quickly.
examples.ja: はやく中に入ろう。

examples.en: Is Rachel in this group?
examples.ja: このグループの中に、レイチェルはいますか？

examples.en: A woman in a bikini came out of the river.
examples.ja: 川の中からビキニの女が出てきた。

2520.meaning_mnemonic: When the <kanji>middle</kanji> kanji is used as a word, it means <vocabulary>inside</vocabulary>. When you're in the middle of something, it means you're <vocabulary>in</vocabulary> that thing!
2520.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word:

There's a sound coming from <kanji>inside</kanji> the wall. It sounds like a knock, knock, knock noise. You break down the wall, and there's some creepy dude standing inside. He is the <reading>knocker</reading> (なか).

examples.en: This curry is delicious.
examples.ja: このカレー、中々おいしいですね。

examples.en: The test in January was quite difficult.
examples.ja: 一月のテストは中々むずかしかった。

examples.en: This card is rare and it costs about 1,000 dollars.
examples.ja: このカードは中々レアなので一千ドルぐらいしますよ。

2521.meaning_mnemonic:
The 々 symbol just repeats the kanji that comes before it. In other words, 中々 is the same as 中中. Easy! So with 中々, you have <kanji>middle</kanji> x2. When something is more middle than middle itself, it's <vocabulary>rather</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>fairly</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>quite</vocabulary> something. Why? I guess because those are all good middle-level intensifiers.

中々 can be used in positive or negative ways. In a positive way, it usually means something is better than expected, like 中々おいしい (quite delicious). But it's really versatile and could also mean "a little," "very," or "completely" depending on the situation. It might even sound condescending, so be careful how you use it! In a negative sense, you can use it when something is more difficult than expected, like in 中々できない (can't be done easily).
2521.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this word is the kun'yomi reading, since it's like putting two single kanji together rather than a true jukugo word. To learn the kun'yomi reading, take a look at this mnemonic: 

From the middle of the middle comes a sound. It is a knocking sound. Knock. Knock. Knock. You open up the walls around this thing. Then you open up the second set of walls (middle of the middle). Inside is an old man, who identifies himself as "the knocker." You go inside of him and find another knocker as well. That's why it's a <reading>knocker knocker</reading> (なかなか).

examples.en: On May 1st, I returned to New York.
examples.ja: 五月一日にニューヨークへかえりました。

examples.en: I'm planning to propose on Mt. Fuji in May.
examples.ja: 五月にふじ山でプロポーズするつもりなんです。

examples.en: May in Japan is known for "Golden Week."
examples.ja: 日本で五月といえばゴールデンウィークです。

2522.meaning_mnemonic: The moon kanji also represents a month, so when you have five of these months, what month of the year is it? That would be <vocabulary>May</vocabulary>, the greatest month of the year (because it has towel day in it!).
2522.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 月 has two on'yomi readings, but it always uses the がつ reading in the names of the months, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember that:

<vocabulary>May</vocabulary> is when you and your buddies get together to eat <reading>Go</reading>dzilla <reading>guts</reading> (ごがつ). You go hunting for Godzilla just for his delicious guts, and then eat them with your friends. Yummy.

examples.en: Is the 5th okay for the meeting?
examples.ja: ミーティングは五日でもだいじょうぶ？

examples.en: There are five days left until the event.
examples.ja: イベントまであと五日。

examples.en: Oh, that girl? I got dumped five days after we went out on a date.
examples.ja: ああ、あの女の子？デートして五日でフラれたよ。

2523.meaning_mnemonic: <vocabulary>Day five</vocabulary> or the <vocabulary>fifth day</vocabulary>. No matter how you look at this word, it makes a lot of sense.
2523.reading_mnemonic:
Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it uses kun'yomi readings for both the kanji. Think about this word this way:

On the <vocabulary>fifth day</vocabulary> I have to <reading>eat</reading> (いつ) five <reading>ca</reading>rs (か). Now imagine yourself eating five cars. How did you manage to get past the first one? I'm impressed.

examples.en: I only walked fifty meters.
examples.ja: 五十メートルしかウォーキングしなかった。

examples.en: Mom turned fifty on the 8th.
examples.ja: ママは八日に五十になった。

examples.en: Portland's Caucasian population is higher than 50%.
examples.ja: ポートランドの白人人口は五十パーセントよりも上なんです。

2524.meaning_mnemonic: What happens when you have ten five times? You get <vocabulary>fifty</vocabulary>!
2524.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. That's the case for this word too, which means you should already know how to read this word.

examples.en: I got five chocolates on Valentine's Day.
examples.ja: バレンタインデーにチョコレートを五つもらった。

examples.en: Let's divide into five groups.
examples.ja: 五つのグループにわかれましょう。

examples.en: It's impossible to collect five eyeballs in one day.
examples.ja: 一日で目玉を五つもあつめるなんてムリですよ。

2525.meaning_mnemonic: From previous number + つ words, you can probably guess that this word means <vocabulary>five things</vocabulary>.
2525.reading_mnemonic:
The reading of this word is the kun'yomi reading of the kanji <kanji>五</kanji>, meaning you didn't learn it when you learned the parent kanji reading. To remember this word, think of it this way:

You have <vocabulary>five things</vocabulary>. What do you have to do with them? You need to <reading>eat</reading> (いつ) them. Just imagine having five delicious things to eat, sticking each on one finger of your hand, and then eating them one after another. And make sure to count down from five while doing it!

examples.en: This smartphone screen size is five inches.
examples.ja: このスマホのスクリーンの大きさは五インチです。

examples.en: One of the five floors is a cafeteria.
examples.ja: 五フロアのうちの一フロアはカフェテリアです。

examples.en: After five games, finally there was a first score.
examples.ja: 五ゲームおわって、やっとファーストスコアが入った。

2526.meaning_mnemonic: This vocab is made from a single kanji, which means it shares the same meaning as the parent kanji: <vocabulary>Five</vocabulary>.
2526.reading_mnemonic: Since numbers are an exception, this word is read using the on'yomi reading even though it's made from a single kanji all alone. Luckily for you, you learned the reading for this word when you learned the parent kanji.

examples.en: There are six spoons.
examples.ja: スプーンが六つあります。

2555.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. That said, this reading can be easy to confuse with other similar words, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

The <vocabulary>princess</vocabulary> is named <reading>Jo</reading>-Ann Jr. (じょ), or Jo for short , and she loves making people say "Ohh, Jo!" (王女) by sneaking up and scaring them. Whenever you think of the princess now, imagine how many times people have screamed "Ohh, Jo!" at her.

examples.en: It's the day to put out the recycling.
examples.ja: リサイクルのゴミを出す日です。

examples.en: Please take out a notebook.
examples.ja: ノートを出して下さい。

examples.en: I handed a hundred yen to the convenience store cashier.
examples.ja: コンビニのレジで百円を出した。

2556.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You already learned that 出る means "to <kanji>exit</kanji>," and this is the transitive version of that. In other words, you're doing the action of causing something else to exit, so this word means <vocabulary>to take out</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to hand out</vocabulary>. Think of it like this: when you take out your wallet, you're causing it to exit your pocket.
2556.reading_mnemonic:
The part of the word that you have to learn how to read is the だ portion, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

What are you going <vocabulary>to take out</vocabulary> at the cash register when you need to pay for something? Your <reading>da</reading>d's (だ) credit card, obviously! You love <vocabulary>to hand out</vocabulary> your dad's credit card left and right whenever it's time for a shopping spree. Thanks, Daddy!

examples.en: Please leave using that exit.
examples.ja: あちらの出口から出てください。

examples.en: It looks like you have to sneeze, but can't.
examples.ja: くしゃみが出そうで出ない。

examples.en: Let's get out of the restaurant.
examples.ja: レストランから出よう。

2557.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means "exit," so what is the verb form of that? It's <vocabulary>to exit</vocabulary>.
2557.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You want <vocabulary>to exit</vocabulary> the room you're in. Why? Because it has a <reading>de</reading>ad (で) body in it. Seriously. You should exit before someone tries to pin this dead body on you. Quick, leave now!

examples.en: That is not an exit.
examples.ja: そこは出口ではありません。

examples.en: The exit is over there.
examples.ja: 出口はあちらです。

examples.en: This bathroom doesn't have an exit.
examples.ja: このトイレ、出口がないよ。

2558.meaning_mnemonic: The mouth you exit out of is just a doorway (I hope), but an easier way to describe this word or concept is to call it an <vocabulary>exit</vocabulary>.
2558.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 出口 is an exception to this rule, however, and uses its kun'yomi readings. There's no particular reason why this is, but oftentimes a "body part" word (like mouth) changes a word to use kun'yomi readings instead of on'yomi ones. You already know the kun'yomi reading for 口 (くち) from learning the vocab, but to remember the reading for 出 you can think the following:

If I exit out this mouth, I'll end up in the ocean (you were swallowed by a whale) and I will surely end up <reading>dea</reading>d (で).

Also keep in mind that because of rendaku, くち becomes ぐち.

examples.en: Please don't water the tree on the right.
examples.ja: 右の木は水をあげないで下さい。

examples.en: Click the button on the bottom right.
examples.ja: 右下のボタンをクリックしてね。

examples.en: On your right is a chart showing the Japanese population.
examples.ja: 右は、日本の人口のチャートです。

2559.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2559.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Look to the <vocabulary>right</vocabulary>. There are <reading>me</reading>at <reading>gee</reading>se (みぎ) over there. What are meat geese, you ask? They're geese made of meat, that sit to the right of you, trying to get you to do bad things. Like the devil/angel motif you see in cartoons. Well there's nothing on your left. And on your right? Just meat geese. Watching you. Waiting. Geese made of meat. Telling you not to do the right thing.

examples.en: My right hand's feeling weak.
examples.ja: 右手に力が入らないんです。

examples.en: It's hard to type with just your right hand.
examples.ja: 右手だけで入力するのは、むずかしいです。

examples.en: Please compare the size of your right hand and your left hand.
examples.ja: 右手の大きさと左手の大きさをくらべて下さい。

examples.en: The mountain on the right-hand side is Mt. Fuji.
examples.ja: 右手の山はふじ山です。

2560.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>right</kanji> <kanji>hand</kanji> is your <vocabulary>right hand</vocabulary>! This word can also be used to mean <vocabulary>right arm</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>right-hand side</vocabulary>.
2560.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. This word, however, uses the kun'yomi readings. This is possibly because of 手, because body parts often use kun'yomi. You learned both readings with the individual words, so you should be able to read this.

examples.en: Please give me four tomatoes.
examples.ja: トマト四こ下さい。

examples.en: There were four class sections in my international school.
examples.ja: わたしのインターナショナルスクールには四クラスありました。

examples.en: There's a short message written on the fourth page of this book.
examples.ja: この本の四ページには、小さいメッセージがかいてあります。

2561.meaning_mnemonic: This vocab word has the same meaning as its parent kanji (single alone kanji usually do that!), meaning it means <vocabulary>four</vocabulary>.
2561.reading_mnemonic:
When a vocab is alone like this with no okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) it usually uses its kun'yomi reading. Numbers are an exception, though, and use the on'yomi reading. However, four and seven actually use both. We're going to go with the kun'yomi reading here, and since you haven't learned this reading yet, here's a mnemonic to help you:

You have to count to <vocabulary>four</vocabulary>. But you're tired. One... two... three... *<reading>YAWN</reading>* ... four. There, you did it. But *yawn* now you can't stop yawning. You're so, so sleepy. Four is too high a number to count without falling asleep.

By the way! Both the reading よん and し are pretty common, but because the on'yomi reading し sounds just like the word for "death," it isn't used as much. Generally when you're just counting (for example, "1, 2, 3, 4..."), you will use the reading し. But when you are counting things or people, you'll use よん. There are exceptions to this, but you'll learn them as they come up.

examples.en: April 1st is April Fool's Day.
examples.ja: 四月一日はエイプリルフールです。

examples.en: Only three more days until April.
examples.ja: 四月まで、あと三日だ。

examples.en: In April, I will try really hard to do my best.
examples.ja: 四月は、力いっぱいがんばります。

2562.meaning_mnemonic: 月 in Japanese means "moon" but it also means "month." Why? Probably because the moon takes about a month to get through its cycles. So, what's the fourth moon of the year? Here's a hint, it's the same as the fourth month of the year: <vocabulary>April</vocabulary>.
2562.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 月 has two on'yomi readings, but it always uses the がつ reading in the names of the months, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember that:

In <vocabulary>April</vocabulary>, you habitually eat <reading>shee</reading>p <reading>guts</reading> (しがつ). It's a tradition you started many years ago, and now you just can't stop eating sheep guts every April. Delicious!

examples.en: The date on the 4th got canceled.
examples.ja: 四日のデートは中止になった。

examples.en: July 4th is an important day for the United States.
examples.ja: 七月四日はアメリカにとって大切な日です。

examples.en: It returned to its original position in four days.
examples.ja: 四日で元のポジションにもどった。

2563.meaning_mnemonic: <vocabulary>Fourth day</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>day four</vocabulary>. No matter how you look at this combination of kanji, the meaning of the word makes a lot of sense!
2563.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Counting days, however, is an exception (at least up to ten). You need to use the kun'yomi readings to read this word. You already know the kun'yomi reading for 四, so that's fine (the ん gets turned into a small っ, though). Think of it this way:

On the <vocabulary>fourth day</vocabulary> of being lost in the wilderness, you start yelling "<reading>Yo</reading>, <reading>ca</reading>r (よっか)!" out of desperation, never getting an answer. You keep marching on, occasionally yelling "Yo, car!", but no car ever comes to help you.

examples.en: Four milkshakes, please.
examples.ja: ミルクシェイク、四つ下さい。

examples.en: There were four ice cubes in water.
examples.ja: 水に氷が四つ入っていた。

examples.en: This apartment has four ovens in place of closets.
examples.ja: このアパート、クローゼットのかわりにオーブンが四つもある。

2564.meaning_mnemonic: Any number with a つ attached is a word that means "NUMBER Things." In this case, it's <vocabulary>four things</vocabulary>.
2564.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can assume it uses the kun'yomi reading. The ん part of よん gets converted to a small っ though, so watch out for that.

examples.en: I hit four thousand followers.
examples.ja: フォロワーが四千人になりました。

examples.en: This mountain is about 4000 meters tall.
examples.ja: この山は、およそ四千メートルです。

examples.en: You can't buy someone's heart for 4,000 yen, you know.
examples.ja: 四千円で他人の心は、かえないよ。

2565.meaning_mnemonic: You have four and you have thousand. Multiply them together and you have <vocabulary>four thousand</vocabulary>.
2565.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. That's true for the 千 part, but the 四 reading is kun'yomi. You should know how to read this word as long as you've been studying your kanji!

examples.en: I was in New York on the day I turned forty.
examples.ja: 四十才になった日、ニューヨークにいました。

examples.en: Cut this tablecloth to 40 cm, please.
examples.ja: このテーブルクロス、四十センチに切って下さい。

examples.en: I've had forty smartphones in my life.
examples.ja: 人生で四十台ものスマホをかってきた。

2566.meaning_mnemonic: What do you get when you have four tens? You get <vocabulary>forty</vocabulary>.
2566.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. The only exception to this is 四, which uses the kun'yomi reading, since the on'yomi reading sounds too much like the word for "death." Luckily you know these reading already, so there's nothing new to learn!

examples.en: The left contact lens is missing.
examples.ja: 左目のコンタクトレンズがない。

examples.en: I’m left-handed.
examples.ja: わたしは、左ききです。

examples.en: The entrance is the door on your left.
examples.ja: 入り口は左のドアですよ。

2567.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2567.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Imagine hearing someone to your <vocabulary>left</vocabulary> saying, "<reading>Hi Da'ri</reading>!" (ひだり) which is supposed to be "Hi There," or "Hi Dearie." You turn left and there's no one there. You hear it again, "Hi Da'ri!" Keep turning to the left until you find the person saying hi to you.

examples.en: I held a spoon with my left hand.
examples.ja: 左手でスプーンをもった。

examples.en: Please raise your left hand.
examples.ja: 左手を上げて下さい。

examples.en: My left hand is a little bit stronger than my right hand.
examples.ja: 左手の方が右手よりも力が少しあるみたい。

examples.en: What you can see on your left-hand side is the Sky Tree.
examples.ja: 左手にみえるのが、スカイツリーです。

2568.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>left</kanji> <kanji>hand</kanji> is your <vocabulary>left hand</vocabulary>! This word can also be used to mean <vocabulary>left arm</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>left-hand side</vocabulary>.
2568.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. This word, however, uses the kun'yomi readings. This is possibly because of 手, because body parts often use kun'yomi. You learned both readings with the individual words, so you should be able to read this.

examples.en: This book, please.
examples.ja: この本、下さい。

examples.en: This book has hints on how to get better at taking quizzes.
examples.ja: この本にはクイズが上手になるためのヒントがかいてある。

examples.en: My oven has a lot of books in it.
examples.ja: うちのオーブンには本がたくさん入ってるんです。

2569.meaning_mnemonic: This vocab word is exactly the same as its parent kanji, including its meaning as well: <vocabulary>book</vocabulary>. It doesn't have those other meanings though, when it's just 本 alone, it's just a book.
2569.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the single kanji it comes from.

examples.en: Japanese curry is delicious.
examples.ja: 日本のカレーはおいしいです。

examples.en: I'm going to Japan in October.
examples.ja: 十月に日本にいきます。

examples.en: What is the population of Japan?
examples.ja: 日本の人口は、どのくらいですか？

2570.meaning_mnemonic: Remember the secondary meaning of 本 being "origin"? That technically makes this <kanji>sun</kanji> <kanji>origin</kanji>. Does that sound familiar? Japan is known as the "land of the rising sun", which is why this means <vocabulary>Japan</vocabulary>!
2570.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. The 本 is read just how you learned it, but the 日 reading is sort of an exception here, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You've finally arrived in <vocabulary>Japan</vocabulary> and immediately fall down on your <reading>knee</reading>s (に). After two excruciatingly long flights, you've finally made it. You're here. This is Japan. Now get up off your knees, people are starting to stare.

examples.en: Mom is always right.
examples.ja: ママはいつも正しい。

examples.en: It's true that I went into the hotel on the 3rd.
examples.ja: ぼくが三日にホテルに入ったというのは正しいです。

examples.en: Would you like me to show you how to enter an entrance properly?
examples.ja: 入り口の正しい入り方をおしえてあげましょうか？

2571.meaning_mnemonic: Ending with an い tells you that this word is an い-adjective. So since you know that the kanji <kanji>正</kanji> means "<kanji>correct</kanji>," what is the adjective version of that word? Well, it's also <vocabulary>correct</vocabulary>.
2571.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses a reading you didn't learn from the kanji. You have to remember the ただ portion in order to read this word, so think about it this way:

After you get the answer <vocabulary>correct</vocabulary> a clown jumps out of nowhere yelling "<reading>Ta-da</reading> (ただ)!!!" Imagine it scaring the crap out of you, too.

examples.en: My task is to correct system errors.
examples.ja: タスクはシステムエラーを正すことです。

examples.en: I corrected the position of the logos on left and right.
examples.ja: 左右のロゴのポジションを正した。

examples.en: That person is a programmer who's dedicated for correcting errors.
examples.ja: あの人はエラーをひたすら正すプログラマーです。

2572.meaning_mnemonic: This word is made up of a kanji with some hiragana attached, ending in an う sound. That means this word is a verb. The kanji itself means "correct," so what is the verb form of that? It would be <vocabulary>to correct</vocabulary>.
2572.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

After you correct something for someone, you yell out <reading>ta-da</reading> (ただ) very excitedly. Go ahead and imagine yourself doing this a few times to help you to remember.

examples.en: What is this ball?
examples.ja: なんだ、この玉？

examples.en: Pochi was a dog that looked like a round ball.
examples.ja: ポチは、まるで丸い玉のような犬でした。

examples.en: Please kick this ball with all your strength.
examples.ja: この玉を力いっぱいキックして下さい。

2573.meaning_mnemonic:
As a single kanji vocab on its own, you know this vocab word has the same meaning as its parent kanji: <vocabulary>ball</vocabulary>.

玉 can be used for round objects traditionally recognized in Japanese culture, like beads, marbles, pearls, snowballs, and pachinko balls. For balls used in sports, people typically use the katakana word ボール.
2573.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the same reading as the one you learned with the kanji: <reading>たま</reading>.

examples.en: Marbles are small, round balls.
examples.ja: ビー玉は小さい丸い玉です。

examples.en: There is a big marble race on February 3rd.
examples.ja: 二月三日に大きなビー玉のレースがあります。

examples.en: Mom, your eyeball is beautiful like a marble.
examples.ja: ママの目玉、ビー玉みたいできれいだね。

2574.meaning_mnemonic: When you see a katakana word, it's a safe bet that it is a foreign loan word from somewhere else. This one's interesting, because it combines katakana and kanji! The first <vocabulary>marble</vocabulary> came to Japan from Portugal, so the ビー part of the word is short for "vidro," which means "glass" in Portuguese. Anyway, don't get thrown off by that ビー. Maybe just imagine that your favorite marble is black and yellow like a bee.
2574.reading_mnemonic: If you know katakana as well as the reading that you learned when you learned the kanji <kanji>玉</kanji>, you should be able to read this. Just watch out for the rendaku.

examples.en: Please give me the round onion.
examples.ja: その丸い玉ねぎ下さい。

examples.en: When I cut the onions, I teared up.
examples.ja: 玉ねぎをきっていたら、なみだが出てきた。

examples.en: Curry without onions is not curry.
examples.ja: 玉ねぎが入ってないカレーはカレーじゃない。

2575.meaning_mnemonic: ねぎ means "onion" in Japanese. But, there are different kinds of onions, right? This happens to be a "ball onion," which is just one of those round ones, like a Walla Walla Sweet <vocabulary>Onion</vocabulary>. Do you know?
2575.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can guess it will probably use the kun'yomi reading. Luckily, that's the reading you learned with the only kanji in this word, so you should be able to read it!

examples.en: I'm planning to get a toy poodle that will be born this month.
examples.ja: 今月、生まれるトイプードルをかうつもりです。

examples.en: My mother was born in the United States.
examples.ja: 母はアメリカで生まれた。

examples.en: Newborns drink milk too.
examples.ja: 生まれたばかりの子もミルクをのみますよ。

2576.meaning_mnemonic: Since this is a kanji with hiragana attached that ends with an う sound, you know that this word is a verb. What's the ultimate verb version of the kanji 生? That would be <vocabulary>to be born</vocabulary>, the very beginning of <kanji>life</kanji> as we know it!
2576.reading_mnemonic:
You have to remember the う part of this word to read it. To remember that, let's use a mnemonic: 

Something is about to be born, and when you lean in for a closer look… it’s an <reading>u</reading>ni (う). Yes, a sea urchin. You weren’t expecting that. Close your eyes and imagine what the process of an uni being born might look like, to help you remember this reading.

examples.en: Money breeds fraud.
examples.ja: お金は不正を生む。

examples.en: The owner of this restaurant is the chef who made Italian cuisine popular in Japan.
examples.ja: このレストランのオーナーが、日本のイタリアンの人気を生んだシェフです。

examples.en: Even though it wasn't my husband's, I had no choice but to give birth to the baby.
examples.ja: 主人の子ではなかったが、生むしかなかった。

2577.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means "life" so what is the verb form of that? Would it be "to do life"? No, probably not. In this case it is <vocabulary>to give birth</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to produce</vocabulary>.

You'll have to differentiate this one from the word 生まれる as well. Just remember that when you give birth, you're the one who has to actually <reading>mo</reading>ve (む) your body by finding the right position and pushing with every ounce of strength you can muster. In contrast, when you're being born, you can just kind of lie there and enjoy the ride.
2577.reading_mnemonic:
You have to remember the う part of this word to be able to read it. You already learned this reading with 生まれる, but here's a mnemonic for you just in case you forgot: 

Imagine yourself giving birth, but not to a baby. Instead, it's an <reading>u</reading>ni (う) you're delivering. Luckily, uni aren't fully formed with their spikes at birth so it shouldn't be a problem. Ooof! What a relief!

examples.en: Do you have a message for people living in this generation?
examples.ja: このジェネレーションを生きる人々にメッセージはありますか？

examples.en: My grandpa lived to be one hundred years old.
examples.ja: わたしのおじいちゃんは百才まで生きました。

examples.en: I can't believe I'm not off tomorrow; I may lose my will to live.
examples.ja: あした休みじゃないなんて、生きる元気がなくなりそうだよ。

2578.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means "life," making this word mean "<vocabulary>to live</vocabulary>."
2578.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use a kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn the い reading with this kanji though, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

What does it mean <vocabulary>to live</vocabulary>? Life is pretty <reading>icky</reading> (いき ... the き comes from the hiragana part), but you have to take that ickiness and roll with it if you want to have a good life... if you want to live!

examples.en: One draft beer, please.
examples.ja: 生ビール、一つ下さい。

examples.en: Are raw peppers tasty?
examples.ja: 生のパプリカは、おいしいですか？

examples.en: Grandma has seen The Beatles in person.
examples.ja: おばあちゃんはビートルズを生でみたことがある。

2579.meaning_mnemonic:
Normally a single kanji alone like this would mean the same thing as its parent kanji, but in the case of <kanji>生</kanji> it's a little different (but still related). When you think of something that has life, it's <vocabulary>fresh</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>raw</vocabulary>. Think sashimi or sushi, for example. You want that to be as close as possible to life as you can, so you eat it when it's fresh and raw. This word can also be used to describe a <vocabulary>live</vocabulary> event, like a concert or sporting event. 

You'll see this word at the beginning of other words. For example, 生たまご is "raw egg."
2579.reading_mnemonic:
This uses one of the kun'yomi readings. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

After eating <vocabulary>raw</vocabulary> fish, my yoga teacher and I say <reading>nama</reading>ste (なま) to the sushi chef, bowing low to show our appreciation.

examples.en: There are many frogs in the rice fields.
examples.ja: 田にはカエルがたくさんいますよ。

examples.en: This rice field is Koichi's.
examples.ja: この田はコウイチさんのものです。

examples.en: Could you finish ploughing the rice fields before you propose to me?
examples.ja: プロポーズは田をたがやしてからにしてくれる？

2580.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
Just keep in mind that compared to 田んぼ, which you learned earlier, this word is more formal and less colloquial.
2580.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When you learned the kanji that makes up this word, all you learned was the kun'yomi reading, so you should be good to go.

examples.en: My wedding dress is white.
examples.ja: わたしのウェディングドレスは白です。

examples.en: This white is a creamy white.
examples.ja: この白はクリームっぽい白ですね。

examples.en: White and pink are apparently my lucky colors.

2587.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means "stand" and this means <vocabulary>to stand something up</vocabulary>. It also can mean <vocabulary>to make something</vocabulary>, both in a physical sense, like making a sound, and a mental sense, like making a plan. 

Don't confuse this with 立つ. 立てる means that you're standing something up. As in, "I stood up the action figure" or "I will erect the flag." You're doing the action to something else.

2591.reading_mnemonic:

You have to work in one of those mall <reading>kio</reading>sks (きょう). Just think about how sad you are that you have to do this today. What a crummy day. It's sunny outside and you're stuck in a mall manning this hermit crab kiosk.

Use this to get yourself close, and then use your own brain grapes to get the rest of the way there. This one won't be as easy as most of the others, but do some good old fashioned memorization and you should be okay. I won't ask you to do this much, fortunately. :)

2598.meaning_mnemonic:
This word means <vocabulary>to understand</vocabulary>, which might surprise you if you remember that the kanji 分 means <kanji>part</kanji>. Think of it this way: to understand something you have to break it down into its parts to see how it works.

Watch out, though, because whereas in English you understand something, in Japanese the thing you understand is the grammatical subject (it's doing the action). So, a more literal meaning for this is <vocabulary>to be understandable</vocabulary>. In other words, there's no object, and 分かる is intransitive, meaning it happens on its own. The かる ending is a hint, because verbs with かる as okurigana (kana added to the kanji) are usually intransitive.
2598.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Whenever you try <vocabulary>to understand</vocabulary> something, you just start screaming "<reading>WAAAAAAAAAHHHH</reading>" (わ). It helps you focus and concentrate on what you’re trying to understand, to the dismay of everyone around you. WAAAAAAAAAHHHH.

2599.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う (in this case る) sound, you know this word is a verb. One of the kanji meanings is <kanji>divide</kanji>, which makes this <vocabulary>to divide something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to separate something</vocabulary>. Depending on the context, it can also mean <vocabulary>to share</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to classify</vocabulary>.

Be careful not to confuse this with 分かる, a similar word with a different meaning. Think of it this way: You "separate" what you care (ける) about from everything else. You want to separate those special things you care about from all the other things you don't care about.
2599.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You already know this reading from 分かる, but here’s a mnemonic in case you forgot:

Whenever you need <vocabulary>to divide something</vocabulary>, you can’t help screaming "<reading>WAAAAAAAAAHHHH</reading>" (わ). You hate having to divide things, or people, so you always end up screaming "WAAAAAAAAAHHHH" in agony.

This word has the same meaning that you learned with the kanji: <vocabulary>part</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>portion</vocabulary>. By extension, it can also mean <vocabulary>content</vocabulary>, as in "alcohol content" because that's the portion of alcohol in a drink.

This word is used for fractions, too, as in one third or one quarter. Again, you can see how this links to "parts" and "portions", right?
2600.reading_mnemonic:
This word is usually combined with a word or phrase indicating whose part or portion you're referring to. That's probably why this single kanji vocab word uses the on'yomi instead of the kun'yomi reading. Check out the common word combinations to see what we're talking about!

And when it means <vocabulary>part</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>portion</vocabulary>, it's read ぶん. Probably because your buns come in two parts. Ohoho.
