This is an intransitive verb. That means it does not take a direct object. The kanji means <kanji>cut</kanji> so this generally means that something is cut. Something breaks or snaps. No direct object here. That's why this verb means <vocabulary>to be cut</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to snap</vocabulary>. The kanji meaning for <kanji>少</kanji> is <kanji>few</kanji>, and the meaning of the vocab form is <vocabulary>a little</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>a few</vocabulary>.
2607.reading_mnemonic: Did you know that this word created an English word you probably already know? Have you ever heard someone say "just a skosh"? That's <vocabulary>少し</vocabulary>! Hopefully you know this English word and therefore know this Japanese word as well.

examples.en: There are few Caucasians and Asians in this area.
examples.ja: このエリアには白人やアジア人は少ないです。

examples.en: Let's cherish the toilet paper as there's not much left.
examples.ja: のこり少ないトイレットペーパー、大切にしよう。

examples.en: It's not a bad thing to have few friends.
examples.ja: 友人が少ないことは、わるいことじゃない。

2608.meaning_mnemonic: This word has a single kanji with hiragana attached, ending in a い. This means you know it's an adjective. What is the adjective form of <kanji>few</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>few</vocabulary>.
2608.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this one is fairly difficult, as it's the kun'yomi reading (you can tell it's kun'yomi because of all the hiragana attached). You have to remember the すく part to remember the reading of this word. Think of it this way: 

You have a <vocabulary>few</vocabulary> of something. This something is <reading>suck</reading>ers (すく). Imagine putting all (three-ish) of them in your mouth at once. How does it taste? Can you taste the flavors from each of the few?

examples.en: Vivid pink is an eye-catching color.
examples.ja: ビビッドピンクは人の目を引くカラーです。

examples.en: Pull this lever with all your strength.
examples.ja: このレバーを力いっぱい引いて。

examples.en: Ten minus two is eight, right?
examples.ja: 十引くニは八でしょ？

2609.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>pull</kanji> and the verb version vocab means <vocabulary>to pull</vocabulary>.

This word can be transitive or intransitive. You use 引く in a transitive way to say you pull something, for example. But it can also mean <vocabulary>to withdraw</vocabulary> when you talk about things that pull back, like water that recedes, pain that subsides, soldiers that withdraw, or even your body recoiling when something puts you off.
2609.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. The reading (ひ) is the same as the one you learned for the kanji, meaning you should already know it!

examples.en: Dad has a big heart.
examples.ja: パパは心が大きい。

examples.en: Cupid's arrow struck my heart.
examples.ja: キューピッドの矢が心にささった。

examples.en: "Good morning, prince," I said in my mind.
examples.ja: 「おはよう、王子」と、心の中でいった。

2610.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2610.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Imagine a giant <vocabulary>heart</vocabulary> sitting in a rowing boat. It's also drinking cocoa. Focus on all three of these parts and associate them into one story / memory. Once you've done that, sing the "<reading>cocoa row</reading>" (こころ) song! I don't know what that song is, but I want you to make one up and actually sing it, out loud. If you do, I bet you won't forget this word's reading too easily.

examples.en: The design of this apartment's doorway is cute.
examples.ja: このアパート、戸口のデザインがかわいいですね。

examples.en: This doorway is a little small.
examples.ja: この戸口、少し小さいね。

examples.en: Why are you always standing in the doorway?
examples.ja: なんで、ずっと戸口に立ってるの？

2611.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>door</kanji>'s <kanji>mouth</kanji> is the <vocabulary>doorway</vocabulary>! 

戸口 is mostly used for doorways that lead outside. It has an old-fashioned feel to it and is becoming less common these days, especially in spoken Japanese.

You might notice that this word resembles 出口 (exit) and 入り口 (entrance). Like in those words, the character 口 just represents an opening here.
2611.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this one is mixed. You get the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, even though it's a combo (jukugo) kanji. Since 戸's only reading is the kun'yomi reading you should know it. Also, you should know the kun'yomi reading for 口 as well from level 1. That means as long as you remember that this is a kun'yomi fest over here, you should be able to read this word. Also watch out for the rendaku (also known as sequential voicing). That just means the く becomes the voiced ぐ.

examples.en: There is a shopping mall in the North.
examples.ja: 北の方にショッピングモールがありますよ。

examples.en: Do you know how to make chocolate cake?
examples.ja: チョコレートケーキのつくり方は分かりますか？

examples.en: Which is better?
examples.ja: どっちの方がいい？

2612.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

You learned 方 means <vocabulary>direction</vocabulary>, but it can also mean <vocabulary>way</vocabulary>, as in この方がいい (this <vocabulary>way</vocabulary> is better) or やり方 (the <vocabulary>way</vocabulary> of doing something). 

Interestingly, 方 can also be used to refer to people politely, like こちらの方 (this person). This is because, in traditional Japanese, people—especially noble ones—were often referred to indirectly, as if indicating their presence from a direction.
2612.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading, but it can actually use kun'yomi or on'yomi depending on the context. Here are a couple mnemonics to help you remember both readings and how they're most often used:

You can always remember which <vocabulary>direction</vocabulary> your <reading>ho</reading>me (ほう) is in. It's in こっちの方 (this direction)!

And the best <vocabulary>way</vocabulary> to get there is with a <reading>cata</reading>pult (かた). Just climb in the catapult and launch yourself there — it's the best やり方.

examples.en: Cars stop at this white line.
examples.ja: この白いラインで車が止まる。

examples.en: I couldn't stop on the skating rink.
examples.ja: スケートリンクの上で、止まることができなかった。

examples.en: The bus almost stopped.
examples.ja: バスは、もう少しで止まりそうでした。

2613.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>stop</kanji>, so the verb 止まる means <vocabulary>to stop</vocabulary>. 

But this is the intransitive version, so it doesn't take a direct object. A train stops, or you stop at a red light. See? No direct object. You can remember this because you often have to stop when you see a 丸 (まる), a.k.a. a circle. Think about it — red lights, the cancel symbol, and no trespassing signs are all 丸. Even stop signs are… sort of 丸?
2613.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading when you learned the 止める, so you should be able to read it already!

examples.en: This is the button to stop the fire.
examples.ja: 火を止めるボタンはこれです。

examples.en: I rushed to stop the water.
examples.ja: いそいで水を止めた。

examples.en: Fugu said "Huh?," and stopped their hand cutting the tomato.
examples.ja: フグは「はっ？」といって、トマトを切る手を止めた。

2614.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>stop</kanji>, so the verb vocab version of that is <vocabulary>to stop something</vocabulary>. Alternatively, it can also mean <vocabulary>to stop doing something</vocabulary>.
2614.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. This word has two different readings for its slightly different meanings, so here's a couple mnemonics to help remember which is which:

When you need <vocabulary>to stop something</vocabulary> from moving, you use your <reading>toe</reading> (と). For most people, this would just lead to a stubbed toe, but you have toes of iron — sturdy enough to stop even speeding locomotives in their tracks.

On the other hand, when you need <vocabulary>to stop doing something</vocabulary> — you know, a bad habit or whatnot — you call over the <reading>Ya</reading>nkees (や). Imagine the whole New York Yankees squad cheering you on (or threatening you with their bats). You'd be able to quit immediately.

examples.en: Is the karaoke contest on the 5th canceled?
examples.ja: 五日のカラオケコンテストは中止ですか？

examples.en: I'm hoping that the concert won't be canceled.
examples.ja: コンサート、中止しないでほしいな。

examples.en: Due to a scandal involving one of the members, the tour has been canceled for a while.
examples.ja: メンバーの一人にスキャンダルがあったため、ツアーはしばらく中止だ。

2615.meaning_mnemonic: You're in the <kanji>middle</kanji> of something when someone yells "<kanji>stop</kanji>!" They hit you with a <vocabulary>cancellation</vocabulary> order and demand the immediate <vocabulary>discontinuation</vocabulary> of all your activities. Welp, it looks like you've been canceled — better go find something else to do.
2615.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This cow has a lot of hair.
examples.ja: この牛、毛がたくさんですね。

examples.en: I had hair since I was born.
examples.ja: 生まれたときから毛がありました。

examples.en: I can't wear a white shirt because of the dog fur.
examples.ja: 犬の毛のせいで白のシャツはきれないんです。

2616.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2616.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Look down! You're holding something covered in <vocabulary>fur</vocabulary>. It's a furry <reading>ke</reading>ttle (け)! It's the weirdest kettle you've ever seen, but presumably it keeps the water hot for much longer.

examples.en: My father is German.
examples.ja: わたしの父は、ドイツ人です。

examples.en: This tie matches my father's.
examples.ja: このネクタイは、父とおそろいなんです。

examples.en: My father was a drummer.
examples.ja: 父はドラマーでした。

2617.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This is the polite and humble form of <vocabulary>father</vocabulary>. You use this when you're talking about your own <vocabulary>dad</vocabulary> to other people in formal settings, especially if you aren't very close to them.
2617.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned when learning the kanji.

examples.en: I emailed my dad.
examples.ja: お父さんにメールした。

examples.en: Dad likes apples.
examples.ja: お父さんはリンゴがすきです。

examples.en: Dad, did you understand?
examples.ja: お父さん、分かった？

2618.meaning_mnemonic:
This word begins with an honorific (お), making whatever comes after it more elevated. Then there's 父, which you know means <kanji>father</kanji>. Lastly, we have the honorific name-ender <ja>さん</ja>. So this is a nice way to say <vocabulary>father</vocabulary>. 

You'll want to use this when you're addressing or calling out to your own <vocabulary>dad</vocabulary>, or when you're talking about him or someone else's dad in a casual setting.
2618.reading_mnemonic:
The part you have to learn to read is the 父 portion. It uses the kun'yomi, but not the one you initially learned with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember this new reading:

The thing your <vocabulary>father</vocabulary> loves the most is <reading>とう</reading>きょう. He will not stop talking about とうきょう to you, and you just have to listen. とうきょう this, とうきょう that. To really get this picture in your head, make sure to imagine your dad incessantly droning on about とうきょう.

examples.en: There are many cows.
examples.ja: 牛がたくさんいますね。

examples.en: Which would you like, a beef steak or a chicken steak?
examples.ja: 牛のステーキとチキンステーキ、どっちがいい？

examples.en: My pet is a cow.
examples.ja: うちのペットは牛です。

2619.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are the same. This word is a bit broader than <vocabulary>cow</vocabulary> though, and can also be used to be <vocabulary>bull</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>ox</vocabulary>.
2619.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you to remember it: 

You're leading the cows around the field. To get them to move, you yell out "<reading>USH</reading>, USH, USH!" (うし) because you have a speech impediment and want to say "MUSH MUSH MUSH." Go ahead and say this out loud, yelling it if you can.

examples.en: I have two older brothers.
examples.ja: 兄が二人います。

examples.en: My brother is a project manager.
examples.ja: 兄はプロジェクトマネジャーです。

examples.en: I drove my brother's car to Atlanta.
examples.ja: 兄の車でアトランタまで行きました。

2620.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This implies that it is your older brother, by the way. Not somebody else's.
2620.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Your <vocabulary>older brother</vocabulary> is different from everyone else's. He has odd powers... some would say powers of the force. Do you know what his name is? It's <reading>Ani</reading> (あに), short for Anikin... wait a sec, does that sound familiar?

examples.en: That man is Yamada's older brother.
examples.ja: あの男の人が、山田さんのお兄さんです。

examples.en: My older brother is big and he also has a masculine demeanor.
examples.ja: 私のお兄さんは体が大きくて、仕草も男の子らしいです。

examples.en: Hey there! Your shirt has some blood on it!
examples.ja: ちょっと、そこのお兄さん！シャツに血がついてますよ！

2621.meaning_mnemonic: This word starts with an お to make it more polite. Then it has the kanji <kanji>兄</kanji> which you already know. Lastly, it has さん which is an honorific to elevate people and be polite. This is basically the formal way of saying <vocabulary>older brother</vocabulary> (versus plain old 兄). It can also be used to refer to a <vocabulary>guy</vocabulary> that you don't know who has a youthful appearance.
2621.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this one is pretty tricky, and I'd consider it an exception. To remember it, you have to learn the 兄 part, and everything else will fall into place. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

Your (kind) <vocabulary>older brother</vocabulary> pushes you down on the ground. You stand up and look at your <reading>knee</reading> (にい), which is all bloody. "Why'd you do that to my knee!?" you ask. "You're supposed to be a nice older brother, that's why I call you お兄さん!"

2622.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

2623.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2623.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. You already learned that reading with the kanji, so you should be good to go here!

examples.ja: JLPTまで、あと一日半しかないよ。

examples.ja: このキッチンの大きさは、およそ二メートル半です。

2624.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2624.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it's supposed to use the kun'yomi reading. But, there is no useful kun'yomi reading for this kanji, so even the single kanji vocab word version uses the on'yomi reading, which you've already learned!

examples.en: This dress is old.
examples.ja: このドレスは古いです。

examples.en: The old tablet sold for 9,000 yen.
examples.ja: 古いタブレットが九千円でうれた。

examples.en: I like old things like antiques and whatnot.
examples.ja: アンティークとか古いものがすきなんです。

2625.meaning_mnemonic:
This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>old</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>old</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>ancient</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>out-of-date</vocabulary>.

This word is used for things like clothes, food and friendships, but not for people! So a 古い友人 (old friend) is someone you've been friends with for a long time, not an elderly friend.
2625.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji with some hiragana attached, it's going to use the kun'yomi reading. You learned the on'yomi when learning the kanji portion, so let's use a mnemonic to help you with the reading of this word: 

If you're <vocabulary>old</vocabulary>, you're also <reading>full</reading> (ふる) of memories. And you're probably full of old secrets. And you're full from old people food.

examples.en: This Benz is secondhand.
examples.ja: このベンツは中古です。

examples.en: I bought used jeans.
examples.ja: 中古でジーンズをかった。

examples.ja: 中古ショップには本やマンガがたくさんありますよ。

2626.meaning_mnemonic: The combination of kanji doesn't make perfect sense, but it's alright. Take something that's <kanji>middle</kanji> <kanji>old</kanji> and you have something that's <vocabulary>used</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>secondhand</vocabulary>. It's not 100% old yet... it's still in the middle, meaning you can give it to someone else to use, like your younger siblings.
2626.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

2627.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

2628.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

2629.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.ja: パソコンを十台オーダーした。

2630.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Let's barbecue outside.
examples.ja: 外でバーベキューしよう。

examples.en: There is a big cherry blossom tree outside.
examples.ja: 外に大きなサクラの木があります。

examples.ja: 外と中、どっちがすき？

2631.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

Note that 外 doesn't always simply indicate the physical position of something. It can also be used figuratively to refer to what's outside of one's inner circle or home.
2631.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

You look <vocabulary>outside</vocabulary>, it's totally frozen. You throw <reading>salt</reading> (そと) outside to melt the ice.

examples.en: We had a double date with a foreign couple.
examples.ja: 外人カップルとダブルデートをした。

examples.en: There are lots of foreigners at the after party.
examples.ja: アフターパーティーには外人がたくさんいた。

examples.en: The foreigner at the bar bought me a glass of whiskey.
examples.ja: バーにいた外人さんがウィスキーをおごってくれたんです。

2632.meaning_mnemonic: An "outside person" is a <vocabulary>foreigner</vocabulary>. This word is fairly common, though it's not super polite, either. It's okay most of the time, but it can be used derogatorily depending on the situation. The more polite version is 外国人 (outside country person) but you won't learn that until you learn the kanji for 国.
2632.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Who's the <vocabulary>foreigner</vocabulary>? Well obviously the <reading>guy</reading> wearing <reading>jean</reading>s (がいじん)!

examples.en: No matter how many times I threw the darts, they wouldn't hit the dartboard, and in the end, they were all misses.
examples.ja: 何回矢を投げてもダーツボードに当たらなくて、結局全部外れだったよ。

examples.en: The teacher's prediction was completely off the mark.
examples.ja: 先生の予想は完全に外れでした。

examples.en: The man lived in a small house on the forest's periphery.
examples.ja: 男は森の外れの小さな家に住んでいた。

examples.en: The princess was wearing a dress that doesn't suit the season.
examples.ja: 王女は、季節外れのドレスを着ていた。

2633.meaning_mnemonic:
外れる is "to come off" or "to be off." And this is its noun form — <vocabulary>a miss</vocabulary>, aka something that's <vocabulary>off the mark</vocabulary>. Whatever it is, it's completely off the original goal or intended target.

This word refers to something that falls outside of what's expected, central, or correct. Like something that didn't match your hopes or expectations — a losing lottery ticket or a disappointing purchase. It can also describe a place on the <vocabulary>periphery</vocabulary> or the <vocabulary>outskirts</vocabulary> — since you're "off the mark" from somewhere more central.
2633.reading_mnemonic: You shoot, but it's <vocabulary>a miss</vocabulary>. Way <vocabulary>off the mark</vocabulary>. Better put on your <reading>haz</reading>mat (はず) suit because you hit a toxic waste barrel instead of the target. Put your hazmat suits on, everyone!

examples.en: The wind was strong, and the arrow missed the target.
examples.ja: 風が強くて矢がターゲットから外れてしまった。

examples.en: I thought it would rain today, but my prediction was off.
examples.ja: 今日は雨だと思ったのに、予想が外れた。

examples.en: Since he came unplugged, Mr. Robot was no longer able to say, "thank you," anymore.
examples.ja: プラグが外れたので、Mr.ロボットは「ありがとう」と言えなくなった。

2634.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

You already learned 外す, which is used when YOU remove something. 外れる, on the other hand means <vocabulary>to come off</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to be off</vocabulary>. It's used when something ends up outside of where it's supposed to be — like a plug coming out of a socket. 

To remember the difference with 外す, just think of how <reading>rare</reading> (れる) it is for a plug to come out on its own, compared to when you intentionally remove it. It's kind of rare, right?

More figuratively, 外れる can also describe when your expectations are off — the results have ended up "outside" of what you were hoping for.
2634.reading_mnemonic: When something is about <vocabulary>to come off</vocabulary>, you better hurry and put on your <reading>haz</reading>mat (はず) suit. Who knows what kind of toxic matter could spray out when this thing comes off. Better take all necessary precautions.

examples.en: What is the population of Manila City?
examples.ja: マニラ市の人口はどのくらいですか？

examples.en: Hikone City's yuruchara is "Hikonyan."
examples.ja: ひこね市のゆるキャラは、「ひこにゃん」です。

2635.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned when learning the kanji.

So this word means <vocabulary>Seattle</vocabulary>, or more specifically <vocabulary>City of Seattle</vocabulary>.
2637.reading_mnemonic: This word uses on'yomi reading, which you learned with the kanji.

2638.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the reading you learned in the kanji section: ひろ, making this <reading>ひろ</reading>い.

2639.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they both mean mother. 母 is a formal and humble way to say "my mother" when talking to others. By using the plain form and omitting respectful language toward your own mom, you actually sound more humble, which makes a polite impression on the person you're speaking to. You wouldn't, however, use it when talking to your mom or when talking about someone else's mom — it would come off as too blunt for that!
2639.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading, but this is the reading you learned with the kanji. Just remember, your <vocabulary>mother</vocabulary> is a terrible person and won't stop laughing at you: "<reading>HA HA</reading> HA HA HA!"

examples.en: Where’s mom?
examples.ja: お母さんはどこ？

examples.en: My mother is always on a kale diet.
examples.ja: うちのお母さん、いつもケールダイエットしてるんです。

examples.en: Oh, I got a LINE message from my mom.
examples.ja: あ、お母さんからLINEだ。

2640.meaning_mnemonic:
This word begins with an honorific (お), which generally adds a nuance of respect or politeness to what comes after it. Then there's 母, which you know means <kanji>mother</kanji>. Lastly, we have the honorific name-ender さん. So this is a nice way to say <vocabulary>mother</vocabulary>. You use it when talking about the <vocabulary>mom</vocabulary>s of friends or casual acquaintances, when talking about your own mom in a casual social setting, or when talking to your own mom.

In more formal settings, you'll want to use 母 (pronounced はは) to talk about your own mom and the super respectful お母さま to talk about someone else's mom.
2640.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. You have to remember the かあ portion. Here's a mnemonic to help you to remember it: 

What does your super nice <vocabulary>mother</vocabulary> do for you (this is why you're so polite to her!)? She drives you all around in her <reading>car</reading> (かあ) taking you wherever you need to go... soccer, kendo, whatever. What a nice mother you have!

examples.en: This is a machine used for fitness training.

examples.en: Depending on the person, the tools they use are different.

2641.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>task</kanji> or <kanji>use</kanji>. You can think of this verb as a more formal way to say <vocabulary>to use</vocabulary>, and that is <vocabulary>to utilize</vocabulary>.
2641.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you to learn the もち portion of もちいる: 

What will you <vocabulary>utilize</vocabulary> to get the job done? You have <reading>mochi</reading> (もち) in your hand, so you'll use that. Now go think of some kind of imaginary task you'll complete with mochi, making it as ridiculous as possible.

examples.en: I’m coming to Paris now on official business.
examples.ja: 今、公用でパリにきています。

2642.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>public</kanji> <kanji>task</kanji> is going to be <vocabulary>government business</vocabulary>. You have to think of this public as government to know the meaning of this word easily.
2642.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This is an archery arrow.

2643.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2643.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned when learning the kanji.

examples.en: There's no class today.
examples.ja: 今日はクラスが休みです。

examples.en: I go for drives with my dog ​​on my days off.

2644.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji <kanji>rest</kanji> has a little hiragana attached, but it's nothing that would suggest it's anything but a noun (it is!). It means the same thing as the kanji, <vocabulary>rest</vocabulary>.
2644.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji with some hiragana, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

So, do you want a <vocabulary>rest</vocabulary> from work or school? You should say "<reading>YAASS</reading> (やす)!"

examples.en: Should we skip today's class?
examples.ja: 今日のクラス、休む？

examples.en: I rested in bed for four and a half days.
examples.ja: ベッドで四日半で休みました。

examples.en: The only time I can rest during the day is when I’m in the bathroom.
examples.ja: 一日で休むことができるのは、トイレにいるときだけだ。

2645.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji 休 means <kanji>rest</kanji>, so what's the verb version of that? It's <vocabulary>to rest</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to take time off</vocabulary>.
2645.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You need <vocabulary>to rest</vocabulary>, right? Don't just answer with a "yes," this deserves a "<reading>YAASS</reading>" (やす)! YAAASSS let's RESSST!!!

examples.en: These classes have been temporarily discontinued.
examples.ja: しばらく、このクラスは休止です。

examples.en: News of the popular rock band's hiatus came to my attention.
examples.ja: 人気のロックバンドの休止のニュースが目に入った。

examples.en: My first kiss happened in an elevator that was stuck.
examples.ja: わたしのファーストキスは休止中のエレベーターの中だったんです。

2646.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>stop</kanji> that's just a <kanji>rest</kanji> (aka not permanent) isn't a straight up stop. You're planning on continuing again. That's why this is a <vocabulary>pause</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>suspension</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>hiatus</vocabulary>.

This is a fairly formal word, and it's often used when an activity or a service is temporarily suspended. For example, you could use it to talk about a class being suspended, a machine suspending its operation, or a pop band going on a hiatus. Check out our common word combinations below for more example usages.
2646.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I drink wine on holidays.
examples.ja: 休日はワインをのみます。

examples.en: Today is a holiday, so I came for a picnic.
examples.ja: 今日は休日なので、ピクニックにきました。

examples.en: Please do not email me on my days off.
examples.ja: 休日にメールしてこないで下さい。

2647.meaning_mnemonic: When you have a <kanji>rest</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji> you have a <vocabulary>holiday</vocabulary>.
2647.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 日 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Every <vocabulary>holiday</vocabulary>, you eat not one, but two <reading>cu</reading>cumbers. <reading>Gee, two</reading> (きゅうじつ)? Take it easy!

examples.en: First, cut the tomatoes.
examples.ja: 先ず、トマトを切ります。

examples.en: First, draft beer. Then, rice.
examples.ja: 先ずは、生ビール。それから、ごはん。

examples.en: Why don't you date a little more first, and then propose?
examples.ja: 先ずはもっとデートしてからプロポーズしたら？

2648.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji means <kanji>previous</kanji>. This is an adverb version of that word. It's a little thing you can begin sentences with. You can't start your sentences with "previous" but you can start it with "<vocabulary>First of all</vocabulary>" or "<vocabulary>to start with</vocabulary>."

This is usually written without kanji though, so keep that in mind.
2648.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. In fact, the reading for this word is very rare, and kind of an exception. We'll use a mnemonic that uses both the kanji part and the hiragana attachment part. 

<vocabulary>First of all</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to start with</vocabulary>, you have to make it through this <reading>maze</reading> (まず).

examples.en: The tip of the pen got crushed.
examples.ja: ペンの先がつぶれた。

examples.en: Please go first.
examples.ja: お先にどうぞ。

examples.en: There's a restaurant just ahead of us.
examples.ja: この先にレストランがある。

examples.en: Nobody knows what the future holds.
examples.ja: 先のことはだれにも分かりません。

2649.meaning_mnemonic:
Everything that happened to you <kanji>previous</kanji>ly is just the <vocabulary>tip</vocabulary> of the iceberg, and the important stuff is <vocabulary>ahead</vocabulary> of you, in your <vocabulary>future</vocabulary>. So make sure you put that stuff <vocabulary>first</vocabulary>!

The original meaning of this word is the tip of something, like a pen or a finger. From that meaning, it's expanded into all sorts of meanings, like ahead, first, and future, depending on the context and where it is in the sentence. It can also mean "previous" in formal contexts (and we'll accept that meaning too, but we're not teaching it here because it's more advanced).
2649.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Just <vocabulary>ahead</vocabulary> of you are the <vocabulary>tip</vocabulary>s of a <reading>saw</reading> and a <reading>key</reading>(さき). You have no idea what they're doing there, but both saws and keys have very sharp tips, so watch out you don't hurt yourself. Imagine yourself edging carefully past those saw and key tips.

You can differentiate this from 先ず (まず) because it doesn't have any hiragana on the end.

examples.en: I went to Cuba the month before last.

examples.en: There was a big hurricane in Florida the month before last.
examples.ja: 先々月、フロリダで大きなハリケーンがあったそうだ。

examples.en: Please look at the receipt from the month before last.
examples.ja: 先々月のレシートを見て下さい。

2650.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>previous</kanji> <kanji>previous</kanji> <kanji>month</kanji> (remember that 々 just repeats the kanji before it) is the <vocabulary>month before last</vocabulary>.
2650.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Last month was June.
examples.ja: 先月は六月でした。

examples.en: We met in New York last month, right?
examples.ja: 先月、ニューヨークでおあいしましたよね？

2651.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 月 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

As of <vocabulary>last month</vocabulary>, your <reading>cen</reading>taur <reading>gets</reading> (せんげつ) up every night and comes to sleep in your bed. Apparently, he gets really bad nightmares. Poor little centaur.

examples.en: Thank you so much for the other day.
examples.ja: 先日はどうもありがとうございました。

examples.en: The party the other day got canceled.
examples.ja: 先日のパーティー、中止でしたね。

examples.en: Did you like my idea from the other day?
examples.ja: 先日のアイディアは気に入っていただけましたか？

2652.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>previous</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji> isn't necessarily yesterday. It can be any recent day, which is why this word means <vocabulary>the other day</vocabulary>.
2652.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 日 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

<vocabulary>The other day</vocabulary>, you saw two <reading>cen</reading>taurs! <reading>Gee, two</reading> (せんじつ) of them?! You're lucky you're still alive!

examples.en: The teacher said "good morning."
examples.ja: 先生は「おはよう」といった。

examples.en: That woman is Tanaka-sensei.
examples.ja: あの女の人は、田中先生です。

examples.en: Koichi is my teacher in life.
examples.ja: コウイチは、わたしの人生の先生だ。

2653.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Previous</kanji> <kanji>life</kanji>... So we're talking about someone who has a previous life, or maybe previous life experience? When you have previous life experience, you can teach others about it, making you qualified to be some kind of <vocabulary>teacher</vocabulary>.

先生 is often used for school teachers, but it's also used to show respect to doctors, lawyers, authors, and other respected experts. It's used as a standalone word or a name ender like トム先生.
2653.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My father is a frisbee expert.
examples.ja: 父はフリスビーの名人です。

examples.en: What should I do to become an expert skier?
examples.ja: スキーの名人になるには、どうしたらいいですか？

examples.en: That woman is not only a chess master, but also a master of blackjack.
examples.ja: あの女の人はチェスの名人であるだけでなく、ブラックジャックの名人でもある。

2655.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>name</kanji> of this <kanji>person</kanji> is well known, but why? It's because they're an <vocabulary>expert</vocabulary> in their field, or a <vocabulary>master</vocabulary> of something. If you're an expert or a master of something, people are going to know your name — even if you're just an expert at being an idiot.
2655.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Did you know that every <vocabulary>expert</vocabulary> has their own pair of <reading>May</reading> <reading>jean</reading>s (めいじん)? A true <vocabulary>master</vocabulary> of anything has a specific pair of jeans they wear only in the month of May. That's what makes them so good at what they do.

examples.en: My surname is "Tanaka."
examples.ja: 名字は「田中」です。

examples.en: Please enter your last name here.
examples.ja: 名字は、ここに入力して下さい。

examples.en: Please call me by my first name, not my family name.
examples.ja: 名字じゃなくて、ファーストネームでよんで下さい。

2656.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>name</kanji> written in <kanji>letter</kanji>s is the <vocabulary>surname</vocabulary>. Back in the day your surname was the important name (it's your family name after all, and family was king back in the day). This is the name you'd write out in kanji... aka in letters. So, that's why this combination of kanji means "surname."
2656.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 名 uses an alternate on'yomi reading here that you haven't learned yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

Imagine you and your significant other are about to get hitched, and you're trying to decide your future <vocabulary>surname</vocabulary>. "Let's just combine 'me' and 'you' and go with <reading>Myou</reading> (みょう)," you say. Yes, from now on, you two will share the surname Myou.

examples.en: That's a cute letter.
examples.ja: かわいい字ですね。

examples.en: Is this character "n"? Or is it "so"?
examples.ja: この字は「ン」ですか？それとも「ソ」ですか？

examples.en: Please increase the size of the character more.
examples.ja: 字の大きさを、もっと大きくしてください。

2657.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2657.reading_mnemonic: You only learned one reading for the kanji that makes up this word, and it's the same as the reading for this word (of course). That means you should already know the reading.

examples.en: Make this character bold, please.

examples.en: Is this a bold point pen?
examples.ja: これは太字のペンですか？

2658.meaning_mnemonic: What do you think a <kanji>fat</kanji> <kanji>letter</kanji> is? If I were to guess, I'd say a <vocabulary>bold letter</vocabulary>. You know, like <vocabulary>bold text</vocabulary> on a screen.
2658.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this one is a bit odd. It combines the kun'yomi ふと from 太 with the on'yomi じ from 字. You learned both these readings with the kanji, so you should be OK here. You'll just have to remember it's a weird mix of kun'yomi and on'yomi. It kind of makes this word stand out… as if it were written in bold letters.

examples.en: The letters are too small.
examples.ja: 文字が小さすぎる。

examples.en: The katakana characters for "ku" and "wa" look very similar.
examples.ja: カタカナの「ク」の文字と「ワ」の文字は、そっくりだ。

examples.en: The tree has some alphabet letters written on it.
examples.ja: 木にアルファベットの文字がかいてある。

2659.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>writing</kanji> <kanji>letter</kanji> is simpler than it sounds. It's really just a <vocabulary>letter</vocabulary>, right? You're reading 文字 right now, in fact!
2659.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. The reading of 文 is a bit of an exception here. It uses a shortened version of the on'yomi もん, which is も. Here's a mnemonic to remember this:

You know all the <vocabulary>letters of the alphabet</vocabulary> only because of <reading>Mo</reading>e (も). If it wasn't for your buddy Moe teaching you all the letters, you probably wouldn't even be able to read today. Thanks Moe!

examples.en: The girl got angry and her mouth pursed into a straight line.
examples.ja: 女の子は、おこって口を一文字にむすびました。

examples.en: The salmon has a straight line cut across it.
examples.ja: サーモンに一文字の切り目が入ってます。

examples.en: Quite a few drones were flying in a straight line.
examples.ja: たくさんのドローンが一文字になってとんでいる。

2660.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned 文字 means "letter (of the alphabet)" or "character." And what does the kanji character for <kanji>one</kanji> look like in Japanese? A <vocabulary>straight line</vocabulary>!

Think of this word as meaning "the 一 character." In Japanese, it's most often used to describe the straight line a person's lips make when they're pressed together in concentration, frustration, or silence.
2660.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 文 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Anyone who goes around with his mouth in a <vocabulary>straight line</vocabulary> is probably a <reading>mon</reading>ster (もん). How could anyone walk around with such an uninviting expression on their face? Basically, anyone who isn't smiling constantly is a monster, as far you're concerned. And that includes those monsters with 一文字-shaped mouths.

examples.en: All uppercase letters for the title, please.
examples.ja: タイトルは、全て大文字でおねがいします。

examples.en: Only the T is uppercase, and others are lowercase letters.
examples.ja: Tだけ大文字で、他は小文字です。

The reading for this word is the kun'yomi reading, which you did not learn when you learned the kanji. You have to remember the はや portion to be able to read this word. In order to do that, here's a mnemonic: 

You're <kanji>fast</kanji>! You're <kanji>early</kanji>! Your chop comes down onto your opponent's neck so quickly! As you chop him, you yell "<reading>HAYA</reading>!" (はや)

2669.meaning_mnemonic: Essentially you have the kanji 早 twice, because 々 is the repeater kanji. When you do something doubly <kanji>early</kanji>, there must be some kind of urgency to it, right? So you need to take action <vocabulary>as soon as</vocabulary> you finish whatever it is you're doing.
2669.reading_mnemonic:
This word has two possible readings, each with a different nuance, so here are some mnemonics to remember them by:

そうそう is for when you do something quickly or immediately after something else, like 早々にホテルを出る (to leave a hotel quickly) or オープン早々 (as soon as a shop opens). You can remember this because <vocabulary>as soon as</vocabulary> you get to work, you do everything really <vocabulary>quickly</vocabulary>, so your work performance is just <reading>so-so</reading> (そうそう).

はやばや is for when you do something earlier than usual, like going to bed or closing up shop before the usual time. It often appears as 早々と. You can remember this because when you want to close up shop <vocabulary>early</vocabulary>, you say "<reading>Hiya… bye-ya</reading>!" (はやばや) to all the customers who come in. Saying both hi and bye when they walk in is the best way to hint that you're trying close early. Hiya, bye-ya! Yeah, they get the hint.

examples.en: That line is kinda like something a villager would say in "Animal Crossing," isn't it?
examples.ja: なんか「どうぶつのもり」の村人っぽいセリフだよね。

2691.meaning_mnemonic: You have a <kanji>village</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji>. That isn't someone dancing while wearing construction worker clothes, that's a <vocabulary>villager</vocabulary>.
2691.reading_mnemonic: This word uses double kun'yomi for its reading, probably because it's like two separate words (village and person) put together into one big word. You should know these two kun'yomi readings (it's the main reading for 村 that you learned and you should know 人 by now), though you will need to look out for the rendaku'd びと reading.

examples.en: Who's that guy?
examples.ja: あの男は、だれ？

examples.en: The two men had a knife.
examples.ja: 二人の男はナイフをもっていた。

examples.en: You're such a quiet man.
examples.ja: ほんと、あんたって大人しい男。

2692.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

Just be aware that this word used alone can sound a bit rude. You'll learn a more neutral option very soon.
2692.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you to remember it: 

There is a <vocabulary>man</vocabulary>. Think of the manliest man you can. He works in an auto shop. As a child, he was an <reading>auto 子</reading> (おとこ), working at the auto shop from an early age. This turned him into a man very quickly. 

Like other mnemonics that aren't lined up quite perfectly, your goal here is to get close enough to remember the true reading. Step, step, step, jump!

examples.en: Gas stations in this town are small.
examples.ja: この町のガソリンスタンドは小さい。

examples.en: Dr. Yamashita is a popular doctor in town.
examples.ja: 山下先生は、町で人気のドクターです。

examples.en: I often go out to the neighboring town on my days off.
examples.ja: となりの町には休みの日によく出かけます。

2693.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2693.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

You walk into this town. You hate it (because it's vocab, and who doesn't hate vocab?). So what do you do? You pull out a <reading>match</reading> (まち) and burn this town to the ground. Whoa, you some kind of psycho?

examples.en: Sunflowers are very beautiful.
examples.ja: ヒマワリの花はとてもきれいです。

examples.en: I want to give some flowers to my mother.
examples.ja: 母に花をプレゼントしたいんです。

examples.en: Seeing flowers gives you positive energy.
examples.ja: 花を見ると元気になりますね。

2694.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2694.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. This is the reading you learned when you learned the kanji, so you're good to go. Don't forget to stop and smell the roses on the way, though.

examples.en: At this beach, there are fireworks in August.
examples.ja: このビーチでは八月に花火があります。

examples.en: I want to have a barbecue with fireworks at the river.
examples.ja: 川でバーベキューと花火したいなぁ。

examples.en: Seems like today's fireworks have been canceled.
examples.ja: 今日の花火は中止だってさ。

2695.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>flower</kanji> <kanji>fire</kanji>... what looks like flowers on fire? That would be <vocabulary>fireworks</vocabulary>. Totally makes sense, right?
2695.reading_mnemonic: The readings for the kanji that make this word are the kun'yomi readings, where fire's ひ changes to び. You already learned the kun'yomi reading for 花 when you learned the kanji, so it's only a matter of remembering to use the kun'yomi for 火. If you do, you should be able to read this word.

examples.en: Let's do cherry blossom viewing on April 1st.
examples.ja: 四月一日、花見しましょう。

examples.en: I had some beer while viewing the cherry blossoms under the tree.
examples.ja: 木の下で花見をしながらビールを口にした。

examples.en: Many people come to this town during cherry blossom season.
examples.ja: 花見シーズンには、この町にたくさんの人が来ます。

2696.meaning_mnemonic:
When you have <kanji>flower</kanji>s that you can <kanji>see</kanji>, you are viewing flowers. But not just any flowers. What flowers do Japanese people love viewing? That's right, this word refers to <vocabulary>viewing cherry blossoms</vocabulary>.

The focus of 花見 is on the act of appreciating blossoming trees, often accompanied by outdoor gatherings, picnics, or parties. Although cherry blossoms are the most commonly associated flowers, the term can encompass other flower-viewing experiences as well.
2696.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this vocab is all kun'yomi, but you learned the kun'yomi readings of both these when you learned their kanji. So no worries there. You can spend the extra time viewing the cherry blossoms.

examples.en: I looked outside and saw a white dog.
examples.ja: 外を見ると、白い犬がいた。

examples.en: Did you see the news the other day?
examples.ja: 先日のニュース、見ました？

examples.en: Please look left and right carefully before making a U-turn.
examples.ja: よく左右を見てからUターンして下さいね。

2697.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>see</kanji> so the vocab here means <vocabulary>to see</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to look</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to watch</vocabulary>.

Seeing, looking, watching — 見る doesn't care. No need to squint over word choice here.
2697.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the reading you learned with the kanji (kun'yomi) so you should be able to read this.

examples.en: The volcano is visible from here.
examples.ja: ここから火山が見える。

examples.en: Can you see the villager over there?
examples.ja: あそこの村人が見えますか？

examples.en: I'm really curious about how I seem to others.
examples.ja: 自分が他人からどう見えるのかがすごく気になる。

2698.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>see</kanji>, and 見える is <vocabulary>to be visible</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to be in sight</vocabulary>, though it's often more naturally translated into English as <vocabulary>can see</vocabulary>. It's used when you don't actively intend to see something, it just happens.

This verb can also mean <vocabulary>to seem</vocabulary>, when talking about how you perceive something you can see.
2698.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned with the kanji (the kun'yomi reading). So as long as you know that you should be able to read this word as well.

examples.en: It's not a kitchen that I would show to others.
examples.ja: 人に見せるほどのキッチンじゃないですよ。

examples.en: Show me the notebook.
examples.ja: そのノート、見せて。

examples.en: Would you like me to show you my Pokémon card collection as a thank you for lunch today?
examples.ja: 今日のランチのお礼にポケモンカードのコレクション見せてあげようか？

2699.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. It's related to the meaning of the kanji 見 "see," but this one is about having someone else see something. In other words, it means <vocabulary>to show</vocabulary>.
2699.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one that you learned with the kanji, so you should be able to read it.

examples.en: I tell the brothers apart by their eye colors.
examples.ja: 兄弟を目の色で見分ける。

examples.en: It's impossible to tell whether what the man said is true.
examples.ja: あの男が言ったことが本当かどうか見分けるなんてムリだよ。

examples.en: Are you able to distinguish between diamonds and stones?
examples.ja: ダイヤモンドと石ころを見分けることは出来ますか？

2700.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>see</kanji> something, then you "separate" (分ける) it. This is the same thing as <vocabulary>to distinguish</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to tell apart</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to recognize</vocabulary>. This verb is transitive, so you're doing the action to something. You're distinguishing between things or people.
2700.reading_mnemonic: You should know the reading of 見 already. The second part, 分ける is a word you should have learned in the previous level. Combine that knowledge together and you get the reading for this word.

examples.en: Do you know how to look at this chart?
examples.ja: このチャートの見方、分かる？

examples.en: That perspective is valid.
examples.ja: その見方は正しい。

examples.en: If you see it from a different point of view, half of life is like an elevator.
examples.ja: 他の見方をすれば、人生の半分はエレベーターみたいなものだ。

2701.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>see</kanji>ing <kanji>way</kanji> is your <vocabulary>way of seeing</vocabulary> something. This is like when someone has a dumb opinion and you're like, "oh, okay, so that's one way of seeing it..."
2701.reading_mnemonic:
This uses the kun'yomi readings from the vocab words 見る and 方. The 方 reading here (かた) wasn't the main one you learned though, so here's a mnemonic to help it stick:

You've been told your <vocabulary>way of seeing</vocabulary> things is a little narrow, so in order to gain a broader <vocabulary>perspective</vocabulary>, you decide to <reading>cata</reading>pult (かた) yourself in the air. That'll certainly give you an interesting <vocabulary>viewpoint</vocabulary>.

examples.en: October is moon-viewing season.
examples.ja: 十月は、月見のシーズンですね。

examples.en: Proposing while looking at the moon? How romantic.
examples.ja: お月見しながらプロポーズだなんて、ロマンチックだね。

examples.en: One order of udon with an egg, please.
examples.ja: 月見うどん、一つ下さい。

2702.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>moon</kanji> <kanji>see</kanji> something, you're doing a <vocabulary>moon viewing</vocabulary>.

月見 is a traditional autumn event in East Asia where people admire the full moon and enjoy seasonal treats, which in Japan include moon-shaped dumplings, sweet potatoes, and chestnuts. 月見 also often pops up in the names of foods that resemble the moon in some way, like a 月見バーガー — a hamburger whose fried egg topping is playfully compared to a full Harvest Moon.
2702.reading_mnemonic: This word uses kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You learned the つき reading with the 月 vocab word, and the み reading with the kanji 見 (and with some of its vocab, like 見る). You probably won't have trouble remembering the み part, so here's a mnemonic just for the つき bit: Every year when it's moon viewing time, you get out two keys (つき). The first key lets you out onto the veranda, where you do the actual moon viewing, and the second key unlocks your pantry full of moon-viewing snacks. These two keys are key to enjoying moon viewing at your house.

examples.en: There are many shellfish in the river.
examples.ja: 川には、たくさん貝がいる。

examples.en: Shellfish pasta or shiitake mushroom pasta, which one should I get?
examples.ja: 貝のパスタとシイタケのパスタ、どっちがいいかな？

examples.en: It's ramen made with red shellfish dashi.
examples.ja: 赤い貝のダシでつくったラーメンです。

2703.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2703.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned with the kanji, meaning you should be able to read this already.

examples.en: Ketchup's red color comes from red tomatoes.
examples.ja: ケチャップの赤はトマトの赤です。

examples.en: Do you like red peppers?
examples.ja: 赤パプリカは、すきですか？

examples.en: Stop the car when that light turns red.
examples.ja: あのライトが赤になったら、車を止めて下さい。

2704.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2704.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

examples.en: A baby will be born in May.
examples.ja: 五月に赤ちゃんが生まれる。

examples.en: This cute baby girl is Emma.
examples.ja: このかわいい女の子の赤ちゃんはエマちゃんです。

examples.en: This is baby formula.
examples.ja: これは赤ちゃんのミルクです。

2705.meaning_mnemonic: ちゃん is the honorific you put on a child's name. So, who is this mysterious child you're calling <kanji>red</kanji>? When a baby is born, what color are they? You got it, they're all red. And, because you want to be nice and cute you add ちゃん to that. That's why あかちゃん is a <vocabulary>baby</vocabulary>.
2705.reading_mnemonic: If you know the reading of the kanji <kanji>赤</kanji> you should know the reading of this too.

examples.en: I wonder if ten kilograms is enough.
examples.ja: 十キログラムで足りるかな。

examples.en: I don't have enough toilet paper!
examples.ja: トイレットペーパーが足りない！

examples.en: There never seem to be enough holidays.
examples.ja: 休みは、いくらあっても足りない。

2706.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>leg</kanji> or <kanji>sufficient</kanji>, and we're going with the "sufficient" meaning for this word! This word means <vocabulary>to be enough</vocabulary>.
2706.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember the た portion. Whenever we need to remember the た we use the word "taco." 

What do you have enough of? What is sufficient? Turns out it's <reading>ta</reading>cos (た). Your bunker is filled with them and it's going <vocabulary>to be enough</vocabulary> to last the winter.

examples.en: I have a tattoo on my leg.
examples.ja: 足にタトゥーがある。

examples.en: I am not a fan of bugs with a lot of legs.
examples.ja: 足がいっぱいある虫は、すきじゃないです。

examples.en: My shoe size is 25 cm.
examples.ja: 足のサイズは25センチです。

2707.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are almost exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. A <kanji>foot</kanji> is a <vocabulary>foot</vocabulary>, you know?

Although this word is more commonly used for feet, sometimes it can also refer to <vocabulary>leg</vocabulary>s. Now you've got a leg up in understanding 足!
2707.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

If you remember in the radical/kanji mnemonic, you kick someone with your foot. But what happens after you kick them? Turns out they were made of fire, and you just burned your foot off, turning it to <reading>ash</reading>es (あし). Imagine this happening.

examples.en: Last year, there was a water shortage in this area.
examples.ja: このエリアでは去年、水が不足しました。

examples.en: There has been unauthorized access due to my insufficient skills. I'm sorry.
examples.ja: 不正アクセスがあったのは、わたしの力不足のせいです。すみませんでした。

examples.en: Where is this portion of the shortage coming from?
examples.ja: この不足分は、どこで生まれたんだろう？

2708.meaning_mnemonic:
You have something that's <kanji>not</kanji> <kanji>sufficient</kanji>. When something isn't sufficient, you have an <vocabulary>insufficiency</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>shortage</vocabulary>.

This word is more commonly used in formal contexts. In more casual, everyday conversations, 足りない is often preferred to express something being insufficient.
2708.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My father's car is a Benz.
examples.ja: 父の車はベンツです。

examples.en: I wonder if somebody could give us a ride.
examples.ja: だれか車出してくれないかな？

examples.en: It takes about a day and a half by car to Florida.
examples.ja: フロリダまで車で一日半くらいかかるよ。

2709.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2709.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

You visit your mom who lives inside of a <kanji>car</kanji>. It's sad, and you feel bad. The first thing that pops out of your mouth is: "<vocabulary>Cool Room, Ma</vocabulary> (くるま) because you don't know what else to say about your ma's living situation. 

Be sure to sort of cut off the last letters of the first two words... something like "coo' roo' ma!" Sad thing is, there is only one room in this car your mom calls home.

examples.en: There are many people in the car.
examples.ja: 車内に人々がたくさんいます。

examples.en: There was no driver inside the bus.
examples.ja: バスの車内にはドライバーがいなかった。

examples.en: Last month, I left my smartphone in a taxi.
examples.ja: 先月、タクシーの車内にスマホをわすれたんです。

2710.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>car</kanji> <kanji>inside</kanji> is simply that, <vocabulary>inside the car</vocabulary>. This can be used for other means of transport too, so it can also mean <vocabulary>inside the train</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>inside the bus</vocabulary>.
2710.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This app still isn’t world famous.
examples.ja: このアプリは、まだ世に出ていません。

examples.en: There are all kinds of people in the world, right?
examples.ja: 世の中には色々な人がいるもんですね。

examples.en: In Japanese, "this world" refers to the current world while living, and "the other world" refers to the world after death.
examples.ja: 日本語で「この世」とは生きている時の今の世界、「あの世」とは死後の世界のことです。

2711.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2711.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you to remember it: 

Since you have generations of people making up this <vocabulary>world</vocabulary>, think of the rapper generation. What do they say all the time (obviously I don't know anything about rap)? They say "<reading>Yo</reading> yo yo!" (よ).

examples.en: My mother is a second generation American who was born in Japan.
examples.ja: 母は日本で生まれたアメリカ人の二世です。

examples.en: Elizabeth II was the Queen of England.
examples.ja: エリザベス二世はイギリスの女王でした。

examples.en: Few second-generation celebrities are popular.
examples.ja: 二世タレントで人気の人は少ないです。

2712.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Charles III has become the King of England.
examples.ja: チャールズ三世がイギリスの王になりました。

examples.en: My father is a third-generation Japanese born in the United States.
examples.ja: わたしの父はアメリカで生まれた日本人の３世です。

examples.en: I take pride in being the third generation.
examples.ja: わたしにだって三世としてのプライドがあります。

2713.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>three</kanji> <kanji>generation</kanji> is the <vocabulary>third generation</vocabulary>. Depending on the context, you can sometimes use this alone to say you're third generation Japanese. Usually, though, you'll want to specify whether you're third generation Japanese or another nationality.
2713.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Unauthorized access was mainly from Europe.
examples.ja: 不正アクセスは主にヨーロッパからでした。

examples.en: Japan's population is primarily Asian.
examples.ja: 日本の人口は主にアジア人です。

examples.en: I mainly spend my holidays in the mountains or at the river.
examples.ja: 休日は主に山か川にいます。

2714.meaning_mnemonic: 主 means <kanji>main</kanji> so when you add に it becomes the adverb <vocabulary>mainly</vocabulary>.
2714.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You <vocabulary>mainly</vocabulary> spend your time talking to your master Moe. But you mainly address him like, "<reading>Oh Moe</reading> The Great!" (おも). That's because he's above you. Imagine yourself saying "OH MOE THE GREAT!" as you walk into his room, bowing low.

examples.en: This person is my husband.
examples.ja: この人は、わたしの主人です。

examples.en: Is your husband working remotely today?
examples.ja: 今日ご主人はリモートワークですか？

examples.en: Master, the ten-meter blanket is too big.
examples.ja: ご主人さま、十メートルのブランケットはさすがに大きすぎますよ。

2715.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>master</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji> isn't just a master. You have to think back to when they were making these kanji. Who was the master? It was the <vocabulary>head of household</vocabulary>. This head of household probably told servants what to do and was all bossy and stuff. He was the master person. 

Also, this often means <vocabulary>husband</vocabulary>. Because, I guess the head of household back in the day was the husband. Those sexist ancient people!
2715.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

In Japan, tradition says the head of a household must slide down a <reading>chu</reading>te in only <reading>jean</reading>s (しゅじん). Whenever you need to speak to the head of the household, they'll come sliding down a chute wearing nothing but jeans. What a sight!

examples.en: I'm not very good at controlling it.
examples.ja: コントロールの仕方が下手です。

examples.en: This is how people greet each other in France.
examples.ja: これがフランスのあいさつの仕方なんです。

examples.en: The book "How To Catfish Without Being Caught" was a bestseller in 2020.
examples.ja: 「バレないキャットフィッシングの仕方」という本は２０２０年のベストセラーとなった。

2716.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>doing</kanji> <kanji>way</kanji> is basically a "way of doing" something. More simply put, this is the <vocabulary>method</vocabulary>. "What's your way of doing this?" No no no. "What's your METHOD." There we go.
2716.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the on'yomi reading for 仕 (no surprises there), but the kun'yomi reading for 方, so watch out for that! You're probably more familiar with the on'yomi for 方, so here's a mnemonic to help with the kun'yomi:

Your <vocabulary>method</vocabulary> of <reading>cata</reading>pulting (かた) anything you don't like into the air is definitely the best <vocabulary>way of doing</vocabulary> things.

examples.en: It's no use even if you kept standing over there.
examples.ja: そこにずっと立っていても仕方がないよ。

examples.en: There's nothing you can do about coming to Japan when there's no flight available.
examples.ja: フライトがなくて日本に来られないのは仕方がない。

examples.en: There were not many rainy days, this year's water shortage couldn't be helped.
examples.ja: 雨の日が少なかったんだから、今年の水不足は仕方がないよ。

2717.meaning_mnemonic: You’ve already learned 仕方, which you know means "method" or "way of doing." When you don’t (that’s the がない part) have a way of doing or achieving something, you could say it can’t be helped, it’s no use, or there’s no other way. Makes sense, right? This is a popular phrase in Japanese, so we're sure you'll encounter it a lot!
2717.reading_mnemonic: You already know how to read this from having learned 仕方, so you should be good to go!

examples.en: No other staff are here right now.
examples.ja: 他のスタッフは今いません。

examples.en: The other first-graders raised their hands.
examples.ja: 他の一年生の子は手を上げた。

examples.en: Do you have any other ideas?
examples.ja: その他にアイディアはありますか？

2718.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2718.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

You need to go for a drive to the public gardens, but you aren't going to get your normal car, you're going to get your <kanji>other</kanji> car. Your <reading>hoe car</reading> (ほか)! It's a car made entirely out of garden hoes. You can drive it and hoe with it at the same time! Your other car can't do that!

examples.en: As a stranger, can you understand?
examples.ja: 他人のあなたに分かりますか？

examples.en: Don't only listen to the advice of others.
examples.ja: 他人のアドバイスばかりきくな。

examples.en: I'm worried about the eyes of others, so there's no way I can cosplay outside.
examples.ja: 他人の目が気になって、どうしても外でコスプレができません。

2719.meaning_mnemonic:
When you have an <kanji>other</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji>, you really have <vocabulary>another person</vocabulary>.

他人 has a sense of unfamiliarity or distance, and suggests that the person isn’t well-known, or is different from you or a specific group of people. It doesn't usually mean "another person" in the sense of an additional person, or another person distinct from the one you’re talking about.
2719.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

<vocabulary>Another person</vocabulary> just stole your <reading>ta</reading>co and your <reading>Nin</reading>tendo (たにん). This complete <vocabulary>stranger</vocabulary> just walked up and took your taco and your Nintendo console straight out of your hands. Yoink.

examples.en: I'll swap shifts with Jenny.
examples.ja: ジェニーとシフトを代わる。

examples.en: If you don't mind, can I take your place?
examples.ja: もしよければ、代わりましょうか。

examples.en: This boy is a genius to replace Steve Jobs.
examples.ja: この少年はスティーブ・ジョブズに代わる天才です。

2720.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>substitute</kanji>, and the verb 代わる means <vocabulary>to substitute for</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to take over for</vocabulary>. Use it when one player substitutes for another in sports, for example, or when someone takes over for you at work. 

代わる is usually intransitive, but sometimes it can be transitive and take a direct object. Kind of like "to take over" in English — someone can take over your shift (transitive), or just take over for you (intransitive).
2720.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember the か part:

You need something <vocabulary>to substitute for</vocabulary> your <reading>car</reading> (か). It's getting repaired, so you can't use it now. I guess you can substitute your bike for your car?

examples.en: After a generation, that Italian restaurant has closed.
examples.ja: あのイタリアンレストランは一代でクローズしてしまった。

examples.en: The owner has made this hotel the best hotel in Japan in one generation.
examples.ja: オーナーは一代でこのホテルを日本一のホテルにしました。

examples.en: In one generation, my father turned a small convenience store into a big department store.
examples.ja: 父は一代で小さいコンビニエンスストアを大きなデパートにしたんです。

2721.meaning_mnemonic: This word has the kanji for <kanji>one</kanji> and <kanji>period</kanji>. You only have one period to live in so this is the only <vocabulary>lifetime</vocabulary> you get. Unless you're reborn, but that will probably be in the next age, not this one. So one lifetime for you!
2721.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I substituted sour cream with yogurt.
examples.ja: サワークリームをヨーグルトで代用しました。

examples.en: Is this garlic a substitute for onions?
examples.ja: このニンニクは、玉ねぎの代用ですか？

examples.en: There are many people who use a balance ball in place of an office chair.
examples.ja: オフィスチェアの代用で、バランスボールを用いる人がたくさんいます。

2722.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>substitute</kanji> <kanji>task</kanji> is a <vocabulary>substitution</vocabulary>.

Note that this word has a slightly formal feel to it.
2722.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Can I copy your notes from today's class?
examples.ja: 今日のクラスのノート、写してもいい？

examples.en: Cameras are fine, but please do not take photographs of others.
examples.ja: カメラは平気ですが、他の人は写さないで下さいね。

examples.en: You copied my signature, didn't you?
examples.ja: わたしのサイン、写したでしょ？

2723.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>copy</kanji> so you know this means <vocabulary>to copy</vocabulary>. You know this word means "to copy" because it ends with す. You're copying the documents you need to <reading>sue</reading> (す) someone who screwed you over.
2723.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You have to remember the うつ part. To remember that, think of yourself as a beatboxer. You're saying <reading>うつ</reading>うつうつ over and over again. Thing is, the other beatboxer is going <vocabulary>to copy</vocabulary> everything you do. That's why you're suing him.

examples.en: My father doesn't like to be in videos.
examples.ja: 父はビデオに写るのがきらいです。

examples.en: White flowers are not in the wedding photo.
examples.ja: 白い花は、ウェディングフォトに写っていない。

examples.en: You can take good pictures of trees and mountains with this camera.
examples.ja: このカメラでは、木や山がよく写る。

2724.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>copy</kanji>, but what is a copy? It's basically a photograph, which is why this word means <vocabulary>to be in a photograph</vocabulary>. 

In other words, this is the word you use when you point at a photo and say, "hey, I'm in this!" You know it means "to be in a photograph" because every time you appear in a photo, you're doing something <reading>ru</reading>de (る), like sticking your tongue out or giving someone the finger.
2724.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned that reading with the 写す vocab, but here's a refresher just in case:

You're going <vocabulary>to be in a photograph</vocabulary> in the newspaper. Why? Because you caused a scene by rudely beatboxing out in public: <reading>うつ</reading>うつうつ. You're probably going to appear in people's photos all over social media too. Too bad those photos won't be able to convey the phat beats you were うつうつうつing into everyone's eardrums.

examples.en: The ticket for the Nozomi No.3 was 30,000 yen.
examples.ja: のぞみ三号のチケットは三万円でした。

examples.en: The Thomas train is quite spacious inside.
examples.ja: トーマス号の車内は、とても広いです。

examples.en: Masked Rider 1 is a hero to everyone.
examples.ja: かめんライダー一号は、みんなのヒーローです。

2725.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

This word is generally added to the end of a number, as in 三号 ("number 3"). It can also go together with other words to give things like train car numbers, as in ２号車 ("car 2"), and room numbers. When used on its own, it indicates the edition number of magazines and the like.
2725.reading_mnemonic: This word is made up of a single kanji all alone, but it uses the on'yomi reading. This is probably because you'll usually see this word attached to other things, like numbers. This shows the edition or number of an item. So, even though it's alone, it's usually used like jukugo, which is why the reading for this one is the same as the reading you learned when you learned the kanji.

examples.en: Mami is on the left, Jenny is in the center, and on the right is Michael.
examples.ja: 左がマミ、中央がジェニー、右がマイケルです。

examples.en: Don't stand at the center of the stage.
examples.ja: ステージの中央に立たないで下さい。

examples.en: I put a card in the center of the table.
examples.ja: テーブルの中央にカードをおいた。

2726.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>middle</kanji> of the <kanji>central</kanji>... that is really, really in the <vocabulary>center</vocabulary> if you ask me (and is very <vocabulary>central</vocabulary> as well). This is one of those "overdid it on the meaning" words.
2726.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That mountain is flat.
examples.ja: あの山、平らですね。

examples.en: This is a machine that flattens the ground.
examples.ja: これは土を平らにするマシンです。

examples.en: Can I race marbles even on a flat surface?
examples.ja: 平らなところでもビー玉のレースはできますか？

2727.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same with a little hiragana sticking out. Because the hiragana doesn't really indicate what it is, it's okay to assume that they share meanings as well.
2727.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a kanji plus some hiragana attached, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Something is very, very <vocabulary>flat</vocabulary>. Perhaps someone who doesn't eat much, like a model? Which model? Let's imagine it's <reading>Tyra</reading> (たいら) Banks.

examples.en: I mainly have curry for dinner on weekdays.
examples.ja: 平日のディナーは主にカレーです。

examples.en: Which would be okay, a weekday or a holiday?
examples.ja: 平日と休日、どちらなら平気ですか？

examples.en: My husband has off on weekdays.
examples.ja: 主人は平日が休みです。

2728.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>flat</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji>s are boring. They're the same. One day after another. That's definitely not your exciting weekends... that's your boring, flat <vocabulary>weekdays</vocabulary>.
2728.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 日 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

<vocabulary>Weekdays</vocabulary> are flat, but you do at least earn two entire bales of <reading>hay</reading>. <reading>Gee, two</reading> (へいじつ) of them! What a hard worker you are.

examples.en: I want to be an expert at hitting home runs.
examples.ja: ホームランを打つ名人になりたい。

examples.en: My teacher is quick with a keyboard.
examples.ja: ぼくの先生は、キーボードを打つのがはやい。

examples.en: Let's take action before it's too late.
examples.ja: 今のうちに手を打っておこう。

2729.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>hit</kanji> so the vocab is <vocabulary>to hit something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to strike something</vocabulary>. It can also mean <vocabulary>to type</vocabulary>.

You can use this word to describe bumping a part of your body on something, hitting a ball or a nail, or typing on a keyboard. It can also describe hitting a person, but that use is less common and sounds a bit literary.
2729.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi reading, which you haven't learned yet, but never fear! A mnemonic is here:

If you’re planning <vocabulary>to hit</vocabulary> an <reading>u</reading>ni (う), you’re going to need a special bat or hammer. I don’t know why you’d want to hit a sea urchin, but make sure you have the right equipment if you do, because those things are spiky!

examples.en: It was a powerful hit.
examples.ja: 力いっぱいの一打でしたね。

examples.en: Did that golf ball land on the green in one stroke?
examples.ja: あのゴルフボール、一打でグリーンの上に？

examples.en: I took a hit from boxing.
examples.ja: ボクシングで一打をくらった。

2730.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>One</kanji> <kanji>hit</kanji> is simply… <vocabulary>one hit</vocabulary>!
