"I want you <vocabulary>to come</vocabulary> to the <reading>coo</reading>l (く) side, Luke," says Darth Vader.
"What?" replies Luke.

Just replace this line into the famous line from Star Wars. Say it out loud. Do the Vader voice. It'll help you to remember.

examples.en: Is the piano competition next month?
examples.ja: ピアノのコンクールは来月ですか？

examples.en: We're having a party next month. Please come, Kanae.
examples.ja: 来月、パーティーをするので、かなえさんも来て下さい。

examples.en: The number of new staff members who will join the company next month is about ninety.
examples.ja: 来月入社するスタッフは大体九十人です。

2825.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>next</kanji> <kanji>month</kanji> is the <vocabulary>next month</vocabulary>! It isn't this month or the month before, it's the next one!
2825.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 月 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

<vocabulary>Next month</vocabulary> is when <reading>rye</reading> <reading>gets</reading> (らいげつ) into your diet! You're going to eat only rye bread and drink only rye beer for all of next month. Bet you can't wait!

examples.en: Next year is the year 2000.
examples.ja: 来年は２０００年です。

examples.en: I will be eighteen next September.
examples.ja: わたしは来年の九月に十八才になります。

examples.ja: 先生に「あなたは、まだ全力を出してない」と言われてしまった。

examples.en: If I try to go to the pantry, please stop me with your full power.
examples.ja: もし私がパントリーの方に行こうとしたら、全力で止めて下さい。

2855.meaning_mnemonic: When you put <kanji>all</kanji> your <kanji>power</kanji> into something, you're putting your <vocabulary>full effort</vocabulary> into it. Hopefully that's what you put into your kanji learning as well!
2855.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 力 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

With your <vocabulary>full effort</vocabulary>, you were able to produce a <reading>Zen</reading> <reading>lock</reading> (ぜんりょく). It's a lock imbued with the power of Zen, meaning no one and nothing could possibly break it. It's the one lock to rule them all.

examples.en: The population of all of Japan is mainly Asian.
examples.ja: 全日本の人口は主にアジア人です。

examples.en: The All Japanese women's volleyball team is good.
examples.ja: 全日本の女子バレーボールチームは上手です。

examples.en: Mt. Fuji is popular among all the mountains in Japan.
examples.ja: 全日本の山の中でも、ふじ山は人気です。

2856.meaning_mnemonic: You know 日本 means "Japan." So, now you have the kanji for <kanji>all</kanji> added to it, making this word <vocabulary>All Japan</vocabulary> (as in "All Japan Railways" or something like that).
2856.reading_mnemonic: You know the reading of 日本. Now just add the on'yomi reading of 全 and you should be able to read this word.

examples.en: Is this tree house safe?
examples.ja: このツリーハウスは、安全ですか？

examples.en: It's important to hike safely even for adults.
examples.ja: 大人でも、ハイキングは安全に行うことが大切です。

examples.en: The safety of all of Japan depends on you.
examples.ja: 全日本の安全はあなたにかかってます。

2857.meaning_mnemonic: When you are <kanji>all</kanji> <kanji>relax</kanji>ed you are finally <vocabulary>safe</vocabulary> and in <vocabulary>safety</vocabulary>.
2857.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Which direction is the entrance?
examples.ja: 入り口の方向はどちらですか。

examples.en: You will be able to see the moon in the direction of that mountain over there.
examples.ja: あの山の方向に月が見えます。

examples.en: The man ran to the direction of the convenience store.
examples.ja: 男は、コンビニの方向に走った。

2858.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>direction</kanji> <kanji>yonder</kanji> over there is still just the <vocabulary>direction</vocabulary> of something, though a complicated way to say it, I think. This direction is the "what direction did he go in?" sort of direction.
2858.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Fruit in Cameroon is very cheap.
examples.ja: カメルーンのフルーツはとても安い。

examples.en: I'm fine with a cheap hotel.
examples.ja: 私は安いホテルでも平気ですよ。

examples.en: Welcome to the cheapest supermarket in Japan!
examples.ja: 日本一安いスーパーマーケットへ、ようこそ！

2859.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い at the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. One of the meanings of 安 is <kanji>cheap</kanji>, so this is just that as an adjective, <vocabulary>cheap</vocabulary>. Time to go to a 100円 shop and get some 安い goods, ammiright?
2859.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

"Would you like this item for <vocabulary>cheap</vocabulary>?" 

"<reading>YAASS</reading> (やす), please!"

examples.en: That’s a relief.
examples.ja: これで安心です。

examples.en: I was relieved to see that my friend was just fine.
examples.ja: 元気な友人を見て安心しました。

examples.en: I'm a professional pilot, so don't worry.
examples.ja: 私はプロのパイロットなので、どうぞご安心を。

2860.meaning_mnemonic: When your <kanji>heart</kanji> is <kanji>relax</kanji>ed, how do you feel? What if this is after something startling happens? You would feel <vocabulary>relief</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>peace of mind</vocabulary>.
2860.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'm a little anxious to go abroad alone.
examples.ja: 一人で外国に行くのは少し不安です。

examples.en: I'm worried if I will be able to get into a college.
examples.ja: 大学に入学できるか不安です。

examples.en: Are you worried about your child's independence?
examples.ja: お子さんの自立について、不安は有りますか？

2861.meaning_mnemonic: When you're <kanji>not</kanji> <kanji>relax</kanji>ed, what do you feel? <vocabulary>Uneasiness</vocabulary> is what you'd feel.
2861.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Today was a peaceful day.
examples.ja: 今日は一日、平安な日でした。

examples.en: The best love story in Japanese literature was born during the Heian period.
examples.ja: 日本文学一のラブストーリーは平安に生まれました。

examples.en: When I'm in this forest, my heart becomes peaceful.
examples.ja: この林の中にいると、心が平安になります。

2862.meaning_mnemonic:
Something is <kanji>flat</kanji> and <kanji>relax</kanji>ed. That is you. What words does that describe? To me, that would be <vocabulary>peace</vocabulary>. Just imagine something that is flat and relaxed, like a field of grass with happy people in it. It's so <vocabulary>peaceful</vocabulary>!

This is the way you write the <vocabulary>Heian</vocabulary> period of Japanese history, which is probably where you'll see this word the most.
2862.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I was born in the state of Idaho.
examples.ja: 私は、アイダホ州の生まれです。

examples.en: Can you name all ten provinces in Canada?
examples.ja: カナダにある十の州、全て言えますか？

examples.en: Due to the state's rule, you can't enter with a car here.
examples.ja: 州のルールで、ここは車で入れません。

2863.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2863.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the on'yomi reading that you learned with the kanji, probably because it normally gets added on to other things, like the names of the state. Examples: カリフォルニア州, ニューヨーク州, etc.

examples.en: Have you ever been to Kyushu?
examples.ja: 九州に行ったことはありますか？

examples.en: Mangoes from Kyushu are delicious.
examples.ja: 九州のマンゴーは、おいしいです。

examples.en: Kyushu dialect is popular among men nationwide.
examples.ja: 九州の方言は、全国の男の人から人気です。

2864.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>nine</kanji> <kanji>states</kanji>. This refers to a section of Japan from a long time ago that was presumably made up of nine states. Now it's just one big island, though, and that island is <vocabulary>Kyuushuu</vocabulary>. Go take a look at a map and find this giant island, it's a cool part of Japan!
2864.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What is the population of Honshu?
examples.ja: 本州の人口は何人ですか？

examples.en: Mt. Fuji is located in Honshu.
examples.ja: ふじ山は、本州にあります。

examples.en: I came from Honshu by ferry last night.
examples.ja: 夕べ、フェリーで本州から来ました。

2865.meaning_mnemonic: You have your <kanji>origin</kanji> <kanji>state</kanji>. For Japan (since this is a Japanese word), that would be the main island, the big one in the middle: <vocabulary>Honshu</vocabulary>. You'll have to know some minor Japanese geography for this. Go look at a map of Japan and study it over real quick to see where I'm talking about if you don't know already.
2865.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This song is popular in the United States.
examples.ja: この曲はアメリカで人気です。

examples.en: Do you have any recommended songs?
examples.ja: おすすめの曲はありますか？

examples.en: What's great about this rock band is not their music, but their looks.
examples.ja: このロックバンド、曲じゃなくて見た目がいいんですよ。

2866.meaning_mnemonic: This almost shares the meaning with the kanji. It's essentially the same thing, though when it's alone it refers to a specific <vocabulary>piece of music</vocabulary> (aka a <vocabulary>tune</vocabulary>).
2866.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji as well, so you should be able to read it.

examples.en: This is a jazz masterpiece.
examples.ja: これはジャズの名曲です。

examples.en: My father made a famous song that's also popular for small children.
examples.ja: 父は、小さい子どもにも人気の名曲を作った。

examples.en: Beethoven’s "Smoked Salmon" is a masterpiece.
examples.ja: ベートーベンの「スモークサーモン」は名曲だ。

2867.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: We still have a little mayonnaise.
examples.ja: マヨネーズなら、まだ少し有る。

examples.en: Do you have money for university enrollment?
examples.ja: 大学入学のためのお金は有りますか？

examples.en: Right now we only have one car.
examples.ja: 今は車が一台しか有りません。

2868.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>have</kanji>, so this verb version means <vocabulary>to have</vocabulary>. An alternative meaning is <vocabulary>to exist</vocabulary>, because having something means that it exists for you.

The kanji isn't used too often for this word, so just use the kana when you write it. But you'll see the kanji used sometimes, so it's important to be able to recognize it!
2868.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

<vocabulary>To have</vocabulary> something is very nice. But now, the only thing you possess are screams. Imagine this. You are in a totally empty room with no possessions. You open a little box and look inside. It contains screams that yell: "<reading>AAAAHHHH</reading>" (あ).

examples.en: Nicholas Cage is famous in Japan too.
examples.ja: ニコラス・ケイジは日本でも有名です。

examples.en: What's known as a famous mountain in Japan is Mt. Fuji.
examples.ja: 日本で有名な山と言えば、ふじ山です。

examples.en: Have you ever met a celebrity?
examples.ja: 有名人に会ったことある？

2869.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>have</kanji> a <kanji>name</kanji> (that is known to people) or you <kanji>have</kanji> <kanji>famous</kanji>ness, you are probably someone who is <vocabulary>famous</vocabulary>.
2869.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Let's go with the next bus.
examples.ja: 次のバスで行きましょう。

examples.en: Do you have the day off on the next day?
examples.ja: 次の日は、お休みですか？

examples.en: It's your turn next.
examples.ja: 次は、あなたです。

2870.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2870.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Someone yells out "NEXT!" because the first thing didn't work on you. That was a single guillotine. Now they are going to try <reading>two gui</reading>llotines (つぎ) and see how that works on your thick neck. NEXXXXT!

examples.en: When is the next time?
examples.ja: 次回は、いつですか？

examples.en: Many people are coming to the next meeting.
examples.ja: 次回のミーティングには、たくさんの人が来ますよ。

examples.en: There's no next time. We only live once.
examples.ja: 次回なんてないんだよ。人生は一回しかないんだから。

2871.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>next</kanji> <kanji>time</kanji> you look at this kanji, you should know that it means <vocabulary>next time</vocabulary>.
2871.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: First, please look at the table of contents of the book.
examples.ja: 先ず、本の目次を見て下さい。

examples.en: Even just looking at the table of contents tells you a little about the book.
examples.ja: 目次を見るだけでも、本の中について少し分かりますよ。

examples.en: Next is a page for the table of contents.
examples.ja: 次は、目次のページです。

2872.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>eye</kanji> is on what's <kanji>next</kanji>. How is this possible to see what's coming up? That's because you're looking at a <vocabulary>table of contents</vocabulary>.
2872.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: This year's annual convention came to a successful end.
examples.ja: 今年の年次大会は無事終了いたしました。

examples.en: That information was in the annual report mailed to stockholders.
examples.ja: その情報は株主に郵送された年次報告書に記載されていました。

examples.en: At our company, unused yearly paid leave cannot be carried forward to the following year.
examples.ja: 当社では、未消化の年次休暇は次の年に繰り越すことができません。

2873.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>year</kanji> that is <kanji>next</kanji> is coming up. What will you do in the year that is next that you did this year too? What do you do that is <vocabulary>annual</vocabulary>?

年次 is a formal term typically used in business settings, such as in 年次報告書 (annual report) or 年次休暇 (annual leave).
2873.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Most insects die with this spray.
examples.ja: このスプレーで大体の虫は死ぬ。

examples.en: Every day, I live to my fullest power as if I'm dying.
examples.ja: 毎日、死ぬ気で力いっぱい生きています。

examples.en: There is chance you may die if you enter the mountain alone at night.
examples.ja: 夜に一人で山に入ったら、死ぬかもしれないよ。

2874.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>death</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to die</vocabulary>.
2874.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: Dead bodies of the two were found in a mountain.
examples.ja: 二人の死体は、山で見つかった。

examples.en: A cow corpse is in the ground.
examples.ja: 牛の死体が、土の中にあります。

examples.en: There is a corpse in the trunk of that car over there.
examples.ja: あの車のトランクに死体が入ってます。

2875.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji for <kanji>death</kanji> and <kanji>body</kanji> put together make for a <vocabulary>dead body</vocabulary>. Hopefully you don't have to use or see this vocab too much.
2875.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: No one died in this flight.
examples.ja: 今回のフライトで、死亡した人はいませんでした。

examples.en: Is it true that coffee lowers the risk of death?
examples.ja: コーヒーで死亡のリスクが下がるって、本当？

examples.en: The news of the death of two Japanese people came in.
examples.ja: 日本人二人死亡のニュースが入ってきた。

2876.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Death</kanji> and <kanji>deceased</kanji>. That's a lot of death. This is <vocabulary>mortality</vocabulary>.
2876.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This sheep's fur is white.
examples.ja: この羊の毛は白いです。

examples.en: Let's make mutton curry tonight.
examples.ja: 今夜は羊のカレーにしましょう。

examples.en: We have both lamb and calves.
examples.ja: うちには子羊と子牛が両方います。

2877.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well — <vocabulary>sheep</vocabulary>!

羊 can also mean <vocabulary>ram</vocabulary> in some contexts. After all, a ram is just a male sheep.
2877.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Imagine a <vocabulary>sheep</vocabulary> fighting with Jesus. The first thing it does is <reading>hits Je</reading>sus (ひつじ) in the stomach with its fists, then hits Jesus again with its horns. Try to imagine this playing out, with an announcer calling the shots as well.

examples.en: I got a wool blanket as a Christmas present.
examples.ja: クリスマスプレゼントに、羊毛のブランケットをもらいました。

examples.en: Wool is fluffy.
examples.ja: 羊毛はふわふわです。

examples.en: What, this bra is made out of wool?
examples.ja: えっ、このブラ、羊毛で出来てるんですか？

2878.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: There is blood on your shirt.
examples.ja: シャツに血がついていますよ。

examples.en: Yikes, blood is coming out of my ankle!
examples.ja: うわ、足首から血が出てる！

examples.en: My father is not related to me by blood.
examples.ja: 父は、私と血がつながってません。

2879.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2879.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

You cut yourself and there's <vocabulary>blood</vocabulary> everywhere. You need to stop the bleeding with something, but the only thing nearby is a block of <reading>chee</reading>se. You grab the cheese and stuff it into your gash, but the blood comes out the holes (it is Swiss cheese, blargh!). Imagine this in great detail to be able to remember it well.

examples.en: Bleeding doesn't stop.
examples.ja: 出血が止まりません。

examples.en: There is still bleeding on both hands.
examples.ja: まだ両手に出血があります。

examples.en: The bleeding was so bad that I couldn't use much power.
examples.ja: 出血がひどくて、大した力も出せなかった。

2880.meaning_mnemonic: When the thing that is <kanji>exit</kanji>ing is <kanji>blood</kanji>, you are probably <vocabulary>bleeding</vocabulary>.
2880.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. 

Note that the しゅつ from 出 gets shortened to しゅっ. That's a small つ there, not a big one.

examples.en: Which country are you from?
examples.ja: お国はどちらですか。

examples.en: I was born in a country called Bulgaria.
examples.ja: 私はブルガリアという国の生まれです。

examples.en: This country is safe for a woman to go out alone at night.
examples.ja: この国は夜に女の人が一人で出かけても安全ですよ。

2881.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2881.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Tell me about your <vocabulary>country</vocabulary>. Now imagine that everyone in your country has <reading>coo</reading>l <reading>knee</reading>s (くに). That's because the national dress code is shorts, so everyone's knees get chilly. That why they have cool knees. You could also imagine cool knees in the sense of trendy knees. What makes for cool knees, in your opinion?

examples.en: China's population is larger than Japan.
examples.ja: 中国の人口は日本よりも大きい。

examples.en: There are many famous mountains in China.
examples.ja: 中国には有名な山がたくさんあります。

examples.en: My massage instructor is a Chinese person.
examples.ja: 私のマッサージの先生は中国人です。

2882.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>middle</kanji> <kanji>country</kanji>... who could that be? Let's think about it. Who invented kanji and therefore probably thinks they're the middle of the world? Who also is just a huge country that ruled much of Asia? That would be none other than <vocabulary>China</vocabulary>.
2882.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just make sure you watch out for the rendaku.

examples.en: This is a message to my mother in heaven.
examples.ja: これは、天国にいる母へのメッセージです。

examples.en: This is like a paradise for cosplayers.
examples.ja: ここは、まるでコスプレイヤーの天国だ。

examples.en: I'm disappointed that heaven was like this.
examples.ja: 天国がこんなとこだったなんて、がっかりです。

2883.meaning_mnemonic: This is <kanji>heaven</kanji> <kanji>country</kanji>. Where is that? Probably just in <vocabulary>heaven</vocabulary> (or if you want to be fancy, the <vocabulary>kingdom of heaven</vocabulary>).
2883.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The 国 is changed to the reading ごく though because of rendaku. Even heaven changes a little bit.

examples.en: Right now, there are many people with flu nationwide.
examples.ja: 今、全国でインフルエンザの人が多いです。

examples.en: I want to go to mountains all over Japan.
examples.ja: 日本全国の山に行きたいです。

examples.en: That band is apparently going on a nationwide tour next year.
examples.ja: あのバンド、来年に全国ツアーをするそうですよ。

2884.meaning_mnemonic: When something involves <kanji>all</kanji> the <kanji>country</kanji> you know it's <vocabulary>nationwide</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>national</vocabulary>.
2884.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I still haven’t been to Shikoku.
examples.ja: 四国にはまだ行ったことがありません。

examples.en: Have you gotten used to life in Shikoku yet?
examples.ja: 四国での生活にはなれましたか？

examples.en: Shikoku has beautiful mountains and delicious udon noodles.
examples.ja: 四国には、きれいな山と、おいしいうどんが、あります。

2885.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>four</kanji> <kanji>country</kanji> is another section of Japan. It's quite nice, too. Look on a map and try to find it. So, the meaning of this word is also the reading, which you should be able to figure out because it's all on'yomi: <vocabulary>Shikoku</vocabulary>.
2885.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've learned them already, so you should be able to read this on your own!

examples.en: I have never been to a foreign country yet.

What's a <vocabulary>bright</vocabulary> color? <reading>赤</reading> (あか), aka "red," obviously. Think of a really bright あか color when you see 明るい.

2896.meaning_mnemonic: When it's <kanji>not</kanji> <kanji>bright</kanji>, you can't see what's around you. In the dark, everything feels <vocabulary>unknown</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>unclear</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>uncertain</vocabulary>.
2896.reading_mnemonic:

Everything feels particularly <vocabulary>unknown</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>unclear</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>uncertain</vocabulary> in <reading>May</reading> (めい) because May is when you suddenly realize you still don't know what you're doing this year — your plans are as foggy as morning mist. 2898.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>East</kanji> <kanji>North</kanji> area of Japan is called <vocabulary>Tohoku</vocabulary>, or the <vocabulary>Tohoku region</vocabulary>. It was the region hit by the 2011 Tohoku Earthquake. 

This can also mean <vocabulary>northeast region</vocabulary> when talking about China or Japan, but for other countries (and for the compass direction), we'd use 北東.
2898.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You haven't seen the on'yomi reading for 北 (ほく) yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

In <vocabulary>Tohoku</vocabulary> there's a lot of <reading>hocu</reading>s (ほく) pocus going on. Basically, if you're in Japan's northeast, watch out… A lot of mountain hermits live up in those parts, practicing their weird hocus pocus. Don't let 'em getcha.

2899.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>middle</kanji> of the <kanji>east</kanji> is more simply known as the <vocabulary>middle east</vocabulary>.

If you're in Japan but craving a taste of the <vocabulary>Middle East</vocabulary>, you should go to <reading>とう</reading>きょう. とうきょう's a very international city, so it's full of great spots to enjoy food from the Middle East. Turkish cuisine, Lebanese cuisine, Persian cuisine — you name it, とうきょう's got it.

2901.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>walk</kanji> so the verb version means <vocabulary>to walk</vocabulary>.
2901.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You have to remember the ある portion. Imagine yourself going <vocabulary>to walk</vocabulary> outside. But, as you walk, you walk like a pirate. You have a peg leg, a parrot, and a hook. Lastly, you say "<reading>arrrrr</reading>" (ある). Go ahead, say it out loud while walking around your room like a pirate. It will help.

2902.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. Remember how 直 can also mean <kanji>fix</kanji>? Well, this word uses that meaning, so it's <vocabulary>to fix</vocabulary>. This is when you're fixing something, as in doing the actual physical action of fixing.
2902.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You need <vocabulary>to fix</vocabulary> something <reading>now</reading> (なお)! Seriously, it's urgent! If you don't fix it now, it's going to cause big problems for everyone, so get to it right NOW!!!

meanings: To Be Back In Working Order

examples.en: I think the internet router will be fixed soon.
examples.ja: もうすぐ、インターネットのルーターが直ると思う。

examples.en: The bleeding stopped and the pain in the ankle went away.

2903.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You already learned that 直す means "to fix," where someone actively does the fixing. Well, 直る puts the focus on the thing getting fixed, so it means <vocabulary>to be fixed</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be back in working order</vocabulary>.

In other words, don't use it to say "I fixed it," but do use it to say "It's fixed!" or "It's back to normal!" To remember this, imagine a British person excitedly shouting, "My loo (る) was broken, but now it's fixed!”
2903.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with 直す, but here's a mnemonic in case you forgot:

Something needs <vocabulary>to be fixed</vocabulary> <reading>now</reading> (なお)! Seriously, it's urgent! You need this thing <vocabulary>to be back in working order</vocabulary> right now!

2904.meaning_mnemonic: It's always <kanji>correct</kanji> to say something <kanji>straight</kanji> to another person's face. This is called being <vocabulary>honest</vocabulary>. Are you an honest person?

Be completely <vocabulary>honest</vocabulary>, what's the strangest sound you've ever heard? The <reading>Shou</reading>gun (しょう) going "<reading>jiki</reading> jiki (じき)"?! <vocabulary>Honestly</vocabulary>, it sounds really strange... Maybe it's some kind of new samurai battle cry?

2905.meaning_mnemonic:
You proceed <kanji>straight</kanji> ahead to <kanji>go</kanji> somewhere because you're <vocabulary>going directly</vocabulary> there. You're making a <vocabulary>nonstop</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>direct</vocabulary> trip — no pitstops or detours.

直行 is commonly seen in transportation contexts, especially when talking about flights. It's also often used in business settings to describe traveling directly to a destination without making any stops, like visiting a client’s office straight from your home.
2905.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word and uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. The ちょく of 直 is shortened with a small っ, though, so make sure to take note of that.

<vocabulary>After</vocabulary>. Everything happens after. It's a cause and effect chain. One thing happens, and then another thing happens after. This is life. This is the universe. Everything is after. It's an <reading>auto</reading>matic (あと) cycle that just keeps going and going and going.

Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Did you know the Aries cluster of <vocabulary>star</vocabulary>s used to be called the <reading>Hoe Shee</reading>p (ほし) constellation? 2939.meaning_mnemonic:

2941.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji portion means <kanji>fault</kanji>, so you would think the verb version is "to fault." It's a little different, though. Think of it this way, if you "fault" something, you're messing up. What's a great way to mess up? By losing something. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to lose</vocabulary>. 

Pretend like you are supposed to hold on to someone's wedding ring. You make the biggest fault of all. You lose it. Ouch.
2941.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

So how did you lose the wedding ring anyway? Well... it was eaten by a cow. The <reading>牛 now</reading> (うし + なう) has to have it surgically removed. What a mess!

2942.meaning_mnemonic:
When you do something that's your <kanji>fault</kanji> and then you say "<kanji>thanks</kanji>" after you do it, that's super-duper <vocabulary>rude</vocabulary>, wouldn't you say? Imagine doing something like this and then thinking to yourself after... wow, I was really rude.

This is also often used to mean <vocabulary>excuse me</vocabulary>, typically followed by ですが or します. Occasionally, it’s also used just on its own, usually when the speaker holds a higher or equal status to the person being spoken to. This particular usage is more prevalent among older generations and is commonly associated with masculine speech.
2942.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Please be sure to come to the next class.
examples.ja: 次のクラスは、必ず来てください。

examples.en: I'll surely complete WaniKani before I die.
examples.ja: 死ぬ前に、必ずワニカニをコンプリートします。

2943.meaning_mnemonic: This word looks like a verb but it's not (sorry!). It's an adverb. The kanji itself means <kanji>certain</kanji> and the vocab version means all sorts of variations on that: <vocabulary>surely</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>certainly</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>without exception</vocabulary> to name a few.
2943.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Ra, the Egyptian god asks you: "Can you do it? Are you <vocabulary>certain</vocabulary> you can build the pyramids?" 

"Yes I <reading>can ra</reading> (かなら). Yes I can," you reply.

examples.en: Mom is frantic about losing weight.
examples.ja: お母さんは、ダイエットに必死だ。

examples.en: I ran desperately, but the bus had already left.
examples.ja: 必死に走ったが、バスはもう出てしまった。

examples.en: It was a desperate proposal, but it wasn't successful.
examples.ja: 必死のプロポーズだったが、ダメだった。

2944.meaning_mnemonic:
Your future consists of <kanji>certain</kanji> <kanji>death</kanji>. How would you feel in this situation? Probably very <vocabulary>frantic</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>desperate</vocabulary>. 

Another translation for this word is simply <vocabulary>certain death</vocabulary>, though I'd rather you learn one of the first two before this one if you can.
2944.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the on'yomi readings, though 必 (ひつ) gets shortened to ひっ. In your <vocabulary>desperate</vocabulary> situation just imagine that you're trying to get out of it, and to do so you move the つ only to find a smaller っ blocking your way. It is certain death.

examples.en: I have never been abroad.
examples.ja: 未だ海外に行ったことが有りません。

examples.en: It is still unknown where my husband is.
examples.ja: 主人がどこにいるのか、未だ不明です。

examples.en: I bet no one has lived up to 200 years old.
examples.ja: 未だ、二百才まで生きた人はいないでしょう。

2945.meaning_mnemonic: This is the adverb version of <kanji>未</kanji>, so it means the same thing: <vocabulary>not yet</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>still</vocabulary>, depending on the context.
2945.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn it with this kanji, so here a mnemonic to help you:

Someone's telling you "<vocabulary>not yet</vocabulary>... not yet.... not yet...". You have some food on your nose, but you're not allowed to eat it <reading>今</reading> (いま).

Note that this word can also be read まだ. However, いまだ is often written in kanji, while まだ is almost always written in kana. So when you see 未だ, it's a safe bet to read it as いまだ!

examples.en: I don't know the future.
examples.ja: 未来のことは分かりません。

examples.en: If I could time travel, I’d want to go to the future.
examples.ja: タイムスリップできるなら、未来に行きたいな。

examples.en: I hope the future of Japanese children today is bright.
examples.ja: 今の日本の子の未来は明るいといいな。

2946.meaning_mnemonic:
What has <kanji>not yet</kanji> <kanji>come</kanji>? The <vocabulary>future</vocabulary>.

未来 is usually used to talk about the distant future, and it implies that the future can’t be foreseen. So you can use it to speculate about what might lie ahead, but you probably wouldn’t use it to discuss more concrete plans, goals or predictions.
2946.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: After a leave of absence, I became a company president in Kyushu.
examples.ja: 休学の末、私は九州で社長になりました。

examples.en: It's the end of the world to me, as a writer, that AI can make a sentence like this.
examples.ja: AIがこんな文も作れるなんて、ライターの私にとっては、世も末ですよ。

examples.en: My youngest sister is still five years old.
examples.ja: 末の妹は、まだ五才です。

2947.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. Throw a "the" in there if you'd like, as well.
2947.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

You've reached <vocabulary>the end</vocabulary> of the universe. Nothing is there. You step out, and you're surprised because you get greeted by an old Canadian man. <reading>Sue, eh?</reading>(すえ) he asks you, over and over. The poor man is looking for his wife Sue, and he's searched to the end of the universe. That's true love. As he walks off into the distance, you hear him calling out, "Sue, eh? Sue, eh? Sue, eh?"

examples.en: In Japan, we eat buckwheat noodles at the end of the year.
examples.ja: 日本では年末にソバを食べます。

examples.en: At the end of the year, the town is full of life.
examples.ja: 年末は、町の中に活気があふれます。

examples.en: At the end of the year, there is a culture of cleaning for the entire year.
examples.ja: 年末は、一年分のクリーニングをする文化があります。

2948.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>year</kanji> <kanji>end</kanji> is the <vocabulary>year end</vocabulary> aka the <vocabulary>end of the year</vocabulary>.
2948.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: By the end of the month, I will leave this apartment.
examples.ja: 月末までに、このアパートを出ます。

examples.en: The party is at the end of the month.
examples.ja: パーティーは月末です。

examples.en: The money from the part-time job comes in at the end of the month.
examples.ja: バイトのお金は月末に入ります。

2949.meaning_mnemonic: You know how 月 can also mean <kanji>month</kanji>? If you add 末 on there you have the "month end" aka the <vocabulary>end of the month</vocabulary>.
2949.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 月 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

When it's the <vocabulary>end of the month</vocabulary>, everybody <reading>gets</reading> <reading>mats</reading> (げつまつ). We don't pay people in money at Tofugu, but everyone gets mats at the <vocabulary>month end</vocabulary> instead.

examples.en: It only takes 10 minutes to get to the high school if you drive.
examples.ja: 高校まで、車で行けば十分ですよ。

examples.en: My younger sister is a junior in high school this year. Next year, there will be a university entrance test.
examples.ja: うちの妹は、今年高校二年生です。来年、大学の入学テストが有ります。

examples.en: When I was in high school, I didn't really understand geography and science.
examples.ja: 高校の時は、地理や科学のことが、あまりよく分かりませんでした。

2950.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>tall</kanji> <kanji>school</kanji> is for when your kids get about as tall as they're going to get. That's <vocabulary>high school</vocabulary>, when most people stop growing taller.
2950.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I go to school on weekdays.
examples.ja: 平日は学校に行きます。

examples.en: Rachel is a friend from my school.
examples.ja: レイチェルは私の学校の友人です。

examples.en: In my school, there are four class groups for third graders.
examples.ja: 私の学校は、三年生のクラスが四組あります。

2951.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>study</kanji> <kanji>school</kanji> is obviously a place where people study and learn. In English, that's simply a <vocabulary>school</vocabulary>.
2951.reading_mnemonic: This jukugo word consists of on'yomi readings, except 学 (がく) is shortened with a small っ to make it <reading>がっこう</reading>.

examples.en: What reminds me of summer is draft beer and fireworks.
examples.ja: 夏と言えば、生ビールと花火です。

examples.en: In summer, I sometimes eat two bowls of shaved ice a day.
examples.ja: 夏は、かき氷を一日二つ食べることもあります。

examples.en: The 1900 Summer Olympics were held in Paris.
examples.ja: 1900年の夏のオリンピックはパリで行われました。

2952.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2952.reading_mnemonic: The reading you learned with the kanji is the same as the reading for the vocab.

examples.en: July and August are summer vacation.
examples.ja: 七月と八月は夏休みです。

examples.en: I played games a lot during summer vacation.
examples.ja: 夏休み中に、たくさんゲームをしました。

examples.en: During the summer vacation, I go to my grandmother's house in Shikoku every year.
examples.ja: 夏休みは、毎年四国のおばあちゃんの家に行きます。

2953.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 夏 means <kanji>summer</kanji> and 休 means <kanji>rest</kanji>. What is a "summer rest" though? It's a <vocabulary>summer break</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>summer vacation</vocabulary>.
2953.reading_mnemonic: The readings are kun'yomi readings because this word is essentially two separate words put together into one word. You should know the reading for 夏 from the kanji and the reading for 休み from the vocab.

examples.en: My house is near a mountain.
examples.ja: 私の家は山の近くにあります。

examples.en: Secondhand houses are very popular in the United States.
examples.ja: アメリカでは中古の家がとても人気です。

examples.en: Sorry, I haven't left home yet.
examples.ja: すいません、まだ家を出てないんです。

2954.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2954.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with the kanji. But there's a second reading you haven't learned yet, so here's a mnemonic for both:

What do you do in your <vocabulary>house</vocabulary>? You <reading>ea</reading>t <reading>e</reading>ggs (いえ). You love to eat eggs at <vocabulary>home</vocabulary>. But it has to be on the 内 (うち), a.k.a. the inside, of your house. For some reason you can only eat eggs in the 内 of your house.

Both readings relate to house and home, but いえ is a bit more for the physical building (the house) while うち is more for your personal sense of home, including your family and household.

examples.en: That man is a famous bestselling author.
examples.ja: あの男の人は、有名なベストセラー作家です。

examples.en: I got an autograph from the writer of this book.
examples.ja: この本の作家さんから、サインをもらいました。

examples.en: Many of the fans of this writer are women over thirty years old.
examples.ja: この作家のファンは、三十才以上の女の人が多いです。

2955.meaning_mnemonic:
This is a strange one, but only at first glance. You <kanji>make</kanji> a <kanji>house</kanji>. You'd think this would mean something like "building a house" or "construction" or something. Instead, it means writer. Think of it this way: A <vocabulary>writer</vocabulary> <kanji>makes</kanji> (writes and creates works) in their <kanji>home</kanji>. Writers don't make their word magic in a corporate office!

作家 is generally used to refer to someone who writes professionally as an occupation, especially in the field of literature. It can also be used more broadly to refer to a creator who produces individual works of art or craft.
2955.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since the さく reading of 作 becomes さっ here, we've made a mnemonic for you to remember this reading:

<vocabulary>Writer</vocabulary>s love <reading>soccer</reading> (さっか). In fact, playing soccer is how they get their inspiration. Try playing some soccer, maybe you'll become a <vocabulary>creator</vocabulary> too!

examples.en: My father is physically weak.
examples.ja: 父は体が弱いんです。

examples.en: Even if the strength of your hands and feet are weak, you can get good at badminton.
examples.ja: 手と足の力が弱くても、バドミントン上手になれますよ。

examples.en: Even with a small light of fire, it has become a little brighter around.
examples.ja: 弱い火の光でも、辺りが少し明るくなりました。

2956.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>weak</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>weak</vocabulary>.
2956.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You just got beaten up because you're <vocabulary>weak</vocabulary>. Then the bully asks you: "<reading>Yo! Why</reading> (よわ) you so weak?"

examples.en: My weakness is that I can't stand insects.
examples.ja: 虫がキライなことが、私の弱点です。

examples.en: I exercised every day to get rid of my weaknesses.
examples.ja: 弱点をなくすために、毎日エクササイズしました。

examples.en: The two covered each others' weaknesses.
examples.ja: 二人は、弱点をカバーし合った。

2957.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: At that time, I think my father was 50 years old.
examples.ja: あの時、父は五十才だったと思います。

examples.en: Did you do any sports when you were little?
examples.ja: 小さかった時、何かスポーツはしていましたか？

examples.en: "Please stop the time," he said towards heaven.
examples.ja: 「時を止めて下さい」と天を向いて言いました。

2958.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2958.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

What <vocabulary>time</vocabulary> is it? It's time <reading>to key</reading> (とき) your enemy's car. Imagine yourself looking at your watch, waiting until the correct time to perform a synchronized keying of someone's car. Who do you hate the most? Whose car would you like to key?

examples.en: I eat lunch at one in the afternoon.
examples.ja: ランチは午後一時に食べます。

examples.en: Can you email me by one o'clock?
examples.ja: 一時までにメールをいただけますか？

examples.en: It's not normal to visit someone's home at one in the morning.
examples.ja: 午前一時に家に来るなんて、おかしいですよ。

2959.meaning_mnemonic: When it's <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>o'clock</kanji> it's <vocabulary>one o'clock</vocabulary>. It's time to eat lunch, or take a nap, or something.
2959.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It's already 2:30 now.
examples.ja: 今、もう二時半ですよ。

examples.en: Today, I have a science class at 2:30.
examples.ja: 今日は二時半から科学のクラスです。

examples.en: The next bus to Yamagata is at 2:30.
examples.ja: 次の山形行きのバスは、二時半です。

2960.meaning_mnemonic: When it's <kanji>two</kanji> <kanji>o'clock</kanji> and a <kanji>half</kanji> what time do you think it is? That would be <vocabulary>two thirty</vocabulary>.
2960.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What time is the flight to New York?
examples.ja: ニューヨーク行きのフライトは何時ですか？

examples.en: What time do you go to school every day?
examples.ja: 毎日、何時に学校に行きますか？

examples.en: For our date on the 5th, what time shall we meet in Meguro?
examples.ja: 五日のデートは、目黒で何時に会う？

2961.meaning_mnemonic: This is a good word to know to ask for the time. <kanji>What</kanji> is the <kanji>time</kanji>? This is how you ask <vocabulary>what time</vocabulary> it is.
2961.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The two lights became bright at the same time.
examples.ja: 二つのライトが同時に明るくなった。

examples.en: I'm sorry. I can't do dog sitting and baby sitting at the same time.
examples.ja: すみません。ドッグシッターとベビーシッターは同時にできません。

examples.en: At the same time as the teacher entered the classroom, there was a sound of the chime.
examples.ja: 先生が教室に入ると同時に、チャイムの音がしました。

2962.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>same</kanji> <kanji>time</kanji>? Okay, let's say what we think this word means at the <vocabulary>same time</vocabulary>. Whoops, I just said it, sorry.
2962.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Put the paper and pen on the table.
examples.ja: 紙とペンをテーブルの上に出してください。

examples.en: The Japanese 10,000 yen bill is money made out of paper.
examples.ja: 日本の一万円札は紙のお金です。

examples.en: This is how to make a doll using paper and thread.
examples.ja: これが、紙と糸を用いた人形の作り方です。

2963.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2963.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading, but lucky for you that's the reading you learned with the kanji, meaning you should be able to read this vocab too.

examples.en: It is a letter from my father.
examples.ja: それは、父からの手紙です。

examples.en: Perhaps, it didn't have enough stamps. A letter from the school still hasn't arrived.
examples.ja: 切手が足りなかったのか、学校からの手紙が中々来ません。

examples.en: Can you teach me how to mail out a letter to a foreign country?
examples.ja: 外国への手紙の出し方を教えてくれませんか？

2964.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>hand</kanji> <kanji>paper</kanji> is a <vocabulary>letter</vocabulary> because letters are generally written by hand on paper.

If you want a more graphic image, imagine writing a letter on your hand, and how much it would hurt to chop off your hand and send it.
2964.reading_mnemonic: The reading is double kun'yomi. Think of 手紙 as two words mashed together — a letter is a thing you write by hand (て) on paper (かみ). You've learned those readings already, so you should be able to read this! Just watch out for the rendaku on がみ.

examples.en: Please do not look at the diary on the table.
examples.ja: テーブルの上の日記は見ないで下さい。

examples.en: It takes about 30 minutes to write a journal every day.
examples.ja: 毎日、日記をかくのに三十分くらいかかります。

examples.en: The cover of this diary was 10,000 yen.
examples.ja: この日記のカバーは一万円でした。

2965.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>write down</kanji> your <kanji>day</kanji> (and do it every day) that's your <vocabulary>diary</vocabulary>.
2965.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 日 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

When you write down your day in your <vocabulary>diary</vocabulary>, in fact you write only about <reading>Nicky</reading> (にっき). You love Nicky so much, your diary is full of Nicky this, Nicky that. Ah, Nicky is just the best.

examples.en: Many cars pass by.
examples.ja: たくさんの車が通る。

examples.en: When I go to the company, I pass through the bamboo forest.
examples.ja: 竹の林を通って、会社に行きます。

examples.en: I pass by the convenience store in 3-chome every day.
examples.ja: 三丁目のコンビニの前は、毎日通りますよ。

2966.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>pass through</kanji> so the verb vocab version means things like <vocabulary>to pass through</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to pass</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to travel along</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>to stop by</vocabulary>.
2966.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

There's something in front of you that you have <vocabulary>to pass through</vocabulary> but you can't. It's a wall. In order to pass through it, you decide to kick it as hard as you can to knock it down. Unfortunately, it is way stronger than you, and your toe explodes on contact. You yell: "<reading>TOE! OH!</reading>" (とお) and then just scream a lot.

examples.en: Please be careful with car traffic.
examples.ja: 車の交通に十分と気をつけて下さい。

examples.en: Please wear your seatbelt for traffic safety.
examples.ja: 交通安全のためにシートベルトをしてください。

examples.en: Transportation options in this town are bus and taxi.
examples.ja: この町の交通のオプションは、バスとタクシーです。

2967.meaning_mnemonic: Even though it gets <kanji>mix</kanji>ed up as it <kanji>passes through</kanji> itself, modern <vocabulary>traffic</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>transport</vocabulary> systems are pretty amazing. This word refers to traffic and transport for pedestrians, bikes, cars, buses, trains, planes... anything that gets us from A to B.
2967.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: There's the HQ in that tall building over there.
examples.ja: あの高いビルの中に本社があります。

examples.en: This car is expensive, but it has a good design.
examples.ja: この車は高いですが、デザインがいいです。

examples.en: A million yen for a business suit is too expensive.
examples.ja: ビジネススーツに百万円は、高すぎるよ。

2968.meaning_mnemonic:
This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>tall</kanji> or <kanji>expensive</kanji>? It's the same: <vocabulary>tall</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>expensive</vocabulary>. 

Weird that this word means both of these things, yeah? Just imagine money piled up to be really tall. That money is tall because it needs to buy something expensive.
2968.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Being <vocabulary>tall</vocabulary> is really <vocabulary>expensive</vocabulary> because you have to buy a <reading>ta</reading>ll <reading>car</reading> (たか). If it's not a tall car then your tall body won't fit inside, and those tall cars are expensive!

examples.en: All Japanese women's volleyball teams are strong.
examples.ja: 全日本の女子バレーチームは、中々強い

examples.en: The fact that it was a tie means that both teams were strong.
examples.ja: 同点だったということは、両方強いチームだったということだ。

examples.en: It's very windy today, so it's better not to go out today.
examples.ja: 風が強いから、今日は外に出るのはやめた方がいい。

2969.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>strong</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>strong</vocabulary>.
2969.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

If you wanna be <vocabulary>strong</vocabulary>, you need to be able to use <reading>two yo</reading>-yos (つよ) at a time. Like, as weapons. And I don't mean with two hands. I mean one hand wielding two yo-yos. Now that's strong.

examples.en: This hair dryer is quite powerful.
examples.ja: このヘアドライヤーは、かなり強力だ。

examples.en: All bugs died with some strong spray.
examples.ja: 強力なスプレーで虫は全て死にました。

examples.en: Pikachu leveled up and has more power now.
examples.ja: ピカチュウはレベルアップして、強力になった。

2970.meaning_mnemonic: You have <kanji>strong</kanji> <kanji>power</kanji>. You are <vocabulary>strong</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>powerful</vocabulary>. Feel your <vocabulary>strength</vocabulary>.
2970.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 力 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Nothing is as <vocabulary>strong</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>powerful</vocabulary> as the <reading>きょう</reading>と <reading>lock</reading> (りょく). It's a legendary lock produced in ancient きょうと, rumored to be the strongest lock in existence. What magical powers do you think lie behind the <vocabulary>strength</vocabulary> of the きょうと lock?

examples.en: I always teach my child the importance of saying "thank you."
examples.ja: 私はいつも子どもに「ありがとう」と言う大切さを教える。

examples.en: Please tell me how to live abroad.
examples.ja: 海外生活の仕方を教えて下さい。

examples.en: The geography teacher taught me how to distinguish the volcanos.
examples.ja: 地理の先生が、火山の見分け方を教えてくれました。

2971.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>teach</kanji> so the verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to teach</vocabulary>. It's also used to mean <vocabulary>to tell</vocabulary> in a more general sense.
2971.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Think about your favorite teacher. Now think about them teaching you the following: "Today I'm going to teach you about the <reading>ocea</reading>n (おし)." It is big. Really big. Inside it are krakens, space aliens, and lost cities. 

Here is where you continue the lesson in your head, making it the most ridiculous lesson about the ocean you've ever heard. Focus in on the ocean part, since that's the reading, always coming back to it.

examples.en: This is a classroom for first-graders.
examples.ja: ここは、一年生の教室ですよ。

examples.en: A substitute teacher still hasn't come to the classroom.
examples.ja: 代わりの先生が中々教室に来ません。

examples.en: Today, I'm going to the class to make muffins.
examples.ja: 今日は、マフィンを作るための教室に行きます。

2972.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Next is the psychology class.
examples.ja: 次は、心理学のクラスです。

examples.en: In psychology, you learn about human hearts.
examples.ja: 心理学では、人の心を学びます。

examples.en: I want to take advantage of psychology to communicate with people better.
examples.ja: 心理学を活用して、人とのコミュニケーションが上手になりたいです。

2973.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>reason</kanji> your <kanji>heart</kanji> does what it does is all psychological. The <kanji>study</kanji> of that is <vocabulary>psychology</vocabulary>.
2973.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I went to college to learn geography.
examples.ja: 地理を学ぶために大学へ行きました。

examples.en: In geographical books, I also learned about volcanoes  and rivers.
examples.ja: 地理の本の中で、火山や川についても学びました。

examples.en: I'm sorry, I don't know my way around here.
examples.ja: すみません、この辺の地理は分からないんです。

2974.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>reason</kanji> the <kanji>earth</kanji> is the way it is is because of the <vocabulary>geography</vocabulary> of it. Though it may seem kind of strange that geography is bringing reason to the earth, if you think of geography as a study, then you can think about how you try to get reason through that, as well.
2974.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I divided nine people into three groups.
examples.ja: 九人を三組のグループに分けた。

examples.en: Are you Koichi from grade three class two?
examples.ja: あなた、三年二組のコウイチくん？

examples.en: This man is the leader of a famous yakuza organization.
examples.ja: この男は、有名なヤクザの組のリーダーですよ。

2975.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2975.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. That's the reading you learned with the kanji so you should be able to read this one too. If you need a refresher, here's a mnemonic to help you:

You're part of a special <vocabulary>group</vocabulary>. It is the <reading>cumi</reading>n group, and they deal with all things cumin (the spice or seed). Smell the cumin. Touch it. Taste it. You live and breathe the stuff, because you are the president of this cumin group.

P.S. This can also be spelled 組み (same reading: くみ) when it's a counter for groups, like ひと組み or ふた組み.

examples.en: This is a boat going to Shikoku.
examples.ja: こちらは四国に行く船です。

examples.en: What time is the next ship leaving?
examples.ja: 次の船は、何時に出ますか？

examples.en: The sunrise seen from aboard the ship is beautiful.
examples.ja: 船の上から見る日の出はきれいです。

2976.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2976.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

You're riding in a boat. It's great. Imagine it being the best time you've had in your life. You tell everyone: "This is <reading>fun, eh</reading>?" (ふね). You're on a Canadian ship, which is why you add the "eh" in there. Say this out loud wherever you are right now while imagining the sea smell, the wind, and the excitement of boats.

examples.en: You can see many balloons in the sky.
examples.ja: 空に、たくさんの風船が見えます。

examples.en: That clown made a dog out of a balloon for me.
examples.ja: あのピエロが、風船で犬を作ってくれたんだ。

examples.en: I thought it was a balance ball so I stood on it and realized it was just a big balloon.
examples.ja: バランスボールかと思って上に立ったら、ただの大きな風船だったんです。

2977.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>wind</kanji> <kanji>boat</kanji>. This is a strange one for sure. You may assume this is like one of those giant balloons you can go ride around in, and you'd be partly right. Really, this word covers the general word <vocabulary>balloon</vocabulary>, though it especially has to do with the toy-style balloons (or smaller balloons). It's a little round wind ship!
2977.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Last week, my company was closed.
examples.ja: 先週は、私の会社はお休みでした。

examples.en: You sure have grown a lot! You were still tiny last week though.
examples.ja: 大きくなったねー。先週はまだあんなに小さかったのに。

examples.en: Could you show me your notebook because I didn't go to class last week?
examples.ja: 先週のクラス休んじゃったから、ノート見せてくれない？

2978.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: There is a big test this week.
examples.ja: 今週は大きなテストがあります。

examples.en: It looks like it will be raining all this week.
examples.ja: 今週は、ずっと雨のようです。

examples.en: Is it okay to have a meeting this week?
examples.ja: ミーティングは、今週でもいいですか？

2979.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: On weekends, I'm on a bed or sofa.
examples.ja: 週末は、ベッドかソファの上にいます。

examples.en: I want to take a rest on weekends and save my physical energy.
examples.ja: 週末はゆっくり休んで、体力をセーブしたいと思います。

examples.en: I will go to the river with my friends on the weekend.
examples.ja: 週末に友人と川に行きます。

2980.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>end</kanji> of the <kanji>week</kanji> is the <vocabulary>weekend</vocabulary>... that is, unless you work on the weekend, but we can't cater to everyone here.
2980.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Have you ever seen snow?
examples.ja: 雪を見たことがありますか？

examples.en: When I went outside, there was white snow everywhere.
examples.ja: 外に出ると白い雪が広がっていました。

examples.en: Every year in December, I go to snowy mountains to ski.
examples.ja: 毎年十二月に雪山にスキーしに行きます。

2981.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2981.reading_mnemonic: The reading you learned with the kanji is the same as the reading for this vocab word. Enjoy the snow!

examples.en: This is a fish called "koi."
examples.ja: これは、「コイ」と言う名の魚です。

examples.en: I'm not good at cutting fish.
examples.ja: 魚を切るのが下手です。

examples.en: In Japan, people eat raw fish.
examples.ja: 日本では生の魚を食べます。

2982.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2982.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Imagine a <vocabulary>fish</vocabulary>. Now imagine the fish playing soccer, while wearing a nun's outfit. This is a <reading>soccer nu</reading>n (さかな).

examples.en: Is this a goldfish? Is it carp?
examples.ja: これは、金魚ですか？コイですか？

examples.en: Please give me a goldfish with red and white dots.
examples.ja: 赤と白の点が入ってる金魚を下さい。

examples.en: Are there any goldfish in the river?
examples.ja: 川に、金魚はいますか？

2983.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>gold</kanji> <kanji>fish</kanji> is really just gold in color, but it's still called a <vocabulary>goldfish</vocabulary>.
2983.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Is salmon a saltwater fish? Or is it a freshwater fish?
examples.ja: サケは海魚ですか？それとも川魚ですか？

examples.en: Can sea fish be pets?
examples.ja: 海魚はペットに出来ますか？

examples.en: If you go into the sea by scuba diving, you can see various sea fish and jellyfish.
examples.ja: スキューバダイビングで海の中に行くと、色々な海魚やクラゲを見ることができます。

2984.meaning_mnemonic:
An <kanji>ocean</kanji> <kanji>fish</kanji> is simply an <vocabulary>ocean fish</vocabulary>. They also happen to be the most delicious kind of fish.

海魚 is often used in contrast with 川魚 (river fish), especially when talking about fish as food.
2984.reading_mnemonic: You might think this is all going to be on'yomi, which it can be, but we'd actually like you to focus on the kun'yomi reading うみざかな here. Using the on'yomi is also correct, but sounds formal and scientific, while うみざかな is much more colloquial, so try to remember this reading instead! You already know the individual kun'yomi readings for this, but do watch out for the rendaku.

examples.en: That bird is an American eagle.
examples.ja: あの鳥は、アメリカンイーグルです。

examples.en: The birds in the sky look like dots.
examples.ja: 空にいる鳥が点のように見えます。

examples.en: Dad, there's bird poop on the car.
examples.ja: お父さん、車に鳥のフンがついてるよ。

2985.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2985.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

When you think about birds, what is the most common bird you can think of? What bird do you hate the most or like eating the most? Either one will work. Now, imagine yourself going up to that bird. You did something terrible. You <reading>tore</reading> (とり) off its wing and started eating it (pretend it's cooked first, if that makes you less nauseous).

examples.en: Swan wings are white and beautiful.
examples.ja: 白鳥の羽は、白くてきれいです。

examples.ja: 毎年、近くの川に白鳥がたくさん来ます。

examples.en: In addition to the swan, there are ducks too.
examples.ja: 白鳥の他にも、アヒルがいますね。

2986.meaning_mnemonic: There are many <kanji>white</kanji> <kanji>bird</kanji>s out there, for sure, but one really stands out if you ask me. That bird is the <vocabulary>swan</vocabulary>. It's big, it's white, and it's majestic.
2986.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
