examples.ja: 私のレインコートは黄色です。

examples.en: There are many yellow flowers growing on the grassland.
examples.ja: その草地には黄色の花がたくさん生えています。

examples.en: My mother is wearing a yellow shirt.
examples.ja: お母さんが黄色いシャツを着ています。

2987.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the same as the readings you learned with the kanji meaning you should be able to read this word right off the bat.

examples.en: A black pen, please.
examples.ja: 黒いペン、下さい。

examples.en: I'm thinking of going to the prom in a black dress.
examples.ja: プロムには黒いドレスで行こうと思う。

examples.en: Since our pet dog's fur is black, we do not have any white wool sweaters.
examples.ja: ペットの犬の毛が黒いので、うちには白い羊毛のセーターが有りません。

2988.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>black</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>black</vocabulary>. Special Note: The noun version of black also exists in Japanese. It is just 黒 with the same pronunciation, but minus the い which makes it adjective-tastic.
2988.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Think of black things. One very common black thing is the common <reading>crow</reading> (くろ). Associate those two together.

examples.en: Toronto has a big community of Black people.
examples.ja: トロントには、大きな黒人のコミュニティがあります。

examples.en: There are still not many shampoos and foundations for Black people in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本には、まだまだ黒人用のシャンプーやファンデーションが少ない。

examples.en: My mother is Black and my father is Asian.
examples.ja: 母は黒人で、父はアジア人です。

2989.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>black</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji> is simply a <vocabulary>Black person</vocabulary>, kind of like how a 白人 is a "White person," but a different  color.
2989.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Imagine a <vocabulary>Black person</vocabulary> you know well wearing <reading>coke</reading> <reading>jean</reading>s (こくじん). Yep, jeans made entirely from coke bottles. That's actually a thing. Look it up if you don't believe me.

examples.en: Can I give that horse carrots and apples?
examples.ja: あの馬に、ニンジンやリンゴをあげてもいいですか？

examples.en: There are many white horses in the meadow.
examples.ja: 草地には、白い馬がたくさんいます。

examples.en: It's fun to see horses running at full power.
examples.ja: 馬が全力で走るのを見るのは楽しいです。

2990.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
2990.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Imagine someone riding a horse. Who is that person? It's <reading>Uma</reading> (うま) Thurman, the famous actress.

examples.en: Sports cars have high horsepower.
examples.ja: スポーツカーは、高い馬力を持っています。

examples.en: I bought an air conditioner that has some horsepower for the company.
examples.ja: 会社用に馬力があるエアコンを買った。

examples.en: How much power is actually in one horsepower?
examples.ja: 一馬力の力の大きさは一体どのくらいですか？

2991.meaning_mnemonic: This word was probably made pretty recently. A <kanji>horse</kanji>'s <kanji>power</kanji>? That is <vocabulary>horsepower</vocabulary>.
2991.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 力 has two common on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Cars with high <vocabulary>horsepower</vocabulary> are usually driven by <reading>Ricky</reading> (りき). Ricky is well-known for loving all cars with a lot of horsepower, so he's often seen driving around in fancy sports cars. Vroom vroom Ricky!

examples.en: The staff's thought is to continue supporting the president.
examples.ja: スタッフは、これからも社長を支える考えだ。

examples.en: My father went to work every day to support my mother and me.
examples.ja: 父は母や私を支えるために毎日仕事へ行った。

examples.en: This rock does not have the power to support a tree any bigger than this.
examples.ja: この石に、これ以上大きな木を支える力はありません。

2992.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>support</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to support</vocabulary>.
2992.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You need <vocabulary>to support</vocabulary> someone. In order to support them, you grab two saws. One saw and another saw. It's a <reading>saw saw</reading> (ささ) combination good enough to do all the supporting you need - and maybe cut some supports too.

examples.en: I go to the branch in that town every day.
examples.ja: 私は毎日、その町の支店に通っています。

examples.en: My brother bought a used car at the branch.
examples.ja: 兄は、その支店で中古の車を買いました。

examples.en: My husband is the branch manager of the New York branch.
examples.ja: 私の主人は、ニューヨーク支店の支店長です。

2993.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>support</kanji> <kanji>shop</kanji> is the <vocabulary>branch office</vocabulary>. Presumably this is because the regular "shop" is the "shop" and anything that supports it is the local (branch) office.

If it helps, this word has the same meaning as 支局 which you will also be learning in this level.
2993.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'm planning to live in Tokyo next year.
examples.ja: 来年から、東京に住むつもりです。

examples.en: Can people who live abroad make a Japanese credit card?
examples.ja: 海外に住んでいる人でも、日本のクレジットカードは作れますか？

examples.en: When I was living in China, my youngest sister was born.
examples.ja: 中国に住んでいる時に、末の妹が生まれました。

2994.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>dwell</kanji>, so the verb version means <vocabulary>to live</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to reside</vocabulary>, or of course <vocabulary>to dwell</vocabulary>. Basically, someone is living somewhere. Where do you live?
2994.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You have a place to live... but not for long. You are being <reading>sue</reading>d (す) out of your house and home so you will have nowhere <vocabulary>to dwell</vocabulary>.

examples.en: There are a lot of residents in this apartment.
examples.ja: このアパートには、たくさんの住人がいます。

examples.en: Residents in town have a cherry blossom viewing party every April.
examples.ja: 町内の住人たちは、毎年四月に花見パーティーをします。

examples.en: Apparently, the resident of Room 202 is a famous manga artist.
examples.ja: ２０２号室の住人、有名なマンガ作家らしいよ。

2995.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>dwell</kanji> somewhere and you’re a <kanji>person</kanji>, that makes you a <vocabulary>resident</vocabulary>.
2995.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

All the <vocabulary>resident</vocabulary>s in my area care about is <reading>jew</reading>els and <reading>Nin</reading>tendo (じゅうにん). Their houses are crammed full of jewels and Nintendo stuff. How about the residents of your town? I bet they all love jewels and Nintendo too.

examples.en: Many residents in this town are grandmas and grandpas.
examples.ja: この町の住民は、おばあちゃんとおじいちゃんが多いです。

examples.en: I want to have a pizza party with the residents of the apartment.
examples.ja: アパートの住民たちで、ピザパーティをしたいんです。

examples.en: Many residents lost their homes in the 2011 tsunami.
examples.ja: ２０１１年のつなみでは多くの住民が家を失いました。

2996.meaning_mnemonic: They <kanji>dwell</kanji> here, these <kanji>people</kanji>. So what are they? They’re <vocabulary>residents</vocabulary>.
2996.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I went into the river to help the horse.
examples.ja: 私は、その馬を助けるために川に入りました。

examples.en: I am one yen short. Can you help me?
examples.ja: お金が一円足りないんです。助けてもらえませんか？

examples.en: Thanks to you saving me on that rainy day, I am who I am today.
examples.ja: あなたが、あの雨の日に助けてくれたおかげで、今の私がいます。

2997.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>help</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to help</vocabulary>. Don't confuse this with 助かる which means "to be helped." You know that 助ける is "to help" because you're doing the helping. You know that you're doing the helping because you <reading>care</reading> (ける).
2997.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You need <vocabulary>to help</vocabulary> someone. Someone is hanging off a cliff and out of reach. They ask you, the person standing above them, to <reading>toss</reading> (たす) them a rope, but you refuse. "TOSS IT!" they yell. "I WILL NOT TOSS IT," you respond. You're a jerk.

examples.en: That's thanks to help of my father.
examples.ja: 父の助力のおかげです。

examples.en: This was only possible with the help of others.
examples.ja: 他人の助力が有ったから出来たことです。

examples.en: With the help of a friend, it seems like I can get out of college after four years.
examples.ja: 友人の助力で、四年間で大学を出ることが出来そうです。

2998.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>help</kanji> with your <kanji>power</kanji>, you are providing <vocabulary>assistance</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>support</vocabulary>.

Note that this is a formal word that’s mostly used in professional situations. It implies that someone has done something substantial for you.
2998.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 力 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

You really need some <vocabulary>assistance</vocabulary> with this <reading>lock</reading> (りょく). You are certain that world peace and eternal happiness lie behind this one lock. But no one is willing to <vocabulary>support</vocabulary> you in opening it. What a cruel world.

examples.en: My brother is an assistant of a psychologist.
examples.ja: 弟は心理学者の助手です。

examples.en: My assistant is also the mother of three children.
examples.ja: 私の助手は三人の子の母でもあります。

examples.en: As the president's assistant, I do things like getting coffee and answering the phone for them.
examples.ja: 社長の助手として、コーヒーを買ってきたり、電話に出たりします。

examples.en: If I'm the assistant to an assistant who was just fired, does that mean that I’m fired too?
examples.ja: 仮に私が首になった助手の助手だとしたら、それってつまり私も首になっちゃったってこと？

2999.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 手 can mean a "doer" in some words? What do you think your <kanji>help</kanji> <kanji>doer</kanji> is? It’s someone who helps you, so it’s your <vocabulary>assistant</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>helper</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>aide</vocabulary>.
2999.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You learned the on'yomi reading of 手 with the vocabulary word 投手.

examples.en: This is advice from my dad.
examples.ja: これは、お父さんからの助言です。

examples.en: The president gave useful advice to all the staff.
examples.ja: 社長は全てのスタッフに役に立つ助言をしました。

examples.en: My mother advised me about being independent.
examples.ja: 母は私に自立するための助言をしてくれました。

examples.en: I will give you advice, if you give me that chocolate.
examples.ja: そのチョコレートをくれたら、助言をあげるわ。

3000.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>help</kanji> with what you <kanji>say</kanji>, you're giving <vocabulary>advice</vocabulary>.

This word is commonly found in formal or professional contexts. In more casual settings, you can just use アドバイス (advise) instead.
3000.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It costs money to enter a medical university.
examples.ja: 医大に入るにはお金がかかります。

examples.en: My former partner was a teacher at a medical school.
examples.ja: 元パートナーは医大の先生でした。

examples.en: Not all students at med school become doctors.
examples.ja: 医大の学生がみんな医者になるわけではないですよ。

3001.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen 大学 to mean "college." So take the 大 and put it with <kanji>medicine</kanji> to create "medicine college", or <vocabulary>medical university</vocabulary>.
3001.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 大 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Your local <vocabulary>medical university</vocabulary> really prides itself on its <reading>ea</reading>gle <reading>dye</reading> (いだい). It's the only dye in the world made straight out of eagles. A bit strange for a medical university, but impressive nonetheless!

examples.en: I study medicine at university.
examples.ja: 大学では医学を学びます。

examples.en: Thanks to medical technology, my mother is still alive and healthy today.
examples.ja: 医学のテクノロジーのおかげで、私の母は今日も元気に生きています。

examples.en: From your perspective as a teacher who knows a lot about medicine, what do you think?
examples.ja: 医学にくわしい先生の見方としては、どう思いますか？

3002.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>study</kanji> of <kanji>medicine</kanji> is <vocabulary>medical science</vocabulary>. It can also be called <vocabulary>medicine</vocabulary>, but make sure to think of it as the "medicine" where it has to do with "medical science."
3002.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I have to go see a doctor today.
examples.ja: 今日は医者に行かなくちゃいけない。

examples.en: As a physician my mission is to make people healthy.
examples.ja: 私の医者としてのミッションは人々を元気にすることです。

examples.en: I don't like seeing blood, but can I still be a doctor?
examples.ja: 私は血を見るのがきらいですが、医者にはなれますか？

3003.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This town was once a monarchy.
examples.ja: この町はかつて君主国だったそうです。

examples.en: A monarchy is a country where the leader is a king or queen.
examples.ja: 君主国は王や女王がリーダーの国のことです。

examples.en: Denmark is a monarchy.
examples.ja: デンマークは君主国です。

3004.meaning_mnemonic: One <kanji>ruler</kanji> is the <kanji>master</kanji> of this entire <kanji>country</kanji>. Why, this sounds quite like a <vocabulary>monarchy</vocabulary> to me.
3004.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Are you perhaps Koichi's younger sister?
examples.ja: 君、もしかしてコウイチの妹？

examples.en: The curry you make is the best in Japan.
examples.ja: 君の作るカレーが日本一だよ。

examples.en: You taught me the importance of taking a shower every day, right?
examples.ja: 君は私に毎日シャワーをあびる大切さを教えてくれたじゃないか。

3005.meaning_mnemonic: Okay, so the kanji itself means <kanji>buddy</kanji> and so does the word, but it also means <vocabulary>you</vocabulary> as well. This is one of the several ways to say "you" in Japanese, and this one is kind of an "affectionate" you. Maybe you'd say it with someone you're close to. Maybe you'd say it with a girlfriend or boyfriend. You wouldn't want to use it with your boss or teacher, though. Make sure to keep that in mind. It's kind of like saying "hey buddy" or "hey you," after all.
3005.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Who's your <vocabulary>buddy</vocabulary>? It's <reading>Kimmy</reading> (きみ)! If you know a Kimmy, imagine her. If you don't, find a famous Kimmy or make up a Kimmy to imagine. You ask... is it you?? Wait, you're my buddy?

examples.en: Michael has no brothers.
examples.ja: マイケル君には兄弟がいません。

examples.en: Tanaka-kun, you look well today.
examples.ja: 田中君、今日も元気そうだね。

examples.en: Yamashita-sensei calls both male and female students with "-kun."
examples.ja: 山下先生は、男女両方の学生に「〜君」を付けます。

3006.meaning_mnemonic: Add this to the end of someone's name, it's like saying ______<kanji>buddy</kanji>. It's generally used as a name ender (like さん) for boys and young men. Don't use this on people who are higher ranked than you (socially or literally). As in, you wouldn't use it on your boss. Use it on your younger male subordinates as well as boys who aren't adults yet.
3006.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji (on'yomi), probably because it usually is attached to other words (aka names, like こういち君) making it act more like jukugo words do.

examples.en: How much is the rate of the yen compared to the dollar now?
examples.ja: ドルに対する円のレートは、今いくらですか？

examples.en: Above is my perspective on diplomacy with the United States.
examples.ja: 以上が、米国との外交に対する見方です。

examples.en: Please tell me your thoughts on robot engineering.
examples.ja: 先生のロボット工学に対する考えを教えて下さい。

examples.en: It’s clear now that their relationship will never work because their opinions on Star Trek are the complete opposite.
examples.ja: あいつらの関係が修復不可能だってことは明らかだね。だって、スタートレックに対する意見が全く違っているんだから。

3007.meaning_mnemonic:
When you do (する) <kanji>versus</kanji>, you choose <vocabulary>to face</vocabulary> an opponent. It’s where your attention and efforts are going to <vocabulary>be directed toward</vocabulary>. Alternatively, you can use this word <vocabulary>to contrast</vocabulary> one thing with another.

This word is used to help point out the relationship between two things in a sentence, where one thing is focusing on another thing. This is all a little vague and perhaps confusing, so check out the collocations and context sentences to get a better grasp of this word!
3007.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji, so you should be able to read this word no problem.

examples.en: This company is focusing on business overseas.
examples.ja: この会社は対外のビジネスに力を入れています。

examples.en: The president always says he wants to improve our public image.
examples.ja: 社長は、いつも「対外へのイメージを上げたい」と言っています。

examples.en: There is no concern about external communication.
examples.ja: 対外コミュニケーションについて不安はありません。

3008.meaning_mnemonic:
Something is <kanji>versus</kanji> the <kanji>outside</kanji>. Back in the day, everything was a battle with the outside. You had the Mongols... the rebels... and the foreigners. So, when you say something is "versus the outside" you're just saying it's something compared to where you are right now. It's something that's <vocabulary>foreign</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>external</vocabulary>.

This is a formal word typically used at the beginning of compounds to indicate that the subject is related to foreign affairs, such as 対外政策 (foreign policy) or 対外貿易 (foreign trade).
3008.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Those sisters are still confronting each other.
examples.ja: あの姉妹はまだ対立している。

examples.en: I want to stop the conflict between my father and my brother.
examples.ja: 父と兄の対立を止めたいです。

examples.en: Please tell me the reason for the conflict.
examples.ja: 対立の理由を教えて下さい。

3009.meaning_mnemonic:
If it's you <kanji>versus</kanji> someone else and you're <kanji>stand</kanji>ing in each other's way, you're in <vocabulary>conflict</vocabulary>. Better hope they're not bigger than you, or this <vocabulary>confrontation</vocabulary> might turn out to be a bad idea…

対立 is when two sides are in conflict, usually because their ideas, goals, or interests just don't match. It's the kind of <vocabulary>opposition</vocabulary> where neither side wants to back down, and they just keep standing against each other.
3009.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'm opposed to the idea.
examples.ja: その考えには反対です。

examples.en: Um, your right and left sandals are on opposite feet.
examples.ja: あの、そのサンダル、右と左が反対ですよ。

examples.en: My father was opposed to me proposing in a Walmart.
examples.ja: 父は、私がウォルマートでプロポーズすることを反対した。

3010.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>anti</kanji> <kanji>versus</kanji>... You'd think this would be a double negative, but it's like a lot of other words where you have two similar words combined... it just means the same thing as those two words. In this case, the anti-versus of something would be the <vocabulary>opposite</vocabulary>. 

反対 refers to something that's opposite in direction, position, or nature. In some cases, it can also mean <vocabulary>opposition</vocabulary> because disagreeing or resisting to something means someone is taking the opposite side on a matter.
3010.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I often see the news on this station.
examples.ja: この局のニュースをよく見ます。

examples.en: You can mail out letters overseas at the post office.
examples.ja: ゆうびん局では海外に手紙を出すことが出来ます。

examples.en: The North American Bureau mainly does diplomacy with the United States and Canada.
examples.ja: 北米局では、主にアメリカとカナダとの外交をします。

3011.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3011.reading_mnemonic: The kanji and the vocab are exactly the same, even the reading. This one uses the on'yomi probably because it's often attached to other words (specifying a bureau, for example), so that's why it follows jukugo conventions despite being all alone.

examples.en: Please head back from the Tokyo branch to headquarters in Portland.
examples.ja: 東京支局からポートランドの本社にもどって下さい。

examples.en: Last year, I went to the Tokyo branch of the passport center.
examples.ja: 去年、パスポートセンターの東京支局へ行きました。

examples.en: Does TV Tokyo have overseas bureaus?
examples.ja: テレビ東京には、海外支局はありますか？

3012.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>support</kanji> <kanji>bureau</kanji> is the group that supports a business. It is the <vocabulary>branch office</vocabulary>. 

If it helps, this word has the same meaning as <vocabulary>支店</vocabulary> which you will also be learning in this level.
3012.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'll be on a diet for a role.
examples.ja: 役のためにダイエットします。

examples.en: The role of Romeo is Leonardo DiCaprio.
examples.ja: ロミオ役はレオナルド・ディカプリオです。

examples.en: Part-time workers at convenience stores play a more important role in Japanese society than you think.
examples.ja: コンビニのアルバイトは、日本社会にとって、あなたが思ってるよりも大切な役です。

3013.meaning_mnemonic: If you have a certain <kanji>duty</kanji> then it's your job to play that <vocabulary>role</vocabulary>. You have to play the <vocabulary>part</vocabulary>. Like in a play!
3013.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji you learned, meaning you should be able to read this one as well.

examples.en: A public official came today.
examples.ja: 今日、役人が来ましたよ。

examples.en: If you graduate from college and pass all tests, you can become a government official.
examples.ja: 大学を出て、全てのテストに通れば、役人になれます。

examples.en: Even the official is a human with a heart.
examples.ja: 役人だって、心のある一人の人間なんですよ。

3014.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>duty</kanji> this <kanji>person</kanji> has? It's to the government, which makes them a <vocabulary>public official</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>government official</vocabulary>.
3014.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

A <vocabulary>public official</vocabulary> recently declared that all the <reading>yak</reading>s at <reading>Nin</reading>tendo (やくにん) are going to be kicked out. You didn't know that Nintendo has resident yaks? Well it does, but not for much longer. But who will take care of all the Nintendo yaks now?! Maybe you could take one in!

examples.en: Masking tape is useful for various things.
examples.ja: マスキングテープは、色々なことの役に立つ。

examples.en: Yamashita-sensei's advice is helpful for life.
examples.ja: 山下先生の助言は、人生の役に立つ。

examples.en: I'm sorry that I couldn't be much help.
examples.ja: あまりお役に立てず、すみませんでした。

3015.meaning_mnemonic: When duty (役) comes calling, those willing to stand (立つ) and accept it are the ones who are going <vocabulary>to be useful</vocabulary> to society. Don't run from your duties — stand up, face them, and prove yourself a useful member of the human race!
3015.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 役 is the one you learned with the kanji. The 立つ reading is that of the 立つ vocabulary, which you should be familiar with by now.

examples.en: Being a teacher at this school is a great duty.
examples.ja: この学校の先生になることは、大役ですよ。

examples.en: Thanks to getting a big role in the drama series, I became popular nationwide.
examples.ja: ドラマの大役になったおかげで、全国で人気になりました。

examples.en: Being a leader at the Middle East bureau is an important role!
examples.ja: 中東局でリーダーになるなんて、大役ですよ！

3016.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>duty</kanji> is a <vocabulary>great duty</vocabulary>. It can also be an <vocabulary>important task</vocabulary>. Think about some kind of big duty you have. Then, think about what an important task it is too. Feel proud of your important task.
3016.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 大 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

You've been assigned the <vocabulary>important task</vocabulary> of taking care of the local <reading>tie</reading> <reading>yak</reading>s (たいやく). Where you're from, tie-wearing yaks are incredibly important, so don't take this great duty lightly!

examples.en: Well then, we're going to take a vote.
examples.ja: それでは、決を採りたいと思います。

examples.en: It seems that it's taking a while to make a decision, right?
examples.ja: なかなか決が出ないみたいだね。

examples.en: After this, the president makes a decision.
examples.ja: この後、社長が決を下します。

3017.meaning_mnemonic:
Noun version of <kanji>decide</kanji>? It's a <vocabulary>decision</vocabulary>.

決 is a formal word that refers to a decisive <vocabulary>verdict</vocabulary>. It's used in formal phrases like 決を採る (to take a vote) or 決を下す (to pass a judgment), both of which are about making decisions or delivering verdicts.
3017.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the kanji!

examples.en: It takes time to decide which tie to wear every day.
examples.ja: 毎日、ネクタイを決めるのに時間がかかります。

examples.en: I decided to enroll in a private university.
examples.ja: 私立大学に入学することに決めました。

examples.en: Have you decided on the restaurant you'll go to with Koichi tonight?
examples.ja: 今日の夜、コウイチと行くレストランは、もう決めましたか？

3018.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>decide</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to decide</vocabulary>.
3018.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You have <vocabulary>to decide</vocabulary>. You have two <reading>key</reading>s (き) in front of you. You have to decide on one of them and use it to unlock the door to get away from the monster. Why do monster attacks always come down to keys and doors?

examples.en: I determined to propose on Mt. Fuji.
examples.ja: ふじ山の上でプロポーズすると決心した。

examples.en: My determination to "become a hero" is strong.
examples.ja: 私の「ヒーローになる」という決心は強いです。

examples.en: Have you found the resolve to study chemistry at university?
examples.ja: 大学で化学を学ぶ決心はつきましたか？

3019.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>decide</kanji> with your <kanji>heart</kanji> you have true <vocabulary>determination</vocabulary>, unlike when you decide with your mind.
3019.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just make sure you take note of the shortened つ. So, けつ goes to けっ.

examples.en: Pending court cases can be a major source of stress for the parties involved.
examples.ja: 未決状態の裁判は、当事者にとって大きなストレスです。

examples.en: This project cannot officially proceed yet because the budget is undecided.
examples.ja: このプロジェクトは、予算が未決のため、まだ正式には進められません。

examples.en: The final decisions on the unresolved matters are scheduled for next month.
examples.ja: 未決事項についての最終決定は、来月行われる予定です。

examples.en: That case has been put on hold as pending due to a lack of evidence.
examples.ja: その事件は、証拠不足のため未決のまま保留されています。

3020.meaning_mnemonic:
Something that is <kanji>not yet</kanji> <kanji>decide</kanji>d... it is <vocabulary>pending</vocabulary>!

未決 is a formal term, typically used in legal or administrative contexts to refer to matters that are still <vocabulary>unresolved</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>undecided</vocabulary>.
3020.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It is said that they chose mass suicide rather than surrendering to the enemy.
examples.ja: 彼らは敵に降伏するよりも、集団自決を選んだとされています。

examples.en: Even during wartime, forcing someone to take their own life is considered a serious violation of human rights.
examples.ja: 戦時下においても、自決を強制する行為は、重大な人権侵害と見なされています。

examples.en: Historically, many peoples have fought for self-determination.
examples.ja: 歴史上、多くの民族が自決を求めて闘争を続けてきました。

3021.meaning_mnemonic:
When your <kanji>self</kanji> <kanji>decide</kanji>s on something, that's called <vocabulary>self-determination</vocabulary>. But the word is mainly used in Japan as a euphemism for <vocabulary>suicide</vocabulary>. It's kind of important that you know that.

This word is very formal and generally used in historical contexts, such as referencing suicides that occurred during wartime.
3021.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I investigated my shortcomings.
examples.ja: 自分の欠点を究明しました。

examples.en: I want to get to the bottom of the cause of the accident.
examples.ja: 事故の原因を究明したいんです。

examples.en: I investigated the weaknesses of aluminum batteries.
examples.ja: アルミ電池の弱点を究明した。

3022.meaning_mnemonic:
If you do <kanji>research</kanji> to <kanji>bright</kanji>en a subject area, you're probably doing some kind of <vocabulary>investigation</vocabulary> that illuminates the unknown.

This word is usually found in academic and scientific contexts, and suggests a thorough investigation meant to ascertain or clarify something.
3022.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You've seen those readings in other compounds, so hopefully you know how to read this one.

examples.en: This is psychology research.
examples.ja: これは、心理学の研究です。

examples.en: According to research, tea makes people healthy.
examples.ja: 研究によると、お茶は人を元気にします。

examples.en: There was no answer in this investigation.
examples.ja: 今回の研究では答えが出ませんでした。

3023.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>sharpen</kanji> <kanji>research</kanji> you're just doing a <vocabulary>study</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>investigation</vocabulary>. Or in other words, you're doing <vocabulary>research</vocabulary>!
3023.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: There are many students in this lab every time.
examples.ja: この研究室には毎回たくさんの学生がいます。

examples.en: We plan to conduct a new chemical experiment in the laboratory tomorrow.
examples.ja: 明日、研究室で新しい化学実験を行う予定です。

examples.en: This hamster was born in the lab.
examples.ja: このハムスターは研究室で生まれました。

3024.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 研究 means "research"? Well the <kanji>room</kanji> where you do research is a <vocabulary>laboratory</vocabulary>!

研究室 refers to a <vocabulary>lab room</vocabulary>, often within a larger institution like a university or college.
3024.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This is a ball throwing exercise.
examples.ja: これは、ボールを投げるエクササイズです。

examples.en: How far the Frisbee goes depends on the strength of the person who throws it.
examples.ja: フリスビーがどこまで行くかは、投げる人の力によります。

examples.en: It's rude to throw money at people.
examples.ja: 人に向かってお金を投げるのは失礼ですよ。

3025.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>throw</kanji> so the verb version means <vocabulary>to throw</vocabulary>.
3025.reading_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached, so you can bet it uses the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn this reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You're at a baseball game watching people <vocabulary>throw</vocabulary> balls around. But you're hungry so you call for a snack from a vendor. You raise your hand and they throw some <reading>na</reading>chos (な) at you. Oh no! Oh ouch! The nachos are hot and they hit you in the face. The vendor just threw a bunch of hot, sauced nachos at you! WHY?!

examples.en: Let's do yoga every day for your mind and body.
examples.ja: 心身のために毎日ヨガをしましょう。

examples.en: The balance of mind and body is important.
examples.ja: 心身のバランスが大切です。

examples.en: My mind and body were not well so I decided to take a leave of absence.
examples.ja: 心身が元気でなくなってしまい、休学することにしました。

3026.meaning_mnemonic: Technically this kanji is <kanji>heart</kanji> and <kanji>somebody</kanji>, but think about it this way. Where does everything come from inside somebody? The heart! It keeps things going by pumping blood, providing the foundation for both a good <vocabulary>mind and body</vocabulary>.
3026.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My body is fine, but my heart is tattered.
examples.ja: 身体は元気ですが、心はボロボロですよ。

examples.en: My mother has had a weak constitution since she was born.
examples.ja: 母は生まれた時から身体が弱いんです。

examples.en: Doing sports is important, but resting your body is even more important.
examples.ja: スポーツも大切ですが、身体を休めることはそれ以上に大切です。

3027.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Somebody</kanji>'s <kanji>body</kanji>. This refers to the very general word <vocabulary>the body</vocabulary>. As in, "the human body" or something like that. This can also refer to <vocabulary>health</vocabulary> as well.
3027.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

This word can also be read からだ, which is irregular but shouldn't be too hard to remember because it's the same as the reading you already learned for 体! You'd usually use this reading in casual contexts, and when the word is on its own, rather than in a compound word. In formal situations and compounds, you'd want to stick to the regular old on'yomi reading.

examples.en: Please spray over your whole body once a day.
examples.ja: 一日に一回、全身にスプレーして下さい。

examples.en: Every day, I go to work in a business suit from head to toe.
examples.ja: 毎日、全身ビジネススーツで会社に行きます。

examples.en: I had a lot of red dots throughout my body due to a crab allergy.
examples.ja: カニのアレルギーで全身にたくさんの赤い点が出てしまった。

3028.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: There are many large trees in this forest.
examples.ja: この森には大きい木がたくさん有ります。

examples.en: Walking in the woods is very fun.
examples.ja: 森の中を歩くのは、とても楽しいです。

examples.en: I want to build a house where you can see the forest.
examples.ja: 森が見える場所に家を作りたいと思っています。

3029.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3029.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading, but that's the reading you learned with the kanji so you should be able to read this one too.

examples.en: Both people's thoughts are not the same.
examples.ja: 両者の考えが同じじゃない。

examples.en: With the power of both people, I think you can reach the right answer.
examples.ja: 両者の力で、正しい答えが出せると思うんです。

examples.en: The game ended in a tie, with both sides scoring the same.
examples.ja: そのゲームは、両者同点の引き分けでした。

examples.en: A year and a half later, a deal was finally struck between the two parties.
examples.ja: 一年半後にようやく両者の間で取引が行われた。

3030.meaning_mnemonic: When you have <kanji>both</kanji> <kanji>someone</kanji>s, you have <vocabulary>both people</vocabulary>. You'll notice over time that 者 is often used to indicate a person or type of person, so keep that in mind for future words as well!
3030.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I want to meet the author of this book.
examples.ja: この本の作者に会いたいです。

examples.en: That song is filled with the feelings of the composer.
examples.ja: その曲には作者の思いがこもっています。

examples.en: I heard that the artist graduated from art university and became a macramé artist.
examples.ja: あの作者はアートの大学を出て、マクラメ作家になったそうです。

3031.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Someone</kanji> who <kanji>make</kanji>s is someone who creates things. Back in the day, a creator like this may have been known as many things, but the big one that stands out is an <vocabulary>author</vocabulary>.

Wondering about the difference between 作者 and 作家? Basically, 作者 just refers to the creator of a particular creative work, such as a book, article, artwork, piece of music, etc., while 作家 refers to someone who creates those things as an occupation.
3031.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 作 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Your favorite <vocabulary>author</vocabulary> is also a <reading>sack</reading> <reading>sha</reading>man (さくしゃ). They do all sorts of weird magic involving sacks, and you just love reading about it. Maybe one day, you can become a sack shaman and <vocabulary>writer</vocabulary> yourself.

examples.en: My father is a scholar of psychology.
examples.ja: 父は心理学の学者です。

examples.en: The writer of this book is a famous scholar.
examples.ja: この本の作家は有名な学者です。

examples.en: The scholars are doing research about Hello Kitty every day.
examples.ja: 学者たちは毎日ハローキティについて研究しています。

3032.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Someone</kanji> who does <kanji>study</kanji> for a living. That is a <vocabulary>scholar</vocabulary>.
3032.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That man is a famous engineer.
examples.ja: あの男の人は有名な工学者です。

examples.en: Who is the robotics engineer who created the Roomba?
examples.ja: 「ルンバ」を作ったロボット工学者は一体だれですか？

examples.en: Can I become an engineer without going to college?
examples.ja: 大学に行かなくても、工学者になれますか？

3033.meaning_mnemonic: Do you remember 工学 from a couple levels ago? This is <kanji>someone</kanji> who is in 工学. If 工学 is "engineering" then 工学者 is an <vocabulary>engineer</vocabulary>.
3033.reading_mnemonic: The readings are just the on'yomi readings of the kanji. All things you should know now.

examples.en: In my case, that worked out well for me.
examples.ja: 私の場合は、それでうまくいきました。

examples.en: What should I do in this situation?
examples.ja: この場合は、どうすればいいですか？

examples.en: I think in that case, it's better to call a professional.
examples.ja: その場合はプロを呼んだ方がいいと思う。

3034.meaning_mnemonic: What <kanji>location</kanji> <kanji>suit</kanji>s a situation the best? That always depends on the <vocabulary>case</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>circumstance</vocabulary>. You can't know the suitability of the location until you have all the facts about the circumstances.
3034.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You didn't learn these readings with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

There are few <vocabulary>case</vocabulary>s where you want to <reading>baa</reading> (ば) while making <reading>eye</reading>s (あい) at someone. In the <vocabulary>circumstance</vocabulary> of a sheep looking for love, it may be acceptable, but in any other <vocabulary>situation</vocabulary> it's probably not appropriate behavior.

examples.en: This is the spot where the corpse was visible from the soil.
examples.ja: 土の中から死体が見えたのが、この場所です。

examples.en: Excuse me. Could you tell me the location of a nearby ATM?
examples.ja: すみません。近くのATMの場所を教えてくれませんか。

examples.en: Where was the location of your first kiss?
examples.ja: ファーストキスの場所はどこですか？

3035.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>location</kanji> <kanji>place</kanji> is either a <vocabulary>place</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>location</vocabulary>, just like the kanji it's made from.
3035.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi reading for the first kanji and the on'yomi reading for the second. You haven't learned this reading for 場 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

What is this <vocabulary>place</vocabulary> you're in? You look around and listen. You hear, "<reading>Baa</reading> (ば) baa baa!" You must be in a <reading>ba</reading>rn!

examples.en: Please buy a ticket before you enter.
examples.ja: 入場する前にチケットを買って下さい。

examples.en: Today's admission is from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.
examples.ja: 今日の入場は、午前十時から午後八時までです。

examples.en: Admission costs 1000 yen.
examples.ja: 入場には千円かかります。

3036.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>enter</kanji> a <kanji>location</kanji>, that's your <vocabulary>entrance</vocabulary>.

This is a common word for admission into public events or venues, like a concert hall, a sports stadium, or a theme park.
3036.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: This town has a large factory.
examples.ja: この町には大きな工場があります。

examples.en: Factory staff come to work every day at 6 a.m.
examples.ja: 工場のスタッフは毎日午前六時に出社します。

examples.en: Since I was injured in a wine factory, I only noticed the bleeding a day later.
examples.ja: ワインの工場でケガをしたため、出血に気がつくのが一日後になりました。

3037.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>construction</kanji> <kanji>location</kanji> is a <vocabulary>factory</vocabulary>. A factory is a place where you or machines do a bunch of construction!
3037.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: If there’s a spot you don’t understand, please raise your hand.
examples.ja: 分からない所があれば、手を上げてください。

examples.en: See you at the same place as last time.
examples.ja: 前回と同じ所で会いましょう。

examples.en: My friend came over just as my mother was doing squats.
examples.ja: お母さんがスクワットをしている所に、友人が来てしまった。

3038.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

Wondering about how 所 differs from 場所? While 場所 only refers to a physical location, 所 can also refer to an abstract place, such as a point in time, a situation, or a condition. Hence, 所 usually needs some context to clarify what kind of place you are talking about.
3038.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Here's the <vocabulary>place</vocabulary>! Either you have to <reading>talk or row</reading> (ところ). If you talk, maybe you can talk your way out of this problem you're in. If you row, you may be able to escape. Either way, this is the place for it.

examples.en: My grandma joined the group home in March.
examples.ja: 私のおばあちゃんは、三月にグループホームに入所しました。

examples.en: I had an entrance test for a model agency today.
examples.ja: 今日はモデルエージェンシーの入所テストでした。

examples.en: Be sure to check the rules before your admission.
examples.ja: 入所の前に必ずルールをチェックしておいて下さい。

3039.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>enter</kanji> a <kanji>facility</kanji>. So this is your <vocabulary>admission</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>entrance</vocabulary> into that facility. 

入所 is for entering facilities or institutions, often those with names ending in 所, like a 研究所 (research institute). It's also used in prison contexts. You might gain "admission" to prison for not doing your WaniKani reviews, for example, at least in countries ruled by Crabigators...
3039.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My husband is being released tomorrow morning.
examples.ja: 主人の出所は明日の午前中です。

examples.en: What's important is what happens after one is released from prison.
examples.ja: 大切なのは出所した後のことです。

examples.en: What is the source of this quote?
examples.ja: この引用の出所は何ですか？

3040.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>exit</kanji> a <kanji>facility</kanji>. It's your <vocabulary>release from prison</vocabulary>!

出所 commonly refers to leaving or being released from facilities ending in 所, particularly 刑務所 (prisons). It can also be a slightly formal word for <vocabulary>source</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>origin</vocabulary>, often used in discussions of copyright to specify the origin of cited information, images, or content.
3040.reading_mnemonic:
The reading follows on'yomi protocols, but you just have to be careful of the shortened しゅつ which becomes しゅっ.

Note: There is also the reading <reading>でどころ</reading> for the meanings <vocabulary>origin</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>source</vocabulary>. This version is generally used in spoken language, often to emphasize the significance or curiosity about where something came from.

examples.en: Not here, let’s go to another store somewhere else.
examples.ja: ここじゃなくて、どこか他所の店に行こうよ。

examples.en: Their house, their rules. Our house, our rules.
examples.ja: 他所は他所、家は家！

examples.en: My mother is from around here. Don't say she's a person from somewhere else.
examples.ja: 私の母はこの辺の生まれです。他所の人間だなんて言わないで下さい。

3041.meaning_mnemonic: When you're talking about some <kanji>other</kanji> <kanji>place</kanji> you're talking about <vocabulary>another place</vocabulary>.
3041.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which you would normally expect to use the on'yomi readings from the kanji. With this word, however, the on'yomi readings are rarely used now, so they sound rather out of date. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember the more common reading in contemporary Japanese:

Another place <reading>you saw</reading> (よそ) always seems better. In other words, the grass is greener somewhere else you saw!

examples.en: Tokyo Tower is one of Japan's famous places.
examples.ja: 東京タワーは、日本の名所の一つです。

examples.en: Are there any famous spots you recommend around here?
examples.ja: この辺に、おすすめの名所は有りますか？

examples.en: This town is a famous spot for cherry blossom viewing.
examples.ja: この町は、花見の名所です。

3042.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>famous</kanji> <kanji>place</kanji> is a <vocabulary>famous place</vocabulary>. When traveling around Japan, you should ask about the 名所 if you can.
3042.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Next, please enter your address.
examples.ja: 次に、住所を入力して下さい。

examples.en: I'd like to mail out a letter, but can you tell me the address of the house?
examples.ja: 手紙を出したいんですが、家の住所を教えてもらえませんか？

examples.en: The address of the company is 3-chome.
examples.ja: 会社の住所は三丁目です。

3043.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>dwell</kanji> in a <kanji>place</kanji>, that place is your <vocabulary>address</vocabulary>.
3043.reading_mnemonic: This word is made up of the on'yomi readings that you've already learned with the kanji. Have at it!

examples.en: It's already morning.
examples.ja: もう朝ですよ。

examples.en: In the morning before going to work, we have coffee and tea.
examples.ja: 朝、出社する前にコーヒーとお茶をのみます。

examples.en: I went to a popular bakery early in the morning.
examples.ja: 人気のベーカリーに朝早く行きました。

3044.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3044.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Hopefully this means you won't have to wake up too early in the morning to study kanji, now.

examples.en: My breakfast everyday is bacon and bread.
examples.ja: 毎日の朝ごはんはベーコンとパンです。

examples.en: I always go to work without eating breakfast.
examples.ja: 私はいつも朝ごはんを食べずに出社します。

examples.en: After breakfast, I run.
examples.ja: 朝ごはんの後、ランニングをします。

3045.meaning_mnemonic: ごはん is a food or meal (maybe you'll learn the kanji for it later, but it's not usually used, so you're learning it this way now). What is your <kanji>morning</kanji> meal? That is <vocabulary>breakfast</vocabulary> (not to be confused with second breakfast, you hobbit).
3045.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 朝 is the same as the one you learned with the kanji, meaning you should be able to read everything here.

examples.en: I do yoga in the bright morning sunshine.
examples.ja: 明るい朝日の中、ヨガをします。

examples.en: The rising sun seen from the mountain is very beautiful.
examples.ja: 山の上から見る朝日は、とてもキレイです。

examples.en: Morning sunlight and birdsong don't wake me, so I make sure to set my alarm before going to bed.
examples.ja: 朝日と鳥の声では目がさめないので、ベッドに行く前にアラームは必ずセットします。

3046.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>morning</kanji> <kanji>sun</kanji> is not only the <vocabulary>morning sun</vocabulary>, but it's the <vocabulary>rising sun</vocabulary> as well (because that's when the sun rises, right?).
3046.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, which is convenient since you've learned both of them by now with the words 朝 (あさ) and 日 (ひ). Put them together and what do you get? あさひ!

examples.en: Please tell me the ticket number.
examples.ja: チケット番号を教えて下さい。

examples.en: My student number is 4890.
examples.ja: 私の学生番号は４８９０です。

examples.en: Tanaka-san's phone number is in my smartphone.
examples.ja: 田中さんの電話番号はスマホに入ってます。

3047.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>number in a series</kanji> plus a <kanji>number</kanji>. You know what happens when two kanji with basically the same meaning get combined into one by now, right? It just turns out to be the same meaning, basically. This word means <vocabulary>number</vocabulary>, and it's used in contexts like phone numbers, exam numbers, and serial numbers.
3047.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The most important thing to me is money.
examples.ja: 私にとって一番大切なのはお金です。

examples.en: I want to get the highest score on this week's test.
examples.ja: 今週のテストで一番高い点数をとりたいです。

examples.en: This is the most popular song in all of America right now.
examples.ja: これが、今全米で一番人気の曲ですよ。

3048.meaning_mnemonic:
When you're the number <kanji>one</kanji> in a <kanji>number in a series</kanji>, you're <vocabulary>number one</vocabulary> ba-bay!

This word can refer to something ranked <vocabulary>first</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>best</vocabulary> in comparison to other things, or it can specifically refer to something marked with the number one, like an athlete with the number one on their jersey.
3048.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I am entry number two.
examples.ja: 私はエントリーナンバー二番です。

examples.en: Today is the second-longest day of the year.
examples.ja: 今日は一年の中で二番に長い日です。

examples.en: We won second place in the high school regatta.
examples.ja: 高校のボートレースで二番になりました。

3049.meaning_mnemonic:
When you're number <kanji>two</kanji> in a <kanji>number in a series</kanji> you're <vocabulary>number two</vocabulary>. Not quite as good as being 一番, but take what you can get, you know?

This word can refer to something ranked <vocabulary>second</vocabulary> in comparison to other things, or it can specifically refer to something marked with the number two, like an athlete with the number two on their jersey.
3049.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: There were a lot of German shepherds in front of the police box.
examples.ja: 交番の前に、たくさんのジャーマンシェパードがいました。

examples.en: Grandma, who always loses her way home, is a heavy user of the police box.
examples.ja: いつも家までの道が分からなくなってしまうおばあちゃんは、交番のヘビーユーザーです。

examples.en: Ironically, I feel uneasy if there's a police box too close to my house.
examples.ja: 皮肉なことに、家から交番が近すぎると、反対に不安です。

3050.meaning_mnemonic:
This word is a little tricky — at first, the combination of <kanji>mix</kanji> and <kanji>number in a series</kanji> doesn't seem to add up to <vocabulary>police box</vocabulary>, but there's a catch. This word is actually an abbreviated combo of two other words: The 交 comes from 交替 (in rotation) and the 番 comes from 立番 (standing watch).

A <vocabulary>police box</vocabulary> is basically a tiny community police station staffed by one or two officers. It's something that is not common in many Western countries, but it is pretty much all over Japan.
3050.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The correct answer of "three plus four" is "seven."
examples.ja: 「三足す四」の正しい答えは「七」です。

examples.en: Please pick an answer from A, B, C or D.
examples.ja: 答えは、A・B・C・Dの中から、えらんで下さい。

examples.en: I don't know the answer, so I'll get advice from the teacher.
examples.ja: 答えが分からないので、先生に助言をもらいます。

3051.meaning_mnemonic: You can guess this is a noun version of the kanji because the hiragana sticking out of it isn't an う-related sound or an い-related sound. So, what is the noun version of <kanji>answer</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>answer</vocabulary>.
3051.reading_mnemonic: The reading is kun'yomi, but this is also the reading you learned with the kanji so you should be able to read this and then give your 答え correctly.

examples.en: It took a little time to answer "yes."
examples.ja: 「はい」と答えるのに少し時間がかかった。

examples.en: In return for answering the questionnaire, I got ice cream.
examples.ja: アンケートに答えた代わりに、アイスクリームをもらいました。

examples.en: When I answer the phone, I first answer "hello" and say my name.
examples.ja: 私は電話に出る時、先ず「もしもし」と答えて、自分の名前を言います。

3055.reading_mnemonic:

For example, the どう in Judo is the soft "way." There are many words that end with 道, and you'll see them later on. 3058.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. 

Don't confuse this with 〜間 which is similar in meaning but different in reading. The 〜間 means it's attached to something. This is a standalone word.
3058.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. 間 has two common kun'yomi readings, あいだ and ま. You haven't learned these readings yet, so here's an explanation of each reading and mnemonics to help you remember them:

間 is usually read as あいだ for a longer interval of time or general space between things. It's read as ま for a short burst of time or when defining a specific area, like a 茶の間 (the older name for a Japanese living room).

You can remember this because time feels longer in <reading>Ida</reading>ho (あいだ). Any interval of time you spend there feels so long, because Idaho life moves so slowly. As soon as you cross the border and enter a new state, you call your <reading>ma</reading> (ま) to tell her you're finally out of that slooooow state, and the intervals of time feel shorter.

examples.en: One more day until the JLPT. I don't have enough time.
examples.ja: JLPTまで、あと一日。時間が足りません。

examples.en: In this holiday, I have plenty of time to play games.

examples.en: It took three whole hours by bus to get to Disneyland.
examples.ja: ディズニーランドまで、バスで３時間もかかった。

3059.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>time</kanji> <kanji>interval of time</kanji> is just the <vocabulary>time</vocabulary>. As is often the case, if two similar meaning kanji are combined into one word, they tend to produce a word with a similar meaning. Excuse me, friend, what's the 時間?

Note that 時間 can also be used as a unit of time measurement to mean <vocabulary>hour</vocabulary>(s). In this case, it's always used as a suffix — usually following a number or the question word 何 (なん).
3059.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: You can go to convenience stores anytime, twenty-four hours a day.
examples.ja: コンビニは２４時間いつでも行くことが出来ます。

examples.en: The dollar increased by thirty yen in one year.
examples.ja: 一年間でドルが三十円も上がりました。

examples.en: Can you let me be in the bathroom for only three minutes?

3060.meaning_mnemonic:
When you stick this onto the end of another word that talks about an <kanji>interval of time</kanji> in some way, you're indicating the <vocabulary>amount of time</vocabulary> that has gone past. For example, 二年間 is "two years." 一時間 is "one hour." Any amount of time + 〜間 will make it an "amount of time" instead of just a specific time.

Note that 〜間 can be omitted, especially in conversations, when it's clear that you're talking about a duration of time from the context. However, the exception is 時. You always say 〜時間 to refer to the amount of hours, to differentiate from 〜時 (〜o'clock).
3060.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. This should save you at least 二分間.

3061.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, and the reading of 間 is a bit of an oddball, here's a mnemonic to help you:

Did you know that the <vocabulary>human</vocabulary>s who work for <reading>Nin</reading>tendo are all called <reading>Gen</reading>ji (にんげん)? Yep, that's right, every single human ever hired by Nintendo is called Genji, without exception.

examples.en: It will be open soon!

3062.meaning_mnemonic:
The もなく part is like saying "there isn't even." So, when "there isn't even <kanji>an interval of time</kanji>," things will happen <vocabulary>soon</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>before long</vocabulary>.

You'll probably hear this the most in train announcements letting you know your train will <vocabulary>shortly</vocabulary> be arriving in Tokyo or wherever.
3062.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this one is weird, though. It's a second kun'yomi reading (there is also あいだ), read as ま. So what is happening <vocabulary>soon</vocabulary>? Your <reading>Ma</reading> is going to be here <vocabulary>before long</vocabulary>. You better hurry and prepare, because your room looks terrible... 

"間もなく, your mom is about to show up!"

3082.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

As a vocab word on its own, 事 usually refers to an intangible or abstract <vocabulary>thing</vocabulary>, like いい事 (good thing) or する事 (things to do). 

Depending on the context, it can also mean <vocabulary>matter</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>occurrence</vocabulary>, like 大切な事 (important matter) or きのうの事 (what happened yesterday).
3082.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned that reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

You've done all kinds of <vocabulary>thing</vocabulary>s in your <reading>coat</reading> (こと). If you think about it, you only wear a coat when you have things to do. Try to remember all the things you've done in a coat. It's a lot! Symbolically, your coat = all the things and <vocabulary>occurrence</vocabulary>s you've experienced, and all the <vocabulary>matter</vocabulary>s you've had to deal with in life.

Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn with the kanji. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

Right now it's time <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary> <reading>Haj</reading> (はじ). (Haj is the fifth pillar of Islam, and is a pilgrimage to Mecca during the month of Dhu al-Hijja). You need to start Haj right now!

3098.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means start, and this verb means to begin or to start. 始まる is the intransitive version, so it doesn't take a direct object. A war begins, for example, or the new school term starts. No direct object, right? Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
3098.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 始める.
