examples.ja: 父は事実、それを知っていました。

3103.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>occurrence</kanji> of <kanji>truth</kanji> is a <vocabulary>fact</vocabulary>.

事実 is primarily used as a noun, but it can also be used to say something is <vocabulary>factual</vocabulary>. Additionally, in relatively formal writing it can be used as an adverb to mean <vocabulary>in fact</vocabulary>.
3103.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Even if I used all of my true strength, it was still a draw.
examples.ja: 全ての実力を出しても、同点の引き分けでした。

examples.en: The younger brother seems to be worried about why he cannot be a professional, despite his true strength.
examples.ja: 弟は実力があるのに、なぜプロになれないのか不安に思っているようです。

examples.en: Koichi's hula dancing abilities are genuine.
examples.ja: コウイチのフラダンスの実力は本物です。

3104.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>truth</kanji> behind someone's <kanji>strength</kanji> is their <vocabulary>true strength</vocabulary>. It is also their <vocabulary>true ability</vocabulary>.
3104.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 力 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Your <vocabulary>true strength</vocabulary> is sealed behind two locks. <reading>Gee, two</reading> <reading>lock</reading>s (じつりょく)?! People must have been scared of your <vocabulary>true power</vocabulary> to seal it behind two locks!

examples.en: Those clothes are cute.
examples.ja: その服、かわいいね。

examples.en: My mother's lucky color is red, so she always wears red clothes.
examples.ja: うちの母は、ラッキーカラーが赤なので、いつも赤い服をきています。

examples.en: Why is it that I never have enough clothes no matter how many I own?!
examples.ja: どれだけ持っていても服が足りないのは、なぜ？！

examples.en: Put all the clothes in the drawer.
examples.ja: 服を全部引き出しの中に入れてください。

3105.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3105.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the reading you learned with the kanji and uses the on'yomi even though it's a single word. Very strange, but convenient for you so long as you remember this exception reading word.

examples.en: Swimming in the sea is not safe because the typhoon is approaching.
examples.ja: 台風が近づいてるので、海で泳ぐのは安全ではありません。

examples.en: I want to swim like a mermaid someday.
examples.ja: いつか人魚みたいに泳ぎたいんだ。

examples.en: Even though it's a municipal pool, it still costs money to swim.
examples.ja: 市立プールだからといって、泳ぐにはお金がかかります。

examples.en: Hey, your eyes are shifty.
examples.ja: あんた、目が泳いでるよ。

3106.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>swim</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to swim</vocabulary>.
3106.reading_mnemonic: The reading is kun'yomi (see that hiragana sticking out?) but that's the reading you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: There are too many things in this house.
examples.ja: この家には物がありすぎます。

examples.en: We don't have food for tomorrow, so I'm going to the supermarket.
examples.ja: 明日食べる物がないので、スーパーに買いに行ってきます。

examples.en: The other day, I found something I lost a year ago.
examples.ja: 先日、一年前に失くした物を見つけたんです。

3107.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. Besides <vocabulary>thing</vocabulary>, it has the related meanings of <vocabulary>object</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>item</vocabulary>.
3107.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading, but you haven't learned it yet. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

What game has the most <vocabulary>thing</vocabulary>s in it? <reading>Mono</reading>poly (もの). You can choose from a bunch of random things to play as, you know? And no one actually knows what those things are. What's a thimble anyway? Just call it a thing.

examples.en: Is this lettuce perhaps real?
examples.ja: このレタス、もしかして本物なの？

examples.en: I bought these Nike sneakers thinking they were real.
examples.ja: このナイキのスニーカー、本物だと思って買いました。

examples.en: Real rich people won't even complain about their duty of paying taxes.
examples.ja: 本物の金持ちは税金を払う義務について悪口なんて言わないよ。

3108.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>real</kanji> <kanji>thing</kanji> is the <vocabulary>real thing</vocabulary>, aka the <vocabulary>real deal</vocabulary>. 

If you learned 本 as <kanji>book</kanji> you can also think of this word as the "book thing." What is this book thing? Is it the real version of the book? Is it the real deal? If so, I'll pay you a million.
3108.reading_mnemonic: The readings are on'yomi plus kun'yomi (kun'yomi is 物). You learned the reading of the kanji 本 and also the vocabulary reading of 物, so you should be able to read it.

examples.en: What are Kyushu's local specialties?
examples.ja: 九州の名物は何ですか？

examples.en: Koichi is the famous president of Tofugu.
examples.ja: コウイチは、トーフグの名物社長です。

examples.en: Portland's specialties are hipsters, old carpets, and delicious coffee.
examples.ja: ポートランドの名物は、ヒップスターと、古いカーペットと、おいしいコーヒーです。

3109.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>famous</kanji> <kanji>thing</kanji> of an area is their <vocabulary>famous product</vocabulary>, but it sounds better in English if you say it's the <vocabulary>local specialty</vocabulary>. When you're traveling around Japan, be sure to be on the lookout for the 名物! It's always fun.
3109.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: My father likes bitter coffee.
examples.ja: 父は苦いコーヒーを気に入ってます。

examples.en: Is there a bitter fruit in this world?
examples.ja: 苦いフルーツなんて、この世の中に有るんですか？

examples.en: Be careful not to let the caramel burn or it will taste bitter.
examples.ja: カラメルは、こがさないように気を付けてください。でないと、苦い味になってしまいます。

3110.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji for 苦 means <kanji>suffering</kanji>. This word, however, is a bit different, but you'll see how it's related. It means <vocabulary>bitter tasting</vocabulary>. Think of putting the most <vocabulary>bitter</vocabulary> thing in the world in your mouth. You feel sick, your mouth gets all weird, and you try to spit it out but the bitterness remains. Obviously eating bitter tasting things will cause you to suffer.
3110.reading_mnemonic:
This reading of the kanji is unique to this meaning of the word, so here's a mnemonic to help you out!

The taste is so <vocabulary>bitter tasting</vocabulary> that you fall to your knees really, really hard. Luckily, you were wearing your <reading>knee gua</reading>rds (にが). Feel the relief that you were wearing them. Ack, no relief now. It's still bitter in your mouth.

examples.en: I ate so much that I'm in pain.
examples.ja: 食べすぎて苦しい。

examples.en: These jeans have been uncomfortably tight since about a month ago.
examples.ja: 一ヶ月前くらいから、このジーンズ、苦しいんだ。

examples.en: Remembering what happened back then still makes my heart ache.
examples.ja: あの時のことを思い出すと、今でも心が苦しい。

examples.en: In the village, there was not enough food in winter, and all the villagers lived in hardship.
examples.ja: 村では、冬になると食べ物が不足して、村人はみんな苦しい生活を送っていました。

3111.meaning_mnemonic:
This word ends in い, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. In fact, it ends in しい, which makes it even more likely it's an adjective. Since the kanji 苦 means <kanji>suffering</kanji>, this word is the adjective version of that: <vocabulary>painful</vocabulary>.

苦しい usually describes a painful or <vocabulary>distressing</vocabulary> feeling that's ongoing and hard to endure, rather than a physical sensation of pain. For example, you can use 苦しい when it's hard to breathe, when you feel emotional pain, or even when your finances are <vocabulary>strained</vocabulary>.
3111.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Everything is really <vocabulary>painful</vocabulary> right now. Why? You have something heavy on top of you, <reading>cru</reading>shing (くる) you.

examples.en: There are days when I get on the bus to go to the office.
examples.ja: 会社へ行くのに、バスに乗る日もあります。

examples.en: I couldn't get on a flight going to Tokyo.
examples.ja: 東京行きのフライトには乗れませんでした。

examples.en: The dog on that surfboard is cute!
examples.ja: あのサーフボードに乗ってる犬、かわいいね！

3112.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>ride</kanji> so the verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to ride</vocabulary>.
3112.reading_mnemonic: The reading is kun'yomi (see that hiragana?) but that's the reading you learned with the kanji. Enjoy the ride!

examples.en: In Japan, is it possible to take a dog with you in a taxi?
examples.ja: 日本では、犬をタクシーに乗せることは出来ますか？

examples.en: I loaded a suitcase into the vehicle.
examples.ja: 今、車内にスーツケースを乗せました。

examples.en: It's rude to put your feet on a table.
examples.ja: テーブルに足を乗せるのは失礼ですよ。

3113.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>ride</kanji> so this word has to do with riding. There's another word that's similar (乗る which means to ride). This particular one is transitive, meaning there is a direct object. The action is done to someone or something. So this means <vocabulary>to give someone a ride</vocabulary> when it's used for people, and <vocabulary>to place something on</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to load something</vocabulary> when it's used for things. 

Use the せ as a hint. The せ is a "sail" (せ) that you use on your boat to give someone a ride. How nice of you.
3113.reading_mnemonic: The reading is kun'yomi (see that hiragana?) but that's the reading you learned with the kanji so you should be okay with this. Allow me to give you a ride to the next item to study.

examples.en: I got motion sickness.
examples.ja: 乗り物よいしちゃった。

examples.en: I loved riding things when I was little.
examples.ja: 小さいころ、ボクは乗り物に乗るのが大好きでした。

examples.en: I feel like old vehicles smell like time itself.
examples.ja: 古い乗り物には、時間のにおいがする気がするんだよね。

examples.en: In Japan, it is considered good manners to set your smartphone to silent mode and refrain from making calls on public transportation.
examples.ja: 日本では、公共の乗り物の中ではスマホはマナーモードにして通話はしないのがマナーです。

3114.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 乗り has something to do with <kanji>riding</kanji> and that 物 is a <kanji>thing</kanji>. So what is a "riding thing?" Nowadays, at least, that would be a <vocabulary>vehicle</vocabulary>.
3114.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, but you know them both now, so you should be able to read this too!

examples.en: When a customer comes in, you'll hear the sound of this bell.
examples.ja: お客さんが入ってくると、このベルの音がします。

examples.en: I served tea to the customer.
examples.ja: お客さんにお茶を出しました。

examples.en: You are one of our precious WaniKani customers.
examples.ja: あなたは大切なワニカニのお客さんの一人なんですよ。

3115.meaning_mnemonic: The さん on the end is the name honorific さん. It's there to show some respect. It's like saying "Mr. Guest!" or something like that. But that sounds dumb in English. We'll just call this word <vocabulary>guest</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>visitor</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>customer</vocabulary>. You'll hear this word a lot when you're at a store or you're a customer somewhere in Japan. You are the お客さん, in that situation. Alternatively, you'll also hear お客さま which is a more polite version of this word (because it ends in さま and not さん).
3115.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the reading you learned with the kanji. Just add the hiragana on the end and you'll be good to go.

examples.en: The guest room was large and had two beds.
examples.ja: 客室は広く、ベッドが二つありました。

examples.en: Sure enough, rooms with ocean views are expensive.
examples.ja: 海が見える客室は、やはり高いです。

examples.en: At this hotel, all the rooms have concierge service.
examples.ja: このホテルでは全ての客室にコンシェルジュサービスが付いてきます。

3116.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>guest</kanji>'s <kanji>room</kanji> is the <vocabulary>guest room</vocabulary> (the room you put guests in, duh!).
3116.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: When I was little, I wanted to work in a cake shop when I became an adult.
examples.ja: 小さい時は、大人になったらケーキ屋さんになりたいと思ってました。

examples.en: There is a famous tonkotsu ramen shop in this town.
examples.ja: この町には有名なとんこつラーメン屋があります。

examples.en: The other day, a man I met at the bakery asked me for my phone number.
examples.ja: この前、パン屋で会った男の人に電話番号をきかれたんです。

3117.meaning_mnemonic: You'll see this attached to other words... like "meat" or "fish." When you see this, you'll know it is a ___ store, making this word mean <vocabulary>store</vocabulary> (same as the kanji).
3117.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading. Don't type the 〜 out when writing the answer. It's just there to let you know that there's usually something attached to this word.

examples.en: There's a bed in my room.
examples.ja: 私の部屋にはベッドがあります。

examples.en: The room is facing south, so it gets good sunlight.
examples.ja: 南を向いた部屋なので、日当たりがすごくいいんです。

examples.en: I plan to clean the room this afternoon.
examples.ja: 今日の午後は部屋のクリーニングをする予定です。

3118.meaning_mnemonic: If you have a <kanji>part</kanji> of a <kanji>roof</kanji>, that part is your <vocabulary>room</vocabulary>. Just imagine a roof divided into sections in a house, with the sections going all the way down to the ground. Each section is its own room, right?
3118.reading_mnemonic:
部屋 is a bit tricky because it's one of the few Japanese words that use the へ reading for 部. You'll just have to remember this one is special. Here's a mnemonic to help you out:

Imagine you're renting out a <vocabulary>room</vocabulary>, but all you hear at night is a constant "<reading>heh</reading> (へ)… heh... heh... hehehe". An incessant snickering, coming from somewhere inside your room. Hehehe.

examples.en: I bought 400 grams of beef at the butcher shop.
examples.ja: 肉屋さんで牛肉を四百グラム買いました。

examples.en: Japanese butchers sell croquettes and cutlets.
examples.ja: 日本の肉屋さんでは、コロッケやカツなどが売ってますよ。

examples.en: In the small town where I was born, there was a vegetarian restaurant named "Butcher." Now that I recall it, it's kind of a sarcastic name.
examples.ja: 私の生まれた小さい町には「お肉屋さん」と言う名前のベジタリアンのレストランがあったの。今思い出すと、なんだか皮肉な名前よね。

3119.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>meat</kanji> <kanji>shop</kanji> is a place that sells meat. Who sells meat? A <vocabulary>butcher shop</vocabulary>!

肉屋 often refers to the butcher shop, but it can also mean the actual butchers who work there. You might also see this as お肉屋さん, but that won't change the meaning — it can still be either the shop or the butcher, depending on context!
3119.reading_mnemonic: For 肉 you use the にく reading (which you learned with the kanji). For 屋 you use the kun'yomi, which you learned with the kanji. Basically, if you learned the kanji readings, you can read this word!

examples.en: This town has an old tea house.
examples.ja: この町には古い茶屋があります。

examples.en: Would you like to go into the teahouse and take a little break?
examples.ja: 茶屋に入って少し休みませんか？

examples.en: There is a bamboo grove in front of the teahouse, and there is also a red Japanese umbrella.
examples.ja: 茶屋の前には竹林があって、赤い和風のパラソルもあります。

3120.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>tea</kanji> <kanji>shop</kanji> is a <vocabulary>tea shop</vocabulary>. Mmm, delicious, delicious tea.

Traditionally, a 茶屋 was a Japanese <vocabulary>teahouse</vocabulary> where travelers could rest and enjoy tea and snacks. These kinds of 茶屋 are less common today, but the term is still often used for cafes or restaurants designed to evoke the charm of historical Japanese teahouses.
3120.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the readings you learned with the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: We bought some raw salmon at a fish shop.
examples.ja: 魚屋さんで生のサーモンを買いました。

examples.en: The fish shop will cut the fish you buy.
examples.ja: 魚屋さんは買った魚を切ってくれますよ。

examples.en: The owner of that fish shop runs the shop during the day, but at night he's the drummer in a rock band.
examples.ja: あそこの魚屋さんのご主人、日中は魚屋さんだけど、夜はロックバンドのドラマーなんですって。

3121.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>fish</kanji> <kanji>shop</kanji> is a <vocabulary>fish shop</vocabulary>, a place from which you buy fish. Especially in Japan, very important.
3121.reading_mnemonic: The kun'yomi reading is used for the 魚 (so it's さかな) and the kun'yomi reading is used for 屋 (や). You'll have to use the reading of 魚 from the vocabulary from a couple levels ago to remember the reading of this one.

examples.en: My friend is a designer in Nagoya.
examples.ja: 私の友人は名古屋でデザイナーをしています。

examples.en: The breakfast culture in Nagoya is famous all over the country.
examples.ja: 名古屋の朝ごはん文化は全国で有名です。

examples.en: Which is the highest building in Nagoya City?
examples.ja: 名古屋市内で一番高いビルはどれですか？

3122.meaning_mnemonic: The place that's <kanji>famous</kanji> for <kanji>old</kanji> <kanji>roof</kanji>s. I don't know why, but it's the city of <vocabulary>Nagoya</vocabulary>. Just associate the two things together and it'll be hard to forget (so long as you've heard of Nagoya before - if not, read up about it!).
3122.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji (except for 名 and 屋, which are kun'yomi here). If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. For な just think to 名前 (なまえ) which uses the な reading. The "name" (名前) of this city is what? It's <reading>Na</reading>goya. Watch out for rendaku changing こ to ご too.

examples.en: Okay, then let’s do it next time.
examples.ja: じゃあ、やっぱり今度にしよう。

examples.en: I'm planning to go see the cherry blossoms with my friends this time.
examples.ja: 今度、友人と花見に行く予定です。

examples.en: This summer vacation I'm going to Shikoku.
examples.ja: 今度の夏休みは四国に行くつもりです。

3123.meaning_mnemonic: In the <kanji>now</kanji> <kanji>occurrence</kanji> you'll learn your kanji, no? This word means <vocabulary>this time</vocabulary>. Despite being "this time" it has the feeling of <vocabulary>next time</vocabulary>, though. It's like saying "okay, this time we'll get it" where "this time" really means "next time," making it a little bit different from 今回.
3123.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I just got out of the bath.
examples.ja: 丁度、おふろから出たところです。

examples.en: The size of these clothes is just right.
examples.ja: この服の大きさが丁度いいです。

examples.en: I was just looking for that book.
examples.ja: 丁度その本を探していたんです。

examples.en: Oh! I was planning to call you just now!
examples.ja: あら！今丁度あなたに電話をしようと思っていたところよ！

3124.meaning_mnemonic: Okay, we're going to cheat a little bit to remember the meaning of this word. Let's say you take the temperature of the <kanji>street</kanji>. It is exactly one hundred <kanji>degree</kanji>s. That's <vocabulary>exactly</vocabulary> what it is. <vocabulary>Just</vocabulary> 100 degrees, not one degree more or less. You put your eggs on the street and watch them cook.
3124.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Every time, I get the same error.
examples.ja: 毎度、同じエラーが出るんですよ。

examples.en: Of course, I always ignore hateful replies.
examples.ja: もちろんクソリプは毎度スルーだよ。

examples.en: This always happens, but it’s taking a long time for Kyoko to decide on what to wear today too.
examples.ja: 毎度のことだが、キョーコは今日も服を決めるのに時間がかかっている。

3125.meaning_mnemonic: When something happens at <kanji>every</kanji> <kanji>occurrence</kanji> and at <kanji>every</kanji> <kanji>degree</kanji>, it's something that happens <vocabulary>frequently</vocabulary>. It happens <vocabulary>each time</vocabulary>.
3125.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It took a while to get the angle right.
examples.ja: 正しい角度にするのに時間がかかりました。

examples.en: I would like to think about this from various angles.
examples.ja: これについては、色々な角度から見て考えてみたいと思います。

examples.en: Each angle is sixty degrees, which means it's an "equilateral triangle."
examples.ja: 一つの角度が全て六十度ということは、それは「正三角形」ですよ。

3126.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>angle</kanji> <kanji>degree</kanji> is just an <vocabulary>angle</vocabulary>. 90 degrees? 160 degrees? They're all still angles when you come down to it.
3126.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: In Tokyo in summer, there are many days where it gets above thirty degrees.
examples.ja: 東京の夏は、三十度以上になる日が多いです。

examples.en: First, heat the oven to 190 degrees.
examples.ja: 先ず、オーブンを１９０度にして下さい。

examples.en: The angle here is ninety degrees.
examples.ja: ここの角度は、９０度です。

3127.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji <kanji>degree</kanji> can mean both degree in terms of angles and degree in terms of temperature. This word is how you talk about these things. Just attach it to a number and you have yourself the number of <vocabulary>degrees</vocabulary> that something is. After the numbers 1, 2 and 3 (and in some other situations) this can also mean <vocabulary>times</vocabulary>.
3127.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji reading you learned. When writing out the answer to this reading, omit the 〜 as it's only there to let you know that some other word should come before it.

examples.en: My mother is waiting for me at home.
examples.ja: お母さんが家で私を待っています。

examples.en: I'll be waiting at the airport.
examples.ja: 空港で待ってますね。

examples.en: Wait! I might have forgotten my wallet at home.
examples.ja: ちょっと待って！財布を家に忘れたかも。

3128.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>wait</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to wait</vocabulary>.
3128.reading_mnemonic: You need <vocabulary>to wait</vocabulary> for your <reading>ma</reading>ma (ま) all the time. You want to go out? You have to wait for mama to drive you. Want to eat dinner? You have to wait for mama to make you food. Hmm. Maybe all this waiting is really a you problem.

examples.en: It's not good to keep people waiting.
examples.ja: 人を待たせるのは良くないよ。

examples.en: How much longer are you going to make me wait?
examples.ja: 一体いつまで待たせるつもりですか？

examples.en: Sorry for making you wait so long. I had to wait for the bus for such a long time.
examples.ja: お待たせしてすみません。いや〜バスにえらく長いこと待たされましてね。

3129.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>wait</kanji> so this word has something to do with waiting. Use the たせ as a hint. Someone "tossed" a ball off into a ditch, and then they had to find it. They made you wait for them to get the ball too, even though it's a cheap piece of crap. Feel upset about this. That'll help you remember that this means <vocabulary>to make someone wait</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to keep someone waiting</vocabulary>.
3129.reading_mnemonic: You learned this reading from 待つ, congrats!

examples.en: I decided to have my own car before I turned thirty.
examples.ja: 三十才になるまでに自分の車を持つと決めたんです。

examples.en: What is that man holding in his left hand?
examples.ja: あの男、左手に何を持ってるんですか？

examples.en: When you go out in the summer, be sure to carry water and a towel.
examples.ja: 夏に出かけるときは、水とタオルを必ず持っていきましょう。

3130.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji itself means <kanji>hold</kanji> and the verb version is <vocabulary>to hold something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to carry something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to own something</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to keep something</vocabulary>.

This is a transitive verb, meaning it takes a direct object. You hold something, like chopsticks, have something, like power, or keep something, like your friend's book over the weekend.
3130.reading_mnemonic: If you try <vocabulary>to hold something</vocabulary> in your hand long enough it will <reading>mo</reading>ld (も). And then that mold will cover your hand, then your arm, then your entire body. Basically, you should never hold anything for too long or you'll become a mold person.

examples.en: There are lots of rich people's houses around here.
examples.ja: この辺は金持ちの家が多い。

examples.en: It's the kind of school where rich people would go to.
examples.ja: そこは金持ちが行くような学校だよ。

examples.en: I used to run small errands for a wealthy neighbor of mine to make money when I was young.
examples.ja: 若い頃、お金を稼ぐために、近所のお金持ちの人たちの使い走りをしていました。

3131.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>hold</kanji> <kanji>gold</kanji> you are a <vocabulary>rich person</vocabulary>.
3131.reading_mnemonic: Do you remember the word お金? This is the 金 in that word. The reading for 持ち is the も you learned with 持つ. So, combine the かね of お金 and the 持ち and you have the reading of this word. Note that just like お金, you'll often see this with the honorific prefix お in front of it as well.

examples.en: I know exactly how you feel.
examples.ja: あなたの気持ちはよく分かります。

examples.en: I've been feeling sick since I woke up in the morning.
examples.ja: 朝起きた時から気持ちわるいんです。

examples.en: Here’s a little something for you. This is just a small token of my appreciation. Go ahead, open it.
examples.ja: これ、つまらないものですが。ささやかな感謝の気持ちです。どうぞ、開けてみてください。

3132.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>energy</kanji> you <kanji>hold</kanji> in your body is your <vocabulary>feeling</vocabulary>s. It can take the form of all kinds of things. Good feelings, bad feelings, that "strange feeling."
3132.reading_mnemonic: 気 is on'yomi and you learned that with the kanji. 持ち, though, is kun'yomi, which you learned with the word 持つ. One of those weird exception readings, but the ち on the end of 持ち is a clue that it uses the kun'yomi.

examples.en: The world is big, so I want to go to various countries.
examples.ja: 世界は広いから、色々な国に行きたいです。

examples.en: This documentary has become a popular masterpiece worldwide.
examples.ja: このドキュメンタリーは全世界で人気の大作になりました。

examples.en: Many artists have a world of their own.
examples.ja: アーティストは、自分の世界を持ってる人が多いです。

3133.meaning_mnemonic: Both kanji mean <kanji>world</kanji>, so it should be easy to guess this is a word for <vocabulary>the World</vocabulary>. It also means <vocabulary>society</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>the Universe</vocabulary>.
3133.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You know the on'yomi reading for 界, but you didn't learn this on'yomi reading of 世, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember:

What's the most hated vegetable in <vocabulary>the world</vocabulary>? <reading>Ce</reading>lery (せ), probably. The world is divided into those who love celery and those who hate celery. Which one are you?

examples.en: "Handmade Cheesecake" is on sale starting today!
examples.ja: 今日から「手作りチーズケーキ」の発売です！

examples.en: This is an announcement to all our fans. Our merchandise will be released online first.
examples.ja: ファンのみんなにお知らせです。私たちのグッズが先ずはオンラインで発売されることになりました。

examples.en: My sister has been in front of the store since twelve hours before the release of the new smartphone.
examples.ja: 私の姉は、新しいスマートフォン発売の十二時間前から、お店の前にいます。

3134.meaning_mnemonic: You want things to <kanji>depart</kanji> from your store so you have to <kanji>sell</kanji> them. You put all these things up for <vocabulary>sale</vocabulary>. You are <vocabulary>selling</vocabulary> these items.
3134.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Can you tell me the pronunciation of "Otolaryngology"?
examples.ja: 「Otolaryngology」の発音を教えてくれませんか？

examples.en: After the teacher corrected my pronunciation of L and R, I became able to pronounce them well.
examples.ja: 先生がLとRの発音を正してくれてからは、上手に発音出来るようになりました。

examples.en: I am training in pronunciation to improve my speaking skills.
examples.ja: スピーキング力を上げるため、発音のトレーニングをしています。

3135.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sound</kanji> that <kanji>departs</kanji> from your mouth is you talking. Imagine yourself saying things and words departing your mouth. They are bent in different ways and have different colors, highlighting your <vocabulary>pronunciation</vocabulary> of certain words and phrases.
3135.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I found a caterpillar on a tree.
examples.ja: 木の上に毛虫を発見しました。

examples.en: If you live in a foreign country, you'll make discoveries every day.
examples.ja: 外国で生活をしていると、毎日発見があります。

examples.en: With this old map, you may be able to find some treasure.
examples.ja: この古い地図があれば、宝を発見することが出来るかもしれない。

3136.meaning_mnemonic: You make <kanji>departure</kanji> from your home off into the great beyond. You will go to <kanji>see</kanji> the unseen, and hopefully make a great <vocabulary>discovery</vocabulary>.
3136.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You know the はつ part, which gets shortened to はっ. The 見 is unlike what you learned with 見, though. 

In order to remember that this is けん, imagine you're going out to make a discovery of some strange new lands. With strange new lands, there comes strange new people. This one has a samurai named <reading>Ken</reading> (けん) on it. He's trying to discover new things too!

examples.en: Hey, I have something I want to discuss with you.
examples.ja: ねえ、相談があるんだけど。

examples.en: Home loan consultation is from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m.
examples.ja: 家のローン相談は、午後六時から午後九時です。

examples.en: When I consulted the doctor, I was told, "First, try to live a life without stress."
examples.ja: 医者に相談したら「先ずはストレスのない生活をして下さい」と言われました。

3137.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>mutual</kanji> <kanji>talk</kanji>. Both sides are talking to each other and the feelings are mutual. Imagine you're discussing a problem. You want to get help with it, so you get some <vocabulary>consultation</vocabulary> from your friend. This <vocabulary>discussion</vocabulary> was very helpful.
3137.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The opponent of this game seems to be strong.
examples.ja: 今回のゲームの相手は強そうだ。

examples.en: My mother's companion for chatting is her pet caterpillar.
examples.ja: 母の話し相手は、ペットの毛虫です。

examples.en: How about thinking carefully about the person you're proposing to with a flash mob?
examples.ja: フラッシュモブでプロポーズされる相手のことも、きちんと考えなよ。

3138.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 手 can mean a "doer"? Now, what do you think your <kanji>mutual</kanji> <kanji>doer</kanji> might be? It’s someone who shares the same activities or tasks with you. This person could be your <vocabulary>partner</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>companion</vocabulary>, or even an <vocabulary>opponent</vocabulary> in certain situations.
3138.reading_mnemonic:
The readings are the kun'yomi readings. For 手, that's no problem for you. For 相, that's more of an issue since you learned the on'yomi reading for it. Think of it this way: 

Your partner wouldn't be your partner without you. Your partner is: <reading>I</reading> (あい) and you. Remember that as you gaze into your partner's eyes. "I and you."

examples.en: What prefecture are you from?
examples.ja: 何県の出身ですか。

examples.en: I have been to Ishikawa prefecture three times.
examples.ja: 石川県には三回行ったことがありますよ。

examples.en: Yamaguchi prefecture's specialty is puffer fish.
examples.ja: 山口県の名物はフグです。

3139.meaning_mnemonic: Attach this word onto the end of a prefecture place name and you have the <kanji>prefecture</kanji> portion of _____ <vocabulary>prefecture</vocabulary>. These are a lot like states or provinces.
3139.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this is the same as what you learned with the kanji, probably because it's always attached to things (so it's like jukugo). Don't write the 〜 when you're writing in the answer, just the けん portion, and you'll get this one correct.

examples.en: This blue flower is very beautiful.
examples.ja: この青い花、とても美しいですね。

examples.en: The river called "Shimanto River" in Shikoku is one of Japan's beautiful rivers.
examples.ja: 四国の「四万十川」という名の川は日本の美しい川の一つです。

examples.en: The eyes of this doll are beautiful like jewels.
examples.ja: この人形の目は、宝石のように美しいですね。

3140.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. More precisely, it has しい on the end, which makes it even more likely it's an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>beauty</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>beautiful</vocabulary>.
3140.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you. It's a long reading for a mnemonic, but try your best. 

You look at someone who is <vocabulary>beautiful</vocabulary>. What an easy life they've lived. No hard work and all they do is pamper themselves to stay beautiful. Feel disgusted. You walk up to this person and say: "<reading>U too cushy</reading>! (うつくしい). 

Sorry for adding the whole word in there for the reading mnemonic, but I thought it worked out better that way. Just know that the word isn't うつくしいしい or something weird like that. The hiragana on the end is part of the mnemonic as well.

examples.en: That woman is a very elegant beauty.
examples.ja: あの女の人は、とてもエレガントな美人ですね。

examples.en: When I asked for her phone number, I just couldn't say, "You're a beautiful woman."
examples.ja: 電話番号をきく時、「あなた美人ですね」ってどうしても言えなかったんだよ。

examples.en: He said, "I don't need anyone's advice," but then he said he would welcome advice from beautiful women.
examples.ja: あいつ、「だれの助言もいらない」って言ってたのに、美人の助言はウェルカムなんだとよ。

3141.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>beautiful</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji> is a <vocabulary>beautiful woman</vocabulary>. Wait, why isn't this a beautiful person? In fact, this word used to have a broader meaning, but for some reason it's generally only used for women in modern Japanese.
3141.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Where you're from, every <vocabulary>beautiful woman</vocabulary> wears <reading>bee</reading> <reading>jean</reading>s (びじん). That's right, jeans made out of bees. Beauty knows no pain after all!

examples.en: My brother is always worried about losing.
examples.ja: 兄は、いつも負けることを不安に思っています。

examples.en: Even if you lose with your body, don't lose with your heart.
examples.ja: 体は負けても、心は負けないで。

examples.en: "What should we eat?" "It's your call. I lost in rock-paper-scissors."
examples.ja: 「何食べようか？」「あなたが決めてよ。私はじゃんけんに負けたんだから。」

3142.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>lose</kanji> so the verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to lose</vocabulary>.
3142.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You lose your tournament/soccer game/whatever (you decide something applicable to you). You're sad about this. Who's there to comfort you? Your <reading>Ma</reading> (ま). She's a nice lady.

examples.en: The match was a draw.
examples.ja: 勝負は引き分けだった。

examples.en: I think this year is the year of challenges.
examples.ja: 今年は、私にとって勝負の年だと思っています。

examples.en: You only have one shot at this, so please give it your all.
examples.ja: これは一発勝負なので、全力を出して下さいね。

3143.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Win</kanji>, <kanji>lose</kanji>... both will happen in tonight's <vocabulary>match</vocabulary>! What a <vocabulary>showdown</vocabulary> it will be!

Note that 勝負 can also describe situations where one takes a significant risk or makes a bold move— <vocabulary>a gamble </vocabulary>—with high stakes involved.
3143.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just remember that ふ becomes ぶ because of rendaku here.

examples.en: Tom always wins with skill.
examples.ja: トムはいつも実力で勝つ。

examples.en: I did a lot of training in order to win.
examples.ja: 勝つために、たくさんトレーニングをしました。

examples.en: Maria is always working hard to win.
examples.ja: マリアはいつも勝つためにがんばっている。

3144.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>win</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to win</vocabulary>.
3144.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

What did you just <vocabulary>win</vocabulary>? You won a new <reading>ca</reading>r (か)!

examples.en: The winners of this race will get some money.
examples.ja: このレースの勝者はお金がもらえますよ。

examples.en: Only the winner can proceed to the next stage.
examples.ja: 勝者だけが次のステージにすすめます。

examples.en: The idea that going to a famous university will make you a winner in life is an old way of thinking.
examples.ja: 有名な大学に行ったら人生の勝者になれるだなんて考え方、古いですよ。

3145.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The book about successful marriage proposals is likely to be a bestseller this year.
examples.ja: プロポーズ必勝の本が今年のベストセラーになりそうです。

examples.en: Thinking she would definitely win, my sister spent 20,000 yen on the lottery.
examples.ja: 姉は必勝すると思い、宝くじに二万円を使った。

examples.en: Can I really win if I use this "Pachinko Surefire Win Manual"?
examples.ja: この『パチンコ必勝マニュアル』を使えば本当に勝てるのでしょうか？

3146.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>certain</kanji> <kanji>win</kanji> sounds like a great thing. When these two kanji are put together, a <vocabulary>certain victory</vocabulary> is inevitable.
3146.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Take note that the つ in ひつ is turned into a small っ, though.

examples.en: This test was a piece of cake.
examples.ja: 今回のテストは、楽勝だったね。

examples.en: ”How was the JLPT5?" "Thanks to WaniKani, it was easy peasy."
examples.ja: 「JLPT5はどうだった？」「ワニカニのおかげで、楽勝だったよ。」

examples.en: That game is such a piece of cake that it's just kinda boring.
examples.ja: あのゲームは楽勝すぎて、なんかつまらないんだよね。

3147.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>win</kanji> that was an <kanji>ease</kanji>. That is an <vocabulary>easy victory</vocabulary> or an <vocabulary>easy win</vocabulary>. Don't hope for a lot of these, though. Hope for tough wins instead, they actually make you better.

Note that this can be used both literally, to describe an easy victory at a game or contest; or more figuratively, to describe something as “easy” in general.
3147.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: At the end of every year, I send a handmade postcard to my friends.
examples.ja: 毎年、年末には友人に手作りのポストカードを送る。

examples.en: I'll send you the video from earlier via LINE.
examples.ja: さっきのビデオ、LINEで送るね。

examples.en: Let’s call it a day. I’ll walk you home.
examples.ja: 今日は、ここまでにしよう。家まで送るよ。

3148.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>send</kanji>, and the vocab verb version is <vocabulary>to send something</vocabulary>. If the object of this verb is a person, it means "to send" in the sense of <vocabulary>to escort someone</vocabulary>, maybe to the station, or to the door.
3148.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You need to send an entire <reading>oak</reading> (おく) tree in the mail, but it's too big. Imagine yourself dragging one to the post office. They tell you that you can't send that here... Go to the oak sending facilities.

examples.en: This TV drama will be broadcast for the first time in ten years.
examples.ja: このドラマが放送されるのは、十年ぶりです。

examples.en: Are we really broadcasting this clip?
examples.ja: このクリップ、本当に放送するんですか？

examples.en: President Koichi's important announcement will be broadcast on television tonight.
examples.ja: コウイチ社長は今晩テレビで重大な決定を放送することになっている。

3149.meaning_mnemonic:
You are going to <kanji>release</kanji> and <kanji>send</kanji> something out. Imagine this message going out through the sky to everyone around you. You are going <vocabulary>to broadcast something</vocabulary> to the world! 

The する is on there to make this noun a verb. Without the する it would be the noun "broadcast."
3149.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This suitcase is heavy.
examples.ja: このスーツケースは重いですよ。

examples.en: I want to use this big, heavy rock as a bench.
examples.ja: この大きくて重い石を、ベンチの代わりに使いたいと思います。

examples.en: Now that I remember today's exams, I feel reluctant to go to school.
examples.ja: 今日の試験のことを思い出すと、学校への足が重い。

3150.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>heavy</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>heavy</vocabulary>.
3150.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You're lifting something that's really <vocabulary>heavy</vocabulary>. Oof! You lift it above your head. You're so awesome. You scream: "<reading>OH! MO</reading>RE!" (おも) they put more. You yell it again: "OH, MORE!" and again: "OH, MORE!" Go ahead and act this out wherever you are, pretending like you're holding a couch or two or three over your head, saying "OH MORE!"

examples.en: The important thing is to be healthy.
examples.ja: 重要なのは、元気でいることです。

examples.en: When I was in elementary school, I thought it was important to make friends at school.
examples.ja: 小学生の時、私は学校で友達を作ることが重要だと思っていました。

examples.en: It was an important announcement for the people.
examples.ja: それは、国民にとって重要なお知らせでした。

3151.meaning_mnemonic: When something has a <kanji>heavy</kanji> <kanji>need</kanji>, you know that that thing is <vocabulary>essential</vocabulary>. It is <vocabulary>important</vocabulary>.
3151.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What is Anna’s body weight in kilograms?
examples.ja: アンナさんの体重は、何キロですか？

examples.en: Our dog ​​got fat last year, but she lost the weight all at once on a desperate diet.
examples.ja: うちの犬は去年太ったが、必死のダイエットで一気に体重が下がりました。

examples.en: Excuse me. This weight takes my contact lenses into account too, right?
examples.ja: すみません。この体重、コンタクトレンズの分も入ってますよね？

3152.meaning_mnemonic: How <kanji>heavy</kanji> is your <kanji>body</kanji>? Figure that out and you'll have your <vocabulary>body weight</vocabulary>.
3152.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Please draw a double line under characters you're not sure about.
examples.ja: 分からない文字の下に、二重のラインを引いて下さい。

examples.en: This fish has a strong smell, so I'll double wrap it.
examples.ja: この魚はニオイが強いので、ラップを二重にしておきますね。

examples.en: This is an exercise to get rid of double chins.
examples.ja: これは、二重アゴをなくすためのエクササイズです。

3153.meaning_mnemonic:
When you have <kanji>two</kanji> <kanji>heavy</kanji> things, you have <vocabulary>double</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>dual</vocabulary> the heavy (compared to one, at least).

3156.reading_mnemonic:

<vocabulary>If</vocabulary> you don't mind, could you <reading>carry</reading> (かり) this for me? <vocabulary>Supposing</vocabulary> it's not too much trouble, of course.

examples.en: Does this book have kana?
examples.ja: この本には、ふり仮名がついてますか？

3157.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>temporary</kanji> <kanji>name</kanji>s. These are the <vocabulary>kana</vocabulary> (that's hiragana and katakana). Why are kana the "temporary names" though? Maybe they were just meant to be a temporary way to write the names of the kanji you didn't know how to write yet. That's just a guess, but it should help you remember that this word means "kana."
3157.reading_mnemonic:
Okay, so 仮 uses the rare kun'yomi reading か, which you haven't learned yet, but luckily it's the same as the on'yomi you have learned! And 名 also uses a kun'yomi reading that you learned with the vocab word 名 (な). So you sort of know these readings already, but it's a lot to take in, so here's a mnemonic to help: 

The reading is so tricky for <vocabulary>kana</vocabulary> that it makes you say <reading>かな</reading>… (I wonder…) whenever you try to read it. You keep thinking, "Is the reading kana, かな? Or could it be something else, かな?" You're just not sure.

examples.en: It is not a assumption, but the truth.

仮定 refers to making tentative assumptions about a specific situation to discuss what might happen under certain conditions, such as "if we <vocabulary>assume</vocabulary> I dropped my wallet here yesterday...”
3158.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

3161.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

3164.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this is just the vocab 日本's primary reading plus the on'yomi you learned for 酒, put together.

3167.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>end</kanji>, so this verb means <vocabulary>to end</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be over</vocabulary>.

Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive, and 終わる is usually intransitive too. But sometimes it can be transitive and take a direct object. Kind of like "to end" in English — you can say the class ends (intransitive) or a teacher ends their class (transitive).

examples.en: What's the name of the last stop on this Amtrak leaving from Chicago?

examples.en: The endpoint of this hiking trail is roughly around here on the map.
examples.ja: このハイキングコースの終点は、地図で見ると、大体この辺りです。

examples.en: No matter what I say, no matter what I do, please do not let me get out of the train until it gets to the last stop. Okay?

3168.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>end</kanji> <kanji>point</kanji> is where everything ends... but for this example, think of a map with a route on it. The last spot on the route is the "last point." It is the <vocabulary>last stop</vocabulary>.
3168.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

3169.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.ja: ボールが転がる音がした。

3172.meaning_mnemonic: You know the kanji here means revolve. The verb version of this is similar. It means to roll or to tumble. You have to be revolving in order to roll or tumble, right? 転がる is intransitive, so it doesn't take a direct object. A ball rolls down a hill. A tumbleweed tumbles. No direct object, right? Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
3172.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

What should you do when you want <vocabulary>to roll</vocabulary> down a hill? Become a bottle of <reading>Coro</reading>na (ころ). Just imagine yourself as a bottle of Corona, rolling down a hill. You're a Corona bottle, so you roll super easily. Now feel the grass under your glass as you roll down that hill. Nice, isn't it?

examples.en: Excuse me. Is there bicycle parking around here?
examples.ja: すみません。この辺に自転車のパーキングはありますか？

examples.en: I'll buy you a new bicycle. I don't need anything in return!
examples.ja: 自転車を買ってあげるよ。お返しは要らないからね！

You'd think this would be a regular car, but <vocabulary>bicycles</vocabulary> were probably introduced before cars were, meaning the self revolving car is the bicycle, not the car. Just imagine yourself on a bike, and you don't even have to move the pedals. They revolve themselves, but now you're going too fast and it's scary.
3173.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

転送 is often used in the context of logistics or communication systems, like transferring packages or forwarding e-mails.
3175.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

3177.meaning_mnemonic:
