3177.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

In order <vocabulary>to advance</vocabulary>, you must <reading>sue Sue</reading> (すす) for her misdeeds against you. Imagine her standing in your way, literally. She keeps saying, "You'll have to sue me if you want <vocabulary>to move forward</vocabulary>!" So you do — you sue Sue. That way, you can finally move on with your life.

examples.en: Cosplay culture continues to evolve day by day.
examples.ja: コスプレ文化は日々進化し続けている。

examples.en: Evolved scientific technology supports our lives.
examples.ja: 進化した科学テクノロジーが私たちの生活を支えています。

examples.en: Hey, mom. What will humans become when we evolve?
examples.ja: ねえ、ママ。人間は進化したら何になるの？

3178.meaning_mnemonic: Think of things that <kanji>advance</kanji> and <kanji>change</kanji>. Does this sound familiar? Does this sound like <vocabulary>evolution</vocabulary>?
3178.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The construction of the road is progressing.
examples.ja: 道の工事が進行しています。

examples.en: The other day, I reported on the progress status of the project.
examples.ja: 先日、プロジェクトの進行ステータスをリポートしました。

examples.en: The new vaccine made from blowfish extract has suppressed the progression of the disease.
examples.ja: フグのエキスから作られた新しいワクチンが病気の進行を止めました。

3179.meaning_mnemonic:
When something <kanji>advance</kanji>s and <kanji>go</kanji>es, it is moving forward. So this means <vocabulary>advance</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>progress</vocabulary>.

進行 can be used to describe various situations, like when a project progresses; but also when an illness advances to a more serious stage.
3179.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Did you hear the snow falling just now?
examples.ja: 今、雪が落ちる音がしませんでした？

examples.en: My brother fell off the tree trying to catch insects.
examples.ja: 弟は虫を取ろうとして、木から落ちてしまいました。

examples.en: A lot of colorful leaves have fallen on the ground.
examples.ja: 土の上にはカラフルな葉がたくさん落ちていました。

3180.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>fall</kanji> and the vocab verb version means <vocabulary>to fall down</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to fall</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>to drop</vocabulary>. It can also mean <vocabulary>to fail</vocabulary>, in the sense of failing an exam.
3180.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

If you start <vocabulary>to fall down</vocabulary>, what do you yell? "<reading>OHHHH</reading> (お)!"

examples.en: Last summer, we went to a mountain with beautiful fresh leaves.
examples.ja: 去年の夏、青葉が美しい山へ行きました。

examples.en: Three days ago, I found a small white flower in the greenery
examples.ja: 三日前、青葉の中に小さな白い花があるのを見つけた。

examples.en: It's good for your eyes to see greenery.
examples.ja: 青葉を見るのは目にいい事ですよ。

3181.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>young</kanji> <kanji>leaf</kanji> is exactly what you'd expect, although most people usually just call them <vocabulary>fresh leaves</vocabulary>.

Remember how there's some overlap between blue and green in Japanese? 青葉 is another example!  That's why 青 is used to describe fresh and lush green leaves, especially those on trees during early summer.
3181.reading_mnemonic: The readings for the kanji in this word are the kun'yomi readings. Since you've already seen the word 青, hopefully you can just combine it with 葉 (you learned the reading for this part with the kanji). Be sure to pay attention to the rendaku, though. は goes to ば in this word, making it <reading>あおば</reading>.

examples.en: This cushion is very light.
examples.ja: このクッション、すごく軽いですね。

examples.en: I eat light snacks such as fruits and cereal every day for breakfast
examples.ja: 毎日の朝ごはんは、フルーツやシリアルといった軽い物を食べています。

examples.en: With some light exercise, my stress has disappeared.
examples.ja: 軽いエクササイズで、ストレスがなくなりました。

3182.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>lightweight</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>lightweight</vocabulary>.
3182.reading_mnemonic: The reading you learned with the kanji is the reading you'll be using here. Because of that, this word is kind of a <vocabulary>lightweight</vocabulary>.

examples.en: I saw a bird carrying a part of the tree.
examples.ja: 鳥が木の一部を運ぶのを見ました。

examples.en: I brought tea to the customer's room.
examples.ja: お茶を、お客さんの部屋に運びました。

examples.en: What? Did you carry all three suitcases by yourself?
examples.ja: えっ、一人で三つのスーツケースを運んだんですか？

3183.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>carry</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to carry</vocabulary>.
3183.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Imagine you have <vocabulary>to carry</vocabulary> a <reading>har</reading>d<reading>co</reading>re (はこ) music fan home after a concert. They spent all night moshing to hardcore sounds, and now they’re too tired to walk. But you? You’re a hardcore friend, so you’re happy to carry them.

examples.en: It's lucky to win a lottery.
examples.ja: 宝くじが当たるなんて、運がいいよ。

examples.en: You're lucky to win 100,000 yen from slots.
examples.ja: スロットで十万円勝つなんて、お前は運がいいよ。

examples.en: We were lucky as there were no deaths or injuries from this typhoon.
examples.ja: 今回の台風では、死人もケガ人も出ず、本当に運がよかった。

3184.meaning_mnemonic: The いい portion means "good." So, when what you <kanji>carry</kanji> is good you are <vocabulary>lucky</vocabulary>. Just think of it in terms of luck being a physical item you carry in your hands. Now imagine yourself carrying it. Now think to yourself "what I'm carrying is good, it's lucky!"
3184.reading_mnemonic: The reading for the kanji in this vocab is the same as the one you learned with the kanji, meaning you should be able to read this.

examples.en: When I opened the door, the wind came in from outside.
examples.ja: ドアを開けると、外から風が入ってきた。

examples.en: "Hey. Can you open this wine?" "Of course. It's a piece of cake."
examples.ja: 「ねぇ。このワイン、開けてもらえないかな？」「もちろん。そんなの楽勝さ。」

examples.en: It is a big role to open a fish shop every single morning without missing a day.
examples.ja: 一日も休まずに、毎朝魚屋開けるというのは大役です。

3185.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>open</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to open something</vocabulary>.
3185.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You go <vocabulary>to open</vocabulary> the door. When you do, a huge scream comes out: "<reading>AAAHHH</reading>!" (あ). Imagine giant あ characters flying out of the door you opened as well.

examples.en: The new drama will be released in March of this year.
examples.ja: 新しいドラマの公開は今年の三月です。

examples.en: It's been almost twenty years since this work was released.
examples.ja: この作品が公開してから、間もなく二十年です。

examples.en: The celebrity's private phone number has been released.
examples.ja: 有名人のプライベートの電話番号が公開されてしまった。

3186.meaning_mnemonic: When something is <kanji>public</kanji> <kanji>open</kanji> it is <vocabulary>open to the public</vocabulary>. You can go look at things that are 公開. You can also use this when you're <vocabulary>releasing</vocabulary> something to the public, which means you’re making it publicly accessible.
3186.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I am the company president, but I've just started the company and I have no money.
examples.ja: 私は社長ですが、開業したばかりで、お金がありません。

examples.en: My brother is going to start a marketing company next month.
examples.ja: 私の兄は来月、マーケティングの会社を開業する予定です。

examples.en: The business that my friend started abroad has been greatly successful, and this time they're going to do the same in Japan.
examples.ja: 友人が海外で開業したビジネスが大成功し、今回は日本でも同じような事をするつもりだそうです。

3187.meaning_mnemonic:
This is one of those words that has kanji that basically tell you the meaning. You <kanji>open</kanji> a <kanji>business</kanji>... aka <vocabulary>opening a business</vocabulary>.

While this can be used for opening any sort of business, it’s commonly associated with doctors, lawyers, and other professionals opening their own practice or office.
3187.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This town is currently under development.
examples.ja: この町は今、開発中です。

examples.en: The leader of the development team is such a big role.
examples.ja: 開発チームのリーダーなんて、大役じゃないか。

examples.en: This company is fully focused on the development of new products.
examples.ja: この会社は新しいプロダクトの開発に全力で集中しています。

3188.meaning_mnemonic: You are now <kanji>open</kanji> for <kanji>departure</kanji>. You get on your boat and leave this place. You are going to another place to start its <vocabulary>development</vocabulary>, where you will create a new world.
3188.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I like collecting old marbles.
examples.ja: 私は古いビー玉を集めるのが、すきです。

examples.en: We collected beautiful flowers from all over the country and made handmade bouquets.
examples.ja: 全国から美しい花を集めて、手作りのブーケを作りました。

examples.en: We are collecting feedback from users.
examples.ja: ユーザーからのフィードバックを集めています。

3189.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>collect</kanji> and this verb is transitive, meaning the action is done to something or someone. So this verb means things like <vocabulary>to collect something</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to gather something</vocabulary>.
3189.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You have one of something, but that's not much of a collection. What should you get if you want <vocabulary>to collect something</vocabulary>? <reading>Ah, two</reading> (あつ)! Two of that thing! Yes, when you have enough to say "Ah, two…" you know you've really begun to collect something. Ah, two Crabigator trading cards! See?

examples.en: Let's concentrate during the exam.
examples.ja: 試験の間は、集中しましょう。

examples.en: You should not talk to Dad when he is concentrated in a game.
examples.ja: パパがゲームに集中している時は、話しかけない方がいいよ。

examples.en: I was too focused on the meeting that I've just remembered that I haven't had my breakfast yet.
examples.ja: ミーティングに集中しすぎて、朝ごはんをまだ食べてないことを今思い出しました。

examples.en: In Japan, the population is concentrated in large cities such as Tokyo.
examples.ja: 日本は、東京などの大きな町に人口が集中しています。

3190.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>collect</kanji> to the <kanji>middle</kanji> of yourself, you are collecting towards your brain. All energy is going towards there, massing up in the middle, giving you extreme <vocabulary>concentration</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>focus</vocabulary>.
3190.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Today is the day of money collection.
examples.ja: 今日は集金の日です。

examples.en: Hello, I'm calling to notify you for the collection of money.
examples.ja: もしもし、集金のお知らせでお電話しました。

examples.en: When I went to collect money the other day, the client didn't have enough money, so I got two onions instead.
examples.ja: 先日、集金に行ったら、お客さんのお金が足りなかったので、代わりに玉ねぎを二つもらってきました。

3191.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>collect</kanji> <kanji>gold</kanji> you are <vocabulary>collecting money</vocabulary> (or doing <vocabulary>money collection</vocabulary>). Of course, back in the day gold was like money, which is why this word works the way it does. Hopefully you don't have to deal with too much 集金 in your daily life. We'll try to keep WaniKani nice and reasonably priced for you.

集金 often refers to collecting bills, dues, or fees in person or through a designated representative. This can be carried out by a business, an organization, or even just a small group of people.
3191.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My mother drinks tea every day.
examples.ja: 母は毎日お茶を飲む。

examples.en: My brother drank some whiskey and his face turned red all at once.
examples.ja: 兄は一気にウイスキーを飲んで顔が赤くなった。

examples.en: Can you drink this tap water?
examples.ja: この水道水は飲めますか？

examples.en: What would you like to drink? Gin, vodka, beer, wine, sake, or chuhai? You name it, we’ve got anything that has alcohol in it.
examples.ja: 何をお飲みになりますか？ ジン、ウォッカ、ビール、ワイン、日本酒、それともチューハイ？ 何でも言ってくださいね。お酒なら何でもありますから。

3192.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>drink</kanji> so the vocab verb version is <vocabulary>to drink</vocabulary>.
3192.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Go have a drink in the great Allicrab's name!

examples.en: This is Mr. Nakayama, an industrial designer.
examples.ja: こちらは、工業デザイナーの中山さんです。

examples.en: It's an industrial area near the house, so there are many factories around.
examples.ja: 家の近くは工業エリアなので、多くの工場があります。

examples.en: With the progress of industrial technology, robots have been used as pets in recent years.
examples.ja: 工業テクノロジーの進歩により、近年はロボットがペットとしても活用されています。

3193.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I like the shape of the "eye" kanji.
examples.ja: 「目」という漢字の形が気に入ってます。

examples.en: This is not the kanji I learned in elementary school.
examples.ja: これは、小学校で学んだ漢字じゃないよ。

examples.en: Most people from China know kanji, so it is a little easier for them to learn Japanese.
examples.ja: 中国出身だと、漢字を知ってる人がほとんどなので、日本語を学ぶのが少し楽です。

3194.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>Chinese</kanji> <kanji>letter</kanji>s... you're finally learning the word for them, the thing you've been studying this whole time for so long! This is <vocabulary>kanji</vocabulary>, your new best friend (they came from China, which is why they're Chinese letters).
3194.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: American roads are wide.
examples.ja: アメリカの道路は広いですね。

examples.en: I can't drive through this paved road as there's always construction.
examples.ja: ここは、いつも道路の工事をやってて車が通れません。

examples.en: Please be careful not only for vehicles, but also for bicycles and pedestrians on the road.
examples.ja: 道路には車両だけでなく、自転車や歩いてる人もいるので、気を付けて下さいね。

3195.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>road</kanji> <kanji>road</kanji> is obviously the best kind of road. It's double road, after all. So, what is this ultimate road? It is a <vocabulary>paved road</vocabulary>.
3195.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Never go on the railroad tracks, no matter what.
examples.ja: 線路には、何があっても入らないで下さい。

examples.en: There is a train track in front of the house, so the noise from the train is loud.
examples.ja: 家の前に線路があるので、電車の音が大きいです。

examples.en: My older brother always gets on the last car of the train so that he can see the train tracks.
examples.ja: 兄は必ず線路が見えるよう、電車の後ろの車両に乗ります。

3196.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>line</kanji> that runs on a <kanji>road</kanji> is a <vocabulary>railroad track</vocabulary>. First you have to get into your mind that the "line" in question is a railway line. Then, what railway line runs on a road and what kind of road is it? It's a <vocabulary>railroad track</vocabulary>.
3196.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Many cats live in the alley of the downtown area.
examples.ja: 下町の路地には、たくさんのネコが住んでいます。

examples.en: The fish store is in an alley just off of Western Street.
examples.ja: その魚屋は、西通りから少し路地に入った所にあります。

examples.en: Be careful for your safety when you walk in an alley around here at night.
examples.ja: この辺の路地、夜に歩く時は、安全に気を付けてね。

3197.meaning_mnemonic: If you think about it, an <kanji>earth</kanji> <kanji>road</kanji> isn't going to be the main road. It will be the road less traveled. You could call it a <vocabulary>path</vocabulary> (you know, like a dirt path!) or a <vocabulary>dirt road</vocabulary>. Alternatively, another less traveled street that would probably be made out of dirt back in the day (before everything was paved) would be an <vocabulary>alley</vocabulary>. Imagine yourself walking down a dirt alley at night with no shoes. Scary!
3197.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You've learned these readings already, so you should be able to read this word too! And remember, that it's the じ reading that you learned with 生地 here.

examples.en: At school, we learned about the lifestyle of long-ago peasants.
examples.ja: 学校で、むかしの農民のくらしを学びました。

examples.en: The farmers always began working before the sun rose.
examples.ja: いつも農民たちは、朝日がのぼる前からはたらき出しました。

examples.en: The farmers swung their hoes every day until the sun went down.
examples.ja: 農民たちは、毎日、日がくれるまでクワをふるいました。

examples.en: The farmers' hands were steeped in the smell of soil.
examples.ja: 農民の手は、土のにおいにそまっていました。

3199.meaning_mnemonic:
In the olden days, the <kanji>peoples</kanji> who worked in the <kanji>farm</kanji> were the <vocabulary>peasants</vocabulary>.

農民 means <vocabulary>farmers</vocabulary>, but usually not in the modern sense of people who do farm work as their day job. Instead, it refers to the <vocabulary>farming class</vocabulary> — people who were born into a life of farming, often in historical contexts.
3199.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: In our town, there are many people who are farming rice.
examples.ja: 私たちの町では、米の農業をしてる人々が多いです。

examples.en: Agriculture is hard work, but it is important for people's lives.
examples.ja: 農業はハードワークですが、国民の生活にとって大切です。

examples.en: I came from Ireland to learn about the culture of Japanese agriculture.
examples.ja: アイルランドから、日本の農業の文化を学びに来ました。

examples.en: The agriculture method called Biodynamics is popular now.
examples.ja: 今、バイオダイナミックという農業の方法が人気です。

3200.meaning_mnemonic: What's another way to call the <kanji>farming</kanji> <kanji>business</kanji>? If you encapsulated it into one word (assuming we're talking about plant farming, here), you could call it <vocabulary>agriculture</vocabulary>.
3200.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I went to college using a subway called "Tokyo Metro."
examples.ja: 私は「東京メトロ」という地下鉄を使って大学へ行っていました。

examples.en: There are subway exits in various places.
examples.ja: 地下鉄の出口は色々な所にあります。

examples.en: There are many different kinds of people on the New York subway.
examples.ja: ニューヨークの地下鉄には本当に色々な人が乗ってますね。

3201.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>ground</kanji> <kanji>below</kanji> <kanji>iron</kanji> is iron under the ground. It isn't a deposit of iron, though. It's man-made. And what's made of iron? Trains. In this case, because it's underground, it's a <vocabulary>subway</vocabulary>. Depending on where you live, you might call it <vocabulary>the Underground</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>the Tube</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>the Metro</vocabulary>
3201.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Our president is a strong man who comes to work after a triathlon.
examples.ja: うちの社長はトライアスロンの後に出社するような鉄人です。

examples.en: This famous female professional wrestler is strong like a badass.
examples.ja: この有名女子プロレスラーは鉄人のように強いです。

examples.en: That man is a French chef, who was once also called the "Iron Chef."
examples.ja: あの男の人は、かつては「鉄人シェフ」とよばれたフレンチシェフです。

examples.en: I saw a tough guy playing peak-a-boo with a baby in a grocery store.
examples.ja: スーパーで赤ちゃんに「いないいないばぁ」をしている鉄人を見てしまった。

3202.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>man</kanji> made of <kanji>iron</kanji> is a <vocabulary>strong man</vocabulary>... aka a huge <vocabulary>badass</vocabulary>. Have you seen "Iron Chef?" The Japanese translation is 料理の鉄人, which means "Chef Iron Man" aka "Chef Badass," at least in my book.
3202.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Check out the <vocabulary>strong man</vocabulary> wearing nothing but <reading>jean</reading>s (じん). He looks like a badass in his jeans, flexing his pecs. Very impressive, but also slightly terrifying.

examples.en: When I grow up, I want to join an electric railway company.
examples.ja: 大人になったら、電鉄会社に入社したいです。

examples.en: Keio Electric Railway's blue train cars are cool.
examples.ja: 京王電鉄の青い車両はカッコイイですよね。

examples.en: The nickname for the Enoshima Electric Railway is "Enoden."
examples.ja: えのしま電鉄のニックネームは「えのでん」です。

3203.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>electricity</kanji> <kanji>iron</kanji> sounds scary, but if you think to back in the day and to where iron was used a lot, you probably think of the railway systems... big hunky pieces of iron on the ground to make the railway. So, you can advance this by adding electricity instead of coal, creating an <vocabulary>electric railway</vocabulary>.
3203.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This is a Japanese song, isn't it?
examples.ja: これって、日本の歌ですよね？

examples.en: Do you know the name of the song that was playing at the shopping mall today?
examples.ja: 今日ショッピングモールでかかってた歌の名前、知ってますか？

examples.en: It's a song I made for you.
examples.ja: 君のために作った歌だよ。

3204.meaning_mnemonic: One of the kanji's meanings is <kanji>song</kanji> and this word means exactly that: a <vocabulary>song</vocabulary>.
3204.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Think about a song... but not just any song... think about the <reading>utter</reading> (うた) song, and make it up right now and sing it out loud. What does the utter song sound like? Why do you love utterances so much that you made a song about them?

examples.en: I want to quit the company and become a singer right now.
examples.ja: 会社をやめて、今すぐ歌手になりたい。

examples.en: There was a Japanese pianist and singer at the restaurant.
examples.ja: レストランには日本人のピアニストと歌手がいました。

examples.en: Cindy Lauper is a famous singer from New York.
examples.ja: シンディ・ローパーはニューヨーク出身の有名な歌手です。

3205.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how  手 can sometimes mean “doer”? What do you think a <kanji>song</kanji> <kanji>doer</kanji> is? A <vocabulary>singer</vocabulary>, of course
3205.reading_mnemonic: The readings are on'yomi readings. You've learned them both already (you learned 手's on'yomi reading with word 投手), so you should be able to read this like a <vocabulary>singer</vocabulary> sings with a bunch of <reading>cashew</reading>s かしゅ in their mouth. FAST AND LOUD!

examples.en: The teacher of arithmetic is Tanaka-sensei.
examples.ja: 算数の先生は、田中先生です。

examples.en: Do you have all the tools you need for tomorrow's arithmetic class?
examples.ja: 明日の算数のクラスに必要な道具は全部持ったの？

examples.en: If you don't know the answer on the arithmetic test, you can just say one or four and it'll be just fine.
examples.ja: 算数のテストで答えが分からない時は、とりあえず一か四と答えておけば平気です。

3206.meaning_mnemonic: What is it called when you <kanji>calculate</kanji> <kanji>numbers</kanji>? That is the study of <vocabulary>math</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>arithmetic</vocabulary>.
3206.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Right now, could you calculate the number of people who came today?
examples.ja: 今日の入場人数を今すぐ算定してもらってもいいですか？

examples.en: My mother is good at calculating the money going in and out of the house every month.
examples.ja: 母は毎月の家のお金の出入りを算定することが上手です。

examples.en: We calculated the sales of shaved ice and balloons from the fireworks display.
examples.ja: 花火大会の時のかき氷と風船の売り上げを算定しました。

3207.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>calculate</kanji> and <kanji>determine</kanji> (the calculation), you are determining the calculation. That's why this word is <vocabulary>to calculate</vocabulary>.

Unlike 計算する, which means “to calculate” in general, 算定する is a formal word that focuses more on the final value of a calculation, instead of the process of calculating itself.
3207.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I listen to the radio every day.
examples.ja: 私は毎日ラジオを聞く。

examples.en: I'm sorry to ask you this. Do you have some money on you?
examples.ja: こんな事聞いて、すみません。今お金持ってますか？

examples.en: Why the hell can you as an adult not listen to a person, when five-year-old child can listen to their teacher?
examples.ja: 五才の子でも先生の話をよく聞けるのに、大人のあなたが人の話を聞けない理由は一体何なんですか？

3208.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>hear</kanji> so the vocab verb version is <vocabulary>to hear</vocabulary>.

This can also mean <vocabulary>to ask</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to listen</vocabulary>, like asking someone a question or listening to what others are saying. It basically covers anything that involves the act of letting something in through the 門 (gates) of your 耳 (ears).
3208.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You need <vocabulary>to hear</vocabulary> something very important, but you can't. In order to hear, you have to take a <reading>key</reading> (き) and unlock the doors covering your ears. Go ahead and imagine yourself doing that, focusing on the key that lets you hear.

examples.en: I want to be a newspaper reporter.
examples.ja: 新聞ジャーナリストになりたい。

examples.en: In recent years, I check news from the newspaper online.
examples.ja: 近年、新聞のニュースはオンラインでチェックします。

examples.en: Famous newspapers nationwide are, for example, the Asahi Shinbun and the Mainichi Shinbun.
examples.ja: 全国で有名な新聞は、「朝日新聞」や「毎日新聞」などがあります。

3209.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>new</kanji> <kanji>hear</kanji> is what it sounds like. It's new things that you're hearing about in your ear... at least that's what it was back a long time ago. Now those new things that get to your ear get to you via other mediums. In this case, a <vocabulary>newspaper</vocabulary>.
3209.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I go to a Japanese classroom once a week.
examples.ja: 週に一回、日本語の教室に通っています。

examples.en: Does this book have a Japanese version?
examples.ja: この本は日本語バージョンもありますか？

examples.en: I am studying Japanese with a book called "GENKI" and an app called "WaniKani."
examples.ja: 「GENKI」という本と、「ワニカニ」というアプリで日本語を学んでいます。

3210.meaning_mnemonic: You know 日本 is "Japan." So, when you add <kanji>language</kanji> onto the end of that you have <vocabulary>Japanese language</vocabulary>.
3210.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the vocab word 日本 (にほん) plus the on'yomi that you learned for 語. Combine them together to get the reading for this word.

examples.en: I went to college to learn French.
examples.ja: フランス語を学ぶために大学に行きました。

examples.en: Your French is great and I thought you were a French person.
examples.ja: フランス語が上手なので、てっきりフランス人かと思ってました。

examples.en: There are not many French books in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本には、フランス語の本はあまりありません。

3211.meaning_mnemonic: I bet you can guess that フランス means "France." So what happens when you add <kanji>language</kanji> to it? You get the "France Language" aka the <vocabulary>French Language</vocabulary>.
3211.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the on'yomi reading for 語 which is the reading you learned with the kanji. This is probably because it gets added onto a lot of other words so it's treated like a jukugo. For example: 日本語 = "Japanese Language." 中国語 = "Chinese Language." スペイン語 = "Spanish Language."

examples.en: I taught my friend Spanish.
examples.ja: 友人にスペイン語を教えてあげました。

examples.en: Apparently, the pronunciation of Spanish is about the same as Japanese pronunciation.
examples.ja: スペイン語の発音は、日本語の発音と大体同じらしいですよ。

examples.en: Garlic in Spanish is "ajo," which is pronounced "aho." "Aho" means "stupid" in Japanese.
examples.ja: ニンニクはスペイン語で「ajo」っていうんだけど、「アホ」って発音されるんだよ。「アホ」は日本語で「stupid」って意味だよ。

3212.meaning_mnemonic: You can probably figure out that スペイン is "Spain" just by reading it. Add the kanji <kanji>language</kanji> on there and you have the <vocabulary>Spanish language</vocabulary> (or just <vocabulary>Spanish</vocabulary>), if you'd like.
3212.reading_mnemonic: The reading for the kanji portion is just the reading you learned with the kanji. Since it's attached to something, it's like a jukugo word.

examples.en: This tale is very long.
examples.ja: この物語はとても長いですよ。

examples.en: I'll read the Andersen story for you.
examples.ja: アンデルセン物語を読んであげましょう。

examples.en: There are many stories about yokai in various parts of Japan.
examples.ja: 妖怪にまつわる物語は、日本各地にたくさんあります。

3213.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>language</kanji> about <kanji>thing</kanji>s. This is a confusing one. Just think of it more like someone talking about things, anything, really. Someone who just talks about things is someone who tells stories. So, this word means <vocabulary>tale</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>story</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>legend</vocabulary> (not the Tom Cruise one, though).
3213.reading_mnemonic:
Both kanji take the kun'yomi here. For 物, that's もの, which you learned with the vocabulary 物. You learned the kun'yomi for 語 with the verb 語る, but here it becomes がたり because of rendaku, and the り is tucked inside the kanji.

Maybe you've already heard the word ものがたり too. It's in some film and book names. If you haven't, and you find this reading hard to remember, think of a story about an infamous <reading>Gatling</reading> (がたり) gun that wandered the land, mowing everything down in its path. It's a terrible legend, but what if it were true???

examples.en: What is the subject of this sentence?
examples.ja: この文の主語は何ですか？

examples.en: I learned how to use subjects in Japanese class last week.
examples.ja: 先週の日本語のクラスで、主語の使い方を学びました。

examples.en: In Japanese, even if you don't say the subject every time, the listener would often get it.
examples.ja: 日本語では、いちいち主語を言わなくても相手に分かってもらえる事が多いんですよね。

3214.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>main</kanji> thing you talk about in your <kanji>language</kanji> becomes the <vocabulary>subject</vocabulary> of the sentence.
3214.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I have no time to read a book when I'm at home.
examples.ja: 家にいる時は本を読む時間がありません。

examples.en: I don't think I have the ability to read fast.
examples.ja: 私には速く読む力が足りないと思うんです。

examples.en: After joining the company, I read newspapers on the train every morning.
examples.ja: 入社してからは、毎朝電車で新聞を読んでいます。

3215.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>read</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to read</vocabulary>.
3215.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Go read something else, now.

examples.en: Excuse me. Could you tell me how to read your name?
examples.ja: すみません。お名前の読み方を教えてもらってもいいですか？

examples.en: I can speak French, but I don't know how to read French.
examples.ja: フランス語は話せるけど、フランス語の読み方は知らない。

examples.en: Does this kanji have four ways to read?!
examples.ja: この漢字には読み方が四通りもあるんですか？！

3216.meaning_mnemonic: You know that this has something to do with <kanji>read</kanji>ing and you know that 方 means <kanji>way</kanji> or <kanji>method</kanji>. So, when you think of a "way of reading" you can think of a couple other better words, such as <vocabulary>reading</vocabulary> (aka the reading of a word) or <vocabulary>pronunciation</vocabulary>. Anytime you need to know how something sounds, this is what you'll ask for.
3216.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi readings from the vocab words 読む and 方. So as long as you're okay with those, you can apply that knowledge over here.

examples.en: We hear the birds chirping outside.
examples.ja: 外から鳥が鳴く声がしますね。

examples.en: The puppy is barking.
examples.ja: 子犬がワンワン鳴いています。

examples.en: The sound of chickens saying "cock-a-doodle-doo" starts the morning of the farm.
examples.ja: ニワトリが「コケコッコー！」と鳴く音が農場の朝を始めます。

3217.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>chirp</kanji> but the verb has the broader meaning <vocabulary>to make an animal sound</vocabulary>. Variations of this include <vocabulary>to bark</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to chirp</vocabulary>, but this can be used for any animal sound.
3217.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same reading as the one you learned with the kanji. So, spend more time chirping and less time memorizing, okay?

examples.en: All of the lines are crooked.
examples.ja: 全ての線が、曲がってます。

examples.en: What does this line on the map represent?
examples.ja: 地図上の、この線は一体何を表しているんですか？

examples.en: Please have the incorrect spots marked with double lines.
examples.ja: 正しくない場所は、二重線でマークしておいて下さい。

examples.en: The Yamanote train line can take you to many places in Tokyo.
examples.ja: 山手線の電車で、東京の色々な場所に回ることができます。

3218.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This also works for "train lines" as well. You'll see this attached onto the ends of names describing them.
3218.reading_mnemonic: The reading you learned with the kanji is the same for this vocab word. Enjoy it!

examples.en: The caterpillar was running next to the tree.
examples.ja: 毛虫が木の横を走っていました。

examples.en: There's a fence made of wood standing next to the house.
examples.ja: 家の横に木で出来たフェンスが立っています。

examples.en: Don't just sit by, you help too!
examples.ja: 横でボーっと見てないで、あんたも助けてよ！

3219.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. Please note that this word refers to "the side of something." Not "the left side," for example. That would be 左側.
3219.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this vocab is the same as the one you learned with the kanji, lucky you!

examples.en: How are you today?
examples.ja: 今日の調子はどうですか？

examples.en: I will help with housework this week because your mother is not in good shape.
examples.ja: お母さんの調子がよくないので、今週は家事を手伝います。

examples.en: To men who only say flattering things, you should just text them back a heart-shaped emoji.
examples.ja: 調子のいいことばっかり言う男には、ハート形の絵文字だけ返しておけばいいのよ。

3220.meaning_mnemonic: Imagine yourself <kanji>investigating</kanji> a <kanji>child</kanji>. You heard this child was having a rough time, so you need to come check on the <vocabulary>condition</vocabulary> of his home and life. You find the condition to be terrible, and you tell the parents you have to take the child away because of these conditions (imagine them being ridiculously bad... perhaps they raise raccoons in their kitchen?).
3220.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The teacher emphasized important points.
examples.ja: 先生は、重要なポイントを強調しました。

examples.en: I want to emphasize that safety is the most important thing during construction.
examples.ja: 工事の時は、何よりも安全が重要だという事を強調したい。

examples.en: I said the same thing many times to emphasize my thoughts.
examples.ja: 自分の考えを強調するために、何度も同じことを言いました。

examples.en: I feel like Barbie dolls twenty years ago were still emphasizing body lines.
examples.ja: 二十年前のバービー人形は、まだボディラインを強調するものが多かった気がします。

3221.meaning_mnemonic: If you use a <kanji>strong</kanji> <kanji>tone</kanji> on certain words, then you are putting <vocabulary>emphasis</vocabulary> on whatever it is you're talking about. It's the <vocabulary>stress</vocabulary> you put on things that are important because your tone gets stronger on those words or syllables.
3221.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It is my routine to check the weather in Germany, where my younger sister is, every morning.
examples.ja: 毎朝、妹がいるドイツの天気を調べるのが私のルーティンです。

examples.en: If you are not willing to look it up yourself, ask Alexa now.
examples.ja: 自分で調べる気がないなら、早くアレクサに聞いてください。

examples.en: An American genius scientist came to Japan to examine bird dung.
examples.ja: アメリカ人の天才科学者が、鳥のフンを調べるために日本に来ました。

examples.en: Can you research capybaras and see if they are edible?
examples.ja: カピバラが食べられるのかどうか、ちょっと調べてくれない？

3222.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>investigate</kanji> so the vocab verb version means <vocabulary>to investigate</vocabulary>.
3222.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You are hired <vocabulary>to investigate</vocabulary> someone's wife. It is said that <reading>she love</reading>s (しら) another man... but you need to investigate her to find out if that's true, for her husband of course.

examples.en: Both parents of this puppy are German Shepherds.
examples.ja: この子犬の親は両方ジャーマンシェパードです。

examples.en: I have to get a signature from my parents.
examples.ja: 親にサインをもらわないといけない。

examples.en: If the parents are both swans, the child should also be a swan, right?
examples.ja: 親が白鳥だったら、子も白鳥のはずでしょ？

3223.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3223.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Just imagine your parents saying <reading>oh yah</reading> (おや) over and over at you. What did you do at school today? I beat up this kid. "Oh yah?"

examples.en: I've only told this to close friends.
examples.ja: まだ親しい友人にしか話してないの。

examples.en: I ran into a teacher who I was close with in college on the street.
examples.ja: 大学生の時に親しかった先生に、道でバッタリ会ったんです。

examples.en: No matter how close you are, you shouldn't come into the bathroom.
examples.ja: いくら親しいからって、トイレに入ってきちゃダメだよ。

3224.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with some kana and an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>intimacy</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>intimate</vocabulary>! Depending on the context, this also means <vocabulary>friendly</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>close</vocabulary>.
3224.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Those who are most <vocabulary>intimate</vocabulary> with you hang out with you even when you're doing gross things, like sitting on the <reading>sh*tter</reading> (した). Gross, your family is.

examples.en: Thank you for always being kind.
examples.ja: いつも親切にしていただいて、ありがとうございます。

examples.en: A young lady on the street kindly helped me find my lost wallet.
examples.ja: 道にいたお姉さんが、失くした財布を親切に見つけるのを助けてくれた。

examples.en: When I got to their home, Michael's mom always kindly offered me some tea.
examples.ja: 家に行くと、マイケルのママはいつも親切にお茶を出してくれる。

3225.meaning_mnemonic:
When your <kanji>parent</kanji>s <kanji>cut</kanji> you you'd think they are being mean... but they're not. They are bleeding all the bad blood out of you. They are truly being <vocabulary>kind</vocabulary>. 

Just think of how crazy it would be for your parents to cut you... then think about some kind of twist to make it so they are being kind instead.
3225.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I opposed my best friend's thoughts.
examples.ja: 親友の考えに反対した。

examples.en: We are more than friends but less than best friends, don't you think?
examples.ja: 私たちって、友人以上、親友以下よね。

examples.en: I met Rachel last summer and soon became best friends with her.
examples.ja: レイチェルとは去年の夏に出会って、すぐに親友になりました。

examples.en: I'm thinking of giving my best friend a llama as a birthday present.
examples.ja: 親友のバースデープレゼントに一頭のラマをあげようと思ってるんです。

3226.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>friend</kanji> who is like one of your <kanji>parent</kanji>s is someone who will look out for you. They are like family, in fact! That's why this word means <vocabulary>best friend</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>close friend</vocabulary>. Just imagine someone who watches over you like a parent would. This is the way to describe them.
3226.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: You have something like a thread on your head.
examples.ja: 頭に何か糸のような物が付いてますよ。

examples.en: This apartment isn't that tall, so watch your head, please.
examples.ja: このアパートは高さがあまりないので、頭の上に気をつけてください。

examples.en: What kind of person is a "smart person"?
examples.ja: 「頭がいい人」というのは、一体、どういう人の事ですか？

3227.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3227.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading which you learned with the kanji earlier. No problem!

examples.en: The red face is due to drinking alcohol.
examples.ja: 顔が赤いのは、アルコールのせいです。

examples.en: I can't remember the face of my teacher from elementary school.
examples.ja: 小学校の時の先生の顔が思い出せません。

examples.en: I should probably drop by at the townspeople's next cherry blossom viewing.
examples.ja: 今度の町民たちの花見には、顔を出しておこうかな。

3228.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3228.reading_mnemonic: The reading is kun'yomi, since it's a kanji all alone with nothing attached. Luckily, that's also the reading you've already learned, so associate that with this vocab word.

examples.en: You look more relaxed than before.
examples.ja: この前より、顔付きがリラックスしてるね。

examples.en: This bulldog has a girly facial expression.
examples.ja: このブルドッグ、顔付きが女の子っぽいですね。

examples.en: You look like a person with a big heart.

Every <vocabulary>sick person</vocabulary> enjoys playing on their <reading>Nin</reading>tendo (にん). You have the nastiest flu, but you've still got your Nintendo, so everything is fine.

3233.reading_mnemonic:

Think of <vocabulary>the most</vocabulary> ridiculous <reading>motto</reading> (もっと) you've ever heard. Now imagine a motto that's even more ridiculous. "It's Not for Women" "If It Doesn't Get All Over the Place, It Doesn't Belong in Your Face" and of course, "Why Not Enjoy the Go?"

examples.en: Please don't argue about me!

Your views conflict with someone else's so you're going to compete with them to see who's right.
3238.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You're starting <vocabulary>to compete</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to argue</vocabulary> with someone, who is yelling at you: "You <reading>are so</reading> (あらそ) stupid!". You might want to imagine this in an accent that gets you closer to the Japanese pronunciation.

3239.meaning_mnemonic: You have <kanji>war</kanji> and <kanji>conflict</kanji>. Of course, conflict comes with war, so this word just means <vocabulary>war</vocabulary>.
3239.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

3240.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>compete</kanji> to the point of <kanji>conflict</kanji>, you know that this person / entity is your <vocabulary>competition</vocabulary>. Gotta beat out that competition. For example, in order to beat out the competition, WaniKani has a mascot that can eat every other small furry animal that the competition has for their mascot. Case closed.
3240.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Koichi and I are companions from the same company.
examples.ja: コウイチとは同じ会社の仲間です。

examples.en: I got this shirt from my golf buddy.
examples.ja: このシャツはゴルフ仲間にもらったんだ。

examples.en: My group of friends and I relaxed after a hard day at school.
examples.ja: 学校での厳しい一日を終えて、仲間たちとリラックスをした。

3241.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>relationship</kanji> <kanji>interval</kanji> is very short between you and your <vocabulary>comrade</vocabulary>s. You are <vocabulary>companion</vocabulary>s who have been through thick and thin together, so there's no distance between you.

仲間 is one of those very Japanese words that's hard to translate directly into English. It's a warm word that refers to people you share something with, like work, hobbies, goals, or even struggles. 仲間 aren't necessarily friends in the "get a coffee and chat" sense, but they're people with whom you've built a strong and special bond based on a shared experience or sense of purpose.
3241.reading_mnemonic:
You know the readings for both of these kanji. 仲 uses the same reading as always, and 間 uses the ま reading, which you learned with 間もなく. Since 間 has a few different readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember to use the ま one:

Think through all your companions in your life. Imagine one of them is your <reading>Ma</reading> (ま). She's on your pirate crew, and a pretty awesome pirate.

3242.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading since it's a single kanji, all alone, but this is the reading you learned with the kanji, so you should be okay and have a great relationship with this word going forward.

examples.en: Let's make up.

3243.meaning_mnemonic: 直り is the noun form of 直る, which you already know means "to be fixed." When a <kanji>relationship</kanji> is fixed, you get <vocabulary>reconciliation</vocabulary>. In other words, you're <vocabulary>making peace</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>making up</vocabulary> with someone. Good on you.
3243.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the kun'yomi readings. 仲 is the same as always, and 直り uses the reading from 直る. Nice and easy!

examples.en: I think they are just pretending to be intimate friends and they don't actually like each other.

examples.en: The other day, I received an email from a close friend who lives in Japan.

examples.en: Those kids are really good friends, aren't they?

3244.meaning_mnemonic:
When your <kanji>relationship</kanji> with someone is really <kanji>good</kanji>, you naturally become <vocabulary>good friend</vocabulary>s. You're always palling around together and acting <vocabulary>buddy-buddy</vocabulary>, so everyone can tell how close your friendship is.

仲良し describes close friends or people who get along really well. The word has a friendly, cute vibe and is often used for kids, families, or anyone with a warm bond.
3244.reading_mnemonic: Both the readings here are kun'yomi, which you already know. Just be careful with 良 — in 良い, it can be read よ or い, but in 良し it's always read as よ.

examples.en: Could we meet up? I wouldn't be able to convey my message over an email.

3245.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>transmit</kanji>, but 伝える is mostly used for "transmitting" information, feelings, or messages to someone else. So it means <vocabulary>to convey</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to tell</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to pass down</vocabulary>.

In technical contexts, 伝える can also mean <vocabulary>to transmit</vocabulary>, in the sense that copper transmits heat or air transmits sound.
3245.reading_mnemonic: You want <vocabulary>to convey</vocabulary> your knowledge to your apprentice, so you make them the best <reading>two</reading> <reading>ta</reading>cos (つた) you've ever made. They just wanted you <vocabulary>to tell</vocabulary> them the recipe, but you believe showing it is a better way <vocabulary>to pass down</vocabulary> that skill.

共同 is used when two or more people or groups do something together with a <vocabulary>shared</vocabulary> purpose or responsibility. 共同作業 (collaborative work) means you share tasks with others, for example, and 共同生活 (shared living) means living together with someone, whether it's a partner or a roommate.

3250.reading_mnemonic:

This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>become</kanji> so the vocab verb version would be <vocabulary>to become</vocabulary>.

3252.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

3254.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Every <vocabulary>old person</vocabulary> has <reading>roe</reading> <reading>jean</reading>s(ろうじん), a special pair of jeans smeared with roe that they wear when they go out on the town. Some elderly people have cod roe jeans, some have salmon roe jeans… But tofugu roe jeans (adorned with the roe of the lesser spotted tofugu) are the most fashionable of all.

You look down and very <vocabulary>low</vocabulary> to the ground is a man, looking up at you. Your friend is there too, but you don't know this little man. Your friend says "<reading>He coo'</reading>, he coo," referring to the low to the ground man.

examples.en: That drama show was the worst!

3259.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

3262.meaning_mnemonic: The の is there to indicate that it is the difference of something. For example this is like saying "the <vocabulary>separate</vocabulary> ______" or "the <vocabulary>different</vocabulary> _____" or "<vocabulary>another</vocabulary> ______". 別 by itself just means separate, different, or another.

examples.en: As long as there's coffee, I wouldn't mind going to any cafe in particular.

3263.meaning_mnemonic:
If someone asks if you want a <kanji>separate</kanji> knee (に), you'll say <vocabulary>not particularly</vocabulary>. I mean, you've never thought about it, but do you really need more knees? <vocabulary>Not really</vocabulary>...

In this first meaning, 別に is often used on its own, or with a negative verb or adjective, as in 別に長くない (not particularly long).

However, when 別に is used with a positive verb, it often simply means <vocabulary>separately</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>in addition to</vocabulary>. After all, when you have to do something separately, you have to do it in addition to something else. Like learning this meaning in addition to the first one. What a chore!
3263.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the reading you learned with the kanji. Well done!

examples.en: Koichi has become a changed man ever since he quit drinking.
examples.ja: コウイチはお酒をやめてから、すっかり別人になったね。

examples.en: I thought it was my friend Koichi when I called out to him, but it was a different person.

examples.en: Koichi used to diss AKB48 pretty often, but now he's a crazed AKB48 fan. It’s as though he's a different person.

3264.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>separate</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji> is someone who is different from who they were before. I saw you a year ago and you were someone else. Now you're a <vocabulary>different person</vocabulary>, in a good way! You're a <vocabulary>changed man</vocabulary>.

3265.meaning_mnemonic:
When you say <kanji>separate</kanji> <kanji>separate</kanji>, you're putting things off into their own areas. So 別々 means <vocabulary>separate</vocabulary>. 

Note that this word is typically used in reference to multiple separate items, as opposed to 別の, which refers to a single separate or different thing. It's also used a lot as an adverb with the particle に to mean "separately."
3265.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the べつ reading you know, twice.

3267.reading_mnemonic: What works so well? Your special <reading>key</reading> (き) that can unlock anyone and anything's potential. Imagine putting it into a key slot in someone's back. 3275.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>fate</kanji> <kanji>orders</kanji> are the orders you get from above. You are <vocabulary>order</vocabulary>ed and <vocabulary>command</vocabulary>ed to carry out said orders.

3276.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>ocean</kanji>/<kanji>sea</kanji> <kanji>coast</kanji> is the <vocabulary>seashore</vocabulary>. Then again, it could also be the <vocabulary>coast</vocabulary> as well.

examples.en: Thirty minutes later, Koichi finally released my hand.

examples.ja: この辺りに、犬を放してあそばせられるドッグランみたいなとこはありますか？

examples.en: Every time I let Fugu loose in the sea, he swims off and when I call him he doesn't listen. What should I do to teach him to not run away?
examples.ja: フグを海に放すといつも、泳いで逃げちゃって、私が呼んでも知らんぷりするの。どうすれば逃げないように教えることができるのかしら。

3277.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>release</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to release</vocabulary>, as in <vocabulary>to set free</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to let something go</vocabulary>.

放す often suggests that you've released something in a way that gives it freedom to move or go where it wants. Think of letting your dog run in the field — it's not just that you let go of the leash, but that the dog is now free to run around as it pleases.
3277.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You need <vocabulary>to release</vocabulary> your pet <reading>花</reading> (はな). It's a monstrous, carnivorous 花 that you keep in a cage in your backyard. You think it's super cute, but your neighbors say it scares them, so you need <vocabulary>to set free</vocabulary> your beloved 花. Hopefully it doesn't eat anyone on its way back to the wild.

examples.ja: 昔、一回だけ、テレビ画面にキスしたことがあるよ。

3279.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. むかし sounds like a kun'yomi reading, doesn't it? It's so long.

3280.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>electricity</kanji> <kanji>wave</kanji> is a wave of electricity going through the air. There are many words you can use to describe this, but the easiest one is <vocabulary>reception</vocabulary> (like the reception on your phone, for example).

Other more technical meanings are <vocabulary>radio wave</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>electromagnetic waves</vocabulary>. Which one you like is up to you, but reception is going to be the most common meaning on the street. Luckily people in Japan don't have AT&T, otherwise you'd hear this word a lot more…
3280.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The は from 波 rendakus to ぱ, so be careful. Maybe it's your <reading>pa</reading> who has bad reception every time you try to call him?

examples.en: Did you pour olive oil in my coke by any chance?

examples.ja: 高校生になったらアルバイトに全力を注ぎたいです。

examples.en: Can you pour a little more wine?
examples.ja: もう少しワインを注いでいただけますか？

3281.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>pour</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to pour</vocabulary>.
3281.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You are going <vocabulary>to pour</vocabulary> some <reading>sauce</reading> (そそ).

examples.en: I'm worried that he might be heading in a bad direction. I cautioned him, but he won't listen at all.

3282.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>pour</kanji> your <kanji>ideas</kanji> into something, you're thinking a lot about it. You're paying close <vocabulary>attention</vocabulary> and using <vocabulary>caution</vocabulary>. You'll see this on a lot of <vocabulary>warning</vocabulary> signs marking dangerous things in Japan, so be sure to pay attention to them!
3282.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

It's a formal <vocabulary>request</vocabulary> to get this new thing (imagine it being something you're excited about ordering right now, and imagine yourself ordering it by pouring writing onto an order form).
3283.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

3284.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This cactus is growing well.
examples.ja: このサボテン、元気に育ってるね。

examples.en: Love grew between the dog and Koichi.
examples.ja: いつの間にかその犬とコウイチの間には愛が育ちました。

3285.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>raise</kanji> so the verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to be raised</vocabulary>. 

P.S. This word is for when you are being raised, not when you are doing the raising of someone. That's <vocabulary>育てる</vocabulary>. You'll learn it later.
3285.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

When you were raised, you were raised completely on <reading>soda</reading> (そだ). That's all you drank. No water, no juice... just tons and tons of soda. Imagine this.

examples.en: Today, we are going to the education center.
examples.ja: 今日は教育センターに行きます。

examples.en: In Japan, you're obligated to receive elementary school education and junior high school education.
examples.ja: 日本では、小学校教育と中学校教育を受けなければなりません。

examples.en: Do you remember who said, "It is a thousand times better to have common sense without education than education without common sense?"
examples.ja: 「教育があって常識がないよりも、教育がなくて常識がある方がはるかによい。」って誰の言葉だっけ？

3286.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Teach</kanji> and <kanji>nurture</kanji>. That's what your <vocabulary>education</vocabulary> is supposed to do.
3286.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I volunteered for a year to pick up trash on the beach.
examples.ja: 海岸でゴミを拾うボランティアを一年間やりました。

examples.en: I just picked up a 500 yen coin on the sidewalk.
