examples.en: There was an abandoned sofa on the roadside and it looked still usable, so I picked it up.
examples.ja: 道端にソファを捨ててあったんだけど、まだ使えそうだったから、拾ってきたよ。

3287.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>pick up</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to pick something up</vocabulary>.
3287.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Nicely done!

examples.en: The compass arrow is pointing at the direction of North.
examples.ja: コンパスの矢が北の方向を指しています。

examples.en: In Japan, it's rude to point at people with your finger.
examples.ja: 人を指で指すのは、日本では失礼です。

examples.en: I haven't done my homework... What if the teacher points at me?
examples.ja: 宿題やってないよ、、。先生に指されたらどうしよう。

3288.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji means <kanji>finger</kanji>. So, if you "to finger" something, what are you doing? You're pointing. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to point</vocabulary>.
3288.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You are pointing at something in fear. It is a <reading>saw</reading> (さ). Thing is, you're pointing at this saw with a missing finger. It just cut off your finger and you're freaking out, trying to point with a bloody non-finger.

examples.en: You have such beautiful fingers.
examples.ja: 指がきれいですね。

examples.en: Why do we have five fingers and also five toes?
examples.ja: なんで手の指も足の指も五本なんだろう？

examples.en: I just had a sudden pain in my middle finger.
examples.ja: 突然中指が痛くなったんだけど。

3289.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are almost exactly the same. The only difference is that this word can mean <vocabulary>finger</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>toe</vocabulary>. What are toes but small, walking fingers?
3289.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: 

What do you use your <vocabulary>finger</vocabulary> for the most? For pointing, of course! Imagine going up to people and saying, "What will <reading>you be</reading> (ゆび) when you grow up?" Point your finger at the next person, "What will you be?" Keep going until you're just saying, "You be? You be?" with your finger out.

examples.en: Why do you extend your pinky when you drink from a glass?
examples.ja: なんでグラスで飲み物を飲む時に小指を立てるの？

examples.en: Ouch! I just hit my right pinky toe on the corner of the dresser.
examples.ja: いってぇー、そこのタンスの角に右足の小指ぶつけた。

examples.en: What happened? Your pinky finger is injured, isn't it?
examples.ja: どうしたの？小指、ケガしてるじゃん。

3290.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>small</kanji> <kanji>finger</kanji> is your <vocabulary>little finger</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>pinky finger</vocabulary>. Makes sense, but it's also used for the pinky on your feet. You know, your <vocabulary>pinky toe</vocabulary>.
3290.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings from both kanji, probably because it includes body parts. You know them both already, so now you know this too!

examples.en: The meeting place was designated by the client.
examples.ja: ミーティングの場所は、お客さまが指定しました。

examples.en: May I assign my own flight?
examples.ja: 自分でフライトを指定してもいいですか？

examples.en: This painting is designated as a national treasure in Japan.
examples.ja: この絵は日本に国宝に指定されてます。

3291.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>determine</kanji> and use your <kanji>finger</kanji> to point at someone or something, you're going <vocabulary>to appoint</vocabulary> them. Just imagine yourself determining who's the best for the job then pointing with your finger. That is who you will appoint. The する on the end makes it a verb, so <vocabulary>指定</vocabulary> would be "appointment" or "designation" or something along those lines. Cool how する works.
3291.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I put butter in udon to give it a western-style twist.
examples.ja: バターを入れて、うどんを洋風にアレンジしました。

examples.en: Oh, is it a song from a Japanese artist? It sounded kind of like a western-style melody.
examples.ja: えっ、日本のアーティストの曲なの？なんだか洋風なメロディだね。

examples.en: My house is entirely furnished in the Western style, so there are no tatami mats.
examples.ja: 私の家は、家具を全て洋風に揃えているので、畳はありません。

3292.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 風 can mean "style" as in 和風? Well, this is now <kanji>Western style</kanji> <kanji>style</kanji>, more simply put as <vocabulary>Western style</vocabulary>.

洋風 is used to describe things with a Western look or influence, like 洋風の部屋 (Western-style room) or 洋風スープ (Western-style soup).
3292.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It's important to check the size before buying clothes.
examples.ja: 洋服を買う前にサイズをチェックをするのは大切です。

examples.en: Should I wear Japanese clothes for today's date? Or should I wear regular clothes?
examples.ja: 今日のデートは和服にしようかな？洋服にしようかな？

examples.en: You should get dressed really quickly or you’ll be late for school.
examples.ja: 早く洋服を着ないと、学校に遅れるわよ。

3293.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Western style</kanji> <kanji>clothes</kanji> is just <vocabulary>Western clothing</vocabulary> (or <vocabulary>Western style clothes</vocabulary>). But nowadays, because Japanese people wear Western clothing all the time, we use it to just mean <vocabulary>clothes</vocabulary>. We're talking things that aren't kimonos, etc.
3293.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Can I get to the Pacific Ocean from here?
examples.ja: ここから太平洋まで車で行けますか？

examples.en: After all, fish from the Pacific Ocean taste good.
examples.ja: 太平洋の魚はやっぱり味が良いんだよな。

examples.en: The Pacific Ocean is shiny and beautiful.
examples.ja: 太平洋の海はキラキラしてて綺麗ですね。

3294.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>fat</kanji> <kanji>peace</kanji> <kanji>ocean</kanji> is the <vocabulary>Pacific Ocean</vocabulary>. The Japanese language thinks this ocean is peaceful, just like English does (the word 太平 actually means "peace").

Note that we're using the alternative meaning of 洋 here! If you didn't learn that with the kanji, just imagine that to get to Western-style places you need to cross the ocean from Japan.
3294.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You've seen the たい reading for 太 in 太陽, but here's a mnemonic refresher for it just in case:

When you cross the <vocabulary>Pacific Ocean</vocabulary>, you must wear a <reading>tie</reading> (たい). Your tie is uncomfortably tight as you watch the Pacific slide by under you. But you want to look your best on this momentous journey, don't you? Doesn't matter if you're going by boat or plane, you wear a tie when you cross the Pacific.

examples.en: I ate a Neapolitan Spaghetti at the Western food restaurant.
examples.ja: 洋食レストランでナポリタンスパゲティを食べました。

examples.en: I'm working part-time at a so-called old fashioned Western family restaurant.
examples.ja: いわゆる昔ながらの洋食屋さんで、バイトをしています。

examples.en: Oh, did you eat the western-style lunch set at that restaurant? Hahaha. No wonder you still feel full.
examples.ja: ええっ！あそこのレストランで洋食ランチセットを食べたの？ははは。どおりでまだお腹がいっぱいなはずだわ。

3295.meaning_mnemonic: Western-style eats just means Western-style food. You can call this Western food for short, but in Japan it actually refers to a Japanese genre of food inspired by European dishes. Think omurice (omelette rice) or Napolitan pasta (spaghetti and ketchup). You know, Western-style food.
3295.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This house has three small western style rooms.
examples.ja: この家には小さな洋室が三つあります。

examples.en: There are beds and desks in the western style room.
examples.ja: 洋室にはベッドとデスクがあります。

examples.en: My room is a six-tatami-sized, western style room, with my favorite shade of light blue on the walls.
examples.ja: 私の部屋は六畳の洋室で、壁の色は私の好きな水色です。

3296.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>Western style</kanji> <kanji>room</kanji> is a <vocabulary>Western style room</vocabulary>. We're talking something that's not a tatami mat filled room. Good to know this word if you're staying in hotels or ryokans and prefer not to sleep on a futon, etc.
3296.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Do you think the gods exist somewhere?
examples.ja: 神はどこかにいると思いますか？

examples.en: I wish there were a call center where I could consult with God.
examples.ja: 神に相談できるコールセンターがあったら良いのに。

examples.en: God may be able to walk on water, but I can swim in the meadow.
examples.ja: 神様は水の上を歩けるかもしれないけど、俺は草地の上を泳ぐことができるんだぜ。

3297.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3297.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

Do you know the word "Kamikaze"? Also, do you remember the word 風 from a previous level? Kamikaze means "divine winds" or "godly winds." If you know the word "Kamikaze" you can apply it to this single word, that means "god" or "gods." Use your prior knowledge to remember this reading.

examples.en: Shinto doesn't really have specific teachings.
examples.ja: 神道には特に教えがないんですよ。

examples.en: Koichi just kept talking about Shinto.
examples.ja: コウイチは、ひたすら神道について語った。

examples.en: Why doesn’t Shinto have an absolute God?
examples.ja: どうして神道には絶対的な神がいないのですか。

3298.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>way</kanji>/<kanji>road</kanji> of the <kanji>god</kanji>(s) is, as you can probably guess, a big Japanese religion. There's two, and I'll give you a hint, this one isn't Buddhism (that would probably have the kanji for Buddha in it, no?). So what's the other big one? It's <vocabulary>Shinto</vocabulary>. If you're having trouble remembering this because you've never heard of it before, skip to the reading. The reading will help.
3298.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a bit wonky. 神 should be no problem. 道 on the other hand is almost the one you learned (どう) but now it's とう for some reason. Perhaps the gods took away the dakuten to make it とう, who knows. All I know is that it's best not to question said gods. If you already know of Shinto in English, though, this reading should be really easy. If you don't, perhaps you can use this reading to help you to remember Shinto the religion.

examples.en: There are lots of small shrines around here.
examples.ja: この辺は小さい神社が多いですね。

examples.en: Have you ever drawn a fortune slip at a shrine?
examples.ja: 神社でおみくじを引いたことはありますか？

examples.en: Many influencers are taking selfies at shrines these days.
examples.ja: 最近は神社で自撮りするインフルエンサーが多いんですよ。

3299.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>God</kanji> <kanji>company</kanji>... think of this as "what 'company' does the god's work?" Well, the answer to that is a shrine, probably. In this case a <vocabulary>Shinto shrine</vocabulary> because of the しん in 神.
3299.reading_mnemonic: But wait! 神 is read じん in this word for some reason. Darn those gods, always messing around, adding dakuten. Maybe this will help, though: Imagine yourself at a Shinto shrine. You are praying to the gods, asking for food. Out from the sky rains <reading>ginger</reading> (じんじゃ). You are pelted with it and not sure if you should be happy or upset.

examples.en: I sent a LINE message to Koichi and he replied to me in a second lol.
examples.ja: コウイチにラインしたら秒で返事きたw

examples.en: When I go to bed, I usually fall asleep in three seconds.
examples.ja: 大体いつも、ふとんに入ったら三秒でねてる。

examples.en: Your pronunciation can reach native-level in just twelve seconds.
examples.ja: あなたの発音をたったの十二秒でネイティブレベルにしてみせますよ。

3300.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well - that is the unit of time, <vocabulary>second</vocabulary>.
3300.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as you learned with the kanji. It's presumably because it's usually attached to other things, like numbers, making it act more like a jukugo word would. Anyway, you should only need a <vocabulary>second</vocabulary> to learn this reading, since you should already know it.

examples.en: I can't accept such a high-class gift.
examples.ja: こんな高級なプレゼントもらえません。

examples.en: This is a famous high-end tea in China.
examples.ja: これは中国で有名な高級茶なんですよ。

examples.en: That luxury restaurant is exclusive for VIPs, and to enter, you'll need an invitation or a referral.
examples.ja: あの高級レストランはVIP専用で、入店には招待状か紹介状が必要なんだって。

3301.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>tall</kanji> <kanji>grade</kanji> item is really just a <vocabulary>high grade</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>high-class</vocabulary> item.
3301.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'm moving to the intermediate level class from the beginner level class next week.
examples.ja: 来週、初級から中級にレベルが上がります。

examples.en: This course is divided into three levels: beginner, intermediate and advanced.
examples.ja: このコースは、初級、中級、上級の三つのレベルに分かれています。

examples.en: My Japanese is still at an elementary level, but I’m working hard at it.
examples.ja: 私の日本語はまだ初級レベルですが、一生懸命勉強しています。

3302.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>first</kanji> <kanji>level</kanji> of something is the <vocabulary>beginner level</vocabulary>. Compare this to 中級 and 上級 (vocab from this level) to get a fuller understanding.
3302.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What kind of level is an intermediate level?
examples.ja: 中級とは、どういったレベルですか？

examples.en: I want to join the intermediate Japanese class.
examples.ja: 中級の日本語クラスに入りたいんです。

examples.en: There are only a few people who are intermediate English speakers at this company.
examples.ja: この会社には英語が中級の人たちは少ない。

3303.meaning_mnemonic: Something at the <kanji>middle</kanji> <kanji>level</kanji> or <kanji>grade</kanji> is at an <vocabulary>intermediate level</vocabulary>.
3303.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I can't follow the advanced level class.
examples.ja: どうしても上級クラスについていけません。

examples.en: Koichi is a senior student at my school.
examples.ja: コウイチは私の学校の上級生です。

examples.en: Some non-native speakers speak English at a native or advanced level, while others do not.
examples.ja: 英語が母国語でない人で、ネイティブレベルや上級の英語を話す人もいれば、そうでない人もいます。

3304.meaning_mnemonic: When you are at an <kanji>above</kanji> <kanji>level</kanji>, you are at an <vocabulary>advanced level</vocabulary>. This is referring to things like proficiency in Japanese, or things like that.
3304.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I am not good at following women.
examples.ja: 女の人を追うのが下手なんですよ。

examples.en: Koichi is always following the latest fashion trends.
examples.ja: コウイチは、いつも最新のファッショントレンドを追っている。

examples.en: I will keep following my dreams, no matter how hard it gets.
examples.ja: どんなに大変でも、私は自分の夢を追い続けるつもりなの。

3305.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>follow</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to follow</vocabulary> (it's also <vocabulary>to chase</vocabulary>, because when you follow something you are chasing it too).
3305.reading_mnemonic: You've learned this reading already, so you should know how to read this word!

examples.en: Dad always loses his battles with Mom.
examples.ja: 父は、いつも母との戦いに負ける。

examples.en: I don't like conflicts.
examples.ja: 戦いはきらいです。

examples.en: Stop fighting unnecessary battles!
examples.ja: ムダな戦いはやめろ！

examples.en: He went straight for a Big Mac after the bloody fight.
examples.ja: 彼は血みどろの戦いの後、そのままビッグマックを食べに行った。

3306.meaning_mnemonic: Don't let this word confuse you. It may end in い, but it's not an adjective, it's a noun. There are no rules in war, after all. This word describes what happens in <kanji>war</kanji>. Those things are <vocabulary>battle</vocabulary>s, <vocabulary>fight</vocabulary>s, and <vocabulary>conflict</vocabulary>s.
3306.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

In a fierce <vocabulary>battle</vocabulary>, there's always a lot of collateral damage. One of the things that gets destroyed is your car. But you can't do anything about it, it's battle time! So you wave goodbye to your car saying, "<reading>Ta-ta ca</reading>r (たたか)!" as you punch some jerk in the face.

3310.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You really have <vocabulary>to compete</vocabulary> for <reading>key so</reading>ap (きそ). These days everyone wants their keys as clean as possible, and the special key soap they use is pretty hard to come by. Whenever it's in stock again people try to compete over it. Just imagine all those shoppers fighting over some key soap…

examples.en: I think that idea is very good!

3311.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>good</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>good</vocabulary>.
3311.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember:

A <vocabulary>good</vocabulary> way to pass the time is with a <reading>yo</reading>-yo (よ). But it better be a good yo-yo. A bad one will just fall apart.

Note that よい is a more formal or literary way of saying "good," the more common one being いい. To distinguish the different readings, the latter version is usually written in just kana too!

examples.en: Do you think you'll be on good terms with Satomi?
examples.ja: さとみちゃんとは、仲良くなれそう？

3312.meaning_mnemonic: When the <kanji>relationship</kanji> is <kanji>good</kanji>, that means you're <vocabulary>friendly</vocabulary> with that person. You're also on <vocabulary>good terms</vocabulary>.

3315.meaning_mnemonic:
*Ahem.* This is the <kanji>convenience</kanji> <kanji>facility</kanji>. What place above all others should be convenient to get to? You know, just in case? That would be the <vocabulary>restroom</vocabulary>. You might also call it the <vocabulary>bathroom</vocabulary>, the <vocabulary>toilet</vocabulary>, the lavatory, or the facilities.

This word is casual and can often sound gruff, so you won't normally see it on official signs or hear it in polite conversation. It's worth knowing so you can understand it in casual speaking and writing though.

examples.ja: なんで休日も働かなきゃいけないの？

examples.en: Do you have any opinions about this plan?

3317.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>idea</kanji> you <kanji>see</kanji> in your head is your <vocabulary>opinion</vocabulary>. As the dude once said... "That's just, like, your 意見, man."
3317.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is all on'yomi, meaning 意 is just fine. 見's on'yomi (けん) is a reading you didn't learn with the kanji because it's so much less useful, but you do have to know it here. You've seen it with 発見 a couple levels ago, so that should help. Still, here's a mnemonic to help you remember:

In this case, just think about how <reading>Ken</reading> the samurai has an <vocabulary>opinion</vocabulary> on everything. Ken is such a know-it-all, and you're better off agreeing with his opinions. He's a samurai after all!

3326.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

This is a magic <vocabulary>root</vocabulary> that turns you into a horse. You take a bite and let out a loud <reading>neigh</reading> (ね)!

examples.en: My father and I have fundamentally the same way of thinking.
examples.ja: 私も父も根本の考え方は同じです。

examples.en: I want to relearn English from the ground up.

3329.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>root</kanji> <kanji>origin</kanji> is the <vocabulary>root</vocabulary> of something. Possibly even more root than root, but we'll stick with root.

根本 generally refers to the root cause or fundamental <vocabulary>basis</vocabulary> of something, like "the root of the problem" or "the fundamental principle."
3329.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Careful, 本 is ぽん, which is a weird rendaku. In case you need help with this rendaku reading, here's a mnemonic:

What's the <vocabulary>root</vocabulary> cause of your unhappiness? A <reading>pon</reading>y (ぽん). Getting a pony was basically the <vocabulary>basis</vocabulary> of all your childhood dreams. Unfortunately your parents couldn't afford a pony, so now you're in therapy. Oh yes, you still think of that pony, down there at the root of all your many, many issues…

examples.en: There are many birds on the roof.
examples.ja: 屋根の上にたくさんの鳥が止まっています。

examples.en: I'm happy to have a life with a roof and food.

examples.en: Please be careful as the snow may fall from the roof.

examples.en: Keep studying Japanese persistently and you’ll be fluent someday.

3331.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>root</kanji> of your <kanji>energy</kanji>. 3368.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

球 has a slightly technical sound and highlights the sphere shape of the object you're talking about. It's most commonly used to refer to <vocabulary>sports ball</vocabulary>s (as a more formal alternative to ボール).
3368.reading_mnemonic:
This word is made up of a single kanji, so it should use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You see a <vocabulary>sphere</vocabulary> in <reading>Tama</reading>ra's (たま) hand. You're not totally sure what it is, but it's really spherical. Maybe it's some kind of <vocabulary>sports ball</vocabulary>. Remember Tamara, the local ball girl? It would totally make sense for Tamara to be holding either a sphere or a sports ball, since that's kind of all she does.

You might notice 球 has the same reading as the vocab word 玉. Their meanings are kind of similar too, so this reading should be a bit easier to remember!

3385.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Touch something that's warm... too warm! You pull your hand back and go "<reading>AH ta-ta!</reading> (あたた). People make this noise when they touch something that's hot, I hear. It's almost like saying "hot hot hot" while dropping the "h" sound.

People often pronounce this as あったかい, especially in casual, spoken Japanese. The "correct" reading is still あたたかい though, so keep that in mind when you're trying to type the kanji or taking an important test!

examples.en: I think I left my passport in the car I rented at the airport.
examples.ja: 空港で借りた車の中に、パスポートを忘れた気がする。

3388.meaning_mnemonic: Put aside your steampunk blimp fantasies for a moment. A <kanji>sky</kanji> <kanji>harbor</kanji> is an <vocabulary>airport</vocabulary>, nothing more.
3388.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Tea ceremony is an important part of Japanese culture.
examples.ja: 茶の湯は日本の文化の大切な一部です。

examples.en: I'm looking for a shop where I can buy tools for tea ceremonies.
examples.ja: 茶の湯の道具が買えるお店をさがしています。

examples.en: In the world of tea ceremonies there is a saying, "Ichi-go ichi-e," which means "to treasure every encounter." This saying was also used as the subtitle for Japan’s release of Forrest Gump.
examples.ja: 茶の湯の世界には、「一つ一つの出会いを大切に」という意味の「一期一会」という言葉があります。この言葉は、映画「フォレスト・ガンプ」の副タイトルとしても使われました。

3389.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>hot water</kanji> of <kanji>tea</kanji>. That is part of the ceremony that goes into the <vocabulary>tea ceremony</vocabulary>.
3389.reading_mnemonic: The readings are both the readings you learned with the kanji. Now you can spend a little more time drinking tea at a tea ceremony and a little less time trying to remember kanji readings.

examples.en: Steam is coming out of the kettle.
examples.ja: ケトルから湯気が出てるよ。

examples.en: Be careful of the steam.
examples.ja: 湯気に気を付けてね。

examples.en: To make good sushi rice, using a paddle, you must mix vinegar into steaming hot, freshly cooked rice.
examples.ja: 美味しい寿司飯を作るには、しゃもじを使って、湯気が立つ炊きたての熱いごはんに酢を混ぜる必要があります。

3390.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Hot water</kanji>'s <kanji>energy</kanji> isn't the hot water itself, it's what comes out of it (when it's boiling, for example). This is the <vocabulary>steam</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>vapor</vocabulary>.
3390.reading_mnemonic:
The ゆ part of the reading makes sense. The げ part for 気 is a bit of an exception, so here's a mnemonic to help with that:

No creature likes <vocabulary>steam</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>vapor</vocabulary> more than <reading>ge</reading>ckos (げ). Geckos live in hot places, so wherever you see steam, you'll be sure to see at least one gecko nearby, if you look hard enough.

examples.en: It's fun to climb on a tree.
examples.ja: 木の上に登るのは楽しいです。

examples.en: Do not wear jeans when climbing a mountain.
examples.ja: 山を登るときは、ジーパンをはかないで下さいね。

examples.en: A dream of mine is to climb Mt. Fuji at least once in my lifetime.
examples.ja: 一生の内、少なくとも一度は富士山に登ることが夢なんです。

3391.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>climb</kanji> so the verb vocab version would be <vocabulary>to climb</vocabulary> (or <vocabulary>to ascend</vocabulary>), if that's the kind of thing you're into.
3391.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. This has the same reading as 上る which you learned all that time ago in Level 1. If you can remember that, you can remember this one!

examples.en: Mountain climbing is fun.
examples.ja: 登山は楽しいです。

examples.en: My favorite part of mountain climbing is eating rice balls on the mountain.
examples.ja: 登山の楽しみは山で食べるおにぎりです。

examples.en: "How about we go mountain climbing?" "Well I don’t know about that."
examples.ja: 「登山に行くってのはどう？」「さあ、どうしようかなあ。」

3392.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Note this uses the alternative と reading, not to be confused with とう (actually, very confusing, sorry!). Just imagine you cut your <reading>toe</reading> off with an ice pick while mountain climbing. You know it's a short と because your toe is now short. And さん becomes ざん thanks to our old friend rendaku.

examples.en: Maybe I should wear a coat today.
examples.ja: 今日はコートを着た方がいいかも。

examples.en: Have you ever almost gone out of the house without getting dressed?
examples.ja: 服を着ないで家を出そうになったことある？

examples.en: When I'm in a uniform, I feel refreshed.
examples.ja: 制服を着ると気持ちまで引き締まります。

3393.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>wear</kanji> so this word means <vocabulary>to wear</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to put on</vocabulary>.
3393.reading_mnemonic: What do you want <vocabulary>to wear</vocabulary> today? How about a dress made entirely of <reading>key</reading>s (き)? Feel the metal on your skin and the weight on your shoulders. It's not a comfortable thing to put on. Maybe just stick with wearing a single key around your neck next time.

examples.en: I've just arrived at Narita Airport.
examples.ja: 今、成田空港に着きました。

examples.en: Once you know your arrival time, message me on LINE again.
examples.ja: 着く時間が分かったら、またラインして。

examples.en: The train didn't arrive on time.
examples.ja: 電車が時間通りに着かなかったんです。

3394.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. Remember how 着 can also mean <kanji>arrive</kanji>? This is the verb version of that meaning, so it means <vocabulary>to arrive</vocabulary>.
3394.reading_mnemonic: This uses a different kun'yomi reading than the one you just learned, but 着く (つく) has the same reading as 付く (to be attached). Because when arrive somewhere, it's like you're finally attached to your destination. If that connection doesn't quite click, here's another mnemonic: You wanted to arrive on time but you showed up late. How late were you? Two (つ) hours and two minutes late, to be exact.

examples.en: I like kimono.
examples.ja: 私は着物が好きです。

examples.en: Your kimono is lovely.
examples.ja: ステキなお着物ですね。

examples.en: I bought a kimono at the department store.
examples.ja: デパートで着物を買いました。

3395.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>thing</kanji>s you <kanji>wear</kanji> are your <vocabulary>clothes</vocabulary>. Oh, and Japanese clothes count too. We're talking <vocabulary>kimono</vocabulary>s. Way back when, these could just be called <vocabulary>clothes</vocabulary> because it's all people really wore, but nowadays we know they're specific to the stereotypical kimono you think of when you think "Japan."
3395.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a bit strange using kun'yomi readings. Luckily, we taught you these already, so go put on that kimono of yours and relax at the 温泉 for a bit.

examples.en: The underwear section is over there.
examples.ja: 下着売り場はあちらです。

examples.en: Lately, I often order underwear online.
examples.ja: 最近は、私は下着はネットで注文することが多いです。

examples.en: Oh, is that your special underwear? Looks cool!
examples.ja: おおっ、それって勝負下着？かっこいいね！

3396.meaning_mnemonic: The things you <kanji>wear</kanji> <kanji>below</kanji> your other clothes. That is your <vocabulary>underwear</vocabulary>. You do wear underwear, right?
3396.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this one is all kun'yomi vocab reading, but you should know these by now. 着 uses the reading you learned with 着る, but this word employs that pesky rendaku, so remember that き becomes ぎ here.

examples.en: Did you remember to bring your swimsuit?
examples.ja: 水着、ちゃんと持ってきた？

examples.en: That swimsuit is cute!
examples.ja: あの水着、かわいい！

examples.en: Oh, look. The swimsuits are on sale.
examples.ja: あ、見て。水着がセール中だよ。

3397.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this one is all kun'yomi vocab reading, but you should know these by now. 着 uses the reading you learned with the vocab word 着る, but this word employs that pesky rendaku, so remember that き becomes ぎ here.

examples.en: Isn't that skirt a bit too short?
examples.ja: そのスカート、ちょっと短すぎるんじゃない？

examples.en: The baby's short, flailing arms and legs are so cute!
examples.ja: 赤ちゃんが短い手足をバタバタさせてるのは本当にかわいい。

examples.en: Wah! I didn’t know your tail was shorter than mine.
examples.ja: わぁ！あんたの尻尾が私より短いなんて、知らなかったわ。

3398.meaning_mnemonic:
This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>short</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>short</vocabulary>.

This word is used to describe things that are short in length, not in height, like 短いトンネル (a short tunnel) or 短いスカート (a short skirt). It can also be used for things that are <vocabulary>brief</vocabulary>, like speeches, meetings, or messages.
3398.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Who has <vocabulary>short</vocabulary> hair and always wears shorts? It's <reading>Ms. Ca</reading>rr (みじか)! Everyone always recognizes Ms. Carr because she's the one with the short hair and shorts, no matter the weather. Ms. Carr, the ultimate short style icon!

examples.en: Where did you buy that tanto?
examples.ja: その短刀、どこで買ったの？

examples.en: My brother has a short sword.
examples.ja: 兄は短刀を持っています。

examples.en: A dagger can also be a weapon, so please carry them with caution.
examples.ja: 短刀は武器にもなりえるので注意して所持して下さいね。

3399.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>short</kanji> <kanji>sword</kanji> is the <vocabulary>short sword</vocabulary>. What's another word for a short sword? It's a <vocabulary>dagger</vocabulary>.
3399.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The short-term experiment is over.
examples.ja: 短期の実験が終わりました。

examples.en: What should I do in order to master hiragana and katakana in a short period of time?
examples.ja: 短期でひらがなとカタカナをマスターにするにはどうしたらいいですか？

examples.en: Maybe I should do a short term part-time job during spring break.
examples.ja: 春休みは短期のアルバイトをしようかな。

3400.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>short</kanji> <kanji>period of time</kanji> is the <vocabulary>short term</vocabulary>. You know not to think short term anyways, right? You're learning kanji, after all.
3400.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This is spring water.
examples.ja: これは泉の水です。

examples.en: There is a small spring in this city.
examples.ja: この街には小さな泉があります。

examples.en: Wow! You look beautiful! Did you go on a special diet? Or did you find the Fountain of Youth?
examples.ja: わぁ！すごく綺麗。何か特別なダイエットでもしたの？それとも、若返りの泉でも見つけたとか？

3401.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3401.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You're looking at a natural <vocabulary>spring</vocabulary> in the ground. Water is bubbling up, but then something changes. It looks a bit clogged... something is poking out. Then, all of a sudden, Mario flies out of the springs, falls in front of you and yells: "<reading>izumeeeee</reading> (いずみ), Mario!"

examples.en: The population of this area is only one person.
examples.ja: このエリアの人口は、たったの一人です。

examples.en: How large is the population around here?
examples.ja: こちらの人口はどのくらいですか？

examples.en: Apparently, about 70% of the population is shy.
examples.ja: 人口の70%くらいはシャイなんだって。

3402.meaning_mnemonic: The amount of people with mouths (that you have to feed) is the <vocabulary>population</vocabulary> that you have to feed.
3402.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Here at Tofugu, we measure <vocabulary>population</vocabulary> in <reading>jean</reading>s (じん). Each of us has just one pair of jeans, so if you know the jean count you know the population.

examples.en: This calf is still a little baby.
examples.ja: この子牛は、まだまだ小さい赤ちゃんです。

examples.en: A very healthy calf was born.
examples.ja: とても元気な子牛が生まれたよ。

examples.en: Dear Santa Claus, please bring me a calf as a present.
examples.ja: サンタさん、どうか子牛をプレゼントして下さい。

3403.meaning_mnemonic: You have a child cow. What do you think a child cow is? Probably a <vocabulary>calf</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>baby cow</vocabulary>.
3403.reading_mnemonic: Since you should know the readings of the words 子 and 牛 from the previous level, you should be able to read this word too even though it's using the kun'yomi readings for the kanji.

examples.en: This is an American stamp.
examples.ja: これはアメリカの切手です。

examples.en: Please give me two 40 yen stamps.
examples.ja: 四十円の切手を二つ下さい。

examples.en: My husband is a stamp collector.
examples.ja: 主人は切手コレクターです。

3404.meaning_mnemonic: This is a pretty old word, and in the olden days, everything was <kanji>cut</kanji> by <kanji>hand</kanji>, including <vocabulary>postage stamp</vocabulary>s. Having to cut thousands of <vocabulary>stamp</vocabulary>s each day by hand sounds incredibly laborious, so maybe that's why this word came to be associated specifically with stamps.
3404.reading_mnemonic: You'd think that the reading for this would consist of the on'yomi readings, but human body parts (hand) do funny things to words. In this case, it's the kun'yomi readings of both the kanji. You should know the kun'yomi reading for <kanji>切</kanji> and <kanji>手</kanji> from the previous levels, meaning you should be able to remember the reading for this word fairly easily. Watch out for the small っ, though.

examples.en: Today's game was a tie.
examples.ja: 今日のゲームは引き分けだった。

examples.en: Even when it actually was a draw, in my heart you're the best in Japan.
examples.ja: 本当は引き分けでも、私の心の中では、あなたが日本一です。

examples.en: A draw means that both teams had the same score.
examples.ja: 引き分けとは、両方のチームが同じ点だったということです。

3405.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>pull</kanji> something and "separate" (分ける) it, you are making everything even. In a game, this would be a <vocabulary>tie</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>draw</vocabulary>.
3405.reading_mnemonic: See the hiragana stuck in there? That's hinting that these use the kun'yomi readings. You learned the kun'yomi readings of these two kanji separately in the previous level, so if you know those you should know this word's reading as well.

examples.en: Last year, my mother died.
examples.ja: 去年、母が亡くなった。

examples.en: This is a flower for my friend who has passed away.
examples.ja: これは、亡くなった友人のための花です。

examples.en: My sister said "the lottery..." before her death.
examples.ja: 姉は、亡くなる前に「宝くじ...」と言いました。

3406.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. This word is actually two words put together, though. 亡く means "be deceased." なる means "to become." So put that all together and you have <vocabulary>to pass away</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to become deceased</vocabulary>. It's basically a polite way to say something died (死ぬ).
3406.reading_mnemonic:
To learn to read this kanji you have to remember the な part of 亡く, though our mnemonic will use the whole thing.

If you're about to become deceased, you are probably <reading>knock</reading>ing (なく) on death's door.

examples.en: Life is wonderful.
examples.ja: 人生ってすばらしい。

examples.en: Would you be my partner for life?
examples.ja: 人生のパートナーになってくれませんか？

examples.en: Life is like a banana, you never know how long it will be.
examples.ja: 人生はバナナのようなものさ。どれだけながいのかだれもしらないのさ。

3407.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji for <kanji>person</kanji> and <kanji>life</kanji> combined makes you think about human life. What is your <vocabulary>human life</vocabulary> like?
3407.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 and 生 both have two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you:

Your <vocabulary>life</vocabulary> boils down to just two things: <reading>jean</reading>s and a <reading>sa</reading>ber (じんせい). Your whole life, that's all you've ever needed, jeans and a saber. What are you, some kind of American pirate?

examples.en: A boy was born in 2018.
examples.ja: ２０１８年に男の子が生まれました。

examples.en: Congratulations, mom. It's a cute baby boy!
examples.ja: おめでとうございます、お母さん。かわいい男の子ですよ。

examples.en: That energetic boy will be a first-grader next year.
examples.ja: あの元気な男の子は来年一年生だ。

3408.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>man</kanji> <kanji>child</kanji> is a <vocabulary>boy</vocabulary>.

There's a の particle stuck in the middle of this word. Here it just means the noun before の is modifying the noun after. 

But for now, all you really have to remember is that 男の子 means "boy."
3408.reading_mnemonic: If you know the kun'yomi readings of both of these kanji you should be okay. You have two separate single-kanji words put together by a の. That's why it's the kun'yomi reading - they're separate.

examples.en: There was a caterpillar in the cabbage.
examples.ja: キャベツの中に毛虫がいた。

examples.en: It was not soil. It was caterpillar poop.
examples.ja: 土じゃなくて、毛虫のフンだった。

examples.en: This is Charlotte, my pet caterpillar.
examples.ja: ペットの毛虫のシャーロットです。

3409.meaning_mnemonic: When you think of a <kanji>fur</kanji> <kanji>insect</kanji> what do you think of? My mind immediately goes to a <vocabulary>caterpillar</vocabulary>. Imagine the furriest caterpillar you can and touch it. How does it feel? Furry?
3409.reading_mnemonic: The readings for this word are strange. Both use the kun'yomi readings - 虫 uses the reading you learned with the kanji, so that's easy. The 毛 part is like the vocab word 毛 you learned in the previous lesson.

examples.en: My father was born in a downtown area.
examples.ja: 父は下町で生まれた。

examples.en: I liked the atmosphere and people downtown.
examples.ja: 下町の空気や人々が気に入ったんです。

examples.en: A shitamachi is an old Japanese style of downtown.
examples.ja: 下町とは日本の古いスタイルのダウンタウンのことです。

3410.meaning_mnemonic: You have the <kanji>below</kanji> <kanji>town</kanji>. Does this sort of sound familiar? We have another word for it in English, but it's essentially the same thing: <vocabulary>downtown</vocabulary>. It isn't the downtown you might be used to though. In Japan, this is an old word that was used for the commercial districts literally, physically down (lower than) the main city. So picture an old, urban Japanese area!
3410.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is all kun'yomi despite being jukugo. Just think of sketchy things going on in the downtown, just like how there's sketchy kun'yomi readings for this word. You should know both the kun'yomi readings from the previous level, though, so if you do you know the reading for this word as well.

examples.en: Please enter your email address in all lowercase letters.
examples.ja: Eメールアドレスは、全て小文字で入力して下さい。

examples.en: Please use lowercase letters and uppercase letters in the password.
examples.ja: パスワードには小文字と大文字を入れて下さい。

examples.en: Is this a lowercase L? Or is it a capital letter I?
examples.ja: これは小文字のLですか？それとも大文字のIですか？

3411.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 文字 means "letters". So, what are "small letters"? That would be <vocabulary>lowercase letters</vocabulary>.
3411.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. However, 小 uses the kun'yomi reading and 文 is an exception here, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember this:

You learned your lowercase letters from <reading>子</reading> <reading>Moe</reading> (こも). That's right, after Moe taught you all the letters, his son 子 Moe taught you the lowercase ones. Such teamwork.

examples.en: Tanaka sensei is a man.
examples.ja: 田中先生は男の人です。

examples.en: There were not many boots for men.
examples.ja: 男の人用のブーツは中々ありませんでした。

examples.en: A romantic man tends to do a flash mob when proposing.
examples.ja: ロマンチックな男の人ってプロポーズでフラッシュモブやりがちよね。

3412.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>man</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji> is a <vocabulary>man</vocabulary>. 

There's a の particle stuck in the middle of this word. Here it just means the noun before の is modifying the noun after. 

Don't worry if that's hard to remember though. Just remember 男の人 means "man" (and that it's more polite than plain 男).
3412.reading_mnemonic: This word is actually two separate words combined with a particle. So, since you treat them like separate words, you read each of them with the kun'yomi readings (they are both single kanji words all alone). That being said, in level 4 you learned about the vocab readings for these separate words, so use that knowledge to remember the reading for this word as well.

examples.en: May it be a good year.
examples.ja: いい年になりますように。

examples.en: 2021 was the year of the Olympics.
examples.ja: ２０２１年はオリンピックの年でした。

examples.en: I haven't cut down a tree since that year.
examples.ja: あの年からずっと木を切ってないよ。

3413.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. You can also use this word to talk about someone's <vocabulary>age</vocabulary>.
3413.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

This <vocabulary>year</vocabulary> you plan on <reading>tossi</reading>ng (とし) out all your old stuff as a New Year's resolution. You pronounce it "toshing" though, because it has more vigor that way.

examples.en: Thanks for everything so far.
examples.ja: 今まで、ありがとう。

examples.en: What have you been up to so far?
examples.ja: 今まで何をしていたんですか。

examples.en: What Koichi has been saying until now was true.
examples.ja: 今までコウイチが言ってたことは本当だった。

3414.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 今 means now. What you probably don't know is that まで means "until." So, this word means <vocabulary>until now</vocabulary>.
3414.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the kun'yomi reading which you learned previously when you learned the vocab word 今. You can tell this is a kun'yomi reading because it has hiragana attached. So if you know that, you should be able to read this word as well.

examples.en: November and December are winter vacation.
examples.ja: 十一月と十二月は、冬休みです。

examples.en: There are no big plans during winter vacation.
examples.ja: 冬休みには、大したプランはありません。

examples.en: Every year during winter vacation, I go to Mexico.
examples.ja: 冬休みは毎年、メキシコに行きます。

3415.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>winter</kanji> <kanji>rest</kanji>! Wait, nobody calls it that. This is a <vocabulary>winter holiday</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>winter break</vocabulary>.
3415.reading_mnemonic: The readings for these are both the kun'yomi readings. Hopefully you learned them when you were doing vocab in the previous levels so that all you have to do now is combine the two separate words into one bigger word. Please don't take a winter break until you figure this word out.

examples.en: Please give me some pink wool.
examples.ja: ピンク色の毛糸を下さい。

examples.en: Grandma gave me a wool blanket she made herself.
examples.ja: おばあちゃんが自分で作った毛糸のブランケットをくれました。

examples.en: These jeans are actually made of wool.
examples.ja: このジーンズ、本当は毛糸でできています。

3416.meaning_mnemonic: When you have <kanji>fur</kanji> <kanji>string</kanji> (aka string made of fur) what do you think of? Hopefully <vocabulary>wool yarn</vocabulary>.
3416.reading_mnemonic: The readings for these kanji are the kun'yomi readings. With 毛 you should have learned this reading via the vocab word in the previous level. With 糸 it's actually the main reading for the kanji, so you should already know it.

examples.en: I'm going to the supermarket right now.
examples.ja: 今すぐスーパーにいってきます。

examples.en: Watch the news on TV right now!
examples.ja: 今すぐテレビのニュース見て！

examples.en: I'm going to come pick you up on a private jet right now.
examples.ja: 今すぐプライベートジェットで、むかえに行くよ。

3417.meaning_mnemonic: You'll have to learn this word in two parts. You already know the meaning of 今 because of the kanji, which means "now." The すぐ part, however, is a new word, meaning "soon." すぐ and "soon" even start with a similar sound, so maybe that can help you remember this! If you put 今 and すぐ together, you get "now soon." Put in better English, that's <vocabulary>at once</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>right now</vocabulary>.
3417.reading_mnemonic: Since you already know the vocab word 今 (read いま), you should be able to read this word as well.

examples.en: I was finally able to pass JLPT N1.
examples.ja: やっとJLPTN1にごうかくすることが出来ました。

examples.en: Dinner's ready!
examples.ja: ディナーが出来たよ。

examples.en: Mochi are made from rice.
examples.ja: もちは米から出来る。

3418.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>exit</kanji> and <kanji>come</kanji>, apparently it means <vocabulary>to be able to do</vocabulary>. I think of it like you're leaving a location (出) to do a task and then you come (来る) back after you did it. Perhaps you were waiting in a room training like someone from Dragonball. When you leave the room, you are ready to fight the enemy and win. You train in that room <vocabulary>to be able to do</vocabulary> whatever you need to do, and only leave and come back alive because you were able to do it.

This verb is really common and it has a wide range of meanings. It can also mean things like <vocabulary>to be ready</vocabulary>, for example a meal, and <vocabulary>to be made</vocabulary>, for example when saying what something is made from. It's commonly written in hiragana, but you'll see the kanji version too!
3418.reading_mnemonic: The readings are a bit strange. They're both kun'yomi readings, where 出 is で and 来る is きる. This is different from the reading you originally learned with 来る (くる), though, so be careful. If you can remember that and remember the kun'yomi readings from the previous vocab, you should be able to learn this one's reading as well.

examples.en: How do you say "thanks" in the dialect of this area?
examples.ja: このエリアの方言で「ありがとう」は何と言いますか？

examples.en: In this country, dialects are cherished.
examples.ja: この国では方言がとても大切にされています。

examples.en: Learning Japanese dialects is valuing Japanese culture.
examples.ja: 日本の方言を学ぶことは、日本文化を大切にすることです。

3419.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>way</kanji> you <kanji>say</kanji> things is your <vocabulary>dialect</vocabulary>. It's an entire "way" of speaking. 

You can even think of the  方 as being a "direction." If you go far enough in different directions in a country, you'll discover different regional dialects.
3419.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: This is my younger sister's doll.
examples.ja: これは私の妹の人形です。

examples.en: When I was little, I collected used dolls.
examples.ja: 小さい時、中古の人形をコレクションしていました。

examples.en: The girl cherishes all her dolls — ​​Barbie doll, Mel-chan doll, and Rika-chan doll — as if they're her own children.
examples.ja: その女の子は、バービー人形、メルちゃん人形、リカちゃん人形、全ての人形を自分の子のように大切にしています。

3420.meaning_mnemonic: Something that is <kanji>person</kanji> <kanji>shape</kanji>d that isn't a person? That has to be some kind of <vocabulary>doll</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>puppet</vocabulary>.
3420.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, and the reading of 形 is a bit of an oddball, here's a mnemonic to help you:

Did you know that all <vocabulary>doll</vocabulary>s at <reading>Nin</reading>tendo are made out of <reading>gyo</reading>za dumplings (にんぎょう)? They'll also regularly try to get you to eat them... Mmmm, gyoza dolls. Don't be afraid to take a bite!

examples.en: Is rucksack a foreign word?
examples.ja: リュックサックは、外来語ですか？

examples.en: In fact, "ikura" is a loanword from Russia.
examples.ja: 実は、「イクラ」は、ロシアからの外来語なんです。

examples.en: In present day Chinese, many Japanese words are used as loanwords.
examples.ja: 今の中国語では、たくさんの日本語が外来語として使われています。

examples.en: In Japan, we often use foreign words. Foreign words are becoming so much a part of Japanese culture that sometimes Japanese and foreign words are difficult to tell apart.
examples.ja: 日本では外来語を使う事が多いです。たまに日本語と外来語が見分けられないほど、外来語は日本文化の一部になりつつあります。

3421.meaning_mnemonic: You know the word 外来 to mean "imported." So, combine that with the kanji for <kanji>language</kanji> and you have an imported word, aka a <vocabulary>borrowed word</vocabulary>. There are a lot of these in Japanese, which makes this word important. Almost everything in katakana is a 外来語, in fact.
3421.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This table was handmade by Hayashi.
examples.ja: このテーブルは、林さんの手作りです。

examples.en: A friend gave me a handmade gift.
examples.ja: 友人が手作りのプレゼントをくれました。

examples.en: Handmade pasta is popular in this restaurant.
examples.ja: このレストランでは手作りのパスタが人気です。

3422.reading_mnemonic: The readings for these kanji are the kun'yomi readings. Just think of this word as two separate words put together (手 and 作る). The る in 作る gets changed to り because it's an adjective, and the つ in つくり gets changed to づ because of the way the words are combined with each other. You should know most of the reading that is in this word, though it will probably take a little bit of thinking to sort out the little changes in those readings.

examples.en: Tokyo is a big town.
examples.ja: 東京は大きい町です。

examples.en: You can see the Tokyo Tower from my office.
examples.ja: 私の会社から東京タワーは見えますよ。

examples.en: I'm going from Hawaii to Tokyo.
examples.ja: ハワイから東京に行きます。

3423.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>East</kanji> <kanji>capital</kanji> in Japan is <vocabulary>Tokyo</vocabulary>. If you look on a map and compare it to Kyoto (the old capital), you'll see it lies to the east. That's why this is the east capital, Tokyo.
3423.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You didn't learn the on'yomi for 東 (とう) with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help:

How do you know you've made it to <vocabulary>Tokyo</vocabulary>? The station platform signs will say 東京 — <reading>とう</reading>きょう — Tokyo. Just look for those とうきょう signs if you're headed for the east capital.

examples.en: Red wine goes well with beef.
examples.ja: 牛肉には赤ワインが合います。

examples.en: Is this the right phone number?
examples.ja: この電話番号で合ってますか？

examples.en: Indian cuisine in America is altered quite a bit from how it’s prepared in India to suit American tastes.
examples.ja: アメリカのインド料理は、アメリカ人の口に合うよう、実際のインドでの調理方法とはかなり違った方法で作られている。

3424.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>suit</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to suit</vocabulary>. 

This word also means <vocabulary>to come together</vocabulary> as well. Presumably when something suits something else, it comes together with it flawlessly. That's why this word also has this other meaning (and it will be important for future vocab as well).
3424.reading_mnemonic: You want to find a pet <vocabulary>to suit</vocabulary> your personal style, so you get matched with an <reading>a</reading>ardvark (あ). An aardvark will match the ant mounds you use for chairs and couches, it's the perfect match.

examples.en: There is a little bit of wind today.
examples.ja: 今日は、少し風がありますね。

examples.en: Wind is blowing towards south.
examples.ja: 南向きの風がふいています。

examples.en: The wind is strong today because the typhoon is coming nearby.
examples.ja: 今日は、台風が近くに来ているせいで、風が強いです。

3425.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3425.reading_mnemonic: Do you know the word "kamikaze" from WWII history? Well, it means "divine wind." The "kaze" part is the wind part, and this word uses the same reading, making it <reading>かぜ</reading> as well.

examples.en: Phonetic kanji often used for the slang "maji" is the letter for "serious."
examples.ja: 「マジ」というスラングによく使われる当て字は「本気」です。

examples.en: This book is a bit confusing because it uses a lot of ateji.
examples.ja: この本は、当て字を多く使用しているため、少し分かりにくいです。

examples.en: Japanese ateji are difficult for foreigners to understand.
examples.ja: 日本語の当て字は、外国人にとって分かりにくいです。

examples.en: Just like 亜米利加 (amerika), there's also a way of ateji where kanji are selected solely for their sounds and the meaning is ignored.
examples.ja: 亜米利加 (アメリカ)のように、発音が同じ漢字を使う当て字の方法もありますよ。

3426.meaning_mnemonic:
当てる means "to guess" or "to hit", and 字 means <kanji>letter</kanji>. So these are guessed letters? Kind of, they're so-called <vocabulary>phonetic kanji</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>ateji</vocabulary>.

This refers to cases where kanji are used solely for their sound, but not their meaning. There are also some cases of ateji where kanji are used only for their meaning and not their sound, but this is less common.
3426.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the kun'yomi reading for 当て and the on'yomi reading for 字. You've seen 当てる in the past, so you should be able to read this portion as well. Combine the two together and you have yourself a nice reading.

examples.en: The panda ate one bamboo plant after another.
examples.ja: パンダが次々に竹を食べました。

examples.en: At the last meeting, ideas came up one after another.
examples.ja: 前回のミーティングでは次々にアイディアが出た。

examples.en: People with various hairstyles came to the restaurant in succession.
examples.ja: レストランには色々なヘアスタイルの人が次々に来ました。

3427.meaning_mnemonic:
When things happen in a <kanji>next</kanji>, <kanji>next</kanji> (next, next, next…) way, they happen <vocabulary>one after another</vocabulary>.

Imagine a factory line for item checking. The people there keep shouting "Next! Next!" because items come <vocabulary>in succession</vocabulary> without stopping!
3427.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the word 次 (so it's つぎ), but this time you do it twice. No strange rendaku or anything like that either, which makes everyone happier.

examples.en: What can you see on the other side of the mountains?
examples.ja: 山の向こうには何が見えますか？

examples.en: Let's buy two loaves of bread at the bakery on the other side of the road.
examples.ja: 道の向こうのベーカリーでパンを二斤買いましょう。

examples.en: When I go abroad, I'm inspired by the culture over there every time.
examples.ja: 海外に行くと、毎回向こうの文化にインスパイアされるんですよ。

3428.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 向 means <kanji>yonder</kanji>, and this is its noun version, meaning <vocabulary>over there</vocabulary>.

向こう is used when speaking generally about something distant from yourself, whether it's a place, as in 向こうの山 (the mountain <vocabulary>over that way</vocabulary>), or a person, as in 向こうの人 (the person on the <vocabulary>other side</vocabulary>). Sometimes, it can even be used for time, like 向こう一週間 (the next week ahead).
3428.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned that with 向く, but here's a mnemonic for you in case you forgot:

<vocabulary>Over there</vocabulary>, a cow is saying <reading>moo</reading> (む). It's way over there, though, so you can't see or hear it. Kinda makes you wonder: if a cow moos way over there and no one's around to listen, did it really moo at all?

examples.en: Turn right on this road and you'll find a convenience store.
examples.ja: この道を右に曲がると、コンビニがあります。

examples.en: I feel like my ankle is bent.
examples.ja: 足首が曲がっている気がするんです。

examples.en: Your mustard-colored necktie is a bit crooked.
examples.ja: そのマスタード色のネクタイ、ちょっと曲がってるよ。

3429.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means both music and bend. For this word, we're looking at "bend." So the verb 曲がる is to be bent. It's intransitive, so don't give it a direct object. Use it to say something gets bent or bends: a knee is bent, the road bends — that sort of thing. Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
3429.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You already learned this reading with 曲げる, so you should be good to go!

examples.en: Peru is one of the countries in South America.
examples.ja: ペルーは南米の国の一つです。

examples.en: When I was a student, I went to South America as a backpacker.
examples.ja: 学生時代に、バックパッカーとして南米に行きました。

examples.en: South America is by no means a part of the United States!
examples.ja: 南米は決して米国の一部ではありませんよ！

3430.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 米国 means "America" (the country)? The 米 kanji can actually be used for either of the American continents. In this word we have <kanji>south</kanji> combining with <kanji>America</kanji>, so it must mean… <vocabulary>South America</vocabulary>!
3430.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You haven't seen the 南 reading (なん), so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

In <vocabulary>South America</vocabulary> everyone eats <reading>naan</reading> (なん). You may be surprised, since naan isn't exactly considered South American food. But what is a flour tortilla, really? It's South American naan!

examples.en: This is a popular blockbuster in all of America.
examples.ja: これは、全米で人気の大作です。

examples.en: What is the number one song on the US hit chart now?
examples.ja: 今、全米ヒットチャートでナンバーワンの曲は何ですか？

examples.en: An interview offer came from a nationwide television station.
examples.ja: 全米のテレビ局から、インタビューのオファーが来た。

3431.meaning_mnemonic: Do you remember how 米国 can mean "America?" That 米 means America sometimes. So, when you see <kanji>all</kanji> <kanji>rice</kanji> (I mean, <kanji>America</kanji>), you can think of this word as meaning <vocabulary>All America</vocabulary> (sort of like how 全日本 means "All Japan.").
3431.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: As soon as you get out of the south exit, there is a tea shop.
examples.ja: 南口から出るとすぐにお茶の店があります。

examples.en: It seems that there will be a convenience store at the south exit next summer.
examples.ja: 来年の夏には南口にコンビニができるらしい。

examples.en: The bench at the south exit is a popular dating spot for grandmas and grandpas.
examples.ja: 南口のベンチは、おばあちゃんとおじいちゃんに人気のデートスポットです。

3432.meaning_mnemonic: After learning 北口, 西口, and 東口, it's time for round four! Yep, you guessed it, adding <kanji>south</kanji> to 口 makes this <vocabulary>south exit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>south entrance</vocabulary>.
3432.reading_mnemonic: Just like 北口 and the others, this also uses kun'yomi readings. And just like before, watch out for the rendaku that changes くち to ぐち!

examples.en: I wrote an essay from my summer memories.
examples.ja: 夏の思い出を作文にしました。

examples.en: Memories from when I was little are still precious.
examples.ja: 小さかった時の思い出は、今でも大切です。

examples.en: I'm going to say "goodbye" to memories with my former partner.
examples.ja: 元パートナーとの思い出に「さようなら」を言いたいと思います。

3433.meaning_mnemonic: Do you remember the word 思う? It means "to think." What you are <kanji>think</kanji>ing is <kanji>exit</kanji>ing—it's coming out of your head! You're recalling <vocabulary>a memory</vocabulary> or multiple <vocabulary>memories</vocabulary>.
3433.reading_mnemonic: The readings are both kun'yomi, but based off of previous experience with the two separate words that make up this word, you should be able to read it. Just remember that it's kun'yomi. One hint is the hiragana sticking out of the 思.

examples.en: Don't get any closer to the river!
examples.ja: それ以上、川に近づくな！

examples.en: This dog gets up and says "woof!" if an adult man approaches him.
examples.ja: この犬は、大人の男が近づくと、立ち上って「ワン！」と言います。

examples.en: Next week, a typhoon will be approaching Kyushu.
examples.ja: 来週、九州に台風が近づきます。

3434.meaning_mnemonic: Because this word ends with an う sound, you can tell it's probably a verb. The kanji portion means <kanji>near</kanji>. The verb version of that is <vocabulary>to draw near</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to get close</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to approach</vocabulary>. Essentially, the general idea is that you're getting closer to something. You're becoming more nearby. You're approaching.
3434.reading_mnemonic: There's hiragana attached to this kanji, which means it's probably the kun'yomi reading (and it is). You've seen the kun'yomi reading via the word 近い. So, as long as you know that word, you should be able to read this one as well.

examples.en: I sometimes remember the day when I was proposed to.
examples.ja: たまにプロポーズされた日のことを思い出す。

examples.en: I finally remembered the name of the psychology teacher.
examples.ja: やっと心理学の先生の名前を思い出した。

examples.en: Coming to this area reminds me of when I was small.
examples.ja: この辺りに来ると、小さかった時を思い出します。

3435.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 思う means "to think" and 出す means "to take out." So this is what happens when your brain takes a moment to think and pulls a memory out of storage. It means <vocabulary>to remember</vocabulary>!

You can shout 思い出した！when you recall your keys are in the fridge. (Again?!) You can also say 母を思い出します when something reminds you of your mom. In Japanese, you usually omit what reminded you of the memory because the important thing is the memory itself, filling your heart with touchy-feelies. Oh, mama!
3435.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is the kun'yomi readings. You should know the words 思う and 出す and their readings, so you should be able to read this word if you know those words.

examples.en: Most of the staff here are college students.
examples.ja: ここのスタッフは大体、大学生です。

examples.en: Many college students take a leave of absence from school.
examples.ja: 大学生は休学する人が多いです。

examples.en: Do you know the life of an American college student?
examples.ja: アメリカの大学生の生活を知ってますか？

3436.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 学生 means "student" and you know that 大学 means university/college. Combine the two and you have a <vocabulary>university student</vocabulary> / <vocabulary>college student</vocabulary>.
3436.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The teacher corrected my way of saying "Excuse me."
examples.ja: 先生が「すみません」の言い方を正してくれました。

examples.en: I think that way of speaking is rude.
examples.ja: その言い方は失礼だと思います。

examples.en: You will know where they're from by how they say "Thank you."
examples.ja: 「ありがとう」の言い方で、その人の生まれが分かります。

3437.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>say</kanji>ing <kanji>way</kanji> is… your <vocabulary>way of saying</vocabulary>! This refers to the words you use and how you phrase things, as well as how you say it.
3437.reading_mnemonic:
This uses the kun'yomi readings from the vocab words 言う and 方. You might be more used to the on'yomi for 方 though, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember the kun'yomi (かた).

Your <vocabulary>way of saying</vocabulary> things is to <reading>cata</reading>pult (かた) them right into people's ears. Just catapult those words like you're trying to break through their ear drums.

examples.en: The police went ahead and headed to the white car.
examples.ja: パトカーは先回りして白い車に向かった。

examples.en: I went ahead and made dinner.
examples.ja: 先回りして、夜ごはんは作っておいたよ。

examples.en: The company president is a person who can do various things ahead.
examples.ja: 社長は、先回りして色々なことを行える人です。

3438.meaning_mnemonic: If you get there <kanji>previous</kanji> to something rotating (回り), you are <vocabulary>arriving ahead</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>going ahead</vocabulary> in <vocabulary>anticipation</vocabulary>.
3438.reading_mnemonic: This consists of a couple kun'yomi readings put together. You can tell it's kun'yomi because of the hiragana sticking out at the end. In previous levels, you learned both the words 先 and 回る (verb version of 回り). If you know those, you should be able to put them together to learn the reading of this word as well.

examples.en: My brother is very fast talker.
examples.ja: 兄は、とても早口です。

examples.en: I spoke fast when I made an order, so I got five beers instead of one.
examples.ja: 早口でオーダーしたので、生ビールが一つの代わりに五つ来た。

examples.en: Many Japanese are good at fast-talking.
examples.ja: 日本人は、早口が上手な人が多いですね。

3439.meaning_mnemonic: When you have a <kanji>fast</kanji> <kanji>mouth</kanji>, you're probably a <vocabulary>fast talker</vocabulary>, right motormouth?
3439.reading_mnemonic: Remember how body parts often change even jukugo words to kun'yomi readings? That's what happened here too. Both readings are kun'yomi, making this one <reading>はやくち</reading>.

examples.en: I’m ten yen short.
examples.ja: お金が十円足りないんです。

examples.en: We are one onion short.
examples.ja: 玉ねぎが一つ足りない。

examples.en: I don't have enough strength to raise this sofa to the loft.
examples.ja: このソファをロフトに上げるには力が足りない。

3440.meaning_mnemonic: You know the word 足りる from Level 4. What is this one? it's the opposite (negative form on a verb is ない). So, what is the opposite of 足りる (To be sufficient)? The opposite is <vocabulary>to not be sufficient</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>not enough</vocabulary>.
3440.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 足りる (たりる) which you should have seen in Level 4.

examples.en: My former partner is older than me.
examples.ja: 元パートナーは、私より年上です。

examples.en: My brother is three years older than you.
examples.ja: 私の兄は、あなたより三才年上ですよ。

examples.en: I went on a date with an older woman.
examples.ja: 年上の女の人とデートに行った。

3441.meaning_mnemonic: When you're <kanji>year</kanji>s <kanji>above</kanji> someone else, you are <vocabulary>older</vocabulary> than that person.
3441.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this one is an exception, because it uses kun'yomi readings even though it is a jukugo kanji. You already know the separate kun'yomi readings from the vocabulary of the last level, but you will have to remember to actually use this knowledge when this word comes up.

examples.en: There are all kinds of people in the world.
examples.ja: 世の中には、色々な人がいます。

examples.en: That is the rule of society.
examples.ja: それが世の中のルールだ。

examples.en: Could we say that this world is safe?
examples.ja: この世の中は、安全だと言えるのでしょうか？

3442.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>middle</kanji> of the <kanji>world</kanji> is the <vocabulary>society</vocabulary>. It's what holds everything together, for us humans. You can also call it <vocabulary>the world</vocabulary>.
3442.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the kun'yomi readings. Why? Because this word is really two separate words connected together into one bigger word. You know the kun'yomi readings from vocab practice in previous levels.

examples.en: Mr. Tanaka is off, so a substitute teacher will come.
examples.ja: 田中先生はお休みなので、代わりの先生が来ます。

examples.en: I got onions in return for giving tomatoes.
examples.ja: トマトをあげた代わりに玉ねぎをもらった。

examples.en: I had a hard time finding a substitute person.
examples.ja: 代わりの人は中々見つからなかった。

3443.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen that 代わる means "to substitute for" or "to replace." This is the noun version of that (no う sound on the end). So, what is the noun version of those verb words? It would be <vocabulary>substitute</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>replacement</vocabulary>.
3443.reading_mnemonic: You should be able to figure out the reading from learning 代わる in the previous level.

examples.en: I want to be on a diet this year.
examples.ja: 今年はダイエットをしたいです。

examples.en: My child will be a freshman in college this year.
examples.ja: 私の子は、今年、大学一年生になります。

examples.en: I just came to Japan in April of this year.
examples.ja: 今年の四月に日本へ来たばかりです。

3444.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>now</kanji> <kanji>year</kanji> is which year? It is <vocabulary>this year</vocabulary>.
3444.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for 今年 (ことし) is kinda weird, what with the こ part and all. Just imagine the こん reading you learned for 今 has been shortened to こ here, if that helps. Then the 年 part uses its kun'yomi reading とし. It's an odd combo, so here's a mnemonic:

Your goal <vocabulary>this year</vocabulary> is to treat everyone with <reading>courtesy</reading> (ことし). You're going to be nice and polite to everyone this year, even on social media. After all, there's too much negativity in the world right now. Oh yes, no doubt about it — this year will be one of courtesy.

examples.en: Should we replace this part with gold?
examples.ja: このパーツ、金に代える？

examples.en: Please substitute cow's milk with almond milk.
examples.ja: 牛のミルクをアーモンドミルクに代えて下さい。

examples.en: The life of this puppy cannot be replaced with money.
examples.ja: この子犬の一生はお金に代えることは出来ません。

3445.meaning_mnemonic:
You know the kanji is <kanji>substitute</kanji>, and you know this is a verb. There are other similar ones, but this one means <vocabulary>to replace something</vocabulary>. In order to remember that this particular word means "to replace something" focus in on the え. You have an egg in your hands that you notice isn't any good (it's black and moldy). So, you replace it with another egg (or substitute it with another egg, or exchange it with another egg, etc).

This verb is transitive, meaning it has a direct object. You replace something, like that egg!
3445.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this one is the same as 代わる which you learned in a previous level. As long as you know that one you should be able to learn this one's reading as well.

examples.en: This class has many younger children.
examples.ja: このクラスは年下の子が多いです。

examples.en: I went on a date with a younger boy.
examples.ja: 年下の男の子とデートに行きました。

examples.en: I am ten years younger than my sister.
examples.ja: 私は、姉よりも十才年下です。

3446.meaning_mnemonic: When you have someone who has <kanji>years</kanji> <kanji>below</kanji> your own, this person is <vocabulary>younger</vocabulary> than you.
3446.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this one is kind of strange. It is the kun'yomi reading for both of the kanji. You know the kun'yomi readings from earlier, back when you learned the vocab 年 and 下.

examples.en: Let's meet up soon.
examples.ja: 近々、会いましょう。

examples.en: A baby will be born soon.
examples.ja: 近々、赤ちゃんが生まれます。

examples.en: I will go to China soon.
examples.ja: 近々、中国に行きますよ。

3447.meaning_mnemonic:
When something is <kanji>close</kanji> <kanji>close</kanji> (the 々 character repeats the kanji that was before it) it will happen <vocabulary>in the near future</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>soon</vocabulary>. 

This is pretty vague, and it's up to the person speaking to decide how soon <vocabulary>soon</vocabulary> is. Depending on the person and the situation, it could technically be used for anything up to a few years!
3447.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading twice; that's the one you learn with the vocab word 近い from the previous level. The second 近 gets converted to ぢか, though, so take note of that. To write the character ぢ, type "di" on your keyboard.

examples.en: The blue sky is spreading out today.
examples.ja: 今日は青空が広がっている。

examples.en: We did a cherry blossom viewing under the blue sky.
examples.ja: 青空の下で花見をしました。

examples.en: Many days in May have a blue sky.
examples.ja: 五月は青空の日が多いですね。

3448.meaning_mnemonic: This is simply a <kanji>blue</kanji> <kanji>sky</kanji> (aka a <vocabulary>blue sky</vocabulary>!).
3448.reading_mnemonic:
You'd think that this word would use on'yomi readings to read it, but it doesn't (shake that angry fist at the kanji gods!). Instead, it's double kun'yomi, probably because this word is really like two separate words put together, "blue" and "sky." In the previous level you unlocked these two separate words, learning their readings. That means you should be able to read this as well. 

One quick note is the rendaku-fication of 空 as well. It becomes ぞら.

examples.en: Both brothers are still elementary school students.
examples.ja: その兄弟は、まだ二人とも小学生です。

examples.en: I've been playing basketball since I was an elementary schooler.
examples.ja: 小学生の時から、ずっとバスケットボールをしています。

examples.en: When I was in elementary school, the stone and the marbles were like my friends.
examples.ja: 小学生の時、石ころとビー玉は、友人みたいなものでした。

3449.meaning_mnemonic: You know 学生 is student, so what is a <kanji>small</kanji> student? Think young. That would be an <vocabulary>Elementary School Student</vocabulary>.
3449.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Is this the right way to make macaroni cheese?
examples.ja: このマカロニチーズの作り方は正しいですか？

examples.en: Please teach me how to make curry.
examples.ja: カレーの作り方を教えて下さい。

examples.en: When you don't know how to make it, check it on the Internet.
examples.ja: 作り方が分からない時は、インターネットでチェックしましょう。

3450.meaning_mnemonic: This is the <kanji>way</kanji> to <kanji>make</kanji> something. This is <vocabulary>how to make</vocabulary> something. You'll see this for directions on building something.
3450.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi readings from the vocab words 作る and 方. So as long as you're okay with those, you can apply that knowledge over here.

examples.en: My child is a junior high school student now.
examples.ja: 私の子は、今中学生です。

examples.en: This is an essay I wrote when I was in junior high.
examples.ja: これは中学生のときの作文です。

examples.en: I participated in a piano competition for junior high school students.
examples.ja: 中学生向けのピアノのコンクールに出ました。

examples.en: Oyama-sensei is my teacher from when I was a junior high school student.
examples.ja: 大山先生は、中学生の時の先生です。

3451.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen 学生 (means student). Now let's look at a student who's in the middle. Perhaps we can call this a <vocabulary>middle school student</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>junior high school student</vocabulary>, depending on where you're from.
3451.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Are there any anime that were unpopular this year?
examples.ja: 今年、不人気だったアニメは有りますか？

examples.en: It's an unpopular band in Japan, but I think that song is a masterpiece.
examples.ja: 日本では不人気なバンドですが、私は、あの曲は名曲だと思います。

examples.en: This YouTuber is famous for being unpopular with women.
examples.ja: このYouTuberは、女の人から不人気なことで有名です。

3452.meaning_mnemonic: You already know 人気 which means "popular." And you also know that 不 means "not." So what do you get when you combine the two? Something that's <vocabulary>not popular</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>unpopular</vocabulary>.
3452.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It is important to review the plan once a year.
examples.ja: 一年に一回、プランを見直すことが大切です。

examples.en: This time was a chance to reassess my weaknesses.
examples.ja: 今回は自分の弱点を見直すチャンスになりました。

examples.en: At university, I want to learn literature and reevaluate writers from the Heian period.
examples.ja: 大学では文学を学び、平安時代の作家を見直したいと思っています。

3453.meaning_mnemonic: You know the word 直す from a couple levels ago. It means "to fix." So, when you fix the way you see something, what are you doing? You're reevaluating it. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to reevaluate</vocabulary>.
