3453.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 見る and 直す. Know those and you'll know how to read this word too!

examples.en: I have the exact same idea as you.
examples.ja: あなたと全く同じ考えです。

examples.en: There's no weekdays off at all.
examples.ja: 平日は全く休みが有りません。

examples.en: I pulled the lever with all my strength, but there was no water coming out.
examples.ja: 全力でレバーを引いたが、水は全く出なかった。

3454.meaning_mnemonic: This is the adverb version of the kanji <kanji>all</kanji>. So, it's like you add an 'ly' to it. But, that doesn't work too well (allly? c'mon). So, instead think of this word as <vocabulary>completely</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>entirely</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>truly</vocabulary>.
3454.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

The person who <vocabulary>completely</vocabulary> doesn't understand this vocab word is <reading>Matt</reading> (まった). Be sure to take note of the small っ, too.

examples.en: The length of this bamboo is three meters.
examples.ja: この竹の長さは三メートルです。

examples.en: About how long is one meeting?
examples.ja: 一回のミーティングの長さは大体どのくらいですか？

examples.en: The length of this banana is twenty centimeters.
examples.ja: このバナナの長さは、二十センチです。

3455.meaning_mnemonic: You know the word 長い from a couple levels ago. This is like the word 大きい versus 大きさ, where 大きさ is "size" and 大きい is "big." So, 長い is "long" and 長さ is <vocabulary>length</vocabulary>.
3455.reading_mnemonic: If you know the reading of the word 長い from level 6 you'll know the reading for this word too. Only difference is the さ at the end, which is hiragana so it should be easy to read.

examples.en: The grocery store over there is having a sale for tomatoes this week.
examples.ja: あそこのスーパー、今週はトマトの安売りセールをやってるよ。

examples.en: Thanks to the sale, I could buy this dress for 300 yen.
examples.ja: 安売りのおかげで、このワンピースは三百円で買えたよ。

examples.en: Aren't you selling yourself short?
examples.ja: 自分を安売りしてない？

3456.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>sell</kanji> something <kanji>cheap</kanji>, you're selling it at a <vocabulary>discount</vocabulary>. Alternatively you can remember this word as <vocabulary>sell cheaply</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>bargain sale</vocabulary>. These are good deals!
3456.reading_mnemonic: The hiragana on the end hints that the readings are the kun'yomi readings. Use your memory of 安い and 売る to help you to remember how to read this.

examples.en: The other day, there was a caterpillar on the tree.
examples.ja: この前、木の上に毛虫がいたんです。

examples.en: Until recently, there were flowers, plants, and shiitake mushrooms growing here.
examples.ja: この前までは、ここには花や草やシイタケが生えてたんです。

examples.en: That woman was on a TV show the other day.
examples.ja: この前のテレビ番組に、あの女の人が出てました。

3457.meaning_mnemonic: この means "this", and you know what the word 前  means (front/before). The combination of these words, "this before" if you will, can mean a few different things. If we're talking about when something happened, the "before" meaning kicks in, and it means <vocabulary>the other day</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>recently</vocabulary>. If we're talking about location, then the "front" meaning kicks in, and it means <vocabulary>in front of this</vocabulary>.
3457.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 前 is the kun'yomi, like the reading for the vocabulary word 前. So long as you know that word, you'll be able to read this one too. The reason it's not on'yomi is because it's like two words put together. The word この and the word 前.

examples.en: Is there a convenience store at the east exit?
examples.ja: 東口にはコンビニがありますか？

examples.en: Buses leave from the east exit.
examples.ja: バスは東口から出ます。

examples.en: Let's meet at the east exit.
examples.ja: 東口で会いましょう。

3458.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 北口 and 西口 from a few levels before? This is the <kanji>east</kanji> version of that, so it means <vocabulary>east exit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>east entrance</vocabulary>.
3458.reading_mnemonic: Just like 北口 and 西口, this also uses kun'yomi readings. And just like before, watch out for the rendaku that changes くち to ぐち!

examples.en: There was a flier in the mailbox.
examples.ja: お知らせの紙がポストに入ってました。

examples.en: There's a notice. Please come to the head office right away.
examples.ja: お知らせがあります。今すぐ本社に来てください。

examples.en: And now a word from our sponsor.
examples.ja: ここでスポンサーからのお知らせです。

examples.en: It was announced that the fireworks had been cancelled due to rain.
examples.ja: 雨で花火が中止になったというお知らせがありました。

3459.meaning_mnemonic: This is a strange word, so you'll have to bear with me. You know that 知 means <kanji>know</kanji>. But in the case of this word, what do you know? Look at the second half. らせ sounds a bit like "race." So, you know about a "race." How do you know about this race? You got a <vocabulary>notice</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>notification</vocabulary> about it.
3459.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already with the kanji, so you should be all set. Lucky you!

examples.en: Next, please tell me your name.
examples.ja: 次に、名前を教えて下さい。

examples.en: My name is Yamada.
examples.ja: 私の名前は山田です。

examples.en: Tofugu is the name of the company that makes WaniKani.
examples.ja: トーフグは、ワニカニを作っている会社の名前です。

3460.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>name</kanji> that's in the <kanji>front</kanji>. That is not your last name, that is your regular <vocabulary>name</vocabulary> or your <vocabulary>first name</vocabulary>.
3460.reading_mnemonic: This word uses both kun'yomi readings (oh darn!). That being said, you've seen the kun'yomi readings for both the kanji that make up this word. The word 名 (な) and the word 前 (まえ) both are kun'yomi, so use those words and Voltron them into a single word, なまえ.

examples.en: It took three days for the crafts to be completed.
examples.ja: 工作が出来上がるのに、三日かかりました。

examples.en: Tea will be ready in about five minutes.
examples.ja: お茶は大体五分で出来上がります。

examples.en: The house will be completed at the end of the month.
examples.ja: 家は月末に出来上がります。

3461.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen the word 出来る (to be able to do), which is the first part. Then the second part, 上がる means "to rise." So, think about it this way: once you're able to do something, you rise because you're finished. That's why this verb means <vocabulary>to be finished</vocabulary>.
3461.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a combination of the readings from 出来る and 上がる. So long as you were paying attention in lessons past, you should be able to read this word as well just by combining those other words.

examples.en: Next is a stretch where you bend your ankles.
examples.ja: 次は、足首を曲げるストレッチです。

examples.en: I accidentally bent my father's precious sword.
examples.ja: 父の大切な刀を曲げてしまった。

examples.en: In this YouTube video, Koichi just keeps bending a hundred spoons.
examples.ja: このYouTubeビデオでは、コウイチがスプーンを百本ひたすら曲げつづけます。

3462.meaning_mnemonic: This is a verb because it ends with an う sound. What does the kanji mean? It's <kanji>music</kanji> and <kanji>bend</kanji>. In the case of this word, we're going with the "bend" version. The verb of that is <vocabulary>to bend</vocabulary>. This is when you're doing the bending. You can remember this because げ kind of looks like the <reading>ge</reading>cko you're bending. That gecko looked good before you bent him in half.
3462.reading_mnemonic: How were you able <vocabulary>to bend</vocabulary> this gecko? Solo effort? No way! It actually took both you and your <reading>ma</reading>ma (ま) to make it happen! Just imagine you and your mighty mama, tag-teaming to bend a gecko in half!

examples.en: Black hair is mixed in with the white hair.
examples.ja: 白い毛の中に黒い毛が交じる。

examples.en: Some wool yarn was mixed in with the sandwich I bought at the convenience store.
examples.ja: コンビニで買ったサンドイッチに毛糸が交じっていた。

examples.en: Today I live among many Japanese people.
examples.ja: たくさんの日本人の中に交じって今日も生きています。

3463.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 交ぜる means <vocabulary>to mix</vocabulary> and that the kanji means <kanji>mix</kanji> as well. So, this probably has something to do with mixing things. This word means <vocabulary>to be mixed</vocabulary>. This is when something is mixed but it's not mixed by you. It's just being mixed. Think of it this way - the じ in 交じる is Jesus, who just uses Jesus magic to mix something. So, you're not mixing it. It's just when something is <vocabulary>to be mixed</vocabulary>.
3463.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as with 交ぜる. So long as you know the ま portion of that word's reading, you'll be able to read this word as well.

examples.en: My dog runs around when she sees the snow.
examples.ja: うちの犬は、雪を見ると走り回る。

examples.en: During the summer vacation, there are many small children and adults running around on the beach.
examples.ja: 夏休みは小さい子も大人も、ビーチで走り回る人が多いです。

examples.en: The president is running around in the company today as usual.
examples.ja: 社長は今日も会社の中で走り回っています。

3464.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen the words 走る (to run) and 回る (to revolve). So, when you're running and revolving while you're doing it, you're running in circles. So, the verb form of that is <vocabulary>to run around</vocabulary>.
3464.reading_mnemonic: The readings are those like the words 走る and 回る. Make sure you know those words from before and apply that knowledge to read this word as well.

examples.en: My father is good at guessing if tea is cheap or expensive.
examples.ja: 父は安いお茶と高いお茶を当てるのが上手です。

examples.en: Mr. Ohtani is a genius at hitting the ball with the bat.
examples.ja: 大谷氏は、バットにボールを当てる天才です。

examples.en: I have the power to guess a person's future by their phone number.
examples.ja: 私には電話番号で、その人の未来のことを当てる力があります。

3465.meaning_mnemonic: You know that the kanji 当 means <kanji>right</kanji> or <kanji>success</kanji>. So since this is a verb, you're doing right and success (which doesn't make much sense). Instead, you're guessing something and getting it right. So, this word means <vocabulary>to guess</vocabulary> something. Hopefully you don't have to guess too hard when it comes to the meaning of this word as well.
3465.reading_mnemonic: The reading can be remembered via the word 当たる which you learned a few levels ago. Use that knowledge to remember that this word is read as あてる. The important part is the あ.

examples.en: I'm not good at mingling with various people at parties.
examples.ja: パーティで色々な人と交わるのが下手なんです。

examples.en: The two roads intersect and become one road here.
examples.ja: 二つの道が交わって、ここで一つの道になります。

examples.en: Tofugu is a company where American and Japanese culture mingle.
examples.ja: トーフグは、アメリカと日本の文化が交わった会社です。

3466.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that the kanji means <kanji>mix</kanji> and the word 交ぜる means "to mix," so it probably has something to do with that. This word means <vocabulary>to intersect</vocabulary>, which is kind of like mixing. When two things intersect with each other, they're getting mixed up, so that's where this word gets its meaning. 

To remember that this one means "to intersect," remember the わ as <reading>wa</reading>lk. You're walking around, and then you intersect with some people on the street.
3466.reading_mnemonic: The reading is almost the same as 交ぜる which you should be familiar with by now. It has the ま but it also has an extra じ in there. That じ is there because you intersect with a group of <reading>mage</reading>s (まじ) that catch you on fire as you walk past.

examples.en: Both women and men can be transformed with makeup.
examples.ja: 女も男もメイクで化けることが出来る。

examples.en: Raccoon dogs are good at transforming into human beings.
examples.ja: タヌキは人間に化けるのが上手です。

examples.en: Is it true that a used Porsche turned into ten million yen after three years?
examples.ja: 中古のポルシェが三年後に一千万円に化けたって本当ですか？

examples.en: My house was transformed into a national treasure-level house with a year of renovation.
examples.ja: 私の家は一年間のリノベーションで国宝レベルの家に化けた。

3467.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>change</kanji> so you'd think the verb version is "to change," but it's a bit more specific. This word means <vocabulary>to change form</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to transform</vocabulary>.

化ける means to change into something else, usually in a surprising and magical way. It's often used in stories where animals or spirits take on human forms. It can also describe transformations in real life that are so dramatic they feel unreal.
3467.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You try to transform. You want to turn into something awesome, like a dinosaur, but then *poof* you turn into a sheep. "<reading>Ba</reading>aaa," you say. "Baaa."

examples.en: After the sound of the knock, there was a sound of the doorknob being turned.
examples.ja: ノックの音の後、ドアノブを回す音がした。

examples.en: My brother is a genius at spinning pizza dough.
examples.ja: ぼくの兄はピザの生地を回す天才です。

examples.en: Please pass around more salmon sushi.
examples.ja: もっとサーモンのおすしを回して下さい。

3468.meaning_mnemonic: You've probably seen the word 回る, which means "to revolve." This word is similar, except for you're doing the turning/rotating action on something else. You can simply say <vocabulary>to turn something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to rotate something</vocabulary> when answering this question, but be sure to think of yourself actually turning/rotating something. Remember this by using the す on the end. You've taken your friend <reading>Sue</reading> and put her on a stick. You're rotating her over a fire on a spit because you're a sick cannibal.
3468.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the word 回る (まわ). So long as you know that level 5 word, you'll be able to read this one as well. Use both of these words together to remember their readings.

examples.en: I am an elementary school teacher.
examples.ja: 私は小学校の先生です。

examples.en: There are many foreign-born students in the elementary school in this town.
examples.ja: この町の小学校には、外国生まれの生徒もたくさんいますよ。

examples.en: I am in a volunteer club that reads picture books to elementary school children.
examples.ja: 小学校の子どもたちに、絵本をよむボランティアの会に入ってます。

examples.en: I've been interested in you since we were in elementary school.
examples.ja: 小学校の時から、君のこと、ずっと気になっていたんだ。

3469.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen 学校 from a couple levels ago. Now we're adding a <kanji>small</kanji> to it. What is a "small school"? That's a school for small people, making it an <vocabulary>elementary school</vocabulary>.
3469.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the regular on'yomi reading of 小 plus the vocab word 学校 that you've seen previously. Combine these two things for the reading of 小学校.

examples.en: Go to the right on this street.
examples.ja: この通りを右に行って下さい。

examples.en: Streets in the Shitamachi area have lots of shops, and people come and go throughout the day.
examples.ja: 下町の通りには、たくさんのお店が有って、一日中、人々が行ったり来たりします。

examples.en: There is a street called "Takeshita Street" in Tokyo, which is popular with junior high and high school students.
examples.ja: 東京には、「竹下通り」という名の通りがあって、中学生や高校生に人気です。

3470.meaning_mnemonic: You know the word 通る hopefully by now. That is the verb version of this word, which means "to pass through." So, if this is the noun version, what is it that you use to pass through something? To drive or walk along? That would be an <vocabulary>avenue</vocabulary> (or <vocabulary>street</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>road</vocabulary>, etc). This is a pretty common word in Japan, and good for not getting lost.
3470.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the word 通る, so as long as you know that, you should be able to read this one as well. Mind the strange long お sound!

examples.en: Please be careful of the fire on the stove.
examples.ja: ストーブの火に気を付けて下さい。

examples.en: It might rain today, so be careful and take a raincoat when you go out.
examples.ja: 今日は雨かもしれないから、外出する時は気を付けてレインコートをもってね。

examples.en: Be careful in big cities in this country, because there are many pickpockets.
examples.ja: この国の大きな町では、スリが多いから気をつけてね。

examples.en: It's not so bright around here, so watch your feet.
examples.ja: 辺りは明るくないので、足元に気をつけて下さい。

3471.meaning_mnemonic: This word contains the words 気 (energy) and 付ける (to attach). So, when you <kanji>attach</kanji> <kanji>energy</kanji> to something you're focusing in on it, right? This word is a sort of "order" as well, since it's te-form there at the end. It's a set phrase people say to other people who are doing dangerous things. It's kind of like saying "Attach energy to what you're doing! Stay focused!" A simpler way to translate this would be to say this word means <vocabulary>be careful</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>take care</vocabulary>, though. Learn this word so that you can always show that you're caring for your friends!
3471.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the two words 気 and 付ける. So long as you know those from the previous levels, you should be able to read this one as well.

examples.en: This book is new.
examples.ja: この本は新しいです。

examples.en: The new apartment is clean, spacious, and close to the company.
examples.ja: 新しいアパートはきれいだし、広いし、会社からも近いんですよ。

examples.en: I'm sorry, this white shirt is still new, so could we get white wine instead of red wine today?
examples.ja: ごめんなさい。この白いシャツまだ新しいので、今日は赤ワインじゃなくて白ワインでもいいですか？

3472.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>new</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>new</vocabulary>.
3472.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Your family buys you a <vocabulary>new</vocabulary> Atari! You're so excited! But wait... what's this? This is no Atari. This is an <reading>Atara</reading>... a knockoff video game system :(

examples.en: My little brother is a high school student.
examples.ja: 私の弟は高校生です。

examples.en: When I was in high school, I was in the tennis club.
examples.ja: 高校生の時は、テニス部に入ってました。

examples.en: Today, high school students are coming to tour this bread factory. Let's show them what a bread factory can do!
examples.ja: 今日は、高校生たちが、このパン工場の見学に来ます。パン工場の本気を見せましょう！

3473.meaning_mnemonic: You know 高校 means "high school." So, a "life" that does high school is a <vocabulary>high school student</vocabulary>. This is like how 中学生 are middle school students and 小学生 are elementary school students!
3473.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Use the reading of 高校 from before to learn the reading of this word as well, if it helps.

examples.en: Junior high school students often come to this convenience store.
examples.ja: このコンビニには中学校の生徒がよく来ます。

examples.en: There is also a tea ceremony club in junior high school.
examples.ja: 中学校には茶道のクラブもありますよ。

examples.en: Thanks to my junior high school teacher, I started karate.
examples.ja: 中学校の時の先生のおかげで、空手をはじめたんです。

3474.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 学校 means school. So, people who are in the <kanji>middle</kanji> <kanji>school</kanji> are in... wait for it... <vocabulary>middle school</vocabulary>. 

And, of course, if you're one of those people that call it <vocabulary>junior high school</vocabulary> you can do that too.
3474.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a combination of 学校 and 中. Really, it's all on'yomi too, so you should be able to read this one. Take note of the がく turning to がっ, though.

examples.en: There's no stamp attached to this letter yet.
examples.ja: この手紙には、まだ切手が付いてないですよ。

examples.en: Ugh, some ketchup got on my white tee shirt.
examples.ja: あーあ。白いティシャツにケチャップが付いちゃった。

examples.en: What’s that thing attached to your earlobe?
examples.ja: あなたの耳たぶに付いてるそれ、何？

3475.meaning_mnemonic: You know that the word 付ける means "to attach" and you know that the kanji 付 means <kanji>attach</kanji>. So, this word probably has something to do with attaching. This is the intransitive version, though, where something is attached (and you're not doing the attaching). You can use the く as a hint. You see something attached on the wall. You say "Coo'"
3475.reading_mnemonic: The reading can be derived from 付ける, a word you should have seen a few levels ago. If you know that word's reading you should be able to figure out this word's reading as well (and vice versa).

examples.en: Can you find my mother?
examples.ja: 私の母を見付けることが出来ますか？

examples.en: The other day, I found a gem under that tree.
examples.ja: 先日、あの木の下で宝石を見付けたんです。

examples.en: I was glad I could find a book I like today.
examples.ja: 今日は、自分の気に入った本を見付けることが出来たので、よかったです。

3476.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 付ける means "to attach" and that 見 means "see." So, when you attach your seeing to something, it's like you're looking around trying <vocabulary>to find</vocabulary> something. When you find what you're looking for, imagine your eyeballs flying out and attaching to that item, then yelling "I FOUND IT!"

You'll usually see this word with the 付 in kana, so 見つける.
3476.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 見る and 付ける. If you use those readings, you'll be able to read this word too.

examples.en: People say my younger brother is a wimp.
examples.ja: 弟は弱虫だと言われている。

examples.en: My type is a man with a strong will but is a bit wimpy.
examples.ja: 気は強いけど、ちょっと弱虫な男がタイプです。

examples.en: No matter what you are — whether you're a wimp, or even a caterpillar, you should be just the way you are.
examples.ja: 弱虫だって毛虫だってなんだって、君は君のままでいいよ。

3477.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>weak</kanji> <kanji>insect</kanji>. This is what people call <vocabulary>weakling</vocabulary>s in Japan. This is a good word to know if you're a bully, or something.
3477.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this one is a weird one. It uses the kun'yomi readings for both, meaning you'll have to pull your knowledge of the word 弱い from earlier and apply it here. 虫 should be okay, though, as this is the reading you learned with the kanji.

Just remember, only weak bugs use kun'yomi, and that weak bug is you in this instance.

examples.en: My husband ran with all his might, despite his weak-looking body.
examples.ja: 主人は弱々しい体ながら全力で走った。

examples.en: The vehicle made a frail engine sound.
examples.ja: その車両は弱々しいエンジン音を立てていた。

examples.en: My mother in a weak voice told her grandmother, "Take time to rest."
examples.ja: 母は弱々しい声で、おばあちゃんに「ゆっくり、休んで」と言った。

3478.meaning_mnemonic: Something that is double <kanji>weak</kanji> is probably pretty weak. You also know that this is an adjective because it ends with い. You know that 弱い is weak, so it probably isn't that. Instead, this one is <vocabulary>weak looking</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>frail</vocabulary>. If you know the grammar らしい you can kind of use that as a hint. The しい on the end reminds me of らしい which is like "seems to be." So, "seems to be weak" = "weak looking."
3478.reading_mnemonic: The reading is double kun'yomi, as you can probably guess due to all the hiragana involved. So, you double up on よわ and then add the しい to read this vocabulary word.

examples.en: The mouth of the mug is chipped.
examples.ja: マグカップの口の所が欠けてしまった。

examples.en: The moon was a little bit less than full last night.
examples.ja: 夕べの月、少しだけ欠けてましたね。

examples.en: My grandpa often says things that are rude and lacking in delicacy.
examples.ja: うちのおじいちゃんは、よくデリカシーに欠ける失礼な事を言います。

3479.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji itself means <kanji>lack</kanji>, and this verb has a few meanings related to that. You'll often see it meaning <vocabulary>to get chipped</vocabulary>, like when talking about a teacup or your teeth. I guess a chipped teacup is lacking... a piece of itself?

欠ける can also literally mean <vocabulary>to be lacking</vocabulary>, as in "a good goalie is lacking from their team." You can use it like this when you're short of something, or when something is missing that would complete a set. In these situations, you'll usually see it as 欠けている!
3479.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Something is lacking... it's a <reading>ca</reading>r (か). You can't stop thinking about this because you have to walk 40 miles to get to your destination. If only that car wasn't missing, this would be easier. Imagine the sweat... the pain... the thirst... all because that car's not present.

examples.en: Many people in this town go see the eye doctor.
examples.ja: 町民の中には、目医者に通っている人も多いです。

examples.en: Doesn't every eye doctor wear glasses?
examples.ja: 目医者の先生って、みんなメガネかけてない？

examples.en: Today, I went to an eye doctor and got contact lens with my new prescription.
examples.ja: 今日は、目医者に行って新しい度のコンタクトレンズを作ってきました。

3480.meaning_mnemonic: Do you remember 医者 (doctor)? What happens when you add <kanji>eye</kanji> on there? You have yourself an <vocabulary>eye doctor</vocabulary>.
3480.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the vocab word 医者 (いしゃ) plus the reading 目 (め), the same as the reading you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: Please turn right and enter the first room.
examples.ja: 右に曲がって一番目の部屋に入ってください。

examples.en: On that morning, my older brother was the first to leave the house.
examples.ja: その朝、一番目に家を出たのは兄でした。

examples.en: The first person who I wanted to inform that I would be admitted to the University of Tokyo was my father, who supported me throughout my entrance exams.
examples.ja: 東京大学に入学できる事を一番目に知らせたかった人は、受験中ずっと支えてくれた父でした。

3481.meaning_mnemonic:
You've seen 一番 (number one), so what in the world is this eye on the end? This eye (目) is used to mark something's position in a sequence. So, add this to "number one" and you have <vocabulary>the first thing</vocabulary> or simply <vocabulary>the first</vocabulary>.

Just imagine your collection of eyeballs you have at home. (You have a collection of eyeballs, right?) You have them lined up in a display case and you're explaining the first one to your friend. It's not first because it's the best or anything — you love all your eyeballs equally, after all — but it does happen to come first in sequence in your display right now.
3481.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is just the vocab word 一番 plus the word 目. If you know both of those readings you'll be able to read this one as well.

examples.en: I find it quite annoying, so I wanna get even.
examples.ja: ムカつくから、なんか仕返ししたいな。

examples.en: Seriously, she is the worst! I'll get even with her someday!
examples.ja: 本当に最低の女！いつか仕返ししてやるわ！

examples.en: To get back at him for eating my pudding, I ate Koichi's favorite yogurt.
examples.ja: プリンを食べられた仕返しに、コウイチの好きなヨーグルトを食べてやった。

3482.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>return</kanji> the <kanji>doing</kanji>s of another person, you're doing it to <vocabulary>get even</vocabulary> (whether it's a nice thing or a mean thing).
3482.reading_mnemonic: The readings are a bit weird, here. 仕 gets its on'yomi reading... you should be okay with that. 返し gets the kun'yomi reading, though, which is the reading you saw with the word 返す in level 9. You can tell this part uses the kun'yomi vocab reading because it has that hiragana attached to it. Just remember to distinguish between the two parts of the word to remember the readings.

examples.en: The height of that apartment is thirty meters.
examples.ja: あのアパートの高さは三十メートルです。

examples.en: I can never beat Koichi and Michael when it comes to their level of humor.
examples.ja: ギャグセンの高さでは、どうしてもコウイチとマイケルには勝てないよ。

examples.en: Mt. Fuji has not only height but also beauty.
examples.ja: ふじ山には、高さだけでなく、美しさもある。

3483.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen the word 高い from a couple levels ago. This word is related to that. It's like 大きい versus 大きさ, where one describes the other. In this case, the 高さ is the <vocabulary>height</vocabulary> of something (while 高い is tall). This word isn't "price" though. For that you'd ask いくらですか？ (how much is it?).
3483.reading_mnemonic: Use the reading of 高い (たかい) to help you to learn and remember the reading for this one. They're the same except for the hiragana at the end.

examples.en: I'm looking forward to the date tomorrow.
examples.ja: 明日のデートが楽しみです。

examples.en: It's still January, but I'm looking forward to summer vacation already.
examples.ja: まだ一月ですが、もう夏休みが楽しみです。

examples.en: Sake and draft beer are something I look forward to on my days off.
examples.ja: 日本酒と生ビールが休日の楽しみです。

3484.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen the word 楽しい, which means "fun." This is obviously very similar looking, though this one means <vocabulary>looking forward to</vocabulary>. Why? Because it has a み on the end, saying "who is going to have fun? It's <reading>me</reading>! That's why I'm looking forward to it!"
3484.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just like 楽しい, so make sure you know that and you'll be able to read this one as well.

examples.en: This curry uses spices made for Japanese people.
examples.ja: このカレーは、日本人向けのスパイスを使ってます。

examples.en: This game is intended for beginners.
examples.ja: このゲームはビギナー向けですよ。

examples.en: This book is a picture book for children who are about three years old.
examples.ja: この本は三才くらいの子ども向けの絵本です。

3485.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully seen 向く and 向ける by now. They mean "to face" and "to turn toward." This has a similar idea. When you add 向け to something imagine you're turning it, aiming it at someone. It's aimed at them, meaning it's <vocabulary>made for</vocabulary> them. Turn a book toward someone, now it's <vocabulary>aimed at</vocabulary> them, it's made for them. See the connection?
3485.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the word 向く so work off of that word to be able to read this one.

examples.en: This research institute is famous throughout the country.
examples.ja: ここは、全国でも有名な研究所です。

examples.en: This shampoo was created at a research institute in the United States.
examples.ja: このシャンプーは、アメリカの研究所で、生まれました。

examples.en: On weekdays, I research literature from the Heian era at the laboratory of Japanese language.
examples.ja: 平日は、日本語研究所で平安時代の文学の研究をしています。

3486.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen that 研究 is "research" from previous vocab, and you might remember 所 can mean "facility." So this word means <vocabulary>research institute</vocabulary> or, of course, <vocabulary>research facility</vocabulary>.
3486.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will also help if you know the reading of 研究 already.

Also note that 所 is normal in first reading, but gets rendaku'd in the second reading, meaning しょ becomes じょ. Both readings are valid and they don't affect the meaning, so it just comes down to personal preference!

examples.en: There's a shortcut if you turn down this road to the right.
examples.ja: この道を右に曲がった方が、近道ですよ。

examples.en: Not all shortcuts are safe roads.
examples.ja: 全ての近道が、安全な道という事じゃない。

examples.en: If you take a shortcut, you can go to the cherry blossom viewing venue quickly.
examples.ja: 近道をすると、花見の場所にすぐに行けますよ。

3487.meaning_mnemonic: Taking the <kanji>nearby</kanji> <kanji>road</kanji> will get you to your destination more quickly (because it's more close by!). This is a <vocabulary>shortcut</vocabulary>, aka the <vocabulary>short way</vocabulary>.
3487.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a bit weird in this one. It uses the kun'yomi reading for both kanji, even though it looks just like it should be all on'yomi reading. It's like you're taking a <vocabulary>shortcut</vocabulary> with your kanji readings and doing the native Japanese readings (kun'yomi) instead of the more intellectual Chinese ones (on'yomi). Luckily, you've hopefully seen both of these kanji as vocab already. You have ちか for 近 (short for 近い) and you have 道 (みち), just like the word "street" you learned before. Combine these together and you have the reading for this word. Perhaps it's like this because you're combining a couple concepts together into one word, at least when it comes to "short + way."

examples.en: I'm sure they'll be fine. It's okay.
examples.ja: きっと助かるよ。平気。

examples.en: When I left the house, there was a taxi right in front of my eyes and I was saved.
examples.ja: 家を出たら、目の前にタクシーがいて、助かった。

examples.en: The teacher told us in advance what kind of answers we will be asked for on this test, which was very helpful.
examples.ja: 今回の試験については、どんな答えを聞かれるか、先生が前もって教えてくれたので、とても助かった。

3488.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 助ける means "to help." This word, 助かる, is related, but it's a bit different. It means to be helped or to be saved. It's intransitive, so it doesn't take a direct object. Imagine shouting "I'm saved!" No direct object, right? Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
3488.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 助ける, so hopefully you know that word and can apply that knowledge over here.

examples.en: Do you think I'll make it if I leave now?
examples.ja: 今から出て、間に合うと思う？

examples.en: If we get in a taxi right now, we might still make it on time.
examples.ja: 今すぐタクシーに乗れば、まだ間に合うかもしれません。

examples.en: Sorry! Eating ramen took longer than I thought, and I'm not going to make it to the meeting on time.
examples.ja: ごめん！ラーメン食べるのに思ったより時間がかかって、待ち合わせに間に合いそうにない。

3489.meaning_mnemonic: There is an <kanji>interval</kanji> (of time) that you need "to suit" (合う). To suit that interval, you need to be there before the time in question. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to be in time for</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to make it on time</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be on time for</vocabulary>.
3489.reading_mnemonic: You learned this reading for 間 when you learned 間もなく. And the reading for 合う is just that of the word 合う. If you remember them both, you'll remember this word!

examples.en: I'll be at the office until an email comes back.
examples.ja: メールが返ってくるまで会社にいます。

examples.en: The ball that I threw came back to me with the wind.
examples.ja: 投げたボールが風で返ってきた。

examples.en: Thinking my money would be returned properly was a huge mistake.
examples.ja: 貸したお金がちゃんと返ってくると思ったら大間違いよ。

3490.meaning_mnemonic:
You hopefully know the word 返す, which means "to return" (as in, you're doing the direct action of returning something). This word, on the other hand, is the version where something just returns (and you're not doing the action of returning it). Use the る to help you to remember this. る the Kangaroo is returned to you. You don't do any of the returning, it just happens or someone else does it. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to be returned</vocabulary>.

Note this word is often combined with くる (to come), which reinforces the aspect that something is coming back to you.
3490.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 返す, so as long as you know that you'll be able to apply it here to learn the reading of this word as well.

examples.en: Summer is the season to eat shaved ice and enjoy fireworks.
examples.ja: 夏はかき氷を食べたり花火を楽しむシーズンです。

examples.en: This weekend, I'm planning to enjoy a barbecue with my friends at the river.
examples.ja: 今週末は、友人たちと川でバーベキューを楽しむ予定だ。

examples.en: This trampoline is very popular now. Both adults and children can have fun on it.
examples.ja: このトランポリン、今大人気なんです。大人も子どもも楽しめますよ。

3491.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully seen the word 楽しい, which means "fun." This is basically the verb version (ends in an う sound, right?) of that. That means this is <vocabulary>to enjoy something</vocabulary>, or just <vocabulary>to have fun</vocabulary>.
3491.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the word 楽しい, so be sure to know that word and you'll be able to apply it over here.

examples.en: Hey mom, when will it be decided what we will eat today?
examples.ja: ねえママ、今日は何を食べるか決まるのはいつ？

examples.en: Has the day of enrollment been decided?
examples.ja: いつが入学の日か決まりました？

examples.en: There are too many roommates and the house rules have yet to be decided.
examples.ja: ルームメイトの数が多すぎて、中々家のルールが決まらない。

3492.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully seen the word 決める before. This is similar, except instead of deciding something, something gets decided. Rules are decided, a schedule gets decided — that kind of thing. It's intransitive, so it doesn't take a direct object. So 決まる means to be decided. Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
3492.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 決める, so make sure you know that word so you can apply that knowledge over here.

examples.en: It's rude to throw pebbles at people!
examples.ja: 人に対して小石を投げ付けるなんて、失礼だろ！

examples.en: My father got angry and threw a balloon at my mother.
examples.ja: 父は、怒って母に風船を投げ付けた。

examples.en: The prince tried to throw an onion at the vampire for the time being.
examples.ja: 王子は、とりあえずドラキュラに玉ねぎを投げ付けてみた。

3493.meaning_mnemonic: You know that you're <kanji>throw</kanji>ing something that is <kanji>attach</kanji>ing to something else. How else can you say that? The best way would be to say <vocabulary>to throw against</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to throw at</vocabulary>.
3493.reading_mnemonic: The readings just come from two vocab words you've hopefully seen already: 投げる and 付ける. So long as you know the readings for those words, the reading for this word should be no problem for you.

examples.en: In Japan, raccoons are said to be creatures that bewitch humans.
examples.ja: 日本では、タヌキは人間を化かす生物だと言われている。

examples.en: This fox is a genius at enchanting people.
examples.ja: このキツネは人を化かす天才だ。

examples.en: "I’m sorry I couldn't make it the other day. I was bewitched by a fox." "No worries. Things like that can’t be helped."
examples.ja: 「先日は来れなくて、すみませんでした。キツネに化かされちまってねえ。」「心配しないでください。それはどうしようもない事ですから。」

3494.meaning_mnemonic:
You've seen the word 化ける (to transform) before, and here's a related word: 化かす. This means <vocabulary>to bewitch</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to trick</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to deceive</vocabulary>.

Why? In Japanese folklore, foxes, spirits and other yokai often transform in order to bewitch, trick, or deceive humans. To 化かす them, in other words.

This verb is transitive, so it needs a direct object — you bewitch, trick, or deceive someone. You know this because when a fox wants to bewitch someone, they have to <reading>cuss</reading> (かす). They say a magic cuss word that lets them change forms and fool people. Those tricksy foxes…
3494.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 化ける, so make sure you know that word and you'll be able to learn this word's reading as well.

examples.en: No matter how many times you tell me the same story, I still don't understand.
examples.ja: 同じ話を何回されても、よく分かりません。

examples.en: A talk about Japanese toilets again?
examples.ja: また日本のトイレの話ですか？

examples.en: Could you listen to me for just a little bit?
examples.ja: 少しだけでいいので、話を聞いてもらえないですか？

3495.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji version of 話 means <kanji>talk</kanji>. This word also means <vocabulary>talk</vocabulary>, but it means a few other things as well. This can refer to a <vocabulary>speech</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>story</vocabulary> as well. Basically anything that involves a talking session. So, before you go, I hope you stay awhile and listen to my 話.
3495.reading_mnemonic:
Who tells a great <vocabulary>story</vocabulary>? <reading>Hana, she</reading> (はなし) tells a great story! If you know someone named Hana or Hanna you can use that person to help you to remember this one better too. 

You can also use 話す's reading to help you to remember this one, as well.

examples.en: Turn this way, please.
examples.ja: こっちを向いてください。

examples.en: When you look down, you can see a large river.
examples.ja: 下を向くと、大きい川が見えます。

examples.en: The house faces west, so it gets nice sunlight in the afternoon.
examples.ja: 家は西に向いていて、午後は日当たりがいいです。

3496.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that the kanji means <kanji>yonder</kanji>, which is like "over there." This is the verb version of "yonder." That being said, "to yonder" isn't really a thing, so you have to think of what happens when you "look yonder." This word means <vocabulary>to turn toward</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to face</vocabulary>. You're looking yonder, but you have to turn towards said yonder to look that way.

This word can also mean <vocabulary>to be suitable</vocabulary>, as in a good fit for a job, role, or situation. After all, you turn toward the things you're most suitable for, right?
3496.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You turn <vocabulary>to face</vocabulary> a new direction and look out into the distance. There is a single cow out there. It turns to face you too, and says <reading>moo</reading> (む).

examples.en: Do you know each other?
examples.ja: お知り合いですか？

examples.en: Since I know that person, I'll ask them about it.
examples.ja: 知り合いだから、ちょっと聞いてみるよ。

examples.en: I absolutely don't want it to be known that I'm acquainted with them.
examples.ja: アイツと知り合いだとはゼッタイにバレたくない。

3497.meaning_mnemonic: You've probably seen the words 知る and 合う by now. This is someone you "know" because you have "come together" before, but that's pretty much it. You don't really know them well, you just met them a couple times so you know who they are. This person is an <vocabulary>acquaintance</vocabulary>.
3497.reading_mnemonic: The readings are that of 知る and 合う. So long as you know those words, you should be able to read this one too.

examples.en: Where is the gondola terminal?
examples.ja: ゴンドラ乗り場はどこですか？

examples.en: I'm at the taxi stand now.
examples.ja: 今、タクシー乗り場にいます。

examples.en: At the moment, I’m chilling at the bus stop in front of my house looking at cars passing by.
examples.ja: 今、家の前のバス乗り場で通り過ぎる車を見ながらダラダラしているよ。

3498.meaning_mnemonic: What's a <kanji>ride</kanji> <kanji>location</kanji>? It's a <vocabulary>boarding area</vocabulary>! This word is used widely to refer to any place where you board transportation, such as a <vocabulary>bus stop</vocabulary>, a <vocabulary>taxi stand</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>train platform</vocabulary>.
3498.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings. You didn't learn the kun'yomi reading for 場 with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

At the <vocabulary>boarding area</vocabulary>, you <reading>baa</reading> (ば) at the bus driver to ask if this is the right bus. You're in a country inhabited only by sheep, but luckily you've practiced your Sheepanese well enough to be able to baa for directions at <vocabulary>bus stop</vocabulary>s, <vocabulary>taxi stand</vocabulary>s, and <vocabulary>train platform</vocabulary>s.

examples.en: You should be more careful about how you use language.
examples.ja: もう少し、言葉の使い方に気を付けた方がいいよ。

examples.en: Grandpa always calls because he doesn't know how to use his smartphone or computer.
examples.ja: おじいちゃんはスマホやパソコンの使い方が分からないので、いつも電話をしてきます。

examples.en: How to use Excel? Even my dog knows that.
examples.ja: エクセルの使い方？そんなのうちの犬でも知ってるよ。

3499.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen the word 使う hopefully by now. If you have, you know it means "to use." So, the <kanji>way</kanji> to <kanji>use</kanji> something is the <vocabulary>way of using</vocabulary> (aka <vocabulary>how to use</vocabulary>). This will be a word you see when you're looking at directions for how to use something.
3499.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi readings from the vocab words 使う and 方. So as long as you're okay with those, you can apply that knowledge over here.

examples.en: Since I started a new job, it has only been three days.
examples.ja: 新しい仕事を始めてから、まだ三日です。

examples.en: I won't be able to sign off work until six o'clock today, so stay in a nearby cafe until then.
examples.ja: 今日は六時まで仕事が終わらないから、それまで近くのカフェにいてね。

examples.en: The baby's job is to cry.
examples.ja: 赤ちゃんの仕事は泣くことです。

3500.meaning_mnemonic:
You know 事 means "occurrence," but it can also mean "thing." So when you're <kanji>doing</kanji> <kanji>thing</kanji>s all day, what are you probably doing? A <vocabulary>job</vocabulary>! All jobs really just amount to doing things.

Just like "job" in English, 仕事 can refer to a person's specific <vocabulary>occupation</vocabulary>, to <vocabulary>work</vocabulary> in general, or to a particular task depending on the context.
3500.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi reading for 仕 and the kun'yomi reading for 事. Please note that 事 uses the reading こと, which you didn't learn with the kanji, but you have come across it once or twice by now, and because of the way rendaku works, it's changed to the voiced ごと.

examples.en: That girl's name is Emma.
examples.ja: あの少女の名はエマだ。

examples.en: What is the name of this flower?
examples.ja: この花の名は、なんですか？

examples.en: My husband built a reputation as the "Hotel King."
examples.ja: 主人は「ホテル王」の名をのこした。

3501.meaning_mnemonic: This vocabulary word is the same as the 'name' meaning of the kanji. If you can remember that, you'll have no trouble remembering this word as well.
3501.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: Just think of the first part of the English word <vocabulary>name</vocabulary>. What is it? It's <reading>na</reading> (な), just like this word!

examples.en: I don't think you're a loser.
examples.ja: 私はあなたのことを負け犬だとは思わないよ。

examples.en: If I am living like this, I'll just continue to be a loser in life.
examples.ja: こんな生活をしてたら、ずっと人生の負け犬だよ。

examples.en: I don't want to be called a loser anymore.
examples.ja: 負け犬と呼ばれるのは、もう嫌なんだよ。

3502.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully come across 負ける by now, which means "to lose." So, you can figure out this word means "losing dog." Well, calling someone a dog isn't so nice, so you're probably just calling them a <vocabulary>loser</vocabulary>.
3502.reading_mnemonic: The readings are kun'yomi, but you should be familiar with 負ける and of course 犬 well enough to learn the reading here.

examples.en: I'm currently waiting alone. I wonder if everyone will come?
examples.ja: 今、待ちぼうけ中だよ。 みんな来るのかな？

examples.en: Without realizing I'd been deceived, I ended up waiting alone at a deserted station for three hours.
examples.ja: ダマされてたことに気づかず、さびれた駅で三時間も待ちぼうけをしていました。

examples.en: Make sure to let Misaki know that tomorrow's meeting has been canceled so she doesn't feel stood up, okay?
examples.ja: 待ちぼうけを食らったと思わないように、明日のミーティングが中止になったこと、ミサキさんにもちゃんと教えといてあげてね？

3503.meaning_mnemonic: With <vocabulary>待ち</vocabulary> you know you're waiting, but what's a <vocabulary>ぼうけ</vocabulary>? Turns out it's the long version of ボケ which means idiot. Basically, in this case you're a waiting idiot. Why? because you were <vocabulary>stood up</vocabulary>.
3503.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 待ち comes right from 待つ. You know the drill by now.

examples.en: Japan's team won today's game.
examples.ja: 今日のゲームは日本チームの勝ちでした。

examples.en: The key chain is first come, first served. Let’s get a move on!
examples.ja: キーホールダーがもらえるの早い者勝ちなんだって。早く行こう！

examples.en: If that ace is on the mound, we don't stand a chance of winning.
examples.ja: あのエースがマウンドに立っていたら、私たちには勝ち目がないよ。

3504.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully seen 勝つ by now, which means "to win." This is a nouny version of that. So, what's the noun version of "to win?" It's <vocabulary>a win</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>victory</vocabulary>.
3504.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 勝つ. So as long as you have some understanding of that reading, you should be able to read this one as well.

examples.en: Once they've decided on a name for Koichi's baby, I'll let you know right away.
examples.ja: コウイチの赤ちゃんの名前が決定したら、すぐにお知らせしますね。

examples.en: The winner of the contest has been decided.
examples.ja: コンテストの勝者を決定しました。

examples.en: ROFL! This TV show is hilarious, man. I’ve decided that this is now my new favorite show.
examples.ja: クソワロタwwwこのテレビ番組クソほどおもしろいじゃねーかよ。俺の一番好きな番組に決定したわ。

3505.meaning_mnemonic: A 決定 is a "decision." So, when you add する to it you're making it a verb, meaning this word means <vocabulary>to decide</vocabulary>.
3505.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 決定 with する added. Make sure you know 決定 and you'll know this word as well.

examples.en: In this country, there are not many opportunities to meet Japanese people.
examples.ja: この国では、日本人に出会うチャンスがあまりない。

examples.en: I met various people in this town and they were kind to me.
examples.ja: この町では色々な人に出会って、親切にしてもらいました。

examples.en: Where did you meet your husband?
examples.ja: ご主人とは、一体どこで出会ったんですか？

3506.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>exit</kanji> your house and you <kanji>meet</kanji> someone. You didn’t mean to meet them, but it happened anyway. That’s why this word means <vocabulary>to meet by chance</vocabulary>.
3506.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is that of the word 出る and the word 会う, both of which you've hopefully seen. The 出 portion may be confusing, but you can usually assume that if one part of the word is kun'yomi / vocab reading, the other part is too, which is why 出 uses the vocab reading.

Oh by the way, this word can be written like this too: 出合う. It’s not as common, but you may come across it every now and then, so it’s good to know!

examples.en: There are many people who suffer from long hours at work in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本には長時間労働に苦しむ人が多くいます。

examples.en: I don't want to go to school while suffering from bullying.
examples.ja: いじめに苦しみながら学校に行きたくないよ。

examples.en: Why do innocent people suffer?
examples.ja: なぜ罪のない人が苦しんでいるのか。

3507.meaning_mnemonic: You've already been introduced to the word 苦しい. That word means painful, or agonizing. So, if you turn that into a verb, you have <vocabulary>to suffer</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to struggle</vocabulary>.
3507.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 苦しい, so as long as you're on top of that word, this word should be readable for you as well.

examples.en: It took me some time to realize that the woman was my own mother.
examples.ja: その女が自分の母だと気付くまでに時間がかかりました。

examples.en: When I noticed, it was already time to go to school.
examples.ja: 気づいたらもう学校に行く時間だった。

examples.en: I can’t believe you gave me your ice cream. I didn’t realize that you were so kind until now.
examples.ja: あんたが私にアイスクリームをくれるなんて、本当に信じられないよ。あんたがそんなに優しいなんて今まで気付かなかったわ！

3508.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>attach</kanji> your <kanji>energy</kanji> (imagine someone suddenly looking up at something, attaching their energy to it), you have noticed or realized something. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to realize</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to notice</vocabulary>. 

Don't confuse this with 気を付けて which is similar in that it has all the same kanji. It's just used a little different. Try to remember the difference before moving on.
3508.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the 気 kanji (which you know) and the word 付く which you should know by now. Combine these together and you have the ability to read this word. Take note that the 付く part is rendaku'd, though, so it is a tiny bit different.

examples.en: Which do you like being better? One who sees someone off, or one who is seen off by someone.
examples.ja: 見送る方と見送られる方、どっちが良い？

examples.en: I went to Tokyo to see them off.
examples.ja: 東京まで見送りに行った。

examples.en: He passed up a chance to go abroad.
examples.ja: 彼は海外に行くチャンスを見送った。

3509.meaning_mnemonic: You know the words 見る and 送る by now, hopefully. Here you're "seeing" the "sending." You're seeing someone off, so this verb is <vocabulary>to see off</vocabulary>. This can also mean <vocabulary>to put off</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to pass on</vocabulary>, since it's as though you're just passively seeing someone (or something) off rather than taking action and going with them.
3509.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the vocab words 見る and 送る. Make sure you know those and you'll know this word's reading as well.

examples.en: I go to the convenience store from time to time.
examples.ja: そこのコンビニは時々行きます。

examples.en: Sometimes I wonder what Koichi is doing at the moment.
examples.ja: 時々「コウイチは今何してるかな？」って思うんだよね。

examples.en: Sometimes there were problems with my neighbors.
examples.ja: ご近所とのトラブルは時々ありました。

3510.meaning_mnemonic: You know the single word 時, right? It means <kanji>time</kanji>. This is that twice. So you have one time, and you have another time. They are separate. Things don't happen in every of these times you have. They happen <vocabulary>sometimes</vocabulary>.
3510.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the vocab word 時 twice, with the second one getting rendaku'd.

examples.en: Please first go to the receptionist.
examples.ja: まずは受付に行ってください。

examples.en: Even the reception staff at that gym are ripped.
examples.ja: あそこのジムは受付スタッフまでマッチョだね。

examples.en: Have you already checked in at reception?
examples.ja: 受付の手続きはもうお済みですか？

3511.meaning_mnemonic: Imagine someone <kanji>accept</kanji>ing something and then <kanji>attach</kanji>ing something. This person is a <vocabulary>receptionist</vocabulary>, because they are accepting the call, writing down the information, and then attaching said information to a sticky note for you to read. You say, "No, I'm not available."
3511.reading_mnemonic: For this reading you have to think back to the verb words that get used with this kanji, namely 受ける and 付ける. Then just drop off the るs and put them together. 受 becomes うけ and 付 becomes つけ and you're left with うけつけ. This is what's called a compound word. And now you know it. Nice!

examples.en: I've just done the grocery shopping.
examples.ja: スーパーで買い物をしたばかりです。

examples.en: Let's go shopping at a department store sometime.
examples.ja: たまにはデパートに買い物に行こうよ。

examples.en: We’re going Christmas shopping today! I’m so excited!
examples.ja: 今日はクリスマスの買い物に行くの！すごくワクワクするわ！

3512.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully seen 買う by now and know it means "to buy." So, 買い is going to be similar to that. Add that to <kanji>thing</kanji> and you have a "buying things" sort of word. What does "buying things" describe? It describes <vocabulary>shopping</vocabulary>.
3512.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the kun'yomi, which is usually the case when there's hiragana in the middle. You learned the reading for 買い when you learned the kanji, as well as the word 買う, and you learned this reading of 物 in the word 物!

examples.en: I'm not a big fan of celery.
examples.ja: セロリが苦手です。

examples.en: The drawback about that idol is that she is not a good singer.
examples.ja: あのアイドル、歌が苦手なのが欠点なんだよな。

examples.en: Why does my dog bark only at you? He probably just doesn't like you.
examples.ja: うちの犬がなんでお前にばっかり吠えるかって？たぶん、お前のことが苦手なんだよ。

3513.meaning_mnemonic: A "suffering hand" is a little misleading. Think more in terms of the words 苦い (bitter) and 手 (person... remember how that happens sometimes?). Now think of this word like you're bitter about having to work with someone. Why? Because they are extremely <vocabulary>hard to deal with</vocabulary>.
3513.reading_mnemonic: The reading is that of 苦い (にがい) plus regular old 手 (て). Remember, this is your bitter person, the person who's "hard to deal with." So, it uses the strange にがい reading.

examples.en: Seventy years ago, TV was black and white.
examples.ja: 七十年前、テレビは白黒でした。

examples.en: Let’s put it in very black and white terms.
examples.ja: 白黒ハッキリつけようぜ。

examples.en: Kanae-chan, don't you look a bit like a panda in your black and white outfit today?
examples.ja: カナエちゃん、今日の全身白黒の服は、ちょっとパンダみたいじゃない？

3514.meaning_mnemonic: Something is both <kanji>white</kanji> and <kanji>black</kanji>. It is <vocabulary>black and white</vocabulary> (you can also say <vocabulary>white and black</vocabulary> if you prefer).
3514.reading_mnemonic: The readings are kun'yomi, but you should have seen both 白 and 黒い separately as vocabulary by now. It's the same readings here, so you can apply that knowledge and read this word!

examples.en: My boyfriend is a drinker.
examples.ja: 私の彼氏は酒好きです。

examples.en: That alcoholic is drinking in the morning again today.
examples.ja: あの酒好き、今日も朝から引っかけてやがるぜ。

examples.en: My wife is a drinker and I’m worried about her becoming an alcoholic.
examples.ja: 私の妻は酒好きなので、アル中にならないか心配だ。

3515.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>like</kanji> <kanji>alcohol</kanji> a lot, you're probably a heavy <vocabulary>drinker</vocabulary>.
3515.reading_mnemonic: The reading is all kun'yomi vocab reading here as you can probably guess from the hiragana sticking out on the end. You should know the readings of these as separate words already (酒 and 好き) which means all you need to pay attention to is the rendaku of すき to ずき.

examples.en: My father is also a boozer.
examples.ja: 私の父親も酒飲みなんですよ。

examples.en: Koichi likes drinking, but he isn't like an alcoholic.
examples.ja: コウイチはお酒は好きだけど、酒飲みってほどじゃあないですよ。

examples.en: He’s a heavy drinker but he doesn’t like red wine.
examples.ja: 彼は大酒飲みだが、赤ワインが苦手だ。

3516.meaning_mnemonic: We have <kanji>alcohol</kanji> and a variant form of 飲む (to drink). So you know this has to do with drinking alcohol. It means a <vocabulary>boozer</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>drunkard</vocabulary>, someone who drinks a lot of alcohol!
3516.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the vocab words お酒 and 飲む combined together into one. You can guess it's a kun'yomi reading because of the み on the end of 飲, which should make you think back to vocab words that use these kanji and the kun'yomi readings. If you can do that, you can read this word (and many others, probably!).

examples.en: Have you ever heard the sound of a giraffe?
examples.ja: キリンの鳴き声を聞いたことがありますか。

examples.en: I woke up to the sound of birds chirping in the morning.
examples.ja: 朝、鳥の鳴き声で起きた。

examples.en: I hear a puppy barking under the vending machine.
examples.ja: 自動販売機の下から子犬の鳴き声が聞こえるんです。

3517.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>chirp</kanji> <kanji>voice</kanji> is a sound an animal makes. Sure, it works for birds (which chirp), but it also works with most other animals as well. So, we call this an <vocabulary>animal cry</vocabulary>.
3517.reading_mnemonic: The readings are those that you learned with the kanji. 声 gets changed to ごえ, though, so take note of that in your head. Perhaps you can imagine an animal that does a "GOEEEEE" cry.

examples.en: What's the drink that Koichi's drinking?

3519.meaning_mnemonic:
You've seen 聞く by now hopefully. This is similar, but instead of meaning "to hear" it means <vocabulary>to be hearable</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be audible</vocabulary>. To remember this, just think about how you can hear a こえ (voice) coming from the middle of the word 聞こえる. It's audible to you too, right?

聞こえる is used when sounds reach your ears on their own, like "I can hear music from next door." It's more about what comes to your ears, not what you're trying to listen to. That's why it also means <vocabulary>to be able to hear</vocabulary>.
3519.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 聞く, so if you know the reading of that word, you can apply it here.
