examples.ja: それは予想外でした。

3543.meaning_mnemonic:
If you consider the future <kanji>beforehand</kanji> and <kanji>imagine</kanji> how things will turn out (based on some facts), you will have an informed <vocabulary>expectation</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>prediction</vocabulary> for it.

予想 refers to an expectation or prediction about the future based on current information or trends, like predicting which candidate will win an upcoming election or estimating future economic conditions.
3543.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I really like this retrospective scene in the movie.
examples.ja: この映画のこの回想のシーンがすごく好きなんだよね。

examples.en: Paul was lost in aimless reminiscence at the beach.
examples.ja: ポールはビーチで、とりとめのない回想にふけっていた。

examples.en: I know that Viet sometimes reminisces about his yakuza days during work hours.
examples.ja: ビエトが時々、仕事中にヤクザ時代のことを回想しているのを私は知っている。

3544.meaning_mnemonic:
The past events <kanji>revolve</kanji> around your mind as you <kanji>imagine</kanji> them. That's a <vocabulary>reminiscence</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>recollection</vocabulary> of those times.

回想 refers to the reminiscence or recollection of past experiences or events. It's often used to describe flashback scenes in movies or dramas, as well as moments in literature where characters think back on their past.
3544.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I can't go along with Koichi's ideas.
examples.ja: コウイチの思想にはついていけません。

examples.en: That person seems to hold some kinda strong views, don't you think?
examples.ja: あの人、ちょっと思想が強そうだよね。

examples.en: Of course, each person has the freedom to hold whatever ideas they wish in their heart.
examples.ja: もちろん、内心にどんな思想を持つかはその人の自由です。

3545.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>think</kanji> and <kanji>contemplate</kanji> deeply, you're producing something larger, like an <vocabulary>ideology</vocabulary>. This means having a group of, or a single larger, <vocabulary>thought</vocabulary>(s) or <vocabulary>idea</vocabulary>(s).

思想 refers to the big ideas or beliefs an individual holds about the world and life. It’s often used to talk about one’s thoughts about philosophy, politics, religion, or other such beliefs.
3545.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You haven't learned the on'yomi for 思 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

All your <vocabulary>thought</vocabulary>s and <vocabulary>idea</vocabulary>s are about <reading>shee</reading>p (し) right now. You just can't stop thinking about sheep. Are you thinking about sheep right now? What kind of sheep are they?

examples.en: If you had to lose one of your five senses, which one would you give up? Please also tell me why.
examples.ja: 五感のうちどれか一つを失ってしまうとしたら、どれを選びますか？また、その理由も教えてください。

examples.en: The dishes at our restaurant are designed to be enjoyed with all five senses.
examples.ja: うちのレストランの料理は五感で楽しめる料理となっています。

examples.en: Using all five senses in one's everyday life is very important.
examples.ja: 毎日、五感をしっかり使って生活することはとても大切なことです。

3546.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>five</kanji> <kanji>feeling</kanji>s that you have are what? Sight, sound, taste, touch, and smell (don't count the sixth one where you see dead people). These are <vocabulary>the five senses</vocabulary> that you probably have.
3546.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I agree with that opinion as well.
examples.ja: 私もその意見に同感ですね。

examples.en: I agree with this more wholeheartedly than I've ever agreed with anything in my whole life.
examples.ja: 今までにこんなに同感したことがないぐらい、思いっきり同感しています。

examples.en: "I hate Fugu." "I feel the same way."
examples.ja: 「私、フグのこと嫌い。」「同感だわ。」

3547.meaning_mnemonic:
When you have the <kanji>same</kanji> <kanji>feeling</kanji> as someone else, you are in <vocabulary>agreement</vocabulary> with them. They have an opinion or feeling about something, and you're <vocabulary>feeling the same</vocabulary> way.

同感 is a word used to express agreement, often with a sense of shared feeling. You use it when you hear a thought or viewpoint that really resonates with you — you totally agree with this person's take and feel exactly the same way. Preach!
3547.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Tofugu's drinking parties are so fun!
examples.ja: トーフグの飲み会はとても楽しいですよ！

examples.en: Forcing someone to chug a drink at a drinking party is alcohol harassment.
examples.ja: 飲み会で一気飲みを強要するのはアルハラだよ。

examples.en: My parents say that I can’t go to the drinking party.
examples.ja: うちの親が飲み会には行っちゃダメだって言うんだよね。

3548.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 飲む is drink, so this has to do with <kanji>drink</kanji>ing. Also, 会 means <kanji>meet</kanji>, so when you meet to drink you're getting together with others to drink. It's a <vocabulary>drinking party</vocabulary>!
3548.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the 飲む vocabulary word and the regular kanji reading for 会. Hopefully you know both of those by now so you can apply them to the reading of this word, too!

examples.en: That taxi driver is a good-looking guy.
examples.ja: あのタクシーの運転手、イケメンだね。

examples.en: Please rest assured, as we are renting a bus with a driver.
examples.ja: 運転手付きのバスをレンタルしてるので安心して下さい。

examples.en: The driver seemed okay but his car was totaled in the accident.
examples.ja: 運転手は大丈夫だったみたいだけど、車は事故でめちゃくちゃになっていたよ。

3549.meaning_mnemonic: You know that <vocabulary>運転</vocabulary> has to do with driving, right? And you know that <kanji>手</kanji> often has to do with a person doing something in words like these. So, a person who does driving is what? A <vocabulary>driver</vocabulary>.
3549.reading_mnemonic: The reading is all on'yomi, because it's jukugo. You should know the on'yomi reading of 手 by now just by seeing similar word patterns to this one.

examples.en: Let's collect fallen leaves and start a fire.
examples.ja: 落ち葉を集めて火を起こそう。

examples.en: I made this greeting card from the fallen leaves.
examples.ja: このグリーティングカード、落ち葉で作ったんだよ。

examples.en: I love the feel and sound when stepping on fallen leaves.
examples.ja: 落ち葉を踏んだ時の感触と音が大好きです。

3550.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this one is a bit strange. You'll have to pull from your knowledge of 落ちる and use that for the first half. Then, 葉 is rendaku'd to ば. Because, when a leaf falls, Scrooge says "BAH! Humbug!" (probably because he's losing money).

examples.en: Our father always gives us advice.
examples.ja: 父親はいつも私たちに助言をしてくれます。

examples.en: The father of this child is you.
examples.ja: この子の父親は、あなたです。

examples.en: Everyone in my family loves my dad.
examples.ja: うちの家族はみんな父親のことが大好きです。

3551.reading_mnemonic: The reading here is pretty weird. It's all kun'yomi. My guess is this translates literally to "father parent" (two different words, therefore uses the other readings). You should know the readings of these two separate words, though. It is 父 (ちち) and 親 (おや).

examples.en: My mother is always full of energy.
examples.ja: うちの母親はいつも元気です。

examples.en: This cow's mother was sold a long time ago.
examples.ja: この牛の母親は、とっくに売られてしまったんです。

examples.en: How has your life changed now that you have become a mother?
examples.ja: 母親になってみて、人生はどう変わりましたか？

3552.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this is strange. It's the kun'yomi vocab reading, probably because the literal translation is "mother parent" and therefore consists of a couple words combined together into one concept. So, make sure you know the separate word readings of 母 and 親. If you do, you should be able to read this too.

examples.en: This is probably my third favorite Beatles's song.
examples.ja: この曲、ビートルズの中で三番目くらいにすき。

examples.en: The third child my mom and dad had was my baby brother.
examples.ja: 母と父の間に三番目に生まれたのが弟です。

examples.en: Did you know that Japan has the third highest number of inhabited islands in the world, after Indonesia and the Philippines?
examples.ja: 日本の有人島の多さは、インドネシア、フィリピンに次いで、世界で三番目だってこと、知ってた？

3553.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember 一番目? This is just like that, but with three, making it <vocabulary>the third thing</vocabulary> or simply <vocabulary>the third</vocabulary>.

Again, think about your eyeball collection. This time, you're showing someone the third eyeball in your display case. It just happens to be third in line, but honestly it's just as beautiful as the two that come before it.
3553.reading_mnemonic: Use your knowledge of the reading for 一番目 to remember the reading for this word as well.

examples.en: When I glanced back, he was still looking at me.
examples.ja: チラリと見返ると、彼もまだ私のことを見ていました。

examples.en: As I watched the fluttering of the turquoise butterfly, I suddenly glanced back at Mori-kun.
examples.ja: 青緑色のチョウチョウがヒラヒラしているのを見ながら、私はふと森君の方を見返りました。

examples.en: There was a huge crash and I involuntarily looked behind me.
examples.ja: ガシャーンと大きな音がして、私は思わず後ろを見返った。

3554.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>see</kanji>ing is <kanji>return</kanji>ing on something. This verb can be both transitive and intransitive. When it’s transitive, it means <vocabulary>to look back at</vocabulary>, in the sense of looking back at someone who’s behind you, or looking back at your past. When it’s intransitive, it simply means <vocabulary>to look back</vocabulary>, in the sense of looking over your shoulder.
3554.reading_mnemonic: The readings are just 見 and the vocab word 返る, combined together. So long as you know both of those you should be able to combine them into the reading for this word.

examples.en: The way he talks makes me really annoyed.
examples.ja: 話し方が本当にイライラするのよね。

examples.en: You talk like a Japanese person.
examples.ja: まるで日本人みたいな話し方ですね。

examples.en: I want to learn a persuasive way of talking.
examples.ja: 説得力のある話し方を学びたいです。

3555.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>speak</kanji>ing <kanji>way</kanji> is… your <vocabulary>way of speaking</vocabulary>, or your <vocabulary>speaking style</vocabulary>. This includes your tone of voice, speed, and even how you use gestures when talking. It's more about the whole way you communicate, not just the wording or how you phrase things.
3555.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi readings from the vocab words 話す and 方. So as long as you're okay with those, you can apply that knowledge over here.

examples.en: A small boy fell.
examples.ja: 小さい男の子が転んでしまいました。

examples.en: I almost fell on the street because of the snow.
examples.ja: 雪のせいで道で転んでしまいそうでした。

examples.en: Koichi didn't cry when he fell today.
examples.ja: コウイチ、今日は転んでも泣かなかったね。

3556.meaning_mnemonic: Do you remember the word 転がる? This is kind of similar, instead of rolling, this is more for when something falls and hits the ground. It means <vocabulary>to fall over</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to fall down</vocabulary>. Just imagine someone falling off a chair face first into the dirt and making a ぶ sound.
3556.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 転がる. Hopefully you know that one well enough to associate it with this one, meaning you can read them both.

examples.en: The plan is that all employees will come together on a trip to Kyushu.
examples.ja: 九州への旅行で全社員が集まる予定です。

examples.en: A lot of money was raised through crowdfunding.
examples.ja: クラウドファンディングで、こんなにたくさんのお金が集まりました。

examples.en: Look! A group of miscreants are gathering over there!
examples.ja: 見て！あそこにヤンキーたちがたくさん集まってるよ。

3557.meaning_mnemonic: I bet you remember 集める means "to collect something." But this time you're not collecting something. Instead, something just… collects. In other words, 集まる means to come together or to gather. Friends come together, or fans gather at a venue — that sort of thing. No direct object needed, since this is intransitive. Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
3557.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 集める so if you know that word you'll know how to read this word as well.

examples.en: Oh, you dropped your handkerchief.
examples.ja: あの、ハンカチ落としましたよ。

examples.en: You should immediately stop doing things that will make people lose faith in you.
examples.ja: そんな信用を落とすようなことは今すぐ止めた方がいいよ。

examples.en: Today I bought a book called 'How to Make a Man Fall In Love With You,' but I lost it somewhere on the way back home.
examples.ja: 今日、『男を落とす方法』っていう本を買ったんだけど、帰り道にどこかで落としちゃったみたいなんだよね。

3558.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen how 落ちる means "to fall down." Now you're doing the action of "falling something down," aka you're dropping it. You can remember this because you kind of <reading>toss</reading> (とす) something and it drops to the ground, making this word mean <vocabulary>to drop something</vocabulary>.
3558.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 落ちる. So long as you know that word you can apply that reading over here, too.

examples.en: This is the end.
examples.ja: これで終わりだ。

examples.en: "All is well that ends well," right?
examples.ja: 「終わり良ければ全て良し」でしょ？

examples.en: Work ends this week and Christmas holidays starts next week! Aww I can't wait for that.
examples.ja: 今週で仕事も終わりで、来週からはクリスマス休暇だー！あー、待ちきれない。

3559.meaning_mnemonic: By now you should know that 終わる means "to end" or "to finish." So what is this noun-version of that word? It would be <vocabulary>the end</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>the finish</vocabulary>.
3559.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 終わる. So long as you know that word, you can learn this word's reading as well!

examples.en: What time was the last train?
examples.ja: 終電、何時だっけ？

examples.en: I'll get going as the last train of the JR Line is coming soon.
examples.ja: もうすぐJRの終電だから、行くね。

examples.en: When I miss the last train and take a taxi, it costs about 5000 yen to get home.
examples.ja: 終電を逃してタクシーに乗ると、大体家まで五千円かかります。

3560.meaning_mnemonic: We've seen a few times where 電 refers to a train. They're big deals, after all, and use a ton of electricity. So, the <kanji>end</kanji> train for this word would refer to the <vocabulary>last train</vocabulary>.
3560.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What time does this shop open?
examples.ja: このお店は何時に開きますか。

examples.en: The venue hasn't opened yet, so let's go get a beer for the time being.
examples.ja: 会場はまだ開かないから、とりあえずビールを買いに行こう。

examples.en: Um... Your fly is open.
examples.ja: あの... 社会の窓が開いていますよ。

3561.meaning_mnemonic: You should know 開ける by now. This word is similar to that, except it has to do with when things are just open. It's the same thing, though. The meaning is also <vocabulary>to open</vocabulary>.
3561.reading_mnemonic:
Do you remember the reading for 開ける, which you learned in level 10? That's right, it's あける! So if you know the reading of that word (I hope you do!) then you can apply that knowledge here.

Just a quick side note — 開く can also be read as ひらく, but we're going to focus on the あく reading here. Since ひらく has slightly different meanings, we won't accept it as a reading for this word, so be sure to enter あく!

examples.en: I never expected something like this would happen.
examples.ja: まさかこんなことが起こるなんて、思ってもみなかったよ。

examples.en: Please try thinking through why something like this happened.
examples.ja: どうしてこんなことが起こったのか、よく考えてみてください。

examples.en: It was a huge earthquake, the kind that occurs only once every few hundred years.
examples.ja: それは数百年に一度起こるか起こらないかの大地震でした。

3562.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 起きる means "to wake up", but did you learn its secondary meaning, "to occur"? Well, this word means only <vocabulary>to occur</vocabulary>. Just imagine an incident occurring involving a uranium <reading>core</reading> (こる) to remember that this means <vocabulary>to occur</vocabulary>. After all, uranium core incidents don't wake up, do they?
3562.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji and the same as 起きる too, meaning you should be able to put together the reading on your own.

examples.en: My father is always worried about his brother.
examples.ja: 父は兄のことをいつも心配しています。

examples.en: The staff are worried as the president has not yet come to work, although it's already past eleven o'clock.
examples.ja: 社長が十一時になっても出社してないので社員たちは心配しています。

examples.en: If you have time to worry about sales, make more sales calls!
examples.ja: 売り上げを心配する時間があるならセールスの電話を一本でも多くしてよ！

3563.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 心配 is "a worry." What about the verb version of that? It would be <vocabulary>to worry</vocabulary>.
3563.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes straight from 心配 so try to make sure you know that word so you can read this word! It's also all jukugo on'yomi reading, too, so you should be able to figure it out regardless.

examples.en: Don't worry, it's okay. Everything should work out.
examples.ja: 心配しないで、平気ですよ。全て上手くいくはず。

examples.en: I'm so worried about tomorrow's exam that I can't feel at ease.
examples.ja: 明日の試験が心配で、安心していられません。

examples.en: I'm a little worried because my father doesn't have the energy like he always had.
examples.ja: 父にいつもの元気がないので、少し心配です。

examples.en: I was worried because I could not tell whether the ship was heading east or west.
examples.ja: この船の進行方向が西なのか東なのか分からなくて心配になった。

3564.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>distribute</kanji> your <kanji>heart</kanji> around you, it's like your heart is everywhere at once, but not in your body. You feel frantic, you don't know what to do because your heart is out there. This represents the feeling you have when you have <vocabulary>a worry</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>concern</vocabulary>. 心配しないでね！
3564.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Take note that the ぱい in 配 got rendaku'd from はい, as well.

examples.en: My stomach growled.
examples.ja: お腹が鳴ってしまった。

examples.en: The phone is ringing.
examples.ja: 電話が鳴っている。

examples.en: The door bell rang.
examples.ja: ドアのベルが鳴った。

3565.meaning_mnemonic: You learned 鳴く means "to chirp" (or some other animal sound). 鳴る is similar, but it's used when something just makes a sound, like a phone ringing, a bell jingling, or thunder rumbling. So 鳴る means <vocabulary>to sound</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to ring</vocabulary>. You know this because 鳴る can also be used for when your stomach rumbles: "<reading>rrrr</reading>" (る)!
3565.reading_mnemonic: The reading can come from 鳴く. So long as you know the reading for that word you can know the reading for this word as well.

examples.en: My mother sings in the shower every day.
examples.ja: 母は毎日シャワー中に歌う。

examples.en: I don't like singing in front of people.
examples.ja: 人前で歌うのは好きじゃないんです。

examples.en: I'm going to make dinner today, so could you sing for me?
examples.ja: 今日は僕が夕食を作るから、君は僕のために歌ってよ。

3566.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. One of the kanji's meanings is <kanji>sing</kanji> so the verb vocab version of this is <vocabulary>to sing</vocabulary>.
3566.reading_mnemonic: Awesomely, this uses the same reading as the reading for the vocab words 歌. Just throw the う onto the end and you have yourself the reading. So, sing your heart out and learn this word easily. "IIIIiiIIIiiiII WILLL ALLllwaYYYs Loovvve YoOooOOooooOOOO ♬!"

examples.en: You are so selfish!
examples.ja: ほんと、勝手だよね！

examples.en: Don't say whatever you want.
examples.ja: 勝手なことばっかり言わないでよ！

examples.en: Could you stop opening the fridge or eating chips at someone else's house without permission?
examples.ja: 他人の家で勝手に冷蔵庫を開けたりポテチを食べるの、やめてくれる？。

3567.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>hand</kanji> (or person, as you know 手 often refers to a person) that <kanji>win</kanji>s gets to do <vocabulary>as one pleases</vocabulary> without regard for anyone else.
3567.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this is weird. It's all kun'yomi, which luckily you've seen before, but still strange. I guess when you do <vocabulary>as one pleases</vocabulary> you can read kanji however you want, in this case the kun'yomi readings. Do note that there's a small っ in there before 手, presumably to connect the two readings of the two kanji together.

examples.en: I met Hana-san at the beginning of April.
examples.ja: 花さんとは、4月の初めに出会いました。

examples.en: Our family goes to see the sunrise together at the beginning of each year.
examples.ja: うちは毎年、年の初めに家族みんなで朝日を見に行きます。

examples.en: It was Kaoru who first opened her mouth.
examples.ja: 初めに口を開いたのはカオルだった。

examples.en: You're the one who threw the first punch!
examples.ja: 初めになぐりかかってきたのはそっちだろ！

3568.meaning_mnemonic:
You know 初 means <kanji>first</kanji>, and に can mark a point in time. So 初めに means <vocabulary>at first</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>in the beginning</vocabulary>. 

初めに has a lot of overlap with 始めに. But while 始めに is for the beginning of some larger process, 初めに refers more to doing something first or to the initial point of a certain time frame. You might say 初めにアクビをしたのは私です (I was the one who yawned first), for example, or 今年の初めに (at the start of this year).
3568.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi, which you didn't learn with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you out. What are you beginning? You are beginning <reading>Haj</reading> (はじ). (Haj is the fifth pillar of Islam, and is a pilgrimage to Mecca during the month of Dhu al-Hijja).

examples.en: Is this your first time in Japan?
examples.ja: 日本は初めてですか？

examples.en: I'm struggling with all these new experiences.
examples.ja: 初めてのことばかりで、四苦八苦しています。

examples.en: I've been interested in you since the first time we met.
examples.ja: 初めて会った時から、ずっと気になっていました。

3569.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 初 means "first" This word means <vocabulary>for the first time</vocabulary>. Think of めて as "meet." Then think "when we met <vocabulary>for the first time</vocabulary> ____ happened."
3569.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi, which you didn't learn with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you out. What are you beginning? You are beginning <reading>Haj</reading> (はじ). (Haj is the fifth pillar of Islam, and is a pilgrimage to Mecca during the month of Dhu al-Hijja).

examples.en: The 'Wind God' brought forth the divine wind.
examples.ja: 「風の神様」が、神風を起こしたんだよ。

examples.en: Thanks to the divine wind, Japan experienced a miraculous victory.
examples.ja: 神風のおかげで、日本が大勝利をするミラクルが起きたんだ。

examples.en: Five years ago, Koichi drove Viet’s troops back from his shores where they were swallowed up by a divine wind.
examples.ja: 五年前、神風が吹き、コウイチはビエトの軍隊を海岸から後退させた。

3570.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Wind</kanji> of the <kanji>gods</kanji>. These are <vocabulary>divine winds</vocabulary>. More popularly, this is a word known as <vocabulary>kamikaze</vocabulary>, which became known because of the kamikaze pilots during WWII. This was used before WWII, though, when the entire Mongol fleet was destroyed by a storm, preventing an invasion of Japan. How lucky.
3570.reading_mnemonic: The readings are kun'yomi readings for both, probably because this is two words put together into one. You know the reading of 風 from previous levels, hopefully. Now all you need to do is apply your knowledge of the word 神 to be able to read the rest.

examples.en: Oh, I'll help.
examples.ja: あ、手伝うよ。

examples.en: Sorry, could you help me out a bit?
examples.ja: ごめん、ちょっと手伝ってくれない？

examples.en: I really want to help, but there's nothing I can do.
examples.ja: 手伝ってあげたいのはやまやまなんだけど、私にはどうにもできないんです。

3571.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>transmit</kanji> your <kanji>hand</kanji> to something or someone, you're putting out your hand <vocabulary>to help</vocabulary> them or <vocabulary>to assist</vocabulary> them.
3571.reading_mnemonic: Both of these are the kun'yomi readings that you've already learned! The thing is, the た from 伝's つた changes into だ for who knows what reason. Perhaps you can ask for someone <vocabulary>to help</vocabulary> you to understand this dumb reading change.

examples.en: I am left-handed.
examples.ja: 私は左利きです。

examples.en: Do you have scissors for left-handed people?
examples.ja: 左利きの人向けのハサミはありますか？

examples.en: Are you right-handed? Or are you left-handed?
examples.ja: あなたは右利きですか？それとも左利きですか？

3572.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>profit</kanji> from the <kanji>left</kanji>, you're probably doing everything on the left. That's your good side. You're probably <vocabulary>left handed</vocabulary>.
3572.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the kun'yomi vocab readings, so combine the readings of the words 左 and 利く together to get the reading of this one. It makes sense since this word is like two words put together.

examples.en: We have physical education tomorrow.
examples.ja: 明日は体育があります。

examples.en: Before physical education class, please make sure to trim your nails.
examples.ja: 体育の前には、必ずツメを切って来てください。

examples.en: When is "Health and Sports Day" again? It's in October, right?
examples.ja: 「体育の日」っていつだっけ？十月だよね。

3573.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 教育 means "education?" Well, the 育 here is referring to the education word, but this time it's a <kanji>body</kanji> education. What do you call the body education at school? <vocabulary>Physical education</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>PE</vocabulary>.
3573.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My son is not right-handed.
examples.ja: 私の息子は右利きではありません。

examples.en: Even though I'm left-handed, I accidentally bought a right-handed glove.
examples.ja: 左利きなのに、右利きのグローブを買っちゃったんだ。

examples.en: I really liked her, but things got awkward after I found out she's right-handed. I don't know why.
examples.ja: 彼女のこと、すごく好きだったんだけど、右利きだって分かってからムリになっちゃったんだよね。どうしてかは分からないけど。

3574.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>right</kanji> side of your body is the side you <kanji>profit</kanji> most from. So, you use it a lot more. That's because you're <vocabulary>right handed</vocabulary>.
3574.reading_mnemonic: Both kanji use the kun'yomi vocab readings. So, think to the words 右 and 利く to learn how to read this one. It probably reads like this because it's two separate words come together (right + handed) rather than one word.

examples.en: He is someone who prefers classical music.
examples.ja: 彼はクラシック音楽を好む人です。

examples.en: Koichi likes eating black garlic.
examples.ja: コウイチは、黒ニンニクを好んで食べます。

examples.en: My cat prefers to be alone.
examples.ja: うちのネコは一人でいることを好みます。

3575.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 好き is "like." Although 好き is kind of like a verb already, this is definitely a verb. It can be <vocabulary>to be fond of</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to like</vocabulary>.
3575.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is a strange one, different from anything you've learned, kanji on'yomi or vocab kun'yomi. The reading is この, so think of this: 

What’s something easy <vocabulary>to be fond of</vocabulary>? <reading>子</reading>? <reading>No</reading> (この), not for you. You’re always saying “子? No!” Most people are fond of kids, at least their own, but not you. Noisy, germy, needy 子? No, no thank you!

examples.en: Next, I plan to grow wasabi in the office.
examples.ja: 次はオフィスでワサビを育てるつもりです。

examples.en: Could you raise this puppy instead?
examples.ja: この子犬を私の代わりに育ててくれませんか。

examples.en: What did you raise as a class when you were in elementary school? Our class raised tadpoles, hamsters, and eggplants.
examples.ja: 小学校の時、クラスで何を育ててた？うちのクラスはおたまじゃくしとハムスターとなすを育ててたよ。

3576.meaning_mnemonic: This is similar to 育つ, except now you're doing the raising of someone. This word means <vocabulary>to bring up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to raise</vocabulary>. You can remember this because of the てる. Your version of bringing a child up involves <reading>tear</reading>ing (てる) all their clothes to make them look poor so they can get the cheaper lunch at school. You're rich because of all the tax breaks you get from all the children you're raising, but you could always use more money to fuel your StarCraft addiction (we've all been there).
3576.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 育つ. So long as you know that one, you know how to read this one as well.

examples.en: I think I'll catch up in about five minutes.
examples.ja: あと五分くらいで追い付くと思う。

examples.en: If you can catch up with Kristen in the hundred meter dash, you can compete in the Olympics.
examples.ja: 100メートル走でクリステンに追い付くことができたらオリンピックに出られるよ。

examples.en: I'm still trying to catch up emotionally a bit.
examples.ja: まだちょっと気持ちが追い付いてないんです。

3577.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>follow</kanji> then <kanji>attach</kanji> yourself to whoever you're following is <vocabulary>to catch up with</vocabulary> someone.
3577.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji, but you can also just notice that this word includes 追う and 付く combined.

examples.en: Are you planning to fight alone?
examples.ja: 一人で戦うつもりなの？

examples.en: Japan and America fought in WWII.
examples.ja: 第二次世界大戦で日本とアメリカは戦いました。

examples.en: My brother is fighting against an illness.
examples.ja: 私の兄は病気と戦っています。

3578.meaning_mnemonic: This is the verb version of the vocab word <vocabulary>戦い</vocabulary>, which I'm hoping you learned earlier. The verb version of course means <vocabulary>to fight</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to battle</vocabulary>.
3578.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 戦い a word you've hopefully seen by now. Associate these words together in your mind and you'll be able to read them so long as you know the other one.

examples.en: I have no intention of pursuing Mari.
examples.ja: マリのこと、追いかけるつもりはないよ。

examples.en: He forgot his passport! I have to go after him right now.
examples.ja: あいつ、パスポート忘れてる！今すぐ追いかけなきゃ。

examples.en: I saw a lion chasing a rabbit over there.
examples.ja: あそこで、ウサギを追いかけるライオンを見ました。

3579.meaning_mnemonic: 追う means "to follow" or “to chase” and かける in this case means “to run,” so this word means <vocabulary>to chase</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to pursue</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to run after</vocabulary> someone or something.
3579.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 追う as well as the kanji reading you learned too.

examples.en: I'll order it on Amazon!
examples.ja: Amazonで注文するよ！

examples.en: I ordered wrapping paper covered in silver glitter.
examples.ja: 銀色のラメの入ったラッピングペーパーを注文しました。

examples.en: We could eat out or order takeout. I don’t mind one way or the other.
examples.ja: 外食でも、お持ち帰りで注文しても、僕はどちらでも構わないよ。

3580.meaning_mnemonic: You hopefully have seen the word 注文 (order, request). This is just the verb version: <vocabulary>to order</vocabulary> / <vocabulary>to request</vocabulary>.
3580.reading_mnemonic: If you know the reading of 注文 you should be able to read this one too. Also, it's just all jukugo on'yomi readings, so you should be able to read it anyways.

examples.en: I love you.
examples.ja: 大好きです。

examples.en: No matter what he says, Fugu still likes WaniKani a lot.
examples.ja: なんだかんだ言っても、フグはワニカニのことが大好きなんですよ。

examples.en: I know it's not good for my health, but I really love McDonald's fries.
examples.ja: 体に良くないのは分かってるけど、マクドナルドのポテト、大好きなんだよね。

3581.meaning_mnemonic:
You've hopefully seen 好き by now, which is "to like." So, what happens when you have a 大 (big) like? You <vocabulary>really like</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>like a lot</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>love</vocabulary> something.

This is the same as 好き in that a more literal translation would be <vocabulary>lovable</vocabulary>, but it's generally translated as a verb in English.
3581.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 好き which you've hopefully seen. Then, 大 is the reading you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: This letter conveyed my mother's feelings.
examples.ja: この手紙で母の気持ちは伝わりました。

examples.en: Apparently not all teammates got the message that there won't be practice tomorrow.
examples.ja: 明日が休みなの、チームメイト全員に伝わってなかったみたい。

examples.en: Even though you can't speak Japanese well, if you try to speak with your heart, people will understand.
examples.ja: 日本語が上手に話せなくても心で話せばきっと相手に伝わりますよ。

3582.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means transmit, and this verb version is to be transmitted or to be conveyed. It's intransitive, so it doesn't take a direct object. A message is transmitted, or your feelings are conveyed — that kind of thing. Verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
3582.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 伝える.

examples.en: The balloon escaped from the girl's hands.
examples.ja: 風船が女の子の手から放れた。

examples.en: I wonder how that dog was able to get off its leash.
examples.ja: あの犬はどうやってクサリから放れることができたんだろう。

examples.en: Once our son is off our hands, we are planning to live in the U.S.
examples.ja: 息子が私たちの手から放れたら、アメリカに住むつもりです。

3583.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 放す is "to release"? Now you're learning the intransitive version. Instead of you doing the releasing, something gets released or freed. So this is <vocabulary>to get loose</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to escape</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to be released</vocabulary>.

放れる describes something held in place coming loose and starting to move, like an animal breaking free from its tether or an arrow being released from a bowstring. You know this because it's pretty rare (れる) for something that's restrained to break free from its bonds. Escaping isn't easy, so it only happens on rare occasions.
3583.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same one you learned with 放す. If you can remember that word, you can apply the reading over here as well.

examples.en: I'm in the dentist's waiting room now.
examples.ja: 今、歯医者の待合室にいます。

examples.en: There were many people in the hospital waiting room.
examples.ja: 病院の待合室にはたくさんの人がいました。

examples.en: It was too cold waiting outside for the night bus because there was no waiting room. Please build a waiting room!
examples.ja: 待合室がないので、夜行バスを外で待つのが寒すぎた。待合室作ってくれ！

3584.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>room</kanji> where you <kanji>join</kanji> other people to <kanji>wait</kanji>. This is a <vocabulary>waiting room</vocabulary>.
3584.reading_mnemonic: Remember how you learned 待合 already? Well throw the on'yomi for 室 on the end of that and you have your reading!

examples.en: That person seems unpleasant, don't they?
examples.ja: あの人感じ悪いよね。

examples.en: I really like the retro feel of this cafe.
examples.ja: このカフェ、レトロな感じがすごく好きなんだよね。

examples.en: What’s it feel like to be a company president, Mr. Koichi?
examples.ja: コウイチさん、社長になるって、どんな感じですか？

3585.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned that 感じる means "to feel." This is the noun version, which means a <vocabulary>feeling</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>sense</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>impression</vocabulary>.

感じ is a casual word for the intuitive feeling or vibe something gives off. It doesn't usually refer to deep emotions, but rather the overall sense or atmosphere you get from a situation, person, or thing. This is one of those words you'll hear and use all the time — いい感じ (nice vibe), そんな感じ (something like that), どんな感じ？(what's it like?), and so on.
3585.reading_mnemonic: If you can read 感じる, you should be able to read this too. It uses the same reading — just without る.

examples.en: How one feels varies from person to person.
examples.ja: どう感じるかは人それぞれです。

examples.en: Don't look at it, feel it with your heart.
examples.ja: 見るのではなく、心で感じてください。

examples.en: I feel like my older brother has been giving me the cold shoulder recently.
examples.ja: 最近兄に冷たくされていると感じます。

3586.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>feeling</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to feel</vocabulary>.
3586.reading_mnemonic: Guess what? Even though this would use the vocab kun'yomi reading, usually, the readings for both on'yomi and kun'yomi on this kanji are the same, meaning you can read this word no matter what. Feeling better now?

examples.en: Oh, I want to be moved. Please let me know if you have any recommendations for moving films.
examples.ja: あー、感動したい。感動する映画のおすすめがあったら教えてください。

examples.en: This musical was incredibly moving!
examples.ja: このミュージカル、めっちゃ感動しました！

examples.en: We were also moved when we heard users say they were impressed by the WaniKani system.
examples.ja: ワニカニのシステムに感動したって言ってくれるユーザーさんの声を聞いて、私たちも感動しました。

3587.meaning_mnemonic:
You know this is a verb from the する. Your <kanji>feeling</kanji>s are getting <kanji>move</kanji>d, so it means <vocabulary>to be emotionally moved</vocabulary> — describing how you're deeply affected by something. In English, this is sometimes phrased as <vocabulary>to be moving</vocabulary>, referring to the emotional impact something has, like a heartfelt movie.

感動する is used whenever something reaches you on a deep, genuine level, like when you're moved by an emotional speech, a touching story, or a stunning view.
3587.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: You have such an admirable child.
examples.ja: 感心なお子さんですね。

examples.en: I'm so impressed that you study every single day.
examples.ja: 毎日勉強するなんて、感心、感心。

examples.en: Katie never ceases to impress me.
examples.ja: ケイティには、いつも感心させられっぱなしです。

3588.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>feeling</kanji>s are in your <kanji>heart</kanji>. When your feelings are in your heart they are pure feelings. You can be happy for people and feel <vocabulary>admiration</vocabulary> for their successes. This is a great feeling to have in your heart.

感心 expresses that you are <vocabulary>being impressed</vocabulary> by someone's effort, skill, or good behavior. You'll hear it when someone does something <vocabulary>praiseworthy</vocabulary> and you genuinely admire it, like 感心した (I’m impressed).
3588.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: If you don't mind, please let me know your thoughts.
examples.ja: よかったら、感想を聞かせてください。

examples.en: The homework is a book review for this book.
examples.ja: 宿題はこの本の感想文です。

examples.en: That's just your opinion, isn't it?
examples.ja: それってただのあなたの感想ですよね？

3589.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>feeling</kanji>s you <kanji>contemplate</kanji> about a subject are your <vocabulary>impressions</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>thoughts</vocabulary> on it.

感想 is all about what you think or feel after experiencing something, like after reading a book, watching a movie, or going to an event.
3589.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Let's show our gratitude to everyone on Thanksgiving Day.
examples.ja: 感謝祭の日にはみんなに感謝しましょう。

examples.en: I never say it out loud, but I'm always grateful to my parents.
examples.ja: 言葉には出さないけど、親にはいつも感謝しています。

examples.en: I can't thank everyone enough. It's because of all of you that I'm able to stand here.
examples.ja: 皆さんには感謝してもしきれません。私がここにいる立てるのは、皆さんのおかげです。

3590.meaning_mnemonic: You have <kanji>feeling</kanji>s of <kanji>apologizing</kanji>. Strangely, this word means <vocabulary>thanks</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>gratitude</vocabulary>, though. Perhaps someone did something so nice for you that you want to apologize for how many nice things they're doing for you. You are this grateful to them!
3590.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Even though there are many people in Tokyo, it is well organized.
examples.ja: 東京は人が多いけれど整然としています。

examples.en: Darin always provides well-reasoned explanations.
examples.ja: ダリンはいつも理路整然とした説明をしてくれます。

examples.en: The neatly arranged wine bottles on the shelves of the Tofugu office were all emptied out by Mami.
examples.ja: トーフグオフィスの棚に整然と並べられていたワインボトルを、マミが全部空けてしまった。

3591.meaning_mnemonic:
Something with an <kanji>arrange</kanji>d <kanji>nature</kanji> must be very <vocabulary>orderly</vocabulary>. Nicely arranged, very tidy and orderly!

Note that for this word, you need to add と to the end to make it an adverb, and たる to make it an adjective! It's quite formal, so you'll mostly just see it in literature to describe something that's been arranged in an orderly way.
3591.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: How much is the admission fee?
examples.ja: 入館料はいくらですか？

examples.en: The entrance fee here is too expensive.
examples.ja: ここの入館料は高すぎます。

examples.en: No admission fee is required today.
examples.ja: 今日は入館料はいりません。

3592.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>fee</kanji> for <kanji>enter</kanji>ing a <kanji>public building</kanji> is the <vocabulary>admission fee</vocabulary>. Gotta pay it if you want to get inside.
3592.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Are gas bills expensive in Japan?
examples.ja: 日本はガスの料金は高いですか。

examples.en: Can you show me your fee plan first?
examples.ja: まずは料金プランを見せてもらえますか？

examples.en: No fee is charged for the first time.
examples.ja: 初回は料金はかかりません。

3593.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>fee</kanji> <kanji>gold</kanji> (or money) you have to pay is a <vocabulary>fee</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>charge</vocabulary>.

You've learned 代金, which generally refers to the money paid for physical goods, but 料金 refers to a fee or charge for using a service — think bus fares, highway tolls, entrance fees, monthly service charges, that kind of thing.
3593.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The password is being projected on the screen.
examples.ja: スクリーンにパスワードが映っていますよ。

examples.en: Is it true that you look fatter on TV?
examples.ja: テレビに映ると太って見えるって本当ですか？

examples.en: I wonder if it will properly appear on the screen.
examples.ja: ちゃんとスクリーンに映るかな。

examples.en: Didn't Dad appear on TV just now?
examples.ja: 今、テレビにお父さん映らなかった？

examples.en: During the video call, the dog's face unexpectedly appeared and it was heartwarming.
examples.ja: テレビ電話をしていると、犬の顔がひょっこり映ってほっこりした。

examples.en: I can't forget the beautiful moon reflected in the water that we saw together that night.
examples.ja: その夜、君と二人で見た、あの水に映る美しい月が忘れられません。

3594.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>reflect</kanji>. The verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to be reflected</vocabulary>. You're not doing the reflecting directly. You can remember this by thinking how rude (る) it is that someone's reflecting your image using a mirror for everyone outside the dressing room to see.
3594.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Your reflection is getting reflected onto the mirror. You don't like it, it doesn't look like you. Impostor reflection! You take a hammer and you <reading>打つ</reading> (うつ) it as hard as you can, glass flying everywhere. Then some dubstep starts playing from the broken mirror: <reading>うつ</reading>うつうつうつ. 

You might recall that this reading is the same as <reading>写</reading>る and might wonder if they're related. They are! They both talk about the image of something showing up somewhere else, and use different kanji to distinguish where. In 写る's case, that would typically be in photographs, and for 映る, it's in reflections or projections (which includes the contents of screens, like those of TVs or computers).

examples.en: What kind of movies do you usually watch?
examples.ja: いつもどんな映画を見ますか？

examples.en: Would you like to go see a movie together?
examples.ja: いっしょに映画を見に行きませんか？

examples.en: This is a horror movie.
examples.ja: これはホラー映画です。

3595.meaning_mnemonic: It's a <kanji>reflect</kanji>ion of an <kanji>image</kanji> on a screen, and the image is moving! What is this? It's a <vocabulary>movie</vocabulary>.
3595.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Oh, a new movie theater has been built.
examples.ja: あ、新しい映画館ができてる。

examples.en: I love the caramel butter popcorn at the movie theater.

You're thrown into something <vocabulary>dark</vocabulary> and small. A lid is closed on top of you, and you are confused. What have you been thrown in? 3600.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

3600.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji.

3601.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the reading you learned with the kanji. The second one is ざま however, which plays right into the "various" meaning of the word. There's even various ways to read さま in this word!

Just imagine looking at this signpost in the distance. You know you have to get to it from where you are. That is the goal of your journey.

As you're trekking towards it there are people standing to the side <reading>mock</reading>ing you, telling you you'll never make it to your goal. Imagine this happening.

3604.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3604.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji! No need to burn any 橋s with this word and its kanji.

examples.en: How are you planning to kill that fly?

3605.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>kill</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to kill</vocabulary>.
3605.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You <vocabulary>kill</vocabulary> someone! Oh no, what are you going to do? Where will you put the body? You decide to stuff it into the <reading>core</reading> (ころ) of a nuclear silo. It will melt and disappear in there, right? At least, that's what you think. Imagine opening up the core of the nuclear silo and feel the burn of the radiation. You throw the body in and close the core, then run away. Unfortunately, this nuclear core will kill you too, eventually. Then, it will kill everyone in the area, because the body you threw in will overheat the core, causing a giant explosion.

examples.en: I'm also not good with murder scenes in dramas.

examples.en: Huh, murder at our school!? Is that for real?

examples.en: I don't think this murder plan will go well.

3606.meaning_mnemonic: When a <kanji>person</kanji> is <kanji>kill</kanji>ed, you have yourself a <vocabulary>murder</vocabulary>.

3608.meaning_mnemonic:
If you know <kanji>all</kanji> of something's <kanji>nature</kanji> then you know it <vocabulary>entirely</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>completely</vocabulary>. If you don't, then you know it <vocabulary>not at all</vocabulary>.

This word is weird. It can mean two opposite things depending on what kind of word comes after it. If it's a negative word, it'll mean "not at all." If it's not negative, it'll mean "entirely." Check out the patterns of use and context sentences for examples.
3608.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

Something that's <kanji>right</kanji> by its very <kanji>nature</kanji> is <vocabulary>natural</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>obvious</vocabulary>. 

当然 is also often used as an expression to mean <vocabulary>of course</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>naturally</vocabulary>. It's used when something is expected or goes without saying, like a confident "yeah, that's how it should be."

3610.meaning_mnemonic:
To find your <kanji>self</kanji>'s true <kanji>nature</kanji>, go out into <vocabulary>nature</vocabulary>. Go out into the forests and fields, do some reading and thinking, and find your true nature.

This can also mean "natural" when it's used as a な adjective, like in 自然な日本語 (natural Japanese) or 自然な色 (natural color).
3610.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Wait! Except 自 is し and not じ! That is because when you add the little dakuten you are adding to the し. When it has no dakuten, it is in the form that <vocabulary>nature</vocabulary> intended.

If you haven't run into that word, you've probably run into the kanji 暑 at least. That uses the reading あつ. Two similar concepts, but there are two kanji to differentiate, which gets confusing.

3637.meaning_mnemonic: This is a tricky word that doesn't really have a good translation. The best ways I've seen it done in terms of getting a meaning across are <vocabulary>please</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>please help me</vocabulary>. When you say this word you're kind of saying "please help me out and I'm relying on you and you're kind of awesome too." Anyways, <vocabulary>please</vocabulary> is a pretty good way to do it. So, when you see this word you'll notice it has the <kanji>request</kanji> kanji in it. You can guess you're requesting something. What is that thing? It's help (<vocabulary>please help me</vocabulary>) and you're asking very nicely too (<vocabulary>please</vocabulary>).
3637.reading_mnemonic: You ask for help by saying <vocabulary>please help me</vocabulary>, and that person does try to help you... but the amount they do for you is so <reading>neg</reading>ligible that it hardly does anything to help you at all. Please try to help me again, this time better?

You're important, after all, so you just do what you want and make the other person wait in this giant metropolis while you move along leisurely. This word is usually used in a nicer way, though. As in, "do it at your convenience!"
3649.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for 都 is an exception from what you learned with the kanji. To remember this, just think about someone who does something at their own convenience. They say, I'm going <reading>to go</reading> (つごう) where I want, when I want, at my own convenience.

The 合 (ごう) part is a reading you know from the kanji, though, so if you can get to "to go" with the mnemonic, you should be able to put two and two together to know that it's a long vowel ごう.

3662.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji itself means <kanji>participate</kanji>, so you'd think this word would mean "to participate" but it's a little more complex than that. Think of it as "to participate" but where you have <vocabulary>to come</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to go</vocabulary> in order to do it. This is the humble way to say those things, so you're going to these places with your tail between your legs, just happy you can participate more than anything. By extension, this is also a humble way to say <vocabulary>to visit</vocabulary>, often used if you're visiting something sacred like a shrine or a tomb. 

Historically, this word arose as a humble way to indicate visiting a person of higher social status. In a weird twist, this word has come to also mean <vocabulary>to be defeated</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be at a loss</vocabulary>. Think of it as what can happen when you're trying to participate while in an inferior position to someone or something.

3789.meaning_mnemonic: A thing that gives you <kanji>time</kanji> <kanji>measurement</kanji>s is a <vocabulary>watch</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>clock</vocabulary>. Most people have these in their phones instead of on their wrists now.
3789.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this is pretty weird. 計 is all nice and normal, but 時 is と for some reason. It probably is coming from the vocab word 時 (とき), is my guess. But even if it is, it's shortened, making it a step more complicated. Maybe it's just better to imagine that your <vocabulary>watch</vocabulary> is a walky <reading>talky</reading> (とけい) and run with that?

examples.en: That will be a total of three thousand yen.
examples.ja: 合計で三千円になります。

examples.en: The total of numbers from one to ten is fifty-five.
examples.ja: 1から10までの数字の合計は55です。

examples.en: When we totaled the number of people who came to today's event, it was more than we expected.
examples.ja: 今日のイベントに来た人の人数を合計すると、予想以上の人数でした。

3790.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>join</kanji> all your <kanji>measure</kanji>ments together you have yourself a <vocabulary>total</vocabulary>.
3790.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: We are planning to go to the beach during summer vacation.
examples.ja: 夏休みに海に行こうと計画しています。

examples.en: I like to plan but I don't like to carry out what I've planned.
examples.ja: 計画を立てるのは大好きなんですけど、計画したことを実行するのはきらいなんです。

examples.en: This plan carries risks, but if successful, the rewards are significant.
examples.ja: この計画にはリスクがありますが、成功すれば大きいです。

3791.meaning_mnemonic: You need <kanji>measurement</kanji>s and <kanji>image</kanji>s to make a <vocabulary>plan</vocabulary>. You can't follow a plan without measurements and images to refer to, right? Any good plan has measurements and drawings.
3791.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The reading for 画 is the secondary reading though (かく), so take note of that.

examples.en: He is quick at calculations.
examples.ja: 彼は計算が速いです。

examples.en: Is this calculation correct?
examples.ja: この計算、合ってる？

examples.en: That woman is famous for being calculating.
examples.ja: あの女は計算高いことで有名です。

3792.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>measure</kanji> and then <kanji>calculate</kanji> something, you are making a <vocabulary>calculation</vocabulary>. For example, you measure the length of a frog, then you calculate how many frogs you'd need to reach the moon. What is that? A calculation, of course.
3792.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My father is a former soldier.
examples.ja: うちの父は元軍人です。

examples.en: Look, there are a lot of servicemen over there. I wonder what's going on?
examples.ja: 見て、あそこに軍人さんがたくさんいる。どうしたんだろう？

examples.en: In that war, over 500,000 servicemen lost their lives.
examples.ja: その戦争では、50万人以上の軍人が命を落としました。

3793.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>army</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji> is someone in the army. What are those people called? They're <vocabulary>soldier</vocabulary>s.
3793.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I heard that my grandfather was a sailor in the Navy.
examples.ja: 僕のおじいちゃんは、海軍の軍人だったそうです。

examples.en: This is something used by the British Navy during World War II.
examples.ja: これは、第二次世界大戦の時に、イギリスの海軍が使っていたものです。

examples.en: The Japanese Navy used to eat curry once a week. This curry is now sold as "Navy Curry" even in retort pouches.
examples.ja: 日本の海軍は、週に一度カレーを食べていました。このカレーは、今では「海軍カレー」としてレトルトでも売られています。

3794.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>sea</kanji> <kanji>army</kanji> are the branch of the military that has boats and does ocean/sea things. What's that? The <vocabulary>navy</vocabulary>.
3794.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: How about we go grab a meal sometime?
examples.ja: 今度、飯でも行かない？

examples.en: Hey, still no food? I'm starving.
examples.ja: ねー、飯まだ？ハラペコなんだけど。

examples.en: This employee prefers working to eating three meals a day.
examples.ja: この社員は三度の飯より仕事をするのが好きです。

3795.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. It also refers to <vocabulary>cooked rice</vocabulary>, because you gotta eat cooked rice with every meal, so it's basically synonymous with "meal" itself.

This word has a slightly gruff feel to it so it's used mostly in informal situations.
3795.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You're eating a <vocabulary>meal</vocabulary>... MMmm, delicious! What are you eating? Well, it's a <reading>Mesh</reading> (めし) net. Taste the mesh net. It tastes terrible. This is a bad meal. Feel it in your mouth. It's weird and meshy.

examples.en: I always eat out for lunch.
examples.ja: お昼はいつも外でご飯を食べます

examples.en: Damn it! I just spilled my rice.
examples.ja: しまった！ご飯こぼしちゃった。

examples.en: I wonder what to make for dinner tonight.
examples.ja: 今日の夜ご飯は何を作ろうかな。

3796.meaning_mnemonic: The ご just makes this word more polite and fancy — two important qualities when it comes to food. This has the same meaning as the kanji (<kanji>meal</kanji>), making it <vocabulary>meal</vocabulary>, but it can also just mean <vocabulary>cooked rice</vocabulary>. So, "Come eat your ご飯" can mean either "come eat your rice" or "come eat your meal" — or both, since most Japanese meals come with rice anyway.
3796.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Now how about you "<reading>han</reading>d" me another bowl of rice?

examples.en: I don't want to see her sad.
examples.ja: 彼女が悲しむのは見たくありません。

examples.en: Animals, as well as humans, are saddened by the deaths of their friends.
examples.ja: 人間だけではなく、動物も仲間の死を悲しみます。

examples.en: She was very saddened by the loss of her beloved pet.
examples.ja: 彼女は愛するペットが亡くなってとても悲しんでいます。

3797.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>sad</kanji> and this verb is transitive, so it means <vocabulary>to be sad about</vocabulary> something. Boohoo.
3797.reading_mnemonic: If you're going <vocabulary>to be sad about</vocabulary> something right now, it will be <reading>kana</reading> (かな). Don't use kana when you're trying to learn kanji! You'll be sad forever if you're stuck using kana your whole life, so don't let that habit start now, friend.

examples.en: Ah, I think my own home is the most relaxing place after all.
examples.ja: あー、やっぱり自分の家が一番落ち着くわ。

examples.en: Mom, please listen calmly.
examples.ja: お母さん、落ち着いて聞いてください。

examples.en: Viet is good at soothing babies.
examples.ja: ビエトは赤ちゃんを落ち着かせるのが上手い。

3798.meaning_mnemonic: Hey. <kanji>Drop</kanji> yourself down and <kanji>arrive</kanji> back to me. You're going nuts over there. Lower down. Come back. Arrive. You need to do these things <vocabulary>to calm down</vocabulary>.
3798.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 落ちる and 着く. Hopefully you know these words so you can read this word as well! If you don't, just 落ち着く and everything will be okay.

examples.en: Ah, you startled me! Why are you wearing that mask?
examples.ja: わぁ、びっくりした！何で仮面なんてかぶってるの？

examples.en: Behind her smiling mask, she might actually be crying.
examples.ja: 彼女は笑顔の仮面の下で、本当は泣いているのかもしれないよ。

examples.en: On the Halloween night, I saw Viet wearing the Masked Rider costume and eating a whole box of chocolates.
examples.ja: ハロウィンの日の夜、仮面ライダーのコスプレをしながら、チョコレートを一箱平らげたビエトを見ました。

3799.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>temporary</kanji> <kanji>face</kanji> is something you put over your face to cover it. It's a <vocabulary>mask</vocabulary>.
3799.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I know Viet is involved with a dangerous organization, but I still don't think that he has anything to do with the crime.
examples.ja: ビエトがやばいそしきと係わっているのは知っているけど、そのはんざいに係わっていたとはやっぱり思えないんだよな。

examples.en: Don't get involved with people like that.
examples.ja: あのれん中には係わらない方がいいよ。

examples.en: If you ate blowfish without taking the poison out, it would be a matter of life and death.
examples.ja: もし毒抜きをせずに河豚を食べたら、命に係わりますよ。

3800.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that the kanji means <kanji>connection</kanji>. This is a verb, so one meaning is <vocabulary>to be connected</vocabulary>. It can also mean <vocabulary>to be involved</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to be related</vocabulary>. Basically things that have to do with being connected with something else.

Does this all sound familiar? In fact, this is another way to write 関わる, which you already learned! The two have exactly the same meaning, but this version is a bit less common.
3800.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. It's exactly the same as the reading for 関わる, so here's a reminder of that mnemonic to help you:

Remember the "<reading>Kaw Kaw</reading> (かか) Crow Gang"? They are bad news, always eating from garbage and squawking "kaw kaw"... You don't want <vocabulary>to be involved</vocabulary> with them.

examples.en: The high school I went to was very conservative.
examples.ja: 私の通っていた高校は、とても保守的な学校でした。

examples.en: That artist has many fans with conservative views.
examples.ja: あのアーティストには、保守的な考え方のファンが多い。

examples.en: People tend to become more conservative as they get older, but I don't want to be like that.
examples.ja: 年を重ねるにつれて保守的になる人が多いけど、私はそうはなりたくありません。

3801.meaning_mnemonic: Who are all <kanji>like</kanji> "I want to <kanji>preserve</kanji> and <kanji>protect</kanji> what I have, get out of my business, government!"? <vocabulary>Conservative</vocabulary> people, of course.
3801.reading_mnemonic: The reading doesn't match up for this word's 守. The reading is しゅ, but you can remember that because the conservatives want to protect and preserve their <reading>hoe</reading>s (ほ) and their <reading>chute</reading>s (しゅ) from the government. For some reason those get taxed a lot.

examples.en: Please tell me how to store bananas.
examples.ja: バナナの保存方法を教えてください。

examples.en: Data should be regularly backed up and saved.
examples.ja: データは定期的にバックアップして保存しておくべきです。

examples.en: How long should I keep the receipts for?
examples.ja: レシートっていつまで保存しておけばいいんですか？

3802.meaning_mnemonic: We try to <kanji>preserve</kanji> anything we want to <kanji>exist</kanji> with <vocabulary>preservation</vocabulary>. Want a special sea creature or bird to exist? Up <vocabulary>conservation</vocabulary> efforts! And, if you want to save data (like on a computer), you can use this word for that kind of <vocabulary>saving</vocabulary>, as well.
3802.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It is important for the factory to maintain high quality.
examples.ja: 高いクオリティを保持するのは工場にとって大切なことです。

examples.en: I retained the US title this year too.
examples.ja: 今年も全米タイトルを保持しました。

examples.en: The data will be preserved for one month, then it will be gone.
examples.ja: データは一ヶ月保持された後は、全てなくなります。

3803.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>preserve</kanji> the things you <kanji>hold</kanji> on to, you're <vocabulary>keep</vocabulary>ing them. In other words, you're <vocabulary>hold</vocabulary>ing and <vocabulary>maintain</vocabulary>ing them!

Note that 保持 is a formal word that's commonly used in professional or official contexts.
3803.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Do you have life insurance?
examples.ja: 生命保険、入ってる？

examples.en: Which travel insurance did you choose?
examples.ja: 旅行保険、どこのやつにした？

examples.en: Oh no, I left my health insurance card at home again.
examples.ja: しまった。また家に保険証を忘れてきちゃった。

3804.meaning_mnemonic: When you are able to <kanji>guarantee</kanji> against <kanji>risk</kanji>, it's probably because you bought some good <vocabulary>insurance</vocabulary>! What do you use? The gecko 保険?
3804.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Please keep the warranty certificate safe.
examples.ja: 保証書を失くさないようにしてください。

examples.en: This product comes with a one-year warranty.
examples.ja: この商品には一年間の保証が付いています。

examples.en: I am a lifetime member of WaniKani, but I don't really think I can use it for life, as there is no guarantee that Tofugu will still be around in five years.
examples.ja: 私はワニカニのライフタイムメンバーですが、トーフグが五年後もあるなんて保証はないから本当にライフタイムでワニカニが使えるなんて思っていませんよ。

3805.meaning_mnemonic:
Giving <kanji>evidence</kanji> (or a <kanji>guarantee</kanji>) that you will <kanji>preserve</kanji> something, is giving a <vocabulary>guarantee</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>assurance</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>warranty</vocabulary>.

This word is used when the emphasis is on taking responsibility for something, as in a guarantor, a product warranty, or quality assurance.
3805.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: A life insurance sales manager came home earlier.
examples.ja: さっき生保のセールスマネジャーが家に来ましたよ。

examples.en: When the heck can I get the money from my deceased husband's life insurance?
examples.ja: 亡くなった主人の生保のお金は、一体いつもらえるんですか？

examples.en: If you buy life insurance, you will have peace of mind if anything ever happens to you.
examples.ja: 生保に入れば、万が一自分に何かあったとしても安心です。

3806.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>Life</kanji> <kanji>guarantee</kanji> is something you get on someone else. If their life ends, it's guaranteed with money. That's a <vocabulary>life insurance</vocabulary> policy, for yah! (A.K.A. <vocabulary>life assurance</vocabulary> in some parts of the world!)
3806.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: To keep your physical strength, you have to train every day.
examples.ja: 体力を保つには毎日トレーニングしなくてはいけません。

examples.en: I do yoga and meditation to maintain a healthy heart.
examples.ja: 元気な心を保つために、ヨガやメディテーションをします。

examples.en: I want to live a healthy life and maintain my current weight.
examples.ja: ヘルシーな生活を送って、今の体重を保ちたいと思います。

3807.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>preserve</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to preserve something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to keep something</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to maintain something</vocabulary>.

This is a transitive verb, so it takes a direct object. You preserve something, like your youth.
3807.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

If you want to learn how <vocabulary>to preserve something</vocabulary> like fruits and veggies, you should start with <reading>tamots</reading> (たも), that's slang for delish tomatoes. Once they're preserved, you get to make everyone you love eat those yummy tamots. Mmm!

examples.en: I bought three Buddhist statues in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本で仏像を三体買いました。

examples.en: As many as fifty Buddha statues have been unearthed in the park there.
examples.ja: あそこの公園で、五十体もの仏像が出土されたそうです。

examples.en: Someone sends a Buddhist statue to our office every month. If you are that person, please come forward and identify yourself.
examples.ja: 誰かがうちのオフィスに毎月仏像を一体ずつ送ってくるんです。心当たりのある方は、どうか名乗り出て下さい。

3808.meaning_mnemonic:
You have <kanji>Buddha</kanji> and 像, which you learned mainly as "image" but can also mean <kanji>statue</kanji>. So that makes this a <vocabulary>statue of Buddha</vocabulary>. 仏像 can also just mean an <vocabulary>image of Buddha</vocabulary>, of course.

仏像 refers to statues, paintings, or artistic representations of Buddhist figures used as objects of worship. While it often means Buddha sculptures, it also includes depictions not just of the Buddha himself but other Buddhist deities as well.
3808.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That's quite a classical joke, isn't it?
examples.ja: ずいぶん古典的なギャグだね。

examples.en: It's super shameful that I was deceived by such a classical fraud.
examples.ja: こんな古典的なサギに引っかかってしまって、本当に情けないです。

examples.en: I broke up with the guy I met on a dating app because his views on classic masterpieces were too old-fashioned and didn't align with mine.
examples.ja: デートアプリで出会った彼は、古典的名作に対する考え方が古典的すぎて、私とは意見が合わなかったので別れました。

3809.meaning_mnemonic: When something is "<kanji>old</kanji> <kanji>rule</kanji>s-<kanji>like</kanji>," it is not very modern. It is in the past. It is <vocabulary>classical</vocabulary>.
3809.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This word appears in Buddhist scriptures.
examples.ja: この言葉は、仏典の中に登場します。

examples.en: They have memorized all Sanskrit Buddhist scriptures, Pali Buddhist scriptures, and Chinese Buddhist scriptures.
examples.ja: 彼らはサンスクリット語仏典、パーリ語仏典、漢語仏典を全て丸暗記しています。

examples.en: I love your smile. It feels like it holds more power than several volumes of Buddhist scriptures.
examples.ja: 私はあなたの笑顔が大好きです。あなたの笑顔には、仏典数冊分以上のパワーが感じられます。

3810.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Buddha</kanji> transcribed all of the <kanji>rule</kanji>s of Buddhism in the <vocabulary>Buddhist Scriptures</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>Buddhist Writing</vocabulary>s.
3810.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Note that ぶつ gets shortened to ぶっ.

examples.en: Oh, are dictionaries OK for tomorrow's test?
examples.ja: え、明日のテスト、字典使ってOKなの？

examples.en: I love reading ancient character dictionaries.
examples.ja: 私は古代文字字典を読むのが大好きです。

examples.en: I bought this Japanese-origin kanji dictionary at that secondhand bookstore over there.
examples.ja: この国字字典はあそこの古本屋で買ったんです。

3811.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Letter</kanji> <kanji>rule</kanji>s can be found in a <vocabulary>character dictionary</vocabulary>. In Japanese, one kanji "letter" or "character" can hold a lot of information, so you have dictionaries dedicated to kanji meanings. That's what this is.

This word is a little old-fashioned these days, so you might also see 漢字辞典 used for a character dictionary. (You'll learn 辞典 soon, if you haven't already!)
3811.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What kind of encyclopedia is that?
examples.ja: それ、何の事典？

examples.en: This encyclopedia uses a lot of photographs and illustrations.
examples.ja: この事典には、写真やイラストがたくさん使われています。

examples.en: Every year, I received an encyclopedia from Santa Claus as a Christmas present.
examples.ja: 毎年、サンタさんからクリスマスに百科事典をプレゼントしてもらっていました。

3812.meaning_mnemonic: If you come across a <kanji>matter</kanji> in which the <kanji>rule</kanji>s aren’t clear, you’ll need to have a look in an <vocabulary>encyclopedia</vocabulary>!
3812.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: We should reserve our energy for our adventure tomorrow.
examples.ja: 明日からの冒険のために、力を残しておいた方がいいよ。

examples.en: Wow, this illustration gives off the vibe of an adventurer's tavern, huh?

examples.en: Koichi left his job at WaniKani and embarked on a new adventure with Pikachu.

3813.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>dare</kanji> to do something <kanji>risky</kanji>. It's <vocabulary>adventure</vocabulary> time! Imagine yourself daring yourself to do risky things. Is this an adventure? If not, make it so!
3813.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Please don't say things like that even as a joke.
examples.ja: 冗談でもそんなこと言わないで。

examples.en: She's good at telling jokes and always entertains us.
examples.ja: 彼女は冗談が上手で、いつも楽しませてくれます。

examples.en: Tofugu likes joking on their podcast.
examples.ja: トーフグはポッドキャストで冗談ばかり言っている。

3814.meaning_mnemonic: When you have a <kanji>superfluous</kanji> <kanji>talk</kanji> you aren't being serious, you're telling a <vocabulary>joke</vocabulary>.
3814.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This is the most dangerous job in the world.
examples.ja: これは世界一危険な仕事です。

examples.en: In stations, there is often an announcement that says, "It will be unsafe, so please stay behind the yellow line."

It can also use the on'yomi, though, which you've already learned. When it takes the on'yomi and is used as a standalone word, it usually refers to some kind of institution, like a 幼稚園.

3826.meaning_mnemonic:
This is like a very formal and humble way of saying <vocabulary>to know</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to believe</vocabulary>. Sure, the kanji means <kanji>suppose</kanji>, but think of it this way... When you say "I suppose" it's like a humble way of saying "I know" or "I believe." You're not being as direct about it this way, and in Japanese, that makes you more humble and polite. So, that's why 存じる means <vocabulary>to know</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to believe</vocabulary>.

Note this word is typically used in the polite ます form. When you’re humble, you may want to be as polite as possible, I suppose!

examples.en: It seems like the express train bound for Kyoto departs from platform three.

examples.en: I saw a patrol car rushing somewhere around that corner.

This is often used with trains or subways, so look out for it if you're looking to get somewhere in a hurry. Also be careful in case it doesn't stop at your stop, because 急行 trains don't stop at every station (which is what makes them express!).
3841.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.
