examples.en: Salmon's attitude toward the government is very conservative.
examples.ja: サーモンの政治に対する考えはとても保守的です。

examples.en: Do you know what politics is for? It's to protect the lives of the citizens and to absolutely prevent war.
examples.ja: 政治って何のためのものか分かりますか？国民の生活を守るためと、ゼッタイに戦争をしないためですよ。

3842.meaning_mnemonic: If you want to <kanji>cure</kanji> the <kanji>government</kanji>, you have to get into <vocabulary>politics</vocabulary>. Gotta join 'em to fix them... but can you survive that long without being corrupted yourself?
3842.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I need to think of what to blog about!
examples.ja: ブログに書くこと考えなきゃ！

examples.en: The notes I had written down went somewhere.
examples.ja: せっかく書いたメモがどこかに行ってしまった。

examples.en: Koichi's handwriting is far from being good.
examples.ja: コウイチは、お世辞にも字を書くのが上手だとは言えません。

3843.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>write</kanji> so the verb version means <vocabulary>to write</vocabulary>.
3843.reading_mnemonic: The reading you learned with the kanji is the on'yomi one, but this word is read with the kun'yomi, か. So just be sure to remember the kun'yomi reading to read this word in the <reading>ca</reading>r (か) ... or <vocabulary>to write</vocabulary> it, or whatever.

examples.en: You can return any unsold stock, so would you let us sell our products here?
examples.ja: 残品はこちらで引き取るので、こちらのお店で販売させてもらえませんか。

examples.en: Before we leave the store tonight, let’s go ahead and count the remaining stock.
examples.ja: 今夜店を出発する前に残品を数えておきましょう。

examples.en: We sold the remaining goods at half price.
examples.ja: 残品は半額で処分しました。

3844.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>remainder</kanji> <kanji>product</kanji>s are the things that haven't been sold. They're the <vocabulary>unsold merchandise</vocabulary>. They're the <vocabulary>remaining stock</vocabulary>.

This is a very specific word that is mainly used in the context of inventory management or retail sales.
3844.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Note that ひん changes to ぴん.

examples.en: Medications are needed to cure this disease.
examples.ja: この病気を治すには薬が必要です。

examples.en: Do you know how to heal scratches fast?
examples.ja: キズを早く治す方法を知っていますか？

examples.en: To cure a scratchy throat, it's best to tie a leek around your neck.
examples.ja: ノドのイガイガを治すには、ネギを首にくくっておくのが一番です。

3845.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. 

The kanji itself means <kanji>cure</kanji>, and this verb means <vocabulary>to cure</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to heal</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to ease</vocabulary> something. This particular verb is when someone does the curing. The illness or injury doesn't just get better by itself. How can you remember that? Because when you try to heal someone and you mess up, they can try to <reading>sue</reading> (す) you.
3845.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

I need you <vocabulary>to heal</vocabulary> him, and I need you to heal him right <reading>now</reading> (なお). NOW NOW NOW! 

This also shares the reading for 直す, a very similar word you learned previously, which means "to fix." I'm guessing that the Japanese word なおす was only one word ("to fix" and "to cure" are pretty similar, right?). Then, there were two Chinese words for it (as you can see with the kanji), so the one Japanese word got split into two very similar words.

examples.en: It seems like it will take about six months to fully recover.
examples.ja: 全治六ヶ月みたい。

examples.en: I was hit by a truck and got a bad injury that will take a year to heal completely.
examples.ja: トラックにはねられて全治一年の大ケガをしました。

examples.en: My child got a stress fracture during gym class, and the doctor said it would take two months to heal. But at first, the principal said something like, "Crying over something like this..." Isn't that awful?
examples.ja: うちの子、体育で骨にヒビが入って全治二ヶ月だったんですが、最初は校長先生から「これぐらいでこんなに泣くなんて…」みたいに言われてたんですよ。ありえなくないですか？

3846.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>All</kanji> <kanji>cure</kanji>d! That means you've made a <vocabulary>complete recovery</vocabulary>! You're <vocabulary>completely healed</vocabulary>!
3846.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That disease is currently still considered incurable.
examples.ja: その病気は今はまだ不治の病とされています。

examples.en: He's incurably addicted to social media, so there's no hope for him anymore.
examples.ja: アイツは不治のSNS中毒だから、もうダメだよ。

examples.en: Rather than battling an incurable suffering, I might choose euthanasia.
examples.ja: 私は不治の苦しみと戦うよりも、安楽死する方を選ぶかもしれません。

3847.meaning_mnemonic: When you can <kanji>not</kanji> <kanji>cure</kanji> something, this is a problem of <vocabulary>incurability</vocabulary>.
3847.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My grandmother was born in the Meiji era.
examples.ja: 私のおばあちゃんは明治生まれです。

examples.en: I'm writing an essay about Meiji literature.
examples.ja: 明治文学についての作文を書いています。

examples.en: During the Meiji era, ten thousand yen was a large sum of money.
examples.ja: 明治時代は一万円が大金だったんですよ。

3848.meaning_mnemonic: It’s the era of <kanji>bright</kanji> <kanji>rule</kanji>! If this doesn't make sense, don't worry about it. Focus more on the reading, which is めいじ. Sound familiar? This is the famous <vocabulary>Meiji era</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>Meiji Emperor</vocabulary>. If you don't know about it consider reading up, it's interesting history!
3848.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You didn't learn the on'yomi for 明 (めい) with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

The <vocabulary>Meiji era began</vocabulary> with a lot of changes — and by <reading>May</reading> (めい), the new Japan was already shaped.

examples.en: My dog likes to take showers.
examples.ja: ウチの犬はシャワーを浴びるのが好きです。

examples.en: This is a picture of a morning glory in the morning sun.
examples.ja: これは朝日を浴びるアサガオの写真です。

examples.en: For Christmas, I plan to stay home and watch as much Japanese anime as I can.
examples.ja: クリスマスは家にこもって日本のアニメを浴びるほど見るつもりです。

3849.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>bathe</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to bathe in</vocabulary>.

This verb is transitive, and the object is whatever you're "bathing in". It could be a bath or a shower, but it could also be the sun. So you can both シャワーを浴びる and 日の光を浴びる. More negatively, this can also mean <vocabulary>to be exposed to</vocabulary> something, such as criticism or radioactivity.
3849.reading_mnemonic: You want to know the best way <vocabulary>to bathe in</vocabulary> something? With a bunch of <reading>a</reading>ardvarks (あ) in the water. They use their sticky little tongues to clean all your cracks and crannies.

examples.en: I want to sunbathe on Totoro's big belly.
examples.ja: トトロの大きなおなかの上に乗って日光浴がしたいです。

examples.en: My policy is not to bathe, but to sunbathe on weekdays.
examples.ja: 私は平日は日光浴だけで入浴はしないポリシーなんです。

examples.en: The Tofugu dog loves to sunbathe on the balcony.
examples.ja: トーフグのワンコは、ベランダで日光浴をするのが大好きです。

3850.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 日光 is "sunlight" so when you add <kanji>bathe</kanji> you get "sunlight bathe" ... but that sounds dumb, so let's call this word <vocabulary>sunbathe</vocabulary> instead!
3850.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: We decided, spur of the moment, to take the limited express.
examples.ja: ノリで特急に乗ることに決めました。

examples.en: How much is the limited express fare?
examples.ja: 特急料金はいくらですか？

examples.en: I already got a ticket for you, so if you leave now you can still catch the 3:50 express train.
examples.ja: チケットを先に買っておいたので、今出れば三時五十分の特急に間に合うよ。

3851.meaning_mnemonic: Something that's <kanji>special</kanji> and in a <kanji>hurry</kanji> must be special indeed. This refers to <vocabulary>limited express train</vocabulary>s in Japan. They go fast, they stop at fewer stops (because they're special!) and they hurry. Look out for these if you want to get somewhere in a jiffy.
3851.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just note that the とく goes to とっ.

examples.en: I studied at Beijing University in 2013.
examples.ja: 私は2013年に北京大学に留学しました。

examples.en: When I studied abroad, I practiced speaking Japanese naturally a lot.
examples.ja: 留学先で、日本語を自然にしゃべる練習をたくさんしました。

examples.en: "My older brother didn't obey the orders of our parents and left to study abroad." "Where is he studying abroad?" "It's in the U.S."
examples.ja: 「兄は親の言いつけを守らず、留学してしまいました。」「留学先はどこなんですか？」「アメリカです。」

3852.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>detain</kanji> your <kanji>study</kanji> and take it away to a foreign place. That foreign place is having you <vocabulary>study abroad</vocabulary>.
3852.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The reading for 留 is the りゅう version. You can remember this because <reading>Ryu</reading> (りゅう) from street fighter is doing a study abroad program to learn more karate.

examples.en: Can I post photos of this place on social media?
examples.ja: ここの写真をSNSに上げてもいいですか？

examples.en: Look at this photo. Dad hasn't changed at all since then. Well, he's gained some weight, but nothing else has changed, right?
examples.ja: この写真、見て！お父さん、昔のまんま。変わったことと言えば、ちょっと太ったことくらいじゃない？

examples.en: Koichi's picture from high school was leaked.
examples.ja: コウイチの高校時代の写真が流出してしまいました。

3853.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>copy</kanji> of <kanji>reality</kanji> is a lot like magic. How do you make a copy of reality, though? You take a <vocabulary>photo</vocabulary>.
3853.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Koichi loves pure black garlic.
examples.ja: コウイチは真っ黒なニンニクが好きなんです。

examples.en: Viet came back from the beach in Hawaii with a dark tan.
examples.ja: ビエトはハワイのビーチで真っ黒に日やけして帰ってきました。

examples.en: These colored contacts show up super well, even on pitch-black pupils!
examples.ja: このカラコン、黒目が真っ黒でもめっちゃ発色するよ！

3854.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>reality</kanji> is that it's <kanji>black</kanji>. Like, so black that it's beyond fake black, it's reality black. This is so black it's <vocabulary>pitch black</vocabulary>.
3854.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 真 is the kun'yomi reading, which you haven't learned yet. Think of what is pitch black. It's your poor <reading>Ma</reading> (ま). She is so dark that she sucks in light, like a black hole... wait, she is a black hole, it explains why your Ma is pitch black.

examples.en: The cornflower's (yagurumagiku) flower meaning is 'happiness'.
examples.ja: ヤグルマギクの花言葉は「幸福」です。

examples.en: In my case, I feel like I'd be happier with a job where I don't have to do things I don't want to do, rather than being able to do what I want.
examples.ja: 私の場合は、「やりたいことができる」より「やりたくないことをやらなくていい」仕事の方が幸福度が高い気がします。

examples.en: Even if people walk the same path in life, some may feel happiness while others may feel unhappiness. Whether it's happiness or unhappiness depends solely on "how you perceive that life," that's all there is to it.
examples.ja: 同じ人生を歩んでいても、幸福と感じる人もいれば、不幸と感じる人もいる。幸福か不幸かは、「あなたがその人生をどう切り取って見るか」、それだけなんですよ。

3855.meaning_mnemonic:
With a little <kanji>happiness</kanji> and <kanji>luck</kanji> you can achieve <vocabulary>happiness</vocabulary>, though that goes without saying.

幸福 is often used to discuss happiness in a broader, more abstract sense, like the happiness of a population or the concept of happiness in philosophical contexts.
3855.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This is funny. I laughed out loud.
examples.ja: これは面白い。大声で笑いました。

examples.en: "I had a date with Fugu last night." "How did it go?" "It was fun. I laughed a lot."
examples.ja: 「昨夜、フグとデートをしたの。」「どうだった？」「楽しかった。めちゃくちゃ笑ったわ。」

3856.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>laugh</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to laugh</vocabulary>.
3856.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. You can laugh freely, now!

examples.en: I seriously love your smile!
examples.ja: 君の笑顔がマジで大好きなんだよ！

examples.en: The prince's smile made both the king and queen melt.
examples.ja: 王子の笑顔に、王様も女王様もメロメロでした。

examples.en: I wish you all a wonderful day with a smile on your face...
examples.ja: 皆様が、今日も笑顔でステキな一日になりますように…

3857.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>laugh</kanji>ing <kanji>face</kanji> is a <vocabulary> smiling face</vocabulary> (or just a <vocabulary>smile</vocabulary>!). 笑顔s all around!
3857.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word won't make you <vocabulary>smile</vocabulary>, though. You were smiling, but then you heard about the reading of this kanji. It made you yell out "<reading>EH</reading>??" (え). Just watch out for the rendaku of かお to がお.

examples.en: Where is the trash can?
examples.ja: ゴミ箱はどこですか？

examples.en: We need a trash can in this room.
examples.ja: この部屋にはゴミ箱が必要です。

examples.en: The recycling bin for plastic bottles is next to the trash can.
examples.ja: ペットボトルのリサイクルボックスはゴミ箱の横にあります。

3858.meaning_mnemonic: ゴミ means "garbage." Add a <kanji>box</kanji> to it and you have a garbage box aka a <vocabulary>garbage can</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>garbage bin</vocabulary>.
3858.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the kun'yomi reading, the one you learned with the kanji. Be sure to pay attention to the rendaku though. はこ changes to ばこ.

examples.en: Be careful with this box; it's heavy.
examples.ja: この箱、重いから気をつけてね。

examples.en: This cardboard box contains unwanted clothes.
examples.ja: このダンボール箱には、いらなくなった服が入っています。

examples.en: My husband bought a box of tomatoes, and we are struggling to finish them.
examples.ja: 夫がトマトを箱で買ってきて、食べきれなくてこまっています。

3859.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3859.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: Backpacks are convenient for carrying luggage.
examples.ja: 荷物を持ち運ぶには、バックパックが便利です。

examples.en: She hurriedly packed her belongings into a large suitcase.
examples.ja: 彼女は急いで大きなスーツケースに荷物を入れました。

examples.en: I've sent the package over there! It should arrive in about three days.
examples.ja: 荷物、そっちに送ったよ！三日ぐらいで着くみたい。

3860.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>luggage</kanji> <kanji>thing</kanji> is your <vocabulary>luggage</vocabulary>. It's also your <vocabulary>baggage</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>load</vocabulary> too.
3860.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You'll need to remember the 物 reading as もつ, though. Why? Because all your luggage just got thrown into various <reading>moats</reading> along the countryside. It's going to take you forever to collect your luggage from these moats and by then it'll be all soggy. Dangit...

examples.en: As proof of our friendship, I'll give you this Mt. Fuji keychain.
examples.ja: 友情の証として、このふじ山のキーホルダーをあげます。

examples.en: That's evidence that he cares about you, isn't it?
examples.ja: それって、彼が君のことを大切にしている証なんじゃないかな。

examples.en: Behold! This crystal is the proof of the king's authority!
examples.ja: 見よ。このクリスタルこそが、王の証なのだ！

3861.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3861.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 
Your relentless search for <vocabulary>evidence</vocabulary> has finally uncovered the existence of <reading>a</reading> <reading>car</reading> <reading>shee</reading>p (あかし)! It's a bizarre hybrid, having a car's body but a sheep's head and legs. "Ah, car sheep! I've finally found the evidence proving you're real!"

examples.en: There are no witnesses.
examples.ja: 証人はいません。

examples.en: I am also one of the witnesses.
examples.ja: 私も証人の一人です。

examples.en: He is a Jehovah's Witness.
examples.ja: 彼はエホバの証人です。

3862.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>evidence</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji> is a <vocabulary>witness</vocabulary>, because witnesses are people who provide evidence (you know, with their mouths or something).
3862.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: All of the Tofugu workers testified that they had seen Koichi eat Viet's meatball.
examples.ja: 全トーフグ社員が、コウイチがビエトのミートボールを食べるのを見たと証言しました。

examples.en: Only Michael refused because he didn't want to testify against Koichi.
examples.ja: マイケルだけは、コウイチに不利な証言はしたくないと言って、証言しませんでした。

examples.en: When Fugu allegedly put blowfish poison in the teacher's apple, all of his classmates testified that he did not do it.
examples.ja: フグが先生のリンゴにフグ毒を付けたと疑われた時、クラスメート全員が彼はやってないと証言しました。

3863.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Evidence</kanji> that you <kanji>say</kanji> is <vocabulary>testimony</vocabulary>. You could also say you're providing <vocabulary>verbal evidence</vocabulary>. Hopefully you won't have to give too much of this in your lifetime.
3863.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.ja: 私自身はコーヒーもお茶も両方のみます。

examples.en: I have never cut fish myself.
examples.ja: 私自身で魚を切ったことはありません。

examples.en: I personally have a strong desire to learn archeology, but others don't understand me.
examples.ja: 私自身は考古学を学びたいという思いが強いですが、他の人にはあまり分かってもらえません。

3864.meaning_mnemonic: "When it comes to <kanji>somebody</kanji> like my<kanji>self</kanji>... aka <kanji>I</kanji>..." When you say this you're really saying "<vocabulary>personally</vocabulary>" or "<vocabulary>as for me</vocabulary>."
3864.reading_mnemonic: The readings are a bit weird here. The 私 is わたし and the rest is on'yomi kanji readings. So, it's a mix of both, I'm afraid. "When it comes to me, I like mixing up on'yomi and kun'yomi because I hate myself."

examples.en: This dictionary app is recommended.
examples.ja: この辞書アプリ、おすすめだよ。

examples.en: This is the best selling dictionary in the world.
examples.ja: これは、世界で一番売れている辞書です。

examples.en: Since I like using paper dictionaries, they tend to get worn out quickly.
examples.ja: 私は紙の辞書を引くのが好きなので、すぐにボロボロになります。

3865.meaning_mnemonic: Take all the <kanji>word</kanji>s you use in <kanji>writing</kanji>, put them together and you have a <vocabulary>dictionary</vocabulary>!
3865.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Oh, you're leaving the company?
examples.ja: え、会社辞めるの？

examples.en: I actually quit my part-time job yesterday.
examples.ja: 実は昨日、バイト辞めたんだ。

examples.en: On Sunday nights, all I can think about is "I want to quit my job."
examples.ja: 日曜の夜は「仕事辞めたい」しか考えられない。

3866.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>quit</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to quit</vocabulary>.
3866.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: "Hey, you going <vocabulary>to quit</vocabulary>?" "<reading>Yah</reading> (や) man, I'm going to quit."

examples.en: Koichi is not good at giving insincere compliments.
examples.ja: コウイチは心にもないお世辞を言うのが下手です。

examples.en: I don't like being told that my Japanese is good just to flatter me.
examples.ja: お世辞で日本語が上手だと言われるのは好きではありません。

examples.en: Hmm, there's no way to sugarcoat it: this just isn't well done.
examples.ja: うーん、これはお世辞にも上手とは言えないね。

3867.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>quit</kanji> your current <kanji>generation</kanji> to join an older one, you'll need to use all kinds of <vocabulary>flattery</vocabulary>. Older people love being flattered; so be nice and give them some <vocabulary>compliment</vocabulary>s.
3867.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Just watch out, as the 世 gets shortened from せい to せ! You can memorize this by remembering to be short and sweet with your flattery, don't make it too long and overcomplicated!

examples.en: Koichi's apartment is located about three hours from the Tofugu office, in some faraway woods.
examples.ja: コウイチのアパートはトーフグオフィスから三時間ほど行った、遠い林の中にあります。

examples.en: That condo was really nice but we gave up on buying it, because it was too far from the station.
examples.ja: あのマンション、とてもよかったんですけど、駅から遠すぎて買うのをあきらめました。

examples.en: How far is Tokyo from Portland? Is it too far for me to walk?
examples.ja: 東京は、ポートランドからどれくらい遠いんですか？歩くにはちょっと遠すぎますか？

3868.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>far</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>far</vocabulary> (or it's <vocabulary>far away</vocabulary>).
3868.reading_mnemonic: You want to go <vocabulary>far</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>far away</vocabulary> when you see a <reading>toe... oh</reading> (とお)! You realize there is a zombie toe on the ground and it reminds you of where you can go that's far from here—where the zombie that once had this toe went! (Remember the kanji mnemonic? It's that scooter zombie's toe that makes you say oh and want to go.)

examples.en: Let's start with the introductory course first.
examples.ja: まずは入門コースから始めましょう。

examples.en: I heard he started his training under a famous yoga instructor.
examples.ja: 彼は有名なヨガの先生のところに入門したそうですよ。

examples.en: This book is an introductory text on programming.
examples.ja: この本はプログラミングの入門書です。

3869.meaning_mnemonic: If you are able to <kanji>enter</kanji> the <kanji>gate</kanji> then you have gained <vocabulary>admission</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>entrance</vocabulary> to the facility.  Sometimes you do this to start an <vocabulary>apprenticeship</vocabulary>, where you get an <vocabulary>introduction</vocabulary> to some sweet new skills, like how to make an entrance.
3869.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What is your opinion on this issue?
examples.ja: この問題に関するあなたの意見を教えてください。

examples.en: Sayaka is conducting research on Japanese literature.
examples.ja: サヤカは、日本文学に関する研究を行っています。

examples.en: I have a question regarding Japanese grammar.
examples.ja: 日本語の文法に関して、聞きたいことがあるんです。

3870.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 関 means <kanji>related</kanji>. So, when you add する to it you make it a verb. Now it means <vocabulary>to be related to</vocabulary>.
3870.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: What kind of relationship do you two have?
examples.ja: 二人はどういう関係なの？

examples.en: That's irrelevant now, right?
examples.ja: それは今は関係ないでしょ？

examples.en: It seems like Viet has a deep connection with the yakuza.
examples.ja: ビエトはヤクザとズブズブの関係らしいよ。

3871.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>connection</kanji> <kanji>related</kanji> to another <kanji>connection</kanji> obviously has some kind of <vocabulary>connection</vocabulary>, at least between all those meanings.
3871.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: We're planning to go via the Hanshin train.
examples.ja: 阪神電車で行く予定です。

examples.en: I'm a fan of the Hanshin Tigers.
examples.ja: 私は阪神タイガースのファンです。

examples.en: I am thinking about buying a house in the Hanshin district. About how much is the market price?
examples.ja: 今度、阪神地区に家を買おうと思ってるんですが、相場はいくらぐらいなんですか。

3872.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>slope</kanji>s of the <kanji>god</kanji>s! What could this be? Well, it's mainly just a company, known as <vocabulary>Hanshin</vocabulary>. They're based in the area between Osaka and Kobe. Think of it this way: 大阪 + 神戸 = 阪神! They're everywhere, though, and even have a baseball team (the Hanshin Tigers), so it's good to know.
3872.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The design on the front of this T-shirt is really great.
examples.ja: このTシャツは前面のデザインがすごく良い。

examples.en: The udon soup I had at a restaurant in Canada surprisingly had a strong taste of onions upfront.
examples.ja: カナダのレストランで食べたウドンのスープは、玉ねぎの味が前面に出ている感じで少しびっくりした。

examples.en: At this time, Viet came to stand at the forefront of the movement to make Taco Day a national holiday.
examples.ja: この時、ビエトは「タコスの日」を祭日にしようという運動の前面に立つようになった。

3873.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>front</kanji> <kanji>face</kanji> of something is the <vocabulary>front</vocabulary> or the <vocabulary>front side</vocabulary> of it (kind of like how 外面 is the exterior because it's the outside face). This also means <vocabulary>fore</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>forefront</vocabulary>, especially when used metaphorically.
3873.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: There are many leaves on the ground.
examples.ja: 地面にはたくさんの葉っぱが落ちていました。

examples.en: I'll take the dog for a short walk before the ground gets soaked from the rain.
examples.ja: 雨で地面がビシャビシャになる前にワンコをちょっと歩かせてくるよ。

examples.en: Fugu said that he'd rather live underground than underwater.
examples.ja: 海の中じゃなくて地面の中に住めたらいいのに、とフグは言いました。

3874.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>ground</kanji>/<kanji>earth</kanji> <kanji>face</kanji> is the surface that makes up the <vocabulary>ground</vocabulary> or the <vocabulary>Earth's surface</vocabulary>.
3874.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 面 is what you'd expect. 地 on the other hand is じ, which is a bit different (though close sounding) to what you learned previously. Thank the Chinese and their ever changing language for this one. Think of <reading>Je</reading>sus (じ) laying on the ground, telling you how comfortable the ground is. You say "Jesus, you have to get off the ground, you have a dinner to go to," but he doesn't want to leave.

examples.en: You shouldn’t be fooled by her outward appearance.
examples.ja: 彼女の外面にだまされない方がいいですよ。

examples.en: He has a good outward appearance and always smiles in public.
examples.ja: 彼は外面が良く、人前ではいつも笑顔を見せています。

examples.en: These glasses have a flat curvature on the outer surface of the lens, so there's less distortion and glare in the peripheral areas.
examples.ja: このメガネは、レンズの外面のカーブをフラットにしているので、周辺部のボヤケやユガミが少ないんです。

3875.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>outside</kanji> <kanji>face</kanji> to something is the <vocabulary>external appearance</vocabulary> of that thing.

While 外面 can refer to the outer surface of an object, it’s more commonly used to describe someone's <vocabulary>outward appearance</vocabulary>, behavior, or demeanor on the <vocabulary>surface</vocabulary>.
3875.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji, so this is がいめん. But note that this can also use the kun’yomi readings, which makes it そとづら.

While がいめん is neutral, そとづら is a bit negative, often implying that the person's outward appearance might be deceptive, hiding their true nature.

examples.en: If you stare at computer screens for a long time, your eyesight will get worse.
examples.ja: ずっとコンピューターの画面ばかり見ていると目が悪くなるよ。

examples.en: Can I ask you to turn down the screen brightness a bit?
examples.ja: 画面の明るさをもう少し下げてもらってもいいですか？

examples.en: Lately, images of dogs often pop up on my screen automatically.
examples.ja: 最近、よく犬の画像が自動で画面に出てくるんです。

3876.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>image</kanji> <kanji>surface</kanji> is a <vocabulary>screen</vocabulary>. Just imagine your computer screen. There's an image on the surface, right? It just happens to move around all the time, like most images on screens these days.
3876.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I have something to talk to you about face-to-face. When are you available?
examples.ja: あなたに、面と向かってお話したいことがあります。ご予定は、いつが空いていますか？

3877.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3877.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: That was the funniest thing I’ve ever heard.
examples.ja: それは今まで聞いた中で、一番面白い話でした。

examples.en: This manga is a bit crude but it's very interesting.
examples.ja: このマンガは、ちょっと下品だけどとても面白いんです。

examples.en: He is an amusing guy, his only downside is that he gets angry over the smallest things.
examples.ja: あいつは面白いやつだけど、ちょっとしたことですぐ切れるのがネックだよな。

3878.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>face</kanji> of this object is so <kanji>white</kanji>! Why is it so white compared to everything else? This is so <vocabulary>interesting</vocabulary>...
3878.reading_mnemonic: The reading is unlike what you've learned before, at least with the 面 part (白い is just like the vocab word 白い). When you look at the white face of the object you say to your friend Moe: "<reading>Oh mo</reading>!" (おも) because you want him to come over and look at this. Try to imagine someone you know named Moe, or at least a celebrity or something named Moe.

examples.en: I found a new book at the library.
examples.ja: 図書館で新しい本を見つけました。

examples.en: Library use is free of charge.
examples.ja: 図書館の利用にお金はかかりませんよ。

examples.en: I like studying at the library.
examples.ja: 私は図書館で勉強するのが好きなんです。

3879.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>public building</kanji> where <kanji>writte</kanji>n things are all <kanji>diagram</kanji>ed out in a way that lets you find said written things? That sounds like a <vocabulary>library</vocabulary> to me!
3879.reading_mnemonic: The 書館 part should be readable by you, but it's the 図 that's troublesome with an alternate reading from the one you learned. Imagine yourself at the library. You check out every single book you can about the human <reading>toe</reading> (と). You have a giant stack of books on it, then you drop it... ironically on your toe. You decide to <reading>show Khan</reading> (your buddy) your smashed toe.

examples.en: I think this will take some time to digest.
examples.ja: これは消化するのに時間がかかると思うよ。

examples.en: My cat always struggles to digest fish skin properly.
examples.ja: うちのネコは、いつも魚の皮をうまく消化できないんです。

examples.en: You might want to avoid things that are hard to digest for now.
examples.ja: まだ消化しづらいものはやめといた方がいいんじゃない？

3880.meaning_mnemonic: You know how 消化 is "digestion"? Well, The verb form of that is this word, which is <vocabulary>to digest</vocabulary>.
3880.reading_mnemonic: If you know 消化 you should be able to read this. Also, it uses the readings you learned with the kanji anyways, so no problemo there.

examples.en: This will erase with an eraser.
examples.ja: これ、消しゴムで消えるよ。

examples.en: Digital tattoos don't disappear for a lifetime, you know.
examples.ja: デジタルタトゥーは一生消えないからね。

examples.en: Oh no, all the data is gone!
examples.ja: やばい、データが全部消えちゃった！

3881.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen that 消す is "to extinguish." So, this is another verb version of that. This time, you're not doing the extinguishing, it's just happening. Something is going <vocabulary>to disappear</vocabulary> on its own. How can you differentiate this from 消す? Well, える allows you to notice how the object disappeared into thin <reading>air</reading> (える). You know you didn't do it, so it disappeared on its own, making it <vocabulary>to disappear</vocabulary>.
3881.reading_mnemonic: The reading is different from 消す, unfortunately, so you can't use that. Just think about how after the object in front of you disappears you use a <reading>key</reading> (き) to open an invisible door. That's where everything's disappearing to! You see all your disappeared stuff on the other side of this invisible door which you opened with a magical <reading>key</reading>.

examples.en: This picture is really creepy.
examples.ja: この絵、めっちゃ気持ち悪い。

examples.en: I feel sick from eating too much.
examples.ja: 食べすぎて気持ち悪い。

examples.en: Don't say disgusting things!
examples.ja: 気持ち悪いこと言わないでよ！

3882.meaning_mnemonic: The 気持ち (feeling) is <kanji>bad</kanji>. So, you can imagine how you feel isn't good, it's a <vocabulary>bad feeling</vocabulary>. You're <vocabulary>feeling terrible</vocabulary>, in fact.
3882.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the words 気持ち and 悪い. Hopefully you've seen both and can combine them together to know the reading automatically. No bad feelings with this word, right?

examples.en: The water flowing in the nearby river was very clean.
examples.ja: 近くを流れる川の水は、とてもきれいでした。

examples.en: There, time flowed slowly.
examples.ja: そこでは、ゆっくりとした時間が流れていました。

examples.en: I was surprised when my favorite heavy metal song started playing from her speakers.
examples.ja: 彼女のスピーカーから僕の好きなヘビメタの曲が流れてきて、びっくりしました。

3883.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>stream</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>to stream</vocabulary> (though it's also <vocabulary>to flow</vocabulary>, a very similar word). You can differentiate this from 流す because with 流す you flush something down the toilet, which causes it to overflow so you <reading>sue</reading> (す) the toilet maker. With 流れる you find a <reading>rare</reading> (れる) jewel trying to flow down the river. You grab it, and see it's a rare diamond!
3883.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 流す. So long as you know that you should be able to read this one as well!

examples.en: It's impossible for me to move this piano by myself.
examples.ja: 私一人でこのピアノを動かすのはムリです。

examples.en: I'm going to move the car real quick!
examples.ja: ちょっと車を動かしてくる！

examples.en: I move my body around here and there while doing desk work.
examples.ja: デスクワークをしながら、ちょこちょこ体を動かしています。

3884.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen 動く hopefully, and know it means <vocabulary>to move</vocabulary>. This is similar to that, but now you're moving something else. You know this because as you go <vocabulary>to move something</vocabulary> the thing you're moving starts to <reading>cuss</reading> (かす) you out because it's angry.
3884.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this can come from 動く. If you know that word, you know how to read this word!

examples.en: Do you want to wear earrings like these?
examples.ja: こういうイヤリング、着ける？

examples.en: I'm not really fond of wearing accessories.
examples.ja: 私、アクセサリーを着けるの、あんまり好きじゃないんです。

examples.en: How did you learn speed reading?
examples.ja: どうやって速読を身に着けたんですか？

3885.meaning_mnemonic: Another verb for this kanji! Crazy! I know, I'm sorry. The previous ones were: 着る (to wear), 着く (to arrive), and now 着ける (to put on / to wear). At least it's similar to 着る, right? In this case, this word is like 付ける, which means "to attach." It's used for things you "attach" to your body to wear, like accessories, or a face mask. That's why this is <vocabulary>to put on</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to wear</vocabulary>. Same sound, different kanji, similar ideas.
3885.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 着く's reading, but it might be easier to think it shares a reading with 付ける, which has a similar meaning. Put on clothes, attach on clothes, etc.

examples.en: You must study everyday.
examples.ja: ちゃんと毎日勉強するんだよ。

examples.en: I like to study but I don't like to read.
examples.ja: 勉強することは好きなんですが、本を読むことはキライなんです。

examples.en: School is where you go to study.
examples.ja: 学校は勉強しに行くところですよ。

3886.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen 勉強 (study) by now, right? Well, this is the verb version of that. This is <vocabulary>to study</vocabulary>.
3886.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 勉強. It's also the readings you learned with these kanji.

examples.en: When are you planning to travel?
examples.ja: いつ旅行する予定なんですか？

examples.en: Ah, I want to travel.
examples.ja: あー、旅行したいな。

examples.en: I went there when I traveled to Hokkaido for the first time.
examples.ja: 初めて北海道旅行した時に、そこに行った。

3887.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully seen 旅行 by this point. This is the verb version of that. Instead of "trip" it's <vocabulary>to travel</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to take a trip</vocabulary>. These are fun to do. You should do them!
3887.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 旅行, but it also happens to use the reading you learned with the kanji anyways, so you should be able to read it.

examples.en: Do you want to warm up the onigiri?
examples.ja: おにぎり、温める？

examples.en: I like to heat up milk and drink it.
examples.ja: 牛乳を温めてホットミルクにして飲むのが好きです。

examples.en: That idea is something I've been nurturing for a long time.
examples.ja: そのアイディアは私がずっと温めてきたものです。

3888.meaning_mnemonic: You know that the kanji 温 means <kanji>warm</kanji>, and this verb is related. It means <vocabulary>to heat something up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to warm something up</vocabulary>. It's all about you doing something to another object to make it hot, like putting it in the microwave.
3888.reading_mnemonic:
The kanji reading is the same as 温かい. As long as you know that reading, you should be able to associate it with this word.

Just like you can say あったかい for 温かい, people often say あっためる in conversation. The "official" reading is still あたためる, so when typing out the kanji or taking a test, try to stick to あたためる.

examples.en: Don't wake him up for anything.
examples.ja: ゼッタイ起こすなよ。

examples.en: Can you wake me up tomorrow morning?
examples.ja: 明日の朝、起こしてくれない？

examples.en: That person caused a problem at work and got fired.
examples.ja: その人、仕事で問題を起こして、首になったんだよ。

examples.en: You are absolutely correct, Viet! We should definitely wake Koichi up right now!
examples.ja: ビエットが100%正しいよ。今すぐコウイチ起こすべきだよ。

3889.meaning_mnemonic:
You've seen 起きる which is "to wake up." This is similar, except you are waking someone else up, which makes the meaning of this word <vocabulary>to wake someone up</vocabulary>. How do you differentiate between this and 起きる? Because of the す on the end. You wake someone up violently, wrenching their neck. They turn around and <reading>sue</reading> (す) you, making you wish you never woke them up.

This can also mean <vocabulary>to cause something</vocabulary>. I guess if you wake someone up and they're not a morning person, you could cause something... like trouble.
3889.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 起きる, so as long as you know that word you should be able to read this one. Of course, you can also imagine them yelling "OH!" when you shake them awake too, if that helps.

examples.en: Most of the visitors that come to this ski resort are foreign tourists.
examples.ja: このスキー場に来るのは、ほとんど外国人旅行者です。

examples.en: Universal Studios Japan is crowded even on weekdays because there are many foreign tourists.
examples.ja: ユニバは海外旅行者が多いから、平日でも空いてないんだよ。

examples.en: In many countries, restaurants aimed at tourists tend to be on the expensive side.
examples.ja: どこの国でも旅行者向けの飲食店は高めなことが多いですよ。

3890.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen that 旅行 is "trip." So who is <kanji>someone</kanji> who goes on trips? That is a <vocabulary>tourist</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>traveler</vocabulary>.
3890.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help if you know the reading of 旅行 already.

examples.en: I'm not fond of that person because they're always badmouthing others.
examples.ja: あの人、人の悪口ばっかり言うから苦手なんだよね。

examples.en: It's not considered speaking ill of someone, is it?
examples.ja: それって、悪口じゃなくない？

examples.en: I overheard everyone talking behind my back.
examples.ja: みんなが私の悪口を言っているのを聞いちゃったんだよね。

3891.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>bad</kanji> <kanji>mouth</kanji> produces nothing but <vocabulary>bad-mouthing</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>trash-talk</vocabulary>.

悪口 often targets someone's character, appearance, or abilities, with the intention of hurting them or damaging their reputation, sometimes to their face, but often behind their back. It gives rise to unfavorable information that can spread through gossip.
3891.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is the kun'yomi vocab readings for these two kanji, probably because this word is just two words put together into one (bad + mouth). Use your knowledge of the vocab words 悪い and 口 to learn the reading of this word.

Okay, I lied. You should actually do わるぐち instead. わるくち is possible, but the rendaku version is way more common. Sorry to say such bad things before.

examples.en: Viet's hair style today kind of looks like a delinquent's, don't you think?
examples.ja: ビエト、今日はちょっと不良っぽいヘアスタイルだね。

examples.en: The malfunctioning parts were found.
examples.ja: 不良パーツが見つかりました。

examples.en: That delinquent girl suddenly stopped coming to school, and the next thing we knew, she had apparently joined a gang.
examples.ja: あの不良少女は、いきなり学校に来なくなったと思えば、ギャングに入ったそうなんです。

3892.meaning_mnemonic: Something that's <kanji>not</kanji> <kanji>good</kanji> is <vocabulary>bad</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>substandard</vocabulary>. This usage is more formal and frequently paired with other kanji compounds. Alternatively, it can refer to someone who is a  <vocabulary>delinquent</vocabulary>, in which case it is often used as a standalone word.
3892.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: He is clumsy and struggles to learn new things.
examples.ja: 彼は不器用で、新しいことを学ぶのが苦手です。

examples.en: Despite her clumsiness, she never gave up.
examples.ja: 不器用ながらも、彼女は決してあきらめませんでした。

examples.en: With clumsy words, he expressed his gratitude to his parents.
examples.ja: 彼は不器用な言葉で、親に感謝の気持ちを伝えました。

3893.meaning_mnemonic: You know how 器用 means "dextrous" and "skillful"? Well, this is when you're <kanji>not</kanji> those things. When you're not dextrous, you're <vocabulary>clumsy</vocabulary> and when you're not skillful you're <vocabulary>unskillful</vocabulary>.
3893.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just keep in mind that the reading of 不 changes from ふ to ぶ. If you're clumsy you'll get a lot of <reading>boo</reading>-boos (ぶ), get it?

examples.en: Please! Help me!
examples.ja: お願い！手伝って！

examples.en: I have a favor to ask you, would you hear me out?
examples.ja: ちょっとお願いがあるんだけど、聞いてもらえる？

examples.en: Please, let's stop talking about that.
examples.ja: お願いだから、その話はもうやめて。

3894.meaning_mnemonic: The noun form of <kanji>request</kanji> (don't be tricked by the い on the end, it's not an adjective). So, request goes to <vocabulary>a request</vocabulary>.
3894.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same like お願いします. Hopefully you're able to read that by now so you're able to read this too.

examples.en: It looks like this restaurant has an all-you-can-drink option.
examples.ja: このレストランは飲み放題があるみたいだよ。

examples.en: The all-you-can-drink plans start at 2000 yen.
examples.ja: 飲み放題プランは2000円からです。

examples.en: We booked a course that includes all-you-can-drink.
examples.ja: 飲み放題付きのコースを予約しました。

3895.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Drink</kanji>ing <kanji>as much as you want</kanji> is nice and all, but don't get sick. When you see this word, you know you're at an <vocabulary>all you can drink</vocabulary> place. Tip: Usually there's a time limit, so drink up!
3895.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the word 放題 (ほうだい) and 飲む (のむ). So long as you know those vocab words, you'll be able to read this one as well.

examples.en: This hotel breakfast is all-you-can-eat.
examples.ja: このホテルの朝食は食べ放題です。

examples.en: Let's go to an all-you-can-eat pizza place.
examples.ja: 食べ放題のピザ屋に行こう。

examples.en: In Japan, there are cafes that offer all-you-can-eat cake.
examples.ja: 日本にはケーキ食べ放題のカフェがあります。

3896.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>eat</kanji> <kanji>as much as you want</kanji>, you are getting an <vocabulary>all you can eat</vocabulary> deal.
3896.reading_mnemonic: The reading consists of the readings of 食べる and 放題. If you know those you should be able to read this too.

examples.en: What do you think is necessary for effective communication?
examples.ja: 良好なコミュニケーションをとるために必要なこととは何だと思いますか？

examples.en: To maintain good condition, daily care is essential.
examples.ja: コンディションを良好に保つには、日々のお手入れが欠かせません。

examples.en: After the surgery, everything was fine for a while, but the illness returned a year later.
examples.ja: 術後はしばらく良好でしたが、一年後に病気が再発したんです。

3897.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>good</kanji> <kanji>like</kanji> is something you like really good, if that makes any sense. This thing is a <vocabulary>good</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>favorable</vocabulary> thing.
3897.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've learned them already, so you should be able to read this on your own!

examples.en: That man is a murderer.
examples.ja: その男は人殺しです。

examples.en: No one wants to send their own child to the battlefield to become a killer.
examples.ja: 自分の子を戦場に送り出して、人殺しをさせたい人なんていませんよ。

examples.en: People who speak ill of others on social media should consider that they might be committing murder in a sense.
examples.ja: SNSで悪口を言ってる人は全員、自分が人殺しをしているかもしれないってことを考えた方がいいよ。

3898.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the kun'yomi vocab readings. So, if you know 人's reading as a vocab word and 殺す's reading, you should be able to read this word. Just note that ころし goes to ごろし due to rendaku.

examples.en: This murderer is a notorious serial killer.
examples.ja: この殺人者は、有名なシリアルキラーです。

examples.en: Believe me, my son was just framed as a murderer by someone.
examples.ja: 信じてください。息子は誰かに殺人者に仕立て上げられただけなんです。

examples.en: Have you ever considered the pain of someone whose family member was a murderer?
examples.ja: あなたは家族が殺人者だった人の苦しみについて、考えたことはありますか？

3899.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully seen 殺人 (murder) from level 13. So, <kanji>someone</kanji> who does <kanji>murder</kanji> is what? A <vocabulary>murderer</vocabulary>.
3899.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The ring fit perfectly on her finger.
examples.ja: その指輪は彼女の指にぴったり合っていました。

examples.en: I can't get this ring off of my finger.
examples.ja: 指輪が指から外れなくなってしまいました。

examples.en: "When I get a bonus, I’ll buy you a diamond ring." "You always say that, but words are just words."
examples.ja: 「ボーナスが出たら、ダイヤモンドの指輪を買ってやるよ。」「あなたはいつも口先ばかりでしょ。」

3900.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>finger</kanji> <kanji>ring</kanji> is the kind of <vocabulary>ring</vocabulary> you'd put on your finger. That's just simply a "ring" though, so you'll have to know what "ring" this is via context.
3900.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the individual vocab readings, 指 and 輪. In English we don't distinguish some other ring from a "finger ring" but in Japanese, you can think of this as two separate words coming together to form one word, which is why it uses the kun'yomi vocab readings like this. So, if you know the individual words, you should be able to figure out this word is read as <reading>ゆびわ</reading>.

examples.en: This elastic band is very durable.
examples.ja: この輪ゴムはとても丈夫です。

examples.en: She used a rubber band instead of a hair tie.
examples.ja: 彼女はヘアゴムの代わりに輪ゴムを使いました。

examples.en: If it's rubber bands you're looking for, there should be several on that desk.
examples.ja: 輪ゴムなら、あのデスクの上に何本かあるはずですよ。

3901.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>ring</kanji> of gum (ゴム) (which is what Japanese people call rubber quite often) is a ring of rubber. What is a ring of rubber that people use often? It's a <vocabulary>rubber band</vocabulary>.
3901.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 輪 is the kun'yomi vocab reading, which is わ, making this word <reading>わ</reading>ゴム.

examples.en: I think it will take quite some time to organize all this data.
examples.ja: このデータを全て整理するには、かなり時間がかかると思います。

examples.en: Can I take a moment to organize your story?
examples.ja: ちょっと一回、話を整理させてもらっていいかな？

examples.en: Tell that employee to tidy up their desk!
examples.ja: あの社員に、デスクを整理するよう言っておいて！

3902.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>arrange</kanji> something with <kanji>reason</kanji> you're arranging it. That's why this is <vocabulary>to arrange</vocabulary>.
3902.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This apartment's residents' rooms are all neatly arranged.
examples.ja: このアパートの住民の部屋はみんなきちんと整理されています。

examples.en: I have not yet properly organized my thoughts.
examples.ja: まだ考えがちゃんと整理できていません。

examples.en: Today I organized the photo library on my phone.
examples.ja: 今日はスマホのフォトライブラリーを整理しました。

3903.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>arrange</kanji> something according to <kanji>reason</kanji>, the result is an <vocabulary>arrangement</vocabulary>.
3903.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Oh, do you have to memorize all of this?
examples.ja: え、これ全部暗記するの？

examples.en: By using WaniKani, you can easily memorize Japanese vocabulary.
examples.ja: ワニカニを使えば、日本語の単語を楽に暗記することができます。

examples.en: I have to memorize my lines from the script by tomorrow.
examples.ja: 明日までに、台本のセリフを暗記しなければいけないんです。

3904.meaning_mnemonic: Hopefully you've seen 暗記 before now. It means "memorization." So, turn that into a verb and you have <vocabulary>to memorize</vocabulary>.
3904.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 暗記. It also is the reading you learned with the kanji too.

examples.en: Where are you going to practice?
examples.ja: どこで練習するの？

examples.en: I don't want to regret it later thinking "I should have practiced more," so I'm practicing a lot now.
examples.ja: 後から「もっとたくさん練習しておけば良かった」と思いたくないんで、今たくさん練習しています。

examples.en: I practiced pronouncing the word "meat" for six hours yesterday.
examples.ja: 昨日、肉って言葉の発音を六時間も練習したんだぜ。

3905.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully seen 練習, which means "practice." So, if you make it into a verb, you have <vocabulary>to practice</vocabulary>.
3905.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the kanji as well as from the vocab word 練習. You should be able to read this!

examples.en: Could you project the slides onto the screen for me?
examples.ja: スクリーンにスライドを映してもらえますか？

examples.en: I think others are like mirrors that reflect ourselves.
examples.ja: 他人は自分を映すかがみだと思うんです。

examples.en: Why don't we use this white wall as a screen to project the movie?
examples.ja: この白いカベをスクリーン代わりにして映画を映すのはどうでしょう。

examples.en: What's the intention behind showing a close-up of a bagel at this point in this movie?
examples.ja: この映画、ここでベーグルをアップ映す意図は何なの？

3906.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 映る is "to be reflected." Now you're doing the reflecting, which is really projecting (light). That's why this word is <vocabulary>to project</vocabulary>.
3906.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 映る. So long as you know the reading of 映る you should be able to read this one too.

examples.en: He is a world-renowned chef.
examples.ja: 彼は世界的に有名な料理人です。

examples.en: My girlfriend works as a cook in a restaurant.
examples.ja: 僕の彼女は料理人としてレストランで働いています。

examples.en: Chefs also need to pay attention to the presentation of their dishes.
examples.ja: 料理人は料理のプレゼンテーションにも気を配らなくてはなりません。

3907.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen 料理 and probably know it means "cooking." So, what is a <kanji>person</kanji> who does cooking? That is <vocabulary>a cook</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>chef</vocabulary>.
3907.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: He isn't a famous artist.
examples.ja: 彼は有名な芸術家ではありません。

examples.en: She is a globally renowned artist who has received numerous awards.
examples.ja: 彼女は、多くの賞を受賞している、世界的に名の知れた芸術家です。

examples.en: The artist asked his disciple to look after his house while he was away and left for Europe to study.
examples.ja: その芸術家は、弟子に留守番をたのんで、ヨーロッパに留学しました。

3908.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 芸術 is <kanji>art</kanji> so you'd think that 芸術家 would be something like "art house." Well, it's not. Think of it this way: Who is the person who works for "House Art"? It's the <vocabulary>artist</vocabulary>.
3908.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Huh, is this fully automatic?
examples.ja: え、これ全自動なんですか？

examples.en: I've set up all the data on my smartphone to automatically upload to the cloud.
examples.ja: スマホでのデータは、全て自動でクラウドにアップロードするようにセッティングしています。

examples.en: I didn't even realize it was an automatic door.
examples.ja: 自動ドアだって知らなかったんだよ。

3909.meaning_mnemonic: Something that can <kanji>move</kanji> by its <kanji>self</kanji> is something that's <vocabulary>automatic</vocabulary>.
3909.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This train's doors don't open automatically.
examples.ja: この電車のドアは、自動的には開きません。

examples.en: If that country starts a war, our country will automatically be drawn into the conflict as well.
examples.ja: あの国が戦争を始めると、俺たちの国も自動的に戦うことになるんだよ。

examples.en: The data automatically backed up here is managed by a system that will also automatically delete it after a certain period of time.
examples.ja: こちらに自動的にバックアップされたデータは、今度は一定期間後に自動的に消去されるシステムになっています。

examples.en: This is due to an automatic logout after more than 30 minutes of inactivity.
examples.ja: これは、30分以上何もしなかった場合の自動的なログアウトによるものですね。

3910.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>automatic</kanji><kanji>al</kanji> (自動 + 的) thing of course isn't "automatical." A better way to say it is to cut off the -al and call it <vocabulary>automatic</vocabulary>.
3910.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know the reading of 自動 as well.

examples.en: I generally don't believe in spiritual matters.
examples.ja: 私は基本的にはスピリチュアルな事は信じません。

examples.en: I was told by my boss that I don't even know the fundamentals and that I'm useless.
examples.ja: 上司に、基本的な事も知らない役立たずだと言われました。

examples.en: Basically, I have no interest in politics.
examples.ja: 基本的に政治に関心がないんです。

3911.meaning_mnemonic: The things that are <kanji>basics</kanji> (基本) <kanji>like</kanji> (的) are <vocabulary>basic</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>fundamental</vocabulary>.
3911.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Knowing how to read the word 基本 will be helpful too.

examples.en: He reads books without ever creasing the pages.
examples.ja: 彼はゼッタイに折り目をつけずに本を読みます。

examples.en: Please open the origami again after you fold it in half to add the crease.
examples.ja: 折り紙を半分に折って、折り目をつけてからまた開いてください。

examples.en: Could you put a crease in my trousers?
examples.ja: ズボンには折り目を付けてもらえますか？

3912.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>fold</kanji> you can see with your <kanji>eye</kanji> is a <vocabulary>fold</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>crease</vocabulary> in something.
3912.reading_mnemonic: The readings are both kun'yomi vocab readings. You should have seen 折る by now which should help you to read 折り. Then there's 目, which I'm guessing you won't have a problem with.

examples.en: In Japan, March is graduation season.
examples.ja: 日本では三月が卒業のシーズンです。

examples.en: The WaniKaniko-chan of the idol group TFG48 has announced her graduation.
examples.ja: アイドルグループTFG48のワニカニ子ちゃんが卒業を発表しました。

examples.en: Even after graduation, even after becoming adults, we'll always be best friends, right?
examples.ja: 卒業しても、大人になっても、私たち、ずっと親友だよね？

3913.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>business</kanji> of you <kanji>graduating</kanji> is your <vocabulary>graduation</vocabulary>. If you think about it, it's kind of a big business, getting you graduated from expensive schools. The graduation business focuses on graduations, and getting you there (hint: this business is a school, probably).
3913.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Tomorrow is my graduation ceremony.
examples.ja: 明日は私の卒業式です。

examples.en: Ah, this is a photo from after the graduation ceremony, right? How nostalgic!
examples.ja: あ、これ、卒業式の後の写真だね。なつかしい！

examples.en: Huh? Did you say that Beyoncé came to the graduation and sang for you guys? No way! You must be joking!
examples.ja: はあ？卒業式にビヨンセが来て歌を歌ってくれた？まさか！冗談でしょう？

3914.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 卒業 is <kanji>graduation</kanji> so what about when you add <kanji>ceremony</kanji> to it? That makes it a <vocabulary>graduation ceremony</vocabulary>.
3914.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help if you know how to read 卒業 already as a word, too.

examples.en: Everyone is imperfect.
examples.ja: 人間はみんな不完全です。

examples.en: Aren't incomplete things better than complete things, since they have a humanness about them?
examples.ja: 完全なものよりも不完全なものの方が人情味があってよくない？

examples.en: The Tofugu softball team had an incomplete end to their season when the game they were winning was suspended due to rain.
examples.ja: 勝ち試合が雨で中止になり、トーフグソフトボールチームのシーズンが不完全に終わった。

3915.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 完全 means "complete" or "perfect." So, a <kanji>not</kanji> "complete" or "perfect" is something that is <vocabulary>incomplete</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>imperfect</vocabulary>.
3915.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It also will help if you can read 完全.

examples.en: I went to an art museum workshop.
examples.ja: 美術館のワークショップに行ってきました。

examples.en: We had an art museum date over the weekend.
examples.ja: 週末は美術館デートでした。

examples.en: When I went to the Louvre Museum in Paris, I saw famous artworks like the "Mona Lisa."
examples.ja: パリのルーヴル美術館に行った時に「モナリザ」などの有名なアート作品を見ました。

3916.meaning_mnemonic: You know 美術 is <kanji>fine art</kanji>. So what is a <kanji>public building</kanji> that contains said fine art? It's a <vocabulary>museum</vocabulary>.
3916.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'm a professional origami artist.
examples.ja: 私はプロの折り紙アーティストです。

examples.en: I stockpiled everyday items, cosmetics, groceries, and origami paper during the Amazon sale.
examples.ja: Amazonのセールで、日用品、コスメ、食料品、折り紙を買いだめしました。

examples.en: Today, Koichi found origami instead of food in his bento box.
examples.ja: 今日のコウイチの弁当箱の中には、なぜか食べ物の代わりに折り紙が入っていました。

3917.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 折る is "to fold," so what about "to fold <kanji>paper</kanji>"? Ever heard of something that involves lots of folding of paper that is Japanese? Most likely you have. This is <vocabulary>origami</vocabulary>, aka the <vocabulary>art of paper folding</vocabulary>.
3917.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 折る and the vocab word 紙. As long as you know those you should be able to read this. Also, you probably already know this reading because it's an English word, too.

examples.en: I want to enter a private university.
examples.ja: 私立大学に入学したいです。

examples.en: I thought I'd be able to make a good living if I graduated from a well-known private university.
examples.ja: 有名私立大学を出れば、きっと上手く生きていけると思ったんです。

examples.en: Private universities have many foreign students as well.
examples.ja: 私立大学の学生は外国人も多いです。

3918.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen 私立, which is "private," and you've seen 大学, which is "college" or "university." So, combine them together and you have a <vocabulary>private college</vocabulary> / <vocabulary>private university</vocabulary>.
3918.reading_mnemonic: If you know the readings of the words 私立 and 大学 you'll be able to read this. It's also all jukugo on'yomi readings too, so you can read it that way.

examples.en: We still have hope.
examples.ja: まだ希望はある。

examples.en: Now all hope is lost.
examples.ja: これで、希望は全て失われました。

examples.en: Do you have a seating preference?
examples.ja: お座席のご希望はございますか？

3919.meaning_mnemonic: Both your <kanji>hope</kanji>s and <kanji>wish</kanji>es are held within this vocab word. So, what is the meaning of this word? It is both <vocabulary>hope</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>wish</vocabulary>. Either will work.
3919.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I hope you can get into the university of your choice!
examples.ja: 希望する大学に入学できるといいですね！

examples.en: I'm hoping to study abroad in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本への留学を希望しています。

examples.en: I'll do my best to schedule shifts for you according to your preferences, but sometimes adjustments may be necessary if everyone's preferences don't align. Thank you for your understanding in this matter.
examples.ja: できるだけ希望するシフトでバイトに入ってもらえるようにしますが、みんなの希望が合わない時は調整が必要なこともあるので、そこはよろしくお願いします。

3920.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 希望 is a "wish." When you "do a wish," that means <vocabulary>to wish</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to request</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to hope</vocabulary>.

This is a formal way to say that you wish for something, so you might use it at work to request an opportunity to work abroad, or let them know politely that you're resigning.
3920.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 希望. It's also the on'yomi jukugo reading as well, if that helps any.

examples.en: I'm not a doctor, but I learned surgical techniques from a doctor.
examples.ja: 私は医者ではありませんが、ある医者から、手術の技術を学びました。

examples.en: I learned the latest web development skills from the company I used to work for.
examples.ja: 以前に働いていた会社で、ウエブ開発の最新技術を身につけました。

examples.en: During the presentation, a Google engineer suddenly stood up and started singing karaoke.
examples.ja: プレゼン中、グーグルの技術者が急に立ち上がり、カラオケを始めたんです。

3921.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen 技 as a vocab word meaning "technique," and the kanji 術 means <kanji>technique</kanji>. So this means <vocabulary>technique</vocabulary>! Your technique is also your <vocabulary>craft</vocabulary>, and what’s needed for <vocabulary>technology</vocabulary>.
3921.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'll compromise on 100,000 yen.
examples.ja: 十万円で妥協するよ。

examples.en: Koichi and Viet compromised by going to McDonald's.
examples.ja: コウイチとビエトは、マクドナルドに行くことで妥協しました。

examples.en: After all, you don't want to compromise on the design and interior of your own home, right?
examples.ja: やっぱり、自分の家のデザインやインテリアは妥協したくないじゃん。

3922.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 妥協 means <kanji>compromise</kanji>. So, what happens when you make it a verb? It becomes <vocabulary>to compromise</vocabulary>.
3922.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the vocab word 妥協, so if you know that you should be good (also, just the reading of the kanji works too).

examples.en: I don't want to give in.
examples.ja: 妥協したくないの。

examples.en: I was struggling a bit mentally because I couldn't compromise well.
examples.ja: うまく妥協することができなくて、ちょっとメンタルやられちゃってたんだよね。

examples.en: It's not good to compromise on your work.
examples.ja: 仕事を妥協するのはよくないよ。

3923.meaning_mnemonic: When you have <kanji>gentle</kanji> <kanji>cooperation</kanji> nobody has their way. You're very gently coming towards the middle, coming to a <vocabulary>compromise</vocabulary>. (Whether you like it or not.)
3923.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Our dog has many demands.
examples.ja: うちの犬は要求が多い。

examples.en: Users are demanding cost reductions.
examples.ja: ユーザーは、コストダウンを要求しています。

examples.en: Whether it's a dog or a person, if you give in too readily to their demands, those demands will only escalate.
examples.ja: 犬でも人でも、要求にこたえすぎると、要求がエスカレートしていきます。

3924.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>need</kanji> this <kanji>request</kanji> to happen, so you don't just ask nicely, you <vocabulary>demand</vocabulary> it.
3924.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The man demanded money.
examples.ja: 男は金を要求した。

examples.en: Employees are demanding time off.
examples.ja: 社員が休みを要求しています。

examples.en: Customers are demanding fast responses.
examples.ja: 顧客は速い対応を要求しています。

3925.meaning_mnemonic: You hopefully remember that 要求 means "demand" . When you make that a verb, it becomes <vocabulary>to demand something</vocabulary>.
3925.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the vocab word 要求. It's also the regular on'yomi jukugo reading.

examples.en: Yogurt helps you digest food.
examples.ja: ヨーグルトは食べ物の消化を助けてくれます。

examples.en: Koichi's having a touch of diarrhea, so please have him eat something easy to digest.
examples.ja: コウイチは下り気味だから、消化の良いものを食べさせてあげてね。

examples.en: I haven’t finished digesting the ramen I ate for lunch.
examples.ja: 昼に食べたラーメンをまだ消化しきっていない。

3926.meaning_mnemonic: What is something that will first <kanji>extinguish</kanji> something and then <kanji>change</kanji> it? One thing I can think of is your body. It takes in food, extinguishes it in your stomach, then changes it into things your body can use (and then excrete). That's why this "extinguish-change" process is your <vocabulary>digestion</vocabulary>.
3926.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I feel sick due to indigestion.
examples.ja: 消化不良で気持ち悪い。

examples.en: I consulted with the teacher, but I still can't understand it well, so I'm feeling really frustrated for not digesting it well.
examples.ja: 先生に相談したんだけど、まだよく分からなくて消化不良ですごくモヤモヤしてるんだよね。

examples.en: Isn't it just indigestion? I mean, you did eat a lot of heavy stuff that's hard to digest.
examples.ja: ただの消化不良じゃないですか？ほら、消化に悪い物たくさん食べてたし。

3927.meaning_mnemonic: You've hopefully seen 消化 by now and know that it means "digestion." If you know that, then you can see that the "digestion" is <kanji>not</kanji> <kanji>good</kanji>. When your digestion is not good, what do you have? <vocabulary>Indigestion</vocabulary>. Excuse me, I have to run to the restroom...
3927.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Knowing 消化 and 不良 will help as well.

examples.en: They found out that I'd cheated and I was rejected.
examples.ja: カンニングしたのがバレて不合格になってしまった。

examples.en: If you don't mind, could you tell me the reason I wasn't accepted?
examples.ja: もしよければ、不合格になった理由を教えてもらえませんか？

examples.en: I didn't get accepted into my first-choice public university, but I got into a private university that I applied to as a safety.
examples.ja: 本命の公立大学は不合格だったが、すべり止めで受けた私立大学に合格しました。

3928.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 合格する is "to pass a test," so what's the opposite of that? <vocabulary>Fail a test</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>failure</vocabulary>.
3928.reading_mnemonic: If you know the reading for 合格, all you have to do is add 不 to it! You've learned all these readings, yay!

examples.en: What if I told you that I was planning to graduate from this industry soon?
examples.ja: この業界、そろそろ卒業するつもりなんだって言ったらどうする？

examples.en: I can't wait to finish school, but I don't want to grow up.
examples.ja: 学校は早く卒業したいけど、大人にはなりたくないな。

examples.en: Is it possible to graduate from art school or an art college and still not find a job in art?
examples.ja: 美大や芸大を卒業しても、アートの仕事が見つからないこともあるんですか？

3929.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 卒業 is "graduation." Make it a verb, and you have <vocabulary>to graduate</vocabulary>.
3929.reading_mnemonic: The reading is just the same as the vocab word 卒業.

examples.en: It is not good to leave behind food.
examples.ja: 食べ物を残すのは良くないですよ。

examples.en: I left a comment on your blog.
examples.ja: ブログにコメントを残しました。

examples.en: I intend to be a big name in the world someday.
examples.ja: いつか世に名を残せるような大物になるつもりです。

3930.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>remainder</kanji>, but you can't really "to remainder." What is something that's similar that would make sense? How about <vocabulary>to leave behind</vocabulary>. This is when you're actually doing the leaving behind too. For example, you eat some food and you leave behind your rice because you're a bad child. You can remember this because of す. Every time you leave some food behind your mom would <reading>sue</reading> you, because she was a terrible mom. Imagine this.
3930.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word can come from level 14 item 残る. Associate the two in your mind and you'll be able to read both.

examples.en: This is a recipe for a rare cheese cake that hardens in the microwave without gelatin or flame.
examples.ja: これはゼラチンも火も使わずにレンジでチンして固めるレアチーズケーキのレシピです。

examples.en: Viet takes an hour to make his pompadour hard every morning.
examples.ja: ビエトは毎朝一時間かけてリーゼントをワックスで固めます。

examples.en: Koichi was determined to make WaniKani the best Japanese language learning site in the world.
examples.ja: コウイチは、ワニカニを世界一の日本語学習サイトにする決意を固めた。

3931.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>hard</kanji> so the verb vocab version? <vocabulary>To make something hard</vocabulary>. You need to differentiate this from 固まる, though, which means "to harden" (the hardening happens on its own). This word means "to make something hard," because you're doing the hardening. You can remember this because you want to make something hard. And to do that, you send special "<reading>mail</reading>" (める) to this thing you want to make hard, and this mail does that for you.
3931.reading_mnemonic:
Since the reading for 固 (かた) is different than the one you learned with the kanji, here's a mnemonic to help you:

Why would you want <vocabulary>to make something hard</vocabulary>? Obviously because you want to put it in a <reading>cata</reading>pult (かた). There's no point putting soft things in catapults, after all.

examples.en: An unusual incident happened that year.
examples.ja: その年に、変事が起きたんです。

examples.en: I think we should simulate what to do in case something strange happens.
examples.ja: 変事が発生した場合のシミュレーションをしておくべきだと思います。

examples.en: All WaniKani users were worried that some unusual incident had befallen Tofugu.
examples.ja: トーフグに何か変事が起きたんじゃないかと、全ワニカニユーザーが心配していたんですよ。

3932.meaning_mnemonic:
You know 変 means "change," but it can also mean "strange." So a <kanji>strange</kanji> <kanji>occurrence</kanji> is an incident that is unlikely. In other words, an <vocabulary>unexpected incident</vocabulary> or an <vocabulary>unusual incident</vocabulary>.

変事 is a formal word used to describe sudden and unusual occurrences that disrupt normal conditions, such as natural disasters, emergencies, or crises. You won't see this word often, but may still come across it in formal writing.

With 変事, think of how the 変 comes first to emphasize the strangeness of the incident.
3932.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Dad is very proud because you became an architect.
examples.ja: お父さん、あんたが建築家になったから、鼻が高いのよ。

examples.en: This building was built by French architect Jules Lescas.
examples.ja: こちらはフランス人建築家のジュール・レスカスが建築した建物です。

examples.en: My house was designed by a famous architect.
examples.ja: 私の家は有名な建築家によってデザインされたんですよ。

3933.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 建築 is architecture. So, someone of <kanji>house</kanji> <kanji>architecture</kanji> is someone who does architecture. They are an <vocabulary>architect</vocabulary>.
3933.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will also help if you know how to read 建築 already.

examples.en: Until what year B.C. was the Tyrannosaurus present?
examples.ja: ティラノサウルスがいたのは、紀元前何年ごろまでですか。

examples.en: If time machines existed, I would want to go to 3000 BCE.
examples.ja: もしタイムマシーンがあったなら、紀元前三千年紀に行ってみたいな。

examples.en: Today, Koichi insists that he is a man who has traveled back in time from ancient Rome, B.C.
examples.ja: 今日のコウイチは、自分は紀元前の古代ローマからタイムスリップしてきた男だって言ってきかないんです。

3934.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 紀元後 is "Common Era", or "anno Domini"? Well, this is the opposite because it has <kanji>before</kanji> (前) instead of 後. It's <vocabulary>Before the Common Era</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>Before Christ</vocabulary>.
3934.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will also help if you know how to read 紀元後 already, because then you'll just have to remember the 前.

examples.en: I made ham and cheese sandwiches for breakfast.
examples.ja: 朝ご飯にはハムとチーズのサンドイッチを作りました。

examples.en: For breakfast at my house, it's always rice instead of bread.
examples.ja: ウチの朝ご飯は、パンじゃなくご飯と決まっています。

examples.en: Having cereal for breakfast every morning isn't very good for your health.
examples.ja: 毎朝シリアルを朝ご飯にするのは、あまり体に良くないです。

3935.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>morning</kanji> <kanji>meal</kanji> is the meal you eat in the morning. That is <vocabulary>breakfast</vocabulary>.
3935.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji. It's also like the vocab: 朝 is like the vocab version, あさ and ご飯 is like the word you learned, ごはん.

examples.en: Jenny is British.
examples.ja: ジェニーさんはイギリス人です。

examples.en: This book was created by a team of Brits and Americans.
examples.ja: この本は、イギリス人とアメリカ人のチームがつくりました。

examples.en: Well, British people also drink coffee.
examples.ja: そりゃ、イギリス人もコーヒーをのみますよ。

3936.meaning_mnemonic: イギリス means "Great Britain" or "United Kingdom." So what is a "Great Britain person?" You guessed it — a <vocabulary>British person</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>Brit</vocabulary>.
3936.reading_mnemonic:
Often times, when two kanji come together to form a kanji compound (or jukugo), you use the on'yomi readings. This is similar to that, though instead of another kanji it's a foreign word. This pattern works with almost any country as well. Just add 人 to a country name and you've described the people who live there. You'll see more of these before you're finished here.

And since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: 

As with all words for nationalities, the 人 here is pronounced じん. All nationalities, including <vocabulary>Brit</vocabulary>s, love <reading>jean</reading>s (じん)!

examples.en: Hey, crybaby Ko-chan. Here comes a tunnel you like.
examples.ja: 泣き虫コウちゃーん、ほら、コウちゃんの好きなトンネルだよーっ！

examples.en: Only Koichi knows Viet is a crybaby.
examples.ja: コウイチだけがビエトが泣き虫だということを知っている。

examples.en: My kid's high fever doesn't seem to be coming down. She is usually a crybaby, but it seems like she doesn't even have energy to cry now and I'm worried.
examples.ja: ウチの子の高熱が中々下がりません。いつもは泣き虫なんですが、今は泣く元気も無いようで、心配です。

3937.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen that 泣く is to cry, so you can probably guess that 泣き is just "cry." You've also seen how 虫 is rarely a nice thing to call someone. So what's a mean thing you can call someone who cries? How about a <vocabulary>crybaby</vocabulary>?
3937.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 泣く and 虫. So long as you're okay with those two words you should be able to read this one too.

examples.en: I can hear a baby is crying.
examples.ja: 赤ちゃんの泣き声が聞こえます。

examples.en: Koichi's cry is actually really cute.
examples.ja: コウイチの泣き声って、実はめちゃくちゃカワイイんだよ。

examples.en: If you get irritated by the crying of small children, as an adult, you could just wear headphones with noise cancellation, I think.
examples.ja: 小さい子の泣き声にイライラするなら、大人だったら自分でヘッドフォンしてノイズキャンセルすれば良いのにって思う。

3938.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>cry</kanji> <kanji>voice</kanji> is a sound of <vocabulary>crying</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>sob</vocabulary>. Don't cry! Kanji will get easier someday!
3938.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the vocab words 泣く and 声. So long as you know those two words okay, you should be able to read this word too!

examples.en: Would you like to have dinner at our place?
examples.ja: 晩ご飯、良かったらウチで食べていく？

examples.en: Before the dinner, I drank down a glass of beer in one gulp.
examples.ja: 晩ご飯の前に、ビールを一気にグビッと飲み干しました。

examples.en: Tonight's supper is salted, sun-dried flounder.
examples.ja: 今日の晩ご飯のオカズは、天日干しで作ったカレイの干物です。

3939.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>night</kanji> <kanji>meal</kanji> is the meal you eat at night. That is <vocabulary>dinner</vocabulary>.
3939.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I want to eat curry rice for lunch.
examples.ja: 昼ご飯にはカレーライスが食べたいです。
