examples.en: Why don't we order pizza for lunch?
examples.ja: 昼ご飯は、ピザを注文しない？

examples.en: There was no time for lunch today.
examples.ja: 今日は昼ご飯を食べる時間はありませんでした。

3940.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>noon</kanji> <kanji>meal</kanji> is the meal you eat at noon. What meal is that? It's delicious, delicious <vocabulary>lunch</vocabulary>.
3940.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the words 昼 and ご飯. If you know how to read those words you can read this word as well.

examples.en: She made a wish on the first star.
examples.ja: 彼女は、一番星に願い事をしました。

examples.en: The deity of this shrine is famous for listening to wishes.
examples.ja: こちらの神社の神様は、願い事を聞いてくださることで有名です。

examples.en: The man put his hands together in prayer with his wish in mind.
examples.ja: 男は願い事を心に思いながら、手を合わせて祈りました。

3941.meaning_mnemonic: You know that お願い means "a request," and 事 can mean "thing." Well, a request for some specific thing can also be called <vocabulary>one's wish</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>prayer</vocabulary>. Do you have any 願い事 in your heart right now? Of course you do! Don't worry, you can tell me.
3941.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the words お願い and 事. If you know how to read those you should be able to read this word too. Just remember that 事 is rendaku'd, so it's read as ごと.

examples.en: Sorry, I'm currently syncing data, so please wait a moment.
examples.ja: ごめん、今データ同期中だからちょっと待って。

examples.en: Dropbox always freezes during syncing for some reason. I wonder why.
examples.ja: Dropbox、いつも同期中にフリーズしちゃうんだよね。何でだろう。

examples.en: Yesterday, Google Drive was syncing all morning, so I couldn't get any work done.
examples.ja: 昨日はGoogleドライブがずっと同期中で午前中仕事にならなかった。

3942.meaning_mnemonic: You're making things in two different places be exactly the <kanji>same</kanji> for <kanji>a period of time</kanji>. You're in the <kanji>middle</kanji> of a process called <vocabulary>syncing</vocabulary>. You can see 同期中 a lot in computery contexts, or if you change your device language to Japanese. (Not that I recommend that...)
3942.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: There is an old temple in the town.
examples.ja: その町には古い寺があります。

examples.en: I'm planning to draw a fortune slip at the temple during New Year's.
examples.ja: お正月にお寺でおみくじを引いてみるつもりです。

examples.en: There was a cherry blossom tree standing at the entrance of the temple.
examples.ja: その寺の入り口には、サクラの木が一本立っていました。

3943.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3943.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji too! What good fortune — you must have been praying to Benzaiten at the local お寺.

examples.en: I hope that doesn't happen.
examples.ja: そうならないことを期待するよ。

examples.en: Don't expect too much from me.
examples.ja: あまり期待しないでくださいね。

examples.en: I'm anticipating Valentine’s chocolate from girls other than my mother this year.
examples.ja: 今年は母親以外の女子からのバレンタインのチョコレートを期待しています。

3944.meaning_mnemonic: Hopefully you know the word 期待 by now (expectation). This is the verb version, which makes it <vocabulary>to expect</vocabulary>.
3944.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the word 期待, so make sure you know that to know this one as well.

examples.en: A new conveyor belt sushi shop opened up.
examples.ja: 新しく回転ずしのお店がオープンした。

examples.en: If I go to Japan, I'd like to visit a conveyor belt sushi restaurant.
examples.ja: 日本に行ったら、回転ずしに行って見たいです。

examples.en: I started working part-time at a rotating sushi restaurant.
examples.ja: 回転ずし屋でバイトを始めました。

3945.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 回転 is "rotation" and you probably know what すし is (gets rendaku'd in this word to ずし). So, what is "rotation sushi?" It's <vocabulary>rotating sushi</vocabulary>, also known as <vocabulary>conveyor belt sushi</vocabulary>. Look it up if you don't know what it is.
3945.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 回転, so be sure to know that to know this one. Also, it's just the readings of the kanji you learned too, so shouldn't be too hard.

examples.en: Oh, this chair is a swivel chair.
examples.ja: あ、このイス、回転するイスなんだ。

examples.en: That pitcher is good at spinning the ball.
examples.ja: あのピッチャーはボールを回転させるのが上手い。

examples.en: I gave it my all and answered the quiz questions while my head was spinning.
examples.ja: 頭をフル回転させて、がんばってクイズに答えました。

3946.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 回転 means "rotation" or "revolution." So, what happens when you make it into a verb? It becomes <vocabulary>to rotate</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to revolve</vocabulary>.
3946.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 回転 of level 10. Alternatively, you can just use the readings of the kanji as well. EZPZ.

examples.en: Do you have something to verify your identity?
examples.ja: 何か身分を証明できる物は持っていますか？

examples.en: I need a certified photo with date stamp.
examples.ja: 日付スタンプのある証明写真が必要なんです。

examples.en: Please show me proof that you have finished up to level sixty of WaniKani. If you don't prove it, I won't believe you.
examples.ja: ワニカニのレベル60まで終わったっていう証明を見せてください。証明がないなら信じませんよ。

3947.meaning_mnemonic: Is the <kanji>evidence</kanji> <kanji>bright</kanji> enough to convince me? Is this really <vocabulary>proof</vocabulary> enough to <vocabulary>prove</vocabulary> it?
3947.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You didn't learn the on'yomi for 明 (めい) with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

You need to show me <vocabulary>proof</vocabulary> to make me believe in the month of <reading>May</reading> (めい). Does it even exist? It may or may not be real (that's why it's called May), so you have to <vocabulary>prove</vocabulary> it to me somehow.

examples.en: What day of the week is today?
examples.ja: 今日って何曜日だっけ？

examples.en: I have Japanese lessons on Wednesdays.
examples.ja: 水曜日は、日本語のレッスンがあります。

examples.en: At our place, we have decided on dinner menus for each day of the week.
examples.ja: うちの家では、曜日ごとに夕飯のメニューを決めてるんです。

3948.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>weekday</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji> is the <vocabulary>day of the week</vocabulary>, as in "Monday" or "Tuesday." You'll be learning those on level 18, but first you should learn 曜日 to get you prepared.
3948.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi reading for 曜 and the kun'yomi reading for 日. You've learned both of these already, but be careful because ひ of 日 changes to び here.

examples.en: This blanket feels really good.
examples.ja: このブランケット、気持ちいい。

examples.en: Doesn't it feel good to have a clean house?
examples.ja: 家がきれいだと気持ちいいよね！

examples.en: It looks like I felt so comfortable that I was snoring during the massage.
examples.ja: マッサージ中、気持ち良すぎてイビキをかいてたみたい。

3949.meaning_mnemonic: When you have a "feeling" (気持ち) that is いい (that means "good" by the way), you have a <vocabulary>good feeling</vocabulary>.
3949.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the vocab word 気持ち, so if you know that (or the vocab words 気 and 持ち) you should be A-okay on this one. Maybe even <vocabulary>feeling good</vocabulary> about it?

examples.en: It seems like I am lucky today. I won a lottery.
examples.ja: 今日が運が良いみたいで宝くじが当たったんだ。

examples.en: What matters for gambling is your luck, rather than your ability.
examples.ja: ギャンブルは実力よりも運が大切だ。

examples.en: I might have run out of luck though, and I don't want to use it up on something like this.
examples.ja: こんなことで使い果たしたくはないけど、これで運を使い果たしちゃったかも。

3950.meaning_mnemonic: This takes the <kanji>luck</kanji> meaning from the kanji. Think of it this way: If you're "carrying" you're going to create your own luck. Now nobody will mess with you, kanji gangstah. You carry guns and have a ton of <vocabulary>luck</vocabulary> because of it.
3950.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji! How... shall I say... <vocabulary>luck</vocabulary>-filled?

examples.en: That comedy duo is from the Kansai region.
examples.ja: あのコンビは関西の芸人です。

examples.en: This guy is a total noob in Kansai, so we’ll have to show him around.
examples.ja: こいつは関西は完全に初心者だから、俺らがガイドしてやらないとな。

examples.en: I heard that people from Kanto and people from Kansai don't get along well. Is it true?
examples.ja: 関東の人と関西の人って折が合わないって聞いたんですが、本当ですか。

3951.meaning_mnemonic:
Get <kanji>connected</kanji> to <kanji>west</kanji> Japan by going to <vocabulary>Kansai</vocabulary>! 

関西 is a region in western Japan that includes cities like Osaka, Kyoto, and Kobe. To get to West Japan, you have to pass through (or over) it, so you can think of it as the geographical beginning of western Japan.
3951.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses on'yomi readings. The 西 on'yomi is usually going to be せい, which you've seen before, but in this word it's さい. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember that:

Ugh, tricky readings like the one for <vocabulary>Kansai</vocabulary> really make you want to <reading>sigh</reading> (さい).

examples.en: I was born in Osaka.
examples.ja: 私は生まれは大阪です。

examples.en: Osaka has a lot of delicious food.
examples.ja: 大阪には美味しい食べ物がたくさんあります。

examples.en: I was so excited about the Osaka trip that I totally neglected my studies.
examples.ja: 大阪旅行が楽しみすぎて、勉強がすっかりお留守になってしまっていました。

3952.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>heights</kanji>. What a nice area to be, it's where everyone wants to live! This magical place is <vocabulary>Osaka</vocabulary>. Heard of it before? It's a city, and kind of the rival to Tokyo.
3952.reading_mnemonic: The reading is pretty weird, but then again so are people from Osaka (just kidding, Osakazens!). The 大 reads like おお from おおきい. Then, 阪 uses the kun'yomi reading as well, which you didn't learn. That being said, doesn't this kanji look like 坂, which also means slope? Well, it shares a kun'yomi reading as well, so if you've seen 坂 you can apply that reading over to here, making おおさか. Then again, if you know this word means <vocabulary>Osaka</vocabulary> you probably can figure out how to write it too. Don't forget the double おお though!

examples.en: The steering wheels of Japanese cars are usually on the right side.
examples.ja: 日本の自動車のハンドルは通常右側にあります。

examples.en: My right eye is blurry.
examples.ja: 右側の目がボヤけるんです。

examples.en: There's a lot of salt in the right-hand drawer of Koichi's desk.
examples.ja: コウイチのデスクの右側の引き出しには、塩がたくさん入っています。

3953.reading_mnemonic: The reading is all kun'yomi vocab reading. You should know the reading of the vocab word 右 by now. Also, the 側 reading happens to be the reading you learned with the kanji as well as with the word 側.

examples.en: Everybody stands on the left side on this escalator I guess.
examples.ja: このエスカレーターでは、みんな左側に立っていますね。

examples.en: They drive on the left in Japan the same as they do in England.
examples.ja: 日本は、イギリスと同じで、車は左側通行ですよ。

examples.en: I prefer to lie with my left side down.
examples.ja: 私は左側を下にして横になる方が好きです。

3954.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>left</kanji> <kanji>side</kanji> is the <vocabulary>left side</vocabulary>. Simple as that.
3954.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this is vocab kun'yomi readings. Just take the vocab 左 and add it to 側 to have yourself <reading>ひだりがわ</reading>.

examples.en: To keep the zombies out, we lowered the shutters and locked them out from the inside.
examples.ja: ゾンビを中に入れないために、シャッターを下ろして、内側からカギをかけました。

examples.en: I think I got a splinter in the inside of my right thigh.
examples.ja: 右の太ももの内側にトゲがささったみたいです。

examples.en: She oozes beauty from within.
examples.ja: 彼女は、美しさが内側からにじみ出ている。

3955.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>inside</kanji> <kanji>side</kanji> is the <vocabulary>inside</vocabulary>. A little redundant but makes a lot of sense.
3955.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the kun'yomi readings. With 側 you've already learned it. With 内 you've also already learned the reading. Combine them together and you have うちがわ. In case you've forgotten, here's a mnemonic to help you remember that pesky うち portion. What is it that's drawn you inside? "<reading>Oo, chee</reading>se!" (うち) Cheese has drawn you inside. You're so excited that you exclaim, "Oo, cheese!"

examples.en: I thought this door opened outward, but it actually opens inward, I guess.
examples.ja: 外側に開くと思ったら、内側に開くドアだったんだね。

examples.en: I usually put the key in the outside pocket though....weird.
examples.ja: いつもは外側のポケットにカギを入れておくんですけど...おかしいなぁ。

examples.en: With this takoyaki maker, you can make the outside crispy even on a gas stove!
examples.ja: このタコ焼き器を使えば、ガスコンロでも外側がカリカリにできますよ！

3956.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings from the kanji. Since you learned the kun'yomi reading for 外 with the vocabulary, you should be just fine here.

examples.en: Both of my ears itch immensely.
examples.ja: 両側の耳がかゆくてムズムズします。

examples.en: Escalators are actually safer if you stand still without walking and stand on both sides.
examples.ja: エスカレーターは本当は安全上、歩かずに止まって両側に立つものなんだよね。

examples.en: A picture of Viet, with girls on both sides of him, was sold to the paparazzi.
examples.ja: 両側に女の子をはべらせたビエトの写真がパパラッチに売りつけられた。

3957.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Both</kanji> <kanji>side</kanji>s is <vocabulary>both sides</vocabulary>. Which side? Both sides.

両側 typically refers to both sides in a physical sense, like saying there are houses on both sides of the street or handrails on both sides of a staircase.
3957.reading_mnemonic: The first kanji takes the on'yomi reading and the second takes the kun'yomi reading. Luckily you know both of them already!

examples.en: Mt. Fuji can be seen to the east.
examples.ja: 東側にはふじ山が見えます。

examples.en: The balcony is on the east side of the apartment.
examples.ja: バルコニーはアパートの東側にあります。

examples.en: You can see the sunrise from the windows on the east side.
examples.ja: 東側のマドからは、日の出が見られます。

3958.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings you first learned with each kanji. As long as you remember this is double kun'yomi, you're good to go.

examples.en: A house with yellow on the west side is said to bring good luck for money.
examples.ja: 家の西側に黄色いものがあると金運がアップするそうです。

examples.en: A large poplar tree is planted on the west side of this hotel.
examples.ja: このホテルの西側には、大きなポプラの木が植えられていています。

examples.en: That's news from the western media, right?
examples.ja: それって西側のメディアのニュースでしょ？

3959.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>west</kanji> <kanji>side</kanji> of something is known as the <vocabulary>west</vocabulary> or the <vocabulary>west side</vocabulary>. Sorry, I couldn't think of a good west side story for this mnemonic.
3959.reading_mnemonic: This word uses kun'yomi readings, both of which you happened to learn with the kanji. If you can remember these are kun'yomi here, you'll be good to go!

examples.en: There are hardly any military personnel left in that country anymore.
examples.ja: もうあの国には、兵員はほとんど残っていません。

examples.en: Everyone everywhere is short of troops. It is not just a problem for our country.
examples.ja: どこもみんな、兵員不足は変わりませんよ。ウチの国だけの問題ではありません。

examples.en: How are you going to recruit soldiers when the people don't believe in us?
examples.ja: 国民たちが私たちのことを信じていない中で、どうやって兵員を集めるつもりなんですか？

3960.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>soldier</kanji> <kanji>member</kanji> (or a member of the soldiers) is a person that is of the <vocabulary>military personnel</vocabulary>. It also shows the amount of <vocabulary>military strength</vocabulary> an army has. The more soldier members, the more military strength and military personnel it has!
3960.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This is my ultimate weapon!
examples.ja: これが俺の最終兵器だ！

examples.en: I used to work at a chemical weapons laboratory.
examples.ja: 化学兵器の研究室で働いていたことがあります。

examples.en: We discussed whether using arms was right or wrong.
examples.ja: 私たちは兵器使用の是非について語り合いました。

3961.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>container</kanji>s that <kanji>soldier</kanji>s use aren't just bowls and stuff, they're the things that hold their <vocabulary>arms</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>weapons</vocabulary>. Think spear and sword containers, full of weapons!
3961.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: He is a former soldier.
examples.ja: 彼は元兵士です。

examples.en: Of the 300, only 14 soldiers remain.
examples.ja: 300人のうち、残った兵士はわずか14人です。

examples.en: The soldier's eyes silently informed me of this.
examples.ja: 兵士の目は無言で私にそのことを伝えた。

3962.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Why is that US soldier wearing pince-nez glasses?
examples.ja: あの米兵は、どうして鼻メガネをかけているの？

examples.en: There are many U.S. soldiers passing through here, so please don't be a distraction to the traffic.
examples.ja: ここは米兵がたくさん通るので、通行のジャマにならないようにしてください。

examples.en: The American soldier is looking for land to build a new house.
examples.ja: その米兵は新しい家を建てるために土地を探しています。

3963.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 米国 is "America." Well, more of that again. With 米 representing "America" you can combine that with 兵 (<kanji>soldier</kanji>) to have yourself a <vocabulary>US soldier</vocabulary> / <vocabulary>American soldier</vocabulary>.
3963.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What is the cause of the fight?
examples.ja: ケンカの原因は何ですか？

examples.en: Due to the wildfire of unknown origins, the town has been in such a chaotic situation.
examples.ja: 原因不明の山火事で、町は大変なことになっています。

examples.en: The cause of his illness is said to be work-related stress.
examples.ja: 彼の病気の原因は仕事でのストレスだと言われています。

3964.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>original</kanji> <kanji>cause</kanji> is how you got into this mess. Forget all the things it caused, the first <vocabulary>cause</vocabulary> is the <vocabulary>origin</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>source</vocabulary> of what's going on right now. You can pinpoint one thing that caused all of this!
3964.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I would like to study atomic energy in college.
examples.ja: 大学で、原子エネルギーの勉強をしたいと思っています。

examples.en: What was the atomic number and atomic symbol of this atom?
examples.ja: この原子の原子番号と原子記号は何だったっけ？

examples.en: Everything is made of atoms and molecules.
examples.ja: 全ての物は原子や分子でできています。

3965.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>original</kanji> <kanji>child</kanji> of everything is the <vocabulary>atom</vocabulary>. It is the child from which everything else is created, for it was the original child. Atoms are the building blocks of all things!
3965.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Comic book movies often lose the flavor of the original work.
examples.ja: マンガが原作の映画は、原作の良さを失ってしまうことが多いです。

examples.en: Have you read Shakespeare's original works?
examples.ja: シェイクスピアを原作で読んだことはありますか？

examples.en: I got an autograph from the original author.
examples.ja: 原作者の方にサインをもらいました。

3966.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>original</kanji> thing you <kanji>make</kanji> is the <vocabulary>original work</vocabulary>. It's always better to have the original, rather than a copy, I think.
3966.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I was diagnosed with intrinsic asthma.
examples.ja: 内因性ぜんそくだとしんだんされました。

examples.en: When a traumatic thing happens, endogenous opioids, which are morphine-like substances, will be secreted.
examples.ja: トラウマになる出来事が起きると、その苦しみを和らげるために、内因性オピオイドというのう内ま薬が分ぴつされます。

examples.en: The real reason I’ve been suffering for a long time is apparently because of an endogenous mental illness.
examples.ja: 私が長い間苦しんできた本当の理由は、どうやら内因性の精神疾患のせいらしい。

3967.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>inside</kanji> <kanji>cause</kanji> is an <vocabulary>internal cause</vocabulary>. Internal causes are usually the nastiest causes, if you ask me.

This word is mostly used in the fields of medicine and psychology. You’ll often see it as 内因性, which is a technical term used to talk about factors that originate within a person or an organism.
3967.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What do you think the main cause of inflation is?
examples.ja: インフレの主因って何だと思いますか？

examples.en: The main culprit is ultra-processed food.
examples.ja: 主因はウルトラプロセスフードですよ。

examples.en: The main cause behind the near-miss was that the train sped up when it wasn't supposed to.
examples.ja: ニアミスの主因は、この電車がスピードを上げるべきではないタイミングで上げたことです。

3968.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>main</kanji> <kanji>cause</kanji> is the <vocabulary>main cause</vocabulary> or the <vocabulary>primary cause</vocabulary>.
3968.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: They say "evil begets evil" right? So they just got properly punished.
examples.ja: 悪因悪果って言うだろ？当然のむくいだよ。

examples.en: If you do something bad, you'll get in trouble later because evil breeds evil.
examples.ja: 悪いことをしたら、悪因悪果で後々ひどい目にあうよ。

examples.en: What does the Bible say about karma? Was it like "evil begets evil" or something?
examples.ja: 聖書には、業について何て書いてあるんだっけ？悪因悪果とかだっけか？

3969.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>evil</kanji> <kanji>cause</kanji> yields the <kanji>evil</kanji> <kanji>fruit</kanji>, or more simply, <vocabulary>evil breeds evil</vocabulary>.

This is a Buddhist term, often used together with 善因善果 (virtue breeds virtue) to illustrate the concept of karma. While not a widely known phrase, it a nice saying to remind us of the importance of our actions.
3969.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The last 悪果 gets the 悪 shortened a little bit.

examples.en: Do you want to eat lunch in the cafeteria?
examples.ja: お昼ごはん、食堂で食べない？

examples.en: There are several eateries near my house.
examples.ja: 私の家の近くには、食堂がいくつかあります。

examples.en: When I went to the Tofugu dining hall a while ago, there was free live music from some singer I didn't know.
examples.ja: さっきトーフグ食堂に行ったんだけど、無名の歌手が無料のワンマンライブをしてたよ。

3970.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>eat</kanji>ing <kanji>hall</kanji> is a big room in which you eat. What big rooms do you eat in? How about a <vocabulary>cafeteria</vocabulary>, a <vocabulary>dining hall</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>diner</vocabulary>?
3970.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It might be better with a little more salt.
examples.ja: もう少し塩が多い方が良いかもしれませんね。

examples.en: I love salt ramen.
examples.ja: 私は塩ラーメンが大好きです。

examples.en: Until your baby turns one year old, you shouldn't give them any salt.
examples.ja: 一才になるまで赤ちゃんには塩をあげない方がいいですよ。

3971.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3971.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji, no extra salt needed.

examples.en: I drink salt water every day.
examples.ja: 私は毎日塩水を飲んでいます。

examples.en: Let broccoli soak in salted water for five minutes.
examples.ja: ブロッコリーは、塩水に5分つけておきます。

examples.en: Sea water stings on wounds because it's salty.
examples.ja: 海水は塩水なのでキズにしみます。

3972.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Water</kanji> with <kanji>salt</kanji> in it is <vocabulary>salt water</vocabulary>. Best not to drink 塩水.
3972.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the kun'yomi vocab readings. You know 塩's from the kanji and you know 水's from the vocab word 水. Combine them together and you have <reading>しおみず</reading>.

examples.en: I think it lacks a little saltiness.
examples.ja: 塩味が少し足りない気がします。

examples.en: Lightly-salted potato chips aren't that popular.
examples.ja: うす塩味のポテトチップスは、あまり人気がありません。

examples.en: Salty olives are an essential ingredient in Greek salad.
examples.ja: グリークサラダには、塩味の利いたオリーブが欠かせません。

3973.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>taste</kanji> of <kanji>salt</kanji> is a <vocabulary>salty taste</vocabulary> (it's also when something <vocabulary>tastes salty</vocabulary>).
3973.reading_mnemonic:
The readings are the kun'yomi vocab readings. So, take the readings of 塩 (you learned the reading with the kanji) and 味 and you have yourself <reading>しおあじ</reading>.

If you happen to be a cooking show fan, you might also hear the on'yomi reading of this word - <reading>えんみ</reading>. This word can also be read as <reading>しおみ</reading>, which has more or less the same meaning as the primary reading you learned.

examples.en: No matter what happens, never misuse government money!
examples.ja: ゼッタイに官金に手を出すんじゃないぞ！

examples.en: That politician was blinded by government money.
examples.ja: あの政治家は官金に目がくらんだんだよ。

examples.en: Do you think that taking a child to daycare in a government car is, in a sense, a misuse of government funds?
examples.ja: 保育園まで公用車に子どもを乗せて行くことは、ある意味で官金の私消に当たると思いますか？

3974.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Government</kanji> <kanji>gold</kanji> (aka money) is what makes up <vocabulary>government funds</vocabulary>.
3974.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: He is a former diplomat.
examples.ja: 彼は元外交官です。

examples.en: My father is a diplomat and a diplomat from another country gave him a rare guitar, which is one of only a few that exist in the world.
examples.ja: 私の父は外交官で、世界に数台しかないギターを他の国の外交官からプレゼントされました。

examples.en: The diplomat does not seem to know much about fashion.
examples.ja: その外交官はファッションについては詳しくないようです。

3975.meaning_mnemonic: Someone from the <kanji>outside</kanji> who comes in to <kanji>mix</kanji> with the <kanji>government</kanji> is a <vocabulary>diplomat</vocabulary>. Really, that's what diplomats do, right? They come from the outside (country). They mix with the government, and they do what they're there to do!
3975.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: You should take care of your own feelings before you take care of other people's feelings.
examples.ja: 人の気持ちを察する前に、自分の気持ちを大切にするべきです。

examples.en: Even without telling them, I wanted them at least to guess that it wasn’t the only reason.
examples.ja: 言わなくても、それだけが理由じゃないことくらい察してもらいたかった。

examples.en: When I was in elementary school, I told my name to the mother of the first friend I ever made, and her expression changed. After that, the child suddenly stopped hanging out with me. I was eight at the time, but I understood everything.
examples.ja: 小学生の時、初めて仲良くなった子の母親に名前を言うと、顔色が変わった。それ以後、その子は急に私とつるまなくなった。当時八才だったが、全て察した。

3976.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>guess</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to guess</vocabulary>. Alternatively, you can learn this as <vocabulary>to sense</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to presume</vocabulary>.
3976.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this is actually the same as what you learned with the kanji, but the さつ is shortened to さっ. If you had <vocabulary>to guess</vocabulary> be sure to guess with the shorter つ.

examples.en: She is very good at sensing danger.
examples.ja: 彼女は危険察知能力が高い。

examples.en: He sensed his boss's frustration and stayed as far away from him as possible.
examples.ja: 彼は上司のイライラを察知し、出来るだけ近づかないようにしました。

examples.en: Viet and his foot soldiers seemed to have sensed that the police would raid them.
examples.ja: ビエトと手下たちは、警察の手入れがあることを事前に察知していたようだ。

3977.meaning_mnemonic: Okay, so you <kanji>guess</kanji> but you also kind of <kanji>know</kanji>. You can make an <vocabulary>inference</vocabulary> as to what the answer is... You're not 100% sure, but you think you know, even though you're guessing.
3977.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You know the 察 part, although it gets shortened to さっ here. You didn't learn 知's on'yomi when you learned the kanji, though, so here's a mnemonic to help you with it:

One <vocabulary>inference</vocabulary> everyone can make is that you probably want to eat some <reading>chee</reading>se (ち). Seriously, it's written all over your face. You can try to hide it, but everyone saw how hot and bothered you just got in the dairy section. It doesn't take a mind-reader to <vocabulary>sense</vocabulary> how bad you're jonesing for some cheese.

examples.en: I'm afraid that we request that seated customers please order something from the menu.
examples.ja: おそれ入りますが、お席をご利用されるさいは、メニューから何か一つご注文をお願いします。

examples.en: Let's put everybody's bags on the seat to the right of me.
examples.ja: 私の右側の席にみんなの荷物をおきましょう。

examples.en: "Excuse me. Could you move over and let me sit down, please?" "I’m sorry, this seat is taken."
examples.ja: 「すみませんが、席を詰めて私を座らせてもらえませんか？」「申し訳ないんですが、この席は空いてないんです。」

3978.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
3978.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the on you learned with the kanji. Have a seat and relax.

examples.en: I will be absent tomorrow.
examples.ja: 明日は欠席します。

examples.en: There were zero absences from yesterday's meeting.
examples.ja: 昨日のミーティングの欠席者はゼロでした。

examples.en: I had to miss the graduation ceremony because I got COVID.
examples.ja: コロナにかかってしまったので、卒業式は欠席しなくちゃいけませんでした。

3979.meaning_mnemonic: When a <kanji>seat</kanji> is <kanji>lack</kanji>ing the person it's supposed to have in it, there is an <vocabulary>absence</vocabulary>. Where is Johnny? Another absence? Ugh. Johnny. C'mon.
3979.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Note that the けつ is shortened to けっ as つs often are when in a situation like this.

examples.en: I'm afraid that my attendance will probably be irregular.
examples.ja: すみませんが、出席は不定期になると思います。

examples.en: I'm not planning to attend Koichi's birthday party.
examples.ja: コウイチのバースデーパーティーには、出席しない予定です。

examples.en: Could you put me on another flight? I really have to attend the G7.
examples.ja: 別の便に乗せていただけますか？どうしても、G7に出席しなくてはならないんです。

3980.meaning_mnemonic: The people who <kanji>exit</kanji> their <kanji>seat</kanji>s at the end of the show are the number of people who showed up, not counting empty seats. This is the true <vocabulary>attendance</vocabulary>.
3980.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just note the しゅつ gets changed to しゅっ, as many つs do in this situation.

examples.en: No seats are available on this flight.
examples.ja: このフライトに空席はありません。

examples.en: Are there still many open seats left? If possible, I’d prefer to sit in the front.

examples.en: I went to see a movie on Christmas day in the U.S. and I was surprised to see that the theater was nearly empty.
examples.ja: アメリカでクリスマスに映画を見に行ったら、ほとんど空席でびっくりしました。

3981.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>sky</kanji> <kanji>seat</kanji> is a seat full of sky (aka nothing!). This is an <vocabulary>empty seat</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>open seat</vocabulary>.
3981.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: He is always smiling.
examples.ja: 彼は常に笑顔です。

examples.en: My mother is always running.
examples.ja: 私の母は常に走っています。

examples.en: It takes some kids a while to realize their parents aren’t always right.
examples.ja: 自分の親が常に正しいわけではないことを知るのに、時間がかかる子どももいます。

3982.meaning_mnemonic: The particle に here is a clue that this word is an adverb. An adverb describes actions, so what's a <kanji>normal</kanji> action? It's one you're <vocabulary>always</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>constantly</vocabulary>, doing. That's what makes it normal!
3982.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn. In order to learn it, think of this:

I <vocabulary>always</vocabulary> <reading>tune</reading> (つね) my violin, but today I didn't tune it. So, now I sound terrible. Imagine how terrible my untuned violin sounds, compared to how it always sounds.

examples.en: I want to be able to have daily conversations in Japanese.
examples.ja: 私は日本語で日常会話が出来るようになりたいです。

examples.en: I do my daily shopping on Amazon.
examples.ja: 日常の買い物はアマゾンですませます。

examples.en: I would like to know what the daily life of Koichi is like.
examples.ja: コウイチの日常がどんなものなのか知りたいです。

3983.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Normal</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji>s are what you have in your regular <vocabulary>everyday life</vocabulary>. This is your <vocabulary>normal life</vocabulary>.
3983.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I was relieved that you guys have common sense.
examples.ja: 常識のある人たちばかりで、安心しました。

examples.en: Common sense suggests that the plan won't succeed.
examples.ja: 常識的に考えれば、その計画は成功しないだろう。

3984.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Normal</kanji> <kanji>discerning</kanji> is the discerning you do on a daily basis, without thinking. It is all the things that you do that are <vocabulary>common sense</vocabulary>.
3984.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I think that comedian has definitely been deprived of any chance to appear on television recently. Don't you agree?
examples.ja: あの芸人、ゼッタイ最近干されてるよね。

3985.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>dry</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to dry something</vocabulary>.
3985.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Why do you need <vocabulary>to dry something</vocabulary>? Because someone used a <reading>hose</reading> (ほす) and got everything all wet. Ugh, you shouldn't leave that hose out anymore...

examples.en: It's said that the pond at this shrine had water no matter what kind of dry weather there was.
examples.ja: この神社の池には、どんな干天でもゼッタイに水があったんだって。

examples.en: Here, it suddenly started pouring rain last night, completely different from the dry weather we've had until now.
examples.ja: こちらでは、今までの干天がウソのように、昨夜から急に大雨になっています。

examples.en: Maybe it's because we've had a drought all these years, but the river is not flowing.
examples.ja: ここ最近ずっと干天だったせいか、川の水が流れてないんですよね。

3986.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 天気 is weather (and how 天 often refers to sky things?). Well, when those sky things are dry, you have <vocabulary>dry weather</vocabulary>.

Note that 干天 is quite old-fashioned and you'll find it mainly in formal writing and advanced set expressions.
3986.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: If parents interfere too much in school life, the child may feel stressed.

3987.meaning_mnemonic: When you're <kanji>ford</kanji>ing a stream, and you suddenly feel <kanji>dry</kanji> feelings around you, that doesn't make any sense for something wet. This dryness is an <vocabulary>interference</vocabulary>. It's an <vocabulary>intervention</vocabulary> trying to stop you from fording.
3987.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.ja: この薬を飲むと、幻が見えますよ。

examples.ja: 幻の魚をつかまえたぞ！

examples.en: It was like a phantom.

3988.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. You can add <vocabulary>phantom</vocabulary> to the meanings as well, because phantoms are kind of like <vocabulary>illusion</vocabulary>s.
3988.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You look up to see a crazy <vocabulary>illusion</vocabulary>. You can't believe it's real. Master Roshi, from Dragonball, is standing in front of you (you thought he was a cartoon!). Then, he splits into a million versions of himself, creating a <reading>mob of Roshi</reading>s (まぼろし). This mob goes on to train many people to fight.

examples.en: Isn't that just a hallucination?

examples.en: I've heard that hallucinogenic mushrooms grow in that forest.

3989.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>illusion</kanji> you have when you're <kanji>awake</kanji> is a <vocabulary>hallucination</vocabulary>.
3989.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That is an illusion.

examples.en: The atmosphere of the venue was so beautiful that I felt like I was in a fantasy world.

3990.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>illusion</kanji> that you <kanji>imagine</kanji> is your big <vocabulary>fantasy</vocabulary> (it's also an <vocabulary>illusion</vocabulary>). This makes sense, though, right? An illusion is an illusion, sure. But, when you imagine it, it becomes your fantasy!
3990.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: There’s gum stuck to the bottom of your shoe.

3993.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>river</kanji> <kanji>bottom</kanji> is the <vocabulary>river bottom</vocabulary>, also known as the <vocabulary>riverbed</vocabulary>.
3993.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the readings you learned with the kanji. Just don't forget the rendaku for 底!

examples.ja: ようやくマイホームが建ちました！

3994.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 建てる is "to build." This is similar to that, but it's the version where you're not doing the building. Something is just getting built. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to be built</vocabulary>. You can remember that by thinking about how <reading>two</reading> (つ) buildings were built without you noticing. These two buildings just seemed to pop up out of nowhere and, unfortunately, they're now blocking your view.
3994.reading_mnemonic: The reading is shared with 建てる, so if you know 建てる then you should be able to read this word as well.

examples.en: This is very nicely designed building, isn't it?

examples.en: See that red building over there? That red building is a local art gallery.
examples.ja: あそこに赤い建物があるのが見えますか？あの赤い建物は、地元のアートギャラリーです。

3995.meaning_mnemonic:
This is a <kanji>build</kanji> <kanji>thing</kanji>, or perhaps a <kanji>build</kanji>ing <kanji>thing</kanji>. In other words, a <vocabulary>building</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>structure</vocabulary>. 

建物 is a very general word that can refer to any kind of building, including residential buildings, commercial buildings, or public facilities.
3995.reading_mnemonic: The reading might look a little strange, but makes sense once you get it. You already know that the verb 建てる means "to build", and that a もの is a "thing". Now just remove the る part from the verb to make it a noun, combine it with もの, and we get <reading>たてもの</reading>! Just remember that it’s all kun’yomi since it comes from the verb 建てる.

examples.en: Viet is good at separating his public and private selves.
examples.ja: ビエトは本音と建前を使い分けるのが上手い。

examples.en: They're just pretending that's the case for appearance's sake.
examples.ja: それは建前上、そういうことにしてるだけですよ。

examples.en: It is often said that "the contrast between one’s personal feelings and public behavior" is a uniquely Japanese culture, but it is found in every country in the world.
examples.ja: よく「本音と建前」は日本独特の文化だと言われますが、世界中どこの国にもあるものですよ。

3996.meaning_mnemonic:
We all <kanji>build</kanji> up something in <kanji>front</kanji> of ourselves. It's the front we present to the world, the <vocabulary>public behavior</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>public stance</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>social niceties</vocabulary> that maintain harmony.

建前 is very important in Japan. For example, you might find yourself invited to an acquaintance's home out of courtesy, with the expectation that you’ll decline (also out of courtesy!). A host of a party may say "just bring yourself," but guests know this could be 建前, and considering their own 建前, they bring a small gift anyways.  People can also be reluctant to say "no" to things, like drinks with coworkers when they really want to go home, and may not to show it when they find situations inconvenient or unpleasant. So you might need some guesswork to peek behind the 建前 that people build up in front of themselves!
3996.reading_mnemonic: The reading is pretty strange. It's a lot like 建物 in that it's read as たて, which is like the word 建てる even though the て isn't showing here. So, you'll have to remember it's read like 建てる but the て gets pushed into the kanji.

examples.en: I haven't truly fallen in love yet.

3997.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: Your <vocabulary>love</vocabulary> isn't toward a person, it's toward this giant <reading>Koi</reading> (こい) fish you met the other day. The fish is just so... so... handsome! You get hearts popping above your head every time you think about this koi!

examples.en: This is a song about lost love.

3999.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

4002.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>love</kanji> your <kanji>self</kanji> that is <vocabulary>self love</vocabulary>. 4004.reading_mnemonic:

You lay there on the ground, and the fans around the stadium are disgusted with your performance. Some hipster walks up to you and says: "<reading>Yah, Boo</reading>" (やぶ) referring to how poorly you did. "No boo!", you reply back. "Yah boo", they say again.

examples.en: To be honest, this movie you made is a flop. However, you can’t let it get you down just because you failed once. Someone said that success is the ability to go from one failure to another with no loss of enthusiasm, right?
examples.ja: 正直言って、君が作ったこの映画は失敗作だね。でも、一度失敗したからといって、クヨクヨしてちゃダメだよ。誰かも、「成功とは、失敗から失敗へと熱意を失うことなく進んでいける能力である」って言ってただろ？

4028.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. examples.en: LMAO! You are just terrible at humming.

You know 鼻's reading from the kanji (はな) and you know 歌's reading from the vocabulary word 歌 (うた). Combine them together and you have a very nice humming tune and reading, はなうた.

I guess that blood added a little tenten (it represents the blood coming out of that nose!). Spurt spurt spurt.

examples.ja: 日曜日の朝は、毎週教会に行きます。

examples.en: I got sunburned during Sunday's hike.
examples.ja: 日曜日のハイキングで日焼けをしてしまいました。

4055.meaning_mnemonic: This is a day of the week. You know this because it has 曜日 in it. But what day of the week is it? The <kanji>Sun</kanji> day of the week is <vocabulary>Sunday</vocabulary>. Doesn't get much easier than that for you. Lucky!
4055.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know the word 曜日 as well.

examples.en: Would you like to go out for a drink this coming Monday after work?
examples.ja: 今度の月曜日、仕事の後、飲みに行かない？

examples.en: Monday is the beginning of a new week.
examples.ja: 月曜日は新しい週の始まりです。

examples.en: I always have a hard time getting up on Mondays. I don't want to go to work.
examples.ja: 月曜日はいつも起きるのがツライです。会社に行きたくないんで。

4056.meaning_mnemonic: This is a day of the week. You know this because it has 曜日 in it. But what day of the week is it? The "<kanji>moon</kanji>" day of the week is <vocabulary>monday</vocabulary>. Why? Because "Moon" is pretty much just "Mon," right?
4056.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know the word 曜日 as well.

examples.en: I have piano lessons on Thursdays at six o'clock.
examples.ja: 木曜日は六時からピアノなんです。

examples.en: I am planning to do the cleanup on Thursday.
examples.ja: そうじは木曜日にしようと思ってます。

examples.en: I've been having coughs since Thursday.
examples.ja: 木曜日からセキが出てるんです。

4057.meaning_mnemonic: This is a day of the week. You know this because it has 曜日 in it. But what day of the week is it? The <kanji>tree</kanji> day of the week is <vocabulary>Thursday</vocabulary>. Tree day comes after water day (which is Wednesday, for Water-Wednesday!). Trees need water to grow, which is why the tree comes right after the water.
4057.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know the word 曜日 as well.

examples.en: What we have to do on Wednesday can be roughly split up into three things.
examples.ja: 水曜日にするべきことは、大きく分けて三つあります。

examples.en: I'll get it done by Wednesday.
examples.ja: 水曜日までに終わらせます。

examples.en: Every Wednesday, I go to the pool after school and swim.
examples.ja: 毎週水曜日、学校の後プールに行って泳いでいます。

4058.meaning_mnemonic: This is a day of the week. You know this because it has 曜日 in it. But what day of the week is it? The <kanji>water</kanji> day of the week is where the water flows from. Think of your entire week as a big hill, with Wednesday (hump day) being in the middle. This hump is a hill. What originates from hills? Water! That's why Water day is <vocabulary>Wednesday</vocabulary>.
4058.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know the word 曜日 as well.

examples.en: She is an international student from Canada.
examples.ja: 彼女はカナダからの留学生です。

examples.en: These are support programs available for exchange students.
examples.ja: これが留学生向けのサポートプログラムです。

examples.en: That class's foreign students look kind of innocent, don't you think?
examples.ja: あのクラスの留学生、何だかあどけない感じがするよね。

4059.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 留学, which means "study abroad"? Do you also remember 学生, which is "student"? This word is like those two words mashed together (they share a 学), making it a "study abroad student." What's a better way to say that? How about <vocabulary>exchange student</vocabulary>!
4059.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I like Japanese comedy.
examples.ja: 私は日本のお笑いが好きです。

examples.en: We want to be comedians.
examples.ja: 俺たち、お笑い芸人になりたいんです。

examples.en: Oh, that was hilarious! I never expected it to end up like some kind of comedy!
examples.ja: あー、面白かった。まさかあんなお笑いみたいな結末になるとは、思ってもみなかったよ！

4060.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 笑う is "to laugh." This is a noun version of that, though it's not "a laugh," (that's 笑い). Add お to that and you have the thing that makes you laugh. It's <vocabulary>comedy</vocabulary>. It's the <vocabulary>joke</vocabulary> that's elevated with お because it made you laugh SOOOOO much. Haha!
4060.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same 笑う or 笑い. It's also the same as what you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: I try to put only what I need in my hand luggage.
examples.ja: 手荷物の中には、必要なものだけを入れるようにしています。

examples.en: You can leave your baggage at the front desk.
examples.ja: フロントで手荷物をあずかってもらえるよ。

examples.en: I got stuck at the baggage check!
examples.ja: 手荷物チェックのとこで引っかかっちゃったんだ！

4061.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 荷物 and how it means "baggage" or "luggage." Add a <kanji>hand</kanji> to it and you have <vocabulary>hand baggage</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>hand luggage</vocabulary>.
4061.reading_mnemonic: If you know 荷物 and you know 手, then you should be able to Voltron the two together into one mega reading.

examples.en: Certificates cannot be issued.
examples.ja: 証明書は発行できません。

examples.en: Could I check your ID?
examples.ja: 身分証明書はお持ちですか？

examples.en: I forgot my bag with my graduation certificate in it on the train.
examples.ja: 電車の中に卒業証明書が入ったカバンを忘れてきてしまった。

examples.en: Are you sure you own land on the moon? Do you have some sort of written proof?
examples.ja: あなたが月に土地を所有してるなんて本当なんですか？証明書でもあるんですか？

4062.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 証明 means "proof"? Well, when you <kanji>write</kanji> the proof down on something, you have a <vocabulary>certificate</vocabulary>.

This can be used for different kinds of <vocabulary>written proof</vocabulary>, like a 卒業証明書 (graduation certificate), 身分証明書 (personal ID), and more.
4062.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Knowing 証明's reading will also be helpful.

examples.en: Everybody laughed for some reason when I said that people eat KFC for Christmas dinner in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本ではクリスマスディナーにケンタッキーを食べると言ったら、なぜか笑いが起きました。

examples.en: I don't know what I'm laughing at anymore, but I just can't stop laughing.
examples.ja: もう自分でも何を笑ってるのか分からないけど、ただ笑いが止まらないんです。

examples.en: It’s not like you to cry at movies. You always laugh really hard when there are any serious scenes in them.
examples.ja: 映画を見て泣くなんて、お前らしくないじゃないか。いつもどの映画のどんなシリアスなシーンにも大笑いしてるのに。

4063.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 笑う is "to laugh." This is the noun version, because the う in 笑う turns to い (so don't confuse this as an adjective). What is the noun version of "to laugh"? It's <vocabulary>a laugh</vocabulary>.
4063.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 笑う, so just make sure you know that so you can know this as well.

examples.en: If you write me an IOU, I don't mind loaning you some money.
examples.ja: ちゃんと借用書を書いてくれるんだったら、お金をかしてもいいよ。

examples.en: This illustration was borrowed from Aya of Tofugu.
examples.ja: このイラストはトーフグのアヤさんから借用させてもらいました。

examples.en: English has many loan words from French, and Spanish has many loan words from Arabic.
examples.ja: 英語にはフランス語からの借用語がたくさんありますし、スペイン語にはアラビア語からの借用語が多いんですよ。

4064.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>borrowing</kanji> <kanji>task</kanji> is just another way to say <vocabulary>borrowing</vocabulary>. This is also for when you take out a <vocabulary>loan</vocabulary>.

借用 is a formal word for the borrowing of things like money, facilities, or other goods. You can also use it in a jokingly formal way in everyday conversation though, like ちょっと借用しただけだよ (I just borrowed it for a moment).
4064.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I want to skim the scum off the top, so can I borrow your ladle for a second?
examples.ja: アクを取りたいので、ちょっとお玉を借りてもいいですか？

examples.en: I borrowed one of your loose‐leaf sheets of paper, Kristen.
examples.ja: クリステンのルーズリーフ、一枚借りたよ。

examples.en: "I’m sorry I lost the romance novel I borrowed from you." "Don’t worry about it. I won’t need it anymore anyway. I have a girlfriend now."
examples.ja: 「ごめんね。君から借りていた恋愛小説をなくしちゃったんだ。」「気にしないでいいよ。それはもう必要ないから。彼女ができたんだ。」

4065.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>borrow</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to borrow</vocabulary>.
4065.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Dude, can I borrow your <reading>ca</reading>r (か)? Please?

examples.en: Before I knew it, my debt had reached five million yen.
examples.ja: 気づいたら借金が五百万円になっていた。

examples.en: Once he's paid off his debts, he plans to start a new life.
examples.ja: 借金を返し終わったら、彼は新しい人生を始めるつもりです。

examples.en: Koichi owes Viet 50,000,000 yen.
examples.ja: コウイチは、ビエトに五千万円を借金してます。

4066.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>money</kanji> (and <kanji>gold</kanji>) you <kanji>borrow</kanji> is your <vocabulary>debt</vocabulary>. Be sure to pay it back before the yakuza come for you.
4066.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The しゃく gets shortened to しゃっ though, so beware. Just think of that like the little bit that you lost to the yakuza, because they weren't happy you didn't pay back your debt. *cut*

examples.en: The cost benefit is greater with renting.
examples.ja: コストメリットは借家の方が大きいんですよ。

examples.en: You need to buy a house soon, too, or you'll be a renter for the rest of your life.
examples.ja: お前もそろそろ家を買わないと、一生借家ぐらしになるよ。

examples.en: I built a shed in the yard without permission, even though it's a rental property. I wonder if it's okay.
examples.ja: 借家なのに、庭に勝手に小屋を建てちゃったんですよね。大丈夫かな？

4067.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>borrow</kanji> a <kanji>house</kanji> it's a <vocabulary>rented house</vocabulary>. This could also be a <vocabulary>house for rent</vocabulary>.

You can use 借家 in conversation to formally refer to a rented house or a house for rent. But it's more commonly found in legal contexts, like in laws and regulations.
4067.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji, but in this case the second kanji can be read with either the on'yomi or kun'yomi. This uses a less common kun'yomi of 家, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

If you live in a <vocabulary>rented house</vocabulary>, someone has to give you the keys and let you in and stuff. You're only renting, after all. And when they let you in they'll say, "Here's a <reading>shack</reading>, <reading>yah</reading> (しゃくや) house renter! Enjoy!"

By the way, in the secondary reading しゃっか, the しゃく changes to しゃっ. This reading is mostly used in legal contexts though, so しゃくや is more common.

examples.en: Nalanda Monastery was the Mecca of Buddhism.
examples.ja: ナーランダ僧院は仏教のメッカでした。

examples.en: I climbed up to the Taktsang Monastery on the mountain by myself.
examples.ja: 一人で山上のタクツァン僧院まで登りました。

examples.en: Nice to meet you, I'm Koichi. I am starting to work at this temple from today. Please take care of me.
examples.ja: 初めまして。今日からこの僧院で働くコウイチです。よろしくお願いします。

4068.meaning_mnemonic:
An <kanji>monk</kanji>’s <kanji>institution</kanji> is going to be a <vocabulary>monastery</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>temple</vocabulary>. What a nice place to live, I'm sure!

This word refers to Buddhist monasteries, and it's often used for ones outside of Japan.
4068.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This book is written by a former Buddhist monk.
examples.ja: この本は元仏僧の方が書かれた本です。

examples.en: I am currently researching the lifestyle of Buddhist monks.
examples.ja: 今、仏僧の生活スタイルについて調べています。

examples.en: It's quite a dangerous world when even a renowned Buddhist monk becomes a yakuza, isn't it?
examples.ja: 高名な仏僧がヤクザになるとは、世の中もブッソウになったモンだねぇ。

4069.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This is how we cut out the heart shape.
examples.ja: こうやってハートの形を切り取るんです。

examples.en: Can you clip this coupon for me?
examples.ja: このクーポンを切り取っておいてもらえますか？

examples.en: I am sure the media will only cut out the parts that are newsworthy.
examples.ja: マスコミはきっとニュースになりそうなところだけを切り取るだろ。

4070.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>cut</kanji> and <kanji>take</kanji> something, you are going to cut it right off. So, this verb is <vocabulary>to cut off</vocabulary>.
4070.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 切る and 取る. So, know those words separately and you can combine them into this word.

examples.en: I saw a man take the smartphone out of Michael’s bag.
examples.ja: 男が、マイケルのカバンからスマホを取り出すのを見たよ。

examples.en: The woman took a pen out of her pocket.
examples.ja: 女はポケットからペンを取り出した。

examples.en: Can you take the pufferfish out of the oven for me?
examples.ja: オーブンからフグを取り出しておいてくれない？

4071.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>take</kanji> something and then <kanji>remove</kanji> it, is when you reach in and grab something and choose it and pull it out. This is <vocabulary>to pick out</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to take out</vocabulary>.
4071.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the individual words 取る and 出す. Put them together and you should be able to read this word too.

examples.en: Viet was chuckling softly to himself, especially when Koichi was yelling.
examples.ja: 取り分けコウイチがどなっている時に、ビエトは一人静かに笑っていました。

examples.en: I finally passed JLPT N1 and I'm especially appreciative of Tofugu for that.
examples.ja: ついにJLPT1に合格したんですが、トーフグには取り分け感謝しています。

examples.en: It’s not especially cold today.
examples.ja: 今日は取り分け寒いという訳ではない。

4072.meaning_mnemonic:
You 取り (take) and then 分け (divide) something. But you'll want to be <vocabulary>especially</vocabulary> careful not to give anyone an unequal share. This is especially important because we’re dealing with money, and people will flip out and shoot you under the table if you aren't especially accurate.

Note that this word is usually written in kana.
4072.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the words 取る and 分ける. So long as you know those words you should be able to read this one as well.

examples.en: A button came off.
examples.ja: ボタンが取れちゃった。

examples.en: It might be difficult for this stain to be removed.
examples.ja: このシミは取れないかもしれないね。

examples.en: Renting an office in the business district will be considerably expensive, but it’s important for our image and I think it will pay for itself in about a year.
examples.ja: ビジネス街にオフィスを設けるとなると賃料はかなり高くつきますが、我々のイメージにとって重要な事でもありますし、一年ぐらいで元は取れるのではないかと思うんです。

4073.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

This is an intransitive verb. That means it does not take a direct object. Something comes off. Something is removed. No direct object here. That's why this verb means <vocabulary>to come off</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be removed</vocabulary>.
4073.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 取る.

examples.en: I'm worried about whether they'll obey the agreement.
examples.ja: ちゃんと取り決めを守ってもらえるのか、不安です。

examples.en: You should make living arrangements with your roommate.
examples.ja: ルームメイトと生活上の取り決めをしておいた方がいいよ。

examples.en: According to the contract between our company and Ms. Salmon, it is unfortunate, but we did not make an agreement regarding her appearance in our competitor’s commercials.
examples.ja: サーモンさんと我が社で取り交わした契約によると、残念なことに彼女が競合他社のCMに出演することについて我々は何の取り決めも行っておりませんでした。

4074.meaning_mnemonic: You've <kanji>take</kanji>n a <kanji>decision</kanji> from someone. By doing this, you've created a kind of <vocabulary>arrangement</vocabulary> with them. Imagine yourself pulling this decision out of the person. They don't want to necessarily give it to you, but they're letting you pull it out of them, kind of. When you've pulled it out, you've come to an arrangement, though they've pulled some of your decision out too.
4074.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi reading for both kanji, which you might have guessed already since there's hiragana sticking out of both of them. The 取り comes from 取る and the 決め comes from 決める. Put them together and what have you got? Bibbidi bobbidi とりきめ!

examples.en: He always wants to complain about something.
examples.ja: 彼は何かにつけて文句を言いたがります。

examples.en: I could not complain about the food at that restaurant.
examples.ja: そのレストランの料理には文句のつけようがありませんでした。

examples.en: That's a pickup line, isn't it?
examples.ja: それは口説き文句でしょ？

4075.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>paragraph</kanji> in <kanji>writing</kanji> is what you send someone when you want to submit a <vocabulary>complaint</vocabulary>. You want to make sure these are in writing, though, otherwise you don't have proof of your complaint. Also, don't make it longer than a paragraph, because that's too long and nobody cares about how you think the shop staff mistreated your dog Fluffy.
4075.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Shh! That's a forbidden phrase!
examples.ja: シーッ！それは禁句ですよ！

examples.en: From now on, "Kawaii" is a forbidden phrase, okay?
examples.ja: これからは、「可愛い」は禁句ですよ。

examples.en: In front of our president, phrases like "next time" or "someday" are forbidden. He's a person who follows the policy of doing things today if they can be done today.
examples.ja: ウチの社長の前では「今度」とか「いつか」は禁句です。今日できることは今日やってしまうポリシーの人なんで。

4076.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>paragraph</kanji> that is under <kanji>prohibition</kanji> is under prohibition because it contains a <vocabulary>taboo word</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>taboo phrase</vocabulary>. Do not say this word, please!
4076.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Saki speaks in a cute voice, don't you think?
examples.ja: サキって可愛い声で話すよね。

examples.en: Who does that cute baby belong to?
examples.ja: あの可愛い赤ちゃんは誰の子ですか？

examples.en: This WaniKani icon is so cute!
examples.ja: このワニカニのアイコン、めっちゃ可愛い！

4077.meaning_mnemonic: It's <kanji>possible</kanji> to <kanji>love</kanji> this thing. It's so gosh darn <vocabulary>cute</vocabulary>! Any really cute thing is possible to love.
4077.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is screwed up, though if we're lucky, you already know the word for cute. It seems to have injected itself into American and English culture a decent amount, anyways. If you are one of the lucky ones, you'll know that this word is read as かわいい. If you're not, think of the cute thing being a cow. Then you say, "that <reading>cowはいい</reading>" (かわいい), or "that cow is good" because it's so cute.

examples.en: We have permission from the school.
examples.ja: 学校から許可はもらっています。

examples.en: Who gave you permission to do that?
examples.ja: それって誰が許可したの？

examples.en: The president's permission is required to start a major project.
examples.ja: 大きなプロジェクトを開始するには、社長の許可が必要です。

4078.meaning_mnemonic: I <kanji>permit</kanji> that it is <kanji>possible</kanji>. So, go ahead, do it. I give you <vocabulary>permission</vocabulary>.
4078.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The theme of today's Tofugu podcast is the inseparability of life and death.
examples.ja: 今日のトーフグポッドキャストのテーマは、生と死の不可分性です。

examples.en: English contracts often have a severability clause as one of general provisions.
examples.ja: 英文けい約書には、一ぱんじょうこうの一つに、可分性というじょうこうがよくあります。

examples.en: As a general rule, divisible claims, like savings accounts, do not become the target of divisions of inherited property.
examples.ja: 預貯金などの可分債権は、原則として遺産分割の対象にはなりません。

4079.meaning_mnemonic: When it's <kanji>possible</kanji> to <kanji>separate</kanji> something, it's <vocabulary>divisible</vocabulary>. Just imagine separating things into parts. It's possible. So, if that's possible, it's divisible. Now think of something that's nothing (i.e. "no candy bars"). That is not possible to separate into parts. That is not divisible.
4079.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Glasses are an integral part of my life.
examples.ja: メガネは私の生活に不可欠です。

examples.en: What do you think would be essential to becoming fluent in Japanese?
examples.ja: 日本語がペラペラになるのに不可欠なことは何だと思いますか？

examples.en: When I go to the beach, sunscreen is essential.
examples.ja: ビーチに行く時は、日焼け止めが不可欠です。

4080.meaning_mnemonic: It's <kanji>not</kanji> <kanji>possible</kanji> to <kanji>lack</kanji>. It is <vocabulary> indispensable</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>essential</vocabulary>, so don't lack it!
4080.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I don't have the courage to confess.
examples.ja: 僕には告白する勇気はありません。

examples.en: How many times have you confessed your feelings to someone first?

examples.en: She finally confessed what she had done.
examples.ja: 彼女はついに自分のしたことを告白しました。

4081.meaning_mnemonic:
To <kanji>announce</kanji> something and make it <kanji>white</kanji> is to make a <vocabulary>confession</vocabulary>. Think of a completely blank sheet of paper - your confession clears all the announcements from the sheet of paper, making it white.

This word is often used when someone confesses romantic feelings for someone else.
4081.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The mimosa flower heralds the arrival of spring.
examples.ja: ミモザは春を告げる花です。

examples.en: I bid farewell to my girlfriend.
examples.ja: 恋人に別れを告げました。

examples.en: That hurricane announced the end to our routine.
examples.ja: あのハリケーンで、私達の日常は終わりを告げた。

4082.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>announce</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to announce</vocabulary>.
4082.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: I'd like <vocabulary>to announce</vocabulary>... we're not having one baby, we're having <reading>two</reading> (つ) babies!

examples.en: Did you see the newspaper ad in the Asahi Shimbun this morning?

examples.en: This chocolate was sold at a discount at Costco as a promotional item.

examples.ja: 図書館から借りた本に、スーパーの広告が一枚はさまっていました。

4083.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>announce</kanji> something to a <kanji>wide</kanji> audience, you're just throwing your message out there for everyone to hear. This is just a big wide <vocabulary>advertisement</vocabulary>.
4083.reading_mnemonic: Sorry, you only learned the kun'yomi reading with 広. So, think of it this way when you need to remember this word's meaning: You're advertising something. It's a big <vocabulary>advertisement</vocabulary> to advertise how terrible a person <reading>こう</reading>いち is. Come up with some terrible things he's done so that you can imagine this crazy Koichi advertisement you made and ran on national TV.

examples.en: Did you see the preview for the next episode of that drama?

examples.en: The trailer for that movie often pops up on YouTube.
examples.ja: その映画の予告はYouTubeでよく流れてきます。

examples.en: A death threat was sent to Tofugu's office.
examples.ja: トーフグのオフィスに殺人予告が送られてきたんです。

4084.meaning_mnemonic:
If you <kanji>announce</kanji> something <kanji>beforehand</kanji> you will have <vocabulary>advance notice</vocabulary>. Advance notice is always nice to give.

You'll also see this used as an abbreviation of 予告編, meaning <vocabulary>trailer</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>preview</vocabulary>.
4084.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Did you already see Tofugu's public, financial announcement?
examples.ja: トーフグの決算公告、もう見ましたか。

examples.en: Tofugu decided to put up an important public notice about Koichi in an official telegram.
examples.ja: トーフグは、日本政府の官報にコウイチについての重大な公告をのせることにしました。

examples.en: There is a law in Japan called the Electronic Public Notice Regulation. Do you have anything like that in your country?
examples.ja: 日本には、電子公告規則という法律がありますが、あなたの国はどうですか？

4085.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>public</kanji> <kanji>announcement</kanji> is a <vocabulary>public notice</vocabulary>.

公告 looks and sounds a lot like 広告, but the meanings are different. You might remember 広告 is for advertisements, but 公告 here is for the kind of official statements that companies or governments put out for the public, especially shareholders, creditors, or other stakeholders.

You can remember 公告 is a public notice because the kanji for "public" is 公, and it's not covered by a canopy like the other one. It's uncovered, all out in the open for everyone to see — public!
4085.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Maybe you should report it to the store manager.
examples.ja: 店長に報告した方がいいんじゃない？

examples.en: I have an announcement to make to you all today.
examples.ja: 今日は皆さんにご報告があります。

examples.en: You can leave when you have written your report.
examples.ja: 報告書が書けたら帰っていいですよ。

4086.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>News</kanji> that you <kanji>announce</kanji> becomes a <vocabulary>report</vocabulary>. When someone announces news on a topic, they are giving you a report on the <vocabulary>information</vocabulary>.

報告 is a report given by someone after they've done some investigation or research into the topic. It can be used for class presentations on a topic or a report given to your boss. This differs from 報道, which is a report released by news organizations.
4086.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Smoking is not good for you.
examples.ja: 喫煙は体に良くないです。

examples.en: Is there a smoking room in this area?
examples.ja: この辺りに喫煙室はありますか？

examples.en: None of Tofugu's employees smoke.
examples.ja: トーフグの社員には、喫煙する人が一人もいません。

4087.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I enjoy having the breakfast special at a cafe.
examples.ja: 私は喫茶店でモーニングを食べるのが好きです。

examples.en: The staff at this coffee shop are always smiling.
examples.ja: この喫茶店のスタッフは、いつも笑顔です。

examples.en: A stylish coffee shop has opened in our neighborhood.
examples.ja: ご近所にオシャレな喫茶店がオープンしました。

4088.meaning_mnemonic:
If you <kanji>consume</kanji> <kanji>tea</kanji> in a <kanji>shop</kanji>, it could either be a <vocabulary>cafe</vocabulary>, a <vocabulary>tea house</vocabulary>, or slightly confusingly, a <vocabulary>coffee shop</vocabulary>. Welcome! Sit down. Relax. Have some tea (or coffee).

This word often refers to cafes with a retro feel to them, though they can be modern too. These places usually serve a variety of drinks and light meals.
4088.reading_mnemonic: The readings are what you'd expect except for きつ getting shortened to きっ and 茶, which has this strange さ reading. To remember that it's さ instead of ちゃ, think of this <vocabulary>tea house</vocabulary> you're going in. You think it's nice and pleasant, and it is for a while... until someone starts working a <reading>saw</reading> (さ) outside, ruining the atmosphere. BEWWEEEEHHHEEEHHHHHE gatatatatatat BWEEEHEEE.

examples.en: Where is this information from?
examples.ja: その情報、どこ情報？

examples.en: First, let's organize the information.
examples.ja: まずは情報を整理しましょう。

examples.en: Sorry, I didn't have enough information.
examples.ja: すみません、情報不足でした。

4089.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>feeling</kanji> of <kanji>news</kanji> is that it should give you <vocabulary>information</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>data</vocabulary>, not fluff.
4089.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Rain is forecast for this afternoon.
examples.ja: 今日は午後から雨の予報です。

examples.en: Have you checked the weather forecast?
examples.ja: 天気予報、チェックした？

examples.en: The weather girl said the forecast is calling for hot weather, starting tomorrow.
examples.ja: お天気お姉さんは、明日から暑くなるって予報してたけどね。

4090.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>news report</kanji> that covers things <kanji>beforehand</kanji> (before they happen) is a <vocabulary>forecast</vocabulary>. For example, a weather forecast is a 天気予報.
4090.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I cannot believe what the media reports.
examples.ja: メディアが報じることは信じられません。

examples.en: Only the Associated Press reported the news.
examples.ja: そのニュースを報じたのはAP通信のみでした。

examples.en: Everyone felt relieved when they reported that Koichi was safe.
examples.ja: コウイチの無事が報じられて、みんな胸をなで下ろしました。

4091.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>news report</kanji> so you could try to say "to news report" but that doesn't make sense. What does make sense is "<vocabulary>to report on</vocabulary>," however.
4091.reading_mnemonic: The reading doesn't seem like it's the kanji's on'yomi reading, but it is. What an oddity! Do you think it's worth doing a news report on it? Koichi, reporting in on this strange reading that is readable by you right now. Signing off.

examples.en: Don't report lies!
examples.ja: ウソを報道するな！

examples.en: How will this terrorist attack be reported in Japan?
examples.ja: 今回のテロのことは、日本ではどのように報道されていますか？

examples.en: According to local media reports, a rare trading card of WaniKani was sold at auction for one hundred million yen.
examples.ja: 地元メディアの報道によると、ワニカニのレアトレーディングカードがオークションで一億円で落札されたそうです。

4092.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>News</kanji> travels down the <kanji>road</kanji> by way of a <vocabulary>news report</vocabulary>.

報道 specifically refers to information put out by news organizations or the press in the form of newspaper articles, radio or television broadcasts, etc. Notice that it's different from 報告, which is more general and means the reporting of information by anyone.
4092.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Where did you buy this charm?

examples.en: I always keep a picture of my father in my wallet as a talisman.
examples.ja: 私はいつも父の写真をお守り代わりにサイフに入れています。

examples.en: Apparently, even God has compatibility, so it's not good to wear multiple charms at the same time.
examples.ja: 神様にも相性があるから、たくさんのお守りを同時に付けるのは、良くないんだって。

4093.meaning_mnemonic: You know how 守る is "to protect," right? This is like that, but it's the noun version. It's not really "a protection," though it kind of is. What things can you wear to protect you from things like bad luck, demons, and ancient aliens? That would be an <vocabulary>amulet</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>charm</vocabulary>. You'll see these kinds of things sold at temples and such.
4093.reading_mnemonic: The reading is like that of 守る, so if you know the reading of that word you should be able to read this one as well.

examples.en: I took a housesitting job for 20,000 yen a day.

examples.en: In the U.S., it is not acceptable to leave small children alone at home.

4094.meaning_mnemonic: You know how 留守 means "absence" or "away from home"? Well, now that you're absent from your home, it's someone else's  turn to come to your home and take care of it. This person is the <vocabulary>caretaker</vocabulary>, someone who's <vocabulary>looking after one's house</vocabulary>.
4094.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Knowing 留守 will be important as well.

examples.en: How can you sit seiza for that long?
examples.ja: 何でそんなに長い間正座できるの？

examples.en: Frankly, I am not good at sitting on my knees.

4095.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>correct</kanji> way to <kanji>sit</kanji> is this way: <vocabulary>traditional Japanese sitting</vocabulary> (this is when you sit on your legs and your feet, kneeling). You can also call it <vocabulary>seiza</vocabulary>. Learning the reading will help with the meaning.
4095.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Have you ever done zazen?

examples.en: She relaxes every morning in zazen.

4096.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>sit</kanji> and do <kanji>zen</kanji> you are probably doing <vocabulary>zen meditation</vocabulary>. Hummmmm.
4096.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

4097.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>sit</kanji> <kanji>seat</kanji> is probably going to be a <vocabulary>seat</vocabulary>.
4097.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I am in Ginza now.

4098.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I bought a station lunch at a kiosk.

4099.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 弁当 is "bento"? Well, the 弁 in this word comes from that, so pretend it means "bento."
