As you might think, a train station bento is just a bento that's sold at a train station. Easy!
4099.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: We can't find Koichi's bow anywhere.
examples.ja: コウイチの弓がどこにも見当たらないんだ。

examples.en: You have to stabilize your upper body to draw the bow.
examples.ja: 弓を引くには、まず上半身を安定させなくてはいけません。

examples.en: I don't think you can buy bows and arrows at a convenience store, can you?
examples.ja: コンビニでは弓と矢は買えないと思うよ？

4100.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4100.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

All we need to shoot a <vocabulary>bow</vocabulary> is <reading>you 'n' me</reading> (ゆみ). One person holds the bow, the other fires the arrows. Teamwork makes the dream work. Even for shooting bows. Just you 'n' me.

examples.en: I took up Kyudo last month.
examples.ja: 先月、弓道を始めたんです。

examples.en: Why are Japanese bows for kyudo so powerful?
examples.ja: 日本の弓道の弓って、どうしてそんなに強いの？

examples.en: I got up early and went to the Kyudo club dojo to do Kyudo.
examples.ja: 早起きして、弓道部の道場で弓道をしてきました。

4101.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I almost forgot Koichi's face.
examples.ja: 危うくコウイチの顔を忘れる所だったよ。

examples.en: Sorry, Kanae. We all totally forgot about how much effort you put into it.
examples.ja: ごめんね、カナエちゃん。みんなカナエちゃんがどれだけ努力したのかすっかり忘れちゃってたんだ。

examples.en: Forget about it. There's nothing you can do about it now.
examples.ja: もう忘れなって。今さらどうにもならないんだから。

4102.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>forget</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to forget</vocabulary>.
4102.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You don't want <vocabulary>to forget</vocabulary> anything, because forgetting always makes everything <reading>worse</reading> (わす). Forgot your car keys? Now you can't drive. Forgot someone's name? Now you have to ask again and it'll be awkward. All these situations make your day worse, and probably your life worse too.

examples.en: The year-end party is tomorrow, not today.
examples.ja: 忘年会は今日じゃなくて明日です。

examples.en: I'm already really forgetful, so I don't need a so-called "forget the year party."
examples.ja: 元々忘れっぽいんで、私には「忘年会」は必要ありません。

examples.en: As for what happened at today's year-end party, I'll just let it go.
examples.ja: 今日の忘年会であった出来事は、忘れる事にします。

4103.meaning_mnemonic: Time to get <kanji>together</kanji> and <kanji>forget</kanji> the <kanji>year</kanji>... what a terrible year, good thing a new one is coming. This get together is a <vocabulary>year end party</vocabulary>.
4103.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: In order to write a good article, it is important to make a rough draft.
examples.ja: いい記事を書くためには下書きをすることが大事です。

examples.en: For now, the rough draft of the illustration is complete.
examples.ja: イラストの下書きが完成しました。

examples.en: I always go for it without any drafts; I'm all about one-shot victories!
examples.ja: 俺はいつも下書き無しで、一発勝負なんだよ！

4104.meaning_mnemonic: Something <kanji>below</kanji> your <kanji>writing</kanji> isn't what you want to necessarily publish to the world. It's below your writing, after all. This is merely a <vocabulary>rough draft</vocabulary>.

examples.en: I always try to put my schedule on the calendar as soon as it is made.
examples.ja: いつも予定ができたら、すぐにカレンダーに書き入れるようにしています。

examples.en: I think there should be more space for comments. The current space is not enough.
examples.ja: もっとコメントを書き入れるスペースがあった方がいいと思います。今のスペースだと足りないです。

examples.en: If you could fill in your social security number here in this document, I can take care of the rest.
examples.ja: この書類のここに社会保証番号を書き入れてもらえれば、あとは全て上手くやっておきますよ。

4105.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>insert</kanji> what you <kanji>write</kanji> into something is <vocabulary>to write in</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to fill in</vocabulary>.
4105.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 書く and 入れる. Combine those two words to get the reading of this word.

examples.en: I can't remember how to write this kanji.
examples.ja: この漢字の書き方が思い出せません。

examples.en: Could you teach me how to write business e-mails?
examples.ja: ビジネスメールの書き方を教えてください。

examples.en: I think this way of writing makes it a little difficult to understand the meaning of the sentence.
examples.ja: この書き方だと、ちょっと文の意味が分かりにくいんじゃないかな。

4106.meaning_mnemonic: This is the <kanji>way</kanji> of <kanji>writing</kanji> (kind of like how 見方 is the way of seeing). So this means <vocabulary>way to write</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>how to write</vocabulary>. How's your 書き方 for kanji? Mine is terrible.
4106.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi readings from the vocab words 書く and 方. So as long as you're okay with those, you can apply that knowledge over here.

examples.en: It is not possible to rewrite it now.
examples.ja: 今から書き直すのはムリです。

examples.en: Could you rewrite this part a bit?
examples.ja: この部分を少し書き直してもらえませんか？

examples.en: I rewrote that letter over and over again at the time.
examples.ja: その手紙、当時、何度も何度も書き直したんです。

4107.meaning_mnemonic: 書く means "to write" and 直す means "to fix," right? Well, if you write something and then decide to fix it, you're going to have <vocabulary>to rewrite</vocabulary> it. Yup, the only way to fix that horrible chicken scratch paragraph you've written is to totally rewrite it from the ground up, so you'd better start rewriting ASAP.
4107.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 書く and 直す. Know those and you'll know how to read this word too!

examples.en: Bacon is so tasty that I can eat an unlimited number of strips.
examples.ja: ベーコンは美味しいから、何枚でも食べれるよ。

examples.en: About how many tickets have you sold so far?
examples.ja: チケット、今のところ何枚ぐらい売れたの？

examples.en: How many WaniKani trading cards are there in total?
examples.ja: ワニカニのトレーディングカードって、全部で何枚あるんですか？

4108.meaning_mnemonic: You have <kanji>flat object</kanji>s but <kanji>what</kanji> amount of flat objects? This word is asking that question: "<vocabulary>how many flat objects</vocabulary> are there?" If this doesn't make sense, think back to words like 何回 or 何年 which ask "how many ____" just like this one.
4108.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The minimum order quantity for stickers is one hundred.
examples.ja: ステッカーの注文枚数は、百枚からです。

examples.en: Can you guess how many credit cards Koichi has in his wallet at the moment?
examples.ja: 今コウイチのサイフの中にあるクレジットカードの枚数を当ててみてください。

examples.en: Could you count the number of origami papers?
examples.ja: 折り紙の枚数を数えてもらえますか？

4109.meaning_mnemonic: You have <kanji>flat object</kanji>s. You have a <kanji>number</kanji> of them. These flat objects are flat things, right? Flat things like sheets of paper, perhaps (or other sheets of things). So, this word is <vocabulary>number of sheets</vocabulary>.
4109.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I’ll give you five stickers as a bonus too.
examples.ja: ステッカーを五枚、オマケに付けておきますね。

examples.en: There are only five sheets of copy paper left.
examples.ja: コピー用紙、あと五枚しかないよ。

examples.en: I went to a convenience store and bought five postcards.
examples.ja: コンビニに行って、葉書を五枚買いました。

4110.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 枚 is a <kanji>flat objects counter</kanji>. So, now we're counting! You have <vocabulary>five flat objects</vocabulary>.
4110.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Can I just wash it with water?
examples.ja: 水で洗うだけでいいの？

examples.en: When you return home, please wash your hands and gargle.
examples.ja: 家に帰ったら手を洗ってうがいをしてください。

examples.en: Viet made a clean break from both the yakuza world and drugs.
examples.ja: ビエトは、ヤクザの世界からも、薬物からも、完全に足を洗った。

4111.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>wash</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to wash</vocabulary>.
4111.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You have <vocabulary>to wash</vocabulary> <reading>a ro</reading>ck (あら) you found. It looks shiny, but you can't tell until you wash it.

examples.en: While I waited for the car wash to finish, the part-timer kept yacking at me and it was really annoying.
examples.ja: 洗車が終わるのを待っている間、ガソリンスタンドのバイトがずっとダラダラ話しかけてきて、かなりウザかった。

examples.en: Who would buy a car wash business to launder money?
examples.ja: 誰がマネー・ロンダリングするのに洗車ビジネスなんて買うっていうのさ？

examples.en: If there's someone out there who wants to wash Koichi's car, please email us at hello@tofugu.com.
examples.ja: コウイチの車の洗車をしたいという方がいたら、hello@tofugu.comまでメールしてください。

4112.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>wash</kanji> that washes <kanji>car</kanji>s is a <vocabulary>car wash</vocabulary>.
4112.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Don't confuse this with the same-sounding 戦車 though... unless you're washing your 戦車 in a 洗車...

examples.en: It's a tote bag with a simple and sophisticated design.
examples.ja: シンプルで洗練されたデザインのトートバッグです。

examples.en: Her use of language is very sophisticated.
examples.ja: 彼女の言葉づかいはとても洗練されています。

examples.en: Hmmm... not bad, but maybe a little more refinement would be good?
examples.ja: うーん…悪くはないけど、もう少し洗練した方がいいかな？

4113.meaning_mnemonic: You take your <kanji>practice</kanji> and you <kanji>wash</kanji> it. Slowly chunks fall off and it becomes more and more simple. You are washing away the gunk on the outside to attain <vocabulary>refinement</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>polish</vocabulary> yourself, via practice.
4113.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I started working part-time as a dishwasher in a restaurant.
examples.ja: レストランで皿洗いのバイトを始めました。

examples.en: I saw on TV that there is a ramen shop where you can pay for your meal by washing dishes, is this true?
examples.ja: 食事代は皿洗いでOKなラーメン屋さんがあるってテレビで見たんですけど、本当ですか？

examples.en: While my husband is lying on the living room sofa, I feel really sad doing the piled-up dishes, stealing sideways glances at him.
examples.ja: リビングのソファで横になっている夫を横目に、たまりにたまったお皿の皿洗いをしているとき、とても悲しくなります。

4114.meaning_mnemonic: You know the word 皿 (plate) and the word 洗う (to wash), right? You can probably guess dish washing is happening here, but this is a noun, so it's the idea of <vocabulary>dishwashing</vocabulary>, AKA <vocabulary>doing dishes</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>washing dishes</vocabulary>.
4114.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the individual vocab words (you can tell because there's a bit of hiragana stuck on there). It's the reading for 皿 and 洗う combined.

examples.en: I am going to bake a cheesecake today.
examples.ja: 今日はチーズケーキを焼くつもりです。

examples.en: If you find these in your yard, burn them immediately. They're tick eggs.
examples.ja: これを庭で見つけたら、すぐに焼いてください。ダニのタマゴなんで。

examples.en: Isn't that meat already cooked? Let's move it to the plate before it becomes overcooked!
examples.ja: そのお肉、もう焼けてるんじゃない？焼きすぎになる前にお皿に上げよう！

4115.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>bake</kanji> or <kanji>burn</kanji>. So, the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to bake</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to burn something</vocabulary>, or even <vocabulary>to grill</vocabulary>.

焼く means to apply heat to something to change it in a physical way. It can refer to lightly toasting something, charring it, or even burning it to ashes depending on the context. It's commonly used in cooking contexts to describe baking, grilling, or roasting food. But it can also be used with pottery, film photography, and even sun-tanning.
4115.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the reading you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: You should properly take care of your skin from sunburn.
examples.ja: ちゃんと日焼けケアした方がいいよ。

examples.en: I got suntanned from being on the beach too long.
examples.ja: ビーチにいすぎて日焼けしちゃった。

examples.en: Because I forgot to apply sunscreen, I got sunburnt and turned completely red.
examples.ja: 日焼け止めクリームを忘れたせいで、日焼けで真っ赤になった。

4116.meaning_mnemonic: When the <kanji>sun</kanji> <kanji>burn</kanji>s something, and that something is you, it's giving you <vocabulary>sunburn</vocabulary>.
4116.reading_mnemonic: The readings here are the vocab kun'yomi readings. You have ひ for 日 and や for 焼け (which you learned with the vocab). Combine it with some sunscreen and hopefully you'll prevent the <vocabulary>sunburn</vocabulary>.

examples.en: Do you want to go out for yakitori today?
examples.ja: 今日、焼き鳥食べに行かない？

examples.en: I started working part-time at a yakitori restaurant.
examples.ja: 焼き鳥屋でアルバイトを始めました。

examples.en: Grilled chicken is essential for my life.
examples.ja: 焼き鳥は私の生活に不可欠です。

4117.meaning_mnemonic: A nicely <kanji>bake</kanji>d <kanji>bird</kanji> isn't just any bird, it's <vocabulary>grilled chicken</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>roast chicken</vocabulary>. You may also know it by its Japanese name: <vocabulary>yakitori</vocabulary>.
4117.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the vocab kun'yomi readings. With 焼き, you can use the reading you learned with the kanji. With 鳥 just remember back to the vocab word, とり. Combine and eat.

examples.en: I am in the mood for grilled meat today.
examples.ja: 今日は焼き肉が食べたい気分です。

examples.en: Yesterday, my family and I had yakiniku using a hot plate at home.
examples.ja: 昨日は家族でホットプレートで焼き肉をしました。

examples.en: I find it really irritating when people chew yakiniku loudly.
examples.ja: 私が特にイライラするのは、焼き肉をクチャクチャ音を立てて食べる人です。

4118.meaning_mnemonic: Nicely <kanji>bake</kanji>d <kanji>meat</kanji> is <vocabulary>grilled meat</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>yakiniku</vocabulary>. Mmm, yum! If you go to Japan look out for 焼肉 places (same meaning and reading). They're pretty tasty, if you're into meat at least.
4118.reading_mnemonic: 焼き uses the reading you learned with the kanji. 肉 does too. Put them on the grill and enjoy!

examples.en: This is a photo of a sunset.
examples.ja: これは夕焼けの写真です。

examples.en: I booked a room with an ocean view where you can see the sunset.
examples.ja: 夕焼けが見えるオーシャンビューの部屋を予約しました。

examples.en: Watching the sunset calms my mind.
examples.ja: 夕焼けを見ると、心が落ち着きます。

4119.meaning_mnemonic: When the <kanji>evening</kanji> is <kanji>burning</kanji> with sun, it is the sun going down, getting all close to the horizon and earth. This is the <vocabulary>sunset</vocabulary>, or more specifically, the <vocabulary>evening glow</vocabulary> you can see during a sunset.
4119.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the kun'yomi vocab readings. Combine 夕 and 焼け (you learned the reading via the kanji) and you'll have <reading>ゆうやけ</reading>.

examples.en: Hey! Smoke is coming out of the grill!!
examples.ja: ちょっと！バーベキューグリルから煙が出てるよ！！

examples.en: I woke up to the smell of burnt smoke.
examples.ja: 煙のコゲくさいニオイで起きました。

examples.en: The time of our youth vanished in the blink of an eye, like smoke.
examples.ja: 僕らの青春の時間は、煙のようにアッという間に消えていった。

4120.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4120.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You're standing around a <vocabulary>smoke</vocabulary> machine. It's billowing up smoke. Strangely, your buddy Bill Murray is here too. For some reason, he loves the smoke, and he puts his head in it, breathing it in deeply until he goes into a coughing fit. You decide it's time to stop him. "<reading>Kay, Murray</reading> (けむり), it's time to stop that," you say.

examples.en: I thought I saw black smoke, and turns out there's a fire at that apartment building over there!
examples.ja: 黒煙が見えると思ったら、あそこのマンションで火事だって！

examples.en: I like diesel cars that run with a cloud of black smoke.
examples.ja: 俺は黒煙をモクモク出して走るディーゼル車が好きなんです。

examples.en: The steam locomotive billowing black smoke and running through the winter landscape of Hokkaido was really cool.
examples.ja: 黒煙を上げながら冬の北海道を走るSLは、とてもカッコよかったです。

4121.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Black</kanji> <kanji>smoke</kanji> is <vocabulary>black smoke</vocabulary>. It's also something you should avoid if you can.
4121.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I prayed for the hurricane victims.
examples.ja: ハリケーンのひがい者のために祈りました。

examples.en: I pray that you will pass the national examinations successfully.
examples.ja: 国家試験に無事合格できるように祈っています。

examples.en: I don’t think many Japanese people know Japan’s national sport "sumo" used to be a ritual to pray for a bountiful rice harvest.
examples.ja: 日本の国技である相撲が、かつては米の豊作を祈る儀式だったことを知ってる日本人がたくさんいるとは思えないな。

4122.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>pray</kanji> and this verb is transitive, so it means <vocabulary>to pray for</vocabulary>.
4122.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: "You gotta pray for Christmas presents if you want Santa to bring you some!" "<reading>I know</reading> (いの), I know," you reply as you begin to pray for presents. You should say this out loud to remember it better.

examples.en: That concert was held for the purpose of praying for the recovery from the Great East Japan Earthquake.
examples.ja: そのコンサートは、東日本大震災の復興祈念のためのものでした。

examples.en: In Okinawa, I visited the Peace Memorial Park and the Himeyuri Peace Memorial Museum.
examples.ja: 沖縄では、平和祈念公園と、ひめゆり平和祈念資料館に行きました。

examples.en: We, the employees, would like to offer our prayers for a prosperous and happy new year for all of you.
examples.ja: 皆さまにとって、新年が幸多い年となりますよう、社員一同ご祈念申し上げます。

examples.en: Let's pray for more and more growth and prosperity for Tofugu, cheers!
examples.ja: トーフグの益々の発展と繁栄を祈念して、乾杯！

examples.en: I'll attend the peace memorial service for atomic-bomb victims tomorrow.
examples.ja: 明日は原爆犠牲者慰霊平和祈念式典に出席します。

4123.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>pray</kanji> with your <kanji>thought</kanji>s, making this a <vocabulary>prayer</vocabulary>.

While 祈願 is about formally asking a specific deity for something, 祈念 refers to <vocabulary>praying</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>wishing</vocabulary> in a more silent and personal sense. It's used in formal situations to express hopes for success, safety, peace, or recovery, and often appears in names of monuments or events that combine remembrance and hope, such as 平和祈念公園 (Peace Memorial Park) or 復興祈念イベント (Reconstruction Prayer Event).
4123.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: A safety prayer charm was hanging from the car's rearview mirror.
examples.ja: 車のバックミラーに、安全祈願のお守りがぶら下がっていた。

examples.en: I went to a shrine to pray that I could get my visa without any trouble.
examples.ja: 無事にビザが取れるよう、神社でご祈願してきました。

examples.en: You can offer a prayer at either a shrine or a temple.
examples.ja: ご祈願は、神社でもお寺でもできますよ。

examples.en: Koichi can do the war dance of the Martians.
examples.ja: コウイチは、火星人の戦勝祈願のおどりをおどることができます。

4124.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>pray</kanji> and make a <kanji>request</kanji>, as a <vocabulary>prayer</vocabulary> to some deity at a shrine or temple. 

This usually refers to making a wish or asking for a favor from a deity, like prosperity, good health, or winning an important sports game.
4124.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This is a non-smoking area.
examples.ja: ここは禁煙スペースです。

examples.en: All guest rooms at this hotel are non-smoking.
examples.ja: このホテルは、全客室禁煙です。

examples.en: I quit smoking using a smoking cessation patch.
examples.ja: 僕は禁煙パッチを使って禁煙しました。

4125.meaning_mnemonic: If <kanji>smoke</kanji> is <kanji>prohibite</kanji>d you probably shouldn't smoke. Aka <vocabulary>no smoking</vocabulary>, okay?
4125.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Students are not allowed to work part-time at this school.
examples.ja: この学校では、学生のアルバイトは禁止されています。

examples.en: I believe pets are not allowed in this apartment.
examples.ja: このアパート、たしかペットは禁止だったはずですよ。

examples.en: Viet told his gangsters that gambling was forbidden.
examples.ja: ビエトは手下のヤクザたちに、ギャンブルは禁止だと言い聞かせた。

4126.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Stop</kanji>! That's <kanji>prohibition</kanji> (prohibited)! When something is prohibited and you're forced to stop, that thing is obviously <vocabulary>forbidden</vocabulary>. If you see this you should probably not do the thing it's telling you not to do.
4126.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What's the name of that Zen temple, again?
examples.ja: あの禅寺の名前は何だっけ？

examples.en: I visited Nanzenji temple in Kyoto.
examples.ja: 京都の南禅寺に行ってきました。

examples.en: This temple is a Zen temple built in the 14th century.
examples.ja: このお寺は、十四世紀に建てられた禅寺です。

examples.en: I like the Zen temple in Kyoto called Tōfuku-ji.
examples.ja: 東福寺っていう京都の禅寺が好きなんです。

4127.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>zen</kanji> <kanji>temple</kanji> is just what it sounds like, a <vocabulary>zen temple</vocabulary>. Sounds nice.
4127.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is the two words 禅 and 寺 put together. The てら gets changed to でら, though.

In terms of when it's pronounced ぜんじ, if you put this word onto the end of the name of a 禅寺 the pronunciation changes to ぜんじ. It makes sense - it's more like a jukugo word that way (not that the original isn't, but you can see the separation of words coming together which gives the hint that it's a kun'yomi combo reading). Anyways, you may need a zen temple to keep your mind pure enough to remember this, but it's a good thing to keep in mind if you can.

examples.en: He is a Zen priest.
examples.ja: 彼は禅僧です。

examples.en: That is what some Zen monk said.
examples.ja: それは、どこかの禅僧が言っていた言葉です。

examples.en: How can I become a Zen monk?
examples.ja: 禅僧になるには、どうすればいいですか？

4128.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I want to enroll in a private college.
examples.ja: 私大に入学したいと思っています。

examples.en: Many kids at private universities have a part-time job too.
examples.ja: 私大の学生もバイトしてる子が多いですよ。

examples.en: It costs money to enroll in a private university.
examples.ja: 私大は入学にお金がかかります。

4129.meaning_mnemonic: You know how 私 can mean <kanji>private</kanji> and how 大 is the first half of 大学? Well, combine those together and you have the shortened version of <vocabulary>private college</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>private university</vocabulary>.
4129.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 大 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

You went to a specific <vocabulary>private college</vocabulary> just to study <reading>dye</reading>s (だい). You're so into dyes that you decided to go to this extremely expensive <vocabulary>private university</vocabulary> that specializes in dyes. Good for you!

examples.en: There's a wide variety of different races in this city.
examples.ja: この町には、色々な人種の人がいます。

examples.en: I don't really like racial jokes.
examples.ja: 人種をネタにしたジョークは、あんまり好きじゃありません。

examples.en: Now, race has nothing to do with it, does it?
examples.ja: 今、人種は関係ないですよね？

4130.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>kind</kanji> or <kanji>type</kanji> of <kanji>person</kanji> is when you categorize a person into different types. How do we do that? Well, you categorize by <vocabulary>race of people</vocabulary> (or more simply by <vocabulary>race</vocabulary>).
4130.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That's almost as if you didn't do it.
examples.ja: それは、ほぼやってないに等しいんじゃない？

examples.en: Even for people who aren’t nerds, using uppercase letters on the internet is equivalent to shouting.
examples.ja: オタクだけではなく他の人にとっても、ネット上で大文字を使うことは大声を出すことに等しいですよ。

examples.en: Do you think the left and right balls are equal in weight?
examples.ja: 左の金玉と右の金玉の重さって等しいと思いますか？

4131.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>equal</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>equal</vocabulary> (and also <vocabulary>similar</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>equivalent</vocabulary>). That "similar" one is a bit weird, because "similar" is not equal, though I'd lean more towards equal.
4131.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: What should be equal above all things? I think each <reading>人</reading> (ひと) should be equal!

examples.en: The "equal sign" is called "tōgō"! I didn't know that.
examples.ja: 「イコール」って「等号」って言うんだ！知らなかった。

examples.en: Koichi feels sick if the top and bottom lines of an equal sign are not the same length.
examples.ja: コウイチは等号の上と下の線が同じ長さじゃないと気分が悪くなる。

examples.en: You have to pay attention to whether the formula to the right of the equal sign is plus or minus.
examples.ja: 等号の右側の数式が正か負かについて、注意する必要があります。

4132.meaning_mnemonic:
How do you represent an <kanji>equal</kanji> <kanji>number</kanji>? With an <vocabulary>equal sign</vocabulary>.

It's worth pointing out that this is a pretty formal word that's used in advanced math. In everyday conversation, people would use イコール for the equal sign.
4132.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: How much is the first prize for this lottery?
examples.ja: この宝くじの一等の賞金はいくらですか？

examples.en: I won this bacon keychain when I won first prize in the bacon costume competition.
examples.ja: このベーコンのキーホルダーは、私がベーコンのコスプレ大会で一等賞を取った時にもらったんです。

examples.en: You are in the first-class carriage, yeah? That's so like you, Koichi!
examples.ja: 一等車に乗ってるとは、さすがコウイチだね。

4133.meaning_mnemonic: When you're <kanji>equal</kanji> to <kanji>one</kanji> you are the very top. You are <vocabulary>first class</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>first rank</vocabulary>. In fact, you are <vocabulary>the best</vocabulary>.
4133.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. いち gets shortened to いっ though, so watch out for that if you want to remain <vocabulary>the best</vocabulary>, yeah?

examples.en: This is designed to form an scalene triangle when viewed from above.

examples.ja: この時、以下の不等式が成り立ちます。

examples.en: The car is designed to distribute torque unequally at 41:59 between the front and the rear.
examples.ja: この車は、トルクが前41：後59で不等配分されるようになっています。

4134.meaning_mnemonic: When something is <kanji>not</kanji> <kanji>equal</kanji> is of course <vocabulary>unequal</vocabulary>. It's an <vocabulary>inequality</vocabulary>. You'll usually see this word in technical contexts like math and engineering, but it does pop up in more general formal writing, too.
4134.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Military training for soldiers took place in England.
examples.ja: イギリスで兵士たちの軍事訓練が行われました。

examples.en: That dog is well trained.
examples.ja: あの犬はよく訓練されている。

examples.en: Don't worry, it will work if you follow the training.
examples.ja: 大丈夫、訓練どおりにすれば上手くいくよ。

4135.meaning_mnemonic: You've got your <kanji>instruction</kanji> and you have your <kanji>practice</kanji>. Time to start your <vocabulary>training</vocabulary>, or simply your <vocabulary>practice</vocabulary>.
4135.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: When I think of that person, my heart aches.
examples.ja: あの人のことを思うと、胸が苦しいんです。

examples.en: I have a mole on my right chest.
examples.ja: 私は右胸にホクロがあります。

examples.en: Why did you get fired? Perhaps you should ask your own conscience about that.
examples.ja: どうして首になったかって？それはご自身の胸に聞いてみてはいかがですか？

4136.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4136.reading_mnemonic: This vocab word uses the same reading as the one you learned with the kanji. At least I won't have to bring up the image of you <reading>moon</reading>ing (むね) people with your breasts or whatnot. Oh dang, I just went and did it.

examples.en: Neither CT nor MRI showed any brain problems.
examples.ja: CTでもMRIでも、脳には問題はありませんでした。

examples.en: Did you know that a leech has thirty-two brains?
examples.ja: ヒルには脳が32個もあるって知ってた？

examples.en: You've got to make sure the bacon gets nice and crispy! There have been cases where tapeworms were found in the brains of people who ate it undercooked!
examples.ja: ベーコンはちゃんとカリカリになるまで焼かないと！生焼けで食べた人の脳からサナダムシが発見されたこともあるんだよ！

4137.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4137.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. Don't have to use your <vocabulary>brain</vocabulary> for that.

examples.en: How do you judge if someone is brain dead?
examples.ja: 脳死かどうかはどうやってジャッジするんですか？

examples.en: For now, try doing this exercise without thinking about it.
examples.ja: とりあえず脳死でこのエクササイズやってみて。

examples.en: Brain hemorrhaging may lead to stroke and, finally, brain death.
examples.ja: 脳内出血は、脳卒中につながり、最悪脳死を引き起こすこともあります。

4138.meaning_mnemonic: If your <kanji>brain</kanji> is <kanji>dead</kanji> you have <vocabulary>brain death</vocabulary>.
4138.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Try thinking carefully with what little brain you have!
examples.ja: 少ない脳みそを使ってよく考えてみろ！

examples.en: I'm so tired today, my brains just aren't working.
examples.ja: 今日はつかれすぎて脳みそが全然働いていません。

examples.en: I'm not addicted to my smartphone. When the battery runs out and I don't feel like doing anything, I relax by mindlessly scrolling through my phone with zero brain activity.
examples.ja: スマホ中毒じゃないよ。電池切れで何もしたくなくて、脳みそゼロでできるスマホのスクローリングでリラックスしてるんだよ。

4139.meaning_mnemonic: Do you know みそ Soup and how miso goes in it? This is that miso. It's soft and strange feeling. Now, your <kanji>brain</kanji> <kanji>miso</kanji>, that's your <vocabulary>brains</vocabulary> or your <vocabulary>gray matter</vocabulary>. Essentially, if someone cuts your head open with a katana, this is perhaps what would come out.
4139.reading_mnemonic: Reading is just what you learned with the kanji. Just use your 脳 a bit and it should be easy.

examples.en: That's media brainwashing.
examples.ja: それってメディアの洗脳だよ。

examples.en: They're all brainwashed by the government.
examples.ja: アイツらみんな、政府に洗脳されてるんだよ。

examples.en: The first training you receive after joining Tofugu is brainwashing you into the Tofugu mindset.
examples.ja: トーフグに入社した後、一番最初に受けるトレーニングは、トーフグマインドへの洗脳です。

4140.meaning_mnemonic: Give your <kanji>brain</kanji> a nice <kanji>wash</kanji>. No! Wait! It's not as nice as it sounds. This is <vocabulary>brainwashing</vocabulary>.
4140.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'm fed up with the double-talk of politicians.
examples.ja: 政治家達の二枚舌にはもうウンザリだよ。

examples.en: He has a forked tongue, so you should be careful.
examples.ja: あいつは二枚舌だから気をつけた方がいいよ。

examples.en: My boss is hypocritical, often saying "think for yourself!" and "do as you're told!"
examples.ja: 上司は二枚舌で、「自分で考えろ！」と「言われた通りやれ！」の二つが口グセなんです。

4141.meaning_mnemonic: You have <kanji>two</kanji> <kanji>flat objects</kanji> that make up your <kanji>tongue</kanji>. What kind of tongue is made up of two of anything? That's a tongue that's split, that's a <vocabulary>forked tongue</vocabulary>.
4141.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. That's the case for the first two kanji, but 舌 actually uses the kun'yomi. Not only that, it's read here as じた, and not した.

examples.en: Who did the graffiti here?
examples.ja: ここに落書きをしたのは誰だ？

examples.en: No, no, no, it's just a doodle.
examples.ja: いやいや、ただの落書きですよ。

examples.en: There used to be lot of graffiti along the underground passages at Shinjuku Station a long time ago, but we rarely see them now.
examples.ja: 新宿駅の地下道には、昔、たくさんの落書きがしてありましたが、今はほとんど見当たりません。

4142.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>fall</kanji> into the urge to <kanji>write</kanji>, you just grab whatever's nearby and start <vocabulary>doodling</vocabulary> on it.

落書き means doodling or <vocabulary>scribbling</vocabulary> without much thought, and it also means the scribbles themselves. Imagine a kid doodling in the margins of their notebook in class. <vocabulary>Graffiti</vocabulary> can be 落書き too, but usually this refers to vandalistic graffiti rather than the artistic stuff — think of an "anarchy" symbol under a bridge or a stick figure drawing in a bathroom stall.
4142.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 書, however, is kun'yomi in this case and also has rendaku. So just remember that it's read as が for this vocab and you'll be fine.

examples.en: Can you go put a postcard in the mailbox for me?
examples.ja: ポストに葉書を出してきてくれない？

examples.en: There was a handwritten message on the postcard.
examples.ja: その葉書には手書きのメッセージが書かれていました。

examples.en: She always sends a postcard from her trips.
examples.ja: 彼女は毎回、旅行先から葉書を送ってくれます。

4143.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>writing</kanji> that you put on a <kanji>leaf</kanji> is like something else. Instead of a leaf, think about writing you put on a leafish sized item. A <vocabulary>postcard</vocabulary> perhaps?
4143.reading_mnemonic: The reading is kind of weird, sorry. The reading for 葉 is the は you know and love. Then, 書 is かき despite not having a き on the end like you'd expect. So, it's weird. It's shortened like a postcard is a shortened letter, I suppose? Technically it is the 書き reading, but keep in mind that 書き gets rendaku'd.

examples.en: Kanji characters have both on reading and kun reading.
examples.ja: 漢字には音読みと訓読みがあります。

examples.en: What was the kun'yomi of this kanji?
examples.ja: この漢字の訓読みって何だったっけ？

examples.en: Oh, this is a kun'yomi? I thought it was an on'yomi.
examples.ja: え、これって訓読みだったの？てっきり音読みだと思ってた。

4144.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>instruction</kanji> <kanji>reading</kanji> may not make a lot of sense, but you've heard this word before. Jump to the reading and you'll know what the meaning of this word is.
4144.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the word 読み (like 読む) and the reading you learned for 訓 combined, making <reading>くんよ</reading>み. Sounds familiar? It's that <vocabulary>kun'yomi</vocabulary> reading you've heard so much about.

examples.en: It was a good lesson.
examples.ja: いい教訓になりました。

examples.en: I will not let this lesson be wasted.
examples.ja: この教訓をムダにはしません。

examples.en: I hope to learn from the lessons learned this time and do better next time.
examples.ja: 今回の教訓を活かして、次回はもっと上手くやれるようにしたいと思います。

4145.meaning_mnemonic: At least way back in the day, things that <kanji>teach</kanji> <kanji>instructions</kanji> to people are things that teach a <vocabulary>lesson</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>moral</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>teachings</vocabulary>. Back in the day, lots of learning was done through storytelling, and storytelling taught lessons and morals, thus, this word.
4145.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I still can't forgive him.
examples.ja: 彼のこと、まだ許すことはできないよ。

examples.en: Who said such awful things? It is unforgivable!
examples.ja: 誰がそんなヒドイこと言ったの？許せない！

examples.en: Ladies and gentlemen, please forgive me. I just farted in this car.
examples.ja: みなさん、どうかお許しください。今この車の中でオナラをしてしまいました。

4146.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>permit</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to permit</vocabulary>. It also means <vocabulary>to forgive</vocabulary>, in that "I'll permit it this time... but only this time." Look out for 許さない in TV shows, too. It means "I won't permit this!" or "I won't forgive you!"
4146.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: I'm going to allow it. <reading>You're</reading> (ゆる) allowed to do it this one time, okay?

examples.en: Today, I will try this method.
examples.ja: 今日は、やり方を試みる。

examples.en: The female spy tried to get closer to the man at the bar.
examples.ja: 女スパイは、バーで男の人に近づくことを試みた。

examples.en: I decided to try a new approach.
examples.ja: 新しいアプローチを試みる事に決めました。

4147.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>try</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to try to do something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to attempt something</vocabulary>.

This verb is transitive, meaning it takes a direct object. Here, the direct object is whatever it is that you're trying to do.
4147.reading_mnemonic: You know how when you try to do something you put your whole heart into it? Well, think of that in Japanese. You put your whole <reading>心</reading> (こころ) into it.

examples.en: Try this supplement.
examples.ja: このサプリ、試して。

examples.en: I tried various diets, but none of them worked.
examples.ja: 色々なダイエットを試したけど、どれもダメだったよ。

examples.en: I don’t know if I can lick my elbow, but I’ll give it a try.
examples.ja: 肘を舐めれるかどうかは分からないけど、試しにやってみるよ。

4148.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>attempt</kanji> or <kanji>try</kanji>. The verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to try something out</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to give something a try</vocabulary>. Why don't you try out the meaning of this verb, while you're at it?
4148.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Okay. Here's the deal. We have this wild animal. I want you <vocabulary>to attempt</vocabulary> to <reading>tame</reading> (ため) it. Now, imagine trying to tame this wild animal. Yeehaw!

examples.en: If you don't mind, why don't we play another game together?
examples.ja: 良かったらもう一試合しませんか？

examples.en: How was the soccer game?
examples.ja: サッカーの試合はどうでしたか？

examples.en: "That baseball game was really terrible." "Yeah, tell me about it."
examples.ja: 「あの野球の試合は本当にひどかったね。」「本当にそうだね。」

4149.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>attempt</kanji> to <kanji>join</kanji> together isn't just any get together. Imagine two people boxing. They attempt to knock each other out when they join together. That's why this word is <vocabulary>game</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>match</vocabulary>. Did you watch the 試合 today? No! Don't tell me what happened, I recorded it on the VHS.
4149.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi し for 試 and the kun'yomi あい for 合, which you learned with 場合. So you should be able to put them together!

examples.en: First, just taste it without saying anything.
examples.ja: 先ずは何も言わないで試食してみて。

examples.en: I lost interest in buying this after sampling it.
examples.ja: 試食の後、買う気を失ったんです。

examples.en: It's almost like I'm going to Costco to eat the food samples.
examples.ja: コストコには試食のサンプルを食べるために行くようなものです。

4150.meaning_mnemonic:
Go ahead and <kanji>try</kanji> an <kanji>eat</kanji>. How was that little try? That little <vocabulary>food sample</vocabulary>? That little <vocabulary>taste</vocabulary>?

You know when you walk into the supermarket and have people offering you the tiniest cube of cheese? That's what this is. So this word is commonly used in the context of product demonstrations or food events.
4150.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: He is my friend.
examples.ja: 彼は私の友達です。

examples.en: If you don't mind, would you like to be my friend?
examples.ja: よかったら、私と友達になってくれませんか？

examples.en: I heard from a friend of a friend that Viet is a yakuza!
examples.ja: 友達の友達から聞いたことなんだけど、ビエトってヤクザらしいよ！

4151.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>friend</kanji> that you <kanji>attain</kanji> is your <vocabulary>friend</vocabulary>. This is the most common way to say "friend," so learn it if you want to make any!
4151.reading_mnemonic: The readings for both of these are readings you haven't learned yet, though maybe you already know this word since it's fairly common. Think of it this way. You have your friend <reading>Tom</reading> (とも) Cruise. You like him, and he likes you. You're close enough friends that you can <reading>touch</reading> (だち) each other too. Like, on the shoulder or on the hand or whatever, without it being awkward. So, you like to <reading>Tom touch</reading> (ともだち) when you can, because he has nice skin.

examples.en: My daddy is a pizza delivery driver. He can deliver pizzas faster than anybody else.
examples.ja: 僕のお父さんはピザの配達人です。誰よりも速くピザを配達することができます。

examples.en: Koichi pounded his chest with a fist, saying he would definitely deliver it by six.
examples.ja: コウイチは、ゼッタイに六時までに配達してみせると言って、胸をたたきました。

examples.en: It completely slipped my mind that I have to deliver this flower today.
examples.ja: この花を今日中に配達しなければいけないのを、すっかり忘れていました。

4152.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>distribute</kanji> the goods, they <kanji>attain</kanji> the goods. You are going <vocabulary>to deliver</vocabulary> to everyone.
4152.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My mother's cooking is delicious to the level of a culinary master.

4153.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>person</kanji> who has "<kanji>attain</kanji>ed" is someone who knows much. They are a <vocabulary>master</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>expert</vocabulary>, obviously.
4153.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Due to a miscommunication, we ended up with a pink car.

examples.en: I'm worried about whether what I wanted to say was conveyed properly.

examples.en: I’m researching the neural signal transmissions that occur while people are learning a new language.
examples.ja: 私は、人々が新しい言語を学んでいる時の、ニューロンの信号伝達について研究しています。

4154.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>transmit</kanji> something and you <kanji>attain</kanji> it on the other end, you've done a <vocabulary>transmission</vocabulary>.
4154.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It is quiet today, isn't it?
examples.ja: 今日は静かですね。

examples.en: Excuse me, could you please be a little more quiet?
examples.ja: すみませんが、もう少し静かにしていただけますか？

examples.en: With Koichi and Viet on board, the cab quietly started to move.
examples.ja: コウイチとビエトを乗せて、そのタクシーは静かに動き出した。

4155.meaning_mnemonic: This is the な adjective form of <kanji>quiet</kanji>, which is kind of just like the noun, anyways. What is the adjective version of quiet? It's also <vocabulary>quiet</vocabulary>.
4155.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You need to be <vocabulary>quiet</vocabulary>. <reading>She's</reading> (しず) being nice and quiet, unlike you!

examples.en: First, I'll upload a still image.
examples.ja: まずは静止画をアップします。

examples.en: My cat stands still when I point the camera at her.
examples.ja: ウチの猫はカメラを向けると静止します。

examples.en: After hitting a home run, the batter always pauses just for a moment, right?
examples.ja: ホームランを打ち上げた後、バッターってゼッタイちょこっと静止するよね。

4156.meaning_mnemonic: Everything is <kanji>quiet</kanji> and <kanji>stop</kanji>ped. The world is <vocabulary>still</vocabulary> and everything is <vocabulary>at rest</vocabulary>.
4156.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I am not sure I can keep my composure when so many cute cats are around.

4157.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.ja: このアプリを使えば、すぐにファイルが分類できます。

examples.en: E-mails are automatically sorted by category.
examples.ja: 電子メールは、カテゴリーごとに自動的に分類されます。

4159.meaning_mnemonic:

分類 is a relatively formal word that refers to the act of classifying or categorizing items, organisms, or information into specific groups based on shared characteristics or criteria.
4159.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My dog is on two different medications.
examples.ja: うちの犬は二種類の薬を飲んでいます。

You can differentiate this from the future word 乱す because with れる you know it is <reading>rare</reading> for it to be like this. You aren't doing it, but it just happens on occasion (rarely) so you take advantage of it.

What you'd get is a <vocabulary>personal history</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>resume</vocabulary>. I guess you can think of it as a history of the schools and jobs you've left your footprints at.
4188.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: When you put on your pants, you always jump around, don't you?
examples.ja: ズボンを履く時って、いつもジャンプしながら履くよね？

examples.en: You haven't put your underwear on yet? Hurry up!
examples.ja: まだパンツ履いてないの？早くしなさい！

examples.en: Don't put sneakers on without socks! The sneakers will stink. How many times do I have to tell you this?
examples.ja: くつ下を履かずにスニーカーを履かないで！スニーカーがくさくなるって何度言ったら分かるの？

4189.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>footwear</kanji>. And what do you do with footwear, usually? You put it on! That's why this word is <vocabulary>to put on shoes</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to put on pants</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to put on a skirt</vocabulary>.

Okay, pants and skirts aren't exactly footwear. But 履く is basically used for any garment you wear from the waist down, including socks, shoes, boots, pants, skirts, shorts, and even underpants.
4189.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You decide to put on shoes, and then to put on pants. "Hahahaha!" (は) you laugh. What a ridiculous idea to put on shoes before you put on pants! But you do it every morning, and every morning it makes you laugh. You really crack yourself up.

examples.en: Can I have a bowl of wakame soup, please?
examples.ja: 若布スープを一つ下さい。

examples.en: Today's dinner is wakame rice.
examples.ja: 今日の晩ご飯は若布ご飯です。

examples.en: Wakame and cucumber salad is my favorite.
examples.ja: 若布とキュウリの和え物は私の大好物です。

4190.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>young</kanji> <kanji>cloth</kanji> for some reason is the seaweed <vocabulary>wakame</vocabulary>. If you've never heard of wakame before, go look it up. It's delicious and really good for you. Seaweed is kind of like cloth in the sea, right? Well, this young cloth is nice and soft and thin, like wakame. I imagine young people are soft and thin too, which is why the young cloth gets to be wakame.

Note that this word is more commonly written in kana, like わかめ or ワカメ.
4190.reading_mnemonic:
若い uses the same reading you learned with the kanji, but the reading for 布 is totally irregular. If you can figure out the meaning, you can use that to remember the reading (since they're the same), but here's a mnemonic to help you just in case:

You're eating <vocabulary>wakame</vocabulary> and you suddenly spot a <reading>目</reading> (め) looking up at you. You didn't know seaweed had eyes!

examples.en: It is a colorful and cute fabric.
examples.ja: カラフルでかわいい布ですね。

examples.en: I'm going to make cushion covers with this fabric.
examples.ja: この布でクッションカバーを作るつもりなんです。

examples.en: Oh, you use cloth diapers instead of disposable ones?
examples.ja: え、紙オムツじゃなくて布オムツを使ってるんですか？

4191.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4191.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You take your <kanji>cloth</kanji> and put it on top of your head. It's there because right at <reading>noon</reading> (ぬの) the sun is in the middle of the sky and burns your scalp. So, you cover it with a cloth. Imagine yourself setting an alarm for noon to help you to focus on the noon part.

4192.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>wealth</kanji> <kanji>cloth</kanji> is your <vocabulary>wallet</vocabulary>. Really, a wallet is just a piece of cloth you keep in your pocket that has your wealth in it, right? This can also be your <vocabulary>purse</vocabulary>, especially if you live in the ol' UK.
4192.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Ah, I want to get into my duvet right now!
examples.ja: あー、今すぐ布団に入りたい！

4193.meaning_mnemonic:
Put some <kanji>cloth</kanji> in a <kanji>group</kanji> and you get a <vocabulary>futon</vocabulary>. It’s just the kind of nice, soft <vocabulary>bedding</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>sleeping mat</vocabulary> you’d like to curl up on.

Keep in mind that this word is different from the English version. We’re not talking about sofa-beds for your dorm room here. In Japanese, your 布団 is the traditional bedding you lay out on the floor at night and put away in the daytime. 布団 can refer to the sleeping mat, the <vocabulary>duvet</vocabulary> that covers it, or both items as a set.
4193.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The reading for 団 is the secondary reading that went with the kanji, though, so watch out for that. If you can figure out the meaning of this word, chances are you already know how to spell it, so carry that over to Japanese.

毛布 usually refers specifically to a <vocabulary>wool blanket</vocabulary>, as opposed to comforters for example.
4194.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

4195.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

4197.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>junior</kanji> <kanji>believe</kanji>r is a <vocabulary>believer</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>follower</vocabulary>. examples.en: Would you like bargain coupons?

4199.meaning_mnemonic: When you are able to <kanji>acquire</kanji> whatever you want, you start to see the <vocabulary>benefit</vocabulary>s of everything around you and begin to <vocabulary>profit</vocabulary> from them. Aren't you so amazing?

examples.ja: 彼の言葉にはいつも説得力があります。

4201.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>acquire</kanji> <kanji>theory</kanji> after theory. In doing this, you have a lot of theories in your head. You use all these theories as tools for <vocabulary>persuasion</vocabulary>. These theories will allow you to <vocabulary>convince</vocabulary> anyone of anything.
4201.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The 説 gets shortened to せっ.

examples.en: I've been very busy lately.

examples.ja: 今日は忙しくて、ランチを食べる時間もありませんでした。

4202.reading_mnemonic: You're <vocabulary>busy</vocabulary> because you have to take care of your friend's <reading>ice ogre</reading>s (いそが) this weekend. You don't know why you agreed to this, you were busy enough, but now you'll never get anything done running around taking care of these little ice ogres.

examples.ja: まさか日本の年号がワニカニに改まる日が来るなんて！

examples.en: Don’t be so formal! The president of our company is very friendly.
examples.ja: そう改まるなよ。うちの社長は、とても気さくなんだから。

examples.en: When I looked up at the sky from the top of that mountain, I felt my heart become solemn.

examples.en: I don't see his bad habits changing anytime soon.

examples.en: After hearing everyone's stories, my thoughts have changed.

4204.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji itself means <kanji>renew</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to be renewed</vocabulary>. Like most verbs ending in まる, this is an intransitive verb, meaning it doesn't take a direct object. Something renews or gets renewed, or something changes. See? No direct object.

Although it's not often translated as "renew," 改まる implies a kind of renewal in the changes it's used to describe — whether it's the revision of regulations or the old year changing over to a new one. It can also be used for personal improvements, or describe a shift to a more formal demeanor in social situations.
4204.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You might remember this reading from the transitive verb 改める, but here's a mnemonic just in case: 

<vocabulary>To be renewed</vocabulary> means to be changed into something <reading>新た</reading> (あらた). Out with the old, in with the 新た, right? Picture yourself in a situation where there's been a lot of change. Try to remember how it feels when everything is 新た. Are you nervous, excited, or do you usually move on without noticing?

4214.meaning_mnemonic: You know 梅 is a Japanese plum, and 干す means "to dry something." So when you combine them as 梅干し, you get dried plums, right? Well, sort of. You have to pickle them before you dry them, so we can say 梅干し means <vocabulary>pickled plum</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>pickled ume</vocabulary>. And if you know the Japanese name, you can call it by that too: <vocabulary>umeboshi</vocabulary>.
4214.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this one, like the meaning, is kind of tricky. It uses two kun'yomi readings that you've learned before. So you have うめ plus ほし, which comes from 干す but gets rendaku'd to ぼし here. In other words, うめぼし. I guess the pickling process has mangled the reading of this word. But you'll just have to deal with it, because this food is as common as it is tasty! 

Also, you might often see this written as 梅干, where the し gets shy or something and hides, but the reading stays the same: うめぼし.

4220.reading_mnemonic:

4225.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>entangle</kanji>, but this verb version is usually used in a figurative sense, so it means <vocabulary>to be involved with</vocabulary>, as in 事件に絡む (to be involved with an incident).

絡む can still describe something thread-like winding around something else though, like ツタが木に絡む (the ivy twines around the tree), so it also means <vocabulary>to get tangled</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to entwine</vocabulary>. Note that this use is still intransitive because it focuses on the state of things being entwined, and に marks the location of the action, not a direct object.

To remember that this is intransitive, imagine suddenly hearing a lot of <reading>moo</reading>ing (む) and turning around to find that your cows have somehow gotten entangled. They're all just suddenly in a knot. HOW??

The kanji itself means <kanji>overthrow</kanji> or <kanji>collapse</kanji>, and this is a transitive verb (like most verbs ending in す) related to those actions. It means <vocabulary>to knock over</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to bring down</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to defeat</vocabulary>.

It can be used to talk about physically knocking something over, as well as bringing something or someone down, like a government, or defeating someone, like an enemy.
4261.reading_mnemonic:

4263.meaning_mnemonic: If someone <kanji>overthrow</kanji>s your <kanji>property</kanji>, it'll end in <vocabulary>bankruptcy</vocabulary>. Without property you're sure to <vocabulary>go bankrupt</vocabulary>, unfortunately.
4263.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

4264.reading_mnemonic: You'll want to know the words 借りる and 手 to be able to read this one. Combine them to know the reading.

examples.en: Wow, this wall is very thick, isn't it?

examples.en: European buildings made of stone have very thick walls.

examples.en: This glove has thick memory foam padding, so it seems perfect for long rides!
examples.ja: このグローブは、パッドが低反発でめっちゃ厚いやつなので、ロングライドにも良さそうです！

examples.en: I find that the thicker the slice of bread, the tastier it is. Before I knew it, I started eating a whole loaf of bread every morning.
examples.ja: 私、食パンって厚ければ厚いほど美味しいと思うんですけど、気づいたら毎朝一斤まるまる食べるようになってました。

4265.meaning_mnemonic:
This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>thick</kanji>? Also <vocabulary>thick</vocabulary>.

This is a relatively formal word that is generally used in writing.
4265.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. No <vocabulary>thick</vocabulary> books needed to understand this reading, yeah?

examples.en: When a rocket enters the atmosphere, it is subjected to tremendous pressure.
examples.ja: ロケットが大気に入るときには、ものすごい圧力がかかります。

examples.en: The report was suppressed due to pressure from higher-ups.

examples.en: Japan is often said to be a country where peer pressure is strong.

4266.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>pressure</kanji> <kanji>power</kanji> is the <vocabulary>pressure</vocabulary>. This can also be <vocabulary>stress</vocabulary> as well.
4266.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I have high blood pressure and I take medication for lowering blood pressure.
examples.ja: 私は高血圧なので、血圧下げる薬を服用しています。

examples.en: I am having trouble getting up in the morning because I have low blood pressure. When I had my blood pressure taken today, it was eighty-five over thirty. Can you do something for me, Dr. Koichi?
examples.ja: 低血圧だから朝起きられなくて困っているんです。今日は血圧をはかってもらったら、上が85で下が30でした。コウイチ先生、何とかしてもらえませんか？

4267.meaning_mnemonic: Check the <kanji>pressure</kanji> of your <kanji>blood</kanji>. It's your <vocabulary>blood pressure</vocabulary>.
4267.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Shiatsu improves blood circulation and helps alleviate stress and anxiety.
examples.ja: 指圧は血行を良くして、ストレスや不安を和らげてくれます。

examples.en: Some people say that getting too many shiatsu massages isn’t good for you.
examples.ja: 指圧をしすぎると体に良くないこともあると言う人もいます。

examples.en: Shiatsu is a massage technique born in Japan, and its roots are said to date back to the mythological era.
examples.ja: 指圧は日本で生まれたマッサージ法で、そのルーツは神話時代までさかのぼる事が出来ると言われています。

4268.meaning_mnemonic:
When someone applies <kanji>finger</kanji> <kanji>pressure</kanji>, they're probably practicing <vocabulary>shiatsu</vocabulary>.

Shiatsu is an alternative therapy from Japan, which involves applying pressure with the fingertips to specific spots on the body. This word can also refer to any kind of <vocabulary>finger pressure</vocabulary>, logically enough!
4268.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I don't use social media, so I didn't know that meme existed.
examples.ja: SNSをしないので、そのミームの存在を知りませんでした。

examples.en: Rules exist to be followed.
examples.ja: ルールは守るために存在するんですよ。

examples.en: He has lived so long in space, that he sometimes forgets that gravity exists.
examples.ja: 彼は宇宙生活が長かったので、時々、重力の存在を忘れることがあります。

4269.meaning_mnemonic: I <kanji>exist</kanji>, I <kanji>suppose</kanji>... this is the kind of <vocabulary>existence</vocabulary> I have. I'm not really sure either way, and I don't care. Existence is futile, I suppose.
4269.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Currently, WaniKani has won great popularity.
examples.ja: 現在、ワニカニは大変な人気を呼んでいます。

examples.en: Please tell me the present address of the Tofugu office.
examples.ja: トーフグオフィスの現在の住所を教えてください。

examples.en: About how many emails are you getting a day now?
examples.ja: 現在は、一日に何件ぐらいのEmailを受信してるんですか？

4270.meaning_mnemonic: In the <kanji>present time</kanji> we <kanji>exist</kanji>. What time is it? It's <vocabulary>present</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>now</vocabulary>. It is the <vocabulary>current</vocabulary> time!
4270.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Wolverines really exist, huh?
examples.ja: クズリって、実在するんですね。

examples.en: That Instagrammer doesn't actually exist.
examples.ja: そのインスタグラマー、実在してないんだよ。

examples.en: There’s a rumor that WaniKani’s face was modeled after a real person.
examples.ja: ワニカニの顔は、実在の人物をモデルに作られたというウワサがあります。

4271.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>truth</kanji> is that you <kanji>exist</kanji> in <vocabulary>reality</vocabulary>. This is your <vocabulary>real existence</vocabulary>. Well, that makes sense, I suppose.
4271.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Have you been living abroad for a long time now, Kido-san?
examples.ja: 木戸さんは在外生活、もう長いんですか？

examples.en: But, there are quite a lot of Japanese women living abroad who express a desire to return to Japan, aren't there?
examples.ja: でも、日本に帰りたいと言ってる在外日本人女性ってすごく多いですよね？

examples.en: Given my career so far, and my experience living abroad in America, I believe I can quickly find a job in Japan.
examples.ja: これまでのキャリアとアメリカでの在外経験を活かせば、日本での仕事はすぐに見つかると思っています。

4272.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>exist</kanji> <kanji>outside</kanji> (outside of what? Japan, of course), you are <vocabulary>overseas</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>abroad</vocabulary>.
4272.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: She was so engrossed in the game that she did not hear him.
examples.ja: 彼女はゲームに夢中になっていて、彼の声が聞こえませんでした。

examples.en: I was so engrossed in a TV drama that I forgot to prepare dinner.
examples.ja: テレビドラマに夢中になっていて、夕食の準備を忘れていました。

examples.en: The waitress, pursued by a dishwasher smitten with her, ran home frantically.
examples.ja: そのウェイトレスは、彼女に夢中になっている皿洗いの男に追いかけられ、とにかく夢中で家まで走って帰りました。

4273.meaning_mnemonic:
Even in the <kanji>middle</kanji> of your <kanji>dream</kanji> you're thinking about your body pillows. You're <vocabulary>crazy about</vocabulary> them, wrapped in <vocabulary>absorption</vocabulary>.

Alternatively, this describes doing something <vocabulary>frantic</vocabulary>ally, like running away from somebody or something.
4273.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I woke up in the middle of the night with a nightmare.
examples.ja: 夜中に悪夢で目が覚めました。

examples.en: Yesterday, you were groaning from a nightmare.
examples.ja: 昨日、悪夢にうなされてたよ。

examples.en: It was like having a nightmare.
examples.ja: まるで悪夢を見ているようでした。

4274.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>bad</kanji> <kanji>dream</kanji> is also known as a <vocabulary>nightmare</vocabulary>. Ah! Noooooo!
4274.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Wow, it's like a dream come true!
examples.ja: うわー、夢みたい！

examples.en: My dream is to go and work in Japan.
examples.ja: 私の夢は日本に行って、日本で働くことです。

examples.en: Yesterday, I had a dream that Koichi was giving me a shiatsu massage.
examples.ja: 昨日、コウイチに指圧をしてもらっている夢を見たんだ。

4275.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4275.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: You're having this crazy <vocabulary>dream</vocabulary>. The dream allows you to do anything you want. Every time you ask "hey, can I do this?" The answer is always "<reading>you may</reading>" (ゆめ). Think of some things you'd want to do if you could do anything. Ask permission and get this answer in your imagination.

examples.en: If you don't stop interfering, I'll sue you for obstruction of business operations!
examples.ja: これ以上妨害するのを止めないと、営業妨害で訴えるぞ！

examples.en: Now that we've come this far, the risk of being intercepted by the enemy should be practically zero.
examples.ja: ここまで来れば、敵の妨害の危険はほぼ無いだろう。

examples.en: Someday I want to be arrested for interfering with police officers' duties, like in the movies.
examples.ja: 私はいつか映画のように公務執行妨害で逮捕されてみたい。

4276.meaning_mnemonic: Something that <kanji>obstruct</kanji>s and also does <kanji>damage</kanji> is an <vocabulary>obstruction</vocabulary>. No obstruction is ever good and if left too long it really will cause damage and <vocabulary>interference</vocabulary> as well.
4276.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I heard that company is trying to hamper Tofugu's success.
examples.ja: あの会社は、トーフグの成功を妨げようとしているらしい。

examples.en: You should get rid of things that hinder productivity.
examples.ja: 生産性を妨げるものは、すててしまった方がいいよ。

examples.en: I don’t understand why people try to prevent aliens from reaching the earth.
examples.ja: どうして人々は宇宙人が地球にやってくる事を妨げようとするのか理解できません。

4277.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>obstruct</kanji>, so what is the verb vocab version? It's <vocabulary>to obstruct</vocabulary>.
4277.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You try <vocabulary>to obstruct</vocabulary> a woman coming your way (see kanji). As she gets close, she roars, "I am <reading>Sama(n)tha</reading>!" (さまた) You shall let me pass!" You don't argue with Samanthas. Get out of her way!

examples.en: In this job, it's necessary to wear a helmet for safety.
examples.ja: この仕事では、安全のためにヘルメットを被る必要があります。

examples.en: In this photo, the one wearing the New York Yankees cap is my brother.
examples.ja: この写真でニューヨーク・ヤンキースのキャップを被ってるのが私の弟です。

examples.en: My child always wears a mask of innocence in front of non-family members.
examples.ja: うちの子は、他人の前ではいつも猫を被ります。

examples.en: I saw a man wearing pantyhose over his head running out of the bank with money. I'm glad our timing for entering the bank didn't coincide!
examples.ja: ストッキングを被った男が銀行からお金を持って走って出ていくのを見ました。銀行に入るタイミングが被らなくて良かった！

4278.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>cover</kanji>, so the verb version means <vocabulary>to put on</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to wear</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to cover oneself with</vocabulary>.

被る is used when you wear things that cover your head or face, like hats, helmets, and masks, or when cover yourself with something, like pulling a blanket over yourself. Figuratively, it can also refer to overlapping events — think of it like one event "covering" another on a timeline.

Since the kanji's other meaning is <kanji>incur</kanji>, 被る can also mean taking on a burden or blame — incurring responsibility, in other words.
4278.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Every time you go <vocabulary>to put on</vocabulary> your hat, you yell "<reading>KABOO</reading>M (かぶ)!" Why? Because your hat is da bomb. Go ahead, try it: put on your super cool hat while shouting out "KABOOM!" Is everyone looking at you now? Did they realize the hat you're wearing is da bomb?

examples.en: Today I had a date with my wife.
examples.ja: 今日は妻とデートでした。

examples.en: I wonder if my ex-wife will return the car I gave her as a present.
examples.ja: 元妻にプレゼントした車、返してくれないかな？

examples.en: My wife puts Vaseline on her nostrils every morning before going to work.
examples.ja: 僕の妻は毎朝会社に行く前に鼻の穴にワセリンをぬります。

4279.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This is used to refer to your own wife, though, for the most part.
4279.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: Your <kanji>wife</kanji> does everything for you. She feeds you, she bathes you, she cleans up after you and even wipes your butt when you poop. Really, she is doing <reading>too mu</reading>ch (つま), and you should stop being a baby.

examples.en: That married couple look exactly alike.
examples.ja: あの夫妻は顔がそっくりです。

examples.en: Mr. and Mrs. Otani and Mr. and Mrs. Darvish also attended that BBQ.
examples.ja: そのBBQには、大谷夫妻やダルビッシュ夫妻も参加していました。

examples.en: A doctor couple I know advised me to avoid that particular medication.
examples.ja: 知人のお医者さん夫妻から、あの薬だけはやめといた方がいいって止められたんです。

4280.meaning_mnemonic: You have a <kanji>husband</kanji> and a <kanji>wife</kanji>. Combine them together and they're <vocabulary>husband and wife</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>married couple</vocabulary>. This can also be added to a name to mean <vocabulary>Mr. and Mrs.</vocabulary>.
4280.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Going out to eat with another woman when you have a wife and kids is not okay.
examples.ja: 妻子がいるのに、他の女性と二人でご飯に行くのはダメでしょ。

examples.en: All the male employees in our company are married and have children.
examples.ja: うちの会社の男性社員は全員妻子持ちです。

examples.en: She was crying, saying she had fallen in love with a married man with kids, but I told her firmly, "If you have time to cry, then hurry up and break up."
examples.ja: あの子、妻子のある人を好きになってしまったって言って泣いてたんだけど、泣いてるヒマがあるならさっさと別れなよって強く言っちゃった。

4281.meaning_mnemonic: You have your <kanji>wife</kanji> and you have your <kanji>child</kanji>. These are your <vocabulary>wife and kids</vocabulary>.
4281.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Even if polygamy were to be accepted, without financial stability, it's unlikely that we could halt the declining birthrate, right?
examples.ja: たとえ一夫多妻がOKになっても、お金がなければ少子化は止められないでしょ。

examples.en: Oh, are there people in Japan who practice polygamy?
examples.ja: え、日本で一夫多妻をしてる人達もいるんですか！？

examples.en: Chimera anglerfish, Japanese tree frogs, and honey bees, for example, have a mating system opposite to polygyny, called polyandry.
examples.ja: チョウチンアンコウやモリアオガエル、ミツバチなんかは一夫多妻の反対で、一妻多夫なんですよ。

4282.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>One</kanji> <kanji>husband</kanji>, <kanji>many</kanji> <kanji>wives</kanji>. Sounds a bit sketchy. This is <vocabulary>polygamy</vocabulary>.
4282.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just note that the 一 gets changed to いっ and the 夫 gets changed to ぷ from ふう for some reason. You can imagine that this is because when you are the type that has many wives, you're probably the type who makes them clean up your <reading>poo</reading> for you as well.

examples.en: I would hate to do that for sure.
examples.ja: それはゼッタイ嫌です。

examples.en: My girlfriend's annoying habit is probably when she makes mashed potatoes by putting hot water in potato chips.
examples.ja: 僕の彼女の嫌なところは、ポテトチップスにお湯を入れてマッシュポテトを作るとこかな。

examples.en: If you don't like your job, why don't you quit? It's not good for you to do something you don't want to do.
examples.ja: 仕事が嫌なら、やめたら？嫌なことを嫌々するのは体に良くないよ。

4283.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. The vocab has the added meanings of <vocabulary>eww</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>gross</vocabulary>, and even <vocabulary>reluctant</vocabulary>.
4283.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is pretty weird. It's different than the 嫌い word you will see in this level too. It is いや, so when you think of something you dislike, just think "<reading>iyah</reading> (いや), I dislike it." Also, think about that <vocabulary>eww</vocabulary> feeling it gives you when you think of the thing you dislike most.

examples.en: I hate green peppers.
examples.ja: 私はピーマンが嫌いです。

examples.en: I don't have anyone I don't like.
examples.ja: 僕には嫌いな人はいません。

examples.en: I'm sorry for everything. I know you might think I'm a jerk, but please don't hate me if you can.
examples.ja: 色々とごめんね。俺のこと、嫌なやつと思ってるかもしれないけど、できれば嫌いにならないでほしいな。

4284.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 嫌 means <kanji>dislike</kanji> and this vocab word means the same thing: <vocabulary>dislike</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>hate</vocabulary>!

Though this word is an adjective in Japanese, it usually makes sense to translate it as a verb in English, because of the difference in sentence structure. However, a more literal translation would be <vocabulary>dislikable</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>detestable</vocabulary>.
4284.reading_mnemonic: Of all the things out there to <vocabulary>dislike</vocabulary> the thing I dislike the most is the <reading>killer</reading> (きら) of people. People should never kill people.

examples.en: What kind of mood is mom in today?
examples.ja: 今日のお母さんの機嫌はどう？

examples.en: Grandpa is in a really good mood! What happened?
examples.ja: おじいちゃん、めっちゃ機嫌いいね！どうしちゃったの？
