examples.ja: 父は朝から機嫌が悪い。どうやら仕事で何かあったようだ。

4285.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Machine</kanji>s <kanji>dislike</kanji> everything. Their <vocabulary>mood</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>temper</vocabulary>, is very sour. What about your mood?
4285.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. けん gets changed to げん, though, so don't let that ruin your <vocabulary>mood</vocabulary>.

examples.en: Our suspicion that Viet is a yakuza cannot be wiped away.
examples.ja: ビエトがヤクザだという嫌疑がぬぐえません。

examples.en: That politician is under suspicion of being involved in human trafficking.
examples.ja: あの政治家は人身売買に関わっていた嫌疑をかけられています。

examples.en: It seems like they were deemed "not sufficiently suspicious", huh?
examples.ja: どうやら「嫌疑不十分」とされたみたいだね。

4286.meaning_mnemonic: I <kanji>dislike</kanji> him and I have <kanji>doubt</kanji>s about him. I therefore have much <vocabulary>suspicion</vocabulary> against him as well.
4286.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I left a message on the answering machine.
examples.ja: 留守番電話にメッセージを残しました。

examples.en: I've been calling the Tofugu office over and over again, but I always get the answering machine.
examples.ja: トーフグのオフィスに何度も何度も電話をしていますが、いつも留守番電話なんです。

examples.en: On my answering machine, I got a message from Koichi saying he's flying to Hawaii tomorrow.
examples.ja: 留守番電話にコウイチから明日飛行機でハワイに行くというメッセージが入っていました。

4287.meaning_mnemonic: You hopefully know that this has something to do with <vocabulary>housesitting</vocabulary> (留守番). So, a <vocabulary>telephone</vocabulary> (電話) that does housesitting for you is what? It's your <vocabulary>answering machine</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>voicemail</vocabulary>.
4287.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I believe smoking while walking is pollution.
examples.ja: 私は歩きタバコは公害だと思っています。

examples.en: In Japan, pollution became a huge societal problem between 1950 and 1960.
examples.ja: 日本では1950~1960年代にかけて、公害が大きな社会問題になりました。

examples.en: "Cadmium" is known to have caused one of the four major pollution-related diseases called "Itai-Itai disease."
examples.ja: 「カドミウム」は、四大公害病のひとつ「イタイイタイ病」を引き起こす原因となったことで知られています。

4288.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Public</kanji> <kanji>damage</kanji> is something that affects everyone, the whole public. What is in the air and gets into everything no matter where you are? How about <vocabulary>pollution</vocabulary>?
4288.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It seems that my hometown is in serious trouble due to flooding.
examples.ja: 地元が水害で大変なことになっているようだ。

examples.en: I grew up on a flood-prone island.
examples.ja: 私は、水害の起きやすい島で育ちました。

examples.en: The flood left 5,000 cats homeless.
examples.ja: その水害で、5,000匹の猫が家を失いました。

4289.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Water</kanji> <kanji>damage</kanji> is so bad they call it <vocabulary>water damage</vocabulary>. Doesn't get any clearer than this.
4289.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I wonder if silicone, which has been used in various processed foods lately, is really harmless. It's even used in coffee.
examples.ja: 最近、色んな加工食品に使われているシリコーンって、本当に無害なのかな？コーヒーにも入ってるんだけど。

examples.en: That guy, with such a harmless-looking face, engaging in sexual harassment... It's unbelievable.
examples.ja: アイツ、あんな無害そうな顔してセクハラをするなんて、信じられないよ。

examples.en: As an Asian living in America, I often feel like I'm just overlooked as a harmless extra unless I actively assert my presence.
examples.ja: 私はアメリカに住むアジア人ですが、自ら存在をアピールしないと、ただの無害なモブとしてスルーされるように感じることは多々あります。

4290.meaning_mnemonic: Psh, that guy's <kanji>damage</kanji> is <kanji>nothing</kanji>. He's what I'd call "mostly <vocabulary>harmless</vocabulary>."
4290.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I got a wart on my buttocks.
examples.ja: お尻にイボができました。

examples.en: When I go to high places, my butt itches.
examples.ja: 高いところに行くと、お尻がかゆくなるんです。

examples.en: This is an exercise for the inner muscles of the buttocks.
examples.ja: これはお尻のインナーマッスルのエクササイズです。

4291.meaning_mnemonic: The お is just there to be nice to your butt. This word simply means <vocabulary>butt</vocabulary> (or any other word for it, like <vocabulary>buttocks</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>bottom</vocabulary>).
4291.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: Marilyn's cat's tail is very fluffy.
examples.ja: マリリンの猫の尻尾は、とてもフワフワです。

examples.en: No one had noticed that Tyson had a tail.
examples.ja: だれも、タイソンに尻尾が生えていることには気づいていなかった。

examples.en: That cute Shiba came towards Koichi wagging its tail and jumped on him.
examples.ja: あの可愛い柴犬が、尻尾を振りながらコウイチに近づき、飛びついた。

4292.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>butt</kanji> <kanji>tail</kanji> is just your <vocabulary>tail</vocabulary>, though I wonder why they had to specify that it was your butt tail. Where else do you have a tail, I wonder?
4292.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this word is a bit of an exception. You kind of already know the reading for 尻 from the kun'yomi しり you learned already. Here it gets shortened to しっ. The reading for 尾 is totally different from what you learned, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

The animal with the best <vocabulary>tail</vocabulary> in the world is the <reading>po</reading>lar (ぽ) bear. They're stubby and white and cute. Only polar bears have tails like that!

examples.en: Bows and arrows are used in this Ainu dance.
examples.ja: このアイヌのダンスでは弓矢が使われます。

examples.en: In this game, I always choose to play with a bow and arrow.
examples.ja: このゲームでは、いつも弓矢を選んでプレイします。

examples.en: I made bamboo bows and arrows in the mountains with my father during summer vacation.
examples.ja: 夏休みに父と山で竹の弓矢を作りました。

4293.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>bow</kanji> and an <kanji>arrow</kanji>. Put them together and you have a <vocabulary>bow and arrow</vocabulary>.
4293.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the vocab readings, 弓 and 矢, put together. This is probably because this word is like two separate words put together, thus the "and" in the middle of the English translation.

examples.en: I forget things a lot.
examples.ja: 私は忘れ物が多い。

examples.en: Isn't this something someone forgot?
examples.ja: これ、誰かの忘れ物じゃない？

examples.en: I feel like I forgot something today, but I just can’t remember what it is.
examples.ja: 今日何か忘れ物をしたような気がするんだけど、それが何だったかをどうしても思い出せないんだよな。

4294.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 忘れる is "to forget"? Well, a <kanji>thing</kanji> you've forgotten is a <vocabulary>forgotten item</vocabulary>.

忘れ物 is a casual way to refer to something left behind accidentally, like an umbrella you forgot about and left on the train.
4294.reading_mnemonic: You didn't learn this reading with the kanji 忘, but you did learn it with the vocabulary 忘れる. What was that reading again? You can't remember! It's become a <vocabulary>forgotten item</vocabulary> in some dusty corner of your brain. And really, forgetting how to read 忘? That's <reading>worse</reading> (わす) than leaving your umbrella or keys behind! Come on! Try to hold onto the reading this time — you'll only be making things worse if you don't.

examples.en: What kind of machine is that?
examples.ja: それはなんの機械ですか？

examples.en: Today the machine is not working very smoothly.
examples.ja: 今日は機械の調子があんまり良くないんだよね。

examples.en: Koichi bought a batting cage machine for the office
examples.ja: コウイチは会社用にバッティングセンターの機械を買いました。

4295.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I've already booked the airplane tickets.
examples.ja: 飛行機のチケット、もう取っちゃったんだよね。

examples.en: I dislike airplanes, so I would never be able to go to Japan.
examples.ja: 私は飛行機が苦手なので、一生日本に行けることはないでしょう。

examples.en: When I was seated next to Koichi on the plane, I was so surprised that I thought my eyeballs would pop out.
examples.ja: 飛行機でコウイチのとなりの席になった時、ビックリして目玉が飛び出るかと思いました。

4296.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>fly</kanji> and <kanji>go</kanji> <kanji>machine</kanji> is some machine you get into that flies and goes places. It's an <vocabulary>airplane</vocabulary>.
4296.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Japan is currently facing a crisis that threatens its national survival.
examples.ja: 日本は今、国家存亡の危機にあります。

examples.en: Maybe you should have a bit more sense of urgency.
examples.ja: もうちょっと危機感もった方がいいんじゃない？

examples.en: World War III will lead to a crisis of civilization.
examples.ja: 第三次世界大戦は文明の危機につながります。

4297.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>dangerous</kanji> <kanji>machine</kanji> is walking through your town, destroying everything. This is a huge <vocabulary>crisis</vocabulary>!
4297.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This amulet will surely protect you from disaster.
examples.ja: このお守りが、きっとあなたを災いから守ってくれるでしょう。

examples.en: That doll brought a lot of misfortune to this village.
examples.ja: その人形が、この村に多くの災いをもたらしたんです。

examples.en: The mouth is the source of calamity.
examples.ja: 口は災いの元だよ。

4298.meaning_mnemonic: This is the noun form of <kanji>disaster</kanji>, so it means <vocabulary>disaster</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>misfortune</vocabulary>.
4298.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Think about how, the last time <vocabulary>disaster</vocabulary> struck, it <reading>was a wh</reading>ile (わざわ) before things got back to normal.

Be careful of the い on the end, it can be tricky and make you think it's an adjective when it's a noun.

examples.en: There is nothing scarier than natural disasters.
examples.ja: 自然災害ほどおそろしいものはありません。

examples.en: There is even the possibility that a disaster could occur during your trip.
examples.ja: 旅行中に災害が起こる可能性だってあります。

examples.en: Today I'm going to share with you a life hack that will come in handy during disasters and camping.
examples.ja: 今日は災害やキャンプの時に便利なライフハックをお教えします。

examples.en: It can't be helped, but unless the disaster hits where they live, people just end up considering it someone else's problem. There are lots of things you just don't understand unless they affect you.
examples.ja: しょうがないけど、自分が住んでいる場所で災害が起きないと、結局みんな他人事なんだよ。当事者にならないと、分からないことっていっぱいあるからさ。

4299.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>disaster</kanji> that does <kanji>damage</kanji>. Usually these are <vocabulary>natural disaster</vocabulary>s, though they could also just be regular <vocabulary>disaster</vocabulary>s as well.
4299.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I heard that a fire broke out in that building at dawn.
examples.ja: 明け方、あのビルで火災が発生したそうです。

examples.en: I heard there was a fire at a nuclear power plant, is it true?
examples.ja: 原子力発電所で火災が起きたと聞いたんですが、本当ですか？

examples.en: My father was unconscious for a long time after the fire in his office, but he finally woke up today!
examples.ja: 私の父はオフィスの火災でずっと意識不明でしたが、今日ついに目を覚ましました！

4300.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>fire</kanji> <kanji>disaster</kanji> is a <vocabulary>fire disaster</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>conflagration</vocabulary>.

火災 is a more formal version of 火事. It usually refers to a serious and significant fire that causes extensive damage or loss of life.
4300.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That was a heck of a misfortune, huh?
examples.ja: それはとんだ災難でしたね。

examples.en: That was a tough break earlier. That teacher's always on everyone's case, so you'd do best not to let it get to you.
examples.ja: さっきは災難だったね。あの先生、みんなにうるさいからさ、気にしない方がいいよ。

examples.en: To think I'd come down with the flu during my precious spring break. What a disaster.
examples.ja: せっかくの春休みなのに、インフルになるとは。災難すぎる。

4301.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>disaster</kanji> that is <kanji>difficult</kanji> is particularly difficult, making it more of a <vocabulary>misfortune</vocabulary>. Obviously a disaster that wasn't difficult wouldn't really be that bad, so a difficult one gets the "misfortune" or <vocabulary>calamity</vocabulary> label.
4301.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I still can't forget the trauma I experienced from the day of the earthquake disaster.
examples.ja: 震災にあった日のことが、今でも忘れられないトラウマになっています。

examples.en: A teacher at my school did not return home after the earthquake.
examples.ja: 私の学校の先生は震災で帰らぬ人となりました。

examples.en: The earthquake left the ground full of holes. Here, three months after the earthquake, the ground is still covered with cracks.
examples.ja: 震災で、地面が穴ぼこだらけになってしまいました。ここでは、震災から三ヶ月たった今でも、地面にヒビが入ったままです。

4302.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>earthquake</kanji> <kanji>disaster</kanji> is just that, an <vocabulary>earthquake disaster</vocabulary>. These are no good.
4302.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I thought it smelled smoky, turns out there was a fire in the neighborhood.
examples.ja: なんか煙いと思ったら、近所で火事が起きてたらしい。

examples.en: The smoky fireworks made me cough.
examples.ja: 花火が煙くて、むせてしまいました。

examples.en: It’s so smoky! When the heck are you going to quit smoking? This really smells awful.
examples.ja: 煙いなあ！一体いつになったらタバコやめるんだよ？本当に臭いんだけど。

4303.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>smoke</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>smoky</vocabulary>.
4303.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You sort of did learn this reading with the vocabulary word 煙, but this one is just different enough where we thought we should make a mnemonic for this one: 

All this <vocabulary>smoki</vocabulary>ness is from a terrible <reading>chem</reading>ical (けむ) spill that happened nearby. It was acid, so it burned everything up real good, causing the air to get pretty smoky.

examples.en: Oops, embarrassing! I can't believe I made such a basic mistake!
examples.ja: うわっ、はずかしい！こんな初歩的なミスを犯すとは！

examples.en: Unless we create and adhere to protocols rigorously, the era of AI committing murder might be upon us.
examples.ja: きちんとプロトコルを作ってみんなで守らないと、AIが殺人を犯す時代がやってくるかもしれません。

examples.en: "The ignorance of the law is no excuse" means that even if someone did something without knowing the law, it cannot be claimed that they had no intention to commit a crime.
examples.ja: 「法の不知は許さず」とは、たとえ法を知らずにやってしまったことだとしても、罪を犯す意思がなかったとすることにはできないというものです。

4304.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>crime</kanji> and the verb vocab version can mean <vocabulary>to commit a crime</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to make a mistake</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to rape</vocabulary>, depending on the context.
4304.reading_mnemonic: You go <vocabulary>to commit a crime</vocabulary>. How did it go, you think? Well, I thought it went <reading>oka</reading>y (おか). Imagine yourself committing a crime and it going just okay. Not great, not bad... meh. Okay.

examples.en: The culprit who ate the cookies turned out to be Dad.
examples.ja: クッキー食べた犯人、お父さんだった。

examples.en: I heard they haven't caught the culprit yet.
examples.ja: まだ犯人つかまってないらしいよ。

examples.en: The criminal learned the hard way that speaking carelessly can bring disaster.
examples.ja: その犯人は、口は災いの元だということを思い知った。

4305.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>crime</kanji>  <kanji>person</kanji> is a <vocabulary>culprit</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>criminal</vocabulary>.

Just note that 犯人 is mostly used to talk about the culprit of a specific crime, not criminals in general.
4305.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: They say the accomplice is most likely out of the country.
examples.ja: 共犯者は国外にいる可能性が高いそうだ。

examples.en: My accomplice's son was born in January of the year before last.
examples.ja: 共犯者の息子は、一昨年の一月に生まれました。

examples.en: The accomplice was indeed like a bug that flew into the fire in summer.
examples.ja: あの共犯者は、まさに飛んで火にいる夏の虫だったな。

4306.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Someone</kanji> who does <kanji>crime</kanji> <kanji>together</kanji> with you is your <vocabulary>accomplice</vocabulary> in crime. It's best to "take care of" these before the coppers get to them.
4306.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Do you know how likely it is to win the lottery?
examples.ja: 宝くじに当たる確率がどのくらいか知っていますか？

examples.en: It feels like I have curry on Fridays with a high probability.
examples.ja: なんか金曜日は高確率でカレーを食べてる気がする。

examples.en: I feel like the chances of dating Midori-chan are fifty-fifty, but do you think they're even lower?
examples.ja: ミドリちゃんと付き合える確率、自分では五分五分かなって思ってるんだけど、もっと低いと思う？

4307.meaning_mnemonic: You're <kanji>certain</kanji> there is this <kanji>percent</kanji> chance it will happen? You know that this is the <vocabulary>probability</vocabulary>?
4307.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The male to female ratio in our company is 5:2.
examples.ja: うちの会社の男女比率は、5:2です。

examples.en: Approximately what percentage of GDP is that?
examples.ja: それってGDP比率の何パーセントぐらいですか？

examples.en: When you are trying to learn something, you should consider the ratio of input to output.
examples.ja: 何かを学ぼうとするときは、インプットとアウトプットの比率を考えながら学ぶといいですよ。

4308.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>compare</kanji> the <kanji>percentage</kanji>, figuring out the <vocabulary>ratio</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>proportion</vocabulary> of one thing to another. This can also be expressed as a <vocabulary>percentage</vocabulary>!

比率 usually shows up in cases where you compare two numbers with each other, like the number of male and female students in a classroom.
4308.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I heard that person just gave birth to a baby last winter and that she'll have another one this fall.
examples.ja: あの人、去年の冬に赤ちゃんを産んだばかりなのに今年の秋にもまた赤ちゃんを産むんですって。

examples.en: A lot of baby mantises came out of the egg that the mantis laid.
examples.ja: カマキリが産んだたまごの中からたくさんの赤ちゃんカマキリが出てきました。

examples.en: Okay. You ready to push again? You are going to have twins! Okay, okay, come on, you can do it. You can do it!
examples.ja: よし、もう一度いきむ準備はいいかい？君は双子の赤ちゃんを産むんだよ！ 大丈夫、大丈夫。頑張れ！君ならできるよ！

4309.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>give birth</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to give birth</vocabulary>.

You know another 産む as well (生む). This 産む is more sciency, but both are good to know.
4309.reading_mnemonic: You know another "to give birth" word (生む). Guess what!? They share readings!

examples.en: That is certainly true.
examples.ja: それは確かにそうですね。

examples.en: He is certainly a good leader. But the problem is that sometimes his language is too harsh.
examples.ja: 彼は確かにリーダーに向いていると思います。でも、時々言葉がきついのがネックです。

examples.en: I'm certain I saw Koichi fly about one hundred meters with my own eyes.
examples.ja: コウイチが百メートルほど飛ぶのを、この目で確かに見ました。

4310.meaning_mnemonic: This is an adverb, but it has the same meaning (basically) as the kanji. It means <vocabulary>certainly</vocabulary>, and it can also mean <vocabulary>surely</vocabulary>.
4310.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this one is <vocabulary>certainly</vocabulary> weird. To remember the reading for this word, just think how you're certain that if you s<reading>tash</reading> (たし) the treasure, nobody will find it here.

examples.en: I did the calculations on the computer, so they are accurate.
examples.ja: コンピュータで計算したので、正確ですよ。

examples.en: That reporter's reporting is always very accurate.
examples.ja: その記者の報道はいつもとても正確です。

examples.en: Koichi doesn't know the accurate number of WaniKani users.
examples.ja: コウイチはワニカニの正確なユーザー数を知りません。

4311.meaning_mnemonic: It is <kanji>correct</kanji> and you're <kanji>certain</kanji> of it. When you've done this much checking and you're this sure, your measurements must be very <vocabulary>accurate</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>precise</vocabulary>.
4311.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The backroom of the grocery store is off-limits.
examples.ja: スーパーのバックヤードは立入禁止です。

examples.en: This door says Authorized Personnel Only.
examples.ja: このドアには、関係者以外立入禁止って書かれているよ。

examples.en: When people hear that something is off-limits, they want to go in, don't they?
examples.ja: 立入禁止って聞くと入りたくなっちゃうのが人間でしょ？

4312.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Stand</kanji>ing and <kanji>enter</kanji>ing are both 禁止 (prohibited). If you see this sign, it's essentially saying <vocabulary>do not enter</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>no entry</vocabulary>.

While this type of sign will usually say 立入禁止, you may also encounter variations such as 立ち入り禁止 or 立入り禁止.
4312.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for 立入 is a bit strange, but it might help you to know that it can also be written 立ち入り. The 立ち is the same one you learned with 立ち飲み and the 入り is the reading you learned with 入り口. In our version of the word, the hiragana isn't visible (it's sort of pushed into the kanji), but the word is still pronounced the same way: たちいり.

And 禁止 doesn't have any weirdness going on, so at least you have that!

4314.meaning_mnemonic:

穴場 is for places that are good but relatively unknown. You can use it for any kind of location — restaurants, parks, beaches, fishing spots only the locals know, or even a hidden study spot on campus that you always have to yourself.
4314.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi reading for each kanji. You've seen both of these readings before, but here's a mnemonic in case you need it:

Your town's <vocabulary>hidden gem</vocabulary> is a place where you can <reading>baa</reading> (ば) without shame. It's this great petting zoo no one knows about yet. 4346.meaning_mnemonic:

The kanji is <kanji>fruit</kanji> so the meaning is <vocabulary>really</vocabulary>? Like, really really? Because it sounds like you made that up. I really doubt it means really.

It can also mean <vocabulary>as was expected</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>just as I thought</vocabulary>, but usually we use it as a way to say, "Really? I don't really believe you..."
4346.reading_mnemonic: To remember the reading, just imagine yourself snorting out a sharp "<reading>HA</reading>!" (は) right before saying the phrase: "<reading>HA!</reading> Just as I thought."

examples.en: In kanji, there are many exceptions to both on'yomi and kun'yomi readings, and many characters have multiple readings. Is it really necessary to memorize which readings are on'yomi and which are kun'yomi for each character?
examples.ja: 漢字の音訓って、例外も多いし、それぞれ二つ以上あるものもあるし、いちいちどれが音読みでどれが訓読みなのかを覚える必要ってあるんですかね？

4364.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen (hopefully) 音読み and 訓読み. This is a combination of the two. This is <vocabulary>on'yomi and kun'yomi</vocabulary>, aka the <vocabulary>Chinese and Japanese readings</vocabulary>.
4364.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The people who live in my neighborhood are all big fans of parties.
examples.ja: 私の近所に住む人達は、パーティが大好きな人達ばかりです。

examples.en: Various people have said that people doing WaniKani quickly memorize kanji.
examples.ja: 「ワニカニをしている人達は、漢字をすぐに覚えてしまう」と色んな人達が言っていました。

examples.en: Some people laugh at the fact that my father is a pizza delivery person, but I believe those people are the ones who should be laughed at.
examples.ja: お父さんがピザの配達人であることを笑う人達もいますが、僕はそういう人達こそ笑われるべきだと思っています。

4365.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji 達 pluralizes things sometimes. So, when you have a <kanji>plural</kanji> amount of a <kanji>person</kanji> you have more than one person, you have <vocabulary>people</vocabulary>.

Take note! When using this word, you want to attach it to the type of "people" you are talking about. For example, あの人達 (those people over there). Other examples: 男の人達, その人達, 向こうの人達, etc. You don't use this by itself, instead you use it with something describing what kind of people you're talking about.
4365.reading_mnemonic: The readings are both kun'yomi readings of the kanji. The readings come from the word 人 and the だち of 友達, though now it's たち because it hasn't been rendaku'd. You like to <reading>touch</reading> (たち) people, you perv.

examples.en: During my trip to Kyoto, at a small restaurant I visited, I enjoyed grilled ayu fish while overlooking a calmly flowing stream.
examples.ja: 京都旅行で行った小料理屋では、静々と流れる小川を見下ろしながら、アユの塩焼きをいただきました。

examples.en: Watching the snow silently pile up, I felt like having hot cocoa.
examples.ja: 雪が静々とつもりゆくのを見て、ホットココアが飲みたくなりました。

examples.en: In old Japan, a wife who walked quietly behind her husband was considered a good wife.
examples.ja: 昔の日本では、夫の後ろを静々と歩くような妻が良妻とされてきました。

4366.reading_mnemonic: You know how 静か is しずか? Well, this is the same reading as that. Say it in a whisper with me: "<reading>しずしず</reading>." Shhh!

examples.en: Adding a little salt here enhances the flavor.
examples.ja: ここで少し塩を加えると味が引き立ちます。

examples.en: This application allows you to add animation to your videos.
examples.ja: このアプリを使うと、動画にアニメを加えることができます。

examples.en: Adding just a little extra effort can greatly improve anything, you know.
examples.ja: 何事も一手間加えるだけで、グッと良くなるものなんですよね。

4367.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. 

The kanji itself means <kanji>add</kanji> and this word is the verb version of that: <vocabulary>to add</vocabulary>.

This is a transitive verb, meaning that you are doing the adding to something else. You add a nose to your snowman, for example.
4367.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You decide <vocabulary>to add</vocabulary> something and then <vocabulary>to add</vocabulary> something else, and you end up with quite a <reading>qua</reading>ntity (くわ) of things. Just keep adding and adding forever. What a huge QUANTITY you now have!

examples.en: Here's how to participate.
examples.ja: 参加方法はこちらです。

examples.en: Why don't you participate in Tofugu's end-of-year party? It will be fun!
examples.ja: あなたもトーフグの忘年会に参加しませんか。きっと楽しいですよ。

examples.en: On Sunday, I attended a zazen session at a temple in Kyoto.
examples.ja: 日曜日、京都のお寺の座禅の会に参加してきました。

4368.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>participate</kanji>, <kanji>add</kanji>ing yourself to the activity, that is <vocabulary>participation</vocabulary>. Well done, you earn a gold star for participating!
4368.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I was just saying my opinion, but my boss yelled, "don’t complain," at me.
examples.ja: 意見を言っただけなのに、上司に「文句するな」と怒鳴られました。

4369.meaning_mnemonic: You know how 文句 is a <vocabulary>complaint</vocabulary>, right? Well, add する to make it a verb and you have <vocabulary>to complain</vocabulary>. This is a really casual way to complain though, usually used in manga or on social media. Keep your eye out for it!
4369.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I never expected my house to burn down in a fire.
examples.ja: まさか火事で家が焼けるとは思っても見ませんでした。

examples.en: This bread is toasted well.
examples.ja: このパンはこんがりとよく焼けています。

examples.en: "This meat is thick, so I think it'll be a while until it's cooked." "I think it'll cook while you're doing the dishes."
examples.ja: 「この肉は厚いから、焼けるまでに時間がかかりそうだね」「あなたが皿洗いをしている間に、焼けると思うけど」

4370.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 焼く is "to bake," "to burn something," or "to grill"? 焼ける is just the intransitive version. That means no direct object needed! So this verb means <vocabulary>to get baked</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to get burned</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to get grilled</vocabulary>. 

焼ける is used when something is heated and transformed by the heat. Depending on the context, it can refer to anything from a muffin getting baked, fish being grilled, or pottery being fired. You can even use it when your skin gets a tan or a house burns down. Well, that last one is kinda sad. I hope it never happens.

You can distinguish 焼ける from 焼く because when cooking, you always <reading>care</reading> (ける) to ensure the food gets baked or grilled really well. You want to make sure it's properly 焼ける'd (heated through) to be safe!
4370.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 焼く, so just use that knowledge and apply it here to be able to read this too.

examples.en: No electronic devices are allowed in this room.
examples.ja: この部屋への電子機器持ち込みは禁止されています。

examples.en: In this factory, workers manually check each electronic device one by one at the end of the process to make sure there are no problems.
examples.ja: この工場では、電子機器に問題がないか、最後に作業員が一つずつ手作業でチェックしています。

examples.en: I can smell electricity, you know. Young people these days are constantly using electronic devices, so I often smell electricity around them.
examples.ja: 私、電気のニオイが分かるんですよね。最近若い方は電子機器を常に使っているので、電気のニオイがプンプンします。

4371.meaning_mnemonic:
You have an <kanji>electronic</kanji> (電子) <kanji>container</kanji> <kanji>machine</kanji>. This is just a machine that contains electricity and electric parts. So basically, an <vocabulary>electronic device</vocabulary>, or more generally, <vocabulary>electronic equipment</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>electronics</vocabulary>.

電子機器 refers to complex electronic devices like computers, smartphones, medical devices, control systems, and more. So while it can be used to refer to a wide range of electronic devices, it's usually not used for things like simple household appliances like toasters or kettles.
4371.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'll get in touch with you after I'm fired.
examples.ja: 会社を首になったら連絡するよ。

examples.en: I want to cut ties with you, so please never contact me again.
examples.ja: あなたとはエンを切りたいので、もう連絡してこないでください。

examples.en: Sorry, I’ve gotta go. I'll check my schedule and get back to you.
examples.ja: ごめん、行かなきゃ。予定を調べて、後で折り返し連絡するよ。

4372.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>take along</kanji> a message and <kanji>entangle</kanji> it into the telephone. From there it buzzes off to the person in order for you <vocabulary>to contact</vocabulary> them.
4372.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Oh, you have a brother and a sister. That's unexpected.
examples.ja: あなた弟と妹がいるの？意外だね。

examples.en: Unexpectedly, my weight has dropped.
examples.ja: 意外と体重は落ちてた。

examples.en: Liking soft pasta that's been cooked too long was an unexpected aspect of Canadian culture.
examples.ja: ゆですぎの柔らかいパスタを好んで食べるのは、カナダの意外な文化でした。

4373.meaning_mnemonic: Something <kanji>outside</kanji> your normal <kanji>idea</kanji> of how things work will come as <vocabulary>unexpected</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>surprising</vocabulary> to you.
4373.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: He's not interested in others, you know.
examples.ja: アイツは他人に関心がないんだよ。

examples.en: In our case, my father had absolutely zero concern in parenting.
examples.ja: うちの場合は、父親の子育てへの関心がゼロだったんですよね。

examples.en: Everyone, please take more interest in politics.
examples.ja: 皆さん、もっと政治に関心を持ってください。

4374.meaning_mnemonic: The things <kanji>related</kanji> to your <kanji>heart</kanji> are the things that <vocabulary>concern</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>interest</vocabulary> you the most.
4374.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What time does the event start?
examples.ja: イベントの開始時間は何時ですか？

examples.en: A new project will start tomorrow.
examples.ja: 明日から新しいプロジェクトが開始します。

examples.en: Did you tell the president that the start time for the meeting will be delayed?
examples.ja: ミーティングの開始がおくれるって、社長にはもう言った？

4375.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>open</kanji> of the <kanji>start</kanji> is the <vocabulary>start</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>beginning</vocabulary>.

Note that 開始 is slightly more formal than 始める.
4375.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Now for the announcement. The winner of the speech contest is Mr. Tanaka!
examples.ja: それでは、発表します。スピーチコンテストの勝者は田中さんです！

examples.en: I participated in the university presentation conference.
examples.ja: 大学のプレゼンテーション発表会に参加しました。

examples.en: Apparently, the president wants to make a very important announcement for the company and the staff.
examples.ja: 社長が会社とスタッフにとって、とても大切な発表をしたいそうです。

4376.meaning_mnemonic: I'm going to <kanji>express</kanji> my <kanji>departure</kanji>. That is my only <vocabulary>announcement</vocabulary>.
4376.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The ひょう changes to ぴょう and the はつ gets shortened, though, so just about everything about this word is weird.

examples.en: The data shows everything.
examples.ja: データは全てを表す。

examples.en: This red ball is called "hinomaru," and represents the sunrise.
examples.ja: この赤い玉は、「日の丸」と言って、日の出を表しています。

examples.en: I made cookies to express my thanks to you, Sensei.
examples.ja: 先生へのお礼を表すために、クッキーを作ったんです。

4377.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>express</kanji> and the verb vocab version is transitive, meaning that it's done to something. So this verb means <vocabulary>to express something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to show something</vocabulary>.
4377.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You're struggling <vocabulary>to express something</vocabulary> to your friends: namely, that you <reading>are a wa</reading>lrus (あらわ). All your friends think you're a human, so they'll be shocked when you express to them the fact that, actually, you are a walrus. You need to get it off your chest though… Your big, blubbery walrus chest.

examples.en: Can you spread both of your legs more?
examples.ja: 両足、もっと広がる？

examples.en: The living room spreads from this entrance.
examples.ja: リビングルームは、この入り口から広がります。

examples.en: The virus quickly spread to all Japan.
examples.ja: ウィルスは、すぐに全日本に広がった。

4378.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 広い? Well this is like that, except a verb. When something does the action of getting wide, it means to spread out, to extend, or to stretch. You already learned 広げる, which is used when you spread SOMETHING. But 広がる is intransitive, so it doesn't take a direct object. Like: The sea spreads out before you. See? No direct object. Actually, verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
4378.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 広い, too, so as long as you knew that you knew this reading as well.

examples.en: This dress makes the curve of the body look beautiful.
examples.ja: このドレスは、体の曲線をキレイに見せてくれる。

examples.en: I like furniture with a curved design.
examples.ja: 曲線を使ったデザインの家具が気に入ってます。

examples.en: Fireworks that look like curved lines have brightened the night sky.
examples.ja: 曲線のような花火が夜空を明るくしました。

examples.en: This road has a lot of curves and it is difficult to drive by car.
examples.ja: この道は曲線が多くて車で走るのがむずかしいです。

4379.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>bend</kanji> in a <kanji>line</kanji> is merely a <vocabulary>curve</vocabulary>.
4379.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: There are five minutes until departure.
examples.ja: 出発まで五分です。

examples.en: I'm going to leave for Tokyo in two weeks.
examples.ja: 二週間後に、東京に出発する予定です。

examples.en: Let's have some tea until the ferry departs.
examples.ja: フェリーが出発するまでの時間、お茶でものみましょうよ。

4380.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>exit</kanji> and then make a <kanji>departure</kanji>. This is just a <vocabulary>departure</vocabulary>.
4380.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The しゅつ gets shortened and はつ changes to ぱつ. No wonder you want to make a departure, you want to get away from crazy readings like this.

examples.en: I participated in a seminar as a jazz critic.
examples.ja: ジャズ評論家として、とあるセミナーに参加してきました。

examples.en: Participating in club activities is optional.
examples.ja: クラブ活動に参加するかどうかは、任意です。

examples.en: I’m participating in the skyscraper observation tour this Sunday.
examples.ja: 今週の日曜日、摩天楼の見学ツアーに参加します。

4381.meaning_mnemonic: You know how 参加 is <kanji>participation</kanji>? Well, make that a verb with する and you have yourself <vocabulary>to participate</vocabulary>.
4381.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Will also help to know the reading of 参加.

examples.en: Surprisingly, the oldest participant of the moviegoer party was 100 years old.
examples.ja: 映画好きのパーティーの最年長参加者は、なんと百才だった。

examples.en: Thanks to one participant, the meeting was thrown into chaos. It was a disaster.
examples.ja: ある参加者が会議を混乱させてしまってね。さんざんだったよ。

examples.en: Koichi's speech received genuine praise from the participants.
examples.ja: コウイチのスピーチは、参加者達から心からの称賛を受けました。

4382.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 参加 is <kanji>participation</kanji>, so <kanji>someone</kanji> who does participation is a <vocabulary>participant</vocabulary>.
4382.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That police officer always says one word too many.
examples.ja: あの警察官はいつも余計な一言が多い。

examples.en: That policeman escaped in the confusion!
examples.ja: あの警察官、混乱にまぎれてバックレやがったぞ！

examples.en: When the police officer found the suspect, he was painting a beautiful landscape on a hilltop.
examples.ja: 警察官が容疑者を発見した際、男は丘の上で美しい風景画を描いていました。

4383.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>police</kanji> (警察) <kanji>government</kanji> is full of <vocabulary>police officer</vocabulary>s. This is the formal way to say "police officer." It is similar to 警官, but has a slightly more official feel to it.
4383.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Don't you realize that such comments disturb everyone's harmony?
examples.ja: そういう発言がみんなの和を乱しているってこと、気づいてないの？

examples.en: Many kids with ADHD don't like having the rhythm of their lives thrown out of order.
examples.ja: ADHDの子どもは、生活のリズムを乱されることをイヤがる子が多いです。

examples.en: I ran with my hair in disarray, but in the end I didn't make my scheduled flight.
examples.ja: 髪を乱して走ったが、結局予定の飛行機には間に合わなかった。

4384.meaning_mnemonic: You know how 乱れる is "to be in disorder"? Well, now you're the one causing this. So, by doing this you are going <vocabulary>to put in disorder</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to throw out of order</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to disturb</vocabulary> whatever it is. Just imagine all the people who will try to <reading>sue</reading> (す) you for your actions.
4384.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 乱れる, so hopefully you know it already.

examples.en: When I was told not to be friends with aliens, it made me want to do it even more.
examples.ja: 宇宙人と友達になってはいけないと言われて、余計になりたくなった。

examples.en: To put it simply, we're aliens too, aren't we?
examples.ja: 平たく言えば、私達も宇宙人だよね。

examples.en: Koichi’s photographs honestly and sympathetically portray aliens who were victims of drought and the Great Depression on Mars.
examples.ja: コウイチの写真は、火星で干ばつと大恐慌の犠牲となった宇宙人たちを正直に、かつ同情を込めてとらえている。

4385.meaning_mnemonic: You know how 宇宙 is <kanji>space</kanji>? Well, a <kanji>person</kanji> from space is an <vocabulary>alien</vocabulary>.
4385.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will also help to know how to read the word 宇宙 on its own, too.

examples.en: The enemy's sudden attack threw the space shuttle into chaos.
examples.ja: 敵からのいきなりのアタックで、宇宙船は大混乱となった。

examples.en: Rigid rules have been established to live in this spaceship.
examples.ja: この宇宙船での生活には、きびしいルールが設けられています。

examples.en: Nearly all of the sixteen space ships were retained and refurbished.
examples.ja: 十六台の宇宙船のほとんど全てが、保持され改装されました。

4386.meaning_mnemonic: You know how 宇宙 is <kanji>outer space</kanji> and how 船 is <kanji>ship</kanji>, right? Well, put those together and you have an outer space ship (better known as a <vocabulary>space ship</vocabulary>).
4386.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know the word 宇宙 beforehand as well.

examples.en: Amazon sent me two more pairs of shoes than I ordered.
examples.ja: アマゾンから、注文より二足余計に履き物が送られてきました。

examples.en: When you write "Please take shoes off here" and "Please take kimonos off here" in hiragana, they look exactly the same.
examples.ja: 「ここで履き物をぬいでください」と「ここでは着物をぬいでください」を平仮名で書くと全く同じになる。

examples.en: In Japanese, indoor footwear is called "uwabaki" and outdoor footwear is called "sotobaki."
examples.ja: 日本語で、屋内の履き物は「上履き」、屋外の履き物は「外履き」と呼ばれます。

4387.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 履く is "to put on shoes" and 物 means "thing"? Well, combine them and you have a word for things you put on your feet, a.k.a. <vocabulary>footwear</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>shoes</vocabulary>.

You might know that 履く is used for lots of different clothes you wear below the waist, but be careful: <vocabulary>履き物</vocabulary> only refers to footwear and shoes.
4387.reading_mnemonic: The reading is that of 履く and 物 put together. Just know those separately and you should be able to figure this one out as well.

examples.en: In order to become a rock musician, I need to persuade my dad.
examples.ja: ロックミュージシャンになるには、親父を説得する必要がある。

examples.en: I persuaded my wife not to buy unnecessary things.
examples.ja: 余計な物を買いすぎないよう、妻を説得しました。

examples.en: It wasn't easy to convince my brother to bail out of the bacon-trafficking business.
examples.ja: ベーコンの密売ビジネスから足を洗うよう兄を説得するのは、容易なことではなかった。

4388.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 説得 is <kanji>persuasion</kanji>, so what is the verb version of that? <vocabulary>To persuade</vocabulary>.
4388.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will also immensely help to know the reading of the word 説得.

examples.en: The roads are pretty busy at that time, aren't they?
examples.ja: その時間だと道路はかなり混んでいますよね？

examples.en: Farmers' markets get quite crowded around noon, so I try to go shopping as early in the morning as possible to avoid the crowds.
examples.ja: ファーマーズマーケットはお昼ごろになるとかなり混むので、人混みをさけるためにできるだけ朝早く買い物に行くようにしています。

examples.en: The train is crowded every morning, but it’s not your fault. There’s no need to blame yourself.
examples.ja: 電車は毎日混みますが、あなたのせいではありません。自分を責める必要はありませんよ。

4389.meaning_mnemonic: This one is a little strange. You have 混じる (to get mixed up in), 混ぜる (to mix), 混ざる (to get mixed), and now this: 混む, <vocabulary>to be crowded</vocabulary>. It makes sense that when everyone's all mixed up it's going to be crowded, but how to differentiate between this and the other 混 words? Just think of how cows <reading>muuuuu</reading> (む) get all bunched up and crowded, which is why this word is <vocabulary>to be crowded</vocabulary>.
4389.reading_mnemonic: Hey, <reading>come</reading> (こむ) out of that crowd of cows. It's going <vocabulary>to be crowded</vocabulary> in there.

examples.en: The radio signal was weak, and noise was mixed in, so it was difficult to hear.
examples.ja: ラジオの電波が弱く、ノイズが混じって聞こえにくかった。

examples.en: My sister's brown eyes occasionally appeared to be mixed with green or yellow.
examples.ja: 妹の茶色の目には、時折、緑や黄色が混じって見えることがあった。

examples.en: The messages from the devil are a mixture of lies and truths meant to confuse us.
examples.ja: 悪魔からのメッセージには、我々を混乱させるために嘘と真実が入り混じっている。

4390.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji means <kanji>mix</kanji>, and you already learned its transitive and intransitive pair: 混ぜる (to mix) and 混ざる (to get mixed). 混じる is another intransitive verb, but it means <vocabulary>to be mixed in with</vocabulary>.

So how are 混ざる and 混じる different? 混ざる is used to talk about things that become mixed together as part of the same whole — like blended colors or intermingled groups. 混じる, on the other hand, is less about blending smoothly and more about something getting mixed in when it doesn't quite belong — static in your audio, scattered strands of gray in your dark hair, or even some random stranger sitting at your group's table.

You can remember this by thinking about how this out-of-place thing getting mixed in makes you want to <reading>jeer</reading> (じる): "Boo, get out of here! You don't fit in!"
4390.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned that reading with 混ぜる, but here's a mnemonic in case you forgot:

Who doesn't want gray hair <vocabulary>to be mixed in</vocabulary> with their dark hair? Your <reading>ma</reading> (ま). Sadly for your ma, age and the stress of raising YOU have led to a lot of gray already starting to be mixed in. Poor ma…

examples.en: Many users got confused when WaniKani's subscription fee decreased.
examples.ja: ユーザーの多くは、ワニカニのサブスクリプションが安くなったことに混乱した。

examples.en: During the Great East Japanese Earthquake, people around Tokyo didn't panic, they just did what they could.
examples.ja: 東日本大震災では、東京周辺の人々は混乱することもなく、ただ自分にできることをしていた。

examples.en: You’ll probably get confused, but my brother is striving to overcome his fear of death right now, so please leave him alone.
examples.ja: 君はおそらく混乱すると思うけど、弟は今、死への恐怖を克服しようと必死で努力しているところなの。だから、そっとしておいてあげてくれないかな？

4391.meaning_mnemonic: If 混乱 is <kanji>confusion</kanji> then making it into a verb would cause it <vocabulary>to be confused</vocabulary>.
4391.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 混乱 so no reason for you <vocabulary>to be confused</vocabulary>, right?

examples.en: I had my teacher decrease the number of homework assignments I was given.
examples.ja: 先生に宿題をちょっとだけ減らしてもらいました。

examples.en: I asked them to reduce the amount of cream, but they didn't accept my request.
examples.ja: クリームの量を減らすようお願いしたんですが、聞き入れてもらえませんでした。

examples.en: The plague reduced the number of blowfish to half its previous level.
examples.ja: その疫病は、河豚の数をそれまでの水準の半分に減らした。

4392.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>decrease</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to decrease something</vocabulary>. You can differentiate this from 減る because with this one, you are the one that is going to be doing the decreasing. The <reading>rush</reading> (らす) of decreasing something fills your veins.
4392.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 減る, so if you know that reading you should know this one.

examples.en: I will continue WaniKani forever ♡
examples.ja: これからもずっとワニカニを続けるつもりです♡

examples.en: Why do you all keep criticizing me?
examples.ja: どうしてあなた達は私のことを批判し続けるのですか？

examples.en: Weekends are awesome because I can continue to sleep all day long.
examples.ja: 一日中寝続けられるので、週末は最高だ。

4393.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>continue</kanji>, so 続ける means <vocabulary>to continue something</vocabulary>. It's a transitive verb, so it takes a direct object. You can 続ける your work, for example, and you should 続ける your WaniKani lessons at a pace that works for you!

Although it has the same 続 kanji, this word is a bit different from 続く, which is used for when something just continues on its own (like rain, or trends). It can be hard to remember the difference, so here's a mnemonic to help you with 続ける:

You only <reading>care</reading> (ける) about things that you can continue through your own actions. For those other things that just continue on their own, you're like, That's <reading>coo</reading>' (く), but you’re not that interested.
4393.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 続く, so be sure to know that so you can know this.

examples.en: You can’t use proper nouns in the game Shiritori.
examples.ja: しりとりに固有名詞は使えません。

examples.en: How are proper nouns different from nouns?
examples.ja: 固有名詞と名詞はどうちがいますか。

examples.en: I eagerly looked up a word that I didn't recognize in the dictionary, but couldn't find it and it turned out it was just a proper noun.
examples.ja: 分からない単語を辞書で一生懸命探してたんだけど、見つからないと思ったら、固有名詞だった。

4394.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>noun</kanji> (名詞) that <kanji>has</kanji> <kanji>hard</kanji>ness is a noun that can't be budged. It's a big noun, so big that you have to capitalize these kinds of nouns in English. It is a <vocabulary>proper noun</vocabulary>.
4394.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know the word 名詞 as well.

examples.en: Wait, was that politician a conservative?
examples.ja: あれ、あの政治家って、保守主義だっけ？

examples.en: This country is strongly conservative, so change is slow.
examples.ja: この国は保守主義が強いので、変化が遅いんです。

examples.en: My parents are both teachers and extremely old-fashioned conservatives.
examples.ja: 私の両親は、二人とも教師で、めちゃくちゃ古風な保守主義者です。

4395.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 主義 is "-ism." Add that ism to people who want to <kanji>protect</kanji> and <kanji>conserve</kanji> their country so it stays just the way it is (forever). That's <vocabulary>conservatism</vocabulary> and they're <vocabulary>conservative</vocabulary> people.
4395.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the reading of 保守的 for the first half and then the regular kanji readings for the second half. Combine those things and you'll be a master of righteousness and / or kanji.

examples.en: Transitive verbs take objects.
examples.ja: 他動詞は目的語を取ります。

examples.en: Please change all of these transitive verbs into intransitive verbs.
examples.ja: ここに書いてある他動詞を全部自動詞に書きかえてください。

examples.en: Is memorization the only way to learn if the verb is transitive or intransitive?
examples.ja: その動詞が他動詞か自動詞かを学ぶには、まる暗記するしかないのかな。

4396.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 動詞 means "verb"? When the verb is done to some <kanji>other</kanji> thing, it's a <vocabulary>transitive verb</vocabulary>.

That means it takes a direct object. Verbs like 食べる, 使う, and 上げる are transitive verbs because they need a direct object, an "other" thing, to receive their action.
4396.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Not that you asked me, but I think you should leave the yakuza.
examples.ja: 余計な事を言うようだけど、暴力団から足を洗った方がいいと思うよ。

examples.en: My dad will never approve of my joining a gangster organization.
examples.ja: 父は私が暴力団に入ることを認めてくれないでしょう。

examples.en: What’s the difference between the Yakuza and Kanto Rengo?
examples.ja: 暴力団と関東連合の違いは何ですか？

4397.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>group</kanji> that has <kanji>power</kanji> using <kanji>violence</kanji>? Sounds like a <vocabulary>crime syndicate</vocabulary> to me, probably the <vocabulary>Yakuza</vocabulary> or some other <vocabulary>gangster organization</vocabulary> .
4397.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The suspect admitted his guilt.
examples.ja: 容疑者は、自分の罪を認めた。

examples.en: The suspect conveyed a message of optimism to the teenagers.
examples.ja: その容疑者は、十代の若者たちにオプティミズムのメッセージを伝えた。

examples.en: Apparently Satoshi is wanted as a suspect in the Sweet Dumpling Poisoning Case.
examples.ja: サトシはみたらし団子毒殺事件の容疑者として指名手配されたらしいよ。

4398.meaning_mnemonic: I have a <kanji>suspicion</kanji> (容疑) about <kanji>someone</kanji>. That someone is my main <vocabulary>suspect</vocabulary>.
4398.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Will help to be able to read 容疑 first, though.

examples.en: The motorcycle gang confessed that they had run over the raccoon.
examples.ja: 暴走族は、アライグマをひいたことを認めた。

examples.en: I will never ever acknowledge your joining of a biker gang.
examples.ja: 暴走族に入るなんて、ゼッタイにゼッタイに認めませんよ。

examples.en: Mr. Viet, I would be grateful if you could reply as soon as possible about your time spent in a biker gang.
examples.ja: ビエトさん、あなたが暴走族をしていた頃のエピソードについて、早急にお返事いただけると幸いです。

4399.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>tribe</kanji> that <kanji>runs wild</kanji> (暴走) is what the Japanese call a <vocabulary>biker gang</vocabulary>. Just imagine them riding around on their bikes, running wild. They're also close, like a family. How nice!
4399.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Tofugu holds a drinking party every night to help stimulate the economy.
examples.ja: トーフグが毎晩飲み会を設けているのは、経済活性化のためです。

examples.en: My great grandfather told me he had to "economize because he's broke." Apparently "economizing" means being thrifty with your money.
examples.ja: ひいおじいちゃんが、「金欠だから経済しないと」って言ってたけど、なんか経済するって節約するって意味らしいよ。

examples.en: Since Koichi was inaugurated as President, the US economy has continued to recover at a rapid pace.
examples.ja: コウイチが大統領に就任してからというもの、アメリカの経済は急ピッチで回復している。

4400.meaning_mnemonic: When a <kanji>passage of time</kanji> <kanji>comes to an end</kanji>, you look back on it and see how well you did. Did we make more money? Did we make less? That's all <vocabulary>economics</vocabulary>, baby (that's money, baby!).
4400.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The さい changes to ざい, though, so watch out for that.

examples.en: That's enough! You've made too many errors in judgement recently.
examples.ja: いい加減にしろ！最近判断ミスが多すぎるぞ。

examples.en: Cut the BS, refs!
examples.ja: 審判のやつら、マジでいい加減にしろ！

examples.en: Viet was so angry that he couldn’t restrain himself from punching Koichi and screaming, "Cut it out!"
examples.ja: ビエトはあまりにも怒っていたので、コウイチを殴って「いい加減にしろ！」と叫ばずにはいられなかった。

4401.meaning_mnemonic: You know how いい加減 is unfounded or pointless? Because if you <kanji>add</kanji> and then <kanji>decrease</kanji> you haven't really done anything? Well, this is like saying "do the pointless!" Okay, that doesn't make any sense. This is a phrase that means something similar to <vocabulary>cut it out</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>cut the BS</vocabulary>!
4401.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as いい加減, which you (hopefully) learned earlier.

examples.en: Everybody wants to avoid troublesome formalities!
examples.ja: みんな、面倒な手続きはしたくないよ！

examples.en: Last week I finished the process of enrolling my child in school.
examples.ja: 先週、子どもを学校に入学させる手続きを終えました。

examples.en: The procedure was very complicated and I got so confused that I didn't know what to do.
examples.ja: 手続きが複雑で、頭が混乱してどうしていいか分からなくなりました。

4402.meaning_mnemonic: Someone takes your <kanji>hand</kanji> and shows you how to <kanji>continue</kanji>. "This is the <vocabulary>procedure</vocabulary>," they say. Move your hand like this. Verrrryyy goood. Good procedure. Good!
4402.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi vocab readings of 手 and 続く put together into one. Darn these body parts making everything kun'yomi.

examples.en: "Which side are you on, Fugu? Are you my enemy?" "I’m on your side, Salmon."
examples.ja: 「フグ、あなたはどっちの味方なの？私の敵なの？」「僕は君の味方だよ、サーモン。」

examples.en: Viet took matters into his own hands and headed to the enemy's hideout.
examples.ja: ビエトは自分だけの判断で、敵のアジトに向かった。

examples.en: I wish to exact revenge on that person for the sake of my parents someday.
examples.ja: いつかアイツに、親の敵を討ちたいんです。

4403.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

敵 means <vocabulary>enemy</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>opponent</vocabulary>, whether in war, sports, competitions, or other conflict situations. Just keep in mind that 敵 can sound a bit strong!
4403.reading_mnemonic:
The main reading is the same one you learned with the kanji. But there's also a secondary かたき reading you haven't seen yet, so here's a mnemonic for that:

You love to call your <vocabulary>enemy</vocabulary>'s <reading>car tacky</reading> (かたき). They're always driving around in some tacky sports car, you can't stand it. Every time they drive by you shout, "Your car is tacky, enemy!"

Note: In terms of differences, the てき reading just means "enemy," whereas かたき typically refers to someone you hold a deep grudge against, often on behalf of another.

examples.en: I find him attractive because of his enthusiasm for helping others.
examples.ja: カレの他の人を助けたいっていう熱意が、素敵だなって思うのよね。

examples.en: I noticed some mushrooms living among the beautiful flowers.
examples.ja: 素敵な花に交じって、キノコが生えているのを見つけました。

examples.en: This is such a lovely open air bath!
examples.ja: とっても素敵な露天風呂ですね。

4404.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>element</kanji> of your <kanji>enemy</kanji> that bugs you the most is how <vocabulary>lovely</vocabulary> they are. You wish you were as <vocabulary>charming</vocabulary> as them… and maybe that's why you insist on being their enemy. You just can't deal with how <vocabulary>wonderful</vocabulary> they are.

素敵 is the kind of word you use when something makes your heart flutter — when it feels delightful, admirable, or even inspiring. For example, 素敵な人 can mean someone who's attractive, but it can also refer to someone you admire, respect, or feel drawn to because of their attitude, values, character, or vibe.
4404.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 素 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Oh wow, you look really <vocabulary>lovely</vocabulary> in that <reading>su</reading>it (す). Yes, I can see you through the Internet, and I have to say, that suit is just <vocabulary>dreamy</vocabulary>! Don't ever take it off.

examples.en: Who do you think is Wanikani's rival?
examples.ja: ワニカニの大敵はだれだと思いますか？

examples.en: Our arch enemy finally acknowledged their defeat.
examples.ja: オレたちの大敵が、ついに敗北を認めたぞ。

examples.en: As you all know, carelessness is man's greatest enemy. People say "even monkeys fall from trees," right?
examples.ja: 分かっていると思うけど、油断大敵だよ。「サルも木から落ちる」って言うだろう？

4405.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>enemy</kanji> is your worst enemy. Your <vocabulary>arch enemy</vocabulary>.

大敵 is for a powerful or dangerous opponent, whether it's a <vocabulary>formidable adversary</vocabulary> in battle or competition, or something abstract, like calling carelessness your <vocabulary>great enemy</vocabulary>.
4405.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Both kanji have a couple different on'yomi readings though, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember which ones to pick:

Your <vocabulary>arch enemy</vocabulary> is the <reading>tie techie</reading> (たいてき). Who's the tie techie? He's the tech support guy at work who always wears the same tie and never helps you. He just says "try restarting your computer" to every problem, which isn't helpful. He's not just a great enemy, he's basically your nemesis. You hate that tie techie.

examples.en: Koichi is invincible at Shiritori.
examples.ja: しりとりで、コウイチは無敵だ。

examples.en: I wanna get plastic surgery to make people think that I'm an adorable, unrivaled woman.
examples.ja: 整形して、みんなから可愛すぎる無敵な女だって思われたい。

examples.en: Our son admires invincible heroes.
examples.ja: うちの息子は、無敵のヒーローに憧れています。

4406.meaning_mnemonic: You have <kanji>nothing</kanji> when it comes to <kanji>enemies</kanji>. Why? It's not because you're super kind and everyone likes you. No, it's that you've defeated anyone who's tried. You are <vocabulary>unrivaled</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>invincible</vocabulary>.
4406.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Work just came to an end.
examples.ja: 今やっと仕事が済んだところだよ。

examples.en: Let's get together in the cafeteria once we're done with this work!
examples.ja: この作業が済んだら食堂に集まろうぜ！

examples.en: I apologized, but he told me apologizing wouldn't end the problem, so I got angry and slapped him in the face.
examples.ja: 謝ったんだけど、「これは謝って済む問題じゃない」なんて言われちゃって、それで頭にきて彼の顔をひっぱたいちゃったのよね。

4407.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>come to an end</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to come to an end</vocabulary>.
4407.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Your romp finally has <vocabulary>to come to an end</vocabulary> when someone decides to <reading>sue</reading> (す) you for all your romping.

examples.en: That committee member has good judgment, doesn't she?
examples.ja: あの委員は、すぐれた判断力を持っていますね。

examples.en: Morishima-kun is the head of the committee.
examples.ja: その委員会の委員長は、森島君です。

examples.en: The school’s disciplinary committee decided that teachers don’t need to teach students about wet dreams in the physical education class.
examples.ja: 風紀委員は、保健体育の授業で教師が夢精について生徒たちに教える必要は無いと判断した。

4408.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>committee</kanji> <kanji>member</kanji> is a <vocabulary>member of a committee</vocabulary> (or a <vocabulary>committee member</vocabulary>).
4408.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: When the teacher said that, many hands were raised.
examples.ja: 先生がそう言うと、たくさん手が挙がった。

examples.en: Tom's name was mentioned at the time, wasn't it?
examples.ja: その時にトムの名前が挙がってましたね。

examples.en: I can’t believe that I’m nominated for the Mustache Award.
examples.ja: 自分がヒゲ大賞の候補に挙がっているなんて、信じられないよ。

4409.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>raise</kanji> something you are causing it <vocabulary>to be raised</vocabulary>. This verb can also mean things like <vocabulary>to be listed</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be nominated</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to rise</vocabulary>. For these additional meanings, you might want to imagine something rising up onto a list or someone rising up to a nomination, because lists and nominations are always high up.
4409.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

The reading for this is the same as the other "to rise" word, 上がる. Nice how that works, right? So, just associate the two and you have yourself a reading.

examples.en: Don't try to confuse me by bringing up things that don't have to do with the election.
examples.ja: 選挙の話と関係のないことを持ち出して、頭を混乱させるのは止めてくれ。

examples.en: Many people have been critical of the results of this election, and they say the whole thing should be redone.
examples.ja: 今回の選挙結果には多くの人が批判的で、もう一度選挙し直すべきだと言っています。

examples.en: Koichi lost his voice from singing the blues during his election speech.
examples.ja: コウイチは、選挙演説中にブルースを歌って声がつぶれた。

4410.meaning_mnemonic: You have to <kanji>choose</kanji> someone and <kanji>raise</kanji> them up to office. This is an <vocabulary>election</vocabulary>.
4410.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I ordered my personal seal at a seal store.
examples.ja: 判子屋さんで、判子を注文しました。

examples.en: Please sign here and put your seal there.
examples.ja: ここにはサイン、そこには判子をお願いします。

examples.en: This document was officially sealed by Koichi.
examples.ja: この書類には、コウイチによって公的な判子が押されています。

4411.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>child</kanji> of a <kanji>judge</kanji> is the thing he puts on his judgements. What does he put on his judgments? His <vocabulary>seal</vocabulary>, you know, to make it all official and stuff.
4411.reading_mnemonic: 判 is the reading you learned. 子 is the kun'yomi vocab reading, which I bet you know pretty well by now as well. You just have to remember to use it here.

examples.en: That baseball commentator doesn't have a very good reputation.

4425.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>establish</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to establish</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to set up</vocabulary>.

設ける is a formal word that suggests setting up something in order to prep for future needs or events. If you want to ensure smooth operation or governance, for example, you might set up rules (ルールを設ける) or establish an office (オフィスを設ける). You can even use it to say you’ll arrange a drinking party (酒の席を設ける), in which case it probably means the party has a more formal purpose like networking or discussion.
4425.reading_mnemonic: What are you going <vocabulary>to establish</vocabulary>? How about a system for <reading>mow</reading>ing (もう) lawns? It's very important that lawns are mowed according to an established system, you know. How do you mow yours?

設定する is a little formal, but does get commonly used for device, system, and game settings. It's also often used in more official contexts, like for setting prices for products or establishing project goals.
