An <kanji>occurrence</kanji> of some <kanji>matter</kanji> is really just something that happens. It's an <vocabulary>incident</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>case</vocabulary>. 

事件 often refers to significant or serious occurrences like crime cases or accidents. It can also be used playfully — "There was a 事件 at the party!" — to dramatize an event like someone asking out your classmate.
4437.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I don't want to be a bridesmaid because the dresses are too flashy.
examples.ja: ドレスが派手すぎるから、ブライズ・メイドにはなりたくないんだよね。

examples.en: Showy fashion was the trend about 30 years ago in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本では三十年ほど前は派手なファッションが流行していました。

examples.en: That girl may look gaudy, but despite appearances she's actually very sensitive on the inside.
examples.ja: あの子、見た目は派手だけどああ見えて中身はとても繊細なのよ。

4438.meaning_mnemonic: This is a weird one. Just think about the <kanji>sect</kanji> of <kanji>hand</kanji>s. They are always doing jazz hands and things like that, trying to be all <vocabulary>showy</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>flashy</vocabulary>. Ugh, what a dumb sect, you think.
4438.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji, though て goes to で.

examples.en: That company is only admirable on the surface.
examples.ja: あの会社、うわべだけは立派だよね。

examples.en: You've become such a splendid movie critic.
examples.ja: お前も立派な映画評論家になったもんだなぁ。

examples.en: My cat grew very handsome whiskers, so I named him Hige.
examples.ja: 私の猫は立派な髯を生やしているので、「ヒゲ」と名付けました。

4439.meaning_mnemonic:
People are <kanji>stand</kanji>ing and forming a <kanji>sect</kanji> for you because of the <vocabulary>splendid</vocabulary> things you say and do. Your <vocabulary>admirable</vocabulary> conduct has brought them to their feet, and now they're worshipping you like some new age guru.

立派 is a slightly formal word used to say something or someone is <vocabulary>impressive</vocabulary>. For example, you might call someone who achieved something great a 立派な人, or describe an elegant, expensive-looking building as a 立派な建物. Even a fine, majestic mustache could be called a 立派なヒゲ!
4439.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The りつ shortens to りっ though, so keep an eye on that you splendid frood you. Oh and は changes to ぱ too. Because rendaku and all that.

examples.en: My father is from Okayama Prefecture.
examples.ja: 私の父は岡山県出身です。

examples.en: The earthquake brought utter chaos to Okayama prefecture.
examples.ja: 岡山県は、地震で大混乱となりました。

examples.en: The suspect admits that he stole the money in Okayama prefecture.
examples.ja: 容疑者は、岡山県で金を盗んだことを認めています。

4440.meaning_mnemonic: Okayama (岡山) <kanji>Prefecture</kanji> is a prefecture in Japan. Learning the reading will help you to remember the meaning of this word since half of it is in Japanese.
4440.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi readings of the first two kanji. Luckily you learned them when you learned the kanji. Then, stick 県 on there and you should be good to go!

examples.en: Yesterday's concert was wonderful!
examples.ja: 昨日のコンサート、素晴らしかったです！

examples.en: The opening of that film and the camera work were truly magnificent.
examples.ja: あの映画のオープニングとカメラワークは実に素晴らしかった。

examples.en: A magnificent view extended out from the mountaintop.
examples.ja: 山頂には素晴らしい景色が広がっていた。

examples.en: "Don’t sell yourself short like that. You’re a magnificent woman."
examples.ja: 「そんな風に自分を安売りしないで。君は素晴らしい女性だよ。」

4441.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>element</kanji> of <kanji>clear up</kanji> (like the sky clearing up!) is so <vocabulary>wonderful</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>splendid</vocabulary>. Sort of a weird word, but very useful. Just think of that wonderful feeling you get when the sun breaks and things clear up and it's awesome.
4441.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a bit weird, too. Luckily, you've learned both of them already. 晴れる is はれる. That's the reading you use here, though は goes to ば.

examples.en: Aya was right in her decision to go with that raw material.
examples.ja: その素材を選んだアヤの判断は正しかった。

examples.en: In this restaurant, seasoning is kept to a minimum for you to enjoy the natural taste of the ingredients.
examples.ja: このレストランでは、素材そのものの味を楽しんでもらうため、味付けはひかえめにしています。

examples.en: I'm looking for copyright-free materials.
examples.ja: 著作権フリーの素材を探しています。

4442.meaning_mnemonic: When you want to use the most basic <kanji>element</kanji>s of a <kanji>material</kanji>, you end up with <vocabulary>raw material</vocabulary>s. Maybe it's the raw materials you're going to use to build a house. Maybe it's the raw materials you need to make a good soup. Either way, they haven't been touched much (yet).
4442.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The reading for 素 is the そ reading, so be careful. You can remember by thinking how you have to <reading>sew</reading> the building together using these raw materials.

examples.en: Do you think I should refuse the job?
examples.ja: その仕事、断るべきだと思う？

examples.en: Viet was appointed as the next Secretary of State, but he refused.
examples.ja: ビエトは次期国務長官に任命されたが、断った。

examples.en: I was asked to be the chief umpire for a baseball game, but I rejected the offer. I would have done it if it was for the chief referee of a soccer game though.
examples.ja: 野球の試合の主審を頼まれたけど、断りました。サッカーの試合の主審だったら引き受けたんだけどね。

4443.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>cut off</kanji>. What happens when you do the action of cutting someone off? You're going <vocabulary>to refuse</vocabulary> them whatever it is they want.
4443.reading_mnemonic: Deciding <vocabulary>to refuse</vocabulary> something unfortunately starts a <reading>coat war</reading> (like a pillow fight, but everyone hits each other with coats instead of pillows). Coats to the ready, and let the coat war commence!

examples.en: My judgment was wrong.
examples.ja: 私の判断は間違っていた。

examples.en: If I hadn't made the wrong decision then, I would have gotten extremely rich.
examples.ja: あの時、判断を誤らなければ、大金持ちになれていたのに。

examples.en: It is difficult for an amateur to judge whether a mushroom is edible or poisonous.
examples.ja: 食用キノコか毒キノコの判断は、素人には難しい。

4444.meaning_mnemonic: I <kanji>judge</kanji> to <kanji>cut off</kanji> your head. That is my <vocabulary>judgment</vocabulary>!
4444.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Japanese language teachers also seem to think highly of Tofugu.
examples.ja: 日本語の先生たちも、トーフグのことを高く評価してくれているようです。

examples.en: I did not expect this film to receive criticism.
examples.ja: この映画が批判的な評価を受けるとは思わなかった。

examples.en: My family doctor has a low rating because he is always in a rush, is unwilling to listen to patients who have researched a medical problem they have, and often dismisses their worries.
examples.ja: 私のホームドクターは、いつも急いでいて、自分の症状について調べてきた患者の話を聞かずにけんもほろろに追い出すので、評価が低い。

4445.meaning_mnemonic: Let's <kanji>evaluate</kanji> the <kanji>value</kanji>. What is this also known as? An <vocabulary>evaluation</vocabulary>.
4445.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This critique is pretty cohesive.
examples.ja: この評論はよくまとまっているね。

examples.en: Don't let the words of someone who can only write second-rate criticism get to you.
examples.ja: あんな二流の評論しか書けないやつの言葉、気にするなよ。

examples.en: It’s so cute to see a ten year old girl make a critique in a movie, don't you think?
examples.ja: 映画の中で十歳の女の子が評論をしているのが可愛いよね。

4446.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Evaluate</kanji> my <kanji>theory</kanji>. Then, when you evaluate, please give me <vocabulary>critique</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>criticism</vocabulary> to help me get better?
4446.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Could you kindly ask Koichi to review this book for me, please?
examples.ja: コウイチにこの本の書評をお願いしてもらえませんか？

examples.en: That book review is widely recognized as being well-reasoned.
examples.ja: その書評は、妥当なものとして広く認められています。

examples.en: There are so many critical reviews about that book that I lost interest in buying it.
examples.ja: その本についての批判的な書評があまりにも多いので、買う気が失せたよ。

4447.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>writing</kanji> that has been <kanji>evaluate</kanji>d has gotten a <vocabulary>book review</vocabulary>.
4447.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Sometimes you can’t help but be the subject of criticism.
examples.ja: 批判の的となっても仕方がないと思っている。

examples.en: I'm trying to look at everything as critically as possible.
examples.ja: できるだけ批判的な目であらゆる物事を見るよう心がけています。

examples.en: Viet was severely criticized for taking bribes from the yakuza.
examples.ja: ビエトは暴力団から賄賂を受け取ったことを厳しく批判されました。

4448.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>criticism</kanji> is when you <kanji>judge</kanji>. It is still just a <vocabulary>criticism</vocabulary>.
4448.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: You can follow me on a voluntary basis.
examples.ja: フォローは任意です。

examples.en: Please choose any 8-digit number.
examples.ja: 任意の八ケタの数字を選んでください。

examples.en: Do I legally have to tell you my name and address, or is it optional?
examples.ja: 名前と住所は法律で答えなくてはいけないと決まっているものですか？それとも任意ですか？

4449.meaning_mnemonic: My <kanji>idea</kanji> of <kanji>duty</kanji> is that you don't really have to do it. It's <vocabulary>optional</vocabulary>, you know?
4449.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I received a checkup at the hospital.
examples.ja: 病院で検査を受けました。

examples.en: Upon inspection, we could not find anything wrong with the engine.
examples.ja: 検査の結果、エンジンには何も問題ありませんでした。

examples.en: I'm surprised pinworm tests aren't commonly administered in North America.
examples.ja: 北米でギョウ虫検査があまり一般的ではないなんて、驚きです。

4450.meaning_mnemonic: We're going to need to <kanji>examine</kanji> and <kanji>inspect</kanji> you for our annual <vocabulary>checkup</vocabulary>, mmk? Now drop your pants and cough, please.
4450.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Hey look, the police are examining people over there.
examples.ja: ほら、あそこで警察が検問しているよ。

examples.en: While the police were inspecting my car, my heart was racing.
examples.ja: 警察が私の車を検問している時、ドキドキしました。

examples.en: Some of the security guards who inspect people at Narita Airport's checkpoints are undergoing training.
examples.ja: 成田空港の検問所で検問している警備員の中には、トレーニング中の警備員もいます。

4451.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>examine</kanji> the <kanji>problem</kanji>. In order to do this, you need <vocabulary>to inspect</vocabulary> it or <vocabulary>to examine</vocabulary> it. And if you're inspecting people like this, you're probably the police.
4451.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I’m not only a referee, but also a sports analyst.
examples.ja: 私は審判でもあり、スポーツ解説者でもあります。

examples.en: That sports college has established a refereeing course too.
examples.ja: そのスポーツ大学には、審判コースも設けられています。

examples.en: Passing judgment wasn't as easy as I'd expected.
examples.ja: 審判を下すのは思ったよりも簡単な事ではなかった。

4452.meaning_mnemonic: This word has <kanji>judge</kanji> and <kanji>judge</kanji> in it, so it has something to do with <vocabulary>judgment</vocabulary>. It's usually used in sports, so it's the <vocabulary>referee</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>umpire</vocabulary>, depending on your sport of choice.
4452.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just watch out for rendaku turning はん into ぱん (as is so often the case after ん).

examples.en: My older brother took out three books on the Treaty of Paris and two on Treaty of Versailles from the library.
examples.ja: 兄は図書館からパリ条約に関する本を三冊とヴェルサイユ条約に関する本を二冊借りてきました。

examples.en: This treaty was made based on the committee's conclusion.
examples.ja: この条約は、委員会の判断に基いて取り決められたものです。

examples.en: Koichi’s New Year’s resolution is memorizing the entire text of the Treaty of Versailles.
examples.ja: コウイチの今年の抱負は、ベルサイユ条約の全文を暗記することです。

4453.meaning_mnemonic: There are many <kanji>clause</kanji>s about the <kanji>promise</kanji>s you make in this contract considering it's supposed to be a <vocabulary>treaty</vocabulary>.
4453.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: "I should have checked it out myself." "Don’t blame yourself. It wasn’t your fault."
examples.ja: 「自分でちゃんとチェックするべきだったよ。」「そんなに自分を責めないで。あなたのせいじゃないわよ。」

examples.en: The typhoon disrupted the train schedule, so blaming Michael is unreasonable.
examples.ja: 台風で電車のダイヤが混乱してただけなんだから、マイケルさんを責めるのはおかしいよ。

examples.en: Our kid had a fever, but I messed up and didn't take him to the hospital, so he ended up with pneumonia. My wife later reproached me harshly.
examples.ja: 子どもが熱を出したんだけど、判断を誤って病院に連れて行かなかったら肺炎になっちゃってね。後で妻からひどく責められたよ。

4454.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>blame</kanji> so this also means <vocabulary>to blame</vocabulary>. Additionally, this can also mean <vocabulary>to criticize</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to reproach</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to accuse</vocabulary>.
4454.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Are you going <vocabulary>to blame</vocabulary> me for eating your <reading>ce</reading>lery (せ)? You should know I'm the wrong person to blame because I don't even like celery!

examples.en: Japanese salarymen tend to hate taking responsibility.
examples.ja: 日本のサラリーマンは責任を取る事を嫌がることが多い。

examples.en: When the clock struck seven, I awoke from a terrible dream that Koichi was forcing me to take responsibility for all of my WaniKani errors.
examples.ja: 時計が七時を打つ音で、コウイチからワニカニのエラーの全ての責任を負わされるというおそろしい夢から目覚めました。

examples.en: Why don't we reserve judgement on whoever's responsibility it was, and just start by making up for lost time?
examples.ja: 責任が誰にあるかの判断は一旦保留にして、まずは遅れを取り戻そう。

4455.meaning_mnemonic: You can <kanji>blame</kanji> <kanji>duty</kanji> all you want, but you still have a <vocabulary>responsibility</vocabulary> as well, no matter what your duty dictates.
4455.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I've been very busy these days, so I've been skipping meal prep and just buying to-go dinners.
examples.ja: 最近はとても忙しいので、夕食を作る手間を省いてテイクアウトばかりしています。

examples.en: A lot of the explanations were left out, so I couldn't understand it.
examples.ja: 説明がたくさん省かれていたので理解できませんでした。

examples.en: This robot was supposed to save us a lot of labor, but the situation remains unchanged.
examples.ja: このロボットが多くの人手を省くはずだったが、状況は変化しないままである。

4456.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>conserve</kanji>... but why stop there when you could try <vocabulary>to omit</vocabulary> everything and <vocabulary>to eliminate</vocabulary> everything? Just take exactly what you need, conserve it, and omit everything else.
4456.reading_mnemonic: You <reading>have</reading> (はぶ) what you have, and omit what you don't need. Perfect life.

examples.en: I’ve been reflecting on it, so please don’t be so hard on me.
examples.ja: 反省しているので、そんなにきつく当たらないでください。

examples.en: My younger brother reconsidered it even more than I did.
examples.ja: 弟は、私よりも余計に反省していた。

examples.en: President Koichi and Vice President Viet held a postmortem meeting.
examples.ja: コウイチ大統領とビエト副大統領は反省会を開いた。

4457.meaning_mnemonic: If you're <kanji>anti</kanji> <kanji>conserve</kanji>, I'm going to ask you to do some heavy <vocabulary>reconsideration</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>reflection</vocabulary>, and see if that's really the right way to be. If you change your thinking, you might even end up showing <vocabulary>regret</vocabulary>.
4457.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for 反 is all good. The reading for 省 is an on'yomi reading you haven't seen yet. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

I'm standing in front of you, forcing a <vocabulary>reconsideration</vocabulary> of your anti conserve stance, with my <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい) to your throat. I better see some reflection on your face or you won't have one in a second.

examples.en: Over the past few years, Viet’s daily amount of alcohol has been considerably increasing.
examples.ja: ここ2、3年、ビエトが一日に飲むお酒、かなり増えてるんだよね。

examples.en: It would be nice if the constructive criticism increased a bit.
examples.ja: もう少し建設的な批判が増えるといいんだけど。

examples.en: It felt like the number of gray hairs mixed into my mom's black hair had increased since I last saw her.
examples.ja: 母の黒髪に交じった白髪の量が、以前より増えている気がした。

4458.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>increase</kanji>, so the vocabulary verb version means <vocabulary>to increase</vocabulary>. This is when something is just increasing on its own, and you're not doing the increasing. You know this because you like to <reading>err</reading> (える) on the side of caution and not touch anything when it's increasing, therefore you're not doing any of the increasing yourself (it's just happening).

This is an everyday word that refers to an increase in number or quantity, but keep in mind that it cannot be used to express an increase in degree.
4458.reading_mnemonic: It would be <reading>foo</reading>lish (ふ) of you to touch anything while things are increasing anyways. You don't want to mess up a good thing, do you? Don't be a fool.

examples.en: Crimes have been increasing steadily since Viet left town.
examples.ja: ビエトがこの町を去ってから、 犯罪は着実に増加している。

examples.en: The number of Japanese restaurants have been increasing around here.
examples.ja: この辺りでは、日本食レストランの数が増加しています。

examples.en: I ate way too much mochi on New Years and my weight increased by 50 kilos.
examples.ja: お正月に餅を食べ過ぎて、体重が五十キロも増加した。

4459.meaning_mnemonic:
An <kanji>increase</kanji> will <kanji>add</kanji> to what you had before. This is an <vocabulary>increase</vocabulary>.

This word refers to an increase in number or quantity, often used in formal contexts, reports, or news articles.
4459.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What do you think about the sudden increase in the number of young people who lack self-control in recent years, Dr. Fugu?
examples.ja: 近年の、自制心が欠けている若者の急増について、フグ先生はどうお考えですか。

examples.en: I feel that there's been a sudden increase in the number of people who can't accept even the slightest criticism.
examples.ja: ちょっとした批判も受け入れられない人が急増している気がします。

examples.en: The number of children who dream of being a choreographer has increased suddenly.
examples.ja: 振り付け師になるのが夢だという子どもが、急増しています。

4460.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>sudden</kanji> <kanji>increase</kanji> is just that, a <vocabulary>sudden increase</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>surge</vocabulary>!
4460.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I will never accept a tax increase.
examples.ja: 増税するなんて、ゼッタイに認めません。

examples.en: Because of the tax increase, I had to pay an extra 50 yen.
examples.ja: 増税のせいで、五十円余計にかかった。

examples.en: In the bill that just came, my property tax has been increased by 50%, but that’s a mistake, right? At least I hope it is.
examples.ja: さっき届いた請求書の固定資産税が、50%も増税されてたんだけど、間違いだよね。そうであってほしい。

4461.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>increase</kanji> <kanji>tax</kanji> you're doing a <vocabulary>tax increase</vocabulary>.
4461.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It's completely unacceptable that he uses our tax dollars for golf, right?
examples.ja: 税金でゴルフに参加するとか、ありえなくない？

examples.en: I wanted to study taxes, but it looks like it's too difficult for a blowfish like me.
examples.ja: 税金の勉強をしたかったのですが、どうやらフグの私には難しすぎたようです。

examples.en: My parents only adopted you because they needed the tax deduction.

4464.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>solve</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to be solved</vocabulary>. In a similar vein, this can also mean <vocabulary>to be cleared</vocabulary>, like with misunderstandings or tension in a room.

解ける is an intransitive verb, so it doesn't take a direct object. In other words, you use it to say something is solved or gets solved. You can remember this because you don't <reading>care</reading> (ける) enough to solve things yourself, you just let things get solved on their own.
4464.reading_mnemonic: You already learned how to read 解く, and this uses the same reading for the kanji. Lucky you!

4465.meaning_mnemonic:
You sit down to <kanji>solve</kanji> an issue and firmly <kanji>decide</kanji> on your course of action. This process is called <vocabulary>solving</vocabulary>, and it leads to a <vocabulary>solution</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>settlement</vocabulary>.

解決 is about finding a resolution or bringing a matter to a close. It can be used either for small-scale personal problems or for large-scale problems like social and political issues.

Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>recognize</kanji> or <kanji>acknowledge</kanji>, so the verb also means <vocabulary>to acknowledge</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to recognize</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to perceive</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to admit</vocabulary>, among others.

This can be used to mean recognizing somebody or something visually, as well as in the sense of "to acknowledge" or "to admit". So you can use this verb to recognize someone's presence, achievements, marriage, or your own defeat. That said, you'll usually see 認める in the sense of "to acknowledge".

examples.ja: 地震の被害者の多くは家を失ってしまったので、今は体育館で生活しているんです。

4487.meaning_mnemonic: You learned 被害 means "damage," and this is about <kanji>someone</kanji> who suffers damage, so this means <vocabulary>victim</vocabulary>.
4487.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Remembering the word 被害 might help you out too.

examples.en: Alright, I'm gonna go to bed. Sleep well. See you in the morning.
examples.ja: よし、そろそろ寝るね〜。おやすみ〜。また明日〜。

examples.en: Good night, darling <3 Sleep tight.
examples.ja: おやすみ、ダーリン<3 ぐっすり寝てね。

examples.en: I once went to Tofugu's office on a Sunday to find Koichi sleeping on the floor.
examples.ja: 日曜日にトーフグのオフィスに行くと、コウイチが床の上で寝ていたことがあった。

4488.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>sleep</kanji> or <kanji>lie down</kanji>, so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to sleep</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to lie down</vocabulary>—just like what you do when you decide <vocabulary>to go to bed</vocabulary>.
4488.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the reading you learned with the kanji. So, you can go ahead and lie down for a moment before moving on to the next item.

examples.en: I'm going to take a little nap.
examples.ja: ちょこっと昼寝してくるねー。

examples.en: When I woke up from my nap, it was already past 7 p.m.
examples.ja: 昼寝から目覚めると、すでに夜の七時を回っていた。

examples.en: Koichi is napping at the moment. Please be seated and wait for a moment.
examples.ja: コウイチはただ今昼寝中です。おかけになって少々お待ちください。

4489.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>noon</kanji> <kanji>sleep</kanji> is sleep you do during the day, also known as a <vocabulary>nap</vocabulary>.
4489.reading_mnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You learned them when you learned the kanji, so you should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: "So are you going to work overtime again today?" "Well actually, I was kind of hoping to get off work early today because I’ve been missing out on a lot of sleep."
examples.ja: 「今日も残業するつもりなの？」「えっと…ですね、今日は寝不足なのでどちらかというと早く上がりたいと思っています。」

examples.en: I didn't get enough sleep last night since I waited up for my husband until two in the morning.
examples.ja: 昨日は午前二時まで夫の帰りを寝ないで待っていたので、寝不足です。

examples.en: I was reprimanded by my boss for showing up to work looking sleepy.
examples.ja: そんな寝不足な顔して会社に来るなって上司に怒られた。

4490.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 不足 is a physical shortage? Well, now you have a physical shortage of <kanji>sleep</kanji>. That's a <vocabulary>lack of sleep</vocabulary>.
4490.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. However, the first kanji 寝 actually uses its kun'yomi ね. 不足 is on'yomi as you'd expect, but the ふ in 不 changes to ぶ, so hopefully you've been getting enough sleep.

examples.en: Don't go back to sleep - you'll oversleep! Don't ever go back to sleep.
examples.ja: 二度寝は危ないよ〜寝坊しちゃうよ！ゼッタイに二度寝しちゃダメだよ。

examples.en: I’m afraid no one in the Tofugu office is available at the moment. Every worker overslept today.
examples.ja: あいにくですが、トーフグのオフィスには今、ご対応できる者がおりません。社員がみんな寝坊してしまったのです。

examples.en: I frequently overslept and was late, so I was transferred to a rural branch office.
examples.ja: 寝坊で遅刻することが多すぎて、田舎の支店に飛ばされました。

4491.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>sleep</kanji> like a <kanji>monk</kanji>, as in you never stop sleeping (because you sleep while you meditate). When you sleep like a monk like this you're constantly <vocabulary>oversleeping</vocabulary>, probably because you're up late doing sutras or something. You're a <vocabulary>late riser</vocabulary>.
4491.reading_mnemonic: These are the readings you learned with the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Summer was over and the leaves on the trees were beginning to change color.
examples.ja: 夏が過ぎ、木の葉が色づき初めていた。

examples.en: All the Tofugu employees waited at the office for the typhoon to pass.
examples.ja: トーフグの社員達はみんな、台風が過ぎるのをオフィスで待った。

examples.en: I couldn't get to sleep last night because I ate too much supper.
examples.ja: 昨晩は、晩ご飯を食べ過ぎて、どうしても寝られませんでした。

4492.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>surpass</kanji>, but this verb is intransitive, meaning we’re not focussing on who did the action, but on the action itself. So this means <vocabulary>to pass</vocabulary>, as in “the storm passed”, <vocabulary>to be over</vocabulary> as in “winter’s over”, or <vocabulary>to be too much</vocabulary>.
4492.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

In order for the storm <vocabulary>to pass</vocabulary> you’re going to have to <reading>sue</reading> (す) it. Sadly storms won’t pass unless you take legal action these days.

examples.en: My eyes have never watered from onions before.
examples.ja: 玉ねぎが目にしみたことは過去に一度もありません。

examples.en: Moving forward, I've decided to face the events in my past in my own way.
examples.ja: これから、自分なりに、過去の出来事にしっかり向き合っていくつもりです。

examples.en: That man hasn't paid rent for the past 10 years.
examples.ja: あの男は、過去十年にも渡って、家賃を滞納しているんです。

4493.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>surpass</kanji> the <kanji>past</kanji> then you're going backwards in time (at least if you're coming from the "present"). If this is the case, then you are definitely in the <vocabulary>past</vocabulary>.
4493.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. But 去 has two on'yomi readings and you haven't seen this one yet, so here's a mnemonic to help:

In the <vocabulary>past</vocabulary>, you were a <reading>子</reading> (こ). You're not really a 子 anymore, but in the past you definitely used to be a 子!

examples.en: I can’t believe that all the students in the class received punishment for cheating.
examples.ja: クラスの生徒全員がカンニングで罰を受けたなんて、信じられない。

examples.en: Is it true that Tiger Woods was penalized two shots per hole for playing with a Pokémon sticker on his driver?
examples.ja: タイガー・ウッズがドライバーにポケモンのシールを付けてプレイしていたせいで、一ホールにつき二打の罰が科されたって本当？

examples.en: A widespread movement is underway to make doping violations by athletes subject to criminal penalties.
examples.ja: アスリートのドーピング違反に、刑事罰を導入する動きが広まっています。

4494.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4494.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the reading you learned with the kanji... and you thought I was about to punish you because it was a single kanji vocab word. Now get over here. Time for a dirty spanking for thinking such a thing.

examples.en: We’ll contact you shortly about the fine.
examples.ja: 罰金については、また追って連絡します。

examples.en: The police saw me glancing at my phone while driving and gave me a 6,000 yen fine.
examples.ja: 運転中にスマホをチラ見したところを警察に見られて、六千円の罰金を取られた。

examples.en: There was a proposal to have late employees pay a fine.
examples.ja: 遅刻した社員に罰金を払わせようという提案がありました。

4495.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Penalty</kanji> <kanji>gold</kanji> is the money you pay when you get a penalty. It's for <vocabulary>a fine</vocabulary>.
4495.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The ばつ gets changed to ばっ though, so don't get it wrong (or you'll get a 罰金!).

examples.en: I’m kind of disappointed about this penalty game, but I’m also a little excited.
examples.ja: この罰ゲームについて、がっかりもしてるんだけど、ワクワクしてもいるんだよね。

examples.en: As punishment from the batsu game, I had to sleep eight hours every night for a week.
examples.ja: 罰ゲームで、一週間毎日八時間寝ることになりました。

examples.en: I can tell you this now, but back when I confessed my feelings for you, it was only because of a batsu game.
examples.ja: 今だから言えるけど、あの時お前に告白したの、ただの罰ゲームだったんだよ。

4496.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>penalty</kanji> <kanji>game</kanji> (ゲーム) is a fun kind of game you see on Japanese television a lot. When you mess up, you are punished. Usually it hurts. You can call this a <vocabulary>batsu game</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>penalty game</vocabulary>. Don't call it anything else, though, or you know what happens...
4496.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The athlete was clearly doping, yet he wasn't punished.
examples.ja: その選手は明らかにドーピングをしていたのに、罰せられなかったんだ。

examples.en: If a child is lying, you should first ask why before punishing them.
examples.ja: ウソをついている子どもがいたら、罰する前にまず理由を聞いてあげるべきです。

examples.en: Koichi punished the employees who leaked Tofugu’s secrets.
examples.ja: コウイチはトーフグの秘密を漏らした従業員を罰した。

4497.meaning_mnemonic: When you do a <kanji> penalty</kanji> to someone you are trying <vocabulary>to punish</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to penalize</vocabulary> them.
4497.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. Just remember that the つ becomes a small っ so I don't have <vocabulary>to punish</vocabulary> you.

examples.en: How did Tofugu come about?
examples.ja: トーフグはどうやって誕生したんですか？

examples.en: The man was born in the United States in 1985.
examples.ja: その男は、一九八五年にアメリカで誕生した。

examples.en: My birthday is April 8th, which is the same birthday as Buddha’s.
examples.ja: 私の誕生日は四月八日で、お釈迦様の誕生日と同じ日です。

4498.reading_mnemonic:
The 誕 reading is what you'd expect. But for 生, this uses the slightly less common secondary reading, so here’s a mnemonic to help you:

Just imagine the <vocabulary>birth</vocabulary> of your friend <reading>Joe</reading> (じょう), the local farmhand. He’s such a massive guy, it must have been quite the ordeal...

examples.en: Oh, does everyone in Japan take their shoes off in the house?
examples.ja: え、日本ではみんな家の中でクツを脱ぐんですか？

examples.en: I usually spend Sundays in my pajamas.
examples.ja: 日曜はたいていパジャマを脱がずに過ごします。

examples.en: "Alright, I'll take my clothes off no matter what the temperature is." "Good! That's the spirit."
examples.ja: 「分かったよ。気温が何度だろうが、服を脱いでやるよ。」「いいぞ。その意気だ。」

examples.en: Jonathan instructed employees to remove their hats while in the office.
examples.ja: ジョナサンは、社員達にオフィスの中では帽子を脱ぐよう指示しました。

4499.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>undress</kanji> and the verb is <vocabulary>to undress</vocabulary>.
4499.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: When you go <vocabulary>to undress</vocabulary> your goal is to become <reading>nu</reading>de (ぬ).

examples.en: The conversation got sidetracked.
examples.ja: 話が脱線しました。

examples.en: The train was derailed, but nobody was injured.
examples.ja: 電車が脱線しましたが、ケガ人はありませんでした。

examples.en: Sorry, I got sidetracked again.
examples.ja: すいません、また脱線してしまいました。

4500.meaning_mnemonic:
When something <kanji>escape</kanji>s from the <kanji>line</kanji> it should be on, that's a <vocabulary>derailment</vocabulary>.

脱線 can refer to train derailments (no surprise there), but often gets used figuratively to mean a <vocabulary>digression</vocabulary>, like in speech or writing. Do you ever derail conversations with your digressions?
4500.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Oh, no. There's one missing character!
examples.ja: あっ、ヤバい。一字脱字がある！

examples.en: Can you see where the missing characters are in this article?
examples.ja: この記事の中の、どこに脱字があるか分かりますか？

examples.en: Don’t be afraid to let me know if you find misspelled or missing words, please.
examples.ja: 誤字脱字を見つけたら、遠慮せずに教えてくださいね。

4501.meaning_mnemonic:
You've got an <kanji>escape</kanji>d <kanji>letter</kanji>, in other words, an <vocabulary>omitted character</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>omitted letter</vocabulary>.

脱字 refers to the kind of typos where letters, characters, or even whole words are accidentally omitted from what you're writing.
4501.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: How did you manage to break out?
examples.ja: どうやって脱走に成功したの？

examples.en: We built a fence to prevent the dog from escaping.
examples.ja: 犬が脱走しないように、フェンスを作りました。

examples.en: Apparently, our kid has tried to escape from school.
examples.ja: うちの子、学校から脱走しようとしたみたいなんだよね。

examples.en: The criminal, who had received a heavy sentence, broke out of prison.
examples.ja: 重い刑罰を言い渡された犯罪者が、刑務所から脱走した。

4502.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>escape</kanji> and <kanji>run</kanji> the hell out of there. Basically, you're trying <vocabulary>to escape</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to flee</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to break out</vocabulary>. Pretty simple.

脱走する specifically refers to escaping from a controlled or confined environment, like escaping from prison, a military base, or a guarded facility.
4502.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The だつ changes to だっ, though, so be careful of that.

examples.en: I didn't intend to evade taxes.
examples.ja: 脱税するつもりはなかったんです。

examples.en: Oh no, I might have been caught evading taxes.
examples.ja: ヤバイ、脱税してたのがバレたかもしれない。

examples.en: The tax evasion was at the direction of Mr. Mori.
examples.ja: 脱税は森氏の指示でした。

examples.en: When I was little my parents taught me to be a kind person, but they were arrested on charges of tax evasion.
examples.ja: 私は小さいころ、両親から親切な人になるよう教わりましたが、二人は脱税容疑で逮捕されました。

4503.meaning_mnemonic: You're trying to <kanji>escape</kanji> from <kanji>tax</kanji>es? You scared of them? Huh? That's <vocabulary>tax evasion</vocabulary>, buddy. You're going to jail for that.
4503.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That monk has American blood in him.
examples.ja: あの坊さんには、アメリカ人の血も混じっているんですよ。

examples.en: Appearances can be deceptive. For example, he looks like a yakuza, but he is actually a monk.
examples.ja: 人は見かけだけでは判断できないよ。例えば、アイツはヤクザみたいな見た目をしているけど、実は坊さんなんだぜ。

examples.en: Man, I can’t compete with the monks she goes out with. They’re on a whole other level.
examples.ja: くそ、彼女が付き合ってる坊さんたちには太刀打ちできねーよ。あいつら俺とはかなりレベルが違うんだ。

4504.meaning_mnemonic: さん is what you put on people's names. It's sort of like "Mr." So a "Mr. Monk" is a monk — specifically a Buddhist monk. 坊さん is a casual term for monks. Even in its more polite form, お坊さん, it's still a bit too informal to use when speaking directly to a monk. So it's okay to use when you're talking about them, but not to them!
4504.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the one you learned with the kanji. <reading>ぼう</reading>さん！

examples.en: We already tried feeding him, changing him, and burping him. Well, how can we get this baby to stop crying?
examples.ja: ミルクもあげてみたし、オムツもかえてみたでしょ。それに、ゲップもさせてみた。あーどうしたら赤ん坊を泣き止ませることができるんだろう。

examples.en: Most people can't help but think "cute" when they see a pet or a baby.
examples.ja: たいていの人は、ペットや赤ん坊を見ると、思わず「可愛い」と思ってしまう。

examples.en: "Is the baby sleeping or awake?" "He’s sleeping off a cold.”
examples.ja: 「赤ん坊、寝てる？起きてる？」「風邪を引いて寝てるよ。」

4505.meaning_mnemonic: Here's a weird one for you. You have a <kanji>red</kanji> <kanji>monk</kanji>. What is this? It's a <vocabulary>baby</vocabulary>. Think about it. Babies, when they come out, are all red. Also, they have a shaved head, just like a monk would. So, a "red monk" is really just a baby. I wonder who's getting the shorter end of the stick here, the monk or the baby? Probably the monk.
4505.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi vocab reading of 赤 (you learned this with the kanji) and the reading you learned for 坊 as well.

examples.en: Before becoming a Buddhist priest, I shaved my head.
examples.ja: 坊主になる前に頭を坊主にした。

examples.en: Tomorrow, I'll shave my head with clippers.
examples.ja: 明日、バリカンで坊主にする。

examples.en: Hey, son. You have to be realistic. Isn’t it about time you followed in my footsteps and became a Buddhist priest?
examples.ja: 息子よ。現実的になれ。いい加減俺の後を継いで坊主になったらどうなんだ？

4506.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>monk</kanji> <kanji>master</kanji> is still a monk, and this is used for a <vocabulary>Buddhist monk</vocabulary> specifically. Keep in mind this isn't a word you'd use to address monks directly though, so don't use it when you're speaking to them!

This word also is used for describing a <vocabulary>shaved head</vocabulary> (you can probably guess why). That might be why it can also be a casual way of addressing a young <vocabulary>boy</vocabulary>, since in the old days a shaved head was the default hairstyle for boys in Japan.
4506.reading_mnemonic: The 坊 reads like you'd expect. Unfortunately 主 is an exception and read ず. Just think of a <reading>zoo</reading> that holds <vocabulary>Buddhist monk</vocabulary>s in captivity. How sad for those Buddhist monks.

examples.en: My husband is so busy with the imperial court service that I haven’t seen him for four weeks.
examples.ja: 主人は宮仕えでとても忙しくしており、私は四週間も顔も見ていません。

examples.en: My dream is to become a temple and shrine carpenter like my father.
examples.ja: 僕の夢は、お父さんみたいな宮大工になることです。

examples.en: Our babies are now one month old, so we took them to the shrine for a blessing.
examples.ja: うちの赤ちゃんたちが生後一か月になったので、お宮参りに行ってきました。

4507.meaning_mnemonic:
This <kanji>Shinto shrine</kanji> you're visiting? Turns out if you go inside it's magically turned into the <vocabulary>imperial palace</vocabulary>. Wow! Feels like I’m a member of the <vocabulary>imperial family</vocabulary> now.

宮 is a historical word that generally refers to Japanese imperial palaces, the Japanese imperial family, or the imperial family members. Depending on the context, it can also refer to a Shinto shrine or its buildings.
4507.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji reading you learned.

examples.en: Koichi and Viet ordered a burger and a hot dog, respectively.
examples.ja: コウイチとビエトは、各々ハンバーガーとホットドッグを注文しました。

examples.en: Well, each of us has our reasons for doing things, right?
examples.ja: まあ、各々、色々と都合がありますからね。

examples.en: It seems that each person has their own way of eating potato chips.
examples.ja: どうやら各々独自のポテトチップスの食べ方があるようだ。

4508.meaning_mnemonic: You have <kanji>each</kanji> <kanji>each</kanji> which is <vocabulary>each</vocabulary> (or <vocabulary>every</vocabulary>, or "<vocabulary>respectively</vocabulary>"). Kind of goes along the lines of "each and every" in English.
4508.reading_mnemonic: The reading is weird. So sorry. Just imagine you look at <vocabulary>each</vocabulary> item. Every single one is messed up in some way. Possibly they are robots all accidentally programmed to need to kill humans. You say "<reading>oh no oh no</reading>" in quick succession because this is a bad situation.

examples.en: There should be an usher standing at each location.
examples.ja: 各場所に、案内係が立っているはずです。

examples.en: First, choose a representative for each team.
examples.ja: まず始めに、各チームの代表者を決めて下さい。

examples.en: This store offers a variety of types of bacon.
examples.ja: こちらのお店では、ベーコンが各種取り揃えられています。

4509.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4509.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji, though it's kind of like an add-on for other words in a sense, which makes it behave like jukugo, I think. Don't confuse this with 各々 though. That one does use the kun'yomi reading, which is strange when you consider this one doesn't. Every kanji has its own "perks" I suppose.

examples.en: Wanikani users are in various areas of the world.
examples.ja: ワニカニのユーザーは世界各地にいます。

examples.en: When I turned on the TV, they were just reporting today's weather in each area.
examples.ja: テレビを点けると、ちょうど各地の今日の天気が伝えられているところだった。

examples.en: My family had to move from place to place because of my dad’s job.
examples.ja: 父の仕事の都合で、私の家族は各地を転々としなくてはいけませんでした。

4510.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Each</kanji> <kanji>ground</kanji> is its own ground. It is <vocabulary>each area</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>various areas</vocabulary>.
4510.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: You need to bring your own bento box for the school trip.
examples.ja: 遠足には、各自お弁当を持参してください。

examples.en: When I entered the Tofugu office, each worker was lying in a comfortable position.
examples.ja: トーフグのオフィスに入ると、各自が楽な姿勢で横になっていました。

examples.en: The only thing we can do at this point is let each person decide on their own.
examples.ja: 後は各自の判断に任せるしかないよ。

4511.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My friend guided me to the prefectural pool.
examples.ja: 友人が、県営プールまで案内してくれました。

4519.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

価 refers to the monetary value or the price of goods in a transaction. Although it's somewhat old-fashioned and less common these days, you may still see it used in advanced phrases like 価をつける (to set a price) or 一文の価もない (not even worth a penny).

Note that あたい can also refer to a numerical value in mathematics, such as the value a variable or function takes, but it's more commonly written with the kanji 値 in this use.
4519.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: Okay, this is a great <vocabulary>value</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>price</vocabulary>. Wait, what is? <reading>A tie</reading> (あたい). Get a tie, and it will make you more professional which will help you to get a better job. Great value, right there, just for a tie.

examples.en: In Japan, it seems that prices have finally begun to go up, too.

examples.en: Inflation, or a sharp rise in prices, has occurred, and this has caused the value of money to drop.

examples.en: Japanese tourists are increasingly choosing to travel to Thailand and Vietnam instead of expensive and distant North America and Europe since they are close by and affordable.

4520.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Thing</kanji>s with <kanji>value</kanji> have <vocabulary>prices</vocabulary>.

物価 refers to the prices of goods and services in a place — the <vocabulary>prices of commodities</vocabulary>, a.k.a. the <vocabulary>cost of living</vocabulary>. It's used when discussing how expensive it is to live somewhere or when talking about inflation.
4520.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The ぶつ changes to ぶっ, though, so hopefully that doesn't change the price you're willing to pay for this vocab? Right? Please give me your money.

4548.meaning_mnemonic:

Generally, あたい refers to a numerical value in math, while ね is a formal word for "price."

4563.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: And what was your mother's reaction to that?
examples.ja: で、それに対して、お母さんはどんな反応だったの？

examples.en: Could you tell me how to force quit an unresponsive application, please?
examples.ja: 反応しないアプリケーションを強制終了する方法を教えてくれませんか？

examples.en: The doctor diagnosed me with an acute rejection of Japanese language study.
examples.ja: 医者から、日本語の勉強に拒絶反応を起こしていると診断されました。

4564.meaning_mnemonic: Whoops, this one comes out weird. You have <kanji>anti</kanji> <kanji>respond</kanji> though the meaning of this word is <vocabulary>a reaction</vocabulary>. Maybe you're "anti respond" but you have no choice, you have to give <vocabulary>a response</vocabulary> despite that fact?
4564.reading_mnemonic: The 反 reading is all good and merry, but the 応 reading gets a bit wonky, turning おう into のう. This is probably because it's just way easier to say はんのう and sounds basically the same too. So, はんおう goes to はんのう and everyone's happy. Do you have <vocabulary>a response</vocabulary>?

examples.en: "So what did you think of the proposal?" "Well, I think it was just okay."
examples.ja: 「提案はどうだった？」「うーん。まあまあって感じかな。」

examples.en: I wonder if it's worth proposing this idea when it's going to be rejected anyway.
examples.ja: どうせ提案してもボツになるのに、このアイディアを提案する価値はあるのかな、って思っちゃうんだよね。

4565.meaning_mnemonic: Please <kanji>present</kanji> your <kanji>plan</kanji> in the form of a <vocabulary>proposition</vocabulary>.
4565.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Oh right! I had to submit my passport as well.
examples.ja: そうだ！パスポートも提出しなきゃいけないんだった。

examples.en: I couldn't decide if the answers were correct, but the time was up, so I handed them in anyway.
examples.ja: 答えが合っているのか判断がつかなかったが、とりあえず時間が来たので提出した。

examples.en: Could you tell me what a Tofugu writer applicant needs to submit and what skills are required?
examples.ja: トフグライターへの応募者の提出物について教えて頂けますか？また、必要なスキルは何ですか？

4566.meaning_mnemonic:
Go ahead and <kanji>present</kanji> then <kanji>exit</kanji>. This will be your <vocabulary>presentation</vocabulary> of the materials.

Perhaps it's the <vocabulary>submission</vocabulary> of your resignation, or the <vocabulary>filing</vocabulary> of a complaint, which explains why you exit so quickly afterwards. You could also just be <vocabulary>handing in</vocabulary> your homework, though.
4566.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Your assistance is vital to the success of this fart project.
examples.ja: このオナラ計画の成功には君の援助が必要です。

examples.en: I heard that some international students are able to attend college with government assistance, is this true?
examples.ja: 政府からの援助を受けて大学に通うことができる外国人留学生もいるって聞いたんですが、本当ですか？

examples.en: When I was in need of money, the president offered me a helping hand.
examples.ja: お金が無くて困っていると、社長が援助の手を差し伸べてくれた。

4567.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>aid</kanji> and <kanji>help</kanji> someone you are giving them <vocabulary>assistance</vocabulary>. How kind!
4567.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Thank you for your hearty support.
examples.ja: 心あるご支援、有難うございます。

examples.en: I joined a volunteer group that supports the elderly in the community.
examples.ja: 地域のお年寄りを支援するボランティアグループに参加しました。

examples.en: Rumors spread throughout Portland that Viet was supporting the Yakuza.
examples.ja: ビエトがヤクザを支援しているというウワサが、ポートランド中に広まった。

4568.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Get a grip! The situation isn't as bad as you think.
examples.ja: しっかりしろよ。状況はお前が思っているほど悪くないみたいだぜ。

examples.en: Please explain in detail the situation when you turned the thief over to the police.
examples.ja: どろぼうを警察に渡した時の状況についてくわしく教えてください。

examples.en: Bill is good at analyzing situations.
examples.ja: ビルは状況の分析をするのが上手い。

4569.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>condition</kanji> <kanji>condition</kanji> is the <vocabulary>condition</vocabulary>. It's also the <vocabulary>circumstances</vocabulary> if you can remember that. It's like saying "What's the condition!??" which is similar to saying "What's the circumstances?"
4569.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My little sister told me about her unstable state of mind.
examples.ja: 妹は、メンタルの状態が不安定なことを私に打ち明けた。

examples.en: What, was it like this in its original state?
examples.ja: え、元の状態って、こんな感じだったっけ？

examples.en: Hiroshi and I are currently keeping things at a distance.
examples.ja: ヒロシと私は今距離を置いてる状態なの。

4570.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>condition</kanji> that something is in and the <kanji>appearance</kanji> of it is the <vocabulary>condition</vocabulary> / <vocabulary>state</vocabulary> of that object.
4570.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I heard a rumor that you're a pervert, is it true?
examples.ja: 君が変態だっていうウワサを聞いたんだけど、本当？

examples.en: Why do those employees respect the perverted president's judgment so much?
examples.ja: どうしてあの社員達は、変態社長の判断をそんなにリスペクトしてるのかな？

examples.en: I'm a pervert who gets excited when I see a caterpillar metamorphose into a butterfly.
examples.ja: 僕は毛虫がチョウに変態するところを見るとテンションが上っちゃう変態なんです。

4571.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>appearance</kanji> is <kanji>strange</kanji>. You're <vocabulary>abnormal</vocabulary>. Oh, and you're a <vocabulary>pervert</vocabulary> because you look so abnormal. Though you could just be a caterpillar going through your <vocabulary>metamorphosis</vocabulary> to become a butterfly. You just look really weird while the changing is going on.
4571.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This plate looks like it has a crack in it, but it's designed that way on purpose!
examples.ja: このお皿、ヒビが入ってるみたいに見えるけど、態とそういうデザインなの！

examples.en: I suspect that the current prices are deliberately inflated.
examples.ja: 今の価格って、態とつり上げられたものなんじゃないかと思ってるんです。

examples.en: She pretended to be indifferent toward him on purpose.
examples.ja: 彼女は、彼に態と気のないふりをした。

4572.meaning_mnemonic:
So this doesn't quite make sense in terms of the meaning of the kanji... but you'll be okay. This means <vocabulary>on purpose</vocabulary>. Perhaps when you do something that has the <kanji>appearance</kanji> of doing what you wanted to do, you're doing it on purpose.

態と is usually written in kana in modern writing, but you'll occasionally see it in kanji too.
4572.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: "You did that to me <vocabulary>on purpose</vocabulary>? <reading>Whaza</reading>pp with that?"

examples.en: That staff member had a reeeally bad attitude, and it irritated me.
examples.ja: すっごく態度の悪いスタッフで、イライラしたよ。

examples.en: I can’t trust him because his attitude takes a 180 degree turn depending on who he’s talking to.
examples.ja: あいつ、ダレと話をしているかによって、態度を180度変えるからね。信じられないよ。

examples.en: I behaved badly to my husband, though it can't be helped that he comes home late because of work.
examples.ja: 仕事で遅くなるのは仕方の無いことなのに、つい夫にひどい態度を取ってしまいました。

4573.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>appearance</kanji> has many <kanji>degree</kanji>s. You turn it up a dial, and you show off one <vocabulary>attitude</vocabulary>. Then you turn it down a degree and you have another <vocabulary>behavior</vocabulary>. So many <vocabulary>manner</vocabulary>s to show off.
4573.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The president made a huge blunder and he tried to cover it up, but it backfired.
examples.ja: 社長は大失態を犯し、それをごまかそうとしたが、それがかえってアダとなった。

examples.en: Since the 2017 fiasco, Koichi has locked himself in his room and refuses to come out.
examples.ja: ２０１７年の失態から、コウイチは部屋に引きこもって出てこなくなってしまった。

examples.en: The president, who had made a terrible political blunder, could not hide his frustration.
examples.ja: とんでもない政治的失態を演じた大統領は、苛立ちを隠せないでいた。

4574.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>appearance</kanji> of <kanji>fault</kanji> is a huge <vocabulary>blunder</vocabulary> on our family. At least do not have the appearance of fault.
4574.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The しつ gets shortened to しっ, though, so don't make that <vocabulary>blunder</vocabulary>.

examples.en: I sent a congratulations card to my nephew when he passed his high school entrance exam.
examples.ja: 甥っ子が高校の入学試験に合格した時に、祝賀状を送りました。

4575.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji> Congratulations</kanji> on your <kanji>condition</kanji>. I'll send you a <vocabulary>greeting card</vocabulary> to make it official. Though this kind of card is almost always in the form of a <vocabulary>New Year's Card</vocabulary>.
4575.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The local train has just passed through a tunnel.
examples.ja: この各駅停車はちょうどトンネルを通り過ぎたところです。

4576.meaning_mnemonic:
At  <kanji>each</kanji>  <kanji>station</kanji> someone keeps  <kanji>halt</kanji>ing the  <kanji>car </kanji>. What is this, a <vocabulary>local train</vocabulary>?! Yes, yes it is. You’re on a local train. People use it when they get on (or off) at the smaller stations.

If you’re not used to train travel, just remember that a "local train" is one that stops at every station on a line.
4576.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The police have a system to verify information in real time.
examples.ja: 警察には、情報をリアルタイムで確認するシステムがある。

examples.en: Wouldn't it be better to confirm with a lawyer?
examples.ja: 弁護士に確認してみた方がいいんじゃない？

examples.en: I was so relieved when I confirmed that our company finally got out of the red.
examples.ja: 我が社がついに赤字を脱したことを確認した時、私は胸を撫で下ろしました。

4577.meaning_mnemonic: 確認 is confirmation. When that's a verb, you have <vocabulary>to confirm</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to verify</vocabulary>.
4577.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help immensely if you know the word 確認 already as well.

examples.en: I often get my shopping done online.
examples.ja: 買い物はオンラインで済ますことが多いです。

examples.en: I went to the bathroom at the law office.
examples.ja: トイレは法律事務所で済ましてきました。

examples.en: What? Do you think just a "sorry" will be enough?
examples.ja: えっ、「ごめん」で済ますつもり？

4578.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 済む and how it means "to come to an end." This is like that, but slightly different. This is <vocabulary>to finish something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to settle something</vocabulary>, because this is when you're doing the coming to an end action. You can remember this because you're coming in to finish the score uno <reading>mas</reading> (ます) time. This is the last time.
4578.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with 済む, so if you know that you'll be able <vocabulary>to finish</vocabulary> this vocab.

examples.en: With this number of people, wouldn't it be more economical to take a taxi?
examples.ja: この人数なら、タクシーで行く方が経済的じゃない？

examples.en: Since I am in a difficult financial position, I’m working full time 5 days a week while also working part time 6 days a week.
examples.ja: 私は経済的に苦しい立場にあるため、週五日フルタイムの仕事をしているうえに、週六日パートタイムでも働いています。

examples.en: Although we do not have the financial means to do so, we try to save as much as possible in case of emergency.
examples.ja: 経済的な余裕は無いが、万が一に備えてできるだけ貯金をするようにしています。

4579.meaning_mnemonic: 経済 is economics. So, something that has to do with economics is the <vocabulary>economic</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>financial</vocabulary> situation.
4579.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know 経済 as well.

examples.en: I just can't understand why some people would skip such a fun committee meeting.
examples.ja: あんなに楽しい委員会の会議をサボる人がいるなんて理解できない。

examples.en: I was given a big job as chair of the budget committee.
examples.ja: 予算委員会の委員長という大役をおおせつかった。

examples.en: You should stop flip-flopping on important issues in the committee, it’s irresponsible. Everyone finds it annoying.
examples.ja: いい加減、委員会での重要な問題に対して意見をころころ変えるのをやめてくれないか。みんなにいい迷惑だよ。

4580.meaning_mnemonic: There are member(s) of a committee (委員) all getting together to <kanji>meet</kanji>. This is the <vocabulary>committee</vocabulary> itself.
4580.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Of course it will help to know 委員 as well, since it's 2/3rds of the word.

examples.en: We elect a Tofugu Chairman every year.
examples.ja: トーフグの会長を毎年選挙しています。

examples.en: The government announced the date for electing the next leader.
examples.ja: 政府は次のリーダーを選挙する日を発表しました。

examples.en: Every year at our school, there's an event to elect the student council president.
examples.ja: うちの学校では、毎年、生徒会長を選挙するイベントがあります。

4581.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Election</kanji> is 選挙 so when you make that word into a verb, you have <vocabulary>to elect</vocabulary>.
4581.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Also, the reading just comes from 選挙 so if you know that you know this as well.

examples.en: It's difficult to judge whether it's an edible or poisonous mushroom.
examples.ja: 食用キノコか毒キノコかを判断するのは難しい。

examples.en: It's often said you shouldn't judge people by their appearance, but do you think that's really true?
examples.ja: よく人を見た目で判断してはいけないと言いますが、それは本当に正しいことだと思いますか？

examples.en: Judging from what I've heard, the best seems to have been saved for last.
examples.ja: これまでに聞いたことから判断すると、どうやら真打ちは最後にあるようだね。

4582.meaning_mnemonic: 判断 is judgement. Make that into a verb and you have <vocabulary>to judge</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to conclude</vocabulary>.
4582.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know 判断 before learning this, but if you don't I won't judge you (the Crabigator will).

examples.en: Koichi is a man who’s filled with a sense of responsibility.
examples.ja: コウイチは、責任感のかたまりのような男だ。

examples.en: Tofugu's employees are all responsible people.
examples.ja: トーフグの社員は責任感がある人達ばかりです。

examples.en: He may have a strong sense of responsibility, but to me he seemed a little rude and selfish.
examples.ja: 彼は責任感が強いのかもしれないけど、私には少し失礼で自分勝手な気がしました。

4583.meaning_mnemonic: 責任 is <kanji>responsibility</kanji>. If you add 感 you get a "feeling of responsibility." That's not really a thing people say. What people do say, however, is <vocabulary>sense of responsibility</vocabulary>. Do you have one?
4583.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Does this bus stop at that bus stop?
examples.ja: このバス、あのバス停で止まりますか？

examples.en: If it's bus number 29, it should come to this bus stop.
examples.ja: ２９番のバスなら、このバス停に来るはずですよ。

examples.en: At the bus stop, I accidentally got on the express bus.
examples.ja: バス停で、間違えて直通のバスに乗ってしまいました。

4584.meaning_mnemonic: This is where the <kanji>bus</kanji> (バス) halts. It's the <vocabulary>bus stop</vocabulary>.
4584.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: For me, the biggest problem in the world right now is the stoppage of WaniKani sticker production.
examples.ja: ワニカニのステッカーの生産停止は、私にとって、今世界で一番大きな問題です。

examples.en: I try to pause videos during meal time.
examples.ja: 食事中は動画を停止するようにしています。

examples.en: My brother once went into cardiopulmonary arrest, but his heart started beating again after the surgeon performed a cardiac massage.
examples.ja: 私の兄は一度心肺停止にまで至ったんですが、外科医が心臓マッサージを施した後に、心臓が再び脈動しだしたんです。

4585.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Halt</kanji> and <kanji>stop</kanji>. When something does this, it's in a <vocabulary>stoppage</vocabulary>.
4585.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Did Kawasaki City not lose power?
examples.ja: 川崎市は停電しなかったの？

examples.en: Why do I keep flipping light switches on and off if I know that there is still a power outage.
examples.ja: どうしてまだ停電してるって分かってるのに、電気のスイッチを何度も付けたり消したりしちゃうんだろう。

examples.en: Because of the blackout, all of the ice cream in the freezer melted.
examples.ja: 停電のせいで、冷凍庫のアイスクリームが全部とけちゃった。

4586.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>halt</kanji> <kanji>electricity</kanji> you experience a <vocabulary>power outage</vocabulary>. Makes sense. When the electricity stops you don't have any more power.
4586.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That vampire is so negative about everything, it's getting on my nerves.
examples.ja: あの吸血鬼は、何事に対してもマイナス思考で、こっちがイライラしてくるよ。

examples.en: The vampire rushed back to where he sleeps.
examples.ja: 吸血鬼は、あわてて寝どこに帰っていった。

examples.en: That vampire bastard is seriously unforgivable! He told me that he wouldn’t even suck my blood because I am too much of a phony.
examples.ja: 吸血鬼の野郎、マジ許せねえ！俺の事、血を吸いたくない程インチキ臭すぎるって言うんだ。

4587.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>demon</kanji> that <kanji>suck</kanji>s <kanji>blood</kanji>? What mythological creature can you think of that sucks blood? How about a <vocabulary>vampire</vocabulary>? Them Sparklzzzz!
4587.reading_mnemonic: 吸血 should be easy for you to read. The 鬼 part uses the reading you already learned with the kanji, き. Easy, no?

examples.en: I can't keep up with the speed at which young people absorb knowledge.
examples.ja: 若者の知識の吸収スピードにはついていけないよ。

examples.en: Our tenugui absorbs a great deal of liquid.
examples.ja: うちの手ぬぐいは、水分の吸収力がすごいんです。

examples.en: When plants get water, how long does it take for them to absorb it?
examples.ja: 植物が水分を取り入れる時って、どれくらいのスピードで吸収するんですか？

examples.en: If you want to be comfortable on your menstrual days, we recommend choosing a pad with a higher absorption rate.
examples.ja: 生理の日を快適に過ごすなら、より吸収量の多いナプキンを選ぶのがおすすめです。

4588.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>suck</kanji> something in and <kanji>obtain</kanji> it. Shhheewwwwww! When you suck something in and obtain it into your body, you have done <vocabulary>absorption</vocabulary> because it's been sucked inside of you.
4588.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Can you issue the receipt again?
examples.ja: もう一度領収書を発行してもらえませんか？

examples.en: I’d like to return this, is that okay? Here’s the receipt.
examples.ja: すいません、これを返品したいんですけど、できますか？これが領収書です。

examples.en: I think you should really turn in your receipts to get reimbursed.
examples.ja: いい加減そろそろ領収書を出して、経費を払い戻してもらった方がいいんじゃない？

4589.meaning_mnemonic: I <kanji>obtain</kanji> some <kanji>territory</kanji>, so I want a <kanji>writte</kanji>n record of it. How will I get a written record of my obtained territory? How about with a <vocabulary>receipt</vocabulary>? Emailing one will do just fine.
4589.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That person doesn't have much income but always spends lavishly.
examples.ja: あの人、収入があまりないのに、いつも贅沢しているんです。

examples.en: When I opened up about my actual income, I got dumped.
examples.ja: 本当の収入を打ち明けたら、フラれたんだ。

examples.en: If I take the job overseas, my income will probably be half what it is now.
examples.ja: その海外での仕事に就けば、おそらく収入が半分になるだろう。

4590.meaning_mnemonic: Please <kanji>enter</kanji> what you've <kanji>obtain</kanji>ed in here. We'll divvy it all up later. But we have to enter it all here so we know our <vocabulary>income</vocabulary>.
4590.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I won't be sending out New Year's cards this year.
