examples.en: I got a New Year's greeting card with Koichi's picture from Tofugu.
examples.ja: トーフグから、コウイチの写真付きの年賀状が送られてきました。

examples.en: Let's have Aya draw the illustration for the New Year's card next year.
examples.ja: 来年の年賀状のイラストをアヤにかいてもらおう。

examples.en: In Japan, there is a tradition of sending each other New Year's cards.
examples.ja: 日本では、新年に年賀状を送り合う伝統があります。

4591.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>year</kanji> <kanji>congratulation</kanji>s <kanji>condition</kanji> is when you tell the world about your condition for the new year. What's a better way to tell them than by using a <vocabulary>New Year's Card</vocabulary>?
4591.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This is not real leather.
examples.ja: これは本物の革じゃありません。

examples.en: I processed the hides into leather in order to make a leather bag.
examples.ja: 革のカバンを作るために、皮を革に加工しました。

examples.en: Fugu bought crocodile skin sandals in Japan.
examples.ja: フグは日本でワニ革のサンダルを買った。

4592.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4592.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember: 

<vocabulary>Leather</vocabulary> is the skin of a cow, right? How do you say "skin" in Japanese? Remember <reading>皮</reading> (かわ)? It has the same reading as that, and they're both skin, so hopefully that makes it easier to remember.

examples.en: Our revolutionary leader is a very understanding person.
examples.ja: 私達の革命の指導者は、とても理解がある人なんです。

examples.en: You are lucky to see the beginning of this revolution.
examples.ja: この革命の始まりを見ることができたあなたは、幸せですよ。

examples.en: The situation changed for the better after the revolution.
examples.ja: 革命の後、情勢は好転した。

4593.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Leather</kanji>'s <kanji>fate</kanji> is in the hands of a <vocabulary>revolution</vocabulary>. It's the leather revolution! Off with these normal clothes and on with leather ones!
4593.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: After washing it several times, the color of the leather has started to fade. Now I’m wondering if I was even supposed to wash it.
examples.ja: 何度か洗濯したら、皮革の色があせ始めたんだけど、もしかしたら洗っちゃいけなかったのかな。

4594.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Skin</kanji> <kanji>leather</kanji> is really just <vocabulary>leather</vocabulary> because leather is also skin. It's also <vocabulary>hides</vocabulary>.
4594.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should know them both already!

examples.en: I am unemployed again.
examples.ja: また無職になってしまった。

examples.en: I became friends with an unemployed homeless man.
examples.ja: 無職のホームレスの男性と友達になりました。

examples.en: I was unemployed and couldn't pay my bills, so my gas and electricity were shut off.
examples.ja: 無職でお金がはらえずにいたら、ガスと電気を止められました。

examples.en: He would be the perfect husband, save for one thing - he has been unemployed for ten years.
examples.ja: 彼は完璧な夫ですが、一つだけ問題があるんです。十年間ずっと無職なんです。

4595.meaning_mnemonic: When the status of your <kanji>employment</kanji> is "<kanji>nothing</kanji>" then you're probably <vocabulary>unemployed</vocabulary>. You're experiencing <vocabulary>unemployment</vocabulary>.
4595.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What do you think of this workplace?
examples.ja: この職場、どう思う？

examples.en: My workplace is equipped with the most up-to-date computers.
examples.ja: 私の職場には、最新のコンピュータが備えられています。

examples.en: Apparently, I have a secret admirer at work.
examples.ja: どうやら、職場に私のかくれファンがいるみたいなんです。

examples.en: If you want to stay in this workplace, you’ve got to quit your habit of making everything out to be a big deal.
examples.ja: もしこの職場に残りたいのなら、物事をたいそうに考えるクセを無くしてください。

4596.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>employment</kanji> <kanji>location</kanji> is your <vocabulary>place of work</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>place of employment</vocabulary>. It's also your <vocabulary>workplace</vocabulary>.

Are you using WaniKani at your 職場 right now? Wouldn't that be funny.
4596.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the on'yomi reading for the first kanji and the kun'yomi reading for the second kanji. You didn't learn the kun'yomi reading for 場 with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

At your <vocabulary>place of work</vocabulary>, you "<reading>baa</reading>" (ば) to your coworkers as a greeting. Remember that town hall where you had to speak Sheepanese to the clerks? Well, it turns out your "baa" pronunciation was so good that they hired you. Now you can practice baaing all day, and get paid for it too!

examples.en: What profession do you want to have when you grow up?
examples.ja: 大人になったら、どんな職業につきたい？

examples.en: Do you work as a model, perhaps? You have great style.
examples.ja: あなたの職業って、もしかしてモデルなの？スタイルめっちゃいいよね。

examples.en: All WaniKani users know what Viet's secret job is.
examples.ja: ワニカニユーザーは、ビエトの裏の職業が何なのか、みんな知っています。

4597.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>employment</kanji> <kanji>business</kanji> is your <vocabulary>occupation</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>profession</vocabulary>. What is your employment business?
4597.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I’m not a teacher, but I am part of the school staff.
examples.ja: 私は教師ではありませんが、学校職員です。

examples.en: The employees are studying to prepare for an examination too.
examples.ja: 職員達も、試験に備えて勉強しています。

examples.en: Our staff are all good at cracking eggs.
examples.ja: うちの職員は、みんな卵を割るのが上手なんですよ。

4598.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>employment</kanji> <kanji>member</kanji>s of a workplace are the <vocabulary>personnel</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>staff</vocabulary>. Pretty straightforward!

職員 and 社員 are two similar terms, but have different meanings. 社員 generally refers to employees of private companies, while 職員 refers to employees who work in various fields such as civil service, education, government, non-profits, and more.
4598.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The man I met on the internet is in his thirties and has a job, but he is divorced and also has a kid.
examples.ja: 私がインターネットで出会った男性は、三十代で有職ですが、バツイチ子持ちです。

examples.en: In Japanese, we use the word "mushoku" to say "I am unemployed," but we don't use the word "yūshoku" to say "I am employed."
examples.ja: 日本語では、「無職」という言葉を使って「私は無職です」とは言うけど、「有職」という言葉を使って「私は有職です」とは言わないんだよね。

examples.en: Is it really such an important condition for marriage that your potential spouse be employed?
examples.ja: 相手が有職であることって、結婚するのにそんなに大事な条件でしょうか？

4599.meaning_mnemonic:
To <kanji>have</kanji> <kanji>employment</kanji> just means <vocabulary>having a job</vocabulary>. Wow, congrats on <vocabulary>being employed</vocabulary>!

有職 is a formal word for saying that someone has a steady job, as opposed to 無職 (unemployed). You'll often see it in official writing like surveys or articles.
4599.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Do you know any good job hunting websites?
examples.ja: いい求職のサイト、知ってる？

examples.en: There’s a lot of useful information for job hunting on this blog.
examples.ja: このブログには、求職する時に役立つ情報がたくさんのっている。

examples.en: Don’t worry about being unemployed. I’ve been job hunting for almost two years now.
examples.ja: 失業なんて気にするなよ。俺なんてかれこれもう約二年間も求職活動中だぜ。

4600.meaning_mnemonic: Ugh, time to <kanji>request</kanji> <kanji>employment</kanji> again. Time to go <vocabulary>job hunting</vocabulary>.
4600.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The MP will not resign and will continue to be a member of parliament.
examples.ja: その国会議員は辞職しないで議員を続けるそうです。

examples.en: Since my boss clearly told me, "There are plenty of people who can replace you," I resigned from that company.
examples.ja: 上司にはっきりと「あなたの代わりはいくらでもいる」と言われたので、その会社を辞職しました。

examples.en: Mami was forced to resign for the crime of eating Koichi's bacon.
examples.ja: マミはコウイチのベーコンを食べた罪で辞職に追いこまれた。

4601.meaning_mnemonic:
If you <kanji>quit</kanji> your place of <kanji>employment</kanji>, you are putting in your <vocabulary>resignation</vocabulary>, aka <vocabulary>resigning</vocabulary>.

辞職 is a formal term that refers to someone voluntarily leaving their job or post in professional settings.
4601.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Mom was as mad as an ogre yesterday, huh?
examples.ja: 昨日、お母さん、鬼のようにキレてたよね。

examples.en: Let's say that you actually saw an ogre.
examples.ja: あなたが実際に鬼を見たと仮定しましょう。

examples.en: Hey! Stop this weak act and show us your true form, you demon!
examples.ja: おい！下手な芝居はやめて正体を現せ！この、鬼め！

4602.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4602.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: 

<vocabulary>Demon</vocabulary>s are mean. This particular demon bites you on the knee, creating an "O" shape on your knee. He tells you he has cursed you with the <vocabulary>"O" knee</vocabulary> (おに).

examples.en: "Those are the rules. Understand?" "I understand."
examples.ja: 「それが規則だ。分かったか？」「分かりました。」

examples.en: Eating bacon by yourself is against the rules!
examples.ja: 一人でベーコンを食べるのは、規則に反してますよ！

examples.en: Tofugu has established strict workplace rules and regulations.
examples.ja: トーフグには、厳しい就業規則が設けられている。

4603.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>standard</kanji> <kanji>rule</kanji> is just one of the <vocabulary>rule</vocabulary>s or <vocabulary>regulation</vocabulary>s. Nothing weird about these rules.
4603.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Lead a more disciplined life.
examples.ja: もっと規律正しい生活をしなさい。

examples.en: From now on, I will properly follow the rules.
examples.ja: これからは、ちゃんと規律を守ります。

examples.en: I swear I followed the rules and didn’t drink, not even a drop.
examples.ja: 規律に従って酒は一滴たりとも飲んでいないと断言します。

examples.en: Their discipline is so strict that apparently even some Buddhist monks run away.
examples.ja: 規律が厳しすぎて逃げ出す仏僧もいるらしい。

4604.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>standard</kanji> <kanji>law</kanji> is the <vocabulary>rule</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>law</vocabulary> you have to follow. With these standard laws comes <vocabulary>discipline</vocabulary>. If you don't have these it will be chaos!
4604.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The nurse always seemed to have a fake smile on her face.
examples.ja: その看護師はいつも作り笑いをしているように見えた。

examples.en: My husband is critical of my continuing to work as a nurse.
examples.ja: 夫は、私が看護師の仕事を続けることに批判的なんです。

examples.en: Viet told us the obvious lie that he found a girlfriend who’s a nurse.
examples.ja: ビエトは看護師の彼女が出来たという白々しい嘘をついた。

4605.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>expert</kanji> who <kanji>watches over</kanji> and <kanji>defend</kanji>s people at all hours is the <vocabulary>nurse</vocabulary>. That's what nurses do, 24/7. They have to check up on people, defend their health, and watch over them, making sure they're okay. What a tough job.
4605.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The lawyer Goodman faked an illness because he didn’t want to see Walt.
examples.ja: グッドマン弁護士はウォルトに会いたくなかったので仮病を使った。

examples.en: That attorney has finally shown his true colors.
examples.ja: あの弁護士、ついに尻尾を出しやがったぞ！

examples.en: After hearing the amount of the retainer fee, the lawyer changed his attitude.
examples.ja: 報酬の金額を聞いて、弁護士は態度を改めた。

4606.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>samurai</kanji> who uses <kanji>speech</kanji> to <kanji>defend</kanji> people. This samurai does their battle in the court of law. This "samurai" is an <vocabulary>attorney</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>lawyer</vocabulary>.
4606.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Let's think about what we can do to conserve nature.
examples.ja: 自然を保護するために、何ができるか考えてみましょう。

examples.en: The police took the girl who was wandering by herself near Shinjuku Station into protective custody.
examples.ja: 警察は新宿駅近辺を一人で歩いていた少女を保護した。

examples.en: The bird pecking at insects over there is a species that is protected under international agreements.
examples.ja: あそこで虫をついばんでいる鳥は、国際間で保護することが取り決められた鳥です。

4607.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>preserve</kanji> and <kanji>defend</kanji> something is <vocabulary>to conserve</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to protect</vocabulary>. I won't let you destroy this land I'm trying <vocabulary>to protect</vocabulary>!
4607.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I work as a teacher of jurisprudence.
examples.ja: 私は法律学の教師をしています。

examples.en: I don’t like that teacher because he is always flip-flopping on historical facts.
examples.ja: あの教師は歴史認識をころころ変えるからあまり好きじゃない。

examples.en: On the math teacher's desk, there was an answer sheet for the exam that tests understanding.
examples.ja: 数学教師の机には、理解力をテストする試験の解答が置いてありました。

4608.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>teach</kanji>ing <kanji>expert</kanji>/<kanji>teacher</kanji> is a <vocabulary>teacher</vocabulary>.

教師 is a relatively formal word for teachers. Unlike 先生, this word is specifically for people in the teaching profession and cannot be used as a name ender.
4608.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: We've finally got some proof to expose that doctor!
examples.ja: ついにあの医師の尻尾をつかまえたぞ！

examples.en: Oh, that doctor is on TV a lot, right?
examples.ja: あっ、その医師って、テレビによく出てる方ですよね？

examples.en: This doctor appeared on TV twice, though just for short amounts of time.
examples.ja: ほんの短い時間だけでしたが、この医師は二度テレビに出たことがあるんです。

examples.en: According to the doctor, my grandfather's heartbeat became gradually weaker and weaker, then it finally stopped.
examples.ja: 医師によると、祖父の心拍はだんだん弱くなっていって、最後に停止したそうです。

4609.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>medicine</kanji> <kanji>expert</kanji> is someone who knows a lot about medicine. Those people are (I hope) generally <vocabulary>doctor</vocabulary>s.
4609.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Lawyers are experts in law.
examples.ja: 弁護士は、法律のエキスパートです。

examples.en: In Japan, there is no law against walking and drinking in the street.
examples.ja: 日本には、道を歩きながら飲酒をしてはいけないという法律は無い。

examples.en: If you can memorize every legal term within one month, I will pay you a million dollars.
examples.ja: もし一ヶ月の間に全法律用語を覚えることができたら、百万ドルお支払いしてもいいですよ。

4610.meaning_mnemonic: Though there's no law about two kanji with the same meaning producing the same meaning, a <kanji>law</kanji> <kanji>law</kanji> is probably a <vocabulary>law</vocabulary>.
4610.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This music is very rhythmic.
examples.ja: この音楽はとても律動的ですね。

examples.en: Out of the Tofugu team, Kanae was doing the radio gymnastics the most rhythmically.
examples.ja: トーフグチームの中で、一番律動的にラジオ体操をしていたのは、カナエです。

examples.en: This morning, I saw a lot of rabbits jumping rhythmically in my garden.
examples.ja: 今朝、たくさんのウサギが庭で律動的に飛び跳ねているのを見ました。

4611.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>law</kanji> of <kanji>move</kanji>ment is governed by <vocabulary>rhythm</vocabulary>. Imagine moving around to a boss beat. As you move, you start to feel the rhythm in your step. Go ahead and walk around your room and feel this rhythm. 

Note that リズム is a much more common word to use for "rhythm," but you may see the kanji version sometimes in formal writing. One thing you will see more often is 律動的 which means "rhythmic."
4611.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: There is some sort of unwritten rule that says people are only allowed to speak Japanese in this school.
examples.ja: 学校では日本語でしか話してはいけないという不文律のようなものがあります。

4612.meaning_mnemonic: This <kanji>not</kanji> <kanji>writing</kanji> <kanji>law</kanji> is a law that hasn't been written down. It's an <vocabulary>unwritten law</vocabulary>, like taking your shoes off and showering every day.
4612.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Is the answer to "seven divided by two," three with a remainder of one?
examples.ja: 七割る二の答えって、三余り一であってる？

examples.en: I’m sorry, I broke the plate.
examples.ja: ごめんなさい、お皿を割ってしまいました。

examples.en: Koichi showed that he could break one hundred roofing tiles right in half with a karate chop.
examples.ja: コウイチは空手チョップで百枚の瓦を真っ二つに割ってみせた。

4613.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>divide</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to divide</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to split something</vocabulary>.

It can also mean <vocabulary>to break something</vocabulary>, as in ワイングラスを割る (to break a wine glass). After all, you’re technically dividing the object into parts if you break it, right?
4613.reading_mnemonic: The reading you learned with the kanji is the one you'll use here. It's the わ one, though, making it わる.

examples.en: I think my husband is doing a great job in his role as a father.
examples.ja: 私の夫は父親としての役割をしっかり果たしてくれていると思います。

examples.en: The internet will play a more important role in future elections.
examples.ja: インターネットは今後の選挙においてより重要な役割を担っていくでしょう。

examples.en: It's more efficient to divide up the roles and get it done together.
examples.ja: 役割分担をしてみんなで片付ける方が効率がいいよ。

4614.meaning_mnemonic: Let's <kanji>divide</kanji> the <kanji>duty</kanji> up amongst various people. Each person will have their own <vocabulary>role</vocabulary> in completing this duty.
4614.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji. See how we divide up the duty of learning kanji into radicals and kanji and vocab? Makes it nice, right? Each piece is its own 役割.

examples.en: When I write an article, I have someone check it for me when it is about ten percent complete.
examples.ja: 記事を書く時は、一割ほどできたところでだれかにチェックしてもらいます。

examples.en: The number of Christians in Japan doesn't even reach 10%.
examples.ja: 日本でのキリスト教信者の数は一割にもおよばない。

examples.en: "This blowfish is a bit too expensive. Could you give me a discount?" "I’ll give you a 10% discount."
examples.ja: 「この河豚、ちょっと高すぎますよ。まけてもらえませんか？」「一割引きにしてあげましょう。」

4615.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>One</kanji> <kanji>division</kanji> is <vocabulary>ten percent</vocabulary>. You'll just have to imagine this in terms of tens going by. Must be some old Japanese percentage system that carried over or something. Just remember that one wari is ten percent, two waris are twenty percent, and so on.
4615.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the same as what you learned with the kanji. You know much more than ten percent of this word's reading already.

examples.en: The ratio of people who attended was eighty percent.
examples.ja: 出席者の割合は80%だった。

examples.en: I think most of the people who use that term are elderly people.
examples.ja: その言葉を使ってる人の割合は、年配の人がほとんどだと思うよ。

examples.en: Please tell me the ratio of boys to girls among WaniKani users.
examples.ja: ワニカニユーザーの男女の割合を教えてください。

examples.en: I thought it was going to take longer, but it was over relatively quickly.

examples.en: In Japan, noodles that contain one hundred percent buckwheat flour are called jūwari soba.
examples.ja: 日本では、蕎麦粉の割合が100%の蕎麦を十割り蕎麦と呼びます。

4616.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>divide</kanji> something into parts and <kanji>join</kanji> them back together, you are better able to evaluate the <vocabulary>ratio</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>percentage</vocabulary> of these parts in relation to the whole. Think of all these parts, neatly separated and then placed next to one another. It's only because you divided them that you get to see them this way.

割合 usually refers to the ratio of a certain part when compared to the whole, often expressed as a percentage. When used this way it's similar to 比率, but 割合 is more common in everyday language.

Note that 割合 can also be used as an adverb, where it means <vocabulary>comparatively</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>fairly</vocabulary>.
4616.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You've learned them both already, so you should be able to read this already!

examples.en: In a trial it's necessary to judge as fairly as possible.

After your <reading>ban</reading> (ばん) on the WaniKani forums, you now face <vocabulary>trial</vocabulary> before none other than Judge Koichi. He's going to decide whether your ban will be lifted or not. Good luck, there's a lot at stake.

In modern Japanese, this word is not commonly used as a standalone term. However, it is often found as part of proper nouns that refer to geographic locations that have a cape, as well as family names that are associated with capes.

Combine those together and you have <reading>ながさき</reading>. Sound familiar? It should. This is the city of <vocabulary>Nagasaki</vocabulary>, one of the cities in which the A-bombs fell.

You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You have <vocabulary>to provide</vocabulary> your friends with their own <reading>sauna</reading> (そな) because they don't want to use your shower. This requires you to go out and buy a sauna for your house (very expensive) just so you can provide your needy friends with what they want (a sauna). Feel angry you have to provide this.

examples.en: I'm sorry, I gave in to the temptation to sleep in, and couldn't make it in time to prepare for the birthday party.
examples.ja: ごめん。ゆっくり寝たいっていう誘惑に負けちゃって、誕生日パーティーの準備、間に合わなかった。

4626.meaning_mnemonic: When you follow standard procedure to provide what's needed, you make the perfect preparation! Both 準備 and 用意 mean "preparation," but the nuances are different. 準備 is about preparing in advance for an event or situation, often involving planning or setup. 用意 is about making sure specific items or resources are ready and available. For example, as part of the 準備 for a party, you might 用意 food and drinks for the guests. You could use 準備 for the food and drinks too — it would just emphasize that they're part of the overall event setup.

That's the first part. Now, who are you leading? Let's say you're leading a bee back to its nest, via the road. It's a <reading>道 Bee</reading> (みちび)!

Maybe going to the reading will help you after all.

4631.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>stretch</kanji>, and the verb version means <vocabulary>to stretch over something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to spread out</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to be taut</vocabulary>, not to be confused with the type of stretching you do after a workout.

This word is both transitive and intransitive. When it follows を, it emphasizes the physical act of extending something over an area, like stretching a canvas over a frame, unfurling a sail on a ship, or roping off a crime scene. When following が, it expresses the resulting state of having been stretched or spread, like a bloated stomach, a swollen muscle, or a spider web.
4631.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Imagine yourself trying <vocabulary>to stretch</vocabulary> your favorite toy figurine, seeing just how far you can stretch it. With every stretch, you start laughing uncontrollably, <reading>HA</reading> (は) HA HA HA HA HA. Seems a bit cruel. Are you okay?

I'd say it's close enough to make a mnemonic out of in your head.

examples.en: Traveling first class is too extravagant.
examples.ja: ファーストクラスでの旅行なんて、贅沢すぎるよ。

examples.en: In the winter, Koichi comes to the office with a luxurious fugu skin coat.
examples.ja: 冬になると、コウイチは贅沢なフグ皮のコートを着て出社する。

examples.en: I don't want to do anything extravagant for my birthday. If I can just read a good book, I'm happy.
examples.ja: 誕生日だからって贅沢な事は何もしたくないわ。良い本が読めればそれでいいの。

4640.meaning_mnemonic: You live in the most <kanji>extravagant</kanji> of <kanji>swamp</kanji>s, which means you’re completely surrounded by <vocabulary>luxury</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>extravagant</vocabulary> things.
4640.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The law is scheduled to take effect on the fifth of next month.
examples.ja: その法律は来月五日に施行される予定です。

examples.en: Do you remember who is responsible for the enforcement of this law?
examples.ja: この法律の施行の責任を誰が負っていたのか覚えていますか？

examples.en: The implementation of that law hasn’t been finalized yet.
examples.ja: まだその法律の施行が確定したわけではない。

4641.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>carry out</kanji> something and <kanji>go</kanji>, the result is still <vocabulary>enforcement</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>carrying out</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>implementation</vocabulary> of whatever it is. There’s no point hanging around after you’ve enforced something! So you always carry out and go.
4641.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

You might sometimes see せこう as an alternative reading, but しこう is the more common version.

examples.en: If you wait here, I'm sure that tabby cat will show up again.
examples.ja: ここで待っていれば、きっとまたあのトラ猫が現れるよ。

examples.en: I'm glad someone has come along who understands my dreams without laughing at them.
examples.ja: 私の夢を笑わずに理解してくれる人が現れて、うれしいです。

examples.en: Even when he oversleeps, he always shows up to the office playing dumb, with a look on his face that says "What, late? Not me."
examples.ja: アイツはいつも、寝坊しても、遅刻なんてしてませんという顔をして白々しくオフィスに現れる。

4642.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>appear</kanji>, so this word means <vocabulary>to appear</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to emerge</vocabulary>.
4642.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Some kind of paranormal entity starts <vocabulary>to appear</vocabulary> in front of you. "You… <reading>are a wa</reading>lrus (あらわ)!" you scream, terrified. Yes, it seems a ghostly walrus has appeared before you. It has come from beyond the grave to warn you that the Crabigator will get you if you don't do your reviews!

examples.en: Every Tofugu article has unique and interesting figures of speech.
examples.ja: トーフグの記事は、どれも表現がユニークでおもしろい。

examples.en: When I was able to understand artistic expressions that I hadn’t understood before, words can’t express how happy I was.
examples.ja: 以前は理解できなかった芸術表現が理解できるようになった時、言葉では表現できないほどうれしかった。

examples.en: Last night in my dream, our baby told me that it’s time for her baby teeth to come out and she can’t express in words how itchy they are.
examples.ja: 昨夜の夢で、私たちの赤ちゃんに「乳歯が抜けそうだった時、言葉では表現できないほど痒かった」って言われたの。

4643.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>express</kanji> something that's of the <kanji>present time</kanji>, you are saying something that only people of the current time understand. These are <vocabulary>expression</vocabulary>s or <vocabulary>figure of speech</vocabulary>. You say these things during the present time, not the future, not the past, the present time. Otherwise nobody would understand.
4643.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Is this a dream or real?
examples.ja: これは夢か、現実か？

examples.en: It's important to understand the reality first.
examples.ja: まずは、現実を正しく理解することが大切です。

examples.en: "For God’s sake, face reality! This isn’t cake, it’s poop!"
examples.ja: 「頼むから、現実を見てくれよ！これはケーキじゃなくてウンチなんだ！」

4644.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>present</kanji> is the <kanji>truth</kanji>. It is what's going on right now. It is <vocabulary>reality</vocabulary>.
4644.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I hope live streaming can convey how fun the atmosphere is here right now.
examples.ja: ライブストリーミングで、現場の楽しい空気感が伝わればいいなと思っています。

examples.en: If you want to change this rule, please get approval from the on-site workers first.
examples.ja: このルールを変えたければ、まず現場の了解を取ってください。

examples.en: Let's hope that what actually happened at the scene of the crime will come to light soon.
examples.ja: あの犯罪現場で実際に何が起きたのかがすぐに明るみに出ることを期待しよう。

4645.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>present</kanji> <kanji>location</kanji> is the <vocabulary>on-site location</vocabulary>! And you're on the <vocabulary>scene</vocabulary> to check out what's currently going on.

現場 refers to an on-site location where something is happening or has happened. It can refer to a crime scene, an accident site, or a filming location. It may also refer to a construction site or a factory, as these are <vocabulary>workplace</vocabulary>s where more hands-on work or operations take place.
4645.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is a combination of the on'yomi and kun'yomi readings. You didn't learn the kun'yomi reading for 場 with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

At this crime <vocabulary>scene</vocabulary>, a "<reading>baa</reading>" (ば) was apparently heard by witnesses. This can only mean one thing: that infamous arch-criminal, the Lamb-Chopper, has struck again! Baa!

examples.en: Ahhh, the milk's spilled!
examples.ja: あーっ牛乳こぼれてるよー！

examples.en: Good morning. Here’s your milk.
examples.ja: おはよう。はい、牛乳よ。

examples.en: There's nothing better than having some good milk to drink while watching the sunrise.
examples.ja: 朝日を見ながら飲む美味しい牛乳に勝るものはないね。

4646.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Cow</kanji> <kanji>milk</kanji> is <vocabulary>cow's milk</vocabulary>, though most people just call cow's milk <vocabulary>milk</vocabulary>.
4646.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That man dancing over there with chikuwa on each of his nipples is my boss.
examples.ja: あそこで乳首にチクワを付けてダンスしてる人が私の上司です。

examples.en: My nipples are covered with scabs because the baby bites them.
examples.ja: 赤ちゃんにかまれて、乳首がカサブタだらけになってるんです。

examples.en: When I saw all the blood spurting out of your nipples, I couldn't help but panic!
examples.ja: あんたの乳首から血がふき出しているのを見て、思わずパニクッちゃったよ！

examples.en: I've sterilized the feeding bottle nipples with boiling water.
examples.ja: 哺乳瓶の乳首、熱湯消毒しておいたよ！

4647.meaning_mnemonic: What is a <kanji>milk</kanji> <kanji>neck</kanji>? Think about where milk comes from. Now, think of what looks like a little neck on the thing that milk comes from. What is that thing? It's a <vocabulary>nipple</vocabulary>.
4647.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this one is an exception, you already know that 首 is read as くび, but 乳 in this case is read as ち. Here's a mnemonic to help you.

You come across a <vocabulary>nipple</vocabulary> and decide to milk it so that you can make some <reading>chee</reading>se (ち). That's a little bit strange. You should probably find out who this nipple belongs to and ask them if you can do that first.

examples.en: Could you call a taxi for me?
examples.ja: タクシーを呼んでもらえますか？

examples.en: A stranger suddenly called out my name at the airport.
examples.ja: 空港で、見知らぬ人に名前を大声で呼ばれた。

examples.en: He saved your life so you should invite him to your birthday party.
examples.ja: 彼はあなたの命の恩人なんだから、誕生日会に呼んだ方がいいわよ。

4648.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>call</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to call</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to call out</vocabulary>. As in "HEY, YOU!"
4648.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji, so you should be good here. Just imagine yourself  calling out to someone: "<reading>YO</reading> (よ)! You!"

examples.en: Eating and drinking are prohibited in this castle.
examples.ja: この城の中では、飲食は禁止です。

examples.en: The castles that still remain have all become famous sightseeing spots.
examples.ja: 今でも残っているお城は、全て観光名所になっています。

examples.en: If I won the lottery, I would build my own castle in the back yard.
examples.ja: もし宝くじが当たったら、裏庭に自分のお城を建てるね。

4649.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4649.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: That actor has a real attitude problem.
examples.ja: あの俳優は、態度に問題がある。

examples.en: That actress is always fawning over big actors, so other actresses don't like her.
examples.ja: その女優は、いつも大物俳優に尻尾をふっているため、他の女優から嫌われている。

examples.en: My boyfriend is the actor performing the part of the horse in this play.
examples.ja: 私の恋人は、この芝居で馬の役を演じている俳優よ。

4650.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>superior</kanji> <kanji>haiku</kanji> requires someone really famous and well known to read it... it's just on that level. Who is super well known and who deserves to read this superior haiku? A great <vocabulary>actor</vocabulary>, perhaps?
4650.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: A Japanese person wouldn't let these haiku mistakes slide.
examples.ja: 日本人だったら、この俳句のミスは放っておかないよね。

examples.en: I often write haiku while riding my bike.
examples.ja: 私はよく自転車に乗りながら俳句を作ります。

examples.en: The haiku he composed today was so romantic, wasn’t it?
examples.ja: 彼が今日詠んだ俳句、すごくロマンチックだったわよね。

4651.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>haiku</kanji> <kanji>paragraph</kanji> is just a <vocabulary>haiku</vocabulary>. Haikus are little haiku paragraphs.

You will learn kanji
The Crabigator watches
He feeds on reviews
4651.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Students who excel in a particular field can enter this university through a different route.
examples.ja: この大学には、一芸に秀でる学生は別ルートで入学することができる。

examples.en: Satomi excels at expressing her thoughts.
examples.ja: サトミは、自分の考えを表現することに秀でている。

examples.en: The only thing I excel at is picking my nose. In fact, I have never made my nose bleed.
examples.ja: 私は鼻くそをほじくることだけには秀でています。実際、鼻血を出すはめになったこともありません。

4652.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>excel</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to excel</vocabulary>.
4652.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

"<reading>He-e</reading> (ひい) is going <vocabulary>to excel</vocabulary>," you stutter. "He-e is!"

examples.en: Leo is much more capable than I am.
examples.ja: レオは僕なんかよりずっと優秀です。

examples.en: Aya got an award for excellence in an art contest.
examples.ja: アヤは、絵画コンクールで優秀賞をもらいました。

examples.en: Superior system administrators prepare for any possibility of hacking.
examples.ja: 優秀なシステム管理者は、ハッキングによるいかなる攻撃の可能性にも備えます。

4653.meaning_mnemonic:
Something that's <kanji>superior</kanji> will <kanji>excel</kanji>. It is <vocabulary>superior</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>excellent</vocabulary> in every way.

This word is typically used to describe someone's superiority or excellence, often in comparison to others.
4653.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What's the difference between this new product and that old model?
examples.ja: この新製品とあの型落ちした商品の違いは何ですか？

examples.en: There is a need to understand that we all have differences and that we should accept one another.
examples.ja: 私たちは、みんなに違いがあることを理解し、認め合う必要があります。

examples.en: I don’t understand the difference at all between a janitor and an executive vice president.
examples.ja: 清掃員と副社長の違いなんて全く分からないね。

4654.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you'd think it's probably an adjective. However in this case, it's a noun. What's the noun form of <kanji>different</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>difference</vocabulary>.
4654.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Not different at all.

examples.en: Let's try a different approach.
examples.ja: 違うアプローチも試してみましょう。

examples.en: I felt as if I had met the person  before, but apparently I was wrong.
examples.ja: 今の人、どこかで会った気がしたんですが、違ったみたいです。

examples.en: Compared to veteran employees, the base pay of new employees isn’t very high.
examples.ja: ベテラン社員とは違って、新入社員の基本給はあまり高くない。

4655.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>different</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to be different</vocabulary>... and of course, to be different is also <vocabulary>to be wrong</vocabulary> in Japan. Don't be different!
4655.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the reading you learned with the kanji. It's not different at all.

examples.en: Today is the day for burnable garbage, isn’t it?
examples.ja: 今日は可燃ゴミの日だよね。

examples.en: Could you not put non-burnable trash in with the burnable trash please?
examples.ja: 可燃ゴミの中に不可燃ゴミを交ぜないでくれませんか？

examples.en: The only thing you’re getting for Christmas from me is burnable garbage.
examples.ja: あなたが私から貰うクリスマスプレゼントは、可燃ごみだけだよ。

4656.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Possible</kanji> to <kanji>burn</kanji> ゴミ (garbage). This is <vocabulary>burnable garbage</vocabulary>.
4656.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Our cafe is opening for business as of today.
examples.ja: 私たちのカフェは、今日から営業するんです。

examples.en: This shop should have still been in business last month…
examples.ja: このお店、先月は営業していたはずなんだけど...。

examples.en: Do you know how much money a fortune teller doing business on the street makes?
examples.ja: 道ばたで営業する占い師が、どれくらいのお金を稼ぐのか知ってる？

4657.meaning_mnemonic: The word 営業 is <kanji>business</kanji>. The verb version of that (to do a business) becomes <vocabulary>to run a business</vocabulary>.
4657.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Also, it shares the reading with 営業.

examples.en: Japan has a lot of traditional culture.
examples.ja: 日本には伝統的な文化がたくさんあります。

examples.en: This festival is a traditional event, but it now incorporates a modern essence as well.
examples.ja: このお祭りは伝統的な行事ですが、今では現代的なエッセンスも加えられています。

examples.en: Kimono are Japan’s traditional attire, and fundoshi are the traditional Japanese underwear for men.
examples.ja: 着物は日本の伝統的な衣装で、褌は、伝統的な日本の男性用下着です。

4658.meaning_mnemonic: If 伝統 is "tradition," then adding a 的 (<kanji>-al</kanji>) to it would make it <vocabulary>traditional</vocabulary>.
4658.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Why don’t you at least let yourself relax on your birthday?
examples.ja: 誕生日ぐらい、肩の力をぬいたら？

examples.en: I was the only one not invited to WaniKani's birthday party, so I felt left out.
examples.ja: 私だけワニカニの誕生日会に呼んでもらえなくて、無視された気分になった。

examples.en: "Can I bring a friend to your birthday party?" "Of course! The more people we have, the more fun it will be."
examples.ja: 「君の誕生日会に友達を連れて行ってもいい？」「もちろん！ 人数が多ければ多いほど楽しいしね。」

4659.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 誕生 is <kanji>birth</kanji>? If you add <kanji>day</kanji> on there, you have a <vocabulary>birthday</vocabulary>. Happy birthday!
4659.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji, but with this word 日 uses the kun'yomi ひ, which is turned into び due to rendaku.

examples.en: I overslept and wasn't able to properly warm up my shoulders before the match.
examples.ja: 寝坊して、試合前に肩をちゃんと作れなかったんだ。

examples.en: I overslept too often, so the president finally advised me to resign.
examples.ja: 寝坊しすぎて、ついに社長から肩をたたかれた。

examples.en: I thought, "Oh no! I overslept," but thankfully, it was Sunday.
examples.ja: 「しまった！寝坊した！」と思ったんですが、有り難いことに日曜日でした。

4660.meaning_mnemonic: 寝坊 is <kanji>oversleep</kanji>. Make that into a verb and you have <vocabulary>to oversleep</vocabulary>.
4660.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It also just takes the reading from 寝坊.

examples.en: Please change this i-adjective into the past tense.
examples.ja: この形容詞を過去形に変えてください。

examples.en: Don’t you use the past tense in this case?
examples.ja: この場合は過去形は使わないんですか？

examples.en: Can you explain the difference between the past tense and the past perfect tense in a simple way?
examples.ja: 過去形と過去完了形の違いをやさしく説明してくれますか。

4661.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>past</kanji> <kanji>shape</kanji> is how things were in the past. To describe those things (like you would with an adjective, aka 形容詞), you'd use <vocabulary>past tense</vocabulary>.
4661.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My child has too much on his mind and has trouble focusing on one thing.
examples.ja: うちの子は、気が多過ぎて一つのことに集中するのが苦手なんです。

examples.en: I will pick you up shortly after 5 o'clock.
examples.ja: 五時過ぎにむかえに行きます。

examples.en: You get paid way too much for working such short hours.
examples.ja: 短時間の仕事で良い給料をもらい過ぎだよ。

4662.meaning_mnemonic: 過ぎる is <vocabulary>to pass</vocabulary>. When you pass what is needed, what are you left with? Just this word: <vocabulary>too much</vocabulary>. This can also mean <vocabulary>after</vocabulary>, as in "after 5pm", and <vocabulary>past</vocabulary>, as in "past sixty".
4662.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 過ぎる. Know that and you know <vocabulary>too much</vocabulary>. Dial it down to get 過ぎ.

examples.en: What counter measures for earthquakes are you taking at your house?
examples.ja: あなたの家ではどんな地震対策をしていますか。

examples.en: It is said that the Japanese government is taking measures to address the declining birthrate, but aren't all of these measures somewhat inadequate?
examples.ja: 日本政府は少子化対策を進めているって言うけど、どの対策もビミョーなものばかりじゃない？

examples.en: When I tried to make coffee and pressed the button, the coffee maker caught fire. We need to find the cause of this malfunction and take preventive measures to avoid it happening again.
examples.ja: コーヒーを入れようとしてボタンを押したら、コーヒーメーカーが火を噴いたの。不具合の原因を見つけて、再発防止対策を講じなきゃいけないわ。

4663.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>versus</kanji> <kanji>plan</kanji> is to attack back. They've already attacked you once, so now it's time for your <vocabulary>counter plan</vocabulary>.
4663.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I guess the values of young people are getting updated more and more.
examples.ja: やっぱり、若者たちの価値観はどんどんアップデートされていってるよね。

examples.en: I have no intention of attending a party with people who have different values than my own.
examples.ja: 私は価値観の違う人達のパーティに出席する気はありません。

examples.en: I think it’s quite important to share similar values with your spouse.
examples.ja: 結婚相手と価値観が近いことって結構大切だと思うんだよねー。

4664.meaning_mnemonic: These <kanji>view</kanji>s that have <kanji>merit</kanji> (価値) are your <vocabulary>values</vocabulary>.
4664.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: When I was in middle school I was a member of the cheering section for the baseball club.
examples.ja: 中学校の時は野球部の応援団の一員でした。

examples.en: Koichi just shrugged his shoulders when asked about the Tofugu rooting section.
examples.ja: コウイチは、トーフグ応援団について聞かれても、肩をすくめるだけだった。

examples.en: Hey, you're the leader of the cheer squad, right? I’ve heard a lot about you.
examples.ja: ああ、君が応援団長だね？噂はかねがね伺っておるよ。

4665.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>group</kanji> that <kanji>roots for</kanji> you is your <vocabulary>rooting section</vocabulary> or <vocabulary> cheer squad</vocabulary>. Go go go you!

応援団 tend to wear black school uniforms and support their team with lively chants and energetic performances. They can also have cheerleaders with pom-poms, but those are usually just called チアリーダー.

4695.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>touch</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to touch something</vocabulary>.

触る is used when someone does the touching. It's not used to describe objects touching each other.

Note that 触る can be used with either the particle に or を, like 手に触る or 手を触る (to touch a hand). Using に simply marks the location you touch, while using を highlights your action of touching that specific area or object. So the former is intransitive and the latter is transitive, though there's some debate about that.

4714.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>distinction</kanji>, and the verb version here means… a million things. Let's just focus on a few common meanings. Things with distinction tend to stick out from the others. They tend <vocabulary>to shine</vocabulary>, you know? And if you imagine shining a beam of light on something, that light tends <vocabulary>to project</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to extend outward</vocabulary>. It sticks out, shines on something, then makes that thing more distinct too. 

That's why you can say 光が差す (light shines), かげが差す (a shadow is cast), 指差す (to point at), or even カサを差す (to open and raise an umbrella). Basically, 差す usually has to do with causing something <vocabulary>to appear</vocabulary>, either by shining or projecting outward.

examples.ja: 仕事で限界まで自分を追いつめてしまい、今はちょっと休みを取っています。

examples.en: The baseball player retired when he felt that he had reached his limit.
examples.ja: その野球選手は、自分の限界を感じて引退した。

4744.meaning_mnemonic:
As you reach the <kanji>limit</kanji> of your <kanji>world</kanji>, you face your <vocabulary>limit</vocabulary> and confront your <vocabulary>limitations</vocabulary>.

This word refers to the maximum extent or limit that something can reach or endure. It conveys the idea of reaching the utmost point beyond which a situation or condition cannot be sustained.
4744.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This service is limited to lifetime members.
examples.ja: これはライフタイム会員限定のサービスなんです。

examples.en: This restaurant offers seasonally limited course meals.
examples.ja: このレストランでは、季節限定のコース料理が提供されています。

examples.en: Mom, I really want the limited edition Tofugu dolls, so can’t you give me one million dollars?
examples.ja: お母さん、あの限定販売のトーフグ人形が欲しいんだけど、百万ドルくれない？

4745.meaning_mnemonic:
A specific <kanji>limit</kanji> has been <kanji>determine</kanji>d. This is the <vocabulary>limit</vocabulary> of a certain thing, which can’t be exceeded.

This word means placing a particular limit or restriction on the quantity, scope, or availability of something for a special or exclusive purpose. This is often used for things like sales or products that are only available for a limited time or in restricted quantities.
4745.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: However, it should be noted that the limit is set at one million yen per person.
examples.ja: ただし、一人当たり１００万円を限度とする。

examples.en: Even though you are generous, there is a limit.
examples.ja: いくら気前がよくても限度というものがある。

examples.en: I forget what my limit is on this credit card.
examples.ja: このクレジットカードの限度額がいくらだったか忘れちゃったんだよね。

4746.meaning_mnemonic:
A certain <kanji>limit</kanji>’s <kanji>degree</kanji> is how far it can go. It’s the <vocabulary>limit</vocabulary>; turn it up one more degree and it’s out of <vocabulary>bounds</vocabulary>. Keep it right where it is and it’s perfect.

This word refers to the maximum extent or range of something, beyond which it cannot be surpassed. While similar to 限界, 限度 often implies a predetermined acceptable or tolerable limit, while 限界 is more closely associated with an absolute or ultimate limit.
4746.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: After all, nothing beats Tofugu when it comes to learning Japanese.
examples.ja: やっぱり、日本語の勉強はトーフグに限るよ。

examples.en: It’s only at times like these that I forget something.
examples.ja: こういう時に限って、忘れ物をしてしまう。

examples.en: The food at that new restaurant is good, but the menu is limited.
examples.ja: あの新しいレストランは、料理は美味しいけどメニューが限られている。

examples.en: It's not limited to just this time that Viet was chased by the police.
examples.ja: ビエトが警察に追われるのは今回に限ったことではない。

examples.en: Nothing beats beer after a bath!
examples.ja: お風呂の後はビールに限る！

4747.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>limit</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to limit</vocabulary>. It is often used in the passive form 限られる, which means <vocabulary>to be limited</vocabulary>, implying that the limiting is being done by someone else.

This is a formal word used to define the limits of time, space, or quantity, or to set restrictions on things. It is also used casually when emphasizing something in particular or considering something to be the best.
4747.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: <vocabulary>to limit</vocabulary> things, you have something called a <reading>ca</reading>r (か) <reading>guillotine</reading> (ぎ) which you drive around limiting everything with.

examples.en: I made sure that the time bomb was neatly placed in the drawer.
examples.ja: 時限爆弾がきちんと引き出しの中にしまわれていることを確認した。

examples.en: The final class today was actually a lecture by Koichi from Tofugu!
examples.ja: 今日の最後の時限は、なんとトーフグのコウイチのレクチャーだったんだよ！

examples.en: I ate beans during fourth period cooking class, so a time bomb might be set to go off soon.
examples.ja: 四時限目の調理実習で豆を食べたから、もうすぐ僕の時限爆弾が爆発するかもしれない。

examples.en: In Canada, a temporary restriction has been established that prohibits non-Canadian citizens from purchasing residential real estate for a period of two years, starting from January 1st, 2023.
examples.ja: カナダでは、2023年1月1日から2年間、カナダ人以外が住宅用不動産を買うことが禁止される時限的な制限が設けられました。

4748.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>time</kanji> <kanji>limit</kanji> is a <vocabulary>time limit</vocabulary>, but not any old time limit. This is usually used at the beginning of compound words, especially 時限爆弾 (time bomb).
4748.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: When was the essay due?
examples.ja: レポートの提出期限、いつだっけ？

examples.en: If we don't set a deadline for our work, I don't think it will ever get done.
examples.ja: 期限を設けて仕事をしないと、いつまでたっても終わらないと思うんです。

examples.en: I have to leave Japan next month because my visa will expire.
examples.ja: ビザの期限が切れるので、来月日本を出なくてはいけません。

4749.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>period of time</kanji> <kanji>limit</kanji> is the <vocabulary>deadline</vocabulary> for a certain thing. Alternatively, this can describe a <vocabulary>term</vocabulary> for something, like the repayment of debts, or some sort of <vocabulary>due date</vocabulary>.
4749.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Young people have infinite possibilities.
examples.ja: 若者には、無限の可能性がある。

examples.en: Is anything infinite in this world?
examples.ja: この世に無限なものなんてある？

examples.en: The situation looks bright at the moment, but the demand won’t increase indefinitely, right?
examples.ja: 今は絶好調のように思えるが、需要は無限には増加しないだろう？

4750.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>limit</kanji> is <kanji>nothing</kanji>. What? No limit? That means it will never stop! It is <vocabulary>infinite</vocabulary>!
4750.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Is Koichi out of his mind, offering WaniKani for free?
examples.ja: 無料でワニカニを提供するなんて、コウイチ、気は確かなのかな？

examples.en: This program is presented courtesy of the following sponsors.
examples.ja: この番組はごらんのスポンサーの提供でお送りします。

examples.en: How can I register to become an organ donor in Japan?
examples.ja: 日本で臓器提供者になる同意書にサインをするには、どうすればいいですか？

4751.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>present</kanji> something and <kanji>offer</kanji> it to someone, you're kindly <vocabulary>offering</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>providing</vocabulary> it to them.

提供 is a relatively formal word that refers to offering or providing something you have for someone else's benefit — like giving resources, services, funds, or information.
4751.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Please tell me how to offer moon-viewing dango.
examples.ja: 月見だんごを供える方法を教えてください。

examples.en: It's so nice of him to leave an offering of Ichiro's Malt that my dad liked.
examples.ja: 親父が好きだったイチローズ・モルトを供えてくれるなんて、アイツは本当に気が利くやつだよ。

examples.en: Can you buy some flowers to place on the graves tomorrow on your way home?
examples.ja: 明日お墓に供える花を、帰りに買ってきてくれない？

4752.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>offer</kanji>, and this verb version means <vocabulary>to make an offering</vocabulary>.

供える means <vocabulary>to offer</vocabulary> something, usually to a god, Buddha, or someone who has passed away. For example, you might 花を供える (offer flowers) at a grave or altar.
4752.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. It shares its reading with the word 備える, which you learned a level ago, but in case you need a reminder, here it is:

What's the best way for your servants <vocabulary>to make an offering</vocabulary>? When they <vocabulary>offer</vocabulary> up their sauna (そな)! You really value a warm and relaxing sauna session at the end of the day.

examples.en: I think this movie is not intended for kids, but for grownups.
examples.ja: この映画は子供向けではなく、大人向けだと思うよ。

examples.en: When my child was born, life changed more dramatically than I had expected.
examples.ja: 子供が生まれると、思った以上に生活が大きく変わった。

examples.en: Your child is way too good looking, I can hardly believe he’s your kid.
examples.ja: お前の子供、イケメンすぎて、お前の子供だとは思えねーよ。

examples.en: After the kids have gone to bed, we really want to enjoy some couples time together, but we're usually too tired and end up falling asleep with the kids.
examples.ja: 子供達が寝静まった後に夫婦の時間を楽しみたいのは山々だが、疲れすぎて子供達と一緒に寝落ちしてしまうことがほとんどだ。

4753.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>child</kanji> often has to <kanji>accompany</kanji> someone else when they go places, because they're… a <vocabulary>child</vocabulary>. Can't have all those kids running around unaccompanied, can we?
4753.reading_mnemonic:
The readings for this one are the kun'yomi readings of each kanji. 子 is こ, like the individual vocab word. 供 is ども, however. Remember this by thinking how much <vocabulary>children</vocabulary> love <reading>domo</reading>-kun (ども).

Also, 子ども is kind of more "politically correct" with the kana hanging off there. 子供 is still used in a lot of situations, usually stiff ones. The second kanji means servant, and some people don't like that. The second version pops up a decent amount, so it's good to be familiar with that as well.

examples.en: I took a pencil to the exhibition just in case.
examples.ja: 万一に備えて、展示会にエンピツを持って行きました。

examples.en: I went to an exhibition called the Supermarket Trade Show.
examples.ja: スーパーマーケットトレードショーという展示会に行ってきたんだ。

examples.en: My brother organized his first art exhibition in a cafe.
examples.ja: 私の兄は、カフェで初めての美術展示会を開催した。

4754.meaning_mnemonic: I want to <kanji>expand</kanji> my business. I want to <kanji>show</kanji> my goods. I want to do this in a place where everyone <kanji>meet</kanji>s up to do these things. You can do this in a <vocabulary>trade show</vocabulary>.
4754.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Japan has developed considerably compared to 100 years ago.
examples.ja: 百年前と比べて、日本は大きく発展した。

examples.en: Whether this country will develop or not depends on the youth.
examples.ja: この国が発展するかどうかは、若者にかかっています。

examples.en: When old people catch a cold, it can easily develop into pneumonia.
examples.ja: 年寄りの風邪は肺炎に発展しやすいんだよ。

4755.meaning_mnemonic: Let's <kanji>depart</kanji> from this place and <kanji>expand</kanji> it out. To do that we'll have <vocabulary>to develop</vocabulary> it.
4755.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The はつ gets shortened to はっ, though.

examples.en: That story's development was unexpected.
examples.ja: その話の展開は意外だった。

examples.en: What are the advantages of small businesses expanding overseas?
examples.ja: 中小企業が海外展開をする利点とは何でしょうか。

examples.en: This air bag is dangerous because it doesn’t deploy right away when the car crashes.
examples.ja: このエアバッグは車が衝突してもすぐには展開しないので危険なんです。

4756.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>expand</kanji> and <kanji>open</kanji>. Just imagine something happening like this. This is when something is <vocabulary>unfolding</vocabulary> or in <vocabulary>development</vocabulary>.
4756.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Alright, I'll send it as a confidential letter then.
examples.ja: じゃあ、親展で送るね。

examples.en: The test results will be sent to you later, marked “confidential.”
examples.ja: 検査結果は後日、親展で送付されます。

examples.en: Did you open it even though it's marked “confidential”? If you opened it without permission, that could count as a crime.
examples.ja: 「親展」って書いてるのに、開けたの？これ、勝手に開けると、罪に問われるんだよ。

examples.en: Can you buy me an envelope with the characters for "confidential" printed on it?
examples.ja: 親展の文字が印刷された封筒を買って来てくれない？

4757.meaning_mnemonic:
If <kanji>intimacy</kanji> <kanji>expand</kanji>s to something, that thing is <vocabulary>confidential</vocabulary>. Try visualizing intimacy as a sort of gooey liquid, expanding and covering a letter, and making that letter confidential.

親展 is generally written on the front of envelopes to indicate that only the intended recipient should read its contents.
4757.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Of course you know that Tofugu sells various goods online, right?
examples.ja: トーフグがオンラインで色んなグッズを販売しているのはもちろん知っていますよね？

examples.en: Sales of Tofugu stickers are strong.
examples.ja: トーフグのステッカーの販売は好調です。

examples.en: Many of the salespeople at our company are taking time off work in August.
examples.ja: 我が社の販売員の多くは、八月に休暇を取ります。

4758.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Sell</kanji>, <kanji>sell</kanji>, sell. This is the attitude you need if you want to work in <vocabulary>sales</vocabulary> or do <vocabulary>sales</vocabulary>. You have to work on your <vocabulary>selling</vocabulary>.
4758.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which means you need to know the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You know them both, hurray!

examples.en: I don't feel inclined to install a vending machine in the Tofugu office.
examples.ja: トーフグオフィスに自動販売機を設置することには、あまり気が乗りません。

examples.en: All vending machines at this station seem to be empty.
examples.ja: この駅の自動販売機は全部空になっているみたいだ。

examples.en: The October twenty-third meeting about the vending machines has been rescheduled for October twenty-fourth due to Koichi’s birthday party.
examples.ja: 10月23日の自動販売機に関する会議は、コウイチの誕生日会のため、10月24日に変更されました。

4759.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Automatic</kanji> (自動) <kanji>sell</kanji> <kanji>sell</kanji> <kanji>machine</kanji>. The machine sells things by itself, basically. This is a <vocabulary>vending machine</vocabulary>. There is a shorter version of this, but good to learn the long one first :)
4759.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Remember those, and you'll be fine here.

examples.en: The mail order catalog arrived.
examples.ja: 通販のカタログが届いた。

examples.en: I’ve never bought anything through mail order before, but I’ll give it a shot.
examples.ja: 今まで通販で買い物したことないけど、ちょっとやってみるよ。

examples.en: I got complaints so many times that I quit my mail-order online shop.
examples.ja: 何度もクレームが発生したんで、ネットショップで通販するのはやめました。

4760.meaning_mnemonic: Things you <kanji>sell</kanji> that <kanji>pass through</kanji> the world to get to you are probably <vocabulary>mail order</vocabulary>. You order them and they get zoomed off to you, passing through all kinds of space to arrive at your door.
4760.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The stock that I had been sitting on for so long finally went up and I feel relieved.
examples.ja: ずっと塩づけになっていた株がやっと上がって、気が楽になりました。

examples.en: I can't understand at all why Viet bought the bio-venture company's stocks.
examples.ja: ビエトがどういうつもりでバイオベンチャーの株を買ったのか、全然分からないんだよね。

examples.en: Koichi made tons of money on the stock market and decided to swag out his car with big wheels and leather seats.
examples.ja: コウイチは株でガッポリもうけたので、車のタイヤをどでかいホイール・タイヤに変えて、シートも革張りにしてカッチョ良くしちゃおうと決めた。

4761.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4761.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji.

examples.en: Koichi braced himself up for the further decline in stock prices.
examples.ja: コウイチは、株式のさらなる下落に備えて気を引きしめた。

examples.en: I'm not very enthusiastic about the idea of buying stocks as a company.
examples.ja: 会社で株式を買うという考えにはあまり気が進まないよ。

examples.en: The news that the stock market seemed to go into a bottomless decline was a great blow to him.
examples.ja: 株式市場が底なしの下落に陥ったようだというニュースは、彼に大きな精神的ダメージを与えた。

4762.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>stock</kanji> <kanji>ritual</kanji> is the dance we do in the modern world around <vocabulary>stock</vocabulary>s and <vocabulary>share</vocabulary>s of different companies. Buy! Sell! Buy! Sell!
4762.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: This diaper is excellent, as it can absorb any amount of pee without any issue.
examples.ja: このオムツはどんな量のおしっこでも難なく吸収してくれる優れものです。

examples.en: That new worker can absorb anything new very quickly, so his nickname became "sponge."
examples.ja: あの新人、新しいことを何でもすぐに吸収しちゃうから、あだ名がスポンジになったんだ。

examples.en: This is a great opportunity for all of the workers to absorb knowledge about the new system.
examples.ja: 全社員が新システムに関する知識を吸収する良い機会です。

4763.meaning_mnemonic: If 吸収 is "absorption" the verb version is <vocabulary>to absorb</vocabulary>.
4763.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The glass fugu ornament fell off the table and broke.
examples.ja: ガラス製のフグの置物が、テーブルから落ちて割れてしまった。

examples.en: Regarding the approach to the project, the members' opinions were completely divided into two.
examples.ja: プロジェクトの進め方について、メンバーの意見が真っ二つに割れてしまった。

examples.en: "Something terrible happened!" "What's wrong?" "When I woke up, my butt was split up into two!" "Oh, that's not a big deal. My butt is split up into five."
examples.ja: 「大変なことが起こった！」 「どうしたの？」「朝起きたらおしりが二つに割れていたんだ！」「なんだ、そんなこと？私なんか五つに割れているわよ。」

examples.en: We finally uncovered the identity of the criminal!
examples.ja: ついに犯人の身元が割れたぞ！

examples.en: He needed to poop so badly that he almost broke the door from pounding on it with his fists.
examples.ja: 大便がしたくてたまらなかった彼は、ドアを拳で割れるほど強く叩いた。

4764.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 割る is "to divide"? Now you're learning the intransitive version. Instead of you doing the dividing, something just gets divided or split up. So this is <vocabulary>to be divided</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be split</vocabulary>.

It can also mean <vocabulary>to break</vocabulary>, as in ワイングラスが割れる (the wine glass breaks). After all, when an object breaks, it’s divided into parts, right?
4764.reading_mnemonic: The reading is shared with 割る.

examples.en: I'm sure that it had a tag saying 20% off.
examples.ja: 二割引の値札が付いてたはずですよ。

examples.en: At this supermarket, on Tuesdays, people who have a student ID get a 5% discount.
examples.ja: このスーパーでは、火曜日は学生証を持っている人は5%割引になります。

examples.en: I want to buy that large-sized refrigerator. Would you please add a discount? 10% would be enough for me.
examples.ja: あの大きな型の冷蔵庫を買いたいんですが、一割でもいいんで割引してもらえませんか。

examples.en: I’ll set about adding a discount coupon to the website.
examples.ja: ちょうどホームページへ割引クーポンの追加をしようと思ってたところだよ。

4765.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Divide</kanji> that price and <kanji>pull</kanji> it apart. You only have to pay for one part! What a <vocabulary>discount</vocabulary>.
4765.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji. き from ひき kind of just gets stuffed into the 引 and hidden away like that strange collection of fingernails you have hidden in your closet drawer inside of a 35mm film container. Also remember that the reading gets changed to びき here because of that pesky rendaku.

examples.en: Since it's Friday, I need to prepare a bento.
examples.ja: 今日は金曜日だからお弁当を準備しなくちゃ。

examples.en: Finish your breakfast before getting ready.
examples.ja: 準備する前に先に朝ご飯食べちゃいなさい。

examples.en: About how much does it cost to prepare a new home?
examples.ja: 新居を準備するのにかかる費用はいくらぐらいですか。

4766.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen that 準備 is <kanji>preparation</kanji>. This is the verb version, so it means <vocabulary>to prepare</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to get ready for</vocabulary> something.
4766.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 準備.

examples.en: Hang in there, you can do this.
examples.ja: 「そのまま頑張って。あなたなら大丈夫よ。」

examples.en: Recently, he's been trying his best to button his shirts by himself.
examples.ja: 最近は、自分でシャツのボタンを掛けようと頑張っています。

examples.en: My doctor advised me to lead a regular life and eat regularly, so I'm working hard on that.
examples.ja: 医者から規則正しい生活をして規則正しく食事をするようアドバイスされたので、今頑張っているんです。

4767.meaning_mnemonic: 張る is <kanji>to stretch</kanji>. You're <kanji>stubborn</kanji> and want to stretch out what you're doing right now. Although you're stubborn, you keep doing it. You persevere. That's why this word is <vocabulary>to persevere</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to do one's best</vocabulary>.
4767.reading_mnemonic:
This word gets its reading from the kanji 頑 and the verb 張る put together, but the 張る part gets rendaku'd to ばる. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember that rendaku:

When you have <vocabulary>to persevere</vocabulary>, you always scream <reading>baa</reading> (ば)! Not sure why, you just think when someone has <vocabulary>to do one's best</vocabulary>, screaming "baa!" is a great motivator. Kinda like how weightlifters and tennis players grunt when they're doing their best, you know? Baa!

examples.en: Can you leave out the wasabi?
examples.ja: ワサビは抜いてもらえますか？

examples.en: I want to pull out a splinter, do you know where the tweezers are?
examples.ja: トゲを抜きたいんだけど、ピンセットどこにあるか知らない？

examples.en: Today I had four wisdom teeth extracted at once.  They popped out like pulling a cork out of a bottle of wine!
examples.ja: 今日は親知らずを一気に四本抜きました。ワインのコルクを抜くみたいに、ポンッと抜けたよ！

examples.en: Well, I never thought you could overtake the first place runner! I'm surprised.
examples.ja: いやー、まさかお前が一位のランナーを抜くことができるとは！びっくりだよ。

examples.en: I was so preoccupied with airing out the air mattress that I forgot to drain the water from the bathtub.
examples.ja: エアマットレスの空気を抜くのに気を取られて、バスタブの水を抜くの忘れてた。

4768.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>pull out</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to pull something out</vocabulary>.

This word often implies that the pulling out requires force or effort. It's a pretty versatile word, and can also cover things like letting the air out of something, draining the water out of something, and even overtaking someone or pulling through difficulties.
4768.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Just go ahead and extract it out of your memory so you can use it here.

examples.en: A part-time worker at my company got arrested for punching a person.
examples.ja: うちの会社のアルバイトが人をなぐって捕まってしまったんだ。

examples.en: No matter how many times I called there had been no answer, but then I finally caught Ashley.
examples.ja: 何度電話をしても出なかったけど、やっとアシュリーが捕まった。

examples.en: At first I was just stopped for speeding, but I ended up being caught for drunk driving.
examples.ja: 最初スピード違反で止められたんだけど、その後飲酒運転で捕まっちゃったんだよ。

4769.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>catch</kanji>, so this intransitive verb version is <vocabulary>to be caught</vocabulary>.

This is often a literal, physical catch, but 捕まる can also be used when someone's been gotten ahold of in a figurative way, like when you've finally managed to contact them.
4769.reading_mnemonic: The reading is つか, so to remember that with <vocabulary>to be caught</vocabulary>, think about how you're a police officer chasing some criminals. Unfortunately, they split up into <reading>two ca</reading>rs (つか), meaning they can't both be caught. Guess you should have called for backup...

examples.en: My grandpa made a model airplane for me.
examples.ja: おじいちゃんが、模型の飛行機を作ってくれたんだ。

examples.en: My little brother is good at assembling models.
examples.ja: 弟は模型を組み立てるのが得意です。

examples.en: My grandfather started his business as a one-person model retail shop.
examples.ja: 祖父は、最初は従業員一人の小売模型店からこのビジネスを始めました。

4770.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>imitation</kanji> <kanji>model</kanji> is obviously not the real thing. It's (usually) a <vocabulary>plastic model</vocabulary> or just a <vocabulary>model</vocabulary> figure or something.
4770.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That book has influenced the lives of many people.
examples.ja: その本は、多くの人の人生に影響を与えました。

examples.en: I granted permission to the part-time student worker to access the company database.
examples.ja: アルバイトの学生に会社のデータベースにアクセスする権限を与えた。

examples.en: People will dislike you if you keep making remarks that cause harm to others.
examples.ja: 人にダメージを与えるような発言ばかりしていると、嫌われますよ。

examples.en: Today let's practice responding to small talk in a way that gives a good impression to the other person.
examples.ja: 今日は、相手にいい印象を与えるようなスモールトークの受け答えの練習をしましょう。

examples.en: First and foremost, I would like to express my sincere thanks for taking time out of your busy schedules to be here and for granting me the fantastic opportunity to give this presentation.
examples.ja: まず初めに、お忙しい中足をお運び頂き誠に有り難うございます。また、このような素晴らしいプレゼンテーションの機会を与えて頂いたことにも、感謝申し上げます。

4771.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>give</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to give</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to grant</vocabulary>.

This is a relatively formal word that is generally used in writing. In conversations, people commonly use more relaxed words like あげる or くれる.
4771.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You go <vocabulary>to give</vocabulary> a bone to your dog. <reading>Atta</reading> (あた) boy, Sparky! <reading>Atta</reading> boy.

examples.en: I felt the urge to study after hearing about the bonus.
examples.ja: 賞与金の話を聞いて、急に勉強する気になりました。

examples.en: You got this much bonus? Your company is generous, yeah?
examples.ja: こんなに賞与金を出してくれるなんて、お前の会社は気前が良いんだなぁ。

examples.en: Our paydays are the fifth and the twentieth of every month, and a bonus may be paid at the end of the year depending on how well the company has done.
examples.ja: 給料日は毎月五日と二十日で、会社の業績次第で賞与金が年末に支払われます。

4772.meaning_mnemonic:
It's a <kanji>prize</kanji> where you are <kanji>give</kanji>n <kanji>gold</kanji>. In business, this is called a <vocabulary>bonus</vocabulary>. You didn't expect it (not your salary) and it is given to you (and is gold, if you're lucky).

Note that you’ll more commonly see its shorter version 賞与.
4772.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This price includes consumption tax.
examples.ja: この料金は、消費税を含みます。

examples.en: Please separate the trash containing mercury from the other trash.
examples.ja: 水銀を含むゴミは別に分けて出してください。

examples.en: This margarine does not contain trans fats.
examples.ja: このマーガリンには、トランス脂肪酸は含まれていません。

examples.en: What kinds of benefits does a hot spring containing alkali have?
examples.ja: アルカリを含む温泉にはどのような効能があるのですか？

4773.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>include</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to include</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to contain</vocabulary>.

While 含む can be used in everyday conversation, it’s a relatively formal word that is generally used in explanatory sentences.
4773.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

They don't want <vocabulary>to include</vocabulary> you in their game? Well, "<reading>F***</reading> (ふく) you!" you yell at them, because they wouldn't include you.

examples.en: The use of language can sometimes create a political implication.
examples.ja: 言葉の使い方によって、政治的な含意が生じることがある。

examples.en: I wonder what implication the author put into this title.
examples.ja: 作者はこのタイトルにどんな含意を込めたのだろうか。

examples.en: There was a significant implication in the prime minister's visit to that country with that timing.
examples.ja: そのタイミングで首相がその国を訪問したことには、大きな含意があった。

examples.en: It is difficult for anyone to pick up on implications, but it can be said that people who are good at reading the implications in others’ words tend to succeed in their careers.
examples.ja: 誰にとっても含意を汲み取るのは難しいことだが、やはり人の言葉の含意を読み取ることが上手い人は出世しやすい傾向にあると言えるだろう。

4774.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Include</kanji> your <kanji>idea</kanji>s here, but think about the <vocabulary>implication</vocabulary>s they will result in too, especially considering you're just including them now. They have implications!

This word is quite formal, and therefore commonly used in academic or professional contexts.
4774.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: "Is it a ghost by any chance?" "No, it's just a shadow."
examples.ja: 「もしやお化け？」「いや、ただの影でしょ。」

examples.en: A black shadow creeped up to Koichi's back.
examples.ja: コウイチの後ろに黒い影がしのびよった。

examples.en: "I haven’t seen Fugu for weeks." "Oh, look. Here comes Fugu right now." "Well, speak of the devil. Hi, there. We were just talking about you."
examples.ja: 「私、もう何週間もフグを見てないわ。」「ほら、見て。ちょうど今フグが来たわよ。」「あら、噂をすれば影がさす、ね。こんにちは。私たち、今ちょうどあなたのことを話していたのよ。」

4775.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4775.reading_mnemonic: Just imagine the <vocabulary>shadow</vocabulary> of a <reading>cage</reading> (かげ). Lots of long bars. Looks good.

examples.en: Due to the effects of the recession, many companies went bankrupt.
examples.ja: 不況の影響で、多くの企業が倒産した。

examples.en: The price of gold tends to rise during recessions.
examples.ja: 不況時に金の価格は上昇しやすい。

examples.en: As a Japanese language learning site with a distinctive ideology, WaniKani resembles a type of cult, and even in times of economic downturn, its devotees provide support.
examples.ja: ワニカニは独特の思想を布教する一種のカルトのような日本語学習サイトなので、不況の中でも信者たちが支えてくれている。
