4776.meaning_mnemonic: A "<kanji>not</kanji> <kanji>condition</kanji>" is where nothing is going well. How are things going? Not well. The condition is bad. We're in a <vocabulary>recession</vocabulary>.
4776.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: In Vietnam, it's difficult to even cross a street.
examples.ja: ベトナムでは道を渡るのも一苦労です。

examples.en: Please use the pedestrian crossing to cross the street properly.
examples.ja: ちゃんと横断歩道を渡ってください。

examples.en: After crossing the bridge, please turn right.
examples.ja: 橋を渡り終わったところで、右に曲がって下さい。

examples.en: Hey, give it up, Koichi. Even if Viet would help you out, it's impossible to swim and cross the pacific ocean.
examples.ja: コウイチ、やめときなよ。いくらビエトが手伝ってくれるからって、泳いで太平洋を渡るなんて無理だって。

4777.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>transit</kanji>, which is just another word for crossing through or crossing over. That's why this word is <vocabulary>to cross</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to cross over</vocabulary>.
4777.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: When he handed me the pen my heart was pounding.
examples.ja: 彼が私にペンを渡してくれた時、胸がどきどきした。

examples.en: When I handed in my resignation to the boss, my hands were shaking.
examples.ja: 上司に辞表を渡す時、手が震えました。

examples.en: I dialed the number that she had given me, but I couldn't reach her.
examples.ja: 渡された番号に電話を掛けてみたが、つながらなかった。

4778.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>transit</kanji>. It's also in the verb 渡る, which means "to cross." But with 渡す, it's more like you're sending something across instead, usually to another person. So 渡す means <vocabulary>to hand over</vocabulary>.

It can also mean <vocabulary>to ferry something across</vocabulary> a river, or <vocabulary>to lay something across</vocabulary> an expanse, like when you lay a plank over a pothole or build a bridge across a river.

To remember the す in 渡す, think of suing someone. When you <reading>sue</reading> (す) them, you have to hand over the papers to let them know you're suing. If you don't 渡す the papers, you can't sue!
4778.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: My father's low voice echoed throughout the room.
examples.ja: 父の低い声が部屋中に響いた。

examples.en: The singing voice of Ariana Grande reverberated in my heart even long after the video ended.
examples.ja: 動画が終わった後も、アリアナ・グランデの歌声が私の心にずっと響いていました。

examples.en: To win a major contract, we’ll need a great business proposition that resonates in our customers’ hearts.
examples.ja: 大きな契約を勝ち取るには、顧客の心に響く素晴らしい提案書が必要だ。

4779.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>echo</kanji> so the verb is <vocabulary>to echo</vocabulary>.
4779.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: <reading>He be</reading> (ひび) echoing... <reading>He be</reading> (ひび) echoing... <reading>He be</reading> (ひび) echoing... <reading>He be</reading> (ひび) echoing... <reading>He be</reading> (ひび) echoing...

examples.en: Even if I quit my job now, it doesn't have influence on my life.
examples.ja: 今、私が仕事を辞めても生活に影響はない。

examples.en: If Tofugu was swallowed up by a big business, what influence do you think it would have on us?
examples.ja: トーフグが大企業に吸収されたら、私達にはどんな影響があると思う？

examples.en: You should consider that working extra hours may have a negative influence on your health.
examples.ja: 残業は健康に悪影響を及ぼす可能性があるということを考えた方がいいですよ。

4780.meaning_mnemonic: In the <kanji>shadow</kanji>s you still <kanji>echo</kanji>. Your echo leaves the shadows and hits people, creating an <vocabulary>influence</vocabulary> on them. You're like the shadow person pulling the strings, making things do what you want... influencing them.
4780.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: They were a hundred votes short of getting elected.
examples.ja: 当選にはあと百票届かなかった。

examples.en: How did you get such a large amount of votes?
examples.ja: どうやってそんなに大量の票をゲットしたの？

examples.en: The idol smiled happily when she became the top vote recipient in the general election.
examples.ja: そのアイドルは、総選挙で自分が得票数１位になったとき、とてもうれしそうに笑った。

examples.en: Koichi defeated the other candidate with a majority of the votes and became the President of the United States of America.
examples.ja: コウイチは票の大半を得て相手候補者に圧勝し、アメリカ合衆国の大統領となった。

4781.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. It can also be <vocabulary>a vote</vocabulary>, because that's what ballots tend to do.
4781.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: Are you planning to vote at this election as well?
examples.ja: 今回の選挙でも投票するつもり？

examples.en: I forgot to transfer my residency, so I can't vote in this town yet.
examples.ja: 住民票を移すのを忘れてたので、この町ではまだ投票できないんです。

examples.en: In this company, every year all the workers have to vote to choose the CEO.
examples.ja: この会社では、毎年CEOを選ぶために全社員が投票することになっている。

4782.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Throw</kanji> a <kanji>ballot</kanji> in the ballot box <vocabulary>to vote</vocabulary>.
4782.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. You may have to think back to some other words using 投 to remember the on'yomi reading, 投資 for example.

examples.en: It's a sight I see every day, and yet I didn't notice it at all up until then.
examples.ja: 毎日のように見ている光景なのに、それまで全く気づかなかったよ。

examples.en: Please tell me about a scene that deeply lingers in your heart.
examples.ja: みなさんの心に深く残っている光景を教えてください。

examples.en: I've never seen such a beautiful spectacle before.
examples.ja: このような絵のように美しい光景は今までみたことがありません。

examples.en: Ahaha, this is quite a surreal sight, isn't it?
examples.ja: あはは、これは中々シュールな光景だね。

4783.meaning_mnemonic:
When <kanji>light</kanji> shines on a <kanji>scene</kanji>, it's still a <vocabulary>scene</vocabulary>. The light is here to create some drama, also making this a <vocabulary>sight</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>spectacle</vocabulary>.

光景 refers to a scene or sight that leaves an impression, whether it's unfolding in front of you or recalled in your mind. It's often used in a poetic way to describe moments that are especially vivid — whether touching, beautiful, striking, or painful.
4783.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It will be a long time before business confidence in Japan improves significantly.
examples.ja: 日本の景況感が大きく上向くのは、まだまだ先のことだろう。

examples.en: I called a friend who works at a securities company and asked about the business climate.
examples.ja: 証券会社で働く友人に電話を掛けて、景況を聞きました。

examples.en: This report summarizes the business climate of domestic, small and medium-sized enterprises.
examples.ja: 本レポートは、国内中小企業の景況動向について取りまとめたものです。

examples.en: Koichi wouldn't tell me about the economic climate at Tofugu, so I had Mami tell me about it secretly instead.
examples.ja: コウイチに聞いても教えてくれないので、マミにトーフグの景況についてこっそり教えてもらいました。

examples.en: Mr. Jim Rogers likely came to Japan to confirm the actual economic conditions, known as the "street corner sentiment," of the country.
examples.ja: ジム・ロジャーズ氏は、日本の実際の景況感、いわゆる「街角景況感」を確認するために来日したのでしょう。

4784.meaning_mnemonic: Take a look at this <kanji>scene</kanji> and the <kanji>condition</kanji> it’s in. This is the climate of the situation, but more specifically the <vocabulary>business climate</vocabulary>. This word is really only used to talk about the state of business and economic stuff, and tends to appear in technical writing.
4784.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Many towns in Germany value their cityscapes.
examples.ja: ドイツには、景観を大切にしている町が多い。

examples.en: Oh, that's going to ruin the scenery, isn't it?
examples.ja: あーあ、あれじゃあ、せっかくの景観が台無しだね。

examples.en: I really like Kyoto’s scenery.
examples.ja: 私は京都の景観がとても好きです。

examples.en: In Kyoto, an ordinance has been established to protect the cityscape.
examples.ja: 京都では、景観を守るための条例が定められています。

examples.en: The local government of this city has a solid landscape plan.
examples.ja: この市の自治体は景観計画をきちんと立てています。

4785.meaning_mnemonic:
Quite the <kanji>scene</kanji>, this <kanji>view</kanji> is. So what you're looking at is a <vocabulary>landscape</vocabulary>. This often refers to a <vocabulary>cityscape</vocabulary> or the general <vocabulary>scenery</vocabulary> of an area.

This is a formal word that’s commonly used in the context of urban planning or environmental design.
4785.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: You can see the whole city from here.
examples.ja: ここから、町の全景が見わたせるんです。

examples.en: If you have a drone, you can take a picture of the whole city!
examples.ja: ドローンがあれば、この都市の全景を写した写真がとれますよ！

examples.en: Well, I can't get a good picture of the whole building from this information.
examples.ja: うーん、この情報だけだと、建物の全景がうまくイメージできないな。

examples.en: I was expecting a breathtaking panorama of Mt. Fuji, but the reality of it was pretty pathetic.
examples.ja: 私は息を飲むような富士の全景を期待していたが、実際はかなりお粗末なものだった。

4786.meaning_mnemonic:
When you can see <kanji>all</kanji> the <kanji>scene</kanji> you have a <vocabulary>complete view</vocabulary>.

This is not a common word in everyday conversations, but it can be found in literature, art, film, photography, and travel writing to describe a panoramic or comprehensive view of a scene.
4786.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I’ll blur the foreground a bit.
examples.ja: 前景をちょっとぼかしてみます。

examples.en: Can you make this foreground layer invisible?
examples.ja: この前景レイヤー、見えなくしてみて。

examples.en: Isn't the tree standing in the foreground too prominent?
examples.ja: 前景に立っている木、目立ちすぎじゃない？

examples.en: How can I focus on something in the foreground with this camera?
examples.ja: このカメラでは、どうすれば前景の被写体にピントを合わせることができるんですか？

4787.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>front</kanji> <kanji>scene</kanji> is the <vocabulary>foreground</vocabulary>.

This word primarily refers to the visual foreground in art, photography, or theater. Unlike "foreground" in English, it’s not commonly used in a figurative sense to describe the most prominent aspect of situations.
4787.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The journalist persistently appealed against gender inequality in society through their articles.
examples.ja: その記者は、記事を通して男女不平等について社会に訴えつづけました。

examples.en: My direct supervisor was let go because many female workers complained about his sexual harassment.
examples.ja: 多くの女子社員がセクハラを訴えたため、私の直属の上司は首になりました。

examples.en: Salmon decided to sue Fugu's adulterous partner.
examples.ja: サーモンはフグの不倫相手を訴えることにした。

4788.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>sue</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to sue</vocabulary>.
4788.reading_mnemonic: <reading>YOU TA</reading>KE (うった) MY THINGS, I AM GOING <vocabulary>TO SUE</vocabulary> YOU!

examples.en: Apparently they are filing a criminal complaint against Viet's yakuza group.
examples.ja: あいつら、ビエトの組に対する告訴の手続きをしているみたいだぜ。

examples.en: I don't know yet because I haven't heard the details of the criminal complaint.
examples.ja: まだ告訴内容を聞いていないので分かりません。

examples.en: I won't take legal action as long as you pay me every month.
examples.ja: 毎月きちんとお金を払って頂けるなら、告訴はしません。

4789.meaning_mnemonic:
I've <kanji>announce</kanji>d I'm going to <kanji>sue</kanji> you. To do this, I need to file a <vocabulary>criminal complaint</vocabulary> against you. What's the nature of my complaint? Uh... You suck.

告訴 is a legal term used when someone submits a criminal complaint to the authorities and formally asks them to investigate and prosecute a crime. It's not just any old complaint or accusation — it's an official legal action that carries serious weight.
4789.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I lost all of my delicious bacon to that litigation.
examples.ja: あの訴訟のせいで、かくしていた美味しいベーコンを全て失った。

examples.en: Lawsuits are very time-consuming and expensive.
examples.ja: 訴訟には時間とお金がめっちゃかかるよ。

examples.en: The documents related to the lawsuit have all been properly filed by the lawyer.
examples.ja: その訴訟に関する書類は、弁護士によって全てきちんとファイルされている。

4790.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>sue</kanji> and bring about a <kanji>lawsuit</kanji>, you are bringing about a <vocabulary>lawsuit</vocabulary>.
4790.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Viet was arrested for cheating Koichi out of his money.
examples.ja: ビエトは、コウイチをペテンにかけて金を巻き上げた罪で逮捕された。

examples.en: My friend who works for the Portland City Police secretly told me information that Viet is likely to be arrested soon.
examples.ja: ポートランド市警で働いている友達が、ビエトがそろそろ逮捕されるらしいという情報をこっそり教えてくれた。

examples.en: I was almost arrested by mistake for molestation on the rush hour train.
examples.ja: ラッシュ時の電車内で痴漢行為を働いたとして、危うく誤認逮捕されるところだった。

4791.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>apprehend</kanji> and <kanji>catch</kanji> someone, that leads to an <vocabulary>arrest</vocabulary>.
4791.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Of course, my allowance from my parents wasn't enough, so I worked part-time to supplement my living expenses.
examples.ja: もちろん、親からの仕送りだけでは足りなかったので、生活費はアルバイトで補っていました。

examples.en: Can we make up for the lack of vegetables by drinking vegetable juice?
examples.ja: 野菜ジュースで、野菜不足を補うことはできるのでしょか。

examples.en: To compensate for the empty spot, I joined the bowling game.
examples.ja: 欠員を補うために、ボーリングゲームに参加しました。

examples.en: People lose about 2500 ml of fluids per day. To make up for it, you need to take in the same amount of fluids from food or drinks.
examples.ja: 人は1日に約2500mlの水分を失います。それを補うためには、食べ物や飲み物から同じ量の水分を取り入れる必要があります。

4792.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>supplement</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to supplement</vocabulary>.

Note that this word is generally considered relatively formal in tone.
4792.reading_mnemonic: Do we need <vocabulary>to supplement</vocabulary> the team with more specialists? “<reading>Oh</reading>, <reading>Gee</reading>ks? <reading>Nah</reading>! (おぎな) We have plenty of those already, and <vocabulary>to compensate for</vocabulary> the lack of workers, we can just make them work longer hours. They'll love that.

examples.en: All of the candidates wore glasses.
examples.ja: 全ての候補者がメガネを掛けていた。

examples.en: There was a famous model among the applicants.
examples.ja: 候補者の中には、有名なモデルもいました。

examples.en: Academically speaking, the candidate would be very useful, but he has such a bad personality.
examples.ja: 学歴的には、候補者として十分通用するはずが、彼は性格に難があるからね。

4793.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>candidate</kanji> is <kanji>someone</kanji> who's a <kanji>supplement</kanji> to the entire political system. Despite being a supplement, they're still a <vocabulary>candidate</vocabulary> nonetheless, unless they can win!
4793.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: In my retirement, I want to live in Hawaii, known for its mild climate.
examples.ja: 老後はおだやかな気候で知られるハワイに住みたいです。

examples.en: How different are the climates of Portland and Tokyo?
examples.ja: ポートランドと東京の気候はどのぐらい違いますか。

examples.en: Due to the effects of global warming, the climate in the Arctic region is changing.
examples.ja: 地球温暖化の影響により、北極圏の気候が変化しています。

examples.en: I got off to a good start with my new job, considering the threatening climate.
examples.ja: 気候は荒れ模様だが、新しい仕事ではいいスタートが切れた。

4794.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>energy</kanji> of the <kanji>climate</kanji> is the <vocabulary>climate</vocabulary>. High energy? Climate. Low energy. Climate.
4794.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The schedule for the day depends on the weather.
examples.ja: 当日の予定は、天候に左右されます。

examples.en: It appears that the weather won't be good for a month.
examples.ja: ここ一か月は天候が優れないみたいです。

examples.en: The weather was favorable on that day.
examples.ja: 当日は、天候に恵まれました。

examples.en: All flights have been cancelled due to bad weather conditions.
examples.ja: 悪天候のため、全便欠航となりました。

examples.en: I know there will be extra costs if we travel during peak season, but the weather will be the best around that time.
examples.ja: 繁忙期に旅行をすれば費用が嵩むのは分かっているけど、そうはいっても天候もその時期が一番いいからね。

4795.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Heaven</kanji>'s <kanji>climate</kanji> is <vocabulary>the weather</vocabulary>.

Compared to 天気, this is a more formal term used to describe the weather over the period of one day, multiple days, or even weeks.
4795.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Seasonal greetings change depending on the month.
examples.ja: 時候のあいさつは月によって変わります。

examples.en: It's now the season where colorful leaves dance with joy, riding the northern wind. How is everyone doing?
examples.ja: 北風にノッて、カラフルな木の葉がダンスを楽しむ時候となりましたが、みなさまお元気ですか？

examples.en: People usually begin letters with a seasonal greeting in Japan. This website has many example sentences for it, so please have a look when you have time.
examples.ja: 日本では、通常手紙は時候の挨拶から書き始められます。このウェブサイトには、時候の挨拶の例文がたくさん載っているので、時間のある時に確認してみて下さい。

examples.en: In Japanese, 時候 means "season", whereas in Chinese it means "time".
examples.ja: 日本語では「時候」は「季節」の意味で使われますが、中国語では「時候」は「時」の意味で使われます。

4796.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>time</kanji>'s <kanji>climate</kanji> is the <vocabulary>seasonal climate</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>seasonal weather</vocabulary>.

You’ll almost always see this word used in the context of 時候のあいさつ (seasonal greetings). It's a customary practice to start a letter by discussing something related to the current season before addressing the main topic.
4796.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Recently, I've been so busy with work that I haven't been able to spend any time with my kids at all.
examples.ja: 最近仕事が忙しくて、全然子供に構ってあげられてないんだよね。

examples.en: I don't mind what you think about me, but could you please stop badmouthing my friends as well?
examples.ja: 君が僕のことをどう思おうと構わないけど、友達のことまで悪く言うのはやめてくれるかな？

examples.en: I don't want to be an attention seeker.
examples.ja: 構ってちゃんにはなりたくないなあ。

examples.en: "This one will cost about a million yen more." "I still don’t mind. I’ll take it."
examples.ja: 「こちらの品は百万円ほどお高くなります。」「それでも構わないよ。それを頂くよ。」

4797.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>care</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to care about</vocabulary>.

This word generally implies a more direct physical or verbal expression of care, rather than just mentally caring about someone or something. The exception is when it's used in the negative, like 構わない (I don't mind).
4797.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Do you care a lot about grammar? I don't care, unless it has to do with <reading>comma</reading>s (かま). Then I do flip out.

examples.en: This movie is composed of two parts.
examples.ja: この映画は二部構成になっている。

examples.en: What is your family structure?
examples.ja: あなたの家族構成を教えてください。

examples.en: Even if the plot is well structured, it won't be interesting if the dialogue is trite.
examples.ja: 構成のしっかりしたプロットでも、台詞がありきたりだと面白くなくなる。

examples.en: I'd never seen the grammar that makes up this sentence before.
examples.ja: この文を構成する文法は今まで見たことがありませんでした。

4798.meaning_mnemonic:
If you <kanji>set up</kanji> something so that it <kanji>become</kanji>s a certain way, that's the <vocabulary>composition</vocabulary> of this thing. That's its <vocabulary>structure</vocabulary>.

構成 refers to the process of assembling several elements to create a cohesive whole or the assembled whole itself. It can be applied to various contexts, such as social structures, family compositions, artistic works, or the configuration of materials.
4798.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Oh wow, it's quite big. I wonder if I can carry it home.
examples.ja: うわっ、結構大きいですね。持って帰れるかな？

examples.en: This has a fairly fancy price, yeah?
examples.ja: 結構なお値段がするんですね。

examples.en: "Would you like something to drink?" "No, thank you. I'm good."
examples.ja: 「何か飲みますか？」 「いいえ、結構です。」

examples.en: "Would you like anything else today?" "No, that's all. Thank you."
examples.ja: 「今日は他には何か、ございませんか？」「いいえ。それだけで結構です。」

examples.en: "Do you think there would be less crime if bacon was free?" "I'd say it would make quite a difference."
examples.ja: 「ベーコンを無料にすれば、犯罪は減ると思いますか？」「結構効果はあると思います。」

4799.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Bind</kanji> and <kanji>set up</kanji> everything so it is <vocabulary>fine</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>fairly</vocabulary>  <vocabulary>sufficient</vocabulary>. 

This word is often used to express that something is adequate or satisfactory, to politely decline an offer or invitation, or to indicate a relatively high degree or extent of something, like:

"No thank you" 結構です
"That's fine, no more" もう結構です
"It's fairly big" 結構大きい
etc.
4799.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The けつ shortens to けっ.

examples.en: My wife likes patterns with small flowers.
examples.ja: 私の妻は、小さな花の模様が好きです。

examples.en: I want to change the layout of my room soon.
examples.ja: そろそろ部屋の模様替えをしたいな。

examples.en: Koichi is trying to make a curtain with a pattern of his face on it, but it's probably best to stop him, right?
examples.ja: コウイチが、コウイチの顔の模様のカーテンを作ろうとしてるんだけど、さすがにやめさせた方がいいよね？

4800.meaning_mnemonic: 様 uses its alternative meaning "manner" here, so we have an <kanji>imitation</kanji> <kanji>manner</kanji>. An imitation of the same manner over and over creates a <vocabulary>pattern</vocabulary>.
4800.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You might remember the on'yomi for 様 from the vocab 〜の様に, but here's a mnemonic for it just in case:

You see a <vocabulary>pattern</vocabulary> in your <reading>yo</reading>gurt (よう). Could this be a divine message? Or maybe this yogurt is just way past its expiration date. Either way, a pattern in your yogurt is something you ought to pay attention to.

examples.en: What size of attendance are you expecting for this event?
examples.ja: このイベントの集客人数の規模って、どのくらいを見てますか？

examples.en: I am a little anxious because I have only participated in small-sized projects.
examples.ja: 規模が小さいプロジェクトにしか参加したことがないので、ちょっと不安です。

examples.en: It may be just a small scale firm to you, but I’m proud of my parents’ company.
examples.ja: あなたにとってはただの規模の小さな会社かもしれませんが、私は両親の会社に誇りをもっています。

4801.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>standard</kanji> of <kanji>imitation</kanji> is to imitate to the <vocabulary>scale</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>scope</vocabulary> of the original.
4801.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Can you go to a fish shop and get fresh tuna?
examples.ja: 魚屋さんに行って、新鮮なマグロを買ってきてちょうだい。

examples.en: Today, I went to a mountain and breathed some fresh air.
examples.ja: 今日はちょっと山に行って新鮮な空気をすってきました。

examples.en: I always worked overtime at my last job until I was told to stop, so it’s very new to me to leave work at five o’clock every day.
examples.ja: 前の職場では、止めろと言われるまでいつも残業していたので、毎日五時に退社するのはとても新鮮です。

4802.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>New</kanji> and <kanji>fresh</kanji> is <vocabulary>fresh</vocabulary> (has to be new if you want it to be fresh, after all).

This word is used to describe fresh vegetables, fish, air, and new ideas or experiences, but is not commonly used to describe freshly made food or drinks. This is because the word emphasizes the inherent freshness of the thing being described, rather than its recent production.
4802.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: "That's a very vivid-colored shirt, yeah?" "Your socks are really vivid, too"
examples.ja: 「ずい分と鮮やかな色のシャツですね。」「あなたのくつ下も実に鮮やかですね。」

examples.en: The new personnel manager brilliantly solved the problem regarding mandatory overtime without pay.
examples.ja: 新しい人事部長は、強制的なサービス残業に関する問題を鮮やかに解決してのけた。

examples.en: Viet splendidly slipped through a police dragnet.
examples.ja: ビエトは、警察の捜査網を鮮やかにくぐり抜けた。

4803.meaning_mnemonic: Alright, so it's not quite the same, but something that is <kanji>fresh</kanji> is also <vocabulary>vivid</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>splendid</vocabulary>. I know those are a couple things I'd associate with freshness. Try to make the connection here before moving on.
4803.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: This <vocabulary>vivid</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>splendid</vocabulary> fresh fish is MINE! You grab the <reading>other</reading> (あざ) one that's not as vivid and splendid. This one is mine.

examples.en: People were lining up at the fresh fish section at the grocery store for some reason.
examples.ja: なぜかスーパーの鮮魚コーナーに列ができていました。

examples.en: We always try to procure natural fresh fish.
examples.ja: いつも天然の鮮魚を仕入れるようにしています。

examples.en: Our platter with five kinds of sashimi is made with just-caught fresh fish, delivered directly from the central market, so it's delicious.
examples.ja: うちのお造り五種盛りは、中央市場から直送してもらった獲れ立ての鮮魚で作ってるから、美味しいよ。

examples.en: Employees cannot waive their right to receiving fresh fish as a benefit as long as they work for my fish shop.
examples.ja: 俺の魚屋で働いている限り、従業員は福利厚生として鮮魚をもらう権利を、放棄することはできないぜ。

4804.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Fresh</kanji> <kanji>fish</kanji> is <vocabulary>fresh fish</vocabulary> (and the best fish, nom nom nom).

This is a fairly specialized word that you’d mostly see at a market. To describe fresh fish more generally, you can just say 新鮮な魚.
4804.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The medicine is finally starting to take effect.
examples.ja: やっと薬が効いてきた。

examples.en: I heard that this hot spring is very effective for stiff shoulders.
examples.ja: この温泉は肩こりによく効くらしいです。

examples.en: No, the brakes didn't work!
examples.ja: いや、ブレーキが効かなかったんだよ！

examples.en: I wonder if the advertisement has finally started to have an effect?
examples.ja: ようやく広告が効いてきたのかな？

examples.en: It seems that Koichi's ear-bashing yesterday was effective for Michael.
examples.ja: コウイチの昨日のお説教がマイケルに効いたみたいです。

4805.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>effective</kanji>. The verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to be effective</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to work effectively</vocabulary> (since "to effective" doesn't make sense).

This word is used to describe something that works effectively and as intended, such as medicine that achieves the desired effect or brakes that effectively stop the car.
4805.reading_mnemonic: What is particularly effective? It's your <reading>key</reading> (き). It's effective at opening your house door.

examples.en: Anything will show its effect by continuing it.
examples.ja: 何事も、続けることで、効果が現れてくるものです。

examples.en: I wonder if these measures are really effective.
examples.ja: 果たしてこの対策に効果はあるのだろうか。

examples.en: This medicine has the effect of relieving pain.
examples.ja: この薬には痛みを和らげる効果があります。

examples.en: I heard swimming at the gym is the most effective way to lose weight.
examples.ja: ジムで水泳をすることが、最も効果的なダイエット方法だと聞きました。

4806.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>fruit</kanji> of something that's <kanji>effective</kanji> is <vocabulary>an effect</vocabulary>.
4806.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Isn't it more efficient for the two of us to do it together rather than you doing it by yourself?
examples.ja: 一人よりも二人でやった方が効率いいでしょ？

examples.en: Koichi is always thinking on how he can efficiently proceed with his work.
examples.ja: コウイチは仕事を効率よく進めるためにどうすればいいのか常々考えています。

examples.en: Keep in mind that efficiency is our top priority.
examples.ja: 効率が第一だということを、しっかり心に刻んで置いてください。

4807.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>effective</kanji> <kanji>percent</kanji> shows how effective you are. If you're at an effective percent of 80%, that's your <vocabulary>efficiency</vocabulary>.
4807.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That treaty will cease to be in effect from tomorrow.
examples.ja: その条約は明日で効力を失う。

examples.en: Your presentation today seemed like it was a bit weaker in its effectiveness compared to the last one.
examples.ja: あなたの今日のプレゼンテーションは、前回に比べて効力が少し弱いような気がしました。

examples.en: If you take this medicine, you will be able to fly in the sky. However, please be careful because if the effect of the medicine wears off while you are flying, it could be very dangerous.
examples.ja: この薬を飲むと、あなたは空を飛べるようになります。でも、飛んでいる時に薬の効力が切れると大変なので、気をつけてくださいね。

examples.en: When a mediation agreement is reached, the mediation report created thereafter holds the same legal effect as a court judgment.
examples.ja: 調停が成立したときに作成される調停調書は、判決と同様の効力を有します。

4808.meaning_mnemonic:
Something's <kanji>effective</kanji> <kanji>power</kanji> is its <vocabulary>effectiveness</vocabulary>. If it has effective power, it remains <vocabulary>in effect</vocabulary>.

This word usually refers to the legal force or effectiveness of a law, agreement, contract, or treaty, but it can also be used to talk about the efficacy of other things, such as medicine.
4808.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I am not affiliated with an entertainment agency.
examples.ja: 私は芸能事務所には所属していません。

examples.en: Koichi belongs to a kendo team in Portland.
examples.ja: コウイチはポートランドの剣道チームに所属しています。

examples.en: When you're absent due to illness, you should turn in a doctor's note to your department just in case.
examples.ja: 病欠のときは、念の為、所属部署に診断書を提出しておいた方がいいよ。

4809.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>place</kanji> of <kanji>belong</kanji>ing describes your <vocabulary>affiliation</vocabulary>. It’s where you <vocabulary>belong to</vocabulary>. 

This is often used to describe a person’s affiliation or membership to a particular organization, team, or group.
4809.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I am not a type of person who belongs to a group.
examples.ja: グループに属するのは私のガラじゃないんです。

examples.en: Whose group were you in when you were in grade four?
examples.ja: 四年生の時は誰のグループに属していたの？

examples.en: Tulips are flowers that fall under the Liliaceae family.
examples.ja: チューリップはユリ科に属する花です。

examples.en: The starting month of the service will be the month in which the service start date belongs to. The service start date will be the day on which we confirm that the customer has received the SIM card.
examples.ja: サービス開始月は、サービス開始日が属する月となります。サービス開始日は、お客様がSIMカードの受け取られたことを弊社が確認した日となります。

4810.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>belong</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to belong to</vocabulary>.

属する is a formal term for describing someone or something’s belonging to or being part of a group, category or classification.
4810.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the one you learned with the kanji. This kanji is going <vocabulary>to belong to</vocabulary> you.

examples.en: I am allergic to metal.
examples.ja: 私には金属アレルギーがあります。

examples.en: Michael stood a metal ladder against the roof.
examples.ja: マイケルは、屋根に金属のハシゴを掛けた。

examples.en: The metal-plating factory is thriving despite the challenging business climate.
examples.ja: 厳しい景況にもかかわらず、あの金属メッキ工場は成長を続けている。

4811.meaning_mnemonic: Even <kanji>gold</kanji> <kanji>belong</kanji>s to a family... the family of <vocabulary>metal</vocabulary>s!
4811.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: She is a capricious woman, but I’ve gotten used to it.
examples.ja: あいつは気の代わりやすい女だけど、もう慣れたよ。

examples.en: Have you already gotten accustomed to the new environment?
examples.ja: 新しい環境にはもう慣れましたか。

examples.en: Could you bring the hem up for me? I’m not really used to sewing.
examples.ja: 裾上げをお願いできますか？自分ではあまり縫い物に慣れてなくて。

4812.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>accustomed</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to become accustomed</vocabulary>.
4812.reading_mnemonic: What have you <vocabulary>become accustomed to</vocabulary>? All the <reading>Na</reading>rwhals (な) you hang out with. They take some getting used to.

examples.en: Nail biting is one of my bad habits.
examples.ja: ツメをかむのは、私の悪い習慣の一つです。

examples.en: I have made a habit of jogging every day.
examples.ja: 私は毎日ジョギングをすることを習慣にしています。

examples.en: Stretching before work is a good habit that can increase productivity.
examples.ja: 仕事の前にストレッチをすることは、生産性を高める良い習慣です。

examples.en: "I thought you quit smoking." "Well, they say old habits die hard."
examples.ja: 「たばこ、止めたんじゃなかったの？」「まあ、ほら、『古い習慣はなかなかなくならない』って言うだろ。」

4813.meaning_mnemonic: I've <kanji>learn</kanji>ed to be <kanji>accustomed</kanji> to this. It has become my <vocabulary>custom</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>habit</vocabulary>.
4813.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Compared to 80 years ago, Japan has become really wealthy.
examples.ja: 80年前と比べると、日本は本当に豊かになりました。

examples.en: Kyushu is a place that's rich in nature.
examples.ja: 九州は自然が豊かな所です。

examples.en: Reading books will enrich your mind.
examples.ja: 本を読むと心が豊かになりますよ。

4814.meaning_mnemonic:
This is the same as the kanji 豊, making it <vocabulary>plentiful</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>abundant</vocabulary>. It can also mean <vocabulary>rich</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>wealthy</vocabulary>.

豊か is a versatile and nuanced word that conveys a sense of abundance and richness in various aspects of life. It implies a positive and prosperous state, going beyond just material wealth or great quantity, and encompassing overall well-being and fulfillment.
4814.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You discovered <vocabulary>plentiful</vocabulary> <reading>yu</reading>rt <reading>ta</reading>cos (ゆた) inside the yurt you’re staying in. Picture yourself savoring the richly flavored yurt tacos beside your yurt while being immersed in the abundant nature around you.

examples.en: I like a woman with a round body, rather than a skinny one like a model.
examples.ja: モデルみたいに細い人より、豊満な体つきの女性の方がタイプです。

examples.en: I like to draw women with plump figures and ample busts.
examples.ja: 私はふくよかで豊満なバストをもつ女性の絵をかくのが好きなんです。

examples.en: She has full breasts and always has lovely cleavage.
examples.ja: 彼女は豊満な胸をもっており、いつも美しい谷間を覗かせている。

4815.meaning_mnemonic: If you're plentiful and full, you could say you're plump or full-figured... in other words, you're not a snack, you're the Whole. Damn. Meal. This is a literary expression used to describe the physical appearance of a woman's body, often focusing on a well-endowed chest.
4815.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It seems that the very satisfactory result made our president very happy.
examples.ja: 満足な結果が得られて、社長は本当にうれしそうでした。

examples.en: My dad nodded with a happy face when he saw the beautiful scenery.
examples.ja: 父は、その美しい景色を見て、満足そうな顔をしてうなずいた。

examples.en: My business is doing well so I finally feel satisfied.
examples.ja: ビジネスが順調なので、ようやく満足しています。

4816.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just remember that the reading for 足 in this one is ぞく because of that pesky rendaku.

examples.en: The stars are beautifully visible on a night with a full moon.
examples.ja: 満月の夜は、星がきれいに見えます。

examples.en: Fugu has such a round face like a full moon, doesn't he?
examples.ja: フグって、満月の様に真ん丸い顔をしてるよね。

examples.en: I heard that tomorrow night will be a full moon. I hope it’s not cloudy.
examples.ja: 明日の夜は満月なんだって。曇らないといいね。

4817.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: If possible, I don’t want to take a jam-packed bus.
examples.ja: できれば満員のバスには乗りたくない。

examples.en: The concert hall was a full house as expected.
examples.ja: コンサート会場はやっぱり満員だった。

examples.en: I hate that I have to stand in a packed train until I arrive at Shinjuku station every morning.
examples.ja: 毎朝、新宿駅に着くまで、満員電車の中に立っていなくてはいけないのが苦痛です。

4818.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Full</kanji> of <kanji>member</kanji>s, so sorry, no more room. This place is a <vocabulary>full house</vocabulary>. That means there is <vocabulary>no vacancy</vocabulary> here.
4818.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: When I get a perfect score, my teacher draws a flower on the paper.
examples.ja: 満点をとったら、先生に花丸をもらえるの。

examples.en: How could you eat such a bountiful breakfast?
examples.ja: よくこんなにボリューム満点の朝ご飯が食べられるよね。

examples.en: I found an effective way of studying, and thanks to that I've got a perfect score on that test.
examples.ja: 効果的な勉強方法を見つけたおかげで、テストで満点を取ることができました。

examples.en: After watching a movie that was full of thrills, I got hungry. Let's go eat a nutritionally packed set meal!
examples.ja: 迫力満点の映画を見たらお腹がすいたよ。栄養満点の定食でも食べに行こうぜ！

4819.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Full</kanji> <kanji>point</kanji>s are when you get a <vocabulary>perfect score</vocabulary>.

満点 can also be used to describe a state of being at the pinnacle of a certain quality or standard, such as サービス満点 (excellent service) or 栄養満点 (highly nutritious).
4819.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: First, check your own level of obesity!
examples.ja: まずは自分の肥満度をチェックしてみましょう！

examples.en: The major cause of your obesity is probably a lack of exercise.
examples.ja: 肥満の主な原因は、おそらく運動不足でしょうね。

examples.en: There is an increasing number of people with "hidden obesity" who have a body weight within the standard range but have a high body fat percentage.
examples.ja: 体重は標準範囲内だけど体脂肪率が高い「隠れ肥満」の人が増えています。

4820.meaning_mnemonic: Does being <kanji>obese</kanji> mean you're always <kanji>full</kanji>? Of course not. But clearly that's what the people who coined the Japanese word for <vocabulary>obesity</vocabulary> thought... You can see there are some implicit biases in these kanji!
4820.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I spread manure in the rice field.
examples.ja: 田んぼに肥料をまきました。

examples.en: Cow poop will become good fertilizer.
examples.ja: 牛のフンはいい肥料になるんだよ。

examples.en: I had no idea how to handle the conflict among the workers at the fertilizer factory.
examples.ja: 肥料工場での社員間のいざこざについて、どう対処していいか全くわかりませんでした。

4821.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>fee</kanji> for being <kanji>obese</kanji> is lots of <vocabulary>manure</vocabulary> coming out of your butt. If you eat a lot you'll poop a lot of manure.
4821.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I wonder why ramen shop workers often wrap a towel around their heads.
examples.ja: どうしてラーメン屋さんはタオルを頭に巻いてることが多いのかな？

examples.en: I wanted to make rice balls wrapped in meat, but I had trouble wrapping the meat around them.
examples.ja: 肉巻きおにぎりを作りたかったんだけど、お肉がうまく巻けなかったの。

examples.en: This is how we make sushi - we roll it up in seaweed like this... roll, roll, roll.
examples.ja: こんな感じで、お寿司を海苔でクルクル巻いていきます。

examples.en: I spent two hours curling my hair, but it still doesn’t curl well.
examples.ja: 二時間かけて髪を巻いたが、それでもあまりうまく巻けなかった。

4822.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>scroll</kanji>. But, you don't "to scroll." What do you do to scrolls, though? You roll them up, making this word "<vocabulary>to roll</vocabulary>."

This word can also mean <vocabulary>to wind</vocabulary>, like when winding thread or a watch, or <vocabulary>to wrap</vocabulary> when involving a rolling or coiling motion, like wrapping sushi in seaweed or wrapping a cozy scarf around your neck.
4822.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: The thing you are rolling up is your <reading>ma</reading> (ま). She's going wild again, so you throw her into a blanket and roll her up to hold her down.

examples.en: I only have one volume of this manga.
examples.ja: このマンガ、一巻しか持っていないんだよ。

examples.en: The first volume of this novel was really interesting, but you know…
examples.ja: この小説、一巻はすごく面白かったんだけどね。

examples.en: Of course, I have all the volumes from the first to the latest!
examples.ja: もちろん一巻から最新巻まで全部揃ってるよ！

examples.en: In the first volume, all sources are cited in the footnotes.
examples.ja: 一巻では、全ての引用に脚注がつけられ出典が記されています。

4823.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>One</kanji> <kanji>scroll</kanji> is one scroll back in the day, but now it refers to books and means <vocabulary>one volume</vocabulary>.
4823.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. いち goes to いっ.

examples.en: This economics textbook has the first volume and the last volume.
examples.ja: この経済学の教科書は上巻と下巻があるんだよ。

examples.en: I thought I bought the first volume, but it was actually the last volume.
examples.ja: 上巻を買ったつもりが下巻を買ってしまっていた。

examples.en: In the final volume, rural scenery is the main topic.
examples.ja: 下巻では、主に田舎の景色について語られています。

4824.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>scroll</kanji> that's <kanji>below</kanji> is the last scroll you read, making it the <vocabulary>last volume</vocabulary>.
4824.reading_mnemonic: The 下 uses the alternative reading of げ but 巻 is all good and normal.

examples.en: Since it was a light novel, I was able to finish the first volume in thirty minutes.
examples.ja: 肩のこらない小説だったので、上巻は三十分で読めた。

examples.en: The first volume was full of stereotyped expressions.
examples.ja: 上巻には、型にはまったような事ばかりが書かれていたよ。

examples.en: The ending of the first volume was a real cliffhanger.
examples.ja: 上巻の終わりは、すごく続きが気になる感じで終わった。

4825.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>above</kanji> <kanji>scroll</kanji> is the top scroll, the one you read first. It's the <vocabulary>first volume</vocabulary>. Many Japanese books come in parts, so look for this if you want to get the first one.
4825.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I am glad because the second volume of the novel that I was looking forward to is finally on sale.
examples.ja: 楽しみにしていた小説の第二巻が発売されてうれしい。

examples.en: Why do you have two volumes of the same book?
examples.ja: どうして同じ本を二巻も持ってるの？

examples.en: In the second volume, they made an appendix for all sources that are cited.
examples.ja: 二巻では、引用の出典に関する別表が作成されました。

4826.meaning_mnemonic: The number <kanji>two</kanji> <kanji>scroll</kanji> is the <vocabulary>second volume</vocabulary>. With Japanese books, they often come in pieces with groups of three being common. This represents the <vocabulary>second volume</vocabulary>.
4826.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I’m searching for my grandmother. She has Alzheimer's and hasn’t come home since yesterday.
examples.ja: 祖母を捜しているんです。アルツハイマーがあって、昨日から家に帰ってないんです。

examples.en: Since yesterday, the police and townspeople have been searching for a missing boy in the mountains, but it seems that he hasn't been found yet.
examples.ja: 昨日から、警察や町の人たちが、山で行方不明の男の子を捜しているんだけど、まだ見つかってないらしいよ。

examples.en: I will definitely find the real culprit.
examples.ja: 真犯人は必ずオレが捜し出してみせるさ。

examples.en: I am a private detective in a very niche field, and my job is to search for paintings that have been stolen from art museums.
examples.ja: 私はすごくニッチな分野の探偵で、美術館から盗まれた絵画を捜す仕事をしています。

4827.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>search</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to search for</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to seek</vocabulary>.
4827.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You're searching all around for a "<reading>sagger</reading>" (さが) on your body. This is a flap of skin that is sagging on your body really far, and you probably should get it removed.

examples.en: When I cooperated with the police investigation, I received a hard candy as a token of gratitude.
examples.ja: 警察の捜査に協力したら、お礼にアメをもらいました。

examples.en: The police are investigating the case caused by Viet's subordinate.
examples.ja: 警察は、ビエトの部下が起こした事件について、捜査しています。

examples.en: Viet and his gang deftly evaded the police manhunt.
examples.ja: ビエト達は、警察の捜査の手をたくみにかわした。

examples.en: The investigation revealed that the suspect's alibi was false.
examples.ja: 捜査により、犯人のアリバイが偽物だと判明しました。

examples.en: I’m going to draw up some important documents for a criminal investigation today.
examples.ja: 本日は捜査に関する重要書類を作成する予定です。

4828.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>search</kanji> and <kanji>inspect</kanji> things, you are probably part of a <vocabulary>criminal investigation</vocabulary>. You may even be subject to a <vocabulary>manhunt</vocabulary>.
4828.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: "You almost strangled that guy to death!" "I’m sorry. I went too far."
examples.ja: 「あんた、もう少しであの男を絞殺しかけたのよ！」「ごめん。やりすぎたよ。」

examples.en: When Viet was able to avoid being killed by strangling, he dropped to his knees and breathed heavily.
examples.ja: 絞殺をまぬがれたビエトは、ひざをついて、肩で息をした。

examples.en: However, the culprit was found strangled to death on the beach.
examples.ja: しかし、犯人は絞殺死体となって海岸で発見された。

examples.en: The cause of death was determined to be "strangulation" according to the autopsy results.
examples.ja: 検死の結果、死因は「絞殺」と断定されました。

4829.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>strangle</kanji> <kanji>kill</kanji> is <vocabulary>murder by strangling</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>strangling to death</vocabulary>.

This is a pretty formal word that you’d see most in police reports and detective novels.
4829.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I put a kettle on the stove while pumping out my breast milk.
examples.ja: 母乳を絞りながら、コンロにやかんをかけました。

examples.en: I can't believe that you eat food with hands that you didn't wash after wringing out a dust cloth.
examples.ja: ぞうきんを絞った手を洗わないでそのまま食べ物を食べるなんて信じられない！

examples.en: I rack my brain every day about how to manage my relationship with my mean boss.
examples.ja: 意地悪な上司との関係をどうやって保つか、毎日知恵を絞っています。

4830.meaning_mnemonic: You've learned that the kanji 絞 means <kanji>strangle</kanji>. 絞る, on the other hand, means <vocabulary>to wring out</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to squeeze</vocabulary> something like a towel, or <vocabulary>to narrow down</vocabulary> ideas.
4830.reading_mnemonic: Your friend wants <vocabulary>to wring out</vocabulary> a towel, but before she does so <reading>she bow</reading>s (しぼ) to the towel to show her respect for it.

examples.en: I always feel tense when I talk to that senior.
examples.ja: あの先輩と話をすると、いつも肩がこるんだよね。

examples.en: Don't get bothered by it and just ignore whatever that older graduate says about you, okay?
examples.ja: 先輩に何を言われても、気にせず無視すればいいんだからね。

examples.en: My superior isn’t a bad guy, but he and I just haven’t been able to hit it off.
examples.ja: 俺の先輩、悪い人では無いんだけどさ、ただちょっと俺とは反りが合わないんだよね。

4831.meaning_mnemonic: My <kanji>comrade</kanji> who came <kanji>before</kanji> me is my <vocabulary>senior</vocabulary>, my senpai (せんぱい).
4831.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well, but just remember that the second kanji is read as ぱい because of the rendaku on はい.

examples.en: Oh, this guy is my junior from high school.
examples.ja: あ、コイツ、オレの高校の時の後輩。

examples.en: Tomorrow, I'm planning to go for drinks with my junior colleague from work.
examples.ja: 明日、会社の後輩と飲みに行く予定なんだ。

examples.en: I don't really like the formalities of senior-junior relationships. We're only one year apart in age, so you can speak casually.
examples.ja: 先輩後輩の関係って、堅苦しくて好きじゃないんだよね。年、一つしか変わらないんだし、タメ語でいいよ。

examples.en: I’ll take care of you, no matter what happens because you’re my favorite underclassmen.
examples.ja: お前は俺のお気に入りの後輩だから、どんなことがあってもちゃんと面倒みてやるよ。

4832.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The reading for 後 is the long こう reading, though. Just think of your junior being <reading>こう</reading>いち.

examples.en: Apparently, this café is popular with the older crowd.
examples.ja: このカフェは年輩の方に人気だそうです。

examples.en: Next to me, an elderly woman was drinking coffee by herself.
examples.ja: となりの席では、ご年輩の女性が一人でコーヒーを飲んでいらっしゃいました。

examples.en: The other driver in the accident was a 70 year old elderly person.
examples.ja: 事故の相手の運転手は70才くらいの年輩者でした。

4833.meaning_mnemonic:
For <kanji>year</kanji>s and years, your <kanji>comrade</kanji>s have been with you, but now they're all <vocabulary>elderly</vocabulary>.

This is a less common version of 年配, but you'll still sometimes encounter it.
4833.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. As this vocab is identical to 年配, it's also read the same. Just remember that the はい turns into ぱい!

examples.en: Koichi locked the door and then hid the key.
examples.ja: コウイチはドアにかぎを掛けた後、そのかぎを隠した。

examples.en: Mito Komon concealed his true identity while he was traveling.
examples.ja: 水戸黄門は本当の身分を隠して旅をしていた。

examples.en: The entrance to the Secret Garden is hidden.
examples.ja: 秘密の花園への入口は隠されている。

4834.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>hide</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to hide something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to conceal something</vocabulary>.
4834.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Hide your <reading>cock</reading> (かく)! You have a ton of roosters but you don't want people to know about them, so you gotta hide your cocks. What did you think I was talking about?

examples.en: My father has been enjoying his retirement.
examples.ja: 私の父は隠居生活をエンジョイしていますよ。

examples.en: This village used to be a popular place for retreats.
examples.ja: この里は、かつては隠居の地として人気がありました。

examples.en: Do you really want to retire?
examples.ja: お前は本当に隠居したいのか？

4835.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>hide</kanji> away but you're <kanji>alive</kanji>. You've lived your life, so now it's time to hide and enjoy your <vocabulary>retirement</vocabulary> by making your <vocabulary>retreat</vocabulary> from working life.

This word refers to life after someone retires, and usually implies being retired from active life and having a quiet, maybe even secluded, lifestyle. It can also imply handing over the reins to your successors. The word is a little old-fashioned, but you'll still see it in modern writing.
4835.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The new curtains that Aya had designed were hung at the Tofugu office.
examples.ja: トーフグのオフィスに、アヤがデザインしたカーテンが掛けられました。

examples.en: Koichi is like a TV show producer because he always puts his sweater across his shoulder.
examples.ja: コウイチっていっつもセーターを肩から掛けてて、プロデューサーみたいだよね。

examples.en: Since his death, I don’t know where I should hang the picture he gave me.
examples.ja: 彼が死んでから、もらった絵をどこに掛けたらいいか分からなくて困っているんです。

examples.en: That dried food store hangs kale skillfully on a fence so that it gets plenty of sunlight, resulting in delicious dried kale.
examples.ja: あの乾物屋さんは、日光がよく当たるように上手にケールをフェンスに掛けるので、とても美味しい乾燥ケールが出来上がるんですよ。

4836.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>hang</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to hang something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to hang up something</vocabulary> (as in to hang it up by a hook).

You can remember this because you must <reading>care</reading> (ける) about the way you hang something up. Without care, it won't stay hanging for long.
4836.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: I exchanged dollars to yen at Narita Airport.
examples.ja: 成田空港でドルを円に替えました。

examples.en: Just watch. I can change my shirt in one second!
examples.ja: 見てろよ。オレは一秒でシャツを替えられるんだ！

examples.en: I already asked dad to change the light bulb.
examples.ja: お父さんに電球を替えるようにもう頼んだよ。

4837.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>replace</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to replace</vocabulary>. You know that you're doing the replacing because of the <reading>air</reading> (える). You're replacing the air as quickly as you can because if you don't you wouldn't be able to breathe in this small room.

替える means to replace something with another item of the same kind or equivalent, rather than changing its state. Wondering how it differs from 代える? While 代える stresses that you’re using someone or something “in place of another,” 替える simply indicates the act of swapping one thing for another similar thing.
4837.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: I stopped watching Doraemon after the voice actor was replaced.
examples.ja: ドラえもんの声優が替わってから、観なくなってしまった。

examples.en: The government will be replaced as a result of this election.
examples.ja: 今回の選挙で政権が替わることになりました。

examples.en: If it's not too much trouble, could you switch seats with me? I'm with my girlfriend, but we're seated separately.
examples.ja: もしご迷惑でなければ、席を替わってもらえませんか？彼女と一緒なんですが、席が別々になってしまったんです。

4838.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>replace</kanji>, and this word means <vocabulary>to be replaced</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be substituted</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>to be switched</vocabulary>.

Wondering about the difference between 代わる and 替わる? 代わる is used when someone or something takes the place of another, like filling in for a sick coworker. Whereas 替わる is used when things or situations switch places or are replaced with something new, like when talking about generations changing or a new governmental cabinet taking over.

This verb is intransitive, meaning it doesn't take a direct object. You'll sometimes see it with the particle を, though, because the を is showing a "path" rather than a direct object in this case. For example, 席を替わる (to switch seats) indicates your location is moving from one seat to another. Likewise, 電話を替わる indicates that a call is being handed off to another person.
4838.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: Nothing was impossible for invincible Superman.
examples.ja: 無敵のスーパーマンに、不可能なことは何もなかった。

examples.en: It's impossible to be a political observer when you aren't interested in politics.
examples.ja: 政治に関心が無いのに政治評論家になるのは不可能だ。

examples.en: In the poker tournament, I had a bad feeling, but it wasn’t possible for me to fold my hand.
examples.ja: あのポーカーのトーナメントで、悪い予感はしてたんだけど、捨てるのは不可能な手札を持っていたんだよ。

4839.meaning_mnemonic: You already know how 可能 means possible. So when you add <kanji>not</kanji> it becomes <vocabulary>impossible</vocabulary>.
4839.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know how to read 可能 first as well.

examples.en: Is it possible to make a reservation for three people at seven o'clock on a Friday night?
examples.ja: 金曜の夜の七時に三人で予約って可能ですか？

examples.en: If possible, I would like to order an illustration of my dog!
examples.ja: もし可能なら、ウチのワンコのイラストをお願いしたいです！

examples.en: If it's okay for a delivery tomorrow afternoon, I think it's possible.
examples.ja: 明日の午後のデリバリーでよければ、可能だと思います。

4840.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>ability</kanji> is there, so it is <kanji>possible</kanji>... wait, there's enough ability to make this <vocabulary>possible</vocabulary>? Let's do it!
4840.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I don't want to criticize you, but this is just terrible.
examples.ja: 君を非難するつもりは全くないんだけど、これはひどすぎるよ。

examples.en: I was blamed by the other club members for not going to the summer training camp.
examples.ja: 夏の合宿に参加しないことを、他の部員達から非難されました。

examples.en: The kids criticized their parents for hiding the scandal.
examples.ja: 子どもたちは両親が不祥事を隠したことを非難した。

4841.meaning_mnemonic: Know how 非難 is a criticism? Make it a verb and you have the word <vocabulary>to criticize</vocabulary>.
4841.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Of course, it will be really helpful to know the word 非難 to start.

examples.en: What food do you really hate?
examples.ja: 大嫌いな食べ物は何ですか。

examples.en: I heard that there are some people in the world who hate Tofugu.
examples.ja: 世の中には、トーフグのことが大嫌いな人もいるらしい。

examples.en: Mr. Viet will meet with you instead of Mr. Koichi because Mr. Koichi really hates you.
examples.ja: コウイチはあなたのことが大嫌いなので、彼に代わってビエトがお会いします。

4842.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 嫌い is to <kanji>dislike</kanji>? When that dislike is <kanji>big</kanji>, you really dislike it. That means you <vocabulary>hate</vocabulary> (or <vocabulary>really hate</vocabulary>) it.

As with 嫌い, a more literal translation is <vocabulary>detestable</vocabulary>.
4842.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the reading for 大, and the reading for 嫌い is like the one you learned with 嫌い in level 20.

examples.en: When I woke up, a tree had fallen in front of my house. It was probably toppled by the wind.
examples.ja: 起きたら家の前に、木が倒れていたんです。おそらく風で倒れたんでしょうね。

examples.en: He got knocked down in the 1st round.
examples.ja: アイツは第一ラウンドで倒れちまったんだよ。

examples.en: The marathon runner collapsed from exhaustion right before the finish line.
examples.ja: そのマラソン選手は、ゴールの直前で疲れきって倒れてしまいました。

4843.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen how 倒す is "to knock over." But this is when something gets knocked over by itself. You know that you're not doing anything here, because when you're not touching all these fine glass items, it's very <reading>rare</reading> (れる) that anything gets knocked over (because you're not touching anything, you clumsy dumsy). It's also when you or someone else collapses. You didn't push yourself over, you just kind of fell by yourself.
4843.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same like 倒す. If you knew 倒す you will know the reading of this one too.

examples.en: Don't skip over my turn!
examples.ja: 僕の順番を飛ばさないでよ！

examples.en: When Koichi cracks a boring joke, Viet gets grumpy.
examples.ja: コウイチがつまらない冗談を飛ばすと、ビエトは不機嫌になる。

examples.en: Fugu sent a triple flying over center field.
examples.ja: フグは、センターオーバーの三塁打をかっ飛ばした。

4844.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 飛ぶ is to fly? Well this word is for when you make some thing fly. So, this word is <vocabulary>to let something fly</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to send something flying</vocabulary>. It also means <vocabulary>to skip over something</vocabulary>, such as someone's turn or a question on a test.
4844.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is just like 飛ぶ, so if you know that reading you're close. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember the second part:

You can use your strength <vocabulary>to let something fly</vocabulary>, and that something is a <reading>bus</reading> (ばす). You're that buff!

examples.en: You should make sure the door is properly locked.
examples.ja: ちゃんとドアにカギをかけたかどうか確かめた方がいいですよ。

examples.en: Verify that the alcohol content has been completely removed.
examples.ja: アルコール分がちゃんと飛んだかどうか、確かめてくださいね。

examples.en: Kanae always checks the dictionary to make sure there are no mistakes in word use.
examples.ja: いつも、カナエさんが単語の使い方に間違いが無いか、辞書で確かめてくれています。

4845.meaning_mnemonic: Like with 確か, which means <kanji>certain</kanji>, this is the verb version of that. So when you "do certain" you are going <vocabulary>to make sure of</vocabulary> something or you're going <vocabulary>to verify</vocabulary> something.
4845.reading_mnemonic: This one is kun'yomi followed by okurigana. If you remember the reading you learned with 確かに, you should know this one!

examples.en: Taking a shower every day is such a bother.
examples.ja: 毎日シャワーするのって、本当に面倒臭い。

examples.en: There's nothing more annoying than listening to people complain.
examples.ja: 人のグチを聞くことほど面倒臭いことは無い。

examples.en: I've started going gray, but it's too much bother to color it.
examples.ja: 白髪が出てきちゃったんだけど、白髪染めをするのは面倒臭いんだよね。

4846.meaning_mnemonic: Something is a trouble (面倒) and it is smelly (臭い). So what is something that's smelly and a trouble? Well, something that's <vocabulary>troublesome</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>a bother</vocabulary>, I suppose. Basically you can ignore the smelly part. For some reason someone threw that back in, but smelly things are a bother, I suppose.
4846.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is the words 面倒 plus 臭い added together, so it is めんどうくさい!

Although the proper reading is めんどうくさい, be aware that people often just say めんどくさい when speaking. That extra う is just such a bother, you know?

examples.en: The temperature fell suddenly.
examples.ja: 気温が急に下がった。

examples.en: Today's highest temperature will be 40 degrees.
examples.ja: 今日の最高気温は四十度です。

examples.en: The temperature difference between the morning and night is intense.
examples.ja: 朝と夜の気温の差が激しいんです。

4847.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>energy</kanji> of the <kanji>warm</kanji>th will cause the <vocabulary>temperature</vocabulary> to go up and down. Energy goes up? Higher temperature because of more movement and activity. Energy goes down? Well, temperature gets colder and slower.
4847.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I learned the conjugated form in the previous class.
examples.ja: その活用形は、前回のクラスで学びました。

examples.en: The last presentation didn't go well, but I think it will be okay this time.
examples.ja: 前回のプレゼンはダメでしたが、今回は平気だと思います。

examples.en: At the last event, I didn't get the writer's autograph.
examples.ja: 前回のイベントでは、作家のサインはもらえなかった。

4848.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>before</kanji> <kanji>time</kanji> was <vocabulary>last time</vocabulary> or the <vocabulary>previous time</vocabulary>
4848.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Even in this era, there are fax machines in Japan.
examples.ja: 今の時代でも、日本にはファックスが有ります。

examples.en: This is a book of a love story from the Heian period.
examples.ja: これは、平安時代のラブストーリーの本です。

examples.en: In the current time period, the Internet will tell you everything.
examples.ja: 今の時代、インターネットが全てを教えてくれます。

4849.meaning_mnemonic: You have a <kanji>period</kanji> of <kanji>time</kanji> and it's called a <vocabulary>period</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>era</vocabulary>! Simple!
4849.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'm going to participate in a discussion held by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs sometime soon.
examples.ja: 今度、外務省のディベートに参加してくるよ。

examples.en: I heard a rumor that Michael has a friend who is a big shot in the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications.
examples.ja: マイケルの友達の中には、総務省のおえらいさんもいるってウワサだよ。

examples.en: Mr. Viet, Senior Deputy Director General, International Bureau, Ministry of Finance, is on a diet right now and substitutes sugar with saccharin, so don't use sugar in his meal.
examples.ja: ビエト財務省国際局次長は現在ダイエット中であり、砂糖の代わりにサッカリンを用いているため、彼の食事には砂糖を使用しないでください。

4850.meaning_mnemonic:
What should you establish to <kanji>conserve</kanji> a country? The <vocabulary>Ministry of</vocabulary>… well, any ministry really. In Japanese, 〜省 often gets tacked on to the names of government ministries. Like the Ministry of Finance (財務省), the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (外務省), and the mouthful that is the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (文部科学省). Whew!

〜省 is also the suffix used for Chinese <vocabulary>province</vocabulary>s, such as 広東省 (Guangdong Province), so keep this in mind when reading about international affairs.
4850.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I have to finish this article about economics by the end of this month.
examples.ja: この経済学についての記事を、今月末までにあげないといけないんです。

examples.en: He's a genius who finished writing his graduation thesis on economics in only one day.
examples.ja: ヤツは、この経済学についての卒論をたった一日で書き上げた天才です。

examples.en: I don't know the first thing about economics, so I decided to go to school.
examples.ja: 経済学の「け」の字も知らないので、学校に行くことにしたんです。

4851.meaning_mnemonic: You know how 経済 is economics, right? Well, add <kanji>study</kanji> to that and you have the study of economics, aka <vocabulary>economics</vocabulary>.
4851.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know 経済 as well.

examples.en: If you use this coupon, it'll be ten dollars cheaper when you do your checkup.
examples.ja: このクーポンを使えば、検査する時に10ドル安くなります。

examples.en: I had a doctor examine my ears yesterday.
examples.ja: 昨日、お医者さんに耳を検査してもらいました。

examples.en: I'm going to have the quality of my tap water tested next time.
examples.ja: 今度、水道水の水質を検査する予定です。

examples.en: After first examining the condition of the teeth and gums, we will proceed with cleaning off the plaque and tartar.
examples.ja: 初めに歯と歯ぐきの状態を検査してから、プラークと歯石のクリーニングを行います。

4852.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 検査 is inspection, so the verb version of that would be <vocabulary>to inspect</vocabulary>.
4852.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know 検査 already as well.

examples.en: If I were to give examples, it would be endless.
examples.ja: 例を挙げるとキリがないですよ。

examples.en: When I call your name, please raise your hand.
examples.ja: 名前を呼んだら、手を挙げてください。

examples.en: I held my wedding ceremony in city hall, and I’m not ashamed of that.
examples.ja: 私は結婚式を市役所で挙げましたが、そのことを恥ずかしいとは思っていません。

4853.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji means <kanji>raise</kanji>, and this verb is when you do that to something. It's transitive. So this means <vocabulary>to raise something</vocabulary>. It actually has a pretty wide meaning, and can also mean "raise" in the sense of <vocabulary>to cite something</vocabulary>, like an example. It can even mean <vocabulary>to hold something</vocabulary>, like an event.
4853.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 挙がる, so if you know that reading you should know this one as well.

examples.en: It took me a while to understand Tofugu's American jokes.
examples.ja: トーフグのアメリカン・ジョークを理解するのに時間がかかりました。

examples.en: I strive to ensure that the lessons can be understood by everyone.
examples.ja: 皆さんに本当に理解してもらえるようなレッスンになるよう、心がけています。

examples.en: I understand that you love him, but I don't want him to kiss you.
examples.ja: お前がアイツのことを好きなのは理解するけど、あいつがお前にキスをするのはイヤだよ。

examples.en: In order to get along well, it is important to understand the other person's position and feelings.
examples.ja: 仲良くするためには、相手の立場や気持ちを理解することが大切です。

4854.meaning_mnemonic: 理解 is "understanding," so the verb version would be...? How about <vocabulary>to understand</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to comprehend</vocabulary>? Well, do you?
4854.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Of course, if you know 理解 already this one is easy to comprehend.

examples.en: My boyfriend always gives me a hard candy after criticizing me.
examples.ja: 私の彼は、私を批判すると、いつも後でアメをくれる。

examples.en: Everyone said the same thing and criticized the man.
examples.ja: みんなは口をそろえて男のことを批判した。

examples.en: You're always finding fault with other people, aren't you?
examples.ja: お前って、他人の批判してばっかりだよな。

4855.meaning_mnemonic: 批判 is <kanji>criticism</kanji> so the verb version of that would be <vocabulary>to criticize</vocabulary>.
4855.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will be much easier to read this if you know 批判, as well.

examples.en: We really should increase the number of writers who have some literary talent.
examples.ja: もっと文才のあるライターを増やすべきだ。

examples.en: We want to increase the number of Tofugu fans. What do you think we should do?
examples.ja: トーフグのファンをもっと増やしたいんだけど、どうしたらいいかな？

examples.en: I save all my homework for the weekend so I can spend more time with my family on weekdays.
examples.ja: 平日に家族と過ごす時間を増やすために、宿題は全部週末にやることにしてるんだ。

4856.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 増える is "to increase" (as in, something just increases, you aren't doing the increasing yourself). This one is that one, where you're doing the increasing. So, this word means <vocabulary>to increase something</vocabulary>. You know you're doing the increasing because you said "yes" (やす) to increasing something, and did it yourself.
4856.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same like 増える. If you know that vocab word you probably can read this one as well.

examples.en: I like solving puzzles.
examples.ja: パズルを解くのが好きなんです。

examples.en: That boy genius was able to solve the mystery in three minutes.
examples.ja: その天才少年は、そのナゾを３分で解くことができました。

examples.en: He said, "I can solve this kind of problem in three minutes!" but even after three weeks, he still hasn't sent me the answer.
examples.ja: 「こんな問題、三分で解けるさ！」って言ってたのに、三週間たってもまだ解答が送られてこないんだよね。

examples.en: We are currently looking for clues to solve this code.
examples.ja: 私たちは今、この暗号を解くためのヒントをさがしています。

4857.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>solve</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to solve</vocabulary>. You know this verb is for when you are doing the solving because you think it's super <reading>coo</reading>' (く) to solve things.
4857.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

There's something you've been trying <vocabulary>to solve</vocabulary> for your entire life: your <reading>toe</reading> (と). Why is it shaped like that? Why is it a little crooked? What's it scheming? Maybe one day you'll solve the mystery of your toe…

examples.en: This means that there's no longer any way to escape.
examples.ja: これでもう逃げ道は断たれてしまった。

examples.en: I know that I should cut out alcohol and cigarettes. My doctor also told me to cut them out, but there’s no way I could do so right away.
examples.ja: お酒とタバコを断つべきだってのは、自分でも分かってます。医者にも断つように言われたんですが、すぐには無理ですよ。

examples.en: At that time, I said goodbye with a gut-wrenching feeling.
examples.ja: あの時は、はらわたを断つ思いで別れを告げたんだ。

examples.en: The goal of feminism is to sever the chains that bind women. It is not about forcing women to "lose their femininity," but about resisting the oppression of "this is how women are supposed to be.”
examples.ja: フェミニズムの目的は、女性を縛る鎖を断つことです。「女性らしさを失う」ことを押し付けるのではなく、「女性はこうあるべきだ」という抑圧への抵抗なんです。

4858.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>cut off</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to cut off</vocabulary>.

This is often used metaphorically to describe cutting off things that tie us down mentally or societally. This includes ending bad habits, so it also means <vocabulary>to quit doing something</vocabulary>.

Don't confuse this with 断る which means "to refuse." You know this is to cut off because of the つ, which hints that you have had <reading>two</reading> (つ) too many chocolates, and it's time to cut you off.
4858.reading_mnemonic: URGH! The reading isn't even the same as 断る, how frustrating. <vocabulary>to cut off</vocabulary> is read as たつ. Instead of eating too many chocolates and getting cut off, maybe you're eating too many tater <reading>tots</reading> (たつ). Don't eat so many of those, it's unhealthy. You have <vocabulary>to cut off</vocabulary> tater tots from your diet so you don't get fat.

examples.en: At this sports facility you can swim, skate, and play tennis.
examples.ja: このスポーツ施設では、スイミングやスケート、テニスなどができます。

examples.en: There are many museums and other cultural facilities in this town.
examples.ja: この町には美術館などの文化施設がたくさんあります。

examples.en: In a medical facility, doctors and nurses examine and care for patients.
examples.ja: 医療施設では、医者や看護師が患者さんを診察したり看護したりします。

examples.en: I’d like to quit my job at the children’s home because it’s too hard, but, at the same time, I don’t want to go burning any bridges.
examples.ja: 児童養護施設の仕事がきついので辞めたいんですが、一方で今まで築き上げてきた関係も壊したくはないんです。

4859.meaning_mnemonic: Go ahead and <kanji>carry out</kanji> the task and <kanji>establish</kanji> the <vocabulary>institution</vocabulary>. To carry out and establish something is to institute it too. What do you institute? An institution.
4859.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Do you know the phone number of the prime minister's office?
examples.ja: 総理府の電話番号を知っていますか？

examples.en: The Deputy Director General of the Prime Minister's Office was looking for you.
examples.ja: 総理府次長がお前のことをさがしていたぞ。

examples.en: I knew nothing about her except that she worked in the prime minister’s office.
examples.ja: 彼女のことについては、総理府で働いているという以外には何も知らなかった。

4860.meaning_mnemonic:
The prime minister's (総理) <kanji>government</kanji> is where he does all his governmenting. It's where the Japanese <vocabulary>Prime Minister's Office</vocabulary> (aka the <vocabulary>Cabinet Office</vocabulary>) is located as well.

総理府 was actually renamed 内閣府 in 2001, so you'd generally only use 総理府 to talk about the Cabinet Offices from back in the day.
