examples.ja: 私の最近の趣味は、手作りのビールを造ることなんですよ。

4978.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji means create, and this word is for the creation of big things. So it means to construct or to build or to make, and it's usually used with ships, bridges, buildings, and other large-scale work. It can also mean to brew, as in brewing sake. I guess brewing is like constructing, since it involves carefully choosing and mixing ingredients to get those sip-worthy creations!
4978.reading_mnemonic: The reading is like 作る, which means "to make." They have very similar meanings, but different kanji. Use 作る to help you to remember the reading of this word.

examples.en: Actually, the production methods for these two products are almost the same.
examples.ja: 実は、この商品とこの商品の製造方法はほぼ同じなんですよ。

examples.en: I received permission from Koichi to manufacture fugu kamaboko at the factory.
examples.ja: コウイチから、フグのかまぼこを工場で製造する許可をもらいました。

examples.en: I made a video explaining the automobile manufacturing process.
examples.ja: 自動車の製造プロセスを解説するビデオを作りました。

4979.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My friend is in graduate school studying landscape architecture.
examples.ja: 私の友達は大学院で造園について学んでいます。

examples.en: Salmon is a big fan of Fugu's landscaping style.
examples.ja: サーモンはフグの造園スタイルの大ファンなんですよ。

examples.en: When I graduated from the college, I had a job offer from a landscape gardening company.
examples.ja: 大学を卒業した時、造園会社から内定をもらっていました。

4980.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Create</kanji> a <kanji>garden</kanji>? You'll have to know a lot about <vocabulary>landscape gardening</vocabulary>.
4980.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That's cool, right? I renovated the garage into a children's room.
examples.ja: すごいだろ？ガレージを改造して子供部屋にしたんだ。

examples.en: This is embarrassing to say, but the guy riding the modded motorcycle is my brother.
examples.ja: 言うのは恥ずかしいんですが、あの改造バイクに乗ってるのは私の兄です。

examples.en: Prime Minister Koichi has no intention of reshuffling his cabinet.
examples.ja: コウイチ総理には、内閣を改造する気はさらさらありませんよ。

examples.en: For my physical transformation, I'm putting in effort through running and dietary restrictions .
examples.ja: 肉体改造のために、今ランニングと食事制限で頑張ってるんです。

4981.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Renew</kanji> it by <kanji>creat</kanji>ing something anew. This is <vocabulary>remodeling</vocabulary> because you're creating something and changing something that exists already, renewing it.
4981.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The diplomat was stabbed by Android No.18.
examples.ja: その外交官は人造人間十八号に刺された。

examples.en: Countries and money are both human-made constructs, right?
examples.ja: 国もお金も、人間が作った人造物だろ？

examples.en: Unlike 人造大理石 (terrazzo), 人工大理石 (artificial marble) doesn't have any natural stone components at all.
examples.ja: 「人造大理石」と違って、「人工大理石」には天然石の成分は一切含まれていません。

4982.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>person</kanji> <kanji>create</kanji>d item is <vocabulary>man made</vocabulary>. It's <vocabulary>synthetic</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>artificial</vocabulary>.

Wonder what makes 人造 different from 人工? While 人工 means "artificial" in general, 人造 specifically refers to something that is produced or constructed by humans. It's not as commonly used as 人工 and is often found in creative writing when talking about 人造人間 (androids).
4982.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: There are many brewing companies in this town.
examples.ja: この町には酒造会社がたくさんあります。

examples.en: We used to run a distilling business.
examples.ja: うちは元は酒造業を営んでたんですよ。

examples.en: Aoki Shuzo is a traditional sake brewery that has been in operation since its founding in 1717.
examples.ja: 青木酒造は、1717年に創業してからずっと酒づくりを続けている、伝統のある酒造会社です。

examples.en: I like working for this brewing company because they offer all these perks like free gym membership, free food, and even free sake.
examples.ja: ジムの会員権や食事だけではなく酒まで無料の特典として提供されるので、私はこの酒造での仕事が好きです。

4983.meaning_mnemonic: The act of <kanji>alcohol</kanji> <kanji>creat</kanji>ion is done via <vocabulary>brewing</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>distilling</vocabulary>.
4983.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Kanae sometimes comes into office while doing some crazy dance.
examples.ja: カナエは、たまに気違いじみたダンスをしながらオフィスに入ってくる。

examples.en: I drew a picture of "A Mad Tea-Party" from Alice in Wonderland.
examples.ja: 不思議の国のアリスの「気違いのお茶会」の絵をかいてみました。

examples.en: Dancing around in a snow storm in nothing but your underpants is just too crazy.
examples.ja: この吹雪の中、パンツ一丁で踊るなんて、気違いにも程がある。

4984.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>energy</kanji> is ... well ... <kanji>different</kanji>. That's the nice way to put it. You're <vocabulary>crazy</vocabulary>, actually.

WARNING: We're teaching you this word because it's used quite a bit still (especially online) and we want you to be able to understand it if you see it. But please keep in mind that this is considered to be a discriminatory word against people with mental illnesses, so we strongly recommend you do not use or direct this word toward anyone. Think of it like a really inappropriate swear word that makes you really uncool if you say it. Please!

While you still see the kanji version, this word is commonly written in katakana.
4984.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 気 plus 違い.

examples.en: It was a case of mistaken identity. I apologize.
examples.ja: 人違いでした。すみません。

examples.en: Viet isn't a yakuza. He is a poor victim of mistaken identity.
examples.ja: ビエトはヤクザじゃありません。人違いで疑われたかわいそうな被害者なんですよ。

examples.en: I thought I had given my wife a bonus, but it seems like I made a mistake and gave it to the wrong person.
examples.ja: 妻にボーナスを渡したつもりだったんですが、どうやら人違いだったようです。

examples.en: Yes, we are also conjoined twins, but I’m afraid you are mistaking us for a different set of twins.
examples.ja: はい、私達も結合双生児ではありますが、申し訳ありませんがあなたは人違いをしていると思います。

4985.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>person</kanji> who is <kanji>different</kanji> from the person you thought it was is a <vocabulary>mistaken identity</vocabulary>. Whoops, sorry, I thought you were someone else. 人違い!
4985.reading_mnemonic: The readings are 人 and 違い put together.

examples.en: I made the most embarrassing reading mistake today.
examples.ja: 今日、超恥ずかしい読み違いをしてしまった。

examples.en: The culprit laughed at me for misreading the search warrant.
examples.ja: 捜査令状の読み違いで、犯人に笑われた。

examples.en: Misreading of names is common even among Japanese.
examples.ja: 名前の読み違いは日本人の間でもよくあることですよ。

examples.en: It seems that I completely misinterpreted his intentions.
examples.ja: どうやら私は彼の意図について、完全に読み違いをしていたようです。

4986.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>read</kanji> something in a <kanji>different</kanji> way from the way you're supposed to it's a <vocabulary>misreading</vocabulary>.

This word can also be used figuratively, like when you misread a situation or someone’s intentions, and your expectations turn out to be incorrect.

Note that 読み間違い can also be used to mean the same thing.
4986.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi readings from the vocab words 読む and 違い. As long as you remember those, you can apply that knowledge here as well.

examples.en: Certainly, there's a big difference between hearing and seeing, isn't there?
examples.ja: やっぱり、聞くと見るでは大違いだね。

examples.en: It makes a big difference whether or not you pour maple syrup over a pancake.
examples.ja: ホットケーキにメープルシロップをかけるのとかけないのとでは大違いだよ。

examples.en: Yamada-san's husband is very different from my husband.
examples.ja: 山田さんのご主人は私の夫とは大違いだ。

examples.en: There is a big difference between a hard wooden chair and a soft cushy chair.
examples.ja: 堅い木の椅子と柔らかい快適な椅子じゃあ大違いだよ。

4987.meaning_mnemonic: 違い is <kanji>difference</kanji>, so a <kanji>big</kanji> one of those is a <vocabulary>big difference</vocabulary>.
4987.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 違い plus 大 of 大きい (おお) put together. You can remember this because when you see the difference (the BIG difference), you say "oohhhhh" (お), because you were surprised you didn't see it before.

examples.en: My younger brother has a dream to be an acupuncturist.
examples.ja: 私の弟には、針医になるという夢があります。

examples.en: I'll send you the phone number of my favorite acupuncturist!
examples.ja: お気に入りの針医の電話番号を送るね！

examples.en: It’s amazing to think that acupuncturist techniques have come this far.
examples.ja: 針医の技術の進歩には驚くばかりです。

4988.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Needle</kanji> <kanji>medicine</kanji> is when you stick needles into people to cure them. This is done via an <vocabulary>acupuncturist</vocabulary>.
4988.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi reading for 針 and the on'yomi reading for 医. You haven't learned this reading for 針 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

If you do <vocabulary>acupuncture</vocabulary> and stick a bunch of needles in your back it's going to look really <reading>hairy</reading> (はり). Needles look just like metal hairs when they're coming out of someone. Just picture hairy little needles all over your body and you'll never forget this reading!

examples.en: The wire was on the floor, you know.
examples.ja: 針金が床に落ちていたよ。

examples.en: Let's use a wire to fasten it.
examples.ja: 針金を使って留めましょう。

examples.en: This is art made by bending hanger wire.
examples.ja: これはハンガーの針金を曲げて作ったアートです。

4989.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>needle</kanji> made of <kanji>gold</kanji> is a <vocabulary>wire</vocabulary>. Perhaps wires were made from gold mostly back in the day? And they were thin like needles? That's my guess.
4989.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading of both. You already know both of these, just watch out for the rendaku on 金!

examples.en: I couldn't sleep, so I spent the night watching the second hand of the clock.
examples.ja: ねむれなかったので、時計の秒針を見て夜を過ごしました。

examples.en: The ticking sound of the second hand is so loud and annoying, it's frustrating.
examples.ja: 秒針のチクタクチクタクいう音がうるさくてイライラする。

examples.en: My wrist watch's second hand has been broken.
examples.ja: 腕時計の秒針が折れちゃってるの。

4990.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>second</kanji> <kanji>needle</kanji> is the thin hand that indicates seconds on your clock. That's the <vocabulary>second hand</vocabulary> of a clock.
4990.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I bought a weight that is made of lead.
examples.ja: 鉛でできたおもりを買いました。

examples.en: I’m so unmotivated today, my body feels as heavy as lead.
examples.ja: 今日はすごくやる気が無くて、体が鉛のように重く感じる。

examples.en: I was completely caught by a trick question that asks which one is heavier, 1kg of lead or 1kg of iron.
examples.ja: 1kgの鉛と1kgの鉄だったらどっちが重いか、という引っ掛け問題に見事にハマってしまった。

4991.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
4991.reading_mnemonic: Lots of <vocabulary>lead</vocabulary>, all in bullet form. That's what it was like in <reading>nam, 'arry" (なまり).</reading>

examples.en: A key made of lead was placed inside a lead pipe.
examples.ja: 鉛管の中に鉛製のカギが置かれていた。

examples.en: Lead piping was once often used in plumbing systems.
examples.ja: 水道の配管には、かつては鉛管がよく使われていました。

examples.en: Some parts of this house still use lead pipes, so do not drink hot water from the tap, okay?
examples.ja: この家のパイプの一部はまだ鉛管になっているから、水道から出るお湯を直接口にしてはいけないよ。

4992.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>lead</kanji> <kanji>pipe</kanji> is a <vocabulary>lead pipe</vocabulary>. Don't hit people with this in the knees.
4992.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Pencils do not contain lead, so there's no toxicity from them.
examples.ja: 鉛筆には鉛は入っていないので、鉛毒はありません。

examples.en: Is it true that the meat of a deer killed with a rifle may still contain lead and is toxic?
examples.ja: ライフルで仕留められたシカの肉には、鉛毒が残っている可能性があるって本当ですか？

examples.en: Face powder used to contain white lead, so many actors during and before the Taisho era suffered from lead poisoning and died from lead toxicity.
examples.ja: 白粉には鉛白が使われていたため、大正時代以前の役者さんには、鉛中毒に苦しみ鉛毒死した人がたくさんいたんですよ。

4993.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Lead</kanji> <kanji>poison</kanji> is <vocabulary>lead toxicity</vocabulary>.

This word generally refers to the toxicity of lead. While it can also refer to <vocabulary>lead poisoning</vocabulary>, 鉛中毒 (なまりちゅうどく) is the more common word for that.
4993.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'm sorry. I apologize if I offended you.
examples.ja: ごめん。気に障ったのなら、あやまるよ。

examples.en: Over drinking and over eating will hinder your health.
examples.ja: 暴飲暴食は体に障るよ。

examples.en: It'll hinder my job, so I can't reveal my face.
examples.ja: 仕事に差し障るので、顔出しは出来ません。

examples.en: Sometimes her shrill voice can be really irritating.
examples.ja: 彼女の金切り声が時々癪に障るんだよね。

4994.meaning_mnemonic:
This is the verb version of <kanji>hinder</kanji>, but it's what happens when you hinder someone else enough. You'll start <vocabulary>to irritate</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to annoy</vocabulary> them. 

Note that this word isn't used by itself, but in phrases like 気に障る (to hurt one's feelings) or 体に障る (<vocabulary>to be bad for</vocabulary> one's health). Check out the Common Word Combinations for more examples!
4994.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

If you want <vocabulary>to irritate</vocabulary> me, all you have to do is make what I'm eating <reading>sou</reading>r (さわ). Did you know sour food is known <vocabulary>to be bad for</vocabulary> you, too? Don't make that sour face, stop eating sour things!

examples.en: When you arrive, I will probably be replacing the shoji screens.
examples.ja: あなたが着くころには、障子のはり替えをしてると思います。

examples.en: When I was sleeping at night, I was frightened by the reflection of a shadow on the shoji.
examples.ja: 夜寝ていたら、障子に人影が映ってこわくなった。

examples.en: I like being woken up by the sunlight filtering gently through shoji screen.
examples.ja: 障子から差し込む光で、朝目を覚ますのが好きです。

4995.meaning_mnemonic:
It can <kanji>hinder</kanji> a <kanji>child</kanji>, but that's about it. This is a <vocabulary>shoji screen</vocabulary>, which is a type of <vocabulary>Japanese sliding door</vocabulary>. They're typically covered with thin paper, so, you know, an adult can go through it but a child would be hindered by it.

Shoji are made of thin paper stretched across a wooden lattice frame. They're lightweight and designed to let in some natural light.
4995.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The 子 is changed from し to じ, though, so be careful.

examples.en: WaniKani is currently undergoing maintenance due to a system malfunction.
examples.ja: ワニカニはシステム障害でメンテナンス中です。

examples.en: I suffer from panic disorder.
examples.ja: 私はパニック障害に苦しんでいます。

examples.en: My younger brother has a mild intellectual disability.
examples.ja: 私の弟には軽度の知的障害があるんです。

examples.en: When it leaked out that I have a disability, the job offer I had was cancelled.
examples.ja: 障害があることがバレて、内定が取り消された。

4996.meaning_mnemonic: There is <kanji>damage</kanji> that <kanji>hinder</kanji>s you from doing things normally. This is a <vocabulary>disability</vocabulary>.
4996.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What kind of social security is there in Japan?
examples.ja: 日本にはどんな社会保障がありますか。

examples.en: Tomorrow, I will attend the National Security Council.
examples.ja: 明日は、国家安全保障会議に出席する予定です。

examples.en: At school, I learned about safeguarding basic human rights.
examples.ja: 学校で、基本的人権の保障について学びました。

4997.meaning_mnemonic:
If you <kanji>preserve</kanji> and don't <kanji>hinder</kanji>, you're providing <vocabulary>security</vocabulary>, you're <vocabulary>safeguarding</vocabulary> something.

This word is used in contexts where the emphasis is on protecting from harm. For example, you'll see it in compound words like 社会保障 (social security) 安全保障 (security) and 人権保障 (safeguarding human rights).
4997.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I plan to spend New Year's Day alone and relax.
examples.ja: お正月は一人でゆっくりして過ごす予定です。

examples.en: I spent Sunday watching movies with friends.
examples.ja: 日曜日は友達と映画を観て過ごしました。

examples.en: I lead a busy life every day in the U.S.
examples.ja: 私はアメリカで毎日忙しい日々を過ごしています。

examples.en: Our electricity stopped because we fell three months behind on our utility bill, so we had to spend the hot day without an air‐conditioner.
examples.ja: 電気料金の支払いが三ヶ月遅れて電気を止められちゃって、あのクソ暑い日をエアコン無しで過ごさなきゃならなかったんだ。

4998.meaning_mnemonic:
過ぎる means "to pass," and 過ごす is <vocabulary>to pass time</vocabulary>.

過ごす refers to how you live through or experience your time. So it usually needs some extra context when you use it, like what you do while passing time, who you pass it with, or what was it like. Check out the collocations and context sentences to get a better grasp of this word!
4998.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as  過ぎる. If you know it, it's OK <vocabulary>to pass time</vocabulary> relaxing for a bit! If you don’t know it, maybe it's good <vocabulary>to spend time</vocabulary> reviewing…

examples.en: Madam, we have mail for you!
examples.ja: おくさーん、郵便ですよー！

examples.en: There was a bright red mailbox there.
examples.ja: そこには明るい赤色の郵便ポストがありました。

examples.en: What is the postal code?
examples.ja: 郵便番号は何番ですか？

examples.en: Efficiency and speed are everything in mail service.
examples.ja: 郵便業においては、効率とスピードが全てだ。

4999.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Mail</kanji> (or <kanji>post</kanji>) has <kanji>convenience</kanji> because it is sent for you in the <vocabulary>mail</vocabulary> (or the <vocabulary>post</vocabulary>!).

郵便 originally referred to the postal system, but eventually also came to refer to mail itself as a shorthand for 郵便物.
4999.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. The reading for 便 here (びん) isn't the on'yomi you learned with the kanji though, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

You get a lot of junk <vocabulary>mail</vocabulary>, so you throw it in the waste <reading>bin</reading> (びん). The waste bin is where that mail goes.

examples.en: I am such a coward, so I can't talk back even if I wanted to.
examples.ja: 私は腰抜けだから言い返したくても言い返せないの。

examples.en: The next time you call me a coward, I will not forgive you!
examples.ja: 次にオレを腰抜けと呼んだら、許さないぞ！

examples.en: It doesn't bother me one bit what those cowards say.
examples.ja: 腰抜け共に何を言われても痛くもかゆくもないよ。

examples.en: There are too many coward employees who resign before being promoted to management.
examples.ja: 管理職に昇進する前に辞職する腰抜け社員が多すぎる。

5000.meaning_mnemonic: You learned that 抜ける is "to fall out." If your <kanji>waist</kanji> falls out, you can't remain standing. You have to curl up on the ground, like a <vocabulary>coward</vocabulary>.
5000.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, which you've learned already. Go you!

examples.en: Necessary particles are missing from this sentence.
examples.ja: この文では必要な助詞が抜けていますよ。

examples.en: It was in the fall of 2020 that Viet said he wanted to leave the Yakuza group.
examples.ja: ビエトがヤクザグループから抜けたいと言ったのは２０２０年の秋のことだった。

examples.en: I'm busy right now. I'm watching a video of a balloon being deflated.
examples.ja: 今、忙しい。風船の空気が抜けるところのビデオを見てるの。

examples.en: The Tooth Fairy won't come to you in Japan if your teeth fall out.
examples.ja: 日本では歯が抜けてもトゥースフェアリーは来ないよ。

examples.en: As we passed through the forest, a bright blue ocean was spread out before us.
examples.ja: 森を抜けると、そこには真っ青な海が広がっていました。

5001.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 抜く means "to pull something out"? 抜ける describes something coming out of where it was, so it means <vocabulary>to come out</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to fall out</vocabulary>. 

This can be used for air coming out of a balloon, hair falling out, or pages missing from a book. It also means passing through places or leaving a group you were a part of.

To distinguish this word from 抜く, imagine a bunch of <reading>kale</reading> (ける) coming out of the ground on its own! Nobody pulled it out, it just came out by itself.
5001.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. Also, it is the same as 抜く.

examples.en: Apparently, Mr. Tanaka intends to catch the culprits using these plastic bottles.
examples.ja: 田中さんは、このペットボトルを使って犯人を捕えるつもりだそうです。

examples.en: ”Pokemon" is a game in which players catch various Pokemon by using Pokeballs, etc., and make the captured Pokemon fight, grow, and become stronger.
examples.ja: 『ポケモン』は、モンスターボールなどで色んなポケモンを捕え、その捕えたポケモンを戦わせて育てて強くしていくゲームです。

examples.en: An idol's job may be to capture the hearts and minds of fans, but my job is to catch idols on dates with my camera.
examples.ja: アイドルの仕事はファンの心を捕えることかもしれませんが、私の仕事は、アイドルのデート現場をカメラで捕えることです。

examples.en: Catching mice is my cat’s specialty.
examples.ja: 私の猫は鼠を捕えることが得意なんです。

5002.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji itself means <kanji>catch</kanji>, and 捕える means <vocabulary>to capture something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to catch something</vocabulary>. 

捕える is often used in writing to describe having someone captured to keep them from escaping. But it can also be used in more abstract contexts, like capturing a moment in a photograph, grasping a concept or idea, or seizing an opportunity.

You can remember the meaning for this because everyone wants to capture <reading>el</reading>ves (える). Sorry, elves… You're just so cool, people want to capture and keep you forever.
5002.reading_mnemonic: You recently learned 捕まる, which uses the same kanji, but this word has a totally different reading. To remember it, just think about how the meaning of 捕える kind of resembles the verb 捉える that you learned a while ago. 捕える is mostly for capturing things, and 捉える is mostly for grasping ideas. So it kinda makes sense that they'd have the same とらえる reading, right?

examples.en: I'd like to hang the clock here, but I'm not sure if it will hang right.
examples.ja: 時計をココに掛けたいんだけど、うまく掛かるかな。

examples.en: A man's silk hat was hung on a pole hanger.
examples.ja: ポールハンガーには、男性のシルクハットが掛かっていた。

examples.en: When I went to the Louvre, the Mona Lisa was hanging crooked.
examples.ja: ルーヴル美術館に行った時、モナリザが曲がって掛かっていた。

examples.en: Oh, fish got hooked!
examples.ja: お、魚が掛かったぞ！

5003.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 掛ける is "to hang something"? Well, 掛かる focuses on the fact that something is hanging, without specifying who did it. So it means <vocabulary>to be hung</vocabulary>. Use it to say a picture is hung on the wall, for example. 

掛かる can also mean <vocabulary>to be hooked</vocabulary>, whether it's the picture hooked to the wall or a fish that happens <vocabulary>to be caught</vocabulary> on a hook. 

These uses are all intransitive, so you don't need a direct object them. A hint for this is that 掛かる ends with okurigana that rhyme with ある, and those kinds of verbs tend to be intransitive.
5003.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 掛ける, so as long as you know that you know this too.

examples.en: This seems to be a good place to hide for hide and seek!
examples.ja: ここ、隠れんぼで隠れるのにいいかも！

examples.en: Oh, the moon has hidden away.
examples.ja: あー、お月様が隠れちゃった。

examples.en: Under his shirt, there is a hidden tattoo of KFC chicken.
examples.ja: アイツのシャツの下には、KFCのチキンのタトゥーが隠れている。

examples.en: "Oh no. I think I just saw my ex. Quick, hide!" "What? You mean Fugu?" "No. Shark." "Shark? Who’s Shark? You have way too many exes!"
examples.ja: 「やばい。多分あれ元彼だ。速く隠れなきゃ。」「まじで？フグってこと？」「違うよ。サメだよ。」「 サメ？サメって誰のこと？てか、あんた元カレ多すぎだっつーの！」

5004.meaning_mnemonic:
隠す is "to hide something." 隠れる is <vocabulary>to hide oneself</vocabulary> or just <vocabulary>to hide</vocabulary>. You know this because when someone is hiding, it's <reading>rare</reading> (れる) for anyone else to find them. They take this hide-and-seek thing pretty seriously, you know!

This word can also mean <vocabulary>to be hidden</vocabulary> because sometimes the subject is an inanimate object, as in 月が雲に隠れる (the moon is hidden in the cloud).
5004.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 隠す. So as long as you know that you know this as well.

examples.en: There was no price written on this item.
examples.ja: この商品には値段が書かれていませんでした。

examples.en: Buying without even looking at the price, you are indeed the president of the company.
examples.ja: 値段を見もせずに買うなんて、さすが社長ですね。

examples.en: It’s true that we are working on our TV tie-in book, but the price hasn’t been decided yet.
examples.ja: テレビとタイアップした書籍を手がけているのは本当だが、まだ値段は決まっていない。

examples.en: Of course, we cannot put a price on human life. But there are times when it is necessary to calculate the price of someone's life. Do you know when that is?
examples.ja: もちろん、人の命に値段はつけられません。でも、誰かの命の値段を算出する必要がある時もあります。皆さんは、それがどんな時か分かりますか？

5005.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>value</kanji> is in various <kanji>steps</kanji>. Each step is a different amount, and each amount is a <vocabulary>price</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>cost</vocabulary>.

値段 refers to the price attached to something you can buy, like in stores or markets. For example, you could use 値段 to ask how much something costs at a shop or when talking about the price of a particular meal.
5005.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading for 値 plus the on'yomi reading for 段. Combine them together to get the reading here. You've learned both of these readings already, so just remember 値 is ね because you <reading>neigh</reading> (ね) when you see a good <vocabulary>price</vocabulary>.

examples.en: Nothing is better than good health.
examples.ja: 健康に勝るものは何もないですよ。

examples.en: I started swimming for my health.
examples.ja: 健康のために水泳を始めました。

examples.en: This virus rarely affects healthy people.
examples.ja: このウィルスは、健康な人にはほとんど心配いりません。

examples.en: Is company-paid health insurance included in the fringe benefits?
examples.ja: 会社側が負担する健康保険は、諸手当の中に含まれているのでしょうか。

5006.meaning_mnemonic: You're so <kanji>healthy</kanji> it puts you at <kanji>ease</kanji>. That's your <vocabulary>health</vocabulary>! So healthful, go you!
5006.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Is amnesia an incurable disease?
examples.ja: 健忘症は不治の病なんでしょうか。

examples.en: Last year, Mr. Arita suffered from transient amnesia.
examples.ja: 去年、有田さんは一過性の健忘症になってしまった。

examples.en: The doctor told me that he suspected amnesia.
examples.ja: お医者さんに健忘症の疑いがあると言われました。

examples.en: I have a relative who is suffering from amnesia.
examples.ja: 健忘症に苦しんでいる親戚がいます。

5007.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>healthy</kanji> bit of <kanji>forget</kanji>ting <kanji>symptom</kanji>s means you might have <vocabulary>amnesia</vocabulary>.

健忘症 often refers to short-term <vocabulary>memory loss</vocabulary>, either full or partial, but some people might also use it in a sort of joking way for everyday <vocabulary>forgetfulness</vocabulary>.
5007.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Well, your team is efficient but not effective, don’t you think?
examples.ja: でも、あなたのチームは効率的だけど効果的ではないよね。

examples.en: Where are the pressure points that are effective at shaking off drowsiness?
examples.ja: 眠気を覚ますのに効果的なツボはどこですか。

examples.en: It is said that walking is most effective in the morning.
examples.ja: ウォーキングが最も効果的なのは、朝だと言われています。

examples.en: To effectively lose weight, it is important to get a good night's sleep.
examples.ja: 効果的にやせるには、睡眠時間をしっかり確保することが大切です。

examples.en: Performance based salaries are the most effective and fairest ways to attract good workers.
examples.ja: 成果主義の給与制度は、良い社員を引き込む最も効果的で公平な方法である。

5008.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 効果 means "effect"? Add <kanji>~like</kanji> to that and it's <vocabulary>effective</vocabulary>!
5008.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Why do you want to get a position at a company that pays you per diem?
examples.ja: どうして日当で給与を支払う会社に就きたいの？

examples.en: I wonder what kind of jobs we all will end up getting.
examples.ja: みんなどんな仕事に就くことになるのかな。

examples.en: This would definitely make Prince Joffrey take the throne.
examples.ja: これでジョフリー王子が王位に就くのは間違いないね。

examples.en: Who do you think will take Tofugu's president position after Koichi?
examples.ja: コウイチの後、誰がトーフグの社長のポジションに就くと思う？

5009.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>get a position</kanji>. The verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to get a position</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to get a job</vocabulary>.

Note that 就く is used with another word that indicates a position or a job, like 王位に就く(becoming a king) or 仕事に就く (finding employment).
5009.reading_mnemonic: If you want <vocabulary>to get a position</vocabulary>, there are <reading>two</reading> (つ) interviews. Just pass the two interviews to get a job!

examples.en: Congratulations on finding a job!
examples.ja: 就職おめでとう！

examples.en: We're going to celebrate my friend's new job tomorrow night.
examples.ja: 明日の夜、友達の就職祝いをします。

examples.en: I am worried about whether I will be able to find a job after graduation.
examples.ja: 卒業後、ちゃんと就職できるか不安なんです。

examples.en: "I’ve had several job interviews, but I haven’t received any job offers yet.” “Join the club.”
examples.ja: 「いくつか就職の面接をしたんだけど、まだどこからも内定が出ないんだ。」「お互い大変だな。」

5010.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Getting a position</kanji> of <kanji>employment</kanji> means <vocabulary>finding employment</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>getting a job</vocabulary>.
5010.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What are Mr. Hayashi's working hours?
examples.ja: 林さんの就業時間を教えてください。

examples.en: We meet on a monthly basis to discuss employment regulations.
examples.ja: 就業規則についての話し合いをするために、 私たちは月一のペースで会っている。

examples.en: When I go to Hello Work (employment service center), they only recommend part-time jobs to me.
examples.ja: ハローワークに行っても、就業形態がパートのみの仕事しかすすめてもらえないんだよ。

examples.en: The working population refers to the number of individuals within the labor force who are employed and earning income. The working population can be further categorized into two groups: those who are actively working, and those who are on leave and not working due to various reasons.
examples.ja: 就業人口とは、労働力人口の中で、職業に就いて収入を得ている人の数のことです。 就業人口は、就業中の就業者と、何らかの事情により就業していない休業者に分けられます。

5011.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>get a position</kanji> in some <kanji>business</kanji>, you’re considered <vocabulary>working</vocabulary>.

就業 is a formal word that can refer to both <vocabulary>being employed</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>being at work</vocabulary> for the day. It’s commonly used in kanji compounds, such as 就業時間 (working hours) and 就業規則 (employment regulations).
5011.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I couldn't even go out because of the injury, it was such a boring week.
examples.ja: ケガのせいで外出もできなかったので、かなり退屈な一週間でした。

examples.en: I was bored, so it was good timing.
examples.ja: 退屈していたのでちょうどよかったです。

examples.en: Lately, my work has become monotonous and I'm very bored.
examples.ja: 最近、仕事が単調になっちゃって、すごく退屈なんだよ。

examples.en: Beneath the endless sky, students had to listen to the principal’s endless and boring speech.
examples.ja: 果てしなく続く空の下で、生徒たちは果てしなく長くて退屈な校長の話を聞かなくてはならなかった。

5012.meaning_mnemonic: I <kanji>retreat</kanji>! I <kanji>yield</kanji>! I can't take it anymore, it's so <vocabulary>boring</vocabulary>. Just imagine yourself giving up on whatever you're doing because you're so darn bored. You can't stand it. You have to retreat. You are ready to yield. Booooooring.
5012.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What a huge green bell pepper!
examples.ja: なんて巨大なピーマンなんだ！

examples.en: A gigantic Tofugu doll has arrived in the office.
examples.ja: 巨大なトーフグ人形がオフィスに届きました。

examples.en: There is a possibility of a huge earthquake, like one from the Nankai Trough occurring while you are traveling in Japan, right?
examples.ja: 日本に旅行してる時に、南海トラフみたいな巨大地震が来る可能性もあるでしょ？

examples.en: I strongly suggest that you schedule the appointment with him well in advance because he is the president of an enormous company and he is very, very busy.
examples.ja: 彼はとっても忙しい巨大企業の社長さんなんだから、アポの約束は絶対に早目に取っておいた方がいいよ。

5013.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>giant</kanji> <kanji>big</kanji> thing is something that is <vocabulary>huge</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>gigantic</vocabulary>.

巨大 is often used in writing to describe something <vocabulary>enormous</vocabulary>. It can be for anything of immense scale, not just physical objects like buildings or monsters, but also abstract things like the impact of a natural disaster or even a person's influence.
5013.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: To insects, humans are giants, right?
examples.ja: 虫にとっては、人間も巨人でしょ。

examples.en: What, are you a Giants fan?
examples.ja: えっ、巨人ファンなんですか？

examples.en: That basketball player has gigantism.
examples.ja: あのバスケットボール選手は巨人症です。

5014.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I heard that Koichi will host a rolled sushi party this Friday.
examples.ja: 今度の金曜日にコウイチが巻きずしパーティーをするんだって。

examples.en: Why is it that American makizushi has the seaweed rolled on the inside?
examples.ja: どうしてアメリカの巻きずしはのりが内側に巻かれているんですか。

examples.en: There are Japanese people who have never made makizushi too.
examples.ja: 日本人でも巻きずしを作ったことがない人はいるよ。

examples.en: "You should try the sushi roll. I'm sure you'll like it." "Okay, if you say so."
examples.ja: 「君も巻きずしを食べてみるべきだよ。きっと気に入ると思うよ。」「わかったわ。あなたがそう言うのなら。」

5015.meaning_mnemonic:
巻く is "to roll." ずし is すし. This is <vocabulary>rolled sushi</vocabulary>.

Makizushi refers to cylindrical rolled sushi, which is commonly served in bite-sized pieces. If it's shaped like a cone, it's known as 手巻きずし (temakizushi).
5015.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 巻く.

examples.en: No matter how many times I make them, my spring rolls always get stolen.
examples.ja: 作っても作っても春巻きをぬすまれるんです。

examples.en: "Did you eat my spring rolls?" "Sorry, I did."
examples.ja: 「私の春巻き食べたでしょ？」「ごめん。その通りだよ。」

examples.en: My favorite food is fresh spring rolls.
examples.ja: 私の大好物は生春巻きです。

5016.meaning_mnemonic: 巻く is "to roll up." If you roll up spring, you get a roll that's spring flavored. These are known as <vocabulary>spring rolls</vocabulary>.
5016.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 春 and 巻く.

examples.en: Do your best Japan! Hang in there Japan!
examples.ja: 頑張れニッポン、負けるなニッポン！

examples.en: You'll be fine, Haru-chan. I'm sure you'll pass the test. Good luck!
examples.ja: 大丈夫だって。春ちゃんならきっと受かるよ。頑張れ。

examples.en: Hang in there, help is almost here!
examples.ja: 頑張れ、あとちょっとで助けが来るぞ！

examples.en: Well, don’t worry about the results, just try your best!
examples.ja: まあ、結果を気にせずに、頑張れよ！

5017.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 頑張る means “to persevere” or “to do one’s best”? This time you're telling someone to 頑張る, so this word means something like <vocabulary>do your best</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>hang in there</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>good luck</vocabulary>! Speaking of which, 頑張れ, you!
5017.reading_mnemonic:
The reading comes from 頑張る. Just watch out for that rendaku on 張る! You've seen it before, but here's a mnemonic in case you need a refresher:

Remember how when it's time to 頑張る (to persevere), you always scream "baa"? Not sure why, but it's a great motivator for you. So you do the same when you cheer for others. When you tell them <vocabulary>Do your best</vocabulary>, you also scream <reading>baa</reading> (ば) at them. When you tell them <vocabulary>Hang in there</vocabulary>, you scream "baa!" If it makes you persevere, it must work the same for others, right? Baa!

examples.en: Mr. Yamazaki has a habit of inflating his nostrils when he gets angry.
examples.ja: 山崎さんは怒ると鼻の穴を大きくふくらませるクセがあるんです。

examples.en: It's weird. I don't think I had said anything that would make him mad.
examples.ja: おかしいな？別に怒らせるようなこと言ったつもりはないんだけど...。

examples.en: I'm sorry. Please don't get so angry.
examples.ja: ごめんってば。そんなに怒らないでよ。

examples.en: "Fugu, you don’t understand why Salmon is mad at you, do you?" "No, I have no idea." "That’s what I thought."
examples.ja: 「フグ、どうしてサーモンがお前のことを怒っているのか分からないんだろ？」「うん。さっぱり分からないよ。」「そうだと思ったよ。」

5018.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>angry</kanji>, the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to get angry</vocabulary>.
5018.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You're starting <vocabulary>to get angry</vocabulary> about something. It's mostly this <reading>ok</reading>ra (おこ). It tastes terrible.

examples.en: I really don't like people who yell at others.
examples.ja: 私、怒鳴る人、ホントに嫌なんだよね。

examples.en: My boss yells at me so much that I got a hole in my stomach.
examples.ja: 上司に怒鳴られてばっかりで、胃に穴が空いちゃったよ。

examples.en: Mr. Fujisaki has very mild personality, so I have never seen him shout at somebody.
examples.ja: 藤崎さんは温厚な性格で、怒鳴っているところを見たことがありません。

examples.en: "Kinnikuma yells a lot." "Yeah, but don’t worry. His bark is worse than his bite."
examples.ja: 「キンニクマってよく怒鳴るよね。」「そうだね。でも、心配しないで。彼は口は悪いけど根は悪い人ではないから。」

5019.meaning_mnemonic:
An <kanji>angry</kanji> <kanji>chirp</kanji> is a type of shout. The verb version is <vocabulary>to yell</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to shout</vocabulary>.

怒鳴る suggests anger, as you can tell from the kanji, so it's used when someone yells or shouts to scold others or to express anger or frustration.
5019.reading_mnemonic: This one is a bit tricky, as it uses the on'yomi reading you learned for 怒 and the kun'yomi reading for 鳴る, so try to keep that in mind!

examples.en: You seem like you don't have any worries at all, huh? That must be nice.
examples.ja: あんたは何の悩みもなさそうでいいよね。

examples.en: I've been bothered by how easily my stockings get runs.
examples.ja: ストッキングがすぐに伝線しちゃうのが悩みなんです。

examples.en: In the past, my concern was not being able to confide in others, but now I can talk about anything.
examples.ja: 昔は悩みを人に打ち明けることができないのが悩みでしたが、今では何でも言えるようになりました。

examples.en: I don't mind hearing about your troubles, but I'm running out of money. If you want to eat out with me, it's your treat.
examples.ja: 悩み事の相談に乗るのは構わないんだけど、金欠なんだよね。外食したいなら、あんたの奢りだよ。

5020.meaning_mnemonic: This is the noun version of <kanji>worry</kanji>, making it <vocabulary>a worry</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>a trouble</vocabulary>.
5020.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the one you learned with the kanji. Nicely done, no need to have <vocabulary>a worry</vocabulary> about it.

examples.en: Many women wonder whether to continue working after giving birth.
examples.ja: 出産後も仕事を続けるかを悩む女性は多い。

examples.en: I am troubled by harassment from my neighbors.
examples.ja: 近所の人からの嫌がらせに悩んでいます。

examples.en: You are still young, what do you need to be so worried about?
examples.ja: まだ若いのに、何をそんなに悩む必要があるんだよ！

examples.en: "Hey! What’s troubling you?" "My girlfriend dumped me last night."
examples.ja: 「どうしたの？何を悩んでいるの？」「昨日、彼女に振られたんだ。」

5021.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>worry</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to worry</vocabulary>.

悩む is often intransitive, like 彼はいつも悩んでいる (he's always worrying). But it can also be transitive, in which case it'll take a direct object, like 彼女のことを悩む (to worry about her).
5021.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji, so no need <vocabulary>to worry</vocabulary> about it.

examples.en: I'm still baffled by trivial things at my age.
examples.ja: 俺は、この年になっても、まだくだらないことに惑うよ。

examples.en: It's curious, isn't it? I wonder what could be making people feel so lost.
examples.ja: 不思議ですね。何が人を惑わせるんでしょうね。

examples.en: People were crying out and fleeing frantically.
examples.ja: 人々は泣き叫び、逃げ惑っていた。

examples.en: That angel has deliberately led you astray.
examples.ja: その天使は、お前が惑うようにわざと仕向けたのだよ。

examples.en: Right now, I just feel at a loss in life.
examples.ja: 今は、なんというか、人生に惑うような気分です。

5022.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>misguided</kanji>, but the verb version is usually used to describe how you feel after being misguided — <vocabulary>to be at a loss</vocabulary>!

惑う usually refers to being in a quandary or a state of confusion. Using 惑う is kind of old-fashioned, but other forms like 惑わせる and 逃げ惑う (to flee frantically) are still fairly common in modern Japanese.
5022.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: If you are going <vocabulary>to be at a loss</vocabulary> you're going to be <reading>mad</reading> (まど) about it, most likely. Nobody likes to feel at a loss, so imagine how mad you feel when you are.

examples.en: There is an annoying person, and it’s troubling me.
examples.ja: 迷惑な人がいて、困ってるんです。

examples.en: If it's not too much trouble, is it okay to leave it to you?
examples.ja: ご迷惑じゃなければ、お願いしてもいいですか？

examples.en: Lately, I have been getting a lot of junk mail.
examples.ja: 最近、迷惑メールがたくさん送られて来るようになった。

examples.en: I am bad at Japanese, so I might be an inconvenience to you.
examples.ja: 日本語が下手なので、あなたに迷惑をかけてしまうかもしれません。

5023.meaning_mnemonic:
You've been led <kanji>astray</kanji> and you've been <kanji>misguided</kanji>. What a <vocabulary>trouble</vocabulary>, and indeed a <vocabulary>troublesome</vocabulary> <vocabulary>inconvenience</vocabulary> all this is.

迷惑 refers to a <vocabulary>nuisance</vocabulary> that bothers others, like trimming your toenails or speaking loudly on the phone in public.
5023.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I succumbed to a sweet temptation and ended up eating cake.
examples.ja: あま〜い誘惑に負けて、ケーキを食べてしまった。

examples.en: What? My boyfriend wouldn't do something as flirtatious as hitting on someone else! You probably seduced him, didn't you?
examples.ja: はあ？私の彼氏がナンパなんてチャラいことするはずないじゃない。どうせあんたが誘惑したんでしょ？

examples.en: What do you think is the best way to prevent your child from being tempted and led astray by bad influences?
examples.ja: 自分の子供が、悪いヤツらに誘惑されて悪いことに手を出すのを防ぐには、どうすればいいと思いますか？

examples.en: Fugu could not resist the temptation to kiss Salmon.
examples.ja: フグは、サーモンの唇を奪いたいという誘惑に抗うことはできなかった。

5024.meaning_mnemonic:
You're being <kanji>invited</kanji>, but you're also being <kanji>misguided</kanji>. This is <vocabulary>seduction</vocabulary> that's talking. A misguided invitation is never a good thing!

This word also translates to <vocabulary>temptation</vocabulary>, but keep in mind that 誘惑’s focus is more on an external factor that entices someone into succumbing to temptation.
5024.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Mr Suto is good at seeing people's true nature.
examples.ja: 首藤さんは人の素質を見抜くのがうまいんですよ。

examples.en: My mother is great at seeing through my father’s lies.
examples.ja: うちの母親は父親のウソを見抜くのがうまい。

examples.en: I knew that oil supplies have been dwindling in recent years, but I wasn't able to find out why.
examples.ja: 近ごろ石油の供給が少なくなってきているのは知っていましたが、その理由は見抜けませんでした。

5025.meaning_mnemonic:
You know 抜く means "to pull something out." Whenever you <kanji>see</kanji> something and pull something out of it, you're able <vocabulary>to see something's true nature</vocabulary>. You're able <vocabulary>to see through</vocabulary> things like situations, lies, and people.

見抜く often suggests figuring something out instinctively, with sharp insight or keen perception, especially when it comes to understanding the essence or true nature of something.
5025.reading_mnemonic: This is the reading for 見る and 抜く put together.

examples.en: I'm too dumb to have noticed. Thanks for telling me.
examples.ja: オレ、間抜けだから、気づかなかったよ。言ってくれてありがとう。

examples.en: You idiot!
examples.ja: この間抜け野郎！

examples.en: I feel ashamed of the stupid reply I sent.
examples.ja: 間抜けな返事をしてしまい、はずかしく思っています。

examples.en: Did you see his dumb face?
examples.ja: アイツの間抜けヅラ、見た？

examples.en: I don’t want him to think of me as a stupid country bumpkin.
examples.ja: 彼に間抜けな田舎者のお上りさんだと思われたくないの。

5026.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned that 抜ける is "to fall out." If an <kanji>interval of time</kanji> falls out of you, you're totally spaced out. You won't learn anything and you'll become an <vocabulary>idiot</vocabulary>.

間抜け can refer to both a person who does something foolish and to the foolish actions themselves. It's often used to criticize <vocabulary>dumb</vocabulary> behavior.
5026.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the ま reading of 間 and from 抜く.

examples.en: Is there a function in Excel to extract only the month part of a date?
examples.ja: エクセルで日付の月の部分だけを抜き出す関数ってありますか？

examples.en: Q4: What is the reason why Tomoko started crying? Answer the question by selecting seventeen characters from the text.
examples.ja: 問4： 友子が泣き出した理由は何ですか。文中の言葉を17字で抜き出して答えなさい。

examples.en: What do you do with your old computer or smartphone? If you take them to a recycling shop, there is a risk that a malicious third party could extract the data, right?
examples.ja: いらなくなったパソコンとかスマホってどうしてる？リサイクルショップとかに持っていったら、悪意ある第三者にデータを抜き出される危険性があるよね？

examples.en: He secretly started to pull a gun out of his business suit.
examples.ja: 彼は背広から銃をそっと抜き出した。

5027.meaning_mnemonic:
You know 抜く means "to pull something out" and 出す means "to remove," so this word also means <vocabulary>to pull something out</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to extract</vocabulary>.

More specifically, 抜き出す means to pull something out from a larger set of something. For example, this could mean taking a single bill out of your wallet, or selecting specific data from a large dataset.
5027.reading_mnemonic: The readings are from 抜く and 出す, combined together. Know those two and you'll be able to read this word as well.

examples.en: We plan to invite a hundred clients to this party.
examples.ja: 今回のパーティーには、クライアントを百名招く予定です。

examples.en: It's called "beckoning" to use your hands to invite people in.
examples.ja: 人を手を使って招くことを「手招きする」って言うんですよ。

examples.en: It would be great if we could invite him as our CEO.
examples.ja: 彼をうちのCEOとして招くことができれば最高なんだけどな。

examples.en: Eh, I thought it was the weak yen that causes inflation, but a strong yen can also cause inflation sometimes?
examples.ja: え、インフレを招くのは円安だと思ってたんですが、円高がインフレを招くこともあるんですか？

examples.en: I wrote a song to summon the spirits of the dead.
examples.ja: 死者の霊魂を招く歌を作ってみた。

5028.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>beckon</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to beckon</vocabulary>. 

Since 招く conjures up the image of someone beckoning, it also means <vocabulary>to invite</vocabulary>, and is a relatively formal word. Figuratively, it can also mean <vocabulary>to cause</vocabulary>, as in inviting some undesirable outcome or situation.
5028.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You move <vocabulary>to beckon</vocabulary> your friend over. You can't see him well, so that's why you invite him to come closer. He is hiding something, and it turns out to be his long, luxurious horse <reading>mane</reading> (まね). Why does he have a mane!? Horse steroids?

examples.en: Charlie said he's inviting me to the chocolate factory next time!
examples.ja: チャーリーが、今度チョコレート工場に招待するよって言ってくれたんだ！

examples.en: I was invited to the Tofugu Christmas party, but I caught the flu and couldn't go.
examples.ja: トーフグのクリスマス会に招待されたが、インフルエンザにかかって行けなかった。

examples.en: How many people are you planning to invite to the wedding party?
examples.ja: ウェディングパーティーには何人ぐらい招待するつもりなの？

examples.en: Have you decided which friends to invite over for your birthday party?
examples.ja: どのお友達を誕生日会に招待するか決めましたか。

5029.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>beckon</kanji> someone to come to you, but then you <kanji>wait</kanji>. This is because they aren't really near you, so your beckon is more like an invitation. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to invite</vocabulary> .

招待する is a formal word for inviting someone, particularly to formal events or places.
5029.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Still can't find any clues?
examples.ja: 手掛かりはまだ見つからないのですか。

examples.en: We are currently searching wholeheartedly for clues that will lead us to a solution.
examples.ja: 今は全力で、問題解決の糸口となるような手掛かりを探しています。

examples.en: Have the police found any clues regarding the mystery of the vanishing bacon?
examples.ja: 警察は消えたベーコンの謎について何か手掛かりを見つけましたか？

examples.en: Mr. Fujikawa's statement provided a clue to the culprit's trickery.
examples.ja: 藤川さんの発言が、犯人のトリックを見抜く手掛かりになりました。

5030.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned that 掛かる can mean "to be hooked." If you're doing something physical like climbing and your <kanji>hand</kanji> hooks onto something, that thing is called a <vocabulary>handhold</vocabulary>.

Figuratively, this can also mean <vocabulary>clue</vocabulary>, since a clue is something you grasp onto, much like a handhold, to help you progress in solving a crime or mystery. This figurative use of 手掛かり is actually the most common!
5030.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 手 plus 掛かる put together. Just watch out for that rendaku.

examples.en: You'll be alright. The sun will rise again.
examples.ja: 大丈夫。日はまた昇るさ。

examples.en: In the distance, we saw a long, thin plume of smoke rising into the sky.
examples.ja: 遠くの方に、細長い煙が空に昇っていくのが見えました。

examples.en: I felt like I was ascending to heaven as I read my college acceptance letter over and over.
examples.ja: 私は天にも昇る気持ちで、大学からの合格通知を何度も読み直した。

5031.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>ascend</kanji> so the verb vocab version must be <vocabulary>to ascend</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to rise</vocabulary>.

昇る is commonly used to talk about things like the sun and the moon rising, or smoke rising from a fire.
5031.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi reading, but it's pretty easy. How do you read all the other "to climb" words? 登る is one example. 上る is another. They're all <reading>のぼ</reading>る, and so is this. Unlike the other climbing words, though, this suggests there's no effort involved. That's why you're "ascending" and not climbing, because climbing is a bit of work.

examples.en: "Guess what? I got a promotion at work!" "Really? That’s awesome! Congrats!"
examples.ja: 「聞いて聞いて、昇進したんだ！」「本当？すごいね！おめでとう！」

examples.en: What? Isn't the pace of your promotions really fast?
examples.ja: え、お前の昇進のペース、めっちゃ早くない？

examples.en: I missed out on my long-awaited chance of promotion.
examples.ja: 折角の昇進のチャンスを逃してしまった。

examples.en: Mr. Tasaki quit his job one month after he got promoted. What happened to him?
examples.ja: 田崎さんは昇進してから一か月で会社を辞めてしまいました。何があったんでしょう？

5032.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Ascend</kanji> and <kanji>advance</kanji>! Congratulations, you ascend and advance by getting a new <vocabulary>job promotion</vocabulary>.
5032.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I draw manga in my spare time.
examples.ja: 暇な時にマンガをかいています。

examples.en: I admire Mr. Mimura's constant study of stocks in his spare time.
examples.ja: 三村さんは暇さえあれば常に株の勉強をしていて感心します。

examples.en: Lately, work has been so slow, you know? It's so idle that I feel like I'm going to die.
examples.ja: 最近仕事が暇でさー、暇すぎて死にそうなんだよね。

examples.en: We sell home electronic appliances like air purifiers, but not many customers come in and honestly, I have a lot of free time at the store.
examples.ja: 私達は空気洗浄機とか家電を販売してるんですが、お客さんがあまりこないので、お店では正直暇してます。

5033.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

暇 means the <vocabulary>spare time</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>free time</vocabulary> you have when you're <vocabulary>not busy</vocabulary> with work, school, or other obligations. It can also indicate a slow period for a business or a time when you have nothing to do, often suggesting a sense of boredom.
5033.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember: 

In your <vocabulary>spare time</vocabulary> you like to drink <reading>hima</reading> (ひま), an off brand version of Zima.

examples.en: How far in advance do you usually make vacation plans?
examples.ja: いつもどのくらい前から休暇の予定を立てますか？

examples.en: I'm thinking of taking a slightly longer vacation this year.
examples.ja: 今年はちょっと長めに休暇を取ろうと思ってるんです。

examples.en: The day before the Christmas holidays ended, I got the flu.
examples.ja: クリスマス休暇が終わる前日にインフルエンザになってしまった。

examples.en: I wonder where I should go for my summer vacation this year.
examples.ja: 今年の夏季休暇はどこに行こうかな。

examples.en: Oh no! It's only August and I've already used up all my paid vacation days.
examples.ja: やばい！まだ八月なのに、有給休暇、もう全部使い切っちゃった。

5034.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>spare time</kanji> is your <vocabulary>vacation</vocabulary>. It is your <vocabulary>holiday</vocabulary>.

休暇 is a relatively formal word that commonly refers to <vocabulary>time off</vocabulary> from work, ranging from a day off to seasonal vacation to temporary leave.
5034.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I want to play UFO catcher, but I can't find a change machine.
examples.ja: UFOキャッチャーしたいのに、両替機が見つからない。

examples.en: Could you exchange this 10,000 yen bill for 1,000 yen bills?
examples.ja: この一万円札を千円札に両替してもらえませんか？

examples.en: Sorry, I’m afraid we don’t break bills.
examples.ja: すみません、両替はお断りしているんです。

examples.en: I’ll review today’s lesson about how to exchange money in Japanese later.
examples.ja: 後で、今日習った日本語での両替の仕方について復習したいと思います。

examples.en: I wanted to exchange money at Kansai Airport, but the exchange counter was closed.
examples.ja: 関西空港で両替しようと思ったんですが、両替所がしまっていました。

5035.meaning_mnemonic:
Coins? Bills? <kanji>Both</kanji> can be <kanji>replace</kanji>d if you want to <vocabulary>change money</vocabulary> at this <vocabulary>money exchange</vocabulary>. Just don’t do your <vocabulary>currency exchange</vocabulary> at the airport — the rates aren’t so great.

You'll probably see this word the most in arcades where you can go to the 両替 machine and get coins to feed your crane game addiction.
5035.reading_mnemonic: The reading here is a bit weird. Instead of just being か (it changes to が for the rendaku), it is がえ. Just think that if you want change exchanged, I'm your <reading>guy</reading> (がえ).

examples.en: I will replace this trash can bag with a new one!
examples.ja: このゴミ箱のゴミぶくろ、新しいのに取り替えるね！

examples.en: Hey, hey, can you swap my broccoli for that sausage?
examples.ja: ねえねえ、そのソーセージと私のブロッコリー、取り替えてくれない？

examples.en: Today, I learned from my father how to replace the toilet bowl.
examples.ja: 今日、お父さんから便器の取り替え方を教えてもらいました。

examples.en: We should gradually replace all of the office automation equipment for the latest versions.
examples.ja: そろそろ我々のOA機器を最新のものに取り替える方がいいんじゃないでしょうか。

5036.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Take</kanji> and <kanji>replace</kanji> something. That is <vocabulary>to replace</vocabulary> something with something else.

取り替える generally means <vocabulary>to swap out</vocabulary> something with a new or different item of the same kind, like replacing an old gas meter with a new one, or exchanging books with your friend after you've both read your own.
5036.reading_mnemonic: The readings are 取る and 替える put together into one. If you know those words you'll be able to read and understand this one as well.

examples.en: My mother apologized for forgetting to bring me a change of clothes.
examples.ja: 母は、私の着替えを持ってくるのを忘れた事を謝りました。

examples.en: It's time to change into your pajamas!
examples.ja: パジャマにお着替えする時間だよー！

examples.en: My son is going through the "terrible twos" right now, so even just changing his clothes is a big pain.
examples.ja: 今うちの息子イヤイヤ期だからお着替えするだけでも一苦労だよ。

examples.en: Of course I brought a change of clothes for the kids, but I didn't expect to need a change of clothes for myself, so I had to buy some at Wal-Mart.
examples.ja: もちろん子供の着替えは持ってきていたけど、まさか自分の着替えが必要になるとは思ってもいなかったから、ウォルマートで買う羽目になったよ。

5037.meaning_mnemonic: You know how 替える is "to replace"? Well, you're replacing what you <kanji>wear</kanji>. That's a <vocabulary>change of clothes</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>spare clothes</vocabulary>.
5037.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 着る and 替える put together. The か goes to が.

examples.en: I'm gonna master making the ultimate ramen before I die.
examples.ja: 死ぬまでに、究極のラーメンを極めるつもりです。

examples.en: Which kanji do you think is the ultimate in difficulty?
examples.ja: 皆さんは、究極に難しい漢字ってどれだと思いますか？

examples.en: Tomoko spent a half day on beating the ultimate-level monster.
examples.ja: 知子は究極レベルのモンスターを倒すのに半日を費やした。

examples.en: Even Mr. Sakaki congratulated me on finding out the ultimate fundamental truth of the universe.
examples.ja: あの榊氏までもが、私が宇宙の究極の原理を解明したことに祝いの言葉を述べてくれました。

5038.meaning_mnemonic: You are trying to <kanji>research</kanji> the <kanji>extreme</kanji>s. If you do that, you'll be able to figure out the <vocabulary>ultimate</vocabulary> weapon. Just researching the safe middle-ground stuff won't get you ultimate. Extreme research, however, will.
5038.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meanings: To Reach The Peak Of Something

examples.en: Koichi went to Japan to attend a kanji dojo to master the art of kanji.
examples.ja: コウイチは漢字の道を極めるために、日本に行って漢字道場に通いました。

examples.en: I'm a master at cheesecake, you know.
examples.ja: 私、チーズケーキは極めてるからさ。

examples.en: It is no easy task to master the Japanese language.
examples.ja: 日本語を極めるのは、生易しい事ではない。

examples.en: Due to the bad weather, the rescue operation became extremely challenging.
examples.ja: 天候が悪かったので、レスキュー作業は困難を極めました。

examples.en: My dream was to enter the legal profession and master the law, but I've just become extremely busy with work.
examples.ja: 法律関係の職に就いて法律を極めることが夢でしたが、それよりも仕事で多忙を極めることになりました。

5039.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji itself means <kanji>extreme</kanji>. The verb vocab version isn't "to extreme" because that wouldn't make sense. Instead, you bring something to extremes, making this <vocabulary>to reach the peak of something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to perfect</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to reach the extreme</vocabulary>.

極める commonly means reaching the highest level of proficiency or excellence in a particular skill, art, or field. It can also mean taking something to the extreme, like being crazy busy.
5039.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

When you go <vocabulary>to reach the peak of something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to perfect</vocabulary> something, you tend to go a little overboard, so there has to be a <reading>key</reading> <reading>wo</reading>rd (きわ) that other people can say to remind you to calm down a little. “PINEAPPLE! PINEAPPLE!”

examples.en: I entered the hot springs and felt a blissful feeling.
examples.ja: 温泉に入って極楽気分を味わいました。

examples.en: If you do bad things, you can't go to paradise.
examples.ja: 悪いことをしてたら、極楽に行けないよ。

examples.en: The novel about a man who went to paradise by mistake was made into a movie.
examples.ja: 間違いで極楽に行った男についての小説が、映画化されました。

examples.en: Gokuraku Tombo (dragonfly in paradise) is a term used to mockingly describe people who are unaware of the seriousness of a situation and take it lightly. However nowadays, most people only know it as the comedy duo's name.
examples.ja: 「極楽とんぼ」とは、事の重大さに気づかず、のんきに構えている人のことをあざけて言う言葉です。でも、今では芸人さんのコンビ名としてしか知らない人がほとんどですね。

5040.meaning_mnemonic:
This place has <kanji>extreme</kanji> <kanji>comfort</kanji>. It is <vocabulary>paradise</vocabulary>.

極楽 is a short for 極楽浄土 (the Pure Land in Mahayana Buddhism). While it might sound a bit old-fashioned, you can still use it to describe something heavenly. For example, if you're soaking in a cozy, relaxing hot spring, you could say, "Ahhh…極楽!"
5040.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. 極 has two on'yomi readings, though. So here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

In <vocabulary>paradise</vocabulary>, you meet <reading>Goku</reading> (ごく) from Dragon Ball Z. He grins and tells you he's taking a break from extreme battles and enjoying the extreme comfort of this heavenly paradise.

examples.en: My parents have decided to go to Antarctica this summer.
