examples.en: My life may be incomplete, but I would've never dreamt of joining the mafia.
examples.ja: 俺は中途半端な生き方をしてきたかもしれないけど、マフィアに入りたいって思ったことは一度もないよ。

5062.meaning_mnemonic: Take the <kanji>middle</kanji> <kanji>route</kanji>, <kanji>half</kanji> to the <kanji>edge</kanji>. You don't do anything the full way. Just to the middle. Just to the half. Not to the edge. This was really <vocabulary>half finished</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>half assed</vocabulary> of you.
5062.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The ぱ at the end is the only tricky part here since that isn't a common reading (or the one you learned before) for the kanji. Just think of your ol' <reading>Pa</reading> (ぱ), who is the biggest half-asser you know.

examples.en: Mr. Takei, you're being quite extreme by quitting the company just because something unpleasant happened, don't you think?
examples.ja: ちょっと嫌なことがあったからって会社を辞めるなんて、武井さんも極端ですねぇ！

examples.en: When you put it in extreme terms, isn't pension basically a system where 'the lucky survivors' make the young people pay for it?
examples.ja: 年金ってさ、めっちゃ極端に言えば「生き残れたラッキーな人に対して、若い人にお金を出させる」仕組みでしょ？

examples.en: I think uniforms are fantastic to be honest. In extreme terms, I believe that everyone wearing the same clothing makes their individual personalities stand out.
examples.ja: 私は制服って素晴らしいと思ってるんです。極端な話、皆が同じ服を着ることで、それぞれの中身の個性が際立つと思うんですよ。

examples.en: You may be able to perform miracles, but I want you to avoid doing extreme things.
examples.ja: 君は奇跡を起こすことができるかもしれない。でも、僕は君には極端なことは避けてもらいたいんだよ。

5063.meaning_mnemonic:
At the <kanji>extreme</kanji> <kanji>edge</kanji>, which is just the <vocabulary>extreme</vocabulary>.

極端 means something is taken to the extreme without moderation, so it generally has a negative connotation.
5063.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Your pay will be deposited in the bank on the fifth day of every month.
examples.ja: 給料は毎月五日に銀行に振りこまれます。

examples.en: You're not doing your job at all. You salary thief!
examples.ja: お前、全然仕事できてねーじゃん。この給料どろぼう！

examples.en: With only my salary, we’re in the red if we continue with our current lifestyle.
examples.ja: 私の給料だけだと、今の生活スタイルのままじゃ赤字なんだよね。

examples.en: "I heard your boss is going to give you a raise." "Really? That’ll be the day."
examples.ja: 「君の上司が、君の給料を上げるつもりだって聞いたよ。」「まさか！そんなことあり得ないよ。」

5064.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>salary</kanji> <kanji>fee</kanji> are the moneys you get for your <vocabulary>salary</vocabulary>. These are your <vocabulary>wages</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>pay</vocabulary>.
5064.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What is the monthly take-home pay that you receive?
examples.ja: 月にもらえる給与は手取りでいくらぐらいですか。

examples.en: I heard that the topic of salary is taboo in corporate America, is that true?
examples.ja: アメリカの企業では給与の話題はタブーだと聞いたんですが、本当ですか？

examples.en: We will transfer your monthly wages to the designated bank account.
examples.ja: 毎月の給与は、指定の銀行口座にお振り込みいたします。

examples.en: Frankly, I think it would be quite difficult to find a job that meets your desired salary level.
examples.ja: 正直、ご希望の給与水準に見合うお仕事を見つけるのは、かなり難しいかと思います。

5065.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>salary</kanji> I <kanji>give</kanji> you is your <vocabulary>salary</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>wages</vocabulary>. It is the <vocabulary>pay</vocabulary> you earn.

Curious about the difference between 給与 and 給料? 給与 is generally considered the formal version of 給料, but there is another minor difference in nuance. 給料 often refers to your base pay, while 給与 refers to the total amount of <vocabulary>compensation</vocabulary> you receive, including overtime, bonuses, etc.
5065.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The water supply has finally resumed.
examples.ja: 水の供給がようやく再開されました。

examples.en: Our maximum priority is to stabilize the supplies.
examples.ja: 最優先事項は供給を安定させることだ。

examples.en: For a stable supply of electricity, it is important to efficiently combine power generation methods such as thermal, hydroelectric, nuclear, and renewable energy sources.
examples.ja: 電力の安定供給には、火力、水力、原子力、再生可能エネルギーなどによる発電を効率的に組み合わせることが重要です。

examples.en: To ensure a stable food supply to the citizens, it is necessary to secure agricultural land and utilize it to the maximum extent possible.
examples.ja: 食料を国民に安定的に供給するには、農地を確保し、それを最大限に有効利用する必要があります。

5066.meaning_mnemonic:
If you can <kanji>offer</kanji> a <kanji>salary</kanji> to someone, it means you've got plenty of <vocabulary>supply</vocabulary>. The bigger the salary you can offer, the bigger your supply is, probably. That's why those big tech companies can pay so well — they have an endless supply of paying customers or ad revenue, I guess. 

供給 is a somewhat formal word you'd generally hear in the context of economics — like <vocabulary>supplying</vocabulary> goods, energy, or food where there's demand. You wouldn't use it for art supplies or the food you buy every day.
5066.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: What was the reason for the pay cut?
examples.ja: 減給の原因は何だったんですか？

examples.en: Isn't this essentially a pay cut?
examples.ja: これって、実質的には減給じゃないですか？

examples.en: I never expected a pay cut, so I stayed at a first-rate hotel to round off my journey.
examples.ja: まさか減給があるなんて思いもしなかったから、旅の締めくくりに一流ホテルにとまっちゃったんだよね。

examples.en: I got a pay cut and my boss is mean so I’m seriously thinking of quitting and looking for a different job.
examples.ja: 減給されるし、上司も嫌なヤツだし、会社を辞めて転職先をさがすことを本気で考えてるんだよね。

5067.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I’m worried about whether or not I can get a raise.
examples.ja: 昇給できるかどうかが気にかかっているんです。

examples.en: I got a raise, but I now have to work more to make up for it.…
examples.ja: 昇給したのはいいんですが、その分もっと働かないといけなくなってしまって…。

examples.en: At my previous company, I received regular raises every year and a bonus twice a year.
examples.ja: 前の会社では、毎年定期昇給があって、賞与も年に2回出ました。

examples.en: When the industry made an economic comeback I applied for a raise, but it didn’t work out.
examples.ja: 業界の景気回復に伴い、昇給を願い出たんだが、うまくいかなかったよ。

5068.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>ascend</kanji> in <kanji>salary</kanji> you get a <vocabulary>pay raise</vocabulary> at work.

Note that this is a relatively formal word to talk about <vocabulary>getting a raise</vocabulary>.
5068.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It’s strange, I wonder why those countries entered into a peace treaty so suddenly.
examples.ja: どうしてあの国が突然平和友好条約を締結したのか不思議に思うよ。

examples.en: We spent a considerable amount of time to ratify this treaty.
examples.ja: この条約を締結するのにかなり長い時間を費やした。

examples.en: We decided to sign a partnership agreement with the supplier.
examples.ja: 供給元とパートナーシップ協定を締結することにしました。

examples.en: When a foreign country and Japan enter into a treaty, the Diet ratifies the treaty, and then the Cabinet concludes it.
examples.ja: 外国と日本が条約を結ぶ時は、国会が条約を承認し、内閣が条約を締結するんです。

5069.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>tighten</kanji> things up and <kanji>bind</kanji> things together, it's hard to separate them again. That's why this word is used <vocabulary>to conclude</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to enter into</vocabulary> important agreements, like treaties and contracts.

Note that this word is quite formal, which makes sense, given the contexts it’s usually used in.
5069.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Did you tightly turn off the gas?
examples.ja: ガスの元栓、ちゃんと締めた？

examples.en: I'm wondering what words would be good to wrap up the speech.
examples.ja: どんな言葉でスピーチを締めるべきか迷っているんだ。

examples.en: Wait a minute. I haven't fastened my seatbelt yet!
examples.ja: ちょっと待って。シートベルト、まだ締めてない！

examples.en: I don't know how to put on a tie, but leave it to me to tighten the screws!
examples.ja: ネクタイの締め方は分からないけど、ネジを締めるのは任せて！

5070.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>tighten</kanji> so the verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to tighten</vocabulary>, like a screw, or to tie, like a necktie or towel.

締める can also mean <vocabulary>to wrap up</vocabulary> when used in reference to a speech or some other occasion. In Japanese culture, people often 締める a situation with some shared action, like clapping in rhythm to end a celebration or having a final bowl of ramen to close out a night. You call it 締める because it's like you're tying off the event and giving it a sense of closure.
5070.reading_mnemonic: You go <vocabulary>to tighten</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to tie</vocabulary> your captive up, and you realize you don't have anything to do it with. Then you see a sheep standing nearby. Okay. You take the <reading>shee</reading>p (し), pull its wool, and tie the sheep and your captive up together around a tree. Problem solved!

examples.en: He succeeded in obtaining the organizational votes in the presidential election.
examples.ja: 彼は、大統領選挙で組織票をゲットすることに成功した。

examples.en: I heard they finally issued an arrest warrant for that criminal organization.
examples.ja: ついにあの犯罪組織に逮捕状が出たらしいよ。

examples.en: President, what kind of organization do you think a good organization is?
examples.ja: 社長は、いい組織とはどんな組織を指すとお考えですか？

examples.en: I’m Sakuraba, the man responsible for making the promotion decisions for this organization.
examples.ja: 私がこの組織で昇格の決定を担っている桜庭と申します。

5071.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>group</kanji> that's <kanji>weave</kanji>d together so tightly with hierarchy and everything else is a little more complicated than a group. It's an <vocabulary>organization</vocabulary>.
5071.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You didn't learn that reading for 組, so here's a mnemonic to help: 

You start an <vocabulary>organization</vocabulary> for <reading>so</reading>ap (そ). You're all about soap and making it more effective through your organization. So you call it the Soap Organization for Antiseptic Progress, or S.O.A.P. for short.

examples.en: We mostly weave by machine, but we sometimes weave by hand.
examples.ja: 機械で織ることがほとんどですが、手で織ることもありますよ。

examples.en: I'm weaving a lap blanket with wool from Ms. Sheep.
examples.ja: 羊さんの羊毛で、ひざ掛けを織っているんです。

examples.en: Wow, did you weave this fabric Ken-san?
examples.ja: うわー、この布地、ケンさんが織ったんですか？

examples.en: Lately, my mother has been really into using a handloom to weave carpets.
examples.ja: 私の母親は、最近手織り機でカーペットを織ることにはまっているんです。

5072.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>weave</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to weave</vocabulary>.
5072.reading_mnemonic: When you have <vocabulary>to weave</vocabulary> the only thing you can weave is an <reading>O</reading> (お) shape. That's it. Just O's.

examples.en: My stomachache got worse and I was hospitalized, so I spent a month at the hospital.
examples.ja: 胃痛がひどくなって入院し、病院で一ヶ月過ごしました。

examples.en: Please give me the medicine that works well for stomachaches.
examples.ja: 胃痛によく効く薬をください。

examples.en: When you experience severe stomach pain after eating raw fish, please go to the hospital immediately! It could be anisakiasis.
examples.ja: 生魚を食べて激しい胃痛が出た時はすぐに病院へ行ってください！アニサキス症かもしれません。

examples.en: Since I quit smoking my intense stomach aches have also stopped.
examples.ja: 禁煙してから、激しい胃痛も治まっている。

5073.meaning_mnemonic:
When your <kanji>stomach</kanji> <kanji>hurts</kanji> you have yourself a little <vocabulary>stomachache</vocabulary>.

Try to remember this isn't for general abdominal pain. 胃痛 is specifically for pain or discomfort in the stomach (the internal organ) — a literal stomachache.
5073.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: You are getting a little fat around the belly, aren’t you?
examples.ja: お前ちょっと腹が出てきたんじゃねぇか？

examples.en: Ms. Shimazaki was holding her belly with laughter.
examples.ja: 島崎さんは腹をかかえて笑っていました。

examples.en: These days, I have been bothered by my beer belly, so I finally decided to go on a diet.
examples.ja: 最近ビール腹が気になって、とうとうダイエットをすることにしました。

examples.en: I've been experiencing stomach pain for quite some time now.
examples.ja: ここ最近、ずっと腹が痛いんだ。

5074.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
5074.reading_mnemonic:
If anyone tries to touch your <kanji>belly</kanji>, that's <reading>hara</reading>ssment (はら). Unless you're cool with it, obviously. But if you're not, make sure to yell "harassment!" when they touch your belly. You should also shout what kind of harassment it is: 腹ハラ (腹 harassment).

Note: This word will often get rendaku'd when it's combined with other vocab, like in ビールばら (beer belly) or 別ばら (separate stomach for dessert).

examples.en: I've had a bit of a stomachache since this morning.
examples.ja: 朝から、ちょっとお腹が痛いんです。

examples.en: In my forties, I've started to get a potbelly.
examples.ja: 四十代になってお腹がぽっこり出てきた。

examples.en: Since I ate until I was completely full of delicious food today, I feel like I can work hard again starting tomorrow.
examples.ja: 今日はおいしいものをお腹いっぱい食べたから、また明日から仕事がんばれそうだよ。

examples.en: "Supper is ready! Come and get it." "Oh, thank god! I'm starving!"
examples.ja: 「お夕飯の支度ができましたよ！いらっしゃい。」「ああ、よかった！お腹ペコペコだよ。」

5075.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

It's common to see this word written in kanji, but you'll also see it written in hiragana, especially in casual contexts.
5075.reading_mnemonic: The reading is an exception, but it isn't too hard to remember. It's the same as <reading>中</reading> (なか), so if you think about it it makes sense. It's your insides, just like your <vocabulary>belly</vocabulary> is your insides!

examples.en: It makes me so mad. They are in the way of our practice!
examples.ja: 本気で腹立つんだけど。練習のジャマだわ！

examples.en: There's something about the way she talks that makes me angry.
examples.ja: 彼女の話し方には、何か腹立つものがある。

examples.en: While hiding her angry feelings, she pretended to be calm and chose her words carefully.
examples.ja: 腹立つ感情を隠しつつ、彼女は冷静をよそおって言葉を選んだ。

examples.en: It's completely natural to feel angry at someone who doesn't keep their promises.
examples.ja: 約束を守らない人に腹立つのは、極めて自然なことである。

5076.meaning_mnemonic: What's that feeling when your <kanji>belly</kanji> <kanji>stands</kanji> up? It's that feeling where something jumps up into your throat (in this case your belly) and you get all pissed off. This word means <vocabulary>to get mad</vocabulary>.
5076.reading_mnemonic:
The readings are 腹 plus 立つ put together. The たつ becomes だつ as a standard reading though.

While はらだつ is the standard reading for 腹立つ, it's usually found in more formal settings or writing. You'll probably hear はらたつ more often in everyday conversations, as it’s a shorter, more colloquial way of expressing 腹が立つ!

examples.en: It hurts just to think about seppuku, doesn’t it?
examples.ja: 切腹とか考えるだけで痛いよね。

examples.en: How did Japanese samurai warriors come to commit seppuku?
examples.ja: どうして日本の武士は切腹をするようになったのでしょうか？

examples.en: Yesterday, I dreamed that I became a samurai and committed ritual suicide.
examples.ja: 昨日、サムライになって切腹する夢を見た。

examples.en: The old samurai insisted on committing ritual suicide.
examples.ja: その年老いた武士は、切腹をすることに固執した。

5077.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>cut</kanji> your <kanji>abdomen</kanji> you are committing <vocabulary>seppuku</vocabulary>. It will help if you already know the word "seppuku" from English, since it's also the reading here.

切腹 is a form of <vocabulary>ritual suicide</vocabulary> by self-inflicted disembowelment, often performed by samurai to restore honor.
5077.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. But it's got shortening and rendaku going on, so you have to remember those if you want to get it right. Or just know the word seppuku already since it's pretty popular. That works too.

examples.en: The feudal lord ordered the low-grade samurai to perform ritual suicide.
examples.ja: 大名はその下級武士に腹切りを命じた。

examples.en: The word "harakiri" might have spread more among foreigners because the sound of it has a strong impact.
examples.ja: 外国人に「腹切り」という言葉の方が広まったのは、響きにインパクトあったからかもね。

examples.en: The word harakiri feels somehow more visceral than seppuku, doesn’t it?
examples.ja: 腹切りって言葉、なんだか切腹よりも生々しい感じがするよね。

examples.en: The movie based on samurai harakiri will be released next week.
examples.ja: 侍の腹切りをテーマにした映画は来週公開されます。

5078.meaning_mnemonic:
If your <kanji>abdomen</kanji> is getting <kanji>cut</kanji>, and you're the one doing the cutting, there's a good chance you're committing <vocabulary>harakiri</vocabulary>, a form of <vocabulary>ritual suicide</vocabulary>.

腹切り sounds blunt and colloquial compared to the more formal 切腹. Kind of like you're just saying the words "belly cutting" — not very refined! This is often the case with synonym pairs like this: the one with kun'yomi readings will sound more casual, while the one with on'yomi readings will sound more formal.
5078.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 腹 and 切る. If you're lucky, you already know the word harakiri as it's made its way into English as well.

examples.en: You should call her before visiting.
examples.ja: 家を訪ねる前に、電話してみた方がいいよ。

examples.en: Nobuko, don't open the door even when a stranger visits the house.
examples.ja: 信子ちゃん、知らない人が訪ねてきてもドアを開けたらダメよ。

examples.en: Someday, I want to take a trip to visit the natural beauty of Canada using a camper van.
examples.ja: いつか、キャンピングカーを使って、カナダの自然を訪ねる旅がしたいんです。

examples.en: I visited a truant student every day after school.
examples.ja: 私は、放課後毎日、不登校の生徒を訪ねました。

5079.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>visit</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to visit</vocabulary>.
5079.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You want <vocabulary>to visit</vocabulary> your friend <reading>Taz</reading> (たず), the Tasmanian Devil. He's your best bro, so imagine visiting him and having a good time and saying you're going to visit him again.

examples.en: Is there something that got on your nerves when I visited you the other day?
examples.ja: この間の訪問の際、何かお気に触るようなことをしてしまいましたか？

examples.en: Don't you have a home-visit care service that is a bit cheaper?
examples.ja: もうちょっと安い訪問サービスはないんですか？

examples.en: Home visits are for teachers to visit students' homes, observe the home environment, and have conversations with parents.
examples.ja: 家庭訪問は、先生が生徒の家庭を訪ね、家庭環境を観察し、保護者と話すためのものです。

examples.en: In Japan, you usually can't get all your dental treatment done in just one visit.
examples.ja: 日本では、通常歯医者に一回の訪問で治療を済ませてもらうことはできません。

5080.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>visit</kanji> <kanji>problem</kanji> is when someone makes <vocabulary>a visit</vocabulary>, because you're the type of person who doesn't like visitors, since they're usually so inconsiderate and you have to feed them. That's why <vocabulary>a visit</vocabulary> is a visit problem.
5080.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I find it difficult to ask friends to hang out.
examples.ja: 私、友達を誘うのが苦手なんです。

examples.en: I was enticed by the pleasant weather and went for a walk.
examples.ja: 陽気に誘われ、ウォーキングに出かけた。

examples.en: What should we do? Should we also invite Saori to karaoke?
examples.ja: どうする？サオリもカラオケに誘う？

examples.en: If my boss asks me to go eat ramen, I have no choice but to go, right?
examples.ja: 上司にラーメンを食べに行かないかと誘われたら、行くしかないっしょ。

examples.en: I finally asked Sayako out on a date and she said yes, so we're going out for dinner tonight.
examples.ja: ついにサヤコをデートに誘ったんだけど、なんとOKの返事をもらえたんだよ。だから、今夜、食事をしに出かけるんだ。

5081.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>invite</kanji>. The verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to invite</vocabulary>.

誘う refers to casually inviting someone to a place, an event, or an activity. If it's an invitation to something tempting, it can also mean <vocabulary>to tempt</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to entice</vocabulary>.
5081.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Everyone is excited to <vocabulary>invite</vocabulary> you to their home for a demo because you've just invented <reading>saw</reading> <reading>so</reading>ap (さそ). What's saw soap? It's a soap that cuts through all the grime!

examples.en: I'm sorry, but my parents have told me not to lend money to people.
examples.ja: すみませんが、人にお金を貸すな、と親に言われているんです。

examples.en: Renting out apartments or houses isn't as easy as you might think. Depending on the tenant, it can become really stressful.
examples.ja: アパートや家を貸すのって、思ってるほど楽じゃないよ。テナントさんによって、ほんとストレスになるんだから。

examples.en: I guess it can't be avoided. Just this time, I'll lend you a hand.
examples.ja: しょうがねーな。今回だけ、手を貸してやるよ。

examples.en: "Can you lend me your car?" "Absolutely not. You don’t have a license yet."
examples.ja: 「君の車を貸してくれない？」「絶対にだめだよ。まだ免許持ってないじゃないか。」

5082.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>lend</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to lend</vocabulary>.
5082.reading_mnemonic: Allow me <vocabulary>to lend</vocabulary> you some advice. The reading you learned from the kanji can be used here.

examples.en: Our company chartered a plane and we went to Bermuda.
examples.ja: 会社で飛行機を貸し切りにしてバミューダまで行きました。

examples.en: Tokyo Disneyland sometimes has days reserved for celebrities only.
examples.ja: 東京ディズニーランドは時々芸能人貸し切りになる日があります。

examples.en: The inn has a private hot spring.
examples.ja: この宿には、貸し切りの温泉があります。

5083.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>lend</kanji>ing gets <kanji>cut</kanji> right away when you make a <vocabulary>private reservation</vocabulary>.

貸し切り means reserving a space exclusively, like renting out a restaurant for a birthday party or chartering a bus, cruise, or jet.
5083.reading_mnemonic: It's the reading of 貸す and 切る put together. Know those two readings and you know this one as well. Sometimes you'll see this word as 貸切り or 貸切 as well.

examples.en: I pressed him to pay back the money, but he ran away.
examples.ja: 彼に金を返すよう迫ったが、逃げられてしまった。

examples.en: If you only look at the surface, you will never close in on the essence of the matter.
examples.ja: 表面的なことだけを見ていては、物事の本質に迫ることはできません。

examples.en: It appears that danger is imminent.
examples.ja: どうやら危険が迫っているようですね。

examples.en: I am currently being pressed to make a big decision.
examples.ja: 私は今、大きな決断を迫られています

examples.en: I was quite surprised to see Koichi's face, which was five meters away from me a second ago, suddenly looming right in front of me.
examples.ja: 一秒前には五メートル先にあったコウイチの顔が急に目前に迫ってきてかなりびっくりした。

5084.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>urge</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to urge</vocabulary>.

At its core, 迫る means <vocabulary>to approach</vocabulary>, like a deadline or danger drawing near. This idea extends to urging someone because it's like you're coming really close to them, <vocabulary>to press</vocabulary> them into action.
5084.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Do you prefer <vocabulary>to urge</vocabulary> people to do something, or <vocabulary>to press</vocabulary> them to do it? It depends on how you want <vocabulary>to approach</vocabulary> them. But it's all <reading>sema</reading>ntics (せま) because they're basically the same.

examples.en: For some reason, I feel a tight pressure on my chest since last weekend.
examples.ja: 何故か週末から胸が圧迫される感じがあるんです。

examples.en: My friend Hanako is practicing for stress interviews in order to pass the test to become a broadcaster.
examples.ja: 友達の花子ちゃんは、アナウンサー試験に合格するために圧迫面接の練習をしています。

examples.en: Sending money to my son is putting a strain on our finances.
examples.ja: 息子への仕送りが家計を圧迫しています。

examples.en: I gave up my dream to become an astronaut because I couldn’t stand the pressure.
examples.ja: 圧迫に耐えないので、宇宙飛行士になる夢を諦めた。

5085.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>pressure</kanji> is <kanji>urge</kanji>d upon you. It's the <vocabulary>pressure</vocabulary>, so much pressure!

圧迫 refers to a tight pressure caused by strong compression, or to the act of pressing down itself. Figuratively, it can also mean <vocabulary>constriction</vocabulary>, like tuition fees putting a strain on a household budget, or <vocabulary>oppression</vocabulary>, such as people being subjugated.
5085.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The あつ turns into a small っ, and はく goes to ぱく.

examples.en: I think all people should learn the history of persecution and discrimination in the world.
examples.ja: 全ての人々が、世界の迫害と差別の歴史を学ぶべきだと思います。

examples.en: We fled to this country because there was a possibility of persecution if we stayed in our homeland.
examples.ja: 私達は自国にいると迫害を受ける可能性があったので、この国に逃げて来たんです。

examples.en: The Rohingya refugees are referred to as "the most persecuted minority in the world.”
examples.ja: ロヒンギャ難民は、「世界で最も迫害された少数民族」と呼ばれています。

5086.meaning_mnemonic:
Someone has an <kanji>urge</kanji> to <kanji>damage</kanji> things. If that person wants to harm you, you might be facing <vocabulary>persecution</vocabulary>.

As you might guess, this word is quite formal.
5086.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: His situation must be pretty dire.
examples.ja: ヤツの状況はかなり切迫しているはずです。

examples.en: With an urgent expression on his face, Koichi said, "I need to go to the bathroom right now, or it's going to be bad.”
examples.ja: コウイチは切迫した表情で、「俺、今すぐトイレに行かなきゃヤバイんだ」と言った。

examples.en: I’m facing an imminent crisis so I need to borrow money from the yakuza.
examples.ja: ヤクザからお金を借りなければいけないという切迫した危機に直面している。

examples.en: I was hospitalized for three weeks due to threatened premature labor, and being hospitalized for such conditions is really difficult.
examples.ja: 切迫早産で三週間入院したけど、切迫の入院って、本当に辛いんだよ。

5087.meaning_mnemonic:
We're <kanji>cut</kanji> right down to the end, reaching that <kanji>urge</kanji> position where <vocabulary>urgency</vocabulary> is so strong.

切迫 is used to describe the tension in a situation where a time limit is <vocabulary>drawing near</vocabulary>, or to describe something bad or dangerous as <vocabulary>impending</vocabulary>.
5087.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The せつ of 切 gets shortened to a small っ. The はく becomes ぱく.

examples.en: My mother often gets lost.
examples.ja: 私の母はよく道に迷うんです。

examples.en: I'm torn between buying a Mario figurine or a Luigi figurine.
examples.ja: マリオの人形とルイージの人形、どちらを買おうか迷っています。

examples.en: There will be a bunch of people there I don't know, so to be honest, I'm still not sure whether I'll go.
examples.ja: 知らない人がたくさんいるだろうし、正直まだ行くかどうか迷ってるんだよね。

examples.en: I'm not sure if I should buy unsweetened coffee.
examples.ja: 無糖珈琲を買おうかどうか迷っています。

5088.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>astray</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to go astray</vocabulary> (because you don't just "to astray" now do you?). You can use it if you ever happen <vocabulary>to get lost</vocabulary>. 

Beyond physically getting lost, 迷う is also for times when you waver between different choices or hesitate to take a decisive step.
5088.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

If you are going <vocabulary>to go astray</vocabulary>, one way to do it would be to eat wayyyy too much <reading>mayo</reading> (まよ). I can't think of a worse way to go astray, personally.

examples.en: I heard that at Disneyland, they don't broadcast for lost children.
examples.ja: ディズニーランドでは迷子の放送がないそうですよ。

examples.en: Even Japanese people often get lost at Shinjuku Station.
examples.ja: 日本人でも、新宿駅で迷子になる人は多い。

examples.en: I wasn't attentive, and I almost got lost at Universal Studios Japan.
examples.ja: ボーッとしてたら、USJで迷子になりかけた。

examples.en: I was just trying to find the parents of a lost child, but I was accused of attempted kidnapping.
examples.ja: 迷子の子どもの両親を探してあげようとしていただけなのに、誘拐未遂で起訴されてしまいました。

5089.meaning_mnemonic:
After going <kanji>astray</kanji>, the <kanji>child</kanji> becomes a <vocabulary>lost child</vocabulary>. Let's help them find their way home.

Keep in mind that 迷子 isn't only for lost children; it applies to anyone who's lost, such as a <vocabulary>lost person</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>stray animal</vocabulary>.
5089.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 迷 is an exceptional reading. The ご comes from こ. Think of the まい as the child asking: "Where is <reading>my</reading> (まい) mommy???"

examples.en: The map for the maze is hidden somewhere.
examples.ja: どこかに、迷路の地図が隠されています。

examples.en: Nobody found their way out of the maze.
examples.ja: 誰一人としてその迷路の出口を見つけることができませんでした。

examples.en: Haruko and Akiko compete against each other at a corn maze every year. I wonder which one will win this year.
examples.ja: 春子ちゃんと秋子ちゃんは毎年トウモロコシばたけの迷路で競争しているんだけど、今年はどっちが勝つかな。

examples.en: My son loves mazes.
examples.ja: 私の息子は迷路が大好きです。

5090.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>road</kanji> where you're <kanji>astray</kanji> is a road that goes all around in different ways, tricking you and making you lost. This is a <vocabulary>maze</vocabulary>.
5090.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Anyhow, it's probably a kind of superstition.
examples.ja: どうせ迷信の一種でしょう。

examples.en: I don't believe in the superstition and kept using a cracked mirror up until now.
examples.ja: 私は迷信を信じないので、今でも割れた鏡を使っています。

examples.en: It's discriminatory to say that old people are more likely to believe in superstitions.
examples.ja: 年寄りは迷信を信じやすいというのは差別だ。

5091.meaning_mnemonic: Led <kanji>astray</kanji> in what you <kanji>believe</kanji> by all these <vocabulary>superstition</vocabulary>s. These superstitions will lead you astray, don't believe them!
5091.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It's too early to retire from active duty.
examples.ja: 現役を退くには、まだ早過ぎますよ。

examples.en: The player chose to retire from the front lines and become a coach.
examples.ja: その選手は第一線を退いて、コーチになる道を選びました。

examples.en: Facing the wolf, Mika retreated two or three steps back.
examples.ja: オオカミを前にして、ミカは二、三歩退いた。

examples.en: How do you think you would have gotten the enemy soldiers to retreat in this situation?
examples.ja: お前なら、どうすればこの状況で敵兵を退かせることができると思う？

examples.en: Koichi finished his term and stepped down from the position of president.
examples.ja: コウイチは任期を満了し、大統領の座を退きました。

examples.en: Even after you resign from your position, you must not disclose or misuse personal information obtained in the course of your work.
examples.ja: 職を退いた後も、仕事で得た個人情報を他人にもらしたり、悪用してはいけません。

5092.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>retreat</kanji>, and the verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to retreat</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to withdraw</vocabulary>.

退く can also mean <vocabulary>to resign</vocabulary>, since resigning is a kind of a figurative retreat, like from a professional role or the forefront of some field or industry.
5092.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You need <vocabulary>to retreat</vocabulary> because <reading>she re-zo</reading>ned (しりぞ) where you are standing. Now this is a no standing zone. Who is she? The re-zoner, duh.

examples.en: I hope I will be released from the hospital soon.
examples.ja: すぐに退院することができるといいんだけど。

examples.en: We do not know yet when he will be able to leave the hospital.
examples.ja: いつ退院することができるのかはまだ分かりません。

examples.en: Ms. Murata's mother left the hospital six hours after she had her baby.
examples.ja: 村田さんのお母さんは、赤ちゃんを産んだ後、六時間で退院しました。

examples.en: When Dad gets discharged from the hospital, let's celebrate.
examples.ja: お父さんが退院したらみんなでお祝いをしよう。

5093.meaning_mnemonic: Time to <kanji>retreat</kanji> from the <kanji>institution</kanji>. Basically, you are leaving an institution, particularly institutions like hospitals, asylums, etc. When you are leaving one of these places, it means you are <vocabulary>to be discharged</vocabulary>.
5093.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Why don’t you leave school early with me?
examples.ja: 一緒に学校を早退しない？

examples.en: Because I had a severe stomachache, I left work early and went to see a doctor.
examples.ja: 激しい胃痛があったので、会社を早退して医者に行きました。

examples.en: I submitted an early leave form at work, but it doesn't seem to be approved yet.
examples.ja: 会社に早退届を出したのですが、まだ受理されていないようです。

examples.en: I left school early and my friends said I was cheating. Is it wrong to leave early?
examples.ja: 学校を早退したら、友達にずるいって言われたんだけど、早退は悪いことなの？

5094.meaning_mnemonic:
An <kanji>early</kanji> <kanji>retreat</kanji> means that you <vocabulary>leave early</vocabulary>.

Note that 早退 means leaving school or work earlier than usual. It's not used for leaving hangouts or parties early.
5094.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Can you stop by a grocery store and buy some tofu on your way home?
examples.ja: 途中でスーパーによっておとうふを買って来てちょうだい。

examples.en: I was in the middle of eating lunch when I got a phone call.
examples.ja: 昼ご飯を食べてる途中で、電話がかかってきた。

examples.en: Oh, I stopped playing that game halfway through.
examples.ja: あ、そのゲーム、途中で止めちゃったんだよね。

examples.en: That painting is still only half done.
examples.ja: その絵はまだ途中です。

examples.en: "Can you come over right now?" "Sure, I’m actually on my way now." "Huh? Do you know where you’re going?" "Nope, I don’t."
examples.ja: 「今すぐに来られますか？」「ええ。今向かっている途中です。」「え？ということは、場所をご存知なんですね？」「いいえ、分かりません。」

5095.meaning_mnemonic:
If you're on a <kanji>route</kanji>, right in the <kanji>middle</kanji>, you're <vocabulary>on the way</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>en route</vocabulary>.

途中 can also be used figuratively to say you're <vocabulary>in the middle of</vocabulary> doing something or something is <vocabulary>half done</vocabulary>.
5095.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: How are you planning to arrest them?
examples.ja: どうやって逮捕するつもりですか？

examples.en: We finally arrested the culprit.
examples.ja: ついに犯人を逮捕した。

examples.en: I've never been arrested before.
examples.ja: これまでに逮捕されたことはありません。

examples.en: You should be careful because the criminal is still free.
examples.ja: 犯人はまだ逮捕されてないみたいだから、気を付けた方がいいよ。

examples.en: If you don’t leave now, I’ll arrest you for violating laws against interfering with a public servant in the line of duty.
examples.ja: もし今この場を去らなければ、公務執行妨害で逮捕するぞ。

5096.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 逮捕 is an "arrest" or "capture"? This is the verb version, and it is <vocabulary>to arrest</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to capture</vocabulary>.
5096.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Will also be helpful to know the word 逮捕 already as well.

examples.en: I just don't like the way that bastard speaks.
examples.ja: あの野郎の物の言い方が気に入らねぇんだよ。

examples.en: The guys were making a ruckus at the party.
examples.ja: パーティーでは野郎どもがどんちゃんさわぎをしていた。

examples.en: You rascal, how dare you!
examples.ja: この野郎、よくもやったな！

examples.en: That bastard got promoted to sales manager. I’m sick to my stomach.
examples.ja: あのクソ野郎がセールス・マネージャーに昇進するなんて本当に気に食わねぇ。

5097.meaning_mnemonic:
Ugh, that <kanji>field</kanji> <kanji>guy</kanji>. He's the worst. Always in the fields, making us look bad, quite the <vocabulary>bastard</vocabulary>. Really though, he's just this guy, but for some reason I sometimes don't like him.

While 野郎 can be a casual term for a man, it's usually used to insult or show annoyance towards someone. So it's best to avoid using it unless you're really sure it's okay!
5097.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I am having trouble because my kid loses his shoes quickly.
examples.ja: 子供がすぐ靴をなくすから困っているんです。

examples.en: Perhaps it is because my walking style is bad, but my shoes get worn out within a year of buying them.
examples.ja: 歩き方が悪いせいか、靴を買っても一年たたないうちにはきつぶしてしまう。

examples.en: It's time to get new shoes.
examples.ja: そろそろ新しい靴を買わなきゃ。

examples.en: "Ah, my feet are killing me." "Told you so! That’s why I told you to wear more comfortable shoes."
examples.ja: 「ああ、足が棒だよ。痛くて死にそう。」「言わんこっちゃない。だから、もっと歩きやすい靴を履けって最初に言ったじゃないか。」

5098.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
5098.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. Huzzah!

examples.en: It says three pairs of socks for 500 yen. That’s so cheap!
examples.ja: 靴下三足で五百円だって！めっちゃ安いっ。

examples.en: I don't like nylon socks because they are slippery.
examples.ja: ナイロンの靴下はすべるから好きじゃない。

examples.en: Hey, did you know? In English, those socks that Santa Claus fills with gifts on Christmas are called "Christmas stockings"!
examples.ja: ねえ、知ってた？クリスマスにサンタさんがプレゼントを入れてくれる靴下のこと、英語では 「クリスマスストッキングズ」って言うんだって！

examples.en: I tried to reach the top shelf to get a pair of pink socks, but I wasn’t tall enough.
examples.ja: ピンクの靴下を取ろうと一番上の棚に手を伸ばしたが、背丈が足りずに届かなかった。

5099.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You've learned them already, so you should be able to read this word too!

examples.en: There is a famous shoe store in front of Mr. Takahashi's house.
examples.ja: 高橋さんの家の前には有名な靴屋さんがあります。

examples.en: We always buy shoes from the same shoe shop.
examples.ja: うちは、いつも同じ靴屋で靴を買うんだよ。

examples.en: Don't you have to go all the way to Italy to study abroad, just because you want to work as a craftsman in a shoemaker's shop?
examples.ja: 靴屋で職人として働きたいからってわざわざイタリアまで留学しなくてもよくない？

examples.en: I was offered a job at the shoe store, but I politely declined.
examples.ja: 靴屋での仕事に内定が出たが、丁重にお断りさせてもらったよ。

5100.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>shoes</kanji> <kanji>shop</kanji> is one that sells shoes. It's a <vocabulary>shoe store</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>shoe shop</vocabulary>.
5100.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: Koichi, you always wear Pikachu rain boots on rainy days, don't you?
examples.ja: コウイチはいつも雨の日はピカチュウの長靴をはいてくるよね。

examples.en: I always thought rain boots are for kids, but these days, there are fashionable rain boots for adults too, aren't there?
examples.ja: 長靴って子供のものだけかと思ってたんだけど、最近じゃ大人用のお洒落な長靴も売ってるんだね。

examples.en: While laying in his hospital bed, he decided he would get a nice pair of riding boots for his wife the next day.
examples.ja: 病院のベッドに横になりながら、彼は明日妻にいい乗馬用の長靴を買ってやろうと思った。

5101.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Long</kanji> <kanji>shoes</kanji> aren't long in that the feet part are long (that wouldn't make sense). Instead, the top part is long to keep you dry when it's raining. Yes, these are <vocabulary>rain boots</vocabulary>.

In modern Japanese, 長靴 is most commonly used to mean rain boots or <vocabulary>rubber boots</vocabulary>. It can occasionally mean <vocabulary>riding boots</vocabulary> as well. But if you're referring to fashion boots or boots in general, you can just call them ブーツ.
5101.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a bit weird. Double kun'yomi, so think along the lines of 長い and 靴 getting added together. 靴 is the reading you learned with the kanji, however. It also gets rendaku'd.

examples.en: That man was a bad influence on all of us.
examples.ja: あの男がみんなに悪影響を与えたんだよ。

examples.en: She cried as she realized that her bad influence filtered down to her children.
examples.ja: 悪影響が自分の子どもにまで及んでいたことに気が付き、彼女は泣き出した。

examples.en: YouTube is convenient, but we need to be careful because some videos may be harmful to children.
examples.ja: YouTubeは便利だけど、子供に悪影響が出そうな動画もあるから注意が必要だよね。

examples.en: I think the negative impact that smartphones have had on humanity is immeasurable.
examples.ja: スマホが人類にもたらした悪影響は計り知れないと思うよ。

5102.meaning_mnemonic: 影響 is "influence," so an <kanji>evil</kanji> <kanji>influence</kanji> is a <vocabulary>bad influence</vocabulary>.
5102.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I had some stomach trouble and that forced me to retire.
examples.ja: 胃病のせいで、隠居することになりました。

examples.en: My father is retired in a farming village.
examples.ja: 私の父は農村で隠居しています。

examples.en: I was fed up with my working life, so I decided to sell all my stocks and go into retirement.
examples.ja: 社会人生活に嫌気がさしたので、持っている株を全て売って隠居することにしました。

5103.meaning_mnemonic:
隠居 is "retirement". Make that a verb and you have <vocabulary>to retire</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be retired</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to go into retirement</vocabulary>.

Like 隠居, this word emphasizes life after retiring, and usually implies having a quiet, maybe secluded, lifestyle. It's a bit of an old-fashioned word, but you'll still see it in modern writing.
5103.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Do you have any recommendations for a good izakaya?
examples.ja: おすすめの居酒屋とかってありますか？

examples.en: That izakaya manager is really funny.
examples.ja: あの居酒屋の店長、本当に面白いよね。

examples.en: Cheaper chain izakayas are more relaxing than upscale izakayas.
examples.ja: 高級居酒屋よりも安いチェーン居酒屋の方がほっとする。

examples.en: The door opened and an old woman walked into the izakaya by herself.
examples.ja: 扉が開き、居酒屋の中に老婆が一人ぼっちで入ってきた。

5104.meaning_mnemonic:
An <kanji>alive</kanji> <kanji>alcohol</kanji> <kanji>shop</kanji> is a place that serves a lot of alcohol. In Japan, these places are often <vocabulary>izakaya</vocabulary>. If you don't already know what an izakaya is, you can consider it to be a casual <vocabulary>Japanese Style Bar</vocabulary>.

An izakaya is a pub or tavern where you can enjoy drinks and tasty bar food like yakitori and gyoza, usually at quite affordable prices. Cheers!
5104.reading_mnemonic:
The readings here are all kun'yomi, but this is the first time you've seen the さか reading for 酒, which rendaku then turns into ざか here. If you know what an izakaya is already, you can probably remember the reading, but if not here's a mnemonic to help:

When you need recommendations for a good <vocabulary>izakaya</vocabulary> (a <vocabulary>Japanese style bar</vocabulary>), you ask your friend <reading>Zacha</reading>ry (ざか). He knows all the best spots. You even call him Izakaya Zachary. He doesn't like that, but too bad. In your mind, Zachary will always be tied to Japanese style bars.

examples.en: Please follow the arrows.
examples.ja: 矢印にそって進んでください。

examples.en: What does the arrow road sign mean?
examples.ja: あの矢印の道路標識は何という意味ですか。

examples.en: How do you make the arrow symbols appear?
examples.ja: 矢印ってどうやって出すの？

examples.en: The blue arrow road sign means "left turn allowed," and the sign with a white arrow on a blue background means "one-way"!
examples.ja: 青い矢印の標識は「左折可」で、青地に白抜きの矢印の標識「一方通行」だよ！

5105.meaning_mnemonic: 矢印 combines the kanji <kanji>arrow</kanji> and the vocab word 印 (mark), giving us the type of arrow you use for pointing at things, like these: →↑↓←. It could be an arrow on a sign, or on a piece of paper, or a document. We can just call it an <vocabulary>arrow</vocabulary>, or an <vocabulary>arrow symbol</vocabulary>.
5105.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 矢 and 印 put together into one. The 印 is like the actual vocab word 印, but watch out for rendaku changing it from しるし to じるし.

examples.en: We are almost at the spectacular viewpoint!
examples.ja: もうすぐ絶景ポイントですよ！

examples.en: I'm looking forward to seeing the spectacular view from the top of the mountain.
examples.ja: 山の上から、絶景を見るのが楽しみです。

examples.en: From the observation deck, the view was even more spectacular than expected.
examples.ja: 展望台からは、予想以上に素晴らしい絶景が広がっていました。

examples.en: There is a famous facebook page that introduces lots of stunning views from around the world.
examples.ja: 世界の息を飲むような絶景をたくさん紹介している有名なFacebookページがあります。

5106.meaning_mnemonic: All good things are fleeting. When a <kanji>scene</kanji> in front of you <kanji>dies out</kanji>, it is gone. But, it was beautiful, it was amazing, it was a <vocabulary>spectacular view</vocabulary>.
5106.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Today at school we learned about series circuits and parallel circuits.
examples.ja: 今日は学校で、直列回路と並列回路について学びました。

examples.en: At that station, the express train and local train were stopped side by side.
examples.ja: その駅では、特急電車と各駅電車が並列して停車していた。

examples.en: I am not good at doing multiple things simultaneously, like doing housework while watching TV...
examples.ja: 私はテレビを見ながら家事をしたり…みたいなマルチタスクの並列処理が苦手です。

5107.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Line up</kanji> everything in a <kanji>row</kanji>. When you do that, they're all in <vocabulary>parallel</vocabulary>.

並列 is specifically used to describe items being arranged in a parallel way, like in parallel circuits or when vehicles are parked parallel to each other.
5107.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'm not good at doing things in parallel.
examples.ja: 私、並行して何かをするのは苦手なんです。

examples.en: I am currently writing two novels at the same time.
examples.ja: 今、二つの小説を同時並行で書いています。

examples.en: I like the scene where the train runs parallel with the bicycle, along a section of track that's side by side with the road.
examples.ja: 線路と道路が並行している区間を、電車と自転車が並行して走るシーンが好きなんです。

examples.en: I heard that studying multiple languages at the same time is more efficient than only studying one.
examples.ja: 複数の言語を並行して勉強することは、ひとつだけを学習するよりも効率的だと聞いたことがあります。

5108.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Line up</kanji> and <kanji>go</kanji> together. If you did that, you'd be <vocabulary>in parallel</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>going abreast</vocabulary> with someone.

並行 refers to two or more things placed or moving parallel to each other, like buses or trains running side by side. It's also used to describe two or more activities happening at the same time.
5108.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I can’t believe that people wait in line for twelve hours just to get some eco-friendly bags.
examples.ja: エコバッグを買うために十二時間も行列に並ぶなんて信じられないよ。

examples.en: It's dangerous, so please line up inside the white line.
examples.ja: 危ないですから白線の内側にお並びください。

examples.en: Please don't push in. We were here first. Everybody is waiting in line, so you should take your place in the queue like everyone else too. The end of the line is that way.
examples.ja: 割りこまないで下さい。私達が先ですよ。みんな並んでいるんですから、あなたもちゃんと並ぶべきです。列の最後尾はあちらです。

5109.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji itself means <kanji>line up</kanji>, and this is the intransitive verb version of that, which makes this <vocabulary>to line up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be lined up</vocabulary>. You can remember this because you keep saying <reading>boo</reading> (ぶ), why is everyone already lined up? If you were the one in charge of lining things up, you wouldn't have <vocabulary>to stand in line</vocabulary> yourself…

Figuratively, this can also mean <vocabulary>to be on par</vocabulary>, as in someone or something matches or is comparable in ability, status, or ranking to another (as if they are aligned side by side in comparison).
5109.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Only for you, when you visit <reading>Nara</reading> (なら), the deer there are <vocabulary>to be lined up</vocabulary> for you to inspect, as you are the deer inspector. If you don't know about Nara and its deer, you should look it up, they're pretty awesome.

examples.en: We have an ordinary and a luxury makizushi set. Which one would you like?
examples.ja: この巻きずしセット、並と上があるんだけど、どっちがいい？

examples.en: You can't achieve this level of success with just ordinary effort.
examples.ja: 並の努力では、ここまで成功することはできないよ。

examples.en: He had average reflexes, but a great mind.
examples.ja: 運動神経は並だったが、頭はすこぶる良かった。

5110.meaning_mnemonic:
The things that <kanji>line up</kanji> are <vocabulary>ordinary</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>average</vocabulary> things. Because the majority of things (or people) fall into the average category, you could say most of them line up side by side with each other.

This might be why 並 is often used in restaurants to refer to standard (or average) portion sizes. And in sushi restaurants, 並 can refer to a standard set, as opposed to a more luxurious or premium one.

Note that when describing something as 並 outside of a restaurant or commercial context, it could have a slightly judgmental tone. Most people wouldn't love it if you called their work (or them) ordinary and average, you know?
5110.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember:

You're at the coast, looking out at the <reading>波</reading> (なみ), which are all very <vocabulary>ordinary</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>average</vocabulary>. Nothing exceptional about those waves.

examples.en: I'm planning to go to university again and earn a master's degree properly.
examples.ja: もう一度大学に行って、ちゃんと修士の学位を取るつもりなんです。

examples.en: I'm studying to get my master's degree while working part time.
examples.ja: アルバイトをしながら、修士号を取るために勉強しています。

examples.en: Last year, I completed my master's degree in applied linguistics.
examples.ja: 昨年、応用言語学の修士課程を修了しました。

5111.meaning_mnemonic: A degree of <kanji>mastering</kanji> equal to a <kanji>samurai</kanji> is required for a <vocabulary>master's degree</vocabulary>. You'll have to master your chosen skill to the level of a samurai in order to obtain such a degree… Sounds tough.
5111.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I don't know how to repair clocks.
examples.ja: 時計の修理の仕方が分かりません。

examples.en: If you send it in for repair, won't the repair cost a lot of money?
examples.ja: 修理に出したら、修理代、高くつくんじゃない？

examples.en: I contacted the manufacturer, but they said they no longer have the parts and it is beyond repair.
examples.ja: メーカーに問い合わせましたが、もう部品がなく修理不能だそうです。

examples.en: "Hey, repairman. Can you fix this right now?" "You mean, you guys' relationship? Sorry. No can do."
examples.ja: 「おい、修理屋。これはすぐに直せるか？」「って、君たちの関係ってこと？悪いけど、それはできないよ。」

5112.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>repair</kanji> things for a <kanji>reason</kanji>, you'll be able to <vocabulary>repair</vocabulary> just about anything! Just remember, always be repairing for a reason.
5112.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The training session is set to begin at 3 p.m.
examples.ja: その研修は午後3時に始まる予定です。

examples.en: Oh, will Mori-san be training the new employees?
examples.ja: えっ、森さんが新人社員を研修するんですか？

examples.en: Does this company have an employee training program?
examples.ja: この会社には、社員研修の制度はありますか？

5113.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>sharpen</kanji> your <kanji>mastering</kanji> of a specific skill. One could say that you're <vocabulary>training</vocabulary>. Additionally, when you sharpen someone else's mastering, you <vocabulary>give training</vocabulary>.
5113.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: When is the deadline for handing in the rhetoric essay?
examples.ja: 修辞学のレポートの締め切りはいつですか？

examples.en: This rhetoric book is not only interesting but also useful.
examples.ja: この修辞学の本は、面白い上に有益です。

examples.en: I have a crush on my rhetoric teacher.
examples.ja: 私は修辞学の先生に恋をしています。

5114.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>mastering</kanji> <kanji>word</kanji>s field of <kanji>study</kanji> is also known as <vocabulary>rhetoric</vocabulary>.

修辞学 is specifically for the study and theory of rhetoric. Rhetoric as an academic field, in other words. If you're just talking about the way people persuade each other with words, the more colloquial term is レトリック.
5114.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Why don't you bring an umbrella?
examples.ja: 傘、持っていったら？

examples.en: I forgot my umbrella at the kindergarten.
examples.ja: 幼稚園に傘を忘れてきちゃった。

examples.en: I barely see any people walking with umbrellas in America.
examples.ja: アメリカでは、傘をさして歩いている人をあまり見かけません。

examples.en: I left my umbrella in the cloakroom.
examples.ja: 私は傘をクロークに預けました。

5115.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
5115.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: I left the restaurant, forgetting my umbrella in the stand where I had placed it.
examples.ja: レストランの傘立てに傘を入れたまま忘れて出てきてしまいました。

examples.en: If you put your umbrella in the umbrella stand at a convenience store, it often gets stolen.
examples.ja: コンビニの傘立てに傘を立てると、ぬすまれることが多い。

examples.en: Please do not put a wet umbrella in the umbrella stand.
examples.ja: 傘立てに濡れた傘を立てないで下さい。

5116.meaning_mnemonic: This is when you take your <kanji>umbrella</kanji> and you <kanji>stand</kanji> it up. Wait, how is an umbrella standing up? Good question, my dear Crabling, you are putting your umbrella in an <vocabulary>umbrella stand</vocabulary>.
5116.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the readings for 傘 (learned with the kanji) and 立つ (to stand).

examples.en: This is my colleague, Hayashi-san.
examples.ja: こちらは同僚の林さんです。

examples.en: My colleague is a cold-hearted man.
examples.ja: オレの同僚は冷たいヤツなんだよ。

examples.en: It would have been nice to have a boss or colleagues to turn to for advice when there was trouble.
examples.ja: 困ったときに相談できるような上司や同僚だったら良かったんだけどね。

5117.meaning_mnemonic:
We work at the <kanji>same</kanji> place and are <kanji>colleague</kanji>s, making us <vocabulary>colleague</vocabulary>s or <vocabulary>coworker</vocabulary>s.

As you might guess from the 同 kanji, 同僚 generally refers to people working in the same workplace with the same rank or status. In other words, you wouldn't usually call your boss your 同僚!
5117.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: He comes from a bureaucratic background, but he's humble and a good guy.
examples.ja: 彼は官僚出身だけど、腰が低くていいやつだよ。

examples.en: I'm sure they all think something like, "It's our rightful privilege as career bureaucrats to secure cushy post-retirement jobs."
examples.ja: きっとアイツらみんな、我々キャリア官僚が天下りするのは当然の権利だとか思ってるんじゃない？

examples.en: Just as bureaucratism inevitably spreads in a large nation, every large organization ends up suffering from what we call "big company syndrome." It's what you might refer to as a bureaucratic organization.
examples.ja: 大きくなった国家に必ず官僚主義がはびこるように、大きくなった組織は、みんな大企業病にかかるんです。いわゆる官僚組織ってやつですよ。

5118.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>government</kanji> <kanji>colleague</kanji> is someone who works for the <vocabulary>bureaucracy</vocabulary>, making them a <vocabulary>bureaucrat</vocabulary>.

Just like the word bureaucracy in English, 官僚 often carries a negative connotation, suggesting red tape, inefficiency, or the power and influence that senior civil servants might wield within the government.
5118.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My sister works at a children's welfare center.
examples.ja: 私の姉は、児童相談所で働いています。

examples.en: Isn't Harry Potter a children's book? I always thought it was a book aimed at children.
examples.ja: ハリー・ポッターって、児童書じゃないの？てっきり児童向けの本だと思っていたよ。

examples.en: Recently, there has been an increase in the number of students wandering about during class.
examples.ja: 最近、授業中に立ち歩く児童生徒が増えています。

examples.en: Ninety percent of the children were absent.
examples.ja: 児童の九割が欠席しました。

5119.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>child</kanji> who is a <kanji>juvenile</kanji> is just a <vocabulary>child</vocabulary>. A group of them is <vocabulary>children</vocabulary>.

児童 refers specifically to children who are of elementary school age, typically from around 6 to 12 years old. It's often used in formal contexts, like in legal documents or when referring to <vocabulary>school children</vocabulary> in educational settings.
5119.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I think that game is still too advanced for preschoolers.
examples.ja: そのゲームは、幼児にはまだ早いんじゃないかな？

examples.en: Early childhood is a special time, and early childhood education is very important.
examples.ja: 幼児期は特別な時期で、幼児教育ってすごく大事なんです。

examples.en: It's really cute when toddlers speak toddler language!
examples.ja: 幼児が幼児語しゃべってるのって、本当に可愛いよね！

5120.meaning_mnemonic:
An <kanji>infancy</kanji> <kanji>child</kanji> is a <vocabulary>toddler</vocabulary>. The kanji are kind of deceptive since this isn't really used for infants. It's more for small children, from toddlers on up to <vocabulary>preschooler</vocabulary>s.

幼児 is sort of formal, but it's commonly used to talk about small children from about one to six years old, or about that specific period of early childhood.
5120.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Misaki's hands are so cold!
examples.ja: ミサキちゃんの手、めっちゃ冷たいね！

examples.en: You should eat the soup soon, or it will end up cold.
examples.ja: 早く飲まないと、スープが冷たくなっちゃうよ。

examples.en: We call cold coffee "ice coffee" in Japanese.
examples.ja: 冷たいコーヒーのことを、日本語では「アイスコーヒー」と呼びます。

examples.en: I may sound cold, but I'm under tight control from above, and that makes many things difficult.
examples.ja: 冷たいことを言うようですが、こちらも上からの締めつけがきびしくて色々と難しいんです。

5121.meaning_mnemonic: Something that is <kanji>cool</kanji> is <vocabulary>cold</vocabulary>. This refers to something that is <vocabulary>cold to the touch</vocabulary>, not the weather or something like that (which is 寒い).
5121.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's mnemonic to help you: Something that is really <vocabulary>cold</vocabulary> to the touch is cold enough <reading>to ma</reading>ke ice cream with.

examples.en: I tried to speak in as calm a tone as possible.
examples.ja: できるだけ冷静な口調で話すようにした。

examples.en: Let's calm down! Let's compose ourselves a bit.
examples.ja: 落ち着いて！ちょっと冷静になろう。

examples.en: How can you stay calm after something like this?
examples.ja: こんなことが起きて、冷静でいられる訳がないだろ！

5122.meaning_mnemonic: You're <kanji>cool</kanji> and <kanji>quiet</kanji>. That's you, daddio. Nice and <vocabulary>cool-headed</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>calm</vocabulary>. So much <vocabulary>composure</vocabulary>
5122.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Our freezer is always full.

examples.en: Geez, I forgot to close the freezer!
examples.ja: げっ、冷凍庫、閉め忘れてた！

examples.en: I hope you find a good freezer.
examples.ja: 良い冷凍庫が見つかるといいですね。

examples.en: There is a mysterious block in our freezer. What is that?
examples.ja: 冷凍庫の中に怪しいカタマリが入っているんだけど、あれ何？

5123.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>cool</kanji> <kanji>frozen</kanji> <kanji>storage</kanji> is one which is really cold on the inside, so cold it can freeze things. This is called a <vocabulary>freezer</vocabulary>, not to be confused with 冷蔵庫, which is refrigerator, and doesn't have the kanji for "freeze" in it.
5123.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Do soap bubbles freeze?
examples.ja: シャボン玉って凍るの？

examples.en: If it’s venison, I have it frozen in the freezer.
examples.ja: シカ肉なら、冷凍庫で凍らせてあるよ。

examples.en: Have you ever made ice cubes by freezing orange juice?
examples.ja: オレンジジュースを凍らせて氷を作ったことはありますか。

examples.en: Please be careful because the road is still frozen solid.
examples.ja: 道路はまだガチガチに凍ってるから気を付けてね。

examples.en: I was really horrified. It was a spine-chilling experience.
examples.ja: ほんと、ゾッとしましたよ。背筋が凍る思いでした。

5124.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>frozen</kanji>, so the vocab version is <vocabulary>to freeze</vocabulary>.
5124.reading_mnemonic: The reading actually comes from the word 氷, which means "ice." You can kind of see where the origins of these words come from, now... really cold frozen things. So, think back to こおり, then change the り to a る and put it outside the kanji. That makes the reading for this <reading>こお</reading>る, in all (or most) of 氷's glory.

5126.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

5127.meaning_mnemonic:
I can <kanji>deal with</kanji> it, no matter what the <kanji>reason</kanji>. I swear I can <vocabulary>deal with</vocabulary> this problem on my own!

処理 is a relatively formal word for <vocabulary>handling</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>processing</vocabulary> a problem or task to bring it to a resolution. It covers all kinds of tasks, from administrative work and data processing to practical challenges like waste disposal and complaint handling. It can even apply to defusing unexploded bombs.
5127.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

5128.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>deal with</kanji> trash, you have to <kanji>divide</kanji> it into different types before you can get to its <vocabulary>disposal</vocabulary>. Whenever you deal with and divide something, you’re preparing to dispose of it.

処分 means getting rid of things you don’t want, like trash or old furniture. Sometimes, it can also mean <vocabulary>punishment</vocabulary>, like suspension from school for breaking the rules. This connection makes sense because both disposal and punishment involve handling something unwanted—whether it's an item or a behavior.
5128.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

We're going to <kanji>deal with</kanji> it by <kanji>put</kanji>ting this up your butt and giving you the <vocabulary>treatment</vocabulary> you need. Kancho!

処置 is commonly used when treating injuries or illnesses. It can also refer to deciding how to handle a situation or the act of handling it, but in these cases, people usually use 処理 instead.

The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

券 is a standalone word that means <vocabulary>ticket</vocabulary>, but it's commonly used as a suffix to form words like 入場券 (admission ticket), 割引券 (discount <vocabulary>coupon</vocabulary>), or 定期券 (commuter <vocabulary>pass</vocabulary>).
5130.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. Usually it's attached to things, because it tells you what kind of ticket something is.

旅券 is a formal term for a passport. It's commonly used in official documents and formal settings, like when dealing with government paperwork. In less formal contexts, you can simply say パスポート!

回数券 refers to a book or set of prepaid tickets that are often sold at a discount and can either be physical or digital. They are commonly used for public transportation, like buses or trains, and can also be issued by other businesses that people frequent, such as hot springs and public baths.
5133.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

5139.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>gambling</kanji> <kanji>hit</kanji> can be multiple things. 5139.reading_mnemonic: The reading is weird on this one, but gambling is weird, I guess. はく goes to ばく, maybe because you're playing some gambling <reading>back</reading>gammon. 微妙 can also just mean <vocabulary>delicate</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>subtle</vocabulary>, like 微妙な立場 (a delicate position that requires careful handling) or 微妙なニュアンスの違い (a subtle nuance difference that's hard to pinpoint).
