The kanji means <kanji>infancy</kanji>. The adjective version describes someone who is <vocabulary>very young</vocabulary>, like little kids in their early childhood or babyhood!

Depending on the context, it can also describe behaviors or ideas that are <vocabulary>childish</vocabulary> or immature, often with a negative connotation.
5147.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

When you were <vocabulary>very young</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>childish</vocabulary> you were sent off to do prayers to ask for forgiveness. One of the things you had to do was sing "<reading>hosanna</reading> (おさな) in the highest."

examples.en: Isn't "Childhood" a book about Tolstoy's childhood memories?
examples.ja: 『幼年時代』って、トルストイの幼年時代の思い出について書かれた本じゃないんですか？

examples.en: At that moment I realized that those happy childhood days would never come back.
examples.ja: その時私は、あの幸せな幼年時代は、もう二度と帰ってはこないんだと実感しました。

examples.en: I always spent my childhood summers at my cousin's place in Kyushu, so the flat stag beetle is a memorable bug for me.
examples.ja: 幼年時代の夏は、いつも九州の従兄弟のところで過ごしたから、ヒラタクワガタは思い出の虫なのだ。

5148.meaning_mnemonic:
You have 時代 as a "period" of time you're talking about. What period? The <kanji>infancy</kanji> <kanji>year</kanji>s. Those years are not just when you're a baby, but when you were growing up, too. That was your <vocabulary>childhood</vocabulary>.

幼年時代 specifically refers to your <vocabulary>early childhood</vocabulary> years. It's a formal word you mostly see in writing with a slightly stiff tone, often appearing in literature, autobiographies, or memoirs looking back on someone's younger years.
5148.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Don't worry. The money is kept in the warehouse.
examples.ja: 心配するな。金は、庫の中に入れてある。

examples.en: The door to the granary is securely locked.
examples.ja: 庫の戸には、ちゃんとカギがかかってある。

examples.en: I saw a boy go into the storehouse.
examples.ja: 男の子が庫の中に入っていくのを見たぞ。

5149.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji means <kanji>storehouse</kanji>, and the vocab is also <vocabulary>storehouse</vocabulary>! Specifically, this usually refers to a traditional Japanese storehouse, which is typically a two story building used to store personal property or merchandise.
5149.reading_mnemonic: What do you put in your <vocabulary>storehouse</vocabulary>? Nothing that nice. Just your totally <reading>cra</reading>shed (くら) car. So sad, it was a nice car, too and now it's all crashed and stored in your warehouse.

examples.en: Do you have a safe in your home?
examples.ja: 家に金庫はありますか？

examples.en: Apparently Mami keeps her bacon in a safe-deposit box.
examples.ja: マミは貸金庫にベーコンをあずけているらしいよ。

examples.en: That bank vault is very sturdy.
examples.ja: あの銀行の金庫はとても頑丈です。

5150.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Gold</kanji> <kanji>storage</kanji> is where you put your gold. You want it to be safe, so you put it in <vocabulary>a safe</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>vault</vocabulary>.

金庫 can refer to various types of secure storage. Depending on the context, it can mean a personal safe, a bank vault, or a safety deposit box.
5150.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Two BMWs were parked in a row at the garage.
examples.ja: 車庫には、二台のBMWが並列して停められていました。

examples.en: They have a rather unusual apartment complex with a train garage under the apartments.
examples.ja: アパートの下に電車の車庫がある、ちょっと変わった団地があるそうです。

examples.en: When I was backing my parents’ car into the garage I ran it into a pole.
examples.ja: 両親の車を車庫に入れる時に、柱にぶつけてしまいました。

examples.en: A "shako shomei" is a document that certifies a parking space has been secured for a vehicle, and obtaining one is mandated by the Garage Act.
examples.ja: 車庫証明とは自動車の保管場所が確保されていることを証明する書類のことで、車庫法で取得が義務付けられています。

5151.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Car</kanji> <kanji>storage</kanji> is where you store your car. It's your <vocabulary>garage</vocabulary>.

車庫 literally means vehicle storage, so it's used for everything from home garages to large depots for public transportation. It carries a bit more of a formal tone than the katakana word ガレージ (garage).
5151.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The weather has been improving, hasn't it?
examples.ja: 天気、回復してきたね。

examples.en: This rehabilitation is designed to recover brain function.
examples.ja: このリハビリは、脳の機能を回復するためのものです。

examples.en: The doctor told me that he is not likely to regain consciousness.
examples.ja: 彼が意識を回復することは難しいだろうと医者に言われました。

5152.meaning_mnemonic: 回復 is <kanji>recovery</kanji>. Make it into a verb and you have <vocabulary>to recover</vocabulary>.
5152.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 回復, but you can also figure it out via the readings of the kanji as well.

examples.en: Don't give up. We still have a faint hope.
examples.ja: あきらめないで。まだ微かな望みが残っているよ。

examples.en: A faint sound could be heard echoing through the silent snowy mountains.
examples.ja: シンと静まり返った雪山に、微かな音が響くのが聞こえました。

examples.en: I heard that Koichi studied Japanese by the dim light of a candle, which worsened his eyesight, so that's why he's wearing glasses.
examples.ja: コウイチはロウソクの微かな明かりで日本語を勉強してたせいで目が悪くなってメガネを掛けているらしいですよ。

5153.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji means <kanji>delicate</kanji>, and so does this word. Something that's <vocabulary>delicate</vocabulary> is probably also <vocabulary>faint</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>indistinct</vocabulary>. So use 微か to describe things like faint sounds, delicate breezes, and indistinct memories.
5153.reading_mnemonic: You should speak in a <vocabulary>delicate</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>faint</vocabulary> voice when you <reading>cuss</reading> (かす). So delicate that the cuss words are <vocabulary>indistinct</vocabulary> to other people, even. It's the only acceptable way to cuss.

examples.en: This ghostly shaped microorganism is "Daphnia magna."
examples.ja: このお化けのような形の微生物は「ミジンコ」です。

examples.en: What time is the the microbiology specialist scheduled to come?
examples.ja: 微生物学の専門家は何時に来る予定ですか。

examples.en: Miso is actually made through the activity of microorganisms.
examples.ja: ミソって実は、微生物の働きによって作られているんですよ。

examples.en: Mr. Kadota had been researching on reading the minds of microbes until two years ago.
examples.ja: 門田さんは二年前まで微生物の心を読み取る研究をしていました。

5154.meaning_mnemonic: You've learned 微 can mean "delicate," but it can also mean <kanji>tiny</kanji>. Combine that with 生物, which you might remember is "living thing," and what do you get? A tiny living thing…? Well, that's a <vocabulary>microorganism</vocabulary>. The tiniest kind of living thing there is.
5154.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Isn't that a violation of the Constitution?
examples.ja: それって憲法違反じゃないですか？

examples.en: I'm trying to memorize the full text of the Constitution through rote memorization.
examples.ja: 憲法の全文を丸暗記しています。

examples.en: Freedom of expression is guaranteed by the Constitution.
examples.ja: 表現の自由は憲法で保証されています。

examples.en: I'm busy reviewing the constitutional amendment.
examples.ja: 憲法改正案の見直しで忙しい。

5155.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>constitution</kanji> <kanji>law</kanji>s are what makes up the <vocabulary>constitution</vocabulary>.
5155.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: She is the youngest prime minister in Thailand's constitutional history.
examples.ja: 彼女は、タイの憲政史上最も若い首相です。

examples.en: I am doing a study comparing the constitutional systems of Japan and China.
examples.ja: 私は日本と中国の憲政を比較する研究をしています。

examples.en: Politics conducted by means of a constitution is called "kensei" or "rikken-seiji."
examples.ja: 憲法によって行う政治のことを「憲政」や「立憲政治」といいます。

5156.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>constitution</kanji> <kanji>government</kanji> is a <vocabulary>constitutional government</vocabulary>.

憲政 is a formal word that might come up in discussions about democracy or constitutional frameworks, especially in advanced writing.
5156.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I got so absorbed into a game, that I was completely losing myself in it.
examples.ja: ゲームに熱中しすぎて、無我夢中の状態になっていた。

examples.en: "Shoot! Fire!" Viet shouted frantically.
examples.ja: 「撃て！撃つんだ！」とビエトは無我夢中でさけんだ。

examples.en: To be honest, I don't remember anything because I was completely absorbed in it.
examples.ja: 正直、無我夢中だったので、何も覚えていません。

examples.en: Working feverishly, he built his house in his twenties and built his tomb in his thirties.
examples.ja: 彼は無我夢中で働き、二十代で家を建てたが、三十代で墓を建てることとなった。

5157.meaning_mnemonic: You already know that 無我 is "selflessness" and 夢中 is "crazy about." So this means something like <vocabulary>total absorption</vocabulary>. You're so into something that you’ve started losing your sense of self. Just like 夢中, this can also describe doing something <vocabulary>frantic</vocabulary>ally, like running away from somebody or something.
5157.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I managed to communicate to Japanese people with gestures.
examples.ja: 日本人の人たちと、身振り手振りで何とかコミュニケーションをとることができた。

examples.en: That girl is always exaggerating her gestures and body language.
examples.ja: あの子って、いつも身振り手振りが大げさなんですよね。

examples.en: Viet motioned to his men to hide somewhere.
examples.ja: ビエトは部下に、どこかに隠れるよう身振りで合図した。

examples.en: The man shrugged his shoulders, making a gesture that meant, "So what? I don't know anything about it, okay?"
examples.ja: 男は肩をすくめて「それで？オレは知らねーよ？」という意味の身振りをした。

5158.meaning_mnemonic:
The way your <kanji>body</kanji> <kanji>shake</kanji>s is how you use <vocabulary>body language</vocabulary> or how you <vocabulary>gesture</vocabulary>.

身振り generally refers to gestures in terms of body movements that make communication more expressive or help bridge language barriers. You'll often encounter this together with 手振り (hand gestures) in the phrase 身振り手振り.
5158.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this is the kun'yomis for 身 and 振る put together, where the 振り gets rendaku'd to ぶり.

examples.en: Please add the furigana for your name in katakana.
examples.ja: 名前にはカタカナで振り仮名をつけてください。

examples.en: We don't use furigana since Wanikani is a site to study kanji.
examples.ja: ワニカニは漢字を勉強するサイトなので、振り仮名は使いません。

examples.en: I found a job where I add small kana characters to kanji.
examples.ja: 漢字に振り仮名を振る仕事を見つけました。

5159.meaning_mnemonic: 振る is "to shake." 仮名 is kana. This word refers to <vocabulary>furigana</vocabulary>, which is the little kana that's put next to kanji for the people who don't use WaniKani and can't read anything. As to why it's called "shake kana"? I have no clue. Just imagine putting little kana next to kanji and watching them shake around, though, and you should be good to go.
5159.reading_mnemonic: The readings are 振る and 仮名 put together into one. If you know those words, you won't need no furigana to help you with this word.

examples.en: I found a job as an interviewer who conducts interviews during the interview examination process with exam candidates.
examples.ja: 面接試験で受験生を面接する面接官の仕事を見つけました。

examples.en: I checked out the homepage of the company that I'm gonna have a job interview with a day after tomorrow, and found out it's definitely a yakuza company.
examples.ja: 明後日面接する会社のホームページをのぞいたら、バリバリのヤクザ会社だった。

examples.en: It looks like the final interview will be a one-on-one interview with the president of this company. I hope I can get there.
examples.ja: 最終面接は社長面接で、この企業の社長と一対一で面接するみたいです。そこまでたどり着けるといいんだけど。

5160.meaning_mnemonic:
面接 is an <kanji>interview</kanji>. Make that into a verb and you have to <vocabulary>interview with</vocabulary>.

Remember that 面接 is an interview for a job or admission to a school, not an interview for a magazine or a TV show. インタビューする is the more appropriate word for a media interview.
5160.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Will help to know the word 面接 as well.

examples.en: Don’t move. Hold still or you’ll be shot!
examples.ja: 動くな。じっとしていないと、撃つぞ！

examples.en: No, there's no need to shoot that bear.
examples.ja: いや、あのクマを撃つ必要はないだろ。

examples.en: In the real battle, you have to win even by shooting the enemy from the rear.
examples.ja: 実戦では、敵を後ろから撃ってでも勝たなければいけない。

examples.en: I know it sounds paradoxical, but I shot you to protect you.
examples.ja: 逆説めくが、私はお前を守るために撃ったんだ。

5161.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>to attack</kanji>, but 撃つ means <vocabulary>to shoot</vocabulary>.

This can mean <vocabulary>to fire</vocabulary> a weapon such as a gun or to shoot a projectile, like an arrow. It can also mean to shoot a person or animal.
5161.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

What are you going <vocabulary>to shoot</vocabulary> at? <reading>U</reading>ni (う)! Why? Because this area is overrun with those black, spiky sea urchins. You need to cull them by shooting them down.

examples.en: The server is under cyber attack.
examples.ja: サーバーがサイバー攻撃を受けている。

examples.en: The enemy will probably attack the megacities first.
examples.ja: 敵はまず巨大都市を攻撃してくるだろう。

examples.en: You are such a coward to make a surprise attack from the back.
examples.ja: 後ろから攻撃を仕掛けてくるなんて、ひきょうだぞ！

examples.en: It was the sexiest missile attack I've ever seen.
examples.ja: 今まで見た中で一番セクシーなミサイル攻撃だったよ。

examples.en: Yesterday, an armed attack was launched.
examples.ja: 昨日、武力攻撃が開始された。

5162.meaning_mnemonic:
With <kanji>aggression</kanji> you <kanji>attack</kanji> the enemy. This is an <vocabulary>attack</vocabulary>.

攻撃 usually refers to <vocabulary>attacking</vocabulary> someone or something with the intent of causing direct harm or damage, either physically or verbally. You'll hear it used in the context of war, games, arguments, or even things like media criticism or cyberattacks.
5162.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Tomorrow, we will attack the enemy's castle.
examples.ja: 明日、敵の城を攻めるぞ。

examples.en: Thank you for your question. You’re tackling a rather difficult point.
examples.ja: ご質問ありがとうございます。中々難しいところを攻めてきますね。

examples.en: That pitcher often assaults batters with curve balls.
examples.ja: そのピッチャーはバッターを変化球で攻めることが多い。

examples.en: Setting logic aside, I just kept pushing and pushing relentlessly.
examples.ja: 理屈は抜きにして、とりあえず攻めて攻めて攻めまくりました。

5163.meaning_mnemonic:
You don't say "to aggression." When you do aggression on someone, you're probably doing something to hurt them in some way. This is an attack, making this word <vocabulary>to attack</vocabulary>.

攻める means to attack or advance on an enemy in battle, but it can also apply to making a strong or proactive move in competitions like sports, business, or games. It can also be used to describe taking bold actions, like moving ahead with a risky plan.
5163.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

<vocabulary>To attack</vocabulary> someone, use a <reading>ce</reading>lery (せ) stick. Celery is not a deadly weapon but most people hate it, so it's perfect to casually attack someone, especially those who hate celery.

examples.en: What is your major?
examples.ja: 専攻は何ですか？

examples.en: I'm majoring in fine arts.
examples.ja: 私はファインアートを専攻しています。

examples.en: She is an anthropology student of this university.
examples.ja: 彼女はうちの大学の、人類学専攻の学生なんだよ。

5164.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>specialty</kanji>, which you focus on with <kanji>aggression</kanji>, is your <vocabulary>major</vocabulary> in college (your <vocabulary>college major</vocabulary>). Study hard, young grasshopper.
5164.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: At the same time, the Soviet Union launched a counter-offensive.
examples.ja: これと同時に、ソ連が反攻を開始しました。

examples.en: In 1944, the Allied forces shifted to a counteroffensive.
examples.ja: 1944年に連合軍は反攻に転じました。

examples.en: Of course, our army is preparing for a counter-attack. However, we are not yet ready and are in a situation in which we cannot launch a counter-attack.
examples.ja: もちろん我が軍は、反攻を準備している。しかし、まだ準備が整っておらず、反攻を行うことができない状況にあるのだ。

5165.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Anti</kanji> <kanji>aggression</kanji> is when you receive some aggression, then respond to it with anti aggression, aka your <vocabulary>counterattack</vocabulary>.
5165.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Could you explain the process of how you came to that diagnosis?
examples.ja: どうしてその診断結果になったのか、診断のプロセスを説明してもらえませんか？

examples.en: Do you know the personality test called MBTI assessment?
examples.ja: MBTI診断っていう性格診断テスト、知ってる？

examples.en: Doctor Nishimura is believed to be the best doctor in terms of their diagnosis of breast cancer.
examples.ja: 西村医師は乳がんの診断においては右に出る者はいないと言われています。

examples.en: My son was diagnosed with asthma when he was four.
examples.ja: 私の息子は四歳の時に喘息だと診断されました。

5166.meaning_mnemonic:
To <kanji>diagnose</kanji> is to (metaphorically) <kanji>cut off</kanji> all the possibilities you don't believe to be likely. That's how you get a <vocabulary>diagnosis</vocabulary>!

診断 is primarily used in medical contexts to mean the act of <vocabulary>diagnosing</vocabulary> or the diagnosis itself. In non-medical contexts, it can also mean an <vocabulary>assessment</vocabulary> used to evaluate something, like a 性格診断 (personality test).
5166.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I just saw a mitten crab on the beach!
examples.ja: さっき、浜でモクズガニを見ました！

examples.en: The beach winds felt nice.
examples.ja: 浜風が気持ちよかった。

examples.en: What, were you also on the beach that day, Hama-san?
examples.ja: え、浜さんもこの日、浜にいたんですか？

5167.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. It's worth mentioning that a more common way to say beach is ビーチ, and many people actually say 海 even though this literally means "sea."
5167.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: Could you give me a ride to Yokohama please?
examples.ja: 横浜まで乗せてもらえませんか？

examples.en: I once lived in Yokohama for about three months.
examples.ja: 私は三ヶ月ほど横浜に住んでいたことがあります。

examples.en: Is it true that people born and raised in Yokohama are called “Hamakko”?
examples.ja: 横浜生まれ、横浜育ちの人のことを「浜っ子」って言うって本当ですか？

5168.meaning_mnemonic: It's the <kanji>side</kanji> of the <kanji>beach</kanji>! Well, wait, what is it? This will make better sense when you look at the reading for the word, since it's a place: <vocabulary>Yokohama</vocabulary>.
5168.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 横 and 浜 put together into one nice word, <reading>よこはま</reading>.

examples.en: But apparently only those with pure hearts can see it.
examples.ja: でも、心の清い人にしか見えないんだって。

examples.en: My motto is "Purity, Honesty, Beauty."
examples.ja: 「清く正しく美しく」が私のモットーです。

examples.en: You know how they say, "If the water is clear, the fish won't live there"?
examples.ja: 「水清ければ魚住まず」って言うでしょ？

5169.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>pure</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>pure</vocabulary>.
5169.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: "In order to stay <vocabulary>pure</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>clean</vocabulary>, you shouldn't ever do anything dirty or bad. That is the <reading>key, yo</reading> (きよ)."

examples.en: We're supposed to keep our kitchens clean, right?
examples.ja: キッチンは清潔にしておくものでしょ？

examples.en: The restaurant was clean and well kept, and the food was delicious.
examples.ja: おそうじの行き届いた清潔なお店で、ご飯も美味しかったです。

examples.en: That clinic is very clean.
examples.ja: あそこのクリニックはとても清潔です。

examples.en: My type is a guy who is actually clean but looks dirty and sketchy.
examples.ja: 実際には清潔だけど、見た目は汚らしくてちょっと影がある男の人がタイプです。

5170.meaning_mnemonic:
Something so <kanji>pure</kanji> it's <kanji>pure</kanji> twice. It must be really <vocabulary>clean</vocabulary>! <vocabulary>Cleanliness</vocabulary> is next to pure...liness, after all. I'm sure that's how the saying goes.

清潔 is a relatively formal word that refers to <vocabulary>sanitary</vocabulary> conditions in personal hygiene, public health, or medical settings. It can refer to both physically clean places and hygienic practices. In literature, 清潔 can also describe a person as morally pure.

examples.en: Among the candy shops, there are several types, such as Japanese sweet stores and Western sweet stores.

5194.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Koichi's piggy bank is much bigger than mine, to the point where you can't even compare them.

5195.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 貯金 means "savings"? Well, a <kanji>box</kanji> you put said savings in is a <vocabulary>savings box</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>piggy bank</vocabulary>.
5195.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.ja: この本は、児童文学にしては比較的難しい言葉を使っているね。

examples.en: As a matter of fact, Japan is one of the G7 countries with relatively low taxes.
examples.ja: 実は日本って、G７の中では税金が比較的安い方なんです。

5196.meaning_mnemonic: 比較 is a comparison. Add 的 to it and you have <vocabulary> comparatively</vocabulary>.
5196.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Will help if you know the word 比較.

examples.en: My daughter lacks physical strength compared to the other girls at her age.
examples.ja: 同じ年の女の子と比較すると、私の娘は体力があまりありません。

examples.en: Let us now compare the two sets of data.
examples.ja: では、次に二つのデータを比較してみましょう。

examples.en: Stop comparing me to your ex-girlfriend!
examples.ja: 元カノと比較するの、やめてよ！

5197.meaning_mnemonic: 比較 is <vocabulary>comparison</vocabulary>. So, verb version of that? It's <vocabulary>to compare</vocabulary>.
5197.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Will help a lot to know the word 比較 as well.

examples.en: Isn't that shirt on backwards?
examples.ja: そのシャツ、前と後ろが逆じゃない？

examples.en: Koichi has the complete opposite personality of his older brother, doesn't he?
examples.ja: コウイチって、お兄さんとは真逆な性格をしてるよね。

examples.en: I wanted to loosen the screw, but I ended up turning it in the opposite way and tightened it instead.
examples.ja: ネジをゆるめたかったのに、逆に回して締めつけてしまっていた。

examples.en: Are there more and more people driving on the wrong side of the road recently? There was a truck driving the wrong way on the highway just now!
examples.ja: 最近、道路を逆に走る人、増えてない？さっきも高速道路を逆走しているトラックがいたよ！

5198.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

Keep in mind that 逆 often implies something is the <vocabulary>reverse</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>opposite</vocabulary> of what it should be. For example, you use 逆 when you're going in the opposite direction of your destination or wearing your shirt backwards.
5198.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji as well. Lucky! <kanji>Reverse</kanji> face time!

examples.en: Isn't that counterproductive?
examples.ja: それ、逆効果じゃない？

examples.en: I wanted to cheer him up, but it had the opposite effect.
examples.ja: 励ますつもりが、逆効果になってしまった。

examples.en: I expected to capture his heart by filling his stomach, but it backfired.
examples.ja: 胃ぶくろを満たしてハートをつかむはずが、逆効果だった。

5199.meaning_mnemonic: 効果 means "effect," so the <kanji>opposite</kanji> of said effect is the <vocabulary>opposite effect</vocabulary>. Or in other terms, something <vocabulary>counterproductive</vocabulary>.
5199.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as  well. Will help to know 効果 as well.

examples.en: You're going against your parents?
examples.ja: お前、親に逆らうつもりか？

examples.en: After all, no one can go against the current of the times.
examples.ja: やっぱり、誰も時代の流れに逆らうことはできないんだよ。

examples.en: Fugu was moved by Salmon who was swimming upstream against the river's flow.
examples.ja: フグは流れに逆らって川を上って行くサーモンに感動を覚えた。

5200.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an <ja>う</ja> sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>opposite</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to go against</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to oppose</vocabulary>.

逆らう refers to resisting natural or social forces, like 逆らって進む (to go against the tide), or to opposing specific people, like 親に逆らう (to defy one's parents). It means actively resisting something, whether it's a flow, a trend, or authority, highlighting a conscious choice to take a different path.
5200.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Just like when you play <reading>soccer</reading> (さか). You never play right, causing you <vocabulary>to go against</vocabulary> all things you're supposed to do and shoot goals into your own goalie's net.

examples.en: That legislator often uses paradoxical logic.
examples.ja: あの議員は、逆説の論理をよく使います。

examples.en: This manga is a paradoxical story that makes us think about life through the battles between those who have become immortal.
examples.ja: このマンガは、不死の存在となった者同士の戦いを通じて命について考える、逆説的な物語です。

examples.en: Excellent people want to go to places where they can grow, so companies that aim "high" have a lot of talented people. Paradoxically, companies that do not attract good people have low goals.
examples.ja: 優秀な人は成長できる場に行きたがるんで、「高い目標」を目指している企業には、良い人材が多いんです。逆説的に言えば、良い人が集まらない企業は、目標が低いんですよ。

5201.meaning_mnemonic: It is <kanji>reverse</kanji> to the <kanji>theory</kanji>! What is going on? Things aren't right. There must be some kind of <vocabulary>paradox</vocabulary> going on, where all theories are reversed! D:
5201.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Those who think they can get by if they just smile and laugh are very mistaken.
examples.ja: ニコニコ笑っておけば何とかなるでしょって思ってる人は大間違いですよ。

examples.en: The original big mistake was that we tried to record outdoors.
examples.ja: そもそも、野外で録音しようとしたのが大間違いだった。

examples.en: If you think this is the end of summer, you are mistaken! The real summer is yet to come.
examples.ja: これで夏が終わったと思ったら大間違いだよ！本当の夏は、まだまだこれからなんだから。

examples.en: I asked her to go out with me, but it was a big mistake.
examples.ja: 彼女をデートに誘ったが、それは大間違いだった。

5202.meaning_mnemonic:
A 間違い is a mistake. A <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>mistake</kanji> is a <vocabulary>big mistake</vocabulary>.

大間違い is less about factual errors and more about someone being way off in their assumptions or expectations. It suggests things didn't go according to plan — like you assumed a smile would fix everything or expected a date to go well, only for things to turn out completely wrong.
5202.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 大 and 間違い put together into one not so mistaken word.

examples.en: Is there a post office in this area?
examples.ja: この辺に郵便局はありますか？

examples.en: Could you get ten stamps at the post office for me?
examples.ja: 郵便局で切手を十枚買ってきてくれない？

examples.en: My uncle is the postmaster of that post office.
examples.ja: 私のおじは、あの郵便局の郵便局長なんです。

examples.en: I made a complaint about the post office’s service.
examples.ja: 郵便局のサービスに対して苦情を言いました。

examples.en: How many digits are there in an American zip code?
examples.ja: アメリカの郵便番号は何ケタあるんですか？

5204.meaning_mnemonic: You know that a 郵便 is the <kanji>mail</kanji> and that a 番号 is a <kanji>number</kanji>. So a "mail number," what is that? Usually refers to your <vocabulary>post number</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>postal code</vocabulary>. It is also often referred to with a symbol, which is 〒, so look out for that.
5204.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: How could this book fit in my small mailbox?
examples.ja: どうやって私の小さな郵便箱にこの本が入ったんだろう。

examples.en: There was one mailbox mounted next to the nameplate in front of my house.
examples.ja: 僕の家の前の表札の横には、郵便箱が一つ取り付けてあった。

examples.en: This mailbox has a camera in it!
examples.ja: この郵便箱、カメラがついてるよ！

examples.en: Since so many love letters are delivered to Koichi, we use a gigantic tanker as a mailbox instead.
examples.ja: コウイチあてのラブレターがあまりにもたくさん届くので、巨大なタンカーを郵便箱の代わりに使っています。

郵便 is the "mail." A <kanji>box</kanji> that's used with said mail is a <vocabulary>postbox</vocabulary>.

郵便箱 used to refer specifically to a public <vocabulary>collection box</vocabulary> where you drop off your mail to be sent. But now, some people use it for their home <vocabulary>mailboxes</vocabulary> too! Don't worry — you can usually tell which is which from context.
5205.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

5206.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>record</kanji> of <kanji>sound</kanji> is a <vocabulary>sound recording</vocabulary> of some kind. Might be minidisk, might be CD, might be digital. Whatever it is, it's still the record of sound.
5206.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Have you completed your resident registration already?
examples.ja: 住民登録はもうお済みですか？

examples.ja: 三宅結花です。携帯電話を変えたので、新しい電話番号とメールアドレスの登録をお願いします。

5207.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Climb</kanji> up and <kanji>record</kanji> your information here. This is <vocabulary>registration</vocabulary>. examples.en: I heard that Kitayama-san is a world record holder in swimming!
examples.ja: 北山さんって、水泳の世界記録保持者なんだって！

examples.en: This book contains testimonies from Japanese soldiers who decided to remain in Palau even after the Pacific War had ended.
examples.ja: この本には、太平洋戦争終了後もパラオに残ることを決意した日本兵の証言が記録されています。

5208.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Write down</kanji> a <kanji>record</kanji> of the events so we have a <vocabulary>record</vocabulary>, please. Don't want people to forget about this momentous occasion, when King Felix got his perfect game.

記録 refers to the act of putting something on record or to the record itself. Just like English "record," it can also refer to the best performance or most remarkable event of its kind that's been officially measured and noted, like the record for fastest baseball pitch.
5208.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I do not believe that there is any country that does not need to have an army.
examples.ja: 私は、軍隊を持つ必要の無い国は存在しないと思っています。

examples.en: Many men of this generation have military experience.
examples.ja: この世代の男性は軍隊経験がある人が多いんです。

5209.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>army</kanji> <kanji>squad</kanji> is <vocabulary>an army</vocabulary>. It's also just the <vocabulary>army</vocabulary>. It refers more to "an" army rather than "the" army. Just a group of people who do army things.

examples.en: What kind of things would I have to do if I became a member of the Tofugu party?

examples.en: I am the captain of a small animal rescue team.

5210.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

隊 is commonly used as a suffix to refer to an organized group or unit, often one that works together toward a specific goal or purpose, like a レスキュー隊 (rescue <vocabulary>squad</vocabulary>), 軍の部隊 (military <vocabulary>unit</vocabulary>), or 登山隊 (mountaineering <vocabulary>team</vocabulary>)!
5210.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji reading you learned, probably because this is stuck onto things, describing various squads.

examples.en: The soldiers wandered the woods aimlessly.
examples.ja: 兵隊達は、気の向くままに森を歩いていた。

examples.en: Our sons have recently become really into playing soldiers.
examples.ja: うちの息子達は、最近兵隊ごっこをすることにハマっています。

5211.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>soldier</kanji> in a <kanji>squad</kanji> is a real <vocabulary>soldier</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>sailor</vocabulary>, unlike those "soldier" who are not in a squad. They don't have jobs, and can't be called real soldiers.
5211.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I never thought there would be an interview for the enlistment test.

<kanji>Enter</kanji>ing into a <kanji>squad</kanji> is called <vocabulary>enlistment</vocabulary>!

入隊 can refer to <vocabulary>enlist</vocabulary>ing in any group that ends with 隊 (squad), like the 軍隊 (military) or an 音楽隊 (marching band). These are indeed the most common uses.
5212.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Our laundry hasn't dried yet.

examples.en: The soil in the planter was getting dry, so I gave it some water.
examples.ja: プランターの土が乾いてきたので水をやりました。

examples.en: "Looks like I got shot in the leg three times," Viet said in a dry voice.
examples.ja: 「足を三発撃たれたみたいだ」と、ビエトは乾いた声で言った。

5213.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>dry</kanji>, so this verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to get dry</vocabulary>. You're not doing the drying here — it's happening on its own. To remember this, just think about how <reading>coo</reading>l (く) it is that something can become dry all by itself. It's just, like, the magic of nature — how cool is that?
5213.reading_mnemonic: The <reading>川</reading> (かわ) has started <vocabulary>to get dry</vocabulary>. Need to use less water around here otherwise it'll become completely dry.

examples.en: Currently it's the height of the dry season here.

examples.en: I recommend going during the dry season if you are planning to travel to the Philippines.

examples.en: In this region, the dry season lasts from May to October.
examples.ja: この地域では、乾季が5月から10月まで続きます。

examples.en: By now it's usually the dry season already, but it still continues to rain this year.
examples.ja: いつもはこの時期は既に乾季になっているが、今年は未だ雨が降り続けている。

5214.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>dry</kanji> <kanji>seasons</kanji> is the <vocabulary>dry season</vocabulary>.

乾季 is a formal term typically used in geographical climate discussions, especially for regions with clear wet and dry seasons like Southeast Asia, Africa, and South America.
5214.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.ja: 少しおくれるので、先に乾杯して始めてください。

examples.en: Alright, cheers cheers! Hey, bottoms up!
examples.ja: さあ、乾杯、乾杯！それ、ぐいと一杯、飲み干したまえ。

5215.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>dry</kanji> out your <kanji>cup of liquid</kanji> after saying <vocabulary>Kanpai</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>cheers</vocabulary>!

乾杯 means <vocabulary>toast</vocabulary>ing with your drink and is how you say "Cheers!" in Japanese. It literally means "dry your cup" (drink up), so traditionally, people would finish their drink after saying it. But it's much more relaxed nowadays—most people just take a sip for 乾杯.
5215.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just watch out for the はい turning into ぱい!

examples.en: The teacher encouraged the students to ask more questions.
examples.ja: 先生は生徒にもっと質問をするよう促した。

examples.en: It seems that the news prompted people to take action.
examples.ja: そのニュースが人々に行動を促すきっかけとなったようです。

examples.en: The doctor urged me to quit smoking, but I struggled to follow through.
examples.ja: 医者は禁煙を促されたが、なかなか実行に移せなかった。

examples.en: This campaign aims to promote eco-friendly actions.
examples.ja: このキャンペーンは、環境に優しい行動を促すことを目的としています。

5216.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>urge</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to urge</vocabulary>.

促す means <vocabulary>to encourage</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to prompt</vocabulary> someone to take action or proceed with something. Depending on the context, it can also mean <vocabulary>to promote</vocabulary> the growth, development, or change of something.
5216.reading_mnemonic: Someone with a weird accent is trying <vocabulary>to urge</vocabulary> you to eat "<reading>Unagah</reading>" (うなが). This person really means "unagi," and this person also doesn't realize how delicious unagi is (and thinks he's tricking you). You ask him what "Unagah" is. Go ahead and say it out loud.

examples.en: It's been a week and I still haven't received a call, so I plan to send a follow-up email.
examples.ja: 一週間経っても電話がかかってこないから、催促のメールを入れるつもりです。

examples.en: Kaneko-san urged me to return the money, but I don't remember borrowing any.
examples.ja: 金子さんにお金を返してくれと催促されましたが、借りた覚えがありません。

examples.en: My cat’s face when demanding food is just too cute—take a look!
examples.ja: うちのネコがご飯を催促してくるときの顔が可愛すぎるんで、見てください。

examples.en: How can I press a customer to take action on his overdue payment politely but also strongly?
examples.ja: どうすれば顧客に未払分の支払手続きを丁寧かつ強く催促することができるのでしょうか。

5217.meaning_mnemonic: I'm so for this I'm willing to <kanji>sponsor</kanji> you. I am going to <kanji>urge</kanji> you to do this until you do it, so much so I'll give you money. This is one great <vocabulary>urge</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>press for</vocabulary> you to do this!
5217.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I've finally received the final notification.
examples.ja: ついに、最終催告を送り付けられてしまいました。

examples.en: Since I could not respond to the payment notification, my credit card got suspended.
examples.ja: 催告に応じることが出来ず、クレジットカードが止められてしまった。

examples.en: I received a demand notice because I couldn't pay the mortgage.
examples.ja: 住宅ローンが払えなかったため、催告書がきてしまいました。

examples.en: A consumer credit company has been sending me notification letters over and over, demanding that I pay back my debt.
examples.ja: サラ金から、借金の返済を求める催告状が何度も何度も届いています。

5218.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>sponsor</kanji> an <kanji>announce</kanji>ment, you're allowing those you're sponsoring to create some kind of <vocabulary>notice</vocabulary> for all those they want to get in contact with.

催告 refers to the act of <vocabulary>officially notifying</vocabulary> someone with a <vocabulary>formal notice</vocabulary>, urging them to take action within a specified time frame. It's a technical term mainly used in legal or business contexts, like reminding someone to fulfill obligations such as payments or contracts.
5218.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I wonder what a golf tournament hosted by a celebrity is like.
examples.ja: 芸能人主催のゴルフ大会ってどんなのなんだろう？

examples.en: This event is hosted by the local chamber of commerce.
examples.ja: このイベントは、地元の商工会が主催しています。

examples.en: Actually, the host of this concert is a well-known music producer.
examples.ja: 実はこのコンサートの主催は、とある有名な音楽プロデューサーなんです。

examples.en: The racetrack turf symposium was able to happen because of city government sponsorship.
examples.ja: 競馬場の芝についてのシンポジウムが市当局の主催で開かれた。

5219.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>master</kanji> <kanji>sponsor</kanji> for an event is the host who's <vocabulary>hosting</vocabulary> (and possibly sponsoring) it. 

主催 is a formal term often used in business, official events, or public gatherings. While it can imply sponsorship, it mainly refers to the act of leading and organizing an event or activity, as well as the person or group hosting it.
5219.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My child accidentally broke the glass WaniKani ornament.
examples.ja: 子供が、ガラス製のワニカニの置物を壊してしまったんです。

examples.en: I was careful with my choice of words because I didn't want to damage the relationship.
examples.ja: 関係を壊したくなかったので、言葉選びには気をつけました。

examples.en: Continuing an extreme diet may harm your health.
examples.ja: 無理なダイエットを続けると、体を壊す可能性があります。

examples.en: I cooked this blowfish in my own way and it wrecked my stomach.
examples.ja: この河豚を自分なりに料理してみたんですが、お腹を壊してしまいました。

5220.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>break</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to break something</vocabulary>, because you're doing the breaking. You know this because someone is trying to <reading>sue</reading> (す) you for the things you broke of theirs.
5220.reading_mnemonic: The thing you broke? A beautiful ceramic <reading>koa</reading>la (こわ). Watch it shatter to the ground, because you threw it there. What a jerk you are.

examples.en: Something came out of the completely destroyed building.
examples.ja: 全壊したビルの中から何か出てきました。

examples.en: I had my own house, but it was completely destroyed by the typhoon.
examples.ja: マイホームを持っていたんですが、台風で全壊しちゃったんですよ。

examples.en: Our house was almost totally destroyed by the tornado, but my family is all safe.
examples.ja: トルネードで自宅はほぼ全壊ですが、家族はみんな元気です。

examples.en: Among the houses that suffered from this earthquake, the number of completely destroyed houses was 835.
examples.ja: この地震で被害を受けた家のうち、全壊家屋は全部で835戸だった。

5221.meaning_mnemonic:
When <kanji>all</kanji> of something <kanji>breaks</kanji>, every last bit of it is broken. It's <vocabulary>complete destruction</vocabulary>!!!

全壊 is a formal term used when buildings or structures are completely destroyed by disasters like earthquakes, fires, or accidents. It's often seen in news reports or insurance assessments to describe the <vocabulary>total destruction</vocabulary> of property.
5221.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I just saw a news ticker saying "London Bridge collapses due to a terror attack"! Could it be true?
examples.ja: 今、『テロでロンドンブリッジ倒壊』のテロップが流れてきたよ！本当かな？

examples.en: There were reports that Tokyo Tower might collapse due to the impact of the major earthquake.
examples.ja: 大地震の影響で東京タワーが倒壊するかもしれないとの報道があった。

examples.en: The fire-fighting team rescued a girl from the collapsed building.
examples.ja: 消防隊は、倒壊したビルの中から少女を助け出した。

examples.en: My grandparents' house is so old that it could collapse under the weight of the snow.
examples.ja: 私の祖父母の家はとても古いので、雪の重みで倒壊しかねません。

5222.meaning_mnemonic:
When something <kanji>collapse</kanji>s and <kanji>break</kanji>s, it is when a <vocabulary>collapse</vocabulary> happens. Something big collapsing or <vocabulary>falling down</vocabulary> will probably result in its <vocabulary>destruction</vocabulary>.

倒壊 is a formal word often found in news or official documents. It's used to describe buildings or structures collapsing, usually from destructive forces like natural disasters or bombings.
5222.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I have three daughters.
examples.ja: 私には娘が三人います。

examples.en: I heard Matsumoto's daughter is going to be a university student this year!
examples.ja: 松本さんのとこの娘さん、今年大学生になるんだって！

examples.en: It's dangerous for young women to be walking around at this time of night, you know?
examples.ja: こんな時間に若い娘さんたちだけで歩いてたら危ないよ？

examples.en: "My daughter is a mermaid." "Whoa! Does that mean you married a fish?"
examples.ja: 「私の娘は人魚なんだ。」「ええっ、それってつまり、あんた魚と結婚したってことか？」

5223.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

娘 primarily means <vocabulary>daughter</vocabulary> but can also refer to a <vocabulary>young woman</vocabulary> (often unmarried). This is because its original form is 産す女 (むすめ), or "a woman who gives birth." Over time, it came to represent both daughters and young women.
5223.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: Klara is the only daughter of the Sesemann family.
examples.ja: クララはゼーゼマン家の一人娘です。

examples.en: He has an only daughter.
examples.ja: 彼には一人娘がいます。

examples.en: Ms. Hayashi is raising her only daughter by herself.
examples.ja: 林さんは女手ひとつで一人娘を育てています。

5224.meaning_mnemonic: An "alone" (一人) <kanji>daughter</kanji> is a daughter with no other daughter siblings, making her the <vocabulary>only daughter</vocabulary>.
5224.reading_mnemonic: The readings are 一人 plus 娘 put together into one, single (daughter) word.

examples.en: He is interested in various religions.
examples.ja: 彼はさまざまな宗教に関心があります。

examples.en: For many people, religion is a part of their daily lives.
examples.ja: 多くの人々にとって、宗教は生活の一部です。

examples.en: Sometimes, I feel like WaniKani seems a bit like a cult.
examples.ja: 時々、ワニカニってカルト宗教みたいだと思うことがあります。

examples.en: She will be the secretary who records the transactions of the world religions meeting.
examples.ja: 彼女が、世界宗教会議の記録を取る書記を務めます。

5225.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>religion</kanji> <kanji>teach</kanji>ings are what makes up a <vocabulary>religion</vocabulary>. If you don't have the teachings of the religion, nobody will learn about it, and it will stop being a religion.
5225.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: People of all denominations got together at the meeting.
examples.ja: その会議には、あらゆる宗派の人々が集いました。

examples.en: There are various sects in Buddhism.
examples.ja: 仏教にはさまざまな宗派があります。

examples.en: Even within Christianity there are many denominations, each with slightly different doctrines.
examples.ja: キリスト教といっても多くの宗派があって、それぞれ教義が少し違うんです。

5226.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>religion</kanji> <kanji>sect</kanji> is a sect within religion, most likely, but it can be simply referred to as a <vocabulary>sect</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>denomination</vocabulary>.
5226.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: In Zen Buddhism, they teach you to empty your mind and focus on the present moment.
examples.ja: 禅宗では、心を無にして今に集中することを教えています。

examples.en: To calm my mind, I went to a Zen temple and tried Zen meditation.
examples.ja: 心を落ち着けるために、禅宗の寺に行って座禅をしてみました。

examples.en: Following the teachings of Zen Buddhism, he tries to live a simple life.
examples.ja: 禅宗の教えに従って、彼はシンプルな生活を心がけています。

5227.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>zen</kanji> <kanji>religion</kanji> is a part of Buddhism. It is the <vocabulary>Zen sect</vocabulary> of Buddhism, or <vocabulary>Zen Buddhism</vocabulary>.

Practitioners of 禅宗 follow 禅 (Zen) practices like meditation and mindfulness to achieve enlightenment. That's why it's called 禅宗!
5227.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'm going to be the organizer of the next banquet.
examples.ja: 今度の宴会の幹事をすることになりました。

examples.en: I need to reserve a banquet hall for the year-end party.
examples.ja: 忘年会のための宴会場を予約しなくてはいけません。

examples.en: I joined the dinner party after wrapping up my work.
examples.ja: 仕事の締めくくりをつけてから、宴会に参加しました。

examples.en: Drinking alcohol with someone you don’t like at a dinner party is a much more tedious task than recording the proceedings of a meeting.
examples.ja: 宴会で嫌な奴とお酒を飲むのは、会議で議事録を記録するより退屈な仕事だ。

5228.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>banquet</kanji> <kanji>meet</kanji>ing is when you meet together for a <vocabulary>banquet</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>dinner party</vocabulary>.

宴会 refers to a gathering where people share food and drinks to celebrate something or deepen their social bonds. It's generally not used for casual dinner parties among friends, but rather for formal or semi-formal social events involving a larger group of people, such as farewell parties for colleagues or workplace holiday parties.
5228.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The prince was shot dead during the feast.
examples.ja: 王子は、宴の最中に撃たれて死んだ。

examples.en: The banquet this evening is truly fun, isn't it?
examples.ja: こよいの宴は実に楽しいものですな。

examples.en: Alright, it's party time! Everyone, drink up, drink up!
examples.ja: さぁ、宴じゃ宴じゃ！みんな、飲め飲め！

5229.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

宴 is an old-fashioned word for 宴会. It refers to large, festive feasts in traditional settings, often involving lots of sake and the enjoyment of traditional performing arts. You may see it used in literature or in song lyrics to evoke scenes of grand, lavish banquets from ages past.
5229.reading_mnemonic: At a <vocabulary>banquet</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>party</vocabulary>, you don't only get food, you also <reading>歌 GE</reading>T (うたげ), which is you getting a song from a singer. After all, entertainment is just as important as the food when you're at a wild <vocabulary>bacchanal</vocabulary> such as this!

examples.en: You shouldn't go on a diet in an unhealthy way.
examples.ja: 不健康なやり方でダイエットをするのはよした方がいい。

examples.en: Now that I've become a parent, I'm thinking of reevaluating my unhealthy lifestyle.
examples.ja: 私も親になったから、これまでの不健康な生活を見直そうと思ってるんです。

examples.en: This show is violent and contains a lot of unwholesome content, so I don't want my kids watching it.
examples.ja: この番組は暴力的で、不健康な内容が多いので子供には見せたくないんですよね。

5230.meaning_mnemonic: If 健康 is "health," then something that is <kanji>not</kanji> this is <vocabulary>unhealthy</vocabulary>.
5230.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Will help to know 健康 first.

examples.en: The president's joke helped ease the tension.
examples.ja: 社長のジョークに緊張の糸がほぐれました。

examples.en: My hands wouldn't stop sweating from nervousness during the interview.
examples.ja: 面接のときは、緊張で手汗が止まりませんでした。

examples.en: Amidst the palpable tension in the room, she quietly stood up.
examples.ja: 緊張感がただよう会場の中、彼女は静かに立ち上がった。

examples.en: "I have a job interview tomorrow. I'm a little nervous." "Oh, really? Well, I'm sure you'll do fine."
examples.ja: 「明日、就職の面接があるんで、ちょっと緊張してるんだよね。」「え〜そうなの？うまくいくといいね。」

examples.en: I've been having trouble sleeping lately due to stress and tension from work.
examples.ja: 仕事から来るストレスと緊張で、最近よく眠れないんです。

5231.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>tense</kanji> body begins to <kanji>stretch</kanji> tighter and tighter as <vocabulary>nervousness</vocabulary> takes over.

緊張 describes that nervousness you feel before a big event or during a stressful moment. It can also refer to other things that feel tight or strained, like muscle <vocabulary>tension</vocabulary>, or even global tensions and strained relations between countries.
5231.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My wrath will not go on for more than three minutes.
examples.ja: 私の怒りは三分以上続かない。

examples.en: Naoko felt intense anger at Kazuki's words.
examples.ja: 直子は和希の言葉にとてつもない怒りを覚えた。

examples.en: Anger often bubbles up slowly after the fact, doesn't it?
examples.ja: 怒りって、後からフツフツわいてくることが多いよね。

5232.meaning_mnemonic: This word looks a lot like 怒る, doesn't it? But this word isn't a verb, so you can think of it as referring to <vocabulary>anger</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>wrath</vocabulary> itself.
5232.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

I have a lot of <vocabulary>anger</vocabulary> because <reading>I ca</reading>rry (いか) all of my own things (books, luggage, drinks) and no one will ever carry them for me. Plus, the more things I carry, the more anger I carry inside. Ahh!

examples.en: Walking down a dark road is a bit scary.
examples.ja: 暗い道を歩くのはちょっと怖いな。

examples.en: I'm not good with dogs, and I get scared when they come near.
examples.ja: 犬が苦手で、近づかれると怖いんです。

examples.en: That movie was so scary! I couldn't sleep alone at night.
examples.ja: あの映画、本当に怖かった！夜、一人で眠れなかったよ。

examples.en: It seems that a magnitude 7 earthquake occurred on Mars. Scary!
examples.ja: 火星でマグニチュード7の地震が起きたんだってさ。怖いね！

5233.meaning_mnemonic:
This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>scary</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>scary</vocabulary>.

怖い is commonly used in everyday language to describe something that's scary on a more immediate or personal level.
5233.reading_mnemonic: You know what's really <vocabulary>scary</vocabulary>, like double scary (because kanji and vocab both mean scary)? How about your <reading>cowo</reading>rkers (こわ). They are all insane, and you know it. Absolute nutjobs they are.

examples.en: She was unable to say anything out of sheer terror.
examples.ja: 彼女は恐怖のあまり、何も言えなくなった。

examples.en: Oh, Minami-senpai, when you suddenly called out to me, I was filled with nothing but fear.
examples.ja: いやー南先輩、先輩に突然呼び出されたときは、恐怖でしかなかったですよ。

examples.en: I'm afraid of heights, so when I went up the CN Tower, my legs froze with fear.
examples.ja: 高い場所が苦手なので、CNタワーに上った時は、恐怖で足がすくみました。

examples.en: When a yakuza told me that the change I gave him was 100 yen short, I felt an incredible amount of fear.
examples.ja: ヤクザにお釣りが百円足りないと言われた時に、とてつもない恐怖を感じました。

5234.meaning_mnemonic: I <kanji>fear</kanji> it. It is <kanji>scary</kanji>. It is pure <vocabulary>terror</vocabulary>.
5234.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My dad and I are both afraid of heights.
examples.ja: 私も父も高所恐怖症です。

examples.en: I'm claustrophobic, so I have difficulty taking elevators.
examples.ja: 閉所恐怖症のため、エレベーターに乗るのが苦手です。

examples.en: Because of the power harassment I experienced from my boss, I've developed social anxiety.
examples.ja: 上司からパワハラを受けたせいで、対人恐怖症になってしまいました。

examples.en: I studied kanji on WaniKani too much, and while it was great that I learned kanji, I ended up developing a phobia of alligators and crabs.
examples.ja: ワニカニのやり過ぎで漢字を覚えたのはいいけれど、ワニとカニ恐怖症になってしまった。

5235.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned 恐怖 means "terror," and 〜症 can mean "disease." So what's a terror disease? Well, it's a <vocabulary>phobia</vocabulary>.

In Japanese, 恐怖症 is mostly used as a suffix for specific phobia names, like 高所恐怖症 (acrophobia, or fear of heights). Do you have any 恐怖症?
5235.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Have you ever had the experience of waking up in the middle of the night after a terrifying dream?
examples.ja: 恐ろしい夢を見て、真夜中に目が覚めた経験はありませんか？

examples.en: I've never seen Viet with such a terrifying look in his eyes.
examples.ja: あんなに恐ろしい目をしたビエトは見たことがありません。

examples.en: We must never forget the terrors of war.
examples.ja: 我々は、戦争の恐ろしさを忘れてはいけません。

5236.meaning_mnemonic:
This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>fear</kanji>? When you really feel fear, you think something is <vocabulary>terrifying</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>frightening</vocabulary> or even <vocabulary>dreadful</vocabulary>.

恐ろしい can describe something that inspires deep fear or awe, often beyond normal feelings of fear. Since it can be used to create a dramatic or intense atmosphere, you might find 恐ろしい more often in literature.
5236.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

How <vocabulary>terrifying</vocabulary> is it? It's <reading>Oh so</reading> (おそ) terrifying!

examples.en: "Let’s go for a drink." "Sounds like a plan."
examples.ja: 「ちょっと一杯飲みに行かない？」「いいね。」

examples.en: When I was a child, I watched a movie called "One Cup of Soba Noodles in Broth" just once.
examples.ja: 子供の時に「一杯のかけそば」という映画を一度だけ観たことがあります。

examples.en: My mind was so full of the following year's budget that I didn't feel like having even one drink that night.
examples.ja: 次年度の予算のことで頭が一杯な状態だったので、その夜は一杯もお酒を飲む気にはなれなかった。

5237.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>One</kanji> <kanji>cup of liquid</kanji> is equal to <vocabulary>one cup</vocabulary>. It could just be <vocabulary>a drink</vocabulary>, but if you're measuring exactly one cup, it needs to be <vocabulary>full</vocabulary> to the brim. That's <vocabulary>a lot</vocabulary> of liquid—so be careful not to spill!

一杯 mainly refers to the amount that fills a container, like a cup, glass, bowl, or even spoon. It can also describe something being "full," such as a full stomach or a theater at capacity (like how a cup is filled to the brim!). Depending on the context, it can also mean "a lot," as fullness implies abundance. When it uses that meaning, you'll also often see it written in just kana (いっぱい).
5237.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just remember that 一 becomes いっ, and 杯 becomes ぱい.

examples.en: I had two glasses of cold lemonade at the beach.
examples.ja: 浜辺で冷たいレモネードを二杯飲んだ。

examples.en: Mixing two teaspoons of olive oil into this sauce will make it smoother.
examples.ja: このソースに小さじ二杯のオリーブオイルを混ぜると、まろやかになります。

examples.en: I ate two bowls of ramen, and now I'm stuffed.
examples.ja: ラーメンを二杯も食べてしまって、お腹がいっぱいです。

examples.en: I had two cups of coffee while the railroad operation was suspended.
examples.ja: 電車が運行を見合わせている間に、コーヒーを二杯飲みました。

5238.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Two</kanji> <kanji>cups of liquid</kanji> is equals to <vocabulary>two cups</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>two drinks</vocabulary>. It can also mean <vocabulary>two glasses</vocabulary>, depending on what your drink is in!

〜杯 is a counter used to count the amount that fills a container, such as a cup, glass, bowl, or even a spoon! The contents don't have to be liquid—you can use 二杯 for two bowls of rice or two spoons of sugar as well.
5238.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Now, add three tablespoons of honey here.
examples.ja: ここで、大さじ三杯のハチミツを入れます。

examples.en: The cream of corn soup at this restaurant was so delicious that I ended up having three bowls.
examples.ja: この店のコーンポタージュが美味しすぎて、三杯も飲んでしまった。

examples.en: I have a habit of drinking three cups of coffee a day—do you think that's caffeine addiction?
examples.ja: 私、一日にコーヒーを三杯飲むのが習慣になってるんですが、これってカフェイン中毒だと思いますか？

examples.en: I was depressed at the time, so I chugged three glasses of beer.
examples.ja: その時ちょっとへこみ気味だったもんで、ビールを三杯一気飲みしちゃったんだよね。

5239.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Three</kanji> <kanji>cups of liquid</kanji> is equals to <vocabulary>three cups</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>three drinks</vocabulary>. It can also mean <vocabulary>three glasses</vocabulary> depending on what your drink is in!

〜杯 is a counter used to count the amount that fills a container, such as a cup, glass, bowl, or even a spoon! The contents don't have to be liquid—you can use 三杯 for three bowls of rice or three spoons of sugar as well.
5239.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just watch out for 杯, which becomes ばい thanks to our old friend rendaku.

examples.en: I cut a wooden plank with a saw.
examples.ja: ノコギリで木の板を切りました。

examples.en: What are you going to use this plastic board for?
examples.ja: このプラスチックの板、何に使うの？

examples.en: I'm looking for a marble board that matches this ornament.
examples.ja: この置物に合う大理石の板をさがしています。

examples.en: I posted some comments on a forum about baseball on 2chan, but I was told it was the wrong board.
examples.ja: 2chの野球板に書き込みをしたんですが、板違いだと言われてしまいました。

5240.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

板 generally refers to something thin, flat, and solid, like a board, plank, slab, or plate. In some contexts, it can also refer to stock market boards that display trading prices, or bulletin boards used for posting messages in online forums.
5240.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Who can make good use of various <vocabulary>board</vocabulary>s? An avid <reading>eater</reading> (いた)! If you’re an avid eater, you’ll need lots of (cutting) boards to prepare all the delicious food you’re going to eat. This makes boards and eaters the perfect match.

examples.en: The signboard of this restaurant is big and very eye-catching.
examples.ja: このレストランの看板は大きくてよく目立ちます。

examples.en: The billboard was blown away by the typhoon.
examples.ja: 台風で看板が飛ばされてしまいました。

examples.en: She is the face of this store.
examples.ja: 彼女はこの店の看板です。

examples.en: There is a dent in the store sign because some drunk guy punched it.
examples.ja: 酔っぱらいの男が殴ったせいで、お店の看板がへこんでいるんです。

5241.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>watch over</kanji> <kanji>board</kanji> is a board that's put up and watches over everything. What kind of board watches over everything from up high? One that gets the most visibility, so probably a <vocabulary>signboard</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>billboard</vocabulary>.

看板 typically refers to physical signs, such as <vocabulary>store sign</vocabulary>s or billboards. But it can also mean the figurative symbol or face of a business, like 看板メニュー (signature dish) or 看板娘 (popular female employee).
5241.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meanings: To Get To The Bottom Of

examples.en: It is difficult to identify the best time to buy stocks.
examples.ja: 株の買い時を見極めるのは難しい。

examples.en: I want to see the truth with my own eyes.
examples.ja: 自分のこの目で真実を見極めたいんです。

examples.en: To truly assess his abilities, you should give him more tasks to handle.
examples.ja: 彼の能力を見極めるには、もっと仕事を任せてみるべきだ。

examples.en: Koichi can identify whether a dictionary has a good or bad index just by looking at its cover.
examples.ja: コウイチは、辞書の表紙を見ただけで、その辞書の索引が良い索引か悪い索引かを見極めることができる。

5242.meaning_mnemonic:
極める is "to carry to extremes." If you take the action of <kanji>see</kanji>ing something to the extremes, you're going <vocabulary>to get to the bottom of</vocabulary> whatever it is. You'll be able <vocabulary>to identify something</vocabulary>, like the truth.

見極める primarily involves the careful examination and discernment of the underlying aspects or truth of a matter. It emphasizes the thoroughness and effort required to make well-informed decisions or judgments, particularly when the situation is complex or difficult to understand.
5242.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the words 見る and 極める put together. Get to the bottom of this word and learn it.

examples.en: This issue is extremely important.
examples.ja: この問題は極めて重要です。

examples.en: This medicine has extremely few side effects.
examples.ja: この薬は副作用が極めて少ないです。

examples.en: We are facing an extremely dangerous situation.
examples.ja: 我々は、極めて危険な状況に直面しています。

examples.en: It’s extremely obvious that you don’t have any idea how we can solve this problem.
examples.ja: 君がこの問題の解決方法について具体的には何も考えていないというのは、極めて明白な事実だ。

5243.meaning_mnemonic: 極める is "to carry to extremes." So, 極めて is something similar. It's used to refer to something that's <vocabulary>extremely</vocabulary> _______.
5243.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 極める.

examples.en: Japanese food is popular even in the West.
examples.ja: 日本の食べ物は欧米でも人気があります。

examples.en: The hotel's main customers are Westerners.
examples.ja: このホテルの主なお客様は、欧米の方々なんです。

examples.en: Can you name all the countries included in "Europe and the US"?
examples.ja: 「欧米」に含まれる国を全部挙げることができますか。

examples.en: I'm searching for a place in Europe and America that grows pink roses.
examples.ja: 欧米でピンクのバラを栽培している所がないか探しているんですが。

5244.meaning_mnemonic:
You have <kanji>Europe</kanji> and <kanji>America</kanji>. This word refers to <vocabulary>Europe and America</vocabulary>. 

When people use 欧米 in Japan, they usually mean Western countries in general (<vocabulary>the West</vocabulary>), including North America and Western Europe. You'll often see it in news reports related to Western countries or in topics comparing Japanese and Western cultures, customs, or trends.
5244.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Among Central European countries, I would like to visit the Czech Republic.
examples.ja: 中欧の国だったら、チェコに行ってみたいです。

examples.en: I had been thinking that Germany was a part of Western Europe, but it was actually one of the Central European countries, wasn't it?
examples.ja: ドイツは西欧だと思っていたんですが、中欧の国の一つだったんですね。

examples.en: This summer, I took a solo trip through Central Europe.
examples.ja: この夏は、中欧をひとり旅してきました。

examples.en: I’ve wanted to travel around Central Europe for a really long time.
examples.ja: 中欧を旅してみたいなと随分長い間思っていたんですよ。

5245.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>middle</kanji> part of <kanji>Europe</kanji> is <vocabulary>Central Europe</vocabulary>, wherever that is.
5245.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Mizuno-san goes back and forth from Japan to Europe a lot for her work.
examples.ja: 水野さんは仕事で日欧を行き来することが多い。

examples.en: Since there's a time difference between Japan and Europe, it's hard to coordinate meetings.
examples.ja: 日欧間の時差があるので、会議の時間を調整するのが大変です。

examples.en: The Japan-Europe cultural exchange festival will be held next month.
examples.ja: 来月、日欧文化交流フェスティバルが開催されます。

examples.en: The meeting concerning trade between Europe and Japan was sidetracked due to the moderator’s absence.
examples.ja: 日欧貿易に関する会議は、司会者の不在によって横道に逸れてしまった。

5246.meaning_mnemonic:
The 日 refers to "Japan" (It's the 日 of 日本). So, you have Japan and <kanji>Europe</kanji>, which makes this <vocabulary>Japan and Europe</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>Japanese-European</vocabulary>.

日欧 is a fairly formal word commonly found in newspapers or official reports, where it’s often used for brevity when referring to Japan and Europe together, like in 日欧関係 (Japanese-European relations).
5246.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The Edo period lasted for about 260 years.
examples.ja: 江戸時代は約260年間続きました。

examples.en: Please tell me the characteristics of Edo-style sushi.
examples.ja: 江戸前ずしの特徴を教えてください。

examples.en: The diorama that replicates the townscape of Edo is a highlight of this museum.
examples.ja: この博物館では江戸の町並みを再現したジオラマが見ものです。

examples.en: Stop mucking around and go upstairs and do your homework. You said you gotta write an essay about the Edo period in Japan, right?
examples.ja: だらだらしてないで、さっさと二階に行って宿題をしなさい。日本の江戸時代についてレポートを書かないといけないって言ってたでしょ！

5247.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>bay</kanji> <kanji>door</kanji> isn't what you might think, it refers to <vocabulary>Edo</vocabulary>, which is what Tokyo was called back in the day. You'll still see references to it everywhere, though, so it's good to learn. You can also call this <vocabulary>Tokyo</vocabulary> if you want, but I'd prefer if you answered "Edo," instead.
5247.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji. Just watch out for that rendaku on 戸, which changes the reading to ど. Of course, it will be easy if you already know the word <vocabulary>Edo</vocabulary>!

examples.en: We swam in a quiet cove.
examples.ja: 静かな入り江で泳ぎました。

examples.en: Mr. Irie told me that dolphins often visit this cove.
examples.ja: この入り江にはイルカがよくあそびに来ると入江さんが言っていた。

examples.en: I was proposed to by someone I didn’t know in a cove north of the Baltic Sea. It was so romantic that I couldn't help accepting.
examples.ja: バルト海の北の入り江で知らない人からプロポーズされたんですが、とてもロマンチックだったのでつい承諾してしまったんです。

5248.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>enter</kanji> an <kanji>inlet</kanji>, you've gone into the <vocabulary>inlet</vocabulary>. It's also where water goes inside of the inlet (it's entering the inlet from the ocean, or whatever), so that's another way to think about it.
5248.reading_mnemonic: For this reading, just imagine this as 入り with 江 pushed on at the end! Also note this is commonly written as 入江, but the reading stays the same!

examples.en: Garnishing ice cream with a mint leaf gives it a bit of a stylish touch.
examples.ja: アイスクリームにミントの葉っぱを添えると、少しオシャレな感じになりますよ。

examples.en: I gave the present with a message card attached.
examples.ja: プレゼントにメッセージカードを添えて渡しました。

examples.en: What do you think about a man who puts his hand on your waist even though you're not in a relationship?
examples.ja: 付き合ってもないのに、腰に手を添えてくる男性ってどう思いますか？

5249.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. When <kanji>append</kanji>ing something, you basically want <vocabulary>to add something to</vocabulary> something, or <vocabulary>to include something</vocabulary> with it. 

添える means to add something alongside the main thing, often as a thoughtful touch to complement or support it. For example, you might say 添える when including a letter with a gift to add a personal touch, or when garnishing a dish with parsley to enhance its appearance. It's also used when you feel inclined to add a second hand to hold a bowl carefully.
5249.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: One way <vocabulary>to add something to</vocabulary> something else is to just <reading>sew</reading> (そ) it on!

examples.en: As for Koichi's plans, please check the attached schedule.
examples.ja: コウイチの予定につきましては、添付のスケジュールをご確認ください。

examples.en: WaniKani emails often have funny GIFs attached.
examples.ja: WaniKaniのメールには、よく面白いGIFが添付されています。

examples.en: Where is the list of the necessary attached documents for a green card application?
examples.ja: グリーンカード申請に必要な添付書類のリストはどこにありますか。

examples.en: Dear hiring manager, please have a look at the resume attached to this email. Thank you for your time.
examples.ja: 人事部長様、 恐れ入りますが、このEメールに添付された履歴書にお目通し頂けますでしょうか。お忙しいとは存じますが、よろしくお願い申し上げます。

5250.meaning_mnemonic: Append and attach this document to your email. That’s called attachment. 添付 refers to the act of attaching something supplementary to another document, like attaching a file to an email or attaching a map to an invitation.
5250.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 添 is what you'd expect. The reading for 付 is the on'yomi reading ふ, which you've learned with 付近. But for this word it becomes ぷ from the rendaku fairies. Just think of an <vocabulary>attachment</vocabulary> where instead of a document or something, you get an attachment of <reading>poo</reading>p (ぷ). What a gross attachment. Your friend who likes to send poop attachments is dumb.

examples.en: My first impression of Miyazaki-san when we met was very striking.
examples.ja: 初めて会った時の宮崎さんの印象は、とても強烈でした。

examples.en: The midsummer sun in Japan was so intense that it stung and felt painful.
examples.ja: 真夏の日本の日差しは強烈で、ヒリヒリして痛いくらいでした。

examples.en: His shocking remark instantly froze the atmosphere in the room.
examples.ja: 彼の強烈な発言で、会場の空気が一気に凍りつきました。

examples.en: I had a cigarette for the first time in ages, and I got hit hard with a nicotine buzz.
examples.ja: ひっさびさにタバコ吸ったら、強烈なヤニクラくらっちまったよ。

5251.meaning_mnemonic:
Things that are <kanji>strong</kanji> and <kanji>intense</kanji> are <vocabulary>very strong</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>intense</vocabulary>.

強烈 describes something so strong or intense that it leaves a lasting impression and is often <vocabulary>shocking</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>striking</vocabulary>. It can refer to vividly bright colors, a blinding flash of light, extreme heat, or unusually bold or impactful comments.
5251.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: He finished the work at an intense speed.
examples.ja: 彼は猛烈なスピードで仕事を終わらせました。

examples.en: She studied intensely and passed the exam.
examples.ja: 彼女は猛烈に勉強して、試験に合格しました。

examples.en: Yesterday's concert was ferociously fun!
examples.ja: 昨日のライブ、猛烈に楽しかった！

examples.en: I seriously regret that I volunteered to be the leader of this project now.
examples.ja: このプロジェクトのリーダーを買って出たことを、今猛烈に後悔しています。

5252.meaning_mnemonic:
If you're <kanji>fierce</kanji> and <kanji>violent</kanji> then you are <vocabulary>fierce</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>violent</vocabulary>.

猛烈 is used to describe <vocabulary>intense</vocabulary> things, like fierce storms, or actions done with great intensity, like working like mad. Its strong tone can feel a bit comical in casual use, so people also use it playfully to exaggerate things like how hungry they feel.
5252.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The venue was filled with passionate fans of the band.
examples.ja: そのバンドの熱烈なファンが会場をいっぱいにしていた。

examples.en: I was moved by his impassioned love letter, and decided to start dating him.
examples.ja: 彼からの熱烈なラブレターに感動して、付き合うことにしたんです。

examples.en: He is a fervent supporter of that author's works.
examples.ja: 彼はその作家の作品を熱烈に支持している。

examples.en: The woman said, "I'm an ardent fan of Tofugu," and gave Koichi a passionate kiss.
examples.ja: その女性は、「トーフグの熱烈なファンなんです」と言って、コウイチに熱烈なキスをした。

5253.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>fever</kanji> turns <kanji>violent</kanji> when you express your <vocabulary>fervent</vocabulary> feelings.

熱烈 is a relatively formal word that describes someone being fervently absorbed in something or someone and showing <vocabulary>ardent</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>passionate</vocabulary> behavior, like 熱烈に応援する (support fervently).
5253.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: He studied fiercely and passed the university entrance exam.
examples.ja: 彼は猛勉強して、大学に合格しました。

examples.en: A fierce blizzard piled up about three meters of snow.
examples.ja: 猛ふぶきで雪が三メートル程積もりました。

examples.en: That dog suddenly dashed at me fiercely, and I was shocked!
examples.ja: あの犬、急に猛ダッシュしてきたからびっくりしたよ！

examples.en: The motorcycle came rushing forward at breakneck speed.
examples.ja: バイクが猛スピードで突っ込んできた。

5254.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. You can put this on other words to say that it's a "<vocabulary>Fierce</vocabulary> ____" or "<vocabulary>Intense</vocabulary> _____," or something along those lines. If you see this, you know that something is being done really fiercely or intensely.

猛 is used in compounds to emphasize fierceness or intensity, like 猛暑 (intense heat) or 猛勉強 (intense studying). It can also be used in expressions like 猛アプローチ (relentlessly pursuing someone romantically — a fierce "approach"). In casual uses like this, the strong tone is often intentionally goofy or comical.
5254.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji, probably because it's stuck onto things making it all jukugo and such.

examples.en: Young Japanese people tend to abbreviate words and phrases.
examples.ja: 日本の若者はすぐ単語やフレーズを略したがる。

examples.en: Please write your full name without abbreviating it.
examples.ja: 略さずにフルネームを書いてください。

examples.en: As an outsider, I have no idea what you are talking about when you speak in abbreviated form.
examples.ja: 略して話されても部外者の私には何のことか全然分かりません。

examples.en: I apologize, but we cannot skip the procedure.
examples.ja: 恐れ入りますが、手続きを略すことはできないんです。

5255.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.
