The kanji itself means <kanji>abbreviation</kanji>, so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to abbreviate</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to shorten</vocabulary>. In some cases, it can also mean <vocabulary>to omit</vocabulary> something for the sake of simplicity.
5255.reading_mnemonic: The reading is, strangely, the same as the reading you learned with the kanji. <reading>りゃく</reading>す.

examples.en: In Japanese conversation, it is the default to omit grammatical subjects except when necessary.
examples.ja: 日本語の会話では、必要なとき以外は文法上の主語を省略するのがデフォルトです。

examples.en: This is an important point, so don't omit anything and write everything down.
examples.ja: ここは大切なポイントだから省略しないで全部書くように。

examples.en: It says "Ma" at the expiry date, but I wonder if this is an abbreviation of "March" or "May".
examples.ja: 賞味期限の所に「Ma」って書いてあるんだけど、「March」の省略かな、それとも「May」の省略かな？

examples.en: I have to omit the details for now due to time constraints, but I’ll explain it to you later.
examples.ja: 時間の都合上、今は詳細については省略せざるを得ませんが、また後ほどご説明させて頂きます。

5256.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Conserve</kanji> those letters with <kanji>abbreviation</kanji> and now you're <vocabulary>omitting</vocabulary> all the extra fluff! 

省略 is a relatively formal word used when you are intentionally <vocabulary>leaving out</vocabulary> something for the sake of brevity or simplicity, like an unneeded explanation or a long-winded greeting. It can also sometimes refer to the <vocabulary>abbreviation</vocabulary> of a word or phrase.
5256.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: "Kōkō" is an abbreviation of "kōtōgakkō (high school)."
examples.ja: 「高校」は「高等学校」の略語です。

examples.en: Takeshita-san loves to speak using creative abbreviations.
examples.ja: 竹下さんはクリエイティブな略語を使って話すのが大好きです。

examples.en: I don't understand the abbreviations that young people use recently. They are too difficult.
examples.ja: 最近の若者が使う略語は、難しすぎてよく分かりません。

examples.en: Can I borrow your dictionary of acronyms and abbreviations?
examples.ja: 略語辞典を貸してもらえませんか？

5257.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'll draw a rough map from your house to mine and email it to you.
examples.ja: あなたの家からうちまでの略図をかいて、メールでお送りします

examples.en: Could you show me the rough diagram you made?
examples.ja: あなたが作った略図をちょっと見せてもらえませんか？

examples.en: I feel uneasy with just the rough map, so I'll use GPS as well, just in case.
examples.ja: 略図だけでは不安なので、念のためGPSも使います。

5258.meaning_mnemonic:
An <kanji>abbreviation</kanji> version of a <kanji>diagram</kanji> doesn't include all the details. It's more like a <vocabulary>rough diagram</vocabulary> that shows only the essentials.

While 略図 can be used for any simplified diagram, it most commonly refers to a <vocabulary>rough map</vocabulary> that gives a basic overview of an area.
5258.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Just a rough summary is fine, so can you tell me what the meeting was about?
examples.ja: 大略でいいので、会議の内容を教えてくれませんか？

examples.en: Can you explain the outline of the incident first?
examples.ja: まずは事件の大略を説明してくれないか？

examples.en: I understood the gist of his story, but I'm still unclear on the details.
examples.ja: 彼の話の大略は理解できたけど、細かい部分はまだよく分かりません。

examples.en: The broad outline of this project has been decided, so let's work out the details next.
examples.ja: この企画の大略は決まったので、次は詳細を詰めていきましょう。

5259.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>abbreviation</kanji> is where you take everything and abbreviate it down to show the big picture. This abbreviation is the <vocabulary>broad outline</vocabulary> of something bigger.

大略 is a relatively formal word commonly found in writing. It generally refers to a broader, rougher <vocabulary>outline</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>overview</vocabulary> rather than a detailed summary.
5259.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: There's no pain in particular.
examples.ja: 特に痛みはありません。

examples.en: I hope that my kid will grow up to become an adult who understands others’ pain.
examples.ja: 子供には人の痛みが分かるような大人に育ってほしいです。

examples.en: I have a hard spot and pain in my breast. Should I have it examined for breast cancer?
examples.ja: 胸にしこりみたいなものと痛みがあるんだけど、乳がん検査した方がいいかな？

examples.en: Apparently, my aunt had a sharp pain in her chest while pooping and called 119.
examples.ja: 俺の伯母さん、クソしてる時に胸にするどい痛みが走って、119に電話したんだって。

5260.meaning_mnemonic: 痛い is "painful." This is the noun version, it is <vocabulary>a pain</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>pain</vocabulary>.
5260.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 痛い. No pain here.

examples.en: I had a bad headache, so I took a painkiller.
examples.ja: 頭痛がひどいので、痛み止めを飲みました。

examples.en: The painkiller is starting to take effect, and I feel a bit better.
examples.ja: 痛み止めが効いてきて、少し楽になりました。

examples.en: Could you pick up some painkillers for me from the pharmacy?
examples.ja: 薬局で痛み止めを買ってきてもらえませんか？

examples.en: He took a painkiller and kept plowing the field.
examples.ja: 彼は痛み止めを飲んで、また畑を耕し始めた。

5261.meaning_mnemonic: 痛み is "pain." 止める is "to stop." What stops pain if you use it? How about a <vocabulary>painkiller</vocabulary>.
5261.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 痛み and 止める put together into one word. Not too painful, right? Just remember the rendaku on the ど.

examples.en: The pumps I bought over the weekend don't fit properly, and my heels hurt.
examples.ja: 週末に買った靴が合わなくて、かかとが痛むんです。

examples.en: Lately, my mother has often been complaining about her knees hurting.
examples.ja: 母は最近よくヒザが痛むと言っていました。

examples.en: It was heartbreaking to see the bears, emaciated and searching for food.
examples.ja: やせ細ってエサを探し回るクマの姿を見て、胸が痛みました。

examples.en: I've had a bad toothache since last night, so could you check that for me please?
examples.ja: 昨日の夜から歯が酷く痛むんですが、診てもらえますか。

5262.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how <ja>痛い</ja> is "painful"? This is the verb version of that, so it means <vocabulary>to ache</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to hurt</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to be in pain</vocabulary>.

痛む is an intransitive verb that suggests an ongoing sensation of pain or aching. It's a little more descriptive than 痛い, so you might see it used in writing or to describe a more persistent or recurring condition. It's also often used figuratively, especially in expressions like 心が痛む (my heart aches).
5262.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi reading, which you learned already!

examples.en: These days, I can't sleep well due to stress.
examples.ja: 最近ストレスでよく眠れないんです。

examples.en: She likes to sleep with the lights on.
examples.ja: 彼女は電気をつけながら眠るのが好きです。

examples.en: Of course, I try to sleep, but it's pretty hard to fall asleep on a plane, don't you think?
examples.ja: もちろん、眠ろうと努力はするけど、飛行機の中ってなかなか眠れないじゃないですか？

examples.en: "Did you sleep well?" "Yeah, I crashed."
examples.ja: 「ぐっすり眠れた？」「ああ。爆睡したよ。」

5263.meaning_mnemonic: 眠い is "sleepy." The verb version of this is to sleep, or to fall asleep. yawn While 寝る can mean lying down or going to bed (not just sleeping), 眠る only refers to falling asleep or being in a state of sleep.
5263.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 眠い.

examples.en: Sleeping potions are often featured in fairy tales to make people fall asleep.
examples.ja: 童話には、眠り薬を使って人を眠らせる話がよく出てきます。

examples.en: Oh no! I lost the bottle with the sleeping pills!
examples.ja: 大変！眠り薬が入ったビンを無くしてしまったわ！

examples.en: The man grinned and pulled out the sleeping drugs from his pocket.
examples.ja: 男はニヤリと笑って、ふところから眠り薬を取り出しました。

5264.meaning_mnemonic:
Some kind of <kanji>sleep</kanji>ing <kanji>medicine</kanji>? That's a <vocabulary>sleeping potion</vocabulary>!

眠り薬 is often found in storytelling contexts to refer to some kind of sleep-inducing concoction. But it can also be used as a less medical and more colloquial term for actual sleeping medication.
5264.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is 眠い plus 薬 put together in one ... zz zzzzzZZZzz
Just remember that くすり turns into ぐすり here because of rendaku.

examples.en: I can't sleep without sleeping pills.
examples.ja: 睡眠薬が無いと眠れないんです。

examples.en: I couldn't sleep last night, so I took a sleeping pill.
examples.ja: 昨夜、眠れなかったので、睡眠薬を飲みました。

examples.en: Sleeping pills can be dangerous if you don't stick to the prescribed amount.
examples.ja: 睡眠薬は決められた量を守って飲まないと危険ですよ。

examples.en: I'm so uncoordinated right now because of the sleeping pill I took a little bit ago.
examples.ja: さっき飲んだ睡眠薬のせいで、手足が思うように動かないんだけど。

5265.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Drowsy</kanji> <kanji>sleep</kanji> <kanji>medicine</kanji> sounds a little goofy, but it's exactly what you'd expect it to be: <vocabulary>sleeping pills</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>sleeping medication</vocabulary>.
5265.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It snows, but it doesn’t usually accumulate much.
examples.ja: 雪はふるんですが、あまり積もることはないです。

examples.en: I plan to clean up all the dust that piled up throughout the year at the end of the year.
examples.ja: 年末に積もりに積もったホコリを全部そうじするつもりです。

examples.en: They say "little by little, dust becomes a mountain," so I'll keep working hard every day!
examples.ja: 「ちりも積もれば山となる」って言うし、毎日コツコツ頑張るよ！

examples.en: The frustration that had built up over the years suddenly overflowed all at once.
examples.ja: 長年積もりに積もった不満が、一気にあふれ出しちゃったんです。

5266.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>accumulate</kanji> and the verb version is <vocabulary>to accumulate</vocabulary>.

積もる is used to describe when something continuously collects or piles up over time, like snow on the ground or dust in a room. It can also be used in a more emotional way, like when feelings or thoughts quietly build up inside someone.
5266.reading_mnemonic: If something accumulates, you can start with one, but you need at least <reading>two</reading> (つ) things to say it has accumulated. If you don't, then there's nothing accumulating at all.

examples.en: Are the methods for calculating the area of a rectangle and a square the same?
examples.ja: 長方形と正方形の面積を求める方法は同じですか。

examples.en: How large of an area is Koichi's yard?
examples.ja: コウイチの家の庭の面積はどれくらいですか？

examples.en: The area of his forehead is 100 square meters.
examples.ja: 彼のおでこの面積は100平方メートルある。

5267.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>surface</kanji> that <kanji>accumulate</kanji>s into one area is a particular <vocabulary>area</vocabulary>. This has to do with math. When you add all the surfaces together by accumulating them into one calculation, you get yourself the area!
5267.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Find the volume of this cube.
examples.ja: この立方体の体積を求めなさい。

examples.en: The volume of water can change depending on the temperature.
examples.ja: 水の体積は温度によって変わることがあります。

examples.en: The volume of a rectangular prism can be calculated as "length × width × height," and the volume of a cube can be calculated as "side × side × side."
examples.ja: 直方体の体積は、「たて×横×高さ」、立方体の体積は、「１辺×１辺×１辺」で計算できます。

examples.en: My dad told me to measure the volume of our garage, but I don't know why. It seems kind of weird to me.
examples.ja: 父さんにガレージの体積を測るように言われたんだけど、理由は知らないよ。何か変だよね。

5268.meaning_mnemonic: See how much liquid this <kanji>body</kanji> can <kanji>accumulate</kanji> in order to calculate its <vocabulary>volume</vocabulary>. It can be the body of a cup, the body of a bucket, or the body of a body. Whatever it is, the body accumulation represents its volume. (You know, how much space it takes up. Wasn't math class fun?)
5268.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'll look it up on the Internet later.
examples.ja: 後でネットで検索してみるよ。

examples.en: The search engine I use most often is Google.
examples.ja: 私がよく利用する検索エンジンはグーグルです。

examples.en: This book has an index for easy reference.
examples.ja: この本には検索しやすいように索引がついている。

examples.en: I have so many cookbooks, but I end up searching on Cookpad.
examples.ja: こんなにたくさんの料理本を持っているのに、結局クックパッドで検索しちゃうんですよね。

5269.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>examine</kanji> then <kanji>search</kanji>. These are the steps you take in order to perform a <vocabulary>lookup</vocabulary> of some kind. Or, as the case may be in modern times, do an <vocabulary>internet search</vocabulary>.

検索 originally referred to looking up information in books or using indexes and reference cards, like in a library. These days it's almost always used for digital and online searches.
5269.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I don't know how to look at the index.
examples.ja: 索引の見方が分かりません。

examples.en: Wouldn't it be faster to look it up in the index?
examples.ja: 索引を引いた方が速いんじゃない？

examples.en: All of the terms in the index are listed in alphabetical order.
examples.ja: 索引にはすべての用語がアルファベット順に並んでいます。

examples.en: We should make an English index too.
examples.ja: 英語索引も付けた方がいいんじゃないかな。

5270.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>search</kanji> then <kanji>pull</kanji> items from the <vocabulary>index</vocabulary> — you know, that list of keywords in alphabetical order at the end of a nonfiction book. Or in 五十音順 order, if you're fancy enough to be reading Japanese!
5270.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just think of the first part of the word <reading>in</reading>dex (いん). Where do you search? In the index.

examples.en: My dad had to undergo emergency surgery.
examples.ja: 父は緊急手術を受けることになりました。

examples.en: An urgent matter came up, so I have to leave immediately.
examples.ja: 緊急の用事ができたので、すぐに帰らなければならなくなってしまいました。

examples.en: We also need you to provide a phone number for an emergency contact who is not a family member.
examples.ja: 緊急連絡先として、家族以外の方の電話番号も書いていただく必要があります。

examples.en: Three seconds after receiving an emergency earthquake report on my cellphone, the earthquake occurred.
examples.ja: 緊急地震速報を携帯で受信した三秒後に、地震が起きました。

5271.meaning_mnemonic: Things are <kanji>tense</kanji> and we have to <kanji>hurry</kanji>! This is quite the <vocabulary>urgent</vocabulary> <vocabulary>emergency</vocabulary>!
5271.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: When is the deadline?
examples.ja: 締切はいつですか？

examples.en: The application deadline is in three days.
examples.ja: 申込の締切日は三日後です。

examples.en: At this rate, I might not make the deadline.
examples.ja: このままじゃ締切に間に合わないかもしれない。

examples.en: Did you have any luck with putting the deadline off till tomorrow?
examples.ja: うまく締切を明日まで延ばせたの？

5272.meaning_mnemonic:
Things 締める (tighten), and eventually 切る (cut off), meaning you’ve reached the <vocabulary>deadline</vocabulary>! You can associate this with the feeling of your chest tightening once you approach the <vocabulary>due date</vocabulary> for something.

Note that you'll often encounter this written with okurigana like 締め切り as well. You might even see it with a simplified version of the 締 kanji written 〆切, which is relatively common in handwriting!
5272.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this is the stem form of both verbs, so 締め (しめ) and 切り (きり), put together!

examples.en: This seat belt tightens on its own.
examples.ja: このシートベルトは自動的に締まってくれます。

examples.en: Mr Onishi's body is well toned isn't it!
examples.ja: 大西さんの体はよく締まっていますね〜。

examples.en: This is my first managerial position and I’m very tense.
examples.ja: 初めての管理職ということで、身の引き締まる思いをしています。

5273.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>tighten</kanji>, so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to tighten</vocabulary>.
5273.reading_mnemonic:
What can you do if you want something <vocabulary>to tighten</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to become tight</vocabulary>? You need to hug your <reading>shee</reading>p (し) really close until...

The sheep tightens into a tiny little ball. Cute!

examples.en: The minister's statement was widely covered in the news.
examples.ja: 大臣の発言がニュースで大きく取り上げられました。

examples.en: The Finance Minister announced next year's budget plan.
examples.ja: 財務大臣が来年度の予算案を発表しました。

examples.en: With all due respect, Minister, I believe you should listen more carefully to the voices of the people.
examples.ja: お言葉ですが、大臣は、国民の声をもっとしっかりと聞くべきだと思います。

examples.en: She was fired because she forgot to hand out the documents to the cabinet members before the meeting.
examples.ja: 彼女は大臣たちに会議の前に資料を配るのを忘れてしまったために、首になっちゃったんだよ。

5274.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>servant</kanji> is a really important servant — you know, one who serves a king or some other political leader. What do we call a big, highfalutin servant who prances around doing jobs for the leader? A <vocabulary>minister</vocabulary>.

大臣 refers to high-ranking government officials who oversee ministries or departments, and it can be translated in different ways depending on the country and its political system, such as <vocabulary>cabinet minister</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>state minister</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>secretary of state</vocabulary>.
5274.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Where did you learn aerial navigation?
examples.ja: どこで空中航法を学んだんですか。

examples.en: My grandmother can do navigational calculations for airships.
examples.ja: 私のおばあちゃんは、飛行船の航法計算ができるんです。

examples.en: I heard that the navigator used to sit in the back of this aircraft to navigate.
examples.ja: この機体の後ろのところに航法士が乗ってナビしてたんだって。

examples.en: Thanks to my knowledge of celestial navigation, I was able to arrive at the port without getting lost.
examples.ja: 天則航法を学んでおいたおかげで迷わずに港に着くことができました。

5275.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>navigation</kanji> <kanji>method</kanji>s are the methods used for <vocabulary>navigation</vocabulary>.

航法 is a technical term for navigation, specifically referring to the techniques and methods used to guide a ship, aircraft, or spacecraft from one place to another.
5275.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I studied aerospace engineering in the Department of Aerospace Engineering at Japan Aviation University.
examples.ja: 私は日本航空大学の航空工学科で、航空工学について学びました。

examples.en: The number of flight routes from America to Haneda Airport increased and has made travel more convenient.
examples.ja: アメリカから羽田空港の航空路線が増えてより便利になりました。

examples.en: I always use this app to search for cheap airline tickets.
examples.ja: 私はいつもこのアプリを使って格安航空券をさがしています。

examples.en: That airline company is adding a new route in April.
examples.ja: あの航空会社は四月に新路線を増やす予定だ。

5276.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Navigation</kanji> in the <kanji>sky</kanji> is <vocabulary>aviation</vocabulary>. Vroom vroom, sky flying!

On its own 航空 refers to aviation, but you'll usually see it in compound words like 航空機 (aircraft) and 航空会社 (airline company).
5276.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This ship is on a direct voyage to Kobe Port.
examples.ja: この船は神戸港に直航します。

examples.en: My children are still small, so I would like to take a direct flight if possible.
examples.ja: 子供がまだ小さいのでできれば直航の飛行機で行きたいと思っています。

examples.en: This flight doesn't go directly from Portland to Tokyo; it makes a stop in Alaska along the way.
examples.ja: この便はポートランドから東京まで直航せず、途中でアラスカに寄港します。

5277.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 直行 is "nonstop"? Well, with 直航 it's the same thing, but it's only used for flights and boat trips, making this a <vocabulary>nonstop flight</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>direct voyage</vocabulary>.
5277.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This shopping street has a lot of small traditional shops.
examples.ja: この商店街には、昔ながらの小さなお店がたくさんあります。

examples.en: This shopping street is popular with tourists and is always bustling.
examples.ja: この商店街は観光客にも人気で、いつもにぎわっています。

examples.en: Traditional shopping streets are rapidly disappearing due to the opening of large stores.
examples.ja: 大型店の出店で、昔ながらの商店街がどんどん姿を消しています。

examples.en: Could you grab about three croquettes from the butcher shop in the shopping street by the station?
examples.ja: ちょっと駅前の商店街のお肉屋さんでコロッケを３個ほど買ってきてくれない？

5278.meaning_mnemonic:
If there are <kanji>merchandise</kanji> <kanji>shop</kanji>s filling the <kanji>streets</kanji>, then you must have wandered into a <vocabulary>shopping district</vocabulary>. Hope you remembered to bring your wallet!

商店街 generally refers to a pedestrian-friendly street or area with lots of local shops and small businesses. Many 商店街 are covered with a roof, in which case they become <vocabulary>shopping arcade</vocabulary>s.
5278.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This main road with a row of trees is my relaxation spot.
examples.ja: この並木街道は私のいこいの場です。

examples.en: If you take this highway straight for a while, you will eventually arrive at Kyoto.
examples.ja: この街道をずっとまっすぐ行くと、そのうち京都に着きますよ。

examples.en: I'm traveling by bike along the highways, visiting various places across Japan.
examples.ja: 僕は街道を自転車で旅して、日本各地を回っています。

examples.en: Tokai-do Road, Nakasen-do Road, Nikko-kaido Road, Koshu-kaido Road, and Oshu-kaido Road are called Gokaido, which were the five principal routes used during the Edo period.
examples.ja: 東海道、中山道、日光街道、甲州街道、奥州街道は、五街道と呼ばれ、江戸時代の五大陸上交通路であった。

5279.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>street</kanji> <kanji>road</kanji> is as wide as a street and a road combined together. So cool! So wide! It must be a <vocabulary>main road</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>highroad</vocabulary>!

Keep in mind 街道 isn't a generic term for main roads. It usually refers to important routes that connect different regions of Japan, especially those from the Edo period, like 日光街道 (Nikkōkaidō) and 中山道 (Nakasendō). But it can also refer to main roads with historical significance in other countries, like アッピア街道 (the Appian Way) in Italy or オックスフォード街道 (Oxford Street) in the UK.
5279.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. One thing to note though:

This word uses the かい reading for 街 (not がい). And even when 街道 is a suffix, it never gets rendaku'd! Remember this by imagining every <vocabulary>main road</vocabulary> being full of <reading>kay</reading>aks (かい) for some reason. Just a traffic jam of kayaks up and down the 街道.

examples.en: When the doctor examined me, I was told it was just a cold.
examples.ja: 医者に診てもらったら、ただのカゼだと言われました。

examples.en: My child got injured, so I went to get them checked out right away.
examples.ja: 子供がケガをしたので、すぐに診てもらいに行きました。

examples.en: If these symptoms persist, you should get diagnosed by a doctor soon.
examples.ja: この症状が続くなら、早めにお医者さんに診てもらったほうがいいよ。

examples.en: I want a doctor to examine my baby to see if she's growing well.
examples.ja: 赤ちゃんがちゃんと育っているのか、お医者さんに診てもらいたいんです。

5280.meaning_mnemonic: In order to <kanji>diagnose</kanji> a patient, you must first go <vocabulary>to examine a patient</vocabulary>. When you examine them you know what's wrong with them and then you can diagnose them, which is why this verb is <vocabulary>to examine</vocabulary>.
5280.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 見る, which you have to do when you are examining a patient. So, you look and see all you can about the patient while you examine them, making this reading <reading>み</reading>る as well.

examples.en: I'm going to have a medical examination at the hospital today.
examples.ja: 今日は病院で診察を受けます。

examples.en: I asked the doctor various questions during the examination.
examples.ja: 診察中に、医者に色々と質問しました。

examples.en: I wonder how much the doctor's visit will cost.
examples.ja: 診察代、いくらぐらいになるかな？

examples.en: The doctor has a jam-packed medical exam schedule.
examples.ja: 先生は診察の予定がみっちり詰まっています。

5281.meaning_mnemonic:
I will <kanji>diagnose</kanji> you by making an informed <kanji>guess</kanji> during this <vocabulary>medical exam</vocabulary>. 

診察 is what a doctor does when they take a look at you — a <vocabulary>medical examination</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>medical consultation</vocabulary>. Keep in mind this doesn't refer to specific medical tests you might undergo to help the doctor diagnose you. (For those, you'd use 検査.)
5281.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I forcefully stuffed a lot of clothes into the suitcase.
examples.ja: たくさんの服をスーツケースに無理やり詰めました。

examples.en: If you overpack it, the zipper won't close.
examples.ja: あんまり詰めすぎると、ファスナーが閉まらなくなるよ。

examples.en: Excuse me, could you move a bit closer together to make some space for me?
examples.ja: すいません、もう少し詰めてもらえませんか？

examples.en: Can you put some rice in my bento box for me?
examples.ja: お弁当にご飯を詰めといてくれない？

5282.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>stuffed</kanji>, this word means <vocabulary>to stuff in</vocabulary>, as in you're doing the stuffing. You know this because you're a <reading>mail</reading> (める) carrier, and you always have to stuff mail into people's packed mailboxes. Why don't these people check their mail more? It’s hard work trying to cram in all this junk mail!

詰める refers to tightly fitting something into an available space, like cramming clothes into a suitcase, putting jam into a jar, or even scooting over to make room, as you're squeezing yourself into a narrower space.
5282.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned that reading with the kanji, so you should have no troubles here.

examples.en: When I go outside, my allergies stuff up my nose, but when I'm at home, I feel stuffy.
examples.ja: 外に出るとアレルギーで鼻が詰まるけど、家にいると息が詰まるんだよね。

examples.en: Today is packed with things to do, so I'm really busy.
examples.ja: 今日はやることが詰まっていて、とても忙しい。

examples.en: Even though you didn't use toilet paper, the toilet still got clogged. Just how big was the turd you took?!
examples.ja: トイレットペーパーを使ってないのにトイレが詰まるって、どれだけでかいウンコしたんだよ？！

examples.en: I got a fish bone stuck in my throat.
examples.ja: 魚の骨が喉に詰まっちゃった。

5283.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>stuffed</kanji>. The vocab word is <vocabulary>to be stuffed</vocabulary>, as in something is stuffed and you're not doing the stuffing. You know this because when it comes to まる the cat, he stuffs himself into boxes on his own, so you don't have to stuff him into boxes for him. It just happens, and you can watch and be entertained (obviously you need to go watch some Maru videos if you haven't on YouTube, just saying).
5283.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the reading you learned with the kanji!

examples.en: Even though Ms. Matsumoto knows that I am on a diet, she always tempts me to go to a cake shop together.
examples.ja: ダイエットしてるって知ってるのに松本さんはいつもケーキ屋さんに行こうと誘惑してくる。

examples.en: The snake tempted Eve to eat the fruit from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
examples.ja: ヘビはイブを善悪の知識の木の実を食べるように誘惑してしまったのだ。

examples.en: She is a devil who seduces many men.
examples.ja: 彼女はたくさんの男を誘惑する悪魔だ。

5284.meaning_mnemonic: If 誘惑 is seduction or temptation, then the verb version would be <vocabulary>to seduce</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to tempt</vocabulary>.
5284.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Will help to know the word 誘惑 first, though.

examples.en: I desperately needed money, so I borrowed some from a loan shark, but then they demanded an exorbitant sum from me and my situation got even worse.
examples.ja: お金に困ってヤミ金から借りたら、法外な金額が請求されて余計困りました。

examples.en: I'd like to request a cancellation of this bill because I believe the amount on it is incorrect.
examples.ja: 請求書の金額が間違っていると思うので、請求の取り消しをお願いしたいです。

examples.en: I'm told that I can claim a reimbursement later for the parcel's shipping cost.
examples.ja: 荷物の送料は後で請求可能だと言われています。

5285.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>request</kanji> then you <kanji>request</kanji> again… Yep, this sounds like a <vocabulary>request</vocabulary to me.

請求 isn't just any old casual request — it's used when formally requesting something from another party. It often involves payment requests (like a <vocabulary>charge</vocabulary>), but can also refer to asking for things like application forms or informational materials. It can even refer to the kind of <vocabulary>claim</vocabulary> you file in court.
5285.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Please click this petition link and sign it.
examples.ja: こちらの請願のリンクをクリックして署名してください。

examples.en: The person who is petitioning has to show up in person.
examples.ja: 請願するご本人に来ていただかないといけないんですよ。

examples.en: If you wouldn't mind, would you please sign this petition?
examples.ja: もしご迷惑でなければ請願書に署名して頂けませんでしょうか。

5286.meaning_mnemonic: I <kanji>request</kanji> and then I <kanji>request</kanji> again. So many requests, but nobody will listen to me. My last hope is to get a bunch of people who have the same ideas together and make a <vocabulary>petition</vocabulary>.
5286.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Because we have a lack of hands in our project, we have requested some help.
examples.ja: プロジェクトの人手が足りないので応援を要請しました。

examples.en: Unfortunately, Manager Tamura's request for additional workers was seemingly not accepted.
examples.ja: 残念ながら、田村マネージャーの追加人員要請は受理されなかったようです。

examples.en: The labor unions demanded a wage increase.
examples.ja: 労働組合は賃上げを要請した。

5287.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>need</kanji> something so you <kanji>request</kanji> it. But, since it's such a strong need, it's not really a request, it's more of a <vocabulary>demand</vocabulary>.
5287.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Undertaking this project is risky, but I want to give this challenge a try.
examples.ja: この案件を請けるのはリスクが高いですが、チャレンジしてみたいです。

examples.en: She often willingly takes on last-minute requests, which is really helpful.
examples.ja: 彼女は急な注文でも快く請けてくれることが多いので、本当に助かっています。

examples.en: I only took this project so that you could save face.
examples.ja: お前の顔を立てるためだけにこのプロジェクトを請けたんだからな。

examples.en: When taking on a job, I first consider whether it's something the employees will be happy to do. If you don't put profits as a secondary concern, you won't be able to deliver quality work.
examples.ja: 仕事を請けるときは、社員が喜んで受ける仕事かを考えて、請けるか決めるんです。売り上げは二の次にしないと、いい仕事はできませんからね。

5288.meaning_mnemonic:
Someone <kanji>request</kanji>s something, and you're the one <vocabulary>to take on</vocabulary> their request. Wow, how nice of you <vocabulary>to accept</vocabulary> that request!

請ける is a formal word often used in business contexts to describe someone willingly accepting a job, task, or request. For example, you might use 請ける when taking on a new project or accepting customer orders.
5288.reading_mnemonic: What's another word for "to accept" or "to receive"? How about 受ける? They share a reading!

examples.en: This isn't mine, it's a rental bike.
examples.ja: これは私のじゃなくて、貸し自転車なんです。

examples.en: I’m living in a rental warehouse now.
examples.ja: 今は貸し倉庫で寝泊まりしているんです。

examples.en: We are planning to spend the coming holidays at a rental cottage.
examples.ja: 今度の休暇は貸し別荘で過ごす予定です。

5289.meaning_mnemonic: To lend or to rent is 貸す. This is the noun version of that, used as a prefix. It is something that has been rented, a "<vocabulary>rental</vocabulary> ____," like a 貸しビル (rental office building) or 貸しボート (rental boat).
5289.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 貸す.

examples.en: I’m good at getting lost.
examples.ja: 私は道に迷うのが得意です。

examples.en: It was my first time in the area, so I got lost.
examples.ja: 初めての場所だったので、道に迷ってしまいました。

examples.en: I was looking at the map, but I still ended up getting lost.
examples.ja: 地図を見てたのに、結局道に迷ってしまった。

examples.en: I got lost, but a kind person helped me, and I safely arrived at my destination.
examples.ja: 道に迷ったけど、親切な人に助けてもらって無事に目的地に着きました。

5290.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 迷う? It means "to get lost." If you get lost on a <kanji>road</kanji>, you are still lost, wandering around looking for the correct turn. This word means <vocabulary>to be lost</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to get lost</vocabulary>.
5290.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the words 道 and 迷う.

examples.en: All of the cabinet ministers are opposed.
examples.ja: 閣僚たちは、みんな反対しています。

examples.en: The cabinet meeting is held once a month.
examples.ja: 閣僚会議は月1回ですよ。

examples.en: An internal whistleblower revealed the communication between the cabinet ministers regarding this issue.
examples.ja: 内部告発者により、この件に関する閣僚間のやりとりが明るみに出ました。

5291.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>cabinet</kanji> <kanji>colleague</kanji>s are the <vocabulary>cabinet ministers</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>cabinet secretaries</vocabulary>. They're the people in the Cabinet who are all colleagues with each other, making them <vocabulary>cabinet members</vocabulary>. Depending on the country, they're also called ministers or secretaries.

閣僚 is a formal term that refers to the collective group of high-ranking officials in a cabinet, but it can sometimes refer to an individual cabinet member as well.
5291.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This was already decided in the cabinet meeting.
examples.ja: これはもう閣議決定されたことです。

examples.en: Did you watch the Digital Minister's press conference after yesterday's cabinet meeting?
examples.ja: 昨日のデジタル相の閣議後の会見、見ましたか？

examples.en: What did we discuss at the cabinet meeting held earlier today? I forgot.
examples.ja: さっきの閣議では何が議題だったんだっけ？忘れちゃった。

examples.en: Most of the cabinet members cast an opposing vote at this cabinet meeting.
examples.ja: 今回の閣議では閣僚のほぼ全員が反対に回った。

5292.meaning_mnemonic: When <kanji>the cabinet</kanji> meets for <kanji>deliberation</kanji> they are having a <vocabulary>cabinet meeting</vocabulary>. So governmenty.
5292.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: His actions were truly heroic.
examples.ja: 彼の行動はまさに英雄的だった。

examples.en: I’m pissed off at that guy who only has luck and no real ability, but pretends as if he were a hero.
examples.ja: あいつは運だけで実力もないくせに英雄気取りで本当にムカつく。

examples.en: That soccer player instantly started being treated like a hero after scoring that last goal in the game, huh?
examples.ja: あのサッカー選手、あの試合の最後のゴールで一気に英雄あつかいされるようになったね。

5293.meaning_mnemonic:
You've learned 英 means "England," but it can also mean <kanji>excel</kanji>. So what kind of person excels at being <kanji>brave</kanji>? A <vocabulary>hero</vocabulary>!

英雄 is a relatively formal word often used to describe historical or legendary heroes, like William Wallace or King Arthur. In more casual contexts, like when talking about superheroes or referring to your dad as your hero, ヒーロー is more common.
5293.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I visited South Korea last year.
examples.ja: 私は去年、韓国を訪れました。

examples.en: I wonder if this Korean drama series will be rebroadcasted.
examples.ja: この韓国ドラマ、再放送されるのかな。

examples.en: In South Korea, there are many Koreans who learn Japanese.
examples.ja: 韓国には日本語を学ぶ韓国人がたくさんいます。

5294.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>Korea</kanji> <kanji>Country</kanji> is <vocabulary>Korea</vocabulary>, of course... well, <vocabulary>South Korea</vocabulary> that is.
5294.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This custom is frequently seen in both Japan and Korea.
examples.ja: この風習は日韓両国でよく見られます。

examples.en: Learning about the history between Japan and Korea is very important.
examples.ja: 日韓の歴史について学ぶことは、とても重要です。

examples.en: Japan-Korea soccer matches always turn into intense battles.
examples.ja: 日韓のサッカー試合はいつも熱い戦いになります。

examples.en: In 1965, The Japan-Republic of Korea Basic Relations Treaty became in effect.
examples.ja: 1965年に日韓基本条約が締結されました。

5295.meaning_mnemonic:
Take the 日 from 日本 (Japan) and the 韓 from 韓国 (Korea), and stick 'em together to get an abbreviation for <vocabulary>Japan and South Korea</vocabulary>.

日韓 is a bit formal, so you'll usually see it in newspapers or reports referring to Japan and South Korea together. Think international relations and soccer matches.
5295.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It's hard to describe her charm in just one word.
examples.ja: 彼女の魅力を一言で表すのは難しい。

examples.en: The appeal of this restaurant lies in its affordability and generous portions. The taste is also quite good.
examples.ja: このレストランは安さと量が魅力です。味もなかなかですよ。

examples.en: The appeal of city life is definitely its convenience and exciting lifestyle.
examples.ja: 都会の魅力といえば、やはり便利さと刺激的な生活ですね。

examples.en: I became obsessed with the charm of golf.
examples.ja: 私はゴルフの魅力に取り憑かれてしまいました。

5296.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Why did it take you so long to line up the bowling pins?
examples.ja: ボーリングのピンを並べるのにどうしてそんなに時間がかかったんですか。

examples.en: Many luxury wine bottles are lined up at Mr. Hoshino's house.
examples.ja: 星野さんの家にはたくさんの高級ワインボトルが並べられている。

examples.en: We brainstormed ideas, wrote them on post-its, and laid them out on a whiteboard.
examples.ja: ブレインストーミングで出たアイディアを、ポストイットに書いてホワイトボードに並べました。

examples.en: Please set the plates on the table.
examples.ja: お皿をテーブルに並べてください。

5297.meaning_mnemonic: 並ぶ is when something is lining up. 並べる is when you're lining something up. In other words, 並べる is transitive. It means <vocabulary>to line something up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to put something in order</vocabulary>. You know this because when it comes to <reading>bear</reading>s (べる), you have to line them up yourself, because they won't be doing it for you, that's for sure.
5297.reading_mnemonic: The reading of the kanji is same as for 並ぶ, so if you know that you can figure out the reading for this one as well.

examples.en: Greenery is scarce in this town.
examples.ja: この町は緑が乏しい。

examples.en: I don't know if I can handle this job with my lack of experience in company management.…
examples.ja: 会社経営の経験に乏しい私に務まるかどうか...。

examples.en: Efficiency is key for survival in resource-limited companies.
examples.ja: リソースが乏しい企業では、効率化が生き残りのカギです。

examples.en: Not only are my Japanese abilities lacking, but my personal abilities are too.
examples.ja: 日本語能力だけじゃなく、対人能力も乏しいんです。

5298.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>scarce</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>scarce</vocabulary>.
5298.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: When things are <vocabulary>scarce</vocabulary>, you have <reading>to bo</reading>at (とぼ) all the way across the lake to find any resources or food, as your side of the lake is picked dry.

examples.en: How can I know if I’m deficient in Vitamin D?
examples.ja: ビタミンDが欠乏しているかどうかはどうすれば分かりますか。

examples.en: Because I don't like veggies or fruits, I became vitamin deficient.
examples.ja: 野さいもフルーツも嫌いなので、ビタミン欠乏症になってしまった。

examples.en: She has a congenital lack of melanin, commonly known as "albinism."
examples.ja: 彼女は先天的にメラニンが欠乏している、いわゆる「アルビノ」なんだよ。

examples.en: When I went to the doctor, I was diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia.
examples.ja: お医者さんに行ったら、鉄欠乏性貧血って診断されました。

5299.meaning_mnemonic: We are <kanji>lack</kanji>ing and things are <kanji>scarce</kanji>. We have a <vocabulary>lack</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>scarcity</vocabulary> of resources.
5299.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I forgot to chill the juice, so I'll add ice.
examples.ja: ジュースを冷やすのを忘れたので、氷を入れますね。

examples.en: The beer is chilled, so why don't you have some of that?
examples.ja: ビールを冷やしてあるからそれを飲んだら？

examples.en: Cool your head and think well about what you have done.
examples.ja: 自分が何をしたのか頭を冷やしてよく考えなさい。

examples.en: My finger got caught in the door and I'm chilling it with ice now.
examples.ja: 指をドアで挟んじゃって、今氷で冷やしてるの。

5300.meaning_mnemonic: 冷たい is "cold." This is the verb version, so you're making something cold. This word is <vocabulary>to chill something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to cool something</vocabulary>.
5300.reading_mnemonic: <vocabulary>To chill something</vocabulary>, you need to apply cold, not <reading>hea</reading>t (ひ).

examples.en: Thoughts on marriage vary from person to person.
examples.ja: 結婚についての考え方は、人によってさまざまです。

examples.en: Not everybody wants to have a kid right after they get married, right?
examples.ja: 結婚したからって、みんながすぐに子供を作りたい訳じゃないでしょう。

examples.en: My agency tells me that I should keep my marriage hidden.
examples.ja: 事務所から、結婚のことは隠すように言われてるんです。

examples.en: "Shark, how did you know that I got married to Fugu?" "You know. I just heard it through the grapevine."
examples.ja: 「シャーク、私がフグと結婚したってどうして分かったの？」 「ただ人づてに聞いただけさ。」

5301.meaning_mnemonic: Let's <kanji>bind</kanji> this <kanji>marriage</kanji> up with a <vocabulary>marriage</vocabulary>. No better way to make a marriage happen than a marriage, right?
5301.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'm thinking of proposing soon.
examples.ja: 近いうちに求婚しようと思うんだ。

5311.reading_mnemonic: This word's reading is pretty weird. We're going to think back to a couple different words to put this one together. The word for heart (心), is こころ. The word for good is よい (or いい, but for this word's sake, よい). A "good heart (feeling)" is one where your heart feels nice and warm and fuzzy (figuratively, not literally. If it's literal, go to the hospital please). That is a <vocabulary>pleasant</vocabulary> feeling. A こころよい feeling.

When you're <kanji>renew</kanji>ing what you're saying, you're adding onto it, which makes this <vocabulary>furthermore</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>further</vocabulary>. 

This is one of those good paragraph or sentence-starting essay words, which is how you'll often see it used!
5325.reading_mnemonic:
The kanji stands by itself with a particle, meaning that this uses the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn with the kanji. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

You know a person that starts every other sentence by saying "<vocabulary>Furthermore</vocabulary>," and that's... <reading>Sarah</reading> (さら). Really feel yourself getting annoyed with this Sarah for starting every other sentence with "Furthermore, ...!"

Just note that 更に is often written in kana, as さらに, especially in casual writing!

examples.en: It's rare for perpetrators of domestic violence to naturally reform themselves.

 更生 generally refers to rehabilitation from various issues such as addiction, crime,  delinquency, or personal struggles. Ideally, this leads to <vocabulary>reforming oneself</vocabulary> and reintegrating into society.

examples.en: Why don't we talk about the ukiyo-e?

5331.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>float</kanji>ing <kanji>world</kanji> <kanji>painting</kanji> is what you call an <vocabulary>ukiyo-e woodblock print</vocabulary> in Japan. The "floating world" refers to an evanescent world that is impermanent (floating), just as beauty and entertainment are. Back in the day, this type of art was made into woodblock prints and paintings. Unfortunately, we don't have a name for these in English because they're so unique and special, but they come up more than you'd think, so get used to ukiyo-e!
5331.reading_mnemonic: The readings don't really line up perfectly, but they're close (although mixed in terms of what has what reading). Take a look at the word and break everything down. 浮 takes the kun'yomi うき (from 浮く), 世 also takes the kun'yomi よ, and then 絵 takes the on'yomi え. Put that all together and you have うきよえ! Or if you already know the word ukiyo-e, that works too!

5333.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Go grab a cup of water so you don't become dehydrated, okay?

5335.meaning_mnemonic:
Something is <kanji>leak</kanji>ing and whatever is leaking is <kanji>exit</kanji>ing what it was in before. This is when a <vocabulary>leak</vocabulary> occurs.

漏出 is a formal word that means <vocabulary>leakage</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>spillage</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>seepage</vocabulary>. It's often used for physical leaks of substances like liquids, gases, or other materials.
5335.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

5336.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>leak</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to leak</vocabulary>.

漏れる can be used for both physical and abstract leakage, like water or gas leaking, sound or light seeping out, or information or emotions being revealed unintentionally.
5336.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Causing you <vocabulary>to leak</vocabulary> all over the floor (we're talking blood, here) is your friend <reading>Moe</reading> (も). If you know someone named Moe, imagine them doing this. If you don't, think of a famous Moe.

5337.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>illuminate</kanji>, so this means <vocabulary>to illuminate</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to shine light on</vocabulary> something.

But don't get it confused with 照れる, which is "to feel embarrassed" — that would be embarrassing. You know this is "to illuminate" because you get a <reading>rash</reading> (らす) every time something shines on you too much.
5337.reading_mnemonic: Speaking of things that illuminate, your <reading>hand</reading>s (手) illuminate all the time for some reason.

照れる means <vocabulary>to be bashful</vocabulary>, often in situations where the embarrassment stems from modesty rather than serious discomfort. It's used to describe feeling self-conscious in an endearing way, such as blushing due to praise, attention, or being teased in a lighthearted manner.
5338.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: The thing you feel the most embarrassed about is your <reading>手</reading> (て). It's all blue and scary looking.

5348.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>cut</kanji> <kanji>token</kanji> is a token you cut out from a sheet of paper into smaller sheets, and each of these pieces is a <vocabulary>ticket</vocabulary>.
5348.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 切る cut short to きっ, then ふ rendaku'd to ぷ. It's a bit of a troublesome word, so concentrate on this now a bit so you can get it in the reviews.

5349.meaning_mnemonic: You put <kanji>one cup of liquid</kanji>... no, one full cup of liquid <kanji>spirit</kanji> into what you're doing. None of this half-cup garbage. A full one. That means you're going at it <vocabulary>with all one's might</vocabulary>.

examples.ja: この子には、今は精神的なケアが必要だと思うんです。

examples.ja: トーフグのブログが、入院中の私の精神的な支えになっていました。

examples.en: He had quit his job due to mental stress.
examples.ja: 彼は精神的ストレスが原因で仕事を辞めることになりました。

examples.en: When I was mentally troubled, I was wandering aimlessly around the park alone every day.
examples.ja: 精神的に病んでいた時、毎日一人で公園をブラブラしていました。

5350.meaning_mnemonic: Your 精神 is your spirit or your mind. If you add 的 to it, you get <vocabulary>mental</vocabulary>. It can mean <vocabulary>spiritual</vocabulary> too, but it more often shows up in reference to a person's mental or <vocabulary>emotional</vocabulary> state.
5350.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: My father is suffering from a mental illness and is in hospital.
examples.ja: 父は精神病をわずらって入院しています。

examples.en: Mental illness is closely related to physical health.
examples.ja: 精神病と身体の健康は深く関係しています。

examples.en: My cat started acting weird, and I wondered, "Is this a mental illness?"
examples.ja: 猫が急に変な動きをしていて、「これって精神病かな？」と思っちゃった。

5351.meaning_mnemonic:
精神 is your spirit or mind, the non-physical part of you. When it's <kanji>sick</kanji>, it's a <vocabulary>mental illness</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>mental disorder</vocabulary>.

Note that the term 精神病, when used on its own, carries a stigma and is considered a bit disrespectful and outdated.
5351.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Will help if you know 精神 already, though.

examples.en: There are a lot of Korean Americans living in my town.
examples.ja: 私の町には韓国系アメリカ人がたくさん住んでいます。

examples.en: I like romance-type movies, but I'm not good with horror ones.
examples.ja: 私は恋愛系の映画が好きだけど、ホラー系は苦手です。

5352.meaning_mnemonic:
Trace something back through its <kanji>lineage</kanji> to determine what <vocabulary>type</vocabulary> of thing it is. 

〜系 is a suffix you can attach casually to a word to classify it as a <vocabulary>genre</vocabulary> or group, like 理系 (science-oriented fields), おしゃれ系 (trendy or stylish people), or 日系 (Japanese descendants).
5352.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji, probably because this word gets stuck onto other things to describe tribes and groups.

examples.en: Many Japanese Americans live in Los Angeles.
examples.ja: ロサンゼルスには多くの日系アメリカ人が住んでいます。

examples.en: What are the merits of working for a Japanese company in America?
examples.ja: アメリカで日系企業につとめるメリットは何ですか。

examples.en: I only use Japanese airlines.
examples.ja: 私は日系の飛行機しか乗らないようにしています。

examples.en: My wife is a third-generation American of Japanese descent.
examples.ja: 私の妻は日系アメリカ人の三世です。

5353.meaning_mnemonic:
The 日 stands for 日本 here, making it mean "Japanese." So what's a more common way of saying Japanese <kanji>lineage</kanji>? That would be <vocabulary>Japanese descent</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>Japanese origin</vocabulary>.

日系 can be used for both people and entities, such as 日系アメリカ人 (Japanese-American) or 日系企業 (Japanese-operated company).
5353.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Around where in the Milky Way is the solar system located?

examples.en: At the center of the solar system is, of course, the Sun.

examples.ja: 太陽系には惑星はいくつあるんだっけ？

5354.meaning_mnemonic: You know 太陽 means "sun," so hopefully you can guess what a sun <kanji>system</kanji> is. That's right — it's the <vocabulary>solar system</vocabulary>!
5354.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Will help to know 太陽.

examples.en: I am thinking about buying a book that summarizes economic theories systematically.
examples.ja: 経済学の理論について、体系的にまとめた本を買いたいと思っています。

examples.en: Prof. Baba and Prof. Morimoto are conducting systematic research on communication theories.
examples.ja: 馬場教授と森本教授はコミュニケーション理論について体系的な研究をしている。

examples.en: Organizing problems systematically leads to early solutions.
examples.ja: 問題を体系的に整理することで、早期の解決につながります。

examples.en: We are offering systematic Japanese learning material.
examples.ja: 私達は、体系的な日本語学習教材を提供しています。

5355.meaning_mnemonic:
Give a <kanji>body</kanji> to a <kanji>system</kanji> to make it a real, structured system, you know? Then add 的 to it to make it <vocabulary>systematic</vocabulary>.

体系的 is a formal word for something that follows a clear structure or framework, often used in academic contexts. For example, you might hear it when discussing a systematic approach to solving a problem or organizing information systematically.
5355.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: We are very grateful for the uninterrupted supply of electricity and water.
examples.ja: 電気や水が絶えることなく供給されているのはとてもありがたいことです。

examples.en: It's sad, but Koichi's life has ended here.
examples.ja: 悲しいけど、コウイチの命はここで絶えてしまったんだ。

examples.en: Since Tofugu members ate a mushroom called "panaeolus papilionaceus," there has been no end to the laughter in the Tofugu office.
examples.ja: トーフグメンバーが笑い茸と呼ばれるキノコを食べてからというもの、トーフグのオフィスでは、笑いが絶えることはない。

5356.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>die out</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to die out</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to come to an end</vocabulary>.

絶える is mostly used for when something that was ongoing comes to an end, like breath stopping, laughter fading away, a supply being cut off, or foot traffic dying down. You know this because when something dies out, nothing is left but thin air (える).
5356.reading_mnemonic: The reading can come from 絶つ, so as long as you know that word you know this one as well.

5357.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>The next</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji> is just that, <vocabulary>the next day</vocabulary>.
5357.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I joined the company in April, and training started the following month
examples.ja: 4月に入社し、翌月に研修が始まった。

examples.ja: 彼はガンで入院し、翌月に退院しました。

examples.en: The accident occurred in August, and safety measures were reinforced the following month.

examples.en: When I woke up the next morning, I had a hangover with a throbbing headache.

5359.reading_mnemonic: This word uses a mix of on'yomi and kun'yomi readings, but, lucky for you, those are the readings you learned with the kanji. Use the readings you learned, and you shouldn't have any problem!

examples.en: Mr. Hino started his business the year after he returned to Japan from America.

5361.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
5361.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Where you're from, everyone measures their <vocabulary>height</vocabulary> in <reading>ce</reading>lery (せ). No inches or centimeters for you, it's celery sticks only. How many celery sticks tall are you?

examples.en: I made a list of Japanese words that I want to memorize.
examples.ja: 覚えたい日本語の単語の一覧を作りました。

examples.ja: アフリカの歴史書をまとめて一覧できるようにしてみました。

examples.en: I'm struggling to find my boss's name on my contact list.
examples.ja: 連絡先の一覧から中々上司の名前が見つからないんだけど。

5362.meaning_mnemonic:
With just <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>look at</kanji> something you're able to take in all the info you need, because that something is <vocabulary>a list</vocabulary>. A nice list that gives you <vocabulary>an overview</vocabulary> at a glance. Perfect for all that <vocabulary>looking over</vocabulary> you have to do. You busy consumer of information, you.

一覧 usually refers to a neat list you can skim over easily to get the info you need, like a guest list or a data table. With する, it becomes a pretty formal verb for looking over something in a quick way, like skimming through a report or casually checking out a place.
5362.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Please enjoy watching the show!
examples.ja: それではショーを楽しんでご覧ください。

examples.en: As you can see, I am all better now.
examples.ja: ご覧の通り、今はもうすっかり元気になりました。

examples.ja: 今ご覧いただいたドキュメンタリーは1996年にアメリカで製作されたものです。

examples.en: Have you seen your daughter's examination results yet?
examples.ja: 娘さんの試験の結果はもうご覧になられましたか。

5363.meaning_mnemonic:
ご覧 is the polite noun form of 見る and means <vocabulary>looking at</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>seeing</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>watching</vocabulary>. It's often paired with 〜になる, as in ご覧になる, which is a respectful way to describe someone else's 見る action.

Some other common phrases you might hear are ご覧ください (please take a look) or ご覧のとおり (as you can see). They're formal but common in polite speech, such as in customer service or business presentations. ご覧 can even be used on its own as a gentle command, like ほら、そこをご覧 ("Hey, look over there").
5363.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji. Go look at the next lesson, now.

examples.ja: 観覧席はもう満席になりました。

examples.en: Photography is prohibited during the viewing.
examples.ja: 観覧中は写真撮影が禁止されています。

examples.en: Throw it properly! I didn't come to see you throw a practice ball!

examples.en: I watched the TofuguTV filming.
examples.ja: トーフグテレビの撮影現場を観覧しました。

5364.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>view</kanji> and <kanji>look at</kanji> something, you are <vocabulary>viewing</vocabulary> that thing, or <vocabulary>watching</vocabulary> it.
5364.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.ja: ずいぶんシメサバについて詳しいんですね。

examples.en: That person looks like they know a lot about computers.
examples.ja: あの人はコンピューターについて詳しそうだ。

examples.en: Wow! Really? Tell me everything.
examples.ja: おお、マジかよ？ 詳しく教えてくれよ。

5365.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>detailed</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>detailed</vocabulary>.
5365.reading_mnemonic: When something is <vocabulary>detailed</vocabulary> it is made up of a huge <reading>qua</reading>ntity (くわ) of little things. And if you're an <vocabulary>expert</vocabulary> on something, you'll have a huge quantity of knowledge, too.

examples.en: This user often sends us very detailed feedback.

examples.ja: このトピックについては詳しくないので、あまり詳細についてはコメントできません。

5366.meaning_mnemonic: Things that are <kanji>detailed</kanji> and... <kanji>detailed</kanji> are, well, the <vocabulary>details</vocabulary>.
5366.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.ja: その人物は、年も性別も全てが不詳だった

5367.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.ja: 私の日本語のボキャブラリーはまだまだ貧しいです。

examples.en: Her life may be poor, but her heart is very rich. I find her much more likable than someone who is wealthy but poor in spirit.

5368.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>poor</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>poor</vocabulary>.
5368.reading_mnemonic: You know the word 先ず (まず)? It means something along the lines of "first of all." So, if you're <vocabulary>poor</vocabulary>, <reading>first of all</reading> (まず), you're going to want to get some help. Second of all, learn how to play the guitar and make funny jokes.

examples.en: I was so poor as a student that I ate cup noodles every day.
examples.ja: 学生時代はずっと貧乏で、毎日カップラーメンばっかりだった。

examples.en: Being poor doesn't mean you have to give up on your dreams.
examples.ja: 貧乏だからといって、夢をあきらめる必要はありません。

examples.en: Poverty doesn't necessarily mean unhappiness.
examples.ja: 貧乏が必ずしも不幸を意味するわけではありません。

5369.meaning_mnemonic: You are <kanji>poor</kanji> and money / food is very <kanji>scarce</kanji> for you, making you <vocabulary>poor</vocabulary>.
5369.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'm considering purchasing new software.
examples.ja: 新しいソフトウェアの購入を検討しています。

examples.en: After purchasing, returns are only accepted if the item is unused.
examples.ja: 購入後の返品は、未使用の場合に限ります。

examples.en: Please be sure to get a receipt when making a purchase.
examples.ja: 購入の際には、必ず領収書を受け取ってください。

examples.ja: この店で偽のシャネルN°5を購入しました。

5370.meaning_mnemonic:
When your <kanji>purchase</kanji> <kanji>enter</kanji>s into effect, you have made your <vocabulary>purchase</vocabulary>.

購入 is a relatively formal word for the act of purchasing something.
5370.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Let’s create a new marketing strategy based on this purchasing data.
examples.ja: この購買データをもとに、新しいマーケティング戦略を立てましょう。

examples.en: My colleague who works at the purchasing department is my best friend.
examples.ja: 会社の購買部につとめている同僚は私の親友です。

examples.en: Buying bread at the school store is something I look forward to every day.
examples.ja: 学校の購買でパンを買うのが、毎日の楽しみなんだよね。

examples.en: I’m researching customer appetites.
examples.ja: 私は消費者の購買意欲について研究をしています。

5371.meaning_mnemonic: You purchase and buy something? That's some serious purchasing. 購買 is a formal term for the act of purchasing goods or services, mostly in business or economic contexts. It's often combined with another word, like in 購買意欲 (consumer appetite) or 購買力 (purchasing power). In some contexts, 購買 can also refer to a school shop or campus store, especially in high schools or universities.
5371.reading_mnemonic: The reading is on'yomi, which is great for 購 but not as great for 買. Luckily, the reading for 買 is <reading>buy</reading> (ばい), which is the same as the meaning, which is a pretty awesome coincidence.

examples.en: The number of subscribers to this online news site is increasing year by year.
examples.ja: このオンラインニュースサイトの購読者数は年々増加しています。

examples.en: I cancelled my subscription to a magazine, as I no longer read it.
examples.ja: 購読してた雑誌、読まなくなったから解約しちゃった。

examples.en: Get your subscription to the Tofugu Newspaper here!
examples.ja: トーフグ新聞の定期購読はこちらから！

examples.en: The rumor that all American people subscribe to the Tofugu newsletter spread throughout Japan.
examples.ja: 全アメリカ人がトーフグのニュースレターを購読しているという噂が、日本中に広まった。

5372.meaning_mnemonic:
This is a <kanji>purchase</kanji>d <kanji>read</kanji> — especially one that comes regularly. In other words, a <vocabulary>subscription</vocabulary>.

購読 specifically refers to paying for a subscription to some kind of reading material, like a newspaper or magazine, so be sure not to use it for free subscriptions!
5372.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The on'yomi for 読 (どく) is the same as the reading in 読者. In case you forgot, think about how you just got a subscription to <reading>dock</reading> (どく) magazine. It's all about docks and dock related things. How exciting.

examples.en: Isn't that overstepping your authority? You don't have the legal power to do that to begin with, right?

examples.en: During your trip, you can leave your luggage at the hotel front desk.
examples.ja: 旅行中は荷物をホテルのフロントに預けることができます。

examples.en: I leave my kid at a nursery school during my work.
examples.ja: 仕事をしている間は子供は保育園に預けています。

examples.en: By depositing money in the bank, you can keep it safe.
examples.ja: 銀行にお金を預けることで、安全に管理することができます。

5381.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>deposit</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to deposit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to entrust</vocabulary>. 

You use 預ける when you leave something in someone else's care for a while, expecting to get it back. For example, you can use 預ける when you deposit money in a bank, leave your coat in a cloakroom, or even when you park your bicycle in a parking area. You can also use it when you leave your child with grandparents or leave your dog at a pet hotel.
5381.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

In terms of places where you want <vocabulary>to deposit</vocabulary> your money, the last place on your list should be <reading>a zoo</reading> (あず). I mean seriously, you know the animals are just gonna munch up all your dolla bills.

examples.en: I deposit part of my salary every month.

5385.meaning_mnemonic:
The 電 is what powers electric things. Many times, these electric things light up (especially back in the day, when electricity did this a lot more than other things). So, you have "lighting." Then, you have <kanji>decorate</kanji>. So, if you decorate with lighting, you have <vocabulary>decorative lighting</vocabulary>.

This is quite a specific word that is generally used as a product category for decorative lighting. It’s a less common word than other expressions, such as デコレーションライト or イルミネーションライト.

examples.en: Someone was being noisy late at night, and the police were called.

5386.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji is <kanji>boisterous</kanji>. The verb version is <vocabulary>to make noise</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be boisterous</vocabulary>. Basically, you're being boisterous when you make a lot of noise, so that's where it comes from.
5386.reading_mnemonic: You're always going <vocabulary>to make noise</vocabulary> and be boisterous when you eat something <reading>sour</reading> (さわ). Imagine stuffing lemon slices, sour candy, and umeboshi into your mouth. All at once. See how much noise you make? They're so sour, and they make you so boisterous.

The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

When this kanji is a word on its own, it's actually very often written in hiragana. Still, the kanji version of the word is worth knowing, too!
5389.reading_mnemonic:

There's something inside and you wanna get to what's within. Look inside. <reading>Ooh, chee</reading>se (うち)! Your favorite. Ooh cheese, how I love you.

5390.meaning_mnemonic:
我 is me, so two of me makes <vocabulary>we</vocabulary>! Or <vocabulary>us</vocabulary>!

You've learned that 我 is an old-fashioned pronoun. 我々 is similar in that it feels formal and authoritative. This means it's often used in situations that require official representation, like company statements, business meetings, or political speeches. Check out our context sentences for some examples!

examples.en: In Kyoto, I bought a beautiful piece of fabric as a souvenir.
examples.ja: 京都で、お土産に美しい織物を買いました。

examples.en: Can we make something out of this woven cloth?
examples.ja: この織物を使って何か作れないかな？

examples.en: This region is famous for its traditional textile production.

examples.en: I'm majoring in politics, but somehow I started working for a fabric company.

5391.meaning_mnemonic:
If you <kanji>weave</kanji> a <kanji>thing</kanji>, you get a <vocabulary>textile</vocabulary>.

examples.en: It is seen as having no direct influence on health.

5392.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Will help if you know 直接 already.

怒気 looks simple, but it's a pretty advanced term more commonly used in literature, typically to describe a character's anger as expressed through their voices, facial expressions, attitudes, or the surrounding atmosphere.

examples.ja: 腹が減ったなぁ。何か作ってよ。

examples.en: You just ate a little while ago, and you're already hungry again?
examples.ja: さっき食べたばっかなのに、もう腹が減ったの？

examples.en: I’m hungry. Would you like to continue this over lunch?
examples.ja: 腹が減ったな。この件については、昼飯を食べながら話さないか？

5394.meaning_mnemonic:
When your <kanji>belly</kanji> has <kanji>decreased</kanji> in the amount of stuff inside it, you become <vocabulary>hungry</vocabulary>.

腹が減った is a casual way of saying <vocabulary>I'm hungry</vocabulary> in Japanese, often with a bit of a rough or masculine tone.
5394.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is 腹 plus 減る put together. With these two combined, you have はらがへった.

In casual speech, you might hear 腹減った without the が more often. The version with が is more common in writing or fixed expressions like 腹が減っては戦ができぬ (you can't fight on an empty stomach).

examples.ja: お店によく置かれている招き猫は、左手を上げています。これは、左手が「お客さんを招く」とされているためです。

examples.en: On the other hand, a maneki neko with its right paw raised is said to "beckon money and good fortune," so they are often displayed in offices or homes.
examples.ja: 一方、右手を上げている招き猫は「お金や幸運を招く」とされているので、オフィスや個人宅にかざられることが多いです。

5395.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>beckoning</kanji> <kanji>cat</kanji> is a <vocabulary>beckoning cat</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>maneki neko</vocabulary>. 

招き猫 are the cat statues believed to bring good luck and fortune to their owners. They're often placed in front of shops with one paw raised, as if beckoning and saying, "Hey, come on in!"
5395.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, which you know already!

examples.en: We will be setting up a shop in Ginza.
examples.ja: 今度、銀座に店を構えることになりました。

examples.en: Try holding the camera with both hands and positioning it diagonally like this.
examples.ja: こんな風に、カメラを両手で持って、ななめに構えてみてください。

examples.en: When you play poker it’s important to prepare patiently.
examples.ja: ポーカーをする時は、気長に構えることが大切です。

examples.en: As both opponents positioned their fists in front of their chests, the starting bell of the match rang out.
examples.ja: 両者が拳を胸の前に構えると、試合開始のゴングが鳴り響いた。

5396.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji itself means <kanji>set up</kanji>, so this means <vocabulary>to set up</vocabulary>, as in establishing something in an orderly manner.

This can also mean <vocabulary>to assume a stance</vocabulary>, like taking a fighting posture, or to hold in preparation, such as a weapon, while preparing to engage in a fight.
5396.reading_mnemonic: The reading is like 構う, so as long as you know that you know this too.

examples.en: It has been three years since I have visited here.
examples.ja: ここを訪れるのは三年ぶりです。

examples.en: This is a picture of my first visit to Rome.
examples.ja: これは、初めてローマを訪れた時の写真です。

examples.en: But then a turning point came.
examples.ja: しかし、そんな時に転機が訪れたんです。

examples.en: If you want to visit the ramen factory you should make your reservations as far in advance as possible.
examples.ja: もしあのラーメン工場に訪れたいのであれば、できるだけ早くに予約を入れる方がいいですよ。

5397.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>visit</kanji> and the verb vocab version is also <vocabulary>to visit</vocabulary>.

What makes it different from 訪ねる, though? With 訪ねる, you're going somewhere or visiting someone with a clear purpose. With 訪れる, the emphasis is on the act of visiting a place (and not a person), regardless of purpose. So, if you're simply saying that you're going to go visit the Kiyomizu Temple in Kyoto, you could say 訪れる. On the other hand, if you're visiting the Kiyomizu Temple to discover something, or you're going to pay a visit to a teacher in Kyoto for some advice, you could use 訪ねる.

Those uses we just described for 訪れる are for when it is transitive. However, it can also be intransitive, if the action is done by something rather than someone. In that case, it means "to come", as in "winter comes" (冬が訪れる) or "peace comes" (平和が訪れる). 訪ねる, on the other hand, cannot be used in this way.
5397.reading_mnemonic: The reading isn't the same as 訪ねる, though, I'm afraid. It's おとず. Remember how this means just visiting a place? Unfortunately, you completely forgot what you were visiting. When you finally remember, it's because you were looking down to think. It's to look at the toes of the giant Buddha statue. "<reading>Oh Toes</reading>!" (おとず), you exclaim.

examples.en: I booked a plane ticket.

examples.en: Why are plane tickets so expensive?

examples.en: Not only did I lose my plane ticket, but my passport was eaten by my dog.

5398.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>aviation</kanji> (航空) <kanji>ticket</kanji> is the kind of ticket you need to fly on an airplane. That's an <vocabulary>airplane ticket</vocabulary>.
5398.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: A plan to attack the enemy base is underway.
examples.ja: 敵の基地を攻撃する計画が進行中だ。
