examples.ja: 彼らは夜明け前に突然攻撃された。

examples.en: It is not good to attack individuals during a discussion. Let's focus on ideas.
examples.ja: 議論中に、個人を攻撃するのは良くないですよ。アイディアに集中しましょう。

5399.meaning_mnemonic: 攻撃 is an <kanji>attack</kanji>. Make that into a verb and you have <vocabulary>to attack</vocabulary>.
5399.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know 攻撃 as well.

examples.en: Oh, we met earlier at the convenience store too, didn't we?
examples.ja: あれ、先程コンビニでもお会いしましたよね？

examples.en: Who is the old man sitting over there from a little while ago?
examples.ja: 先程からあそこに座っているご老人はだれですか。

examples.en: As I told you earlier, your reservation was cancelled.
examples.ja: 先程も申しましたように、お客様の予約はキャンセルされました。

examples.en: I read the letter from you earlier today.
examples.ja: 先程あなたからの手紙を読ませて頂きました。

5400.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>previous</kanji> <kanji>extent</kanji> of time was <vocabulary>a little while ago</vocabulary>. Just think to a previous extent of time that was indeed a little while ago. Now, associate!

先程 is limited to a relatively brief time frame within the same day. So it can be used for something mentioned earlier in a speech or at an event from <vocabulary>earlier in the day</vocabulary>, but not for something from a few days ago. 先程 is also polite and formal, so it's generally used in professional or respectful settings.
5400.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the words 先 and 程, put together.

examples.en: His bureaucratic way of speaking annoyed me a little.
examples.ja: 彼の官僚的な話し方に、少しイラっとしました。

examples.en: Many people get frustrated dealing with bureaucratic red tape.
examples.ja: 官僚的なたらい回しにあって、イライラする人は多い。

examples.en: There are too many bureaucratic processes in the world.
examples.ja: 世の中には官僚的なプロセスが多すぎます。

examples.en: There's too much bureaucratic red tape in this company.
examples.ja: この会社では官僚的な形式主義がまかり通りすぎている。

5401.meaning_mnemonic: If 官僚 is "bureaucracy," then adding a 的 to it would make it <vocabulary>bureaucratic</vocabulary>.
5401.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Knowing 官僚 will help a lot too.

examples.en: My nasal congestion is so bad that I can't sleep.
examples.ja: 鼻詰まりがひどくて眠れません。

examples.en: Because of my stuffy nose, I can't really taste things.
examples.ja: 鼻詰まりのせいで味がよくわかりません。

examples.en: I'm suffering from a terrible fever and stuffy nose.
examples.ja: 私は高熱と鼻詰まりに苦しんでいます。

5402.meaning_mnemonic: 詰まる is "to be stuffed." So, if your <kanji>nose</kanji> is <kanji>stuffed</kanji>, then you have a <vocabulary>stuffy nose</vocabulary>.
5402.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 鼻 and 詰まる put together. the 詰まり is rendaku'd, probably because you're trying to say this word with a stuffy nose.

examples.en: By obsessing over the failure, I became even more anxious.
examples.ja: 失敗を思い詰めることで、ますます不安になってしまったんです。

examples.en: Sometimes, talking to someone about the feelings you've been preoccupied with can make you feel a little better.
examples.ja: 思い詰めていた気持ちを誰かに話すことで、少し楽になったりすることもあるんだよ。

examples.en: I'm between jobs, but I'm not worrying too much about it.
examples.ja: 私は失業中ですが、そのことを思い詰めてはいません。

examples.en: I was so absorbed in thinking about her, but then I realized. Love starts with taking care of yourself.
examples.ja: 彼女のことを思い詰めていたけど、気づいたんだ。愛は自分自身を大切にすることから始まるんだって。

5403.meaning_mnemonic:
詰める is "to stuff in." If you're really stuffing in your thoughts (<kanji>think</kanji>), you're thinking very deeply and seriously. So this is <vocabulary>to brood</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to dwell on</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to take something to heart</vocabulary>.

思い詰める suggests you're pondering deeply over something serious or distressing, bordering on overthinking.
5403.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 思い and 詰める put together into one reading.

examples.en: Secretly staring at your crush—so youthful, isn't it?
examples.ja: 好きな人をこっそり見詰めるのって、青春っぽいよね。

examples.en: Sometimes you can communicate just by staring… I hope.
examples.ja: 見詰めるだけで通じることもある（と信じたい）。

examples.en: The cat stared at me so intensely, I had to give it a treat.
examples.ja: ネコにジッと見詰められたから、おやつを差し出してしまった。

examples.en: The dog was staring intently at the balloon flying straight up, higher and higher.
examples.ja: その犬は、真っすぐ上へ上へと飛んで行く風船をじっと見詰めていた。

5404.meaning_mnemonic: When you really <kanji>stuff in</kanji> (詰める) what you are <kanji>see</kanji>ing, you're really looking at something, causing you <vocabulary>to stare at</vocabulary> whatever it is you're stuffing your seeing into.
5404.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 見 and 詰める.

examples.en: That male dog has been full of energy since he was a puppy.
examples.ja: その雄犬は子犬のころから元気いっぱいだった。

examples.en: This product is a toilet for male dogs only.
examples.ja: こちらの商品は、雄犬専用のトイレになります。

examples.en: I believe the cost of neutering a large male dog at that veterinary clinic was around 30,000 yen.
examples.ja: あそこの動物病院、大型の雄犬の去勢手術は三万円ぐらいだったはず。

examples.en: The male dog that had escaped has just been safely captured.
examples.ja: 脱走していた雄犬が、先程無事に保護されました｡

5405.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>male</kanji> <kanji>dog</kanji> is a <vocabulary>male dog</vocabulary>.

It's worth mentioning that you'll see this most often written in katakana, as both オス犬 and オスの犬.
5405.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the kun'yomi readings, which is probably A-Okay for 犬, but for 雄 you'll want to think about how a male dog is probably pretty pushy, always trying <reading>to push</reading> (押す) other dogs around, being male and moody and all that.

meanings: To Put An End To Something

examples.en: She never let her smile die out.
examples.ja: 彼女はいつも笑顔を絶やすことがなかった。

examples.en: Make sure the fire doesn't go out during the night.
examples.ja: 夜の間、火を絶やさないように気をつけるんだぞ。

examples.en: To keep the flickering light of life from going out, he ordered a pizza.
examples.ja: 今にも消えそうな命の灯を絶やさないために、彼はピザを注文した。

examples.en: We must not let Japan's traditions fade. Please think with me about how we can protect our culture.
examples.ja: 日本の伝統を絶やしてはなりません。どうすれば私たちの文化を守ることができるのか、共に考えてください。

5406.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 絶える means "to die out?" Well 絶やす is its transitive version, meaning <vocabulary>to let something die out</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to put an end to something</vocabulary>. 

絶やす is used when you stop something from continuing, like ending a family line, letting a tradition fade, or allowing a fire to go out. You know this because if you're putting an end to something, you probably don't like it, so you say "<reading>YAASS</reading>" (やす) with a big evil grin as you let it die out.

Note that 絶やす often appears in its negative form 絶やさない, because it's commonly used to describe the intent not to let something precious or important come to an end.
5406.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 絶える.

examples.en: It's common to get nervous before a match.
examples.ja: 試合前に緊張するのはよくあることです。

examples.en: I was nervous on my first date.
examples.ja: 初めてのデートで緊張した。

examples.en: I was so nervous that my hands started shaking.
examples.ja: 緊張しすぎて、手がふるえました。

examples.en: I'm very nervous for an important presentation.
examples.ja: 大事なプレゼンなので、とても緊張しています。

5407.meaning_mnemonic:
緊張 means "nervousness" or "tension." So, the verb version is <vocabulary>to feel nervous</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to get tense</vocabulary>.

People often use 緊張する when they're about to do something important, like giving a speech or taking a test. In formal contexts it can also be used to talk about muscles physically getting tense.
5407.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Cultural blending always leads to the creation of new value.
examples.ja: いつだって、文化の融合は、新しい価値を生み出します。

examples.en: This is architecture that fuses tradition and modern technology.
examples.ja: これは伝統と現代技術が融合した建築です。

examples.en: Our band plays music that is a fusion of jazz and rock.
examples.ja: 俺たちのバンドは、ジャズとロックを融合させた音楽を演奏しています。

examples.en: Don't you think medical school is more of a fusion of the sciences and humanities rather than just science?
examples.ja: 医学部は理系と言うより、文理融合系だと思いませんか？

5408.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Dissolve</kanji> and then <kanji>join</kanji> together again to create a reaction, a <vocabulary>fusion</vocabulary> reaction.

融合 is a relatively formal word that describes two or more things blending together to become a unified whole. It can describe fusion in the scientific sense (like nuclear fusion) or in a more figurative sense, such as the fusion of ideas, cultures, styles, or technologies.
5408.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I applied for a loan for a new business.
examples.ja: 新しい事業のために融資を申請しました。

examples.ja: 銀行の融資を受けるのは思っていたよりも難しかったです。

examples.en: Loan screening takes time.
examples.ja: 融資の審査には時間がかかります。

examples.en: I received a detailed explanation of the loan conditions.
examples.ja: 融資条件について詳しく説明を受けた。

5409.meaning_mnemonic:
Someone <kanji>dissolve</kanji>s their <kanji>resources</kanji> in order to more easily give them to you, because they are <vocabulary>financing</vocabulary> you with a <vocabulary>loan</vocabulary>. This someone is an investor, and they want to see your business succeed!

融資 is a formal word for <vocabulary>lending money</vocabulary>. It's used when a financial institution lends money to an individual or a business to help with things like starting a company, buying property, or handling expenses.
5409.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It's hard to be away from my pet for a while.
examples.ja: ペットとしばらく離れるのがつらい。

examples.en: It's a little ways from my house to the station.
examples.ja: 家から駅まで少し離れているんです。

examples.en: Leaving your hometown is a little sad, don't you think?
examples.ja: やっぱりふるさとを離れるのは、さびしいでしょ？

examples.en: Being away from my parents and living by myself was easier than I thought.
examples.ja: 親元から離れて一人暮らしをすることは思っていたよりも簡単でした。

5410.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an <ja>う</ja> sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>detach</kanji>, but what happens when something detaches? It causes it <vocabulary>to become separated</vocabulary>, aka <vocabulary>to separate</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to move away</vocabulary> from something else.

You use 離れる when two things that were together separate and become distant from one another. This can refer to a physical detachment, but it can also describe someone moving away from a place, group, or role, or even people drifting apart emotionally. You also use it to describe places that are far from each other.
5410.reading_mnemonic: For the reading, think about what it means <vocabulary>to be separated</vocabulary>. Imagine how all the cherry blossom <reading>花</reading>s (はな) separate from their branches and fall to the ground after blooming in the spring. Ah, to separate is so sad, and yet so beautiful!

examples.en: In Japan, you can get divorced easily just by submitting a divorce paper, right?
examples.ja: 日本では離婚届を提出するだけで簡単に離婚ができるんでしょ？

examples.en: The day after our divorce, I got flowers for our anniversary.
examples.ja: 離婚した翌日、結婚記念日の花が届いた。

examples.en: We had an amicable divorce, and we're still like friends even now.
examples.ja: 私たち、円満離婚だし、今でも友達みたいな関係なの。

examples.en: "I'm going to divorce him." "Don't be so rash. Think carefully before you make a decision."
examples.ja: 「彼とは離婚するつもりなの。」「ちょっ…早まらないで。決断する前によく考えて。」

5411.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Do you get why the separation of church and state is important?
examples.ja: なぜ政教分離の原則が大切か分かりますか？

examples.en: I'm going to try and google how to separate cream from milk.
examples.ja: クリームを牛乳から分離させる方法をググってみるよ。

examples.en: I recorded a video of a dangerous car driving on the median strip.
examples.ja: 中央分離帯を走る危険な車をビデオに撮りました。

examples.en: In Japan, on April 20, 1868 (March 28 in the old calendar), the order to separate Shinto and Buddhism was issued.
examples.ja: 日本では、1868年の4月20日（旧3月28日）に、神仏分離令が出されたんです。

5412.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>divide</kanji> and <kanji>detach</kanji> things from each other, you're creating <vocabulary>separation</vocabulary> between them. Makes sense, right?

分離 is a word you might hear in science when discussing how different substances, like oil and water, don't mix and separate from each other.

Additionally, 分離 can also be a formal term used to describe separating groups of people, often in discussions about serious topics like social <vocabulary>segregation</vocabulary>.
5412.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I couldn't complete the procedure because I forgot my seal.
examples.ja: 印鑑を忘れて手続きができなかった。

examples.en: Apparently, you need a seal to open a bank account.
examples.ja: 銀行口座を作るのに印鑑が必要なんだって。

examples.en: You need an officially sealed document.
examples.ja: 公的な印鑑が押された書類が必要になります。

examples.en: In Japan, you can't get married or divorced without a seal? Seriously?
examples.ja: 日本では印鑑がないと、結婚も離婚もできないってマジ？

5413.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>seal</kanji> that's <kanji>model</kanji>ed after you is a useful <vocabulary>seal</vocabulary> indeed — it's your very own <vocabulary>personal seal</vocabulary>!

印鑑 is a small stamp with your name carved into it. In Japan, people use it on official documents instead of signing their name. It's like your legally recognized "signature stamp," and it's something most adults in Japan need to have.
5413.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: This microwave breaks a lot.
examples.ja: この電子レンジ、よく壊れるんですよ。

examples.en: My watch is broken so I'm going to send it in for repair.
examples.ja: 時計が壊れたので修理に出すつもりです。

examples.en: My Nintendo DS, which I had been using with great care, finally broke.
examples.ja: 大事に使っていたニンテンドーDSがついに壊れてしまった。

examples.en: I overslept, missed my breakfast, and then my car broke down. It's really not my day today.
examples.ja: 寝過ごして朝ごはんを食べ損ねた上に、車が壊れたんだ。本当に今日はついてないよ。

5414.meaning_mnemonic: 壊す is "to break something." 壊れる is when something just gets broken or is broken, and you're not doing the breaking. This is <vocabulary>to be broken</vocabulary>.
5414.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 壊す, so try not to break any of your memories and remember this.

examples.en: This is a fragile item, so be careful!
examples.ja: これ、壊れ物だから、気をつけてね！

examples.en: When carrying a box with fragile items, hold it firmly with both hands.
examples.ja: 壊れ物が入っている箱を持つときは、両手でしっかりと持ってください。

examples.en: The move was really difficult because there were so many fragile items.
examples.ja: 壊れ物がたくさんあったせいで、引っ越しがとても大変だった。

examples.en: Should I write down "Fragile - Handle with Care" on the package?
examples.ja: 小包に、「壊れ物、取扱注意」って書いておいた方がいいかな。

5415.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>thing</kanji> that could <kanji>break</kanji> easily, is a <vocabulary>fragile thing</vocabulary>. Be careful with things like this.
5415.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 壊れる and 物 put together.

examples.en: The payment has already been completed.
examples.ja: 既に支払いは完了しています。

examples.en: I have already mentioned this matter to the department manager.
examples.ja: この件について、部長には既に一言伝えてあります。

examples.en: The meeting has already started, so please hurry and join.
examples.ja: 会議は既に始まっていますので、急いで参加してください。

examples.en: He had already left his office when I called him.
examples.ja: 私が電話した時、彼は既に退社してしまってました。

5416.meaning_mnemonic:
Something that <kanji>previously</kanji> happened has <vocabulary>already</vocabulary> happened.

既に is relatively formal. Use it as a neutral way to describe actions or states that are already complete. By comparison, もう is more casual and might sometimes carry a sense of surprise or regret that something has happened sooner than expected.
5416.reading_mnemonic: The reading is different from what you learned with the kanji. But as I told you <vocabulary>already</vocabulary>, I'll be there on <reading>Su-day</reading> (すで). It's like Sunday, but not quite the same. Imagine your confusion when someone says this over and over, but you don't know what Suday is.

examples.en: Any of them are fine, so please open an existing file.
examples.ja: どれでもいいから、既存のファイルを開いてみてください。

examples.en: The existing design just suddenly changed. Is this a sign of something?
examples.ja: 既存のデザインが突然変わったけど、これって何かのサイン？

examples.en: It seems that additional features will be added to WaniKani's existing services!
examples.ja: ワニカニの既存のサービスに、追加機能が加えられる予定らしいよ！

examples.en: What's more, I heard there's a special discount only for existing members.
examples.ja: しかも、既存のメンバーだけに特別な割引があるんだって。

5417.meaning_mnemonic:
Something that <kanji>previously</kanji> <kanji>exist</kanji>ed is probably still <vocabulary>existing</vocabulary> now.

既存 is a relatively formal word that is often used in official contexts to talk about things that are already in place, like existing systems, facilities, or ideas.
5417.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This issue is settled.
examples.ja: この問題は既決です。

examples.en: It's already decided, so we can't change it.

examples.en: We don't have time to discuss the decided matters.
examples.ja: 既決の事について話し合う時間はありません。

examples.en: Please proceed according to the existing rules.
examples.ja: 既決のルールに従って進めてください。

5418.meaning_mnemonic:
It was <kanji>previously</kanji> <kanji>decide</kanji>d, which means it's been <vocabulary>decided</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>settled</vocabulary>.

既決 is a formal word that means something has already been decided or settled. You'll come across it in official settings, like when a company meeting wraps up and certain topics are marked as 既決.
5418.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Isn't it just normal?
examples.ja: 別に、普通じゃない？

examples.en: A normal person wouldn't do something like this.
examples.ja: 普通の人はこんなことしないだろう。

examples.en: If you think about it normally, it's an unbelievable story.
examples.ja: 普通に考えると、ありえない話だよね。

examples.en: It's generally believed that people are influenced by others.
examples.ja: 普通、人間は他人に影響されるものだと考えられています。

5419.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>pass through</kanji> like completely <kanji>normal</kanji>. You are <vocabulary>normal</vocabulary>. You do things <vocabulary>normally</vocabulary>, normally.
5419.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: How do you usually spend your weekends?
examples.ja: 普段、週末はどんな風に過ごしているの？

examples.en: What is Koichi's usual fashion style?
examples.ja: コウイチの普段のファッションはどんな感じですか？

examples.en: I apologized to my mother for not calling her more regularly.
examples.ja: 私は普段殆ど電話をしないことを、母に謝りました。

5420.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>normal</kanji> <kanji>steps</kanji> are the ones that are totally <vocabulary>usual</vocabulary>. They're the ones you <vocabulary>usually</vocabulary> do, unlike those weird not usual steps.
5420.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: My mom knitted a scarf for me.
examples.ja: 母が私のためにマフラーを編んでくれた。

examples.en: My dad was really good at knitting sweaters.
examples.ja: 私の父は、セーターを編むのがとても上手だった。

examples.en: What inspired you to knit bras?
examples.ja: ブラジャーを編んでみようと思ったきっかけはなんですか。

examples.en: One morning, when I woke up, my grandmother was silently knitting a pair of black gloves at the kotatsu.
examples.ja: ある朝、目が覚めると、おばあちゃんがコタツで、だまって黒い手ぶくろを編んでいた。

5421.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>knit</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to knit</vocabulary>.
5421.reading_mnemonic: When you start <vocabulary>to knit</vocabulary>, you always end up with the same thing every time when you're done, no matter what you're trying to make: The letter "<reading>A</reading>" (あ). It's so frustrating that you can't knit anything else.

examples.en: Why did it take you an hour to edit a blog article?
examples.ja: どうしてブログ記事を編集するのに一時間もかかったんですか。

examples.en: I finally finished writing the article, so I sent it in for editing.
examples.ja: ようやく記事が書き上がったので編集に回しました。

examples.en: We are currently looking for someone to shoot and edit Koichi's wedding video.
examples.ja: ただ今、コウイチの結婚式のビデオを撮影、編集してくれる人をぼ集しています。

5422.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Knit</kanji> and <kanji>gather</kanji> everything back together, which you knit. When you do this to fix things and bring it back together, this is an <vocabulary>edit</vocabulary>.
5422.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Who is the editor of this book?
examples.ja: この本の編者は誰ですか？

examples.en: I think he can become a good editor.
examples.ja: 彼なら、良い編者になれると思います。

examples.en: I consulted the editor, but I haven't received a reply yet.
examples.ja: 編者に相談しましたが、まだ返事がありません。

examples.en: This is Mr. Maruyama, who worked as the editor for this magazine.
examples.ja: こちらの雑誌の編者を務めてくれた丸山君です。

5423.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>knit</kanji> <kanji>someone</kanji> is one who knits words together and makes them better. This someone is an <vocabulary>editor</vocabulary>.
5423.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Did you see the Foreign Minister's speech at the UN yesterday?
examples.ja: 昨日の外務大臣の国連でのスピーチ、見た？

examples.en: The guy who said "I'm aiming to be foreign minister" now apparently works at a convenience store.
examples.ja: 「俺、外務大臣目指してる」って言ってた彼、今コンビニで働いてるみたい。

examples.en: Until the wind settles down, the ship carrying the foreign minister is said to remain in the harbor.
examples.ja: 風が収まるまで、外務大臣を乗せた船は港にとどまるそうだ。

examples.en: Anyway, to make a long story short, Fugu and I had an argument about the Minister of Foreign Affairs and I haven't seen him since.
examples.ja: とにかく、手短に言うとね、フグと僕は外務大臣について口論をして、それ以来、僕は彼に会っていないんだ。

5424.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>outside</kanji> <kanji>task</kanji>s <kanji>minister</kanji> (大臣) is someone who is tasked with dealing with things that are outside the country. This is the <vocabulary>minister of foreign affairs</vocabulary>.
5424.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I heard that my grandpa used to be the prime minister.
examples.ja: ぼくのおじいちゃんは昔、総理大臣だったんだって。

examples.en: After a forty-year career in politics, I finally became prime minister.
examples.ja: 政治家のキャリア40年にしてようやく総理大臣にまで登りつめました。

examples.en: Hey y’all. Prime Minister Koichi is in da house, yo! Check it out!
examples.ja: よぉみんな！コウイチ総理大臣がここに登場だぜ！チェケラ！

5425.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>whole</kanji> <kanji>reason</kanji> our country is still running is because of our "minister" (大臣). Which minister? The <vocabulary>prime minister</vocabulary>, of course. Without our prime minister, we'd all be doomed I say. DOOMED!

Unlike 首相, which can be used for any prime minister, this word is used only for the <vocabulary>Japanese prime minister</vocabulary>.
5425.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. It also contains a vocab word you've learned recently, 大臣!

examples.en: Sayuri is so gorgeous, isn't she?
examples.ja: サユリってすごく華やかだよね。

examples.en: I want to go to a glamorous cocktail party in a beautiful dress someday.
examples.ja: いつか綺麗なドレスを着て、華やかなカクテルパーティーに行ってみたいな。

examples.en: At glamorous parties, I always feel like I'm the only one left out.
examples.ja: 華やかなパーティーでは、いつも一人だけ取り残されたような気分になる。

examples.en: You always manage to cover everything up with that bright and beautiful smile of yours. I'm jealous!
examples.ja: あなたはそうやって何でも華やかな笑顔でごまかせちゃうもんね。うらやましい！

5426.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji means <kanji>showy</kanji>, and this word is basically a super positive version of that — it means <vocabulary>bright and showy</vocabulary>. 

華やか describes the kind of elegant beauty that brightens a room. A little showy, maybe, but in an uplifting way rather than just gaudy. It can describe <vocabulary>gorgeous</vocabulary> clothes, like 華やかなドレス (a gorgeous dress) or bright, <vocabulary>festive</vocabulary> colors and atmospheres.
5426.reading_mnemonic: For the reading, think about something that's <vocabulary>bright and showy</vocabulary>... in particular, <reading>花</reading>s (はな). Flowers are super showy, always showing off their colors and stuff.

examples.en: I ate too much Chinese food and got chased by fried rice in my dreams.
examples.ja: 中華を食べすぎて、夢の中でチャーハンに追いかけられた。

examples.en: Chinese restaurants are usually affordable and give you huge portions, don't you think?
examples.ja: 中華屋って基本、リーズナブルなうえにボリュームがすごいよね。

examples.en: While we were eating our way through Chinatown, my girlfriend said, "I came here with my ex," and after that, I couldn't taste a thing.
examples.ja: 中華街で食べ歩き中、彼女に「ここ、前の彼氏と来た」って言われて、そこから何も味がしなくなった。

examples.en: I'm in the mood for Chinese. Do you want to go out to eat Chinese with me tonight?
examples.ja: 中華料理が食べたい気分なんだけど、今夜一緒に中華食べに行かない？

5427.meaning_mnemonic: 中国 is China, right? That's what this 中 represents. And, of course the Chinese are known for being super showy, which is why you have <kanji>showy</kanji> there.
5427.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It's raining, wanna go to the underground mall?
examples.ja: 雨だし、地下街行かない？

examples.en: I'm off to the underground shopping mall.
examples.ja: ちょっくら地下街に行くところだよ。

examples.en: Today, I relaxed with a coffee at a café in the underground shopping area.
examples.ja: 今日は地下街のカフェでゆっくりコーヒーを飲んだ。

examples.en: I always make sure never to look up at the ceiling in the underground mall. Do you know why?
examples.ja: 僕は地下街の中で一度も天井を見上げないようにしているんだ。何故だか分かるかい？

5428.meaning_mnemonic:
You're "underground" (地下) in the <kanji>streets</kanji>, but don't worry, you're not in some post-apocalyptic sci-fi novel — most of the underground streets and areas in Japan are just <vocabulary>underground shopping mall</vocabulary>s.

地下街, or <vocabulary>underground shopping center</vocabulary>s, are common in big cities in Japan, especially near train stations, where you'll find lots of shops, restaurants, and walkways below street level.
5428.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Is it okay for me to have such luxurious blowfish sashimi?
examples.ja: こんなに豪華なフグのおさしみをいただいてもいいんですか？

examples.en: For my birthday this year, I had my father rent me a luxury cruise ship.
examples.ja: 今年の誕生日に父に豪華客船を貸し切ってもらいました。

examples.en: Wow! That’s splendid. They look delicious. (Kansai-ben)
examples.ja: うわっ！めっちゃ豪華やん。美味しそう。（関西弁）

5429.meaning_mnemonic: Oh wow, that is <kanji>exceptional</kanji>ly <kanji>showy</kanji>! Whatever that thing is, it is <vocabulary>luxurious</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>splendid</vocabulary> and I want one.
5429.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: There's a rumor that he's under police surveillance.
examples.ja: 彼は警察に監視されているというウワサがあります。

examples.en: She quietly slipped away, evading the observant eyes.
examples.ja: 監視の目をかいくぐって、彼女は静かに立ち去ったんです。

examples.en: Do you ever feel like your online activity is being monitored by the government?
examples.ja: 時々、オンラインでのアクティビティが政府に監視されていると感じることはありませんか？

examples.en: I have a surveillance camera, but I haven't checked the tape yet. I wonder if it's working properly.
examples.ja: 監視カメラは持ってるんですが、まだテープを確認した事はないんですよね。ちゃんと撮れてるのかな。

5430.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>oversee</kanji> and <kanji>look at</kanji> all that is in your domain. You are conducting <vocabulary>surveillance</vocabulary>.

監視 is the active <vocabulary>observation</vocabulary> of someone or something to ensure safety or compliance, or to detect suspicious activity. It can also refer to the people who carry out this <vocabulary>monitoring</vocabulary>, either directly or through the use of things like cameras.
5430.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I supervised a final exam today at work.
examples.ja: 今日は仕事で期末試験を監督しました。

examples.en: The coach's leadership led the team to victory.
examples.ja: 監督のリーダーシップが、チームを優勝に導きました。

examples.en: Michael is comparing movies directed by Hayao Miyazaki to other anime movies.
examples.ja: マイケルは、宮崎はやお監督の映画を他のアニメ映画と比べています。

examples.en: I can't remember the name of that movie director. What was his name?
examples.ja: あの映画監督の名前が思い出せないんだけど。何て名前だっけ。

5431.meaning_mnemonic:
The one who <kanji>oversee</kanji>s and <kanji>direct</kanji>s is the one who gives <vocabulary>supervision</vocabulary>. 

監督 refers to the act of supervising or to the person who supervises, such as the <vocabulary>head coach</vocabulary> of a sports team or a movie <vocabulary>director</vocabulary>.
5431.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: The appraisal confirmed it was genuine.
examples.ja: 鑑定の結果、本物だと判明しました。

examples.en: He specializes in art appraisal.
examples.ja: 彼は美術品の鑑定を専門にしています。

examples.en: When I had my wedding ring appraised by an appraiser, it turned out to be a cheap one.
examples.ja: 鑑定士に結婚指輪を鑑定してもらったら、実は安物だったことが判明した。

examples.en: You should take a DNA test to find out if you are his real father.
examples.ja: お前が赤ん坊の本当の父親かどうかを調べるために、DNA鑑定を受けた方がいいんじゃないか。

5432.meaning_mnemonic:
When a <kanji>model</kanji> human <kanji>determine</kanji>s something, that's an <vocabulary>appraisal</vocabulary> you should probably pay attention to. This isn't just some random nobody off the street — they're a model determiner, so they're really giving you an <vocabulary>expert judgment</vocabulary>.

鑑定 often refers to evaluating the authenticity or value of things like art, antiques, or real estate. It's also used in contexts like fingerprint analysis, or in legal settings where court-appointed experts provide technical evaluations to help judges make decisions.
5432.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Everyone except him attended the meeting.
examples.ja: 彼を除く全員が会議に参加した。

examples.en: Everyone's off tomorrow! Excluding me…
examples.ja: 明日はみんな休み！俺を除いて…ね。

examples.en: I go for a walk every day, except when it rains.
examples.ja: 雨の日を除けば、毎日散歩している。

examples.en: Fold all the papers, excluding the red one, to meet the crease.
examples.ja: 赤い紙を除く全ての紙を、その折り目まで折ってください。

5433.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>exclude</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to exclude</vocabulary>.
5433.reading_mnemonic: You would like to exclude your <reading>nose</reading> (のぞ) because you don't like your nose. Imagine your strong feelings about your nose as you decide to exclude it.

examples.en: It's my habit to clean on the weekends.
examples.ja: 週末に掃除をするのが私の習慣です。

examples.en: I love how the room feels brighter after cleaning.
examples.ja: 掃除の後、部屋が明るく感じるのが好きです。

examples.en: Once the cleaning is done, maybe I'll have some tea.
examples.ja: 掃除が終わったら、お茶でも飲もうかな。

examples.en: First things first. Let's start by cleaning your room.
examples.ja: まずやるべきことをやらなくてはね。部屋の掃除から始めようか。

5434.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Sweep</kanji> and <kanji>exclude</kanji> all that dirt from the floor, please. When you do this a lot, it becomes <vocabulary>cleaning</vocabulary>.

掃除 is a common word you'll hear often in daily life, and it can mean anything from quickly vacuuming your room to doing a full-on deep clean of your entire house.
5434.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. For this one though, you have to remember to read the 除 part as じ. Just keep in mind that <kanji>cleaning</kanji> (cleanliness) is next to godliness and so is <reading>Je</reading>sus (じ). So, Jesus is like cleaning. Easy.

examples.en: Could you tell me the reason for the exclusion?
examples.ja: 除外理由を教えてもらえませんか？

examples.en: The horse was excluded from the race due to shin soreness.
examples.ja: その馬はソエにより競争除外となりました。

examples.en: In that case, it seems it will be excluded.
examples.ja: その場合はどうやら適用除外になってしまうみたいですね。

examples.en: However, there seems to be an exemption rule, so please be careful.
examples.ja: ただし、除外規定があるみたいなので、気をつけてください。

5435.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Exclude</kanji> this one and put it <kanji>outside</kanji> what we're considering. This is the <vocabulary>exception</vocabulary>.
5435.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: As for this, I think the quickest way is to ask him directly.
examples.ja: これは彼に直接尋ねるのが一番早いと思います。

examples.en: Please try researching it yourself before asking others.
examples.ja: 人に尋ねる前に、まずは自分で調べてみてください。

examples.en: I was going to ask about the store hours, but there was no one there.
examples.ja: お店の営業時間を尋ねるつもりだったが、誰もいなかった。

examples.en: No matter what I ask, my husband always gives evasive answers... it's like talking to a brick wall.
examples.ja: 何を尋ねても、夫はいつも逃げるような答えを返すばかりで…のれんに腕押しってやつですよ。

5436.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>inquire</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to inquire</vocabulary>, or simply <vocabulary>to ask</vocabulary>.

尋ねる is the polite, slightly formal word you use when you directly ask someone for information you don't know — like directions or details.
5436.reading_mnemonic: You want <vocabulary>to inquire</vocabulary> about some serious matters, but <reading>Taz</reading> (たず), your Tasmanian Devil friend, keeps interrupting <vocabulary>to ask</vocabulary> silly questions instead.

examples.en: The police questioned everyone who was involved.
examples.ja: 警察は関係者全員を尋問しました。

examples.en: During the questioning of a witness, the witness must always tell the truth.
examples.ja: 証人尋問の際、証人は常に真実を述べなければならない。

examples.en: The defense attorney conducted a cross-examination of the witness.
examples.ja: 弁護人は証人に対して反対尋問を行った。

examples.en: During the cross-examination, the lawyer conducted leading questions to the witness and steered the testimony to their advantage.
examples.ja: 反対尋問の際、弁護士は証人に対して誘導尋問を行い、証言を有利に導きました。

5437.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>inquire</kanji> about a <kanji>problem</kanji>, you tend to do <vocabulary>interrogation</vocabulary>-style <vocabulary>questioning</vocabulary> to get to the bottom of it. Why is it like this? What happened? Is it bigger than a breadbox?
5437.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: How much is this?
examples.ja: これはお幾らですか？

examples.en: No matter how much I searched, I couldn't find it.
examples.ja: 幾ら探しても、見つからなかった。

examples.en: There were some troubles, but it ended safely somehow.
examples.ja: 幾らかのトラブルはありましたが、何とか無事に終わりました。

examples.en: Could you tell me how much the shipping will be, please?
examples.ja: 送料が幾らになるのか教えていただけませんでしょうか。

5438.meaning_mnemonic: This has the same meaning as the kanji, specifically the <vocabulary>how much</vocabulary> meaning. To remember this, just think about how <reading>Ra</reading>, the Egyptian God, is always asking "<vocabulary>How much</vocabulary> will it cost to build this pyramid?" Ugh, too much, let's hire some slaves.
5438.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already so you should be able to read it!

examples.en: Can you count how many apples there are in that parcel?
examples.ja: その小づつみの中にリンゴが幾つ入っているか数えてもらえる？

examples.en: How many mics do you know of that are adequate for recording?
examples.ja: 録音に適したマイクを幾つ知っていますか。

examples.en: How old are you, little girl?
examples.ja: おじょうちゃんは幾つかな？

5439.meaning_mnemonic:
This has the same meaning as the kanji, specifically the <vocabulary>how many</vocabulary> meaning. You know this because you ask "how many" and they answer "つ." This can also be used to ask <vocabulary>how old</vocabulary> someone is, but generally only for children's ages.

This word is usually written in kana in modern writing.
5439.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from what you learned in the kanji, nice job.

examples.en: Did you get an A+ on the geometry test? That's amazing, you did really well!
examples.ja: 幾何学のテストでAプラス取ったの？すごいじゃん、よくやったね！

examples.en: I want a carpet with a geometric pattern.
examples.ja: 幾何学模様のカーペットが欲しいんだよね。

examples.en: I used a compass and ruler to draw a geometric shape.
examples.ja: 幾何学的な図形を描くために、コンパスと定規を使いました。

examples.en: Geometry is a branch of mathematics that studies the properties of shapes and the structure of space.
examples.ja: 幾何学とは、図形の性質や空間の構造を研究する数学の一分野です。

5440.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>How many</kanji>? <kanji>What</kanji>? In this area of <kanji>study</kanji>, you ask these questions a lot. This area of study is <vocabulary>geometry</vocabulary>, because you have to ask how many sides and how much the area is or something (can you tell I don't remember any maths?).
5440.reading_mnemonic: The 学 is read correctly, in terms of what you learned. The 幾 and 何 is weird, though. Just think how when you're asking a question in Japanese, you end the sentence with か. So, it's like, "何か????" and that's why it becomes <reading>か</reading>. Then, for 幾 think about how the <reading>key</reading> (き) to answering geometry questions correctly is figuring out "how many" sides something has. So, "do you have the <reading>key</reading>か?"

examples.en: Please don't run in the hallway.
examples.ja: 廊下で走らないでください。

examples.en: The hallway lights were off, and it was a bit scary.
examples.ja: 廊下の電気がついていなくて、少しこわかった。

examples.en: I passed my ex-boyfriend in the hallway. I did my best to pretend to be a door.
examples.ja: 廊下で元カレとすれちがった。こっちは全力でドアのフリした。

examples.en: When she saw him slip on a banana peel in the hallway, without thinking she burst out laughing.
examples.ja: 彼が廊下でバナナの皮に滑るのを見て、彼女は思わず吹き出してしまった。

5441.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>corridor</kanji> is <kanji>below</kanji>. What do you call a corridor that's below? Well, really it's still just a <vocabulary>corridor</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>hallway</vocabulary>.
5441.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: She opened her own picture gallery.
examples.ja: 彼女は自分の画廊を開いた。

examples.en: A new art gallery opened near the station.
examples.ja: 駅前に新しい画廊ができた。

examples.en: That gallery is kind of hard to enter, isn't it?
examples.ja: あの画廊、ちょっと入りづらいよな。

examples.en: The gallery owner confidently said, "This piece will definitely go up in value," and gave a sly grin. Clearly suspicious.
examples.ja: 画廊のオーナーは「この作品、必ず上がりますよ」と断言して、ニヤッと笑った。明らかにあやしい。

5442.meaning_mnemonic:
An <kanji>image</kanji> <kanji>corridor</kanji> is a corridor in which there are images hanging on the wall. This is a <vocabulary>picture gallery</vocabulary>.

Note that 画廊 generally refers to a physical <vocabulary>art gallery</vocabulary>, where artworks are exhibited for in-person viewing.
5442.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Sweeping the yard every morning is part of my routine.
examples.ja: 毎朝、庭を掃くのが日課です。

examples.en: He prefers sweeping with a broom rather than using a vacuum cleaner.
examples.ja: 彼は掃除機をかける代わりに、ほうきで掃くのが好きなんです。

examples.en: Could you sweep the meeting room before the meeting starts?
examples.ja: 会議が始まる前に、会議室をちょっと掃いておいてもらっていいかな。

examples.en: I realized while sweeping the trash that a broom might actually make for a good stretch.
examples.ja: ゴミを掃きながら気づいたんだけど、ほうきって意外といいストレッチになるかも。

5443.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>sweep</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to sweep</vocabulary>.
5443.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: While you <vocabulary>sweep</vocabulary> you laugh. "<reading>HA</reading> (は) HA HA!" Just imagine yourself doing this, or do it for real if you want to clean up a bit.

examples.en: My feet were covered in mud.
examples.ja: 足元が泥だらけになってしまった。

examples.en: My feet got stuck in the mud, and it was hard to move forward.
examples.ja: 泥に足を取られて、前に進むのが大変だった。

examples.en:
"Hey, wait a minute! You just got mud on the floor, didn't you?"
"Eh! I didn't get mud on it. But I did get chocolate on it."
examples.ja: 「おい、ちょっと待て！お前今、床に泥を付けただろ？」「えっ！泥なんて付けてませんよ。チョコレートなら付けましたが。」

examples.en: You can't eat a radish with mud on it as it is, right? So instead of thinking "I want you to accept me as I am," it's better to put in the effort to improve yourself.
examples.ja: 泥のついた大根なんて、そのまま食べられないでしょ？だから「ありのままの私を受け入れてほしい」なんて思わず、自分をよくする努力をした方がいいわ。

5444.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
5444.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with the kanji, but here's a mnemonic in case you need a refresher:

You may know of Dora the Explorer. But have you heard about her dirty, <vocabulary>mud</vocabulary>dy brother, <reading>Doro</reading> (どろ)? They're like a team. And because of all the exploring he does, Doro is always covered in mud.

examples.en: The water in that river has completely turned into muddy water.
examples.ja: その川の水はすっかり泥水に変わってしまった。

examples.en: I can't believe someone would swim in muddy water.
examples.ja: 泥水の中で泳ぐなんて、信じられない。

examples.en: The thought of drinking muddy water makes me feel sick.
examples.ja: 泥水を飲むなんて、考えただけで気分が悪くなるよ。

examples.en: "Hey! Did you spill coffee on my magazine?" "Ah, sorry! My bad!" "Aww... now it looks like there is a muddy water stain right on Johnny Depp's crotch."
examples.ja: 「ちょっと！今私の雑誌にコーヒーをこぼしたでしょ？」「ああ、ごめん！悪かったよ。」「あ〜ぁ〜…ジョニーデップの股間のところに泥水みたいな染みができちゃったじゃない！」

5445.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Mud</kanji> <kanji>water</kanji> is <vocabulary>muddy water</vocabulary>. Don't step in it, if you can help it.
5445.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the kun'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

There's another way to read this word that uses both on'yomi readings (でいすい). It's mostly used in more formal or technical situations though, so we're focusing on the どろみず reading here!

examples.en: What is this stick for? Is this stick for the tent?
examples.ja: この棒、何の棒？テントの棒？

examples.en: I made a craft using ice cream sticks.
examples.ja: アイスの棒を使って、工作をしました。

examples.en: The dog grabbed the stick in his mouth and ran over to me, looking happy.
examples.ja: 犬が棒をくわえて、嬉しそうに走ってきた。

examples.en: First, let's stand the pole here and use it as a marker!
examples.ja: まずはここに棒を立てて、目印にしよう！

5446.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

棒 refers to anything that's long, thin, and solid, whether it's a <vocabulary>pole</vocabulary>, a <vocabulary>rod</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>stick</vocabulary>. It can be used for a wide variety of objects, from tree branches to popsicle sticks.
5446.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: Seriously? That's surprising.
examples.ja: マジで？それは驚くわ。

examples.en: I pretended to be surprised at the surprise party.
examples.ja: サプライズパーティーに驚くふりをしました。

examples.en: My sister said, "I got a new boyfriend," and I was surprised that she had brought home my ex's dad.
examples.ja: 妹が「新しい彼氏できた」と言って連れてきたのが、元カレの父親で驚いた。

examples.en: "Fugu? Is that you, Fugu?" "Salmon? I'll be damned. I haven't seen you since high school. How are you?"
examples.ja: 「フグ？お前、フグか？」「サーモンか？こいつは驚いた。高校以来だね。元気かい？」

5447.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>surprised</kanji>, so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to be surprised</vocabulary>.
5447.reading_mnemonic: What are you so surprised by? Your friend's <reading>odor</reading> (おどろ). Think of a friend that you wouldn't expect to be so smelly. Then, be surprised by the odor. Eww, bro, you have to take a shower.

examples.en: Everyone felt wonder at his performance.
examples.ja: 彼の演技には、皆が驚嘆した。

examples.en: One can only admire the amount of knowledge she has.
examples.ja: 彼女の知識量には驚嘆するしかありませんよ。

examples.en: I was amazed at the size of the solar power plant.
examples.ja: その太陽光発電所の規模に驚嘆しました。

examples.en: He marveled and murmured, "This world is really well made."
examples.ja: 彼は驚嘆して、「この世界、本当によくできてる」とつぶやいた。

5448.meaning_mnemonic: I'm so <kanji>surprised</kanji> it caused me to <kanji>sigh</kanji>. This is like when you run into a movie star, and you go in surprise shock. Then, you breathe out in a sigh because of your great amount of <vocabulary>admiration</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>wonder</vocabulary> for this person.
5448.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Isn't it about time you stopped lamenting your fate?
examples.ja: 自分の運命を嘆くのは、そろそろやめにしないか？

examples.en: He didn't lament his poverty; instead, he worked hard. That's exactly why he succeeded.
examples.ja: 彼は貧乏を嘆くのではなく、努力した。だからこそ、成功したのだ。

examples.en: I lamented that no one ever asked why I wore the same clothes every day.
examples.ja: 私は、毎日同じ服を着ている理由を誰も聞いてくれないことを嘆いた。

examples.en: No matter how much you grieve, time won't turn back, so let's stop worrying and move forward!
examples.ja: どんなにくよくよ嘆いていても、時間はもどらないんだから、嘆くのはやめて前に進もうよ！

5449.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>sigh</kanji>, you feel a certain type of emotion. A type that makes you feel sad and causes you <vocabulary>to lament</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to grieve</vocabulary>.
5449.reading_mnemonic: For the reading, just think about this feeling you're having (this lamenting grieving one). Then, decide you're done with it. <reading>投げ</reading>る (throw) it out the window. You don't want these feels anymore!

examples.en: She sighed and then handed a lunchbox to someone under the desk.
examples.ja: 彼女は嘆息をついた後、デスクの下の誰かにお弁当を渡した。

examples.en: He let out a strange, sharp sigh and stared at the empty stroller.
examples.ja: 彼はギュッというような変な嘆息をもらして、空のベビーカーを見つめた。

examples.en: After sighing in a way unbefitting a toddler, Jacob slowly toppled the building blocks.
examples.ja: ジェイコブは幼児らしからぬ嘆息をこぼしてから、ゆっくりとつみ木をくずした。

examples.en: When he realized that his legs were much shorter than other peoples' he sighed deeply and headed to the Japan Short Leg Association.
examples.ja: 他人よりも自分がずっと短足だと気づいた時、彼は深々と嘆息を落として、日本短足協会へと向かった。

5450.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Exclamation marks are used to express strong emotions.
examples.ja: 感嘆符は強い感情を表すときに使います。

examples.en: I have a friend who puts an exclamation mark at the end of every single sentence in her emails.
examples.ja: メールで語尾に必ず感嘆符を付ける友達がいます。

examples.en: Am I the only one who feels like "thank you" without an exclamation mark feels kind of cold?
examples.ja: 感嘆符なしで「ありがとう」って、なんか冷たく感じるのは私だけ？

examples.en: Saying "Good morning!!!" with that many exclamation marks is way too hyper for the morning, lol.
examples.ja: 「おはよう！！！」って、朝から感嘆符多用でテンション高すぎて草。

5451.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>feeling</kanji> where you <kanji>sigh</kanji> is one in which you're surprised by something, and can't believe it, so you sigh. Ugh, *sigh*. What <kanji>token</kanji> represents this in writing? An <vocabulary>exclamation mark</vocabulary>!!!!
5451.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: That warehouse shouldn't be in use by anyone right now.
examples.ja: あの倉庫、今は誰も使っていないはずだよ。

examples.en: I walked into a warehouse and found a time machine.
examples.ja: 倉庫に入ったら、タイムマシンがあったんだよ。

examples.en: This is the card game I played with Koichi when the two of us were trapped in the warehouse.
examples.ja: これは、倉庫にコウイチと二人で閉じ込められた時にプレイしたカードゲームです。

examples.en: You need to lift the lever until you hear a click to lock the warehouse.
examples.ja: 倉庫の鍵を閉めるには、カチッという音が聞こえるまでレバーを上げる必要があります。

5452.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>storage</kanji> <kanji>warehouse</kanji> is some kind of <vocabulary>warehouse</vocabulary>, or some kind of <vocabulary>storehouse</vocabulary>.

Curious about the difference between 倉庫 and 庫? While 庫 refers to traditional Japanese storehouses, 倉庫 is used for modern warehouses and storehouses (both the commercial and personal kind).
5452.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I unfolded the map I found in the storehouse.
examples.ja: 倉で見つけた地図を広げてみた。

examples.en: This warehouse stores a lot of rice.
examples.ja: この倉には米がたくさん保管されています。

examples.en: It was cool and pleasant inside the storehouse.
examples.ja: 倉の中はひんやりしていて気持ちよかった。

examples.en: Jiro got locked in the warehouse again? That's the third time!
examples.ja: ジローがまた倉に閉じこめられた？3回目だぞ？

5453.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji means <kanji>storehouse</kanji>, and the vocab is also <vocabulary>storehouse</vocabulary>!

Wondering what the difference between 倉 and 庫 is? Long ago, 倉 were places to store grain, while 庫 used to be associated with places to store vehicles, as the kanji composition suggests. These days, they're both used for general storage, but also refer to places to store goods and merchandise. Between the two, 倉 is much more commonly used.
5453.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the other storehouse reading you learned earlier with 庫. They're basically the same thing, and lucky for you they share the same reading too (<reading>くら</reading>).

examples.en: He is a descendant of the imperial family.
examples.ja: 彼は宮家の子孫です。

examples.en: I wonder if the day will come when my descendants realize my intentions.
examples.ja: 子孫たちが、私の意図に気づく日は来るのだろうか？

examples.en: I heard that figure skater is a descendant of Oda Nobunaga!
examples.ja: あのフィギュアスケート選手、織田信長の子孫なんだって！

examples.en: Don't you want to know where the descendants of historical figures are and what they are doing now?
examples.ja: 歴史的な人物の子孫たちが、今どこで何をしているのか知りたいと思いませんか？

5454.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>child</kanji> who is the <kanji>grandchild</kanji> of someone else is a <vocabulary>descendant</vocabulary> of that person.
5454.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Ever since my grandchild was born, every day has been lively.
examples.ja: 孫が生まれてから、毎日がにぎやかになりました。

examples.en: My grandchild asked me, "When you die, can I have your Switch?" and some water started flowing from my eyes.
examples.ja: 孫に「死んだらSwitchくれる？」って聞かれて目から水が流れ出した。

examples.en: I comforted my crying grandchild, only to learn it was just because YouTube stopped.
examples.ja: 孫が泣いてるからなぐさめたら、「YouTube止まっただけ」だった。

examples.en: Hooking up a new computer is a cinch for my grandchild.
examples.ja: 新しいコンピューターを接続することは、 私の孫にとってはお茶の子さいさいだ。

5455.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
5455.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You are the <vocabulary>grandchild</vocabulary> of your grandfather. His favorite thing is to call you a <reading>maggo</reading>t (まご). Your grandfather was in the military and is very hard on you, maggot.

examples.en: The bird is building a nest in the tree.
examples.ja: 鳥が木の上に巣を作っている。

examples.en: There's an insect caught in the spider's web.
examples.ja: クモの巣の中に虫が引っかかっている。

examples.en: There's a bee's nest nearby, so be careful while walking.
examples.ja: 近くにハチの巣があるから、気をつけて歩いてね。

examples.en: There were five baby swallows chirping in the nest.
examples.ja: 巣の中では、ツバメの雛が五羽、ぴいぴい鳴いていました。

examples.en: The apartment was shabby, but it was certainly a love nest just for the two of them.
examples.ja: そのアパートは、オンボロだけど、確かに二人だけの愛の巣だった。

5456.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

巣 refers to all kinds of animal homes — a bird's <vocabulary>nest</vocabulary>, a spider's web, a mouse's burrow, or even a beehive. Sometimes, it can be used figuratively to describe places where people hole up, whether that be a cozy home for lovers or a shady hideout for gangs…
5456.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: I am a little sad that the day has finally come for my children to leave the nest.
examples.ja: ついに子供達の巣立ちの日がやってきてしまい、ちょっとさびしいです。

examples.en: Why do birds leave the nest before they can fly?
examples.ja: どうして鳥は飛べるようになる前に巣立ちをするのですか。

examples.en: Since the birds have been chirping a lot since the morning, I looked outside and saw that a baby sparrow was just about to leave the nest.
examples.ja: 朝から鳥がたくさん鳴いているので、外を見てみたら、ちょうど、子スズメが巣立ちをするところでした。

examples.en: When a user reaches level 60 and it comes time to leave WaniKani behind, Koichi always quietly whispers "Congratulations."
examples.ja: ユーザーがレベル60を達成してワニカニから巣立ちをすることになったら、コウイチはいつもこっそり「おめでとう」ってつぶやくんです。

5457.meaning_mnemonic: When you live in a nest (巣), there's only one reason for you to stand up (立つ), and that's to <vocabulary>leave the nest</vocabulary>. Your mother may be sad about this, but everyone needs to <vocabulary>become independent</vocabulary> someday.
5457.reading_mnemonic: The readings are from the words 巣 and 立つ put together. Just watch out for the rendaku that changes たつ to だつ!

examples.en: Even if you find a beehive, please don't go near it because it's dangerous.
examples.ja: ハチの巣を見つけても、危ないので近づかないでください。

examples.en: My friend had brought delicious honeycomb, and I was envious.
examples.ja: 友達がおいしいハチの巣を持ってきていて、私は羨ましかった。

examples.en: There are a lot of bees buzzing around the beehive.
examples.ja: ハチの巣の周りで沢山のハチがブンブン飛び回っている。

examples.en: This morning, there was a little piece of honeycomb on the plate of breakfast my mom gave me. But she just said, "The usual."
examples.ja: 今朝、母に出された朝食の皿にハチの巣がチョコンとのっていた。でも母は「いつもの」と言った。

5458.meaning_mnemonic: ハチ is a bee. Buzz buzz. Just imagine "eight bees" combining into one bee, making it a "hachi." Then, there's a <kanji>nest</kanji>. What is a nest for bees? A <vocabulary>beehive</vocabulary>.
5458.reading_mnemonic: 巣 is a standalone word here, so it uses the same reading that you learned when you learned the vocabulary.

examples.en: Oh, there's a spider web!
examples.ja: あ、クモの巣ができてる！

examples.en: The abandoned house was full of spider webs.
examples.ja: 空き家の中はクモの巣だらけだった。

examples.en: In our house, even if we find a spider web, my mom says, "This is art!" and won't let us clean it.
examples.ja: うちの家では、クモの巣を見つけても、母が「これは芸術よ！」って言って掃除させてくれないんです。

examples.en: I found my grandpa's unfinished painting covered in cobwebs in the attic.
examples.ja: 屋根裏部屋で、クモの巣が掛かった祖父の未完成の絵を見つけたんです。

5459.meaning_mnemonic: クモ is a spider. Add a <kanji>nest</kanji> to it, and you have a spider nest. What do spiders call their nests? They call it a <vocabulary>spiderweb</vocabulary> (that is, if they can talk).
5459.reading_mnemonic: 巣 is a standalone word here, so it uses the same reading that you learned when you learned the vocabulary.

examples.en: It's difficult to care for a white obi.
examples.ja: 白い帯はお手入れが大変です。

examples.en: He holds a black belt in karate, and is a master of martial arts.
examples.ja: 彼は空手で黒帯を持っている、武道の達人です。

examples.en: I watched how to tie an obi belt on YouTube and practiced it.
examples.ja: 帯の締め方はYouTubeで見て練習しました。

examples.en: When I looked up, a band of clouds covered the sky.
examples.ja: 見上げると、帯状の雲が空をおおっていた。

5460.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are the same, except that this isn't just any type of <kanji>belt</kanji>. It's an <vocabulary>obi</vocabulary>, a wide cloth <vocabulary>belt</vocabulary> worn with traditional clothes like kimono and yukata.
5460.reading_mnemonic: The reading is obi (おび), so if you know the meaning, you know the reading as well! If you need an extra reminder, ask yourself "What is the first letter in belt?" Hmm, I can't remember. <reading>OH! "B"</reading> (おび)! I remember now.

examples.en: This is a safe zone for everyone but you.
examples.ja: ここは、あなた以外には安全地帯です。

examples.en: This region is an agricultural zone, with vast fields stretching out.
examples.ja: この地域は農業地帯で、広い畑が広がっています。

examples.en: In the industrial zone, factories line the streets, and many people work there.
examples.ja: 産業地帯では、工場が立ち並んでおり、多くの人が働いています。

examples.en: When the new road opens, access to this zone will be improved.
examples.ja: 新しい道路が開通すると、この地帯のアクセスが改善されます。

5461.meaning_mnemonic: This <kanji>earth</kanji> <kanji>belt</kanji> is the area within the belt, which holds this area of earth in. It is separate from the rest of the earth, making it its own <vocabulary>zone</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>district</vocabulary>.
5461.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The diameter of this circle is ten centimeters.
examples.ja: この円の直径は10センチです。

examples.en: The diameter of the Earth is about 12,742 kilometers.
examples.ja: 地球の直径は約12,742キロメートルです。

examples.en: The cake was labeled as twenty cm in diameter, but the actual one was five mm short!
examples.ja: ケーキの直径20センチって書いてたのに、実物は5ミリ短かったんです！

examples.en: A new, gigantic species of jellyfish with a 100 foot diameter oozed onto the beach.
examples.ja: 直径100フィートもある巨大な新種のクラゲが、ビーチをドロドロにしてしまいました。

5462.meaning_mnemonic: Draw a <kanji>straight</kanji> line across the <kanji>diameter</kanji> of a circle, then measure it. This gives you the <vocabulary>diameter</vocabulary>. Whoa, look out everyone — we've got a geometry whiz in the room!
5462.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji, you'll know how to read this as well — just look out for ちょく getting shortened to ちょっ.

examples.en: The radius of this circle is ten centimeters.
examples.ja: この円の半径は10センチです。

examples.en: There are five convenience stores within a five kilometer radius.
examples.ja: 半径5km以内にコンビニが5つもあります。

examples.en: I'm the type of person whose mental health falls apart if there's no cat within a fifty centimeter radius.
examples.ja: 僕、半径50cm以内に猫がいないとメンタルがボロボロになる体質なんです。

examples.en: What is the volume in cubic centimeters of a sphere with a radius of three centimeters?
examples.ja: 半径3cmの球体の体積は何立方センチメートルですか。

5463.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Be sure to check the route to your destination in advance using Google Maps!
examples.ja: 事前にGoogleマップで目的地までの経路をチェックしておいてくださいね！

examples.en: I wonder how these small incidents make their way into the news.
examples.ja: こういう小さい事件って、どういう経路でニュースになるんだろうね。

5464.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>pass through</kanji> the <kanji>road</kanji>s, you are figuring out which roads to use, when to use them, and essentially coming up with the <vocabulary>route</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>course</vocabulary> to take to get to wherever you're going.
5464.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I called an ambulance because someone was injured.
examples.ja: ケガをした人がいたので、救急車をよびました。

examples.en: I stayed with the person and talked to them while waiting for the ambulance.
examples.ja: 救急車が来るまで、声をかけながら待っていた。

examples.en: I heard the sound of an ambulance, and when I looked outside, the person being taken away was making a peace sign and streaming on Instagram Live.
examples.ja: 救急車の音が聞こえて、外を見たら、運ばれてる人がピースしてて、インスタライブしてた。

examples.en: The ambulance suddenly took off and hit a guy, so we needed another ambulance.
examples.ja: 救急車が急発進して男性にぶつかったため、もう一台別の救急車も必要になった。

5465.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Rescue</kanji> in a <kanji>hurry</kanji> using this <kanji>car</kanji>. What kinds of cars can do this? How about an <vocabulary>ambulance</vocabulary>.
5465.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: They work every day to save people.

examples.en: Local volunteers have saved many lives.
examples.ja: 地元のボランティアが多くの命を救いました。

examples.en: Because you saved me, I am who I am now.
examples.ja: あなたが私を救ってくれたから、今の私がいるんです。

examples.en: I did everything I could to save him until the ambulance arrived.
examples.ja: 救急車が来るまで、彼を救うためにできることをしていました。

5466.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>rescue</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to rescue</vocabulary>.
5466.reading_mnemonic: The すく in the reading is a lot like the <reading>scue</reading> (すくう) part of <vocabulary>to rescue</vocabulary>, don't you think? Hopefully you do, so you can make the connection.

examples.en: Because it's distracting, let's turn off the TV and get to work.
examples.ja: 気が散るから、テレビを消して作業をしよう。

examples.en: The cherry blossoms scattered in the wind, creating a pink carpet on the ground.
examples.ja: サクラの花が風に散って、地面にピンクのカーペットができました。

examples.en: Sparks scattered, and a few embers flew towards me.
examples.ja: 火花が散り、少しだけ火の粉が飛んできました。

examples.en: The way the colored leaves fall is like saying goodbye to a lover, painful and beautiful.
examples.ja: 色づいた葉っぱが散る様子は、まるで恋人との別れのように、切なくて美しい。

5467.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>scatter</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to be scattered</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to get scattered</vocabulary>. 

散る is an intransitive verb, meaning something is scattering on its own. It's commonly used to describe when things like petals or leaves fall, fluttering down and scattering across the ground. It can also be used more abstractly, such as a crowd suddenly dispersing, your concentration breaking, your dreams falling apart, or even a soldier "falling" in battle.

You know 散る is intransitive because you rue (る) your decision not to go see the cherry blossoms when they were in bloom; now the petals have all scattered to the wind and you've missed your chance. Darn.
5467.reading_mnemonic: Think about something scattering. That something is <reading>chee</reading>se (ち), scattering all over the floor, going everywhere, getting in everything. Ugh, you hate how cheese scatters, don't you?

examples.en: The weather is nice today, so I'm thinking of going for a walk.
examples.ja: 今日は天気がいいので、散歩に出かけようと思っています。

examples.en: I enjoyed a café latte at a café I found while walking my dog.
examples.ja: 犬の散歩中に見つけたカフェで、カフェラテをエンジョイしました。

examples.en: When I go for a walk, I only carry small change.
examples.ja: 散歩をする時は、小銭しか持ち歩きません。

examples.en: These are my walking shoes and these are my running shoes.
examples.ja: こっちが散歩用のシューズで、こっちがランニング用のシューズなんです。

5468.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Scatter</kanji> around the ground and <kanji>walk</kanji>. When you walk in a scatter all around, you're going for <vocabulary>a walk</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>a stroll</vocabulary>.
5468.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The ほ goes to ぽ, though.

examples.en: What are the advantages and disadvantages of dissolving the House of Representatives?
examples.ja: 私達にとって、衆議院を解散するメリットとデメリットは何ですか？

examples.en: Thanks for the support, everyone! The Tofugu band is breaking up today, but I will forever cherish the memories I made with you guys at the show!
examples.ja: みんな、応援ありがとう！今日でトーフグバンドは解散するけど、みんなとライブで作った思い出は一生大切にするから！

examples.en: The drinking party broke up while you were stuck in the bathroom.
examples.ja: トイレにこもっているうちに飲み会は解散しちまったぜ。

5469.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Untie</kanji> and <kanji>scatter</kanji> everything. This will cause the <vocabulary>dissolution</vocabulary> the <vocabulary>breakup</vocabulary>, and indeed the <vocabulary>breaking up</vocabulary> of whatever is being untied then scattered.
5469.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Do you have grated parmesan cheese?
examples.ja: 粉チーズある？

examples.en: If you use this powder, the cake will turn out soft and fluffy.
examples.ja: この粉を使うと、ケーキがふわっと仕上がります。

examples.en: Be careful not to let the powder form clumps when sifting it.
examples.ja: 粉をふるうときは、ダマができないように気をつけてください。

examples.en: This bread is kind of floury and doesn't taste good.
examples.ja: このパン、なんか粉っぽくて美味しくない。

5470.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. Can also mean <vocabulary>flour</vocabulary>.
5470.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember:

Just imagine there's <vocabulary>powder</vocabulary> all over <reading>Cona</reading>n's (こな) hands and face. Detective Conan, that is. Conan has been investigating some kind of bakery murder. He had to dig through sacks of flour to find the hidden murder weapon (rolling pin, naturally) and now Conan is just covered in the white, starchy powder.

examples.en: This is something made by kneading wheat flour.
examples.ja: これは麦粉をこねて作ったものです。

examples.en: At home, we only had a very small amount of wheat flour left.
examples.ja: 家にはもう、ほんの少しの麦粉しか残っていませんでした。

examples.en: In Mesopotamia, they used to knead wheat flour with water to make flatbread to eat.
examples.ja: メソポタミアでは、麦粉を水でねって平焼きパンにして食べていたそうです。

examples.en: Today I opened a bag of wheat flour for the first time in long time and found a bunch of green worms wriggling in it.
examples.ja: 今日久々に麦粉が入った袋を開けたら、緑色のクネクネした幼虫が大量発生していました。

5471.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings. Since you didn't learn that reading for 粉 with the kanji, here's a mnemonic to help you out. What sort of people like <vocabulary>wheat flour</vocabulary> the most? <reading>子</reading>! 子 like wheat flour the most since it is both fun to eat and to play with. Silly 子, wheat flour is a food, not a toy.

examples.en: I got medicine for hay fever at the doctor's office.
examples.ja: 病院で花粉症の薬をもらいました。

examples.en: I heard that propolis helps with hay fever.
examples.ja: プロポリスが花粉症に効くって聞いたよ。

examples.en: My hay fever is so bad that at this point I could probably do without spring forever.
examples.ja: 花粉症やばすぎて、もう春いらないかも。

examples.en: My hay fever is so bad that I seriously thought, "If I get reincarnated, I want to be a piece of concrete."
examples.ja: 花粉症がつらすぎて、「生まれ変わったらコンクリートになりたい」と本気で思った。

5472.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>flower</kanji> <kanji>powder</kanji> <kanji>symptom</kanji>s are when you start sneezing from flower powder, aka pollen that comes from all sorts of flowers, which is pretty much all plants. This word, however, refers to the most common version of this sickness, which is <vocabulary>hay fever</vocabulary>.
5472.reading_mnemonic: The reading is all on'yomi readings, which you learned for all but 花. Instead, 花 is か, and to remember that you can think about how the only way to escape the <vocabulary>hay fever</vocabulary> is to jump in your <reading>ca</reading>r and turn on the filter. Sweet, sweet relief.

examples.en: This is a crayon that has been turned into powder.
examples.ja: これはクレヨンを粉状にしたものです。

examples.en: Finally, sprinkle the powdered chocolate on top.
examples.ja: 最後に、粉状にしたチョコレートを振りかけます。

examples.en: When shiratamako is in a fine powder form, it has more area exposed to the air, which makes it easier for its quality to deteriorate.
examples.ja: 白玉粉は、サラサラの粉状にすると空気と接触する部分が多くなって、品質が落ちやすいんですよ。

examples.en: I have a fresh red hot chili pepper but I want powdered chili pepper and I'm not sure how to do that.
examples.ja: 新鮮な鷹の爪があるので粉状の唐辛子にしたいなと思っているんですが、やり方がよく分かりません。

5473.meaning_mnemonic:
Something that is in a <kanji>powder</kanji> <kanji>condition</kanji> is something that has been <vocabulary>powdered</vocabulary>. Puff!

粉状 is a relatively formal word that is used to describe something being in powder form.
5473.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

You can also use kun'yomi for 粉 and say こなじょう. This reading is more common in casual speech.

examples.en: Firstly, I plan to start by expanding my local network of contacts.
examples.ja: まずはローカルの人脈を広げるとこから始めるつもりです。

examples.en: Then, I'm considering starting a business by leveraging this network.
examples.ja: それから、人脈を活かして、何かビジネスをスタートしようと思ってます。

examples.en: Networking is a very important skill for most business people, but it’s especially true for entrepreneurs.
examples.ja: 人脈作りは、ビジネスに関わる殆ど全ての人にとってとても重要なスキルですが、事業家にとっては殊更です。

examples.en: The Himalayan Mountain range is rich with a wide variety of nature.

5476.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Blood</kanji> flows through your <kanji>vein</kanji>s, carrying the stories of your <vocabulary>lineage</vocabulary>, your <vocabulary>bloodline</vocabulary>.

Note that this word is quite formal and literary.

examples.en: I got discounted vegetables at the supermarket.
examples.ja: スーパーで見切り品の野菜を安く買えた。

examples.en: My child says, "When I grow up, I want to become a vegetable."
examples.ja: うちの子、「大きくなったら野菜になりたい」って言うんです。

examples.en: No matter how full I am, I can eat vegetables.

5477.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>field</kanji> <kanji>vegetable</kanji> is still a <vocabulary>vegetable</vocabulary>, whether it comes from the field or not.
5477.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

5478.meaning_mnemonic: If you eat <kanji>vegetable</kanji> <kanji>food</kanji> you are on a <vocabulary>vegetarian diet</vocabulary>.
5478.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: This cargo is scheduled to be shipped tomorrow.

examples.ja: 毎日札幌貨物ターミナルと福岡貨物ターミナル間を走行する貨物列車があります。

5479.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the 物 reading that's もつ. You can know this because you have to carry the freight and cargo (持つ it!).

examples.en: I am quite familiar with this currency.

examples.en: Currency rates change daily.

examples.en: Many European countries use the euro as their currency.
examples.ja: ヨーロッパの多くの国ではユーロが通貨として使われています。

5480.meaning_mnemonic: The thing that will <kanji>pass through</kanji> <kanji>freight</kanji> is <vocabulary>currency</vocabulary>. Why? Because when you want freight to be your own, you have to put money through it and to the person who owns it. When you do that, it becomes yours. Use that currency!
5480.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Did the continent of Mu really exist?

examples.ja: ヨーロッパ大陸には、歴史的な建造物がたくさんあります。

examples.en: Let's go for a drive to feel the vastness of the North American continent.
examples.ja: 北アメリカ大陸の広さを感じるために、ドライブしてみようよ！

examples.en: Wait, you've already crossed a continent? Can that really be done in one day?
examples.ja: え、もう大陸を横断したの？それって本当に一日でできることなの？

5481.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>land</kanji> is the biggest types of land on this earth that there are. That is a <vocabulary>continent</vocabulary>.
5481.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: For some reason, my name was listed in that army record.
examples.ja: その陸軍の記録に、なぜか私の名前が記されていたんです。

examples.en: Whenever the army is mentioned, my father silently leaves the room.
examples.ja: 陸軍の話になると、父は必ずだまって部屋を出る。

examples.en: We're just here to observe the army training.
examples.ja: 私達は陸軍訓練を見に来たただの見学です。
