5482.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>land</kanji> <kanji>army</kanji> is the <vocabulary>land army</vocabulary>, also known as the plain old <vocabulary>army</vocabulary>.
5482.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: These pants look like the ones I've been trying to find for a while.
examples.ja: このズボン、私がずっと探してたズボンに似てる。

examples.en: Couples who have been together for a long time often end up looking alike.
examples.ja: 長く付き合うカップルは顔が似てくることが多い。

examples.en: At first I thought she looked like her mother, but then she started to look like her father too!
examples.ja: 最初はお母さんに似ていると思っていたけど、だんだんお父さんにも似てきたね！

examples.en: Isn't it unlikely that they look this similar by coincidence? I think it's fair if people call it a rip-off.
examples.ja: たまたまここまで似るのは流石になくない？パクリって言われてもしょうがない気がする。

5483.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>resemble</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to resemble</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to look like</vocabulary>.
5483.reading_mnemonic:
You should have learned this reading with the kanji, but here's a mnemonic to help you, just in case:

What are you trying <vocabulary>to resemble</vocabulary>?? Is that... oh no. A <reading>knee</reading> (に) face resemble surgery, where you make your face look like your knee and vice versa? Do you know how dangerous that surgery is?

examples.en: I am having trouble because my four-year-old daughter imitates everything she sees.
examples.ja: 四歳になる娘が、見るもの全てを真似するので困っています。

5484.meaning_mnemonic: You're taking <kanji>reality</kanji> and trying to <kanji>resemble</kanji> it. To do this, you have to do an <vocabulary>imitation</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>mimicry</vocabulary>, or an <vocabulary>impersonation</vocabulary>.
5484.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi reading for 真 and an irregular reading for 似. You've already learned the reading for 真, but here's a mnemonic to help you with 似:

What are you doing an <vocabulary>imitation</vocabulary> of? A horse! You gallop around <reading>neigh</reading>ing (ね) at the top of your lungs! That's a pretty good imitation.

examples.en: The average price of a meal at that restaurant is 1,500 yen.
examples.ja: そのレストランの食事の平均価格は1500円です。

examples.en: The average grade for 2014's National Center Test for University Admissions was revealed.
examples.ja: 2014年のセンター試験の平均点が出ました。

examples.en: The cafe's coffee was average, but the staff was really friendly.
examples.ja: そのカフェ、コーヒーは平均的だったけど、店員さんがすごくフレンドリーだったよ。

examples.en: The average height in Japan is about 170 cm for men and 157 cm for women.
examples.ja: 日本の平均身長は、男性が約170cm、女性が約157cmです。

5485.meaning_mnemonic: Something that's <kanji>flat</kanji> and <kanji>equal</kanji> to everything around it, all those flat things around it, are <vocabulary>average</vocabulary>. They're the <vocabulary>mean</vocabulary> (same as average).
5485.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Please cut them so that the sizes are as equal as possible.
examples.ja: 大きさがなるべく均等になるように切ってください。

examples.en: My job is to use a bulldozer to level the soil evenly.
examples.ja: ブルドーザーを使って、土を均等に平らにするのが私の仕事です。

examples.en: Career opportunities should be given equally to both men and women.
examples.ja: キャリアを積む機会は、男女に均等に与えられるべきです。

examples.en: Furthermore, the inheritance shares among siblings are divided equally as a general rule.
examples.ja: それから、兄弟姉妹の相続分は原則として均等に分けます。

5486.meaning_mnemonic: This is <kanji>equal</kanji> and that is <kanji>equal</kanji>. They're both the same, amazing! They carry <vocabulary>equality</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>uniformity</vocabulary>,  and <vocabulary>evenness</vocabulary>.
5486.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: She has a very well proportioned body.
examples.ja: 彼女はとても均整のとれた体形をしている。

examples.en: I couldn't help but sigh at the beautifully balanced and symmetrical architecture.
examples.ja: 均整のとれた美しい建築に思わずためいきが出た。

examples.en: Johnny's idols often have a prince-like, well-balanced appearance, don't they?
examples.ja: ジャニーズのアイドルって、均整のとれた王子様っぽい子が多いよね。

examples.en: Chopin's Polonaise No. 11 in G minor, even though it was composed when he was seven years old, is truly a well-balanced piece, isn't it?
examples.ja: ショパンのポロネーズ第11番ト短調って、7才の時に作曲した作品なのに実に均整がとれている作品ですよね。

5487.meaning_mnemonic: Things are <kanji>equal</kanji> in how they're <kanji>arrange</kanji>d. They have perfect <vocabulary>symmetry</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>balance</vocabulary>.
5487.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Our family graves are in Okayama Prefecture.
examples.ja: うちの家のお墓は岡山県にあります。

examples.en: I went to visit the family graves with my parents on Friday.
examples.ja: 金曜日に両親と墓参りに行ってきました。

examples.en: When visiting the family graves, the first thing we do is clean them.
examples.ja: お墓参りでは、まず最初に墓の掃除をします。

examples.en: I've always dreamed of placing our graves on a small island in the Pacific.
examples.ja: 僕たちの墓を太平洋に浮かぶ小さな島に作ることを、いつも夢見てきたんだよ。

5488.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

墓 means <vocabulary>grave</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>tomb</vocabulary>. Since you want to be respectful when talking about someone's eternal resting place, it's common to add the honorific お and say お墓.
5488.reading_mnemonic: You went to your <vocabulary>grave</vocabulary> because you were a <reading>hacker</reading> (はか). You made a lot of powerful enemies with all your hacker exploits, and before you knew it, you were six feet deep.

examples.en: When entering a cemetery, I hold my breath without thinking.
examples.ja: 墓地に入るとき、なんとなく息を止めてしまうんです。

examples.en: There was a sign saying "Welcome!" at the entrance of the cemetery…
examples.ja: 墓地の入口に「いらっしゃいませ」って看板があったんだけど…。

examples.en: I walked through the cemetery with Grandma — she knew everyone.
examples.ja: おばあちゃんと一緒に墓地を歩いたら、知り合いばっかだった。

examples.en: Our garden is adjacent to a cemetery.
examples.ja: うちの庭は墓地に隣接している。

5489.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>grave</kanji> <kanji>ground</kanji> is an area with lots of graves in the ground. This is a <vocabulary>cemetery</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>graveyard</vocabulary>.

墓地 is the standard word for a designated and organized cemetery.
5489.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The tallest mountain in Japan is Mount Fuji.
examples.ja: 日本一高い山は富士山です。

examples.en: When I said I was going to climb Mount Fuji, Mom made me a bento.
examples.ja: 富士山に登るって言ったら、ママが弁当を作ってくれた。

examples.en: Grandma said she used to do yoga on Mount Fuji all the time when she was young, is that true?
examples.ja: おばあちゃんが、若いころはよく富士山でヨガしてたって言ってたけど、本当かな？

examples.en: On the way down from Mount Fuji, I saw a sign that said "Welcome." It wasn't there when I was going up... Why!?
examples.ja: 富士山の下山中に見た看板、「ようこそ」って書いてあった。登りのときはなかったのに…。何故！？

5490.meaning_mnemonic: Did you know that the <kanji>mountain</kanji> that is <kanji>rich</kanji> in <kanji>samurai</kanji> happens to be Japan's most famous mountain? It makes sense considering samurai are probably Japan's most famous thing as well. Combine the two most famous things and you have <vocabulary>Mt Fuji</vocabulary> (or <vocabulary>Mount Fuji</vocabulary> if you'd rather write it that way).
5490.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The appeal of this website lies in its rich variety of content.
examples.ja: このサイトの魅力は、バラエティに富むコンテンツだ。

examples.en: That entrepreneur is not only intellectually gifted but also socially adept.
examples.ja: あの起業家は、知性だけでなく社交性にも富んでいてる。

examples.en: We are searching for individuals who can work flexibly even in a highly dynamic environment.
examples.ja: 変化に富んだ環境でも、フレキシブルに仕事ができる人材を探しています。

5491.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>rich</kanji> so the verb vocab version would be <vocabulary>to be rich in</vocabulary>.

富む is a formal word that's commonly used in writing. While it can refer to material wealth, it's more commonly used figuratively to describe an abundance of a certain quality, a place rich in nature or specific resources, or emotional richness or fulfillment.
5491.reading_mnemonic: Think about the richest person you know. That person is <reading>Tom</reading> (とむ). Imagine Tom as being super rich. If you don't know a Tom, think of a famous Tom, like Tom Cruise, who definitely is pretty rich.

examples.en: In the past, I wanted to gain both fame and wealth, but now all I want to gain is wealth.
examples.ja: 昔は名声も富も得たいと思っていましたが、今得たいのは富だけですね。

examples.en: It is not just money that brings wealth. True wealth is something felt when the heart becomes rich.
examples.ja: 富をもたらすのは、お金だけじゃないよ。真の富は、心が豊かになることで感じるものだからね。

examples.en: Making a fortune of millions is not as easy as I thought.
examples.ja: 巨万の富を築くことは思ったより簡単ではありません。

examples.en: They say that 90% of the world's wealth is actually in the possession of a small group of powerful people who make up the Cult of the Crabigator.
examples.ja: 世界の富の９割は、実はクラビゲーター教団を構成する少数の権力者たちが持っていると言われている。

5492.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are almost exactly the same. Someone who is <kanji>rich</kanji> has <vocabulary>wealth</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>riches</vocabulary>, right?
5492.reading_mnemonic: For the reading, think about the person you know with the most <vocabulary>wealth</vocabulary>. It is <reading>Tommy</reading> (とみ) Hilfiger.

examples.en: The Maldives is a highly popular resort destination among the wealthy class.
examples.ja: モルディブは富裕層の間で人気の高いリゾート地です。

examples.en: Coming from a wealthy family, you wouldn't understand.
examples.ja: 富裕な家庭出身のあなたには分からないでしょうね。

examples.en: I heard that WaniKani has elite club-like content accessible only to a small number of wealthy individuals. Is that true?
examples.ja: ワニカニには少数の富裕者だけがアクセスできるエリートクラブ的なコンテンツがあると聞いたのですが、本当ですか？

examples.en: Why do we separate people into the rich and the poor?
examples.ja: どうして人は富裕層と貧困層に分けられるのでしょうか。

5493.meaning_mnemonic: If you're <kanji>rich</kanji> and <kanji>abundant</kanji>, you are super <vocabulary>wealthy</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>affluent</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>rich</vocabulary>.
5493.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: There are moral education classes at school.
examples.ja: 学校では道徳の授業があります。

examples.en: The movie taught children the importance of morality.
examples.ja: その映画は、子供たちに道徳の大切さを教えました。

examples.en: As we grow up, we may have fewer chances to think about morality.
examples.ja: 大人になると、道徳について考える機会は少なくなるかもしれない。

examples.en: Why are you so sure that animals have no sense of morality?
examples.ja: どうして動物には道徳感がないって断言できるの？

5494.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>way</kanji> of <kanji>virtue</kanji> is the way you take if you have <vocabulary>morals</vocabulary>. Hopefully you have some.
5494.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Who is Ieyasu Tokugawa?
examples.ja: 徳川家康って誰？

examples.en: Doesn't my dog kind of look like someone from the Tokugawa family?
examples.ja: うちの犬、徳川家っぽい顔してると思わない？

examples.en: I said I wanted to go back to the Tokugawa era — Mom took my phone.
examples.ja: 徳川の時代にもどりたいって言ったら、ママにスマホ取り上げられた。

examples.en: She likes Japanese history and is very familiar with the Tokugawa Shogunate.
examples.ja: 彼女は歴女で、徳川幕府にはとても精通しています。

5495.meaning_mnemonic: This is one of those words that makes more sense when you look at the reading. The "Virtue River" isn't some virtuous river, it's in fact the <vocabulary>Tokugawa</vocabulary> family name, made famous by the Tokugawa shogunate. They ran Japan for a while, you know?
5495.reading_mnemonic: The readings are 徳 and the vocab 川 put together into one word. Once you can read this, you'll know the meaning too, so focus on the reading for this one. Just watch out for the rendaku that changes かわ to がわ!

examples.en: I haven't been to Tokushima yet, but I'd love to visit someday.
examples.ja: 徳島県にはまだ行ったことがないけど、いつか行ってみたいんだよね。

examples.en: I picked up a tourism pamphlet for Tokushima at the station.
examples.ja: 徳島県の観光パンフレットを駅でもらいました。

examples.en: I was surprised that Tokushima was more urban than I expected.
examples.ja: 徳島県、思ったより都会でびっくりした。

examples.en: Governor, in what ways would you change Tokushima Prefecture? I think I like things just the way they are.
examples.ja: 知事は、徳島県をどういう風に変えていくおつもりですか？私は今のままがいいと思うのですが。

5496.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>virtue</kanji> <kanji>island</kanji> <kanji>prefecture</kanji> is <vocabulary>Tokushima prefecture</vocabulary>. The reading will give away the meaning of this one, so long as you knew "prefecture."
5496.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the individual kanji. Put them together and you'll know this is <vocabulary>Tokushima Prefecture</vocabulary>.

examples.en: I'll help you look for your contact lens!
examples.ja: コンタクト、探すの手伝うよ！

examples.en: I looked online for a cheap hotel.
examples.ja: ネットで安いホテルを探してみた。

examples.en: I looked for the remote for ten minutes. It was in the toaster.
examples.ja: 10分探したリモコン、トースターの中にあった。

examples.en: A three legged dog walked into a bar and said, "I'm searching for the man who shot my paw. He looks like half fugu and half tofu."
examples.ja: 三本足の犬がバーにやって来てこう言った。「俺の足を撃った男を探しているんだ。半分河豚で半分豆腐みたいな男なんだが。」

5497.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>look for</kanji> and the verb version of the kanji is <vocabulary>to look for</vocabulary>.


Curious about the difference between 捜す and 探す? While there is some overlap between the two, 捜す is typically used in official, thorough searches for something or someone that is thought to concretely exist and has disappeared or cannot be easily found. In contrast, 探す can also be used for personal searches for things that one desires or is looking for.
5497.reading_mnemonic: You are looking for a <reading>sagger</reading> (さが) amongst the products you're shipping off overseas. The saggers are the boxes that have weird lumps sagging out of them, which means they broke and are getting things wet. So, find the saggers. Go <vocabulary>to search for</vocabulary> them, because they could ruin the whole shipment.

examples.en: Continuing to have an inquisitive mind is the key to growth.
examples.ja: 探究心を持ち続けることが、成長のカギです。

examples.en: WaniKani was created through researching how to learn kanji and vocabulary efficiently.
examples.ja: どうすれば効率よく漢字やボキャブラリーが習得できるのかを探究して出来上がったのがワニカニです。

examples.en: Only through inquiry can we discover new possibilities and perspectives.
examples.ja: 探究を通じてのみ、私たちは新しい可能性と視点を発見することができるんです。

examples.en: This book documents my research into religion, that is, a record of the search for truth.
examples.ja: 本書は私の宗教の探究、すなわち真理の探究の記録である。

5498.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Look for</kanji> something. <kanji>Research</kanji> answers. This is an <vocabulary>academic inquiry</vocabulary>, or in other words, <vocabulary>research</vocabulary>.
5498.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Maybe you've been watching detective dramas a bit too much?
examples.ja: 探偵ドラマの見すぎじゃない？

examples.en: She ended up becoming a private detective.
examples.ja: 彼女は結局探偵になりました。

examples.en: My grandpa says, "I used to be a detective," but I wonder if it's true.
examples.ja: おじいちゃんが「オレは昔、探偵だった」って言ってるんだけど、本当かなぁ？

examples.en: Our dog loves playing detective. He's always sniffing shoes. It's so cute, isn't it?
examples.ja: うちの犬、探偵ごっこが大好きなんです。ずっとクツをクンクンかいじゃって、かわいいですよね。

5499.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>look for</kanji> things and you <kanji>spy</kanji> on people. Your job isn't as glamorous as it sounds. You're a <vocabulary>private detective</vocabulary>.
5499.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: When do the police conduct their secret internal investigation?
examples.ja: 警察はどんな時に内偵捜査をするのですか。

examples.en: I heard that restaurant was secretly investigated by the tax office.
examples.ja: あのレストラン、税務署の内偵調査が入ったらしいよ。

examples.en: I asked a detective agency to secretly investigate my husband's affair.
examples.ja: 探偵事務所に夫の浮気の内偵調査をお願いしました。

examples.en: I heard the Kyoto Prefectural Police have started a covert investigation.
examples.ja: 京都府警が内偵を開始したらしいよ。

5500.meaning_mnemonic:
When you go <kanji>inside</kanji> somewhere to quietly <kanji>spy</kanji> on someone, you're doing a <vocabulary>secret investigation</vocabulary>.

内偵 is a formal word for investigations where the target doesn't know they're being investigated. It can mean an <vocabulary>undercover investigation</vocabulary> by police, or it can be a secret check on a business partner, a new hire, or even a suspicious spouse by companies or detectives.
5500.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: This dish is very delicious.
examples.ja: この料理はとても美味しいです。

examples.en: The croissants from that bakery were delicious.
examples.ja: そのベーカリーのクロワッサンは、とても美味しかったです。

examples.en: Honestly, working with this team at this company is quite fortunate.
examples.ja: 正直、この会社のこのチームで働けるのはかなり美味しいです。

5501.meaning_mnemonic:
Something with a <kanji>beauty</kanji> <kanji>taste</kanji> is something that is really <vocabulary>tasty</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>delicious</vocabulary>. Mmmm, yum!

While 美味しい mostly describes tasty food, you may also occasionally see it being used for a sweet deal or situation that benefits you.
5501.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this makes no sense at all. You'll have to learn it straight up, that is, unless you know the word おいしい already, which many people do as it's used in every other sentence in every Japanese variety show. If you don't know this word already, just think of yourself eating something <vocabulary>delicious</vocabulary>. It's so delicious it makes you mad, I have no idea why. You yell at the chef: "<reading>OI</reading> (おい). OI! WHY IS THIS SO DELICIOUS????"

examples.en: It was a very beautiful starry sky.
examples.ja: とっても綺麗な星空でした。

examples.en: Kawaguchi-san's house is always clean and tidy.
examples.ja: 川口さんの家は、いつも綺麗に片付いています。

examples.en: I can't trust people who only say things that sound good.
examples.ja: 綺麗事ばっかり言う人は信じられません。

examples.en: "Salmon, you're the most beautiful woman I've ever met." "Fugu, that's such a lie."
examples.ja: 「君みたいに綺麗な女性に会ったのは初めてだよ、サーモン。」「フグったら、ウソばっかり。」

5502.meaning_mnemonic:
Things that are <kanji>beautiful</kanji> and <kanji>lovely</kanji> are very <vocabulary>beautiful</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>pretty</vocabulary>, and often <vocabulary>clean</vocabulary>, too. You can call someone 綺麗. You can also mention how clean something is with 綺麗. Gives you some insight as to what "beauty" is in Japan, I suppose. Take your baths, folks.

Wondering what the difference is between 綺麗 and 美しい? 美しい is more dramatic, so it implies you’re really blown away by something’s (or someone’s) beauty. 綺麗, on the other hand, is a more everyday word that covers anything that’s beautiful, pretty, or even just clean. In other words, the bar is a bit lower for 綺麗!
5502.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Because of my layoff, physically and mentally I'm torn apart.
examples.ja: 会社を首にされ、身も心もズタズタです。

examples.en: Blowfish are a white-fleshed fish.
examples.ja: フグは白身の魚です。

examples.en: At that time, my mother had a gold bracelet on.
examples.ja: その時、母は金のブレスレットを身につけてました。

5503.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>somebody</kanji>, but the word is <vocabulary>body</vocabulary>. I guess somebody is somebody's body, so they are similar at least. It also refers to <vocabulary>animal flesh</vocabulary> sometimes, meaning the non-bone edible parts of animals, including seafood. It's the "mi" in sashimi!

Wonder about the difference between 体 and 身? 体 refers to physical human and animal bodies, often describing their condition, appearance, etc. While 身 can also mean "physical human body," it can also refer to the self as an individual and be used to indicate one’s social standing or position. That's why you might see 身 used in idiomatic phrases like 身につく, which refers to acquiring or mastering something, like a skill.
5503.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: Who is that somebody? Who is that <vocabulary>body</vocabulary>? Why, of course it is <reading>me</reading> (み).

examples.en: I'll be transferring to a new department starting next month.
examples.ja: 来月から新しい部署に移ることになりました。

examples.en: Now, let's shift to the next discussion.
examples.ja: それでは、次の話題に移りましょう。

examples.en: I haven't been able to make even one friend since I relocated to this town.
examples.ja: この町に移ってきてからまだ友達が一人もできません。

examples.en: I don't like yakiniku because the smell gets on your clothes.
examples.ja: においが服に移るから、焼肉は好きじゃないの。

5504.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>shift</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to be shifted</vocabulary>. You know that this is the one where something is shifted (and you're not doing the shifting), because it's really <reading>ru</reading>de (る) to be shifted, and you don't like it when people do it to you (because it happens quite a lot, strangely).
5504.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 移す, so use that to remember this!

examples.en: "It’s tomorrow, but I think we should still cancel our wedding." "You took the words right out of my mouth."
examples.ja: 「もう明日だけど、でも、やっぱり、私たちの結婚式を中止するべきだと思うの。」「僕もそれを言おうと思っていたんだ。」

5505.meaning_mnemonic: If 結婚 is <kanji>marriage</kanji>, then a marriage <kanji>ceremony</kanji> is a <vocabulary>marriage ceremony</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>wedding</vocabulary>.
5505.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: If you have to push a button to open the doors, can you still call them automatic doors?
examples.ja: 押しボタン式のドアでも、自動ドアって呼ぶのかな。

5506.meaning_mnemonic: If 押し is <kanji>push</kanji>, and a ボタン is a button, then you have yourself a <vocabulary>push button</vocabulary>.
5506.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 押す.

examples.en: Please feel free to use the futon in the closet if you wish.
examples.ja: 押入れの布団、良ければ使って下さいね。

5507.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>push</kanji> things to make them <kanji>enter</kanji> the <vocabulary>closet</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>cupboard</vocabulary>.
5507.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 押し (push the し inside the 押) plus 入れる's reading.

examples.en: Although he is a famous fiction writer, he sometimes self-publishes his books.
examples.ja: 彼は有名な小説家だが、時々自費出版することもあるんだよ。

5508.meaning_mnemonic: If 出版 is <kanji>publishing</kanji>, then the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to publish</vocabulary>.
5508.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 出版, so if you know that you know this. Also, it's just the kanji readings too, so no problemo for a person like you, I'm sure.

examples.en: You have to show your ID card to enter the publishing company.
examples.ja: その出版社では、入館の際に身分証明書を提示しなければなりません。

5509.meaning_mnemonic: If 出版 means <kanji>publishing</kanji>, then a <kanji>company</kanji> that does said publishing is a <vocabulary>publishing company</vocabulary>.
5509.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Will help to know the word 出版 as well, though.

5557.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>acid</kanji> <kanji>element</kanji> is <vocabulary>oxygen</vocabulary>. In German it’s the same as in Japanese - it’s called “Sauerstoff”, including “sauer”, the word for “sour”. The noun version is “Säure” which means both “sourness” and “acid” (which again is the same in Japanese, the same kanji is used in both words). The word “oxygenium” in Greek/Latin literally means “acid maker”. Long ago chemists thought oxygen was a defining characteristic of acids, later they found out there are also acids without oxygen like hydrochloric/muriatic/salt acid and the defining characteristic actually is hydrogen. But the name stuck.

Or you could just imagine all the oxygen you breathe has turned into acid (oh no!), and it sucks to breathe. Whatever works for you.

5608.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned 漏れる means "to leak." 漏らす is the transitive version, which means it takes a direct object. So this means <vocabulary>to let something leak</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to leak something</vocabulary>. The reason you let something leak is because you <reading>rush</reading>ed (らす) the job (because you did it yourself)!

Even though it's transitive, 漏らす often implies an unintentional leak, as in おしっこを漏らす (wet one's pants) or 水を漏らすな (don't let water spill). It's also used figuratively, like 秘密を漏らす (leak a secret), 不満を漏らす (express dissatisfaction), or ためいきを漏らす (let out a sigh).

This is very similar in meaning to 越える. Both can refer to overcoming some physical object or passing beyond a certain amount of time. However, 越す tends to sound a little less intense, while 越える really focuses on the physical or emotional challenge of overcoming a certain milestone. For example, while 山を越す simply refers to crossing a mountain, 山を越える gives the impression that crossing the mountain is a difficulty you've overcome.

5703.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned 迷う means "to go astray," and 迷わす is its transitive version, meaning it takes a direct object. So it means <vocabulary>to lead someone astray</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to perplex someone</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to mislead someone</vocabulary>.

While 迷わす can mean literally causing someone to get lost, it's more commonly used for the act of confusing someone — for example, overwhelming them with difficult choices or intentionally misleading them in a malicious way.

You know this verb is transitive because there's nothing <reading>worse</reading> (わす) than purposefully misleading someone. Intentionally leading someone astray is worse than anything!
5703.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 迷う, so use that so you aren't lead astray too.

examples.en: It will take a little time to load the luggage, so wait there!
examples.ja: 荷物を積むのに少し時間がかかるから、そこで待ってて！

examples.en: He steadily and diligently accumulated experience and earned his current position.
examples.ja: アイツは地道にコツコツ経験を積んで、今の地位を手に入れたんだよ。

examples.en: Now please grab a partner and begin loading the truck with turkey.
examples.ja: それじゃあ2人組を作って、トラックに七面鳥を積み始めて下さい。

examples.en: His "to-be-read" list had many books piled up.
examples.ja: 彼の積ん読リストには、たくさんの本が積まれていた。

5704.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned that 積もる (to accumulate) is used when something like snow or dust piles up over time. 積む is the transitive version, so it means <vocabulary>to pile something up</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to stack up</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to load</vocabulary>. You know this because you are the one <reading>mo</reading>ving (む) things to pile them up!

積む is often used for physical actions like stacking boxes or loading luggage, but it's also used in more abstract ways, such as building up experience or skills. Think of it like "stacking up" experience points to level up in your life!
5704.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 積もる, so pile up your knowledge and remember it that way.

examples.en: This event is hosted by the city.
examples.ja: このイベントは市が主催するものです。

examples.en: Our school is hosting a karaoke party this Saturday. Would you like to join us?
examples.ja: うちの学校で土曜日にカラオケパーティーを主催するんだけど、よかったら来ない？

examples.en: How many users do you think would join if WaniKani hosted a kanji boot camp?
examples.ja: ワニカニが漢字合宿を主催したら、参加してくれるユーザーさんはどれくらいいると思いますか？

examples.en: Some elderly ladies in the neighborhood hosted a bingo tournament, and the first prize was gold dentures.
examples.ja: 近所のおばあちゃんたちがビンゴ大会を主催してくれたんだけど、一位の景品は金の入れ歯でした。

5705.meaning_mnemonic:
If 主催 means "host" or "hosting," the verb version of that would be <vocabulary>to host</vocabulary>.

主催する refers to hosting events, especially formal ones like conferences, concerts, or company parties. It's not just about "doing" an event — it shows that the person or group is the main sponsor and organizer, the one really in charge of making it happen.
5705.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know the word 主催 already as well.

examples.en: I can't forget the face of the gorilla urging for a banana.
examples.ja: バナナを催促するゴリラの顔が忘れられない。

examples.en: I pressed my sister for a reply on LINE, and she just sent a sticker.
examples.ja: 妹にLINEの返事を催促したら、スタンプだけ返ってきた。

examples.en: My girlfriend pushed me to propose… I'm not ready.
examples.ja: 彼女にプロポーズを催促された。まだ心の準備が…

examples.en: I'm sorry to be so demanding, but can you take some pictures of Tokyo Tower and send them to me by Monday please? Thanks.
examples.ja: 催促するようで申し訳ありませんが、東京タワーの写真を何枚か撮って月曜日までに送ってもらえませんでしょうか。

5706.meaning_mnemonic: If 催促 is <kanji>urge</kanji>, then the verb version would be <vocabulary>to urge</vocabulary>.
5706.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Will help to know 催促 first.

examples.en: The training to become a burglar is as hard as boot camp.
examples.ja: 泥棒になるためのトレーニングは、ブートキャンプ並にハードです。

5707.meaning_mnemonic: I don't know why a <kanji>mud</kanji> <kanji>pole</kanji> is a <vocabulary>robber</vocabulary>, but for some reason it is. Just imagine a robber covering himself in mud and standing behind a pole to hide, then jump out, then rob you of everything you've got.
5707.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 泥 plus the reading for 棒 put together.

examples.en: Glasses suit Koichi better than contact lenses.
examples.ja: コウイチにはコンタクトよりもメガネが似合います。

examples.en: I think a denim jacket would totally go with that dress.
examples.ja: そのワンピには絶対デニムのジャケットが似合うと思うよ。

examples.en: Unfortunately, it's not always the case that one's favorite color will suit one.
examples.ja: 残念ながら、自分の好きな色が必ずしも自分に似合うとは限らないのよね。

5708.meaning_mnemonic: It <kanji>resemble</kanji>s you! It <kanji>suit</kanji>s you! Wow, your good looks really cause this scarf <vocabulary>to suit</vocabulary> you, you know?
5708.reading_mnemonic: The reading is from 似る and 合う, put together.

examples.en: The 23-year-old new recruit surprised everyone who works with him by marrying the 82-year-old CEO.
examples.ja: 23歳の新入社員は82歳のCEOと結婚して、一緒に仕事をする人全員を驚かした。

5709.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 驚く is "to be surprised"? This is when you are surprising someone else, doing the surprising, making this word <vocabulary>to surprise</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to shock</vocabulary>.
5709.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 驚く. Don't be surprised if you remember the reading of this word because of your past knowledge.

examples.en: "I’ve been awake since four this morning." "No way! What have you been doing?" "Well, just cleaning around the house."
examples.ja: 「今朝は4時から起きてるよ。」「嘘でしょ？いったい何してるの？」「えっと…家を大掃除してるの。」

5710.meaning_mnemonic: 掃除 is <kanji>cleaning</kanji>, so the verb version would be <vocabulary>to clean</vocabulary>.
5710.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Also, it'll help to know the word 掃除 as well.

examples.en: I love you so much. I need you. Could you please dry my wet shirts right now, Mr. Sun? Please!!!!
examples.ja: あなたを愛しています。僕にはあなたが必要なんです。太陽さん、どうか僕の濡れたシャツを今すぐ乾かしてくれませんか？お願いします！！！

5711.meaning_mnemonic: 乾く is "to be dried." This is the version where you're doing the drying, making this <vocabulary>to dry something</vocabulary>. You know this because it's annoying to have to dry something yourself, so you <reading>cuss</reading> (かす) endlessly as you do it. "#$@%! Why do I have to waste my time drying this %&$# thing?!"
5711.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 乾く.

examples.en: Why am I so good at making a mess?
examples.ja: 俺、どうしてこんなに散らかすのが得意なんだろう？

examples.en: Every day, I clean up the toys my child scattered before going to bed.
examples.ja: 私は毎日、子供が散らかしたおもちゃを片付けてから寝ます。

examples.en: Leaving trash scattered about is bad manners, you know.
examples.ja: ゴミを散らかしたままにするのは、マナー違反ですよ。

examples.en: Even if I cleaned them up, I would just make a mess again the next day.
examples.ja: 掃除しても、次の日にはまたすぐ散らかしちゃうんだよね。

examples.en: I mean, everyone says "hage-chirakasu" (balding in a scattered, patchy way), but baldness isn't something that "scatters" or that you can "tidy up." That kind of expression is just rude.
examples.ja: いや、みんな「ハゲ散らかす」ってよく言うけど、ハゲは別に「散らかす」も「片付ける」もできないものだから！そんな言い方、失礼だろ。

5712.meaning_mnemonic:
散る is "to be scattered." 散らかす on the other hand is when you're doing the scattering. So it means <vocabulary>to scatter</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to make a mess</vocabulary>.

You often hear it when someone talks about making a room messy or leaving things all over the place. You can remember it easily because after a <reading>ruckus</reading> (らかす), people often leave a mess behind.
5712.reading_mnemonic: The reading of the 散 comes from 散る. So, go ahead and scatter more memories around your brain, you got this already.

examples.en: It's dangerous to take your eyes off your child while swimming!
examples.ja: 水泳中は、子供から目を離すと危ないよ！

examples.en: Shouldn't we put this microwave and toaster a little farther apart from each other?
examples.ja: この電子レンジとトースター、もうちょっと離して置いた方がいいんじゃない？

examples.en: Sorry, I'm in the middle of something. I'll call you back. Okay?
examples.ja: ごめん。いま手が離せないんだ。後でかけ直してもいいかな？

examples.en: That marathon runner is said to have cruised across the finish line, a full hundred meters ahead of the runner-up.
examples.ja: あのマラソン選手は、二番手を百メートルも離して余裕でゴールインしたそうです。

5713.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 離れる means "to separate," where something separates or moves away from something else? Well, 離す is the transitive version, so it takes a direct object and means <vocabulary>to separate something</vocabulary>. You can remember this because if you try to separate two people who don't want to be separated, they might sue (す) you in response!

離す is used when you detach or put space between people or objects. This could be literal, like when you 離す your bed from the wall, or more figurative, like when you carelessly 離す your eyes from something important. 

It can also mean <vocabulary>to let go</vocabulary> of something, because you're "separating" your hand from it. This use is very similar to 放す, but it doesn't have that nuance of setting something free — it's just the neutral act of letting go of something.
5713.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 離れる.

examples.en: The plural of sheep is sheep.
examples.ja: Sheepの複数形はsheepです。

examples.en: My friend said, "You don't even know the plural of this word?" and laughed at me, and I was very hurt.
examples.ja: 「この単語の複数形も知らないの？」って友達に笑われて、とても傷つきました。

examples.en: In Japanese you don’t need to change things to the plural form as often as in English.
examples.ja: 日本語では英語に比べて単語を複数形にすることは少ないです。

5714.meaning_mnemonic: If 複数 is <kanji>multiple</kanji>, and 形 is <kanji>shape</kanji>, then when something is in a "multiple shape," it has more than one version of itself. It's the <vocabulary>plural</vocabulary>, or the <vocabulary>plural form</vocabulary>.
5714.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Will help to know the word 複数 as well.

examples.en: Understood.
examples.ja: 了解しました。

examples.en: Got it! I'll head over there right now.
examples.ja: 了解！今すぐそっちに向かうよ。

examples.en: Understood. Let's take time to discuss it tomorrow.
examples.ja: 了解です。明日ゆっくり話し合いましょう。

examples.en: At our office, there's a tacit understanding that we should not eat Mami's bacon without her permission.
examples.ja: うちのオフィスには、マミのベーコンを勝手に食べてはいけないという暗黙の了解がある。

5715.meaning_mnemonic:
When you've <kanji>finish</kanji>ed <kanji>solv</kanji>ing something, you've come to a point of <vocabulary>understanding</vocabulary>. 

了解 is often used to show your understanding of information or instructions that have been communicated to you, similar to "<vocabulary>Got it</vocabulary>" or "<vocabulary>Understood</vocabulary>." It can also be used to show agreement, approval, or consent, since those things naturally depend on mutual understanding too.
5715.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I am the owner of that wallet.
examples.ja: そのサイフの持ち主は私です。

examples.en: Did you find the owner who’d lost it?
examples.ja: 落とし主は見つかりましたか？

examples.en: I recognized the owner of the voice easily, even without seeing his face.
examples.ja: 顔を見なくても、声の主はすぐ分かりました。

examples.en: This pond is home to a large tree frog called the Lord of the Old Pond.
examples.ja: この池には、古池の主と呼ばれる大きなトノサマガエルが住んでいます。

5716.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>master</kanji> is the <vocabulary>owner</vocabulary> who has dominance or control over something.

主 is usually used with other words to indicate a person who owns something or who is principally involved in an action. That might sound a little vague, so check out the collocations and context sentences to get a better grasp of this word!
5716.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is of course different from what you learned with the kanji. Think of this:

The <vocabulary>owner</vocabulary> of those <reading>nu</reading>de <reading>shee</reading>p (ぬし) doesn’t even need their wool, he just likes owning nude sheep. So he keeps them as pets and shaves them every day. He’s not interested in sheep with fur. Only nude sheep for this owner!

examples.en: Social rules are important.
examples.ja: 社会のルールは大切だ。

examples.en: I am worried about the Japanese social system.
examples.ja: 日本社会のシステムに不安があります。

examples.en: Foreigners are members of the society too.
examples.ja: 外国人も社会のメンバーです。

5717.meaning_mnemonic: Not to be confused with 会社, which is a company, this is <vocabulary>society</vocabulary>. When a <kanji>company</kanji> <kanji>meet</kanji>s together, it's like a bunch of people, who are in groups, who come together to live in one world. That is a <vocabulary>society</vocabulary>.
5717.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I have a kind of telephone phobia and my heart starts beating very fast whenever I talk on the phone.
examples.ja: 電話恐怖症みたいなのがあって、電話で話をする時に心臓がバクバクするんです。

5718.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>heart</kanji> <kanji>internal organs</kanji> is the <vocabulary>heart</vocabulary>, of course.
5718.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: My grandfather died of inflammation of the lungs.
examples.ja: 私の祖父は肺臓炎で亡くなりました。

5719.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: They take the internal organs out of deer in my neighbor’s garage.
examples.ja: ご近所さんのガレージで鹿の内臓を取り出すんです。

5720.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Inside</kanji> <kanji>internal organs</kanji> are your <vocabulary>internal organs</vocabulary>, though you'd think the second kanji would give a hint to that without the 内.
5720.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: "Dad, Fugu and I are getting married and moving to Japan." "Not while I’m alive, you won’t."
examples.ja: 「パパ、フグと私、結婚して日本に引っ越すつもりよ。」「俺の目の黒いうちはそんなことはさせないぞ。」

5721.meaning_mnemonic: 越す is "to go beyond." Now you're going beyond your home and <kanji>pull</kanji>ing everything with you to go to another home. You are trying <vocabulary>to move</vocabulary> / <vocabulary>to move homes</vocabulary>.
5721.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 引く and 越す put together. Careful of that っ.

examples.en: I always wave my hand to say hi whenever I pass other bikers.
examples.ja: 他の自転車走者を追い越す時、いつも挨拶代わりに手を振ります。

5722.meaning_mnemonic: 越す means "to go beyond." 追 is <kanji>follow</kanji>. If you are following someone, and then you go beyond them, you have overtaken them. That's why this word means <vocabulary>to overtake</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to surpass</vocabulary>.
5722.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 追う and 越す put together into one. You can overtake this word now that you know that.

examples.en: My grandparents still see their pediatrician.
examples.ja: 私の祖父母はまだ小児科医にかかっています。

5723.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 祖父 is grandfather and 祖母 is grandmother. This is both combined. Is it some hybrid grandmapa monster you've created in your lab? Hardly, it just refers to your <vocabulary>grandparents</vocabulary>.
5723.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 祖父 and 祖母, which are exceptional readings on their own, so you'll need them in order to be able to read this one too.

examples.en: If a dog’s owner had chickenpox, could the dog get it too?
examples.ja: もし犬の飼い主が水疱瘡になったら、その犬も水疱瘡になる可能性はあるんでしょうか。

5724.meaning_mnemonic: You know that to 飼う is "to keep a pet." If you're the <kanji>master</kanji> that is <kanji>keeping a pet</kanji> (飼う), then you are the <vocabulary>pet owner</vocabulary>.
5724.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi readings for both. You'll need to remember the words 飼う and 主 to be able to remember the reading of this word.

examples.en: Aren’t I too young to be called a middle-aged woman? I’m hurt.
examples.ja: おばちゃんって呼ばれる年齢かなあ。傷つくなあ。

5725.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 傷 is "wound"? Now a wound is つくing to you, or in other words, is getting attached to you. If you get a wound attached to your body, you are probably going <vocabulary>to get hurt</vocabulary>.
5725.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the word 傷.

examples.en: I might have scratched my contact lens.
examples.ja: コンタクトレンズを傷つけちゃったかも。

examples.en: We may also be hurting people without knowing it.
examples.ja: 私たちも知らないうちに人を傷つけているかもしれません。

examples.en: Who the heck damaged my Mercedes with an iron bar?! They'll pay for this!
examples.ja: 誰だよ？俺のベンツに鉄棒で傷つけやがったのは？！見つけたらただじゃおかねえぞ！

5726.meaning_mnemonic: You つける (attach) a <kanji>wound</kanji> to someone or something. In other words, this means <vocabulary>to hurt someone</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to scratch</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to damage</vocabulary> something.
5726.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 傷. If you remember the reading for that you got this too.

examples.en: For me, disposable pocket warmers are indispensable in winter.
examples.ja: 私にとって、使い捨てカイロは冬には無くてはならないものです。

5727.meaning_mnemonic: After you <kanji>use</kanji> it you <kanji>throw away</kanji> it, making whatever it is you used a <vocabulary>disposable</vocabulary> item.
5727.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 使う and 捨てる, combined into one.

examples.en: I threw my alarm clock away when it went off at six this morning.
examples.ja: 今朝、六時に目覚ましがなった時に、その時計を投げ捨ててしまいました。

5728.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>throw</kanji> and <kanji>throw away</kanji> something. That's why this means <vocabulary>to throw away</vocabulary>.
5728.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 投げる and 捨てる, combined into one garbage inducing dump of a word.

examples.en: I didn’t have enough time to load rounds into the shotgun.
examples.ja: ショットガンに弾を込める時間がなかったんだ。

examples.en: Put more emotion in your performance! Are you really a professional theatrical actor?
examples.ja: もっと気持ちを込めて演技しろよ！それでもプロの劇団員か？

5729.meaning_mnemonic: You know the kanji 込 means <kanji>into</kanji>. This verb is transitive, meaning you are doing the action. If you “do something into something” you are putting it into that thing. So this means <vocabulary>to put in</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to load something</vocabulary>.
5729.reading_mnemonic:
Lucky for you, the reading you learned with the kanji is the one you use here. In case you need a hand with the okurigana, here’s a mnemonic for you:

You always try <vocabulary>to put in</vocabulary> your emotions into the <reading>mail</reading> (める) you send. You don't just load your mail with words, but also with emotions, to make it truly heartfelt mail.

examples.en: I forgot to apply for the JLPT exam.
examples.ja: JLPTのテストに申し込むのを忘れてしまった。

5730.meaning_mnemonic:
I must <kanji>say humbly</kanji> that I want to get <kanji>into</kanji> this position, so I'm planning <vocabulary>to apply</vocabulary> for it and <vocabulary>to submit an application</vocabulary>.

申し込む isn't just about applying, though. It's about officially communicating desires, whether you want <vocabulary>to propose</vocabulary> marriage, challenge someone to a game of tennis, or even offer a donation to a good cause.
5730.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the word 申す and the kanji 込, stuck together... humbly.

examples.en: He hooked up my PlayStation to his TV before leaving our house to commit suicide by jumping in front of a train. Do you think it means something?
examples.ja: あいつ、飛び込み自殺をするために家を出る前、俺のプレイステーションをあいつのテレビに繋いだんだよな。何か意味があったのかな？

5731.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>fly</kanji> <kanji>into</kanji> something and "commit suicide" (自殺) is <vocabulary>suicide by train</vocabulary>. Unfortunately, this is a term you should probably be familiar with because it comes up from time to time on the news and around train stations. (Hopefully someday it will no longer be a term you need to know and we can remove it forever.)
5731.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 飛ぶ, 込, and 自殺. Combine them together to read this entire word.

examples.en: You better hurry up and fill out an application. The office will close in ten minutes.
examples.ja: 急いで申込書に書き込んだ方がいいよ。あと十分で事務所は閉まっちゃうんだから。

5732.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 書く is "to write" and the kanji 込 is into, so this means <vocabulary>to write in</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to fill out</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to jot down</vocabulary>.

書き込む focuses more on the physical action of writing than 書く on its own. This is because 込む stresses that you’re putting words INTO some space, either on paper or on computer.
5732.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the word 書く and the kanji 込 combined into one.

examples.en: I can't go into the middle of a crowd of people because I'm scared.
examples.ja: 怖くて人込みの中に行けません。

examples.en: When I walk inside Shinjuku Station, I always get frustrated with the crowds of people.
examples.ja: 新宿駅構内を歩く時は、人込みでいつもイライラする。

examples.en: After saying so, the man vanished into the crowd.
examples.ja: 男はそう言うと、人込みにまぎれて消えてしまった。

5733.meaning_mnemonic:
When a <kanji>person</kanji> goes <kanji>into</kanji> a place (then another person goes into the place, and then another person and another person), that place eventually gets filled with a <vocabulary>crowd of people</vocabulary>.

Note that this word is more commonly written 人混み.
5733.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the word 人 and the kanji 込. Just keep in mind that the こ changes to ご and you'll be fine.

examples.en: Couldn’t you find some way to remove this stain?
examples.ja: この染みなんとか取れないかなあ。

5734.meaning_mnemonic: This is the noun version of 染. A dye would seem like the right answer, but what else is a dye? If you get it on you when you don't want to get it on you, it becomes a <vocabulary>stain</vocabulary>.
5734.reading_mnemonic: The reading is unlike what you learned with this kanji before. 5747.meaning_mnemonic:
This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. This adjective describes things that are <kanji>valuable</kanji> in a way that transcends monetary worth, so it means <vocabulary>noble</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>invaluable</vocabulary>.

While 尊い is used for things you honor from the heart, 貴い leans toward a dignified, noble kind of value — the kind tied to high status or social rank. Because of that, you may encounter 貴い in stories about historical class systems or old social hierarchies. It doesn't appear as commonly as 尊い in modern Japanese, but you may still see it in descriptions of someone's noble presence or the sense of dignity they give off.
5747.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. This has the same reading as 尊い (revered, noble), so if you remember that, you can read 貴い too! In case you forgot, here's a mnemonic to help you: 

How can you tell if someone comes from a <vocabulary>noble</vocabulary> background? Just check their <reading>toe toe</reading> (とうと). Most noble families are pretty inbred, so a lot of their members will have a big toe (the long とう) with another small toe growing out of it (short と). This is a common birth defect among inbred aristocrats. Of course, from their point of view, it's <vocabulary>invaluable</vocabulary> proof of how noble and superior they are.

P.S. You'll often see some gangstah thug call a higher ranking gangstah thug (one that acts like an older brother to all the other gangstah thugs) this. It's like family within the gang.

5749.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>valuable</kanji> <kanji>formal name ender</kanji>. It's like saying "the valuable great you"... or something. Anyways, this means <vocabulary>you</vocabulary>, but it isn't as nice as it sounds.

貴様 used to be a polite way to say "you," but in modern Japanese it's almost always a strong insult, roughly like saying <vocabulary>you bastard</vocabulary>. The tone is dramatic, so you'll hear it from anime villains, but not usually in real conversation unless someone's joking around and pretending to be Vegeta from Dragon Ball.

Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>descend</kanji>, but this word means something closer to <vocabulary>to fall</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to come down</vocabulary>.

This word is often used in a positive context for recommending things, actions, and people by implying or pointing out their charms, merits, or both.

Although 薦める and 勧める are similar, there are subtle differences between the two. 勧める is often used to suggest that someone perform a specific action, often as friendly advice or encouragement. It can also be used when offering something, such as a drink. On the other hand, 薦める is used to recommend a person or thing as suitable for a particular situation, with a focus on endorsing the subject rather than a specific action.

5810.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

5812.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

5813.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji is <kanji>work</kanji> which means this verb has something to do with working. It's not straight up "to work," instead it's "<vocabulary>to work for</vocabulary>" or "<vocabulary>to be employed at</vocabulary>."
5813.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the other word that means "to work as" (務める). Remember this and you'll be able to remember the reading for this word too.

examples.en: Commuting can eat up a lot of time, so I prefer to live near my office.
examples.ja: 通勤は時間を浪費するので、私は職場の近くに住む方がいいですね。

5814.meaning_mnemonic:
The things you <kanji>pass through</kanji> on your way to <kanji>work</kanji> are the things you see and run into during your <vocabulary>commute</vocabulary>.

Note that you can only use this word for commuting to work. You don’t use it to go to school unless you work at a school or something!
5814.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I won’t be able to work full-time for now until my child gets a little older.
examples.ja: 子どもがもうちょっと大きくなるまでは、常勤でのお仕事はちょっと無理かな。

5815.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Normal</kanji> <kanji>work</kanji> is work you do all day long, 8-hours a day, 5 days a week. That is <vocabulary>full time employment</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>full time</vocabulary>.
5815.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

5816.meaning_mnemonic:
Giving <kanji>consent</kanji> to someone is similar to humbly listening to and accepting their words. So this word means <vocabulary>to humbly hear</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to accept</vocabulary>.

承る is a humble version of 聞く. Its past form 承りました is commonly used in professional settings to respectfully acknowledge and accept requests, information, or tasks.
5816.reading_mnemonic: You received (<reading>受けた</reading>) some information. Now, you are going to take that information that you received and then revolve it (<reading>回る</reading>) around in your head to think about it. Hmmm... hmm... Ok, I like what I'm hearing. I am going <vocabulary>to accept</vocabulary> what you said. Thank you.

examples.en: I know it's unreasonable, but I'm still asking you.
examples.ja: 無理を承知でお願いしています。

examples.en: I am sure you are all well aware of this incident, but let me explain again.
examples.ja: この事件に関してはみなさまよくご承知のこととは思いますが、もう一度説明させていただきます。

examples.en: I can’t consent to your marrying my daughter.
examples.ja: わしの娘がお前と結婚することは承知できん。

5817.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>consent</kanji> and <kanji>know</kanji> everything that's going on. You <vocabulary>consent</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>know</vocabulary> about all this. You're <vocabulary>aware</vocabulary> of it.
5817.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You didn't learn 知's on'yomi when you learned the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You need someone's <vocabulary>consent</vocabulary> before you give them <reading>chee</reading>se (ち). Cheese has the power to enrapture a person and leave them in a state of total ecstasy, so you better make sure they consent and <vocabulary>know</vocabulary> what's about to happen before you feed them any cheese.

examples.en: I don't have much confidence that I can get approval from the committee.
examples.ja: 委員会から承認を得られる自信はあまりありません。

examples.en: The new project proposal was successfully approved.
examples.ja: 新しいプロジェクト案は無事承認されました。

examples.en: I dropped my seal of approval in a bonfire while roasting baked potatoes.
examples.ja: 焼き芋を焼いているたき火の中に承認印を落としてしまった。

5818.meaning_mnemonic: I <kanji>recognize</kanji> your <kanji>consent</kanji>. It is an <vocabulary>approval</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>recognition</vocabulary> of what I'm doing.
5818.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: On saying that, Kuroda disappeared into the entertainment district.
examples.ja: 黒田はそう言い残すと、歓楽街へと消えていった。

examples.en: What does the tour of the pleasure quarter include?
examples.ja: 歓楽街のツアーには何が含まれていますか。

examples.en: I have traced the source of the rumour that I work in the pleasure quarter.
examples.ja: 私が歓楽街で働いているという噂の源をつきとめました。

5819.meaning_mnemonic:
You'll find <kanji>delight</kanji> and <kanji>comfort</kanji> in these <kanji>streets</kanji>, because you have entered an <vocabulary>entertainment district</vocabulary>! 

歓楽街 refers to an area in a city where many nightlife entertainment venues, like bars, dance clubs, host or hostess clubs, and sometimes businesses offering sketchy red-light adult services, are clustered together.
5819.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I’m worried that you may ruin your health by working too hard.
examples.ja: 働きすぎてあんたが健康を損なうんじゃないかって、心配してるのよ。

5820.meaning_mnemonic: To do <kanji>loss</kanji> to something means you are doing something to make something have loss. This is <vocabulary>to harm</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to injure</vocabulary>.
5820.reading_mnemonic: In order <vocabulary>to harm</vocabulary> your opponent, you go way overboard. You <reading>soak</reading> (そこ) them in acid. Soaked head to toe. Too far man, too far.

examples.en: I had a loss of $500 in poker.
examples.ja: ポーカーで五百ドル損をした。

5821.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>loss</kanji> will give you a <vocabulary>disadvantage</vocabulary>. So, try not to get any losses... or you'll be at a disadvantage.
5821.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the kanji, so you aren't at a <vocabulary>disadvantage</vocabulary>... this time.

examples.en: The truck crash damaged the cargo, but it was only minor damage.
examples.ja: トラックの衝突で積荷がダメージを受けたが、小さな損害で済んだ。

5822.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>loss</kanji> comes from <kanji>damage</kanji> done to you. This is <vocabulary>damage</vocabulary>.

This word is usually used as a noun. It can occasionally be turned into verb by adding する, but this is very rare!
5822.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I went to a pachinko parlor in the hopes of making a lot of money, but I ended up with a heavy loss instead.
examples.ja: 大儲けするつもりでパチンコに行ったが、結局大損してしまった。

5823.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the おお reading of 大 coupled with the on'yomi reading for 損. Just keep in mind that the そん changes to ぞん and you'll be good here.

examples.en: If it turns out that the car is a total loss, many insurance companies will not pay the full repair cost.
examples.ja: 車が全損してしまった場合、修理代は保険で全額支払われないことが多いです。

5824.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>all</kanji> <kanji>loss</kanji> is when you lose it all. It is a <vocabulary>total loss</vocabulary>.
5824.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The branches were bent by blood red apples.
examples.ja: 枝は真っ赤な林檎でたわんでいた。

5825.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
5825.reading_mnemonic: Since this is a word made up of a single kanji and nothing else, you can assume that this word will use the kun'yomi reading. The reading you learned for this kanji happens to be the kun'yomi reading as well. So if you know the kanji you know the reading.

examples.en: Beans, beans the magical fruit, the more you eat, the more you toot, the more you toot, the better you feel, so eat some beans at every meal.
examples.ja: お豆さん、お豆さん、魔法の野菜。たくさん食べれば食べるほど、たくさん屁が出るぷっぷぷぷ。たくさんぷっぷぷ屁が出れば、気持ちが良くなるウッフフフ。だから毎食お豆を食べなさい。

5826.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
5826.reading_mnemonic: You want your <vocabulary>beans</vocabulary>, but you're also super lazy, so you call for your mom, yelling: "<reading>MAMEYYYYY</reading>, MAMMMEEYYY!" (まめ).

examples.en: Azuki bean paste is made of azuki beans, but it’s pretty high in sugar.
examples.ja: 餡こは小豆から作られているが、けっこう糖分が高い。

5827.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Small</kanji> <kanji>bean</kanji>s refer to a type of bean known as <vocabulary>azuki bean</vocabulary>s. It will help if you've heard of this delicious popular bean, because there's not really anything effective we can do with the meaning mnemonic from this point on. Just know that small beans are azuki beans.
5827.reading_mnemonic: The reading doesn't make sense either. If you know that small beans are <vocabulary>azuki beans</vocabulary>, then you know that this is referring to a thing known as <reading>azuki</reading> (あずき). Other than that, there's not much else to do.

examples.en: Don’t get me wrong. I love Japanese food, but natto is the one thing I just can't eat.
examples.ja: 誤解しないでね。日本料理は大好きなんだけど、納豆だけはどうしても食べられないの。

5828.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>supply</kanji> of <kanji>bean</kanji>s is when you take a bunch of beans, mash them up into a supply, and then ferment them all together to make them into <vocabulary>natto</vocabulary> (also known as <vocabulary>fermented soybeans</vocabulary>).
5828.reading_mnemonic: The reading is an exceptional one. 豆 is okay, and is the on'yomi reading from the kanji. The 納 part is weird though. Instead of being のう it's なっ. But, if you can remember the meaning of this word, you can just think about how you do <reading>not</reading> (なっとう) want to eat <vocabulary>natto</vocabulary>. At least a lot of people don't want to eat it. It's quite the acquired taste.

examples.en: Don’t leave milk out of the fridge because it goes bad easily.
examples.ja: 牛乳は腐りやすいんだから冷蔵庫の外に出しっ放しにしないでね。

5829.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>rot</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to rot</vocabulary>.
5829.reading_mnemonic: Remember the word 臭い, which means "stinky"? When something rots, it becomes stinky, and all <reading>くさ</reading>い.

examples.en: Stainless steel is supposed to withstand corrosion, isn’t it?
examples.ja: ステンレスは腐食作用への耐久性があるんじゃなかったっけ？

5830.meaning_mnemonic: When something <kanji>rot</kanji>s and <kanji>eat</kanji>s away at something, that is <vocabulary>corrosion</vocabulary>. Not a good thing.
5830.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: There was a smell of something decomposing in the air.
examples.ja: そこには、何かが腐敗したような臭いがただよっていた。

examples.en: This additive prevents food from rotting.
examples.ja: この添加物により、食品の腐敗が防げます。

examples.en: Many people are tired of the corrupt political ring.
examples.ja: 多くの人々が腐敗した政治組織にうんざりしています。

5831.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Rot</kanji> and <kanji>failure</kanji> lead to <vocabulary>decomposition</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>rotting</vocabulary>. This word also has the related meaning of  <vocabulary>corruption</vocabulary>, similar to how "rotten" can mean "corrupt" in English.
5831.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Her right pinky nail is six meters long.
examples.ja: 彼女の右の小指の爪の長さはなんと六メートルもあります。

5832.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well, though it adds a few more meanings as well, like <vocabulary>nail</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>talon</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>hoof</vocabulary> or really any hard thing on the ends of fingers or feet.
5832.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: I was trying to clip my dog's nails but my mobile phone distracted me.
examples.ja: 犬の爪を爪切りで切ってあげようとしてたんですけど、つい携帯に気を取られちゃいました。

5833.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>cut</kanji> your <kanji>claw</kanji> you use a <vocabulary>nail clipper</vocabulary>.
5833.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the reading you learned for the kanji 爪 and the word for the reading 切る.

examples.en: I can’t be bothered to cut up the green onion.
examples.ja: 葱を刻むのは面倒くさいよ。

5834.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>carve</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to carve</vocabulary>.
5834.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You don't have a knife for your steak, so you have <vocabulary>to carve</vocabulary> it using the <reading>key za</reading>g (きざ) technique. You take a key and zag it through the steak repeatedly until you're able <vocabulary>to cut up</vocabulary> some zaggy bite-sized pieces.

examples.en: The train schedule is a must-have for commuters.
examples.ja: 通勤・通学者にとって、電車の時刻表は絶対に必要なものです。

5835.meaning_mnemonic:
If you take the <kanji>time</kanji> and <kanji>carve</kanji> it onto a <kanji>surface</kanji>, then you've made a <vocabulary>timetable</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>schedule</vocabulary>.

時刻表 generally refers to a timetable or schedule for transportation, such as trains, buses, or flights.
5835.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: It’s a serious problem that the number of Japanese children with thyroid abnormalities have been increasing.
examples.ja: 甲状腺異常のある日本の子どもたちの数が増えているのは、深刻な問題です。

5836.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>deep</kanji> <kanji>carve</kanji> is very <vocabulary>serious</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>grave</vocabulary>. Just imagine getting cut with a sword. If the carve is deep, well, that's serious.
5836.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: How do you close a browser on a smartphone?
examples.ja: スマホでブラウザってどうやって閉じるんですか？

examples.en: Whoops! I closed the book before putting in the bookmark.
examples.ja: あ！シオリをはさむ前にページを閉じちゃった。

examples.en: The computer screen suddenly closed on its own.
examples.ja: 急にパソコンの画面が勝手に閉じちゃったんです。

5837.meaning_mnemonic:
Another verb version of the kanji 閉! This is a special one that can be either transitive or intransitive, so 閉じる means <vocabulary>to close something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to close</vocabulary>.

閉じる is for returning things that have expanded open back to their closed state. It's used for books, umbrellas, web browsers, and even eyes and mouths. There are some overlaps with 閉める (you can 閉じる or 閉める a gate, for example) but 閉める is mostly used for things like doors, windows, and curtains.
5837.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is different from 閉める or 閉まる. Instead, 閉じる is read とじる.

Why? Because <vocabulary>to close something</vocabulary> that's expanded or spread open, you always use your <reading>toe</reading> (と)! It's easy enough with books, but umbrellas are a real challenge… But you, you can do it! You have the toe-tal control and can close anything expanded to the way it was before.

examples.en: Our oldest son does nothing but play baseball. He doesn’t have a girlfriend either.
examples.ja: うちの長男は野球一筋なのよ。女っ気も無くてさ。

5838.meaning_mnemonic: You have <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>muscle</kanji>, therefore it only does one thing. That's it. It is <vocabulary>single mindedly</vocabulary> doing that one thing. It is <vocabulary>intently</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>earnestly</vocabulary> doing that one thing.
5838.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a bit weird. It's the kun'yomi readings, where 一 is ひと and 筋 is すじ. Look back on the vocab words that use these readings to remember this one.

examples.en: It seems that the lid wasn't properly closed, so there's sauce leaking from one side.
examples.ja: フタがちゃんと閉まっていなかったみたいで、横からソースが垂れている。

examples.en: Something was wrong with the faucet last night, and the sound of dripping water bothered me so much I hardly got any sleep.
examples.ja: 昨夜ジャグチの調子が悪くて、水がポタポタ垂れる音が気になってほとんど寝られなかった。

examples.en: Although Jazz's tail had been drooping the entire time Jiro was out, the moment he heard his car, it sprang straight up and started wagging furiously.
examples.ja: ジャズの尻尾は次郎がいない間ずっと垂れ下がっていたが、彼の車が聞こえた途端、ぴんとはね上がり、激しく振り始めた。

5839.meaning_mnemonic:
If 垂らす is "to dangle something" then 垂れる is <vocabulary>to dangle</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to drip</vocabulary> on its own. So you can use 垂れる to describe your dog's floppy ears hanging down or your ice cream’s melty goodness dripping away. You know this because it's <reading>rare</reading> (れる) to witness the moment something starts dangling or dripping down.

Sometimes, 垂れる can also take a direct object in specific expressions, like 説教を垂れる (to give a preachy lecture), こうべを垂れる (to bow one's head in humility), or the crude slang クソを垂れる (to drop a load).
5839.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 垂らす.

examples.en: Don’t you think that the Japanese government should have declared a state of emergency at the time?
examples.ja: あの時、日本政府は非常事態を宣言するべきだったと思わないかい。

5840.meaning_mnemonic: If 宣言 is a "proclamation," then the verb version will be <vocabulary>to proclaim</vocabulary>.
5840.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: My buddy is ridiculously interesting and he’s great at livening up parties.
examples.ja: 俺の友達はメチャクチャ面白くて、パーティーを盛り上げるのが得意なんだよ。

5841.meaning_mnemonic: 盛る is "to heap up." If you "raise" (上げる) what you heap up, well, that comes with heaping something up, making this word <vocabulary>to heap up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to pile up</vocabulary>. This word is also used when you want <vocabulary>to liven up</vocabulary> some things. Heap up that energy and stir things up!
5841.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 盛る and 上げる. Know those words and you'll be able to read this one too.

examples.en: He is not a traitor. He’s just naturally a little slow.
examples.ja: 彼は裏切り者なんかじゃないよ。ただ、生まれつきちょっととぼけているだけさ。

examples.en: They use this facility to kill traitors.
examples.ja: 奴らは裏切り者を殺すのにこの施設を利用している。

5842.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Someone</kanji> who backstabs (裏切り) someone is a <vocabulary>traitor</vocabulary>.
5842.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 裏切り and an exception reading for 者. Just think about how you'd think of a traitor as a "thing" (物) and not a person.

examples.en: We decided to temporarily close our shop for a bunch of reasons.
examples.ja: 諸々の理由がありまして、しばらく一時的に店を閉めることにしました。

5843.meaning_mnemonic: You have <kanji>various</kanji> <kanji>various</kanji> things. They are <vocabulary>various</vocabulary>. You have <vocabulary>all kinds of</vocabulary> them.
5843.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a bit weird. Just think about how when you have various things, you probably have a lot of things. What do you want? You want <reading>more</reading> (もろ) of those things. <reading>More more</reading> more!

examples.en: Oh come on, it was so obvious! There was no chemistry between you two! You definitely shouldn’t call that girl with the braided hair!
examples.ja: おいおい、頼むよ。明らかにお前たちの相性全然よくなかっただろ！絶対にあの三つ編みの女に電話なんてしない方がいいって！

5844.meaning_mnemonic: 編む is "to knit." When you knit in <kanji>three</kanji>s, you are knitting in a braid style. What do you braid? Hair. That makes this <vocabulary>braided hair</vocabulary>.
5844.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the み from 三つ and つ and 編む combined into one (or should I say three?) braids. Just watch out because this isn't みっつあみ, it's just みつあみ. Listen to the audio a few times to make sure you remember how it's spelled and pronounced!

examples.en: This lid doesn't close properly.

That's why this is <vocabulary>to close</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to shut</vocabulary>. You remember this because the door keeps shutting on your hand, <reading>marr</reading>ing (まる) it over and over again. Ouch.

examples.en: I don't think they will be satisfied with just money.
examples.ja: 金を払うだけで、彼らが納まるとは思えないけどな。

5847.meaning_mnemonic:
If 納める is "to supply" or "to deliver," then this word is when things have been delivered: so it's <vocabulary>to settle into</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be satisfied</vocabulary>. 

納まる means something or someone has found its right place and settled there. It often implies that there was a prior state of uncertainty or dissatisfaction, but now everything is in its right place.

Like most verbs with まる as okurigana, this is an intransitive verb. That means it happens by itself, with no emphasis on the person or thing that's making something settle or be satisfied.
5847.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 納める.

That's why it means <vocabulary>to rehash</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to bring up again</vocabulary>. You're bringing up memories from the past and steaming them up again.

The あした reading is irregular, though you can just think of the あ part as coming from the 明 kanji. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember the whole reading as well:

It'll be a better, brighter day <vocabulary>tomorrow</vocabulary> because you're making <reading>ash ta</reading>cos (あした). Mmm, imagine the taste of those delicious ash tacos you'll be having tomorrow.

5937.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>descend</kanji>, but this verb vocab word is <vocabulary>to get off</vocabulary>, as in, to get off the train, or to get out of the car. If you think about trains back in the day, you had to descend down to the platform to get out of them, which is how this word became what it is. You know that this word is the "to get off" word because once you get off the train, you enter the <reading>real</reading> (りる) world, where hardships are real and not as comfy as the train.

Figuratively, this word also means <vocabulary>to step down</vocabulary>, as in "to give up" or "to resign” from something. For example, you can say ニュース番組を降りる (to step down from a news program) or ゲームを降りる (to drop out of a game).
5937.reading_mnemonic: The reading is unlike anything you've seen with this kanji. Just think about how you have <vocabulary>to get off</vocabulary> at <reading>O</reading>-station. None of the other letters are your stop. Just <reading>O</reading>-Station (お).

5938.reading_mnemonic:

When you want to make a <vocabulary>chicken and egg rice bowl</vocabulary>, you have to ask <reading>Don Brie</reading> (どんぶり) for the rice bowl. He's the mafia boss who hoards all the rice bowls to eat his cheese out of — remember him? Don't get on Don Brie's bad side, or no <vocabulary>oyako-don</vocabulary> for you!

5983.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>change</kanji>, and this verb is <vocabulary>to change something</vocabulary>. If you change one thing for another thing, you are going <vocabulary>to change</vocabulary> it, after all. This word refers to changing one thing for a similar thing.

変える and 代える sound the same and are sometimes used in similar contexts, but are different in nuance. 変える refers to the act of making something different, and involves altering the nature or state of something. For example, changing the layout of a room or changing one's perspective on an issue. 代える means to substitute or exchange one thing for another that is expected to fulfill the same role, use or purpose, such as replacing a worker with a substitute.
