6011.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: Have I ever told you about my supernatural power?
examples.ja: そういえば、私の超自然的な力についてお話したことってありましたっけ？

6012.meaning_mnemonic: Something that is <kanji>ultra</kanji> natural (自然的) is <vocabulary>supernatural</vocabulary>. Too natural! Super!
6012.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: My panda robot can fly at supersonic speeds.
examples.ja: 僕のパンダロボットは、超音速で空を飛べるんだぜ。

6013.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I was told that ultrasonic waves destroy fat cells permanently, so I bought this machine for $3,000.
examples.ja: 超音波なら脂肪細胞を永久に破壊することができると言われたので、この3000ドルもする機械を買ったんですよ。

6014.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Just remember that the は changes to ぱ for 波.

examples.en: "When do you need boiled crabigator by?" "I need it as soon as possible."
examples.ja: 「茹でたワニカニ、いつまでに必要ですか？」「できるだけ早く頼むよ。」

6015.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>trust</kanji>, but the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to ask for</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to rely on</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to request</vocabulary>. When you trust someone you can 頼む them, but only when you trust them. You put it in their hands. You trust them, after all.
6015.reading_mnemonic: But, you're entrusting this task to your friend not because you are busy, but because you want to go have a <reading>楽</reading>しい (fun) time at the waterpark. Sucker!

examples.en: I don’t wanna jump to conclusions because he seems to be pretty trustworthy.
examples.ja: 彼は信頼できるような気がするし、早合点はしたくないね。

6016.meaning_mnemonic: I <kanji>believe</kanji> I can <kanji>trust</kanji> you. That's why I put so much <vocabulary>reliance</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>trust</vocabulary> on you to do well.
6016.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Your request may be turned down, but it never hurts to ask.
examples.ja: 依頼は断られちゃうかもしれないけど、聞くだけ聞いてみたら。

6017.meaning_mnemonic: I am <kanji>reliant</kanji> on you and I <kanji>trust</kanji> you. Therefore, I have a <vocabulary>request</vocabulary> for you that I'd like to <vocabulary>entrust</vocabulary> you with.
6017.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Dependence on foreign countries for resources is dangerous.
examples.ja: 外国の資源に依存するのは危険だ。

examples.en: In Saudi Arabia, much of the country's revenue relies on oil.
examples.ja: サウジアラビアでは、国の収益の多くを石油に依存している。

examples.en: I admit that I’ve become dependent on my cell phone.
examples.ja: 自分が携帯依存症だってことは認めます。

6018.meaning_mnemonic: Being <kanji>reliant</kanji> on something in order to <kanji>exist</kanji> is <vocabulary>dependence</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>reliance</vocabulary>.
6018.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: If you weren’t so stupid, I could explain to you how stupid you are!
examples.ja: お前がそこまで馬鹿じゃなければ、お前がどれだけ馬鹿なのか説明することができるんだけどなあ。

6019.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>horse</kanji> <kanji>deer</kanji> is a <vocabulary>stupid</vocabulary> idea. You're an <vocabulary>idiot</vocabulary> for thinking about it, really. It's quite <vocabulary>dumb</vocabulary>.
6019.reading_mnemonic: You learned both of these readings when you learned the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I drove on the most bumpy road I’ve ever driven on in Kagoshima Prefecture.
examples.ja: 鹿児島県で、今までで運転した中で一番デッコボコの道路をドライブしました。

6020.reading_mnemonic: The readings are part on'yomi, part kun'yomi, but you should know them all if you look at them one by one. Just remember that 児 is read as ご here. Go, Kagoshima Prefecture! Go!

examples.en: I can’t distinguish between male and female deer.
examples.ja: 牡鹿と牝鹿の区別がつきません。

6021.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
6021.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: 

You're staring really closely at this <vocabulary>deer</vocabulary>, but something looks off. You get closer, slowly, and you realize it's a <reading>shee</reading>p in a <reading>ca</reading>r (しか) shaped like a deer. The sheep car deer suddenly turns toward you rushing forward, legs raised. Ahh, get outta there! (The lesson here is to never get too close to a deer. You never know its true form until it's too late.)

examples.en: Sorry to ask for your consent after the decision was made.
examples.ja: 事後承諾になってしまってすみません。

examples.en: Still no word from him on his acceptance?
examples.ja: 彼からの承諾の返事はまだないのか？

examples.en: My father agreed to our marriage without hesitation.
examples.ja: 父は、私達の結婚を二つ返事で承諾した。

6022.meaning_mnemonic: You have my <kanji>consent</kanji> and <kanji>agreement</kanji>. This is my <vocabulary>consent</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>agreement</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>acceptance</vocabulary>.
6022.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Koichi reluctantly agreed to become the president of the United States.
examples.ja: コウイチはアメリカ合衆国の大統領になることを渋々受諾した。

6023.meaning_mnemonic: I will <kanji>accept</kanji> and I have <kanji>agreement</kanji> in the matter. I have come to <vocabulary>acceptance</vocabulary>.
6023.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Please obtain permission from the manager beforehand.
examples.ja: 予め管理人の許諾を得てください。

examples.en: I got the permission from the person in the video before releasing it.
examples.ja: このビデオを公開することは、本人の許諾済みです。

examples.en: If you allow me to marry your daughter, I’ll give you my consent to use our company’s trademark.
examples.ja: もし娘さんとの結婚を許可してくださるのなら、あなたに我が社の登録商標の使用を許諾します。

6024.meaning_mnemonic: I will <kanji>permit</kanji> this, and you have my <kanji>agreement</kanji>. Both of these things combine to be my <vocabulary>permission</vocabulary> and my <vocabulary>consent</vocabulary>.
6024.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: "Please let us know whether this is acceptable or not" is a common phrase used in business letters and emails.
examples.ja: 「諾否を御一報ください」という言葉は、仕事の手紙やEmailなどでよく使われるフレーズです。

6025.meaning_mnemonic: Do we have <kanji>agreement</kanji> or <kanji>no</kanji>? Which is it? <vocabulary>consent or refusal</vocabulary>? <vocabulary>Yes or no</vocabulary>? Choose!
6025.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I switched out my name stamp for an expensive ivory one.
examples.ja: 印鑑を高級な象牙の物に変えました。

6026.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>elephant</kanji> <kanji>tusk</kanji> is the material known as <vocabulary>ivory</vocabulary> (or just an <vocabulary>elephant tusk</vocabulary>).
6026.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Our stock of fake fangs for Halloween is running out.
examples.ja: ハロウィン用の偽物の牙の在庫が切れそうです。

6027.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
6027.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

Using your animal <vocabulary>fang</vocabulary> you are able to eat <reading>kibble</reading> (きば).

examples.en: Haven’t you ever thought about surrendering, even once?
examples.ja: 降参しようと思ったことは今まで一度もないんですか。

6028.meaning_mnemonic: 降参 is "surrender" so the verb version would be <vocabulary>to surrender</vocabulary>.
6028.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. The reading is the same as 降参 as well, of course.

examples.en: I'm living alone and I forgot to set my clock back an hour when the winter time started.
examples.ja: 一人暮らしをしているので、冬時間が始まった時に、時計を一時間遅らせることを忘れてしまいました。

6029.meaning_mnemonic: If 暮らす is "to live" or "to live one's life," then to live one's life as 一人, means you are <vocabulary>living alone</vocabulary>.
6029.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the vocab readings from 一人 and 暮らす, so you should be able to read this on your own. Just note that くらし changes to ぐらし due to rendaku.

examples.en: She is Hana.
examples.ja: 彼女はハナさんです。

examples.en: I went to Disneyland with my girlfriend.
examples.ja: 彼女とディズニーランドに行ってきた。

examples.en: My girlfriend is so cute, isn’t she?
examples.ja: 俺の彼女、めっちゃかわいいだろ？

examples.en: She has good taste in clothes.
examples.ja: 彼女は服のセンスがいい。

6030.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>he</kanji> <kanji>woman</kanji> is <vocabulary>she</vocabulary>. Also could mean <vocabulary>girlfriend</vocabulary>, depending on how it's used.
6030.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this is a bit weird, at least for the 彼 portion. Just think about how <vocabulary>she</vocabulary> (your <vocabulary>girlfriend</vocabulary>) is a <reading>canoe</reading> (かの), and you love that canoe girlfriend more than anything. She is your best friend and your lover, and everyone thinks you're weird. Imagine everyone thinking you're weird as you give kisses to your canoe girlfriend.

examples.en: My brother is such a shameless liar. He told me he had no idea what happened, but he was the one who ate all my bacon.
examples.ja: あの俺の兄貴は恥知らずの嘘つきだ。何の事だかサッパリ分からないなんて言ってたくせに、俺のベーコンを平らげたのはアイツだったんだよ。

6031.meaning_mnemonic: 恥 is a "disgrace." If you 知らず then you don't know something. In this case, you don't know disgrace, and a person who doesn't know disgrace is a <vocabulary>shameless person</vocabulary>, because they don't care what disgraces them and what doesn't.
6031.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 恥 and 知る put together.

examples.en: Studying on the train is common for Japanese students who suffer from exam hell.
examples.ja: 試験地獄に苦しむ日本の学生にとっては、電車で勉強するのは当たり前のことです。

6032.meaning_mnemonic: An "examination hell" is the nickname given to the exams you have to take in Japan all at once. That's why this is <vocabulary>exam hell</vocabulary>.
6032.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that smooshes two previous vocabulary words together into a new one. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I got over my seasickness with this medicine.
examples.ja: この薬で船酔いを克服しました。

6033.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 船 goes to ふな (probably because you're sick and can't spell). The 酔い comes from 酔う.

examples.en: She made her boyfriend cook kimchi hotpot.
examples.ja: 彼女が彼氏にキムチ鍋を作らせた。

examples.en: Have you ever tried soy milk hotpot?
examples.ja: 豆乳鍋を食べてみたことはありますか？

6034.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 鍋 means "<kanji>cooking pot</kanji>"? This is the suffix version of that, so it means ____<vocabulary>hotpot</vocabulary> or ____<vocabulary>stew</vocabulary>. 

Usually 〜鍋 will come after the name of the soup base or main ingredient, like 味噌鍋 (miso hotpot) or キムチ鍋 (kimchi stew).
6034.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: We offer 5% off if you pay with cash.
examples.ja: 現金払いにしていただけるなら、5パーセント引きにさせていただきます。

examples.en: Kanji characters should be written with attention to the stop, brush-up, and brushing-off strokes.
examples.ja: 漢字は止め、跳ね、払いに注意して書きましょう。

examples.en: Did you know that paying insurance premiums annually is more economical than paying monthly?
examples.ja: 保険料は月払いよりも年払いの方がお得なの、知ってた？

6035.meaning_mnemonic:
If 払う is "to pay" or "to brush off," then the noun version is <vocabulary>payment</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>brushing off</vocabulary>.

Usually 払い is tacked on the end of another word, like in カード払い (payment by credit card).

When it indicates a kind of brushing off or brushing away, it appears in words like 足払い (sweeping an opponent's legs in judo) or, more figuratively, せき払い (clearing one's throat).
6035.reading_mnemonic:
The reading comes from 払う, so know that and it will pay forward your knowledge to this one.

Note that when 払い is added to the end of a compound, it becomes ばらい.

examples.en: I bought this oil painting for 1500 yen at a flea market.
examples.ja: この油絵はフリマで千五百円で買ったんですよ。

examples.en: My grandmother used to collect oil paintings.
examples.ja: 祖母は油絵を集めていた。

examples.en: What's the most famous brand of oil paints?
examples.ja: 油絵用の絵の具で有名なブランドは？

6036.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi for 油 (which you learned with the vocabulary) and the on'yomi for 絵 (which you learned with the kanji).

examples.en: During lunch the other day for some reason one of the students pulled a bottle of sweet vinegar out of her desk.
examples.ja: この間、給食の時に生徒が何故か机の中から甘酢の瓶を取り出したのよ。

6037.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Sweet</kanji> <kanji>vinegar</kanji> is <vocabulary>sweet vinegar</vocabulary>. Them Japanese love their sweet things.
6037.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 甘い plus 酢, combined together. It's the kun'yomi readings, but that's probably because we're combing two words into one. It also changes the す to ず so, remember that.

examples.en: Kids can take the most mundane, random things and get so excited.
examples.ja: 子どもっていうのは、どんなささいなことでも手当たり次第に盛り上がることができるのよね。

6038.meaning_mnemonic: 盛り上げる is "to heap up" - this has a similar idea, except now this is more like an excitement or swelling. As excitement heaps up in you, you are going <vocabulary>to get excited</vocabulary>. Note how 上がる is in here. This means something is happening to you (or something else), but you're not doing the action. When you get all sorts of excitement building up in you, you aren't really doing it, it's just happening on its own in reaction to something else.
6038.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 盛り and 上がる. Let the excitement build as you realize you know the reading already.

examples.en: My computer is very slow because it’s running out of hard drive space.
examples.ja: 私のパソコンはハードディスクの容量が無くなってきているので、動作がすごく遅いです。

6039.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>slow</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>slow</vocabulary> (or, if you're slow, you're probably <vocabulary>late</vocabulary>, too).
6039.reading_mnemonic: How <vocabulary>slow</vocabulary> are you? You are <reading>oh so</reading> slow (おそ).

examples.en: Although she was determined to become a stripper, she’s still shy about dancing naked in public.
examples.ja: ストリッパーになると自分で決断したにも関わらず、彼女はまだ人前で裸で踊ることを恥ずかしがっているんだよ。

6040.meaning_mnemonic: 恥ずかしい is "embarrassing." This is the verb version. What happens when someone is embarrassed? They become shy and bashful. That's why this word is <vocabulary>to be shy</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be bashful</vocabulary>.
6040.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 恥ずかしい.

examples.en: Why do my pants always start wearing out in the butt area first?
examples.ja: ズボンのお尻の部分がいつも最初に破れるんだけど、どうしてだろう。

6041.meaning_mnemonic: If 破る is "to tear" or "to rip," then this is <vocabulary>to get torn</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to get broken</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to get ripped</vocabulary>.
6041.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 破る.

examples.en: Whenever I introduce myself, I quickly run out of things to say.
examples.ja: 自己紹介では、いつもすぐ言うことがなくなっちゃうんだよね。

6042.meaning_mnemonic: A one's self (自己) introduction (紹介) is a <vocabulary>self introduction</vocabulary>.
6042.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: It’s hard to choose which girl to introduce to you.
examples.ja: お前にどの娘を紹介するかを選ぶのは難しいよ。

6043.meaning_mnemonic: A 紹介 is an introduction. So the verb version is <vocabulary>to introduce</vocabulary>.
6043.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Helps that I introduced introduction to you earlier.

examples.en: You need a referral letter from a doctor to make an appointment at this hospital.
examples.ja: この病院で予約をするには、お医者さんからの紹介状が要ります。

6044.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how a 年賀状 is a new year's card? This is another kind of card/letter, but this time it's for an introduction (紹介), making it a <vocabulary>letter of introduction</vocabulary>.
6044.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Will help to know 紹介 as well.

examples.en: He asked the waitress three times if there was any soup in the restaurant and she answered no each time. She was bewildered.
examples.ja: あいつ、あのウェイトレスさんに三回もこのレストランに汁物はないのかって聞きやがったんだぜ。ウェイトレスさんその度にありませんって言ってさ、困惑してたよ。

6045.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>soup</kanji> <kanji>thing</kanji> is what you use to refer to <vocabulary>soups</vocabulary>.
6045.reading_mnemonic: The reading is both the kun'yomi readings combined to form one word. So, you'll want to make sure you know the word 汁.

examples.en: "We have to finish eating this miso soup by tomorrow." "Okay, let’s get it over with."
examples.ja: 「明日までに、この味噌汁を飲んでしまわなければならないよ。」「じゃあ、さっさと片付けちまおうぜ。」

6046.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 味噌 is "miso," and that 汁 is "soup." So, combine them together and you have <vocabulary>Miso Soup</vocabulary>.
6046.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 味噌 plus the vocab 汁 put together.

examples.en: My heart was pounding while I was hassled by a drunk last night.
examples.ja: 昨日の夜酔っ払いに絡まれた時、心臓がドキドキしました。

6047.meaning_mnemonic: If you're so <kanji>drunk</kanji> that you'll be <kanji>pay</kanji>ing for it later, it's safe to say you're a <vocabulary>drunk person</vocabulary>. You're way past being tipsy at this point, and you're definitely going to pay for it… with a hangover in the morning.
6047.reading_mnemonic: This is a combination of 酔う and 払い, put together with some small っ and a rendaku added in because you're drunk.

examples.en: I’m hungover and I also have a cramp in my leg. Today is the worst.
examples.ja: 二日酔いだし、足もつるし今日は最悪だよ。

6048.meaning_mnemonic: On the <kanji>second day</kanji>, you experience your <kanji>drunk</kanji>enness a different way... in the form of a <vocabulary>hangover</vocabulary>.
6048.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 二日 and 酔い put together (the reading for that comes from 酔う).

examples.en: How long have you worked at this gas station?
examples.ja: この給油所ではどのくらい働いているんですか？

6049.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>fueling</kanji> (給油) <kanji>place</kanji> is a place where you get things fueled. This can either be a <vocabulary>gas station</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>filling station</vocabulary>.
6049.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Even though she landed a perfect triple axel, her score didn't go up by much.
examples.ja: 彼女は完璧なトリプルアクセルを跳んだのに、スコアはあまり伸びなかった。

6050.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>hop</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to hop</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to jump</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to leap</vocabulary>. Basically anything that gets both feet off the ground via your own foot propulsion.
6050.reading_mnemonic: Know how 飛ぶ means "to fly"? This is a similar idea, though this time you're not flying nearly as much, because you're just hopping or jumping. Anyways, the readings are the same.

examples.en: Which year of Showa were you born in?
examples.ja: 昭和何年生まれですか。

6051.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>shining</kanji> <kanji>peace</kanji> time was a time known as the <vocabulary>Showa Era</vocabulary>. This can also refer to the <vocabulary>Showa Emperor</vocabulary> or just <vocabulary>Showa</vocabulary> itself. Everything Showa is here.
6051.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I know that fisherman because he is my brother in law.
examples.ja: 私はその漁師を知っていますよ。私の義理の兄ですから。

6052.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. The reading is the りょう reading, because you gotta get in your row boat to be a <vocabulary>fisherman</vocabulary>.

examples.en: I had my fishing boat stolen last night.
examples.ja: 昨夜漁船を盗まれました。

6053.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

This verb can also be intransitive (oh my!) and mean <vocabulary>to grow stronger</vocabulary>, usually in reference to some sort of feelings or emotions. Make sure to check out the common word combinations for some example usages!

6067.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned that 執 means "<kanji>tenacious</kanji>," but it can also mean "carry out." The verb version here means <vocabulary>to take up</vocabulary>, like taking up a task or responsibility, or <vocabulary>to carry out</vocabulary>. 

執る is a formal word that means taking something in hand and carrying out an action. 筆を執る means "to take up the pen," for example, but also implies you're starting to write something meaningful. From this, 執る is also often used when someone takes charge of an important task or adopts a firm stance on something, like 指揮を執る (to take command).
6067.reading_mnemonic: Notice how the word "take" is in this verb. If you take something, you might say 取る. This word shares take's reading.

You <kanji>tenacious</kanji>ly <kanji>wear</kanji> something. You have some kind of <vocabulary>attachment to</vocabulary> it. You can't let go. It's an <vocabulary>obsession</vocabulary>, after all, and you just can't stop <vocabulary>clinging to</vocabulary> it!

執着 usually refers to an unhealthy or excessive attachment to something. An obsession with money, dwelling on the past, or even persisting in your own narrow-minded beliefs — these are all kinds of 執着.
6068.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

But not just any writing — this is <vocabulary>professional writing</vocabulary>, so you better get it right!

執筆 is a formal word for the act of writing, especially professional or important work like novels, magazine columns, news articles, or academic papers.

6073.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>crumble</kanji>, and this verb is for when you actively make or let something crumble, so it means <vocabulary>to break down</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to tear down</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to crumble</vocabulary>. It's transitive, so you're the one tearing stuff down. You can remember this because if you go around tearing down people's stuff, they'll probably sue (す).

崩す is for when you break down or loosen something that was solid or properly arranged. You can 崩す a sandcastle at the beach, your posture when you slouch, or even your health when you let yourself get worn down and sick. There are tons of ways to use this tricky word, so be sure check the context section for examples.

6130.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>hug</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to embrace</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to hold</vocabulary> (in one's arms, that is). It can also mean <vocabulary>to hug</vocabulary>, especially in the form of 抱きしめる.

Keep in mind that depending on the context, 抱く can be a euphemism for something way more sexual than just hugging. Not always, of course, but pretty often, so just be careful how you use it! 抱きしめる is the better option if you're talking about regular old hugs.
6130.reading_mnemonic:
What are you going <vocabulary>to embrace</vocabulary>? How about your <reading>da</reading>d (だ)? Or if he's not around, maybe an <reading>e</reading>-<reading>da</reading>d (いだ)? You know, like a digital version of a dad.

The two readings for this word have different nuances. だく is more for physical holding and hugging, as in 赤ちゃんを抱く (to hold a baby). But when it's something you hold in your heart, like an emotion or feeling, use the いだく reading: 疑問を抱く (to hold doubts) or 夢を抱く (to have a dream), for example.

6178.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>accompany</kanji>, so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to accompany</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be accompanied by</vocabulary>.

This word is both transitive and intransitive. So it works both when bringing someone with you, like 助手を伴って来る (to come with an assistant), or when going along with someone else, like 上司に伴って行く (to go with one's boss). When it's about physically accompanying someone, it's often used together with a movement verb.

伴う is also used figuratively to talk about consequences that tend <vocabulary>to go hand in hand with</vocabulary> something, like 変化にはリスクが伴う (change comes with risk). In this case, 伴う is usually used by itself.
6178.reading_mnemonic: When you want your friend <vocabulary>to accompany</vocabulary> you somewhere, you yell "<reading>友, NOW</reading>!" (ともなう) to command them to get ready to go. You're very pushy when it comes to having your friends accompany you places.

6206.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

6208.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

6209.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.ja: 「ご一緒してもよろしいですか？」「全然、構いませんよ。どうぞお座りください。」

6210.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>One</kanji> <kanji>cord</kanji> is enough to tie you <vocabulary>together</vocabulary> with someone. Imagine an invisible cord stretching between you and the people you do things together with. That one cord is like a symbol of your togetherness. Very poetic (or very Death Stranding), right?
6210.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. The 一 becomes いっ.

examples.ja: 私はICレコーダーで会話を内緒で録音します。

6211.meaning_mnemonic: Keep information <kanji>inside</kanji> a <kanji>cord</kanji> that cordons off just you and a few others (or maybe no one else). Only the people you let inside the cord can know, because it's a <vocabulary>secret</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>confidential</vocabulary>.
6211.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The neck of this shirt is pretty loose.
examples.ja: このシャツは首回りが緩いんですよね。

6212.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>loose</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>loose</vocabulary>.
6212.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the one you learned with the kanji, so feel nice and loose and move on to the next item.

examples.ja: そのトンネルのボルトは、何本か緩んできています。

examples.en: Everyone's tension loosened at his joke.
examples.ja: 彼のジョークにみんなの緊張感が緩んだ。

6213.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>loose</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to loosen</vocabulary>. This is when something loosens on its own, and not via your actions. You know this because a cow is loosening things, <reading>moo</reading> (む)...
6213.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji!

examples.en: The stream curves gently towards the east and is a good fishing spot.
examples.ja: その小川が緩やかに東にカーブしているところがあるんだけど、そこが釣りの穴場なんだよ。

6214.meaning_mnemonic: This is the na-adjective version of <kanji>loose</kanji>, so that means this word means <vocabulary>loose</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>mild</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>gentle</vocabulary>.
6214.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from what you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: He says that he did blindfold the guy, but entrusted the rest of the murder to the other assassin.
examples.ja: そいつがさ、男の目隠しまではしたけど、残りの殺人業務は他の暗殺者に委託したって言うんだよ。

6215.meaning_mnemonic: To the <kanji>committee</kanji> I would like to <kanji>consign</kanji> these things. This is what I <vocabulary>consign</vocabulary>.
6215.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: It was a mistake to entrust all of the photos to the detective.
examples.ja: 探偵に写真を全部託したのが間違いでした。

6216.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>consign</kanji> something to someone, you are going <vocabulary>to entrust</vocabulary> them with that item. Here you go, I entrust you.
6216.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this one is unusual, but I will entrust you with the knowledge of why to help you remember it! This uses the on'yomi reading and not the kun'yomi, as you might expect, because the す here is the old-fashioned version of the verb する.

Luckily, you learned this reading when you learned the kanji, so it's unusual but hopefully not too hard!

examples.en: I trusted the investment broker and invested a lot of my money into the mutual fund.
examples.ja: 私はその証券マンを信頼して、投資信託に大金をつぎ込みました。

6217.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>believe</kanji> you can <kanji>consign</kanji> your trust to someone, then you can <vocabulary>trust</vocabulary> them, or you are being <vocabulary>entrusting</vocabulary>.
6217.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Our company undertakes system development projects.
examples.ja: 当社はシステム開発を受託しています。

examples.en: I'm swamped with overlapping contract work.
examples.ja: 受託案件が重なって、手が回らないんです。

examples.en: You do understand how important it is for us to secure that subcontract, right?
examples.ja: 我が社にとってその受託契約を受注することがどんなに重要か、分かっているよな。

6218.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>accept</kanji> and <kanji>consign</kanji> the job. You are going to <vocabulary>be entrusted with</vocabulary> this property for the winter. Don't go into room 237.

受託 is a formal word that means taking on a task someone has entrusted to you. You'll often see it in business contexts to talk about a company taking on work from another, like 業務を受託する (to <vocabulary>undertake</vocabulary> contract work). In legal contexts, it can also refer to being entrusted with physical items or money.
6218.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I plan to gift a watch for Father's Day.
examples.ja: 父の日には時計を贈るつもりです。

examples.en: I send you my gratitude.
examples.ja: 感謝の気持ちを贈ります。

examples.en: The winner of fantasy baseball will be given something as a prize.
examples.ja: ファンタジーベースボールの優勝者には、何か賞品が贈られます。

examples.en: The forest gives me the gift of birdsong.
examples.ja: 森は鳥の歌を私に贈ってくれる。

6219.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>presents</kanji> so if you do presents, you're giving them, making this <vocabulary>to give a present</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to gift</vocabulary>.

贈る is used for the act of giving when it's done with particular thoughtfulness or sincerity — often to express things like gratitude, love, congratulations, or respect. Things you might 贈る include flowers on a birthday, a commemorative item at an event, or even words of thanks. It can also extend to bestowing honors, titles, ranks, or awards, as these are also "gifts" in a sense.
6219.reading_mnemonic:
This word has the same reading as 送る (to send), so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

If you want <vocabulary>to give a present</vocabulary> to someone far away, you're going to need to <reading>送る</reading> (おくる) it to them. Make sure you pay for tracking!

examples.en: When I was three my father taught me to say, "I have nothing to do with the bribery case," to my mother.
examples.ja: 父は、私が三歳の時に、「その贈収賄事件には私は関与していない」と母に言うように教えた。

6220.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>presents</kanji> you <kanji>acquire</kanji> are a <kanji>bribe</kanji>. What? That is <vocabulary>bribery</vocabulary>!
6220.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: It’s impossible to bribe him with anything other than a Big Mac.
examples.ja: 彼にはビッグマック以外の賄賂は効かないよ。

6221.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I don't think my income would be enough to feed my family if we had a baby now.
examples.ja: もし今赤ちゃんができたら、俺の収入だけで家族を賄うのは無理だと思うんだよ。

6222.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>bribe</kanji>, but when you pay a bribe, you are going <vocabulary>to pay</vocabulary> something or <vocabulary>to cover</vocabulary> something, like a meal, or something like that.
6222.reading_mnemonic:
This verb uses the kun'yomi reading of the kanji. You haven't learned that yet, so here's mnemonic to help you:

Your employee always works through dinner time, so <vocabulary>to pay</vocabulary> for their extra work and <vocabulary>to cover</vocabulary> their meal, you <reading>mark</reading> <reading>a</reading> <reading>na</reading>cho (まかな) with their name. That marked nacho will be their dinner. So generous of you to cover their dinner with a free nacho! A pay increase would be better though.

examples.en: While running away from my furious wife, my suit got really torn up.
examples.ja: 怒り狂った妻から逃げ回っているうちに、スーツがボロボロに痛んでしまいました。

6223.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>escape</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to escape</vocabulary>. Also, it can be <vocabulary>to flee</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to run away</vocabulary>. Basically, if you're trying to get away from someone or something, you could be doing this.

逃げる is a general word for escaping that can be used in any situation, from running away from danger, to avoiding responsibility, to simply leaving a place quickly.
6223.reading_mnemonic: You are trying <vocabulary>to escape</vocabulary> from something chasing you, but you can't run fast because of your <reading>knee</reading> (に). You try to run, but it keeps holding you back. Feel the fear and pain of running with a hurt knee, and curse that knee of yours for holding you back.

examples.en: My little brother is so generous that he aided in the criminals’ escape and was arrested for it.
examples.ja: 私の弟は優し過ぎて犯罪者達の逃亡を助けてしまい、そのせいで逮捕されてしまいました。

6224.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>escape</kanji> <kanji>death</kanji> you have, well, an <vocabulary>escape</vocabulary>.
6224.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Although his feet were frostbitten, the missing English teacher safely came back alive.
examples.ja: 行方不明の英語教師は、足が凍傷になっていたものの、無事に生還しました。

6225.meaning_mnemonic: We got <kanji>life</kanji> by <kanji>sending back</kanji> our runner to home plate. That run allowed us more life in this game. Now, maybe we'll win! It was all by <vocabulary>reaching home plate</vocabulary>. Outside of baseball, this means <vocabulary>returning alive</vocabulary> from somewhere.
6225.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Okinawa was returned to Japan from the USA in 1972.
examples.ja: 沖縄がアメリカから日本に返還されたのは1972年のことです。

examples.en: I didn’t know that the championship flag had to be returned every year.
examples.ja: 優勝旗が毎年返還されなくちゃいけないなんて、知らなかったよ。

examples.en: I was just researching opinions on the return of the two islands involved in the Northern Territories dispute.
examples.ja: 今、北方領土問題の二島返還論について調べていたところです。

6226.meaning_mnemonic: If we <kanji>return</kanji> and <kanji>send back</kanji> things, we will have done a <vocabulary>return</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>restoration</vocabulary>.
6226.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: We are going to hold a sale to pass on the benefits of the strong yen.
examples.ja: 我々は円高還元セールを実施します。

examples.en: At our company, if profits exceed expectations, we return them to shareholders as an extra dividend.
examples.ja: 当社では、利益が予想を上回れば、特別配当として株主に還元することになっています。

examples.en: This credit card is offering a bonus cashback points promotion until the end of this month, so if you enroll now you'll get a good deal.
examples.ja: このクレジットカードは、今月の終わりまでポイント還元率アップのキャンペーンをしてるので、今入会したらお得ですよ。

examples.en: Through electrolysis, water is reduced to hydrogen and oxygen.
examples.ja: 電気分解によって、水は水素と酸素に還元される。

6227.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Send back</kanji> to the <kanji>origin</kanji> means you are going to <vocabulary>give something back</vocabulary>. This word is commonly used to mean "giving benefits back to the consumers.” For example, if a company makes more money than usual, they can thank consumers with a 利益還元 sale, lowering prices to "give back" some of the profits.

In the context of chemistry, 還元 also means <vocabulary>reduction</vocabulary>, like reducing an oxidized substance back to its original, unoxidized form.
6227.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: At first, I just tried the boiled tofu out of curiosity, and then I grew to like it.
examples.ja: 最初は、どんなもんかなと思って湯豆腐を食べてみただけなんですが、そしたら好きになっちゃったんですよね。

6228.meaning_mnemonic: 豆腐 is <kanji>tofu</kanji>, and 湯 means <kanji>hot water</kanji>, making it tofu you've put in hot water, aka <vocabulary>boiled tofu</vocabulary>.
6228.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of 豆腐 and the kun'yomi reading of 湯. You should be able to read this on your own. Will of course help to know 豆腐 as well.

examples.en: My kid mischievously overstretched the elastic and made it unusable.
examples.ja: 子供がいたずらでゴムを伸ばしすぎて使い物にならなくなりました。

examples.en: My grandmother reached her hands up to my face and told me "I love you," right before she passed away.
examples.ja: 祖母は死ぬ間際、私の顔に手を伸ばし、「愛してるよ」と言ってくれました。

6229.meaning_mnemonic: If 伸びる is "to be stretched" then 伸ばす is <vocabulary>to stretch something</vocabulary>, where you're doing the stretching. You know this because you took a <reading>bus</reading> and you stretched it out to be an even longer bus.
6229.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 伸びる, so if you know that you should know this.

examples.en: It seems that this typhoon could cause extensive damage to the area.
examples.ja: 今度の台風は、この辺りの地域にじん大な被害を及ぼす可能性があるみたいですよ。

examples.en: Please refrain from making statements that are harmful to child viewers.
examples.ja: 子供の視聴者に害を及ぼすような発言はひかえてください。

examples.en: What effect do people think radioactive contamination has on the human body?
examples.ja: 放射能汚染は人体にどのような影響を及ぼすと考えられているのでしょうか。

6230.meaning_mnemonic: If you have <kanji>reach</kanji>, that means you're able <vocabulary>to exert</vocabulary> a great influence on people. Watch out, though, because it also means you're able <vocabulary>to cause</vocabulary> great harm.
6230.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 及ぶ, so if you know that, you'll be able to read this one too.

examples.en: This security app is for Android OS as well as iOS.
examples.ja: このセキュリティー対策アプリは、AndroidOS及びiOSのどちらでもご利用頂けます。

6231.meaning_mnemonic:
及ぶ means "to reach" or "to amount to." The noun version is more like a grammar thing, as it means "<vocabulary>as well as</vocabulary>." Perhaps if you are reaching a certain point or certain amount, then you are adding things on. That's why this means "as well as".

Note that 及び is a term usually used in formal writing.
6231.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 及ぶ, so if you know that one you know that one <vocabulary>as well as</vocabulary> this one.

examples.en: I think my roommate invades my privacy too much.
examples.ja: ルームメートが、私のプライバシーに踏み込みすぎだと思うのよね。

6232.meaning_mnemonic:
踏む is "to step on" and the kanji 込 means <kanji>into</kanji>, so this means <vocabulary>to step into</vocabulary>.

踏み込む means to step further and harder than usual, like stepping forward to lunge for a ball or stepping hard on the accelerator. Figuratively, it can also mean <vocabulary>to intrude</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to delve into</vocabulary>, like stepping into someone's house without permission or exploring complex topics one step further.
6232.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the word 踏む and the kanji 込, put together.

examples.en: He’s not really the kind of person who talks about their own feelings, so he hid that he was excessively obsessed with me.
examples.ja: 彼はあまり自分の気持ちを言葉で表さない人なので、度を超す程私に執着していることを隠していました。

6233.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>ultra</kanji> or <kanji>super</kanji> so the verb version is what happens when you do something ultra or super much. You start <vocabulary>to exceed</vocabulary> the amount you were meant to do it. If you ultra drive a car, you exceed the speed limit. If you ultra study, you exceed your brain capacity. Get it?
6233.reading_mnemonic: Who likes <vocabulary>to exceed</vocabulary> everything? Your <reading>子</reading> (こ)! Or you, when you were a 子. No bedtimes, parents, or other limitations could stop you! You were able to go over them all!

examples.en: The Japanese government dispatched a team of doctors to the area affected by the disaster.
examples.ja: 日本政府は被災地に医師団を派遣した。

examples.en: The American military deployed a unit to Iraq.
examples.ja: アメリカ軍はイラクに軍を派遣した。

examples.en: The temporary worker quickly got used to the atmosphere of her new office.
examples.ja: その派遣社員は、新しい職場の雰囲気をすぐに掴みました。

6234.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>sect</kanji> of <kanji>dispatch</kanji> helps with all the <vocabulary>dispatch</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>deployment</vocabulary> duties.

When used together with the word 社員, this word can also mean <vocabulary>temporary</vocabulary>, in the sense of a temporary employee, possibly someone working for a company via a temping agency.
6234.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: We're going to burn some fallen leaves and make baked sweet potatoes.
examples.ja: 落ち葉を燃やして焼きイモを作ります。

examples.en: Fugu produced poison gas by burning non-burnable trash.
examples.ja: フグは不可燃ゴミを燃やして毒ガスを発生させた。

examples.en: I really like burning things until they’re reduced to ashes.
examples.ja: 何かを完全に灰になるまで燃やすことが大好きだ。

6235.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>burn</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to burn something</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to set on fire</vocabulary>.
6235.reading_mnemonic: This is when you're burning something. To remember this meaning, you have to remember the も part. So, just think of your friend <reading>Mo</reading>e (も), and how you're going to burn him... uh... just a little bit.

examples.en: Sure enough, the place was yakuza territory.
examples.ja: 案の定、その場所はヤクザの縄張りだった。

6236.meaning_mnemonic: Take your <kanji>rope</kanji> and <kanji>stretch</kanji> it out to show where the cutoff is. This is when you <vocabulary>rope off</vocabulary> something. It shows your <vocabulary>territory</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>turf</vocabulary>. Don't cross this rope I've stretched out, it's my <vocabulary>domain</vocabulary>.
6236.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is 縄 and 張る put together into one word. Just watch out for the rendaku that changes the 張り reading to ばり. Here's a little mnemonic in case you need it:

In order to <vocabulary>rope off</vocabulary> your <vocabulary>turf</vocabulary> you go around screaming <reading>baa</reading> (ば), basically at anyone who gets near your <vocabulary>territory</vocabulary>. You walk around the perimeter of your house or yard and shout, "This is my <vocabulary>domain</vocabulary>! Baa!" Yeah, that'll show 'em.

examples.en: The convenience store in 1-chome has just opened.
examples.ja: 一丁目のコンビニはオープンしたばかりです。

examples.en: Tanaka-san's apartment is in 3-chome.
examples.ja: 田中さんのアパートは、三丁目です。

examples.en: You have no choice but to walk to the company as there's no bus coming to 4-chome.
examples.ja: 四丁目にはバスが来ないので、会社までは歩くしかありません。

6237.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>street</kanji> you can see with your <kanji>eye</kanji> isn't soooo big you can't see it (like a town would be), but it's still pretty big because it has a street. This section of the town is the <vocabulary>district of a town</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>city block</vocabulary> (though specifically one of an irregular size).
6237.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji, so use those and you'll be A-Okay.

examples.en: Can you exchange these shoes for a pair that is one size bigger, please?
examples.ja: 一つ大きいサイズの靴に換えてもらえませんか。

6238.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>exchange</kanji>, so this verb is <vocabulary>to exchange</vocabulary>. If you exchange one thing for another thing, you are going <vocabulary>to exchange</vocabulary> it, after all. This word refers to exchanging one thing for something different.

Wondering about the difference between 替える and 換える? 替える means swapping one thing for another of the same kind, whereas 換える means exchanging or trading one thing for something different, often of similar value. So, you use 替える when switching out light bulbs, but opt for 換える when trading jewelry for cash.

I <kanji>recommend</kanji> this to you, so I'd like to <kanji>invite</kanji> you to try it. This is a <vocabulary>solicitation</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>invitation</vocabulary>.

勧誘 means soliciting someone to buy a product or service or inviting them to join a group or activity, often in a pushy way. It's commonly used to describe what telemarketers and door-to-door evangelists do, or for students recruiting new members for extracurricular activities.

6301.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>bury</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to bury</vocabulary> as well.

埋める can also mean <vocabulary>to fill</vocabulary>, and can refer to filling a hole, vacancy, or gap. Note that this word can be used to refer to filling in figurative holes and gaps too, like a hole in one’s finances!
6301.reading_mnemonic:
You learned this reading with the kanji, how nice for you!

However, you might notice that in addition to うめる, there's another reading too: うずめる. うめる is used for the act of burying something or filling in a hole, while うずめる is used when describing the covering or concealment of something, or when burying one's face in something (like a fluffy cat!)

6305.meaning_mnemonic:
Add an <kanji>honorable</kanji> little 御 for someone to <kanji>look at</kanji> when you want to show respect to them. 御覧になる is the honorific form of 見る, so it still means <vocabulary>to look</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to see</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to watch</vocabulary>, but with a more respectful tone.

You'll often use it when someone of higher status than you is doing the looking and you want to sound like a polite, refined adult who's showing proper respect to them. Keep in mind that the first 御 is often written in kana, like ご覧になる.

6312.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

甲 has traditionally meant <vocabulary>turtle shell</vocabulary>, but these days it appears much more often in expressions like 足の甲 (<vocabulary>instep</vocabulary>) and 手の甲 (<vocabulary>back of the hand</vocabulary>). If you think about it, those body parts kind of resemble turtle shells, don’t you think?
6312.reading_mnemonic: This word is made up of a single kanji, but it uses the on'yomi reading, not the kun'yomi reading. Luckily, you've learned this reading already. Yay!

examples.en: Thanks to his efforts, the newsletter was able to avoid being discontinued.
examples.ja: 努力の甲斐があって、そのニュースレターは廃刊になるのを免れた。

6313.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>turtle shell</kanji> that is <kanji>patterned</kanji> has much more <vocabulary>worth</vocabulary> than a boring non-patterned turtle shell. It probably has a better <vocabulary>effect</vocabulary> too if you throw it at your opponent in a go-kart race or something — give it a shot and see what the <vocabulary>result</vocabulary> is!

甲斐 doesn't mean "worth" in the sense of monetary value, but rather in the sense that some action you took paid off or was worth doing. You'll usually see it paired with verbs or other nouns, like 苦労の甲斐があった (it was worth the trouble) or 頑張った甲斐があった (trying hard paid off).
6313.reading_mnemonic:
You haven't learned this reading for 甲 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

It's <vocabulary>worth</vocabulary> it to chuck turtle shells out of your <reading>ca</reading>r (か) and try to hit other cars. Sure, it's a little dangerous, but the <vocabulary>effect</vocabulary> is that the other cars get slowed down or knocked over, which has the <vocabulary>result</vocabulary> of your car overtaking them. Totally worth it.

6315.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
6315.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the いね reading of this kanji. You can think of it like you're saying "いいね!" at the rice plant you're looking at (just shorten the い).

examples.en: My friend has much bigger rice fields.
examples.ja: 友達はもっと大きい稲田をもっていますよ。

6316.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>rice plant</kanji> <kanji>rice paddy</kanji> is a <vocabulary>rice field</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>rice paddy</vocabulary>.
6316.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses kun'yomi readings for 稲 (いな) and 田 with rendaku (だ). You may not be familiar with the いな reading yet, but it appears in a lot of compounds that use 稲, so it's good to know. Here's a mnemonic to help:

There's a popular road trip game in Japan where every time you pass a rice field, you have to <reading>ea</reading>t <reading>na</reading>chos (いな). See a rice field? Eat nachos. And if you've ever driven through rural Japan, you know how many rice fields (and eaten nachos) that adds up to. I once gained five pounds in two hours on a drive through Niigata… It wasn't pretty. But the rice fields were.

examples.en: He is immersing himself in rice cultivation.
examples.ja: 彼は稲作に没頭しています。

6317.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>make</kanji> a <kanji>rice plant</kanji> then you are doing <vocabulary>rice cultivation</vocabulary>, since you're making it from the seed to the harvest and doing it all!
6317.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses a kun'yomi reading for 稲 (いな) and the usual on'yomi reading for 作. You may not be familiar with the いな reading yet, but it appears in a lot of compounds that use 稲, so it's good to know. Here's a mnemonic to help:

When you do <vocabulary>rice cultivation</vocabulary>, you should <reading>ea</reading>t <reading>na</reading>chos (いな). You need all the calories and carbs from some loaded-up nachos to get ready for the hard work of rice cultivation, you know? Mmm, you'd happily do rice cultivation every day if it meant you could eat nachos.

examples.en: He gave me an old novel that is out of print.

examples.en: The principal doesn’t want to transfer his authority to someone else.

This is a formal term used to describe the legal transfer of rights, properties, or liabilities, so it's most commonly seen in official or legal documents.

6453.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: It’s not like you to abstain from alcohol. Unless maybe, are you pregnant?
examples.ja: お酒を控えるなんてらしくないね。もしかして、妊娠したとか？

6454.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>abstain</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to abstain</vocabulary> as well!

控える is super versatile. It can mean <vocabulary>to refrain</vocabulary> from drinking, <vocabulary>to hold back</vocabulary>  comments, or <vocabulary>to stand by</vocabulary> (abstaining from taking action). In some contexts, it can even mean "to take a memo" because memo-taking is like putting information on standby!
6454.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already, good for you!

6455.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 群れ is a <kanji>flock</kanji>? This is the verb version, and means <vocabulary>to flock</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to crowd</vocabulary> together with a bunch of other people.
6455.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 群れ, so if you know that you can flock together the two memories in your brain.

examples.en: The snow piled up thirty centimeters deep last night and my car got buried.
examples.ja: 昨夜、雪が30cmも積もり、車が埋もれてしまいました。

examples.en: My friend's LINE message got buried in my notifications, so I didn't notice!
examples.ja: 友達からのLINE、通知に埋もれてて、気づかなかった！

examples.en: We have to work hard to keep his talent from being buried!
examples.ja: アイツの才能が埋もれてしまわないように、俺たちが頑張らないと！

examples.en: My brother's room was always overflowing with stuff, and important things often ended up buried somewhere in there.
examples.ja: 兄の部屋はいつも色んなものにあふれていて、大事なものがどこかに埋もれるのはよくあることだった。

6456.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 埋まる is "to be buried." This verb is also <vocabulary>to be buried</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to get buried</vocabulary>. 

However, there's a slight difference between them. 埋まる focuses on the subject itself getting buried or filled, while 埋もれる highlights the sense of something being hidden or obscured by being covered. So you could use it to describe a yard covered in snow or your talent being overshadowed in a competitive environment. 

You can remember this nuance because it's <reading>more rare</reading> (もれる) to see something completely buried and covered up.
6456.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 埋める.

examples.en: I plan to work on my days off to make up for the time I took off due to illness.
examples.ja: 病気で休んだ分を休日に働いて埋め合わせるつもりだ。

examples.en: Do you think it's possible to compensate for a lack of intelligence with money?
examples.ja: 知性が足りないのを金で埋め合わせることはできると思う？

examples.en: Can’t we make up for this loss in some way or another?
examples.ja: どうにかこの損失を埋め合わせることはできないだろうか。

6457.meaning_mnemonic: 埋める is "to bury." 合わせる is "to unify together." If you bury somebody in order to unify them with you, you're almost certainly trying <vocabulary>to compensate for</vocabulary> something.
6457.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 埋める and 合わせる. Combine them into one big happy word.

examples.en: How long before we have to be back to the bus from the bathroom? There is a long line, so I’m worried I’ll be late.
examples.ja: 何時までに御手洗からバスに戻らなくてはいけませんか？行列ができているので、遅れないか心配してるんですが。

6458.meaning_mnemonic: You know 手洗い, right? This is like that, but way more polite sounding. The meaning is still the same though: <vocabulary>restroom</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>bathroom</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>toilet</vocabulary>.
6458.reading_mnemonic: The reading for the 御 is お, the rest is てあらい, even though the い isn't showing on the end. It gets pushed into the 洗い.

examples.en: Do I have to change trains to get to Gifu prefecture?
examples.ja: 岐阜県に行くには、電車の乗り換えが必要ですか？

6459.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen how 岐阜 is "Gifu." Now make it a prefecture to make <vocabulary>Gifu prefecture</vocabulary>.
6459.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

6460.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>employment</kanji> (雇用) <kanji>someone</kanji> is someone who gives you employment, aka an <vocabulary>employer</vocabulary>.
6460.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I’m sorry. We’re sold out of medium sizes for this T-shirt.
examples.ja: 御免なさい。このＴシャツのMサイズは売り切れちゃったんです。

6462.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 御免. The addition is all kana.

6463.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

6467.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I really can’t understand how such an incompetent man like that was able to rekindle her love.
examples.ja: どうしてあの甲斐性無しが彼女の愛を復活させることができたのか、全く理解できないね。

6470.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 甲斐 can mean "worth"? If worth is in your <kanji>nature</kanji>, you're probably a person of some <vocabulary>capability</vocabulary>. You're worth knowing and people appreciate your <vocabulary>dependability</vocabulary>.

甲斐性 means being dependable, responsible, or resourceful, especially in supporting others financially or emotionally. Traditionally it refers to a man's ability to provide for his family, so 甲斐性がない is often used to criticize someone for not making enough money.
6470.reading_mnemonic:
This word combines the word 甲斐 (which you've already learned) with the secondary on'yomi reading for 性. You haven't learned this reading of 性 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help:

Who embodies <vocabulary>capability</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>dependability</vocabulary>? The <reading>Sho</reading>gun (しょう), of course! He feeds his entire clan and army, makes battle plans, and rules a nation — all without breaking a sweat. A true leader, dependable and strong, the Shogun gets a lot of love for his 甲斐性.

examples.en: Rock climbing is what I live for.
examples.ja: ロッククライミングは私の生き甲斐です。

6471.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 生きる is "to live" and 甲斐 is "effect" or "worth." Something that has a good effect on your life and gives it worth is your <vocabulary>reason for living</vocabulary>. From your standpoint, it's <vocabulary>something worth living for</vocabulary>.

Keep in mind 生き甲斐 is mostly used as a noun, so you'll see it in phrases like 仕事が生き甲斐 (my job is my reason for living) or 生き甲斐が欲しい (I want something to live for).
6471.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 甲斐 and 生き, so if you know those you may have a <vocabulary>reason for living</vocabulary>, or at least a reason for doing your kanji study. Be careful of the rendaku changing 甲斐's reading to がい!

examples.en: She is proud that the backs of her hands are so beautiful.
examples.ja: とても綺麗な手の甲を持っていることが彼女の自慢です。

6472.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>hand</kanji>'s <kanji>turtle shell</kanji> is the back of it (see you can make it shaped like a turtle shell if you try hard!). That's why this is the <vocabulary>back of one's hand</vocabulary>.
6472.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the respective vocab readings of 手 and 甲.

examples.en: This job is really worthwhile because I can be useful to other people.
examples.ja: この仕事は、誰かのために役に立つことができるので、とてもやり甲斐があります。

6473.meaning_mnemonic:
やり is from やる, meaning "to do," and 甲斐 means "effect" or "worth." So, if the thing you do has an effect and is worth something, then it is <vocabulary>worth doing</vocabulary>.

やり甲斐 is a noun, so it's often used in phrases like やり甲斐がある (to be worth doing) or やり甲斐を感じる (to feel worthwhile).
6473.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own — just watch out for the rendaku changing 甲斐's reading to がい.

examples.en: I jumped for joy.
examples.ja: 私は小躍りして喜びました。

6474.meaning_mnemonic: If 躍る is "to leap" or "to jump," then this noun version will be <vocabulary>jumping</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>leaping</vocabulary>.
6474.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 躍る.

examples.en: I'd love to stay here and hear his whole speech, but unfortunately I have to go.
examples.ja: 残って最後まで彼の話を伺いたいのは山々なんですが、残念ながらどうしても行かなくてはいけないんです。

6475.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji means <kanji>inquire</kanji>, and the verb version means the same — <vocabulary>to inquire</vocabulary>. Depending on the context it can also mean <vocabulary>to hear</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to visit</vocabulary>. 

伺う is a humble verb, so you can use with people of higher status to show your respect for them. For example, if you ask your professor a question or hear something from them, you can say 教授に伺う. If you visit them, you can say 教授のところに伺う. And in customer service, you'll often hear お伺いします, which is the polite way for a staff member to say they're ready to listen and assist.
6475.reading_mnemonic: Excuse me, I'd like <vocabulary>to inquire</vocabulary> about Chairman Kaga. <reading>Ooh! Kaga</reading> (うかが). How exciting! You're asking questions about Chairman Kaga, the ruler over the Iron Chef kingdom.

examples.en: I am determined to devote myself to gambling.
examples.ja: ギャンブルに徹する覚悟を決めました。

6476.meaning_mnemonic: If you do <kanji>penetrate</kanji>, sure, you can <vocabulary>to penetrate</vocabulary>. But, if you penetrate something you really get into it, like, you are going <vocabulary>to devote oneself</vocabulary>.
6476.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the one you learned with the kanji. Look out for the shortening on this one.

examples.en: It’s just like her to study English all night.
examples.ja: 英語を徹夜で勉強するなんて、いかにもあの子らしいよね。

6477.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Penetrate</kanji> the <kanji>night</kanji> and go on through to the morning. You were up <vocabulary>all night</vocabulary> and had a <vocabulary>sleepless night</vocabulary>, aka an <vocabulary>all nighter</vocabulary>.
6477.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've seen these before, although 夜 can be a little tricky. It's the same や reading as in 今夜 and 深夜. Here's a mnemonic just in case:

You spend <vocabulary>all night</vocabulary> watching the <reading>Ya</reading>nkees (や). You should probably be sleeping, or at least doing your reviews or something, but instead you spend a <vocabulary>sleepless night</vocabulary> watching Yankees baseball games. Are the Yankees really that interesting?

examples.en: She can’t go out until she thoroughly applies her make-up.
examples.ja: 彼女は徹底した化粧を施さないと、外出することができません。

6478.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Penetrate</kanji> to the <kanji>bottom</kanji>. ALL the way to the bottom. Don't stop half way. This is <vocabulary>thoroughness</vocabulary>. This is <vocabulary>completeness</vocabulary>.
6478.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 底 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

<vocabulary>Thoroughness</vocabulary> is important when you're making <reading>ta</reading>ter (てい) tots. Each tater has to be cut carefully into little pieces then smashed back together again. Don't even get me started on the <vocabulary>completeness</vocabulary> I feel when I finish and eat them. Mm.

examples.en: The river is pretty shallow around here, so I’m sure you’ll reach the bottom.

包む can be used in both literal and figurative ways, so it can be used for wrapping up gifts, enveloping someone in love, or even for fog or light enveloping an area. In cultural contexts, it also sometimes implies the act of giving a financial gift, since in Japan things are often wrapped nicely before being given — even stacks of bills.
6526.reading_mnemonic:
You never wrap things once, you always wrap them twice. And then you double that. It's a <reading>two two</reading> (つつ) wrapping technique.

つつむ is the reading we want you to focus on, but it's good to know that 包む can be read as くるむ as well. くるむ is used when you wrap something up carefully and protectively, like a baby in a blanket. つつむ on the other hand, has broader use and is commonly used for wrapping things like presents.

6731.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>sink</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to sink something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to submerge something</vocabulary>.

This is a transitive verb, meaning it takes a direct object. So instead of describing something sinking on its own, you use 沈める when you sink an enemy ship or submerge yourself in a bathtub. 

You know this because you can't sink anything until you get that <reading>mail</reading> (める) saying, "Yes, proceed with sinking!" You've got to have that mail if you want to sink something, or else everyone will blame you for the missing ship — or for you disappearing under the water.
6731.reading_mnemonic: When you sink something, like a battleship, you go on and say: "<reading>she's</reading> (しず) sunk, I sunk her." That's like your tagline, or something. You say it for some reason because you think it's cool.

6732.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>sink</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to sink</vocabulary>.

On a literal level, 沈む refers to physical sinking — a boat sinking into the water or someone's foot sinking into the mud, for example. However, it can also be used metaphorically to talk about things like the sun setting (太陽が沈む), a nation falling into decline (国が沈む), or even someone "sinking" into a depressed mood (気分が沈む).
6732.reading_mnemonic: Your boat is about <vocabulary>to sink</vocabulary>, so you run around yelling, "<reading>She's</reading> (しず) sinking! She's… she's sinking! Abandon ship!" Boats are always female, so be careful not to say "it." If you don't say "she's" sinking, your crew might not get the message.
