6760.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Shake</kanji> plus "to do" is the verb version of shake. That's <vocabulary>to shake</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to rock</vocabulary> slowly.
6760.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 揺る.

examples.en: The swings at the park swayed in the wind.
examples.ja: 公園のブランコが風で揺れた。

6761.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 揺る which means "to shake" or "to jolt"? This is like that, but now you're not doing the shaking and jolting, making it <vocabulary>to be shaken</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be jolted</vocabulary>. You know this because it's really <reading>rare</reading> (れる) for you to be shaken like this.
6761.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 揺る.

examples.en: My kid was really looking forward to the kindergarten sleepover, but he got a cold and I just made him take antibiotics. So, sadly, he'll be absent tonight.
examples.ja: うちの子、幼稚園のお泊まり会をすごく楽しみにしてたんだけど、風邪を引いちゃって、今抗生物質を飲ませたところなんです。だから、残念ながら今夜は欠席させて頂きます。

6762.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 泊まる is "to stay the night." The noun version is a <vocabulary>overnight stay</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>sleepover</vocabulary>.
6762.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 泊まる, so pull from that and you shall know this.

meanings: To Let Someone Stay The Night

examples.en: I don't want to have some stranger stay at our house.
examples.ja: うちに知らない人を泊めるのは嫌です。

6763.meaning_mnemonic: 泊まる is "to stay the night." Now you're letting someone else stay the night, which makes this <vocabulary>to let someone stay over</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to let someone stay the night</vocabulary>.
6763.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 泊まる.

examples.en: I'm making a slide for my nephew's birthday, but I'm a little behind schedule.
examples.ja: 甥っ子の誕生日祝いに滑り台を作ってるんですが、少々予定が遅れ気味なんですよね。

6764.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 滑る is "to slide," and 台 is a counter for machines? In this case, the "machine" you slide down is a <vocabulary>playground slide</vocabulary>, or just a <vocabulary>slide</vocabulary> for short.
6764.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 滑る and 台.

examples.en: Take your time. Other than needing to pee, there is no rush. One day at a time.
examples.ja: 焦るなよ。小便に行きたい以外は、急ぐ必要はないよ。一日一日を着実にな。

6765.meaning_mnemonic: This is a bit of a weird word. The kanji is <kanji>char</kanji>, and a previous word you learned (焦げる) is "to be burned." This, on the other hand, is "to be in a hurry" or "to be impatient." I guess if you're getting burned or have that feeling, you're going <vocabulary>to be in a hurry</vocabulary> and you're going <vocabulary>to be impatient</vocabulary>. You can tell that this is that word because it only has one kana, る, which stands for <reading>ru</reading>de. You're feeling someone is being rude (or maybe you are), which is why you have this feeling of impatience and hurrying.
6765.reading_mnemonic: You're being rude, but you're also being a big <reading>ass</reading> (あせ) with your impatience.

examples.en: I always burn my toast completely black.
examples.ja: いつもトーストを真っ黒に焦がしてしまう。

6766.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 焦げる means "to get burned"? 焦がす is the transitive version, so this time someone is actively doing the burning, making it <vocabulary>to burn</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to scorch</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to char</vocabulary>.

焦がす means to burn the surface of something, usually blackening it to some degree. Unlike 焦げる, it can be for both intentional burning (a nice crème brûlée) and accidental burning (leaving bread in the toaster too long, scorching your sleeve on the stove).
6766.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 焦げる, so if you know that you know this word as well.

examples.en: The fever medicine slipped in with other pills and I’m not sure which one is which.
examples.ja: 解熱剤が他の薬に紛れちゃってて、どれがどれだか分かりません。

6767.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 紛らす means "to divert" or "to distract." This is when you're not doing the action, now, making this word <vocabulary>to be diverted</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be distracted</vocabulary>.
6767.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 紛らす.

examples.en: It was a basketball after all, but it was really misleading. I thought it looked exactly like a pregnant woman’s stomach.
examples.ja: 結局それはバスケットボールだったんですが、とても紛らわしかったです。私は完全に妊婦さんの大きなお腹だと思っていました。

6768.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji is <kanji>distract</kanji> and the adjective version is <vocabulary>confusing</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>misleading</vocabulary>.
6768.reading_mnemonic: You know who is particularly <vocabulary>confusing</vocabulary>? That <reading>maggie</reading> (まぎ) girl. She's confusing because she uses <reading>magi</reading>c (まぎ). Think of a Maggie you know, if possible.

examples.en: That old screen door is so gross!
examples.ja: あの古い網戸は本当に気持ち悪いね。

6769.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>net</kanji> <kanji>door</kanji> is a <vocabulary>screen door</vocabulary>. Makes sense, right? Screen doors are like little meshy nets made into a door shape.
6769.reading_mnemonic: You learned the kun'yomi for 網 when you learned it as a vocabulary word. Take that reading, add the 戸 reading with rendaku, and you have yourself あみど.

examples.en: He is just a young boy who hasn’t been tossed in the stormy seas of life yet.
examples.ja: アイツはまだ社会の荒波に揉まれた事のないただの若造だよ。

6770.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>wild</kanji> <kanji>wave</kanji> will make for some <vocabulary>stormy seas</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>raging waves</vocabulary>. Don't go out in these kinds of waves.
6770.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the kun'yomi readings of the kanji, 荒 (the secondary reading you learned with this kanji) and 波 (just the vocab version).

examples.en: Why are you running around naked with only gloves on? You’re such an idiot!
examples.ja: どうして裸んぼで手袋だけはめて走り回ってるの？あんたは本当に馬鹿ね。

6771.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>hand</kanji> <kanji>sack</kanji> is a sack for your hands... better put, these are <vocabulary>gloves</vocabulary>.
6771.reading_mnemonic: The readings are both the kun'yomi vocab readings, so think of 手 and 袋 as individual words, put together to make hand sacks. Watch out for the rendaku.

examples.en: The novelist finally hit pay dirt with his fifty-fifth novel about dragons.
examples.ja: その小説家は、55冊目の竜を題材にした小説でようやく大儲けすることができた。

6772.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
6772.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: There was a tornado warning and a power outage last night.
examples.ja: 昨夜、竜巻警報が出て、停電にもなりました。

6773.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>dragon</kanji> <kanji>scroll</kanji> is a dragon that's shaped kind of like a scroll, spinning around. This is a <vocabulary>tornado</vocabulary>.
6773.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi readings of the kanji. For 竜 just think about how it's a <reading>stand</reading>ing (立つ) dragon, because it would have to be if it's a <vocabulary>tornado</vocabulary>. Your まき reading comes from 巻く, but the kana is pushed into the kanji.

examples.en: What’s the best way to find dinosaur fossils?
examples.ja: 恐竜の化石を見つけるのに一番いい方法はなんでしょうか。

examples.en: "It's Halloween today, so I'm dressing up as a ninja in dinosaur cosplay." "What the heck. That's confusing."
examples.ja: 「今日はハロウィンなので、恐竜のコスプレをした忍者の仮装をしています。」「何だそれ、紛らわしいな。」

examples.en: That philosopher has four dinosaurs as pets.
examples.ja: あの哲学者は、ペットに恐竜を四匹飼っています。

6774.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>fear</kanji> <kanji>dragon</kanji> is a <vocabulary>dinosaur</vocabulary>. Dinosaurs are much, much scarier than dragons, and that's why dinosaurs are called fear dragons in Japanese.
6774.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The crow is seen as an ominous bird not only in Japan but also in Europe.
examples.ja: カラスは、日本だけでなくヨーロッパでも、縁起の悪い鳥とみなされます。

6775.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>edge</kanji> of <kanji>wake up</kanji> is right before you wake up. And, by wake up I mean you're about to wake up to the truth. But, you're only at the edge, so for now what you see is an <vocabulary>omen</vocabulary>... an omen that will show the truth.
6775.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Just remember that 起 is rendaku'd and becomes ぎ here.

examples.en: This country road is free from traffic jams.
examples.ja: この田舎道は、渋滞とは無縁です。

6776.meaning_mnemonic: If something has a <kanji>nothing</kanji> <kanji>edge</kanji>, it's probably <vocabulary>unrelated</vocabulary> to what you're doing. There's no edge, your stuff always has edges.
6776.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: How dare you to bring me a marriage proposal from a guy who has less than a high school education?!
examples.ja: 高卒以下の学歴の男との縁談を私に持って寄越すなんて、一体どういう神経してる訳？

6777.meaning_mnemonic: Let's take the <kanji>edge</kanji> and <kanji>discuss</kanji> it. That edge is the edge of getting married. But, when you reach that edge, before you jump over, you have to do a <vocabulary>marriage proposal</vocabulary>.
6777.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I am so excited that I get to meet with the left wing movement supporter for an interview.
examples.ja: 取材であの左翼支持者の方とお会いできるのがとても楽しみです。

6778.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>left</kanji> <kanji>wing</kanji> is the <vocabulary>left wing</vocabulary>, as in the "left wing party" or "left wing politics" or something like that.
6778.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 左 is the on'yomi reading, さ. You can remember this because the <vocabulary>left wing</vocabulary> uses <reading>saw</reading>s (さ) to cut down their right wing enemies. Imagine left wing hippies sawing down old right wing conservatives. BBrrrrbbbbbbzzzzz!

examples.en: I feel that I was born with extreme right-wing ideas.
examples.ja: 自分は、極端な右翼思想を持って生まれたように感じます。

6779.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>right</kanji> <kanji>wing</kanji> is the <vocabulary>right wing</vocabulary>. As in, "right wing politics" or "right wing beliefs."
6779.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 右, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Those in the <vocabulary>right wing</vocabulary> love eating <reading>u</reading>ni (う), not because they like the taste, but because uni is expensive. Picture some right-wing people in your mind right now and watch as they try really hard to pretend they like eating uni as they shovel buckets of it down their throats.

examples.en: The bird spread its great wings and flew into the sky.
examples.ja: その鳥は、大きな翼を広げて空へ飛び立ちました。

examples.en: Please pick the wings you want to wear.
examples.ja: つけたい翼を選んで下さいね。

examples.en: I thought I saw black wings on her back.
examples.ja: 彼女の背中に黒い翼が見えた気がした。

examples.en: The seagull's wings brushed the surface of the waves.
examples.ja: カモメの翼が波の上をかすめていった。

6780.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
6780.reading_mnemonic: In each political <vocabulary> wing</vocabulary> there are <reading>two boss</reading>es (つばさ). It's a weird system, but that's how they're doing it these days. Imagine your favorite or least favorite political wings, all with two bosses, arguing with each other.

examples.en: Everyone wants to choose a lucky day for their wedding.
examples.ja: みんな、結婚式の日に吉日を選びたいのよ。

6781.meaning_mnemonic: Having <kanji>good luck</kanji> is a <vocabulary>good omen</vocabulary> to have. Good luck means more good luck, right?
6781.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the きち reading you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: I had such an ominous dream that it made me really worried about you, and that’s why I called.
examples.ja: すごく不吉な夢を見たもんで、あんたのことが心配になってこうして電話をした訳さ。

6782.meaning_mnemonic: Something that is <kanji>not</kanji> <kanji>good luck</kanji> is <vocabulary>ominous</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>sinister</vocabulary>. It's also <vocabulary>bad luck</vocabulary> and an <vocabulary>ill omen</vocabulary>.
6782.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Why do we have to endure their insults, dad?
examples.ja: 父さん、どうして僕たちはアイツらの侮辱を忍ばなきゃならないの？

6783.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>endure</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to endure</vocabulary>.
6783.reading_mnemonic: Those who are able <vocabulary>to endure</vocabulary> are those who have had a lot of training. Who has had the most training of anyone? Ninjas. What group are they part of? The <reading>shino</reading>bi (しの).

examples.en: Koichi beat the ninja fair and square!
examples.ja: コウイチは忍者に、正々堂々と勝負で勝った。

6784.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>conceal</kanji>ed <kanji>someone</kanji> is someone who can conceal themselves. Who's better at that than anyone? A <vocabulary>ninja</vocabulary>.
6784.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Watch out for the rendaku.

examples.en: Don't worry, my patient. I can immediately remove your appendix with the sharp blade of my surgical scalpel.
examples.ja: 心配は要りませんよ、患者さん。私のこの手術用メスの鋭い刃で、すぐに盲腸を取ってあげますからね。

6785.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
6785.reading_mnemonic:
The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. But it also has a secondary reading you haven't learned, so here’s a mnemonic for it:

<vocabulary>Blade</vocabulary> in hand, you charge at your foes hollering "<reading>Yah</reading>! <reading>Eee</reading>! <reading>Baa</reading>!" (やいば). As the blade cuts through them, you cry "Yah! Eee! Baa!" even louder. This battle cry always fuels your fury and doubles the force of your swinging blade. "Yah! Eee! Baa!"

While both readings relate to blades, they have slightly different uses. は is used for any cutting tool's blade or edge, whereas やいば is a little old-fashioned and specifically refers to the blades of swords or knives, often in literary contexts.

examples.en: While brandishing his knife, he said to me in a low voice, "Get over here."
examples.ja: 刃物をちらつかせながら、男は低い声で私に「こっちへ来い」と言いました。

6786.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi readings of the kanji. You learned 刃's reading with the kanji, and you probably remember 物 from so many other words.

examples.en: While putting the edge of the blade in my neck, the guys asked me what it’s like to have people fawning over me all the time.
examples.ja: 刃先を俺の首に当てながら、奴は、皆にいつもご機嫌をとられてるってのはどんな気分なのかと聞いてきたんだ。

6787.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>blade</kanji>'s <kanji>ahead</kanji> is the farthest part of the blade away from you (since it's ahead of you). This is the <vocabulary>edge of the blade</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>blade edge</vocabulary>.
6787.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi readings of the kanji. For 刃 you learned that with the kanji. For 先 that's the vocab version of the kanji.

examples.en: The pitcher threw a peach instead of a ball in the MLB game.
examples.ja: 大リーグの試合で、ピッチャーがボールの代わりに桃を投げました。

6788.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
6788.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: I was embarrassed when my mom came to pick me up in the peach colored van.
examples.ja: 桃色のバンで母親が迎えにきた時は、恥ずかしかったですね。

6789.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from the vocab readings (and kanji readings, actually) of the two kanji.

examples.en: "Omg! My mouth is on fire, but this curry is sooo good!"
examples.ja: 「やばい〜！めっちゃ辛い～！でも、このカレーすっげ〜美味しい！」

examples.en: I can't eat spicy food.
examples.ja: 私、辛いものは食べれないんです。

examples.en: Oh, that's what happened? That's tough.
examples.ja: え、そんなことがあったの？それは辛いね。

6790.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. That being said, this can also mean <vocabulary>difficult</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>painful</vocabulary>, often in a psychological sense, though it can be physical as well. I guess if you're in a spicy situation it's going to be a difficult one.
6790.reading_mnemonic:
Depending on the context, the reading for this word could be からい or つらい. 

The からい reading is the <vocabulary>spicy</vocabulary> one that you learned with the kanji, which you can remember because spicy foods give a <reading>から</reading>て chop to your mouth. 

The つらい reading is the <vocabulary>difficult</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>painful</vocabulary> one. You can remember this because <reading>two Ra</reading>s (つら) are way more difficult to deal with than one Ra.

examples.en: Cumin seed is one of the essential spices for Indian curry.
examples.ja: クミンシードは、インドカレーには欠かせない香辛料のうちの一つです。

6791.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>fee</kanji> for <kanji>fragrance</kanji> and <kanji>spicy</kanji> in your food is the fee of <vocabulary>spices</vocabulary>. If you don't pay your spices fee, you aren't going to have any spice or fragrance in your food. If you do, you'll have those things and your food will be awesome!
6791.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've learned them for 香 and 料, but not for 辛, so here's a mnemonic to help:

The cabinet you keep your <vocabulary>spices</vocabulary> in is in a terrible place on the floor, and you keep banging your <reading>shin</reading> (しん) on it. Ouch!

examples.en: When it comes to oden, Japanese mustard is a must, isn’t it?
examples.ja: やっぱりオデンには辛子でしょ。

examples.en: I only have Japanese mustard in tube form, but is that okay?
examples.ja: 辛子、チューブのやつしかないけどいい？

examples.en: Both Japanese mustard and Western mustard are made from the seeds of the same plant, mustard greens.
examples.ja: 辛子もマスタードも、同じカラシナのタネから作られます。

examples.en: Seeds from a type of mustard green called "Oriental mustard" are used for Japanese mustard, while yellow mustard seeds or brown mustard seeds are used for regular mustard.
examples.ja: 辛子に使われるのはオリエンタルマスタードというカラシナのタネ、マスタードに使われるのはイエローマスタードやブラウンマスタードというカラシナのタネです。

6792.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>spicy</kanji> <kanji>child</kanji> is the child of spicy. So, not as spicy as mamma spicy, but still a bit spicy. This child spicy is <vocabulary>mustard</vocabulary>. Not too spicy, but not too mild.

辛子 generally refers to <vocabulary>Japanese mustard</vocabulary>, which tends to be browner and stronger than マスタード (Western mustard). Sometimes, especially as a prefix, it can also indicate spiciness from red pepper, like 辛子マヨネーズ (spicy mayo).
6792.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 辛い (からい) and the on'yomi reading for 子 combined together. It's one of those weird words that mixes the on'yomi and kun'yomi readings.

examples.en: You may feel a little out of place, but please be patient for me.
examples.ja: 場違いだって思うかもしれませんが、私のためだと思って辛抱してください。

6793.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>spicy</kanji> <kanji>hug</kanji> is a hug that feels not so great. But, it's not really painful all at once, either. As you're receiving a spicy hug, you just have to show <vocabulary>patience</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>endurance</vocabulary> while it lasts.
6793.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji, but you haven't learned this for either 辛 or 抱 yet, so let's use a mnemonic to remember it: 

Think about how much <vocabulary>patience</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>endurance</vocabulary> your <reading>shin</reading>s (しん) need to have to be good at <reading>bo</reading>wling (ぼう). You won't get any strikes with weak shins!

Note that the ぼう reading is the rendaku'd reading for 抱.

examples.en: Tofugu won a narrow victory in a copyright infringement suit.
examples.ja: トーフグは著作権侵害の裁判で辛勝しました。

6794.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>spicy</kanji> <kanji>win</kanji> is a <vocabulary>narrow victory</vocabulary>. Kind of makes sense, right?
6794.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: That part of the movie is always a mystery to me.
examples.ja: あの映画のその場面がいつも謎なんだよね。

6795.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word mean exactly the same thing. That makes this a <vocabulary>mystery</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>riddle</vocabulary>.
6795.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the one you learned with the kanji. No <vocabulary>mystery</vocabulary> there, I suppose.

examples.en: Does anyone understand this riddle?

6796.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings of the kanji you learned, twice. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: "If you don’t like your job as a samurai, why don’t you find another one?" "Easier said than done."
examples.ja: 「今の侍としての仕事が気に入らないのなら、他の仕事を探したら？」 「口で言うほど簡単じゃないよ。」

6797.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
6797.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the meaning and the reading of the kanji: <reading>さむらい</reading>.

examples.en: I'll have a draft beer.
examples.ja: 俺は生ビールにするよ。

examples.en: He's my buddy.
examples.ja: こいつ、俺のツレなんだ。

examples.en: Oh, that's okay, I'll do it.

6804.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. 

朱 refers to <vocabulary>vermilion</vocabulary>, a bright red color with a slight orange tint, and can also be translated as <vocabulary>scarlet red</vocabulary>. It's common in Japanese culture — you'll often see it on shrine gates and lacquerware, for example.
6804.reading_mnemonic:
The reading can be either the on'yomi or kun'yomi reading, so you have a choice there. Since you learned the on'yomi しゅ with the kanji already, let's learn the あけ reading now.

あけ sounds like the beginning of 開ける (to open). So imagine you <reading>開け</reading>る (あけ) a person up, to see what color they are inside. Turns out it's <vocabulary>vermilion</vocabulary>! Uh… you shouldn't open people up like that.

朱 is mostly read しゅ, but it can also be read あけ in certain phrases, like 朱に染まる, which means "to be covered in blood" (literally, "to be dyed in vermilion").

6849.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

6850.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: If the earth is going to be destroyed, why should I resist eating bacon?
examples.ja: 地球がじきに滅びるんだとしたら、どうしてベーコンを食べるのを我慢しなくちゃいけないの？

6852.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>destroy</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to be destroyed</vocabulary>. You know you're not destroying things because of the <reading>beer</reading> (びる). You'd never destroy beer... but someone else might. Grrr.
6852.reading_mnemonic: "THE <reading>HORROR</reading>!" (ほろ) you cry, as your beer is about <vocabulary>to be destroyed</vocabulary>.

examples.en: The new model's expression was a little stiff with nervousness.

examples.en: Did you know that there are stones that are harder than diamonds?
examples.ja: ダイヤモンドよりも硬い石があることは、ご存知ですか？

6853.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>stiff</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>stiff</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>hard</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>firm</vocabulary>.
6853.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as a very similar word, 固い. So, if you can use that word to help you to remember, you'll remember the reading of this word in no time as well!

examples.en: I believe that psychological rigidity can hinder problem solving.
examples.ja: 心理的硬直は問題を解決する妨げになると思われる。

examples.en: The rigidity of society is a problem that we need to fix.
examples.ja: 社会の硬直化は解決しなければならない問題です。

examples.en: I wonder how long after death rigor mortis sets in.
examples.ja: 死後どのぐらいで死後硬直が起きるんでしょうか。

6854.meaning_mnemonic:
Keep something <kanji>stiff</kanji> and <kanji>straight</kanji> and it's naturally going to lead to <vocabulary>stiffness</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>stiffening</vocabulary>.

硬直 commonly describes a person's body becoming stiff, whether from shock or discomfort, or due to the onset of rigor mortis following death.
6854.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Do you know how much more money the incumbent president earns than the former president?
examples.ja: 現職の大統領が、前大統領よりもどれだけ多くのお金を稼いでいるか知っているかい？

6855.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. Can also be <vocabulary>to make money</vocabulary>.
6855.reading_mnemonic: <vocabulary>To earn income</vocabulary>, you decided to start a <reading>car</reading> <reading>sa</reading>le. (かせ) "Every car sale, a step to richness!" was your quirky business mantra.

examples.en: The water in the pond was green yesterday, but it’s totally cleared up now. What happened?

6856.reading_mnemonic: You learned this reading when you learned the kanji.

examples.en: This beautiful spear is made from white gold and platinum.

examples.en: Your skin will be really smooth after bathing in the hot spring.
examples.ja: その温泉に入った後は、お肌がツルツルになるよ。

6858.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well, though you'll want to know that this refers most specifically to <vocabulary>human skin</vocabulary>.
6858.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: I get goosebumps just from hearing the name "cockroach."
examples.ja: 「ゴキブリ」という名前を聞くだけで、鳥肌が立ちます。

6859.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Bird</kanji> <kanji>skin</kanji> is <vocabulary>goosebumps</vocabulary>. Makes sense, since a goose is a bird and a bird's skin is bumpy.
6859.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the individual vocab readings of the two kanji, 鳥 and 肌.

examples.en: This towel is very soft and pleasant to the touch.

examples.en: The names of crayon and colored pencil colors that used to be called "skin tone" have now been changed to "pale orange" or "light orange."
examples.ja: 昔「肌色」って呼ばれてたクレヨンや色鉛筆の色の名前は、今は「ペールオレンジ」とか「うすだいだい」に変わってるんだよ。

6865.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The source of the terrible virus that wiped out half of mankind was a vodka-filled watermelon.

6867.meaning_mnemonic:

元凶 isn't just limited to people, so it can often refer to the <vocabulary>root cause</vocabulary> of a problem too, like 汚染の元凶 (the main cause of pollution). It carries a serious, negative tone and is mostly used in writing about crimes, scandals, or other major issues.
6867.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've learned these, but since 元 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you out:

The <vocabulary>ringleader</vocabulary> of all these problems is <reading>Gen</reading>ji (げん). He's the <vocabulary>main culprit</vocabulary> behind this mess. Remember all that trouble he stirred up by flirting with too many women in "The Tale of Genji"? Everyone admired his beauty, but there's no doubt he was the <vocabulary>root cause</vocabulary> of a lot of chaos.

examples.en: Everyone believed that the atrocious criminal would not fare well in prison.

examples.en: I didn’t know the hunters used the five-day workweek system.

6870.reading_mnemonic: You learned the reading of 狩 when you learned the kanji, but the reading for 人 is totally irregular. Just imagine that you're hunting a reindeer named <reading>Rudo</reading>lph (りゅうど). He has an unusually red nose, which makes him easy to spot and puts him at a bit of a disadvantage.

examples.en: Well, I'll call you again around 7 o'clock.
examples.ja: じゃあ、7時頃また電話しますよ。

examples.en: I was popular back then.

examples.ja: 今日のお昼の三時頃、この公園でツキノワグマが目撃されました。

6871.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. When used as a suffix, it means <vocabulary>approximate time</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>around</vocabulary> (as in "around 3:00").

6873.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 近い and 頃 put together.

examples.en: That kid's always alone, right? He doesn't seem to have friends his age so I can't help worrying about him.

6877.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>young</kanji> <kanji>approximate</kanji> is the approximate age of when you were young. This, approximately, is <vocabulary>one's youth</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>early life</vocabulary>.

若い頃 is often used when fondly remembering the past, like, "When I was younger, I used to…"
6877.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 若い and 頃 combined into one.

examples.en: The video about the little angel and the bacon deeply moved my soul.

6889.meaning_mnemonic:

I guess a ghost goes inside you and makes you feel this inspiration? Oh, wait, you can feel that because you have the <vocabulary>sixth sense</vocabulary>.

6918.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: My family took our puppy to a pet cemetery.
examples.ja: 家族でうちの犬をペット専用霊園に連れて行きました。

6919.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>ghost</kanji> <kanji>garden</kanji> is where many ghosts are harvested and where many ghosts grow. This is a <vocabulary>cemetery</vocabulary>.
6919.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

6920.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: If I am not mistaken, there are a lot of wetlands in Hokkaido, right?
examples.ja: 確か、北海道には湿地が多いんだよね？

6921.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>damp</kanji> <kanji>earth</kanji> is where water seems to congregate, but not so much that there's a lake or ocean or anything like that. Just damp. This is a <vocabulary>wetlands</vocabulary>.
6921.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I don’t like the rainy season in Japan because it’s very humid.
examples.ja: 日本の梅雨は湿気が多いので嫌いです。

6922.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>damp</kanji> <kanji>energy</kanji> is a feeling of dampness. It is <vocabulary>moisture</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>humidity</vocabulary>.
6922.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Just be careful of the shortening, and the irregular reading for 気.

examples.en: I sweat a lot when I was sleeping last night and my bed is a little damp.
examples.ja: 昨日の夜、寝汗をたくさんかいちゃったから、ベッドが何だか湿ってるのよね。

6923.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>damp</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to be damp</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be moist</vocabulary>. Ewww.
6923.reading_mnemonic: You know what's really damp and moist? <reading>Shee</reading>p <reading>me</reading>n (しめ) are. They've been hanging out in a greenhouse and now their wool is all damp. They're going to need a towel to dry off.

examples.en: My wife gets upset with me whenever I wear my socks inside out.
examples.ja: 靴下を裏返しに履いちゃうと、嫁が怒ってうるさいんだわ。

6924.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: Around the time they got married, my son’s wife pretended she was a prude.
examples.ja: 嫁ぎたての頃は、息子の嫁はかまととぶっていました。

6925.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>bride</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to marry</vocabulary>, because you can't really "to bride" someone.

嫁ぐ is often used when describing how someone has or is going <vocabulary>to marry into</vocabulary> another family.
6925.reading_mnemonic: Imagine you're getting married to a valley girl. You're all like. Hey, I'm gonna marry you! And she's all like <reading>Tots</reading> (とつ), we gonna get, like, married! Imagine her saying more "tots" things (tots = short for totally in valley girl speak, at least in my imagination).

examples.en: I found a 10,000 yen bill in a ditch beside a coin operated parking space.
examples.ja: コインパーキングの横の溝に、万札が落ちてるのを見つけたんだよ。

6926.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

溝 is commonly used for physical gaps like drainage ditches, small trenches, or grooves in surfaces. It can also describe metaphorical gaps, like emotional or relational divides between people.
6926.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

If you step in that <vocabulary>gutter</vocabulary> you'll catch <reading>measle</reading>s (みぞ). A gutter or <vocabulary>ditch</vocabulary> has all kinds of dirt and germs in it, including measles, so don't go stepping in it or drinking from it!

examples.en: I wonder if Filipinos know that the spawning place for eels is close to the Philippine Trench.
examples.ja: 鰻がフィリピン海溝の近くで産卵することは、フィリピン人に知られているのでしょうか。

6927.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I fell into a drainage ditch and got injured.
examples.ja: 排水溝に落ちて怪我をした。

examples.en: It's pretty common for even Japanese people to mix up 排水溝 and 排水口, isn't it?
examples.ja: 排水溝と排水口がごっちゃになってる人って日本人でも結構多いよね。

examples.en: It's important to clean the gutters and drainage ditches regularly because it can be a big hassle when they get clogged.
examples.ja: 詰まると大変だから、側溝や排水溝は定期的に掃除しておいた方がいいですよ。

6928.meaning_mnemonic:
You already know that <kanji>emit</kanji>ted <kanji>water</kanji> means "drainage." Add <kanji>gutter</kanji> to that and this becomes a <vocabulary>drainage</vocabulary> in the sense of a <vocabulary>drainage ditch</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>gutter</vocabulary>.

When it comes to the drain in your sink or bathtub, you can use 排水口, which has the same pronunciation but a different kanji.
6928.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The top team will be awarded with a prize of doing aesthetic waterfall meditation.
examples.ja: 一位のチームには、賞品として滝修行が授与されます。

6929.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
6929.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: My grandma told me that it is very dangerous to swim in the rapids.
examples.ja: 祖母に、滝川を泳ぐのは危険だと言われました。

6930.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>waterfall</kanji> <kanji>river</kanji> is a river that's moving like a waterfall! Fast and furious! Water that moves like this are <vocabulary>rapids</vocabulary>.
6930.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi vocab reading of each kanji: 滝 and 川. Careful of the rendaku.

examples.en: "Salmon, let’s get married in Las Vegas this weekend." "Fugu, have you lost your mind?"
examples.ja: 「サーモン、今週末、ラスベガスで結婚しよう。」「フグ、気でも狂ったの？」

6931.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>lunatic</kanji> or <kanji>crazy</kanji>. The verb version of this is <vocabulary>to go mad</vocabulary> (you don't really "go lunatic" now, do you?) or <vocabulary>to go crazy</vocabulary>.
6931.reading_mnemonic: To remember the reading, just think about how when you go crazy, you are <reading>coming</reading> (来る) to crazy town. Just imagine some voice beckoning you to come. Come here! Please come here! Come to crazy town! Give in to the voices!

examples.en: You must be insane to decline that offer.
examples.ja: その申し出を断るなんて狂気の沙汰だよ。

6932.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: It looked just like a phoenix soaring high in the air.
examples.ja: それは、まるで天空を高く翔る不死鳥のようでした。

6933.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>fly</kanji>, so the verb version means <vocabulary>to fly</vocabulary>.
6933.reading_mnemonic: You learned this reading already! You should be able to read this too!

examples.en: I think I want to do something to show my filial piety toward my parents.
examples.ja: 何か両親に親孝行してあげたいと思っています。

examples.en: You should at least do something nice for your mom on Mother's Day!
examples.ja: 母の日くらいは親孝行しようよ！

examples.en: Perhaps true filial piety is spending time with your parents, not spending money on them.
examples.ja: お金じゃなくて、時間を使って一緒に過ごすのが本当の親孝行かもしれない。

examples.en: But isn't the age of robots honoring our parents for us just around the corner?
examples.ja: でも、もうすぐロボットが代わりに親孝行してくれる時代が来るんじゃない？

6934.meaning_mnemonic:
You have the kanji for <kanji>parent</kanji> combined with 孝行, which you know means "filial piety." If you show filial piety toward your parents… well, it's still <vocabulary>filial piety</vocabulary>. Now it's just extra clear who you're showing that filial devotion to! 

While it may feel kind of redundant, 親孝行 tends to be a little more common than 孝行. It's nice to add "parent" for extra love points, you know?
6934.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 孝行 plus the kun'yomi of 親. Put them together and you'll become a good filial child.

examples.en: I hadn’t noticed that there was a loophole in the law until now.
examples.ja: その法律に抜け穴があることを今の今まで見逃していました。

6935.meaning_mnemonic: 逃す is "to let go" or "to let escape." If something escapes your <kanji>see</kanji>ing, then you are going <vocabulary>to overlook</vocabulary> it.
6935.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 見 and 逃す.

examples.en: She chuckled when she saw my new hairstyle. That’s rude, isn’t it?
examples.ja: 俺の新しい髪型を見て、あいつプッと吹き出したんだぜ。失礼だよな。

6936.meaning_mnemonic: If 吹く is "to blow" and 出す is "to remove," then you are removing your blowing. You need <vocabulary>to begin to blow</vocabulary> to do that!
6936.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 吹く and 出す.

examples.en: The reality is that the house is so old that the rain and wind blows in whenever a storm comes.
examples.ja: 家はおんぼろで、嵐が来る度に雨風が吹き込むのが現実です。

6937.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 吹く is "to blow" and the kanji 込 means <kanji>into</kanji>. So this word means <vocabulary>to blow in</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to breathe into</vocabulary>, and it can be used both transitively and intransitively.

It can also be used figuratively to mean to breathe into or<vocabulary>to imbue</vocabulary>, like breathing new life into something, or imbuing someone’s mind with hatred.
6937.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the word 吹く and the kanji 込む.

examples.en: What attracts you to whistling?
examples.ja: 口笛を吹くことにどんな魅力を感じますか。

6938.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 口笛 is "whistling." So, if you're <kanji>blow</kanji>ing your whistle you're going <vocabulary>to whistle</vocabulary>.
6938.reading_mnemonic: The readings are of 口笛 and the reading you learned from 吹.

examples.en: This miso soup is too salty. Can you water down a little bit?
examples.ja: この味噌汁はしょっぱすぎるよ。もうちょっと薄めてもらってもいいかな？

6939.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>dilute</kanji> and the verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to dilute</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to water down</vocabulary>.
6939.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 薄い, so if you know that you'll be able to read this too.

examples.en: I’m thinking about how to escape from zombies if they actually showed up.
examples.ja: 万が一ゾンビが実際に現れた場合を想定して、どうやってゾンビから逃れるのかを考えているんです。

6940.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen 逃げる and 逃す. This one is 逃れる. This one simply means <vocabulary>to escape</vocabulary>. So that's not too bad. The difference between this one and the other escapes is that it has to do more with luck.
6940.reading_mnemonic: This is the same reading you learned for 逃す, so you should be able to read this word as well.

examples.en: Don’t you think pretending that you failed to catch the criminal is a bit overkill?
examples.ja: 犯罪者を取り逃がすふりをするのは、ちょっとやり過ぎじゃない？

6941.meaning_mnemonic: The thing you want to <kanji>take</kanji> has <kanji>escape</kanji>d. Meaning you failed to catch this thing. This word is <vocabulary>to fail to catch</vocabulary>.
6941.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 取る and 逃がす.

examples.en: Let’s go to the party and brush off your depression.
examples.ja: パーティーに行って、憂鬱なんて吹き飛ばしちゃおうぜ。

6942.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 吹く is "to blow" and that 飛ばす is "To let fly." So, if you use your blowing to let something fly, you are going <vocabulary>to blow away</vocabulary> it.
6942.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 吹く and 飛ばす, put together.

examples.en: Could I inquire about your blog's URL, please?
examples.ja: あなたのブログのURLをお伺いしてもよろしいですか？

6943.meaning_mnemonic: If 伺う is "to inquire" or "to visit" then the noun version would be a polite way to say <vocabulary>inquiry</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>enquiry</vocabulary>. In other words, a <vocabulary>question</vocabulary>. It can also mean a <vocabulary>visit</vocabulary>.
6943.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 伺う.

examples.en: We were surprised that fans had gathered to wait for us when we arrived at the airport.
examples.ja: 空港に到着するとファンが群がっていて、驚きましたよ。

6944.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 群れる, which means "to flock" or "to crowd."? This also means that!
6944.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a little different from 群れる, though. There's an extra ら in there. That being said, it's pretty similar, so you should be able to use one to remember the other after a few reps. You can also think about it this way: Everyone is flocking together in one place. Strange thing is, it's to a small <reading>村</reading> (むら). There's a 村 reunion going on, that's why.

examples.en: I saw a mole going underground.
examples.ja: モグラが土の下に潜って行くところを見ました。

examples.en: How long can you stay underwater?
examples.ja: 水の中にどのぐらいの間潜っていられますか。

examples.en: My dog learned a trick to jump through a hula hoop.
examples.ja: うちの犬は、フラフープをジャンプして潜る技を身につけました。

6945.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>conceal</kanji>, but as a verb, this word means <vocabulary>to go under</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to pass through</vocabulary>. Most commonly, this word means <vocabulary>to dive underwater</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to go underground</vocabulary>. Can you see why the kanji for conceal kind of makes sense in these cases? If you're underwater or underground, no one can see you!
6945.reading_mnemonic:
潜る has two possible readings: もぐる and くぐる. The first is used when you mean to dive underwater or go underground.  The second is used when you pass through or under something, sometimes with difficulty, such as crawling under a fence. We want you to focus on もぐる, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Why are you trying to dive underwater again and again? It's to get <reading>mo' goo</reading> (もぐ) to sell on the black goo market. Who knew that sea goo was such a commodity?

examples.en: He's good at matching the pace of others, isn't he?
examples.ja: 彼は相手のペースに合わせるのが上手いよね。

examples.en: I don't have a jacket that goes with this sweater.
examples.ja: このセーターに合わせる上着がない。

examples.en: You don't need to force yourself to fit in with others.
examples.ja: ムリして人に合わせる必要はないよ。

6946.meaning_mnemonic: You know that the alternative kanji meaning for 合 is <kanji>join</kanji>, which is what we're using here. The verb form of join is <vocabulary>to join together</vocabulary>, and it can also mean <vocabulary>to unify</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to match</vocabulary>.
6946.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 合う, so if you know that reading you'll know this reading as well.

examples.en: "Come now, isn’t it about time for bed?" My grandfather used to say that to me every night.
examples.ja: 「さぁ、そろそろ寝床に着く時間じゃぞ。」子供の頃、毎晩祖父にこう言われました。

6947.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>sleep</kanji> <kanji>bed</kanji> is where you sleep. Where do you sleep? In a <vocabulary>bed</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>crib</vocabulary>. Side note, if you're a baby sleeping in a crib, you must really want to learn kanji.
6947.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings of the kanji. You didn't learn the second kun'yomi reading for 床. You take とこ and rendaku it into どこ. How do you remember this? Just think about your bed. Then wonder, "<reading>where</reading> (どこ) is it?"

examples.en: I’m thinking of learning how to become an undertaker because it looks like a pretty secure job.
examples.ja: 中々手堅い仕事みたいだから、葬儀屋になるための勉強をしようかなって思ってるんだよね。

6948.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 堅い is "solid" or "tough." When your <kanji>hand</kanji> is <kanji>solid</kanji> and tough, it's <vocabulary>solid</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>steady</vocabulary>. If your hand is shaky, it's the opposite, or something.
6948.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the two words 手 and 堅い combined together. Watch out for the rendaku.

examples.en: My car was broken into last night and my mac was stolen.
examples.ja: 昨夜車上荒らしにあって、マックを盗まれました。

6949.meaning_mnemonic:
荒れる is "to be stormy" or "to be rough." 荒らす is when you do the stormy rough things. You go wild on everyone, trying <vocabulary>to lay waste</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to mess up</vocabulary> everything around you.

荒らす is all about creating a mess. It can be physical destruction, like a wild pig tearing up a garden or a robber ransacking and messing up a house. Or it can refer to disrupting a peaceful situation, such as trolling an online forum or chat.
6949.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 荒れる.

examples.en: In a wild voice he proclaimed that he was totally “pissed off” at his wife for "pissing" on his face every night while he was sleeping.
examples.ja: 彼は荒々しい声で、寝ている時に奥さんが毎晩顔に小便を掛けてくることに怒り心頭していることを公言しました。

6950.meaning_mnemonic: 荒い is <kanji>rough</kanji>. Double that to 荒々しい and you have the same thing: <vocabulary>wild</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>rough</vocabulary>.
6950.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 荒い. Since you already know that 々 means it repeats, you already know this reading!

examples.en: My mom forbade my dad from collecting tasteless dolls.
examples.ja: 母は、父が悪趣味な人形を集めることを禁止しました。

6951.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 趣味 means "hobby"? Well, if you have <kanji>bad</kanji> hobbies, it probably means you have <vocabulary>bad taste</vocabulary>. 

悪趣味 is often used to describe something that lacks sophistication or sensitivity, like tacky shoes and offensive jokes, as well as someone with that kind of taste.
6951.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: There is braille on this wrapping paper.
examples.ja: この包み紙には点字が施してあるわ。

6952.meaning_mnemonic: A 包み is a <kanji>bundle</kanji> or <kanji>package</kanji>, and 紙 is <kanji>paper</kanji>. What paper goes around bundles and packages? That would be <vocabulary>wrapping paper</vocabulary>.
6952.reading_mnemonic: The reading is 包み and 紙 combined together. Be careful of rendaku.

examples.en: It’s high time we got out of here. Let’s move.
examples.ja: そろそろ潮時だ。引き上げるぞ。

examples.en: It’s high time that you quit smoking. Go get some nicotine patches right now.
examples.ja: 今こそタバコをやめる潮時だ。今すぐニコチンパッチを買いに行くんだ。

examples.en: The man decided to take this as an opportunity to step down from his gig as a legal drug seller, as he knew that he might put himself in danger someday if he continued to do this.
examples.ja: こんなことを続けていては、いつか自分の身を危険にさらすかもしれないと、男はこれを潮時に合法ドラッグの売り子からは身を引く事にした。

6953.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>tide</kanji> <kanji>time</kanji> is the <vocabulary>tidal hour</vocabulary>.

This word is often used figuratively, as in “the perfect time to act”, especially in reference to quitting something or backing away from a situation.
6953.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the individual words, 潮 and 時. Watch out for the rendaku.

examples.en: Where exactly is the basin of the Kuroshio Current?
examples.ja: 黒潮の流域とは正確にはどこになりますか？

6954.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>black</kanji> <kanji>tide</kanji> isn't what you think, most likely. This is the <vocabulary>Japan current</vocabulary>, aka the <vocabulary>Kuroshio Current</vocabulary>. It's a Northern flowing  current on the West side of the Pacific Ocean. Have you heard of the Gulf Stream? It's kind of like that.
6954.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi readings of the two kanji, put together. 黒 and 潮.

examples.en: I was rubbing my eyes because of my allergies and one of my contact lenses was torn.
examples.ja: 花粉症で目を擦ってたら、片方のコンタクトレンズが破けました。

6955.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>rub</kanji> and this verb means <vocabulary>to rub</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to scrub</vocabulary>.
6955.reading_mnemonic:
If you're going <vocabulary>to rub</vocabulary> me like that, I'm going to <reading>sue</reading> (す) you. It's making me very uncomfortable. The <reading>cos</reading>t  (こす) of your rubbing actions will be high.
    
So this word has two readings and both mean “to rub.” But you usually use する for a single action, such as lighting a match or grazing your knee, while こする means doing it repeatedly, like when you’re cleaning or polishing something.

examples.en: This package is just a symbol of our friendship.

examples.en:
Tatami mats come in different sizes such as "Edo-ma," "Kyo-ma," and "Danchi-ma," so even a 6-tatami room can vary in actual size.
If you're not aware of this, you might run into problems like thinking "It's 6 tatami, but it feels small" or "The 6-tatami carpet doesn't fit."

examples.en: I found his inside out, wrinkled dress shirt on the tatami where he threw it.

7130.meaning_mnemonic: Something that is <kanji>bright</kanji> and <kanji>clear</kanji> has great <vocabulary>clarity</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>clearness</vocabulary>. Just look at something with such brightness and such clearness! It has so much clarity!
7130.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: You shouldn’t wear slippers barefoot if you don’t want to get athlete’s foot.

7143.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 歯 and 磨く, put together.

examples.en: I'm in the middle of something. I'll come back later and make the muddy water clear.

examples.en: The Major kept a composed face even when the Colonel was angry with him.
examples.ja: 少佐は、大佐に怒られても澄ました顔をしていた。

7144.meaning_mnemonic:

This can also mean <vocabulary>to strain</vocabulary> when used together with 耳, as in 耳を澄ます, "to strain one's ears".
7144.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji, so if you know that, that'll make this answer clear too.

examples.en: The one hundred erasers that I had collected were melted by the heat and turned into one big lump.
examples.ja: コレクションしていた消しゴム100個が熱で溶けて一つの大きな塊になってしまった。

examples.en: Thanks to your taking care of my kid, Ms. Date, I could do my shopping freely.
examples.ja: 伊達さんがうちの子を見ていてくれたお陰で気兼ねなく買い物ができました。

examples.en: Because of the down quilt that my parents gave me, it’s really hard to get out of bed these days.
examples.ja: 両親がプレゼントしてくれた羽毛布団のお陰で、最近布団から出るのがかなり辛い。

examples.en: Thanks to everyone, we could go to the quarter-finals of the Japan National High School Baseball Tournament held in Koshien stadium.
examples.ja: 皆様のお陰で、我々は甲子園球場で開催されている高校野球のトーナメントで、準々決勝にまで進出することができました。

7148.meaning_mnemonic:
陰 is a shadow, and adding お to it and makes it honorific. It becomes the shadow of someone very important, and means <vocabulary>thanks to</vocabulary>, as in "thanks to you, I was able to pass the test." This originally comes from the idea of being in the shadow of the gods, who are protecting you and helping you out!

If that's hard to remember, think about shade helping you out. Perhaps <vocabulary>thanks to</vocabulary> the <kanji>shade</kanji> you were able to survive the heat of the desert.
7148.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the word 陰. <vocabulary>Thanks to</vocabulary> that other vocab word, you can read this one!

examples.en: The other day, I went to the bookstore with a friend.

examples.ja: 私は新しい本を買うために、前の日から本屋の前でキャンプをしました。

7149.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>book</kanji> <kanji>shop</kanji> is a shop that sells books. A <vocabulary>bookstore</vocabulary>.
7149.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the ones that you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: His handwriting is kind of bad, don't you think?

examples.ja: なんか不味そうなサンドイッチだね。

examples.en: I have never had such a bad tasting avocado soup.
examples.ja: こんなに不味いアボカドスープを飲んだことはありません。

7150.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen 美味しい by this point. This is the opposite of that. Instead of 美 you have 不 (not), so something that does <kanji>not</kanji> have <kanji>flavor</kanji> is something that doesn't taste good. i.e. something <vocabulary>bad tasting</vocabulary>. This can also refer to someone who's <vocabulary>unskillful</vocabulary> at something as well.
7150.reading_mnemonic: The reading doesn't follow any of the rules you've run into. It's まずい. Think about how you're going through this really long <reading>maze</reading> (まず) and how you're promised a really tasty wonderful treat at the end for getting through it (you're a lab rat or something). When you get to the end, there's your treat! What joy! You eat it and... oh man... it is so <vocabulary>bad tasting</vocabulary> you can't even believe it. Be sure to imagine the terrible taste and the terrible disappointment after going through that difficult maze only to get this... this... terribly <vocabulary>unappetizing</vocabulary> cheese.

examples.en: "Achoo!" "Are you all right?"
examples.ja: 「ハックション！」「大丈夫？」

Nothing you need to worry about when you have your super giant husband around to protect you. This is a really useful word, and it is used all the time. If someone asks: "Are you alright?" you could say in response "大丈夫" to mean you're doing all right.

7357.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji means <kanji>royal consort</kanji>, so adding it to someone's name gives you their royal style: "<vocabulary>Princess</vocabulary> ______," or, in some cases, "<vocabulary>Queen</vocabulary> ______."

〜妃 essentially refers to the wife of a crown prince, emperor, or other royal family member. These days, you'll almost always see it used with princesses, like ダイアナ妃 (Princess Diana) or キャサリン妃 (Princess Catherine), but in historical contexts you'll occasionally see it used with queen consorts and empress consorts too.
