examples.ja: 父の弁当は、彩りについて全く考慮がされておらず、全部茶色だったので嫌でしたね。

7439.meaning_mnemonic: This is the noun version of the kanji and has the same meaning as well: <vocabulary>coloring</vocabulary>.
7439.reading_mnemonic: The reading has いろ (like 色) in it, then a ど, so think about an <reading>色 do</reading>g, running around coloring things, because that's what an 色 dog does.

examples.en: Whenever I wake up with a pounding headache, I lament drinking too much the night before.
examples.ja: ガンガン響く頭と共に目を覚ます度に、前日の夜飲み過ぎたことを悔やみます。

7440.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>regret</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to regret</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to mourn</vocabulary>.
7440.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 悔しい.

examples.en: My man is in the middle of the fist fight in the club.
examples.ja: 俺の連れは今クラブで殴り合いの喧嘩の真っ最中さ。

7441.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 殴る, which means "to punch"? Well, add on 合う and you've got <vocabulary>punches</vocabulary> that have <vocabulary>come together</vocabulary> with other punches. By "come together" I mean your fist is coming in contact with someone's face, and their fist is coming in contact with your kidneys. In other words, this is a <vocabulary>fistfight</vocabulary>.
7441.reading_mnemonic: The readings come from 殴る and 合う, punched together.

examples.en: We had an early lunch before the raid.
examples.ja: 殴り込みの前に早めの昼食を取りました。

7442.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Punch</kanji> your way <kanji>into</kanji> a place, and you're launching a <vocabulary>raid</vocabulary>. 

殴り込み usually means a raid by gang members or delinquents, where they barge into someone's home or enemy territory to start a fight.
7442.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the word 殴る and the kanji 込.

examples.en: I thought you are a big spender, and you turned out to be a con artist.
examples.ja: 派手にお金を使っているなぁと思っていたら、詐欺師だったんですね！

examples.en: I heard that there are quite a few real estate scammers out there.
examples.ja: 不動産詐欺師というものが結構いるらしい。

examples.en: "Hey, did you just call me a liar?" "No, but I called you a swindler."
examples.ja: 「ねぇ、今俺のこと、嘘つきって言った？」「そうは言ってないけど、詐欺師とは言ったよ。」

7443.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 詐欺 is "fraud." An <kanji>expert</kanji> in fraud is someone who does this it lot, and possibly for a living. That's a <vocabulary>swindler</vocabulary>, a <vocabulary>con artist</vocabulary>,  or a <vocabulary>scammer</vocabulary>.
7443.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Will help to know the reading of 詐欺 as well.

examples.en: Don’t give up! Accomplish it! You can do it!
examples.ja: 諦めないで！やり遂げるんだ！お前なら出来るよ！

7444.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>accomplish</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to accomplish</vocabulary>.
7444.reading_mnemonic: Everything you've accomplished can be stored in your single little pinky <reading>toe</reading> (と)... you haven't accomplished that much, apparently.

examples.en: I like clothes made of hemp cloth, but they’re rather expensive.
examples.ja: 麻布の服が好きなんだけど、結構お値段が高いんだよね。

7445.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the individual vocab readings of 麻 and 布 combined together.

examples.en: I’ve always dreamed of experiencing the red-light district.
examples.ja: 花柳界を経験してみるのが夢だったんだ。

7446.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>red light district</kanji> (花柳) <kanji>world</kanji> of the red light district is the <vocabulary>red light district</vocabulary>, though this can refer especially to the "<vocabulary>pleasure quarters</vocabulary>" or "<vocabulary>world of the geisha</vocabulary>" as well.
7446.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The man they arrested is suspected of breaking into the rest area.
examples.ja: 逮捕された男は、休憩所に不法侵入した疑いがかけられていた。

7447.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>rest</kanji> (休憩) <kanji>place</kanji> is a <vocabulary>rest area</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>rest stop</vocabulary>.
7447.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Watch out for the rendaku.

examples.en: I removed my dog’s ear wax with a cotton swab and it was kind of sticky. Is it normal?
examples.ja: 綿棒で犬の耳垢を取ったら何だか粘々していたんですが、それは普通ですか。

7448.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Sticky</kanji> <kanji>sticky</kanji> things are really <vocabulary>sticky</vocabulary> and covered with <vocabulary>stickiness</vocabulary>.
7448.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 粘る. I suppose you <reading>never never</reading> want to touch something <vocabulary>sticky</vocabulary>.

meanings: Thank You For Your Hard Work

examples.en: Good job! You worked hard.
examples.ja: お疲れ様！よくがんばったね。

examples.en: Thank you for your hard work, chief. I'll be taking my leave now.
examples.ja: お疲れ様でした、所長。お先に失礼します。

examples.en: Thank you for your hard work, Mr. Mayor. Do you have a moment right now?
examples.ja: 市長さん、お疲れ様です。今、ちょっとお時間よろしいですか？

examples.en: When my wife puts my jacket on the hanger she always says, "Thank you for working hard again today."
examples.ja: 私の妻は私の背広をハンガーに掛ける時に、「今日も一日お仕事お疲れ様でした」といつも言ってくれるんです。

7449.meaning_mnemonic: You are a 疲れ (tired) 様 (honorific that kind of refers to whoever's being mentioned). You say this to people when they've done good work — at the end of a workday or after a hard practice, for example. I guess the idea is that if they're tired, they've done some good work. Tell your coworkers お疲れ様でした when they leave for the day, or just use お疲れ in more casual situations with friends!
7449.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 疲れ and 様, combined together into one word.

examples.en: My uncle's been home feeling melancholy.
examples.ja: 伯父は、鬱気で家でふさぎ込んでいる。

examples.en: This song can really blow the gloom away.
examples.ja: 鬱気を吹き飛ばしてくれるような歌ですね。

examples.en: My depression's bothering me today and I can't get myself to study Japanese.
examples.ja: 今日は鬱気が邪魔をして、日本語を勉強する気になれません。

7450.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>gloomy</kanji> <kanji>energy</kanji> has filled the room. This puts you in a <vocabulary>gloomy mood</vocabulary>. You are now <vocabulary>feeling downcast</vocabulary>.

This word is formal, so you'll mostly just see it in literature.
7450.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Careful of the shortening of 鬱 or you'll feel gloomy.

examples.en: The goal is one step away.
examples.ja: あと一歩でゴールです。

examples.en: I go up one step at a time.
examples.ja: 一歩ずつ上がっていきます。

examples.en: Step back, please.
examples.ja: 一歩、後ろに下がってください。

7451.meaning_mnemonic: If <kanji>歩</kanji> is "walk" and you take <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>walk</kanji>, then really you are just taking <vocabulary>one step</vocabulary>. When there's a number before 歩, it refers to the number of steps you're taking. The most common is this one, and you'll see it on urinals when they kindly ask you to please take one step forward because peeing isn't a game and somebody has to clean up after you.
7451.reading_mnemonic: The reading is pretty standard in its trickiness. The いち shortens to an いっ and the ほ rendakus to ぽ. One step at a time, right?

examples.en: "Which floor?" "Fourth please." "This elevator doesn't stop on the fourth floor."
examples.ja: 「何階ですか？」「四階をおねがいします。」「このエレベーターは四階には止まりませんよ。」

examples.en: There's no wonder, but the view from the sixty-fifth floor is splendid.
examples.ja: さすが六十五階からのビューは見事ですね。

examples.en: My friend lives in a tower apartment with thirty floors.
examples.ja: 友人が三十階建てのタワーマンションに住んでいます。

7452.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that the kanji refers to a <kanji>floor</kanji> (as in the "fifth floor"). This word represents the version that comes after a number, shown with a 〜. Essentially, this has the same meaning as the kanji you learned, making it nice and easy.

Note that floor-counting systems can vary across different countries. In Japan the ground floor is generally called 一階, with the floors above being 二階, 三階, and so on.
7452.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Don't type in the 〜 or you'll get it wrong!

examples.en: These spoons come with a case.
examples.ja: このスプーンはケース付きですよ。

examples.en: Is there a hotel with a pool around here?
examples.ja: この辺にプール付きのホテルはありますか？

examples.en: This room is furnished with a refrigerator and a washing machine.
examples.ja: この部屋は冷蔵庫、洗濯機付きです。

7453.meaning_mnemonic: You know that the kanji 付 means <kanji>attach</kanji> and words like 付く mean "to be attached." This has the same idea. When you see this attached to another word, for example, you might know that something is attached to something else, or perhaps <vocabulary>included</vocabulary> with it. For example, if you stay at a hotel room, maybe it is a breakfast付き, i.e. "<vocabulary>including</vocabulary> breakfast."
7453.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from the reading of the kanji as well as from words like 付く and 付ける.

examples.en: I have ten tickets for the soccer game on Sunday.
examples.ja: 日曜日のサッカーの試合のチケットを十枚持っています。

examples.en: My breakfast is usually just one slice of toast.
examples.ja: いつもは朝ご飯は食パン一枚だけです。

examples.en: I’d like to buy some Tofugu stickers. How much would one be?
examples.ja: トーフグのステッカーを何枚か買いたいのですが、一枚いくらになりますか？

7454.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well, so this is <vocabulary>flat object counter</vocabulary>.

This counter can be used with various "flat" things, such as <vocabulary>clothing items</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>sheets</vocabulary>, paper, stamps, dishes, and more. Notice how they're all kind of flat shaped?
7454.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: There are five trucks here.
examples.ja: ここにはトラックが五台あります。

examples.en: Will fifty people fit in one bus?
examples.ja: バス一台に五十人も入りますか？

examples.en: In our house, three people share one computer.
examples.ja: うちではパソコン一台を三人でシェアしていますよ。

7455.meaning_mnemonic: This counter is used with some kind of <kanji>machine</kanji> or device, usually a fairly large one (so nothing itty bitty). Cars are a good example of this. But it can also be used for things like computers, which were once the size of rooms, but are now nice and small. Thanks technology!
7455.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Be sure to omit the 〜 in your answer as it is only a placeholder for a number.

examples.en: It's 300 yen.
examples.ja: 三百円です。

examples.en: About 300 people came.
examples.ja: 大体三百人が来ました。

examples.en: A year is 365 days.
examples.ja: 一年は三百六十五日です。

7456.meaning_mnemonic: You have <kanji>three</kanji> <kanji>hundred</kanji>s. What does that come out to? <vocabulary>Three hundred</vocabulary>.
7456.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a little bit weird, so be careful. You should already know the on'yomi readings, but the ひゃく rendakus to びゃく. This pattern will repeat itself with 三 + many counter kanjis that can rendaku, so pay attention for it as you read Japanese.

examples.en: A lot of people live in the city.
examples.ja: 都市にはたくさんの人が住んでいます。

examples.en: How about living in a lively city area?
examples.ja: 活気のある都市エリアでの生活はどうですか？

examples.en: Do you know any interesting urban legends?
examples.ja: 何かおもしろい都市伝説を知っていますか？

7457.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>metropolis</kanji> <kanji>city</kanji> is a <vocabulary>city</vocabulary>. When you're referring to just a plain ol' city, sans name, you can use this word.
7457.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I went abroad to learn various languages.
examples.ja: 色々な言語を学ぶために海外へ行きました。

examples.en: A person who can speak many languages ​​is called polyglot.
examples.ja: 多くの言語を話す事が出来る人をポリグロットと言うんですね。

examples.en: I started going to graduate school last year to learn linguistics.
examples.ja: 言語学を学ぶために、去年大学院へ進んだ。

7458.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>say</kanji> words in a <kanji>language</kanji>, you are speaking a <vocabulary>language</vocabulary>. Not sure what that language is, but since you're saying it it must be real.
7458.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: This is a floor above ground.
examples.ja: ここは、地上のフロアです。

examples.en: The rocket is now 3,000 meters above the ground.
examples.ja: ロケットは今、地上三千メートルにいる。

examples.en: You can see the size of the Tokyo Tower if you look up from the ground.
examples.ja: 東京タワーは、地上から見上げると、大きさがよく分かりますね。

7459.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 地下, which is "below ground." Well, this is <kanji>ground</kanji> and <kanji>above</kanji> combined together, so I bet you can guess that this means <vocabulary>above ground</vocabulary>. But usually things above ground don't float (unless you're in space), so it's really <vocabulary>on the ground</vocabulary>.
7459.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I'm going to buy all the apples.
examples.ja: リンゴを全部買うつもりです。

examples.en: I got good test scores in all subjects.
examples.ja: 全部の科目のテストで良いスコアでした。

examples.en: Who the hell ate all my bacon cookies?!
examples.ja: 私のベーコンクッキー全部食べたのは一体だれ！？

7460.meaning_mnemonic: If you take <kanji>all</kanji> <kanji>part</kanji>s and put them together, you have <vocabulary>all</vocabulary> things. The <vocabulary>entire</vocabulary> collection. It is <vocabulary>whole</vocabulary>.
7460.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: See you here at 3:00 p.m. on the 3rd.
examples.ja: 三日の午後三時に、ここで会いましょう。

examples.en: What time is the meeting with the president?
examples.ja: 社長とのミーティングは何時ですか？

examples.en: I do WaniKani reviews in the bathroom at 3:00 p.m. every day.
examples.ja: 毎日午後三時にトイレの中でワニカニのレビューをします。

7461.meaning_mnemonic: If there's a number before 時, it means <vocabulary>o'clock</vocabulary>. For example １時 is 1:00, and ２３時 is 23:00 or 11pm.
7461.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: This actor is popular with everyone.
examples.ja: この俳優は、万人に人気がある。

examples.en: In any case, wouldn't it be better to go with a design that appeals to everyone?
examples.ja: やっぱり万人受けするデザインにする方がいいんじゃない？

examples.en: This seems to be the common impression among everyone.
examples.ja: これは万人に共通の感想だろう。

7462.meaning_mnemonic: If we're talking about <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji>s, then we might as well be talking about <vocabulary>all people</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>everybody</vocabulary>, because that's a lot of people, you know?
7462.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 万 and 人 both have two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which ones to use:

<vocabulary>All people</vocabulary> have been <reading>ban</reading>ned from <reading>Nin</reading>tendo (ばんにん). Apparently they're working on something super secret, so now <vocabulary>everybody</vocabulary> is banned. What could it be?!

examples.en: I thought that at least Tofugu would support me.
examples.ja: トーフグだけは、味方してくれると思ってたんだけどな。

examples.en: Dad pretends to be my big sister's ally, but he's actually always on my side.
examples.ja: お父さんは、お姉ちゃんの味方のフリをするが、いつでも私の味方だ。

examples.en: Just which side are you on?!
examples.ja: お前は一体どっちの味方なんだ？

7463.meaning_mnemonic: You like the <kanji>flavor</kanji> of a particular <kanji>direction</kanji>, so you go that way. Everyone else going in the same flavor direction is your <vocabulary>ally</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>supporter</vocabulary>. They're your flavor direction allies. They have the same tastes and they're chasing the same flavors in life, so naturally they become allies, right?
7463.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the on'yomi reading for 味, but the kun'yomi reading for 方, so watch out for that! You're probably more familiar with the on'yomi for 方, so here's a mnemonic to help with the kun'yomi:

A good <vocabulary>ally</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>supporter</vocabulary> is always ready to <reading>cata</reading>pult (かた) you into the best positions. They believe in you so they want what's best for you.

examples.en: The puppy was like an angel.
examples.ja: 子犬は天使みたいでした。

examples.en: What's charming about Koichi is his angelic smile.
examples.ja: コウイチ君は、天使のようなスマイルがチャームポイントです。

examples.en: Are you really an angel?
examples.ja: 本当に、あなた天使なんですか？

7464.meaning_mnemonic: One who <kanji>use</kanji>s <kanji>heaven</kanji> to their advantage is someone from heaven, like an <vocabulary>angel</vocabulary>.
7464.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: There are ten staff members.
examples.ja: スタッフは十人います。

examples.en: There are four of us in my family.
examples.ja: うちは、四人ファミリーです。

examples.en: A thousand guests are coming to the prince's wedding reception.
examples.ja: 王子のウェディングパーティーには千人のゲストがきます。

7465.meaning_mnemonic: When you see this on a number, for example ７人 or ３人, you're using it to count people. Just remember, both 一人 and 二人 have alternative readings. From 3 and up it's just the number plus にん, like this. ５人 is ごにん, １０人 is じゅうにん, etc. This is the <vocabulary>counter for people</vocabulary>, which makes this word the <vocabulary>number of people</vocabulary>.
7465.reading_mnemonic:
This is a counter, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Just think of the sheer <vocabulary>number of people</vocabulary> at <reading>Nin</reading>tendo (にん). It must be huge. This really is just a <vocabulary>counter for people</vocabulary> that work at Nintendo.

examples.en: Is the Year-End Jumbo Draw Lottery still for sale?
examples.ja: 年末ジャンボ宝くじはまだ発売中ですか？

examples.en: This ice-cream is on sale at convenience stores nationwide.
examples.ja: このアイスは全国のコンビニで発売中です。

examples.en: The June issue of Shonen Jump is now on sale, to critical acclaim.
examples.ja: 少年ジャンプ６月号、ただ今絶賛発売中。

7466.meaning_mnemonic: You have 発売, which means "for sale," and then you have 中 which is <kanji>middle</kanji>. An item that is in the middle of being for sale is <vocabulary>now for sale</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>in stores now</vocabulary> or in other words <vocabulary>now available</vocabulary>. You'll see this for items which have recently been released or when a shopkeeper wants to let you know that they're selling something now, finally, or whatever.
7466.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 発売 and 中 (kanji reading) put together.

examples.en: The restroom is straight and to the left.
examples.ja: お手洗いは、真っすぐ行って左です。

examples.en: James always takes a sip of whiskey before going to the bathroom.
examples.ja: ジェームスはいつも、お手洗いに行く前にウィスキーを一口飲む。

examples.en: I dozed off while sitting in the bathroom doing my business.
examples.ja: お手洗いで用を足しているうちに、座ったまま寝てしまいました。

7467.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 手洗い is "handwashing" (and also a not as polite way to mention a bathroom). When you add お you're suddenly making it polite. Why? Because you're talking about something a little more crass than handwashing. You're talking about the <vocabulary>toilet</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>restroom</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>bathroom</vocabulary>. Ewww. Poop goes there.
7467.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 手洗い, so if you know that you'll know this too!

examples.en: Do something to halt the enemy's advance!
examples.ja: どうにかして敵の進撃をはばんでくれ！

examples.en: Viet advanced on the enemy.
examples.ja: ビエトは敵に進撃した。

examples.en: I’m hooked on Attack on Titan.
examples.ja: 進撃の巨人にはまっています。

examples.en: Wow, isn't that amazing? That Hanshin Tigers' incredible winning streak! I really hope this momentum continues.
examples.ja: いやー、すごいですね！阪神タイガースの快進撃！この進撃、続いてほしいですね。

7468.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>advance</kanji> and <kanji>attack</kanji>! This is a <vocabulary>charge</vocabulary> on someone or something, though it can also be an <vocabulary>advance</vocabulary> on them. Yep, this is the 進撃 from 進撃の巨人, the popular anime and manga. Don't say you never learned anything useful here.
7468.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the ones you learned with the kanji. Advance! Charge! Move on to the next item!

examples.en: My father is a car dealer.
examples.ja: 私の父は自動車のディーラーです。

examples.en: Nowadays, every car manufacturer is putting effort into developing electric vehicles.
examples.ja: 今はどの自動車メーカーも、電気自動車の開発に力を入れています。

examples.en: I want to buy a new car, but which one do you recommend?
examples.ja: 新しい自動車を買いたいんですが、どれがおすすめですか？

7469.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 自動 is <vocabulary>automatic</vocabulary>. So what is an automatic <kanji>car</kanji>? That is an <vocabulary>automobile</vocabulary>, or simply a <vocabulary>car</vocabulary>.
7469.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 自動 and the kanji 車's readings, combined.

examples.en: Please don't erase what's on the blackboard yet.
examples.ja: まだ黒板を消さないでください。

examples.en: Who is it that wedged the blackboard eraser between the classroom door and made it fall?
examples.ja: 誰ですか、黒板消しを教室のとびらの間にはさんで落としたのは？

examples.en: At our high school, we've incorporated lessons using electronic blackboards.
examples.ja: うちの高校では、電子黒板を使った授業を取り入れています。

examples.en: We can’t use the blackboard so I’ll bring in a whiteboard.
examples.ja: 黒板が使えないので、ホワイトボードを持参しています。

7470.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The dirty wash cloth fell into the toilet.
examples.ja: 汚い雑巾が、トイレに落ちていました。

7471.meaning_mnemonic: This is the adjective form of 汚, which is <kanji>dirty</kanji>. This word is the adjective <vocabulary>dirty</vocabulary>, but you can also use it to say things like <vocabulary>filthy</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>foul</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>unclean</vocabulary>.
7471.reading_mnemonic: The reading is different from the other kun'yomi readings you've learned so far with this word. It is きたない. Think of it like you're saying "<reading>来た、な</reading>", as in "it came, huh?" What came? A really dirty looking monster, and it's coming for you.

examples.en: My older brother is a fast crawl swimmer.
examples.ja: うちの兄はクロールで泳ぐのが速い。

examples.en: Isn't this car going too fast?
examples.ja: この車のスピード、さすがに速すぎない？

examples.en: Ohtani is a fast runner, handsome, and he's perfect as a pitcher or a batter.
examples.ja: 大谷君は、足も速いし、顔もイケメンだし、投手としても、バッターとしてもパーフェクトなんだよ。

7472.meaning_mnemonic: Just like the meaning of the kanji (<kanji>fast</kanji>) this adjective also means <vocabulary>fast</vocabulary>.
7472.reading_mnemonic: Remember how 早い means "early"? If you are early to something, it probably means you moved <vocabulary>fast</vocabulary> to get there. These two words share a reading (and have similar meanings, in a way, as well!).

examples.en: You should wipe your glasses.
examples.ja: 眼鏡を拭いた方がいいですよ。

7473.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>eyeball</kanji> <kanji>mirror</kanji> is something that refracts and focuses light into your eyeball in a different way so you can see better. Really, these things are glasses, not eye mirrors, but same sort of things when you get down to it. Just imagine someone wearing mirrors on their eyes, and when you ask them what those are for, they just say they're <vocabulary>glasses</vocabulary>.
7473.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for 眼 is the same as the vocab 眼. The reading for 鏡 is an exception, totally different. It shares a reading with 金 (gold), though, so think of the mirrors on the person's eyes being made of gold. What nice glasses!

This word can also be read as がんきょう, but usually only on official/written documents. If you're speaking and not reading a government document, you should say めがね!

examples.en: Hokkaido is located in the north of Japan.
examples.ja: 北海道は日本の北にあります。

examples.en: Lavender and melon are famous in Hokkaido.
examples.ja: 北海道では、ラベンダーやメロンが有名です。

examples.en: I want to go to Hokkaido during winter vacation and eat some delicious crab, fish, and miso ramen.
examples.ja: 冬休みに北海道に行って、おいしいカニや魚とみそラーメンが食べたいです。

examples.en: My dad loves making the pun "Hokkaido wa dekkai dō." It's a play on the words "Hokkaido" and "dekkai zo" (meaning "it's huge").
examples.ja: 私の父は「北海道はでっかいどう」というダジャレを言うのが大好きです。これは、「北海道」と「でっかいぞ」の言葉遊びです。

7474.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>north</kanji> <kanji>sea</kanji> <kanji>road</kanji> is the road you take to get to the northern sea. This is the big northern island of Japan, actually, and it's called <vocabulary>Hokkaido</vocabulary>. It's a very nice place, so be sure to visit for some of the freshest seafood around.
7474.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. The ほく does get shortened though, so be careful!

examples.en: We will have a big sale in the new year.
examples.ja: 新年に大きいセールを行います。

examples.en: At the start of new year, many people set goals for that year.
examples.ja: 新年になると、多くの人が一年のゴールを立てます。

examples.en: In the new year, many people buy lottery tickets.
examples.ja: 新年は、宝くじを買う人が多いです。

7475.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>new</kanji> <kanji>year</kanji> is a <vocabulary>new year</vocabulary>. Hope you had / have / are having a good one, depending on when you read this.
7475.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I can't buy the Japanese textbook because it's too expensive.
examples.ja: その日本語の教科書は高すぎて買えません。

examples.en: Please don't illegally download textbooks from the web; instead, buy them properly.
examples.ja: 教科書はウェブから不正ダウンロードしないで、ちゃんと買ってくださいね。

examples.en: We were told that tomorrow, I have to bring my math drills and Japanese textbooks.
examples.ja: 明日、計算ドリルと国語の教科書を持って行かなきゃいけないんだって。

7476.meaning_mnemonic: The thing you use to <kanji>teach</kanji> a <kanji>course</kanji> with <kanji>writing</kanji>s is a <vocabulary>textbook</vocabulary>. It's a book of writings you use to teach your course!
7476.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: If you add 1 to 1, that'll be 2.
examples.ja: 一に一を足すと、二になります。

examples.en: Maybe it would be better to add more water to this soup.
examples.ja: このスープ、もう少し水を足した方がいいんじゃないかな。

examples.en: Let's add some white paint.
examples.ja: 白のペンキを足しましょう。

7477.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember 足りる? That is "to be enough." How can you make something be enough? You keep adding things to the pile until you reach that point where there are enough! That's why this verb is <vocabulary>to add something</vocabulary>, because you keep adding things until you 足りる.

This verb is transitive, like most verbs ending in す, which is why you are adding something. It's not getting itself added all by itself. Maybe you add so much that someone tries to <reading>sue</reading> (す) you for that nasty pile of squirrels you keep outside.
7477.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 足りる, so if you know that you can add things up to this.

examples.en: I need more time to think.
examples.ja: 考えるのに、もっと時間が要る。

examples.en: Do you need a bag?
examples.ja: ふくろは要りますか？

examples.en: This is a list of things you need and what you don't need.
examples.ja: これは要る物と要らない物のリストです。

7478.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>need</kanji> and the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to need</vocabulary>.

This one's a little tricky, because although it's usually translated as "to need" in English, it's used more like <vocabulary>to be needed</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be necessary</vocabulary>. That is, it's an intransitive verb in Japanese, so it doesn't take a direct object.
7478.reading_mnemonic: Since the reading isn't like the one you learned, think about what you are going <vocabulary>to need</vocabulary>... like, what you're really going to need, more than anything. Then, think of an <reading>ea</reading>gle, because you really need an eagle. You'll need to come up with the reason why you need an eagle though, so hopefully it's a good one.

examples.en: Hey! That's not a place to sit.
examples.ja: ちょっと！そこ、座るとこじゃないよ。

examples.en: Could you not sit on the important documents?
examples.ja: 大事な書類の上に座らないでもらえますか。

examples.en: Are you okay? Would you like to sit on this chair?
examples.ja: 大丈夫？よかったら、このイスに座る？

7479.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>sit</kanji> so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to sit</vocabulary>.
7479.reading_mnemonic: The reading is unlike the kanji reading, so let's use a separate mnemonic to remember this. Just imagine yourself going <vocabulary>to sit</vocabulary> down. You sit down, and the ground collapses below you and you fall. When you land, you find yourself in a nasty, stinking <reading>sewer</reading> (すわ). It is so gross. Taste the sewage in your mouth. Smell it. Feel gross. You shouldn't have sat down on that spot, it was looking awfully dangerous, now that you think about it.

examples.en: Please tell me what kinds of things we have for parts of speech.
examples.ja: 品詞にはどんなものがあるか教えてください。

examples.en: Today I will teach you how to distinguish parts of speech in English.
examples.ja: 今日は英語の品詞の見分け方をお教えします。

examples.en: I wrote a book about parts of speech and right now I'm thinking about how I can sell a lot of copies.
examples.ja: 品詞についての本を書いたんですが、今、どうすればたくさんの冊数を売ることができるのか考えています。

7480.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>product</kanji> of <kanji>part of speech</kanji> is more <vocabulary>part of speech</vocabulary>. Evil begets evil, so to speak.
7480.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Today’s lesson was on na-adjectives.
examples.ja: 今日のレッスンは形容動詞でした。

examples.en: I mixed up na-adjectives with i-adjectives and now I'm really confused.
examples.ja: 頭の中で、形容動詞と形容詞が混ぜこぜになってしまっていて、かなり混乱しています。

examples.en: I found it difficult to judge whether it was a na-adjective or just an i-adjective.
examples.ja: それが形容動詞なのかただの形容詞なのか、判断に迷いました。

7481.meaning_mnemonic: A 形容詞 is an <kanji>adjective</kanji>. So what about an adjective with a 動詞 (verb) in there? How does that make sense? I'm not entirely sure either, but an adjective with movement in it is a <vocabulary>na adjective</vocabulary>. These are the adjectives that can end with な (便利な, for example). In fact, they're more like nouns than they are verbs, so what gives? Whatever it is, just decide you don't want to deal with this craziness. Just say <reading>nah</reading>, I don't care about this anymore.
7481.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. It will help to know 形容詞 and 動詞 as well, since they're both parts of this word.

examples.en: This vehicle is big.
examples.ja: 車両は大きいですね。

examples.en: The vehicle entered the tunnel.
examples.ja: 車両はトンネルに入った。

examples.en: The train car ahead of this one is car No. 1.
examples.ja: 前の車両は一号車です。

7482.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>car</kanji> has wheels on <kanji>both</kanji> sides, and together they make a <vocabulary>vehicle</vocabulary>.

車両 is a formal word often used in official or technical contexts. It refers not just to standard cars but also to <vocabulary>train car</vocabulary>s and other vehicles that carry people or goods. You'll commonly see it in public transportation terms, on signs like "No vehicles allowed," or in driver's license and traffic law classifications.
7482.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I'm starting to feel like a real parent at last.
examples.ja: ようやく親になる実感が持てるようになってきました。

examples.en: Even when I heard the news that my mother died, it didn't feel real at first.
examples.ja: 母が死んだという知らせを聞いても、すぐには実感できなかった。

examples.en: Only after I went to America did I realize how small Japan really is.
examples.ja: アメリカへ行って初めて、日本はなんと小さい国かと実感した。

7483.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>reality</kanji> <kanji>feeling</kanji> is what you get when something feels real. The <vocabulary>realization</vocabulary> sets in — whatever this thing is, you've got a <vocabulary>real feeling</vocabulary> that it's actually happening.

実感 means a realization that comes from lived experience. For example, when you're expecting a baby, you may understand that you're becoming a parent, but not truly have that realization until the baby is born or you hold them in your arms. It's the sense of something feeling real beyond theory or explanation — when it truly sinks in.
7483.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. The reading for 実 gets changed to じっ so be careful!

examples.en: I spilled curry and got a burn on my hand.
examples.ja: カレーを零して、手に火傷を負った。

7484.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>fire</kanji> <kanji>wound</kanji> is a <vocabulary>burn</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>scald</vocabulary> you got from fire (or other hot things). Ouch!
7484.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this is unlike anything you've seen with these kanji. Try to think about a <vocabulary>burn</vocabulary> (on your arm) being caused by a <reading>yakky do</reading>do (やけど) bird (which is a dodo bird that has yak-like features). Take a look at how weird it is, and wonder why it is burning you. Feel the pain.

examples.en: He strives to write clear and understandable text for readers.
examples.ja: 彼は、読者にとって分かりやすい文章を書くことに心がけています。

examples.en: She loves reading letters and comments from readers.
examples.ja: 彼女は読者からの手紙やコメントを読むのが大好きです。

examples.en: Are you a reader of Tofugu's articles? Oh, you're not familiar with Tofugu? It's a website that provides easy-to-understand articles about Japanese language and culture! They have many helpful articles, so please consider becoming a reader!
examples.ja: あなたはトーフグの記事の読者ですか？え、トーフグを知らないんですか？日本語や日本文化について、分かりやすく記事にしているサイトですよ！役立つ記事ばかりなんで、ぜひ読者になってください！

7485.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>read</kanji>ing <kanji>someone</kanji> is someone who is reading. They are the <vocabulary>reader</vocabulary> (of a book, blog, article, etc).
7485.reading_mnemonic: The reading for 読 is the on'yomi reading, which you didn't learn with the kanji. This reading is どく, and you can remember it by thinking about how you are the <vocabulary>reader</vocabulary>, and as the reader you choose where to read. For you, the best place to read is a peaceful <reading>dock</reading> (どく). Sit on the dock and relax. Be the reader.

examples.en: The teacher’s explanation is really easy to understand.
examples.ja: あの先生の解説はとても分かり易いね。

examples.en: I left at the beginning of the commentary on "The Last Judgment."
examples.ja: 最後の審判の解説の冒頭で席を立ちました。

examples.en: As for Tofugu's equity ratio, the president will explain it later.
examples.ja: トーフグの自己資本比率については、後ほど社長が解説します。

7486.meaning_mnemonic:
Once you've <kanji>solve</kanji>d a <kanji>theory</kanji>, you should be able to give a pretty good <vocabulary>explanation</vocabulary> of it to somebody else. Makes sense, right? 

解説 refers to a detailed and analytical explanation. It's often used when someone, often an expert, provides an in-depth analysis about a topic, like a sports game or news article <vocabulary>commentary</vocabulary>.
7486.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I went to an event for discussions between engineering and psychology scholars.
examples.ja: 工学と心理学の学者の対談のイベントに行きました。

examples.en: Last week, a discussion was held between a famous writer and a genius modern artist.
examples.ja: 先週、有名な作家と天才モダンアーティストとの対談が行われました。

examples.en: This month's issue should have my interview.
examples.ja: 今月号には、私の対談がのってるはずです。

7487.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>versus</kanji> <kanji>talk</kanji> is when you sit down with another person and have a <vocabulary>talk</vocabulary>. As you're talking, it might evolve into a <vocabulary>discussion</vocabulary>. Or perhaps you're there to have an <vocabulary>interview</vocabulary>.

対談 is usually a formal discussion between two or more individuals, often organized ahead of time, and with a specific purpose or topic in mind.
7487.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I showed the will to win a gold medal.
examples.ja: 金メダル獲得に意欲をみせた。

7488.meaning_mnemonic: If you have an <kanji>idea</kanji> of what you <kanji>want</kanji> already, then that's good! You have <vocabulary>will</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>desire</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>ambition</vocabulary>. Those who don't know what they want can't have any of these.
7488.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Please bring some food, Ms. Yasuda.
examples.ja: 安田さんは、食べ物をおねがいします。

examples.en: Is this really food? It looks like a stone.
examples.ja: これは本当に食べ物ですか？石みたいですが。

examples.en: When you waste food, heaven will punish you.
examples.ja: 食べ物を粗末にするとバチが当たりますよ。

7489.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>eat</kanji> <kanji>thing</kanji> (aka "a thing you eat") is <vocabulary>food</vocabulary>. Eat those things. Eat that food. Because it's a "thing" you know it's a noun. Interesting how this kanji can turn a verb like this into a noun, right? Look out for it because this pattern will show up with other verbs as well!
7489.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, but you know them both now, so you should be able to read this too!

examples.en: Today's waves are very high, aren't they?
examples.ja: 今日の波、すごく高いね。

examples.en: Those are the best waves for surfers.
examples.ja: サーファーにとっては最高の波だよ。

examples.en: The ocean today is quiet and has no waves at all.
examples.ja: 今日の海、波が全然なくて静かだね。

7490.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
7490.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember:

You jump on a wave and ride around the world on it. As you ride this wave, it gets bigger and bigger, until it reaches tsu<reading>nami</reading> (なみ) proportions. Imagine looking down from the tsunami at the vast, blue sea all around you. That's quite a wave you're riding.

examples.en: He hit his face hard on the asphalt.
examples.ja: 彼はアスファルトに顔面を強打した。

examples.en: During gym class, I got hit square in the face with a basketball.
examples.ja: 体育の時間、顔面に思いっきりバスケットボールが当たったんです。

examples.en: It appears that there's a slight paralysis in your facial area.
examples.ja: どうやら顔面に少しマヒが出ているようですね。

7491.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>face</kanji> of a <kanji>face</kanji> is a face, but more specifically the <vocabulary>face of a person</vocabulary>. Probably because the most face-like thing you can ever have is a human's face... at least in our eyes (by "our" I mean the human race's eyes, because I am totally with you guys on that one).
7491.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for 顔 isn't the one you learned with the kanji. But, we're going to learn that reading right now.

The worst thing that can happen to a face is if a face disappears. If it becomes totally <reading>gone</reading> (がん). A man that is walking up to you with no face, is a man with a gone face. Those men are men who are a part of the <reading>gone men</reading> (がんめん). Faces, totally gone!

examples.en: Can you teach me the meaning of this word?
examples.ja: この言葉の意味を教えて下さい。

examples.en: It's hard to put into words, but Koichi is a very special person to me.
examples.ja: うまく言葉にできないけど、コウイチは私にとってすごく特別な人なの。

examples.en: I was at a loss for words.
examples.ja: 私は言葉に詰まった。

7492.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>leaf</kanji> of the things you <kanji>say</kanji> is like a leaf from a tree of speaking. That leaf is a part of the whole language, it is a single <vocabulary>word</vocabulary>, though it can add up to be a <vocabulary>language</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>manner of speech</vocabulary>.
7492.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for 言 is one you haven't learned, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Now imagine that there are <vocabulary>word</vocabulary>s all over your <reading>coat</reading> (こと). It's completely covered in words. Which <vocabulary>language</vocabulary> are these words in? Why Japanese, of course! Think about which Japanese words you would want written on your coat.

examples.en: It's not too big or too small. It's just the right size.
examples.ja: 大きすぎず、小さすぎず、本当に丁度いいサイズです。

examples.en: Oh, you came at the right time!
examples.ja: あっ、丁度いいところに来たね！

examples.en: This temperature is just right.
examples.ja: このぐらいの温度が丁度いいですね。

7493.meaning_mnemonic: If 丁度 is "exactly", then "exactly good" is going to be just the right amount, aka <vocabulary>just right</vocabulary>.
7493.reading_mnemonic: If you know the reading for 丁度 you'll know the reading for this too. Your knowledge should be <vocabulary>just right</vocabulary>, as they say inside my head.

examples.en: This music is very rhythmic.
examples.ja: この音楽はとても律動的ですね。

examples.en: Out of the Tofugu team, Kanae was doing the radio gymnastics the most rhythmically.
examples.ja: トーフグチームの中で、一番律動的にラジオ体操をしていたのは、カナエです。

examples.en: This morning, I saw a lot of rabbits jumping rhythmically in my garden.
examples.ja: 今朝、たくさんの兎が庭で律動的に飛び跳ねているのを見ました。

7494.meaning_mnemonic:
Rhythm is 律動, but by adding a 的 in there we get the adjective version of that word, making it <vocabulary>rhythmical</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>rhythmic</vocabulary>.

Note that リズミカル and テンポのいい are much more common words to use for "rhythmical" and “rhythmic” respectively, but you may sometimes see 律動的 in formal writing.
7494.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 律動. The 的 part you should also be able to read by now.

examples.en: I don't want to break up!
examples.ja: 別れるのはイヤ！

examples.en: I broke up with my boyfriend last month.
examples.ja: 先月、彼氏と別れました。

examples.en: Wait, why did you break up?
examples.ja: え、なんで別れたの？

7495.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>separate</kanji>, so you can guess the meaning is <vocabulary>to separate</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be divided</vocabulary>.
7495.reading_mnemonic: Remember the word 分ける? That word means "to separate" too. The reading is similar, though not the same, but we can at least use it as a jumping off point. We go from わける to わかれる. It's like we've "separated" the け and the る and combined them in the middle. け, making a かれ, which gets you to <reading>わか</reading>れる.

examples.en: How do you plan to share that data?
examples.ja: そのデータはどうやって共有するつもりですか？

examples.en: We share it internally using Dropbox.
examples.ja: 社内では、Dropboxを使って共有しています。

examples.en: Do you share images or videos with your family?
examples.ja: 画像やビデオって家族で共有してますか？

7496.meaning_mnemonic: This is the same as 共有 but the verb version.
7496.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 共有 as well as the readings you learned via the kanji.

examples.en: I am worried about keeping a high fluency in Japanese if I go to America.
examples.ja: アメリカに行ったら高い日本語力を保持できるか不安です。

examples.en: It is quite impressive to maintain this quality.
examples.ja: このクオリティを保持するのは中々すごいことなんですよ。

examples.en: You should prioritize maintaining your own country’s status first.
examples.ja: 自国の地位を保持することをまず優先した方がいい。

7497.meaning_mnemonic:
This is the verb version of 保持 (keep), so this means <vocabulary>to keep</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to hold</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to maintain</vocabulary>.

Note that this is a formal word that's commonly used in professional or official contexts.
7497.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as 保持, so if you know that word's reading, you know this one too.

examples.en: Leave it to me.
examples.ja: 僕に任せろ。

examples.en: My younger brother is an elementary school student.
examples.ja: 僕の弟は小学生です。

examples.en: Come with me.
examples.ja: 僕と一緒に行きましょう。

7498.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well!
7498.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the same reading as the one you learned with the kanji. <vocabulary> I</vocabulary> certainly like that and I bet you do too.

examples.en: Since being designated as editor of the book, I’ve been feeling overworked.
examples.ja: その本の編集者として任命されてから、過労気味です。

7499.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>edit</kanji> is 編集. <kanji>Someone</kanji> who does those edits is an <vocabulary>editor</vocabulary>!
7499.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Also, the readings from 編集 should help you.

examples.en: I am currently working as a trainee at the factory.
examples.ja: 私は今、工場で研修生として働いています。

examples.en: What I learned during my time as a trainee has been very useful in my current job.
examples.ja: 研修生の時期に学んだことが、今の仕事にとても役立っています。

examples.en: The new trainees are attending orientation starting today.
examples.ja: 新しい研修生たちが今日からオリエンテーションを受けています。

examples.en: This is the new trainee, Miura.
examples.ja: こちらが、新しい研修生の三浦くんです。

7500.meaning_mnemonic: <vocabulary>研修</vocabulary> is a training or study of some kind. If it's in your current <kanji>life</kanji> (生) that you are doing the training, then you are a <vocabulary>trainee</vocabulary>. This is a lot like how a student is in the status of "study life."
7500.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. The reading from 研修 should also help you too.

examples.en: I get one spam mail after another.
examples.ja: 迷惑メールが次から次へと送られてくる。

examples.en: Lately, I've been getting more spam emails, and it’s really annoying.
examples.ja: 最近、迷惑メールが増えて困っています。

examples.en: I get so much junk mail that my inbox fills up quickly.
examples.ja: 迷惑メールが多すぎて、受信ボックスがすぐにいっぱいになるんです。

examples.en: Emails from Koichi are always found in the junk mail folder. I wonder why.
examples.ja: コウイチからのメールはいつも迷惑メールフォルダに入ってしまうんだけどどうしてなんだろう？

7501.meaning_mnemonic: When you have "troublesome" (迷惑) mail, you have mail you don't want. This is known as <vocabulary>spam</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>spam mail</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>junk mail</vocabulary>. On a more technical level it's <vocabulary>unsolicited mail</vocabulary>.
7501.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 迷惑, so if you know that you know this (and then this vocab word won't be unsolicited as well!)

examples.en: What do foreigners need when they stay in Japan?
examples.ja: 外国人が日本に在留する時に必要になるものは何ですか？

examples.en: Of course, I am residing in Japan with residence status.
examples.ja: もちろん、私は在留資格を持って、日本に在留しています。

examples.en: I have a limited amount of time to stay in this country.
examples.ja: 私がこの国に在留することができる期間は限られているんです。

7502.meaning_mnemonic:
If 在留 is <kanji>residence</kanji>, then the verb version of that would be <vocabulary>to reside</vocabulary>.

Like 在留, this is also a more formal term. You might encounter it at the immigration office, but you probably won't hear it in everyday conversation.
7502.reading_mnemonic: The reading comes from 在留 so you should be able to read this one already!

examples.en: I became friends with an American who was residing in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本在留のアメリカ人と友達になりました。

examples.en: Yesterday, I received my visa and residence card.
examples.ja: 昨日、ビザと在留カードを受け取りました。

examples.en: It seems that the maximum duration of stay for foreign workers engaged in household chores will be extended from five years to seven years.
examples.ja: 家事代行を行う外国人労働者の在留期間が、最長5年から7年に変わるそうです。

7503.meaning_mnemonic:
Where you <kanji>exist</kanji> is the place you're <kanji>detain</kanji>ed. As long as you're in this place, this will be your <vocabulary>residence</vocabulary>, even if you're <vocabulary>staying in a foreign country</vocabulary>.

在留 is an official term used for people residing in a foreign country. You'll find it in phrases like 在留カード (residence card) or 在留外国人 (foreign resident).
7503.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The earth is beautifully blue.
examples.ja: 地球は美しい青色をしています。

examples.en: Where did Koichi go? I think he's somewhere on earth though...
examples.ja: コウイチは一体どこへ行ったのかな？地球の上にはいると思うんだけど...。

examples.en: It is important to protect the environment of the earth.
examples.ja: 地球の環境を守ることは重要です。

7504.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>earth</kanji> <kanji>sphere</kanji>! It's where we live and the planet we call home. It's <vocabulary>the earth</vocabulary>!
7504.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: For some reason, the launch of this product has been cancelled.
examples.ja: 故あって、この製品のローンチが中止になりました。

examples.en: There are many volcanoes here. For that reason, there are often earthquakes too.
examples.ja: ここは火山が多い。それ故に、地震もよく起きる。

examples.en: The mistake was down to his youth. Let's cut him some slack, shall we?
examples.ja: 若さ故の過ちだったんだよ。大目に見てやろうじゃないか。

7505.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
7505.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

When thinking about the <vocabulary>circumstance</vocabulary> of your current situation and the <vocabulary>reason</vocabulary> you're there (which is studying kanji and vocab). Whose fault is it? It's WaniKani's fault! But, your brain has been beaten to a mush from all the studying, so when you say "it's your fault" it comes out as "it's <reading>yue</reading> fault!" Go ahead and say it out loud that way.

examples.en: I aspire to be an actor who can convey emotions through facial expressions.
examples.ja: 表情で演技ができる役者を目指しています。

examples.en: Fugu is studying acting at university.
examples.ja: フグは大学で演技の勉強をしています。

examples.en: That actress’s acting ability is magnificent.
examples.ja: あの女優の演技力は素晴らしい。

7506.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>performance</kanji> <kanji>skill</kanji> allows you to be great at <vocabulary>acting</vocabulary> and doing awesome <vocabulary>performance</vocabulary>s.
7506.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: "Enzuru" is a more formal expression for "enjiru."
examples.ja: 「演ずる」は「演じる」の、よりフォーマルな表現です。

examples.en: You seem to not understand how difficult it is to play the role of a dog that expresses joy with its tail.
examples.ja: 尻尾で喜びを示す犬の役を演ずるのがどんなに大変なことか、あなたは分かってらっしゃらないようですね。

examples.en: I am excited to announce that I have been chosen to play the pivotal role of the United States President in our next YouTube video.
examples.ja: この度、私は、次のYoutubeビデオで、アメリカ大統領という大役を演ずることになりました。

7507.meaning_mnemonic: If 演 is <kanji>performance</kanji> then the verb version of this would be <vocabulary>to perform</vocabulary>.
7507.reading_mnemonic: The reading looks weird, but it's actually just the reading you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: The performance is next week! Let's do our best, everyone!
examples.ja: 演芸会は来週ですよ！みなさん、がんばりましょう！

examples.en: At Tofugu, the one who excels most as an entertainer is Michael.
examples.ja: トーフグで一番演芸に秀でているのはマイケルだ。

examples.en: I would like to join the performing arts club. Do you know how I can do that?
examples.ja: 演芸部に入部したいんですが、どうすればいいかご存知ですか？

7508.meaning_mnemonic:
When you turn <kanji>acting</kanji> into <kanji>art</kanji> you get the <vocabulary>performing arts</vocabulary>. It is <vocabulary>popular entertainment</vocabulary>! Lights, action! Welcome to Broadway!

This word is more traditional and isn't used very much these days.
7508.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Can you explain when and why contraction and expansion of the pupil occurs?
examples.ja: いつ、どうして瞳孔の縮小と拡張が起きるのか、説明できますか？

7509.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>pupil</kanji> <kanji>hole</kanji> is still your <vocabulary>pupil</vocabulary>. It can also be called your <vocabulary>pupillary</vocabulary>.
7509.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the same as the ones you learned with the kanji!

examples.en: It feels so good when you cover your eye sockets with a steamed towel.
examples.ja: 蒸しタオルで眼孔を覆うと気持ち良いですよ。

7510.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>eyeball</kanji> <kanji>cavity</kanji> (hole) is where your eye is held. This is your <vocabulary>eye socket</vocabulary>.
7510.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The contents are way too extreme to be published.
examples.ja: このコンテンツは、過激すぎて掲載することはできません。

7511.meaning_mnemonic: 掲載 is <kanji>publication</kanji> so the verb version of that is <vocabulary>to publish</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to print</vocabulary>.
7511.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Will also help to know 掲載 as well.

examples.en: 1 sun is 1/10th of 1 shaku, which is approximately 3.03 centimeters.
examples.ja: 1寸は1尺の10分の1で、約3.03センチです。

7512.meaning_mnemonic: This <kanji>measurement</kanji> also refers to a specific measurement, a "<vocabulary>sun</vocabulary>", which is about <vocabulary>3.03 centimeters</vocabulary>. You'll hear it brought up from time to time to measure things, though usually with more traditional Japanese items.
7512.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the same as the kanji! Congrats! Now to remember it's three point zero three centimeters.

examples.en: My husband devotes every spare moment to working.
examples.ja: 夫は、いつも寸暇を惜しんで働いています。

7513.meaning_mnemonic: You have a <kanji>measurement</kanji> (3.03 cm!) of <kanji>spare time</kanji>. This isn't much free time, but it's a <vocabulary>free minute</vocabulary> that you have.
7513.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: What, are you commuting from Tokyo to Kyushu every day?
examples.ja: えっ、東京から九州まで毎日通ってるの？

examples.en: Koichi goes to the company by Harley.
examples.ja: コウイチは、会社までハーレーで通っています。

examples.en: My younger sister will attend Tofugu Academy starting in April.
examples.ja: 私の妹は、四月からトーフグ学園に通うことになります。

7514.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>pass through</kanji> but we already know the word 通る which means to pass through. This word means a different kind of passing through, like how you pass through the halls of your school everyday. But we don't say to pass through school, we say <vocabulary>to attend</vocabulary> school, or <vocabulary>to commute</vocabulary> to school.
7514.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use one of the kun'yomi readings. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You live in the middle of three different school districts so you need to decide which of the three schools you want <vocabulary>to attend</vocabulary>. You decide you don't mind that you have <vocabulary>to commute</vocabulary> to the farthest of the three because their mascot is Wile E. <reading>Coyo</reading>te (かよ). He's your favorite Looney Toon because he always has the energy <vocabulary>to go back and forth</vocabulary> after that road runner.

examples.en: The meeting on the 2nd was canceled.
examples.ja: 二日のミーティングは、キャンセルしました。

examples.en: It's been two days since the puppy arrived.
examples.ja: 子犬がきてから二日です。

examples.en: I was in Paris only for a couple days.
examples.ja: パリに二日しかいなかった。

7515.meaning_mnemonic: <vocabulary>Second day</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>day two</vocabulary>. No matter how you look at this combination of kanji, the meaning of the word makes a lot of sense!
7515.reading_mnemonic:
Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it uses kun'yomi readings for both the kanji. Think about this word this way:

The circus is in town this weekend and you can't wait to get there. You want to show off your new <reading>foots car</reading> (ふつか) to all the circus clowns. But you have to use your feet to get it there and it ends up taking you <vocabulary>two days</vocabulary>! Darn this old fashioned foots car!

examples.en: There were many people at the exit.
examples.ja: 出口にたくさんの人々がいた。

examples.en: The people around me don't wear jeans much.
examples.ja: まわりの人々は、あまりジーンズをはきません。

examples.en: Why don't people say "Good morning!" more enthusiastically?
examples.ja: なぜ人々は、もっと力いっぱい「おはよう！」といわないんでしょうか。

7517.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Person</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji>, why, that's more than one person. It's <vocabulary>people</vocabulary>!
7517.reading_mnemonic: The reading is the vocab word 人 twice, with the second one getting rendaku'd, turning it into びと.

examples.en: Three girls were at the river.

examples.en: The book genre I recommend is girl's manga.
examples.ja: おすすめの本のジャンルは、少女マンガです。

examples.en: She's a forty-year-old with a smile like a young a girl.
examples.ja: 少女のようなスマイルの四十才だ。

7518.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>little</kanji> <kanji>woman</kanji> is a <vocabulary>girl</vocabulary>. 

少女 is a relatively formal word that's often used in writing to describe a <vocabulary>young girl</vocabulary>, usually between childhood and adolescence (or between the ages of about five and eighteen).
7518.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.ja: 日本へのチケットは、十万円でした。

examples.en: This dome can fit fifty-thousand people.

examples.en: My blog gets about twenty thousand views per month.
examples.ja: わたしのブログは月にニ万ビューほどあります。

7519.meaning_mnemonic: When a vocab word is a single kanji without okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) it usually has the same meaning as the kanji it's spawned from. If you know the kanji meaning you'll also know the vocab meaning. It's <vocabulary>ten thousand</vocabulary>!
7519.reading_mnemonic: When a vocab word is a single kanji with no okurigana, it usually uses the kun'yomi reading. Numbers are an exception to this. Numbers use the on'yomi reading, which you've already learned by learning the kanji's reading! How nice!

7520.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

7521.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>white</kanji>? <vocabulary>White</vocabulary>, of course!
7521.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the vocab 白 you learned, so you already know the reading. Go you!

7522.meaning_mnemonic: When a vocab word is a single kanji without okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) it usually has the same meaning as the kanji it's spawned from. If you know the kanji meaning you'll also know the vocab meaning. It's <vocabulary>one hundred</vocabulary>!
7522.reading_mnemonic: When a vocab word is a single kanji with no okurigana, it usually uses the kun'yomi reading. Numbers are an exception to this. Numbers use the on'yomi reading, which you've already learned by learning the kanji's reading! How nice!

It isn’t really used for the kind of meeting you have at an office, though. 7523.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

examples.en: I go to work early on weekdays.

7524.reading_mnemonic: Since you already know the reading of the vocab word 早い, you should be able to read this word as well.

examples.en: Their death was too soon.

7525.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
7525.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

Picture your <vocabulary>older sister</vocabulary> (even if you don't have one), her birthday is coming up and there's only one thing she wants from you. <reading>A ne</reading>cklace (あね). She's wanted a necklace for years and you're finally going to give her one. She'll be so happy.

examples.en: I am learning the conjugation forms for the JLPT next summer.

7530.meaning_mnemonic:

That something doesn't just turn on its own. So this verb means <vocabulary>to turn something towards</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to point something at</vocabulary>.

In order to remember that this word means "to turn something towards," focus on the け. You have a bottle of ketchup in your hands and you're turning it toward your worst enemy to spray them. Picture yourself pointing the ketchup toward them.

In other words, you show someone who doubted you or treated you unfairly what you’re really capable of.

There are a couple of other meanings, too. It can mean <vocabulary>to look back over something</vocabulary>, like the answers to your kanji test you want to double check, and sometimes <vocabulary>to return someone’s stare</vocabulary>. Note that you can only attach this to people and animals to make them plural. It can also be used with a person's name, like マリアたち. In that case, it refers to Maria and the group of people she's with! This might sound a little complicated, but you'll get the hang of it with a little practice!

Oh, and don't type the 〜 out when writing the answer. It's just there to let you know that there's usually something attached in front of this word.

This is the transitive version, so it means <vocabulary>to let someone escape</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to let someone go</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to set someone free</vocabulary>. You know this because you'd want to let everyone escape when the place is filled with gas (がす).

逃がす is often about purposely letting someone or something go — like setting a bird free or letting a captive escape quietly. But it can also be used in more unintentional and regretful situations, like failing to catch a criminal or missing a big opportunity.
7558.reading_mnemonic:
You learned the に reading for this kanji when you learned 逃げる but here’s another mnemonic to help you remember:

You decided <vocabulary>to let someone escape</vocabulary> because they were on their <reading>knee</reading>s (に) begging you to set them free.

The reading for ”first day," however, is a big old exception. It doesn’t take the on’yomi or kun’yomi readings, and has its own special (weird) readings. Here’s a mnemonic to help  you remember this one:

On the <vocabulary>first day</vocabulary> of a new relationship you just <reading>tweet a chee</reading>sy (ついたち) line at each other. You're so in love you can't speak normally, so you just use bird calls and cheesy lines to communicate.

Warning! Don't mix this up with きょうは! While they may look the same, they don't mean the same thing. We will only ever ask you for こんにちは, so please try to remember that!

We usually don't use kanji for this, so don't use it when you're writing. But you'll probably run into it in the wild so it's good to know!

病む means to fall ill in more formal or literary contexts. In casual conversation, especially among younger people, 病む is used to describe someone feeling down, so this can also mean to get depressed.

Note that this word can be transitive and take a direct object, like 心を病む (to be mentally unwell), but can also be used intransitively without a direct object.
