examples.en: Could you tell me the depth of this pool?
examples.ja: このプールの深さを教えて下さい。

examples.en: I was surprised by how deep it was.
examples.ja: 意外と深さがあってびっくりしたよ。

examples.en: I climbed down a ladder to a depth of 100 meters.
examples.ja: 百メートルの深さまでハシゴで下りました。

7585.meaning_mnemonic: This is the noun version of the kanji <kanji>deep</kanji>, so it means <vocabulary>depth</vocabulary>.
7585.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You already learned this reading when you learned 深い so you should be able to read this one too!

examples.en: Even yakuza can come to the zoo.
examples.ja: ヤクザだって動物園に来ることもあるさ。

examples.en: The flamingos looked so beautiful when I saw them up close at a zoological garden.
examples.ja: 動物園で間近で見たフラミンゴは、とてもきれいでした。

examples.en: Many koalas congenitally carry a virus called the koala retrovirus, and when they experience stress, it can lead to fatal consequences. Therefore, in zoos, please be careful not to use camera flashes or raise your voice excessively.
examples.ja: 多くのコアラはコアラレトロウィルスというウイルスを先天的に保持しており、ストレスなどを受けると、死につながることがあります。ですので、動物園では、カメラのフラッシュや大声を出すなどしないよう、十分気をつけてください。

7586.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 動物 means animal? Well when you add <kanji>park</kanji> it becomes a <vocabulary>zoo</vocabulary>. It's a park for animals. Except the animals can't leave. Ever.
7586.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I'm planning to go to dinner with him on our anniversary.
examples.ja: 記念日には、彼とディナーに行く予定です。

examples.en: I'm currently reading "Salad Anniversary."
examples.ja: 今は『サラダ記念日』を読んでいます。

examples.en: Today is the anniversary of the broadcast debut of "WaniKani-sama."
examples.ja: 今日は『ワニカニ様』の放送開始記念日です。

7587.meaning_mnemonic:
You should <kanji>write down</kanji> all your <kanji>thoughts</kanji> on this <kanji>day</kanji>, because it's not just any day — it's an <vocabulary>anniversary</vocabulary>!

Wondering how 記念日 differs from 周年? 周年 is usually for a numbered anniversary, like 十周年 (10th anniversary), whereas 記念日 refers to the specific date on which a memorable event took place in the past.
7587.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a combination of on'yomi for the first two and kun'yomi for the last one. That being said, all of the readings for all of the kanji are the readings you've learned already, so you should be able to read this word too. Just watch out because ひ is rendaku'd into び.

examples.en: I cannot trust that man because he changes his opinions so often.
examples.ja: あの男は意見がコロコロ変わるので信用できません。

examples.en: People's ways of thinking change over time, don't they?
examples.ja: 人の考え方は時間とともに変わるものでしょ？

examples.en: Advances in AI have changed the way work is done.
examples.ja: AIの進歩により、仕事のやり方が大きく変わりました。

7588.meaning_mnemonic:
You've seen how 変える means "to change" something. This word means that something changed by itself, so it means <vocabulary>to be changed</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be altered</vocabulary>.

変わる refers to the act of changing into something different, and involves alterations in nature, appearance, or state. For example, it can describe changes in weather or the season, someone undergoing a noticeable change in appearance or behavior, or one's feelings or thoughts evolving over time.

Since 変わる means "becoming something different," you can also use 変わった and 変わっている to describe someone or something that's "different from what's normal." For example, you can say 変わった人 or 変わっている人 to mean "an odd person."
7588.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already so you should be able to read it!

examples.en: There's no need to be so eager. Let's just relax and take it easy.
examples.ja: そんなに勇む必要はないよ。リラックスして行こうぜ。

examples.en: Koichi and Viet came into the office in high spirits.
examples.ja: コウイチとビエトは、勇んでオフィスに入って来ました。

examples.en: That horse is prancing too much for me to bet on it.
examples.ja: あんなに勇んでたら、あの馬は買えないなぁ。

examples.en: "I'm definitely going to pass!" you resolved, your face beaming.
examples.ja: 「絶対に合格するぞ！」と勇む君の顔は、とてもキラキラしていました。

7589.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>courage</kanji> so the verb version is what happens when you have lots of it. Someone with courage is probably the kind of person who is able <vocabulary>to be in high spirits</vocabulary> in the face of something!

勇む means <vocabulary>to be eager</vocabulary> to face something or to face it with bravery and determination. It often indicates proactive and enthusiastic engagement. You'll find it in written expressions like 喜び勇む (to joyfully and eagerly undertake something) or 勇んで出かける (to go out with determination).
7589.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Who is the one person who always seems <vocabulary>to be in high spirits</vocabulary>? <reading>Isa</reading>bel (いさ)! She's so positive and eager, even in the face of a challenge.

examples.en: These grapes are seedless, so they are easy to eat.
examples.ja: このブドウはタネ無しだから食べやすいですよ。

examples.en: Please, no last-minute cancellations, okay?
examples.ja: ドタキャンは無しでお願いしますね！

examples.en: I'm broke, jobless, and am an unattractive guy in my forties. Why would you want to be with someone like me?
examples.ja: オレ、金無し、仕事無し、ブサメンの四十代だぜ。なんでオレなんかと付き合いたいの？

7590.meaning_mnemonic: This is the noun version of the kanji <kanji>nothing</kanji>, so when you have nothing, you are <vocabulary>without</vocabulary>.
7590.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

When you are <vocabulary>without</vocabulary> you don't have anything to eat either, so you end up <reading>gnashi</reading>ng (なし) your teeth together instead.

examples.en: Dogs express joy by wagging their tails.
examples.ja: 犬はシッポをふって喜びを表します。

examples.en: We are happier when we share our joy with others.
examples.ja: 私たちは、他人と喜びを分かち合うことで、より幸せを感じることができます。

examples.en: This robot has no positive emotions such as joy or fun.
examples.ja: このロボットには喜びや楽しさといったポジティブな感情はありません。

7591.meaning_mnemonic: This is the noun version of the kanji <kanji>rejoice</kanji>, so it means <vocabulary>joy</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>delight</vocabulary>. You rejoice because there are lots of reasons for your <vocabulary>glee</vocabulary>.
7591.reading_mnemonic: You already learned this reading when you learned 喜ぶ so you should be able to read this one too!

examples.en: I got some kind of warning message... what should I do?
examples.ja: なんか警告文が出てきたんだけど…どうしよう？

examples.en: I advised him that he should pay back the money he borrowed soon.
examples.ja: 借りた金を早く返すよう警告した。

examples.en: That player gets a yellow card warning in every game.
examples.ja: あの選手はどの試合でも必ず警告のイエローカードを出されるね。

7592.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>announce</kanji> something to <kanji>warn</kanji> somebody, you're <vocabulary>warning</vocabulary> them. Sometimes you're just trying to give them some helpful <vocabulary>advice</vocabulary>.
7592.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The media reported the news daily.
examples.ja: マスコミはそのニュースを連日報道しました。

examples.en: This year, Hokkaido has been experiencing heavy snowfall every day.
examples.ja: 今年の北海道は連日大雪です。

examples.en: Many people came to the event day after day.
examples.ja: そのイベントには連日たくさんの人がやって来ました。

7593.meaning_mnemonic: What happens when you <kanji>take along</kanji> a <kanji>day</kanji>? It becomes <vocabulary>every day</vocabulary>.
7593.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Vampires can control the human mind at will.
examples.ja: ヴァンパイアは人の心を自在にコントロールすることができる。

examples.en: She uses her smartphone as freely as if it were a part of her body.
examples.ja: 彼女はスマホを、まるで体の一部のように自由自在に使いこなします。

examples.en: That singer has the ability to effortlessly manipulate various vocal tones, ranging from powerful high notes to soft low notes.
examples.ja: その歌手は、パワフルな高音からソフトな低音まで、様々な歌声を自在にあやつることができます。

7594.meaning_mnemonic:
When you're all by yourself and only your <kanji>self</kanji> <kanji>exist</kanji>s, you probably have <vocabulary>full control</vocabulary>. You can do whatever you want <vocabulary>freely</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>at will</vocabulary>.

自在 is commonly used with the particle に to form the adverb 自在に. This describes how someone can handle something effortlessly, as if they have full control over it.
7594.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I stitched lace into cloth.
examples.ja: レースを布地にたたきつけた。

examples.en: I made kimono out of green fabric.
examples.ja: 緑色の布地を使って着物を作りました。

examples.en: I fell in love with a textile at the fabric store today, but it was too expensive for me to buy.
examples.ja: 今日生地屋さんで一目ぼれした布地があったんだけど、高すぎて買えなかったよ。

7595.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Cloth</kanji> from the <kanji>earth</kanji> is still <vocabulary>cloth</vocabulary>, just a little dirty.
7595.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a combination of kun'yomi and on'yomi readings. That being said, you've learned them both already!

examples.en: I don't like people who get upset easily.
examples.ja: すぐ不機嫌になる人は嫌だ。

examples.en: Hey, don't make such a sullen face. Let's have fun!
examples.ja: そんな不機嫌そうな顔しないでさ。楽しもうよ！

examples.en: I went to bed late last night and had to get up at five in the morning, so I was grumpy all day today.
examples.ja: 昨日遅く寝たのに朝五時に起きなくてはいけなかったので、今日は一日中不機嫌だった。

7596.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 機嫌 means mood? Well when you add <kanji>not</kanji> it becomes a <vocabulary>bad mood</vocabulary>. It's so bad it's like you have no mood at all.
7596.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: My alcoholic father's hands were always shaking.
examples.ja: アル中の父の手は、いつも震えていた。

examples.en: When I found a painting of great value at a flea market, I trembled.
examples.ja: すごく価値のある絵をフリーマーケットで見つけた時、全身が震えました。

examples.en: I couldn't stop crying when I saw a puppy shivering from the cold.
examples.ja: 寒さで震えている子犬を見ると、涙が止まらなくなりました。

7597.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>earthquake</kanji> so the verb means <vocabulary>to shiver</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to shake</vocabulary>, like you would if there was an earthquake happening right now.
7597.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You start <vocabulary>to shake</vocabulary> in an earthquake because you're really <reading>full</reading> (ふる) from eating lunch. Now your full belly is shaking and quaking with the ground! Ahh it's awful! You never want to be full again!

examples.en: Can you tell me the time of the Lion King performance?
examples.ja: ライオンキングの上演時間を教えて下さい。

examples.en: In Japanese cinemas, Hollywood movies are the ones shown most often.
examples.ja: 日本の映画館ではハリウッド映画が一番多く上演されています。

examples.en: What time will the kabuki performance start?
examples.ja: 歌舞伎の上演は何時からですか。

7598.meaning_mnemonic:
What's <kanji>above</kanji> the stage and involves <kanji>acting</kanji>? A <vocabulary>performance</vocabulary>!

This word does not refer to an actor's acting on stage. Instead, it usually refers to a theatrical or musical presentation in its entirety, so it's used in contexts relating to the act of staging an artistic or dramatic production, or features of the production itself, like its start time or running time (as in 上演時間).
7598.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: What, all this money in cash!?
examples.ja: えっ、この金額を全額現金で！？

examples.en: What does the grand total come out to if we combine the expenses for the wedding and the honeymoon?
examples.ja: ウェディングの費用とハネムーン旅行の費用を合わせると全額でいくらになりますか。

examples.en: Please pay the total amount for the candy yourself.
examples.ja: お菓子代は、全額自己負担でお願いします。

7599.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: When I cast my eye around, I saw that I was surrounded by many police investigators.
examples.ja: 辺りを見渡すと、たくさんの捜査員達に取り囲まれていた。

examples.en: It is necessary for a company president to have the ability to survey their entire company.
examples.ja: 会社の社長には会社全体を見渡せる能力が必要です。

examples.en: The sunflower field went on as far as the eye could see.
examples.ja: 見渡す限り、向日葵畑が続いていた。

7600.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.  The kanji means <kanji>see</kanji> and <kanji>transit</kanji>, but the vocab isn't quite the same. You are going to transit your eyes over an area to take in what you see. So you're really going <vocabulary>to look out over</vocabulary> everything. This word is usually used when you're looking at landscapes or a really large area.
7600.reading_mnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned both of these readings by now so you should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: He's as obedient as a dog.
examples.ja: あいつは犬のように従順だ。

examples.en: Don't you think it's easier to restrain yourself and be submissive?
examples.ja: 我を殺して従順でいる方が楽だと思いませんか？

examples.en: I think it's better to have someone who stands up for themselves a bit, rather than always being obedient to the boss.
examples.ja: 俺はいつも上司に従順な部下より、ちょっとくらい歯向かってくるやつの方がいいと思うけど。

examples.en: Publilius Syrus said "A virtuous wife commands her husband by obeying him."
examples.ja: パブリアス・サイラスが、「従順な妻というものは、夫に従うことで夫を支配する。」って言ってたよ。

7601.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>obey</kanji> <kanji>orders</kanji> people consider you to be an <vocabulary>obedient</vocabulary> person.

This word is relatively formal and somewhat literary.
7601.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I wonder why they can say such terrible things.
examples.ja: 何故そんなヒドイことが言えるんだろう。

examples.en: Why are those ducks crying?
examples.ja: 何故あのアヒルたちは泣いているの？

examples.en: Why were you trying to get revenge?
examples.ja: 何故復讐しようと思ったんですか。

examples.en: Why have you decided to investigate the murder case again now?
examples.ja: 何故今ごろになって、もう一度あの殺人事件の捜査を行うことにしたんですか？

7602.meaning_mnemonic: When you want to know <kanji>what</kanji> the <kanji>circumstances</kanji> are around you, you have to ask <vocabulary>why</vocabulary>. Why do things happen around you? Asking why is very important if you want to understand the world.
7602.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this is an exception. The reading for 何 is just the first な from なに. You can remember the second part this way:

No one knows quite <vocabulary>how</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>why</vocabulary> that big <reading>ze</reading>ppelin (ぜ) crashed in the 1930s. People are still asking today and no one has any answers. We have to keep asking until we get some.

examples.en: "Where are you?" "I'm in the living room now."
examples.ja: 「今、どこ？」「え、今、居間だよ」

examples.en: Dad is watching TV in the living room.
examples.ja: 父は居間でテレビを観ています。

examples.en: You took off your socks in the living room and left them there.
examples.ja: 居間に靴下が脱ぎっぱなしになってるよ。

examples.en: Even when I said, "Dinner is ready!" nobody wanted to move from the sitting room.
examples.ja: 「ごはんできたよー！」と言っても、だれも居間から動こうとしなかった。

7603.meaning_mnemonic:
A room that comes <kanji>alive</kanji> in <kanji>interval</kanji>s is your <vocabulary>living room</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>sitting room</vocabulary>. You don't spend all your time in there, so it can only be alive sometimes.

Note that 居間 is a little old-fashioned. These days, the more common word for a living room is リビングルーム.
7603.reading_mnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned both of these readings by now so you should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The Nobel Prize was awarded to them for their contribution to the development of less developed countries.
examples.ja: 後進国の発展に寄与したとして、ノーベル賞が授与された。

examples.en: Did you know that Tofugu is contributing to world peace?
examples.ja: トーフグが世界平和に寄与していることを知っているかい？

examples.en: The Finnish composer Jean Sibelius made a significant contribution to the formation of national identity through his music.
examples.ja: フィンランドの作曲家であるジャン・シベリウス は、音楽を通じて、国民意識の形成に多大な寄与をしました。

examples.en: Businesses that contribute more to the local community tend to receive grants more easily.
examples.ja: 地域への寄与度が高いビジネスの方が、助成金は下りやすいんです。

examples.en: A project manager award was given to Ms. Hattori for her contributions to cost reductions and the shortening of delivery times for goods in the project.
examples.ja: プロジェクトのコスト削減への寄与と納品日数短縮をもたらした服部さんにプロジェクトマネージャー賞が贈られた。

7604.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>draw near</kanji> to <kanji>give</kanji> something, you are probably giving a <vocabulary>contribution</vocabulary>.

寄与 is a very formal word that refers to significant contributions in professional or official settings. It's commonly used in academic or business contexts to highlight how someone's work contributes to the advancement of a field of study or the growth of a company.
7604.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Even though he failed many times, he didn't give up.
examples.ja: 彼は、幾度失敗しても、諦めなかった。

examples.en: Countless times, humanity has repeated the same mistakes.
examples.ja: 幾度も幾度も人類は同じ間違いをくり返してきた。

examples.en: I keep recalling your fragile smile from that moment, and I deeply reflect on the fleeting and beautiful nature of existence.
examples.ja: その時の君のか細い笑顔を幾度となく思い出しては、僕は存在というもののはかなさと美しさについて、深く考える。

examples.en: It feels as though I've walked the same path countless times. And that path always seemed to lead somewhere distant, yet it continued toward the same landscape.
examples.ja: 幾度となく同じ道を歩んできたように思える。そして、その道は、いつも遠くのどこか、しかしこれもまた同じ風景へと続いていた。

7605.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>How many</kanji> <kanji>occurence</kanji>s is just another way of asking <vocabulary>how many times</vocabulary>.

This word is more literary and formal than 何回 or 何度.
7605.reading_mnemonic: The reading is a combination of kun'yomi and on'yomi readings. That being said, both readings for both kanji are the readings you learned with the kanji so you should be able to read this.

examples.en: My mother is the scariest in the world.
examples.ja: 俺の母親は世界で一番恐い。

7606.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>fear</kanji>? <vocabulary>Scary</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>frightening</vocabulary>. It can also mean <vocabulary>I'm afraid</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>I'm scared </vocabulary> too.
7606.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You know what's really scary? <reading>Koa</reading>las (こわ). Have you ever heard one of those things? They're super scary, don't go near them.

examples.en: I’ve never seen such a tall hobbit before.
examples.ja: こんなに背が高いホビットは見たことがないよ。

7607.meaning_mnemonic: This is the words 背 and 高い put together to make one adjective. When your height is tall it means you are a <vocabulary>tall</vocabulary> person. This word is only used for tall people though, not anything else that's tall like a building or a tree.
7607.reading_mnemonic: This word is actually two separate words combined with a particle. So, since you treat them like separate words, you read each of them with the kun'yomi readings (they are both single kanji words all alone). You've learned both of these readings before now, so you should be able to read this word already!

examples.en: The bakufu slaughtered my family.
examples.ja: 幕府が俺の家族を皆殺しにした。

7608.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>government</kanji> behind a <kanji>curtain</kanji> is the <vocabulary>bakufu</vocabulary>. They didn't let anyone know their government secrets so they would hide behind that curtain and keep everything to themselves.
7608.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 幕 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

If you try to peek through the <vocabulary>bakufu</vocabulary>'s curtain you'll only see someone's <reading>back</reading> (ばく). They all huddle together to discuss things so a row of hunched backs is all you'll get out of the shogunate. That's not helpful.

examples.en: The meeting’s documents were substantially altered.
examples.ja: 会議の資料が大幅に変更されました。

examples.en: The price of vegetables has gone up substantially due to the drought.
examples.ja: 干ばつの影響で野菜が大幅に値上がりした。

examples.en: The development of flu vaccines led to a drastic decrease in the number of deaths.
examples.ja: インフルエンザワクチンの開発は、死亡者数の大幅な減少をもたらしました。

7609.meaning_mnemonic: Something <kanji>big</kanji> in <kanji>width</kanji> is <vocabulary>large</vocabulary>. In fact, it's of a pretty <vocabulary>substantial</vocabulary> size. This word is used to describe a large magnitude or degree of change, increase, decrease, or difference in a given situation.
7609.reading_mnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned both of these readings by now so you should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: A hunter is a very profound occupation.
examples.ja: 狩人とは非常に奥深い職業です。

7610.meaning_mnemonic: If your <kanji>interior</kanji> is <kanji>deep</kanji>, then you're a really <vocabulary>profound</vocabulary> person.
7610.reading_mnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You learned おく when you learned the kanji, and ふかい from 深い, so you should be able to read this on your own. Most of the time the ふ is rendaku'd into ぶ, but it can be read the other way too.

examples.en: It's fine to leave your clothes on.
examples.ja: 衣服は着たままでかまいませんよ。

examples.en: Please put the clothes you've taken off here.
examples.ja: 脱いだ衣服はこちらにおいてください。

examples.en: This material makes any dirt on your clothes stand out.
examples.ja: この素材は、衣服のよごれが目立ちます。

7611.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Clothes</kanji> <kanji>clothes</kanji> are also known as <vocabulary>clothing</vocabulary>!

衣服 is slightly more formal than the everyday word 服. It's kind of like saying "clothing" or "<vocabulary>garment</vocabulary>s" instead of just "<vocabulary>clothes</vocabulary>."
7611.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Do you have any rimless glasses?
examples.ja: 縁が無い眼鏡はありますか？

7612.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

縁 often describes the physical outlines of something, such as メガネの縁 (frames of glasses) or 池の縁 (the <vocabulary>edge</vocabulary> of a pond).
7612.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

The <vocabulary>edge</vocabulary> of the cheese is what we call the <reading>foo</reading>l (ふ) <reading>chee</reading>se (ち) because nobody wants that part.

examples.en: My uncle is a banker.
examples.ja: 伯父は銀行員です。

7613.meaning_mnemonic: Who is the <kanji>chief</kanji> <kanji>father</kanji>? That's your <vocabulary>uncle</vocabulary>. And this uncle is the older brother of your mom or dad because he is the chief father. An uncle who is a younger brother of your parent is 叔父, which is another word for "uncle" you already know!
7613.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this word is an exception. But you already learned the 叔父 which means uncle too. Well they have the same reading! So if you know one uncle, you know them all.

examples.en: On March 9th, that girl turns five years old.
examples.ja: 三月九日に、あの女の子は五才になる。

examples.en: I haven't showered in nine days.
examples.ja: 九日もシャワーをあびてない。

examples.en: I became a Mario Kart master on lesson day nine. Thank you.
examples.ja: レッスン九日でマリオカートのマスターになれました。ありがとう。

7614.meaning_mnemonic: <vocabulary>Ninth day</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>day nine</vocabulary>. No matter how you look at this word, it makes a lot of sense.
7614.reading_mnemonic: Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it uses kun'yomi readings for both of the kanji. You learned this reading for 九 when you learned 九つ, so you should be able to read this one too!

examples.en: I'll be on a vacation in Hawaii from the 8th.
examples.ja: 八日からハワイでバケーションなんです。

examples.en: It took eight days to make tonkotsu ramen.
examples.ja: とんこつラーメンをつくるのに八日もかかったよ。

examples.en: The kimchi diet ended after eight days.
examples.ja: キムチダイエットは八日でおわった。

7615.meaning_mnemonic: <vocabulary>Eighth day</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>day eight</vocabulary>. No matter how you look at this word, it makes a lot of sense.
7615.reading_mnemonic:
Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it uses kun'yomi readings for both the kanji. Think about this word this way:

Every <vocabulary>eighth day</vocabulary> you have to buy <reading>yo</reading>gurt to fuel your <reading>ca</reading>r (ようか). Your car runs on yogurt, but it needs to be refilled every <vocabulary>eight days</vocabulary> to keep running. It's really inconvenient because it's just ONE day more than a week. And a week just feels better. Oh well.

examples.en: There's a sword sale on the 10th.
examples.ja: 十日は刀のセールです。

examples.en: It took me ten days to get to Toronto, Canada.
examples.ja: カナダのトロントへいくのに十日かかった。

examples.en: The highlight of the event on March 10th is karaoke.
examples.ja: 三月十日のイベントの目玉はカラオケです。

7616.meaning_mnemonic: <vocabulary>Tenth day</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>day ten</vocabulary>. No matter how you look at this word, it makes a lot of sense.
7616.reading_mnemonic:
Words that count days use an exceptional reading. Even though this is a jukugo word, it actually uses kun’yomi readings. Think about this word this way:

This marks the <vocabulary>tenth day</vocabulary> since this <reading>talker</reading> (とおか) began talking non-stop. Talkers love talking, but this one is getting quite unbearable… Ten days of talking, can you believe it?

Note that とお, generally pronounced "toh" with a long "o" sound, is not a common spelling, and you’ll only see it with a handful of kanji and vocabulary, like in this case. I mean, how often do you encounter a talker who can go on non-stop for ten days? That's pretty rare, right?

examples.en: My husband is my partner for life.
examples.ja: 主人は一生のパートナーです。

examples.en: If you don't do various things yourself, you'll go your whole life without being independent.
examples.ja: 色々自分でやらないと、一生自立できないよ。

examples.en: Do you intend to be a freshman in college your whole life?
examples.ja: あなたは一生、大学一年生でいるつもりですか？

7617.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>One</kanji> <kanji>life</kanji> is all you get. It's your <vocabulary>whole life</vocabulary>. This can also mean <vocabulary>all through life</vocabulary>, and when it's used as an adjective it means <vocabulary>lifelong</vocabulary>.
7617.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You didn't learn this reading for 生 though, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Who has been in charge of you your <vocabulary>whole life</vocabulary>? The <reading>sho</reading>gun (しょう). He owns everyone and that's how it will stay for your <vocabulary>entire life</vocabulary>.

examples.en: The current British king is Charles III.
examples.ja: 今のイギリスの国王はチャールズ三世です。

examples.en: There is no king in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本には国王がいません。

examples.en: I have performed in front of the king.
examples.ja: 国王の前でパフォーマンスをしたことがあります。

7618.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>country</kanji> <kanji>king</kanji> is still a <vocabulary>king</vocabulary>, just of a bigger area.
7618.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The moon is smaller than Mercury.
examples.ja: 月は、水星より小さい。

examples.en: Mercury does not have an atmosphere.
examples.ja: 水星には大気がありません。

examples.en: You can see Mercury in the west from the top of the mountain.
examples.ja: 山の上から西の方に水星を見ることができます。

7619.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>water</kanji> <kanji>star</kanji> is the planet <vocabulary>Mercury</vocabulary>. That's where we hid all of our secret moon water. Mercury looks enough like our moon, so we put it there so no one could find it.
7619.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: What you can see there is Venus.
examples.ja: あそこに見えるのが、金星です。

examples.en: You can see a bright Venus in the night sky.
examples.ja: 夜の空に明るい金星が見える。

examples.en: Venus can be seen in the east before the sunrise and the west sky after the sunset.
examples.ja: 金星は、日の出前の東の空、または日が入った後の西の空に見ることが出来ます。

7620.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>gold</kanji> <kanji>star</kanji> is <vocabulary>Venus</vocabulary>. It's the only planet in our solar system that's the same color as gold.
7620.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I wonder how much this car can sell for?
examples.ja: この車、いくらで売れるかな？

examples.en: Twenty million of these trucks sell every month.
examples.ja: このトラックは毎月二千万台売れるんです。

examples.en: If you put a thousand yen bill on an online auction for five hundred yen, do you think it will surely sell?
examples.ja: 千円札を五百円でネットオークションに出したら、必ず売れると思う？

7621.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that the kanji means <kanji>sell</kanji> and the word 売る means "to sell something." 売れる is the intransitive version of this, so this word means for something <vocabulary>to sell</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be sold</vocabulary>.

It can also be used for something <vocabulary>to sell well</vocabulary>, that often results in that thing beginning <vocabulary>to be popular</vocabulary>.

You can remember this because it's <reading>rare</reading> (れる) to see something sell really well to the point where it gets popular!
7621.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already, so you should be able to read it! It's the same reading as 売る where you're trying to sell some <reading>U</reading>ni (う)!

examples.en: The hull was big.
examples.ja: 船体は大きかった。

examples.en: This hull is used.
examples.ja: この船体は中古です。

examples.en: It'll take at least a year for all the hulls to be built.
examples.ja: 全ての船体ができあがるまでには、少なくとも一年かかります。

7622.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: This is normal stuff, why can’t you get that?
examples.ja: こんな当たり前のこと、どうして分からないの？

examples.en: It's obvious, but it's important to take a shower every day.
examples.ja: 当たり前のことだけど、毎日シャワーをあびることは大切です。

examples.en: Say thank you every time someone does something for you, without taking it for granted.
examples.ja: 他人にしてもらったことを当たり前のことだと思わずに毎回「ありがとう」と言いましょう。

7623.meaning_mnemonic: You've seen how 当たり means success. If you've experienced success <kanji>before</kanji>, everything after that seems to be pretty <vocabulary>obvious</vocabulary>.
7623.reading_mnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned both of these readings by now so you should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I want to get the water running as soon as possible.
examples.ja: 一日も早く水道から水が出るようにしたいんです。

examples.en: Is it okay for people to drink the tap water in this area?
examples.ja: この辺の水道の水は、人が口にして平気ですか？

examples.en: The water in the pool is about half tap water and half rainwater.
examples.ja: プールの中の水は、水道の水と雨水が大体半分半分です。

7624.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>water</kanji> <kanji>road</kanji> carries your <vocabulary>water supply</vocabulary>. In the old days, these were called <vocabulary>aqueduct</vocabulary>s.
7624.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Does this neighborhood have a convenience store?
examples.ja: この付近に、コンビニはありますか？

examples.en: A doctor nearby helped me.
examples.ja: 付近にいた医者が助けてくれました。

examples.en: Please be careful of snakes near the mountains.
examples.ja: 山の付近ではヘビに気をつけて下さい。

7625.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>attach</kanji> things <kanji>near</kanji> you, they end up being in the same <vocabulary>neighborhood</vocabulary> as you. They're attached <vocabulary>nearby</vocabulary> so they can't go much further.
7625.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You didn't learn this reading for 付 though, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Your <vocabulary>neighborhood</vocabulary> is full of <reading>foo</reading>ls (ふ). Fools everywhere. You're probably one too, since you live <vocabulary>nearby</vocabulary>.

examples.en: I can't do without yoga in my daily life.
examples.ja: 毎日の生活にヨガは欠かせません。

examples.en: Every single member of this team is essential and valuable.
examples.ja: このチームのメンバーは一人も欠かせない、大切なメンバーです。

examples.en: I cannot live without my cell phone.
examples.ja: 私の生活に、携帯電話を欠かすことはできない。

7626.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 欠 means <kanji>lack</kanji>? This verb is related. The 欠かす form is a little tricky, but it's sort of like you're causing yourself to lack something. So it means <vocabulary>to do without</vocabulary>. Depending on the context, it can also mean <vocabulary>to miss an event</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to fail to do</vocabulary> something. Just keep in mind this word is most often used in the negative, like 欠かせないもの (things you can't do without) or 朝のコーヒーは欠かさない (never go without morning coffee).

You can remember 欠かす this way: Since you cause yourself to lack something with this word, it's all your fault. That's why you want to <reading>cuss</reading> (かす). You made yourself miss out on something. Well, $*%!!!
7626.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already so you should be able to read it!

examples.en: I'm looking forward to seeing the old town.
examples.ja: 昔の町を見物するのが楽しみです。

examples.en: The town is full of people who came to see the Christmas parade.
examples.ja: クリスマスパレードを見物しにきた人々で町がいっぱいです。

examples.en: Mom would have gone sightseeing in Tokyo.
examples.ja: 母ちゃんなら、東京見物に出かけたぜ。

7627.meaning_mnemonic: If you try to <kanji>see</kanji> a bunch of <kanji>thing</kanji>s at once, you are probably <vocabulary>sightseeing</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>watching</vocabulary>. This can also refer to the person doing the action, so it can sometimes mean <vocabulary>sightseer</vocabulary> too.
7627.reading_mnemonic: The reading is all on'yomi, and you know how to read 物. 見's on'yomi (けん) is a reading you didn't learn with the kanji because it's so much less useful, but you do have to know it here. You've seen it with 発見 a couple levels ago, so that should help. Just imagine taking the samurai <reading>Ken</reading> on an epic <vocabulary>sightseeing</vocabulary> trip. Think of all the things you and Ken will visit!

examples.en: After tomorrow, my mother will be hospitalized for three days.
examples.ja: 明日から母が三日間入院します。

examples.en: Every day since I got hospitalized, my breakfast has been some yogurt and an apple.
examples.ja: 入院してから毎日朝ごはんはヨーグルトとリンゴでした。

examples.en: During the hospitalization, I watched TV and called my friends.
examples.ja: 入院中は、テレビを見たり、友人に電話をしたりしてました。

7628.meaning_mnemonic: So you're <kanji>enter</kanji>ing an <kanji>institution</kanji>. But we're not talking about any institution, we're talking specifically about hospitals. So this word means <vocabulary>hospitalization</vocabulary>.
7628.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: This is a bamboo leaf.
examples.ja: これは、竹の葉です。

examples.en: You can use tea leaves not only once, but several times.
examples.ja: お茶の葉っぱは、一回だけでなく、何回か使えますよ。

examples.en: In November, the mountains are beautiful with the colors from the leaves.
examples.ja: 十一月になると、木の葉に色がついて山が美しいです。

7629.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
7629.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

examples.en: I knew it would happen, so I prepared ahead of time.
examples.ja: こうなることは分かっていたので、予め用意しておきました。

examples.en: I checked in online on the day before the flight.
examples.ja: 予めフライト前日にオンラインでチェックインしておきました。

examples.en: Preparing the lesson in advance was worthwhile.
examples.ja: 予め予習しておいた甲斐がありました。

7630.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are almost exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

Note that 予め is mostly used in formal contexts like meetings, announcements or notices, and business emails.
7630.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

At the Last Supper, the apostles asked <vocabulary>beforehand</vocabulary>: "Can we order <reading>à la car</reading>te, <reading>Je</reading>sus (あらかじ)?" Jesus said no, but He also knew <vocabulary>ahead of time</vocabulary> that Judas would betray Him by ordering some expensive à la carte dishes. And also by doing that other thing.

examples.en: Can you read hiragana?
examples.ja: 平仮名は読めますか？

examples.en: I want to name my child with hiragana.
examples.ja: うちの子には平仮名の名前をつけたいんです。

examples.en: If you eat this chocolate, you can memorize all of the hiragana.
examples.ja: このチョコレートを食べると平仮名を全部おぼえることができますよ。

7631.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how you learned that 仮名 means "kana?" Well this is <kanji>flat</kanji> kana. Flat kana is just <vocabulary>hiragana</vocabulary>.
7631.reading_mnemonic: You should know the reading for this word because it's the same as the English meaning.

examples.en: This child is literally a genius.
examples.ja: この子は文字通り「天才」だ。

examples.ja: 目と玉という漢字の文字通り、目玉は「eye ball」という意味です。

examples.en: "Tsundere" literally means, "acting cold in public but acting lovestruck in private".
examples.ja: ツンデレとは、文字通り「人前ではツンツンしているけど二人の時はデレデレすること」です。

7634.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

7636.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

価格 refers to something's market value, or to product pricing in a broader sense. It's sort of a formal word, so you might see it on fliers or in business and economic discussions about pricing strategies, for example.

7651.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>machine</kanji> that can quickly generate a <kanji>part of speech</kanji> is handy for remembering <vocabulary>one's lines</vocabulary> on stage. If you forget your <vocabulary>line</vocabulary>, just activate the machine, and it will give you a helpful prompt: "Adjective! Adjective!"

台詞 usually means a line or speech in a play, movie, or drama — something a character says out loud. But it's also used in everyday talk when someone makes a <vocabulary>remark</vocabulary> that's clever, dramatic, or memorable, almost like quoting a line.
7651.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this is an exception. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

One can also use the machine to print out <vocabulary>one's lines</vocabulary> as text, but it only prints in <reading>serif</reading> (せりふ) font. Sorry, Comic Sans folks — you'll have to wait for next year's model.

This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>yield</kanji>, and 屈む means <vocabulary>to bend down</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to crouch</vocabulary>. After all, bending down and crouching are sort of like yielding to gravity, don’t you think?

屈む refers to the act of lowering your head or body, so it can also mean <vocabulary>to duck</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to squat</vocabulary> depending on the context.

examples.en: Saturn is big.

7674.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Just be careful because かつ is being shortened here to かっ. It's a pretty common change for on'yomi ending in つ, so keep your eyes open for more that do this!

7675.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

7680.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>service</kanji> <kanji>location</kanji> is a place that people go when they're in need of a service. The best place for this is the <vocabulary>town hall</vocabulary>. Everyone goes to this one location to voice their complaints, and in return their needs are serviced by the officials in the town hall.

役場 specifically refers to the administrative office of a town (町) or village (村) rather than a city (市). Depending on the location, it may be also be called a 町役場 or 村役場.
7680.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the on'yomi reading for the first kanji and the kun'yomi reading for the second kanji. You didn't learn the kun'yomi reading for 場 with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

At your <vocabulary>town hall</vocabulary>, you say "<reading>baa</reading>" (ば) when you talk to the clerks. You live in a town full of sheep, so you need to speak Sheepanese whenever you run errands at the town hall. "Baa, baa, baa," you say as you submit a big stack of paperwork to the clerk.

7681.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. 

The kanji itself means <kanji>point</kanji> so the verb version is something you need to point your finger to do. Picture pointing your finger and pushing a lightswitch <vocabulary>to turn something on</vocabulary>, in this case the light. You won't be able <vocabulary>to switch something on</vocabulary> if you can't point your finger.
7681.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You aren't able <vocabulary>to turn</vocabulary> the light on with just one finger though, you need to use <reading>two</reading> (つ). Either you have really weak fingers, or that's a really strong lightswitch. Either way, you need two fingers to switch on the light.

Maybe you're going <vocabulary>to tell</vocabulary> a story, or the truth.

This verb is transitive, so it generally takes a direct object in Japanese, even though the English translations might not.

7696.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 言葉 means "language?" Well, the way you "attach" (付き) language to things is your <vocabulary>diction</vocabulary>. Everyone has their own 言葉つき when they speak. How would you describe your 言葉つき?

言葉つき refers to the characteristics of <vocabulary>how one speaks</vocabulary>, including the words they choose, how they say them, and their overall speaking style.
7696.reading_mnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned both of these readings by now so you should be able to read this on your own.

7697.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember 放す (to release) and 放れる (to get loose)? 放つ is another transitive verb of the <kanji>release</kanji> family, but this is a more dynamic kind of releasing, so it means <vocabulary>to fire</vocabulary> off something. 

You can remember this because you usually need つ (two) hands to fire something off properly, whether it's a slingshot or a hit in baseball.

放つ often implies setting something free with force or impact. It's used to describe things like shooting arrows, firing bullets, letting animals loose into the wild, or even strongly emitting something like light or an offensive smell. More figuratively, it can describe the act of releasing something into the world, whether that's a creative work you're unveiling or a hot take you're firing off on social media.
7697.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already so you should be able to read it!

7708.meaning_mnemonic:
You have 最, which means <kanji>most</kanji>, and 後尾, which means something like "back" or "rear" (<kanji>behind</kanji> + <kanji>tail</kanji>). When you're at the most back part of something, you might find yourself at the <vocabulary>end of a line</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>end of a queue</vocabulary>.

最後尾 is often seen on signs at the end of a long line to help people locate where to join the queue.
7708.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. Be careful, because this is 最 + 後尾, and not 最後 + 尾, meaning that 後 is read こう, not ご! You learned the こう reading with the kanji, but this might be your first time seeing it in a word, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

Who's always waiting at the <vocabulary>end of a line</vocabulary>? It's <reading>こう</reading>いち. The dude is always the last one to get to places, and he lines up after literally everybody else, which is why he's at the end of the queue. In middle school the bullies called him "End of the Queue こういち." Poor guy.

7716.meaning_mnemonic:
When you <kanji>pull</kanji> yourself back and <kanji>retreat</kanji>, you're <vocabulary>retiring</vocabulary>. At some point in everyone's lives you just can't do it anymore and it's time to take your <vocabulary>retirement</vocabulary>.

This word focuses on the moment of retiring. It's often used to mean <vocabulary>withdrawing from public life</vocabulary>, when someone ends their career in a particular field, like when celebrities or pro athletes retire. It can also be used for students who stop extracurricular activities like clubs and sports teams ahead of graduation, often to study for their exams.

7721.reading_mnemonic:

The second kanji uses the on'yomi reading. You didn't learn this reading for 気 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

At the height of <vocabulary>showing off</vocabulary>, you bend one arm to your hip and the other out in the air. You pretend to be a <reading>ke</reading>ttle (け). You show off your spirit to all your friends singing "I'm a little ke-ttle, short and stout. Here is my handle, here is my spout. EVERYONE LOOK HOW GREAT I AM!" Your kettle dance is sure to impress them.

Unlike 透ける, which is more for things that are partially transparent due to being thin or sheer, 透き通る describes things that are totally transparent, clear, or pure — think glass, water, a cloudless sky, or even a clear and pure voice.

7741.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You already learned that 通る means to pass, but this is a little different. You aren't the one passing, Sue (す) is. So you have to let Sue pass. In other words, this verb is transitive, meaning it has an object. That's why it means <vocabulary>to let something pass</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to put something through</vocabulary>.

The way this verb is translated into English changes a lot depending on the noun it's paired with. For example 火を通す is literally "to let the fire pass through", and means "to heat through". 針に糸を通す is literally "to put thread through a needle", so means "to thread a needle".

枯らす literally means <vocabulary>to let something dry up</vocabulary>, usually by neglect or lack of water (though too much water can also 枯らす plants). It's often used when someone accidentally lets plants die, but it can also describe intentionally killing plants with a herbicide. You'll also see it used figuratively, like 声を枯らす (to lose one's voice).

8613.reading_mnemonic:
The reading can be either the on'yomi or kun'yomi, and you know both.

Between the two, the on'yomi はんせん is the standard reading. As is often the case with on'yomi compounds, it has a more technical feel, so it is commonly used in formal references to sailing ships either in technical books or fiction.

The kun'yomi ほぶね, on the other hand, has a softer, more traditionally Japanese tone, like how people in the past might have referred to it in everyday life. You'll often see it in older songs or literature, but it can also appear in modern works to convey a nostalgic vibe.

examples.en: The next class is next week.
examples.ja: 次のクラスは来週です。

examples.en: The theme of next week's composition is "the day I was born".
examples.ja: 来週の作文のテーマは「自分の生まれた日」です。

examples.en: I'm building up my stamina by running every day in preparation for next week's marathon.
examples.ja: 来週のマラソンのために、毎日走って体力をつけています。

8698.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>next</kanji> <kanji>week</kanji> is the <vocabulary>next week</vocabulary>. It isn't last week or this week, it's the next one!
8698.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: In junior high school, you will study nine subjects.
examples.ja: 中学では九科目学びます。

examples.en: I got an eighty on the tests for all subjects.
examples.ja: どの科目のテストも全て八十点でした。

examples.en: Mom is a teacher of subjects like science and mathematics.
examples.ja: お母さんは科学や数学などの科目の先生です。

8699.meaning_mnemonic: If you've got an <kanji>eye</kanji> on a certain <kanji>course</kanji>, it's a <vocabulary>subject</vocabulary> you really want to take. Maybe you're in school and that means you'll be taking a lot of <vocabulary>course</vocabulary>s. Maybe you're a teacher and you're planning out your <vocabulary>curriculum</vocabulary>. Either way, you have your eye on the course-prize.
8699.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the on'yomi readings, but you learned the kun'yomi reading for 目 before. So, you have to remember that this word uses もく instead of め. To do that, imagine seeing that the <vocabulary>subjects</vocabulary> you're allowed to take next term are different than everyone else's. The other kids notice, and start <reading>mock</reading>ing (もく) you for it. Think of what those subjects are and how you're being mocked for having to take them.

examples.en: When I give the signal, please jump high.
examples.ja: 私が合図をしたら、大きくジャンプをしてください。

examples.en: Sam gave the signal by raising his thumb up.
examples.ja: サムは、親指を上げて合図を送った。

examples.en: That was the signal to start.
examples.ja: それがスタートの合図でした。

8700.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>diagram</kanji> everyone <kanji>join</kanji>s together to see is a <vocabulary>signal</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>sign</vocabulary>.
8700.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi reading for 合 and the on'yomi reading for 図. You know them both now, so you should be able to read this too!

examples.en: There are various creatures in the sea.
examples.ja: 海の中には、色々な生物がいます。

examples.en: I wonder what that creature was.
examples.ja: あの生物は一体何だったんでしょう。

examples.en: I'm wondering if you can show me your notes from the last biology class.
examples.ja: 前回の生物のクラスのノート、見せてくれないかな。

8701.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>life</kanji> <kanji>thing</kanji> is a <vocabulary>living thing</vocabulary>, a <vocabulary>creature</vocabulary>, or an <vocabulary>organism</vocabulary>.
8701.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The housekeepers take care of most of the housework.
examples.ja: 大体の家事はハウスキーパーの方がしてくれます。

examples.en: I think I don't have enough time to watch TV due to the house chores.
examples.ja: 家事のせいで、テレビを見る時間が不足していると思っています。

examples.en: Housework is not my innate forte, so it takes me some time every day.
examples.ja: 元々私は家事に向いてないので、毎日時間がかかってしまいます。

8702.meaning_mnemonic: You know 事 means "occurrence," but it also means "matter." So you can think of a <kanji>house</kanji> <kanji>matter</kanji> as  as <vocabulary>housework</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>chores</vocabulary>. Housework and chores are really just house matters that you have to deal with, after all.
8702.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading of 家 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

<vocabulary>Housework</vocabulary> done in a <reading>car</reading> (か) is still housework. Think of all the times you've tidied up your car. That's housework too!

examples.en: I remembered this morning, "Oh! The exam is today!"
examples.ja: 今朝になってから「あ！テスト今日じゃん！」って思い出したんです。

examples.en: This morning, it was more winter-ish weather than I expected, so I went to work in my coat.
examples.ja: 今朝は思ったより冬らしい天気だったので、コートで会社に行きました。

examples.en: I got up early this morning and made a handmade breakfast with my dad.
examples.ja: 今朝は早く起きて、お父さんと一緒に手作りの朝食を作った。

8703.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Now</kanji> <kanji>morning</kanji> is just another way of saying <vocabulary>this morning</vocabulary>. It's the closest morning to right now!
8703.reading_mnemonic:
This reading is an exception. Let's use this mnemonic to remember it:

<vocabulary>This morning</vocabulary> you want a <reading>quesa</reading>dilla (けさ) for breakfast. You can't wait until tomorrow morning, you NEED it this morning! Imagine eating a delicious quesadilla first thing this morning. Mmm!

examples.en: There is a harbor in this town, and there are train lines running through it.
examples.ja: この町には港もあるし、電車も通ってます。

examples.en: Don't approach the port when a typhoon comes.
examples.ja: 台風が来たら、港には近づかないで下さい。

examples.en: There was a mysterious ship drifting in the harbor.
examples.ja: 不思議な船が港に漂着した。

8704.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
8704.reading_mnemonic:
This is a single kanji with no okurigana, so it's using the kun'yomi reading. You don't know this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You go down to the <vocabulary>harbor</vocabulary> and speak the secret password <reading>me natto</reading> (みなと) to buy some fresh natto. Imagine the salty air hitting your face as you whisper, "me natto." Now eat that yummy natto by the water! Mmmm!

examples.en: The one over there is a god.
examples.ja: あそこにいるのは神様です。

examples.en: Who comes to your mind when you hear the name "guitar god."
examples.ja: ギターの神様と言えば、誰を思いうかべますか？

examples.en: That's probably just the god of mischief.
examples.ja: あれは多分神様のイタズラだったのだろう。

8705.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>God</kanji> (<kanji>formal name ender</kanji>) is <vocabulary>God</vocabulary>! Or the <vocabulary>gods</vocabulary>, if you're talking to more than one. You have to be polite to them, so you add that ender on there.
8705.reading_mnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned them both already so you should be able to read this too!

examples.en: When is your school's culture festival?
examples.ja: そっちの学校の文化祭っていつ？

examples.en: What time should we start the school festival rehearsal?
examples.ja: 文化祭の練習、何時にする？

examples.en: It seems like a famous person is going to come to our school's culture festival!
examples.ja: うちの文化祭に誰か有名人が来るらしいよ！

8706.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 文化 means "culture?" Well add <kanji>festival</kanji> to it and you end up with a <vocabulary>culture festival</vocabulary>! These happen all the time at Japanese schools, so sometimes they're called <vocabulary>school festival</vocabulary>s too.
8706.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've learned all of these readings already, good for you!

examples.en: Sunny days make me want to go on a picnic.
examples.ja: 晴れの日はピクニックに行きたくなります。

examples.en: It looks like it's going to be sunny again tomorrow.
examples.ja: 明日も晴れみたいだよ。

examples.en: This app says "It will be clear, then cloudy."
examples.ja: このアプリでは「晴れのちくもり」になってるよ。

8707.meaning_mnemonic:
If you say something is going to <kanji>clear up</kanji>, you're usually talking about the weather. That makes this <vocabulary>clear weather</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>sunny</vocabulary>.

Maybe because of those connotations, 晴れ can also be used to describe special occasions that are usually public. For example, a wedding or a big recital might be called a 晴れの場 (special occasion). Similarly, the special clothing you wear to such events is called 晴れ着 (formal attire).
8707.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

examples.en: This area doesn’t have bad public safety, but that area does.
examples.ja: この辺りは治安も悪くないけど、あの辺りは治安が良くないからね。

examples.en: If Japan's birthrate continues to decline, public safety will worsen.
examples.ja: このまま日本の少子化が進むと、治安も悪化するでしょう。

examples.en: I'm actually Superman and I'm the one who keeps the peace around here.
examples.ja: 俺は実はスーパーマンなんだ。この辺りの治安を守っているのはこの俺様なんだぜ。

8708.meaning_mnemonic: If your people can <kanji>relax</kanji> because you <kanji>rule</kanji> over them so well, there is <vocabulary>public order</vocabulary>. You don't want the people you rule being upset or stressed out, you want <vocabulary>public safety</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>public peace</vocabulary> for all!
8708.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I have had a fever since the day before yesterday.
examples.ja: 一昨日から熱が出ています。

examples.en: I woke up early the day before yesterday and went jogging.
examples.ja: 一昨日の朝は、早起きしてジョギングに行きました。

examples.en: The night before last, I was able to see a beautiful starry sky.
examples.ja: 一昨日の夜は、美しい星空を見ることができました。

8709.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how you learned that 昨日 means "yesterday?" Well <kanji>one</kanji> day <kanji>previous</kanji> to that <kanji>day</kanji> is the <vocabulary>day before last</vocabulary>.
8709.reading_mnemonic:
This reading is an exception. Let's use this mnemonic to remember it:

The <vocabulary>day before last</vocabulary> you bought an <reading>"O" toe toy</reading> (おととい). It's a kid's toy in the shape of the letter O that you put on your toe. You know it was the day before last because you wore it all yesterday, and now today your toe is sore. If only you could go back to the <vocabulary>day before yesterday</vocabulary> to tell yourself not to buy that O toe toy! Or at least not to wear it for the whole next day!

examples.en: Entry is prohibited to all but related parties.
examples.ja: 関係者以外の立ち入りを禁じる。

examples.en: I think alcohol should be banned worldwide.
examples.ja: アルコールは世界で禁じられるべきだと思います。

examples.en: Private conversation is prohibited in this room.
examples.ja: この部屋では、私語を禁じます。

8710.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>prohibition</kanji> so the verb version means <vocabulary>to prohibit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to forbid</vocabulary>.
8710.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

examples.en: Next month, our high school's vocal music club will participate in the city's vocal ensemble contest in the high school division.
examples.ja: 来月、うちの高校の声楽部が、市の声楽アンサンブルコンテストの高等学校部門に出場することになりました。

examples.en: In America, the high school enrollment rate is high, with almost all students graduating from high school. What is the high school enrollment rate like in Japan?
examples.ja: アメリカでは、高等学校への進学率は高く、ほぼ全ての学生が高校を卒業します。日本の高等学校への進学率はどれくらいですか？

examples.en: If a foreigner wishes to enroll in a Japanese high school for study abroad, they need to be twenty years old or younger and to have received at least one year of Japanese language education at an educational institution, or to have been educated in Japanese for at least one year.
examples.ja: 外国人が留学で日本の高等学校に入学する場合、20才以下かつ教育機関において1年以上の日本語教育、もしくは日本語による教育を受けている必要があります。

8711.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember when you learned that 高等 means "high class" and 学校 means "school?" Well put them together and you have <vocabulary>senior high school</vocabulary>! It's the most high class school you've got (unless you go to university, but that's considered to be separate). 

Fun fact: 高校 is the abbreviation of this word. Neat, right?
8711.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I use this lifehack in the morning so I can wake up properly.
examples.ja: このライフハックを使うと、朝、すっきり目覚めることができます。

examples.en: It seems that Ken has finally become conscious of his responsibilities as a company president.
examples.ja: ケンはやっと社長としての責任感に目覚めたようだね。

examples.en: To save energy, I set the temperature of the air conditioner to 30℃, so when I woke up, I was drenched.
examples.ja: 省エネのため冷房の温度を三十度に設定しているせいで、目覚めたら汗だくになっていました。

8712.meaning_mnemonic:
If your <kanji>eye</kanji>s are <kanji>awake</kanji> then you're going <vocabulary>to wake up</vocabulary>. Your eyes are usually the first thing to awaken when you're waking up, you know? 

This word can also mean <vocabulary>to awaken</vocabulary> but it's like when you to come to your senses, not literally waking up.
8712.reading_mnemonic:
The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You haven’t learned this reading for 覚 yet, and in this case it also gets rendaku’d, so bear that in mind. Anyway, here’s a mnemonic to help you:

If you start <vocabulary>to wake up</vocabulary> in the middle of the night, it’s because of the C<reading>za</reading>r (ざ) you met that had banned sitting. This cruel, ruthless Czar keeps appearing in your nightmares, causing you to wake up incessantly. Terrifying.

examples.en: Why can't you just obediently say thank you?
examples.ja: どうして素直に有り難うって言うことができないの？

examples.en: "Congratulations on the birth of your baby." "Thank you very much."
examples.ja: 「赤ちゃんのご誕生、おめでとうございます。」「有難うございます。」

examples.en: Thanks to you, I've been accused of tax evasion.
examples.ja: 有難う。お陰で脱税で告訴されたよ。

8713.meaning_mnemonic:
Some people <kanji>have</kanji> a <kanji>difficult</kanji> time saying <vocabulary>thank you</vocabulary>. But not you now that you know how!

This is often written in kana, so you don't need to use the kanji when writing. But you'll sometimes see the kanji used so it's important to be able to recognize them! Did you know this is an abbreviation of 有難うございます? You can also spell it like this: 有難う.
8713.reading_mnemonic: You've heard people say ありがとう before right?!

examples.en: Didn’t you actually say that a while ago?
examples.ja: 現にさっきそう言ったじゃありませんか。

examples.en: Some people were actually killed. How can you say such a thing?
examples.ja: 現に人が死んでるっていうのに、よくそんなことが言えますね。

examples.en: There are actually people suffering from starvation at this very moment, you know.
examples.ja: 現にこの瞬間にも飢餓で苦しんでいる人がいるんですよ？

8714.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>present time</kanji> is the time you're <vocabulary>actually</vocabulary> in. You aren't <vocabulary>really</vocabulary> in any other time, because that's not how time works!
8714.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

examples.en: There are a lot of moles on both my arms.
examples.ja: 両腕にホクロがたくさんあります。

examples.en: Next, please cross both arms.
examples.ja: 次は両腕を交差させてください。

examples.en: There were many burns on both of the cook’s arms.
examples.ja: コックの両腕には、ヤケドの跡がたくさんありました。

examples.en: Both of my arms are numb. They can't take it anymore.
examples.ja: 両腕がしびれています。もう限界です。

8715.reading_mnemonic: This is a combination of the on'yomi reading of 両 and the kun'yomi reading of 腕. You've learned them both, so you know this too!

examples.en: The rain caused the river's water level to increase.
examples.ja: 雨がふって川の水かさが増しました。

examples.en: These days, a rumor that Tofugu is growing a lot is going around in the Japanese language education industry.
examples.ja: 最近、日本語教育業界でトーフグの勢いが増したとウワサになっています。

examples.en: Sugar will make it much sweeter, you know.
examples.ja: 砂糖でさらに甘みが増しますよ。

8716.meaning_mnemonic:
It's another verb with the kanji 増! This one means <vocabulary>to increase</vocabulary> too! But!

Just like 増える, this is when something is just increasing on its own. You can use this word to talk about an increase in number, quantity, or degree, but it’s more literary and less common than 増える, except when referring to an increase in degree.
8716.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet so here's a mnemonic to help you:

What <vocabulary>increase</vocabulary>s with time? Your love for your <reading>ma</reading>ma (ま)! Your love for her will grow and grow the older you get! I love you, mama!

examples.en: I broke my right arm, so I won't be able to work for a while.
examples.ja: 右腕を骨折したため、しばらくの間仕事ができません。

examples.en: She is President Koichi's right-hand person.
examples.ja: 彼女はコウイチ社長の右腕です。

examples.en: I was plucking the hair on my right arm to pass the time, so only this arm is smooth now.
examples.ja: ひまつぶしで右腕の毛をぬいてたので、こっちの腕だけツルツルです。

examples.en: I think that’s supposed to be a dragon tattoo on that guy’s right arm.
examples.ja: 奴の右腕には、龍のタトゥーがあるハズだ。

8717.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, but it uses kun'yomi instead of on'yomi, so watch out for that!

examples.en: My stomach aches from stress.
examples.ja: ストレスで、胃がキリキリします。

examples.en: For the first time in my life, I had a gastroscopy.
examples.ja: 人生で初めて胃カメラを飲んだ。

examples.en: What was the name of the character with the trait of having a weak stomach?
examples.ja: あの胃が弱い設定のキャラクター、何て名前だっけ？

examples.en: I ate too much cake and bacon, and they've been heavy on my stomach.
examples.ja: ケーキとベーコンの食べ過ぎで胃がもたれています。

8718.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

Just keep in mind 胃 is specifically for the internal organ "stomach," not for the general abdominal area "stomach."
8718.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

examples.en: The reason is that tomorrow is the cut-off date for my credit card.
examples.ja: 何故なら、明日がカードの締め日だからです。

examples.en: The reason is simple: it's because it tastes good.
examples.ja: 理由はシンプルで、何故なら美味しいからです。

examples.en: It's because you should use your waiting time more productively.
examples.ja: 何故なら、待ち時間は有益に使った方がいいからです。

examples.en: Because, he was a wizard!
examples.ja: 何故なら、彼は魔法使いだったのです。

8719.meaning_mnemonic:
This is like saying "when it comes to the 何故," which means you're giving a reason, making this <vocabulary>because</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>the reason is</vocabulary>, followed by… whatever you wanna say! 

Note that this is a quite formal way to say "because," so you'll mostly encounter this in writing or formal speech, and almost always at the beginning of a sentence in Japanese.
8719.reading_mnemonic: This reading is an exception but you learned them already because they're the same as the word 何故, which you learned a few levels ago. It just has some kana attached to it!

examples.en: If you have doubts, you should think it over a bit more.
examples.ja: 迷いがあるなら、もう少し考えたほうがいいよ。

examples.en: I sensed some hesitation in his words.
examples.ja: 彼の言葉には、少し迷いが感じられました。

examples.en: I managed to get rid of my hesitation.
examples.ja: なんとか迷いを断ち切りました。

examples.en: I had no hesitation about quitting the company.
examples.ja: 会社を辞めることに迷いはありませんでした。

examples.en: She accepted the project without any hesitation.
examples.ja: 彼女は迷いなく、プロジェクトを引き受けた。

8720.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how you learned that 迷う means "to go astray" or "to get lost?" Well, when you feel like you've gone astray or gotten lost, you might act with <vocabulary>hesitation</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>indecision</vocabulary>. You suddenly have <vocabulary>doubt</vocabulary> about where to go or what to do next.

While 迷う can mean getting lost either physically or mentally, 迷い most often conveys an abstract sense of inner conflict or uncertainty, especially in decision making.
8720.reading_mnemonic: You learned this reading already when you learned 迷う! Just swap the う for an い.

examples.en: Please tell me about the popular games in schools nowadays.
examples.ja: 最近学校で流行っている遊びを教えて下さい。

examples.en: I started playing the piano just for fun, but before I knew it, I had become a professional.
examples.ja: ピアノは遊びで始めたんですが、気づいたらプロになってました。

examples.en: He's a genius when it comes to play and always comes up with fun things to do.
examples.ja: 彼は遊びに関しては天才で、いつも面白いことを思いつきます。

examples.en: Her playful designs are loved by many people.
examples.ja: 彼女の遊び心あふれるデザインは、多くの人に愛されています。

examples.en: That affair wasn't serious; I was just playing around. Really, believe me!
examples.ja: あの浮気は、本気じゃなくてただの遊びだったんだ。本当だよ、信じてくれよ！

8721.meaning_mnemonic: This is the noun version of the kanji <kanji>play</kanji>, so it means <vocabulary>play</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>playing</vocabulary>!
8721.reading_mnemonic: You learned this reading when you learned 遊ぶ. It's the same one!

examples.en: Shouldn't you restrain yourself from wearing a gaudy dress?
examples.ja: 華美なドレスはひかえた方がいいんじゃないですか。

examples.en: It's a very nice piece, with an extravagant design, but also leaves a calm impression.
examples.ja: 華美なデザインなのに、落ち着いた印象もあるとてもいい作品だね。

examples.en: Beneath the lavish chandelier, there was a single potato lying all alone.
examples.ja: 華美なシャンデリアの真下に、ジャガイモが１つだけポツンと落ちていた。

examples.en: Which prefecture is known for being a good market for used cars and for its reputation of not favoring a flashy lifestyle?
examples.ja: 中古車がよく売れる地域としても有名で、華美な生活を好まないことで知られている県は何県でしょう？

8722.meaning_mnemonic:
If something has <kanji>showy</kanji> <kanji>beauty</kanji> then it's going a little overboard and is going to come across as <vocabulary>gaudy</vocabulary> <vocabulary>ostentation</vocabulary>. Too much is too much.

Compared to the similar word 派手 (flashy), 華美 suggests a more refined kind of <vocabulary>splendor</vocabulary> — luxurious and elegant, but a tad excessive. It's a formal word, generally used in writing to describe clothing or decor that's beautiful but verges on being showy.
8722.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: My body feels hot from this high fever.
examples.ja: 高熱で体が火照っています。

8723.meaning_mnemonic: If <kanji>fire</kanji> <kanji>illuminate</kanji>s your face, you're going <vocabulary>to feel hot</vocabulary>. Sometimes you start <vocabulary>to flush</vocabulary> when you're embarrassed and it just feels like there is fire making your face light up.
8723.reading_mnemonic:
The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You haven't learned this reading for 火 yet, but it's easier to remember this with a mnemonic for the whole thing:

When are you going <vocabulary>to feel hot</vocabulary>? When is your face going <vocabulary>to flush</vocabulary>? When I ask you to go to a <reading>hotel</reading> (ほてる) with me!

examples.en: The abnormal weather continues.
examples.ja: 異常気象が続いています。

8724.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I bought this avocado yesterday and it’s already gone bad.
examples.ja: このアボカド、昨日買ったところなのにもう傷んでるよ。

examples.en: It looks like the box was damaged because I put it in a place where it was exposed to sunlight.
examples.ja: 日の光が当たる所に置いていたせいで、箱が傷んでしまったみたい。

examples.en: Fresh cream spoils easily, so please put it back in the fridge as soon as you finish using it.
examples.ja: 生クリームは傷みやすいから、使ったらすぐに冷蔵庫に閉まってね。

8725.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji means <kanji>wound</kanji>, and this verb is intransitive, so it means <vocabulary>to be damaged</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to go bad</vocabulary>. After all, fruit with a wound on it is going bad, isn't it?
8725.reading_mnemonic: This shares the same reading as 痛む. The meanings are similar too, so that should be easy to remember, unless your brain was damaged by these mnemonics or something.

examples.en: Oil prices are rising steeply.
examples.ja: 石油価格が高騰している。

8726.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Oil</kanji> that has <kanji>stone</kanji>s in it is from the ground. It's not olive oil, it's <vocabulary>petroleum</vocabulary>!
8726.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I still have no news about my father.
examples.ja: 依然父の消息は不明です。

8727.meaning_mnemonic:
If you have a <kanji>dependent</kanji> <kanji>nature</kanji>, then even if you go off on your own, you're <vocabulary>still</vocabulary> going to ask for help. Dependent people still need help because that's just how they are.

Note that you need to add と to the end of this word to make it an adverb, and たる to make it an adjective!
8727.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: How would you like to pay?
examples.ja: お支払い方法はどうなさいますか？

examples.en: Please make payments by card.
examples.ja: 支払いはカードでお願いします。

examples.en: Thank goodness, now I can pay my bills!
examples.ja: よかったー、これで支払いができる！

8728.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>pay</kanji> that <kanji>support</kanji>s you is made in <vocabulary>payment</vocabulary>s. Whether you make payments to keep your house or your car, or you get payments from your boss, they keep you going.
8728.reading_mnemonic: This is a combination of the on'yomi reading of 支 and the kun'yomi reading of 払. You've learned them both, so you know this too!

examples.en: I chuckled from the depths of my heart.
examples.ja: 心の奥底でほくそ笑みました。

8729.meaning_mnemonic: Something is in the <kanji>interior</kanji> AND the <kanji>bottom</kanji>? Why, it's in the very <vocabulary>depths</vocabulary>! And if it's in the interior and bottom of you, then it's at the <vocabulary>bottom</vocabulary> of your heart!
8729.reading_mnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You learned them when you learned the kanji, so you should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I went to buy three bunches of grapes.
examples.ja: 葡萄を三房買ってきたわよ。

8730.meaning_mnemonic: Remember when you learned 房? Well it can be used as a counter for clusters of fruit. Like a <vocabulary>section</vocabulary> of an orange or a <vocabulary>bunch</vocabulary> of grapes! Yum!
8730.reading_mnemonic: You learned this reading already when you learned 房!

examples.en: I reluctantly admitted to the things I did.
examples.ja: 渋々自分がやったことを認めました。

8731.meaning_mnemonic: If you bite into something <kanji>bitter</kanji> (twice!) you'll take your next bite <vocabulary>reluctantly</vocabulary>. Because who would want that much of something bitter? Not you.
8731.reading_mnemonic: This is the kun'yomi reading twice. You learned this reading when you learned 渋い. If you remember that, you know this too!

examples.en: I’m collecting dew that’s on the leaves.
examples.ja: 葉っぱの上に乗っている露を集めているんだ。

8732.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
8732.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi reading of the kanji, but you haven't learned it yet. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

<vocabulary>Dew</vocabulary> is just the earth's way of giving water <reading>to you</reading> (つゆ). Rain is too forceful, you may not go to the ocean or a lake, so the earth gives dew to you by putting it on the grass outside your house everyday!

examples.en: Please enter your social security number here.
examples.ja: ここにソーシャルセキュリティナンバーを入力して下さい。

examples.en: These three are data-entry professionals.
examples.ja: この三人はデータ入力のプロだよ。

examples.en: People who can do "Romaji input" and "Kana input" are sexy, right?
examples.ja: 「Romaji入力」と「かな入力」ができる人ってセクシーだよね。

8733.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Enter</kanji> something with all your <kanji>strength</kanji> and you will look down to see that what you're doing is <vocabulary>input</vocabulary>ting data. You're inputting it right now! Into this site! The answers you <vocabulary>enter</vocabulary> into WaniKani with all your strength can be said with this word. Wow. Full circle already, and you're only on level 2. Look at you go!
8733.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 力 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

Where you work, <vocabulary>input</vocabulary>ting things earns you <reading>new</reading> <reading>lock</reading>s (にゅうりょく). Not only is your job only about <vocabulary>enter</vocabulary>ing things into a computer, you're also paid exclusively in new locks. Maybe consider a career change!

examples.en: I knocked on the door.
examples.ja: 戸をノックした。

examples.en: My cat scratches the door.
examples.ja: うちのネコは戸をカリカリします。

examples.en: This door opens and closes hard.
examples.ja: この戸は立てつけがわるい。

8734.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>door</kanji> is a <vocabulary>door</vocabulary> — the kanji and the word are exactly the same.

戸 can refer to any kind of door, but it's more commonly used for <vocabulary>sliding door</vocabulary>s, since those are the traditional style of doors in Japan. For Western-style or high-tech doors, people tend to just say ドア.
8734.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

examples.en: That woman over there? That's Mami.
examples.ja: あの女の人？マミさんだよ。

examples.en: There are many female staff at this restaurant.
examples.ja: このレストランには女の人のスタッフがたくさんいます。

examples.en: I would love to be able to email with women well.
examples.ja: 女の人と上手にメールができるようになりたいなあ。

8735.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>woman</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji> is a <vocabulary>woman</vocabulary>.

The の particle here means the first noun is modifying the second one, so you can probably see why 女の人 (a woman person) really just means woman! It's more polite than saying 女 by itself, so that's all you have to remember.
8735.reading_mnemonic: This word is actually two separate words combined with a particle. So, since you treat them like separate words, you read each of them with the kun'yomi readings (they are both single kanji words all alone). That being said, in level 1 you learned about the vocab readings for these separate words, so use that knowledge to remember the reading for this word as well.
