examples.ja: これが、本来の村の名です。

examples.en: Primarily it is an Italian restaurant, but they also have ramen.
examples.ja: 本来はイタリアンレストランですが、ラーメンもあります。

examples.en: I usually work remote, but today I am at the head office.
examples.ja: 本来はリモートワークですが、今日は本社にいます。

8736.meaning_mnemonic: You want to talk about the <kanji>origin</kanji> where something <kanji>come</kanji>s from. That's where it is from <vocabulary>originally</vocabulary>.
8736.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.ja: 手首にブレスレットをしています。

examples.ja: これは、手首のストレッチです。

examples.en: My husband has a tattoo on his wrist.
examples.ja: 私の主人は手首にタトゥーが有ります。

examples.en: The diamond shines when the sun hits it.
examples.ja: 日が当たると、ダイアモンドは光る。

examples.en: The water in the pool shines with the sunlight.
examples.ja: プールの水が日の光でキラキラと光ります。

examples.en: Didn't the sky shine red just now?
examples.ja: 今、空が赤く光ったよね？

8738.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>light</kanji> or <kanji>shine</kanji>, so the verb is <vocabulary>to shine</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to flash</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to glitter</vocabulary>. Just imagine what happens when something emits light!
8738.reading_mnemonic: Remember how you learned the reading for 光? Well this is almost the same thing. Just change the り to る and you'll know this reading!

examples.en: It's been a few years since I came to Japan.
examples.ja: 日本に来てから、数年です。

examples.en: I met a former partner for the first time in a few years.
examples.ja: 数年ぶりに、元パートナーに会いました。

examples.en: Oh, did you just remember? We met once at a cosplay event a few years ago.
examples.ja: あ、思い出しました？数年前に一回、コスプレのイベントでお会いしたことがあります。

8739.meaning_mnemonic: When a <kanji>number</kanji> of <kanji>year</kanji>s have passed you say that <vocabulary>several years</vocabulary> have passed! You don't want to say how many years, so just say several years.
8739.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Type a message mixed up with some emoji.
examples.ja: 絵文字を交ぜて、メッセージを入力しましょう。

examples.en: Take a closer look at this receipt emoji. Can you see the letters?
examples.ja: このレシートの絵文字、よく見て下さい。🧾文字が見えませんか？

examples.en: Young people in college are good at communicating using emoji.
examples.ja: その大学生の青年は絵文字を使ってコミュニケーションをすることが上手です。

8740.meaning_mnemonic: When you use a <kanji>picture</kanji> to replace your <kanji>letter</kanji>s to type, you're using <vocabulary>emoji</vocabulary>! Those are the faces you send when you text or email.
8740.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: What is the radical of this character?
examples.ja: この字の部首は何ですか？

examples.en: There are many radical names.
examples.ja: 部首の名前はたくさんあります。

examples.en: The radical for the kanji for "cut" is "sword."
examples.ja: 「切」の漢字の部首は「刀」です。

8741.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the <kanji>part</kanji> of your body that makes up your <kanji>neck</kanji>. Are you picturing it? That's a building block that makes up your body. A really important one. If you didn't have that neck, you wouldn't look like a person at all. Sound familiar? It should! Because that part of your neck is a <vocabulary>radical</vocabulary>! Just like part of your neck is a building block of your body, the radical is a building block of kanji. Get it? I sure hope so!
8741.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 首 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

When you need a <vocabulary>radical</vocabulary> to make a new kanji, you just press a button and the radical comes tumbling down the radical <reading>chu</reading>te (しゅ). There's definitely no rhyme or reason to radical picking, it's just whatever pops out of the ol' chute.

examples.ja: 近所の犬が、私の戸口に向かって「ワン！」と大きな声で言うんです。

examples.en: My brother is good and fast at adding.
examples.ja: 私の兄は、足し算が上手で早いです。

examples.en: The answer to this addition is incorrect.
examples.ja: この足し算の答えは正しくありません。

examples.en: There will be a test for additions in the next math class.
examples.ja: 次回の数学のクラスで足し算のテストがあります。

8743.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 足す means "to add?" Add <kanji>calculate</kanji> to that and you'll have <vocabulary>addition</vocabulary>! It's the type of calculation you're doing when you add.
8743.reading_mnemonic: This is the kun'yomi reading for 足 and the on'yomi for 算. And the さん reading is rendaku'd into ざん. This is the same for all the math-ish words (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division), so try to remember that, because you'll see it again!

examples.en: Of course I can do subtraction!
examples.ja: もちろん、わたしは引き算ができます！

examples.en: A subtraction, for example, is "subtracting two from six equals four."
examples.ja: 引き算は、たとえば「六から二を引いて、答えが四」ということです。

examples.en: Although it is a elementary school third grade level subtraction problem, I still can't figure out the answer.
examples.ja: 小学校三年生レベルの引き算なのに、答えがどうしても分からない。

8744.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 引く means "to pull" and "to withdraw"? Well, if you <kanji>calculate</kanji> by pulling or withdrawing one number out of another, you're doing <vocabulary>subtraction</vocabulary>. Kinda like how your bank balance gets lower every time you subtract (withdraw) money from it, you know?
8744.reading_mnemonic: This is the kun'yomi reading for 引 and the on'yomi for 算. And the さん reading is rendaku'd into ざん. This is the same for all the math-ish words (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division), so try to remember that, because you'll see it again!

examples.ja: 学校で生物学のクラスが一番楽しいです。

examples.ja: 川田さんは生物学の学者さんです。

examples.ja: デザイナーになりたいなら、生物学も学んだ方がいい。

8745.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 生物 means "living things?" Well when you <kanji>study</kanji> living things you're studying <vocabulary>biology</vocabulary>.
8745.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Your fingertips are red.

I only had time to get the tip. It used to be on your finger and now it's right here, in my hand. Sorry, I guess. Oh, but don't worry, I'll even things out and get the tip of your toe real quick too.
8746.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings from both kanji, probably because it includes body parts. You know them both already, so now you know this too!

8747.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

The <kanji>lively</kanji> <kanji>move</kanji>s you make are your <vocabulary>activity</vocabulary>.

examples.ja: かわいい！母性本能くすぐられる。

8750.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

8753.reading_mnemonic:

examples.ja: 今日は家庭教師に掛け算を教えてもらいました。

examples.en: I solved 100 multiplication problems today.
examples.ja: 今日は掛け算の問題を100問解いたよ。

examples.en: There’s a multiplication test in cram school tomorrow.
examples.ja: 明日、塾で掛け算のテストがあるんです。

8756.meaning_mnemonic: If you try to <kanji>calculate</kanji> something, but instead you feel the urge to <kanji>hang</kanji> your teacher, you know you're doing <vocabulary>multiplication</vocabulary>. It's hard, guys. Like really hard. The hardest kind of math of them all. But you can do it! No one needs to get hanged. And don't hang your head in defeat either. Multiply those numbers like a boss! Hang the numbers instead!!
8756.reading_mnemonic: This is the kun'yomi reading for 掛 and the on'yomi for 算. And the さん reading is rendaku'd into ざん. This is the same for all the math-ish words (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division), so try to remember that, because you'll see it again!

examples.en: Don't worry! Everyone makes mistakes.
examples.ja: ドンマイ！誰だって間違えることはあるよ。

examples.en: Making a mistake on such a simple question is so frustrating.
examples.ja: こんな簡単な問題を間違えるなんて、悔しいよ。

examples.en: Excuse me, I mistook you for a friend.
examples.ja: すいません、友人と間違えてしまいました。

examples.en: It seems that someone else's child allowance was deposited into my bank by mistake.
examples.ja: 間違えて他人の児童手当が私の銀行に振りこまれていたみたいです。

8757.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 間違い means "a mistake?" Well this is the verb version. It means <vocabulary>to make a mistake</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to mistake</vocabulary>.

This verb is transitive. That means that it takes a direct object. Bear in mind that this one is a bit tricky, though, because although it's transitive in Japanese, the English translation will sometimes be intransitive.
8757.reading_mnemonic: It's read the same as 間違い! Nice and easy!

examples.en: I'm gonna go move my car.
examples.ja: ちょっと車を移動してくるよ。

examples.en: That person is giving off a bad vibe. Do you want to move places?
examples.ja: なんか嫌な感じだね。場所、移動する？

examples.en: We have to transfer Prince Koichi to a safe place.
examples.ja: コウイチ王子を安全な場所へ移動させなくてはいけません。

examples.en: You get worn out when you migrate long-distance by bus.
examples.ja: バスで長距離の移動は疲れる。

8758.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Since searching becomes difficult at night, we plan to temporarily pause and then resume in the early morning.
examples.ja: 夜になると捜索が難しくなるため、いったんストップして早朝から再開する予定です。

examples.en: Recently, drones have been used more frequently for search operations in the mountains.
examples.ja: 最近は、山の中の捜索には、ドローンが使用されることが多くなってきました。

examples.en: The police are continuing their investigation for the missing person.
examples.ja: 警察は行方不明者の捜索活動を続けています。

examples.en: I heard that Kondo-san's daughter hasn't come home for three days, and they've filed a missing person report with the police.
examples.ja: 近藤さんのところの娘さん、もう三日も帰ってきてなくて、警察に捜索願を出したんだって。

8759.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>search</kanji> <kanji>search</kanji> is a more intense <vocabulary>search</vocabulary>, like the official <vocabulary>investigation</vocabulary> for a missing person.

捜索 is a formal term often used by authorities or in news reports. It refers to an official search for a missing person or thing, and is commonly used in police investigations, rescue missions, or other organized searches.
8759.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I lost a button from my suit.
examples.ja: 背広のボタンをなくした。

examples.en: I always send my suit to the cleaners.
examples.ja: 背広はいつもクリーニングに出します。

examples.en: I'm wearing my new business suit today because I have an important meeting.
examples.ja: 今日は重要な会議があるので、新しい背広を着ていきます。

examples.en: I had a new business suit tailored for the upcoming formal marriage interview.
examples.ja: 今度のお見合いのために新しく背広を新調しました。

8760.meaning_mnemonic: If your <kanji>back</kanji> is <kanji>wide</kanji>, you need a nice <vocabulary>business suit</vocabulary> to cover it up when you go to work. Otherwise you'll look completely out of place sitting at a desk like a giant, wide-backed wrestler. Is that what you want to look like? Of course not! You need to go out and buy a fancy suit to cover your wide back up right now!
8760.reading_mnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned them both already so you should be able to read this too! Just watch out for the weird rendaku here making it び not ひ.

8761.meaning_mnemonic: This is a <radical>stick</radical>, sticking straight up. It even looks like a stick.

8762.meaning_mnemonic: This looks a lot like a <radical>gun</radical> pointing to the right. You have a handle on the left, and the barrel pointing to the right. Imagine it hanging in a case on the wall in a museum.

8763.meaning_mnemonic: There's a leaf on top and a stem going down out of it, making this the <radical>leaf</radical> radical. It's a pretty wide and flat leaf, so if it helps you can imagine it as a lily pad leaf.

8764.meaning_mnemonic: Do you know those rice paddy hats? The ones shaped just like this radical? That's why this radical is a <radical>hat</radical>.

8765.meaning_mnemonic: The three horns represent the <radical>triceratops</radical>, one of the most awesome dinosaurs ever.

8767.meaning_mnemonic: Can you see the <radical>horns</radical>? You could put these horns on anything. Donkeys, people, monkeys, and so on. That's exactly what we'll be doing when we learn kanji that have horns too.

8768.meaning_mnemonic: On the ground there are a bunch of <radical>spikes</radical> coming out. You wouldn't want to step on those now, would you?

8769.meaning_mnemonic: On the top part of the head (冂) radical, there is a horn radical with one extra spike in the middle. This is a horned helmet with one extra spike. Who were famous for having horned helmets like that? The Vikings! That's why this radical is called <radical>Viking</radical>.

8772.meaning_mnemonic: There's the bottom of a shoe with spikes coming out of it. Only one kind of shoe is like this, and that's a <radical>cleat</radical>. You know, like those studded shoes athletes wear. Soccer cleats, baseball cleats, running cleats… You knew they were called cleats, right?

8774.meaning_mnemonic: This is the <radical>Chinese</radical> radical. Why? Because it looks like a traditional Chinese pagoda! One of those towers with a bunch of tiered roofs, you know? Sure, lots of Asian countries have pagodas, but let's be honest — the Chinese probably came up with them first.

8775.meaning_mnemonic: You have the radical twenty and the kanji one. Put those together and you get 21. What's another name for 21? That's <radical>blackjack</radical>.

8776.meaning_mnemonic: There's a lid on top of something you're trying to keep private. It's your <radical>trash</radical>. You wouldn't want people going through your private trash, which is why we put lids on our trash cans. It's also illegal to look through someone's trash, so make sure you never do that.

8777.meaning_mnemonic: This is the radical for <radical>bear</radical>, because it looks like the letter B — B for bear! You know this one is "bear" and not "building" because it's all boxy, like a stocky, chunky bear who's all fat and ready to hibernate.

8779.meaning_mnemonic: This is the <radical>spring</radical> radical, because it looks like a new plant shoot has pushed its way up through layers of dirt, snow, and ice to announce the coming of spring. Spring is the season (and the radical) full of new, growing life!

8780.meaning_mnemonic: This is a <radical>cape</radical>, like the kind a superhero would wear. Use your imagination to picture a hero facing left, with a cape tied around their neck and hanging down their back. With that cape on, they're ready to save the world!

8782.meaning_mnemonic: There are two drunkards here. That makes this radical a <radical>bar</radical>. Where else are you gonna drink?

8783.meaning_mnemonic: Don't confuse this with triceratops. <radical>Grass</radical> is closer together, and a little bushier, like this. It's also more random and squished down in parts. If you see a bush of lines like this, it's probably going to be grass.

8784.meaning_mnemonic: This radical has a figure reaching out both hands at you with some dirt on his head. This is a <radical>zombie</radical>, and he must have just recently dug himself out of the grave by the looks of it.

8785.meaning_mnemonic: See the <radical>squid</radical> shape here? There's its pointy head, its eyes, and its tentacles (two, anyway). Pretty squid-like if you ask me!

8793.meaning_mnemonic: This is the left side of the kanji 朝, so we'll call it <radical>morning</radical> too.

8794.meaning_mnemonic: In the water is a barb on the ground. It's <radical>coral</radical>. Coral may look pretty, but if you slip in the water and step on it, you're gonna get scratched up. That stuff is roooough.

examples.en: There were many amulets at the entrance of the village.
examples.ja: 村の入り口にお札がたくさんありました。

examples.en: You should be careful not to show your hand.
examples.ja: 自分の札を見せないようにした方がいいよ。

examples.en: I didn't knock because the vacant room tag was hung.
examples.ja: 空室の札がかかってたので、ノックしなかったんです。

8800.meaning_mnemonic: This word is almost the same as the kanji, but only half of it. It means <vocabulary>tag</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>amulet</vocabulary>. They're about the same shape and size as money, but you can't buy a house with them (...probably).
8800.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word:

You can't find your <vocabulary>tag</vocabulary> anywhere. It was just there, you swear, but now it's nowhere to be found. You search for it everywhere, then you realize... it was right there all along. Seriously? You're such a <reading>foo</reading>l, <reading>duh</reading> (ふだ)!

examples.en: From now on, please email this address.
examples.ja: 以後は、このアドレスにメールして下さい。

examples.en: I'll be careful after this.
examples.ja: 以後、気をつけます。

examples.en: After April 8th, you have to go to school.
examples.ja: 四月八日以後は、学校に行かなければいけません。

8801.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>From</kanji> <kanji>after</kanji>, just means <vocabulary>after this</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>from now on</vocabulary>.
8801.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Excuse me. I don't know how to use this coupon.
examples.ja: すみません。このクーポンの使用の仕方が分からないんです。

examples.en: Do you know how much water is used in a pool?
examples.ja: プールにどれくらいの水を使用か知ってますか？

examples.en: We use new biology technology that utilizes insects.
examples.ja: 虫を利用した新しい生物学テクノロジーを使用しています。

8802.meaning_mnemonic:
Something you <kanji>use</kanji> that has a <kanji>use</kanji> has... well, <vocabulary>use</vocabulary>. You can even use it for practical <vocabulary>application</vocabulary>s.

使用 has a slightly more formal tone compared to 使う, and it’s preferred in situations that require a more precise and less casual choice of words.
8802.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Please take a numbered ticket and wait your turn.
examples.ja: 番号札をとって、お待ちください。

examples.en: Sorry, wasn't there a numbered ticket around here?
examples.ja: すみません、この辺りに番号札はありませんでしたか？

examples.en: I lost the numbered ticket for my suitcase.
examples.ja: スーツケースの番号札を失ってしまった。

examples.en: Let's get a numbered ticket at the shaved ice shop, then go grab some tea while waiting.
examples.ja: かき氷屋さんで番号札をもらって、待っている間にお茶でもしましょう。

8803.meaning_mnemonic: You know 番号 means "number" so add a <kanji>tag</kanji> to it and you have a <vocabulary>numbered tag</vocabulary>.
8803.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word (番号) with a single-word kanji added. That means you have two on'yomi readings from the jukugo word and the kun'yomi reading from the single kanji (ふだ). Put them all together and you have the reading of this kanji!

examples.en: Our boss's painting won the special prize at the contest!
examples.ja: 親分の絵が、コンクールで特選に入賞したぞ！

examples.en: Tonight's dinner is premium Japanese beef shabu-shabu.
examples.ja: 今日のディナーは特選和牛のシャブシャブです。

examples.en: I received a gift of premium rice from the company president.
examples.ja: 社長から特選米をプレゼントしていただきました。

8804.meaning_mnemonic: If something is <kanji>special</kanji> you <kanji>choose</kanji> it. That makes it a <vocabulary>special selection</vocabulary> of yours and it gets a <vocabulary>special prize</vocabulary> that only you could give!
8804.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: This carrot soup is delicious!
examples.ja: この人参スープ、おいしい！

examples.en: I gifted some carrot liqueur to the King who loves alcohol.
examples.ja: 酒好きの王様に、人参リキュールをプレゼントした。

examples.en: I can eat anything, but carrots are the only thing I can't handle.
examples.ja: 何でも食べれるけど、人参だけはムリです。

8805.meaning_mnemonic: What do you use to get a <kanji>person</kanji> to <kanji>participate</kanji> in something? A <vocabulary>carrot</vocabulary>, of course. You've heard of "the carrot and the stick," right? So next time you want a person to participate, offer them a carrot.
8805.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 参 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You're craving a <vocabulary>carrot</vocabulary>, but you can't seem to find any. You look in your fridge, in your garden, and even in the trash. Finally you give up your carrot search and sit down when... ouch! The carrot was in your <reading>jean</reading>s (じん) the whole time!

examples.en: I'm looking for a tag to put on my suitcase.
examples.ja: 旅行カバンに付ける荷札をさがしています。

examples.en: Please tell me how to write a package label.
examples.ja: 荷札の書き方を教えてください。

examples.en: The label is coming off from the parcel.
examples.ja: そのパッケージ、荷札がはがれてるよ。

8806.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>luggage</kanji> <kanji>tag</kanji> is a <vocabulary>tag</vocabulary> you put on luggage. It's also a <vocabulary>label</vocabulary> you can put on a package before you send it, like a <vocabulary>shipping label</vocabulary>.
8806.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi reading for both kanji. You've learned both of these readings already, so you should be able to read this word too.

examples.en: There are almost no goods in the grocery store around this time.
examples.ja: この時間のスーパーには品物がほとんどありません。

examples.en: The store's showcases were filled with many items.
examples.ja: そのお店のショーケースにはたくさんの品物がならんでいました。

examples.en: Sorry, this item has already been reserved.
examples.ja: すいません、こちらの品物はすでにご予約をいただいている物なんです。

8807.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>product</kanji> <kanji>thing</kanji> is any type of general <vocabulary>goods</vocabulary>. It's about as specific as you can get when you're talking about <vocabulary>thing</vocabulary>s like this.
8807.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the kun'yomi readings of the kanji. You've seen those readings before, but the one for 品 (しな) is a little tricky, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember:

Think of the <reading>sheen</reading> (しな) that new <vocabulary>goods</vocabulary> have before you buy them. When you bring them home, that sheen is already gone. But then you go back to the store and, wow! All the goods you don't already own have that sheen! Gotta buy them!

examples.en: This item doesn't have a price tag.
examples.ja: この品物には、値札シールがありません。

examples.en: After checking the price tag, I decided not to buy it.
examples.ja: 値札を確かめた後に、買うのを止めました。

examples.en: The king always buys stuff without looking at the price tags and the queen gets angry at him.
examples.ja: 王様は、いつも値札を見ずに買い物をして、女王様に怒られます。

8808.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You learned the kun'yomi reading for 値 in the vocabulary word 値 (ね). You learned the reading for 札 in the vocabulary 札 (ふだ). Put them together and you have ねふだ.

examples.en: There are many excellent engineers in Japan who are recognized worldwide.
examples.ja: 日本には世界に通用する優れた技術者がたくさんいます。

examples.en: In what ways would you say that WaniKani surpasses other kanji learning materials?
examples.ja: ワニカニはどういう点で他の漢字学習教材より優れていると言えますか？

examples.en: Tofugu surpasses the other Japanese learning materials in terms of uniqueness.
examples.ja: トーフグはユニークさにおいて、他の日本語学習教材より優れています。

examples.en: This movie is an excellent work that beautifully elevates the theme of the original work.
examples.ja: この映画は、原作のテーマを見事に昇華した非常に優れた作品となっている。

8809.meaning_mnemonic:
This is the verb version of the kanji <kanji>superior</kanji>, so it means <vocabulary>to surpass</vocabulary>. Someone who is superior is always going to surpass and <vocabulary>to excel</vocabulary> beyond others. That's what makes them so superior in the first place!

This is a formal word that is often used in writing or formal speech.
8809.reading_mnemonic: If you want to surpass everyone, you have to be super good (すぐ) at stuff. Like, super good at everything. Not pretty good, not really good — super good. Only then can you surpass all the others.

examples.en: The answer will be next week or after.
examples.ja: 返事は来週以降になります。

examples.en: Could you call us again on or after August third?
examples.ja: 八月三日以降にもう一度ご連絡していただけますか？

examples.en: My dad forbids me from going out after 9 p.m.
examples.ja: 夜九時以降の外出は父に禁止されているんです。

8810.meaning_mnemonic: Everything that happened <kanji>since</kanji> you <kanji>descend</kanji>ed some stairs, is <vocabulary>hereafter</vocabulary>. It's all <vocabulary>after</vocabulary> the stairs thing you did, <vocabulary>since</vocabulary> you did it already.
8810.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Why did you put the talisman here?
examples.ja: どうしてここに御札をはっているんですか？

examples.en: This is an amulet that I got from the shrine in my hometown.
examples.ja: これは、地元の神社でもらった御札です。

examples.en: Are there talismans in English-speaking countries, too?
examples.ja: 英語圏の国にも、御札ってあるんですか？

8811.meaning_mnemonic: You learned another vocabulary word 札 as "amulet," but this is a special <kanji>honorable</kanji> <vocabulary>amulet</vocabulary>. It's a <vocabulary>talisman</vocabulary>.
8811.reading_mnemonic: The reading for the 御 is お because ふだ uses the kun'yomi reading. Kun'yomi + kun'yomi = yes.

examples.en: When I buy curry, I always buy the spicy kind.
examples.ja: カレーはいつも辛口を買います。

examples.en: Asahi Super Dry is a dry beer that has a sharp, crisp feeling when it goes down your throat.
examples.ja: アサヒスーパードライはシャープなのどごしの辛口ビールです。

examples.en: Everyone gave harsh opinions, but I am actually a big fan of this drama.
examples.ja: みんなは辛口コメントだったけど、私はこのドラマの大ファンです。

8812.meaning_mnemonic: If you put something <kanji>spicy</kanji> in your <kanji>mouth</kanji> you'll end up with a <vocabulary>spicy taste</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>dry taste</vocabulary> in there. Spice sucks up all your mouth moistness.
8812.reading_mnemonic: This is the kun'yomi readings together. You should have learned them both by now.

examples.en: I washed my sweater in hot water and it shrunk.
examples.ja: セーターをお湯で洗濯したら縮んでしまった。

examples.en: I married him because he said he likes doing laundry, but he still hasn't even done it once.
examples.ja: 洗濯が好きだと言っていたから結婚したのに、今まで一度も洗濯をしてくれたことがありません。

examples.en: "Is my white shirt in the wash?" "Oh, that one had lipstick on it, so I took it to the cleaners."
examples.ja: 「俺のワイシャツ、今洗濯してる？」「ああ、それなら口紅が付いていたので洗濯屋さんに出しておいたわよ。」

8813.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Wash</kanji> <kanji>wash</kanji> <vocabulary>to wash</vocabulary> your clothes. You wash wash your laundry. Hmm wash wash sounds like the sound my laundry machine makes when it's washing my underpants.
8813.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: My father is a professional pitcher.
examples.ja: 父は、プロの投手です。

examples.en: Ohtani is a master pitcher and hitter.
examples.ja: 大谷氏は投手の名人でありバッターの名人でもあります。

examples.en: The pitcher on the Mexican team is very strong.
examples.ja: メキシコのチームの投手はとても強いです。

8814.meaning_mnemonic: You already know that 手 means "hand," but it can also mean "doer," as in someone who performs a particular action or task. Why? Because we use our hands to do things. And when it comes to <kanji>throw</kanji>ing, the <kanji>doer</kanji> is the <vocabulary>pitcher</vocabulary>!
8814.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 手 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

To be a good <vocabulary>pitcher</vocabulary>, all you have to do is put the ball into the <reading>chute</reading> (しゅ). Pitchers don't actually throw the ball. There is an invisible pitching chute right on the mound. You slide the ball into the chute and off it goes!

examples.en: Have you read the pitcher's life story?
examples.ja: あの投手の伝記、読んだ？

examples.en: The stuff that was written in the writer's biography was very surprising.
examples.ja: その作家の伝記に書かれていたことは、とても意外だった。

examples.en: Well, I think I might feel like this because I was influenced by a biography I read recently.
examples.ja: まあ、そう思うのは、最近読んだ伝記の影響かもしれません。

8815.meaning_mnemonic: If you want to <kanji>transmit</kanji> the story of someone's life, you have to <kanji>write down</kanji> all of it in a <vocabulary>biography</vocabulary>.
8815.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Today is a national holiday, so the coffee shop I usually go to was closed.
examples.ja: 今日は祭日だからいつものカフェがお休みだったよ。

examples.en: Do you have to work even though it's a national holiday?
examples.ja: 祭日なのに、仕事なの？

examples.en: I forgot it was a holiday and I came to the office.
examples.ja: 祭日だってことを忘れていて、会社に来てしまった。

8816.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>festival</kanji> <kanji>day</kanji> is obviously a <vocabulary>festival day</vocabulary>. This word technically refers to days for Shinto festivals or rituals, but sometimes people also use it to mean a general <vocabulary>national holiday</vocabulary>. This is because some of the Japanese national holidays are based on those traditional Shinto festival days!
8816.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: That office worker always got tasks done steadily.
examples.ja: その会社員は、いつも着々と仕事をこなしていた。

examples.en: It seems like you're making steady progress on the project.
examples.ja: プロジェクトは着々進んでいるようだね。

examples.en: The project is steadily progressing and is expected to be completed at the end of March.
examples.ja: そのプロジェクトは着々と進行しており、予定通りに三月末に完了する見込みです。

8817.meaning_mnemonic: Something you <kanji>wear</kanji>, and <kanji>wear</kanji> again, is something you <vocabulary>steadily</vocabulary> wear. You do it so often, it's reliable. Also, if you wear something this much it's steadily wearing away too.
8817.reading_mnemonic: This word uses on'yomi readings of the kanji you learned, twice. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Wasn't the school trip scheduled for next week?
examples.ja: 遠足って来週だったよね？

examples.en: My kid just got back from the school trip a little while ago. Seems like they had a blast!
examples.ja: うちの子、さっき遠足から帰ってきたよ。めっちゃ楽しかったみたい！

examples.en: We went on a school trip to the zoo.
examples.ja: 学校の遠足で、動物園に行きました。

8818.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Far</kanji> <kanji>feet</kanji> are feet that have gone on long <vocabulary>excursions</vocabulary>. These feet have been on some <vocabulary>trip</vocabulary>s, man. They've seen some things.
8818.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

8819.meaning_mnemonic:
Someone shoved horns onto your husband and said he has to fight for them now. They turned him into a <radical>gladiator</radical>! Now your husband has to fight for their amusement. Are you not entertained?!

P.S. You know this is a gladiator, not a viking, because the horns are on the gladiator's shoulder pads instead of his helmet, and his helmet has a big crest on it.

8820.meaning_mnemonic: A drop of water will last for an <radical>eternity</radical>. Especially if you drop it into an endless stream that never stops flowing. You can see these streams converging from all directions here, flowing for eternity.

8821.meaning_mnemonic: Oh no, you let the pope's hat get snatched by a lion! You get it back, but it's all crooked, so you've got to make it <radical>straight</radical> again. The pope needs a straight, dignified hat, so you'd better straighten that thing out.

8822.meaning_mnemonic:
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>good</radical>.

Just in case you don't remember this, here's the kanji meaning mnemonic: A <radical>drop</radical> of water to a <radical>root</radical> is <kanji>good</kanji>. It's good for the roots to grow and live and thrive. And what's good for roots is good for our plants and us humans too.

8823.meaning_mnemonic: This is an <radical>elephant</radical> — or at least, a wannabe elephant. Look closely. It's actually a family of pigs, and the mama is wearing an elephant mask on her head for some reason. See the big ears and trunk on top? She wants to be an elephant so badly that she dressed up like one.

8824.meaning_mnemonic: A creeper in a rice paddy? That's just a <radical>scarecrow</radical>!

8825.meaning_mnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>festival</radical>.

8826.meaning_mnemonic: This ice is in the shape of a stick. It's an <radical>icicle</radical>!

8827.meaning_mnemonic: You put your hat on the ground and a flag in your mouth. You're letting the world know that they can use your mouth as a <radical>warehouse</radical>. Your gullet is open for storage business. Need to store some ice cream? Please use my mouth warehouse. ;D ;D ;D

8828.meaning_mnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>chapter</radical>.

8829.meaning_mnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>guy</radical>.

8830.meaning_mnemonic: The products trees make? That's <radical>syrup</radical>. Delicious maple syrup, for example. Mmmm!

8831.meaning_mnemonic: Who wears cleats and takes your measurements for so long that icicles start forming on your body? Your <radical>commander</radical>. The commander is very, very particular. And everyone knows the commander has to get everything exactly right. So taking your measurements takes SO long that icicles grow out of your nose. But that's okay. You have to impress your new commander, darn it!

8832.meaning_mnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>doubt</radical>.

8833.meaning_mnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>rejoice</radical>.

8834.meaning_mnemonic: You're stuck in <radical>prison</radical> with nothing but a <radical>spoon</radical>, and the <kanji>smell</kanji> in here is so bad you’re using the prison spoon to waft it outside as best you can.
8834.reading_mnemonic: You can’t believe how awful these <kanji>smell</kanji>s are. You’re new in prison, so you call them all <reading>neo</reading>-smells (にお). They're neo, they're new to you.

8835.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> is <radical>rejoic</radical>ing. She must be <kanji>glad</kanji> and <kanji>happy</kanji> to rejoice out loud in front of you like this.
8835.reading_mnemonic: "I'm so <kanji>glad</kanji>!" the woman shouts, "Because I found the <reading>key</reading> (き)!" You immediately start to wonder what "the key" is. The key to life? The key to learning Japanese? Then you see she's holding up some car keys.

8836.meaning_mnemonic: Open your <radical>mouth</radical>. A <radical>tiger</radical> fell in there on some <radical>spikes</radical>! That's what you tell everybody, but when they look in your mouth there's nothing there. It's all a big <kanji>lie</kanji>!
8836.reading_mnemonic: <kanji>Lie</kanji> about spikes in your mouth and I'll put soap with spikes in it in your mouth to teach you a lesson. That's why I'm using <reading>u</reading>ni <reading>so</reading>ap (うそ).

8837.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>skewer</radical> radical and the <kanji>skewer</kanji> kanji are exactly the same!
8837.reading_mnemonic: Uh oh, this <kanji>skewer</kanji> is really... <reading>cushy</reading> (くし). It's so soft and cushy you can't get any meat or vegetables onto it.

8838.meaning_mnemonic: Into your <radical>mouth</radical> the <radical>leader</radical> shot an <radical>arrow</radical> with an attached <radical>hook</radical> so that they'd be able to see into your <kanji>throat</kanji>.
8838.reading_mnemonic: From your <kanji>throat</kanji> you hear a voice. Not yours, but one you recognize. It's <reading>こう</reading>いち! What's that rascal doing down in your throat?

8839.meaning_mnemonic: On your <radical>mouth</radical> is a <radical>stamp</radical> that you <kanji>tap</kanji>, <kanji>strike</kanji> and <kanji>slap</kanji> to create a beat! The stamp looks like a little drum, but you're really just hitting your mouth for fun (the stamp was an excuse to make it seem normal).
8839.reading_mnemonic: When you <kanji>tap</kanji> and <kanji>strike</kanji> the stamp on your mouth, you make a <reading>ta-ta</reading> (たた) sound. Imagine yourself making a beat with the little stamp drum on your mouth. Now listen... たた! There! Did you hear it?

8840.reading_mnemonic: This <kanji>candy</kanji> in particular is just drops of hardened, clear sugar that looks like <reading>雨</reading> (あめ) drops.

examples.en: Do you like the smell of leather jackets, senpai?
examples.ja: 先輩、革ジャンの匂いは好きですか？

examples.en: That hot spring smells like banana.
examples.ja: その温泉は、バナナの匂いがする。

examples.en: The odor of this bathroom is so strong that I don't want to breathe through my nose.
examples.ja: このトイレは匂いが強すぎて、鼻で息をしたくない。

8841.meaning_mnemonic:
This the noun version of the kanji for <kanji>smell</kanji>. It also means <vocabulary>smell</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>scent</vocabulary>!

Although 匂う often implies something smells unpleasant, 匂い is more neutral and can refer to any kind of smell.
8841.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with the kanji, so you should be able to read it already!

examples.en: This perfume doesn't smell at all.
examples.ja: この香水は、全く匂わない。

examples.en: Ugh, something smells in this room!
examples.ja: げ、なんかこの部屋、匂う！

examples.en: Hmm, something smells. It smells like a case, Watson!
examples.ja: フーム、匂いますねー。事件の匂いがしますよ、ワトソン君！

8842.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>smell</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to smell</vocabulary>.

Although 匂う is technically a neutral term, it often means <vocabulary>to smell bad</vocabulary>. To emphasize the stinkiness, you can also use the kanji 臭 instead of 匂.
8842.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with the kanji, so you should be able to read it already!

examples.en: As soon as they get pregnant, they will happily let us know.
examples.ja: 子供ができればすぐ、嬉々として報告してくれるだろう。

examples.en: My father saw his old friend for the first time in a long time and they happily caught up with each other.
examples.ja: 父は、久しぶりに旧友に会い、嬉々として近況を語り合った。

examples.en: Koichi returned safely and the village was filled with joyful voices.
examples.ja: コウイチが無事に帰ってきて、村には嬉々たる声が響いた。

8843.meaning_mnemonic:
You're so <kanji>glad</kanji>, you get <kanji>glad</kanji> again. No matter what you're doing, it's undoubtedly in a <vocabulary>state of enjoyment</vocabulary>.

嬉々 itself refers to a <vocabulary>joyful state</vocabulary> where someone happily does something. It's generally used as the adverb 嬉々として, which means “happily” or “gladly.” While less common, it can also serve as an adjective when combined with たる.
8843.reading_mnemonic: This word uses on'yomi readings of the kanji you learned... twice! You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: You look happy today, for some reason.
examples.ja: 今日は何だか嬉しそうですね。

examples.en: When you were born one hundred years ago today, I was happy. Happy birthday.
examples.ja: 百年前の今日、あなたが生まれてくれて嬉しかった。お誕生日おめでとう。

examples.en: Nothing happy has happened to me lately.
examples.ja: 最近、嬉しいことが全然ない。

8844.meaning_mnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of <kanji>glad</kanji>? It's also <vocabulary>glad</vocabulary>!
8844.reading_mnemonic: Whenever you're really <vocabulary>glad</vocabulary> to be alive, you look up at the sun's rays and sing, "<reading>Ooh, ray</reading>s (うれ), I'm so glad you're here!" Then your Uncle Ray comes dancing into the room and sings back, "Ooh, Ray is <vocabulary>happy</vocabulary> you're happy!" The sun's rays and Uncle Ray both make you really happy.

examples.en: It's not true, is it?
examples.ja: 嘘ですよね？

examples.en: My motto is, "I will not tell a lie."
examples.ja: 「嘘をつかない」は私のモットーです。

examples.en: Saying you won 100 million yen in the lottery sounds like a lie, I can't believe that!
examples.ja: 宝くじで1億円当たったなんて、嘘の話みたいで信じられない！

8845.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. A <kanji>lie</kanji> is a <vocabulary>lie</vocabulary>!
8845.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You learned with reading with the kanji, so you should be able to read it already!

examples.en: Usopp is a liar.
examples.ja: ウソップは嘘吐きだ。

examples.en: Apparently, Fuguko has a boyfriend who is a complete liar and they fight quite often.
examples.ja: フグ子ちゃん、大嘘つきの彼氏がいて、よくケンカするんだって。

examples.en: In that era, all liars were to be burned.
examples.ja: その時代、嘘吐きは全員燃やされていた。

8846.meaning_mnemonic: If <kanji>lies</kanji> puke (吐く) out of your mouth, you're a <vocabulary>liar</vocabulary>.
8846.reading_mnemonic:
This is a combination of the kun'yomi readings, one of which you haven't seen yet. You'll usually see this word without the 吐 kanji, as in 嘘つき, but for now let's learn its kanji reading! 

You can't just tell one <vocabulary>lie</vocabulary>, it always turns into <reading>two</reading> (つ). Kind of like a chip or pretzel, you can't just have one. With lies, you have to open your mouth for two more. And then two more.... and... well you get it.

examples.en: We need about a hundred skewers for the BBQ that's coming up.
examples.ja: 今度のBBQには100本くらい串が必要です。

examples.en: Could you skewer the meat and potatoes?
examples.ja: 肉とジャガイモに串を刺してくれませんか？

examples.en: Yakitori is chicken spitted on skewers.
examples.ja: 焼き鳥とは、串に刺さった鶏肉のことです。

8847.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same.
8847.reading_mnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with the kanji, so you should be able to read it already!

examples.en: Lately, I've been into grilled kale skewers.
examples.ja: 最近、ケールの串焼きにはまっています。

examples.en: I had dinner at a grilled skewer place Friday night.
examples.ja: 金曜日の夜は、串焼き屋さんで夕飯を食べました。

examples.en: Our parakeet's catchphrase is, "Don't turn me into grilled skewers!"
examples.ja: うちのインコは「串焼きにしないで！」が口癖です。

8848.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Skewer</kanji>s you grill (焼く) turn into <vocabulary>grilled skewers</vocabulary>.
8848.reading_mnemonic: This is a combination of the kun'yomi readings you already learned. You should be able to read it already!

examples.en: Cats purr with their throats.
examples.ja: 猫は、喉でゴロゴロという音を出します。

examples.en: My throat feels irritated.
examples.ja: なんか喉がイガイガする。

examples.en: I have a sore throat. Can you sing on my behalf?
examples.ja: 喉が痛いので、私の代わりに歌ってくれませんか？

8849.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
8849.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji (and is a body part) it uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Remember the mnemonic from when you first learned this kanji? Well こういち is still in your <kanji>throat</kanji> and he doesn't want to get out. In fact, every time you tug on him, he shouts, "<reading>No Do</reading>- (のど)" but you gag and can't hear the rest. People around you think you're saying "No Do-" but it's really just the weirdo living in your throat now. What a pain...

examples.en: Do you happen to have a throat lozenge?
examples.ja: 喉飴持ってない？

examples.en: Today, I will take water and lozenges to cure my cold, and then take it easy for the rest of the day.
examples.ja: 今日はカゼを治すために、水分とって喉飴なめて、一日ゆっくりします。

examples.en: Don't you think cough drops taste like the science room?
examples.ja: 喉飴って理科室みたいな味がすると思わない？

8850.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Throat</kanji> <kanji>candy</kanji> is the kind of candy that should make your throat feel better. That's right, it's a <vocabulary>cough drop</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>throat lozenge</vocabulary>. Don't just eat regular candy when your throat hurts! Use the right kind.
8850.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You've learned them both already, so you should be able to read this already!

examples.en: That man is an otolaryngologist.
examples.ja: あの方は耳鼻喉頭科の先生です。

examples.en: Laryngeal cancer is often caused by alcohol and tobacco.
examples.ja: 喉頭ガンは酒やタバコが原因で起こることが多い。

examples.en: He underwent laryngeal surgery, but lost his voice and was given an artificial larynx.
examples.ja: 彼は喉頭手術を受けましたが、声を失い、人工喉頭となりました。

8851.meaning_mnemonic: The body part that lives between your <kanji>throat</kanji> and your <kanji>head</kanji> is your <vocabulary>larynx</vocabulary>. Otherwise known as the <vocabulary>voice box</vocabulary>, because your vocal cords live in there.
8851.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You learned 頭's on'yomi reading with 頭部, but here's a mnemonic in case you forgot:

If you really want to get a <vocabulary>larynx</vocabulary> workout, go to <reading>とう</reading>きょう. It's loud, it's crowded, and you have to yell the entire time to get people to hear what you have to say. You also know 18 levels of kanji and you really want to shout them all out, which makes your <vocabulary>voice box</vocabulary> tired (but makes you happy).

examples.en: He plays the drums well.
examples.ja: 彼はドラムを叩くのが上手い。

examples.en: I told you to knock on the door before opening it, didn't I?!
examples.ja: 開ける前に、ドアを叩いてって言ったよね！？

examples.en: I'm not particularly fond of Japanese manzai comedy, where they hit people on the head to deliver punchlines. Wasn't it taught in school that you shouldn't hit others?
examples.ja: 日本のマンザイは、人の頭を叩いてツッコムのであまり好きではありません。人のことを叩いちゃいけないって学校で習わなかったのかな？

8852.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>tap</kanji> or <kanji>strike</kanji>, and the verb version is <vocabulary>to strike</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to tap</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to hit</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to knock</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to beat</vocabulary>.

This verb can be used for both things and people, and the English translation will change depending on what it is you're striking. You'll always have some kind of object, though, since this is a transitive verb. So you might tap someone on the shoulder, knock at a door, or beat a drum.
8852.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. Luckily, you already know this reading from when you learned the kanji!

examples.en: "Kowtow" is what is called "dogeza" in Japan.
examples.ja: 叩頭とは、いわゆる日本の土下座のことです。

examples.en: Everyone in the room got to their knees and bowed to the king, pressing their foreheads on the floor.
examples.ja: 部屋の中にいた全員が、王に向かって叩頭した。

examples.en: Apart from Japanese people watching Chinese historical dramas, most Japanese people may not be familiar with the term "kowtow."
examples.ja: 中国の時代劇を見ている日本人以外は、「叩頭」という言葉はほとんど知らないかもしれませんね。

8853.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Tap</kanji> your <kanji>head</kanji> against the floor to show your subservient respect by doing this deep <vocabulary>bow</vocabulary>. This is the most respectful bow you can possibly do.

叩頭 refers to the traditional Chinese custom where individuals kneel and touch their foreheads to the ground as a gesture of deep respect or submission. You may come across the word 叩頭 in literature and drama set in historical China, particularly in imperial settings.
8853.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 叩 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Who's that <vocabulary>bow</vocabulary>ing before you? It's none other than <reading>こう</reading>いち! He's bowing out of deep respect for you finally hitting level 60 on WaniKani. Congrats!

examples.en: Please give me a hard candy.
examples.ja: 飴を一つ下さい。

examples.en: Is it true that there are curry-flavored hard candies in Japan?
examples.ja: 日本にはカレー味の飴があるって本当ですか？

examples.en: Can you go to the pharmacy and get me some lozenges for my throat?
examples.ja: ドラッグストアでノド飴を買ってきてくれませんか？

8854.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. When we talk about this kind of <vocabulary>candy</vocabulary>, it's usually <vocabulary>hard candy</vocabulary> 🍬 or a <vocabulary>lollipop</vocabulary> 🍭 though.
8854.reading_mnemonic: This word is made up of a single kanji, and it uses the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with the kanji, so you should be able to read it already!

examples.en: My father is a master of sugar sculptures.
examples.ja: 私の父は飴細工の名人です。

examples.en: Have you ever made sugar sculptures?
examples.ja: 飴細工作ったことある？

examples.en: Apparently, the sugar goldfish is similar to real goldfish in shape and taste.
examples.ja: その金魚の飴細工は、形も味も本物の金魚にそっくりなんだって。

8855.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Candy</kanji> made into a <kanji>thin</kanji> <kanji>construction</kanji> is a <vocabulary>sugar sculpture</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>candy sculpture</vocabulary>. It's usually a <vocabulary>sugar animal</vocabulary>, but it can be anything, really.
8855.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi reading for the first kanji and the on'yomi readings for the second two. You haven't learned this reading for 工 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You want your <vocabulary>sugar sculptures</vocabulary> to be made into <reading>coo</reading>kies (く)! Cookies are your other favorite snack, so having a cookie that's really just entirely made of sugar is the absolute best.

Also, watch out for the rendaku on 細, it's easy to miss if you're focusing on remembering this new on'yomi reading.

8856.meaning_mnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>wife</radical>.

8857.meaning_mnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>wild</radical>.

8858.meaning_mnemonic: Next to your <radical>mouth</radical> there are <radical>fins</radical> which react to <radical>alcohol</radical>. If you exceed a certain alcohol <radical>measurement</radical>, they start flapping about, which makes you spread <kanji>rumors</kanji> and <kanji>gossip</kanji> uncontrollably.
8858.reading_mnemonic: The flapping fins are making you slur your words, but that doesn't stop you from spreading <kanji>rumors</kanji> and <kanji>gossip</kanji>: "<reading>Ooo</reading> <reading>whassa</reading>t (うわさ) I hear about so and so having an affair?!"

8859.meaning_mnemonic: You have something to <radical>say</radical>, so you <radical>stand</radical> up, throw in the <radical>towel</radical>, and shout: "I <kanji>GIVE UP</kanji>!" The stand radical looks a little weird in this kanji, probably because you're all tired and ready to give up.
8859.reading_mnemonic: What's making you want to <kanji>give up</kanji>? Well, there's <reading>a killer</reading> (あきら) behind you who's threatening to kill you if you don't.

8860.meaning_mnemonic: Use your <radical>fingers</radical> to grab this guy's <radical>foot</radical> and <kanji>catch</kanji> him! Not physically though, you do grab his foot, but you close your eyes, and catch the idea of him in your mind just by touching your fingers to his foot.
8860.reading_mnemonic: As you touch his foot, you <kanji>catch</kanji> a glimpse of the <reading>Torah</reading> (とら) in your mind. Suddenly, you are able to grasp and understand every single thing written in the Torah. You fall to the ground.

8861.meaning_mnemonic: Under the <radical>moon</radical> beneath a <radical>tree</radical> there is a <radical>hat</radical> filled with <radical>water</radical>. You stare down into the water and decide to stick your <kanji>knee</kanji> in it.
8861.reading_mnemonic: Suddenly, in your <kanji>knee</kanji>, you feel <reading>he</reading>at and a <reading>za</reading>p (ひざ)! Your knee is simultaneously burned and electrocuted by the hot water!!

8862.meaning_mnemonic: You're holding a <radical>flag</radical> on a <radical>stick</radical> above your <radical>eye</radical>s to imitate <kanji>eyebrows</kanji>. You can't grow any of your own, but you really love eyebrows, so this was the best you could do.
8862.reading_mnemonic: Underneath your fake <kanji>eyebrows</kanji> are two slabs of <reading>me</reading>at (み). Meat helps hair grow, according to many Internet specialists who also happen to sell meat. You're waiting for this meat to foster eyebrow hair, and when that sweet day comes you won't need these flags.

8863.meaning_mnemonic: If a <radical>tsunami</radical> hits, it's <radical>rain</radical>ing, and you're outside trying to use a <radical>rake</radical>, you're going to be very <kanji>wet</kanji> and <kanji>damp</kanji>.
8863.reading_mnemonic: You can't stand how <kanji>wet</kanji> and <kanji>damp</kanji> you feel in these clothes so you rip them off and rake in the <reading>nu</reading>de (ぬ)!

examples.en: There are rumors that the man named Cyrus is actually a robot.

8866.meaning_mnemonic: When you <kanji>give up</kanji> and just try to enjoy the <kanji>view</kanji>, that's <vocabulary>resignation</vocabulary>. You know things aren't going well, and you know you can't do anything about it now, so you resign yourself to what's to come.

In <vocabulary>resignation</vocabulary>, you throw all of your <reading>ta</reading>ter (てい) tots onto the ground. Look at the tater tots at your feet. Now they're lying scattered there, a symbol of your feelings of resignation.

examples.en: Even if you die, don't give up on learning kanji!
examples.ja: 死んでも漢字の勉強を諦めないで！

examples.ja: コウイチはついにポケモンマスターになる夢を諦めた。

8867.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. 8867.reading_mnemonic:
You hopefully learned this reading with the kanji, but here's a reminder just in case:

Just before you're ready <vocabulary>to give up</vocabulary> on something, you yell, "<reading>AKIRA</reading> (あきら)!". You don't know anyone named Akira, you just saw it in a movie once and it made sense, you know? So now when you've tried really hard on something, but you have to abandon it anyway, you shout AKIRA into the sky. I just did it while trying to write this mnemonic!

examples.en: A glass filled halfway with water can be perceived as "half empty" or "half full," depending on the person.

8868.meaning_mnemonic:

Try to remember the mnemonic from the kanji with this one, because this word isn't used for physically catching things, but for ideas or meanings that you are able <vocabulary>to grasp</vocabulary>, metaphorically speaking.

examples.en: I like eating pizza off my knees.

examples.en: The hair on my kneecap bothers me so much that I can hardly even sleep.

examples.en: While Koichi was sleeping, I drew eyes on his kneecaps.

examples.en: Apparently, this year Apple is going to start developing kneecap recognition.
examples.ja: 今年アップル社は、膝頭認証の開発を始めるらしい。

8870.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>knee</kanji>'s <kanji>head</kanji> is the <vocabulary>kneecap</vocabulary>. It's also called the <vocabulary>patella</vocabulary>, if you want to get fancy and talk about bone names.
8870.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 頭 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You're walking around in your mom's house, minding your own business, when you slam your <vocabulary>kneecap</vocabulary> right into that <reading>ga</reading>rgoyle <reading>she love</reading>s (がしら). It hurts so bad, you can't even think out that phrase and instead you shout out, "GA SHE RA" and fall to the floor, clutching your searing kneecap (which has probably broken in half).

examples.en: I fell off my bike and my kneecap hurts.
examples.ja: 自転車で転んで、膝小僧が痛い。

examples.en: I recently got a tattoo on my right kneecap.
examples.ja: 最近、右の膝小僧にタトゥーを入れたんです。

examples.en: How's your kneecap?
examples.ja: 膝小僧の調子はどうですか？

8871.meaning_mnemonic:
In your <kanji>knee</kanji> there is a <kanji>small</kanji> <kanji>priest</kanji> named <vocabulary>Kneecap</vocabulary>.

This is a really common, cute way of talking about your kneecap. It's usually used by kids and adults alike, and it's more common in spoken Japanese than 膝頭. Kind of like how we use "kneecap" instead of naming the "patella" bone all the time.
8871.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for 膝 and 小, but the on'yomi reading for 僧, which gets rendaku'd from そう to ぞう, so watch out for that! You've learned all these reading before, so you should be able to read this as well.

examples.en: Eyebrow shape varies from person to person.

examples.en: Did you know paying attention to how eyebrows move makes it easier to perceive facial expressions?

You stare at the beautiful brow on your <reading>Ken</reading> (けん) doll, completely mesmerized. You wish your brow looked as perfectly groomed as his... le sigh~

8876.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>wet</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to get wet</vocabulary>.

examples.en: It's been a couple years since I started saying, "I want to lose weight."

examples.en: Most stray dogs in my village are skinny.

8879.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>thin</kanji> <kanji>body</kanji> type is called <vocabulary>lean</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>slim</vocabulary>. These days this is usually used in the context of <vocabulary>slimming</vocabulary> salons and massages you can get that may or may not work.
8879.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've learned them already, so you should be able to read this on your own!

8880.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Sheep</radical> are always looking at the <radical>next</radical> animal, full of <kanji>envy</kanji> and <kanji>jealousy</kanji>.
8880.reading_mnemonic: The reason the sheep feels such <kanji>envy</kanji> and <kanji>jealousy</kanji> is that the next creature is a <reading>cen</reading>taur (せん)! Who wouldn't be jealous of a creature as noble as a centaur?

8881.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>soul</radical> is going <radical>wild</radical> because you're <kanji>confused</kanji>. If you're confused, it's usually because you don't know what's going on or what to do. This makes the soul inside your body go absolutely wild!
8881.reading_mnemonic: Whenever you're <kanji>confused</kanji>, <reading>こう</reading>いち appears to offer you guidance. He's confused a lot, so he knows how to help. And knowledge offered by こういち is the best medicine for confusion.

8882.reading_mnemonic: Your favorite thing to <kanji>push open</kanji> is your own <reading>eye</reading> (あい). You take the arrow into your fingers and gently push each lid open until you can see.

8883.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>fingers</radical> told you that a <radical>flood</radical> last <radical>evening</radical> would <kanji>draw close</kanji>. There was nothing you could do to stop it, it seemed to be <kanji>be imminent</kanji>, coming in the darkness of the evening.
8883.reading_mnemonic: Luckily whenever you sense a flood starting to <kanji>draw close</kanji>, <reading>Satsu</reading>ki (さつ) prepares a raft. Remember Satsuki? Such a talented little girl. I guess floods are common enough that she's learned to make rafts?

8884.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>axe</radical> radical and the <kanji>axe</kanji> kanji are exactly the same, with one minor difference. This kanji is also used as the <kanji>bread loaf counter</kanji>, probably because bread was so big and hard in the past that they had to use axes to slice them.
8884.reading_mnemonic: You imagined being back in time too good and now you're stuck using an <kanji>axe</kanji> to be a <kanji>bread loaf counter</kanji> for the <reading>Kin</reading>g (きん) of England. You aren't sure which king he is or when in time you are, but he's mean and keeps eating all the bread you cut up with your axe.

8885.meaning_mnemonic: A mix of <radical>spirit</radical> and <radical>reason</radical> helped you invent the <kanji>sleeve</kanji>. Your spirit told you your arms were uncomfortable, stuck to your sides under that shirt. Reason told you that maybe, just maybe, if you made holes for your arms something good would come out of it. And that's how sleeves were born!
8885.reading_mnemonic: And without these <kanji>sleeve</kanji>s, your arms would be <reading>so de</reading>ad (そで). They'd be all exposed and defenseless!

8886.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>ice</radical> <radical>wife</radical> is <kanji>amazing</kanji>. She's also <kanji>terrible</kanji>, because she's very cold and has many ice powers, but that's also part of what makes her amazing!
8886.reading_mnemonic: She turns her <kanji>amazing</kanji> gaze onto your <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい) and hits it with an ice beam. Woah! Instead of turning to ice or shattering, it steals her awful powers. Now your saber is amazing and terrible too!

examples.en: I'm jealous of people who can speak Japanese fluently.

Those <reading>ura</reading>nium <reading>Ya</reading>nkees (うらや) are making you more <vocabulary>envious</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>jealous</vocabulary> by the day. They're the new Yankees team that was manufactured in a lab and fed uranium. Their skills are unparalleled because of their metallic strength. Go ahead and feel envious, they'll definitely be #1 this year.

examples.en: Koichi is a man the world envies.

8888.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>envy</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to envy</vocabulary> someone.

Even though they're gross and hulk-ish, they're really good at baseball, so you're jealous of them.

examples.en: Hachi is a target of jealousy in the dog world.

Usually when you get confused it's because you were already <vocabulary>hurried</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>busy</vocabulary>, and things were <vocabulary>hectic</vocabulary>. So this adjective is what causes your confusion.
