You can guess this is an adjective from the い at the end. The meaning for the kanji is <kanji>noisy</kanji>, so the adjective version is also <vocabulary>noisy</vocabulary>.

喧しい is a casual but emphatic way to say someone or something is too noisy. It's often used in Japanese comedy and variety shows, so depending on the situation there can be a playful vibe to it. You can even use it in a figurative way to describe someone who's being overly picky, fussy, or annoying about something particular (they're being "noisy" about insignificant details). Note that in everyday situations, you'll often just see this word written in kana as やかましい.
8925.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn the やかま reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help:

My <vocabulary>noisy</vocabulary> mom has earned the nickname <reading>yak-a-Ma</reading> (やかま). She's always yakking about my life choices. "Yakka yakka yakka," Ma says.

examples.en: Lately, I've been eating cheese that can be split (AKA string cheese) every morning.
examples.ja: 最近は毎朝、裂けるチーズを食べています。

examples.en: Hey, Kenichi. Your jeans are torn at the crotch.
examples.ja: ねえ、ケンイチ君。ジーンズの股が裂けてるよ。

examples.en: I'm so sad that my heart feels like it will burst apart.
examples.ja: 悲しすぎて、心が裂けちゃいそうだよ。

8926.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>split</kanji>, so this verb has to do with something splitting. 

This is an intransitive verb, so this verb means <vocabulary>to be split</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be torn</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to burst apart</vocabulary>.
8926.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 裂く.

examples.en: Your disease will most definitely be cured.
examples.ja: お前の病気は必ず治る。

examples.en: His injuries have healed, but the scars remain.
examples.ja: ケガは治ったが、キズが残った。

examples.en: Do you know the saying "stupidity can never be cured"?
examples.ja: 「バカは一生治らない」っていうことわざ知ってる？

8927.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji 治 means <kanji>cure</kanji>, but this verb refers to the natural process of getting better: <vocabulary>to get better</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to get well</vocabulary>, or simply <vocabulary>to heal</vocabulary>. This is an intransitive verb, meaning that it happens on its own. Nobody cures you, you just get better.
8927.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn this with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

When you get sick, your mom calls every day to ask, "Are you better <reading>now</reading> (なお)?" How about NOW!? How about NOW!? Jeez Mom, just let me rest!

examples.en: Please don't take this with alcohol as its effectiveness will be diminished.
examples.ja: 効果が薄まるので、お酒と一緒には飲まないで下さい。

examples.en: The pink paint, diluted with water, was left on the palette.
examples.ja: 水で薄まったピンクの絵の具がパレットに残っていた。

examples.en: With just one remark, the inherent value of the letter was diminished.
examples.ja: たった一つの発言でせっかくの手紙のありがたみが薄まった。

8928.meaning_mnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>dilute</kanji>, and this is an intransitive verb, as you can guess from the まる ending. So this verb means <vocabulary>to be diluted</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be diminished</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to become weak</vocabulary>.
8928.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

The reading comes from 薄い, so if you know that you'll be able to read this too. If not, here's a mnemonic to help you:

You don't want your drink <vocabulary>to be diluted</vocabulary>, so <reading>you sue</reading> (うす) anyone who dares pour you a weak drink.

examples.en: I moved the toys close to the wall.
examples.ja: オモチャをカベに寄せた。

examples.en: I pulled the car over and parked.
examples.ja: 車をワキに寄せて停めた。

examples.en: All kinds of comments were posted on this podcast episode.
examples.ja: このポッドキャストには色んなコメントが寄せられた。

8929.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

This is a transitive verb. That means it takes a direct object. The kanji itself means <kanji>draw near</kanji>, and the verb version is about making or letting something draw near to something else. That's why it means <vocabulary>to move something close to</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to pull something over</vocabulary>, and also <vocabulary>to contribute something</vocabulary>.
8929.reading_mnemonic: You want <vocabulary>to move something close to</vocabulary> you, but it's out of reach. The solution, of course, is to take out your trusty <reading>yo</reading>-yo (よ) and lasso that thing and pull it closer!

examples.en: This charm has the power to repel misfortune.
examples.ja: このお守りには、災いを退ける力がある。

examples.en: The council dismissed all of the proposals.
examples.ja: 議会は全ての議案を退けた。

examples.en: It's hard for Japan to reject the opinions of the U.S.
examples.ja: 日本にとってアメリカの意見を退けることは難しい。

8930.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. 

The kanji itself means <kanji>retreat</kanji>, and this verb version is when you make something retreat. In other words, it means <vocabulary>to repel something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to dismiss something</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to reject something</vocabulary>.

This is a transitive verb. That means it takes a direct object. You repel something, like bad luck. You reject something, like a proposal.
8930.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You learned this with its intransitive pair verb 退く, but here's a mnemonic just in case:

Remember the re-zoner? Well, <vocabulary>to repel</vocabulary> bad luck, <reading>she, re-zo</reading>ned (しりぞ) the whole place. No bad luck allowed inside the zone.

examples.en: Did the one hundred million yen fit inside the suitcase?
examples.ja: 一億円、そのスーツケースに収まった？

examples.en: It looks like we'll somehow manage to stay within the budget.
examples.ja: なんとか予算内に収まりそうです。

examples.en: After eating the ice cream, my emotions started to settle down.
examples.ja: アイスを食べたら、感情が収まってきたんだよね。

examples.en: I wanted to eat all five large pizzas, but they couldn't be finished within the all-you-can-eat time limit.
examples.ja: 大きいピザを五枚食べ切りたかったが、食べ放題の時間内に収まらなかった。

8931.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

If you <kanji>obtain</kanji> something, you'll want it <vocabulary>to fit inside</vocabulary> your bag. Otherwise how can you take it home? When talking about problems or emotions, this verb can also mean <vocabulary>to settle down</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to be finished</vocabulary> like a dispute settling down or someone’s anger calming down.

Like most verbs with まる as okurigana, this is an intransitive verb. That means it happens by itself, with no emphasis on the person or thing that's making something fit inside, or settle down.
8931.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You don't fit inside your bed anymore. I guess you've grown? Better get out the trusty <reading>o</reading>ld <reading>saw</reading>s (おさ) and chop off your footboard.

examples.en: I rolled a stone.
examples.ja: 石を転がした。

examples.en: Just when I just rolled the dice, the phone rung.
examples.ja: ちょうどサイコロを転がした時、電話が来た。

examples.en: Dung beetles are called “poop rollers” because they roll poop.
examples.ja: Dung beetleは、フンを転がすことから「フンコロガシ」と言います。

8932.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>revolve</kanji>, and the verb version is when you make something revolve. You roll it. That's why this verb is <vocabulary>to roll something</vocabulary>.

This is a transitive verb. That means you roll something else, like a ball. Or, if you're a dung beetle, poop. 💩 Not to be confused with 転がる, which is intransitive, like so many verbs ending in がる.
8932.reading_mnemonic:
You learned this reading when you learned 転がる, but here's a mnemonic anyway just in case:

When you try <vocabulary>to roll something</vocabulary>, the outside bits may be moving, but its <reading>core</reading> (ころ) stays still. Picture yourself making the earth roll across the floor. The outside parts where the people live are spinning round and round, but the earth's core is in exactly the same place.

examples.en: Don't hurt me anymore!
examples.ja: これ以上、私を苦しめないで！

examples.en: The rice shortage is tormenting all citizens of Japan.
examples.ja: 米不足が全日本の国民を苦しめている。

examples.en: Without realizing it, I was harassing the first-graders every day.
examples.ja: 知らないうちに、毎日一年生を苦しめていた。

8933.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. 

The kanji itself means <kanji>suffer</kanji>, and the verb is all about when you make someone else suffer. That's why it's <vocabulary>to hurt someone</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to torment</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to harass</vocabulary>.

You need to differentiate this from 苦しむ, which is about when YOU suffer. You can remember that 苦しめる is about making someone else suffer with this mnemonic: Who made you suffer? <reading>She ma</reading>de (しめ) me suffer! She's so mean!
8933.reading_mnemonic: By now, you've learned 苦しい and 苦しむ. The kanji in these words all use the same reading! Yay!

examples.en: Playing games too much will hurt your eyes.
examples.ja: ゲームのやりすぎは目を痛める。

examples.en: I ran a full marathon in slippers and injured my ankles.
examples.ja: スリッパでフルマラソンをしたら足首を痛めた。

examples.en: That incident is still breaking mom's heart.
examples.ja: 母は今でもそのことで心を痛めている。

8934.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. 

The kanji itself means <kanji>pain</kanji>, and this verb is transitive, so it means to inflict pain. In other words, it's <vocabulary>to injure something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to hurt someone</vocabulary>.

This verb focuses on the pain involved in an injury, so it can only be used for things that feel pain, like people and body parts.
8934.reading_mnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You learned that reading with the word 痛い.

examples.en: Because of construction work, my usual running route has been extended.
examples.ja: 工事のせいでいつものランニングのコースが延びた。

examples.en: The Tokyo Olympics were delayed to the following year, but they might get canceled.
examples.ja: 東京オリンピックは翌年に延びたがキャンセルになるかもしれない。

examples.en: I hate it when meetings are prolonged because of my boss.
examples.ja: 上司のせいで会議が延びるのが嫌いです。

8935.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

This is an intransitive verb, meaning that it happens on its own, and we're not talking about what makes it happen. So this verb means <vocabulary>to be extended</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be delayed</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to be prolonged</vocabulary>. If you know the word ビル, you can think about how building work is always prolonged or delayed, to help you remember that this is intransitive. We never know why it's delayed, it just happens all by itself!
8935.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 延ばす.

examples.en: A new character will be added soon!
examples.ja: もうすぐ新しいキャラクターが加わるよ！

examples.en: When a little extra effort is put in, it draws out the depth of flavor in the dish.
examples.ja: ひと手間が加わると、料理の味に深みが出ます。

examples.en: The cost of advertising will be added to the ten million yen for the ingredients.
examples.ja: 材料の一千万円に、さらに広告のコストが加わる。

examples.en: When this paint is added to this, the color changes.
examples.ja: これにこの塗料が加わると、色が変わるんです。

8936.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji 加 means <kanji>add</kanji>, and this verb means <vocabulary>to be added to</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to join in</vocabulary>.

It is an intransitive verb, like most verbs ending in わる. That means that it happens by itself, or at least the cause of the adding is not you. Something gets added to something else, perhaps by magic?
8936.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 加える. To help you distinguish between the two, remember that most verbs ending in わる are intransitive.

examples.en: At the moment I farted, a teardrop fell out of my eyes.
examples.ja: おならをした瞬間、目から涙が零れた。

examples.en: Someone spilled tea on the couch! Who's the guilty one?
examples.ja: ソファに紅茶が零れてるんだけど！誰が犯人だ？

examples.en: A beautiful melody spilled out from the window.
examples.ja: 窓から美しいメロディが零れてきた。

8937.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

This is an intransitive verb, so this verb means <vocabulary>to get spilled</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to fall out</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to overflow</vocabulary>.
8937.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 零す.

examples.en: When people come, the security lights turn on.
examples.ja: 人が来ると、セキュリティのためのライトが点くんです。

examples.en: Finally the candles were lit, and the tabletop got brighter.
examples.ja: やっとキャンドルに火が点いて、テーブルの上は明るくなりました。

examples.en: When I say "Alexa, turn the lights on," all the lights in the house turn on.
examples.ja: 「アレクサ、電気を点けて」と言うと、家の全ての電気が点きます。

8938.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji 点 means <kanji>point</kanji>, but this verb actually means <vocabulary>to be lit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be ignited</vocabulary>. Think of it this way, when a flashlight turns on, it points a beam, of light.

You already learned 点ける, which is for when you turn something on. 点く, on the other hand, is an intransitive verb. That means it happens by itself. Like, "Oh look! The lights came on! That's <reading>cool</reading> (く)!"
8938.reading_mnemonic:
You already learned this reading when you learned 点ける but here's a mnemonic just in case:

Every time you count to <reading>two</reading> (つ) a light comes on. How cool that it does it all by itself!!

examples.en: Please continue your interview.
examples.ja: どうぞ、インタビューを進めて下さい。

examples.en: With this snow, we can't move the construction forward anymore.
examples.ja: この雪じゃ、これ以上工事を進められないよ。

examples.en: Please move your work forward at the current pace.
examples.ja: このペースで作業を進めてください。

8939.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>advance</kanji>, and this verb means <vocabulary>to advance something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to move something forward</vocabulary>.

This is a transitive verb, so you act upon something else. You advance something. You move something forward. Like a school project, or your plans for taking over the world.
8939.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn with the kanji. Here's a mnemonic to help:

You are moving your lawsuit forward against Sue. But now she says that YOU'RE the problem. "<reading>Sue, sue me</reading>," (すすめ) you say as you continue to advance the lawsuit. Make sure to say "me" like "mehh," in a really snobbish way.

examples.en: Oh, did you come all the way here alone without anyone accompanying you?
examples.ja: ほう、誰も従えず、一人でここまで来たのかい？

examples.en: The singer came with three bodyguards in tow.
examples.ja: その歌手は三人のボディガードを従えてやってきた。

examples.en: At the age of twenty, he had already become a company president leading over a hundred employees.
examples.ja: 二十才の時には、すでに百人の社員を従える社長になっていた。

8940.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji itself means <kanji>obey</kanji>, but the verb meaning is a bit different. In most contexts, it often just means <vocabulary>to be accompanied by</vocabulary> someone or <vocabulary>to have in tow</vocabulary>. To help you remember this, imagine that everyone you're accompanied by obeys you! You're sort of their leader, so you go everywhere with them following in tow.

従える is a relatively formal word that's often used in literature.
8940.reading_mnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You already learned this reading with 従う. Remember it?

examples.en: Is the rice done cooking?
examples.ja: ご飯、炊けた？

examples.en: Today's dinner is curry spaghetti, not curry rice. I forgot to put the plug in, so the rice isn't cooked.
examples.ja: 今晩はカレーライスじゃなくてカレースパゲッティ。コンセントを差し忘れて、ご飯が炊けてなかったんだ。

examples.en: It's only five minutes left until the daikon gets cooked.
examples.ja: 大根が炊けるまであと五分やで。

8941.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. This is an intransitive verb, so it means <vocabulary>to be cooked</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be boiled</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to be done cooking</vocabulary>. Also a little cultural note — this word is used for both rice, and other foods in western Japan, while it's only used for rice in eastern Japan.
8941.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 炊く.

examples.en: The fried chicken (karaage) is fried up!
examples.ja: 唐揚げ揚がったよ！

examples.en: We waited quietly until the tempura was deep fried.
examples.ja: 天ぷらが揚がるまで静かに待っていた。

examples.en: We'll head out once the flag is up.
examples.ja: 旗が揚がったら出発だ。

8942.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

This is an intransitive verb. The kanji means <kanji>hoist</kanji>, but the verb most commonly means <vocabulary>to be fried up</vocabulary>, ready to eat. Imagine something being hoisted up onto the table because it's fried and ready to eat. The verb can also mean, more logically, <vocabulary>to be up</vocabulary>.
8942.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 揚げる.

examples.en: Yay! I got accepted into a university in Seattle!
examples.ja: やった！シアトル市の大学に受かったよ！

examples.en: If you don't pass next time, you'll have fewer chances of becoming a doctor.
examples.ja: 次回受からなければ、医者になれるチャンスは少なくなるよ。

examples.en: I made a resolution that I won't go out on weekends until I pass my exams.
examples.ja: 試験に受かるまで週末は出かけないって決心したんだ。

8943.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji 受 means accept and this verb is related. It means to get accepted, usually into something good like a university or a new job. It can also mean to pass, often in the context of a test or an exam. This is an intransitive verb, so no direct object is needed. A hint for this is that it ends with okurigana that rhyme with ある, and those kinds of verbs tend to be intransitive. Also, be careful: in English you'd use the transitive expression "pass a test," but in Japanese you'd say 試験に受かる. Kind of like saying you pass in the exam — so it's still intransitive!
8943.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. Here's a little mnemonic to help ya remember:

<vocabulary>To get accepted</vocabulary> into this program, you have to juggle <reading>u</reading>nis (う)—yes, those spiky sea urchins! Handling uni is tough, but if you want <vocabulary>to pass</vocabulary> the test and get accepted, you've got to master the uni challenge.

examples.en: We decided to change the date.
examples.ja: 日を改めることにしました。

examples.en: You should correct that way of thinking.
examples.ja: その考え方は改めた方がいいよ。

examples.en: Just as we discussed, we revised a part of the plan.
examples.ja: 話し合った通りに計画を一部改めた。

8944.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji itself means <kanji>renew</kanji>, and this verb's meaning isn't far off. What do you do if you renew something, usually to make it better? You're going <vocabulary>to change something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to revise something</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to correct something</vocabulary>. This verb is transitive, so it takes a direct object.

改める is a formal word for when you're actively make changes or improvements, like fixing a mistake or reforming a system. You might also use it when you decide to change your behavior or update your way of doing something.
8944.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Usually when we want <vocabulary>to change something</vocabulary>, we want to make it <reading>新た</reading> (あらた), right? Out with the old, in with the 新た, as they say.

examples.en: It was water that spread the virus in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本にそのウィルスを広げたのは水だった。

examples.en: Three adults unfolded a blanket.
examples.ja: 大人三人でブランケットを広げた。

examples.en: As soon as I went inside, I opened the book.
examples.ja: 中に入ってすぐ本を広げた。

8945.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. 

The kanji itself means <kanji>wide</kanji>, and the verb version is what happens when you try to make something wider. How do you make something wider? That's right, you have <vocabulary>to spread something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to unfold something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to open something up</vocabulary>. All of those actions will make a thing wider!

This is a transitive verb. That means it takes a direct object. You spread something. Like a newspaper, or a cloth on a table.
8945.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with the kanji, but here's a reminder mnemonic to help you:

You are going <vocabulary>to spread something</vocabulary>. What are you going to spread? How about your arms, so that you can fly into the sky like the super <reading>hero</reading> (ひろ) that you are! Most heroes can fly when they spread their arms wide!

examples.en: I want to finish work and leave the office by five.
examples.ja: 五時には仕事を終えて会社を出たい。

examples.en: As soon as the princess finished the cake, she had some tea.
examples.ja: 王女はケーキを食べ終えるとすぐに、お茶を飲んだ。

examples.en: Most fish spend their entire life in water.
examples.ja: ほとんどの魚は水中で一生を終える。

8946.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>finish</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to finish something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to end something</vocabulary>.

This is a transitive verb, meaning you finish something, like a long day at work!

You need to differentiate this from 終わる, which is when something just ends on its own. 終える is about when you make something end. Remember it like this: Canadians always end their sentences with "eh" え, right? Well that's how you know they're ending their sentence. Just listen for the "eh," eh?
8946.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn with the kanji. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

You finally finished your school project. <reading>"Oh, A!"</reading> (おえ) you say to yourself, as though you can grade your own project.

examples.en: We're making sure to release the small mantis shrimps back into the sea.
examples.ja: 小さいシャコは海に帰すようにしています。

examples.en: I sent my driver home a little early today.
examples.ja: 今日は少し早く運転手を帰した。

examples.en: They won't send you home unless you finish all of the work.
examples.ja: 作業が全部終わらないと帰してもらえないよ。

8947.meaning_mnemonic:
The hiragana ends with an う sound, so you know this is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>return</kanji>, and this verb is transitive, meaning it takes a direct object. You send someone back. You send them home. And tell them to never come near you again. So this means <vocabulary>to send someone back</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to send someone home</vocabulary>.

In fact, most verbs ending in す are transitive. To help you remember that, think of <reading>su</reading>ing (す) someone to make sure they go home!
8947.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Yay! But since this word has a pair verb, let's think of a way to remember the ending:

What's the most surefire way to send someone home? Threaten to <reading>sue</reading> (す) them if they don't!

examples.en: Suddenly, the window shattered into tiny pieces.
examples.ja: 急に窓ガラスが粉々に砕けた。

examples.en: I like sitting on the beach and watching the waves break on the shore..
examples.ja: 海辺に座って、波が砕けるのを見るのが好きです。

examples.en: When I felt like the tension in the air finally broke, the party was almost over.
examples.ja: 緊張した雰囲気がやっと砕けたと思ったんだけど、パーティはすぐに終わっちゃったんだ。

8948.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

This is an intransitive verb, so this verb means <vocabulary>to be smashed</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be shattered</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to break</vocabulary> (for things like waves and tension!).
8948.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 砕く.

examples.en: They were words that struck a chord in my heart.
examples.ja: それは心に刺さる言葉だった。

examples.en: An arrow embedded itself in his head.
examples.ja: 矢が頭に刺さった。

examples.en: Be careful not to get pricked by a thorn.
examples.ja: トゲが刺さらないように気をつけてね。

8949.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

This is an intransitive verb, meaning that the piercing just happens, without emphasis on what makes it happen. That's why it means <vocabulary>to pierce into</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to stick in</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to stab into</vocabulary>. 

This is a tricky word because its English translations often end up being transitive, but in Japanese we always use this with the particle に, not を, so it's intransitive. You can see this in phrases like 言葉が心に刺さった (the words pierced my heart).
8949.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 刺す.

examples.en: Are the beans cooked well?
examples.ja: 豆、ちゃんと煮えてる？

examples.en: Well, it's about time that the potatoes should be cooked through.
examples.ja: さて、そろそろジャガ芋が煮えるころだ。

examples.en: There was a mysterious soup gurgling and boiling in the pot.
examples.ja: 鍋の中には怪しげなスープがグツグツと煮えていた。

8950.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

You already learned 煮る, which is used for when you purposefully boil something. This verb, on the other hand, is intransitive, meaning that it refers to when something is getting boiled or cooked up, with no emphasis on who put the thing in the pot. That's why this verb means <vocabulary>to be boiled</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be cooked</vocabulary>.
8950.reading_mnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with the kanji. Good for you!

examples.en: I think your banana-only diet lacks balance.
examples.ja: バナナだけの食事はバランスを欠いていると思いますよ。

examples.en: Raw fish can't help but lack freshness three days after purchase.
examples.ja: 生の魚は、買った三日後には、どうしてもフレッシュさを欠きますね。

examples.en: The internet is an indispensable service in our lives.
examples.ja: インターネットは私たちの生活に欠くことのできないサービスだ。

8951.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means lack, and this verb means to lack something. Pretty simple in English, but 欠く is actually kind of advanced and formal in Japanese, so it's mostly just used in writing. Also keep in mind this is a transitive verb, so 欠く takes a direct object — maybe someone lacks knowledge, for example, or you lack concentration. This is a bit different from saying "your concentration is lacking," at least grammatically. (For that, you'd use 欠ける.)
8951.reading_mnemonic:
You learned this reading when you learned 欠ける, but here's a mnemonic just in case:

You never know when you're going <vocabulary>to lack something</vocabulary>. Like a <reading>ca</reading>r (か). Did you plan for it to break? NO! But it happened and now you lack a car in a big way. Not <reading>cool</reading> (く)!

examples.en: Whoa, you're a different person when you take off the mask.
examples.ja: おっマスク外すと別人だね。

examples.en: I missed the target again.
examples.ja: またターゲットを外してしまった。

examples.en: Why did you remove Kyoko from the team?
examples.ja: どうしてキョーコをチームから外したんですか？

examples.en: Let's remove the engine.
examples.ja: エンジンを外しましょう。

8952.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji 外 means <kanji>outside</kanji>, and the meaning of this verb is somewhat related. It means <vocabulary>to remove</vocabulary> something. Think of it like this — if you remove your watch, you are putting it "outside" of its usual spot (your wrist), right?

Like many verbs ending in す, this verb is transitive. It's used for when you intentionally take something and put it outside of where it's supposed to be — so depending on the context, it can also mean <vocabulary>to exclude</vocabulary> someone, or even <vocabulary>to miss something</vocabulary> (like a target). See how all these meanings relate to the idea of something ending up outside its intended spot?
8952.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be a kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this one yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

If you're going <vocabulary>to remove</vocabulary> something from its usual spot, you'd better put on your <reading>haz</reading>mat (はず) suit. You know, those full body yellow onesies people wear to make sure they don't come in contact with any hazardous material. You don't know how long that thing you're removing has been there — or what kind of weird toxic stuff may have accumulated around it — so it's better to be safe than sorry.

examples.en: When are you expecting the baby?
examples.ja: いつ産まれる予定なの？

examples.en: It seems that puppies will be born soon at Ono-san's house.
examples.ja: 小野さんの家では、もうすぐ子犬が産まれるそうだ。

examples.en: Koichi started using WaniKani even before he was born, so by the time he was born, he could already read kanji!
examples.ja: コウイチは、産まれる前からワニカニを始めていたので、産まれた時にはすでに漢字を読むことができたんです！

8953.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

This is an intransitive verb. That means that it just happens, and we're not talking about what makes it happen. So this verb means <vocabulary>to be born</vocabulary>.
8953.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

You know another word that means "to be born" (生まれる), and they both have the same reading!

examples.en: Until the shower water warms up, I'll wait here.
examples.ja: シャワーの水が温まるまで、ここで待ちます。

examples.en: With this heater, it takes so much time for the room to get warm.
examples.ja: このヒーターだと、部屋が温まるのにかなり時間がかかる。

examples.en: After running 1km, my body's getting warmed up.
examples.ja: 一キロ走って、体が温まってきた。

8954.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends in an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji 温 means <kanji>warm</kanji>. So the verb 温まる means <vocabulary>to warm up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to get warm</vocabulary>. 

温まる is intransitive, so no direct object needed. Your cat warms up in the sunlight, for example. No direct object, right? A hint for this is that 温まる ends with okurigana that rhyme with ある, and those kinds of verbs tend to be intransitive!
8954.reading_mnemonic: The kanji reading is the same as 温かい and 温める.

8955.meaning_mnemonic: One way to put <radical>wheat</radical> in your <radical>face</radical> is with <kanji>noodles</kanji>.
8955.reading_mnemonic: Once you're done stuffing noodles in your face, you can use your leftover noodles to make <kanji>noodle</kanji><reading>men</reading> (めん).

examples.en: It's been decided I'll take care of my sister's child on Sunday.
examples.ja: 日曜日に妹の子供を預かることになった。

examples.en: The job of a bank isn't only to take care of money.
examples.ja: 銀行の仕事はお金を預かるだけではありません。

examples.en: I want you to hold onto this for me in case I need it.
examples.ja: 必要になった時のために預かっておいてほしい。

8956.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>deposit</kanji>, and this word is for when someone is depositing something (or someone) with you, because they want you <vocabulary>to look after</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to take care of</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to hold on to</vocabulary> it.

Remember that 預ける is used when you leave something with someone else to take care of temporarily. 預かる, on the other hand, is used when you're the one receiving something to look after. You can remember this because you're great at taking care of cargo (かる). You're always looking after everyone's cargo, but you're happy to hold on to it for them.

Also note that even though 預かる ends with かる and kind of looks intransitive, it's actually an exception! It'll pretty much always have a direct object to specify what you're looking after.
8956.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this before with the pair verb 預ける, but here's a mnemonic to remind you just in case:

You need someone <vocabulary>to look after</vocabulary> your kids for the day. Hey, I have an idea! Leave them with the monkeys at <reading>a zoo</reading> (あず)! Monkeys love kids, and kids love monkeys. Now you can zoom off in your <reading>car</reading>s (か) for the day!

examples.en: That's a mountain echo. Can you hear it?
examples.ja: 山びこだ！きこえる？

examples.en: It was a restaurant named "Mountain Echo."
examples.ja: それは、「山びこ」というレストランでした。

examples.en: The mountain echo was so loud last night I couldn't sleep.
examples.ja: 夕べは山びこがうるさくて、ねれなかったよ。

8957.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 山 means mountain. Add the hiragana びこ to the end and this gives you <vocabulary>echo</vocabulary>. That's because bee children (bee 子) love echos, especially <vocabulary>mountain echo</vocabulary>s! Imagine baby bees buzzing as loudly as they can and hearing their voices echoing back at them through the mountains.

As the kanji suggests, 山びこ is generally used to describe the echo you get if you shout in the mountains. To describe other types of echo, you can use the katakana word エコー.

By the way, there is actually a kanji for the second part of this word, but it's so rare that it's usually written in kana!
8957.reading_mnemonic: You learned this kanji reading when you learned the vocabulary 山.

examples.en: We did our best!
examples.ja: 力いっぱいがんばりました！

examples.en: Please push on the door as hard as you can.
examples.ja: ドアを力いっぱいおしてください。

examples.en: I ran as fast as I could in the relay.
examples.ja: リレーでは力いっぱいはしりました。

8958.meaning_mnemonic:
You've hopefully already learned that 力 means "power." You might have also heard the word いっぱい, because it's used a lot in conversation. It has a few meanings (you'll learn more of them later) but the important one here is "full" or "a lot." Put these two words together and you have <vocabulary>full power</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>with all one's strength</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>as hard as one can</vocabulary>. Remember this one with all your strength!

Just a side note: いっぱい can also be written in kanji, which you'll learn later on! However, in simple words like this one it's usually written in kana.
8958.reading_mnemonic: 力 uses the same reading as you learned with the vocabulary. That's because this is basically two separate words stuck together.

examples.en: The book is on the table.
examples.ja: 本はテーブルの上にあります。

examples.en: Please put three glasses on the table.
examples.ja: テーブルの上にグラスを三つおいてください。

examples.en: I cleaned the table earlier.
examples.ja: さっき、テーブルの上をきれいにしたよ。

8959.meaning_mnemonic: First we have a katakana word, so it's safe to assume that it's a loan word. Like many loan words, it comes from English. Say it out loud and what do you have? That's right, "table". Then comes the particle の, which joins two nouns together. Finally we have 上, which you learned means "up" or "above". Put all of these pieces together and we have a phrase meaning <vocabulary>on the table</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>tabletop</vocabulary>!
8959.reading_mnemonic: In this phrase, 上 is a standalone word, so it uses the same reading that you learned when you learned the vocabulary. Easy to stay on top of that one, right?

examples.en: There are many manga under the bed.
examples.ja: ベッドの下にはマンガがたくさんあります。

examples.en: I don't mop under the bed.
examples.ja: ベッドの下はモップをしないんです。

examples.en: Woah, there's someone under the bed!
examples.ja: うわっ、ベッドの下に人がいる！

8960.meaning_mnemonic: This starts with another katakana word, so you can assume that it's a loan word. This one also comes from English. Can you figure out what it means? That's right, "bed". Then comes the particle の, which joins two nouns together. Finally, we have 下, which you learned means "down" or "below". Put these elements together and you get <vocabulary>below the bed</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>under the bed</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>beneath the bed</vocabulary>. What's under your bed?
8960.reading_mnemonic: 下 is a standalone word here, so it uses the same reading that you learned when you learned the vocabulary.

examples.en: The queen often says, "you're right."
examples.ja: 女王は、よく「そうね」と口にする。

examples.en: Don't say that name.
examples.ja: その名は口にするな。

examples.en: I got drunk off a little whisky.
examples.ja: ウィスキーを口にしたら、よっぱらってしまった。

8961.meaning_mnemonic:
You've already learned that 口 means "mouth" and here it's followed by the particle に, which pinpoints a location. The verb する means "to do" so you're doing something to your mouth! Logically enough, this expression is used to describe lots of actions that you do with your mouth. It's often used to mean <vocabulary>to mention</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to say</vocabulary>, but with an added descriptive nuance that you've said something accidentally or unexpectedly, maybe something you shouldn't have said! 🙊

It can also mean other things done with the mouth, like <vocabulary>to eat</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to drink</vocabulary>!
8961.reading_mnemonic: In this expression, 口 is a standalone vocabulary word, so it uses the same reading that you learned when you learned the vocabulary.

examples.en: Walking on a mountain path requires physical strength.
examples.ja: 山道を歩くのは体力が必要だ。

examples.en: There are many turns on this mountain road, so always keep your feet on the brake of the car.
examples.ja: この山道は曲がる所がたくさんあるので、常に車のブレーキの上に足をおいて下さいね。

examples.en: There are many weeds and insects on this mountain road, so please don't come with tank tops, shorts, or flip-flops.
examples.ja: 山道には草や虫が多いので、タンクトップ、ハーフパンツ、ビーチサンダルで来ないでくださいね。

8962.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>mountain</kanji> <kanji>road</kanji> is a <vocabulary>mountain road</vocabulary>! Or a <vocabulary>mountain trail</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>mountain path</vocabulary>.
8962.reading_mnemonic: Both the kanji in this word use the kun'yomi, which you learned when you learned the vocabulary. When it uses this reading, it sounds casual, and is common in conversation. It can also be read using the on'yomi, though, in which case it has a more formal feel to it. That's typical of on'yomi, which tends to add formality to a word!

8963.meaning_mnemonic: The best kind of flowers to grow in your window? Strawberry, obviously. Yes, there are strawberry flowers — it's actually the flowers that turn into the strawberries, you know. And they're perfect as window flowers because they need a ton of light. That's why all your window flowers are strawberries.
8963.reading_mnemonic: Believe it or not, your <kanji>strawberry</kanji> is the only cure for an <reading>itchy Go</reading>dzilla (いちご).

8964.meaning_mnemonic: You keep your <radical>moon</radical> <radical>weapon</radical> in your <kanji>crotch</kanji>. Where else would you keep it?
8964.reading_mnemonic: Your <kanji>crotch</kanji> has a moon weapon, and it's served you well, so you hope that if you have a <reading>子 </reading> (こ) one day, they'll have one too.

8965.meaning_mnemonic: You've made yourself a <radical>tree</radical> <radical>bookshelf</radical> (that is, a bookshelf cut into a tree), so you build a <kanji>fence</kanji> to keep the riffraff out.
8965.reading_mnemonic: On your <kanji>fence</kanji>, you hang up a <reading>sack</reading> (さく) to accept donations.

8966.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>mouth</radical> has a <radical>tooth</radical> that you use to <kanji>bite</kanji> and <kanji>chew</kanji> with.
8966.reading_mnemonic: Your one tooth is so strong that you can even use it to <kanji>bite</kanji> and <kanji>chew</kanji> up a whole  <reading>ca</reading>r (か).

8967.meaning_mnemonic: One <radical>animal</radical> that is particularly  <radical>good</radical> is the <kanji>wolf</kanji>. Wolves have a bad reputation, but actually they're very, very good animals.
8967.reading_mnemonic: A <kanji>wolf</kanji> might be good, but if you run into one, all you can do is scream <reading>Oh 神</reading>!” (おおかみ).

8968.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>mouth</radical> was <radical>slice</radical>d open by a terrible <kanji>cough</kanji>.
8968.reading_mnemonic: Oddly enough, some people find your <kanji>cough</kanji> <reading>sexy</reading> (せき).

8969.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>fingers</radical> have to <radical>stand</radical> up straight, to protect you from being <kanji>abduct</kanji>ed, or <kanji>pull</kanji>ed away against your will.
8969.reading_mnemonic: Suddenly, someone really is trying to <kanji>abduct</kanji> you. They're <kanji>pull</kanji>ling you away. It's the ancient Egyptian god <reading>Ra</reading> (ら). Help!

examples.en: Eat your noodles quickly or they'll get soft.
examples.ja: 早く食べないと麺が伸びちゃうよ。

examples.en: We've developed strawberry-flavored noodles.
examples.ja: 苺味の麺を開発しました。

examples.en: Next, pour boiling water over the noodles.
examples.ja: 次に、麺に沸騰したお湯を注いでください。

8970.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
8970.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this vocabulary is the same as the reading you learned with the kanji. Go eat some noodles to celebrate!

examples.en: Where did you buy that rolling pin?
examples.ja: その麺棒、どこで買ったの？

examples.en: If you're looking for a rolling pin, it's in that drawer.
examples.ja: 麺棒ならあそこの引き出しに入ってるよ。

examples.en: A large number of rolling pins have been brought in from China.
examples.ja: 大量の麺棒が中国から持ち込まれている。

8971.meaning_mnemonic:
Grab your <kanji>noodle</kanji> <kanji>pole</kanji> and let's make some noodles. What's a noodle pole? It's a <vocabulary>rolling pin</vocabulary>!

You use your rolling pin to flatten out the noodle dough before you slice it into noodles. That's why a rolling pin is so important to make noodles.
8971.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. So just keep rolling.

examples.en: This is my first time eating salmon ramen.
examples.ja: 鮭拉麺なんて初めて食べるよ。

examples.en: What small companies need in order to grow is ramen.
examples.ja: 小さな会社が成長するのに必要なのは、拉麺です。

examples.en: I spilled ramen soup on my crotch.
examples.ja: 股間に拉麺の汁をこぼしてしまった。

8972.meaning_mnemonic:
If you're going to <kanji>abduct</kanji> some <kanji>noodles</kanji>, make sure it's everybody's favorite noodles, <vocabulary>ramen</vocabulary>! The other meaning of the first kanji actually makes more sense here though, because you <kanji>pull</kanji> the dough to stretch it when you make <vocabulary>ramen noodles</vocabulary>. Choose whichever meaning helps you remember it best!

This word is mostly written in kana, usually as ラーメン, but sometimes らーめん. You'll see the kanji version pretty often on packaging and menus, though, so it's worth knowing! The word is also occasionally written as らー麺 or ラー麺.
8972.reading_mnemonic: Both of these kanji take the on'yomi, but the first one has a slightly irregular reading, because it's based on the modern Chinese reading. To remember that it's a long らー, just think how excited you are about these ramen! <reading>Raaaaaa</reading>! Raaaamen! So exciting!

examples.en: Everyone started slurping down the cold somen.

examples.en: My nostrils are itchy.

examples.en: My head is itching because I haven't showered in a week.
examples.ja: 一週間シャワーを浴びてないから頭が痒い。

examples.en: I'm so itchy that I can't sleep at night, and I'm totally sleep-deprived.
examples.ja: 夜も寝れないぐらい痒くて、めっちゃ寝不足なんだよね。

9007.meaning_mnemonic: You can guess this is an adjective from the い at the end. The meaning for the kanji is <kanji>itchy</kanji>, and the adjective version is <vocabulary>itchy</vocabulary> too.
9007.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the same reading as the one you learned with the kanji: かゆ.

examples.en: I'm tormented by feelings of helplessness.
examples.ja: 無力感に苛まれてるんよ。

examples.en: The sweltering heat torments us.
examples.ja: うだるような暑さが私達を苛む。

examples.en: The victims were tormented by the anxiety that something else bad would happen.
examples.ja: 被害者はまた何か悪いことが起こるのではないかという不安に苛まれていました。

9008.meaning_mnemonic: As usual, you can guess this is a verb thanks to the う sound on the end. The kanji means <kanji>frustration</kanji>, and unfortunately frustration tends <vocabulary>to torment</vocabulary> people. This verb is pretty advanced, but still useful to know!
9008.reading_mnemonic: We all know it's not okay to <vocabulary>to torment</vocabulary> each other. So how about we all <reading>sign a</reading> (さいな) contract saying that we'll never torment anyone ever again?

examples.en: This in an image of Uranus.
examples.ja: これは天王星の画像です。

examples.en: The discoverer of Uranus is William Herschel.
examples.ja: 天王星の発見者はウィリアム・ハーシェルです。

examples.en: Uranus takes eighty-four years to complete an orbit.
examples.ja: 天王星は一回りするのに八十四年かかります。

9009.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>heaven</kanji> <kanji>king</kanji> <kanji>star</kanji> is the planet <vocabulary>Uranus</vocabulary>. Knowledge of Greek mythology will definitely help you here, because the English name is a reference to the Greek god of the skies, and the Japanese name is a direct translation of that!
9009.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word and uses the on'yomi, but over time the reading for 王 changed from おう to のう, to make it easier to pronounce. You'll still see that listed as an alternative reading in some dictionaries, but it's pretty much never used nowadays, so we'll only accept the てんのうせい reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember:

Who predicted the discovery of <vocabulary>Uranus</vocabulary>? <reading>No</reading>stradamus (のう), of course!

examples.en: Does Mars have water?
examples.ja: 火星には水がありますか？

examples.en: I would like to go to Mars right now if possible.
examples.ja: できれば今すぐ火星に行きたいと思っています。

examples.en: Apparently, the sunset sky looks blue on Mars.
examples.ja: 火星の日の入りは空が青く見えるそうです。

9010.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>fire</kanji> <kanji>star</kanji> is <vocabulary>Mars</vocabulary>. This should be easy to remember, because Mars is the only planet in our solar system that's the color of fire.
9010.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Have you ever seen Jupiter?
examples.ja: 木星を見たことありますか？

examples.en: What's between Mars and Jupiter?
examples.ja: 火星と木星のあいだには、何がありますか。

examples.en: Jupiter and Saturn were born like that.
examples.ja: 木星や土星はこうして生まれたんですよ。

9011.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>tree</kanji> <kanji>star</kanji> is the planet <vocabulary>Jupiter</vocabulary>. Imagine Jupiter covered in very strange trees — the kind that are able to take root in gas! It's a pretty weird image, but will hopefully help you to remember this word. Alternatively, think about how the clouds around Jupiter make patterns that look a lot like wood grain.
9011.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

9012.meaning_mnemonic: Your <radical>forehead</radical> is in the <radical>sun</radical>, and you start seeing those creatures with <radical>lid</radical>s for heads and  <radical>fins</radical> for feet again. Where on earth did they come from? They must have come from the <kanji>underworld</kanji>. Nothing like that exists in this life.
9012.reading_mnemonic: The sun is unusually hot for the month of <reading>May</reading> (めい), which must be why those underworld creatures are running around.

examples.en: Pluto's orbit is irregular, and it takes about 250 years to go around the sun once.
examples.ja: 冥王星の軌道は不規則で、太陽を一周する期間は約２５０年です。

examples.en: Pluto was discovered on February 18 1930 by astronomer Clyde Tombaugh.
examples.ja: 冥王星は天文学者クライド・トンボーによって、1930年２月18日に発見された。

examples.en: Can you explain why Pluto was demoted from planet to dwarf planet?
examples.ja: 冥王星が惑星から準惑星に降格された理由を説明できますか？

9013.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>underworld</kanji> <kanji>king</kanji> <kanji>star</kanji> is the dwarf planet <vocabulary>Pluto</vocabulary>. Since Pluto was the ruler of the underworld in classical mythology, this makes a lot of sense!
9013.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Only the souls of the dead can enter the underworld.
examples.ja: 冥界に入れるのは死者の魂だけだ。

examples.en: Hecate is the goddess of the underworld in Greek mythology.
examples.ja: ヘカテーは、ギリシャ神話に出てくる冥界の女神です。

examples.en: I can hear a message from the god of the underworld coming from the realm of the dead.
examples.ja: 冥界から、冥界神のメッセージが聞こえる。

9014.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>underworld</kanji> <kanji>world</kanji> is the <vocabulary>underworld</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>Hades</vocabulary>, or the <vocabulary>realm of the dead</vocabulary>.

This word is a bit poetic, and mostly used in writing, particularly in contexts like Buddhism, spirituality, and ancient mythologies. It's usually interchangeable with 冥土 (which is also in this level), but 冥土 is used more in certain set expressions, which we'll mention in the page for that word!
9014.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You learned those with the kanji, so you should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: No matter how much money you make, you can't take it with you to the underworld.
examples.ja: どんなにお金を稼いでも、冥土には持っていけないんだよ。

examples.en: "I'll tell you something that'll be your souvenir for the realm of the dead" said the man, and began to tell me his secret, keeping his gun pointing at me.
examples.ja: 「冥土の土産に教えてやるよ。」と、男は銃を構えたまま秘密を話し始めた。

examples.en: After preparing for the journey to the underworld by dressing the body in Buddhist robes and applying makeup for the deceased, they will go on to the next life.
examples.ja: 仏衣や死化粧などの冥土の旅支度をして、故人は来世へと向かいます。

9015.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>underworld</kanji> <kanji>dirt</kanji> is another word for the <vocabulary>realm of the dead</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>underworld</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>Hades</vocabulary>. Like the word 冥界 (also in this level), it's rather poetic, and mostly used in written contexts involving spirituality, Buddhism, and ancient mythologies.

There are a few set expressions that only use 冥土, though. One example is 冥土の土産, "a souvenir to take to the realm of the dead". It refers to something abstract that is so valuable, it's worth taking to the underworld, such as the solution to a great mystery, or a happy memory.

Another expression is 冥土の旅支度, which means "preparations for the journey to the realm of the dead", and can refer to the preparation of the deceased before a funeral, as wells as certain preparations made by Buddhists while they're still alive.

You'll also see this word written as 冥途 sometimes.
9015.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Drunk driving is a crime.
examples.ja: 飲酒運転は犯罪です。

examples.en: I don't want to drink and drive, so I'll go home by taxi.
examples.ja: 飲酒運転はしたくないから、タクシーで帰るよ。

examples.en: I didn't know it was considered drunk driving with a bicycle, but that makes sense.
examples.ja: 自転車でも飲酒運転とみなされるとは知りませんでしたが、なるほどと思いました。

9018.meaning_mnemonic: You know that 飲酒 is "drinking alcohol" and 運転する is "to drive", so it makes sense that this word means <vocabulary>drunk driving</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>drinking and driving</vocabulary>.
9018.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: What was the main reason you decided to stop drinking alcohol?
examples.ja: 飲酒をやめようと思った一番の理由は何ですか？

examples.en: Drinking is expensive and bad for you, right?
examples.ja: 飲酒はお金がかかるし、体に悪いでしょう。

examples.en: I heard that guy got a minor to drink.
examples.ja: あいつ、未成年に飲酒させたらしいよ。

9019.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Drink</kanji> <kanji>alcohol</kanji> is <vocabulary>drinking alcohol</vocabulary>, or just <vocabulary>drinking</vocabulary>. This always refers to alcohol though.
9019.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading of 飲 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Where's a good place for <vocabulary>drinking alcohol</vocabulary>? An <reading>inn</reading> (いん), of course!

examples.en: I'm from Malaysia.
examples.ja: 私はマレーシア出身です。

examples.en: I'm from Aomori, so I don't know the Kyushu dialect.
examples.ja: 青森出身なので、九州の方言は分かりません。

examples.en: The author of this book is from the same place as me.
examples.ja: この本の作者は私と同じ場所の出身なんです。

examples.en: Where is your husband from?
examples.ja: あなたのご主人はどこの出身なんですか？

9020.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>exit</kanji> that <kanji>somebody</kanji> starts from is <vocabulary>one's origin</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>one's hometown</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>one's birthplace</vocabulary>.
9020.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Just watch out for the つ of 出, which becomes っ.

examples.en: This is a huge problem related to people's everyday lives.
examples.ja: これは人々の生活に関わる大問題だ。

examples.en: I have been involved in many projects, but this one is the most exciting.
examples.ja: 今まで色々なプロジェクトに関わってきましたが、今回のプロジェクトが一番ワクワクします。

examples.en: Allergies are not to be taken lightly. They can be life-threatening!
examples.ja: アレルギーは軽く見たらダメだよ。命に関わることもあるんだから！

9021.meaning_mnemonic: You know that the kanji means <kanji>related</kanji>. As a verb, this often means <vocabulary>to be involved</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be related</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>to be connected</vocabulary>. Basically, things that have to do with being related to something else.
9021.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:  

Ever heard of the "<reading>Kaw Kaw</reading> (かか) Crow Gang"? They are bad news, always eating from garbage and squawking "kaw kaw" ... You don't want <vocabulary>to be involved</vocabulary> with them.

examples.en: This UFO is now at an altitude of 33,000 feet.
examples.ja: このUFOは、今、高度3万3000フィートのところにいる。

examples.en: Michael used advanced techniques to complete one difficult game after another.
examples.ja: マイケルは、高度なテクニックを使って、むずかしいゲームを次々クリアした。

examples.en: When the altitude gets too high, the engine will suddenly stop.
examples.ja: 高度が一気に上ると、エンジンが止まっちゃうんだよ。

9022.meaning_mnemonic:
Something that is <kanji>tall</kanji> in <kanji>degree</kanji>s can either refer to its <vocabulary>altitude</vocabulary>, or to the fact that it's quite <vocabulary>high-level</vocabulary>. 

Note that this can refer to any altitude, even lower ones. But when used to refer to, for example, skills or a technique, it always talks about a high level or degree.
9022.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Greetings are essential for building good relationships.
examples.ja: 良好な人間関係を築くのに、あいさつは欠かせません。

examples.en: Today, let's all think about what we can do to build a better society.
examples.ja: 今日はみんなで、より良い社会を築くためには何をすればいいかを考えましょう。

examples.en: My dream is to build a happy family with you.
examples.ja: 私の夢は、あなたと幸せな家庭を築くことです。

9027.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>construct</kanji> and the verb version is <vocabulary>to build something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to construct something</vocabulary>.
9027.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You want <vocabulary>to build something</vocabulary> called a <reading>key zoo</reading> (きず). Which is a zoo for keys instead of animals. So it's a bunch of keys in cages, basically. Hmm, how artsy of you... Hopefully people get it. Isn't it a bit avant-garde <vocabulary>to construct something</vocabulary> like a key zoo?

9028.meaning_mnemonic: You have a <radical>greenhouse</radical> that is <kanji>endless</kanji>. Imagine your endless greenhouse, which goes on and on, as far as the eye can see. Lucky you.
9028.reading_mnemonic: Your flowers have grown so big that now the only way you can fit into your <kanji>endless</kanji> greenhouse is by lying on your <reading>back</reading> (ばく).

examples.en: Road construction costs huge amounts of money.
examples.ja: 道路建設には莫大な費用がかかる。

examples.en: If this situation continues, the cost could be enormous.
examples.ja: このままでは、コストが莫大になる可能性があります。

examples.en: The crab statue is beautiful, but no one will be happy with the huge amount of funds spent on it.
examples.ja: カニの像は美しいが、莫大な資金が使われたことについてはだれも喜ばないだろう。

9029.meaning_mnemonic:
Something that is <kanji>endless</kanji>ly <kanji>big</kanji> isn't just big, but <vocabulary>huge</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>enormous</vocabulary>.

This word is often used in contexts that involve money, but it can also be used for other things like time, energy, and data.
9029.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The servants who serve in this house are very polite.
examples.ja: この家に仕える使用人は、とても礼儀が正しい。

examples.en: The woman seemed to be a female official in the service of the Meiji Emperor.
examples.ja: その女性は、明治天皇に仕えていた女官のようです。

examples.en: Nice to meet you. I'm an angel who started serving God today.
examples.ja: はじめまして。今日から神に仕えることになった天使です。

9034.meaning_mnemonic:
Everything we're <kanji>doing</kanji> is <vocabulary>to serve</vocabulary> you, you know.

This verb is a bit archaic and therefore has a formal feel to it. It's used to talk about serving emperors, kings, and gods, among others.
9034.reading_mnemonic: <vocabulary>To serve</vocabulary> you well, we've gotten ourselves <reading>two ca</reading>rs (つか). If one breaks down, we can still serve you with the other car.

examples.en: What was it like the first time you fell in love?
examples.ja: あなたの初恋ってどんな感じだった？

examples.en: My first love's name was...I think...Micchan.
examples.ja: 初恋の人の名前は…たしか、ミッちゃんだったかな。

examples.en: Grandpa, when was the first time you fell in love?
examples.ja: おじいちゃん、おじいちゃんが初恋をしたのっていつ？

9035.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>first</kanji> <kanji>love</kanji> is your <vocabulary>first love</vocabulary> or your <vocabulary>first crush</vocabulary>. This usually refers to the first time you fall in love, but it can also refer to the person you fall in love with.
9035.reading_mnemonic: Similarly to 初耳, 初 behaves more like a prefix here, which means that this uses kun'yomi readings. You already know these for both 初 and 恋, so you should be good to go!

meanings: Something Heard For The First Time

examples.en: Huh, that's the first I've heard of it.
examples.ja: ええっ、それは初耳です。

examples.en: Seriously? That's all news to me!
examples.ja: マジ？そんな話、初耳だぞ！？

examples.en: This term may be new to many of you.
examples.ja: この言葉は、初耳の人も多いかもしれませんね。

9036.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>first</kanji> time something reaches your <kanji>ear</kanji>, it's <vocabulary>something heard for the first time</vocabulary>. If it's never entered your ear before, it's <vocabulary>news</vocabulary> to you!
9036.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses kun'yomi instead of on'yomi readings, because 初 behaves more like a prefix here. You already know how to read 耳, but you haven't learned the kun'yomi for 初 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

Whatever it is, this <vocabulary>something heard for the first time</vocabulary>, be sure to hold onto your <reading>hats</reading> (はつ)! It's going to be something big, and I'm pretty sure it's going to be <vocabulary>news</vocabulary> to me, too.

examples.en: Please enter your answer here.
examples.ja: こちらに回答を入力してください。

examples.en: Thank you for your response to the survey.
examples.ja: アンケートへのご回答、ありがとうございました。

examples.en: The president has not yet responded about accepting an interview or not.
examples.ja: 社長はインタビューを受ける事について、まだ回答を出していない。

9037.meaning_mnemonic:
You know 回 means "times," but it can also mean "revolve." You <kanji>revolve</kanji> around an <kanji>answer</kanji> until you're ready to give your <vocabulary>answer</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>response</vocabulary> to the question!

回答 refers to responding to a question, inquiry, or request. For example, you use 回答 when answering a questionnaire or letting someone know whether you can attend a party.
9037.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You didn't learn the on'yomi for 答 with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Give me your <vocabulary>answer</vocabulary> and I'll take you to <reading>とう</reading>きょう. How does that sound? All I need is your reply, and we'll be in とうきょう before you know it.

examples.en: Alright, let's take a look at the answers.
examples.ja: では、解答を見てみましょう。

examples.en: You have five minutes to answer!
examples.ja: 解答時間は５分です！

examples.en: I will now hand out the answer sheets.
examples.ja: それでは解答用紙をくばります。

9038.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>solve</kanji> a problem by working toward the <kanji>answer</kanji>. This is the act of <vocabulary>solving</vocabulary>, which eventually leads to the final <vocabulary>answer</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>solution</vocabulary>!

解答 specifically refers to solving problems and giving answers with a correct solution, often for structured contexts like exams or math problems. It can also refer to the answer or solution itself.
9038.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You learned the on'yomi for 答 with 回答, but here's a mnemonic for it in case you forgot:

The reward for <vocabulary>solving</vocabulary> this problem correctly is… A free trip to <reading>とう</reading>きょう! That's right, if you can work out the correct <vocabulary>solution</vocabulary> to this problem, you and a loved one will get an all-expenses-paid trip to とうきょう. Pretty cool, huh?

examples.en: He is an entomologist.
examples.ja: 彼は昆虫学者です。

examples.en: One day we'll all be eating insects for breakfast.
examples.ja: いつか朝ご飯に昆虫を食べる日が来るだろう。

examples.en: My favorite insect is the antlion larva.
examples.ja: 私の一番好きな昆虫はアリジゴクです。

9039.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>insect</kanji> <kanji>insect</kanji> is... you guessed it! An <vocabulary>insect</vocabulary>.
9039.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi of the kanji. You learned this reading for 昆 when you learned the kanji, but you haven't learned the on'yomi for 虫 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Did you know that <vocabulary>insect</vocabulary>s are <reading>Chew</reading>bacca's (ちゅう) favorite thing? He's fascinated by all types of insects, and keeps them in boxes as pets. There are a good few of them crawling around in his fur, too.

examples.en: The use of insecticides is strictly prohibited on this farm.
examples.ja: この農場では殺虫剤の使用は厳禁です。

examples.en: Pesticides are dangerous if they enter the human body.
examples.ja: 殺虫剤は人体に入ると危険です。

examples.en: Because fireflies are insects, they are vulnerable to cold and insecticides.
examples.ja: 蛍は昆虫なので、寒さや殺虫剤に弱い。

9040.meaning_mnemonic: What <kanji>kill</kanji>s <kanji>insect</kanji>s with one <kanji>dose</kanji>? That's an <vocabulary>insecticide</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>pesticide</vocabulary>.
9040.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The night illumination of Okayama Castle was so beautiful!
examples.ja: 岡山城のライトアップ、めっちゃきれいだったよ！

examples.en: On Sunday, I visited the renovated Okayama Castle.
examples.ja: 日曜日、リニューアルした岡山城に行ってきました。

examples.en: If the weather is good, Okayama Castle will be clearly visible from here.
examples.ja: 天気が良ければ、ここからも岡山城がはっきり見えるんですよ。

9041.meaning_mnemonic: This is the same 岡山 that you learned with 岡山県. So what's Okayama <kanji>castle</kanji>? Yep, <vocabulary>Okayama Castle</vocabulary>!
9041.reading_mnemonic:
When 城 is added to a place name like this, it takes the on'yomi. You haven't learned this yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

The lord of <vocabulary>Okayama Castle</vocabulary> is none other than <reading>Joe</reading> (じょう), your local farmhand friend. How a farmhand like Joe managed to become the lord of a Japanese castle is beyond even us, but it's Lord Joe to you now.

examples.en: This town is close to human habitation.
examples.ja: この町は、人里に近い。

examples.en: There is a house in the mountain far from the village.
examples.ja: 人里からはなれた山に家が有ります。

examples.en: Sometimes, bears show up in villages.
examples.ja: 人里にクマが出てくることがある。

9042.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>person</kanji>'s <kanji>hometown</kanji> is a <vocabulary>human habitation</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>village</vocabulary>. This word has a slightly old-fashioned feel, and it's usually used for small villages in the countryside.

It's often combined with はなれた (separated) to talk about how far away from the nearest human habitation something is.
9042.reading_mnemonic: This jukugo uses the kun'yomi of the kanji instead of the more usual on'yomi. You learned both of these readings when you learned the vocabulary 人 and 里. Just notice that さと becomes ざと, because of rendaku.

examples.en: The Japanese-style taro salad at that izakaya is delicious.
examples.ja: その居酒屋の和風里芋サラダは美味しいよ。

examples.en: What's the best way to preserve taro?
examples.ja: 里芋はどうやって保存するのが一番いいですか？

examples.en: Taro has been eaten in Japan for thousands of years.
examples.ja: 里芋は日本で何千年も前から食べられています。

9043.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>hometown</kanji> <kanji>potato</kanji> is a <vocabulary>taro</vocabulary>. In Japan, taro is the kind of potato that everyone has in their hometown, because it's been around for such a long time and it'll grow anywhere.

In English, "taro" can sometimes be used for other root vegetables too, but just keep in mind this word refers specifically to the <vocabulary>Japanese taro</vocabulary> — a small, starchy, potato-like vegetable.
9043.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the kun'yomi readings of the kanji.

examples.en: I'd like this one to go, please.
examples.ja: これはお持ち帰りでお願いします。

examples.en: What shall we do, eat at a restaurant? Get takeout?
examples.ja: どうする、お店で食べる？お持ち帰りにする？

examples.en: Here's the take-out order for customer number two!
examples.ja: こちら、二番さんのお持ち帰りのオーダーのお品になります！

9044.meaning_mnemonic: When you're <kanji>hold</kanji>ing food and <kanji>return</kanji>ing home with it, you're likely getting <vocabulary>takeout</vocabulary>.
9044.reading_mnemonic: You've already learned how to read both 持つ and 帰る, so you should be able to read this as well.

examples.en: I'll leave everything about this store to your judgment.
examples.ja: この店のことは全て君の判断に任すよ。

examples.en: I'm happy to be entrusted with a big job, but I'm also a little nervous.
examples.ja: 大きな仕事を任されて、うれしいけど少し不安でもある。

examples.en: I'm Tanaka and I've been assigned as project manager. I look forward to working with you all.
examples.ja: 今回、プロジェクトマネージャーを任されることになった田中です。よろしくお願いします。

9045.meaning_mnemonic:
The meaning of this word is the same as 任せる. Both words are pretty common, but 任す is slightly less common than 任せる.

Here's the mnemonic again, just in case you need a refresher:

If you pass a <kanji>duty</kanji> on to someone, that means you're going <vocabulary>to entrust something</vocabulary> to that person, or you're going <vocabulary>to delegate something</vocabulary>. In other words, you're going <vocabulary>to leave something to</vocabulary> them, so that they do it for you.
9045.reading_mnemonic: This uses the same reading you learned with 任せる.

examples.en: Most of the politicians in our country are men.
examples.ja: 我が国の政治家の多くは男性だ。

examples.en: In our country, mandatory vaccination of the population is under consideration.
examples.ja: 我が国では、国民のワクチン接種の義務化が検討されています。

examples.en: Currently, foreigners without resident status are not allowed to enter our country.
examples.ja: 現在、在留資格のない外国人は、我が国への入国が認められておりません。

9046.meaning_mnemonic:
You learned that 我が means "our", so our <kanji>country</kanji> is simply <vocabulary>our country</vocabulary>.

Just like 我が itself, this expression is somewhat old-fashioned and stylized. It comes up a lot in political discourse and other formal contexts.
9046.reading_mnemonic: You learned this reading for 我 when you learned 我が. Just watch out for 国, which you might expect to rendaku here, but doesn't!

examples.en: Today's dinner at our house is deep-fried shrimp.
examples.ja: 我が家の今日のディナーはエビフライです。

examples.en: In the end, everyone loves their own child the most.
examples.ja: だれだって、結局我が子が一番可愛いんだよ。

examples.en: The section chief was saying exactly what you said, as if it were his own words.
examples.ja: 課長、あんたの受け売りをそのまま、我が物顔で言ってたよ。

9047.meaning_mnemonic:
Here we have <kanji>I</kanji> followed by the particle が, giving us a somewhat old-fashioned and stylized way of say <vocabulary>our</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>one's own</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>my</vocabulary>.

One explanation for this is that in ancient Japanese, が was used as a possessive particle, much like の is in modern Japanese.
9047.reading_mnemonic:
You haven't learned this reading for 我 so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Let us present you with <vocabulary>our</vocabulary> <reading>wa</reading>lrus (わ). Well it's <vocabulary>my</vocabulary> walrus really, but I'm happy to share.

examples.en: Where can I buy a bus ticket?
examples.ja: バスの乗車券はどこで買える？

examples.en: Do you offer discount tickets?
examples.ja: 割引乗車券はありますか。

examples.en: I was sure I put my train ticket in my inside pocket, but I can't find it.
examples.ja: 電車の乗車券を内ポケットに入れたはずなのに、見当たらないの。

9048.meaning_mnemonic:
If you want to <kanji>ride</kanji> in a <kanji>car</kanji>, the <kanji>ticket</kanji> you'll need is a <vocabulary>passenger ticket</vocabulary>.

乗車券 is primarily a <vocabulary>ticket</vocabulary> for a train ride, so think of "car" here as a train car. It can also refer to tickets for other rides, like Ferris wheels, cable cars, ropeways, or certain buses that require a prior ticket purchase.
9048.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: There were many passengers on that bus.
examples.ja: そのバスにはたくさんの乗客が乗っていました。

examples.en: Some passengers look forward to chatting with cab drivers.
examples.ja: タクシードライバーとのおしゃべりを楽しみにしている乗客もいる。

examples.en: A female passenger was waiting alone on the platform.
examples.ja: ホームには女性の乗客が一人で待っていた。

9049.meaning_mnemonic: If you take a <kanji>ride</kanji> as a <kanji>guest</kanji> (or a <kanji>customer</kanji>), that makes you a <vocabulary>passenger</vocabulary>.
9049.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You hopefully learned the on'yomi for 乗 with the word 乗馬, but here's a mnemonic to help you just in case:

You notice a <vocabulary>passenger</vocabulary> getting on at your stop. Who is it? The distinct smell of barn animals and manure gives it away immediately: it’s <reading>Joe</reading> (じょう), the farmhand!

examples.en: This morning, I went horseback riding.
examples.ja: 今朝、乗馬をしました。

examples.en: I want to experience horseback riding.
examples.ja: 乗馬を体験してみたい。

examples.en: Recently, I've been attending a horse riding club.
examples.ja: 最近は、乗馬クラブに通っています。

9050.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>ride</kanji> a <kanji>horse</kanji>, that's <vocabulary>horseback riding</vocabulary> or, in some parts of the world, simply <vocabulary>horse riding</vocabulary>.
9050.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 乗, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Know who loves <vocabulary>horseback riding</vocabulary>? That's right, <reading>Joe</reading> (じょう) the farmhand. It makes sense, with him being a farmhand and all.

9051.meaning_mnemonic: Did you know that those strange <radical>geoduck</radical> creatures were once used to make <kanji>page</kanji>s? Okay maybe not, but it makes for a memorable image!

examples.en: This book has more than 500 pages.
examples.ja: この本は五百頁以上ある。

examples.en: This manga is fully colored on all pages.
examples.ja: この漫画は全頁フルカラーです。

examples.en: I cannot see the next page of the PDF because of an error.
examples.ja: PDFの次頁がエラーになって見れません。

examples.en: I read through one page each day.
examples.ja: 毎日一頁ずつ読み進めた。

9052.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji and the vocabulary are exactly the same, so they share meanings as well.

This word is often written in katakana as ページ, especially in informal writing and online. But you'll also see the kanji version, especially to refer to the pages of printed texts and in more formal writing.
9052.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the reading you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: To cure my fatigue and recover quickly, I drank green tea and ate mochi for a week.
examples.ja: 疲れを癒して、早く回復するために、一週間緑茶を飲んだりお餅を食べたりしました。

examples.en: I was healed by Riko-chan's kind smile.
examples.ja: 莉子ちゃんの優しい笑顔に癒された。

examples.en: Ryoichiro quenched his thirst for knowledge through reading.
examples.ja: 諒一郎は読書によって知識への渇きを癒すことができた。

9053.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji means <kanji>healing</kanji> and the verb version means <vocabulary>to heal something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to cure something</vocabulary>, and even <vocabulary>to quench a thirst</vocabulary>, both literally and metaphorically. As you can probably guess, this last use has a poetic feel to it.

Like many verbs ending in す, this verb is transitive, meaning it's being done to something. So you can use it when you cure an illness, heal a broken heart, or quench your thirst for adventure!
9053.reading_mnemonic: <vocabulary>To heal something</vocabulary> it's sometimes necessary to do something <reading>いや</reading> (gross). Even if you dislike it, even if it's gross, you do it anyway, because you want to heal whatever it is.

examples.en: Thank you very much for using our company's service.
examples.ja: この度は弊社のサービスをご利用いただきまして誠にありがとうございます。
