examples.en: In case of cancellation, please contact our company's customer support.
examples.ja: キャンセルの場合は、お手数ではございますが弊社カスタマーサポートまでご連絡ください。

examples.en: This campaign may be terminated without notice depending on our company's circumstances.
examples.ja: 本キャンペーンは、弊社の都合により告知なしに終了する場合がございます。

9054.meaning_mnemonic: An <kanji>evil</kanji> <kanji>company</kanji> is actually <vocabulary>our company</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>our humble company</vocabulary>. We're not going to say our company is virtuous, are we? That wouldn't be humble at all. So instead we call it evil, to show our humility.
9054.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: The Big Dipper is made up of seven stars.
examples.ja: 北斗七星は七つの星で構成されています。

examples.en: On a clear night, we can see the Big Dipper from our window.
examples.ja: 晴れた日には、窓から北斗七星が見えるよ。

examples.en: This photo is the Big Dipper before dawn on November 3.
examples.ja: この写真は、１１月３日未明の北斗七星です。

9055.meaning_mnemonic: What can you see in the <kanji>north</kanji> that looks like a <kanji>ladle</kanji> and is made up of <kanji>seven</kanji> <kanji>star</kanji>s? That's the group of stars we call <vocabulary>the Big Dipper</vocabulary> or, depending on where you are in the world, perhaps <vocabulary>the Plough</vocabulary>.
9055.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji.

examples.en: Eighteen-liter containers are used to store things like detergent and oil.
examples.ja: 一斗缶は洗剤や石油などを保管するためのものです。

examples.en: That store has a promotion on five-gallon containers.
examples.ja: その店では、一斗缶のキャンペーンを行っています。

examples.en: Please stack these eighteen-liter containers in the corner over there.
examples.ja: この一斗缶をあそこのコーナーに積んでください。

9056.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>ladle</kanji> <kanji>can</kanji> is a <vocabulary>eighteen-liter container</vocabulary>, which is also a <vocabulary>five-gallon container</vocabulary>. That must be one big ladle!

If you live in Japan you've probably seen these. They're rectangular shaped containers made of metal that are used mostly for industrial purposes, for storing liquids like paint, fuel and chemicals. The 斗 actually refers to an old Japanese measurement, which is roughly equivalent to eighteen liters.
9056.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. Just watch out for the 一, which gets shortened to いっ.

examples.en: I remember playing cat's cradle when I was a child.
examples.ja: 子供の時、綾取りをしていたのを覚えています。

examples.en: The other day, I tried my hand at cat's cradle.
examples.ja: この間、綾取りに挑戦した。

examples.en: Mami taught us various games such as origami and cat's cradle.
examples.ja: マミさんには折り紙や綾取りなどいろいろな遊びを教えてもらいました。

9057.meaning_mnemonic: One <kanji>design</kanji> that you can <kanji>take</kanji> anywhere with you is <vocabulary>cat's cradle</vocabulary>, the game where you loop string around your hands and fingers to create patterns.
9057.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi for both kanji.

examples.en: Please insert a ten-yen or hundred-yen coin.
examples.ja: 十円または百円硬貨を入れてください。

examples.en: My grandmother saved coins in her wallet.
examples.ja: 祖母は財布の中に硬貨を貯めていました。

examples.en: What are some coins that are no longer being produced?
examples.ja: もう製造されていない硬貨にはどんなものがありますか。

9058.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Stiff</kanji> <kanji>freight</kanji> always has to be paid for in <vocabulary>coin</vocabulary>s, because coins are also stiff. You can't go paying for something stiff with something not stiff, that would make no sense at all.
9058.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: In light of the fact that this is a free service, there will be a limit to the number of participants.
examples.ja: 無料のサービスであることに鑑み、参加人数には制限を設けさせていただきます。

examples.en: Taking into account the global situation, we are making necessary changes.
examples.ja: 世界の状況を鑑みながら、必要な変更を行っています。

examples.en: In light of the importance of diet for health, we will support all citizens to eat a balanced diet.
examples.ja: 健康のための食事の重要性に鑑みて、すべての国民がバランスのとれた食事ができるようなサポートをしていきます。

9059.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You learned this kanji means "model," but it can also mean "<kanji>take into account</kanji>," so the verb version means <vocabulary>to take something into account</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be in light of</vocabulary>.

鑑みる literally comes from the idea of "looking at something closely to judge it." It's a formal word used to describe the act of thoughtfully considering something based on things like prior experiences or surrounding circumstances.

It's a transitive verb, but it can take を or に to mark the thing you're taking into account. Both particles are grammatically correct, but に sounds slightly more formal, which often matches the contexts where this word is used.
9059.reading_mnemonic:
This verb uses the kun'yomi of the kanji. You haven't learned that yet, so here's mnemonic to help you:

If you want <vocabulary>to take something into account</vocabulary>, you'll need to <reading>考</reading>える (かんが) about it really hard first. And when you do that thinking, it has <vocabulary>to be in light of</vocabulary> lots of other factors. Taking all those factors into account will help guide your next move, you know?

examples.en: There was an image of Buddha carved into the stone.
examples.ja: その石には仏像が彫ってありました。

examples.en: In front of this historic shrine, there's a gate with a swan carved on it.
examples.ja: この由緒ある神社の前には、白鳥が彫られた門がある。

examples.en: At the factory, I'm in charge of engraving text using an engraving machine.
examples.ja: 工場で、彫刻機を使って文字を彫る仕事を担当しています。

9060.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>carve</kanji> and the verb version is <vocabulary>to carve something</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to engrave something</vocabulary>.

This is a transitive verb, meaning it can take a direct object. You engrave letters into a stone, and you carve a scary face into a pumpkin. Those letters and that face are your objects.
9060.reading_mnemonic: Imagine trying <vocabulary>to carve something</vocabulary> using a <reading>hoe</reading> (ほ). Its long handle makes it a pretty impractical tool for carving. Now imagine all the trouble you have carving with it.

examples.en: The day before yesterday, I went to my junior high school class reunion.
examples.ja: 一昨日、中学の同窓会に行ってきました。

examples.en: I received an invitation to my elementary school reunion.
examples.ja: 小学校の同窓会の案内が来た。

examples.en: We would like to ask for the cooperation of all alumni in the activities of our alumni association.
examples.ja: 同窓会活動への同窓生の皆さまのご協力をお願いいたします。

9061.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>same</kanji> <kanji>window</kanji> <kanji>meeting</kanji> is a meeting with people who spent a long time gazing out of the same classroom window as you. Who are those people? They're your former classmates, and this is a <vocabulary>class reunion</vocabulary>. It can also mean <vocabulary>alumni association</vocabulary>, which is still something you do with former classmates, so it makes sense.
9061.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You didn't learn this reading for 窓, so here's mnemonic to help you:

If you have a <vocabulary>class reunion</vocabulary> coming up, you'd better work on your <reading>soul</reading> (そう). You want to make a good impression on all your old classmates, right? Well get to work on your soul right now, otherwise they might not be impressed.

examples.en: Big sis, carry me!
examples.ja: 姉ちゃん、抱っこして！

examples.en: My daughter sleeps soundly when I hold her in my arms.
examples.ja: 娘は抱っこをしているとぐっすり寝てくれます。

examples.en: We chose a carrier for our friend's baby.
examples.ja: 友達の赤ちゃんのために、抱っこひもを選びました。

9062.meaning_mnemonic: You know that the kanji means <kanji>hug</kanji> and the verb 抱く means "to hug". This noun is similar, but it usually means carrying by hugging, so <vocabulary>holding in one's arms</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>carrying</vocabulary>. This is one that children use a lot!
9062.reading_mnemonic: You learned this reading when you learned the kanji.

examples.en: Is it true that many male cats are left-handed?
examples.ja: 猫の雄に左利きが多いって本当ですか？

examples.en: Apparently all the puppies that were born were male!
examples.ja: 生まれた子犬、みんな雄だったみたい！

examples.en: The male golden-backed squirrel courts by making a frog-like croaking sound.
examples.ja: タイワンリスの雄は、カエルのような鳴き声を出して求愛します。

9063.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji means male and this also means male. It's mostly used for animals.

Note that this is often written in katakana, as オス.
9063.reading_mnemonic: <vocabulary>Male</vocabulary> animals can be kind of pushy, always trying <reading>to push</reading> (押す) other animals around, trying to be the alpha and all.

examples.en: If you're going to be a freeloader, you should at least learn to cook.
examples.ja: 居候をするなら、せめて料理くらいは覚えた方がいい。

examples.en: I can't say anything too strongly because I'm staying here for free.
examples.ja: 居候の身だから、あんまり強くは言うことはできないんだよね。

examples.en: So I lost my job and started living as a freeloader.
examples.ja: それで、仕事を失って、居候生活を始めたんです。

9064.meaning_mnemonic: To stay <kanji>alive</kanji> in some <kanji>climate</kanji>s, some have no choice but to be a <vocabulary>freeloader</vocabulary>. That is, <vocabulary>a lodger who pays nothing</vocabulary>. If you live somewhere with an inhospitable climate but you can't afford to pay rent, your only option is to live with someone for free.
9064.reading_mnemonic:
This is a slightly unusual case because both kanji use the kun'yomi. You haven't learned that reading for 候 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

What? You've become a <vocabulary>freeloader</vocabulary>? I can't believe you've gone <reading>so low</reading> (そうろう)!

examples.en: My husband does everything at his own pace and has gentle nature.
examples.ja: 夫はマイペースで、温厚な性格です。

examples.en: That person is usually mild-mannered, but when he gets angry, he's scary.
examples.ja: あの人、普段は温厚だけど、怒らせると怖いよ。

examples.en: If anything, I think I am on the mild-mannered side.
examples.ja: どちらかといえば、オレは温厚なほうだと思う。

9065.meaning_mnemonic:
When a <kanji>warm</kanji> temper is applied extra <kanji>thick</kanji>, it leads to a person having a <vocabulary>mild-mannered</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>gentle</vocabulary> personality.

Note that this is a more formal term, so you'll usually encounter it in writing.
9065.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You already know the on'yomi for 温, but not for 厚, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

The most <vocabulary>mild-mannered</vocabulary> Tofugu staff has to be <reading>on</reading>ion <reading>こう</reading>いち. It's an onion that jumps in for こういち whenever he's not at the office. He's the most <vocabulary>gentle</vocabulary> soul you could imagine, never yelling at anyone. The ideal boss, really.

examples.en: Do you know the origin of the name of this place?
examples.ja: この場所の名前の由来を知っていますか？

examples.en: We use ingredients from natural sources.
examples.ja: 自然由来の材料を使っています。

examples.en: This word comes from Latin.
examples.ja: この単語は、ラテン語に由来しています。

9066.meaning_mnemonic: What's the <kanji>reason</kanji> that something <kanji>come</kanji>s into being? Its <vocabulary>origin</vocabulary>, of course. Nothing can come into the world without a <vocabulary>source</vocabulary>, because it's always <vocabulary>coming from</vocabulary> somewhere.
9066.reading_mnemonic:
You didn't learn this reading for 由 so here's a mnemonic to help you:

The best way to get close to the <vocabulary>origin</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>source</vocabulary> of something is to move into a <reading>yu</reading>rt (ゆ). Yurts are easy to move around, so you can always get close to the source, wherever that may be.

examples.en: If you want to go to that restaurant, you can go there via Osaka or Kyoto.
examples.ja: そのお店なら、大阪経由でも京都経由でも行けますよ。

examples.en: Recently, I have been getting a little bit of work via social media.
examples.ja: 最近はSNS経由でちょこちょこお仕事をもらえるようになってきました。

examples.en: I think it's best to book your inn via the internet.
examples.ja: 旅館の予約は、インターネット経由で行うのが一番いいと思う。

9067.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>pass through</kanji> somewhere for a <kanji>reason</kanji>, so you're going <vocabulary>via</vocabulary> that place.
9067.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You learned this reading for 経 with the kanji, and you learned this reading for 由 with the word 由来. If you need an extra reminder for that one, here's a mnemonic just in case:

If you're going via an unfamiliar place, I recommend you seek out a <reading>yu</reading>rt (ゆ) to stay in. Wherever it is you're going via, you can't go wrong if you stay in a yurt.

examples.en: Kiyomizu Temple in Kyoto is a temple with a long history.
examples.ja: 京都の清水寺は由緒あるお寺だ。

examples.en: Just because he has a prestigious lineage, it doesn't make him a nice person.
examples.ja: 由緒ある家の人でも、いい人だとは限らない。

examples.en: It's the oldest and most venerable shrine in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本で最も古い由緒ある神社です。

9068.meaning_mnemonic:
The main <kanji>reason</kanji> behind your <kanji>connection</kanji> to some people is your <vocabulary>lineage</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>history</vocabulary>. Lineage and history tie people (especially families) together.

This word can be used for people with a prestigious family lineage as well as for historic buildings, especially temples and shrines.
9068.reading_mnemonic:
You didn't learn this reading for 由 with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

If you had good <vocabulary>lineage</vocabulary> you'd never make a <reading>U-ey</reading> (ゆい) on the highway. That's dangerous, and people with good lineage and a long history would simply never do such a thing.

examples.en: He is from a family of honorable lineage.
examples.ja: 彼は由緒正しい家系の出身です。

examples.en: This place was originally a venerable shrine.
examples.ja: ここは元々は由緒正しい神社なんですよ。

examples.en: I have fallen in love with a woman of honorable lineage.
examples.ja: 由緒正しい生まれの女性に恋をしてしまった。

9069.meaning_mnemonic: Someone or something whose 由緒 (lineage) is 正しい (correct) is <vocabulary>of honorable lineage</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>venerable</vocabulary> indeed.
9069.reading_mnemonic: You already know the readings for 由緒 and 正しい so you just need to put them together to read this word.

examples.en: It generally takes about two minutes.
examples.ja: 大体、二分くらいかかります。

examples.en: Shall we rest for fifteen minutes?
examples.ja: 十五分休みましょうか。

examples.en: It's about five minutes on foot from my apartment to a convenience store.
examples.ja: 私のアパートからコンビニまでは歩いて大体五分くらいです。

9070.meaning_mnemonic: What's <kanji>part</kanji> of an hour? A <vocabulary>minute</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>minutes</vocabulary>! This word is the suffix version of 分, so it goes after numbers to say how many minutes, and is used for telling the time too.
9070.reading_mnemonic: This uses a different on'yomi than what you learned with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember this reading: How many minutes of fun (ふん) will you have today? Lots and lots of minutes, I hope! Depending on the number before 分, its pronunciation can change to ぷん, because of rendaku. We're looking for the original reading ふん here though!

examples.en: Over there, I received sunflower seeds.
examples.ja: あそこで、ヒマワリの種をもらいました。

examples.en: When are you going to sow those seeds?
examples.ja: その種、いつまくの？

examples.en: Thanks, you've given me a good story to tell.
examples.ja: ありがとう、いい話の種ができたよ。

9071.meaning_mnemonic:
What <kanji>kind</kanji>s of <vocabulary>seed</vocabulary>s are you going to sow? Think about all the different kinds of seeds, and the kinds of plants they'll grow into.

This can also mean <vocabulary>source</vocabulary>, as in a source of worry or joy, or even of a good story.
9071.reading_mnemonic: Choose your <vocabulary>seed</vocabulary>s carefully, because you love to have a <reading>tan eh?</reading> (たね). You love tanning, so you don't want to plant anything that will grow tall and create shade. Choose those seed types carefully, and don't forget about your tan, eh?

examples.en: In this company, even young employees are entrusted with essential tasks.
examples.ja: この会社では、若い会社員にも重要な仕事を任せています。

examples.en: It's really important, so it can't be left to anyone else.
examples.ja: 本当に大事なことなので、他の人には任せられません。

examples.en: If you don't learn to delegate, you'll make things hard for yourself.
examples.ja: 任せることを学ばなければ、自分が大変になりますよ。

9072.meaning_mnemonic: If you pass a <kanji>duty</kanji> on to someone, that means you're going <vocabulary>to entrust something</vocabulary> to that person, or you're going <vocabulary>to delegate something</vocabulary>. In other words, you're going <vocabulary>to leave something to</vocabulary> them, so that they do it for you.
9072.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi of the kanji. You haven't learned that reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

In order <vocabulary>to entrust something</vocabulary> to someone, you need to <reading>make a</reading> (まか) list. It's no good delegating tasks if the person has no idea what to do, so be sure to make a list, okay?

examples.en: Can I leave my hairstyle decisions to you?
examples.ja: ヘアスタイルは、お任せでお願いできますか？

examples.en: I made a reservation for a 5000-yen omakase special.
examples.ja: 五千円のお任せコースで予約したよ。

examples.en: If you need legal advice, you can count on me!
examples.ja: 法律の相談は、私共にお任せください！

9073.meaning_mnemonic:
This word comes from 任せる, but without the る on the end it's a noun. You also have the honorific お on the beginning, which is a clue that you're addressing someone else. So you're entrusting something to the person you're talking to, and this means <vocabulary>leaving decisions to someone else</vocabulary>. This is used a lot in restaurants, where it means <vocabulary>chef's choice</vocabulary> or simply <vocabulary>omakase</vocabulary>. In other words, you're leaving the choice of food to the chef.

It can be used in other contexts, too, like if you leave your haircut up to your stylist or a flower arrangement up to the florist, or even if you follow the recommended program at the gym.
9073.reading_mnemonic: You learned this reading with the word 任せる, so I'll leave this one to you.

examples.en: Yesterday, my daughter was injured at school.
examples.ja: 昨日、娘が学校で怪我をしてしまいました。

examples.en: Even monsters get sick and injured.
examples.ja: 怪獣だって病気や怪我をします。

examples.en: I heard that the cause of that child's serious injury was a banana peel.
examples.ja: あの子の大怪我の原因って、バナナの皮らしいよ。

9074.meaning_mnemonic: Do you know how <kanji>suspicious</kanji> <kanji>I</kanji> get if I have an <vocabulary>injury</vocabulary>? I start suspecting everyone around me of having given me the injury. It was you, wasn't it?
9074.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi for both kanji. It also uses the less common reading け, which you learned with 怪, so here's a mnemonic to help you recall this reading:

Remember the suspicious soul and its <reading>ke</reading>ttle (け)? Yup, turns out this exact kettle is responsible for the <vocabulary>injury</vocabulary>. Suspicious souls and their kettles...

examples.en: I wonder how long it will take to thaw this turkey.
examples.ja: このターキー、解凍するのにどのくらい時間かかるかな？

examples.en: The defrosting method should be written on the packaging.
examples.ja: パッケージに解凍方法が書いてあるはずだよ。

examples.en: To open this file, you will need a file extractor.
examples.ja: このファイルを開くには、解凍ソフトが必要です。

9075.meaning_mnemonic:
If you <kanji>untie</kanji> something that's <kanji>frozen</kanji>, you're <vocabulary>thawing</vocabulary> it. The best way to go about <vocabulary>defrosting</vocabulary> anything is always to untie it first.

In the context of computer files, this word can also mean <vocabulary>unzipping</vocabulary>. We unzip files in English, but in Japanese we thaw them!
9075.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi for both kanji, so you should be able to read this one on your own.

examples.en: The new employee has abundant experience.
examples.ja: 新しい社員には豊富な経験があります。

examples.en: Carrots are a rich source of beta-carotene.
examples.ja: 人参にはベータカロテンが豊富に含まれている。

examples.en: This store has a wide selection of items.
examples.ja: この店は品ぞろえが豊富です。

9076.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi of both kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I'd like to know the opinions of both sides, not just one.
examples.ja: 片方だけでなく、双方の意見が知りたいですね。

examples.en: Marriage requires the consent of both parties.
examples.ja: 結婚には双方の合意が必要です。

examples.en: Both sides' claims are no closer to being reconciled.
examples.ja: 双方の主張は平行線をたどっています。

9077.meaning_mnemonic:
You've got a <kanji>pair</kanji> of <kanji>direction</kanji>s, so this is something that concerns <vocabulary>both parties</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>both sides</vocabulary>. Things are going in two directions, not just one! 

双方 is a relatively formal term that is often used in contexts like <vocabulary>mutual</vocabulary> agreements, negotiations, or discussions where both sides are actively engaged.
9077.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: In many sports, such as rugby, there are rules for substitution.
examples.ja: ラグビーなど、多くのスポーツで交代のルールがあります。

examples.en: My father and mother take turns making dinner every day.
examples.ja: 父と母は毎日交代で夜ごはんを作ります。

examples.en: The other day, there was a change of company president for the first time in sixteen years.
examples.ja: 先日、十六年ぶりに社長交代がありました。

examples.en: Could you switch in for me soon?
examples.ja: そろそろ交代してもらえませんか？

9078.meaning_mnemonic:
If you <kanji>mix</kanji> and <kanji>substitute</kanji> two people, that's a <vocabulary>change</vocabulary> of personnel, or a <vocabulary>substitution</vocabulary>. Perhaps those people are even working in <vocabulary>shift</vocabulary>s, so they mix and substitute each other at regular intervals.

You'll see this word in pretty diverse contexts, because it can refer to anything from a change of political regime, to the substitution of a player during a match, to factory shifts. The underlying meaning is that one person or group is switched out with another.
9078.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 代 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

A <vocabulary>change</vocabulary> calls for a <reading>tie</reading> (たい). If you're the new company president, or you're going in to work to start your shift, you'd better make sure you look the part, so get that tie nice and straight.

examples.en: The alien held down the man's head forcefully with his left hand.
examples.ja: 宇宙人は左手でガッと男の頭を押さえた。

examples.en: These words are important, so make sure to master them!
examples.ja: この単語は大事なので、しっかり押さえておきましょう！

examples.en: What's wrong? You're holding your stomach.
examples.ja: どうしたの、お腹押さえて。

9080.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji means <kanji>push</kanji>, and this verb means things like <vocabulary>to hold something down</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>to grasp something</vocabulary>. This verb is pretty versatile, and you can use it if you're holding down a piece of paper, holding a cloth to a wound, or grasping a concept.
9080.reading_mnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, so hopefully you can read this on your own.

examples.en: I need to start thinking about the menu for tonight.
examples.ja: そろそろ今晩の献立を考えないと。

examples.en: It is difficult to come up with a menu that will please everyone.
examples.ja: 全員に喜んでもらえる献立を考えるのは難しい。

examples.en: I always do my weekly meal plan by looking at the contents of my refrigerator.
examples.ja: 私は、いつも冷蔵庫の中身を見て一週間の献立を立てます。

9081.meaning_mnemonic:
I will <kanji>offer</kanji> you food and <kanji>stand</kanji> here while you eat it, because I curated this <vocabulary>menu</vocabulary> and I want to make sure you enjoy it.

This word doesn't mean the physical menu you get in a restaurant; rather, it refers to a <vocabulary>meal plan</vocabulary>, whether that means the sequence of courses for a single meal or the general meal plan for someone's entire week.
9081.reading_mnemonic:
You didn't learn this reading for 献 with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

The most special thing about the <vocabulary>menu</vocabulary> I curated for you? It's all <reading>con</reading>dor (こん) meat: deep-fried condor wings, condor yakitori, condor foie gras. As scavengers, condors aren't exactly the safest birds to put on a menu, so I'm going to stand here just in case you get sick and keel over mid-meal.

examples.en: This is my karate teacher, Jeff-sensei.
examples.ja: こちらは私の空手の先生、ジェフ先生です。

examples.en: I want to do karate at university too.
examples.ja: 大学でも空手をやりたいと思ってます。

examples.en: There's apparently a new karate dojo at the nearby sports center.
examples.ja: 近くのスポーツセンターに、新しく空手の道場ができたそうですよ。

9082.meaning_mnemonic: What can you do with <kanji>empty</kanji> <kanji>hand</kanji>s? <vocabulary>Karate</vocabulary>, that's what. Karate is practiced without weapons, so with empty hands!
9082.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi of both kanji, and you haven't learned this kun'yomi for 空 yet. As long as you know the meaning, the reading should be easy, but here's a mnemonic to help you just in case:

<vocabulary>Karate</vocabulary> comes from (<reading>から</reading>) Japan!

examples.en: I just arrived at the hotel where I will be staying during the business trip.
examples.ja: 今、出張先のホテルに着いたところだよ。

examples.en: During the business trip, I ate delicious food.
examples.ja: 出張先で、美味しい食べ物を食べた。

examples.en: My father is on an overseas business trip. He said that when business trips get prolonged, he misses his family.
examples.ja: 父は海外出張中なんです。出張が長引くと、家族が恋しくなると言っていました。

examples.en: Speaking of Nagoya, I've been there on a business trip. During the business trip, I was lucky to stay at a nice hotel.
examples.ja: 名古屋なら、出張で行ったことがあるよ。出張中、いいホテルに泊まれてラッキーだったよ。

9083.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji>exit</kanji> the building and <kanji>stretch</kanji> in preparation for your <vocabulary>business trip</vocabulary>. This is the routine you always follow for your business trips: exit, and stretch.
9083.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Just be careful about しゅつ becoming しゅっ here!

examples.en: Are you going to the office alone today?
examples.ja: 今日は一人で出社ですか？

examples.en: I'm sorry, the president hasn't come to work yet.
examples.ja: すみません、社長はまだ出社してないんです。

examples.en: I went to a cafe before going to work.
examples.ja: 出社する前にカフェに行きました。

9084.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>exit</kanji> somewhere in order to go to your <kanji>company</kanji>, that's <vocabulary>going to the office</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>arriving at the office</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>coming to work</vocabulary>.
9084.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Just watch out for  the しゅつ, which gets changed to しゅっ, as many つs do in this situation.

examples.en: Oh, our toilet paper is almost gone.
examples.ja: あ、トイレットペーパー、もうすぐ無くなるよ。

examples.en: I've run out of things to do and I'm bored.
examples.ja: することが無くなっちゃって、ヒマなんだよね。

examples.en: Honestly, since we've become a card-centric society, the need to carry cash has become almost obsolete, hasn't it?
examples.ja: 正直、カード社会になってから、キャッシュを持つ必要性ってほぼ無くなったよね。

9085.meaning_mnemonic:
Here we have <kanji>nothing</kanji>, followed by the verb なる. A verb that means "become nothing"? That'll be <vocabulary>to be gone</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to run out</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be lost</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to disappear</vocabulary>.

This can be translated in various ways depending on the situation, but just remember that it always refers to something changing from being there, to not being there.
9085.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi reading, which you learned with 無し, so you should be good to go.

examples.en: I wish I could get rid of my American accent in Japanese.
examples.ja: 日本語のアメリカなまりを無くしたいな。

examples.en: The most important thing is to do away with stress.
examples.ja: 何よりもストレスを無くすことが大切です。

examples.en: What do you think caused you to lose your self-confidence?
examples.ja: ご自身が自信を無くした原因は何だと思いますか。

9086.meaning_mnemonic:
This word ends with a う sound so you can guess it's a verb. The kanji means <kanji>nothing</kanji>, and you'll end up with nothing if you want to <vocabulary>to get rid of something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to do away with something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to lose something</vocabulary>.

This verb is transitive, so the action is happening to something. So maybe you're getting rid of debt, or discrimination, or stress... Whatever it is, there's a direct object with this verb!
9086.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi, which you already learned when you learned the word 無し.

examples.en: This is a photo that captures the springtime of my life.
examples.ja: これは青春時代の思い出の写真です。

examples.en: It's just like a page out of our youth!
examples.ja: まさに青春の１ページって感じだね！

examples.en: Emi, you're fully relishing your youth!
examples.ja: エミ、めっちゃ青春してるじゃん！

9087.meaning_mnemonic:
The time of <kanji>young</kanji> <kanji>spring</kanji> for humans is really just their <vocabulary>youth</vocabulary>. Just like plants in spring, your <vocabulary>adolescence</vocabulary> is when you start growing to your full potential! You might even say it's <vocabulary>the springtime of one's life</vocabulary>.

This generally refers to the period when you’re an energetic teenager and young adult. It can have connotations of exhilarating experiences and bittersweet feelings, as well as nostalgic memories.
9087.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned the on'yomi for 春 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Don't let your <vocabulary>youth</vocabulary> go to waste, because it will be over <reading>soon</reading> (しゅん)!

examples.en: Recycle the other kinds of trash.
examples.ja: その他のゴミはリサイクルして下さい。

examples.en: There are many other types than this.
examples.ja: その他色々なタイプありますよ。

examples.en: Is there anything else you would like to say to your ex?
examples.ja: その他に元パートナーへ言いたいことはありますか？

9088.meaning_mnemonic: その means "that" or "the", and その plus <kanji>other</kanji> means things like <vocabulary>the others</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>other</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>other than that</vocabulary>, depending on the context.
9088.reading_mnemonic: This has two readings, but luckily you learned one of them when you learned the kanji, and the other one when you learned the word 他. The two readings are usually interchangeable, too.

examples.en: This place is a tonkotsu ramen restaurant.
examples.ja: ここは豚骨ラーメンの店です。

examples.en: This pork bone ramen makes me feel nostalgic.
examples.ja: この豚骨ラーメンを食べると懐かしい気持ちになるよ。

examples.en: By all means, please come to Kyushu to eat tonkotsu ramen.
examples.ja: 是非、九州に豚骨ラーメンを食べに来て下さい。

9089.meaning_mnemonic: Pig bone ramen is tonkotsu ramen or, very logically indeed, pork bone ramen. 豚骨ラーメン is a type of Japanese ramen made with a rich, creamy broth from 豚骨 (pork bones). The bones are simmered for hours to extract the flavors, resulting in a flavorful and hearty soup. It's so delicious, you'll be back for more. Bone appetit!
9089.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You know both of these readings, but in case you need a reminder, here's a mnemonic to help you out:

You really like <vocabulary>tonkotsu ramen</vocabulary> so you just ate a whole <reading>ton</reading> (とん) of it. Imagine how you feel after eating a ton of <vocabulary>pork bone ramen</vocabulary>.

examples.en: There aren't many tonkatsu restaurants around here.
examples.ja: この辺は、豚カツ屋が少ない。

examples.en: I think I'll have the breaded pork cutlet set meal.
examples.ja: 豚カツ定食にしようと思います。

examples.en: Ahhh, why did I eat so much tonkatsu yesterday?
examples.ja: あーーー、なんで昨日あんなに豚カツ食べちゃったんだろう。

9090.meaning_mnemonic:
豚 comes from 豚肉 (pork), and カツ comes from the word "cutlet" and means just that. And a <kanji>pork</kanji> カツ is what any Japanese food fan will probably know as simply <vocabulary>tonkatsu</vocabulary>, a.k.a. <vocabulary>breaded pork cutlet</vocabulary>.

豚カツ is a Japanese pork cutlet coated in crispy panko breadcrumbs and deep-fried, making it light and crunchy. It's usually served with a tasty sweet-savory sauce. It's so good, you'll pig out on it!
9090.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the on'yomi of 豚. You haven't learned that yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You really like <vocabulary>tonkatsu</vocabulary> so you just ate a whole <reading>ton</reading> (とん) of it. Imagine how you feel after eating a ton of <vocabulary>breaded pork cutlet</vocabulary>.

examples.en: I'll add five more Amazon gift cards to the giveaway for every 100 retweets I get!
examples.ja: 100RT毎にプレゼントのアマギフを5枚追加するよ！

examples.en: Right now I'm giving him formula roughly every three hours.
examples.ja: 今は大体三時間毎にミルクをあげてる。

examples.en: We have our car inspected once every year.
examples.ja: うちの車は、一年毎に点検に出しています。

9091.meaning_mnemonic:
Add a に to <kanji>every</kanji> and you get <vocabulary>for every</vocabulary>. This means something happens <vocabulary>at intervals of</vocabulary> a certain time frame or milestone, like <vocabulary>once every</vocabulary> year, month, day, etc.!

Note that this is very frequently written in hiragana, but you'll encounter the kanji version as well, especially when it follows a number.
9091.reading_mnemonic:
This uses the kun'yomi reading of 毎, which you haven't learned yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

<vocabulary>For every</vocabulary> kanji you burn, you <reading>go to</reading> (ごと) Tokyo Disneyland as a reward. It's a bit of an expensive habit, but I think you deserve it.

examples.en: When my mother saw this, she was absolutely furious.
examples.ja: それを見た母は、大激怒でした。

examples.en: He stormed off in a fit of rage.
examples.ja: 彼は激怒してその場を立ち去りました。

examples.en: This movie made significant changes to the original work, which infuriated the fans.
examples.ja: この映画は、原作を改変しすぎて、ファンを激怒させました。

examples.en: Putting one's shoes on a bench may be fine in other countries, but in Japan it would cause indignation.
examples.ja: 土足でベンチに上がるの、海外ならいいかもしれないけど、日本では激怒ものだよ。

9094.meaning_mnemonic:
Being <kanji>fierce</kanji> and <kanji>angry</kanji> means you're filled with <vocabulary>rage</vocabulary>, or for you to <vocabulary>be enraged</vocabulary>.

激怒 is a relatively formal word, often used in literature to describe someone flying into a rage or experiencing intense, uncontrollable anger. Therefore, you’ll frequently encounter this as a suru-verb in the form of 激怒する.
9094.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

9095.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>wing</radical> is something you <kanji>must not</kanji> do anything with. Wings are fragile (think bird's wings and butterfly's wings) and sometimes dangerous (like the wings of a plane) and you must not touch them, or even go near them! You MUST NOT. You. MUST. NOT.
9095.reading_mnemonic: Apart from staying away from wings, the other thing you <kanji>must not</kanji> do is eat <reading>mochi</reading> (もち). Okay, they're not fragile or dangerous, but I love mochi and I don't want you eating them.

examples.en: Of course we have that product in our store.
examples.ja: その商品なら、うちの店にも勿論ありますよ。

examples.en: Of course I want to be able to speak Japanese, but I also want to be able to speak French.
examples.ja: 日本語も勿論ですが、フランス語も喋れるようになりたいです。

examples.en: Needless to say, there are people who can study in between looking after children, but it's difficult for me.
examples.ja: 勿論、子育ての合間に勉強が出来る人もいるだろうけど、私には難しいです。

9096.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>must not</kanji> consider this a <kanji>theory</kanji>, because <vocabulary>of course</vocabulary> it's a fact. <vocabulary>Needless to say</vocabulary>, this is the way things are.

This word is often written in kana, but it's worth knowing the kanji version too.
9096.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the readings you learned with the kanji. <vocabulary>Needless to say</vocabulary>, you should be able to read this on your own!

examples.en: It's wasteful to throw away food, isn't it?
examples.ja: 食べ物を捨てるのは勿体ない事ですよね。

examples.en: It's such a waste that you went to Japan but never got to see a taiko performance.
examples.ja: 折角日本に行ったのに、太鼓の演奏を見ることができないなんて勿体ないですよね。

examples.en: Ayano-chan, you're too good for Ryohei!
examples.ja: 綾乃ちゃんは、亮平には勿体ないよ。

9097.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>must not</kanji> use your <kanji>body</kanji> for anything <vocabulary>wasteful</vocabulary>, because that would be <vocabulary>a waste</vocabulary>. You're <vocabulary>too good</vocabulary> for that!

This word is used in all kinds of situations where there's a feeling that something is going to waste, including food, money, time, talent, and opportunities. You can also use it to say that someone is too good for a job, or even for another person. While it's usually written in kana, you'll see it in kanji too.
9097.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the readings you learned with the kanji, except that もち becomes もっ.

examples.en: Do your best, Eito.
examples.ja: 頑張れよ、瑛斗。

examples.en: The pro athlete Eito Tanaka is over there!
examples.ja: あそこに田中瑛斗選手がいるよ！

examples.en: Singer-songwriter Eito rose to fame on social media.
examples.ja: シンガーソングライターの瑛斗は、ソーシャルメディアで有名になりました。

9098.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>crystal</kanji> <kanji>ladle</kanji> is the Japanese given name <vocabulary>Eito</vocabulary>. If you know the singer-songwriter Eito, imagine him holding a crystal ladle. If not, any Eito will do! Other public figures with the name include pro baseball player Tanaka Eito (田中 瑛斗) and Takarazuka actor Namiki Eito (波輝 瑛斗).
9098.reading_mnemonic:
This name uses the on'yomi for both kanji, and you learned both these readings with the kanji. Get yourself a crystal ladle to celebrate!

Note: This name can also sometimes be read あきと, as is the case for pro baseball player Takabe Akito (髙部 瑛斗).

examples.en: This morning, Ryota-kun appeared in my dream.
examples.ja: 今朝、夢に遼太君が現れた。

examples.en: I heard that Ryota and Ayano are dating.
examples.ja: 遼太と綾乃ちゃん、付き合ってるらしいよ。

examples.en: Ryota, wake up quickly or you'll be late!
examples.ja: 遼太、早く起きないと遅刻するよ！

9099.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Distant</kanji> <kanji>fat</kanji> makes up the Japanese given name <vocabulary>Ryota</vocabulary>. Imagine soccer player Noguchi Ryota (野口 遼太) kicking a fat soccer ball into the distance while voice actor Asari Ryota (浅利 遼太) commentates.
9099.reading_mnemonic:
This name uses the on'yomi for both kanji. You haven't learned this particular on'yomi for 太 yet though, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

<vocabulary>Ryota</vocabulary>'s diet consists only of <reading>ta</reading>cos (た). Tacos, tacos, tacos for breakfast, lunch and dinner. Yum!

examples.en: Ryohei is a popular boy's name.
examples.ja: 亮平は人気のある男の子の名前です。

examples.en: I saw the famous Japanese actor Suzuki Ryohei up close the other day.
examples.ja: この間、日本の有名な俳優の鈴木亮平を間近で見たよ。

examples.en: Ryohei-kun loves manga and he wants to go to Tokyo to study drawing.
examples.ja: 亮平君は漫画が好きで、東京に出て絵の勉強をしたいと思っています。

9100.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Clear</kanji> <kanji>flat</kanji> is one way to write the Japanese given name <vocabulary>Ryohei</vocabulary>. 

Some well-known people with the name include metal sculptor Miyada Ryohei (宮田 亮平), actor Suzuki Ryohei (鈴木 亮平), and model and actor Ōtani Ryohei (大谷 亮平), who acts in both Japanese and Korean films and dramas.
9100.reading_mnemonic: Unlike most Japanese names, this one actually uses the on'yomi of both kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Yay for easy names!

examples.en: When I was a child, I was friends with a very innocent girl called Ayano.
examples.ja: 子供の頃、綾乃というとても無邪気な女の子と友達だった。

examples.en: Ayano called the other day but she didn't leave a voicemail message.
examples.ja: 先日、綾乃さんから電話があったんですが、留守電にメッセージが入っていなかったんです。

examples.en: Ayano-chan and Ryohei-kun are having a fistfight, but what should I do?
examples.ja: 綾乃ちゃんと亮平君が殴り合いをしているけど、どうしよう。

9101.meaning_mnemonic: This is a <kanji>design</kanji> <kanji>from</kanji> <vocabulary>Ayano</vocabulary>. Do you know an Ayano who's good at designing things? A couple creative Ayanos include traditional Okinawan folk singer and sanshin player Uema Ayano (上間 綾乃), and author Takeda Ayano (武田 綾乃) who won the Yoshikawa Eiji Literary Newcomer Award in 2021.
9101.reading_mnemonic: This name uses the readings that you learned with the kanji, so you should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I believe that person's spouse is called Daisuke.
examples.ja: その方の配偶者は大輔さんという方だと思います。

examples.en: Daisuke was deeply impressed.
examples.ja: 大輔はとても感銘を受けた。

examples.en: Do you know what Daisuke-kun's family name is?
examples.ja: 大輔君の苗字は何か知ってる？

9102.meaning_mnemonic:
Who's a <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>help</kanji>? That'll be <vocabulary>Daisuke</vocabulary>!

Famous Daisukes include film director and screenwriter Itō Daisuke (伊藤 大輔), figure skater Takahashi Daisuke (髙橋 大輔), and actor and singer Namikawa Daisuke (浪川 大輔).
9102.reading_mnemonic:
This name uses the on'yomi for 大 and the nanori for 輔. You learned both of these with the kanji, so that should be a big help.

Note: Historically, this name can be read たいふ or おおすけ, as is the case for Heian period poet 伊勢大輔, whose name can be read either いせのたいふ or いせのおおすけ. In modern contexts, you'll only need to know だいすけ though, not to worry!

examples.en: Ryoichiro, do you have a nickname?
examples.ja: 諒一郎って、あだ名とかあるの？

examples.en: I've started going out with Ryoichiro-kun.
examples.ja: 諒一郎君と付き合うことになったんだ。

examples.en: Ryoichiro is out right now.
examples.ja: 諒一郎は今、外出中です。

9103.meaning_mnemonic:
If you only <kanji>comprehend</kanji> <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>guy</kanji>, make that guy <vocabulary>Ryoichiro</vocabulary>.

The name 諒一郎 isn't very common, but it's worth learning because the kanji 諒 is used in lots of names, and both 諒 and 一郎 are names in their own right. So by learning this name, you should be able to read a whole lot of other names, too.
9103.reading_mnemonic: You learned all the readings in this name with the kanji. What could be easier to comprehend?

examples.en: I'm planning to go on a trip to Korea with Riko-chan.
examples.ja: 今度、莉子ちゃんと韓国旅行に行く予定なんだよね。

examples.en: Riko puts on a bit of a good girl act, doesn't she?
examples.ja: 莉子って、ちょっとぶりっ子じゃない？

examples.en: I'm sorry for the trouble our Riko has caused you.
examples.ja: うちの莉子が、ご迷惑をおかけしました。

9104.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Jasmine</kanji> <kanji>child</kanji> is one way to write the girl's name <vocabulary>Riko</vocabulary>. Imagine fashioning a child out of jasmine, and calling her Riko. Examples of people named Riko include pop star and singer Fukumoto Riko (福本 莉子) and idol and actress Nakayama Riko (中山 莉子).
9104.reading_mnemonic: You learned this reading for 莉 with the kanji, and I bet you're very familiar with this reading for 子 by now. A lot of Japanese girls' names that end in 子, too.

examples.en: The king showed up riding his prized fast horse.
examples.ja: 王は、自慢の駿馬に乗って姿を現した。

examples.en: The daimyo was presented with a number of fine horses.
examples.ja: その大名には、数々の駿馬が献じられた。

examples.en: She made a successful bid of 100 million yen for a fine horse with a very good coat.
examples.ja: とても良い毛並みの駿馬を一億円で落札した。

9105.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>speed</kanji> <kanji>horse</kanji> is a <vocabulary>fast horse</vocabulary>, and a <vocabulary>fine horse</vocabulary>. This word isn't very common, but it does come up in horse racing contexts, and creative writing.
9105.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji, which you already know. However, 馬 uses a bit of a special reading here: め. So here’s a mnemonic to help you remember this: 

This <vocabulary>fast horse</vocabulary> is so fast that all you can see whenever it speeds past you are its shiny bright <reading>目</reading> (め). Imagine this fast horse zooming past you over and over, but all you ever see are its white 目.

examples.en: The sky was crimson in the sunset, and it was very beautiful.
examples.ja: 空が夕焼けで茜色に染まっていて、とても綺麗でした。

examples.en: We drank champagne while looking at the madder red sky.
examples.ja: 茜色の空を見ながら、シャンパンを飲んだ。

examples.en: Look, the sky is turning a fiery dark red color!
examples.ja: 見て、空が燃えるような茜色になってきてるよ。

9106.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Rose madder</kanji> <kanji>color</kanji> is more simply called <vocabulary>madder red</vocabulary>, which is a kind of <vocabulary>deep red</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>crimson</vocabulary>. This word is used most often to describe the color of the sky at sunset in literature.
9106.reading_mnemonic: The readings are the same as the ones you learned with the kanji.

examples.en: On Sunday, we plan to walk the Kumano Kodō and see Nachi Falls.
examples.ja: 日曜日は、熊野古道を歩いて、那智の滝を見に行く予定です。

examples.en: This is the best photo I could get of Nachi Falls, which I went to the other day.
examples.ja: これは、この間行った那智の滝で一番よくとれた写真です。

examples.en: Nachi Falls has been designated a national beauty spot.
examples.ja: 那智の滝は、国の名勝に指定されています。

9107.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>What</kanji> <kanji>wisdom</kanji> <kanji>waterfall</kanji> is <vocabulary>Nachi Falls</vocabulary>, one of the most famous (and wisest) waterfalls in Japan.
9107.reading_mnemonic: You learned all three of these readings with the kanji, so you should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Entertainment in the Edo period was joruri and kabuki.
examples.ja: 江戸時代の娯楽は、浄瑠璃や歌舞伎だった。

examples.en: I got a ticket for a ningyo joruri performance.
examples.ja: 人形浄瑠璃のチケットをもらいました。

examples.en: This time, we interviewed a creator of joruri puppets.
examples.ja: 今回は、浄瑠璃人形の作り手にインタビューをしました。

9108.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>cleanse</kanji> a <kanji>lapis lazuli</kanji> rock until it goes <kanji>glassy</kanji>, you can use it in a <vocabulary>joruri</vocabulary> performance. In case you haven't heard of joruri, it's traditional Japanese chanted storytelling, sort of like a <vocabulary>ballad</vocabulary>, that's accompanied by shamisen music, and often puppets.
9108.reading_mnemonic: You learned all these readings with the kanji, so you should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Riko showed up wearing a bright blue dress at the place she was meeting Ryoichiro.
examples.ja: 莉子は、瑠璃色のワンピースを着て諒一郎との待ち合わせ場所に現れた。

examples.en: Bright blue and spherical in shape, the higotai is a very pretty flower.
examples.ja: ヒゴタイは、瑠璃色で丸い形をした、とても可愛い花です。

examples.en: Suddenly, a beautiful bright blue insect that looked like a jewel caught my eye.
examples.ja: ふと、瑠璃色の美しい宝石のような虫が目にとまった。

9109.meaning_mnemonic:
What is <kanji>lapis lazuli</kanji> <kanji>glassy</kanji> <kanji>color</kanji>? It's <vocabulary>bright blue</vocabulary>. If you've never seen the rock lapis lazuli, look it up and you'll see why this means bright blue!

This word is generally used in literature.
9109.reading_mnemonic: You learned all three of these readings when you learned the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Ryota's face turned pale with anger.
examples.ja: 遼太は怒りで顔面蒼白になった。

examples.en: The patient's face was pallid and he looked extremely weak.
examples.ja: 患者は蒼白な顔をしていて、非常に弱々しく見えました。

examples.en: The General, who had been awake all night, sat down to breakfast, looking as pale as a ghost.
examples.ja: 一晩中起きていた元帥は、まるで幽霊のように蒼白な顔をして朝食の席についた。

9110.meaning_mnemonic: If you're <kanji>pale</kanji> <kanji>white</kanji>, you're <vocabulary>pale</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>pallid</vocabulary>. This word is usually used to talk about the <vocabulary>pallor</vocabulary> of someone's face.
9110.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word and uses the on'yomi for both kanji. You learned those readings with the kanji, so you should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Takuya-san is an admirable man.
examples.ja: 拓哉さんは殊勝な男性です。

examples.en: Takuya and Eito shared a hug under the crimson sky.
examples.ja: 茜色の空の下で拓哉と瑛斗は抱擁を交わしました。

examples.en: The celebrity Kimura Takuya is so famous in Japan that everyone calls him by his nickname, Kimutaku.
examples.ja: タレントの木村拓哉は、日本ではとても有名で、キムタクという愛称で親しまれています。

9112.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>cultivation</kanji> of a <kanji>question mark</kanji> is something that only people called <vocabulary>Takuya</vocabulary> can do. Imagine a famous Takuya, like actor and singer Kimura Takuya (木村 拓哉 a.k.a. キムタク), or a Takuya you know, cultivating a huge field of question marks. Rows and rows of question marks. I wonder what he's going to do with all those question marks once they're ready to harvest. Other people who must have an abundance of question marks are pro baseball player Kinoshita Takuya (木下 拓哉 a.k.a. キノタク) and actor, model, and K-Pop star Terada Takuya (寺田 拓哉).
9112.reading_mnemonic: You learned both of these readings with the kanji, so you should be able to read this name on your own.

examples.en: Sugahara's a cool surname, isn't it?
examples.ja: 菅原っていう苗字、なんかかっこよくね？

examples.en: Oh, Sugawara-san, do you have a cold?
examples.ja: あれ、菅原さん、風邪ですか？

examples.en: At Sugawara Shoe Store, I bought a pair of stylish leather shoes.
examples.ja: 菅原靴店で、オシャレな革靴を買った。

9113.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Sedge</kanji> <kanji>field</kanji> is both <vocabulary>Sugahara</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>Sugawara</vocabulary>, the Japanese family names. Sedgefield is a family name (and a place-name) in English too, so that might help you with this one!

This is a very old surname, said to have originated with Nara period scholar Hanishi-no-sukune (土師宿禰) who changed his name to Sugawara-no-furuhito (菅原古人). Historically, the name has been associated with scholars and writers, including prominent Heian period statesman, scholar, and poet Sugawara-no-michizane (菅原道真) and noblewoman, writer, and poet Sugawara-no-takasue-no-musume (菅原孝標女), also known more simply as Lady Sarashina in the English speaking world.
9113.reading_mnemonic:
The only reading you haven't learned for this name is the irregular わら reading for 原, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

<vocabulary>Sugawara</vocabulary>-san went to <reading>war a</reading> (わら) long time ago, but these days he enjoys a quiet life tending to his <kanji>sedge</kanji> <kanji>field</kanji>s.

examples.en: May I pour you some sake?
examples.ja: お酌をさせていただいてもよろしいですか。

examples.en: Manager, it is discriminatory to have female employees fill others' glasses just because they are female.
examples.ja: 部長、女性社員だからという理由で酌をさせるのは差別ですよ。

examples.en: What, you're gonna turn down me pouring you alcohol?!
examples.ja: 何だ、お前、俺の酌を断るのか！？

9114.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>serve</kanji> someone, you're <vocabulary>pouring alcohol</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>pouring sake</vocabulary> for them. You're <vocabulary>filling someone's glass</vocabulary>.
9114.reading_mnemonic: You learned this reading with the kanji. Cheers!

examples.en: In Japanese trials there is something called "making allowances for extenuating circumstances".
examples.ja: 日本の裁判には「情状酌量」とよばれるものがあります。

examples.en: I don't think there's scope to make allowances for extenuating circumstances.
examples.ja: 情状酌量の余地はないと思います。

examples.en: Concluding that the defendant's circumstances should be taken into consideration, the judge commuted the sentence.
examples.ja: 被告人には酌量すべき情状があると判断し、裁判官は刑を減軽した。

9115.meaning_mnemonic: If you <kanji>serve</kanji> someone a certain <kanji>quantity</kanji> of understanding, you're <vocabulary>making allowances</vocabulary>. You're <vocabulary>taking into consideration</vocabulary> all extenuating circumstances.
9115.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi for both kanji. You learned these readings with the kanji, so you should be able to read this on your own.

meanings: To Pour Each Other A Drink

examples.en: Do you remember the day we drank sake here together?
examples.ja: あの日、ここで酒を酌み交わしたこと、覚えているか。

examples.en: Then they poured each other a drink, and drank to a vow of brotherhood.
examples.ja: そして、二人は杯を酌み交わし、兄弟の誓いを立てた。

examples.en: I wonder if one day we'll be able to share a family drink together.
examples.ja: いつか、親子で酒を酌み交わす日が来るのかなあ。

9116.meaning_mnemonic: 酌む means "to serve" and the kanji 交 means <kanji>mix</kanji>. What happens if you serve and mix together? You're going <vocabulary>to pour each other a drink</vocabulary> because you plan  <vocabulary>to drink together</vocabulary>.
9116.reading_mnemonic:
You haven't learned this reading for 交 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

All the bars are closed so you and your friends are going <vocabuarly>to drink together in your <reading>ca</reading>r (か). You set up a little bar in the back of your car and settle down for some drinks. It's cramped but cosy.</vocabuarly>

examples.en: This is a love poem he composed for his girlfriend.
examples.ja: これは、彼が恋人のために詠った愛の詩です。

examples.en: In this epic poem, a grand romance is recited.
examples.ja: この叙事詩では、壮大なロマンが詠われている。

examples.en: She always spun her words as if she was composing a poem.
examples.ja: 彼女はいつも、詠うように言葉を紡いだ。

9117.meaning_mnemonic: The verb form of <kanji>compose</kanji> is <vocabulary>to compose</vocabulary>. This particular verb is usually used in relation to poetry, and can also mean <vocabulary>to recite</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to sing</vocabulary>, though more in the sense of singing someone's praises than singing a song.
9117.reading_mnemonic: This word shares the same origin as 歌う and 唄う, and they share the same readings as well.

examples.en: Everyone, do you know who wrote this poem?
examples.ja: みなさんは、誰がこの詠歌を書いたのが知っていますか？

examples.en: Just before he was assassinated, he had written a poem.
examples.ja: 彼は、暗殺される直前に、一つの詠歌をしたためていた。

examples.en: Chanting Buddhist teachings in the form of a waka poem with a melody is called "goeika".
examples.ja: 仏教の教えを和歌の形にして、旋律に乗せて唱えるものを御詠歌といいます。

9118.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>compose</kanji>d <kanji>song</kanji> is a <vocabulary>poem</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>song</vocabulary>. This can also refer to the act of <vocabulary>composing a poem or song</vocabulary>, which makes a lot of sense given the kanji.

This is used particularly when referring to waka poetry.
9118.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi for both kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I marveled at the beauty of the sunset I saw from the top of that mountain.
examples.ja: その山の頂上から見た夕日の美しさに詠嘆した。

examples.en: This sentence is filled with a deep feeling of "I wonder if this might be the last time."
examples.ja: この文には、「これが最後かもしれないんだなあ」という詠嘆の意味が込められています。

examples.en: The word "keri," often used in waka poetry, is an auxiliary verb of exclamation.
examples.ja: 和歌でよく使われる「けり」という言葉は、詠嘆の助動詞です。

9119.meaning_mnemonic:
If you <kanji>compose</kanji> something with a <kanji>sigh</kanji>, it's because you're experiencing a <vocabulary>deep feeling</vocabulary>. You might express this deep feeling with an <vocabulary>exclamation</vocabulary>, as you <vocabulary>marvel</vocabulary> at the wonders of the world.

This word can be used for a range of deep feelings, good or bad, and can also be used for the expression of those feelings, so you'll notice that the English translation varies quite a bit depending on the context.
9119.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi for both kanji. You should be able to read it on your own.

examples.en: The Azusa River is usually very calm.
examples.ja: 普段の梓川はとても穏やかです。

examples.en: At the weekend, I was soothed by the clarity of the water in Azusa River.
examples.ja: 週末は梓川の水の透明感に癒やされてきました。

examples.en: Of course, Azusagawa-san is a talented singer, but the lyrics of her songs are also really good.
examples.ja: 梓川さんの歌唱力が高いのは勿論だけど、曲の歌詞もすごくいいんだよね。

9120.meaning_mnemonic: <kanji>Japanese birch</kanji> <kanji>river</kanji> is <vocabulary>Azusa River</vocabulary> or simply <vocabulary>Azusagawa</vocabulary>. Azusagawa is both the Japanese name for the Azusa River, and a Japanese family name.
9120.reading_mnemonic: You learned both of these readings with the kanji. You just need to remember that rendaku turns かわ into がわ.

examples.en: This is the story of Yamada someone or other.
examples.ja: これは、山田某の話である。

examples.en: Wasn't it a guy named Suzuki something?
examples.ja: たしか、鈴木某とかいう人じゃなかったっけ？

examples.en: I heard you-know-who from that drama troupe has done it again.
examples.ja: あそこの劇団の某がまた何かやらかしたらしいぞ。

9121.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji means <kanji>certain</kanji>, but when it's used as a standalone word, or after a family name, it means things like <vocabulary>someone or other</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>you-know-who</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>something</vocabulary>. It's basically a vague way to refer to someone who's name you've forgotten, or you don't want to mention for some reason.
9121.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi of the kanji, and you haven't learned that yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You bump into <vocabulary>someone or other</vocabulary>, and just as you're wondering what on earth her name is, her <reading>nanny gashe</reading>s (なにがし) her on the leg. It looks like it hurts. Poor <vocabulary>you-know-who</vocabulary>, whatever her name is. The nanny looks horrified, and is trying to patch her up.

examples.en: I teach in a country that sends a lot of exchange students to Japan.
examples.ja: 日本に留学生を多く送りこんでいる某国で教えています。

examples.en: Azusagawa-san worked as a temporary employee at a certain country's embassy.
examples.ja: 梓川さんは派遣員として某国大使館に勤めていました。

examples.en: We can't shake the suspicion that Sara Sugawara is a spy for a certain country.
examples.ja: 菅原沙羅が某国のスパイであるという嫌疑はぬぐえません。

9122.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi for both kanji, and you learned those readings with the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I went to an event held at a certain place in Tochigi Prefecture.
examples.ja: 栃木県の某所で行われたイベントに行ってきました。

examples.en: Last night, there was a taiko performance by a celebrity at a certain place.
examples.ja: 昨夜、某所にて、有名人による太鼓の演奏会が行われたようです。

examples.en: I was eating at an izakaya in a certain place in Tokyo when I met my girlfriend.
examples.ja: 彼女と出会ったのは、都内某所の居酒屋で食事をしている時だった。

9123.meaning_mnemonic: No surprises here. A <kanji>certain</kanji> <kanji>place</kanji> is <vocabulary>a certain place</vocabulary>.
9123.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi for both kanji, and you learned those readings with the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: I met with one of the judges.
examples.ja: 審査員の某氏に会いました。

examples.en: A certain person close to the president commented, "We've put ourselves in a difficult situation".
examples.ja: 社長に近い立場の某氏は、「難しい状況にしてしまった」とコメントしている。

examples.en: A certain person told me that Koichi is going to conquer the world one day.
examples.ja: 「こういちはいつか世界を征服する」と某氏が語っていた。

9124.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>certain</kanji> <kanji>family name</kanji> belongs to <vocabulary>a certain person</vocabulary>.
9124.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi for both kanji, and you learned those readings with the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: Sara-san and I bowed to each other and parted ways.
examples.ja: 沙羅さんと会釈をして別れました。

examples.en: Sara is going to plant the seedlings with Takuya.
examples.ja: 沙羅は拓哉と一緒に苗を植えるつもりです。

examples.en: Did you know that the impressionist Sara comes from Nagoya?
examples.ja: ものまね芸人の沙羅さんが名古屋出身だって知ってた？

9126.meaning_mnemonic: If <kanji>sand</kanji> is <kanji>spread out</kanji> you get the given name <vocabulary>Sara</vocabulary>. You've written your name in sand, right? Now imagine a Sara you know spreading out sand so that it spells her name. Or imagine a pro athlete, like wrestler Doshō Sara (土性 沙羅), judoka Asahina Sara (朝比奈 沙羅), or ski jumper Takanashi Sara (髙梨 沙羅) spreading out the sand. I bet they'd find some skillful ways to do it.
9126.reading_mnemonic: This name uses the on'yomi for both kanji, and you learned those readings with the kanji.

examples.en: There's a lot of sediment in the riverbed.
examples.ja: 川底にはたくさんの土砂がたまっている。

examples.en: Due to the tsunami, a large amount of earth and sand flowed into the second-floor classroom.
examples.ja: 津波で大量の土砂が二階の教室に流れ込んだ。

examples.en: After an earthquake there's a danger of landslides.
examples.ja: 地震の後には土砂災害の危険があります。

9127.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word and it uses the on'yomi for both kanji. This on'yomi for 砂 is a bit less common, and you haven't learnt it yet, so here's a mnemnonic to help you:

If there's too much <vocabulary>sediment</vocabulary>, you need to speak to a <reading>sha</reading>man (しゃ) about it. Only a shaman has the power to get rid of all that <vocabulary>earth and sand</vocabulary> and get the river flowing again.

examples.en: Asphalt is gravel that's hardened with petroleum.
examples.ja: アスファルトは、砂利を石油で固めたものなんですよ。

examples.en: The uranium mine is at the end of this gravel road.
examples.ja: ウラン鉱山はこの砂利道の先にあります。

examples.en: I think it would be a shame to spread gravel over the garden when we could grow vegetables.
examples.ja: 折角野菜を育てられるのに、庭に砂利を敷いてしまうのはもったいないと思うんだけど。

9128.meaning_mnemonic: If <kanji>sand</kanji> makes a lot of <kanji>profit</kanji>, it swells up and becomes <vocabulary>gravel</vocabulary>. They're like the fat cats of the beach.
9128.reading_mnemonic:
You learned the reading for 利 with the kanji, but the reading for 砂 is irregular, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You're walking through that big fat <vocabulary>gravel</vocabulary>, when a pile of it starts moving, and something suddenly leaps out at you. It's a... <reading>ja</reading>guar (じゃ)! Run!

examples.en: Then I watched the sunrise from Mt. Fuji.
examples.ja: そして、ふじ山から日の出をみました。

examples.en: It's almost sunrise!
examples.ja: もうすぐ日の出だ！

examples.en: It was a beautiful sunrise.
examples.ja: きれいな日の出だったね。

9131.meaning_mnemonic: What do we call the <kanji>sun</kanji>'s <kanji>exit</kanji> from the horizon? That'll be the <vocabulary>sunrise</vocabulary>. Imagine the sun exiting the horizon and climbing up into the sky.
9131.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kanji's kun'yomi readings, which you've already learned. As long as you remember those, you should be good to go!

examples.en: One draft beer, please.
examples.ja: 生ビール、一つ下さい。

examples.en: This is a draft beer dispenser.
examples.ja: これは生ビールのサーバーです。

examples.en: Can I get a draft beer to go?
examples.ja: 生ビールはテイクアウトできますか？

9141.meaning_mnemonic:
You just learned the vocab 生, meaning fresh. Combined with the katakana word for beer makes this draft beer or unpasteurized beer.

Note that while in a lot of countries, "draft beer" refers only to beer that's drawn from a keg, 生ビール can also refer to unpasteurized canned or bottled beer, giving it a shorter shelf-life, but also keeping it fresh.
9141.reading_mnemonic: Be careful to use kun'yomi for 生 here. Other than that, as long as you know your katakana, you should be good to go!

examples.en: This hotel was originally an apartment.
examples.ja: このホテルは元々アパートだったんです。

examples.en: That model used to be a designer, right?
examples.ja: あのモデルさんって、元々はデザイナーだったんでしょ？

examples.en: This house originally had a bathroom and kitchen in it.
examples.ja: 元々この家にはトイレもキッチンもあったんです。

9142.meaning_mnemonic:
It's the <kanji>origin</kanji> of all <kanji>origin</kanji>s, so it's the way it was <vocabulary>originally</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>from the beginning</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>by nature</vocabulary>. You get the idea.

Note that this is frequently written in just hiragana, but you'll encounter the kanji version too!
9142.reading_mnemonic: This is just the kun'yomi reading you learned with 元, but twice, so you should be good to go!

examples.en: I got a text from my ex-partner.
examples.ja: 元パートナーからテキストがきた。

examples.en: Oh, it's the same as my ex-partner's necklace.
examples.ja: あ、それ、元パートナーのネックレスといっしょだ。

examples.en: This is a video of me skiing with my ex-partner at Mt. Fuji.
examples.ja: これは、ふじ山で元パートナーとスキーをしたときのビデオだよ。

9143.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>origin</kanji> partner is a partner you had originally, but don't have anymore. In other words, this is your <vocabulary>ex-partner</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>former partner</vocabulary>.

Like in English, this word is fairly formal, and it covers any kind of ex-partner, including business and romantic partners.
9143.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi of 元 and then it's just kana, so you should know how to read this!

examples.en: This is heartening data!
examples.ja: これは心強いデータですね！

examples.en: It's reassuring to have a professional player as my partner.
examples.ja: プロのプレイヤーがパートナーになってくれるなんて、心強いです。

examples.en: The teacher's advice became a reassuring support for our students.
examples.ja: 先生の助言は、私たち学生にとって心強いサポートとなりました。

9145.meaning_mnemonic: Things that make your <kanji>heart</kanji> <kanji>strong</kanji> are <vocabulary>reassuring</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>heartening</vocabulary> to hear. You can practically feel your heart becoming stronger in your chest.
9145.reading_mnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You learned them when you learned the words 心 and 強い, so you should be able to read this on your own. Just note that つよい gets rendaku'd to づよい!

examples.en: Canada is located in North America.
examples.ja: カナダは北アメリカにあります。

examples.en: Is this river in North America?
examples.ja: これって北アメリカの川ですか？

examples.en: I went camping in the mountains of North America.
examples.ja: 北アメリカの山でキャンプをしました。

9147.meaning_mnemonic:
You already encountered アメリカ in the previous level, so you should know that it means "America." Put <kanji>north</kanji> in front of this and you get <vocabulary>North America</vocabulary>, just like in English!

Note that 北アメリカ refers to the continent of North America, as opposed to the northern part of the USA. アメリカ on its own usually means the USA, but when it has "north" or "south" in front of it like this, it's always referring to the continents.
9147.reading_mnemonic: You might be tempted to read this using the on'yomi readings, but this actually uses kun'yomi. You learned that reading with the kanji, so you should have no problems reading this!

examples.en: I'm at the north exit!
examples.ja: 北口にいるよ！

examples.en: The convenience store is located at the north exit.
examples.ja: コンビニは北口にあります。

examples.en: Can you message me when you get to the north exit?
examples.ja: 北口についたら、メールしてくれる？

9148.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 入り口 means "entrance" and 出口 means "exit"? This vocab is just the 口 part with a direction added to it. This also makes it both an entrance or exit. So when you have the kanji for <kanji>north</kanji>, it makes this both a <vocabulary>north exit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>north entrance</vocabulary>. This is a great word to know if you need to know which side of a train station you need to leave on to go somewhere or meet someone!
9148.reading_mnemonic: Just like 入り口 and 出口, this also uses kun'yomi readings. And just like before, watch out for the rendaku that changes くち to ぐち!

examples.en: This suit jacket doesn't have an inside pocket.
examples.ja: このスーツのジャケットには内ポケットがありません。

examples.en: This notebook fits into the inside pocket of a bag.
examples.ja: このノートは、バッグの内ポケットに入ります。

examples.en: Look, that kid's putting bugs in his inside pocket.
examples.ja: 見て、あの子、内ポケットに虫を入れてるよ！

9150.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>inside</kanji> ポケット is your <vocabulary>inside pocket</vocabulary>.
9150.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi for the kanji. You learned that reading when you learned the word 内.

examples.en: An orange stone entered the river.
examples.ja: オレンジ色の石ころが川に入った。

examples.en: There are a lot of pebbles on this beach.
examples.ja: このビーチ、石ころがたくさんあるね。

examples.en: There are many pebbles in front of the entrance.
examples.ja: 入り口の前は石ころが多いです。

9151.meaning_mnemonic: You've already learned 石, which means <kanji>stone</kanji>. You haven't seen ころ before, but it's sometimes used as a casual suffix for small, round things. Put the two together, and you've got a <vocabulary>small stone</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>pebble</vocabulary>.
9151.reading_mnemonic:
This uses the kun'yomi of 石, which you've already learned, and adds a bit of hiragana, so you should be able to read this! If you need help remembering the ころ bit, though, here's a mnemonic for you:

Even a <vocabulary>small stone</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>pebble</vocabulary> could have something amazing at its <reading>core</reading> (ころ). I mean, anything at all could be in that core! Gold, diamonds… Maybe even a chocolate filling! You'd better gather up some small stones and pebbles and start bashing them open to look at their cores. Otherwise, you could be missing out.

examples.en: The man worked at a gas station on the outskirts of town.
examples.ja: 男は町外れにあるガソリンスタンドで働いていた。

examples.en: I'm staying at a hotel on the outskirts of town, that doesn’t even have a convenience store nearby.
examples.ja: 近くにコンビニすらない町外れのホテルにステイしてるんだ。

examples.en: How did you get this far out of town?
examples.ja: こんな町外れまで、どうやって来たの？

9152.meaning_mnemonic: You already know that 町 means "town" and that 外れ can mean "periphery" or "outskirts." This is just a combination of the two, so it means the <vocabulary>outskirts of town</vocabulary>.
9152.reading_mnemonic: You've already learned both 町 and 外れ, so just combine the two and you get 町外れ not only in meaning, but also in reading!

meanings: To Go Out Into The World
To Be Released To The Public

examples.en: It's a dream come true to have my work published.
examples.ja: 自分の作品が世に出るなんて、夢みたいだ。

examples.en: Once a photo or video goes out in the world, it becomes a digital tattoo and stays on the Internet forever.
examples.ja: 一度世に出た写真やビデオは、デジタルタトゥーとなってずっとネットに残るんだよ。

examples.en: In today's concert, I will perform pieces that have never before been released to the public.
examples.ja: 今日のコンサートでは、今まで世に出る機会がなかった曲たちを演奏します。

9154.meaning_mnemonic: Here we have <kanji>world</kanji> with the particle に, following by the verb 出る (to go out). Put that together and this means <vocabulary>to go out into the world</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to be published</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be released to the public</vocabulary> in some way or another. Once it's out there in the world, there's even a chance for it <vocabulary>to become renowned</vocabulary>.
9154.reading_mnemonic: This uses kun'yomi readings for both kanji, which you should already know by now, so I think you're good to go!

examples.en: Fine, I'll have someone else do it!
examples.ja: いいよ、他の人にしてもらうから！

examples.en: Oh, you don't want it? Then I'll give it to someone else.
examples.ja: え、いらないの？じゃあ、他の人にあげるね。

examples.en: Huh, so you deceived someone else!
examples.ja: へー、それで他の人をだましたんだ！

9155.meaning_mnemonic:
Here you have <kanji>other</kanji> and <kanji>person</kanji> joined together by the particle の, which shows that "other" is describing "person". So this means <vocabulary>someone else</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>other people</vocabulary>.

This is more general than 他人, which you already learned. 他の人 can be anyone that's not the speaker, or not the person being talked about. 他人, on the other hand, has an added implication that the person is someone unknown or unrelated.
9155.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kanji's kun'yomi readings, which you've already learned. As long as you remember those, you should be good to go!

examples.en: The elevator is located at the west exit.
examples.ja: エレベーターは西口にあります。

examples.en: I'll be at the cafe at the west exit!
examples.ja: 西口のカフェにいますね！

examples.en: I always take a cab from the west exit.
examples.ja: いつも西口からタクシーにのります。

9158.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 北口 from a couple levels ago, and how 入り口 means "entrance" and 出口 means "exit?" Combine that 口 meaning with the kanji for <kanji>west</kanji>, and you get <vocabulary>west exit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>west entrance</vocabulary>.
9158.reading_mnemonic: This follows the same pattern as 入り口, 出口, and 北口, so it uses kun'yomi readings. And just like with those, make sure to watch out for the rendaku that changes くち to ぐち!

examples.en: Today, we're going to learn about Napoleon The Third.
examples.ja: 今日は、ナポレオン三世について学びましょう。

examples.en: Napoleon III was born in the year 1808.
examples.ja: ナポレオン三世は1808年に生まれた。

examples.en: Napoleon Bonaparte is more famous than Napoleon III, isn't he?
examples.ja: ナポレオン・ボナパルトはナポレオン三世より有名ですよね。

9159.meaning_mnemonic: Adding "third generation" to someone's name means that they are the third generation of people with that name. In this case, the person's name is ナポレオン (Napoleon), so this means <vocabulary>Napoleon The Third</vocabulary>, also written as <vocabulary>Napoleon III</vocabulary>.
9159.reading_mnemonic: The kanji here are pronounced exactly the same as in the standalone word 三世. That is, it's a jukugo word which uses the on'yomi for both kanji.

examples.en: I took a selfie with my smartphone.
examples.ja: スマホで自撮りした。

examples.en: Oh, I don't have my selfie stick.
examples.ja: あれ、自撮り棒がない。

examples.en: Here are some tips on how to take a good selfie easily.
examples.ja: 簡単に上手な自撮りができるコツをお伝えします。

9160.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi of 自, which you learned with the kanji, and the kun'yomi of 撮, which you learned with the word 撮る. Though it's a bit of an unusual combo, you can probably guess the first one since it's such a common reading, and the second one because of the り on the end. Just watch out for rendaku, which turns とり into どり.

examples.en: The coming-of-age ceremony is an important milestone in one's life.
examples.ja: 成人式は、大切な人生の節目です。

examples.en: Then that year, something happened that would become a major turning point in my life.
examples.ja: そしてその年、人生の大きな節目になる出来事が起こったんです。

examples.en: In hindsight, I guess that was a critical juncture.
examples.ja: 今から思うと、あれが一つの節目だったんだろうね。

9161.meaning_mnemonic: What <kanji>season</kanji>s should you keep an <kanji>eye</kanji> on? The seasons that are <vocabulary>turning point</vocabulary>s in your life. Keep an eye on those seasons, because you don't want to miss the <vocabulary>critical juncture</vocabulary>s and <vocabulary>milestone</vocabulary>s.
9161.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi of both kanji. You haven't learned that yet for 節, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

The real <vocabulary>turning point</vocabulary> in your life was when you got yourself a <reading>few she</reading>ep (ふし). Owning a few sheep was a true <vocabulary>milestone</vocabulary> for you. Now you have all the wool sweaters and cheese you could ever want!

examples.en: Every joint in my body is throbbing somehow.
examples.ja: なんか体の節々がズキズキする。

examples.en: That person makes some harsh word choices, huh?
examples.ja: あの人、言葉の節々にトゲがあるよね。

examples.en: Saori woke up with pains in various joints.
examples.ja: 早織は節々の痛みを感じて目を覚ました。

9165.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>joint</kanji> <kanji>joint</kanji>s are your <vocabulary>various joints</vocabulary>, or even <vocabulary>every joint</vocabulary> in your body, or a specific body part. When we're not talking about the joints in your body, this means something like <vocabulary>various parts</vocabulary>, referring to various parts of a whole.
9165.reading_mnemonic: This is just the kun'yomi of 節, which you learned with 節目, repeated twice. Keep in mind that the second ふし gets rendaku'd to ぶし!

examples.en: I wish I had ten million dollars.
examples.ja: 一千万ドルがほしいなぁ。

examples.en: I won ten million yen in the lottery!
examples.ja: ロトで一千万円ゲットしたんだ！

examples.en: Ten million people came to the concert.
examples.ja: コンサートには一千万人の人がきました。

9166.meaning_mnemonic:
You already know that 一千 is "<kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>thousand</kanji>," and that 万 is "<kanji>ten thousand</kanji>." Add all those zeros together (or multiply 1,000 with 10,000) and you end up with <vocabulary>ten million</vocabulary>. 

You learned that 千 is the more common and default way to say 1,000 and 一千 is sometimes used for emphasis or clarity. Well, to say ten million, you almost always say it as 一千万. I mean, who wouldn't want to emphasize ten million! It's ten million, you know?
9166.reading_mnemonic: You already learned how to read both 一千 and 万, so just put those two readings together and you're good to go!

examples.en: There are a lot of rice paddies in Asia.
examples.ja: アジアには田んぼがたくさんある。

examples.en: This is a rice field for jasmine rice.
examples.ja: これはジャスミンライスの田んぼです。

examples.en: Please do not enter the paddy in high heels.
examples.ja: 田んぼにハイヒールで入らないで下さい。

9167.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that the kanji 田 means <kanji>rice paddy</kanji>, so it should be easy to work out that this word also means <vocabulary>rice paddy</vocabulary>.

田んぼ is a common way to say "rice paddy," especially in casual conversation. You can tell because if you ever came across a ju<reading>mbo</reading> (んぼ) rice paddy, you'd probably say something like, "Whoa, that's one jumbo 田んぼ!" When a 田んぼ is that jumbo, the surprise makes your speech naturally more relaxed and informal.
9167.reading_mnemonic: This word has hiragana attached to the kanji, which is a good sign that the reading is kun'yomi. You learned that reading when you learned the kanji, so you should be good to go.

examples.en: There's a crescent moon today.
examples.ja: 今日は三日月です。

examples.en: You have eyes that are like a crescent moon.
examples.ja: 三日月のような目をしてますね。

examples.en: You can see the crescent moon well from the top of the mountain.
examples.ja: 山の上から三日月がよく見える。

9169.meaning_mnemonic: What's a "third day moon"? It's a <vocabulary>crescent moon</vocabulary>. A crescent moon is the newly visible moon that appears on the third day of the month in the lunar calendar that Japanese people used back in the day.
9169.reading_mnemonic:
The word comes from 三日 and 月, but the readings are slightly different. There's no small つ in the reading for 三日, and you need to rendaku 月, all to make it easier to pronounce. Try reading it aloud yourself to see what I mean!
To write the character づ, type "du" on your keyboard.

examples.en: I went to Nishiki Market in Kyoto on Sunday.
examples.ja: 日曜日に京都の錦市場に行きました。

examples.en: These are chopsticks I bought at Nishiki Market.
examples.ja: これは錦市場で買ったお箸です。

examples.en: I bought tamago-yaki at Nishiki Market and ate it while walking around.
examples.ja: 錦市場で卵焼きを買って食べ歩きをしました。

9170.meaning_mnemonic:
You might already know 市場 means "market," like in 株式市場 (stock market). So is this a <kanji>brocade</kanji> market? Well, "brocade" actually refers to the name of a street here, not brocade fabrics. It's a place name, so we can just call this the <vocabulary>Nishiki Market</vocabulary>!

錦市場 is a famous food market on a street called 錦小路 (Nishiki Kōji) in Kyoto, and it's packed with delicious local specialties. Give it a quick search if you haven't heard of it! Maybe your next travel destination?
9170.reading_mnemonic: As you could probably guess from the meaning, 錦 is read にしき here. 市場 is usually read with kun'yomi when it refers to a real, physical street market.
