You haven't learned this reading for 市場 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you: There's one thing you look for when you visit Nishiki Market: an itchy baa (いちば). Sheep go "baa," and the ones you buy must be exceptionally itchy. Itchy baas produce the best mutton and wool, so you keep an eye out for them whenever you go to Nishiki Market!

examples.en: Oh, I can see the Milky Way!
examples.ja: あ、天の川が見える！

examples.en: On a clear day, you can also see the Milky Way.
examples.ja: 天気の良い日には、天の川を見ることもできます。

examples.en: The two can meet by crossing the Milky Way just once a year. Isn't that romantic?
examples.ja: 二人は年に一回だけ、天の川を渡って会うことができるんです。ロマンチックでしょ？

9174.meaning_mnemonic: You're looking at <kanji>heaven</kanji>'s <kanji>river</kanji>, or the river of heaven. There's only one river in heaven (i.e., the sky), and that's the <vocabulary>Milky Way</vocabulary>!
9174.reading_mnemonic:
This is two individual words connected with a の, so it uses kun'yomi readings. You haven't learned this reading for 天 yet, so we've got a mnemonic to help you. Also watch out for the rendaku on 川, turning it into がわ!

What does the <vocabulary>Milky Way</vocabulary> remind you of? It kind of looks like a shining piece of <reading>armor</reading> (あま). Look at it in the sky, shimmering like a piece of silver armor. Uncanny, no? 

To summarize: The 天 is read あま here, and the 川 gets rendaku'd to がわ. Add a の inbetween and the full reading for this vocab is あまのがわ!

examples.en: Oh, wait a moment!
examples.ja: あ、ちょっとまって！

examples.en: I think it's a little different.
examples.ja: ちょっとちがう気がする。

examples.en: I'll think about it a little.
examples.ja: ちょっと考えてみるよ。

9176.meaning_mnemonic: You <reading>chort</reading>le (ちょっと) <vocabulary>a little</vocabulary> at a silly joke. You can’t help chortling <vocabulary>for a moment</vocabulary>. Go ahead, chortle just a little, for just a moment, to help you remember this word.

examples.en: Good morning, Miho-chan!
examples.ja: ミホちゃん、おはよう！

examples.en: I texted "good morning" to Mike.
examples.ja: マイクに「おはよう」とメールをした。

examples.en: Ugh, I'm sleepy... morning.
examples.ja: うーっ、ねむいー、おはよう。

9177.meaning_mnemonic:
From <reading>Ohio</reading> (おはよう), you shout <vocabulary>good morning</vocabulary>. Why Ohio? Because that's where you woke up this morning. Imagine yourself waking up in Ohio, and wishing everyone "good morning" at the top of your lungs.

おはよう is a casual way to say "good morning." It can also be written in kanji, but hiragana is much more common.

examples.en: Did you book a hotel already?
examples.ja: ホテル、もうとった？

examples.en: I'm just about to check out of the hotel.
examples.ja: 今、ホテルをチェックアウトするところ。

examples.en: Which hotel will you stay at?
examples.ja: どこのホテルにステイするの？

9178.meaning_mnemonic:
ホテル comes from the English word <vocabulary>hotel</vocabulary> and the meaning is exactly the same!

The only thing to watch out for is that the "l" on the end becomes ル, because that's the closest sound in Japanese.

examples.en: This one is Mt Fuji.
examples.ja: これがふじ山です。

examples.en: This is a pen.
examples.ja: これはペンです。

examples.en: Give me two of these, please.
examples.ja: これを二つ下さい。

9179.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Colle</reading>ct (これ) <vocabulary>this one</vocabulary> right here! Go ahead, collect this one.

You can use これ to talk about anything that's close to you. Things that are close to you are easy to collect, after all!

examples.en: What do you want to do for Christmas?
examples.ja: クリスマス、どうする？

examples.en: If you don't, someone else will.
examples.ja: あなたがしなくても、だれかがするよ。

examples.en: Shoot there with all your might.
examples.ja: そこで、力いっぱいシュートをするんだ。

9180.meaning_mnemonic:
It's only <reading>through</reading> (する) doing things that we get better at them, so you need <vocabulary>to do</vocabulary> them as much as you can.

する basically means <vocabulary>to do</vocabulary>, but it’s incredibly versatile and goes beyond its English equivalent. Besides being used alone, it can be put together with a whole range of nouns to turn them into verbs. We call these する verbs and you'll learn a lot of them as we go along!

examples.en: Two apple juices, please.
examples.ja: リンゴジュース、二つ下さい。

examples.en: Do you want an apple or a banana?
examples.ja: リンゴかバナナ、いる？

examples.en: This apple tastes bad!
examples.ja: このリンゴ、まずい！

9181.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Ringo</reading> (リンゴ) just ate your <vocabulary>apple</vocabulary>! You were about to take a bite, and he grabbed it. What is Ringo doing snatching apples? Surely he can afford his own.

Did you know that Ringo Starr once appeared in a Japanese TV commercial for <vocabulary>apple</vocabulary> juice? That might help you remember this word, too!

リンゴ is also commonly written in hiragana, and even in kanji, but you’ll probably see it in katakana the most.

examples.en: Do you want a cup of coffee?
examples.ja: コーヒー、のむ？

examples.en: Should we have a coffee break soon?
examples.ja: そろそろコーヒーブレークにする？

examples.en: One hot coffee, please.
examples.ja: ホットコーヒー、一つ下さい。

9182.meaning_mnemonic:
コーヒー is the katakana version of the English word <vocabulary>coffee</vocabulary>. 

Just watch out for the second syllable, which changes to ヒー in Japanese.

examples.en: Hello Sensei.
examples.ja: 先生、こんにちは。

examples.en: Hello Aya.
examples.ja: アヤちゃん、こんにちは。

examples.en: Hello, I'm Jenny.
examples.ja: こんにちは、ジェニーです。

9183.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Connie Chihua</reading>hua (こんにちは) says <vocabulary>hello</vocabulary>. Connie Chihuahua is an amazing talking chihuahua. She can only say "hello", but that alone is pretty impressive.

こんにちは is a formal way to say "hello". It’s generally used during the daytime, from late morning to early evening. Watch out for the は on the end, which is always pronounced わ.

examples.en: When will you do it?
examples.ja: いつするの？

examples.en: Until when are you in the U.S.?
examples.ja: いつまでアメリカ？

examples.en: From when will you be in Canada?
examples.ja: いつからカナダ？

9184.meaning_mnemonic:
He <reading>eats</reading> (いつ) and eats and eats. <vocabulary>When</vocabulary> does this guy not eat?

いつ is a question word that is used to ask <vocabulary>when</vocabulary>.

examples.en: Which one of these ties shall I give as a gift?
examples.ja: プレゼントのネクタイ、どれにする？

examples.en: Can you tell which ones are tasty onions?
examples.ja: どれがおいしい玉ねぎか、分かる？

examples.en: Hmm, which one should I cut first?
examples.ja: えっと、どれから切ればいい？

9185.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Do re</reading> (どれ) mi fa sol la ti... <vocabulary>which one</vocabulary> of these notes are you going to start singing from?

The question word どれ is used to ask <vocabulary>which one</vocabulary> out of three or more choices.

examples.en: I'm going to speak on TV now.
examples.ja: 今から、テレビでしゃべるんだ。

examples.en: What, you're going on TV?
examples.ja: えっ、テレビに出るの？

examples.en: I'll turn on the TV immediately!
examples.ja: すぐにテレビをつけるよ！

9186.meaning_mnemonic:
テレビ comes from the English word <vocabulary>television</vocabulary>. It’s been shortened, which is really common with loanwords in Japanese. The "vi" sound becomes ビ, too.

テレビ is sometimes written as "TV", but even then it’s usually pronounced テレビ.

examples.en: Yep, let's do that!
examples.ja: うん、そうしよう！

examples.en: Yeah, sorry, that's wrong.
examples.ja: うん、ごめん、ちがう。

examples.en: Yep, it's yummy!
examples.ja: うん、おいしい！

9187.meaning_mnemonic:
Wanna play <reading>Un</reading>o (うん)? <vocabulary>Yep</vocabulary>! 'Course I do. I always wanna play Uno.

うん is a casual way to say <vocabulary>yes</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>yeah</vocabulary>, so you’d generally use it with friends and family, and in other informal situations.

examples.en: "Mr. Chandler." "Yes!"
examples.ja: 「チャンドラーさん」「はい！」

examples.en: Yes, thank you very much.
examples.ja: はい、ありがとうございます。

examples.en: Yes, understood.
examples.ja: はい、分かりました。

9188.meaning_mnemonic:
Want me to write a <reading>hai</reading>ku (はい)? <vocabulary>Yes</vocabulary>, of course!

はい is a formal word for "yes". You can use it to let someone know they’re right, or simply that you’re listening, as well as to respond if someone says your name.

examples.en: If it's that notebook you mean, it's on my desk.
examples.ja: そのノートなら、デスクの上だよ。

examples.en: Did you take good notes on the lesson?
examples.ja: レッスン、ちゃんとノートにまとめた？

examples.en: I need an A4 size notebook, you know.
examples.ja: A4サイズのノートがいるんだよね。

9189.meaning_mnemonic:
ノート is a shortened form of <vocabulary>notebook</vocabulary>, with an extra "o" on the end since you can’t end a word with "t" in Japanese.

You can also use this to mean <vocabulary>notes</vocabulary>, in the context of taking down notes in a class.

examples.en: Goodbye Sensei.
examples.ja: 先生、さようなら。

examples.en: Goodbye January. Hello February.
examples.ja: さようなら、一月。こんにちは、二月。

examples.en: So long, and thanks for all the fish.
examples.ja: さようなら、今までサカナをありがとう。

9190.meaning_mnemonic:
I <reading>saw your Nara</reading> (さようなら), but I then had to say <vocabulary>goodbye</vocabulary>. It was just a short trip, but at least I saw your Nara.

さようなら is a formal way to say goodbye, so a good word to use with colleagues and teachers.

A quick tip before I say goodbye: さようなら often drops its middle う, becoming さよなら.

examples.en: Oh, good evening.
examples.ja: あ、こんばんは。

examples.en: Good evening, everyone.
examples.ja: みなさん、こんばんは。

examples.en: Good evening. Nice work today!
examples.ja: こんばんは〜、おつかれさまです！

9191.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Con ban, wah!</reading> (こんばんは) cries your friend, just as you say <vocabulary>good evening</vocabulary>. There's a report on the evening news about a con ban (yes, that's a ban on conning people). Wah! Exciting stuff.

You can use こんばんは as a greeting from around 5pm or 6pm, in both formal and informal situations.　Watch out for that は on the end, which is pronounced わ here too.

examples.en: That looks fun!
examples.ja: それ、おもしろそうだね！

examples.en: Oh, you're going to go for that?
examples.ja: え、それにするの？

examples.en: That's not candy, that's an eyeball.
examples.ja: それはキャンディじゃなくて目玉です。

9192.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Sorry</reading> (それ), can you grab <vocabulary>that one</vocabulary> for me? Yeah, <vocabulary>that</vocabulary>, thanks!

You can use それ for things that are close to the person you're talking to, or fairly close to both of you.

examples.en: Oh, you work part-time at a convenience store?
examples.ja: え、コンビニでバイトしてるの？

examples.en: Convenience store rice balls are so good!
examples.ja: コンビニのおにぎりっておいしいよね！

examples.en: Oh, there's a convenience store over there!
examples.ja: あ、あそこにコンビニがある！

9193.meaning_mnemonic:
コンビニ comes from the English word <vocabulary>convenience store</vocabulary>, but who has time for all those syllables? That's why they cut it down to "conveni". So much more convenient that way.

Watch out for the “v” sound, which usually becomes “b” in Japanese, and this word is no exception.

examples.en: I'm in the department store restroom right now.
examples.ja: 今、デパートのトイレにいる。

examples.en: They had that at the department store.
examples.ja: それ、デパートにあったよ。

examples.en: I saw Leo at the department store!
examples.ja: レオなら、デパートで見かけたよ！

9194.meaning_mnemonic: デパート comes from  <vocabulary>department store</vocabulary>. Yet another shortened loanword! There's an extra "o" sound on the end of this one, since a word can't end in "t" in Japanese.

examples.en: Oh, excuse me! I'm sorry!
examples.ja: あ、すみません！ごめんなさい！

examples.en: Excuse me, where's the "Ocean Hotel"?
examples.ja: すみません、オーシャンホテルってどこですか。

examples.en: Excuse me, is now a good time?
examples.ja: すみません、今ちょっといいですか？

9195.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Sue me, Ma Sen!</reading> (すみません), you yell at Ma Sen, before quickly adding "<vocabulary>Excuse me</vocabulary>…<vocabulary>I'm sorry</vocabulary>, so <vocabulary> sorry</vocabulary>!" You shouldn't have shouted at Ma Sen like that. You hope she won’t actually sue you.

You can use すみません both to apologize and to get someone’s attention. This expression is really common in Japan, and dropping it in wherever you can will help you blend right in!

examples.en: No, it's not.
examples.ja: いいえ、ちがいます。

examples.en: No, you have the wrong person.
examples.ja: いいえ、人ちがいです。

examples.en: No, it's not England. It's Canada.
examples.ja: いいえ、イギリスじゃないです。カナダです。

9196.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Eeh! Eh?</reading> (いいえ) <vocabulary>No</vocabulary>! You’re so surprised by whatever the question was, you can only manage "Eeh! Eh? No!" in response.

いいえ is a formal word for "no", so you can use it to answer politely in the negative.

examples.en: Is this your blog?
examples.ja: これ、あなたのブログですか？

examples.en: What would you do in that kind of situation?
examples.ja: こんなとき、あなたならどうしますか？

examples.en: I miss you darling.
examples.ja: あなたがいなくてさみしいです。

9197.meaning_mnemonic:
"<reading>A gnat, ah!</reading> (あなた). I’m going to get <vocabulary>you</vocabulary>! Yes YOU," you shout as you swat at that pesky gnat buzzing around your head.

あなた is a lot less common than “you” in English, but you’ll come across it in adverts, online forums, and textbooks, where it’s used to address a general, anonymous audience. Some people also use it with their significant other, in which case it sounds intimate, like "darling". In casual conversations, though, it can come off as standoffish, so it's better to use someone's name or social title (like "teacher") instead.

examples.en: Who's this?
examples.ja: この人、だれ？

examples.en: Please look at this page.
examples.ja: このページを見てください。

examples.en: Sorry, my schedule is full on this day.
examples.ja: ごめん、この日はスケジュールがいっぱいなんだ。

9198.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how これ means "this one"? Well, この simply means <vocabulary>this</vocabulary>. The difference is that これ is used on its own, whereas この goes before a noun. For example, この人 means "this person".

Notice how words like this starting with こ are close to you? We'll be learning a few more of these, and they all follow the same pattern!

examples.en: Isn't that Emily over there?
examples.ja: あれ、エミリーじゃない？

examples.en: That one over there is my house.
examples.ja: あれがオレのうちだよ。

examples.en: That was terrible, to say the least.
examples.ja: いくらなんでもあれはヒドいよ。

9199.meaning_mnemonic:
You need <reading>a le</reading>ns (あれ)? How about <vocabulary>that one over there</vocabulary>? You’re in a camera shop picking out a new lens, and that one over there looks good.

Use あれ to refer to something that's far from both you and the person you're talking to.

examples.en: It says this bread costs $5.
examples.ja: このパン、５ドルだって。

examples.en: Is that U.S. dollars? Or is it Canadian dollars?
examples.ja: それって米ドル？それともカナダドル？

examples.en: The dollar to yen rate finally reached 150 yen to the dollar.
examples.ja: ついにドル円のレートが１ドル＝１５０円になった。

9200.meaning_mnemonic:
ドル is the Japanese version of the English word <vocabulary>dollar</vocabulary>. 

The dollar symbol $ is also common in Japanese, and the pronunciation is still ドル.

examples.en: Which child is Maria?
examples.ja: どの子がマリアちゃん？

examples.en: I wonder which hotel I should stay at.
examples.ja: どのホテルにしようかな。

examples.en: When can you do it?
examples.ja: どのタイミングでできますか？

9201.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how どれ means "which one"? どの has a very similar meaning: <vocabulary>which</vocabulary>. Whereas どれ is used on its own, どの is used before a noun to ask "which" out of three or more options. So for example, どの本 is "which book (out of that pile)?".

Notice how question words often start with a ど? We'll be seeing more of these!

examples.en: I don't have any money at all.
examples.ja: お金がぜんぜんない。

examples.en: Do you have scissors?
examples.ja: ハサミ、ない？

examples.en: I don't have scissors, but I do have a cutter.
examples.ja: ハサミはないけど、カッターならあるよ。

examples.en: "Moommm, I want apple!" "I can't give you what I don't have, Hana-chan."
examples.ja: 「ママぁー、りんご、ほしい！」「ないものはないのよ、はなちゃん。」

9202.meaning_mnemonic: The <reading>kni</reading>fe (ない) is <vocabulary>not there</vocabulary>. It's not here and it's not there. It’s missing. It's nowhere to be found, so don't bother looking for it!

examples.en: Oh, I don't have my bag!
examples.ja: あ、カバンがない！

examples.en: That's funny. I thought I put them in my bag.
examples.ja: おかしいなぁ。カバンに入れたはずなのに。

examples.en: I opted for a larger bag that can hold a lot of stuff.
examples.ja: いっぱい入るよう、大きめのカバンにしたよ。

9203.meaning_mnemonic:
If there's a <reading>ca</reading>r <reading>ban</reading> (カバン), you'll need a nice <vocabulary>bag</vocabulary> to carry all your stuff in. You can't just throw it all in the car, so get yourself a nice bag instead.

カバン is used for bags that you can close and that have a fairly rigid structure, like satchels or briefcases, but not more flimsy bags that don't close, like plastic or paper shopping bags.

This word can also be written in hiragana and kanji. All versions are pretty common, but you'll probably see it in katakana the most.

examples.en: I can't find a cab at all.
examples.ja: タクシーがぜんぜん見つからないんだよね。

examples.en: Shall we take a cab?
examples.ja: タクシーで行く？

examples.en: Don't use me as a taxi!
examples.ja: タクシー代わりにしないでよ！

9204.meaning_mnemonic: タクシー is the katakana version of the English word <vocabulary>taxi</vocabulary>. The "xi" sound becomes クシー to fit better with Japanese pronunciation.

examples.en: That person is famous.
examples.ja: その人、有名人だよ。

examples.en: I'm busy that day.
examples.ja: その日は、いそがしいんだ。

examples.en: At that moment, there was a loud boom.
examples.ja: そのとき、ドーンと大きな音がした。

9205.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how それ means "that one"? その has a very similar meaning: <vocabulary>that</vocabulary>. It's used before a noun that's either close to the person you're talking to, or fairly close to both of you. For example, その本 is "that book", and the book in question might be in the hand of the person you're talking to, or it might be on a shelf not far from you both.

examples.en: I think I've seen that person over there somewhere before.
examples.ja: あの人、どこかで見たことある気がする。

examples.en: Do you remember that day?
examples.ja: あの日のこと、おぼえてる？

examples.en: I should have said "thank you" at the time.
examples.ja: あのとき、「ありがとう」って言えばよかった。

9206.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how あれ means "that one over there"? Well, あの means <vocabulary>that</vocabulary>, and goes before a noun to point out something that is far away from both you and the person you're talking to, such as あの本 (that book over there) or あの子犬 (that puppy over there).

Notice how these words starting with あ are far away from you? We'll be learning a few more of these, and they all follow the same pattern! What's more, you’ll notice that words ending in の tend to go before a noun.

examples.en: But I can't.
examples.ja: でも、できないよ。

examples.en: But are you okay with that?
examples.ja: でも、いいの？

examples.en: But it's 50 percent off, you know?
examples.ja: でも、５０パーセントオフだよ？

9207.meaning_mnemonic:
I want to show you my <reading>demo</reading> (でも), <vocabulary>but</vocabulary> you don't want to see it. <vocabulary>However</vocabulary>, I'm going to show it to you anyway. So there.

Something to watch out for with でも is that it always goes at the beginning of a sentence, not in the middle, like "but" usually does in English. It’s also a fairly casual word, so it’s not normally used in formal situations.

examples.en: I don't know that yet.
examples.ja: それはまだ分からないよ。

examples.en: What, are you still in the bathroom?
examples.ja: え、まだトイレにいるの？

examples.en: If you're looking for Ken, he's still taking a shower.
examples.ja: ケンなら、まだシャワーしてるよ。

9208.meaning_mnemonic:
You've been getting <reading>madder</reading> (まだ) and madder, and you’re <vocabulary>still</vocabulary> mad. You’re <vocabulary>not yet</vocabulary> as mad as you could be, though.

You can use まだ to talk about a situation that started in the past and continues into the present. Wait! Where are you going? I'm still explaining this! I'm not done yet!

examples.en: Let's eat here!
examples.ja: ここで食べよう！

examples.en: If you're looking for your glasses, they're here.
examples.ja: メガネなら、ここにあるよ。

examples.en: Where am I? Who am I?
examples.ja: ここはどこ？私はだれ？

9209.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how words beginning with こ are close to you? It ends with こ too, which is a clue that we’re talking about a place. So ここ means <vocabulary>here</vocabulary>.

examples.en: Today I ate a muffin as a snack.
examples.ja: 今日はおやつにマフィンを食べた。

examples.en: Shall we take a snack break?
examples.ja: そろそろおやつにする？

examples.en: Kaori's snacks are always homemade!
examples.ja: カオリちゃんのおやつは、いつも手作りだよ！

9210.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Oh yah! Two</reading> (おやつ) <vocabulary>snack</vocabulary>s, just for you. Imagine your two snacks. What are they? I bet they're delicious. Oh yah!

おやつ can be anything from candy to cookies to onigiri. Basically, it's anything fairly light that’s eaten between meals.

examples.en: Where are you going?
examples.ja: どこに行くの？

examples.en: Which McDonald's?
examples.ja: どこのマクドナルド？

examples.en: Where do you come from?
examples.ja: どこから来たの？

9211.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how words beginning with ど are often question words, and words ending in こ refer to places? This one's no exception, so どこ means <vocabulary>where</vocabulary>.

examples.en: Hello, this is Yamakawa.
examples.ja: もしもし、山川です。

examples.en: Hello, can you hear me?
examples.ja: もしもし、きこえますか？

examples.en: Hello, what are you doing now?
examples.ja: もしもし、今なにしてるの？

9212.meaning_mnemonic:
Woah, this place is <reading>mossy</reading>, <reading>mossy</reading> (もしもし)! This moss needs clearing up, so you call up the person in charge. <vocabulary>Hello</vocabulary>, says the person on the phone.

もしもし is a <vocabulary>telephone hello</vocabulary>, the standard way to answer the phone in Japan!

examples.en: I've played almost all of the games here.
examples.ja: ここにあるゲーム、ほとんどプレイしたことあるよ。

examples.en: I hardly understand any of this lecture.
examples.ja: このレクチャー、ほとんど分からないんだけど。

examples.en: Most people have smartphones nowadays.
examples.ja: 今どき、スマホなんてほとんどの人がもってるでしょ。

9213.meaning_mnemonic: What can be eaten <reading>hot on dough</reading> (ほとんど)? <vocabulary>Most</vocabulary> things can. <vocabulary>Almost all</vocabulary> things, in fact. <vocabulary>Hardly</vocabulary> anything tastes bad when it's hot and served on dough.

examples.en: Is this pen made of glass?
examples.ja: このペン、ガラスで出来てるの？

examples.en: Wow, it looks like Cinderella's glass slipper.
examples.ja: うわー、シンデレラのガラスのくつみたい。

examples.en: You have bird poop on your windshield.
examples.ja: フロントガラスに鳥のフンが付いてるよ。

9214.meaning_mnemonic:
This comes from the word <vocabulary>glass</vocabulary>, and it refers to the stuff used to make Cinderella's slippers, and windows, in which case it can also mean a <vocabulary>pane of glass</vocabulary>.

We'll learn how to say the other meanings of "glass" later!

examples.en: I met my teacher there.
examples.ja: そこで先生に会ったよ。

examples.en: If you're looking for snacks, they're there.
examples.ja: おやつなら、そこにあるよ。

examples.en: You don't have to say so much!
examples.ja: そこまで言わなくてもいいじゃない！

9215.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how words beginning with そ are either close to the person you're talking to, or fairly close to both of you? And how words ending in こ refer to places? This one's no exception. そこ means <vocabulary>there</vocabulary>.

examples.en: My house is over there.
examples.ja: 私のうちは、あそこだよ。

examples.en: Let's take a short rest over there!
examples.ja: あそこでちょっと休もう！

examples.en: What's that thing over there?
examples.ja: あそこにあるのは何？

9216.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how words beginning with あ show that whatever you're talking about is far away from both you and the person you're talking to? And how words ending in こ refer to places? So what do you think this means? That right, it's <vocabulary>over there</vocabulary>.

Note that even though あそこ means "over there," it's still used to refer to a specific, concrete place, as opposed to a word like 向こう which means "over there" in a broader, more general sense.

examples.en: I lost five kilos in one month.
examples.ja: 一ヶ月で五キロやせました。

examples.en: It is roughly 3 km from our house to the school.
examples.ja: うちから学校まで、大体３キロです。

examples.en: This stone sells for only one yen per kilo.
examples.ja: この石は、キロ当たり１円にしかなりません。

9217.meaning_mnemonic:
キロ comes from <vocabulary>kilo</vocabulary>, and it can mean <vocabulary>kilogram</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>kilometer</vocabulary>, or any unit that starts with "kilo" in English.

You can also use abbreviations like "kg" and "km" in Japanese, and they're often just pronounced キロ too.

examples.en: Oh, I can smell cigarette smoke.
examples.ja: あ、タバコのにおいがする。

examples.en: I've been struggling to quit smoking.
examples.ja: タバコが中々やめられないんだ。

examples.en: It's not good to smoke while walking.
examples.ja: 歩きタバコはよくないよ。

9218.meaning_mnemonic:
タバコ is the Japanese version of the Portuguese word "tabaco." You probably won’t be shocked to learn that タバコ means <vocabulary>tobacco</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>cigarette</vocabulary> in English!

Watch out for the first syllable, which is タ and not ト. タバコ can also be written in hiragana, and even in kanji, but katakana is the most common by far.

examples.en: The service at that restaurant isn't great, is it?
examples.ja: あのレストランのサービス、ビミョーじゃない？

examples.en: It's on the house.
examples.ja: サービスです。

examples.en: Eh, it's just lip service, isn't it?
examples.ja: えー、ただのリップサービスじゃない？

examples.en: When I bought cream buns, they gave me bread crusts for free.
examples.ja: クリームパン買ったら、パンの耳、サービスしてくれた。

9219.meaning_mnemonic: This is the equivalent of the English word <vocabulary>service</vocabulary>. By extension, it's often used to mean a <vocabulary>freebie</vocabulary>. Though it's generally used as a standard noun, it can also be a verbal noun used with する. In this case, it means <vocabulary>giving a freebie</vocabulary>.

examples.en: However, that was a lie.
examples.ja: しかし、それはウソだった。

examples.en: However, it was raining that day.
examples.ja: しかし、その日は雨だった。

examples.en: However, she was found by the queen.
examples.ja: しかし、女王に見つかってしまった。

9220.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>She cashe</reading>s (しかし) in on everything. <vocabulary>However</vocabulary>, this time you're going to stop her. No more cashing in.

しかし is used at the beginning of a sentence, just like "however." It's pretty formal, and you'll see it much more in written Japanese than spoken Japanese.

examples.en: I always eat bread in the mornings.
examples.ja: 朝はいつもパンを食べます。

examples.en: Oh, we're out of bread.
examples.ja: あ、食パン切れてる。

examples.en: It says bread crusts are 100 yen.
examples.ja: パンの耳、百円だって。

9221.meaning_mnemonic:
パン is the katakana version of the Portuguese word "pão" and means <vocabulary>bread</vocabulary> in English.

If you know the Portuguese, Spanish, or French word for bread, you shouldn't have trouble remembering this word. If not, here's a mnemonic to help you:

You use a <reading>pan</reading> (パン) to make all your <vocabulary>bread</vocabulary>. It's your special bread pan, and all the bread you make with it is delicious.

examples.en: Thank you, I am very happy to hear that.
examples.ja: ありがとう、とてもうれしいです。

examples.en: This is a very precious teddy bear.
examples.ja: これは、とても大切なテディベアなの。

examples.en: That teacher's lecture is very easy to understand.
examples.ja: あの先生のレクチャーはとても分かりやすい。

9222.meaning_mnemonic:
Look at this <reading>totem, oh</reading> (とても)! It's <vocabulary>very</vocabulary>, very, very, very lucky, as all totems should be. 

This word has a slightly formal feel to it, and you’ll come across it most in writing.

examples.en: My company is in that office building over there.
examples.ja: うちの会社は、あそこのオフィスビルに入ってるんだよ。

examples.en: I'll call you when I get out of the building.
examples.ja: ビルから出たら、電話するよ。

examples.en: The moon was visible in a gap between the tall buildings.
examples.ja: ビルの谷間に月が見えた。

9223.meaning_mnemonic: ビル is the Japanese version of the English word <vocabulary>building</vocabulary>. It usually refers to buildings that are taller than they are wide, most commonly apartment blocks and office buildings.

examples.en: I've already seen that anime.
examples.ja: そのアニメ、もう見たよ。

examples.en: I'm almost done!
examples.ja: もうそろそろ終わる！

examples.en: I understand. I won't come here anymore.
examples.ja: 分かった。ここにはもう来ないね。

9224.meaning_mnemonic:
You've <reading>mow</reading>ed your lawn (もう) <vocabulary>already</vocabulary>? Wow, you're ahead on your mowing. Good work. You'll have to do it again <vocabulary>soon</vocabulary>, though.

This can also mean <vocabulary>yet</vocabulary> in a question, and <vocabulary>anymore</vocabulary> with a negative.

examples.en: That dress is so cute!
examples.ja: そのワンピース、めっちゃかわいいね！

examples.en: I bought five dresses at a bargain sale.
examples.ja: バーゲンで、ワンピースを五着も買っちゃった。

examples.en: I spilled coffee on my favorite white dress.
examples.ja: お気に入りの白いワンピースにコーヒーをこぼしてしまった。

9226.meaning_mnemonic: ワンピース comes from the English word one-piece, but it generally refers to a casual <vocabulary>dress</vocabulary> in Japanese.

examples.en: We can see the fireworks really well from the balcony of my apartment!
examples.ja: うちのマンションのベランダから、花火めっちゃよく見えるよ！

examples.en: Huh, you'd rather live in an apartment than in your own house? Why?
examples.ja: えーっ、マイホームよりマンションに住む方がいいの？なんで？

examples.en: I'm planning to leave this apartment next month.
examples.ja: 私、来月、このマンションを出る予定なんだ。

9227.meaning_mnemonic: マンション comes from the English word "mansion," but it just means an ordinary <vocabulary>apartment building</vocabulary> in Japanese. Depending on context, it can also mean an individual <vocabulary>apartment</vocabulary>. Either way, it’s definitely not a big, luxurious house in Japanese!

examples.en: This is an onomatopoeia that expresses a sense of softness.
examples.ja: これは、やわらかいイメージを表すオノマトペですね。

examples.en: What is your favorite onomatopoeia and why do you like it?
examples.ja: 好きなオノマトペと、それが好きな理由を教えてください。

examples.en: How do you all learn Japanese onomatopoeias?
examples.ja: 日本語のオノマトペって、みんなどうやって勉強してるの？

9228.meaning_mnemonic:
オノマトペ comes from the French word “onomatopée” which, as you can probably guess, means <vocabulary>onomatopoeia</vocabulary>.

オノマトペ has a wider meaning than its English equivalent, and it also covers <vocabulary>mimetic word</vocabulary>s, which are words that evoke ideas and actions rather than sounds.

examples.en: We're going to play poker, so can you go buy some playing cards?
examples.ja: ポーカーするからトランプ買ってきて！

examples.en: Hey, want to play cards?
examples.ja: ねえ、トランプしない？

examples.en: I'm not very good at shuffling cards.
examples.ja: トランプ切るの、苦手なんだよね。

9229.meaning_mnemonic:
トランプ comes from the English word "trump", as in "a trump card", but it means <vocabulary>deck of cards</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>playing cards</vocabulary> in Japanese.

The Japanese meaning probably comes from card games played by English-speaking Westerners back in the day. Japanese people heard the word "trump" a lot, and assumed it meant a deck of cards.

examples.en: Wow, this bread is so fluffy, isn't it!
examples.ja: うわー、このパン、ふわふわだね！

examples.en: Isn't it cute to see jellyfish floating in the sea?
examples.ja: クラゲが海でふわふわ泳いでるのって、かわいくない？

examples.en: I’m kind of light-headed.
examples.ja: なんか頭がふわふわする。

9230.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Who are who are</reading> (ふわふわ) <vocabulary>fluffy</vocabulary>? I’m thinking puppies, but ask yourself, "who are the fluffiest creatures I know?"

This is an オノマトペ meaning fluffy, like a puppy, a cloud, or a cotton ball. It can also describe the movement of a dandelion puffball or a jellyfish, <vocabulary>floating lightly</vocabulary> in the air or the water. And if you’re <vocabulary>feeling lightheaded</vocabulary>, that’s called ふわふわ too. Basically, anything with light or fluffy vibe!

examples.en: How did you become fluent in Japanese?
examples.ja: どうやって日本語ペラペラになったの？

examples.en: Ah, I want to be able to speak English fluently soon.
examples.ja: あー、はやく英語がペラペラ話せるようになりたい。

examples.en: Hey, you've been blabbing on and on! We're in the library, remember?
examples.ja: ねえ、さっきから、ペラペラペラペラうるさいよ！ここ、図書館だよ？

9231.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Parrot, parrot</reading> (ペラペラ), your speaking is so <vocabulary>fluent</vocabulary>!

ペラペラ is an オノマトペ that describes someone speaking a language fluently, or simply being a real chatterbox.

Related to this, ペラペラ also means <vocabulary>leafing through a book</vocabulary>. And in an extension of that meaning, it can describe something <vocabulary>paper thin</vocabulary> or flimsy, like a piece of paper from that book you're leafing through.

examples.en: Oh man, I'm so nervous.
examples.ja: やばい、めっちゃドキドキする。

examples.en: He was so cool that my heart was pounding.
examples.ja: カッコよくて、ドキドキでした。

examples.en: I could feel your excitement.
examples.ja: ドキドキが伝わってきたよ。

9232.meaning_mnemonic:
<reading>Doc, Doc</reading> (ドキドキ), listen to my <vocabulary>racing heart</vocabulary>. I'm so <vocabulary>excited</vocabulary>, but I'm also a bit <vocabulary>nervous</vocabulary>.

ドキドキ is an オノマトペ used to describe the feeling of your heart beating fast. When does your heart race? When you get excited or nervous, so ドキドキ also expresses those feelings!

examples.en: Apparently, an overnight stay with a breakfast buffet costs 5,000 yen at this hotel.
examples.ja: このホテル、朝食バイキング付きで五千円だって。

examples.en: Would you like to go to an all-you-can-eat cake place with me sometime?
examples.ja: 今度いっしょにケーキバイキングに行かない？

examples.en: The Christmas party will be buffet style.
examples.ja: クリスマスパーティーは、バイキング形式にする予定だよ。

9233.meaning_mnemonic:
バイキング comes from the English word <vocabulary>Viking</vocabulary>, but in Japanese, it often refers to a <vocabulary>buffet</vocabulary>.

バイキング came to mean "buffet" thanks to Japan’s first all-you-can-eat restaurant, "Viking", which was named after a feast scene from a movie called (you guessed it) "Viking".

examples.en: The X-rays showed no abnormalities.
examples.ja: レントゲン写真には、異常は認められませんでした。

examples.en: Let's take a chest X-ray just to be sure.
examples.ja: 念の為、胸部のレントゲンを撮りましょう。

examples.en: Please wait in front of the X-ray room.
examples.ja: レントゲン室の前でお待ちください。

9234.meaning_mnemonic:
レントゲン comes from the German word "Röntgen" meaning <vocabulary>X-ray</vocabulary>, named after their inventor Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen.

If that’s news to you, here’s a mnemonic to help you remember: 

You’re planning to <reading>rent a Gen</reading>ji (レントゲン), but you ask Genji to get an <vocabulary>X-ray</vocabulary> first, just to make sure he’s in good health before signing the rental contract.

examples.en: It's just a fluke.
examples.ja: ただのまぐれだよ。

examples.en: It was just a lucky guess.
examples.ja: まぐれで当たっただけなんだよね。

examples.en: Even if it's a fluke, it's still great!
examples.ja: まぐれでもすごいよ！

9235.meaning_mnemonic:
Somebody tried to <reading>mug Re</reading>mi (まぐれ), your friend, but by <vocabulary>chance</vocabulary> they managed to escape! Their escape was a <vocabulary>fluke</vocabulary>, but what a relief they didn't get mugged.

This word can be written in kanji, but the kana version is way more common. In fact, it'd be quite a fluke if you saw it in kanji.

examples.en: Ah, we're out of staples.
examples.ja: あ、ホッチキスの針、切れちゃった。

examples.en: Wow, that's thick! I wonder if I can staple it together with this stapler?
examples.ja: うわっ、分厚い！このホッチキスでとじれるかな？

examples.en: When stapling Japanese documents, it is common practice to staple the top right corner for vertical writing and the top left corner for horizontal writing.
examples.ja: 日本の書類をホッチキスで止める時は、縦書きの場合は右上、横書きの場合は左上をホッチキスで止めるのが一般的です。

9236.meaning_mnemonic:
This word means <vocabulary>stapler</vocabulary>. It comes from the name of the company that first imported staplers into Japan: Hotchkiss! Here’s a mnemonic to help you remember it:

Ever given a <reading>hot kiss</reading> (ホッチキス) to a <vocabulary>stapler</vocabulary>? Imagine what that feels like, and you'll remember this word forever. Just keep in mind that sometimes it's written as ホチキス, but ホッチキス is more common.

examples.en: In this house, the father is in a weak position.
examples.ja: この家では父が弱い立場にいます。

examples.en: I'm not in a position to say such things.
examples.ja: 私はそんなこと言える立場じゃありません。

examples.en: From a user's standpoint, this app is hard to use.
examples.ja: ユーザーの立場から言うと、このアプリは使いにくいです。

9237.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>stand</kanji> <kanji>location</kanji> is where you stand. In other words, it's your <vocabulary>standpoint</vocabulary>, like in a discussion or on an issue. 

While 立場 can mean a literal standing place, it's almost always used metaphorically — to describe your stance in an argument or the complexities of your <vocabulary>position</vocabulary> within society, a situation, or a relationship.
9237.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. 立 comes from 立ち (the noun form of 立つ), and you learned the kun'yomi reading for 場 with 場所. But here's a mnemonic for both in case you need a refresher:

A sheep is trying to give you its <vocabulary>standpoint</vocabulary> on a <reading>touchy</reading> (たち) subject, but all it can do is say "<reading>baa</reading>" (ば). You're starting to get really offended that it's not baa-thering to take a more nuanced standpoint on such a touchy issue!

examples.en: Dad is good at tennis.
examples.ja: パパはテニスが上手い。

examples.en: A skillful person joined the team.
examples.ja: 上手い人がチームに入った。

examples.en: This composition is pretty well-written.
examples.ja: この作文、なかなか上手いですね。

9238.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 上手 means that you're <vocabulary>good at</vocabulary> something? Well, this word uses the exact same kanji, and means the exact same thing!
9238.reading_mnemonic:
That い on the end is your clue that the reading is different, and you can forget about the readings you learned for each kanji. This is a native Japanese word, and the kanji were assigned to it based on the meaning alone. That means you just have to memorize the reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

When you see that someone's <vocabulary>good at</vocabulary> something, you say, "<reading>Ooh</reading>, <reading>my</reading> (うまい)!" at the top of your lungs. Try it! Think of something that impresses you and say "ooh my!" out loud.

examples.en: Stress is causing the disease to worsen quickly.
examples.ja: ストレスのせいで、病気の悪化が早い。

examples.en: Last night, my flu suddenly got worse.
examples.ja: 昨日の夜、インフルエンザが一気に悪化した。

examples.en: In recent times, there has been a notable decline in the overall safety of this neighborhood.
examples.ja: 最近この辺りは治安がかなり悪化している。

9239.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>bad</kanji> <kanji>change</kanji> is exactly what it sounds like: <vocabulary>deterioration</vocabulary>, aka <vocabulary>getting worse</vocabulary> .
9239.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. The on'yomi readings of the kanji are あく and か, but here they become あっか, to make the word easier to pronounce. Try and say it out loud to see if you agree.

examples.en: You should learn an apple pie recipe from Grandma.
examples.ja: アップルパイのレシピは、おばあちゃんに教わるといいよ。

examples.en: Did someone already teach you hiragana and katakana?
examples.ja: ひらがなとカタカナは、もう教わりましたか？

examples.en: Not everything you've learned in school is useful in life.
examples.ja: 学校で教わったことが全て人生で役に立つわけじゃない。

9240.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

The kanji itself means <kanji>teach</kanji>, and this verb means <vocabulary>to learn something from someone</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be taught something</vocabulary>. When you use this verb, you're not learning something by yourself, you're being taught by someone else.
9240.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this kun'yomi yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

When you want <vocabulary>to learn something from someone</vocabulary>, you say "<reading>Oh</reading>, <reading>so</reading>..." (おそ) and repeat what you've just learned. Saying "oh, so…" helps you make sure you're understanding correctly, and shows you're really paying attention. That's important when you're learning from someone!

examples.en: New Year's is coming soon.
examples.ja: もうすぐ、お正月ですね。

examples.en: When does your New Year's holiday start?
examples.ja: 正月休みは、いつからですか？

examples.en: At this year's New Year sale, all the suits will be 50% off.
examples.ja: 今年の正月のセールでは、スーツが全て五十パーセントオフです。

9241.meaning_mnemonic:
You <kanji>correct</kanji> the <kanji>moon</kanji> because it's a <vocabulary>New Year</vocabulary>. It's the beginning of a fresh year, so you gotta have the moon in the correct position.

This usually refers to the first few days of a new year, and it's one of the biggest holidays in Japan.
9241.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Both of these kanji have a couple of on'yomi readings, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember which ones to use:

At <vocabulary>New Year</vocabulary>, you hate your <reading>Shou</reading>gun's <reading>guts</reading> (しょうがつ). He doesn't celebrate New Year, you see, so none of you get any time off. He even started a war last New Year and ruined everyone's holidays. No wonder you hate that shougun's guts.

examples.en: Dad's an active professional wrestler.
examples.ja: お父さんは現役のプロレスラーです。

examples.en: The author of this manga is still a high school student.
examples.ja: このマンガの作者は、現役高校生なんです。

examples.en: I am thinking of going overseas for a year without enrolling in college straight out of high school.
examples.ja: 現役で大学に入学しないで、一年間海外に行こうと思うんです。

9242.meaning_mnemonic:
At the <kanji>present time</kanji> you're providing a <kanji>service</kanji>, so you're <vocabulary>actively working</vocabulary>. 現役 means you have a certain role (such as school teacher or a high school student, etc.) and you're still <vocabulary>active</vocabulary> in that role, as opposed to being retired or having graduated.

This word is also often used to describe students who are taking or have passed a university entrance exam while they were still high school students.
9242.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You learned the readings for both of these, but 役 uses a less common reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember this:

You're <vocabulary>actively working</vocabulary> at the <reading>駅</reading> (えき) and you plan to remain <vocabulary>active</vocabulary> there forever! You sure do love that 駅, it's like you're inseparable.

examples.en: I can read all the katakana letters from the sa row.
examples.ja: カタカナのサ行の文字は全て読めますよ。

examples.en: A sentence this long won’t fit in a single line.
examples.ja: こんなに長い文、一行には入らないよ。

examples.en: At important times like this, some adults have trouble reading between the lines.
examples.ja: こういう大切な時に行間を読めない大人っているよね。

examples.en: In Excel and other spreadsheets, horizontal lines are called "rows."
examples.ja: Excelやスプレッドシートでは、横方向のラインのことを「行」といいます。

9243.meaning_mnemonic:
You write the word <kanji>go</kanji> on a <vocabulary>line of text</vocabulary>. See the word "go" on that <vocabulary>line</vocabulary>, and think about where you're going.

This word can also be used for <vocabulary>row</vocabulary>s (horizontal lines in Excel and other spreadsheets).
9243.reading_mnemonic:
There are two on'yomi readings for this kanji, but when it's used to mean lines of text, it's pronounced as ぎょう. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember that:

You write out another <vocabulary>line of text</vocabulary> asking for some <reading>gyo</reading>za (ぎょう). You write out that line of text slowly and carefully, in your very best handwriting. Turns out you were going to a gyoza restaurant and you want to make sure you impress the gyoza chef, so that they give you a ton of gyoza.

examples.en: Why do you only suspect me?
examples.ja: なんで私ばかり疑うの？

examples.en: It was a piece of news that would make you doubt your own eyes.
examples.ja: それは自分の目を疑うようなニュースでした。

examples.en: I sometimes suspect that our dog is actually a human on the inside.
examples.ja: たまに、うちの犬の中には人間が入ってるんじゃないかなと疑うことがあります。

9244.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji means <kanji>doubt</kanji>, so this is just that as a verb. So this means <vocabulary>to doubt</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to suspect</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to be suspicious of</vocabulary>.
9244.reading_mnemonic: There's reason <vocabulary>to doubt</vocabulary> that you can teach an <reading>u</reading>ni <reading>Taga</reading>log (うたが), but once you try, it's actually not that hard. They're very good listeners after all.

examples.en: When Masao's glass became empty, Michiko quietly poured wine into it.
examples.ja: マサオのグラスが空くと、ミチコはそっとワインを注いだ。

examples.en: Please let me know the days when your schedule is free.
examples.ja: スケジュールが空いてる日を教えてください。

examples.en: Luckily, there was one available table, so we were able to get seated at the restaurant right away.
examples.ja: ラッキーなことに、テーブルが一つ空いていたのですぐ店に入れました。

9245.meaning_mnemonic:
You have the kanji for <kanji>empty</kanji>, so this verb means <vocabulary>to become empty</vocabulary>. 

It can also have a slightly different meaning when it's read differently, but you'll learn this through other words later on, so don't worry about it for now.
9245.reading_mnemonic: Whenever something is about <vocabulary>to become empty</vocabulary>, you can't help saying "<reading>Ah…</reading>" (あ) to express your disappointment. Your glass of water is becoming empty? Ah… Your bag of chips is becoming empty? Ah… Exclaiming a little "Ah…" is the only thing that helps you cope with the sadness of your favorite things becoming empty.

9246.meaning_mnemonic: You've got a <radical>car</radical>, a <radical>weapon</radical>, and some <radical>thread</radical> lying around. So of course you decide to <kanji>connect</kanji> them all together.
9246.reading_mnemonic: There's only one reason you've <kanji>connected</kanji> all this together: <reading>Tuna</reading> (つな) fishing. Obviously!

examples.en: It took an hour to get connected to the internet.
examples.ja: インターネットが繋がるのに一時間かかった。

examples.en: All failures lead to success.
examples.ja: 全ての失敗が成功に繋がるんだよ。

examples.en: Koichi and I are not related by blood.
examples.ja: コウイチと私は血が繋がってません。

9247.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>connect</kanji>, which makes this <vocabulary>to be connected to</vocabulary>. In other situations, this can also mean <vocabulary>to be tied together</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to lead to</vocabulary>.
9247.reading_mnemonic: You already learned this reading with the kanji, so you should be good to go!

examples.en: This is a stretching exercise that helps relieve stiff shoulders.
examples.ja: これは肩こりが楽になるストレッチです。

examples.en: There is a good massage technique to loosen stiff shoulders.
examples.ja: 肩こりをほぐす良いマッサージがあります。

examples.en: You're experiencing shoulder stiffness because you spend too much time playing smartphone games.
examples.ja: スマホゲームばっかりしてるから肩こりになるんだよ。

9248.meaning_mnemonic:
When your shoulders get a little こり, it means you've got <vocabulary>shoulder stiffness</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>stiff neck</vocabulary>. 

The こり here is a nominalized version of the verb こる, which means "to become stiff," so maybe that'll help you remember this!
9248.reading_mnemonic: You already know the reading of 肩, and this is just that with some hiragana added on!

examples.en: I'm afraid of climbing down the ladder.
examples.ja: ハシゴを下りるのがこわいんです。

examples.en: Dad jumped down from the fence.
examples.ja: お父さんはジャンプしてフェンスから下りた。

examples.en: My fiancé's visa finally got issued.
examples.ja: やっとフィアンセのビザが下りました。

9249.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>below</kanji>, which is a clue to the direction this movement verb takes: this is <vocabulary>to go down</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to descend</vocabulary>. In some cases, this can also mean <vocabulary>to be issued</vocabulary>, mostly in situations where some sort of grant or allowance is issued by an authority.

You might notice that this is similar to 下る (くだる), and you can use either to describe going down a mountain. The difference is that 下る implies a gradual sloping motion, like floating down a stream, whereas you'd say 下りる if you’re jumping out of trees!
9249.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji), you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading, which you didn't learn with the kanji. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

You're stuck on a huge mountain, and the only way <vocabulary>to go down</vocabulary> is by using your <reading>o</reading>bi (お). So you'll have <vocabulary>to descend</vocabulary> this entire mountain with nothing but your obi, acting as a rope. Good luck!

examples.en: The boom will be over soon anyway.
examples.ja: どうせすぐブームは去るよ。

examples.en: That manager left the company last year.
examples.ja: そのマネージャーは去年会社を去りました。

examples.en: Finally, the typhoon has gone away, hasn't it.
examples.ja: ようやく台風が去ってくれたね。

9250.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>past</kanji>, and this verb means <vocabulary>to leave</vocabulary>. It should be easy to remember because you know what people say — you leave past in the past.
9250.reading_mnemonic: You will want <vocabulary>to leave</vocabulary>, if you see a <reading>saw</reading> (さ) pointing at you. You know saws can be deadly weapons, you should immediately leave when someone is brandishing one at you!

9251.reading_mnemonic: To have your <kanji>complete</kanji> fingers back, you gotta run to the hospital <reading>solo</reading> (そろ).

examples.en: It's been five years since everyone gathered together.
examples.ja: 全員が揃うの五年ぶりだね。

examples.en: The Yamada family's shoes are always neatly arranged.
examples.ja: 山田さんちのクツはいつもきれいに揃っている。

examples.en: All the conditions were met. I couldn't help but feel like we would win.
examples.ja: 全ての条件が揃っていた。もう勝てる気しかしなかった。

9252.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

This is an intransitive verb that uses the <kanji>complete</kanji> kanji. It means <vocabulary>to be complete</vocabulary>. It can also be used when you want things <vocabulary>to be uniform</vocabulary>. It feels satisfying to have everything complete and uniform, right?
9252.reading_mnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You learned the kun'yomi reading when you learned the kanji, so you should be able to read this!

examples.en: After how many dates do you usually hold hands?
examples.ja: いつも何回目のデートで手を繋ぐ？

examples.en: Music connects people.
examples.ja: 音楽は人と人を繋ぎます。

examples.en: Nowadays, even without cables, you can connect your computer and digital camera using Wi-Fi.
examples.ja: 今はケーブルがなくてもWi-Fiでパソコンとデジカメを繋ぐことができます。

9253.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>connect</kanji>, and this verb means <vocabulary>to connect something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to tie something to</vocabulary> something else. Like connect people, hold hands, connect a cable to a charger, etc.

Figuratively, when you want to connect something over time, like a conversation, then you want <vocabulary>to maintain</vocabulary> something over time as well.
9253.reading_mnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading, which you already know from the kanji.

examples.en: I open the shutters every morning.
examples.ja: 毎朝、雨戸を開けます。

examples.en: Recently, there are fewer houses with shutters in Japan.
examples.ja: 最近は日本でも雨戸をつけている家が少なくなりました。

examples.en: I woke up in the middle of the night because of the sound of rain hitting the shutters.
examples.ja: 雨が雨戸を叩く音で深夜に起きてしまった。

9254.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>rain</kanji> <kanji>door</kanji> is really just a <vocabulary>shutter</vocabulary>. In Japan, having shutters for rain protection is very common. When there were no glass windows, the shutters were simply like exterior doors in Japan, so "rain door" kind of makes sense as "shutter"! 

This word is usually for <vocabulary>sliding storm shutter</vocabulary>s. For other types of shutters, you can just say シャッター.
9254.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, but it actually uses kun'yomi for both 雨 and 戸. Additionally, the reading for 雨 is actually slightly different from what you've learned, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

A <vocabulary>shutter</vocabulary> is basically just <reading>armor</reading> (あま) for a window. They're both protective, and are often made from metal. Kind of makes sense, right?

examples.en: The man over there is in his thirties.
examples.ja: あの男は三十代です。

examples.en: I joined this company in my thirties.
examples.ja: 三十代で、この会社に入りました。

examples.en: My parents were in their thirties when they had their three children.
examples.ja: 三人の子どもが生まれたとき、父と母は三十代でした。

9255.meaning_mnemonic: You have the number "thirty", and <kanji>age</kanji>. So this refers to <vocabulary>one's thirties</vocabulary>.
9255.reading_mnemonic: This uses on'yomi for all the kanji, so you should be good to go here!

examples.en: I would like to pay for the books by card.
examples.ja: 本の代金はカードではらいます。

examples.en: The massage costs 50 dollars.
examples.ja: マッサージ代金は五十ドルです。

examples.en: We haven't received payment for today's lunch yet.
examples.ja: まだ今日のランチの代金をもらってません。

9256.meaning_mnemonic:
When you buy something, you basically <kanji>substitute</kanji> it with <kanji>money</kanji>. That substitute money is the <vocabulary>cost</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>price</vocabulary> of the thing you're paying for.

There are a lot of money-related synonyms in Japanese, but keep in mind this one refers to the money you pay to get some stuff in return (usually goods), not to an expense, price, or value. It's "substitute money" after all!
9256.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which means it uses on'yomi readings for both of the kanji. You already know those, so you should be good to go!

examples.en: It is a theme that questions the way society and human beings should be.
examples.ja: 社会と人間のあり方を問うテーマです。

examples.en: That player's abilities will likely be tested in next week's match.
examples.ja: その選手は来週の試合で実力が問われるだろう。

examples.en: Currently, the way schools operate is being questioned.
examples.ja: 今、学校のあり方が問われています。

9257.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>problem</kanji> and this verb means <vocabulary>to question something</vocabulary>. That's because when you want to get to the bottom of a problem, you question things.

問う has a formal, literary sound and tends to carry a sense of raising a meaningful or weighty question. You'll see it in essays, news articles, and philosophical writing when someone is considering deeper issues, like questioning values, society, or something's very existence. It can also just mean <vocabulary>to ask</vocabulary>, but will sound stuffier and more old-fashioned than the standard 聞く.
9257.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know it's probably going to use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

It's okay <vocabulary>to question something</vocabulary>, but you should be careful not to step on someone else's <reading>toe</reading>s (と) by doing so. Questioning certain things can offend people, especially if it's something they have strong feelings about! So be careful about those toes.

examples.en: The woman stood under the light of the lamp.
examples.ja: 女はランプの明かりの下に立った。

examples.en: There's not much light around here.
examples.ja: この辺は明かりが少ない。

examples.en: It seems like we can camp with only the moonlight today.
examples.ja: 今日は月の明かりだけで、キャンプができそうです。

9258.meaning_mnemonic:
What makes it <kanji>bright</kanji> around here? It's <vocabulary>light</vocabulary>!

Note: 明かり is mostly used for light coming from a specific source, like a lamp or light bulb. You'll learn a more general word for light in a couple levels.
9258.reading_mnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You already know the reading from the kanji!

9259.reading_mnemonic: Why do you want to <kanji>receive</kanji> all these shellfish? Because it's the <reading>mora</reading>l (もら) thing to do. Oh benevolent, moral king of all the world's shellfish, please receive us.

examples.en: Adults work and receive money, right?
examples.ja: 大人は仕事をしてお金を貰うんでしょ？

examples.en: I received a necklace as a gift.
examples.ja: プレゼントにネックレスを貰いました。

examples.en: I always get energy from your smile.
examples.ja: あなたの笑顔にはいつも元気を貰います。

examples.en: Could I receive some advice about this?
examples.ja: これについてアドバイスを貰えませんか？

9260.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>receive</kanji>, making this <vocabulary>to receive something</vocabulary>, or alternatively, <vocabulary>to get something from someone</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be given something</vocabulary>.
9260.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned that reading with the kanji, so you should be good to go here!

examples.en: After that, we just go back down the way we came.
examples.ja: あとはそのまま来た道を下るだけだ。

examples.en: A man riding a skateboard zoomed down the mountain.
examples.ja: スケボーに乗った男が山を下っていった。

examples.en: In Japan, there is a concept of referring to going north as "ascending" and going south as "descending."
examples.ja: 日本では、北に行くことを「上る」、南に行くことを「下る」と言うことがあります。

9261.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>below</kanji>, so you can guess the direction this movement verb takes: this is <vocabulary>to descend</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to go down</vocabulary>.

As a movement verb, it usually describes a gradual downward movement. For example, you'd use this verb to describe walking down a mountain, driving down a hill, or going down a river in a boat.
9261.reading_mnemonic: This verb uses the exceptional reading that 下さい also uses. So just replace the さい with る and you're good to go!

examples.en: I'll contact the manufacturer.
examples.ja: メーカーに問い合わせるよ。

examples.en: Why don't you try sending an inquiry by email?
examples.ja: メールで問い合わせてみたら？

examples.en: I wanted to inquire in advance, but I couldn't get through on the phone.
examples.ja: 事前に問い合わせたかったんだけど、電話がつながらなかったんだよね。

9262.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 問う means "to question something" and 合わせる means "to join together"? If you're joining your questions together, you're probably trying to <vocabulary>to inquire</vocabulary> about something. Inquiring is much more involved than plain old asking, after all.

問い合わせる is a phrase you can use when contacting a business or government office to request information or resolve an issue. It's a bit formal, but in an everyday business-speak kind of way, and it doesn't have the philosophical or weighty tone that 問う does.
9262.reading_mnemonic:
You probably know how to read 問う and 合わせる already. 問う is still pretty new though, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember the 問 part:

You love <vocabulary>to inquire</vocabulary> with your <reading>toe</reading>s (と). Whenever you fill out one of those online forms to contact customer support with an inquiry, you do all your typing with your toes. They don't know you're making this inquiry with your toes — but you do, and it makes you chuckle.

examples.en: Oh no, I forgot to arrange the documents for the meeting.
examples.ja: しまった、会議の書類を揃えるのを忘れてた。

examples.en: All my kitchen supplies are from the same manufacturer.
examples.ja: キッチン用品は全部同じメーカーで揃えてるんです。

examples.en: Everyone was saying in unison that he is not at fault.
examples.ja: みんな口を揃えてアイツは悪くないって言ってたよ。

9263.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember 揃う, "to be complete"? This is the transitive version of that, and it means things like <vocabulary>to arrange something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to gather something</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>to align something</vocabulary>.

This one is a little tricky to understand and translate well. At its core, this verb describes the act of arranging all of the necessary things for something. But it can also describe aligning certain things in a uniform, matching manner. If this still isn't clear, have a careful look at our context sentences and collocations!
9263.reading_mnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You already know this, so you're all good here!

examples.en: Sheepskin is warm.
examples.ja: 羊の毛皮はあたたかい。

examples.en: This is a leopard fur coat.
examples.ja: これはヒョウの毛皮のコートです。

examples.en: I will never ever wear fur.
examples.ja: 私はゼッタイに毛皮を着ません。

9264.meaning_mnemonic: This word is pretty straightforward. You have <kanji>fur</kanji> and <kanji>skin</kanji>, making a word meaning <vocabulary>fur</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>pelt</vocabulary>, like the kind that can be used to make garments.
9264.reading_mnemonic: This is a special case because both kanji use kun'yomi readings in this word. Luckily, you already know the kun'yomi reading from learning the vocabulary 毛 and 皮 previously. Just be careful with the rendaku on the second kanji, 皮.

9265.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Fire</radical> is one of a <radical>few</radical> things you'll need to <kanji>fry</kanji> things.
9265.reading_mnemonic: You love to <kanji>fry</kanji> things and are also an adventurous <reading>eater</reading> (いた). This means you'll fry and eat just about anything. Fried ostrich, fried alligator, fried chocolate, you name it!

examples.en: Do you really spend thirty minutes sautéing the onions?
examples.ja: 三十分もかけて玉ねぎを炒めるんですか？

examples.en: Be careful not to overcook them, okay?
examples.ja: 炒めすぎないように気をつけてくださいね。

examples.en: Let's quickly stir-fry over high heat.
examples.ja: 強火で手早く炒めていきましょう。

9266.meaning_mnemonic: This is the verb version of the kanji <kanji>fry</kanji>, so it means <vocabulary>to fry</vocabulary>, more specifically <vocabulary>to stir-fry</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to sauté</vocabulary>.
9266.reading_mnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading with the kanji, so you should be good to go!

examples.en: The fireworks will be canceled in case of rainy weather.
examples.ja: 雨天の場合、花火大会は中止です。

examples.en: Can we still do marine sports under a rainy weather?
examples.ja: マリンスポーツは雨天でもできますか？

examples.en: It seems like there's no concern for the rainy weather for now.
examples.ja: 雨天の心配は今のところなさそうです。

9267.meaning_mnemonic:
You see the kanji for <kanji>rain</kanji> being followed by the 天 kanji from 天気 (weather). This word means <vocabulary>rainy weather</vocabulary>.

This has a formal nuance to it, and is often used for event announcements (whether to postpone it in case of rainy weather, etc).
9267.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, so you use on'yomi readings. You should be familiar with the on'yomi reading for 天 already, but not for 雨. So here's a mnemonic to help you remember:

The <vocabulary>rainy weather</vocabulary> won't stop you to go catch some <reading>u</reading>ni (う). You would get wet anyway diving into the ocean to collect uni, the rainy weather doesn't affect you. You can also sell them for <reading>ten</reading> (てん) bucks a piece! The rainy weather isn't at all a problem for a uni hunting if you're making ten dollars for each, you know?

examples.en: Who was the mayor two years ago again?
examples.ja: 一昨年の市長って誰だったっけ？

examples.en: I have been jogging every day since two years ago.
examples.ja: 一昨年から毎日ジョギングをしています。

examples.en: The year before last, I saw a show by the Huis Ten Bosch Revue in Huis Ten Bosch.
examples.ja: 一昨年、ハウステンボスでハウステンボス歌劇団のショーを見てきました。

9268.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 一昨日 means "day before last"? Similarly, <kanji>one</kanji> year <kanji>previous</kanji> to that <kanji>year</kanji> is the <vocabulary>year before last</vocabulary>.
9268.reading_mnemonic: The last time you tossed something into a trash can was the <vocabulary>year before last</vocabulary>. Why? Because you got a trash can with an <reading>auto</reading>  <reading>tossi</reading>ng (おととし) feature. What amazing technology!

examples.en: He has the open-mindedness to accept everything.
examples.ja: 彼は全てを受け入れる心の広さを持っています。

examples.en: People can only grow by accepting themselves.
examples.ja: 人は自分を受け入れることでしか成長できません。

examples.en: This school welcomes international students as well.
examples.ja: この学校はインターナショナルな学生も受け入れています。

9269.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember 受ける (to receive something) and 入れる (to put in)? This just combines those two. You receive something, and put it into your heart. You accept it. So this verb means <vocabulary>to accept something</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to take in</vocabulary>. 

You can use this verb for all kinds of acceptance, such as accepting an apology, accepting exchange students to your school, etc.
9269.reading_mnemonic: You should know how to read both 受ける and 入れる, so you should be good to go!

examples.en: Here's a quick and easy recipe where all you need to do is dip them in the sauce and microwave them.
examples.ja: ソースにつけてレンジでチンするだけのお手軽レシピです。

examples.en: We have created an application that makes it easy to collect "WaniKani Cards".
examples.ja: 「ワニカニカード」が手軽にコレクションできるアプリを作りました。

examples.en: Let's move our bodies with easy exercises.
examples.ja: 手軽にできるエクササイズで体を動かしましょう。

9270.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji>hand</kanji>s are <kanji>light</kanji> because it was a <vocabulary>simple and easy</vocabulary> task, so you didn't get your hands full. This word describes something that's hassle-free and doesn't take much effort, time, or sometimes cost to do.
9270.reading_mnemonic: Both kanji use kun'yomi readings in this word, which you've already learned. Just make sure you rendaku the 軽.

examples.en: The rainy season lasts from June to July in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本の六月から七月は梅雨のシーズンです。

examples.en: The rainy season started in Kanto yesterday.
examples.ja: 関東は昨日梅雨に入ったそうです。

examples.en: I don't like the rainy season because it gets too humid, but I also don't like how it suddenly gets really hot once it ends.
examples.ja: 梅雨はジメジメして嫌だけど、梅雨が明けて一気に暑くなるのも嫌なんだよなぁ。

9271.meaning_mnemonic:
In the <kanji>ume</kanji> season, it <kanji>rain</kanji>s a lot in Japan (and some other East Asian countries). That's why <kanji>ume</kanji> <kanji>rain</kanji> means <vocabulary>rainy season</vocabulary>. It usually happens from the end of May to mid-July, when ume get ready to be harvested. 

Keep in mind this is a seasonal word unique to Japan and East Asia, so you usually don't use it to refer to rainy seasons that happen in other regions of the world.
9271.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses an exceptional reading, so don't try to read this with the kanji readings you already learned. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

<vocabulary>Rainy season</vocabulary> is a special season <reading>to you</reading> (つゆ). All of your favorite things in the year happen during rainy season, like… staying inside all day because all it does is rain! But to you, there's nothing better than rainy season.

examples.en: First, let's begin by roasting the soybeans until they turn golden brown.
examples.ja: まず、大豆をこんがりと炒ることから始めましょう。

examples.en: It smells good when you roast sesame seeds in a pan.
examples.ja: フライパンでゴマを炒ると良い匂いがします。

examples.en: "Iritamago" is a Japanese dish similar to scrambled eggs that is cooked without using much oil.
examples.ja: 「炒り卵」は、油をあまり使わないで卵を炒る日本のスクランブルエッグのような料理です。

9272.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji is <kanji>fry</kanji>. You already know the verb for "to fry" (炒める), so this verb is for a slightly different cooking technique — <vocabulary>to roast</vocabulary>. 

So what's the difference between the two? Generally speaking, 炒める involves the use of hot fat or oil, while 炒る describes a way of cooking that involves less or no oil or fat, often to dry roast things. For example, you'd use 炒める for making fried noodles or fried rice, and 炒る for roasting sesame seeds or beans.
9272.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to use the kun'yomi reading. The tricky part is where this doesn't use the same kun'yomi as 炒める, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember this:

Now that you know the difference between frying and roasting, we're going <vocabulary>to roast</vocabulary> our first dish: <reading>Ea</reading>gle (い)! I heard it's your favorite food, so I just had to prepare this for you. What do you mean, "eww"?!

examples.en: This pond has a lot of people swimming in it, it's like a natural pool.
examples.ja: この池はたくさんの人が泳いでて、まるで天然のプールだ。

examples.en: Would you mind buying a bottle of natural water from the convenience store?
examples.ja: コンビニでペットボトルの天然水を買ってきてくれる？

examples.en: Wild eel and yellow tail are quite expensive.
examples.ja: 天然のウナギやブリは高いです。

9273.meaning_mnemonic:
Something of <kanji>heaven</kanji>'s <kanji>nature</kanji> is indeed <vocabulary>natural</vocabulary>, with no human intervention involved.

Although this word is technically a noun, it's often used as an adjective. That's also what distinguishes it from 自然. So you'll often see 天然 used to say that something is "natural" or "of nature", while 自然 will often be used to talk about nature in general, like saying that nature is beautiful.
9273.reading_mnemonic:
You know the reading for 天, but 然 uses a different reading from what you learned. So here's a mnemonic to help you:

One thing that definitely isn't <vocabulary>natural</vocabulary> are <reading>nen</reading>doroids (ねん). Remember, the little plastic figurines? Have you ever seen an anime figurine growing naturally in a field before? Yup, me neither. Not very natural.

examples.en: It's obvious that your mom really likes wine.
examples.ja: あなたのお母さんがワイン好きなのは明らかです。

examples.en: It turned out that he has some Irish heritage in his blood.
examples.ja: 彼にアイルランド人の血が入ってることが明らかになりました。

examples.en: Koichi is clearly acting strange today.
examples.ja: 今日のコウイチは明らかにおかしい。

9274.meaning_mnemonic: When it's <kanji>bright</kanji> around, things become more <vocabulary>obvious</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>clear</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>evident</vocabulary>.
9274.reading_mnemonic:
Since this is a word that consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it uses kun'yomi. Unfortunately, 明 is a little tricky and has a few of those. So here's a mnemonic to help you remember this one:

It's <vocabulary>obvious</vocabulary> that all you need is <reading>a key</reading> (あき) to open this door. It's like, blatantly <vocabulary>clear</vocabulary>. The lock is right there. You really just need a key. Did you forget it? Of course you did…

examples.en: I love kimchi fried rice.
examples.ja: 私はキムチ炒飯が大好きです。

examples.en: I'll go with the fried rice.
examples.ja: 俺は炒飯にするよ。

examples.en: Making delicious fried rice isn't easy.
examples.ja: 美味しい炒飯を作るのは簡単じゃない。

9275.meaning_mnemonic:
What's your favorite <kanji>fry</kanji> <kanji>meal</kanji>? Surely it's <vocabulary>fried rice</vocabulary>, aka <vocabulary>chahan</vocabulary>! Who doesn't love fried rice?

Note that this word is commonly written in katakana as チャーハン, so you may also see it written that way on a menu or product label!
9275.reading_mnemonic:
You know the reading for 飯, but 炒 uses an exceptional reading that you didn't learn. Here's a mnemonic to help you:

Do you know what would bring your <vocabulary>fried rice</vocabulary> to the next level? Some <reading>char</reading>coal (ちゃー)! Next time, just add a little charcoal to your fried rice, and it'll taste so much better. Trust me on this one.

examples.en: If communication isn't done well, some issues might arise.
examples.ja: コミュニケーションが上手くできていないと、トラブルが生じるかもしれません。

examples.en: From there, many problems emerged.
examples.ja: そこから多くの問題が生じました。

examples.en: Due to system updates, it will be necessary to temporarily halt the system.
examples.ja: システムのアップデートにより一時的にシステムを止める必要が生じます。

9276.meaning_mnemonic: Remember how 生まれる means "to be born"? This word is similar, but it's used for when non-living things are "born". So as an intransitive verb, this means <vocabulary>to occur</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to arise</vocabulary>. When used transitively, it means <vocabulary>to cause something</vocabulary>. You'll probably encounter the intransitive use much more, though.
9276.reading_mnemonic:
You'd think this would use kun'yomi, but it actually doesn't! Like other verbs ending in じる, this takes the on'yomi reading of the kanji. 生 has two of those, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: 

If you wanted anything <vocabulary>to occur</vocabulary> in medieval Japan, you needed to talk to the <reading>Shou</reading>gun. You always needed the Shougun's help <vocabulary>to cause something</vocabulary>. Without the Shougun, nothing would ever happen!

examples.en: We're trying to figure out how to structure our next business.
examples.ja: 次のビジネスの仕組みを考えています。

examples.en: Do you know the inner workings of the world?
examples.ja: あなたは世の中の仕組みを知っていますか？

examples.en: If you press a button on this TV remote three times, it triggers a mechanism to unlock this door.
examples.ja: このテレビのリモコンのボタンを三回おすと、このドアがアンロックされる仕組みになっています。

9278.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Doing</kanji> something as a <kanji>group</kanji> requires a <vocabulary>system</vocabulary>. Without some sort of <vocabulary>structure</vocabulary>, everyone does their own thing, and you would never be able to get stuff done as a group, you know?

仕組み refers to the concept of a "mechanism" or "system." It includes the underlying structure, organization, or framework that governs how something works or operates, highlighting its logic, order, and other often unseen things.
9278.reading_mnemonic:
This is a word with an irregular combination of readings. 仕 uses its on'yomi reading, and 組 uses its kun'yomi reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember this unusual combination:

To be more successful in doing group assignments, you came up with a <vocabulary>system</vocabulary> called "<reading>shee</reading>p <reading>cumi</reading>n (しくみ). Why "sheep cumin"? Sheep are known to be good team players (or herd players, should I say?), so you just sticked it to the name of the group you lead, the cumin group, hoping everyone can work together better, like sheep!

examples.en: Is there a way to receive a pension from overseas?
examples.ja: 海外から年金を受け取る方法ってありますか？

examples.en: I haven't received my ticket yet, even though I'm leaving tomorrow.
examples.ja: 明日出発なのにまだチケットを受け取ってないんです。

examples.en: Since I'm at home, I'll receive the Amazon package on your behalf.
examples.ja: 家にいるから、アマゾンのパッケージ、代わりに受け取っておくよ。

9279.meaning_mnemonic:
You know that 受ける means "to receive something." Combine it with 取る (to take something), and 受け取る… still means <vocabulary>to receive something</vocabulary>.

However, while 受ける generally implies passive reception, 受け取る carries a stronger connotation of actively taking possession of something. It is used when receiving a package or gift, or even when interpreting someone's words as having a specific meaning, such as an insult or compliment.
9279.reading_mnemonic: If you know how to read 受ける and 取る, you should be good to go.

examples.en: Just be honest and admit it.
examples.ja: 素直に認めろよ。

examples.en: I'm glad I could hear your honest feelings.
examples.ja: 君の素直な気持ちが聞けてうれしいよ。

examples.en: It's important to have the openness to accept advice from others.
examples.ja: 人のアドバイスを素直に受け入れられる素直さって大事だよね。

9280.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 直 can also mean "direct?" Well, if someone has an <kanji>element</kanji> of <kanji>direct</kanji>ness to them, they're probably a really <vocabulary>honest</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>upfront</vocabulary> person.

素直 usually describes someone who's sincere, emotionally open, willing to listen, and not stubborn. In some contexts, it can also imply someone is obedient or compliant. For example, a child who always does what they're told without objection might be called 素直.
9280.reading_mnemonic:
The reading for this is a bit of a weird one. It uses on'yomi for 素, then it uses the kun'yomi for 直. You know both readings, but it's all a little strange, so here's a mnemonic help you:

If you're <vocabulary>honest</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>upfront</vocabulary> with yourself, you know it's time to <reading>sue now</reading> (すなお). What that person did to you… they definitely deserve be sued, now. Don't try to brush it off, don't let them silence you. Be <vocabulary>obedient</vocabulary> to your feelings and sue now!

examples.en: I found a ramen restaurant that has a line.
examples.ja: 行列のできるラーメン屋を見つけた。

examples.en: Oh, a line of ants!
examples.ja: あ、アリの行列だ！

examples.en: I lined up in a queue at midnight to buy concert tickets.
examples.ja: コンサートのチケットを買うために、夜中から行列にならびました。

examples.en: I learned about matrices today in math class.
examples.ja: 今日は数学のクラスで行列について学びました。

9281.meaning_mnemonic:
You know the two words that make up this word, 行 and 列, and they both have similar meanings: a line and a row. Put them together and you have a <vocabulary>line</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>queue</vocabulary>.

This usually means a line of people waiting for their turn, for example to enter a restaurant. It can be also used for a line that marches, like a line in a parade. In a mathematics context, it can refer to a <vocabulary>matrix</vocabulary>, which makes sense because they're lines and rows of numbers and stuff.
9281.reading_mnemonic: This word takes the readings of the two words that make it up, so you should be lining up to read it!

examples.en: You have worked hard enough!
examples.ja: あなたは十分がんばりました！

examples.en: There is not enough space here.
examples.ja: ここには十分なスペースがありません。

examples.en: Have you thought this through enough?
examples.ja: 十分に考えたんですか？

9282.meaning_mnemonic: You have <kanji>ten</kanji> <kanji>part</kanji>s out of ten. Which means you have quite <vocabulary>enough</vocabulary>. The amount you have is <vocabulary>sufficient</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>plenty</vocabulary>.
9282.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Walking away without saying a word is not cool.
examples.ja: 何も言わずに立ち去るなんて、ひどいよ。

examples.en: Leave this place now, quickly!
examples.ja: 早くここから立ち去れ！

examples.en: The man quickly left the spot.
examples.ja: 男はその場を足早に立ち去った。

9283.meaning_mnemonic:
You 立つ and then 去る. Makes sense, as in order <vocabulary>to leave</vocabulary>, you'll have to stand up first.

立ち去る describes the physical act of leaving a place, often used when walking away from a scene or departing a place after some kind of incident or event.
