9283.reading_mnemonic: This combines the readings of two verbs you already know, so you should be good to go here!

examples.en: Do you have a regular dentist?
examples.ja: かかりつけの歯科医はいますか？

examples.en: I have a dental clinic appointment at 3 o'clock that day.
examples.ja: その日は三時に歯科クリニックのアポイントメントがあります。

examples.en: I want to become a dental hygienist in the future.
examples.ja: 将来は歯科衛生士になりたいです。

9284.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Tooth</kanji> <kanji>science</kanji> gives you the science of <vocabulary>dentistry</vocabulary>, simple as that!

Note that when used by itself, this word solely refers to the scientific field of dentistry. You'll often see it used in combination with other medical words, so have a look at the common word combinations if you wanna know more!
9284.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 歯 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You know who benefits from great <vocabulary>dentistry</vocabulary>? <reading>Shee</reading>p (し)! Have you seen one smile? Their wool makes a great, endless source of <vocabulary>dental</vocabulary> floss. That's their secret. Just think of the sheep and their perfect teeth and you'll never forget this reading!

examples.en: I work as an associate professor at Kyoto University.
examples.ja: 私は京都大学で准教授として務めています。

examples.en: I believe Asano-sensei is an associate professor.
examples.ja: 確か、浅野先生は准教授のはずです。

examples.en: This is Dr. Kimura, who will be assuming the position of specially appointed associate professor at this center soon.
examples.ja: こちらは、今度このセンターの特任准教授に着任される木村博士です。

9285.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 教授 meaning "professor"? That makes this a <kanji>semi</kanji> professor, or in other words, an <vocabulary>associate professor</vocabulary>.
9285.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

examples.en: It's one more month until Christmas!
examples.ja: クリスマスまであと一ヶ月ですね！

examples.en: I'll be going to school in Japan for one and a half months.
examples.ja: 一ヶ月半、日本で学校に行くんです。

examples.en: I played games at home without going outside for a month.
examples.ja: 一ヶ月間、家から出ずにゲームをした。

9286.meaning_mnemonic: Remember the 〜ヶ月 counter? Replace the 〜 with a <kanji>one</kanji> and this becomes <vocabulary>one month</vocabulary>.
9286.reading_mnemonic: 一 uses the on'yomi you learned with it, but gets shortened, so watch out for that. The rest is as you learned it!

examples.en: Japanese schools only have one month of summer vacation.
examples.ja: 日本の学校の夏休みは一ヶ月しかありません。

examples.en: It took several months to complete this.
examples.ja: これが出来上がるまでに数ヶ月かかりました。

examples.en: How many months old is the baby?
examples.ja: 赤ちゃん、今何ヶ月ですか？

examples.en: My child started crawling at eight months and began walking at nine months.
examples.ja: うちの子は八ヶ月でハイハイをして、九ヶ月で歩き出しました。

9287.meaning_mnemonic:
Alright, so this one's a bit weird. See that oddly small ヶ there? Well, together with 月 (<kanji>month</kanji>), it becomes a <vocabulary>counter for months</vocabulary>. You'll use this when you want to talk about a specific number of months, so not when you're saying January, February, etc.

Note that you'll run into different variants of this. While 一ヶ月 is the most common, you'll also encounter 一か月, 一カ月, and rarely 一箇月. Luckily, they're all read the same, just written differently. Speaking about reading, let's get to it.
9287.reading_mnemonic: The little ヶ might be slightly misleading, as you'll have to read this as か. The rest is easy though, as 月 just takes a normal on'yomi reading. And since we're not talking about specific months, that means it's just げつ, making this 〜かげつ.

examples.en: Could you tell me about the plans for the day after tomorrow?
examples.ja: 明後日の予定を教えてもらえますか？

examples.en: I'm going to Japan for one month starting the day after tomorrow.
examples.ja: 明後日から一ヶ月日本に行くんです。

examples.en: Would it be possible to finish it by the day after tomorrow?
examples.ja: 明後日までに仕上げることはできますか？

9288.meaning_mnemonic: Things will be <kanji>bright</kanji> <kanji>after</kanji> the next <kanji>day</kanji>. Or you can think of it as adding an 後 in between your 明日. And what comes after tomorrow? It's the <vocabulary>day after tomorrow</vocabulary>.
9288.reading_mnemonic:
Unfortunately, the reading for this is irregular, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

"What do you want to eat the <vocabulary>day after tomorrow</vocabulary>?" your mom asks you. You answer, "<reading>Ah, satay</reading> (あさって)?" You're not so confident because you never know what you want to eat the day after tomorrow, but you absolutely love satay, the Indonesian skewers. Ah, satay it is!

examples.en: This is an objective fact.
examples.ja: これは客観的事実です。

examples.en: Objectively speaking, what you just said is not right.
examples.ja: 客観的に見て、今の発言はおかしいです。

examples.en: Without objective data, it lacks persuasiveness.
examples.ja: 客観的なデータがないと説得力に欠けてしまいます。

9289.meaning_mnemonic: Remember 主観的 meaning "subjective"? This is the counterpart to that. And since <kanji>guest</kanji>s' and customers' <kanji>view</kanji>s are always objectively right, this means <vocabulary>objective</vocabulary>.
9289.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I ordered a single commercial-grade iron plate.
examples.ja: 業務用の鉄板を一枚注文した。

examples.en: I enjoy gathering around a teppan grill with everyone and eating okonomiyaki.
examples.ja: みんなで鉄板を囲んでお好み焼きを食べるのが好きだ。

examples.en: This is one of my surefire jokes.
examples.ja: これ、オレの鉄板ネタなんだ。

9290.meaning_mnemonic:
Well, you've got <kanji>iron</kanji> and you've got a <kanji>board</kanji>. You'd probably just call it an <vocabulary>iron plate</vocabulary>, though. But this often isn't just any iron plate. If you could guess from the reading, it's often used in cooking as an <vocabulary>iron griddle</vocabulary>, or a <vocabulary>teppan grill</vocabulary>. Ever heard of Teppanyaki?

Figuratively, it means a <vocabulary>sure thing</vocabulary> or a practically guaranteed success. For example, you can use 鉄板 for a racehorse almost certain to win, or a joke that consistently gets big laughs.
9290.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. Watch out for the rendaku and you should be good!

examples.en: Why don't we go to Kyoto to see the autumn leaves?
examples.ja: 京都に紅葉を見に行きませんか？

examples.en: The autumn foliage season for this year has begun.
examples.ja: 今年も紅葉シーズンが始まりましたね。

examples.en: The Japanese maple in my yard has not yet turned red.
examples.ja: うちの庭の紅葉の木はまだ紅葉してません。

examples.en: "<ja>紅葉の紅葉</ja>" is read "momiji no kōyō."
examples.ja: 「紅葉の紅葉」は「モミジのこうよう」って読むんですよ。

9291.meaning_mnemonic:
You've got some <kanji>deep red</kanji> <kanji>leaves</kanji>. You'll usually see those during autumn, which makes this <vocabulary>autumn leaves</vocabulary>. Just <vocabulary>red leaves</vocabulary> is fine too, though.

Note that this refers not only to the leaves themselves, but also the process of them changing color, so this can also mean <vocabulary>leaves turning red</vocabulary>.
9291.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. As you haven't learned this reading for 葉 yet, here's a mnemonic to help you:

Your favorite pastime during autumn is sitting there admiring the <vocabulary>autumn leaves</vocabulary> while eating some <reading>yo</reading>gurt (よう). There's no better combination than autumn leaves and yogurt.

Note that there's also an additional reading, もみじ, used to refer to the Japanese maple tree, or its leaves, but we'd like you to focus on こうよう for this one.

examples.en: How's your dad?
examples.ja: お前の親父さん、元気？

examples.en: That bearded dude is really stubborn.
examples.ja: あのヒゲ親父、ホント頑固なんだから。

examples.en: I grew up watching my dad's back from a young age.
examples.ja: 俺は小さい頃から、親父の背中を見て育った。

9292.meaning_mnemonic:
One's <kanji>parent</kanji> <kanji>father</kanji> is simply just <vocabulary>one's father</vocabulary>. 

Note that 親父 has a masculine and somewhat vulgar tone to it. It can refer to your own dad, someone else's, or a <vocabulary>middle-aged man</vocabulary> you're friendly with. When not talking about your own father, you'll want to add a さん at the end, making it 親父さん.
9292.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this is unfortunately a bit of an exception. 親 uses the kun'yomi おや, and 父 uses the じ reading which you learned with 叔父. You've learned all these readings before, so as long as you remember them, you're good to go. If you don't, check out the mnemonics for these readings on their vocabularies' pages!

examples.en: I started taking swimming lessons.
examples.ja: 水泳教室に通い始めました。

examples.en: Swimming is an excellent full-body workout.
examples.ja: 水泳はとても良い全身運動です。

examples.en: Swimming classes at school are fun.
examples.ja: 水泳の授業は学校で楽しいです。

9293.meaning_mnemonic:
When you're doing a <kanji>water</kanji> <kanji>swim</kanji>, you're really just… well, <vocabulary>swimming</vocabulary>.

Note that 水泳 will usually refer to swimming as a sport or organized activity. When talking about swimming as a general action, 泳ぎ and 泳ぐ are more commonly used.
9293.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You've learned this reading for 水, but not for 泳, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

The only way you can <vocabulary>swim</vocabulary> is by chasing after <reading>a</reading>corns (えい). If somebody isn't dangling an acorn on a stick right in front of your face, you'd never get the motivation to swim. Good thing you're this into acorns.

examples.en: It is dangerous to stack so many plates.
examples.ja: そんなにお皿を重ねると危ないですよ。

examples.en: The princess became more and more beautiful as she grew older.
examples.ja: プリンセスは、年を重ねるごとに美しくなっていきました。

examples.en: Isn't it a waste of time to have a bunch of discussions about things that don't have answers?
examples.ja: 答えのないことにディスカッションを重ねるのってムダじゃないですか？

9294.meaning_mnemonic:
You've got lots of <kanji>heavy</kanji> things, so the only logical thing is <vocabulary>to stack</vocabulary> them all up. 

Besides heavy physical things, you can also use this word when you're going <vocabulary>to accumulate</vocabulary> things like experience, practice, or years on your back.
9294.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

All the things you've <vocabulary>stack</vocabulary>ed up were in preparation for your new <reading>casa</reading> (かさ). With everything inside boxes and neatly piled up, you're finally ready to move into your new casa. Hooray!

examples.en: This phrasing still conveys the meaning, but it sounds a bit unnatural.
examples.ja: この言い方でも意味は通じるけど、ちょっと不自然かな。

examples.en: I met him through the Internet.
examples.ja: 彼とは、インターネットを通じて知り合いました。

examples.en: Even if we don't share a common language, our hearts can still connect.
examples.ja: 言葉は通じなくても、心が通じることはあります。

examples.en: Nothing I say gets through to that person and nothing they say makes sense either; it's like talking to an alien.
examples.ja: あの人、全然話が通じないんですよ。エイリアンと話してるみたいな感覚になります。

9295.meaning_mnemonic:
You have <kanji>pass through</kanji>, so this is <vocabulary>to pass through</vocabulary>.

This word has a bunch of different meanings, and translations will vary depending on context. In short, it's mostly used figuratively to mean that something, like communication, is passing or coming through successfully. Have a look at our common word combinations and context sentences for some example usages!
9295.reading_mnemonic: Like other verbs that end in じる, this actually uses the on'yomi of the kanji, not kun'yomi! You learned that reading with the kanji, so you should be good to go here.

examples.en: Despite the repeated outpourings of criticism, that YouTuber continued to create content.

examples.ja: その年は、コロナのせいで上映中止が相次ぎました。

examples.en: Due to a series of accidents caused by drunk driving nationwide, the police intensified their enforcement.
examples.ja: 飲酒運転による事故が全国で相次いだため、警察は取り締まりを強化しました。

9296.meaning_mnemonic:
Things that happen <kanji>mutual</kanji>ly right <kanji>next</kanji> to each other are said <vocabulary>to happen successively</vocabulary>. In other words, <vocabulary>to happen one after another</vocabulary>.

相次ぐ is a relatively formal word often used in news reports to talk about multiple events or incidents happening one after another, usually in quick succession.
9296.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi readings. You've learned this reading for 相, but not for 次. Instead of giving you a mnemonic, we think it's easier to remember that 次ぐ being read つぐ comes from the 次 reading つぎ. Not too hard! All in all, that makes this あいつぐ.

examples.en: I didn't have time to eat lunch.
examples.ja: 昼飯を食う時間がなかったんだ。

examples.en: Oh no, my silk suit is being eaten by bugs!
examples.ja: げ、シルクのスーツが虫に食われてる！

examples.en: It was a job that just ate up my time and didn't pay off.
examples.ja: 時間ばっかり食って、割りに合わない仕事だったよ。

9297.meaning_mnemonic:
You know the kanji means <kanji>eat</kanji>, and you also already know 食べる. So what's the deal with this also meaning <vocabulary>to eat</vocabulary>? 

食う carries a more masculine and coarse tone than 食べる, so it can come off as rough or impolite in certain situations. It also has a wider set of usages, for example in saying that something is eating up time or resources, or saying that you were bitten by a bug. You'll come across more of these, but they're all pretty straightforward, so don't worry!
9297.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You do know that reading, but this uses a different one, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

There's nothing you love <vocabulary>to eat</vocabulary> more than <reading>coo</reading>kies (く). You could eat them day and night, but watch out, as that might get a little… time-consuming.

examples.en: The current exchange rate for USD/JPY is 1 dollar = 146.25 yen.
examples.ja: ドル円の現在の為替レートは、1ドル=146円25銭です。

examples.en: The foreign exchange market is a living creature that fluctuates daily.
examples.ja: 為替相場は日々変動する生き物です。

examples.en: I believe that in the context of global employment, the exchange rate risk should morally be borne more by the company than the employees.
examples.ja: グローバル雇用における為替リスクは、モラル的には会社が従業員よりも多めに負担すべきだと思うんです。

9298.meaning_mnemonic: For the <kanji>sake</kanji> of <kanji>exchange</kanji>! What sounds so glorious is really just <vocabulary>currency exchange</vocabulary>.

Why of course, it's celery that's stored, cleaned, and… smoked inside of a car wash. So go get all the currency you have, we have some exchanging to do.

examples.en: The faucet wasn't properly closed!
examples.ja: 蛇口がちゃんと閉まってなかったよ！

examples.en: The faucet of the hose is broken, and the water won't stop.

examples.en: Hey, I've been telling you to stop drinking directly from the tap!
examples.ja: ちょっと、蛇口から直接飲むのはやめてって言ってるじゃん！

9299.meaning_mnemonic: This isn't a literal <kanji>snake</kanji>'s <kanji>mouth</kanji>, but rather a <vocabulary>faucet</vocabulary>. They do kind of have a resemblance though, just think about how the shape of a faucet kind of resembles that of a snake, with water coming out of its mouth.
9299.reading_mnemonic:
This one's a little unique, as it uses on'yomi for 蛇, and kun'yomi (which gets rendaku'd) for 口. You didn't learn this reading for 蛇, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Every time you try to drink from the <vocabulary>faucet</vocabulary>, you get viciously attacked by a <reading>ja</reading>guar (じゃ). Trying to drink from the faucet has become a fight for life and death. You just know the jaguar is hiding right there behind the faucet, guarding it.

examples.en: Let's rest here for ten minutes.
examples.ja: ここで十分間休みましょう。

examples.en: Can I play a game just for ten minutes?
examples.ja: 十分間だけゲームしていい？

examples.en: I think I can do it if I have ten minutes.
examples.ja: 十分間あれば出来ると思いますよ。

9300.meaning_mnemonic:
You've got a <kanji>ten</kanji> <kanji>minute</kanji> <kanji>interval of time</kanji>. That simply makes this <vocabulary>ten minutes</vocabulary>.

Note that, as we mentioned on the page for 〜間, you can omit 間 and this will still mean <vocabulary>ten minutes</vocabulary>! You'll especially see this in conversations and more casual contexts.

You do know all of those, but their behaviour is a little different here. 十 (じゅう) and 分 (～ふん) together actually turn into じゅっぷん here. This is sometimes the case when using ～分 to mean "minute" in combination with certain numbers, so try to pay attention to this!

examples.en: Thank you for your great kindness in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本ではお世話になりました。

examples.en: You're truly a high-maintenance child!
examples.ja: あんたは本当に世話のかかる子だね！

examples.en: Yikes! Taking care of a baby is way tougher than I thought.
examples.ja: ヤバイ！赤子の世話、思ってたよりめっちゃキツイわ。

9301.meaning_mnemonic: Older <kanji>generation</kanji>s mostly <kanji>talk</kanji> about one thing: <vocabulary>care</vocabulary>. Everybody wants to receive care once they're older, don't they?
9301.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Just remember that 世 is せ here, and not せい!

examples.en: Hey, isn't that former Prime Minister Mori?

examples.en: What do you think about the Prime Minister's remarks yesterday?

examples.en: This is where the Prime Minister can really show off their leadership, isn't it?

9302.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>neck</kanji> <kanji>minister</kanji>? This meaning <vocabulary>prime minister</vocabulary> makes sense if you think about the neck being the most important part of the body, kind of like the head!
9302.reading_mnemonic:

The first <vocabulary>prime minister</vocabulary>s of Japan were actually the <reading>sho</reading>guns (しょう)… kind of.

examples.en: Wow, that's amazing! As might be expected of you.

A <kanji>stream</kanji> containing <kanji>stone</kanji>s is like… the most natural thing ever. It's just <vocabulary>as expected</vocabulary>.

9303.reading_mnemonic:
Unfortunately, the reading for this is a total exception that you'll just have to memorize, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Just <vocabulary>as expected</vocabulary>, your <reading>sauce ga</reading>l (さすが) saved the day. The dish you cooked was looking a little bare until your gal poured sauce all over it. It looked a little like a stream flowing over dry rocks when she poured the sauce. Just as you'd expect of your sauce gal.

examples.en: When I click here, the text overlaps and becomes unreadable. Do you think it's a bug?
examples.ja: ここをクリックすると、文字が上に重なるから読めなくなるんだ。バグかな？

examples.en: What should I do? My child's birthday party falls on a work day.
examples.ja: どうしよう、子どものバースデーパーティーと仕事の日が重なってしまった。

examples.en: There's not just one cause. Various factors converged to make it like this.
examples.ja: 原因は一つじゃありません。様々な要因が重なって、こうなってしまったんです。

9304.meaning_mnemonic:
If you remember 重ねる, then you'll recognize this as the intransitive version of that verb. Literally, this means <vocabulary>to be piled up</vocabulary>, but it's often used to mean <vocabulary>to coincide</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to overlap</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to accumulate</vocabulary>.

As is often our recommendation for more complicated or hard-to-translate words like this one, check out our common word combinations and context sentences to see how this word is used!
9304.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned that reading with 重ねる, but in case it's slipped your mind, here's a mnemonic to help you remember:

All these boxes that are <vocabulary>piled up</vocabulary> are here because you've just moved into your new <reading>casa</reading> (かさ). Congratulations! Now it's time to unpack every single box you've <vocabulary>accumulate</vocabulary>d. Have fun.

examples.en: Please unify the writing style into the desu-masu form.

9305.meaning_mnemonic: To <kanji>unite</kanji> as <kanji>one</kanji> is to achieve total <vocabulary>unity</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>uniformity</vocabulary>.

examples.en: I made just one mistake on the test.
examples.ja: テストで一ヶ所だけミスをしてしまった。

Remember the small ヶ acting as a counter? Together with <kanji>one</kanji> and <kanji>place</kanji>, it makes this <vocabulary>one place</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>one spot</vocabulary>.

examples.en: Dedicating time to studying is a very good thing.

In addition to spending money, 費やす can be used to refer to spending other resources like time, effort, energy, and emotions.
9307.reading_mnemonic:

Maybe you should listen to the bird tweeting from inside your wallet a little more.

examples.en: Oh no! I'd forgotten to apply for a visa.

Today you finally submitted your <vocabulary>application</vocabulary> for a new <reading>shin</reading> (しん). Your old one had to be painstakingly removed after you banged it against a table. Anyway, congrats on the application for your new shin!

examples.en: Professionals and amateurs are indeed different!

examples.ja: 唐揚げの味付けと粉の比率は自由ですが、竜田揚げには醤油ベースの下味と片栗粉がマストです。

While 唐揚げ most often refers to fried chicken, it can technically also refer to other deep fried meats, fish, or vegetables. As it's the most common meaning, remembering this as "fried chicken" will be just fine, though.

examples.ja: この村にはもう年配者しか残っていないんですよ。

9330.meaning_mnemonic:
As the <kanji>years</kanji> get <kanji>distribute</kanji>d, you slowly turn into an <vocabulary>elderly</vocabulary> <vocabulary>senior</vocabulary>, proud of your <vocabulary>old age</vocabulary>.

This word is used to politely describe an elderly person, as in 年配の方 or 年配者.
9330.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The はい goes to a ぱい, because… elderly persons love <reading>pie</reading> (ぱい), right?

examples.en: The first product of our collaboration with WaniKani is a WaniKani figure!
examples.ja: 我が社とWaniKaniとのコラボ商品第一弾は、ワニカニのフィギュアです！

examples.en: This illustration is the first one in the Rabbit DJ series.
examples.ja: こちらのイラストは、ウサギのDJシリーズの第一弾です。

examples.en: Let's adjust the contents of the second round by looking at the feedback to the first round of the promotional campaign.
examples.ja: キャンペーンの第一弾の反応を見て、第二弾の中身を調整しましょう。

9331.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>ordinal number prefix</kanji> <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>bullet</kanji> is actually the <vocabulary>first installment</vocabulary> of something. Picture someone firing a gun to let everyone know that, yes, this is indeed the <vocabulary>first round</vocabulary> of… whatever you're doing.

Note that this is quite similar to 第一段. While 第一段 refers to the first phase or step within one larger, continuous process or structure, 第一弾 is used to refer to the first installment or part of a series of events or releases.
9331.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Diving is prohibited in this pool.
examples.ja: このプールでは飛び込みは禁止されています。

examples.en: This is a fence to prevent people from jumping in.
examples.ja: これは飛び込み防止のためのフェンスです。

examples.en: Newcomers must do door-to-door sales every day.
examples.ja: 新人は毎日、飛び込み営業をしなくてはなりません。

9332.meaning_mnemonic:
You’re doing a 飛ぶ and 込む at the same time, or you <kanji>jump</kanji> <kanji>into</kanji>, meaning you're <vocabulary>diving in</vocabulary>. Picture yourself standing somewhere up high, and then jumping to dive into a deep body of water.

Alternatively, this can also refer to doing something, or joining or going somewhere without an appointment, announcement, or prior registration, which is where the <vocabulary>dropping by</vocabulary> meaning comes in. For some use cases of this, check out our common word combinations and context sentences below!
9332.reading_mnemonic: As long as you remember that we're combining the kun'yomi readings of the verbs and then turning them into a noun, you should know how to read this.

examples.en: The clownfish is a saltwater fish.
examples.ja: カクレクマノミは海水魚です。

examples.en: Which is the most popular saltwater fish in this store?
examples.ja: このお店で一番人気のある海水魚はどれですか？

examples.en: After all, I'm worried about the smell of saltwater fish.
examples.ja: やっぱり海水魚はニオイが気になります。

9333.meaning_mnemonic:
You've got a <kanji>sea</kanji> <kanji>water</kanji> <kanji>fish</kanji>, or in other words, a <vocabulary>saltwater fish</vocabulary>.

海水魚 refers to fish that live in the ocean, as opposed to freshwater fish.
9333.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Sorry, I'm planning to hang out with Rento that day.
examples.ja: ごめん、その日は漣斗と遊ぶ予定なんだ。

examples.en: I heard Rento couldn't pay his rent and got kicked out.
examples.ja: 漣斗のやつ、家賃払えなくて追い出されたんだって。

examples.en: Rento-kun, I didn't know that the kanji "漣" in your name means "ripple"!
examples.ja: 漣斗くんの「漣」って漢字、「さざなみ」って意味なんだね！知らなかった。

9334.meaning_mnemonic:
This isn't a <kanji>ripples</kanji> <kanji>ladle</kanji>, but the Japanese given name <vocabulary>Rento</vocabulary>! 

The name Rento is fairly common, but this kanji version is quite unique. Sadly, there aren't any famous 漣斗s we can mention, but you should be proud of yourself for reaching this level in WaniKani and mastering such a high-level name!
9334.reading_mnemonic: This name uses the on'yomi for both kanji, which you already learned. Lucky!

9335.reading_mnemonic: Not only are they moles, all of your <kanji>niece</kanji>s were also born in <reading>May</reading> (めい)!

examples.en: I have a five-year-old niece.
examples.ja: 私には五才の姪がいます。

examples.en: I love my niece very much.
examples.ja: 私は姪っ子が大好きです。

examples.en: I met my niece's husband for the first time the other day.
examples.ja: 先日、姪の夫に初めて会いました。

examples.en: Oh, sorry it's so confusing. My niece's child's name is Mei.
examples.ja: あっ、ややこしくてすいません。私の姪の子供の名前がメイなんです。

9336.meaning_mnemonic: This is just the kanji <kanji>niece</kanji> as a vocab, so this also means <vocabulary>niece</vocabulary>!
9336.reading_mnemonic: As a standalone vocab, this uses the kun'yomi reading. Luckily, that's what you learned with the kanji, so no new reading here!

examples.en: It seems that he injured his head while playing soccer.
examples.ja: 彼は、サッカーで頭部にケガをしたようです。

examples.en: However, it seems that there was no issue with his head X-ray.
examples.ja: でも、頭部のレントゲンに問題はなかったそうです。

examples.en: That guy deliberately aimed for your head!
examples.ja: アイツ、わざとお前の頭部をねらったんだよ！

9337.meaning_mnemonic:
Your <kanji>head</kanji> <kanji>part</kanji>, or the part of your body that's your head, is… well, your <vocabulary>head</vocabulary>!

This is a more formal way of saying "head" compared to just 頭, so you'll encounter this more frequently in medical and other, more formal contexts.
9337.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 頭 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Need a checkup on your head? Then head to とうきょう! They have the best… head doctors in とうきょう, I've heard. So head on over to とうきょう for your next head checkup.

9338.meaning_mnemonic: You're using your <radical>fingers</radical> to do something important for this <radical>ceremony</radical>'s <radical>construction</radical>. What's really important for this ceremony's construction, using your fingers? Well… you <kanji>wipe</kanji> the floors.

examples.en: I bought a tenugui towel in Japan.
examples.ja: 日本で手拭いを買ってきました。

examples.en: How is a tenugui towel different from a regular towel?
examples.ja: 手拭いは、ふつうのタオルとどう違うんですか？

examples.en: Wow, cool! I didn't know there were WaniKani tenugui towels.
examples.ja: うわぁ、かっこいい！ワニカニの手拭いがあるなんて知らなかったです。

9339.meaning_mnemonic:
You have the kanji for <kanji>hand</kanji> and the noun version of the verb for <kanji>wipe</kanji>. With a bit of imagination, that makes this a <vocabulary>hand towel</vocabulary>, or just a <vocabulary>towel</vocabulary>. They're a very specific kind of cloth towel, which is why you'll also often encounter them with their Japanese name <vocabulary>tenugui</vocabulary>.

Unlike お手拭き, which you learned about a few levels ago, 手拭い are always towels — never tissues. These thin, flat cloths are long and narrow, serving a variety of purposes beyond simply cleaning your hands. Their history is fascinating, so be sure to look them up!
9339.reading_mnemonic: You have a standalone vocab (手) combined with the noun version of a verb (拭い from 拭う), which means that this uses kun'yomi readings. You've already learned these, so you should be good to go!

examples.en: Excuse me, could I get a hand wipe, please?
examples.ja: すいません、お手拭きをもらえますか？

examples.en: Oh, feel free to use this hand wipe!
examples.ja: あ、よかったらこのお手拭き使って！

examples.en: When I sit down at a restaurant, I first wipe my hands with a hand wipe.
examples.ja: レストランで席につくと、まずお手拭きで手を拭きます。

9340.meaning_mnemonic:
You have <kanji>hand</kanji> and the noun version of 拭く (to wipe). Put the two together and you get a <vocabulary>hand wipe</vocabulary>!

お手拭き refers to a <vocabulary>wet hand towel</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>wet napkin</vocabulary> used for cleaning your hands, often provided at restaurants in Japan before a meal.
9340.reading_mnemonic: The reading for this uses all kun'yomi. So just put together the kun'yomis of 手 and 拭き (from the verb 拭く) with an honorary お and you're good to go!

examples.en: Wait, you wipe your body with this small towel instead of a bath towel?
examples.ja: えっ、バスタオルじゃなく、この小さいタオルで体を拭くんですか？

examples.en: It's a waste to wipe up spills with tissues. Don't we have something like a dishcloth?
examples.ja: こぼしたものをティッシュで拭くのはもったいないよ。ふきんとかないの？

examples.en: In that case, could you please wipe the table with this, Misaki-san?
examples.ja: じゃあ、ミサキさんは、これでテーブルを拭いといてもらえますか？

9341.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji means <kanji>wipe</kanji>, and this is the verb version of that, making this <vocabulary>to wipe</vocabulary>.

拭く is generally used for actions involving cleaning or drying surfaces by wiping, often with a cloth, towel, or similar item.
9341.reading_mnemonic: Like verbs usually do, this uses the kun'yomi, which you already learned with the kanji. Lucky you!

examples.en: My child still has the habit of wiping their mouth with their sleeve.
examples.ja: うちの子、まだ口をそでで拭うクセがあるんです。

examples.en: After wiping the blood with his shirt, the man started running again.
examples.ja: 男はシャツで血を拭うと、また走り出した。

examples.en: After gently wiping away her tears with a handkerchief, she stood up as though she had made a resolution.
examples.ja: 彼女はハンカチでなみだをそっと拭うと、決心したように立ち上がりました。

9342.meaning_mnemonic:
You have the kanji for <kanji>wipe</kanji>, and this is the verb version of that, which makes this <vocabulary>to wipe</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to mop up</vocabulary>.

You've already learned 拭く, which is a general word for the act of wiping, whether you're wiping a table or wiping your forehead. 拭う, on the other hand, is more commonly used in writing to describe the act of wiping away and removing something specific like sweat, tears, filth, or even doubts.
9342.reading_mnemonic:
This is a verb, so it uses the kun'yomi. However, to differentiate this verb from 拭く, it uses a different reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember this:

What are you trying <vocabulary>to wipe</vocabulary>? Some <reading>nu</reading>de <reading>goo</reading> (ぬぐ)! You spilled nude goo all over your floor, and now you have to mop it all up… pesky nude goo.

9343.meaning_mnemonic: You keep your <radical>mouth</radical> close to your <radical>cross</radical>, praying for all your wishes to <kanji>come true</kanji>. Perhaps some gracious god will <kanji>grant</kanji> what you wish for?
9343.reading_mnemonic: And if you really want your wish to <kanji>come true</kanji>, make sure to write it down in <reading>kana</reading>!

examples.en: I will make this dream come true no matter what!
examples.ja: ゼッタイにこの夢を叶えるんだ！

examples.en: When do you want to achieve that goal by?
examples.ja: あなたは、いつまでにその目標を叶えたいですか？

examples.en: It may not be possible to fulfill all your wishes.
examples.ja: 全ての希望を叶えることはできないかもしれません。

9344.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji means "come true" or <kanji>grant</kanji>, and this is the transitive verb version of that, making this <vocabulary>to grant</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to fulfill</vocabulary>.

叶える refers to making something desired come true, either for oneself or someone else. It's usually used in the context of fulfilling wishes, dreams, or goals, but it can also be used for granting someone's request in more formal contexts.
9344.reading_mnemonic: This is a verb, so it uses the kun'yomi reading. Luckily, you already learned this with the kanji, so you should be good to go here!

examples.en: I hope this wish comes true someday.
examples.ja: いつかこの願いが叶うといいな。

examples.en: Anyway, it was a love that was never meant to be.
examples.ja: どうせ、叶わぬ恋だったんだよ。

examples.en: Don't worry, if you don't give up, your dreams will surely come true!
examples.ja: 大丈夫、あきらめなければ、夢はきっと叶うよ！

9345.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji means <kanji>come true</kanji>, and this is the intransitive verb version of that, making this <vocabulary>to come true</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be fulfilled</vocabulary>.
9345.reading_mnemonic: This is a verb, so it uses the kun'yomi reading. Luckily, you already learned this with the kanji, so you should be good to go here!

examples.en: Be careful with this bug; it has a stinger!
examples.ja: この虫、針があるから気をつけてね！

examples.en: It pinched a bit when the needle went in, but it was fine.
examples.ja: 針を刺す時、ちょっとチクっとしたけど、平気だったよ。

examples.en: What do you call the "hari" of a clock in English, again?
examples.ja: 時計の針のことって、英語でなんて言うんだっけ？

9346.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
9346.reading_mnemonic:
As a standalone vocab, this uses the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

This <vocabulary>needle</vocabulary> is… incredibly <reading>hairy</reading> (はり). And you're about to receive an injection. About the only thing worse than a normal needle is probably a hairy needle. Eww.

examples.en: They say it's the season of harvest in autumn, don't they?
examples.ja: 実りの秋っていいますもんね。

examples.en: Autumn is the season of harvest, so there are lots of delicious things.
examples.ja: 秋は実りの季節ですから、美味しいものがたくさんあります。

examples.en: Thanks to everyone, it turned out to be a very fruitful workshop.
examples.ja: 皆さんのおかげで、とても実り多い研究会になりました。

examples.en: I believe that studying abroad always brings significant rewards.
examples.ja: 海外に出て学ぶことは、必ず大きな実りをもたらすと思っています。

9347.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 実る means "to bear fruit"? This is just the noun version of that word, so it means <vocabulary>harvest</vocabulary>. (A nice harvest is what you get when your crops literally bear fruit!)

Literally speaking, 実り refers to fruit and crops that are ripe and ready to be harvested. It's a bit old-fashioned and poetic, but you might see it in phrases like 実りの秋 (the fruitful season of autumn). Like the verb version 実る, it's more often used figuratively nowadays to refer to the <vocabulary>fruits</vocabulary> of hard work.
9347.reading_mnemonic: This is just the noun version of the verb 実る, which you've already learned how to read, so you should be good to go here!

examples.en: I can't believe this love has come to fruition!
examples.ja: まさか、この恋が実るなんて！

examples.en: A lot of oranges have ripened again this year.
examples.ja: 今年もたくさんのオレンジが実りました。

examples.en: Teacher, your many years of effort have finally paid off!
examples.ja: 先生、長年の努力が実りましたね！

9348.meaning_mnemonic:
You might remember 実 means "truth," but it can also mean <kanji>fruit</kanji>! That's why this verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to bear fruit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to come to fruition</vocabulary>. 

実る literally means <vocabulary>to ripen</vocabulary>, but it's mostly used figuratively to describe when hard work leads to results, like in the phrase 努力が実る (effort pays off).
9348.reading_mnemonic:
This is a verb, so it uses the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

Your experiments have finally started <vocabulary>to bear fruit</vocabulary>. You've fully turned yourself into a <reading>mino</reading>taur (みの)! Your long-term ambitions of turning yourself into a minotaur are finally beginning <vocabulary>to come to fruition</vocabulary>. All hail our new minotaur overlord!

examples.en: The two rivals are finally set to face off.
examples.ja: 二人のライバルがついに対決することになった。

examples.en: Someday, I'd like to go head-to-head with that chef.
examples.ja: いつかあのシェフと1対1で対決してみたいな。

examples.en: Alright, now I have all the items I need for the showdown with the boss!
examples.ja: よし、これでボスキャラとの対決にいるアイテムがそろったぞ！

9349.meaning_mnemonic:
When it's you <kanji>versus</kanji> someone else to <kanji>decide</kanji> it all, you know this is a <vocabulary>showdown</vocabulary>. It's a decisive <vocabulary>confrontation</vocabulary>!

対決 is when two sides go head-to-head in a serious match or showdown. Think rivals <vocabulary>facing off</vocabulary> in a big game or the final battle in an anime. It's tense and dramatic, but also exciting — like, "Alright, this is it. Time to settle things. Who's gonna come out on top?"
9349.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: How is life in the northern country?
examples.ja: 北国のくらしはどうですか？

examples.en: Winter in the northern country is very long.
examples.ja: 北国の冬は、とても長いです。

examples.en: Children in the north are good at playing in the snow.
examples.ja: 北国の子どもたちは雪あそびが上手です。

9350.meaning_mnemonic:
Go <kanji>north</kanji> into the <kanji>country</kanji>. Now you're in <vocabulary>northern country</vocabulary>.

北国 is used to describe northern regions where it gets all cold and snowy in winter, like Hokkaido or Tohoku in Japan or parts of Finland or Canada outside of Japan.
9350.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. Luckily they're readings you've already learned, so you're good to go here. Just watch out for the rendaku that changes くに to ぐに.

examples.en: Tropical countries are warm all year round.
examples.ja: 南国は一年中あたたかいです。

examples.en: I was born in a tropical country.
examples.ja: 私は南国で生まれました。

examples.en: Fruits in southern regions are very sweet.
examples.ja: 南国のフルーツはとてもあまいです。

9351.meaning_mnemonic:
If you go far enough <kanji>south</kanji>, every <kanji>country</kanji> is a <vocabulary>tropical country</vocabulary>. Well, relative to Japan anyway… Probably different if you live in the southern hemisphere. 

In Japanese, 南国 often refers to tropical countries or islands like Thailand, Guam, and Hawaii. Sometimes it can refer to the warmer southern regions of Japan as well, like Okinawa.
9351.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses on'yomi readings for 南 (なん) and 国 (こく, but rendaku'd to ごく here). You've seen those readings before, but the なん reading is still pretty new, so here's a mnemonic just in case:

When you're in a <vocabulary>tropical country</vocabulary>, you always get a craving for <reading>naan</reading> (なん) bread. You could be in any <vocabulary>southern country</vocabulary> with a warm, tropical climate — for some reason the heat just makes you want to nosh on some naan.

examples.en: Rugby is very popular in South Africa.
examples.ja: 南アフリカではラグビーがとても人気です。

examples.en: If I go to South Africa, I want to see lions.
examples.ja: 南アフリカに行ったら、ライオンが見たいです。

examples.en: Elon Musk was born in Pretoria, South Africa.
examples.ja: イーロン・マスクは南アフリカのプレトリアで生まれました。

examples.en: When I was backpacking, I traveled around the countries of Southern Africa by hitchhiking.
examples.ja: バックパッカーをしていた時、ヒッチハイクで南アフリカの国々をまわりました。

9352.meaning_mnemonic:
This combines <kanji>south</kanji> and アフリカ, the word for "Africa." Put them together to get <vocabulary>South Africa</vocabulary>. 

南アフリカ will almost always mean the country of South Africa, but in some contexts it'll occasionally refer to the wider region of <vocabulary>Southern Africa</vocabulary>.
9352.reading_mnemonic: The reading uses the kun'yomi for 南, which you've already learned. Yay for geography! Now which continent was South Africa on again…?

examples.en: I want to go to Western Europe.
examples.ja: 私は西ヨーロッパに行きたいです。

examples.en: Cheese and wine are famous in Western Europe.
examples.ja: 西ヨーロッパではチーズやワインが有名です。

examples.en: I ate so much bread in Western Europe that I gained 5 kilos.
examples.ja: 西ヨーロッパでパンを食べすぎて、５キロも太りました。

examples.en: Wow, Western Europe? That's nice! Which countries did you visit?
examples.ja: へえ〜西ヨーロッパですか。いいですね！どこの国に行ったんですか。

9353.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>west</kanji> bit of ヨーロッパ (Europe) is <vocabulary>Western Europe</vocabulary>. 

Have you ever been to 西ヨーロッパ? You know, places like France, the UK, and Belgium, with all their wine and cheese and beer… Western Europe!
9353.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi reading of 西, which you've already learned, so you should be good to go here!

examples.en: A warm southerly wind is blowing.
examples.ja: あたたかい南風がふいています。

examples.en: The flowers are swaying in the south wind.
examples.ja: 南風で花がゆれています。

examples.en: The south wind feels nice today.
examples.ja: 今日は南風が気もちいいです。

9354.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>south</kanji> <kanji>wind</kanji> is… a <vocabulary>south wind</vocabulary>!

南風 is a wind that blows from the south. In Japan it's associated with the warmer temperatures it carries up from the tropics.
9354.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, which you've seen before. The かぜ reading is the same one you learned with the vocab word 風, so if you can remember that you should have no trouble with this word!

examples.en: A cold north wind is blowing.
examples.ja: つめたい北風がふいています。

examples.en: It was a cold day with a northerly wind blowing.
examples.ja: その日は、北風がふくさむい日でした。

examples.en: The puppies were running around in the north wind with great energy.
examples.ja: 北風の中を、子犬たちは元気に走りまわっていました。

examples.en: I have a date coming up, but the north wind is so strong that my wig looks like a lion.
examples.ja: これからデートなのに、北風が強すぎて、ウィッグがライオンみたいになってしまった。

9355.meaning_mnemonic:
From the <kanji>north</kanji> comes a <kanji>wind</kanji>. Naturally, it's the <vocabulary>north wind</vocabulary>.

北風 blows down from the north, and in Japan is often associated with the colder temperatures it brings.
9355.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. Almost like it's two independent vocab words, 北 and 風, mashed together. You've learned these readings, but the かぜ reading is still pretty new, so here's a mnemonic just in case:

Imagine the <vocabulary>north wind</vocabulary> blowing a kami<reading>kaze</reading> (かぜ) off course. The kamikaze pilot tries to complete his mission, but he can't overcome the wind blowing down from the north. Hear the kamikaze crying out, "Curse you, north wind!" In a way though, it kind of saves his life.

examples.en: The afternoon sun is so bright I can't see the TV.
examples.ja: 西日がまぶしくて、テレビが見えません。

examples.en: The setting sun made the curtains glow orange.
examples.ja: 西日でカーテンがオレンジ色に光りました。

examples.en: The afternoon sun is so strong that the sunroom is like a sauna.
examples.ja: 西日が強くて、サンルームがサウナみたいになっています。

9356.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>west</kanji> <kanji>sun</kanji> is, of course, the <vocabulary>afternoon sun</vocabulary>. 

西日 describes the sun when it's in the western part of the sky. It generally refers to the afternoon sun, but it can also mean the <vocabulary>setting sun</vocabulary> or the <vocabulary>evening sun</vocabulary>. Basically, you can use it for sun or sunlight from mid-afternoon until sunset!
9356.reading_mnemonic: This word uses kun'yomi readings for both 西 (にし) and 日 (ひ). You've seen these readings before, so if you can remember that they're kun'yomi then you're good to go! Just watch out for that rendaku that changes ひ to び.

examples.en: There are many mountains in East Asia.
examples.ja: 東アジアにはたくさんの山があります。

examples.en: Have you ever been to an East Asian country?
examples.ja: 東アジアの国に行ったことはありますか？

examples.en: In East Asia, there are many people who eat rice every day.
examples.ja: 東アジアでは、毎日お米を食べる人が多いです。

examples.en: East Asian food is delicious, but I gained weight from eating too much.
examples.ja: 東アジアのごはんはおいしいけど、食べすぎて太っちゃいました。

9357.meaning_mnemonic: You have the kanji for <kanji>east</kanji> combined with アジア, the word for "Asia" — that makes this <vocabulary>East Asia</vocabulary>. Can you name all the countries in 東アジア?
9357.reading_mnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi reading of 東, which you've already learned, so you should be good to go here!

examples.en: The Atlantic Ocean is very big.
examples.ja: 大西洋はとても大きいです。

examples.en: I have not seen the Atlantic Ocean yet.
examples.ja: 私はまだ大西洋を見たことがありません。

examples.en: The Atlantic Ocean is between America and Europe.
examples.ja: 大西洋はアメリカとヨーロッパの間にあります。

examples.en: I tried to swim across the Atlantic, but gave up after a minute.
examples.ja: 大西洋を泳いでわたろうとしましたが、1分であきらめました。

9358.meaning_mnemonic:
A <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>west</kanji> <kanji>ocean</kanji>, you say? It's gotta be the <vocabulary>Atlantic Ocean</vocabulary>.

If you think about it from Japan's perspective, the Atlantic is a big, faraway ocean to the west, right?
9358.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses on'yomi readings for all three kanji. You've seen these readings before, but the 西 reading (せい) is still pretty new, so here's a mnemonic refresher just in case:

While swimming in the <vocabulary>Atlantic Ocean</vocabulary>, you find a <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい). Yikes, how'd this rusty old saber get here? This thing must have floated across the Atlantic from some seaside battlefield of yore. Those old sabers are always washing up on Atlantic shores, you know.

examples.en: The North Pole is very cold.
examples.ja: 北極はとても寒いです。

examples.en: Polar bears live in the Arctic.
examples.ja: 北極にはシロクマが住んでいます。

examples.en: In summer in the Arctic, the sky is bright even at night.
examples.ja: 北極の夏は、夜になっても空が明るいんです。

examples.en: I saw the northern lights at the North Pole. It was a very gentle light.
examples.ja: 北極でオーロラを見ました。とてもやさしい光でした。

9359.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji>north</kanji>ern <kanji>extreme</kanji> of the world is the <vocabulary>North Pole</vocabulary>, aka the <vocabulary>Arctic</vocabulary>. You know, the pole with the polar bears.
9359.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses on'yomi readings for 北 (ほく) and 極 (きょく). If you remember those readings, you're almost there — just keep in mind the ほく changes to ほっ in this word!

examples.en: There were roads in all directions, and I couldn't decide which to take.
examples.ja: 東西南北に道があって、どちらに行こうかまよいました。

examples.en: He looked in all directions, wondering where he should go.
examples.ja: 彼は東西南北を見回し、どこへ行けばいいのか考えました。

examples.en: Stars sparkled in all directions, and the night sky was like a jewelry box.
examples.ja: 東西南北に星がきらめき、夜空はまるで宝石箱のようでした。

examples.en: The compass will tell you which direction you are facing, east, west, south, or north.
examples.ja: コンパスを使うと、東西南北のどちらの方角を向いているのかが分かります。

9360.meaning_mnemonic:
If something happens in the <kanji>east</kanji>, <kanji>west</kanji>, <kanji>south</kanji>, and <kanji>north</kanji>, then it's happening in <vocabulary>all directions</vocabulary>. What other directions are there? That's literally all of them.

This word usually appears in expressions like 東西南北を見る (to look in all directions). But it can also be used more literally to mean <vocabulary>east west south north</vocabulary>, aka the <vocabulary>cardinal directions</vocabulary>.
9360.reading_mnemonic: This word uses on'yomi readings for all four kanji. You've seen those before, so this shouldn't be too hard. Just watch out for that double rendaku — さい changes to ざい and ほく changes to ぼく.

9361.meaning_mnemonic: "Take your <radical>fingers</radical>. <radical>Now</radical>, put them on your foe's <radical>heart</radical> and <kanji>twist</kanji>." These are the words of your martial arts master as he teaches you his final, ultimate technique: the "finger-heart twister."
9361.reading_mnemonic: The last challenger to appear is… your own master, who taught you the <kanji>twist</kanji> technique. Turns out he's a <reading>nen</reading>doroid (ねん), so he doesn't even have a heart for you to twist. Welp, you're screwed.

9362.meaning_mnemonic: When you hold out your <radical>fingers</radical>, a <radical>person</radical> — and then a second <radical>person</radical> — stomps them into the <radical>dirt</radical>, leaving you with a serious finger <kanji>sprain</kanji>. That wasn't very nice of either person, and now you feel awfully <kanji>discourage</kanji>d about things.
9362.reading_mnemonic: You show your <kanji>sprain</kanji> to a doctor, and he tells you to go see the C<reading>za</reading>r (ざ). In your country, only the Czar has the authority to treat a sprain of this severity.

examples.en: Ugh, this sucks! I might've sprained my wrist.
examples.ja: うわ、最悪！手首、捻挫したかも。

examples.en: Let's stretch properly so we don't sprain anything during the game.
examples.ja: 試合中に捻挫をしないようにしっかりストレッチしよう。

examples.en: The reason I broke up with him was a sprain. Even though it was so bad that I couldn't walk, he was like, "Oh, come on — you're fine!"
examples.ja: 彼と別れた理由は捻挫だったの。歩けないくらいの捻挫だったのに「大したことないじゃん！」って言われて。

9363.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>twist</kanji> <kanji>sprain</kanji> is a <vocabulary>sprain</vocabulary>. You probably shouldn't twist it anymore though — that sprain looks bad enough as it is.
9363.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji, you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: I'm working hard at my part-time job to scrape together money for college.
examples.ja: 大学に行くためのお金を捻出するためにアルバイトを頑張ってます。

examples.en: Even though I had no time, I still managed to come up with five new ideas!
examples.ja: 時間がない中で、新しいアイディアを五つも捻出したんですよ！

examples.en: I'm having a tough time making ends meet as it is, so scrounging up the money to travel to Japan is difficult.
examples.ja: ただでさえ生活が苦しいのに、日本に旅行に行く費用を捻出するのは難しいよ。

9364.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Twist</kanji> your wallet till money <kanji>exit</kanji>s. This is the best way of <vocabulary>scraping together</vocabulary> cash when you're low on funds.

捻出 describes the act of working hard to scrape something together, whether you're <vocabulary>scrounging up</vocabulary> money or free time in a tight situation, or <vocabulary>coming up with</vocabulary> an idea by really racking your brain. Imagine twisting an almost-empty tube of toothpaste to get that last little bit, and that's what 捻出 feels like.
9364.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji, you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It's so sunny — almost like yesterday's typhoon didn't really happen.
examples.ja: 昨日の台風がウソの様に晴れてるね。

examples.en: Our Wi-Fi is as fast as light.
examples.ja: うちのWiFiは光の様に速い。

examples.en: He showed up for our first date riding a horse, as though he were a prince.
examples.ja: 彼は初めてのデートに王子の様に馬に乗って現れたの。

9365.meaning_mnemonic: You learned 様 is a "formal name ender," but it can also mean <kanji>manner</kanji>. When you attach this to another noun with の and add に on the end to make it an adverb, you can describe something that's being done <vocabulary>similarly to</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>in the same way as</vocabulary> something else. In other words, something about it is just <vocabulary>like</vocabulary> that other thing — almost <vocabulary>as if</vocabulary> they were one and the same!
9365.reading_mnemonic:
Even though this word isn't a compound, 様 actually uses the on'yomi here. Since you didn't learn the on'yomi with the kanji, here's a mnemonic to help you out:

Many foods are made <vocabulary>similarly to</vocabulary> <reading>yo</reading>gurt (よう): kefir, skyr, lassi… The list goes on. What's that? Those are just subcategories of yogurt, you say? No, no, no. They're made <vocabulary>in the same way as</vocabulary> yogurt and they taste a lot <vocabulary>like</vocabulary> yogurt, but they're not yogurt. Yogurt stands alone.

examples.en: I'm saving this money for my future self.
examples.ja: このお金は、未来の自分のために貯めるの。

examples.en: Oh, you're saving up miles for your honeymoon trip?
examples.ja: えっ、ハネムーン旅行のためにマイルを貯めてるんですか？

examples.en: Japanese people really love collecting reward points, don't they?
examples.ja: 日本人って本当にポイント貯めるのが好きだよね。

9366.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>savings</kanji>, so the verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to save up</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to store</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to accumulate</vocabulary> something valuable.

貯める is used when you're saving up something useful over time — typically money, loyalty points, or airline miles, for example, but sometimes water and other resources too.
9366.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi reading for 貯, which you haven't learned yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

You have <vocabulary>to save up</vocabulary> for <reading>ta</reading>cos (た). Not only are tacos more expensive these days, you also have a horrible taco addiction that you need to plan ahead and save for every month.

examples.en: Let's wait and see how things go for a little while.
examples.ja: しばらく様子を見ましょう。

examples.en: Seeming anxious, my son said, "I wonder if this will be enough."
examples.ja: 息子は「これで足りるかな？」と不安そうな様子で言いました。

examples.en: Dad's been acting strange since yesterday — I wonder if something happened.
examples.ja: 昨日からお父さんの様子がおかしいんだけど、何かあったのかな？

9367.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>manner</kanji> of your <kanji>child</kanji> changes with the <vocabulary>state of things</vocabulary>.

様子 is a versatile word that refers to the state of things — essentially, how things appear or seem. It can describe a <vocabulary>situation</vocabulary>, someone's <vocabulary>condition</vocabulary>, appearance, demeanor, or manner, or even the atmosphere in a room (the "vibe").
9367.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses on'yomi readings of the kanji. But the す reading for 子 here is less common and you haven't seen it yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

When you're not pleased with the <vocabulary>state of things</vocabulary>, you <reading>sue</reading> (す). Sue the government, sue your neighbors, sue whoever. Yep, suing is the only way to improve the state of things.

examples.en: Please come again when the new greenery is out.
examples.ja: 新緑の時期にまた来てくださいね。

examples.en: April and May are definitely the months when the new foliage is most beautiful.
examples.ja: 新緑が一番きれいなのはやっぱり四月と五月ですよ。

examples.en: I feel like my eyesight improved just from gazing at the mountains covered in new green leaves.
examples.ja: 新緑の山をずーっと見てたら目が良くなった気がするんだ。

9368.meaning_mnemonic:
What's <kanji>new</kanji> and <kanji>green</kanji>? That'd be the <vocabulary>new greenery</vocabulary> you see on trees and other plants every year!

新緑 refers to <vocabulary>new foliage</vocabulary> — fresh green leaves of late spring and early summer, just after they've fully emerged. In Japan, it's seen as a symbol of that time of year, so it often carries a slightly poetic nuance.
9368.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. You've seen them before (remember the りょく reading from 緑茶?), so you should be good to go here.

examples.en: Could you go pick up a bottle of green tea at the convenience store for me?
examples.ja: コンビニでペットボトルの緑茶買って来てくれない？

examples.en: Lately, I've been gargling with green tea every day.
examples.ja: 最近は緑茶で毎日うがいしてるんです。

examples.en: Both have a lot of caffeine, but I prefer green tea over coffee.
examples.ja: 両方ともカフェインが強いけど、コーヒーよりも緑茶の方が好きなんです。

examples.en: Technically speaking, hojicha and matcha also fall into the category of "non-oxidized tea."
examples.ja: 厳密に言うと、ほうじ茶や抹茶も「緑茶」と言うカテゴリーに入ります。

9369.meaning_mnemonic:
<kanji>Green</kanji> <kanji>tea</kanji> is <vocabulary>green tea</vocabulary>.

緑茶 technically refers to all kinds of green tea (i.e., non-oxidized teas). But in everyday Japanese, the word usually means green-colored tea made from leaf infusions, typically sencha.
9369.reading_mnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned the りょく reading for 緑 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

You love your <vocabulary>green tea</vocabulary> so much that you <reading>lock</reading> (りょく) it up in a safe in your house. No one's getting to that green tea except you — it's kept under strict lock and key at all times.

examples.en: Okay, next we'll do a stretch where you twist your body from side to side.
examples.ja: それじゃあ次は、左右に体を捻るストレッチをします。

examples.en: If you give that switch a hard twist, the engine will start.
examples.ja: そのスイッチを強く捻るとエンジンが入りますよ。

examples.en: There was kimchi in the bread, and everyone looked puzzled by it.
examples.ja: パンの中にキムチが入っててさ、みんな首を捻ってたよ。

9370.meaning_mnemonic:
Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>twist</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to twist</vocabulary>.

捻る literally means "to twist," so you can use it for everything from turning the handle of a faucet to twisting your ankle in a soccer game. When combined with other words, it can also take on metaphorical meanings, such as 頭を捻る (to think hard) and 首を捻る (to puzzle over).
9370.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Your horse happened <vocabulary>to twist</vocabulary> his ankle, and <reading>he neigh</reading>ed (ひね) in discomfort. If it were you who had twisted your ankle, you probably would have screamed or shouted an expletive or something, but it's your horse, so he neighed. Poor guy. Put some ice on that thing for him.

Note that this can also be read as ねじる, though this reading is usually written in kana. While ひねる refers to general twisting — like turning or bending to the side — ねじる tends to have a nuance of twisting something multiple times, like a string or wire, often from both ends.

examples.en: I have so many business trips that my miles accumulate really fast!
examples.ja: 出張がたくさんありすぎて、マイルが本当すぐに貯まるよ！

examples.en: As soon as my son has a little pocket money saved up, he goes and buys Pokémon cards at the convenience store.
examples.ja: 私の息子はおこづかいが少しでも貯まると、コンビニにポケモンカードを買いに行くんです。

examples.en: If you don't spend your money while you're alive, it just keeps piling up in the bank — and in the end, you can't take it with you to heaven.
examples.ja: 生きてるうちにお金を使わないと、どんどん銀行に貯まっていくだけだし、結局天国には持っていけないのよ。

9371.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 貯める means "to save up"? This is a lot like that, except the focus is on the thing that's being saved up. That's why it means <vocabulary>to be saved up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to add up</vocabulary>. To remember this is the intransitive version, just think about how it's easy for money to be saved up if you put it in the <reading>mar</reading>ket (まる).

貯まる will often refer to money, like in 資金が貯まる (funds get saved up). But you'll also see it in phrases like マイルが貯まる (frequent flier miles add up).
9371.reading_mnemonic: One thing that tends <vocabulary>to be saved up</vocabulary> is <reading>ta</reading>cos (た). This is because you always make too many tacos, so they have to be saved in the fridge for later. But then you forget about them and make more, so they tend <vocabulary>to add up</vocabulary> even more. It's a vicious taco cycle.

examples.en: The sky at dawn today was pink.
examples.ja: 今日の夜明けの空はピンクでした。

examples.en: Things are tough right now, but a new dawn will come.
examples.ja: 今はつらいけど、いつか夜明けが来るよ。

examples.en: My parents are the generation that experienced the dawn of the internet age.
examples.ja: 私の両親は、インターネット時代の夜明けを経験した世代です。

9372.meaning_mnemonic:
We have <kanji>night</kanji> and the noun version of "to dawn" (明ける). What comes when the night ends and a new day dawns? The <vocabulary>dawn</vocabulary>, of course.

夜明け refers to dawn or <vocabulary>daybreak</vocabulary> in the literal sense, but it can also be used metaphorically to mean the <vocabulary>beginning</vocabulary> of something new, as in 時代の夜明け (the dawn of an era).
9372.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings of the kanji. You know 明け because it uses the same reading as 明ける, but 夜 is a little weird because よる gets shortened to よ. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember this change:

What are you doing when <vocabulary>dawn</vocabulary> comes each morning? Playing with your <reading>yo</reading>-yo (よ), obviously. You want to be the best yo-yoer there's ever been, so you're up with the dawn every morning, practicing your yo-yo skills while the competition sleeps.

Note that in the related phrase 夜が明ける, 夜 is also often read as よ.

examples.en: We're getting further into autumn, and the season for tasty mushrooms is just around the corner now, isn't it?
examples.ja: 秋も更けて、もうすぐキノコが美味しいシーズンですね。

examples.en: And so the night wore on.
examples.ja: こうして夜は更けて行ったのでした。

examples.en: I was writing my kid's name and drawing a picture of his face on each of his diapers for daycare, and before I knew it, it had gotten really late into the night.
examples.ja: 保育園用のオムツ一つ一つに子供の名前と似顔絵をかいてたら、すっかり夜が更けちゃったんだよね。

9373.meaning_mnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means renew, but the verb meaning is a little different. This means to grow late, to wear on, or to deepen. Think of it this way: you only renew stuff that's not new, after time has worn on a bit — your streaming subscriptions, your driver's license, your marriage vows. And with each renewal you feel the passage of time a little more deeply… You'll see 更ける more often in writing, usually in reference to night or autumn, as in 夜が更ける (the night grows late) and 秋が更ける (autumn deepens).
9373.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading.

As it starts <vocabulary>to grow late</vocabulary>, you turn into a <reading>foo</reading>l (ふ). You ever get increasingly delirious and giggly with friends as the night wears on? Yeah, you've been there. The later it gets, the more deeply foolish you become. What is that weird, late-night energy anyway?

examples.en: The Halloween party went on until the wee hours.
examples.ja: ハロウィンパーティーは夜更けまで続いた。

examples.en: It puts me in a tough spot when you show up this late at night.
examples.ja: こんな夜更けに来られても困るよ。

examples.en: "Let's meet again!" With those words, Koichi disappeared into the midnight streets.
examples.ja: 「また会おうな！」そう言ってコウイチは夜更けの街へ消えていった。

9374.meaning_mnemonic: We have <kanji>night</kanji> and the noun version of 更ける (to grow late). Stick the two together, and you get a word that means <vocabulary>late at night</vocabulary>, the <vocabulary>dead of night</vocabulary>, or the <vocabulary>wee hours</vocabulary>.
9374.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings of the kanji. You should remember 更's kun'yomi from 更ける, but 夜 is a little tricky because it uses its less common よ reading. You learned this reading with 夜明け, but here's a mnemonic in case you need a refresher:

You've stayed up <vocabulary>late at night</vocabulary> again playing with your <reading>yo</reading>-yo (よ). There are just so many yo-yo tricks you want to master, so you can't help but stay up practicing, yo-yoing until the <vocabulary>wee hours</vocabulary> every night. Someone ought to take that thing away from you so you can get some sleep.

examples.en: Ramadan will soon be over.
examples.ja: もうすぐラマダーンが明ける。

examples.en: In Japan, when the new year begins, people say "akemashite omedetou."
examples.ja: 日本では年が明けると「明けましておめでとう」って言うんだよ。

examples.en: That new shopping mall seems to get crowded on holidays. Should we go check it out around when Golden Week is over?
examples.ja: 新しくできたショッピングモール、休日は混んでるみたい。ゴールデンウィークが明けるころに行ってみない？

9375.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>bright</kanji>, but the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to dawn</vocabulary>. It gets bright each morning when a new day dawns, so the connection kinda makes sense, right?

While 明ける is commonly used with 夜 to talk about the dawn breaking, it's also often used to talk about other time-related transitions. Because of this, it can mean <vocabulary>to end</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to begin</vocabulary> depending on the situation, as in 冬休みが明ける (winter vacation ends) or 年が明ける (the new year begins). Think of it like a new phase in your life is "dawning."
9375.reading_mnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, it's going to use the kun'yomi reading. In this case, that's あ — just like in 明かり — but since 明's kun'yomi readings can be a little irregular, here's a mnemonic to help you out:

When it starts <vocabulary>to dawn</vocabulary>, you gaze up at the sky and exclaim "<reading>ah</reading>" (あ)! The dawn sky is just so beautiful, and the crisp dawn air feels so fresh in your lungs, you can't help but sigh with delight: "ah!"

examples.en: Staying up late and stress are causes of acne.
examples.ja: 夜更かしやストレスがにきびの原因です。

examples.en: My younger brother's finally gotten into staying up late too — he plays video games until dawn.
examples.ja: うちの弟もついに夜更かしを覚えちゃってさ、夜が明けるまでゲームしてるよ。

examples.en: During the Obon holiday, my dad kept staying up late and my grandma got mad at him.
examples.ja: 私の父は、お盆休み中に夜更かしばかりして、おばあちゃんに怒られてました。

9376.meaning_mnemonic:
Remember how 夜更け meant "late at night"? Well, this is similar to that, but instead of referring to the time of night, it refers to the act of <vocabulary>staying up late</vocabulary>. 

夜更かし typically means staying up well past the time you know you should be going to bed. It's often associated with guilty pleasures like binge-watching TV shows or gaming.
9376.reading_mnemonic: This word uses the same readings as 夜更け. If you can remember that one, you should be fine here as well!

examples.en: The doorbell rang at two in the morning.
examples.ja: 夜中の二時にチャイムが鳴った。

examples.en: What brings you here so late in the night?
examples.ja: こんな夜中に何の用ですか？

examples.en: At my previous job, I sometimes worked overtime until the middle of the night, but now I get home by five.
examples.ja: 前の仕事では夜中まで残業をすることもあったけど、今は五時には家に帰ってますよ。

9377.meaning_mnemonic:
The <kanji>night</kanji>'s <kanji>middle</kanji> is the <vocabulary>middle of the night</vocabulary>. In other words, <vocabulary>late at night</vocabulary>.

夜中 doesn't refer to an exact time, but it generally means the later part of the night, around when most people tend to be asleep.
9377.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. 夜 has a couple kun'yomi readings though, so here's a mnemonic to remember よ is the one you want here:

In the <vocabulary>middle of the night</vocabulary>, you like to play with your <reading>yo</reading>-yo (よ). During the day, it's hard to get any peace and quiet to practice your yo-yo tricks, but in the middle of the night you can finally get some alone time with your precious yo-yo.

9378.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Shellfish</radical> cause <radical>landslide</radical>s because of all their <kanji>bustling</kanji> and <kanji>lively</kanji> underwater activity.
9378.reading_mnemonic: You can't stand <kanji>bustling</kanji> and <kanji>lively</kanji> situations, so you get out your <reading>knee gui</reading>llotine (にぎ). What's a knee guillotine? It's exactly what it sounds like, and you're about to use it on these shellfish to prevent some landslides.

examples.en: On weekends, the shopping mall bustles with shoppers.
examples.ja: ショッピングモールは週末、買い物客で賑わう。

examples.en: Every year, the festivals and fireworks draw lively crowds of people.
examples.ja: 毎年、祭りも花火大会も大勢の人で賑わいます。

examples.en: That cilantro specialty restaurant in the alley over there seems to be doing quite well.
examples.ja: あそこの路地にあるパクチー料理専門レストラン、中々賑わってるらしいよ。

9379.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji itself means <kanji>bustling</kanji> or <kanji>lively</kanji>, so the verb vocab version means <vocabulary>to be bustling</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to be lively</vocabulary>.

賑わう is typically used to describe bustling places or times. You might see it in phrases like 若者で賑わう街 (streets bustling with young people) or 夏に観光客で賑わう (to be crowded with tourists in summer). Since bustling places tend to flourish economically, it can also carry a nuance of prosperity and mean <vocabulary>to thrive</vocabulary>.
9379.reading_mnemonic: This uses the reading you learned with 賑, so you should be good to go here!

examples.en: My family is lively.
examples.ja: うちの家族は賑やかです。

examples.en: With a new child due in November, we're expecting to have a lively Christmas this year.
examples.ja: １１月には子供が増えて、今年のクリスマスは賑やかになる予定です。

examples.en: What with radio calisthenics for the elderly going on and all, the park was really bustling this morning.
examples.ja: 午前中の公園は老人向けのラジオ体操もあってかなり賑やかでしたよ。

9380.meaning_mnemonic:
This shares meanings with the kanji, making it <vocabulary>bustling</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>lively</vocabulary>.

You might see 賑やか used to describe bustling and crowded city streets, a festive celebration, the sound of boisterous laughter, or even just a cheerful, animated person.
9380.reading_mnemonic: This uses the reading you learned with 賑, so you should be good to go here!

9381.meaning_mnemonic: Members of the <radical>tongue</radical> <radical>clan</radical> like to do one thing: <kanji>lick</kanji>. They go around licking everything to mark their tongue clan territory, you know? They even lick each other on the cheek by way of greeting.
9381.reading_mnemonic: Unfortunately, the tongue clan members also <kanji>lick</kanji> your <reading>na</reading>chos (な). You'd been saving those nachos! They were your travel rations. Now each and every nacho has been licked clean.

examples.en: Babies lick everything.
examples.ja: 赤ちゃんは何でも舐める。

examples.en: I can have alcohol as long as it's just a little taste.
examples.ja: お酒は舐めるくらいだったら飲めます。

examples.en: Don't you dare look down on me just 'cause your WaniKani level's higher!
examples.ja: 自分の方がワニカニのレベル高いからって、舐めんじゃねぇよ！

examples.en: Honestly, I underestimated the entrance exam for Tofugu University. Ugh… I should've studied more.
examples.ja: 正直なところ、トーフグ大学の入学試験は舐めてたんです。あーあ、もっと勉強すれば良かった。

9382.meaning_mnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>lick</kanji>, so the verb vocab version is <vocabulary>to lick</vocabulary>.

舐める also has a slang meaning of <vocabulary>to underestimate</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to look down on</vocabulary>. In those cases it'll often be written as ナメる or sometimes なめる. You might see it in manga or hear characters in movies say なめんなよ (don't underestimate me). Think of the slang meaning like this: you'd have to really underestimate someone to think you could just lick them without consequences, right?
9382.reading_mnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned that reading with the kanji, so you should be good to go here!

examples.en: An inclination to learn on one's own is important.
examples.ja: 自ら学ぶ姿勢が大切なんです。

examples.en: Daily yoga is indispensable for my self-improvement.
examples.ja: 自らを高めるため、毎日ヨガは欠かせません。

examples.en: Say what you will, but you're the one who willingly ate the habanero, aren't you?
examples.ja: そんなこと言ったって、自ら進んでハバネロを食べたのは君だろう？

examples.en: It's rare for the president to personally apologize to a customer like that, huh.
examples.ja: 社長自らお客さんに謝るなんて珍しいね。

9383.meaning_mnemonic:
The kanji <kanji>self</kanji> is all by itself! So, naturally, this word means <vocabulary>oneself</vocabulary>. Don't let the ら on the end confuse you, by the way — this word is singular.

Like 自分, 自ら means "oneself," but it's mostly used in formal or literary contexts. It can also be used as an adverb to mean <vocabulary>on one's own initiative</vocabulary> to emphasize voluntary action, or <vocabulary>personally</vocabulary> to highlight direct involvement — for example, 自ら辞める (to quit on one's own initiative) or 自ら謝る (to personally apologize).
9383.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses 自's kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

If one prefers not to drive <vocabulary>oneself</vocabulary>, a great alternative option is the 水-car (みずか). It's a self-driving car that runs entirely on 水, rather than gas, allowing one to fight climate change  <vocabulary>on one's own initiative</vocabulary> while never needing to <vocabulary>personally</vocabulary> take the wheel. Stop by your local dealership and get yourself a 水-car today!

examples.en: Please draw a straight line on the paper.
examples.ja: 紙に直線を引いてください。

examples.en: This shape is made of three straight lines.
examples.ja: この図形は三本の直線でできています。

examples.en: When I glanced ahead, there was a straight row of white stones.
examples.ja: ふと前を見ると、白い石が直線上にならんでいました。

9384.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji>straight</kanji> <kanji>line</kanji> is a <vocabulary>straight line</vocabulary>. You know, the shortest distance between two points and all that.

examples.en: The car was slowly proceeding straight forward.
examples.ja: 車はゆっくり直進していた。

examples.en: When turning right, watch out for vehicles coming straight ahead.
examples.ja: 右に曲がる時は、直進車に気をつけてください。

examples.en: There's a McDonald's 100 meters straight ahead from here.
examples.ja: ここから直進100mのところにマクドナルドがあります。

9385.meaning_mnemonic:
If you make a <kanji>straight</kanji> <kanji>advance</kanji>, you are <vocabulary>going straight ahead</vocabulary>. 

直進 is a slightly formal-sounding word for <vocabulary>direct forward motion</vocabulary>. You'll often hear it in regard to the motion of vehicles, like when your GPS tells you to go straight at a light or an announcement on the train tells you the train will be going straight at the next junction.
9385.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: It started raining right before we left.
examples.ja: 出発の直前に雨がふりだした。

examples.en: I fell down right before the goal.
examples.ja: ゴール直前でこけてしまった。

examples.en: Because it was a last-minute cancellation, I hardly got any money back.
examples.ja: 直前のキャンセルだったので、お金はほとんどもどってこなかった。

examples.en: Just as I was about to eat sushi, I realized there was no soy sauce.
examples.ja: すしを食べる直前にしょうゆがないと気づいたんです。

9386.meaning_mnemonic:
Something happened <kanji>direct</kanji>ly <kanji>before</kanji> this. In other words, it happened <vocabulary>just before</vocabulary> this.

直前 is used to talk about something happening <vocabulary>immediately prior to</vocabulary> something else, like when your date cancels on you just before you were supposed to meet or your doctor tells you not to eat a snack right before bed.
9386.reading_mnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

examples.en: Call a doctor right away.
examples.ja: 直ちに医者を呼んでください。

examples.en: This requires immediate action.
examples.ja: これは直ちに対応が必要ですね。

examples.en: If a problem occurs, please report it right away.
examples.ja: 問題が発生したら、直ちに報告してください。

9387.meaning_mnemonic:
If someone tells you to get <kanji>straight</kanji> to doing something, you ought to do it <vocabulary>right away</vocabulary>. Go on, chop-chop!

直ちに means to do something <vocabulary>immediately</vocabulary>, and it has a nuance of urgency — for example, a tsunami warning asking people to immediately evacuate their homes or your doctor telling you to contact them at once if you experience a certain symptom. However, it can also mean <vocabulary>directly</vocabulary>, like 失敗は直ちに死に繋がる (failure will lead directly to death).
9387.reading_mnemonic:
This word uses a rare reading for 直 that you haven't seen before, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

Every time your boss asks you to do something <vocabulary>right away</vocabulary>, you do it and then yell "<reading>ta-da</reading> (ただ)!!" Imagine how annoying of an employee you must be, yelling "ta-da!" every time you finish a task. You get things done immediately, though, so no one can fire you — even if they probably want to.
